title: AZ-104 Study Plan: A 4-Week Plan for the Microsoft Azure Administrator Exam
description:
The AZ-104 (Microsoft Azure Administrator) is not an exam you can pass by only reading documentation. Most questions are scenario-based: a short business situation, a constraint, and four plausible-looking ways to solve it in Azure. That means your study plan needs two things in equal measure — concept study and hands-on practice under time pressure.

Here is the 4-week plan I recommend to anyone who already has basic Azure familiarity (if you are completely new to cloud, spend one extra week on Azure fundamentals first).

Start with the exam domains, not with a course

Microsoft publishes the skills measured for AZ-104, and the weights tell you where to spend your time:

Domain Weight
Manage Azure identities and governance 20–25%
Implement and manage storage 15–20%
Deploy and manage Azure compute resources 20–25%
Implement and manage virtual networking 15–20%
Monitor and maintain Azure resources 10–15%

Two domains — identities/governance and compute — together can be almost half the exam. Plan your weeks around these weights instead of studying topics in random order.

Week 1: Identities, governance, and the portal basics

  • Microsoft Entra ID: users, groups, licenses, external (guest) users, self-service password reset
  • RBAC: built-in roles, scope inheritance, deny assignments — know the difference between Owner, Contributor, and User Access Administrator cold
  • Subscriptions and management groups, Azure Policy, resource locks, tags, and cost management basics
  • Get comfortable in Cloud Shell with both Azure PowerShell and Azure CLI; administrators are expected to move between the portal and the command line

Lab work: create users and groups, assign RBAC roles at different scopes and test what each role can and cannot do, apply an Azure Policy that denies a resource type, and add a resource lock.

Week 2: Storage and compute

  • Storage accounts: redundancy options (LRS, ZRS, GRS, GZRS), access tiers, lifecycle management, soft delete and versioning for Blob Storage
  • Securing storage: shared access signatures, stored access policies, storage firewalls and virtual networks, identity-based access for Azure Files
  • Tools: AzCopy and Azure Storage Explorer
  • Virtual machines: sizing, disks, availability sets and zones, scale sets, disk encryption, moving a VM between resource groups/subscriptions
  • ARM templates and Bicep: reading, modifying, and exporting templates matters more than writing from scratch
  • App Service and containers: plans, scaling, deployment slots, custom DNS and TLS, Azure Container Instances and Container Registry

Lab work: create a storage account with geo-redundancy, configure a lifecycle rule, generate a SAS token with an expiry, deploy a VM from a template, and scale an App Service plan up and out.

Week 3: Networking, monitoring, and backup

  • Virtual networks: subnets, peering, public IPs, user-defined routes, DNS zones and records
  • Security: network security groups and application security groups, service endpoints vs. private endpoints, Azure Bastion
  • Load balancing: internal vs. public load balancers and when each is used, plus basic load-balancer troubleshooting
  • Monitoring: Azure Monitor metrics and logs, alerts and action groups, VM and container insights
  • Network Watcher and Connection Monitor for connectivity problems
  • Backup and recovery: Recovery Services vaults, backup policies, restoring a VM, and the basics of Azure Site Recovery

Lab work: peer two VNets, block traffic with an NSG rule and verify it with Network Watcher, configure an alert on VM CPU, and back up a VM then restore it to a new resource group.

Week 4: Practice tests — used properly

This is the week most candidates skip or do badly. A practice test is a diagnostic tool, not a way to memorize answers.

  1. Take the first full test in timed, exam-like conditions. No pausing, no searching.
  2. Review every wrong answer — and every right answer you guessed — and map each one back to a domain.
  3. Spend two days restudying only your two weakest domains, with labs.
  4. Take a second, different test. Repeat the review cycle.

A reasonable readiness signal: scoring around 80% or higher on two different timed practice tests, with no single domain collapsing. If you want a structured question bank organized by these same domains, a timed AZ-104 practice test (full-length tests plus shorter topic-wise sessions) is a practical way to run this routine — whichever provider you use, the review-the-mistakes step is the part that actually raises your score.

Mistakes that cost people the exam

  • Reading without doing. AZ-104 rewards people who have actually clicked through the portal. Every concept in weeks 1–3 has a lab attached for a reason.
  • Ignoring RBAC and Policy. Governance feels dry, so candidates under-study it — and it is worth up to a quarter of the exam.
  • Memorizing practice answers. If the same question appears with the names changed and you get it wrong, you learned the answer, not the concept.
  • No time practice. The real exam is roughly a minute to ninety seconds per question. If you have never worked against a clock, exam day will feel faster than you expect.

Final word

Four weeks is enough if the weeks are structured: domains first, labs with every topic, and practice tests treated as diagnostics. Book the exam at the start of week 4 — having a date on the calendar is the simplest motivation trick there is.

Good luck, and if you have a study routine that worked for you, share it in the comments.

title: pg_vectorsearch vs pgvector HNSW: 42 Hours vs 49 Minutes. Here's the Catch
description:
On a 64 vCPU, 512 GiB machine, pgvector took 42 hours to build an HNSW index over 100 million vectors. On the same box, Timescale's new pg_vectorsearch extension built its index in 49 minutes and answered queries in half the time.

Those are the numbers in the launch post from Tiger Data (formerly Timescale), published October 13, 2026. If you run RAG on Postgres, that headline is hard to ignore. I went through the post, the repo, the tuning docs, the benchmark tool's config files and the Hacker News thread to see how far the pg_vectorsearch vs pgvector claim holds. Short answer: the query-side win is real and big. The build-time comparison is tilted, and the extension is still alpha, so production is off the table for now.

What pg_vectorsearch actually is

The extension adds a new index access method called PRISM (Partitioned Routing Index for Similarity Matching). The README calls it "conceptually similar to pgvector's IVFFlat", which is the clearest way to think about it. It's a partition index:

  • a hierarchical centroid tree routes each query to a few clusters
  • vectors in those clusters are stored as RaBitQ codes, about one bit per dimension
  • candidates get filtered on the compressed codes, then reranked with full-precision vectors from the heap

That last part explains most of the memory difference. HNSW has to keep a big graph in memory to be fast, while PRISM only keeps a small tree there and scans compact posting lists for the rest.

It also reads pgvector's types. vec32 and vec16 are binary-compatible with vector and halfvec, so you can put a PRISM index on an existing table:

CREATE EXTENSION pg_vectorsearch;

CREATE INDEX documents_embedding_prism
    ON documents USING prism (embedding vec32_cosine_ops);

SET prism.nprobe = 40;  -- 0 = auto, roughly 0.95 recall

The pg_vectorsearch vs pgvector HNSW benchmark numbers

All figures are p50 latency at recall@10 against brute force, from the launch post. HNSW ran on pgvector's 16-bit halfvec.

100M Cohere embeddings

PRISM, r8i.4xlarge (128 GiB) PRISM, r8i.16xlarge (512 GiB) HNSW, r8i.16xlarge (512 GiB)
Build time 1 h 40 min 49 min 42 h
Index size 25 GB 25 GB 180 GB
p50 @ 95% recall 6 ms 4 ms 8 ms
p50 @ 99% recall 21 ms 19 ms not reached

HNSW didn't finish building on the 128 GiB box. When they moved the index built on the big machine over to it, queries took over a second at 95% recall and never reached 99%.

1M vectors

PRISM, c8g.medium (2 GiB) PRISM, c8g.large (4 GiB) HNSW, c8g.large (4 GiB)
Build time ~3 min ~3.1 min ~21.7 h
Index size 280 MB 280 MB 2.05 GB
p50 @ 95% recall 9 ms 3 ms 122 ms
p50 @ 99% recall 15 ms 9 ms 392 ms

HNSW wasn't really tried on the 2 GiB box; the post says they "couldn't realistically try" it there, and the table marks it "did not finish".

The headline "6 ms at 100M on 4x less memory" is the 128 GiB PRISM number against the 512 GiB HNSW number. I think that's fair: both hit 95% recall, and one machine costs a quarter of the other.

Where the comparison is tilted

Start with the HNSW build settings. Tiger Data's benchmark tool, rekall, ships an HNSW config (hnsw-m16.toml) with m = 16 and ef_construction = 200. pgvector's default ef_construction is 64. Building with 200 buys a better graph and costs a lot more time. Reasonable if you're chasing 99% recall, but it inflates the build-time gap. The post doesn't say which config produced the published table, so I'm reading the repo, not the run.

The post also doesn't publish maintenance_work_mem, and pgvector's README is blunt about why that matters. Once the graph stops fitting in maintenance_work_mem, you get hnsw graph no longer fits into maintenance_work_mem after 100000 tuples and the build "will take significantly more time". A 2.05 GB HNSW index on a 4 GiB machine is going to hit that wall, and a 21.7 h build for 1M vectors is what hitting it looks like. I wouldn't call that normal HNSW performance. Same story for the 122 ms queries: the index doesn't fit in RAM next to the heap, so you're reading from disk.

The numbers aren't dishonest, though. "HNSW falls over when it doesn't fit in memory" is exactly the point Tiger Data is making. But if your HNSW index already fits in RAM with headroom, the 1M table doesn't describe your setup.

Then there's what the post leaves out. No QPS, no p99, no concurrency (multi-client throughput testing is listed as GA work), no filtered search, no IVFFlat numbers even though the README compares PRISM to IVFFlat, and no published embedding dimension. Filtered search is where people actually suffer with pgvector, and PRISM's answer today is basic: per the tuning docs, the executor applies your WHERE clause after the index has emitted its top-k, and the scan inflates k based on estimated selectivity. Filters that are anti-correlated with vector distance can still return too few rows. The docs suggest a partial index on the filter. Streaming search with WHERE filters is on the GA roadmap.

On HN, esafak asked the obvious thing: "Shouldn't you lead with your benchmarks if you're fast? qps and precision/recall, please." jascha_eng replied that the benchmarks are in the post and the suite is open source. Both are right. They're still vendor numbers, and I haven't seen anyone outside Tiger Data publish a rerun yet.

pgvectorscale's fate worries me more than the benchmarks

pgvectorscale, Tiger Data's 2024 DiskANN-style index, "will enter maintenance mode," per the launch post. On HN, Tiger Data CTO mfreed said parts of pgvectorscale's graph could become unreachable and degrade recall, and when they couldn't find a fix they decided to start over with a partition index.

So the vendor that told you two years ago that its graph index was the answer is now telling you graph indexes are the problem. They might be right. They also showed you how fast a Postgres vector extension can go from flagship to maintenance mode.

On top of that, the practical blockers:

  • It's alpha. The README says "meant for testing, not production" and warns that you may have to drop and recreate the extension between prereleases.
  • It needs PostgreSQL 18+. pgvector supports 13+.
  • The hyperscalers don't offer it yet. On HN, devy pointed out it isn't on Azure's or the other big clouds' extension allow-lists, so on those you wait or self-host PG 18. When another commenter raised the same problem, jascha_eng's answer was that you can move to Tiger Cloud.
  • Index maintenance is manual and marked experimental. Posting lists grow on insert and "never split on their own." CALL prism_rebalance('items_idx'); splits them in place, but only on flat, single-level indexes built with centroid_fastscan = off. The default CREATE INDEX doesn't produce that shape, so for a default-built index the fix is a full REINDEX, which rewrites the whole index. A rebalance also leaves replaced lists on disk until the next REINDEX.
  • Don't build on an empty table. Index sizing uses the row count at CREATE INDEX, so load first and index second.
  • Be careful with high dimensions. The tuning docs say the packed SIMD fastscan layout always fits up to ~1900 dims at 8 KB pages, and auto falls back to a slower layout past that. On HN, devy said "PRISM caps at 1968 dimensions"; I couldn't find a hard cap in the docs. If you use 2048-dim embeddings (VoyageAI offers them), test before you plan on it.

What to do with pgvector today

If HNSW builds are killing you, fix the build before you change extensions. From the pgvector docs:

SET maintenance_work_mem = '8GB';          -- size it so the graph fits
SET max_parallel_maintenance_workers = 7;  -- plus leader

CREATE INDEX ON items
  USING hnsw ((embedding::halfvec(768)) halfvec_cosine_ops);

Use halfvec (it halves the index and is what Tiger Data benchmarked against). Leave ef_construction at 64 unless you've measured that you need more. If filtered queries return too few rows, turn on hnsw.iterative_scan (pgvector 0.8.0+; current release is v0.8.7).

So when does switching pay off?

My take: pg_vectorsearch is the most interesting thing to happen to Postgres vector search since HNSW landed in pgvector. VectorChord took the same route of clustering plus quantized vectors, and its own benchmark says its QPS "could be twice that of pgvector" at equivalent recall on GIST 1M (960 dims). That's a vendor number too. Still, when two separate teams build partition indexes and both beat HNSW, I'm inclined to believe the direction.

Try it now, on a replica or a staging box, if:

  • you're past ~10M vectors and your HNSW index doesn't fit in RAM, or you're paying for a huge instance just so it does
  • you need 99% recall and HNSW can't reach it at your size
  • you're on PG 18, self-hosted, and comfortable rebuilding indexes

Stay on pgvector HNSW if:

  • your index fits in memory with headroom (most RAG apps under a few million chunks)
  • you're on RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure or another managed Postgres that doesn't list it
  • you rely on selective WHERE tenant_id = ... filters and can't add a partial index per tenant
  • you have heavy update churn and no time to schedule rebalances

Revisit at GA, when filtered streaming search and automatic, incremental rebalancing are supposed to ship. Until then, 42 hours vs 49 minutes is a great slide and a bad reason to migrate production.

What do you run vector search on right now: pgvector, VectorChord, pgvectorscale, or a dedicated vector DB like Qdrant? And if you've rerun rekall on your own hardware, did the numbers hold up? Tell me in the comments.

Sources

  • pg_vectorsearch tuning docs
  • pg_vectorsearch maintenance docs
  • Tiger Data launch post with benchmarks
  • rekall benchmark tool
  • pgvector README
  • VectorChord vs pgvector benchmark
  • Hacker News discussion

title: A Large-Scale Dataset for Multi-Class Financial News Classification in Brazilian Portuguese
description:
arXiv:2610.20630v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The development of Financial Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems for Brazilian Portuguese is hindered by the scarcity of domain-specific datasets. To address this, we present a large-scale corpus of approximately 160,000 Brazilian Portuguese financial news articles collected from web sources. To establish initial benchmarks for a weakly supervised multi-class classification approach based on semantic similarity, we annotated subsets of this corpus both manually and using a Large Language Model (LLM). We evaluated three similarity-based methods -- cosine similarity, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and FAISS-based nearest-neighbor search -- using multilingual semantic embeddings. Our experiments reveal that the task is highly sensitive to label quality and class distribution. On the manually labeled subset, KNN achieved the best performance (47.3% accuracy, 31.9% F1-score), closely followed by FAISS. Conversely, on the LLM-annotated subset, while accuracy reached approximately 50%, F1-scores dropped to near 20%, highlighting the negative impact of label imbalance and noisy weak annotations. These findings establish foundational baselines for a challenging task, underscoring the critical need for high-quality manual annotations. Ultimately, this dataset and our preliminary results provide a reference point for future research in Brazilian Portuguese Financial NLP.

title: Dusting the Phantom: Gaussian Allocation for Fading Dynamic Content
description:
arXiv:2610.21302v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dynamic Gaussian representations have made high-quality, real-time volumetric video increasingly practical, yet challenging motion can still break their reconstruction: small fast-moving objects may disappear, and fine textures in highly dynamic regions are often lost. In particular, simply training longer or using more Gaussians may still fail to recover small, fast-moving objects. We argue that the key bottleneck is not representational capacity itself, but where and when Gaussian primitives are allocated. Existing allocation strategies rely on current Gaussian locations and often overlook the spatiotemporal destinations of relocated Gaussians. To address these limitations, we introduce two complementary strategies. First, Seed Injection identifies under-reconstructed dynamic regions using temporal appearance changes and reconstruction errors, and initializes new Gaussians at geometrically plausible 3D locations through multi-view observations, independent of existing Gaussian locations. Second, Temporal Biased Relocation uses time-resolved optimization signals to guide the spatiotemporal placement of relocated Gaussians. Both strategies maintain a fixed Gaussian budget without modifying the underlying representation. Experiments across multiple dynamic-scene datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction quality, particularly in highly dynamic regions, recovering small, rapidly moving objects and fine-grained appearance details.

title: Your Placeholder Text Is Lying to You: 4 Layout Bugs Lorem Ipsum Hides
description:
Every mockup I reviewed this year used lorem ipsum. Several of those layouts broke in production - not because the design was bad, but because the placeholder text was too friendly.

Here is what lorem ipsum optimizes for, and what it quietly hides.

1. It has no long, unbreakable strings

Lorem ipsum words are short, lowercase, and separated by spaces. Real content contains things the browser cannot hyphenate: a 90-character signed URL, an address like firstname.lastname@international-partners.example.com, an API token, a German compound noun. Those are what overflow a flex row - flex: 1 will not shrink below the content's min-content width unless you also set min-width: 0 (or overflow-wrap: anywhere). You will never see that bug in a lorem ipsum mock. Paste one long token into your design before you call it done.

2. It never expands

German text runs roughly 30% longer than English, Finnish invents longer compounds, and CJK wraps between any two characters instead of at spaces. A button label that fits at 320px in English can overflow in two languages. Test with the longest realistic translation - or at minimum add 30% to every label and re-check the tight rows.

3. It hides truncation and empty states

Lorem ipsum paragraphs are all the same length, so list rows never collapse, cards never hit their one-line truncation, and -webkit-line-clamp never gets exercised. Real data puts a one-word title and a 300-word title in the same list. Feed the layout a deliberately awkward set of strings - empty string, a single character, one 200-character sentence - and look at each row again.

4. It hides the labels

Placeholder copy tends to be descriptive nouns. Real UI copy is verbs and consequences: "Delete workspace", not "Workspace deletion". If a screen only reads correctly with lorem ipsum in it, the placeholder is doing layout work that the layout should be doing.

When lorem ipsum is the right call

Before the copy exists at all - early explorations where you are deciding spacing, hierarchy, and density. Once the layout is settled, swap in realistic strings. When I need filler fast I use a lorem ipsum generator: it runs entirely in the browser (nothing uploaded, no signup), you choose the paragraph and sentence counts, and the output pastes straight into test fixtures.

The rule I keep coming back to: if your placeholder text would pass a type checker, it is not testing anything.

title: Node.js SMS API Integration — Property Support Server Monitoring Alerts
description:
The decisive trade-off is template ownership: the property-management system should own the meaning, version, audience, and approval record of every message, while an SMS provider should transport an already-authorized rendering. TL;DR: put contact-form classification, queue selection, consent evidence, template versioning, idempotency, and the audit trail behind one application boundary; then evaluate AWS SNS, Twilio, Plivo, and a simple SMS API by how faithfully each can carry that decision across US and EU delivery paths. The provider choice follows from the control boundary. It should not define it.

This distinction matters when a resident submits a form about a leaking pipe, a prospective tenant asks for a viewing, or a property owner requests a statement. Those contacts can land in different support queues, yet an apparently harmless acknowledgment may still become a messaging-compliance event. A fast Node.js integration is useful, but speed to the first outbound request says little about duplicate suppression, replay safety, authorization evidence, or the ability to explain six months later why a particular template reached a particular number.

The same comparison is often framed as server monitoring alerts for a retail curbside pickup system, where an alert may tell staff that an order is waiting or report that a pickup workflow is stalled. The property-support case has a different business event, but it exposes the same architectural mistake: letting an SMS API own the message definition and then treating a successful request as proof that the right communication occurred.

Why should the application own the template?

A routing decision has at least four inputs: the property or portfolio, the contact category, the jurisdiction, and the recipient's messaging status. Treating the provider's template identifier as the decision collapses those inputs into an external configuration surface. A support administrator can then change wording without changing the application release, but the audit record may retain only an opaque identifier whose content has since changed. That is a poor ledger.

Instead, store an immutable template version beside the normalized routing result. The record should say, in application terms, maintenance-emergency routed to after-hours-maintenance, rendered with template version 7, in locale en-US, under a recorded authorization basis. The transport adapter receives the rendered body and a stable dispatch key. If organizational policy requires templates to live in a provider console, preserve the same invariant by exporting an immutable copy or content hash into the dispatch record before sending.

Short records help. Ambiguous records do not.

SPF is relevant only to an email fallback: RFC 7208 defines a DNS-based mechanism by which a domain can authorize hosts to use its identity in mail transfer. It does not establish consent for an SMS message, classify a property inquiry, or prove which application template was rendered. Likewise, CTIA's messaging guidance places messaging practices in an ecosystem of consumer protection and interoperability; transport success must not be mistaken for permission or correct audience selection.

What should a Node.js SMS API prove for server monitoring alerts?

Begin with a durable contact_submission record and assign it a unique identifier at ingress. Normalize the phone number and region according to the application's validated data rules, but keep the original input for audit purposes. Classification then produces a queue and a reason code rather than free-form prose. Only after that decision is committed should an outbox row authorize an acknowledgment.

The useful transaction boundary is narrow: contact, routing decision, selected template version, and outbox intent commit together. Network delivery cannot participate in that database transaction, so the worker must assume it can crash after a provider accepts a request but before the local acknowledgment is stored. Exactly-once delivery is not a promise the worker can honestly make across that boundary. An exactly-once mindset is still valuable: define one business intent, attach one idempotency key, record every attempt, and reconcile ambiguous outcomes rather than creating a second intent.

Consider one concrete sequence. A resident submits an emergency maintenance contact, the application commits the contact, queue decision, template version, and outbox intent, and a worker claims that intent; the SMS transport accepts it, but the worker loses its database connection before recording the returned identifier. On restart, the row still lacks acceptance evidence. Blindly creating another outbox row changes one business intent into two, while marking the first row failed invents certainty the system does not possess. The defensible state is uncertain: preserve the original key, query or reconcile using the evidence the selected API makes available, and require an explicit operational decision if that evidence cannot resolve the outcome. This is a mundane edge case, yet it separates an easy integration demo from an auditable communication system.

One practical state machine is pending -> claimed -> accepted or pending -> claimed -> uncertain; a confirmed rejection can move to failed, while an uncertain attempt requires reconciliation before retry. Do not turn a timeout into immediate evidence that nothing happened. That is where duplicate resident messages are born.

Timeouts are ambiguous.

The following Go sketch is deliberately transport-neutral. A Node.js service can create the same outbox contract; the worker language is irrelevant to the invariant, and the example remains in Go to make the state transitions explicit.

package dispatch

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
)

type Intent struct {
    ID              string
    ContactID       string
    Queue           string
    TemplateVersion int
    RenderedBody    string
    Recipient       string
}

type Receipt struct {
    ProviderMessageID string
}

type Transport interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, intent Intent, idempotencyKey string) (Receipt, error)
}

type Ledger interface {
    ClaimPending(ctx context.Context, intentID string) (Intent, error)
    RecordAccepted(ctx context.Context, intentID, providerMessageID string) error
    RecordUncertain(ctx context.Context, intentID, reason string) error
}

func Dispatch(ctx context.Context, ledger Ledger, transport Transport, intentID string) error {
    intent, err := ledger.ClaimPending(ctx, intentID)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    receipt, err := transport.Send(ctx, intent, intent.ID)
    if err != nil {
        if recordErr := ledger.RecordUncertain(ctx, intent.ID, err.Error()); recordErr != nil {
            return errors.Join(err, recordErr)
        }
        return err
    }

    return ledger.RecordAccepted(ctx, intent.ID, receipt.ProviderMessageID)
}

This code does not claim that every transport honors the supplied key. The adapter contract exposes the application's stable identity; provider-specific testing must establish whether a candidate deduplicates it, returns a queryable message identifier, or requires reconciliation in the application ledger. The distinction belongs in the architecture review, not in an optimistic interface comment.

Test the claim.

Compare ownership and evidence, not headline simplicity

AWS SNS, Twilio, Plivo, and a simple SMS API can all be placed behind the Transport interface, but their names do not answer the operational questions. A fair proof of concept should run the same evidence-oriented tests against each candidate and record observed behavior, using current primary documentation and the accounts, sender types, and destinations that the organization will actually deploy. Regional and account configuration can change the result, so a generic feature checklist is weaker than a reproducible acceptance suite.

Decision criterion Evidence to collect Ownership consequence
Template storage Immutable body, version, locale, and approver visible in the audit record Prefer application ownership unless an external template can be snapshotted reliably
Duplicate handling Repeated dispatch with the same business key under timeout and worker-restart tests Keep deduplication in the application ledger even if transport support exists
Outcome evidence Stable message identifier, normalized status, timestamps, and raw signed callback retained separately Map transport states into a small internal vocabulary without discarding source evidence
US and EU routing Results from the intended sender configuration and representative destination countries Treat geography as deployment data, not a global boolean
Consent and suppression Proof that opt-out and authorization rules are enforced before dispatch Keep eligibility ahead of the adapter so transport changes cannot bypass policy
Operational effort Time to diagnose an uncertain send, rotate credentials, reconcile callbacks, and export audit data Count recurring control work, not merely initial SDK lines

This matrix prevents the comparison from becoming an endorsement. AWS SNS may be candidate A, Twilio candidate B, Plivo candidate C, and the simple API candidate D; none receives a pass from brand recognition or a small quick-start. Each must return enough evidence for the same internal ledger. If a candidate cannot demonstrate an invariant, document the gap and decide whether the adapter can close it without creating a hidden second source of truth.

Price belongs in the evaluation, but as a modeled consequence of the real traffic shape: destination mix, message segments, sender registration or operational requirements, retries, support load, and reconciliation effort. It is not the primary argument. A nominal per-message figure cannot compensate for unclear template provenance or an outcome that operators cannot reconcile.

Cheap is contextual.

Failure handling is part of contact routing

An acknowledgment is downstream of the support route, not a substitute for it. If messaging is unavailable, the contact must remain visible in the correct queue with its service priority intact. This ordering keeps a transport fault from losing a maintenance request and lets the team retry communication without rerunning classification.

Callbacks need the same discipline as payment webhooks. Authenticate them using the selected transport's documented mechanism, retain the original payload under an access-controlled retention policy, deduplicate events, and apply monotonic internal transitions. A late status must not rewrite an accepted message into a new send intent. Nor should a callback's recipient field be trusted to locate a contact when the application already has a provider message identifier mapped to an outbox record.

Observe three layers separately: routing correctness, dispatch processing, and transport outcome. Queue-depth and oldest-pending age reveal worker trouble; counts of uncertain attempts expose the reconciliation burden; outcome distributions segmented by region and template version can reveal a deployment-specific change. Avoid putting phone numbers or rendered message bodies in general-purpose logs. The audit store can be precise while operational telemetry remains minimized and access controlled.

Compliance review should define retention, access, deletion, and authorization evidence for each jurisdiction and business purpose. The CTIA material is an important US industry reference, but it is not a complete legal analysis for every US or EU message. Obtain current legal and carrier-policy review for the actual program before launch, then encode the approved limits as versioned policy rather than worker folklore.

Roll out without changing the business decision

Start by freezing the internal intent schema and creating adapters for the shortlisted transports. Replay synthetic contacts through every category and jurisdiction branch, including duplicate submissions, invalid numbers, worker termination after send, delayed callbacks, and callbacks delivered more than once. Synthetic recipients and clearly marked non-production templates keep this exercise separate from resident data.

Next, shadow only the decision path: produce routing and template selections without sending, and compare them with the existing workflow. Once reviewed, enable a small approved scope, reconcile every intent against transport evidence, and expand by property group or jurisdiction. A transport migration then changes adapter configuration and credentials; it does not rewrite queue rules, consent policy, or template history.

The final selection should be the candidate that satisfies the documented control requirements with an acceptable operational burden for the deployment's US and EU footprint. The durable design choice is application-owned intent and evidence. That conclusion survives a provider change, an SDK rewrite, and the next template revision.

Sources

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • CTIA, Messaging Interoperability SMS/MMS: https://www.ctia.org/the-wireless-industry/industry-commitments/messaging-interoperability-sms-mms

title: VELD-QA: A Large-Scale Dataset for Visual Evidence Grounding and Question Answering in Long Documents
description:
arXiv:2610.20964v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing long-document QA benchmarks rarely combine large-scale human-authored questions with detailed visual evidence annotations, limiting diagnosis of evidence localization and interpretation failures. We present VELD-QA, a large-scale benchmark for Visual Evidence grounding and question answering in Long Documents. It contains 15,000 fully human-authored question-answer pairs across 5,859 real-world PDFs totaling 372,445 pages, balancing chart, table, and complex-layout tasks. Human annotations identify supporting pages and evidence elements and describe cited visual content, enabling separate retrieval and interpretation evaluation. We evaluate nine vision-language models under four evidence settings and seven retrieval-augmented and agentic systems. Our analysis identifies bottlenecks in evidence localization and interpretation. Retrieval-based methods substantially underperform the oracle setting with ground-truth supporting pages; full-document access does not close the gap. Localization alone is insufficient: oracle accuracy peaks at 81.7%, highlighting persistent visual interpretation and reasoning challenges. Enriching inputs with our visual-element annotations narrows the performance gap by 17-24%, demonstrating value beyond evaluation and motivating data enrichment for multimodal document QA. Our code is available at https://github.com/oracle-samples/veld-qa.

title: SMS Alert API Alternatives Explained (Europe GDPR and US Startup Support)
description:
Choose an SMS alert API by the evidence it lets your system retain, not by the apparent simplicity of its send call. For US and EU loan-application updates, my recommendation is to put consent, destination policy, sender eligibility, idempotency, and an append-only audit record in your own critical path; then select a provider whose operating model fits the response-time and channel breadth you actually need. Infrai is workable for plain alerts when polling is acceptable and your application owns the compliance logic. Twilio, Vonage, and Sinch deserve equal consideration when a broader communications suite or provider-specific workflow is the stronger requirement.

Short answer: no provider turns a phone number and a message into a compliance decision. The durable architecture makes that decision before transmission and records enough evidence to explain it afterward.

Which SMS alert API alternatives support US and Europe compliance?

This architecture decision record starts with four invariants. First, a loan update cannot be sent unless the application has a current consent record for the destination and purpose. Second, the country inferred by the application must be allowed by an explicit policy; absence from the policy means deny. Third, one business event produces at most one accepted send operation, even if a worker crashes after the provider accepts it. Fourth, every decision leaves an audit record containing the business event ID, policy version, consent reference, message classification, chosen sender, provider request reference, and final disposition.

The last two invariants are related but not interchangeable. An idempotency key prevents duplicate effects within a defined deduplication window; an audit trail explains what the system believed before, during, and after that window. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window, so I would still make the loan event ID unique in the application database rather than treating provider retention as permanent exactly-once delivery.

Exactly once is an aspiration. The enforceable design is an atomic local transition, an idempotent remote request, and reconciliation.

No evidence, no send.

Failure boundaries matter here. A malformed phone number fails before policy evaluation. Missing consent fails closed. An unknown country never falls through to a default sender. A timeout after submission is ambiguous and must be retried with the same key, while HTTP 429 requires bounded exponential backoff that honors Retry-After. Delivery status is later evidence, not permission retroactively granted.

Sender registration and sender-listing capabilities support production setup where local sender rules apply, but the application still has to choose an eligible sender. Inbound messages are retrieved by polling, which can cover simple STOP and HELP processing but is a poor match for conversational, low-latency support. There is no built-in geographic fence or by-country spend circuit breaker, so both belong before the send operation. I chose an application-owned deny-by-default map because a provider-side sender list answers a different question: what can be used, rather than what this lender has authorized for this event.

The decision is about evidence, latency, and scope

The following comparison is deliberately qualitative. Published prices and country rules move; neither should be frozen into an architecture record without a dated procurement review.

Option Best fit for this decision Boundary to test before adoption
Twilio Teams that want a mature, provider-specific messaging workflow and detailed guidance on SMS segmentation Verify current sender registration, inbound handling, and country obligations for every launch market
Vonage Messages API Teams evaluating SMS alongside a broader messaging API Confirm the exact inbound and status event model, regional processing terms, and sender support for the intended countries
Sinch SMS Teams that want an established SMS platform and are prepared to integrate its callbacks and compliance processes Confirm sender availability, opt-out handling, data location, and evidence retention contractually
AWS SNS Systems already organized around AWS identities, logs, and operational controls Validate origination identities, two-way requirements, country coverage, and the evidence exported to the lender's audit store
Infrai Plain alerting where one REST contract and one key across many backend capabilities reduce integration and reconciliation work Inbound events are pull-based; geo-fencing and country spend controls remain application responsibilities
Amazon SES An email fallback for teams already using AWS; it is not an SMS replacement Keep email consent, domain authentication, suppression, and channel-specific evidence separate from the SMS decision

This is not a feature-count contest. Twilio documents how GSM-7 and UCS-2 affect segmentation, a detail that can alter both delivery behavior and cost when loan status text contains non-GSM characters. The same message-body test belongs in any provider evaluation, including Vonage, Sinch, AWS SNS, and the final option in the table. Separately, GDPR requires a lawful basis, purpose limitation, data minimization, and demonstrable compliance; selecting an EU-capable vendor does not transfer those controller obligations out of the application.

Amazon SES belongs in the table only as an adjacent channel decision. A lender may use email when its product policy permits that fallback, but substituting email does not make an SMS alert requirement disappear, and the email side has its own evidence: authenticated sending domains, suppression state, consent purpose, and delivery events. Keeping that distinction visible prevents a broad “communications” procurement exercise from pretending that all channels have interchangeable sender rules or opt-out semantics.

Infrai's differentiator is breadth behind a consistent REST API: its self-describing discovery catalog reports 295 capabilities across 20 modules under one key, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. Public request and response schemas reduce the friction of reviewing a payload contract before it reaches a regulated workflow; the shared idempotency convention reduces a different kind of friction during retry design. Neither point compensates for polling latency, missing geo controls, or the absence of voice, WhatsApp, RCS, and SMTP relay.

Put policy before the network

The critical path below is a runnable Go client for the one verified send operation, POST /v1/sms/send. It reads the exact JSON payload from SMS_PAYLOAD_JSON because no request fields should be guessed, reads credentials and the deployment base URL from the environment, checks every response, surfaces error bodies, reuses the business event ID as the idempotency key, and applies bounded 429 retry behavior. The compliance gate must run before this client is called.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func send(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, baseURL, key, eventID string, payload []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
            baseURL+"/v1/sms/send", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", eventID)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 { return body, nil }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("sms send returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done(): return nil, ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry limit reached")
}

func main() {
    baseURL, key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    eventID, payload := os.Getenv("LOAN_EVENT_ID"), []byte(os.Getenv("SMS_PAYLOAD_JSON"))
    if baseURL == "" || key == "" || eventID == "" || len(payload) == 0 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, LOAN_EVENT_ID, and SMS_PAYLOAD_JSON")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    body, err := send(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, baseURL, key, eventID, payload)
    if err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err); os.Exit(1) }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

The network client is only half of the guarantee. A real service needs a database uniqueness constraint on the event ID and an outbox or equivalent transaction boundary; otherwise two processes can both submit before either stores its receipt. Store message classification and a content hash when retaining the full body would violate minimization policy; retain the body only when the compliance and support case justifies it. This is the trade-off I would document: more local state and reconciliation work in exchange for evidence that remains coherent through a timeout, a worker restart, or a provider migration.

I initially considered treating an HTTP success as the final ledger event, then rejected that model because its failure story is incomplete. Consider the awkward sequence: the provider accepts loan-1042-approved-v1, the connection drops before the response reaches the worker, and the worker restarts. The local row still says “pending,” yet the external effect may already exist. On restart, the worker reads the same outbox row and resubmits with the same idempotency key; it does not mint a new key for attempt two. If the response is accepted, the worker stores the provider request reference and advances the row. If ambiguity remains, reconciliation polls status rather than guessing. The audit stream records each attempt and its outcome, while the business-event uniqueness constraint ensures that another process cannot create a second logical send. That is why I chose a little more state. A dashboard screenshot cannot reconstruct this sequence, and an application log that expires after a week cannot carry a lender's long-term evidence policy.

Retries preserve identity.

Reconciliation then compares accepted submissions with polled status and inbound records. Because the email and SMS namespaces do not emit webhook events, the polling worker needs a persisted cursor, overlap between windows, deduplication by provider record ID, and an alert for stale progress. A three-minute poll may be perfectly adequate for STOP processing in a low-volume alert service, but that number is an internal service-level choice, not a platform guarantee.

Why reject a provider-owned compliance boundary?

The rejected design sends first and relies on provider dashboards, sender registration, or suppression behavior as the system of record. It is attractive because the initial integration is smaller. It also separates the loan decision from its evidence: the provider can show that a message was submitted, yet the lender may still be unable to show which consent and country policy authorized that submission.

There is a valid use case for the rejected option. A prototype using synthetic recipients, no regulated customer data, and no production traffic can use a provider console to test copy and segmentation before the audit subsystem exists. The boundary must be explicit, short-lived, and incapable of reaching real borrowers.

For production, record consent withdrawal locally before the next send can be admitted. Polling for inbound STOP and HELP messages should feed the same suppression decision, with repeated records handled idempotently. If the product requirement changes from alerts to real-time two-way support, polling becomes the architectural reason to reconsider the provider rather than something to disguise with a tighter loop.

Decision

For a startup delivering loan-application alerts in the US and EU, I would adopt the provider-neutral policy and audit layer first, then choose among Twilio, Vonage, Sinch, AWS SNS, and Infrai after a country-by-country sender and data-processing review. The last option fits when plain SMS alerts, pull-based event handling, and a broad single-contract backend surface are acceptable. It does not fit a design that requires real-time inbound webhooks, managed geographic enforcement, or voice and rich-messaging channels.

The acceptance test is concrete: replay one business event twice and observe one provider submission; deny an unlisted country before any network call; trace an accepted alert back to consent and policy versions; process the same inbound opt-out twice without changing the outcome; and reconcile every ambiguous timeout. Pass those tests before debating unit price.

Policy wins.

References

  • EUR-Lex: General Data Protection Regulation, Article 5
  • Twilio: SMS character limits and message segmentation
  • Twilio: Messaging compliance
  • Vonage: Messages API documentation
  • Sinch: SMS API documentation
  • AWS: SMS messaging with Amazon SNS
  • AWS: Amazon SES documentation
  • FCC: Robotexts and unwanted texts

title: Firefox Developer Edition: What's Different and Why Developers Should Use It
description:
Firefox Developer Edition is a special Firefox build aimed at web developers. It offers features and default settings that make web development faster and more productive. Here's what makes it different from standard Firefox.

What is Firefox Developer Edition?

Firefox Developer Edition (formerly Aurora) sits between Firefox Nightly (daily bleeding edge) and stable Firefox. It contains features 4–8 weeks ahead of stable, with developer-focused defaults:

  • DevTools panels enabled by default (like Remote Debugging, Browser Toolbox)
  • Higher contrast DevTools theme
  • Separate profile from regular Firefox (your bookmarks/logins stay separate)
  • A distinct blue/orange color scheme so you can tell it apart at a glance

Download at: https://www.mozilla.org/firefox/developer/

Developer-Focused Features

Browser Toolbox (Enabled by Default)

The Browser Toolbox lets you inspect Firefox's own UI — including panels, chrome, extensions:

  1. Settings → Advanced Settings → "Enable browser chrome and add-on debugging toolboxes"
  2. Tools → Browser Toolbox
  3. Inspect the Firefox UI like any webpage

In standard Firefox you have to opt in; Developer Edition has it enabled by default.

Remote Debugging Over Network

Debug Firefox on another device or a headless instance from your desktop:

  1. about:config → set devtools.debugger.remote-enabled to true
  2. Set devtools.debugger.remote-host to the IP you'll connect from
  3. Connect from DevTools → Remote Debugging

Standard Firefox supports this too, but Developer Edition enables it for local loopback by default.

CSS Grid and Flexbox Overlay

Both editions have this, but Developer Edition has it enabled more prominently in the Layout panel:

.container {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  grid-template-rows: auto;
  gap: 16px;
}

Open DevTools → Layout → click the grid/flex overlay button next to any element. Overlays show column/row lines, gap areas, and cell names visually on the page.

Responsive Design Mode

DevTools → Responsive Design Mode (or Ctrl+Shift+M):

  • Test exact device dimensions (iPhone 15, Pixel 9, Surface Pro, etc.)
  • Simulate touch events
  • Throttle network to 3G/4G speeds
  • Rotate between portrait/landscape
  • Capture screenshots at device resolution

Developer Edition's Responsive Design Mode has all device profiles pre-loaded.

The Separate Profile

Developer Edition uses a profile named dev-edition-default. This means:

  • Your Dev Edition history/bookmarks won't pollute your stable Firefox
  • You can have incompatible extension configurations in each
  • Different about:config settings without touching your daily driver

To sync between editions, enable Firefox Sync in each and sign in to the same account.

A/B Testing Across Editions

Having both Firefox stable and Developer Edition lets you:

  1. Test your site in both quickly (different profiles = different logins, states)
  2. Verify CSS features work in stable vs. upcoming versions
  3. Compare performance before features ship to stable

about:config Differences

Developer Edition ships with some about:config values that differ from stable:

devtools.chrome.enabled = true     (standard = false)
devtools.debugger.remote-enabled = true (standard = false for localhost)
devtools.theme = "dark" (same as standard, but default dark theme)

You can replicate these on standard Firefox manually.

Performance Profiler

Both Firefox editions include the Performance tab, but Developer Edition promotes it more prominently:

  1. Open DevTools → Performance
  2. Click Record
  3. Interact with your page
  4. Stop recording
  5. Analyze flame graph, call tree, and allocations timeline

Useful for finding layout thrash, forced reflows, and slow JavaScript.

Multi-Process Architecture

Firefox uses multiple processes (Fission, Site Isolation):

  • One process per top-level tab origin
  • One process for Firefox UI (chrome process)
  • One process for GPU rendering

In Developer Edition, about:processes shows all processes with memory usage. This is available in stable Firefox too but is a bit buried.

CSS Features Available Early

Developer Edition ships CSS features 4-8 weeks before stable. Recent examples:

  • CSS Nesting (now in stable, was Dev Edition first)
  • :has() relational pseudo-class
  • @layer cascade layers
  • color-mix() function
  • Container queries and @container

Check MDN's browser compatibility tables — a "Developer Edition" row often appears before the stable Firefox row updates.

WebExtension Debugging

Developer Edition is best for extension development:

  1. about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox — load temporary extension
  2. Click "Inspect" — opens dedicated DevTools for background script
  3. Errors in background scripts appear in the Browser Console
  4. No need to package the extension to test it

For AMO submission, extensions are reviewed against release Firefox, so test in stable before publishing.

Should You Use Developer Edition Daily?

Pros:

  • First access to CSS/JS features
  • Better defaults for dev work
  • Separate profile = clean testing environment

Cons:

  • Occasional instability (it IS a pre-release channel)
  • Some sites may behave differently on pre-release
  • Another browser instance to keep updated

Recommendation: Use it for development, keep stable Firefox for daily browsing. The separate profile makes this easy — two browsers, two use cases.

title: WorldCast: Exploring Intelligent Visual Generation in World State Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.20731v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Humans interpret multimodal observations of the world and forecast how it will evolve. Recent multimodal generative systems have demonstrated similar capabilities: they can integrate multimodal context and synthesize visual outputs that depict changes in the world. To characterize this emerging trajectory, we organize model capabilities into a four-level hierarchy and discover that higher-level tasks remain relatively underexplored despite model progress. To bridge this gap, we explore model performance on multi-step world state prediction, a high-level task that requires models to forecast successive future world states from multimodal observations and diverse references. Such a task requires models to possess entangled understanding and generation capabilities, as well as extensive world knowledge to translate human action sequences, physical transformations, and abstract visual reasoning into coherent visual outputs. We introduce WorldCast, a benchmark comprising 320 manually designed cases across eight categories, and evaluate 12 representative models. The conducted experiments yield three key insights: (a) advances in frontier models are rapidly pushing the boundaries of intelligent world modeling, with the GPT-Image-2.5 System scoring 72.8 and demonstrating early-stage visual state prediction capabilities on real-world tasks; (b) WorldCast reveals substantial gaps between models: even Nano Banana Pro reaches only 42.8 and the best open-source model scores 20.1, with deficits in handling complex context, entangled references, and reasoning-heavy tasks; (c) strong generative models effectively draw on the capabilities of their underlying language models. These findings highlight the need for multimodal generative models that are capable of dynamic planning and reasoning while also being deeply unified to faithfully simulate real-world states.

title: Realtime Host Handoff Recovery: WebRTC Failure Handling for Consultation Rooms
description:
Use a realtime API surface that matches host handoff, then make recovery explicit in the video consultation room. The deciding constraint is trust: a replacement host must receive a narrowly scoped token, while the browser must be able to prove which room state it has actually observed.

Short answer: keep authentication, subscription state, and business events as separate state machines, and reconcile them with stable identifiers after every reconnect.

The experiment: a host handoff is a state transition

Imagine a clinician's browser loses its uplink during a consultation. A second clinician takes over. The simple implementation treats “connected” as proof that the handoff worked. That is the trap. A WebRTC peer connection can be alive while the application subscription is stale, and a valid token can outlive the business event that revoked the first host.

I model the room with three clocks: token expiry, realtime subscription, and the clinical business event. They can disagree. The handoff command carries a server-created room identifier and a monotonically increasing event identifier. The new host asks for current presence, compares that identifier, and only then enables controls. It feels slower than optimistic UI for one frame. It is much easier to audit.

The useful measurement is not a glossy latency number. Measure how often a reconnect converges to one host, how many duplicate events are discarded, and how often an unauthorized client is denied. Your mileage may vary with mobile radio conditions; I’m not sure a lab Wi-Fi test tells you much here.

How should realtime failure handling protect host handoff and token scope?

Start with an explicit state table. “Expired” is not the same thing as “disconnected,” and neither means the consultation ended.

State Client action Server decision
Token expired Stop publishing; request a fresh scoped token Re-check role and room version
Subscription dropped Reconnect with backoff, then fetch presence Replay or return the current stable identifier
Duplicate event Compare event identifier and ignore an old one Keep delivery at-least-once safe
Partial handoff Show read-only controls until reconciliation Reject writes from the old host

This separation also makes authorization tests concrete. Try an expired token, a token for another room, and a valid token with an old role. Then add 400 ms latency and duplicate delivery. A green path is not evidence that the workflow is safe.

A small Node.js reconciliation loop

The presence read is deliberately boring. It is a recovery checkpoint, not a second source of business truth. The route below is the documented presence lookup; the room and event identifiers returned by your application service remain the authoritative records.

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
if (!baseUrl) throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required (use the service's v1 base URL)");

async function readPresence(channel: string): Promise<unknown> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${baseUrl}/realtime/presence/get/${encodeURIComponent(channel)}`,
      {
        method: "GET",
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
      },
    );

    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`presence lookup failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json();
  }
  throw new Error("presence lookup rate-limited after retries");
}

The plain REST shape is useful when the room service is already in Node.js but the mobile client is not: there is no SDK version to coordinate, and any HTTP-capable worker can perform the same checkpoint. Infrai's other practical advantage here is a single key and billing surface for adjacent backend capabilities, while this article's decision still rests on scope and recovery semantics. Keep the key on your server; never forward it to a browser.

Keep it server-side.

Where the common room providers fit

There is no universal winner. The right choice depends on how much of the room lifecycle you want to operate and how much control your authorization model needs.

Option Strength for a consultation room Trade-off to validate
Pusher Familiar pub/sub primitives for broadcasting a handoff event You still own media, token scope, and recovery ordering
Ably Managed realtime delivery with presence concepts Validate retention and replay behavior against your audit requirements
PubNub Broad realtime messaging and presence tooling Provider-specific event semantics can increase migration work later
Plain WebRTC plus your service Maximum control over token scope and business events You operate signaling, reconnect behavior, and observability
Infrai realtime surface One HTTP interface can fit a server-side presence checkpoint without installing an SDK It is not a complete media room by itself; pair it with a WebRTC room layer

The catch is important: a REST presence checkpoint does not replace media negotiation, TURN capacity, or clinical audit storage. Choose a managed room provider when your team cannot operate those pieces. Stick with plain WebRTC when protocol control is the product. Choose the Infrai surface when a small, language-neutral backend checkpoint is the missing piece, not because a single API magically removes the rest of the system.

Run the same scenario against every candidate: clinician A publishes, the network drops, clinician B receives a scoped token, and the old browser retries an event. Assert that the old write is rejected, the duplicate is harmless, and a reconnect converges on one stable room and event identifier. Record authentication failures separately from subscription failures and business-event failures; combining them produces an attractive dashboard that cannot explain a patient-facing incident.

I would ship only after those assertions pass under realistic latency and authorization permutations. The implementation is small. The state contract is the real feature.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://docs.livekit.io/
  • https://www.twilio.com/docs/video
  • https://docs.daily.co/

title: APRiL: An Open-ended Benchmark for Chinese Social Awareness in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20785v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in social interactions, where appropriate responses require recognizing implicit cues, inferring mental states, identifying conflicts, and considering potential consequences. However, existing benchmarks often focus on specific social abilities, constrained task formats, or particular interaction settings, offering limited coverage of social awareness across diverse contexts. To address this gap, we introduce APRiL, an open-ended benchmark for Chinese social awareness with instance-specific rubrics. APRiL contains 2,196 Social Awareness Evaluation Instances across six categories and two complementary tasks: Social Scenario Analysis evaluates models' understanding of social cues, mental states, and conflict structures, while Socially Aware Response assesses whether they can translate this understanding into appropriate, natural responses. Experiments on 12 models from six families reveal a consistent understanding-to-response gap. Higher-quality scenario analyses improve responses, while weak analyses may reduce response quality. APRiL provides a systematic resource for advancing socially aware language models in Chinese contexts. Our data and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/APRiL-05DE/.

title: Evaluating Model Capabilities After Benchmark Saturation
description:
arXiv:2610.20667v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rapid advances in AI capabilities are causing benchmarks to saturate. Once several models approach perfect scores, a benchmark loses its power to differentiate between them, and with it its utility for informing AI safety cases and frontier policies. Yet benchmark items produce far more information than the scores we typically extract from them: a full transcript of how each model solved the task. We investigate whether these transcripts can be used to assess model capabilities even after benchmark scores have saturated. We simulate saturation retrospectively using historical benchmark and model releases, and test whether protocols that access only correctly solved transcripts from saturated benchmarks can predict capabilities measured on held-out, unsaturated items. We evaluate representative contemporary approaches for extracting information from model transcripts: pairwise judging, single-transcript absolute scoring, and predictions from deterministic transcript features or embeddings. We find that saturated transcripts retain capability information beyond benchmark accuracy. Amongst our evaluated protocols, pairwise judging performs best, reducing prediction error by 5.3 times compared to a baseline using only saturated benchmark scores. This capability-relevant information is distributed across transcript sections, but concentrated in specific channels of information such as reasoning and tool-calls. However, the predictive power of protocols does not always generalise across distribution shifts -- for example by underestimating the capabilities of the first reasoning models introduced in early 2025. Saturated benchmarks thus retain capability-predicting signal in their task transcripts, but extending the lifetime of existing benchmarks requires methods designed to extract these signals robustly.

title: ToolBottleneckBench: Measuring Tool-Agent Performance under Controlled Pressures and Fixed Harness Budgets
description:
arXiv:2610.21098v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The success score of a tool agent reflects both its model and the budgets of the harness that runs it. We present ToolBottleneckBench, a benchmark that measures tool-agent performance under controlled pressures and fixed harness budgets. Synthetic enterprise tasks stay fixed while one pressure varies: the registered tool catalog, the visible tool menu, the certified workflow, or the encoding of returned records. An exact grader records the first unmet obligation of each failed episode and the harness limit, if any, that ended it. Across 21 model and harness configurations, the visible menu is the only one of the three pressures that act on the model with a large penalty, and this penalty tracks truncation at the completion cap. Raising the cap sixteenfold removes most of the penalty in the truncation-heavy configurations. Most failures end at a harness limit, and the failure record identifies the assigned pressure no more reliably than a count of tool calls. The repairs that help change which tools reach the model or who issues the calls, and only two repairs, neither improving model behavior, beat every configuration switch. We recommend reporting pressure effects with the harness budgets under which they were measured. We release the benchmark at https://github.com/zichuanxu/tool-bottleneck-bench.

title: Error Tracking for Health Endpoint Checks: 4 Node.js Network Errors
description:
A pricing-rule rollout needs enough evidence to stop a bad release without turning every transient probe error into an incident. Short answer: capture timeout, connection-refused, DNS, and unexpected 5xx outcomes as separate error classes; group repeated events; and correlate them with logs and metrics by service name and timestamp. Keep the flag rollback decision outside the error tracker. For a solo SaaS, this protects the scarce resource that matters most: focused shipping time.

Choice Best fit Main boundary
Sentry Application errors with source maps and rich debugging context More machinery than a narrow server-side probe may need
Datadog One established platform for monitors, logs, metrics, and traces Broad configuration requires a disciplined signal policy
Better Stack Uptime checks plus incident response and status pages Less focused on deep application exception analysis
Healthchecks.io Detecting scheduled jobs that miss a check-in Does not replace exception grouping for active HTTP probes
Infrai A small backend that wants error capture and search over plain REST Lacks source-map decoding, session replay, notification routes, and span-tree queries

My default for this rollout is narrow: use an uptime monitor to run the check, an error tracker to preserve diagnostic errors, and the feature-flag system to control exposure. Infrai is a reasonable error-store choice when avoiding another SDK and credential set has high value. Anything that can send HTTP can use its REST API. Its shared key can also cover SMS and observability, which makes delivery evidence easier to keep with service evidence.

How should Node.js error tracking group health endpoint checks?

Start with four classes because they imply different actions. ETIMEDOUT says the dependency did not answer within the probe budget. ECONNREFUSED says the destination was reachable but nothing accepted the connection. A DNS lookup error points toward naming or resolver configuration. An unexpected 5xx is an application response, so it belongs apart from transport trouble.

Do not group on the full error message. Hostnames, ports, durations, and request identifiers can turn one error mode into thousands of groups. A useful group key is closer to pricing-api:health:timeout than to a raw stack trace. Preserve the original message as event detail, then search stable dimensions. Prometheus gives the same warning for metric labels: every unique label set creates another time series, so unbounded identifiers are a bad dimension. The flag also needs a small release vocabulary: old rule, cohort rule, and full rule. Compare the same four error classes across those cohorts, but avoid customer IDs as group keys. A single timeout is weak evidence. Twenty repeated timeouts from the same service and rollout cohort are stronger, yet no universal count is correct because traffic and probe cadence determine the baseline. Define the threshold from your own normal window, then review it after the first rollout. For a one-person operation, a signal is valuable only when it changes a decision. Revenue per hour beats dashboard density.

Noise wins otherwise.

Ship weekly, learn, tighten.

Correlation without pretending it is tracing

Use the same service name and timestamps in error events, logs, and metrics. If a request already carries trace_id and span_id, retain those fields so a search can connect records. This is field-level correlation, not distributed tracing: there is no span-tree query here.

That distinction matters during a pricing change. A rising 5xx rate tells you the endpoint is unhealthy. A matching error group can expose the repeated exception. A metric split by a bounded rollout cohort can show whether the new rule is implicated. None of those alone proves causality, and a trace-shaped pair of IDs does not magically reconstruct the request path.

Keep clocks aligned and record UTC timestamps.

Tiny detail. Huge debugging payoff.

One key across delivery and diagnostics

A fintech rollout often has a second question beside endpoint health: did the verification message send? With Twilio plus Datadog, that generally means two signups, two credential sets, and custom glue to move provider delivery evidence into the observability context. Infrai exposes both SMS and observability under one base URL and one key. The trade is plain: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface.

The runnable TypeScript below reads request bodies from JSON files. Their exact shapes come from the public discovery schema, so the sample does not freeze guessed fields into an article. The SMS response feeds the error-capture payload through a caller-selected field defined by that schema. It uses two application routes and honors Retry-After on 429 responses.

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const baseUrl = ["https:", "", "api", "infrai", "cc", "v1"].join("/");
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const contextField = process.env.INFRAI_CAPTURE_CONTEXT_FIELD;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
if (!contextField) throw new Error("INFRAI_CAPTURE_CONTEXT_FIELD is required");

type Json = Record<string, unknown>;

async function post(
  path: string,
  body: Json,
  idempotencyKey: string,
  attempt = 0,
): Promise<Json> {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}${path}`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return post(path, body, idempotencyKey, attempt + 1);
  }

  const payload = (await response.json()) as Json;
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`${response.status}: ${JSON.stringify(payload)}`);
  }
  return payload;
}

const otpBody = JSON.parse(
  await readFile("otp-request.json", "utf8"),
) as Json;
const captureBody = JSON.parse(
  await readFile("error-capture-request.json", "utf8"),
) as Json;
const smsResult = await post("/sms/otp", otpBody, crypto.randomUUID());

captureBody[contextField] = smsResult;
await post("/errors/capture", captureBody, crypto.randomUUID());

Generate both JSON files and choose INFRAI_CAPTURE_CONTEXT_FIELD from the live discovery schemas before running this. Do not send the bearer token anywhere except the API base URL. Each logical write gets one key, and every retry reuses it.

This example illustrates the handoff, but capture only a delivery result that represents an error worth diagnosing. Recording every successful OTP as an error would destroy the signal-to-noise ratio. Delivery events and your own diagnostic context can land behind the same API boundary; the useful result is answering "did it send?" without manually joining a carrier dashboard to local logs.

Where does this approach stop?

Infrai does not supply the probe or heartbeat. It also lacks alert and notification routes for thresholds, phone calls, SMS, or webhooks, so you need to poll search results and own the alerting logic. That is a material maintenance cost. Healthchecks.io is the better complement for "the scheduled task never ran," while Better Stack is the cleaner choice when hosted uptime checks and incident workflows should arrive together.

The limitation is decisive: Infrai is not suitable when one product must provide the probe, alert delivery, source-map decoding, session replay, and a distributed span tree. Pick the specialist that owns the missing workflow instead of writing permanent glue merely to preserve a one-key setup.

Choose Sentry when source-map reversal, crash symbolication, or session replay is central. Those capabilities are unavailable here, including Electron minidump parsing. Choose Datadog when your team needs distributed trace exploration, mature monitors, and a broad operations suite more than it needs a small REST surface. Its integrated scope can be an advantage for a team that has time to govern tags and monitors.

Feature flags have another boundary. The available flag surface lacks change audit logs, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, and a recycle bin; clients poll. If pricing-rule governance requires an immutable approval trail, use a dedicated flag product and send only the resulting diagnostic context to the error store.

Logs add constraints too: there is no per-user deletion endpoint, bulk export, or subscription endpoint. Retention and cold-storage errors exist, but no configuration entry point is exposed. Those limits can rule the service out for a fintech data-retention design before developer convenience enters the discussion.

A release rule I can operate alone

I would ship the new pricing rule to a bounded cohort, keep four stable error groups, and watch a short list of metrics that can reverse the rollout decision. Search repeated errors to distinguish an isolated network event from persistent configuration trouble. Correlate by service and time, then use trace fields only as join hints.

The decision rule is deliberately boring: pause expansion when a cohort-specific error class departs materially from its baseline; roll back through the flag system when the evidence repeats; investigate isolated errors without paging yourself. The exact threshold must come from actual traffic. No invented universal number will protect revenue.

This division of labor is easy to remember. The monitor checks. The error store explains. Metrics establish scope. The flag controls exposure. Outsource those undifferentiated pieces, but keep the rollback policy in code and review it every week you ship.

  • AWS Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog error tracking documentation
  • Better Stack uptime documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
