title: Blue Teaming: How Attackers Use AI and Disposable Infrastructure
description:
How Attackers Use AI and Disposable Infrastructure: A Practical View for Blue Teams

If you work on a Cloudflare WAF, you spend much of your day looking at requests that arrive from IP addresses you do not control. Some are scanners. Some are bots. Some are people testing a login form. A smaller group is trying to find a real way in.

This article looks at a question many blue teamers ask: how can an attacker use AI, local models and cheap cloud infrastructure against a company? The goal is not to give a recipe for attacks. The goal is to build a clearer mental model of attacker maturity, so you can choose detections and controls that still work when the source IP changes every few hours.

The short version

Attackers do not need a sophisticated AI pipeline to attack a company. Most successful intrusions still begin with exposed services, weak authentication, stolen credentials, vulnerable software or a trusted third party.

AI changes the economics of some parts of an attack. It can help an operator summarize reconnaissance results, generate variations of phishing content, reason over tool output and repeat a workflow with fewer manual steps. It does not remove the need for an exposed surface, a valid identity or a exploitable bug.

A useful way to think about this is through three levels of attacker maturity.

Level 1: The opportunistic attacker

This attacker wants results with minimal effort. They may use a rented VPS, a script, a public scanner and a small set of wordlists. If they use an AI model, it is often on their own laptop or on the VPS itself.

Their infrastructure is usually simple:

[Attacker machine or VPS] --> [Company]

They care about getting a response, not about building a durable operational setup. The VPS may be paid for with cryptocurrency, but the account, email address, payment pattern and access habits can still create links back to a person.

From the defensive side, this is the easiest profile to detect. You will often see broad scanning, repeated login attempts, unusual request rates, obvious tool fingerprints and traffic from hosting providers or datacenter ASNs.

Useful controls at this level include:

  • Rate limiting on authentication and sensitive endpoints.
  • Managed WAF rules and bot management.
  • Blocklists and reputation feeds for known malicious infrastructure.
  • Strong MFA and protection against credential stuffing.
  • Alerts for scanning patterns and abnormal request volumes.

A Cloudflare WAF is particularly useful here because it can reduce noise before requests reach your application. The important part is to treat WAF rules as one layer, rather than as the whole security program.

Level 2: The organized attacker

This attacker has more patience and more operational discipline. They separate their personal identity from the infrastructure used during the attack. They may use temporary VPS instances, separate accounts and infrastructure that can be discarded after use.

A common conceptual separation looks like this:

[Attacker workstation: AI model and tools]
        |
        | Encrypted or anonymized access
        v
[Disposable VPS: network relay or attack host]
        |
        v
[Company]

The attacker may run the AI model locally and use the VPS only as a network relay. Alternatively, they may run a smaller quantized model directly on the VPS, especially if the workload does not require a GPU. The choice depends on cost, speed and how much they want their own endpoint to remain uninvolved.

At this level, the attacker understands that deleting a VPS does not erase every trace. Provider records, payment data, upstream network logs, backups and ISP records can still exist. For that reason, they try to reduce the number of places where their real identity and their attack infrastructure meet.

For blue teams, the source IP becomes less reliable as a primary indicator. The same operator may use different addresses, while different actors may share common hosting ranges.

More useful signals include:

  • Similar request sequences from different source IPs.
  • Consistent TLS, HTTP or automation fingerprints.
  • Reconnaissance followed by targeted attempts against login, API or administrative surfaces.
  • Short-lived sessions with a narrow focus.
  • Credential use that is technically valid but contextually unusual.

At this stage, behavioral detection matters more than static blocklists. You want to correlate identity, device posture, network origin, request pattern and business context.

Level 3: The mature actor

A mature actor treats infrastructure as disposable and treats identity as a separate problem. They do not rely on one VPS, one payment method or one access path. They may use infrastructure they do not directly own, including compromised systems, rented resources obtained through intermediaries or services that make attribution harder.

Their model is closer to this:

[Isolated operating environment]
        |
[Relay or intermediary infrastructure]
        |
[Attack host or compromised system]
        |
[Company]

The AI component may help with analysis, orchestration or documentation, but it is not the core of the intrusion. The core is still patience, valid access, a vulnerable dependency or a human being who can be deceived.

This type of actor produces fewer obvious indicators. Traffic may be slower, lower volume and more selective. They may use valid credentials, legitimate tools and normal-looking protocols. A single WAF rule will rarely stop them.

Your best defenses are structural:

  • Reduce the number of internet-facing services.
  • Require phishing-resistant MFA for privileged access.
  • Apply least privilege and short-lived credentials.
  • Monitor identity anomalies, not only network anomalies.
  • Keep centralized logs across WAF, identity provider, endpoint, email and cloud platforms.
  • Build detection around chains of behavior, such as reconnaissance followed by authentication followed by privilege changes.

The mature attacker is not necessarily invisible. They are harder to catch through one isolated signal. You need context across time, systems and identities.

Where MCP and AI agents fit

AI agent frameworks can connect a language model to external tools. In a legitimate security context, this can help a pentester run reconnaissance, organize findings and automate repetitive work. In the wrong hands, the same pattern can make an operator faster at working through tool output and repeating tasks.

The important point for defenders is that the AI model is not the attack. It is an accelerator around the attack. If your application has no exposed weakness, no weak identity control and no useful data to reach, an AI agent has little to work with.

That is why AI should not distract you from fundamentals. Patching, identity hardening, least privilege, secure defaults, logging and incident response still decide most outcomes.

What this means for Cloudflare WAF work

A WAF is excellent at reducing automated noise and enforcing rules at the edge. It is less effective as the only control against a patient attacker who uses valid credentials and legitimate-looking traffic.

A practical approach is to use the WAF for what it does well:

  • Filter obvious automated abuse.
  • Enforce rate limits and bot controls.
  • Protect known vulnerable paths.
  • Apply geo, ASN and reputation-based rules where they make sense.
  • Generate high quality logs for downstream analysis.

Then connect those logs to the rest of your detection stack. A blocked request is useful. A pattern of blocked requests, failed logins, new device registrations and privileged access attempts is much more useful.

A better question than “who is behind this IP?”

For a blue teamer, the most productive question is often not “who owns this IP?” It is:

What is this sequence of activity trying to achieve, and which control should have stopped it?

An IP can be rotated. A VPS can be deleted. An AI model can run locally. But poor identity hygiene, exposed services, excessive privileges and missing logging remain durable weaknesses.

Focus on making those weaknesses expensive to exploit. That is where your leverage is.

title: How Self-Driving Car Systems Detect and React: Explained with Code & Diagram
description:
TL;DR Self-driving car systems use cameras and sensors combined with AI models like CNNs and reinforcement learning to detect lanes, obstacles, and make real-time driving decisions. This article breaks down these core technologies with simple code examples and points to a ready-made project perfect for final-year students learning autonomous vehicle detection systems.

Imagine you're just days away from your final year project viva on a self-driving car system, and your demo stalled because the lane detection didn’t work as expected. You wonder, “How do these cars actually see and react to the road?” Let’s clear up common myths and see the reality behind how self-driving cars detect their environment and decide what to do next.

What Challenges Do Self-Driving Cars Face and How Are They Overcome?

Myth: Self-driving cars just drive themselves; they don’t need to “see” or think much.

Reality: Autonomous vehicles face huge challenges in sensing their surroundings and making split-second decisions safely. The main hurdles include:

  • Real-time environment sensing: Cars must continuously process data from cameras, LIDAR, and other sensors instantly.
  • Detecting lanes, obstacles, and pedestrians: This involves accurately identifying road markings, vehicles, people, and unexpected objects.
  • Safe navigation decisions: The system must decide when to steer, accelerate, brake, and avoid hazards, all while obeying traffic rules.

These challenges require a blend of computer vision, AI algorithms, and control systems working in harmony.

How Does Computer Vision Help the Car ‘See’ Its Environment?

Myth: The car just uses simple cameras to “look” and drives automatically.

Reality: Cameras alone don’t solve the problem. Computer vision techniques process raw images to extract meaningful features. Key points:

  • Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs): These AI models analyze camera images to detect lanes, traffic signs, and moving obstacles with high accuracy.
  • OpenCV library: Helps preprocess images—for example, applying edge detection or perspective transforms to highlight lane lines.
  • Example: Detecting lane lines involves converting images to grayscale, filtering edges with the Canny algorithm, and transforming the perspective to a bird’s-eye view for better lane curvature detection.

This combination lets the car “understand” the road ahead, not just see it.

What Role Does Reinforcement Learning and AI Play in Driving Decisions?

Myth: The car’s AI just follows fixed rules for steering and braking.

Reality: Modern self-driving systems use reinforcement learning (RL) where AI agents learn optimal driving policies by trial, error, and rewards. Details:

  • AI models learn how to control steering angle, acceleration, and braking by interacting with driving environments or simulators.
  • RL optimizes decisions for safety, comfort, and efficiency, even in complex or unfamiliar scenarios.
  • Sensor fusion integrates data from cameras, LIDAR, and radar to plan the safest path.

This dynamic approach helps autonomous vehicles adapt to diverse traffic conditions.

Can We See a Simple Code Snippet Showing Lane Detection Basics?

Absolutely! Here’s a straightforward Python snippet using OpenCV that captures video frames from a camera, detects edges to find lanes, and highlights them:

import cv2
import numpy as np

def detect_lanes(frame):
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    blur = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (5, 5), 0)
    edges = cv2.Canny(blur, 50, 150)

    height, width = edges.shape
    mask = np.zeros_like(edges)
    polygon = np.array([[
        (0, height),
        (width, height),
        (width, int(height*0.6)),
        (0, int(height*0.6))
    ]], np.int32)
    cv2.fillPoly(mask, polygon, 255)
    masked_edges = cv2.bitwise_and(edges, mask)

    lines = cv2.HoughLinesP(masked_edges, 2, np.pi/180, 100, minLineLength=40, maxLineGap=50)
    line_image = np.zeros_like(frame)

    if lines is not None:
        for line in lines:
            x1, y1, x2, y2 = line[0]
            cv2.line(line_image, (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (0, 255, 0), 5)

    combined = cv2.addWeighted(frame, 0.8, line_image, 1, 1)
    return combined

cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0)  # Use camera 0

while True:
    ret, frame = cap.read()
    if not ret:
        break

    lane_frame = detect_lanes(frame)
    cv2.imshow('Lane Detection', lane_frame)

    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

cap.release()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

💡 Pro tip: This code focuses on lane detection by combining edge detection and masking to isolate the road region. Real self-driving systems build on this with CNNs for more robust detection.

What Is the Typical Architecture of a Self-Driving Car System?

A typical system has four main layers working together:

Layer Description
Sensor Inputs Cameras, LIDAR, radar, ultrasonic sensors capture environment data.
Perception Layer Uses CNNs and image processing (OpenCV) to detect objects, lanes.
Decision-Making AI models like reinforcement learning plan optimal driving maneuvers.
Control Layer Sends commands to steering, throttle, and braking actuators.

This layered architecture ensures safe and efficient autonomous driving.

Tools & Libraries Commonly Used for Self-Driving Car Projects

  • Python Frameworks: TensorFlow and PyTorch for building CNNs and reinforcement learning models.
  • OpenCV: Essential for image and video processing tasks.
  • Simulation Environments: Tools like CARLA or Gazebo allow testing algorithms safely before on-road trials.

Using these lets you prototype and improve your autonomous vehicle projects effectively.

Where Can You Get a Complete Self-Driving Car Project to Learn and Customize?

If you want a ready-made, well-documented self-driving car project to understand these concepts deeply and prepare for your final year submission, check out the Self Driving Car System at College Project Expert. This project includes:

  • 100% working source code in Python
  • Full project report and documentation
  • PowerPoint presentation and viva preparation support

It's an excellent learning base—so make sure to customize and understand every module before your viva. For related ideas, you can also explore projects like AI Powered Self Driving Car Project With Smart Lane Detection Drowsiness Alert System or Lane Detection For Self Driving Car Using Artificial Intelligence.

FAQ

✅ Viva-ready answer:

Q: How does a self-driving car detect lanes and obstacles in real time?

A: It uses cameras processed by convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and OpenCV functions to analyze images instantaneously and identify lanes, vehicles, and pedestrians around it.

✅ Viva-ready answer:

A: Yes, with provided source code and libraries like OpenCV and TensorFlow, beginners can build and customize self-driving car systems effectively.

✅ Viva-ready answer:

Q: What AI techniques control the vehicle's steering and braking decisions?

A: Reinforcement learning algorithms train models to optimize steering, acceleration, and braking based on continuous feedback from the environment.

title: Emotion Is Not External Knowledge: Internal Attention Signals for Affective State Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.21347v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-turn interactions that require maintaining latent conversational states, not only explicit facts. We study affective state as an implicit state inferred from sparse contextual cues that remain relevant after topic shifts, and ask whether LLMs expose internal attention signals for routing such evidence at inference time. Prior attention interventions rely on labeled in-domain head profiles and externally specified target spans, limiting transfer across affective-evidence distributions. We propose Self-targeted Internal Attention Boosting (SIAB), which localizes sparse affective heads via causal localization (in detail activation patching) on synthetic minimal pairs and boosts, at the answer position, the content tokens these heads already attend to; both edited heads and target tokens are derived from the model's own behavior, enabling the same head set to be reused across tasks.We evaluate on ECC and GoEmotions across three LLMs and multiple prompting settings. Across settings, SIAB improves prompt-matched baselines by up to +10.3 macro-F1 on ECC and +5.5 on GoEmotions. Combined with PASTA-style external supervision, it achieves up to +13.84 accuracy points and +12.51 macro-F1 points, while mechanistic analyses trace the gains to sparse, emotion-enriched heads and show that layer proximity affects additivity.

title: Automatic Sentence Completion Using Bengali Audio Speech with a Transformer-Based Early Speech Recognition System
description:
arXiv:2610.21164v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dementia severely impairs communication abilities and turns everyday conversations into challenging experiences. Individuals affected by dementia frequently struggle to express their thoughts or complete sentences, making it difficult for family members and caregivers to understand their needs. This study proposes a novel approach to assist dementia patients by developing an integrated system that detects signs of dementia through Bangla speech and text analysis and provides sentence auto-completion support during conversations. To achieve this, recorded voices from individuals with and without dementia were analysed, and key acoustic features were extracted to capture vocal patterns associated with cognitive decline. A transformer-based model was employed to transcribe voice signals into text for linguistic analysis. In the classification task, several Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models were evaluated using both acoustic and textual representations, and the LSTM model architectures demonstrated strong capabilities for modelling contextual patterns in speech and language data. For the sentence auto-completion task, a sequential learning model based on a Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) network with an attention mechanism was developed to sequentially complete partially expressed Bangla sentences during conversation. This research bridges the gap in dementia analysis in an underrepresented language and implements a sentence auto-completion framework for cognitive disorders.

title: ReasonUni: Reasoning-Augmented Reconstruction Advances Unified Multimodal Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20781v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Image-to-text (I2T) understanding and text-to-image (T2I) generation are dual tasks in unified multimodal models (UMMs). Reconstructive post-training couples these tasks, but existing reconstruction-based methods remain perception-centric and provide limited supervision for reasoning about structure, intent, and transformation. We propose ReasonUni, a reasoning-augmented reconstructive post-training framework that extends this coupling beyond perception. Given an original image and an editing instruction, the UMM first reasons about what and how to edit and describes the target state, then generates the corresponding target image conditioned on this understanding output. To jointly optimize both modules, we introduce TreeGRPO, a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that samples multiple reasoning paths and candidate images per path, then aggregates visual rewards to update both modules under a unified objective. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains in both understanding and generation, showing that reasoning-augmented reconstruction yields genuine mutual gains for UMMs.

title: AI Gateway now supports asynchronous video generation
description:
Video generation on AI Gateway can now run asynchronously.

By default, generateVideo keeps one HTTP request to AI Gateway open until the result is ready. Because video generation can take seconds or minutes, that request can exceed request timeouts.

With asynchronous generation, your application can receive a webhook, poll for completion, or start a generation and retrieve the result in a later request.

Choose an option based on whether your process can keep running and whether your application can receive webhooks:

Existing generateVideo calls continue to work as before. All four options support text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video, and other video inputs.

Upgrade the SDK

Install the latest versions of the AI SDK and AI Gateway provider:

Use asynchronous video generation

Wait for completion in a Workflow

An easy way to consume the completion webhook is a Workflow SDK. The workflow creates its own webhook URL, passes it to startVideo, and suspends until AI Gateway delivers the completion event. Install the Workflow SDK alongside the AI SDK:

While the video renders, the workflow run is suspended and resumes when AI Gateway delivers the terminal event.

Use a webhook with generateVideo

Pass webhook to generateVideo to wait for a completion event without polling. AI Gateway sends an event when the job completes or fails. The SDK waits for that event, fetches the generated videos, and resolves the original generateVideo call.

The calling process and webhook handler need a shared token and store so the delivery can be matched to the correct generation. generateVideo does not expose the signing secret for this job. See the webhook verification documentation for the complete receiver pattern.

Both the polling and webhook options for generateVideo return result.videos as GeneratedFile objects. The SDK downloads provider-hosted videos, making uint8Array, base64, and mediaType available in either job.

Poll with generateVideo

Add poll to an existing generateVideo call:

AI Gateway starts an asynchronous job, and the SDK sends a short status request at each interval until the job finishes. The calling process must remain running until generateVideo resolves, but no individual request to AI Gateway stays open for the full generation.

Start a job and retrieve it later

startVideo returns an operation as soon as AI Gateway accepts the job, without waiting for rendering to finish. Store that operation and pass it to getVideoStatus later from the same process or another one:

The operation is JSON-serializable, so it can be stored in a database or passed through a queue. Your application controls how long to keep checking the job because it has no built-in timeout.

You can also pass webhookUrl to startVideo to receive a completion event instead of checking the status. The start response includes the signing secret needed to verify the webhook.

Unlike generateVideo, getVideoStatus does not download hosted videos. It returns provider URLs or inline bytes. Hosted URLs can expire, so download any videos you need to keep.

Monitor asynchronous jobs

Every asynchronous generation appears on the AI Gateway Logs page as soon as it starts. Jobs show as Running while generation is in progress and update when they complete or fail.

Under Request Mode, select Async to show only asynchronous jobs. Opening an entry shows the job ID and the request details.

Only asynchronous requests create jobs. A standard generateVideo call appears as a single completed request after the video is ready.

For size limits, idempotency for retried job starts, webhook delivery retries, and other operational details, read the asynchronous video generation documentation or browse all video models.

Read more

title: RAC: A Relational Agent Contract for Constraint-Governed Engineering Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.20935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Engineering agents must produce artifacts that satisfy exact, coupled constraints. Existing solutions often require agents to make semantic decisions and also derive consequences such as precise geometry or timing from those decisions, leading to failures in constraint-governed engineering tasks. In this paper, we introduce RAC, a harness-agnostic contract for the action and feedback layer of engineering agents. It specifies authoritative observations, semantic actions, tool-based realization, independent verification, and repair evidence. The agent decides which relations an artifact should satisfy; specialized tools derive their concrete consequences. On PCB placement, routing, and repair tasks, RAC achieves the highest clean-pass rate for all nine evaluated models, averaging 90.9%, compared with 74.0% for the strongest baseline, requirements-only delegation. In job-shop scheduling, direct relational actions achieve 96.3% quality pass versus 59.6% for code-mediated delivery with access to the same scheduling backend. Our evaluations on 141 embedded-code tasks across four microcontroller identify the action contract as a source of agent capability: preserving semantic control while delegating mechanically derivable outputs improves the reliability of constrained artifacts.

title: RIGen: Beyond Action Following with Reciprocal Interaction in Generative Gameplay
description:
arXiv:2610.20811v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative gameplay requires more than immediate responses to player actions.Actions should have persistent consequences, while the generated world should act according to its own state and rules, shaping the player's situation and subsequent choices. Video generation captures local dynamics, but limited history, partially observed game state, and the need for contextual behavior decisions make such interactions difficult to sustain through audiovisual prediction alone. We introduce \rig (Reciprocally Interactive Generation), a framework for reciprocal interaction in generative gameplay. \rig combines persistent state and configurable rules, contextual interaction reasoning, and action-conditioned audiovisual generation. Together, these components make interaction consequences and actor behavior jointly determine generated content while maintaining consistency between game state and visible outcomes. We construct a Xonotic gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning dynamics and interactions. Further post-training enables \rigarena, an interactive generative first-person shooter (FPS) prototype. Experiments demonstrate more reliable combat outcomes and reciprocal interaction between the player and the generated world. Project page: https://murphylmf.github.io/RIGen/.

title: Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields: Evidence-Grounded Selective Safety for Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20679v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Representation-based safety defenses for vision-language models (VLMs) often learn to separate harmful from benign inputs, but separation alone does not establish what a risk score means or when it should be trusted. We introduce Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields (CNRF), an evidence-grounded framework for selective VLM safety. CNRF constructs context-matched benign-harmful counterfactual pairs, uses their representation differences as capability-related risk directions, and estimates neighborhood support separately from risk. This separation prevents unfamiliarity from being conflated with harmfulness and enables selective intervention rather than blanket rejection. A victim-adaptive interface accommodates different safety observations across VLM architectures and routes selected requests for same-victim response review, which either releases acceptable candidates or produces constrained alternatives with reduced harmful capability. Across three VLMs and five multimodal jailbreak families, CNRF achieves 86.06-89.30% macro defense success rate while retaining substantial benign-task utility. Controlled experiments further show that query-matched references and preserved context-direction correspondence materially improve risk ranking in the low-false-positive regime. CNRF thus reframes representation-based VLM safety from learning harmfulness boundaries to constructing applicable evidence for selective risk decisions.

title: How v0 authenticates to Snowflake without exposing the user's OAuth token
description:
AI-generated applications often need to authenticate to external services on behalf of their users. That creates a problem: generated code shouldn't have access to the user's credentials.

We faced that decision when building the v0 Snowflake integration. It lets users connect Snowflake, inspect schemas, query data, and generate applications that run against their warehouses. That generated code has to authenticate to Snowflake, but it is written by a model and runs without human review, and prompt injection can steer it into exfiltrating whatever it can read, so the user's OAuth token should never enter the environment the code runs in.

We solved this with a Snowflake request proxy for v0 sandboxes, built on the Vercel Sandbox firewall. The sandbox can run normal Snowflake clients, but the real credential is resolved at request time in a server proxy outside the sandbox runtime. This lets existing Snowflake clients work inside the sandbox without exposing the user's credential to generated code.

The harder problem was deciding where the proxy could safely inject the credential. The obvious implementation, replacing a placeholder token wherever it appears, introduces another credential leak.

Isolation doesn't protect secrets

v0 runs generated applications in isolated sandboxes. Isolation protects the rest of the system from untrusted code, but it doesn't protect secrets inside the sandbox.

If a generated app can read a token from the filesystem, that token can be copied into logs, returned in an API response, embedded into generated client code, or sent to another host. Sandbox isolation limits what the application can access, but it does not help once the credential itself is available inside the sandbox.

For Snowflake, the credential represents the Snowflake role the user connected with. v0 should be able to help the user explore and build with data they are authorized to access, but generated code should not receive raw provider credentials just because it needs one.

Every Snowflake request goes through the proxy

The sandbox cannot talk to Snowflake directly. When code inside it sends a request to the user's Snowflake account host, the sandbox firewall forwards that request to the v0 Snowflake proxy:

The firewall terminates TLS with a certificate authority unique to each sandbox, which lets the proxy read and rewrite traffic that would otherwise be encrypted. The sandbox trusts that certificate authority automatically, so the Snowflake SDK and CLI run with their default certificate validation, OCSP included. The proxy then verifies the sandbox's OIDC token, looks up the v0 chat the sandbox belongs to, restores the user session bound to that chat, and retrieves a fresh Snowflake credential for that user.

The sandbox does not choose where a token-bearing request is sent. The proxy derives the Snowflake account host from the server-side credential and rejects invalid account URLs, keeping the credential scoped to the connected Snowflake account rather than trusting host information supplied by generated code.

Compatibility without credential exposure

As a stopgap, the first version of the integration wrote the user's real token into the sandbox's Snowflake token files. The proxy replaced that approach. Ideally, we would remove token files from the sandbox entirely, but Snowflake clients expect credentials in different locations depending on the authentication flow.

Some requests, such as Snowflake SQL API calls, authenticate with an Authorization: Bearer header. Other client flows read local token files and send the token as part of a login request. Once the client has authenticated, subsequent requests use Snowflake-issued session tokens, and the proxy passes those requests through untouched.

To preserve compatibility, v0 still writes a token-shaped placeholder into the sandbox. The placeholder is a fixed, public, 72-byte string that grants no access, and its only job is to let existing Snowflake SDK and CLI flows behave as if a token exists. The proxy never authorizes a request based on the placeholder itself. Instead, the proxy authorizes the request using the sandbox's server-side identity and its binding to the user's chat.

The real OAuth token, the reusable credential that represents the user, is never written into the sandbox. Snowflake does issue session tokens that live inside the sandbox after login, but each of those belongs to a single authenticated session.

Those sessions are short-lived in practice. The Snowflake helper in generated apps destroys its connection after each query, which ends the session right away. Closing the chat does not end a session on its own, but tearing down the sandbox takes the token with it, and Snowflake expires the session server-side after four hours of inactivity by default. When a request reaches the proxy, it decides whether and where to attach the credential.

Why blind replacement fails

The first version of the proxy searched each request for the placeholder and swapped in the real token wherever it appeared:

The problem is that generated code controls parts of the request, including where the placeholder can appear. A SQL statement, for example, is caller-controlled data. If a query contains the placeholder as a string literal, blind replacement turns that query into one containing the real OAuth token. If the database then returns that string, the real token comes back into the sandbox as query output, and the proxy would have leaked the token it was built to keep out.

Stricter matching does not close the hole. The proxy shouldn't inject a credential based on attacker-controlled text. Instead, it needs to know which field in each Snowflake request carries authentication.

Injecting credentials only into authentication fields

Snowflake requests reach the proxy in three shapes, and each shape puts authentication in a different place.

For Snowflake SQL API requests, the proxy sets the OAuth token on the Authorization: Bearer header. The body remains caller-controlled SQL and is not rewritten. If the placeholder appears in the SQL payload, the proxy rejects the request before it reaches Snowflake and logs it as placeholder misuse.

For Snowflake login requests, the proxy parses the JSON request body, sets the token structurally at the login token field, and serializes the body again. If the placeholder remains anywhere else in the request body, the proxy fails closed.

Post-login session requests authenticate with Snowflake-managed session tokens, so the proxy has nothing to inject.

Failing closed

The proxy rejects any request where:

  • The sandbox is not bound to a chat

  • No user-scoped credential can be obtained

  • The Snowflake account host cannot be derived

  • The placeholder appears outside an approved authentication field

  • A structured login body cannot be parsed safely

Requests are also bounded before inspection so that compressed or oversized bodies cannot turn the proxy into an unbounded parser. Every proxied request emits an observability event with the upstream outcome, status, duration, and injection location. This surfaces misuse and integration failures without exposing secrets.

Handling refresh and deploy

Token refresh cannot depend on an ambient browser cookie, because proxy requests originate from the sandbox, not from the user's browser session. v0 binds the user session to the sandbox instead, and the proxy mints and refreshes OAuth credentials from that binding.

The publish path uses Snowflake CLI flows with the same credential boundary. Deploy can write the placeholder into credential files, but never the real token.

After deployment, the application runs in Snowpark Container Services and authenticates as its own service user, with a token that Snowflake manages and rotates automatically, mounted at /snowflake/session/token. The user's OAuth token and the v0 proxy are no longer involved.

The resulting security boundary

For users, none of this is visible. Connect Snowflake, ask v0 to inspect schemas or build an app, preview the result, and deploy when it's ready.

The security model rests on five rules:

  • Credential injection happens only at each endpoint's authentication fields

  • Requests that use the placeholder outside an authentication field are rejected and logged

  • Token-bearing requests go only to the connected Snowflake account host

  • Credentials are minted and refreshed server-side

  • Generated code uses Snowflake without ever reading the user's OAuth token

In its first 15 days in production, the proxy attached credentials server-side for roughly 13,000 requests and recorded zero placeholder-misuse rejections.

Although we built this proxy for Snowflake, the same problem applies to other integrations: generated code often needs to authenticate without receiving the user's long-lived credential. The important part is to inject credentials only into protocol-defined authentication fields, rather than rewriting arbitrary request data.

The v0 Snowflake integration is now available in beta. Get started by reading the integration docs.

title: Diminishing Returns of Data in Sparse Autoencoders: Functional Behavior does not Guarantee Feature Reproducibility
description:
arXiv:2610.20680v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are typically trained on hundreds of millions to billions of activation tokens, yet little work has tested whether this scale is necessary. We study how much activation data SAEs need by training four SAE architectures on three language models with budgets ranging from 5M tokens to a 500M-token reference. We measure two notions of convergence: functional behavior on standard evaluations and one-to-one reproducibility of learned features. Functional data requirements are strongly metric-dependent: reconstruction often approaches the full-data reference at substantially smaller budgets, whereas feature reproducibility continues to improve with data. For Gemma-2-2B BatchTopK, the fraction of strictly matched features rises from 2\% at 5M tokens to 29\% at 50M. Data selection also matters: random sampling better preserves the original activation distribution and generally favors reconstruction, whereas diversity-based sampling frequently improves AutoInterp. A theoretical analysis separates statistical consistency of subsampled training from the stronger identifiability and optimization conditions required for one-to-one feature recovery. Our results show that SAE training can often be made far more data-efficient when budgets are matched to the goal, and feature-level claims are backed by explicit reproducibility checks, paving the way toward cheaper and more reliable SAE research.

title: Modern CSS in 2024: Nesting, :has(), Container Queries, color-mix(), and More
description:
CSS has evolved dramatically. Features that required JavaScript hacks or were impossible a few years ago are now native CSS. Here's a rundown of modern CSS features that are production-ready in Firefox and all modern browsers as of 2024.

CSS Nesting

No more BEM or repeated selectors — nest rules directly:

/* Old way */
.card { background: white; }
.card:hover { box-shadow: 0 4px 20px rgba(0,0,0,0.1); }
.card .title { font-size: 1.25rem; }
.card .title:hover { color: blue; }

/* Modern CSS nesting */
.card {
  background: white;

  &:hover {
    box-shadow: 0 4px 20px rgba(0,0,0,0.1);
  }

  .title {
    font-size: 1.25rem;

    &:hover {
      color: blue;
    }
  }

  @media (max-width: 768px) {
    padding: 12px; /* Media queries nested inside too */
  }
}

Firefox 117+. No preprocessor needed.

:has() Relational Pseudo-Class

Style parents based on their children — the "parent selector" CSS has lacked for decades:

/* Card with an image → show image at full width */
.card:has(img) {
  padding: 0;
}

/* Form field with an error → turn label red */
.field:has(.error-message) label {
  color: red;
}

/* Navigation with a dropdown open → prevent scroll */
body:has(.dropdown:open) {
  overflow: hidden;
}

/* Table row on hover → highlight entire row */
tr:has(td:hover) {
  background: rgba(0,0,0,0.05);
}

Firefox 121+. Also available as :not(:has(X)) — elements without X.

CSS Grid subgrid

Children of a grid item can participate in the grandparent's grid:

.parent {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  grid-template-rows: auto auto;
  gap: 16px;
}

.card {
  display: grid;
  grid-row: span 2;
  grid-template-rows: subgrid; /* Use parent's row tracks */
}

Without subgrid, all cards have independently-sized header/body. With subgrid, they align across the row.

Firefox 71+ (first browser to support it!).

color-mix()

Mix two colors in CSS without JavaScript or preprocessors:

:root {
  --color-primary: oklch(60% 0.2 230);
}

.button-light {
  background: color-mix(in oklch, var(--color-primary), white 30%);
}

.button-dark {
  background: color-mix(in oklch, var(--color-primary), black 20%);
}

/* Mix in different color spaces */
.cool { background: color-mix(in hsl, blue, green 50%); }
.warm { background: color-mix(in srgb, red, yellow 40%); }

Firefox 113+.

@layer Cascade Layers

Explicit priority for CSS blocks:

@layer reset, base, components, utilities;

@layer reset { * { box-sizing: border-box; } }
@layer base { a { color: blue; } }
@layer components { .btn { /* ... */ } }
@layer utilities { .hidden { display: none !important; } }

Later layers override earlier layers regardless of specificity. Firefox 97+.

Container Queries

Style elements based on their container's size, not the viewport:

.card-container { container-type: inline-size; }

@container (min-width: 480px) {
  .card { flex-direction: row; }
}

Firefox 110+.

@property Typed Custom Properties

Register custom properties with a type, enabling animation:

@property --progress {
  syntax: '<number>';
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0;
}

.bar { transition: --progress 0.5s ease; }
.bar.loaded { --progress: 75; }

Firefox 128+.

CSS Logical Properties

Write direction-agnostic CSS that works for both LTR and RTL layouts:

/* Old */
margin-left: 16px;
padding-right: 8px;
border-top: 1px solid;

/* Logical */
margin-inline-start: 16px;  /* left in LTR, right in RTL */
padding-inline-end: 8px;    /* right in LTR, left in RTL */
border-block-start: 1px solid; /* top in horizontal, left in vertical */

/* Even more concise */
margin-inline: 16px;    /* left + right margin */
padding-block: 8px;     /* top + bottom padding */
inset-inline: 0;        /* left + right position */

Firefox 91+. Essential for internationalized sites.

oklch() Color Space

Perceptually uniform colors — consistent lightness across hues:

/* oklch(lightness chroma hue) */
:root {
  /* Same lightness, different hues — looks equally bright */
  --red: oklch(60% 0.25 30);
  --blue: oklch(60% 0.25 250);
  --green: oklch(60% 0.25 140);
}

/* HSL 50% lightness of green looks much brighter than 50% lightness of purple */
/* oklch 60% lightness is visually consistent */

Firefox 113+.

Relative Color Syntax

Derive colors from other colors:

:root { --color: oklch(60% 0.2 230); }

.lighter { background: oklch(from var(--color) calc(l + 20%) c h); }
.darker  { background: oklch(from var(--color) calc(l - 20%) c h); }
.muted   { background: oklch(from var(--color) l calc(c * 0.5) h); }

Firefox 128+. Replaces Sass color functions entirely.

text-wrap: balance and text-wrap: pretty

Prevent typographic widows and orphans:

h1, h2, h3 {
  text-wrap: balance; /* Equal line lengths (max 4 lines) */
}

p {
  text-wrap: pretty; /* No orphan words on last line */
}

Firefox 128+.

Summary: What's Production-Ready in 2024

Feature Firefox Chrome Safari
CSS Nesting 117+ 112+ 16.5+
:has() 121+ 105+ 15.4+
Container queries 110+ 105+ 16+
subgrid 71+ 117+ 16+
@layer 97+ 99+ 15.4+
color-mix() 113+ 111+ 16.2+
@property 128+ 85+ 16.4+
oklch 113+ 111+ 15.4+

All of these are safe to use in production today without any build tools.

title: INCONVENIENT: A Benchmark to Assess LLM Generalization Capabilities from Convenience Samples
description:
arXiv:2610.21038v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning models for tabular prediction typically assume that training data are representative of the population on which they will be deployed. In practice, however, data are often collected based on convenience, availability, or cost, resulting in systematic sampling biases that can distort feature--target relationships and undermine real-world generalization. Existing tabular distribution-shift benchmarks primarily construct out-of-distribution (OOD) settings by partitioning observations across naturally occurring domains. While such partitions may induce changes in P(Y | X), the resulting shifts are neither explicitly controlled nor isolated, and the evaluation distributions themselves are often not representative of the broader target population. We introduce INCONVENIENT, a benchmark designed to study robustness to convenience-sample bias. Rather than relying on naturally occurring domain partitions, INCONVENIENT directly perturbs feature--target relationships in the training distribution while preserving the original population distribution as the deployment environment. This setting more closely reflects real-world scenarios in which models are developed from unrepresentative samples and subsequently deployed on a broader population. The distinction is particularly relevant for large language models (LLMs), whose pretraining may encode population-level knowledge that extends beyond the relationships observed in a biased training dataset. Unlike existing distribution-shift benchmarks, INCONVENIENT provides explicit control over both the direction and severity of relationship shifts, enabling a systematic assessment of robustness to convenience sampling. The benchmark comprises 200 tabular classification and regression datasets spanning diverse application domains and generates around 15,500 shifted training distributions which lead to substantial downstream degradation.

title: Human in the loop means making sure the human is not out of the loop
description:
Agents now act before we ask and reach past what we authorized. A person in the loop isn’t enough if nobody owns the outcome. Here’s what to consider when designing for it.

Agents used to wait for a prompt because everyone though that AI was only chat. Now they triage inboxes, update records, and send messages while we’re in another meeting. That’s the whole point of them, and it’s also where the trouble starts.

Because of this, most agent teams hit the same questions:

  • Should the agent act before the user asks?
  • When the agent does more than anyone authorized, who is liable for the call?

The standard answer is a confirm dialog. Add a human click, and the accountability problem is supposed to vanish. It moves instead, landing on whoever had the least information and the least power over the outcome.

None of this is new.

Eric Horvitz modeled when software should act alone in 1999. Sixteen years earlier, Lisanne Bainbridge warned in Ironies of Automation that automating most of a job leaves people holding its hardest part, the watching. What’s new is volume: Gartner predicts at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously through agents by 2028.

I’m an apologist for artificial intelligence, and I’ll admit some things it isn’t good for.

The proactive question is mostly a decoy.

Initiative isn’t what hurts people; reach is. The better question is a reach test: what can the agent touch, and can a person put it back? The answer also settles liability.

Whoever sets an agent’s reach owns what it does there, and no confirm click should shift that to whoever clicked.

Stop Counting the Clicks

A confirm button records that a person was there; it says nothing about whether they read what they approved.

Kathleen Mosier and Linda Skitka named this automation bias in the 1990s, and it comes in two forms. Errors of commission follow the machine’s wrong suggestion, and errors of omission miss what the machine never flagged.

In Skitka’s 1998 NASA report, Automation: Decision Aid or Decision Maker?, people using an aid were 65% accurate when it was wrong, against 97% for people working without one. My Automation Bias entry at UX Guidelines calls omission the quieter failure, since nothing on the screen ever asks to be doubted.

Anthropic’s study of its own coding agent, Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice, found newer users ran full auto-approve in roughly 20% of sessions, rising past 40% for experienced users.

Those experienced users also interrupted more, in about 9% of turns against 5% for new ones.

Approval is a ritual. Interruption is a judgment, which is good.

Anthropic’s own conclusion is that forcing a human to approve every step adds friction without necessarily adding safety. The per-click version is a cousin of the security theater usually credited to Bruce Schneier: visible, reassuring, and blind to how far the agent can reach afterward. People still belong in the loop, just at the point where judgment holds up: watching a run they can stop, instead of pre-signing a list they can’t read.

Follow the Blame

Madeleine Clare Elish gave this its name in 2019. In Moral Crumple Zones, she showed how responsibility for a failure gets pinned on the human operator closest to the event, even when that person had little control over what the automated system did.

A car’s crumple zone protects the driver. The moral version protects the system, and the operator absorbs the impact.

This is the most telling example. In March 2018, an autonomous Uber test vehicle struck and killed Elaine Herzberg in Tempe, Arizona. A safety driver, Rafaela Vasquez, sat behind the wheel, in the loop by every definition the program used. Granted, Vasquez was watching television on her phone, but that further illustrates the point.

According to CNN’s report on the Uber test driver’s 2023 guilty plea, the federal safety board found Vasquez had looked away for more than a third of the trip, and that an inadequate safety culture at Uber contributed. Uber faced no criminal charges and the driver pleaded guilty to endangerment and got three years of supervised probation.

She paid the price for the human missing the loop.

Being in the loop, it turns out, mostly means being nearest the crash.

None of this excuses the distraction, but it shows where accountability flows when a system is built around a watcher it doesn’t support. The reviewer who clicked approve on step 41 of a 60-step run becomes the crumple zone, while the team that decided step 41 needed no stronger gate stays out of the story.

Price the Unasked Act

Eric Horvitz’s 1999 paper, Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces, still frames when software should act unasked. His rule is decision theory in plain clothes: act only when the expected value beats doing nothing.

His math leaves one variable implicit: whether the action can be undone. Drafting a reply and sending it carry the same chance of being right and very different costs of being wrong.

One way vs. two way doors: Proactivity should scale with reversibility, not with confidence.

An agent that prepares, drafts, flags, and stages work is extending the user’s reach inside a space they can still edit and undo. One that sends, deletes, pays, or commits is spending the user’s authority.

The accuracy an action needs should shape the interaction too. A probabilistic output is a prediction about what’s likely right, while a deterministic one is a certainty.

  • A summary can be a prediction and still be useful, because a reader applies judgment.
  • A decision that routes a claim, approves a payment, or marks a contract compliant has to be a deterministic certainty, coming out the same way every time on the same input. That pushes it toward explicit rules the model applies rather than invents.

Put both behind the same button and a prediction ends up dressed as a certainty. Dan Maccarone quotes a client’s rule in We’re gorging on borrowed trust and it’s going to cost us: “people conclude, machines don’t.”

All of this gets harder with ambient agents, which watch a queue or an inbox and act while nobody is looking.

  • A chatbot waits for a question, so a bad answer at least has a witness.
  • An ambient agent acts on its own schedule, often many times before anyone reads the log, so its mistakes compound quietly.

For ambient work, the reach test has to be answered entirely in advance, and the record becomes the first thing a person sees rather than the last.

Write the Mandate

An agent, in the legal sense, acts for a principal, and the principal answers for what the agent does within the authority it was given. A power of attorney writes that authority down: what it covers, for how long, revocable at will.

We need this because nobody signs one that just reads “use your judgment.”

Agency is the whole value of an agent, and control over that agency is the one thing a principal never hands across. A mandate is the reach test answered in advance, in writing.

In Moffatt v. Air Canada, the airline claimed it couldn’t be held liable for what its website chatbot told a customer about bereavement fares. A British Columbia tribunal called that “a remarkable submission” in 2024 and held the airline responsible for everything on its site. The company set the chatbot’s reach, so the company owned what it said. And that bot only spoke when a customer asked it something. Maccarone’s name for what Air Canada spent is borrowed trust, a brand’s reputation lent to output nobody checked.

A mandate lives in the permissions, not in the conversation.

The Replit incident in July 2025 shows what happens when the mandate exists only as a sentence. SaaStr founder Jason M. Lemkin froze his project and told the agent repeatedly not to change anything. It deleted the production database anyway, then wrongly reported that rollback was impossible.

The fix is decades old: least privilege, enforced by the system at the moment of action. An instruction the agent can ignore is only a preference, not a harness.

Check the Law

I’m not a lawyer, so read this as a designer’s map of where the rules point, not legal advice. Some decisions shouldn’t appear in any mandate at all. Article 22 of the GDPR gives people the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.

Even its exceptions for contracts and consent still require a way to reach a human, state a view, and contest the outcome.

Newer laws push the same way:

  • EU Artificial Intelligence Act. Article 14 requires people overseeing high-risk systems to be able to override the output and stop the system, and it names automation bias outright. A Digital Omnibus in July 2026 pushed those duties for uses like employment to December 2027.
  • California CCPA. The state’s automated decisionmaking rules require notice and an opt-out for significant decisions from January 2027, unless people can appeal to a human who can overturn the decision.
  • Colorado ADMT Act. Colorado replaced its 2024 Artificial Intelligence Act in May 2026 with a law granting human review after an adverse decision, from January 2027 if rulemaking finishes.
  • New York City Local Law 144. Hiring tools have needed bias audits since 2023, yet a December 2025 state comptroller audit found 17 possible violations among 32 companies where the city found one.
The law can require a way back. We have to design one.

These laws cover the second half of the reach test, not the first. What an agent can touch is still a product decision, and my own list goes further.

  • Hire, fire, or discipline. Livelihood decisions need a named person who can explain the call, in court.
  • Deny care or benefits. Refusing a claim or a treatment deserves a human who weighed it.
  • Sign for the organization. Contracts and regulatory filings bind a company in ways no model can answer for.
  • Give advice under a professional’s name. Legal, medical, and financial advice carries a license, and licenses belong to people.
  • Move money past the point of recall. Irreversible payments above a set limit wait for a person.

Design for Ownership

Microsoft Research tested their Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction against 20 products in 2019. Two describe half the job:

  • Scope services when in doubt
  • Provide global controls.

A third matters most once an agent decides rather than suggests: make clear why the system did what it did, which drew one of the highest violation counts in the study.

A decision without an explanation leaves a person who can repeat the call but never defend it, which is why I keep an entry on Explainability at UX Guidelines.

Agents need all three, plus two things a 2019 product rarely needed:

  • The first is a record the agent didn’t write. Replit’s agent misreported its own recovery options.
  • The second is a stop that works mid-flight, on screen while the agent runs, plus an escalation path for when it wants to step past its mandate.

I’ve worked inside a lot of these loops. In legal tech at the companies I managed teams at, we always built guardrails that made lawyers review contract language before it moved. We worked just as hard on making that review easy to do, because a required step that’s painful gets rubber-stamped. Maccarone adds the other half: review holds only when the reviewer has something to lose, like a name or a license.

A rubber stamp is a loop no human truly owns.

So when does human in the loop stop meaning human owning the loop? The moment the person in it can no longer pass the reach test. That happens when approvals outpace reading, when the only fence is a sentence in a prompt, or when the only account of events is the agent’s own. Any one of those is enough to turn a reviewer into a witness.

Keep the Initiative

So, should an agent act before you ask? Often, yes; an agent that never acts first is slower. The useful version gets the work ready while you’re busy, then waits at the edge of anything it can’t take back.

Who is accountable when it does more than you authorized? Not the person who clicked approve on a summary they couldn’t check. Whoever sets the reach owns the result. What happens inside the mandate belongs to whoever granted it. Anything outside it belongs to the team that built an agent able to get there.

That’s less comfortable for builders than a confirm dialog, which is the point. A dialog lets a team ship autonomy and park the liability elsewhere. Elish’s crumple zone is what you get by default when you design around a watcher instead of for one.

Human in the loop was a good phrase for a world where software waited. Agents don’t wait, so the phrase has to carry more than a button can hold. Agency matters, and it stays useful only while the people an agent works for remain in control of it.

Build agents that pass the reach test in plain view, and the loop becomes theirs.

Make These Four Moves

  • Audit the approvals. Measure how long people spend before clicking approve; if most approvals land within seconds, you’ve built a ritual rather than a review.
  • Write the rules. List what the agent may do, on which data, and until when, then enforce it in permissions, not the prompt.
  • Run the reach test. Let the agent act unasked on anything a person can undo in one step, and require a decision for anything they can’t.
  • Keep an independent record. Log actions outside the agent’s own narration, and keep a working stop control on screen while it runs.

Human in the loop means making sure the human is not out of the loop was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: LLM-Based Weak Annotation for Cybersecurity Tweet Classification: A Teacher-Student Framework
description:
arXiv:2610.21254v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) relies on the timely identification of emerging threats, enabling organizations and security analysts to support situational awareness and decision-making. Social media platforms such as X (formerly Twitter) have become valuable CTI sources because vulnerabilities and attack activities are often discussed there before appearing in formal reports. However, the rapid growth of cybersecurity discussions on social media has created more content than domain experts can realistically review and annotate, making labeled data a major bottleneck for developing supervised learning approaches. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as weak annotators in other domains, their effectiveness for cybersecurity tweet classification and downstream training of domain-specific pre-trained language models (PLMs) remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose a Teacher-Student weak supervision framework in which a selected LLM serves as a Teacher to generate weak labels for unlabeled cybersecurity tweets, enabling the training of cybersecurity-specific PLMs without large-scale manual annotation. Experimental results show that PLMs trained solely on LLM-generated labels consistently achieve F1 scores above 0.92, remaining within 3 percentage points of fully human-supervised models across all evaluated architectures. These findings suggest that LLM-based weak annotation offers a practical alternative for constructing cybersecurity-specific training data when expert annotation resources are limited.

title: My React forms expect exactly one error shape: the 422 contract between Laravel and React
description:
I used to handle API errors in React the way most people do: one big try/catch, one generic toast, done. It worked, and every form looked like it was built by someone who had given up.

The fix wasn't a library. It was a contract: Laravel always returns validation failures the same way, so React can always render them the same way.

On the backend, FormRequests do the work. When validation fails, Laravel responds with HTTP 422 and a JSON body shaped like this:

{
  "message": "The email field is required. (and 1 more error)",
  "errors": {
    "email": ["The email field is required."],
    "password": ["The password must be at least 8 characters."]
  }
}

That shape never changes, on any endpoint. That's the whole contract.

On the frontend, my registration form keeps one state object:

const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});

And the catch block is a single if/else:

catch (err) {
  if (err.response?.status === 422 && err.response.data?.errors) {
    setErrors(err.response.data.errors);
  } else {
    setErrors({ general: err.response?.data?.message || 'Registration failed. Please try again.' });
  }
}

Each input renders its own error:

{errors.email && <p className="mt-1 text-xs text-rose-600">{errors.email[0]}</p>}

The input border turns rose via a tiny inputClass(field) helper. And the odd-shaped failures — network down, server 500, a route that doesn't exist — collapse into errors.general, the single banner at the top of the form.

Two deliberate choices worth calling out:

  1. I only take the first error per field (errors.email[0]). Showing three stacked messages under one input looks broken. Laravel orders them by rule priority, and the first one is almost always the one that matters.

  2. Non-422 failures never pretend to be validation errors. A 500 doesn't become "the email is invalid" — it becomes a banner. This is the thing most form code gets wrong: it maps every failure onto the same red box and lies to the user about what happened.

The admin user-edit form in my kit uses the exact same pattern — setFormErrors(err.response.data.errors) on 422, general otherwise. One contract, copied across every form, zero decisions left to make per page.

If you're starting a new Laravel + React project and want to skip wiring all of this yourself — the 422 contract, the AuthContext, the token interceptor — I sell a starter kit that has it done: https://kamranofficial.gumroad.com/l/mhekoig. It's $19, one-time, and it's the same code I copy into client projects.
