title: Find Inactive Users in Jira and Confluence
description:
Atlassian bills every user who has access to an app, whether they log in or not. Their words: users "are automatically counted towards billing even if they don't accept your invite or log in." You can find the inactive ones for free with Atlassian's own export. On 15 October we released Cost Slasher, a beta app that adds per-app inactivity policies and time away on top. It doesn't remove anyone for inactivity until you've verified it on your own site.

Prices went up this week. Since 13 October, Jira Standard's first 100 users cost $9.70 a month each, up from $9.05. So around renewal most Jira admins end up asking the same question. Who here hasn't opened Jira in two months, and why am I paying for them?

Below: the free way to find them, what Cost Slasher does today and what stays switched off, the arithmetic on what an idle seat costs against what the app costs, how to install it, and what I got wrong. The screenshots come from the production install on our demo site, taken the evening it went public.

If I were the admin deciding, I'd want to know this first:

  1. Automatic release ships switched off, and until it's on the app doesn't read your users' last-active dates.
  2. The warning period can't go below 24 hours.
  3. Unknown activity means the seat stays.
  4. A seat counts as reclaimed only when the access is verified gone.
  5. Time away releases your licence for the absence and keeps your place in the seat pool.
  6. JSM agents get a policy but no automatic release.
  7. It isn't cheap at 100 users.

How to find inactive users in Jira without an app, and what the export misses

You don't need any app to find inactive users in Jira Cloud. Atlassian already has the data.

  1. Go to admin.atlassian.com, open your organization, then Directory and Users.
  2. Export the users of the site. The CSV has a Last seen in column per app, which Atlassian defines as "the date the user last viewed the app's workspace for a minimum of 2 seconds." (Export users from a site)
  3. Sort by that column and pick a cut-off (60 or 90 days, your call). Take out admins and service accounts, then anyone you know is on leave.
  4. Remove app access or deactivate them, by hand or in bulk (Atlassian's bulk steps).

You can get the same dates from the Organizations REST API as last-active dates, with one line of fine print: "The data for the last activity may be delayed by up to 24 hours." Atlassian's pricing FAQ gives the same advice I'm giving: "Deactivate inactive users that aren't using your cloud product(s) so they no longer count towards your monthly bill."

That's fine once a year. The second time hurts. Nobody warned the people you removed, so the first you hear of it is "I can't open Jira" from someone back from paternity leave. The spreadsheet doesn't know who is on leave, and unless you keep notes there's no record of who removed whom, or why. Atlassian has no built-in inactivity deactivation that I could find: AX-1169, "Deactivate inactive user based on activity", has sat at Under Consideration since May 2019 and has 781 votes.

In my earlier post on Atlassian license management I had a CogniRunner AI agent do this job from a paragraph of instructions, and I said there that if license management is the only job, a deterministic tool is the simpler path. Cost Slasher is ours.

How Cost Slasher's inactivity policy works: allowance, warning period, restore protection, exclusions

Each app gets its own policy, because someone who reads Confluence daily and opens Jira twice a quarter shouldn't be warned off Confluence. Jira and Confluence seats each get one, and so do JSM agent seats (agent seats only, never customer portal access).

The inactivity allowance is how long someone can go without opening the app before a warning is due (30 days by default). The warning period is how long after the warning reaches them before the seat can go. It defaults to 48 hours and can't be set below 24.

Restore protection keeps a seat safe for a while after someone's access comes back (48 hours by default), so a person who just returned isn't warned again on day one. Exclusions are accounts left out of automatic release for that app, say a finance lead who opens Jira twice a year.

When release is on, activity comes from Atlassian's Organizations API, the same last-active dates as the export, read with your organization's Admin API key. That key can do far more than read dates. It lives in Forge secret storage, scoped to the installation. Cost Slasher doesn't create or rotate it, and our AWS side never receives it. Remove API key in the app takes it out of Cost Slasher and blocks new changes, but it doesn't revoke the key in Atlassian Administration. Do that there.

I put the 24-hour floor in the code as a constant, with the comment "Last-active reporting can lag by one day; every policy must allow that lag." If the data can be a day late, a 12-hour warning could run out and release the seat of someone who used Jira this morning, before Atlassian's data shows the visit.

Why the beta does not remove inactive users from Jira automatically yet

The listing's release notes say: "Automatic release stays off until recovery, warnings, activity and capacity are verified." Off is the default for every new policy. Saving a policy with release switched on is refused until activity, recovery and capacity are verified (plus agent activity, for JSM). Even then, no seat goes until a warning has been confirmed delivered and the full warning period has run.

Here's what each check means on your site. Recovery: you've put Cost Slasher's recovery link into Atlassian's native access-denied message and tested it with a real account that lost its paid seat. Warnings: a warning counts from confirmed delivery, not from the moment it was handed to the mail service. Warnings go out as email through Amazon SES in our AWS Ireland region. Activity: a test account opens the app inside a window of at most 72 hours, and the app must then find that exact visit in Atlassian's activity data for that app. Capacity: the app has finished reading who already holds each managed seat, so it knows the real count before it changes anything.

Until then, the app doesn't read your users' activity for that app. My access shows Activity unavailable, nobody gets an inactivity warning, and if you want a seat back you release it yourself. One kind of release does run on its own, switch or no switch: if a managed account is suspended, leaves the organization or drops out of the eligibility group, the app releases that seat. You do that in People: pick the app, select the accounts, add a reason, preview exactly which accounts change, then apply. The listing summary calls this "Beta; access changes require verified setup."

With release on, unknown activity still stops it. The guide is blunt: "Unknown or unparseable activity is not a never-used account and is not a release candidate." A never-used account is different: if Atlassian's answer is complete and has no date for that app, the allowance counts from the day Cost Slasher granted the seat or, for a seat that was already there when you installed it, from the day the app took it over.

Why so careful? A seat you paid for one month too long is cheap. Removing the release manager's Jira access on release morning isn't. Most of the licence apps I looked at advertise the automatic part first ("Auto-Schedule deactivation/suspension of inactive users", "Deactivate and offboard by inactivity threshold (3 days to 6 months)"). I shipped the off switch first, and you turn it on per app once the checks pass on your site.

Confluence inactive users and JSM agents: one policy per product

Cost Slasher installs on Jira and opens in Confluence on the same site. Confluence is the common case for a separate policy: plenty of people live in Confluence and rarely open Jira, and one site-wide rule would warn the wrong people.

JSM agents are different. You can set an agent policy and limit agent seats. Automatic agent release stays disabled, though. Atlassian's last-active data records a page view of two seconds or more, which can't tell an agent who works tickets from one who glanced at the queue. Agent seats also cost more (Service Collection, the plan JSM is now sold as, is $26.90 per agent a month at Standard for the first 15 agents), so a wrong release costs more too.

What ships today: My access, time away, a seat cap, reports and audit

My access is the page members see first: their access per app, the inactivity allowance, the last observed activity, and a button to check or restore. Checking grants nothing. Restoring is a separate click. It's also how people ask for a seat in the first place.

People who already lost their seat can't open the app, so recovery starts outside it. You paste a generated message into Atlassian's access-denied settings, and it links to a recovery page on cost-slasher.leanzero.net. Signing in there only asks Atlassian who you are, and signing in alone grants nothing. (Other apps offer self-service restore too. miniOrange and OSCi advertise it, for example.)

Time away is the feature I haven't seen on the other licence apps' listings (we read ten). A member enters when they leave and when they're back, previews it, then confirms. The licence is released for the absence, and the return seat stays reserved in the pool, so nobody else takes it. Restore is scheduled to start 30 minutes before the recorded return, and there's an "I'm back early" button. It only works if they're still eligible when they come back.

A seat limit with a queue. Each app's managed group has a seat limit. When it's full, a request waits with an expiry (24 hours by default) and the app picks waiting requests up in order as seats free. The limit covers access granted through Cost Slasher's group. Access granted through other groups isn't counted against it.

Management reports download as PDF, CSV or JSON. They hold aggregates only, with no individual names. Type in a monthly seat price and you get an estimate, which the app labels "a planning estimate" that "does not prove invoice savings".

The audit log records who acted, on which account, through which entry point, and the outcome of each stage. You can filter by period, category, outcome, app, actor or account, and the download holds all matching events, across pages.

There are five roles (Member, Operator, Routing manager, Auditor, Administrator), each scoped to sites and apps, and a REST API with scoped tokens that expire.

If your groups come from SCIM, this part matters. Cost Slasher reads a SCIM-managed group only as an eligibility source and never writes to it. Seats are granted through a separate destination group that the app has verified it can write to, and routing rules (add, mirror or move) show a preview first.

What the Atlassian cloud price increase 2026 does to an idle seat

No customer has run Cost Slasher yet, so this is Atlassian's price list and a calculator, done with their tables on 15 October 2026.

Take a 250-user Jira Standard site on monthly billing, and say 25 people (10%) haven't opened Jira in 90 days. Atlassian prices monthly seats in bands, so the last 150 users pay the 101-250 rate.

Before 13 Oct From 13 Oct
Jira Standard, users 1-100 $9.05 $9.70
Jira Standard, users 101-250 $7.65 $8.20
250 users, monthly bill $2,052.50 $2,200.00
25 idle seats, per month $191.25 $205.00
25 idle seats, per year $2,295 $2,460

If the same 25 people also hold Confluence Standard ($5.45 per user per month in the 101-250 band), that's another $136.25 a month, or $1,635 a year.

Cost Slasher is priced on the Jira user count, $1.32 a month for each of the first 100 users and $0.40 for each user after that up to 5,000. Once those 25 are gone the site has 225 users, which comes to $182 a month, $2,184 a year. That's about the cost of 22 idle Jira seats at $98.40 a year each, or 13 people who hold both Jira and Confluence. Up to 10 users it's free, permanently.

So on Jira alone at 10% idle it's close to break-even, and in this beta the seats are released by you, not by the app. What you'd be paying for is the policy and audit trail around each change, plus time away and the seat queue. Automatic release comes once you've verified it. Atlassian's usage billing from 3 December 2026 also pools allowances such as Rovo credits per paid user, so a removed seat shrinks that pool a little (I measured what 25 Rovo credits per user actually buys).

Annual plans are different. You pay for a tier. You only save when you drop to a lower one at renewal. Jira Standard's 300-user tier is $25,500 a year and the 200-user tier is $18,000, so getting a 280-person site under 200 is worth $7,500 a year. Cost Slasher's annual price at 300 users is $2,120.

And the competition, from each app's live pricing on the same day:

App Vendor Annual, 100 users Annual, 500 users
Manage Users for Jira Cloud Bloompeak $200 $600
License Cost Optimizer for Jira Atlassway $790 $2,700
User Management for Jira & Auto-deactivation miniOrange $850 $2,100
Kantega User Management & License Optimizer Kantega SSO $850 $2,100
User Management for Jira TechTime $1,000 $2,375
Flexible User License OSCi $1,000 $2,375
User Management and License Optimizer resolution $1,000 $3,450
Cost Slasher LeanZero $1,320 $2,920

At 100 users we're the most expensive. At 500 only resolution costs more. Kantega's listing says it is fully hosted on Atlassian's infrastructure, and resolution's says Cloud Fortified. Ours is neither yet. For Jira alone at 100 users I probably wouldn't pay $1,320 for it. If your people also hold Confluence or JSM agent seats, or you lose a day every time someone comes back from leave to a missing licence, I think the sum changes. And if all you want is a sorted list of last-active dates, the export from the first section is free.

Install it and the first ten minutes

First, where your data goes, because a security reviewer will ask before step 4. The app calls api.atlassian.com and cost-slasher.leanzero.net. Recovery sign-in, the controller registry (which tracks each installation's controller), shared organization budgeting and email notifications run in AWS Ireland, behind CloudFront. The Admin API key stays in Forge. Our privacy declaration states that the app doesn't support data residency, so if your organization requires Runs on Atlassian, this isn't the app for you today.

  1. Install Cost Slasher from the Marketplace listing on your Jira Cloud site. The listing has a Try it free button, and sites with up to 10 Jira users pay nothing.
  2. Open Apps → Cost Slasher. Members see My access first. The first site admin to open it gets a setup guide that shows one next step at a time. Opening setup doesn't call Atlassian's organization API or change any licence.
  3. Run Storage safety. It tests the app's own Forge SQL storage on your site with throwaway records and checks they get cleaned up. It touches nothing in Jira. Our demo install passed all 88 units.
  4. Enter your Organization ID, Directory ID and an organization Admin API key.
  5. Request pairing from LeanZero. Recovery runs through our service, so this step needs us. Ask through the support portal.
  6. Map each app: an eligibility group, a destination group that grants the paid app, and a seat limit. Applying a mapping creates a policy with automatic release off and starts a read-only count of who already holds each seat. It doesn't grant anyone a seat.
  7. Look at Policies, Operations and People.

The last setup section, Controller shutdown, is the brake. It freezes new work at the revision you reviewed and cancels only operations proven never to have started. Existing paid access is kept. This short film walks through it on the production app:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cklgkAo2b24

We published four more the same evening, on privacy and release notes, roles and scope, the REST API's scoped tokens and usage coverage.

Where I was wrong while building it

This post. The first draft said Cost Slasher finds your inactive users. Then our red-team pass read the code. With release off, the app doesn't read your users' activity, and off is how the beta ships. The title had to change. So did the excerpt, the hero image and five sentences. A launch post that oversold its own beta was the one thing I'd told myself not to write.

A 204 isn't a freed seat. Removing someone from a group returns 204, but they may still get the same app from another group. In my CogniRunner drill the removal returned 204 and the count did drop, but the agent had no way to read the person's groups back. Cost Slasher counts a seat as reclaimed only after it reads back that effective access is gone, and the 4 October commit that fences inactivity releases added 73 test cases.

Two UX defects only showed up when we recorded the demo films. The empty-list message appeared on the last page of 12 lists and the exclusion picker, as if those lists were empty. And the setup page contradicted itself about recovery pairing when pairing was healthy. Both were fixed on 4 October. I should have clicked through those pages myself.

The demo site's first signed request failed with a 503. This was on 15 October, release day. The new production secrets sat in a different AWS namespace from the one our gateway role could read. A narrow permission grant fixed it. The enrollment tool now refuses a mismatched namespace before it writes anything.

The Marketplace shows version 3.2.0. Inside the app the footer says "App release 0.4.4", which is the same build under our own numbering.

Who should install it now

Ten users or fewer? Install it. It costs nothing.

If you're bigger and want inactive users removed on a schedule tonight, this beta isn't it yet, and I'd rather lose that sale than remove the wrong person. If you want a written inactivity policy per app and time away that keeps someone's place, install it and tell us through the support portal what breaks. The Cost Slasher product page has the full manual.

Originally published on leanzero.net. More Atlassian, Forge and local-AI write-ups at leanzero.net/blog, and if you're planning a migration or a Forge app, that's what we do: leanzero.net/services.

title: Fewer crates.io projects go silent on outside pull requests than npm or PyPI
description:
If you maintain a crate, you probably have a view on whether outside pull requests get a fair hearing in the Rust world. I now have a number to set beside that view, and it comes with enough caveats that I want to list them.

Porchlamp scores open-source projects on how they handle pull requests from people outside the team. This post uses a second cut of the same data, split by ecosystem, from the snapshot of 14 October. I covered the method in an earlier post, so here is only the part you need: a black hole is a project that leaves most of its outside pull requests without a human reply, review or merge for two weeks.

The comparison

Among crates projects that received a decision, 20.0% are black holes. The figure for npm is 30.0%, and for PyPI it is 33.8%. The cut spans six ecosystems, and the Rust subset is 1,065 crates.io projects. In plain terms, one in five of the decided crates projects is a black hole, against roughly three in ten for npm and a third for PyPI.

A decision means Porchlamp could judge the project either way. Undecided projects are not in these percentages.

Those figures reconcile with the headline from the earlier post, which is how I checked this cut ties to the published numbers: across all six ecosystems, 4,297 projects received a decision and 1,133 of them (26.4%) are black holes.

Ecosystem Sampled Decided Black holes Share
maven 1,001 278 54 19.4%
crates 1,065 586 117 20.0%
systems 1,287 573 115 20.1%
go 1,164 609 135 22.2%
npm 3,774 1,283 385 30.0%
pypi 2,709 968 327 33.8%
All six 11,000 4,297 1,133 26.4%

Rust is not first in that table. The JVM sample is a shade better at 19.4%, and the systems sample is within a
whisker at 20.1%. The clean split in this data is between those four and npm and PyPI, and I would rather say so
plainly than let the Rust number do more work than it can.

What you can reasonably conclude

In this sample, a decided crates.io project was less likely to be a black hole than a decided npm or PyPI one, by ten points and nearly fourteen points respectively. If you are choosing where to send a first patch, that is mild encouragement for Rust projects and not a guarantee for any one of them. It is also a single snapshot, and it will change as projects do.

What you should not conclude

Do not read this as a finding about the Rust community's character, and do not read it as a clean verdict on your own crate. There is no control for project size in this cut. Ecosystem is the sampling frame, meaning it describes how projects entered the sample and not why they behave as they do. Elsewhere in the same data the black-hole share rises with stars, from 21% to 39% across the bands I measured, so if one ecosystem's sample leans towards larger or smaller projects, its share moves for reasons unrelated to the ecosystem itself.

A second caveat concerns who is counted. Anything reviewed on Gerrit or a mailing list is undecided, so it sits outside all three percentages. If undecided projects cluster in some ecosystems more than others, the shares would shift, and this cut cannot say whether they do.

Nor should a maintainer feel judged by any of these shares. The measure counts silence over two weeks, which is a narrow window and not a character reference.

Help me get it right

Porchlamp is open source, and this comparison is exactly the sort of claim that benefits from more eyes. Each verdict lists the pull requests behind it, so if a crate is misjudged you can show the evidence and ask for a change. Missing projects can be added, and the code takes patches in the repository. The rankings themselves are on the site.

Would you expect the Rust figure to survive a control for project size, and if not, which way would you guess it moves?

title: DST-Net: Decomposed Spatio-Temporal Network for Time Series Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2610.21123v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Series decomposition has emerged as a widely acknowledged paradigm in deep time series forecasting models. However, existing approaches predominantly employ a homogeneous modeling strategy for all subsequences, thereby overlooking the distinct inductive biases inherent in different components. We identify that the trend component exhibits dominant spatial coupling across channels but carries significant temporal redundancy, whereas the seasonal component is characterized by local temporal evolution but remains susceptible to attention distraction. To address this, we propose a novel disentangled architecture that tailors specific modeling strategies to align with the intrinsic properties of each component. For the trend branch, we design a Latent Graph Block, employing latent graph modeling to capture global topological dependencies and system-wide co-movements. Conversely, for the seasonal branch, we introduce a Gaussian Multi-scale Attention mechanism to mitigate attention distraction. By injecting learnable Gaussian priors, we impose structural constraints that compel the model to focus on multi-granular local contexts, effectively filtering out global noise and accurately capturing local evolutionary phases. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model.

title: Debugging React Apps in Firefox: DevTools, React DevTools Extension, and Profiler Workflow
description:
React developers have access to some of the best debugging tools in the ecosystem. Here's how Firefox DevTools plus the React DevTools extension combine for an effective debugging workflow.

React DevTools in Firefox

Install: Search "React Developer Tools" on addons.mozilla.org (published by Meta).

After installing, two new panels appear in DevTools when you're on a React page:

  • Components: The React component tree with props and state
  • Profiler: Performance recording for React rendering

Components Panel Deep Dive

The Components panel shows:

  • Component tree hierarchy (like React's virtual DOM)
  • Props for each component (hover or click to see values)
  • State and context
  • Hooks (useState, useEffect, useContext, etc.)

Selecting components:
Click any component to see its props and state. The "select element" button (crosshair icon) lets you click on the rendered UI and highlights the corresponding component.

Editing state in DevTools:
Click a component → see its hooks list. Click the edit icon next to a useState hook to change its value in-place. The UI immediately re-renders with the new value.

This is extremely useful for:

  • Testing edge cases without writing test data
  • Verifying how a component responds to different props
  • Checking what state was set after a user action

Searching components:
The search box in the Components panel filters the component tree. Search by component name (e.g., "Button" shows all Button components).

Profiler Panel

Record a profiling session:

  1. Profiler panel → click record (circle button)
  2. Interact with your app (click buttons, navigate, etc.)
  3. Click stop
  4. Analyze the flamegraph

Flamegraph view:
Shows which components rendered during the recording. Each bar represents a component render:

  • Width = time to render
  • Color = time relative to other renders (grey = fast, yellow/red = slow)

What to look for:

  • Components that re-render far more often than expected
  • Parent components triggering child re-renders unnecessarily
  • useEffect or useCallback dependencies causing cascading re-renders

Commit view (bar chart at top):
Each bar is one React "commit" (batch of state updates). Tall bars = expensive commits. Click any bar to see what rendered in that commit.

Firefox DevTools + React: The Combination

React DevTools shows the component tree. Firefox DevTools shows the DOM, network, and performance. They complement each other.

Workflow: debugging a slow render:

  1. Firefox DevTools Performance → record
  2. Trigger the slow action
  3. Stop recording
  4. Check the flame chart for long frames
  5. Switch to React DevTools Profiler
  6. Record the same action
  7. Find which components took the most time to render

Workflow: debugging an API call:

  1. Firefox Network panel → filter to XHR/Fetch
  2. Trigger the action that makes the call
  3. See the request details (payload, response)
  4. Switch to React DevTools → find the component that handles the data
  5. Check its state before and after the call

Firefox-Specific Network Panel Features

For React apps, the Network panel's "Edit and Resend" is useful:

Right-click an API request → Edit and Resend

  • Modify headers, body, or URL
  • Resend to test different responses
  • See how the React app handles error states or different data shapes

This avoids having to mock the backend to test edge cases — just resend with modified data directly.

Console Integration

$r in React DevTools: When you select a component in React DevTools, $r in the browser console references that component instance.

// In Firefox console, after selecting a component in React DevTools:
$r.props  // See all props
$r.state  // See state (class components)

$0 for DOM elements: When you select an element in the regular Inspector panel, $0 references it in the console. Switch to React DevTools after selecting a DOM node to see the corresponding React component.

Debugging Hooks

React DevTools shows all hooks for a selected component. For custom hooks, it shows the hook name and current value.

Common hook debugging patterns:

  • useEffect not running: Check the component in React DevTools. Are the dependencies showing the expected values?
  • useState not updating: Click the component before and after the action. Did the state value change?
  • useContext value unexpected: Check the context provider higher in the tree. Click up the component tree to find the Provider and see what value it's providing.

Browser Console for React

React warns about key issues in console:
Watch the console when developing — React logs useful warnings:

  • "Each child in a list should have a unique 'key' prop"
  • "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component"
  • "Warning: An update to X inside a test was not wrapped in act()"

These warnings appear in Firefox console same as Chrome.

Filtering console messages: The Firefox console filter can filter by "Warnings" to see only React warnings, or by source file.

Strict Mode Behavior

React's StrictMode intentionally renders components twice in development to detect side effects. This appears in DevTools as double renders.

If you're seeing unexpected double renders in the Profiler, check if the component is wrapped in <React.StrictMode> — this is expected behavior, not a bug.

Strict Mode only affects development builds (React strips it from production).

Debugging Context

When using React Context, finding where a context value comes from can be tricky.

In React DevTools Components panel:

  1. Find the consumer component (the one reading from context)
  2. Look at its hooks — useContext hook shows the current value
  3. Click the "jump to definition" button (if available) or navigate up the tree to find the Provider

Tip: name your contexts clearly. MyContext vs unnamed context is much easier to identify in DevTools.

Performance: React.memo and useMemo

React DevTools Profiler shows why components re-rendered. Look for:

  • "Props changed" — expected re-render
  • "State changed" — component's own state changed
  • "Context changed" — subscribed context changed
  • "Parent render" — parent re-rendered (can be prevented with React.memo)

If you see "Parent render" for a component that should be memoized:

  1. Check if React.memo is wrapping it
  2. Check if the props being passed are stable (objects/functions create new references every render)
  3. For objects: use useMemo; for functions: use useCallback

Firefox vs Chrome for React Development

The React DevTools extension is the same in both. Functional differences:

Firefox advantages:

  • Network panel "Edit and Resend" is native (Chrome needs an extension for this)
  • Storage inspector (Local Storage, Session Storage, IndexedDB) in Firefox's Storage panel
  • Screenshot capabilities built into screenshot tool

Chrome advantages:

  • React DevTools performs slightly faster in some cases (Chromium's V8 is very fast)
  • Some React Native debugging tools prefer Chrome

For most React development, Firefox works as well as Chrome. The React DevTools extension provides identical functionality in both.

title: Node.js Duplicate Chat Messages After Reconnect: Trace History and Live Overlap
description:
Short answer: If classroom chat repeats a question after reconnect, overlap history backfill with the live subscription and reconcile both by the same stable message ID. An exact handoff boundary across reconnect is not achievable. For a video lesson, keep this message merge separate from room-token issuance and presence checks. A duplicate delivery does not mean two participants are present.

Option Pick this when Check before committing
Infrai realtime You want a stable REST capability contract while the vendor behind it changes Supply your own history source and test the merge
Ably Dedicated connection recovery and history fit your lifecycle Check recovery behavior and message identity
Pusher Channels Your pub/sub transport is established Pair it with durable history and stable IDs
PubNub Its persistence and presence model fits the roster Test presence separately from message replay

How do you debug duplicate chat messages after reconnect?

Picture an edtech lesson: a teacher starts a video room, issues scoped tokens, and watches the roster while students post questions. A student's connection drops as a question is published. On return, the app loads recent history and resumes live delivery. The question reaches both paths. That's a normal overlap, not evidence that a student sent it twice.

Diagram in words: stored record -> history -> keyed view; that same record -> live event -> the same keyed view. Store and publish the same ID. If each path invents an ID, the client cannot tell that the two arrivals describe one message. A timestamp cutoff won't fix it.

The ID is the boundary.

Keep presence distinct. A roster is not a count of chat events, and a replay does not prove its author is still connected. Scope room tokens and check room membership independently of the displayed message set.

Pick this when the integration boundary matters

Infrai is worth trying for the publish leg if your team wants the backend capability contract to stay put when the vendor behind it changes: one REST API covers multiple backend capabilities with consistent conventions, so changing the provider behind a capability does not require changing your integration code. Infrai uses a single API key across backend services: one key, one wallet, one bill, rather than separate credentials and invoices for each provider. Plain HTTP means no SDK to install. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required; it exposes request and response schemas. Its platform convention also specifies an Idempotency-Key for writes. That gives a publishing integration a concrete way to avoid applying a retried write twice. Neither property removes the need for stable IDs shared by storage and delivery. Define your history source explicitly. The limitation is clear: if your lesson requires a specialist's built-in history and recovery contract, Infrai is not a good fit for that requirement. Ably is the better choice to evaluate first for documented connection recovery and history.

Ably is a stronger candidate when its dedicated realtime recovery and history semantics fit your connection lifecycle. Pusher Channels suits an established channel-event integration where another system owns durable history. PubNub deserves a close look when its persistence and presence semantics align with the lesson roster. Compare those behaviors using your own disconnect sequence, not a generic feature checklist.

For an edtech team that owns its message store and wants one stable integration for realtime publishing alongside room-related capabilities, I recommend trying Infrai for the publish leg, while measuring the client merge and presence independently. Choose a specialist first if built-in recovery or persistence semantics are central to the design.

Run the overlap experiment in Node.js

Use one stored record with ID lesson-42:q-17, one history copy, one live copy, and another distinct record. This runnable TypeScript test operates on normalized data, so it assumes no undocumented provider payload fields. Run it with your TypeScript runner. In production, normalize records from your store and subscription before calling accept. To inspect the associated classroom channel, set INFRAI_API_KEY in your environment; the read-only request below checks its status and surfaces the response body. It does not pretend the channel lookup is a history endpoint or a presence count.

type Message = { id: string; room: string; text: string };

const messages = new Map<string, Message>();
async function inspectChannel(): Promise<string> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY");
  const url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/channel/get/lesson-42";
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
    });
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = response.headers.get("Retry-After");
      const seconds = retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)
        ? Number(retryAfter) : 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, seconds * 1000));
      continue;
    }
    const body = await response.text();
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Channel lookup ${response.status}: ${body}`);
    return body;
  }
  throw new Error("Rate limit retry budget exhausted");
}

function accept(message: Message): void {
  if (!message.id || !message.room) throw new Error("Missing message identity");
  const prior = messages.get(message.id);
  if (prior && (prior.room !== message.room || prior.text !== message.text)) {
    throw new Error(`Conflicting content for ${message.id}`);
  }
  messages.set(message.id, message);
}

const question: Message = { id: "lesson-42:q-17", room: "lesson-42", text: "Can you repeat that?" };
const next: Message = { id: "lesson-42:q-18", room: "lesson-42", text: "Got it." };
for (const event of [question, next, question]) accept(event);
if (messages.size !== 2) throw new Error("Reconnect merge failed");
console.log([...messages.values()]);
inspectChannel().then(console.log).catch(error => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Pass: three arrivals display two messages, and replaying an identical record changes nothing. Fail: a repeated ID with different room or text raises an error rather than silently replacing the stored record. This detects an identity conflict; it does not benchmark any service. The channel lookup is an additional live check and requires a valid key and an existing channel; a lookup error cannot invalidate the local merge assertion.

Don't count callbacks.

Next, repeat with your actual store and transport. Log the ID, room, arrival path (history or live), and whether the ID was already seen. Count unique IDs displayed and conflicting IDs, not callback invocations. Disconnect while a question is sent, then vary which path arrives first on reconnect. Observe the room roster separately; never turn a replayed chat event into a participant join.

What should decide the rollout?

Require the persisted record and the published representation to carry the same ID. The UI must show one item per ID in either arrival order. Independently, check the service's presence observations against the membership behavior your lesson requires. A transport that passes the message merge but fails the roster requirement is not the right choice.

This experiment cannot establish a provider's recovery guarantee, retention policy, or video-room behavior. Verify token scope and presence using the service's documented contract. Keep the message store authoritative for history; a live callback alone is not durable history. In particular, do not mistake a successful channel lookup for an accurate class roster: those are different observations with different failure conditions. A sensible rollout exercises all three independently, including a reconnect just before the history response finishes and another just after the live listener starts. Neither ordering should produce an extra displayed question.

References

  • Ably connection recovery.
  • Pusher Channels events.
  • PubNub Message Persistence.
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0.

Further reading

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai realtime documentation and check the live contract before wiring the adapter.

title: Stable Percentage Rollout Feature Flags — User Hashing for Gradual Backend Releases
description:
A Node.js backend using percentage rollout feature flags needs stable user hashing for a gradual release; otherwise, the same fintech account can switch paths between scheduled imports. When the page says the import completed but the ledger has received no new rows for 47 minutes, the safest response is to set the new importer’s rollout to zero, leave every account on the old path, and investigate without changing the bucket rule.

TL;DR: keep the percentage in the flag service, but decide membership in the backend with a documented deterministic hash of an immutable user or account ID. The same account must stay in the same bucket across requests, workers, and deploys. Treat the percentage change as a reversible routing decision, not as an experiment system. For a scheduled import, separately monitor the age of the last successful result; a feature flag cannot detect a job that never ran.

That separation is the operating model: the provider stores the desired rollout, application code evaluates stable membership, import metrics show whether work produced results, and a heartbeat monitor pages on silence. Each boundary has one job. Rollback remains boring.

What should the page have told us earlier?

The useful signal is not “cron fired.” It is “a scheduled import produced a valid result for this tenant within its expected interval.” A worker can start, retry, or even return success while writing nothing. For an hourly account import, record the completion time only after the durable result is committed, then alert when its age crosses a threshold derived from the schedule and normal runtime.

Use an external dead-man’s-switch service such as Healthchecks for the silent case. Infrai has no heartbeat monitoring or notification routing, so polling its free query APIs and building a pager around them would create another small monitoring system to own. That can be reasonable when a team already has an alert dispatcher, but it is not the least complex choice for “the job should have run and did not.”

The rollout signal answers a different question: which accounts should execute the new importer? Infrai can store and update the rollout percentage through its plain REST API. There is no SDK or client-library version to carry in every worker; any runtime that can make an authenticated HTTP request can use the same surface. I recommend trying Infrai for teams that want a small control-plane boundary for rollout percentages across mixed backend runtimes, because the REST handoff is explicit and its public discovery schema can remove guesswork when wiring the call.

Do not turn that recommendation into an analytics claim. The flag capability does not provide evaluation statistics, advanced targeting governance, dependency graphs, or a change audit log. Document who may change a percentage, preserve changes in your own deployment record, and use a specialist when those controls are requirements.

How should Node.js backends combine percentage rollout feature flags with stable hashing?

A random number per request is not a rollout. It is traffic flicker. An account can reach the new importer on Monday, the old one on Tuesday, and both paths during a retry storm. That defeats rollback analysis and may duplicate side effects.

Keep the cohort still.

Hash a stable identifier with a named, versioned algorithm and map it into a fixed bucket range. The example below uses 10,000 buckets, so a percentage can be expressed in basis points. It uses the first eight bytes of SHA-256 in big-endian order. Those details belong in the runbook; changing any one of them reshuffles users.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/binary"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const bucketCount uint64 = 10_000

func enabled(flagKey, accountID string, rolloutBasisPoints uint64) bool {
    if rolloutBasisPoints > bucketCount {
        rolloutBasisPoints = bucketCount
    }
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(flagKey + ":v1:" + accountID))
    bucket := binary.BigEndian.Uint64(sum[:8]) % bucketCount
    return bucket < rolloutBasisPoints
}

func getDiscovery(ctx context.Context) ([]byte, error) {
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("get discovery: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("get discovery: rate limit retries exhausted")
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    manifest, err := getDiscovery(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("discovery response: %s\n", manifest)

    // Bind the discovered flag schema in production. This fixed value keeps the
    // hashing example runnable without guessing any response fields.
    for _, accountID := range []string{"acct_us_1042", "acct_eu_2088", "acct_us_7711"} {
        fmt.Printf("%s new_importer=%t\n", accountID, enabled("ledger-import", accountID, 2_500))
    }
}

The flag key is part of the hash input so unrelated flags do not select exactly the same cohort. The v1 marker makes the contract visible. Keep it unchanged during a release. If a future migration truly needs new bucketing, create a new flag or version and treat the cohort shift as a separate rollout.

Choose the identifier with equal care. For a fintech import, account ID is usually safer than user ID because the work and its side effects belong to the account. A person joining two accounts should not couple their rollout states. Region is not a substitute for hashing: if US and EU tenants need separate release controls, use separate flag keys or apply a documented eligibility check before bucketing.

The sample deliberately prints the discovery response instead of asserting an undocumented flag JSON field. Before production use, select the flag capability from that manifest, bind its documented response schema to a typed structure, validate the resulting percentage as an integer from 0 through 10,000, and pass it to enabled. The public discovery surface needs no key and describes request and response schemas. Authenticated flag calls use Authorization: Bearer <key>, with the key read from an environment variable rather than stored in source. Every documented capability also includes runnable examples in 10 languages, so the Node.js service and Go worker can implement the same boundary without sharing a vendor SDK.

The application flow is short. Read the rollout percentage from the flag system, validate it, evaluate locally, and attach the flag key, bucket algorithm version, and chosen path to the import’s structured result. Cache policy must match the rollback objective. If workers poll every 60 seconds, the operational promise is “rollout changes converge in roughly one polling interval,” not “rollback is immediate.” Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key; for a team already using adjacent backend capabilities, that means this flag poller does not require another credential distribution path or another client dependency.

One trap deserves a runbook line: do not recompute membership from email, mutable customer labels, process-local hash functions, or map iteration. A language upgrade or profile edit can otherwise move accounts with no percentage change.

Trace the page back to the control boundary

When the no-results page fires, the on-call needs enough context to choose a safe first action. Put the account ID, expected schedule, last successful result time, current importer path, flag key, and bucket version in the alert or its linked dashboard. Avoid customer data in those labels. Cardinality and privacy still count during an incident.

The first action is containment. Set the rollout to zero if evidence points to the new path, then verify that old-path completions resume for previously selected accounts. Because selection is deterministic, zero removes the new cohort without asking operators to identify individual users. Raising the percentage later adds a stable superset of accounts as long as the algorithm and key remain fixed.

Instrumentation should sit after the durable write:

  1. The scheduler dispatches an account import with an idempotency key derived from account ID and schedule window.
  2. The worker reads the rollout percentage and evaluates the stable bucket.
  3. The selected importer writes results idempotently. Retries must not double-apply ledger effects.
  4. Only after commit, the worker reports completion and updates the heartbeat.
  5. The monitor pages when result age exceeds the agreed threshold.

This ordering separates delivery from outcome. Standard queues are at-least-once in practice, so consumer idempotency is mandatory regardless of which flag provider chooses the code path. A flag rollback controls future routing; it does not undo a committed financial write.

Infrai’s rollout operation is POST /v1/flags/rollout/{key}. Keep that control-plane call outside the per-record loop. Its broader platform also specifies idempotency as a first-class convention and publishes request schemas and runnable examples through public discovery, which reduces integration upkeep when the same team already uses the REST surface for adjacent backend work. The trade-off is visibility: there is no built-in evaluation history or flag-change audit log, and clients poll rather than receive streamed updates.

Where do the provider boundaries differ?

Provider choice follows the control burden, not the hash function. Flag specialists own the release decision, while observability products own evidence and paging. Mixing those categories in one score would hide the boundary that matters during rollback.

Option Best fit here Boundary or limitation to plan for
Infrai A rollout percentage behind one plain REST surface, especially across several backend languages Rollout basics only; no evaluation analytics, dependency graph, advanced targeting governance, or change audit log
LaunchDarkly Teams that need a dedicated feature-management product and want evaluation and governance concerns handled by a specialist Introduces a dedicated flag platform into the production path; validate its SDK and operating model against rollback requirements
Unleash Teams that prefer a dedicated, open feature-management platform and want control over how it is operated Self-management choices add ownership; confirm that the chosen deployment and client mode meet polling and audit expectations
ConfigCat Teams seeking a focused hosted feature-flag service with language-specific integration options Still a separate vendor surface; verify evaluation semantics and change controls before using it for financial workflows
Sentry Error investigation around failed importer code paths It does not replace a stable flag evaluator or prove that an absent job ran
Datadog Teams wanting metrics, logs, traces, monitors, and paging in one observability product It is a separate operational surface from the rollout control plane
Grafana Teams composing dashboards and alerts over their chosen telemetry sources Alert quality still depends on emitting the last-success signal correctly
Better Stack Teams wanting hosted monitoring and incident response around scheduled work Keep feature selection in the flag layer rather than coupling it to the pager

This is deliberately not a feature-count verdict. LaunchDarkly, Unleash, and ConfigCat are more natural candidates when flags are a program with targeting policy, experimentation, or governance requirements. Infrai is a stronger fit when the desired boundary is narrower: store a percentage, retrieve it over HTTP, evaluate a stable account bucket in code, and keep the surrounding backend integrations on one consistent API.

LaunchDarkly, Unleash, and ConfigCat do not replace the missing-job detector. Healthchecks is the relevant specialist for a scheduled task that goes silent. Sentry is useful once there is an error to inspect; Datadog, Grafana, and Better Stack are credible alternatives when the team wants the result-age signal integrated with a broader monitoring stack. Likewise, logs carrying trace_id and span_id can help correlate an import, but Infrai does not provide distributed trace queries or a span tree. Use a tracing system when the investigation depends on cross-service causal structure.

One tool rarely owns this whole trace.

Thresholds are part of the rollback design

An alert at exactly 60 minutes for an hourly job sounds precise and pages on ordinary scheduling jitter. An alert at six hours preserves sleep but weakens the rollback window. Set the threshold from the business recovery objective, the schedule, normal queue delay, and observed completion time. Then test it by withholding a heartbeat, not by assuming a dashboard query proves the page route works.

There is a second false-positive cost. During a staged rollout, the new cohort may contain too few scheduled accounts to produce a result in every interval. A global “new importer produced zero rows” alert will fire even when no selected account was due. Compare due-and-selected accounts with successful results, or page on each due account’s result age. This adds state, but the state corresponds to the obligation the business actually cares about.

Roll out in steps that allow at least one meaningful import cycle between changes. Record the percentage, timestamp, operator, bucket version, and observed completion counts in the deployment record because the flag service will not supply that audit history. Stop on ambiguous evidence.

The clean design has two independent rollback levers: percentage zero routes future work to the old importer, while normal deployment rollback restores code. Neither should change the hashing contract. After recovery, reconcile any schedule windows that started before containment using the same idempotency key scheme, then advance gradually only when old-path and new-path result-age signals are comparable.

False positives spend operator attention and train people to distrust silence alerts. False negatives hide missed financial data. That is why the final threshold belongs in an SLO or runbook decision, with an owner and a test cadence, rather than as a convenient constant copied from the cron expression.

Further reading

  • Infrai documentation
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • ConfigCat documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation
  • Better Stack documentation
  • RFC 5424: The Syslog Protocol
  • Electron crashReporter documentation

If this narrow control-plane boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the live rollout schema before wiring the poller.

title: LibreFang 2026.9.14 Released
description:
LibreFang 2026.9.14 Released

v2026.9.14 is a milestone release bringing autonomous goal execution, multi-instance channels, per-agent reasoning modes, and comprehensive configuration tooling to the dashboard and CLI. This release stabilizes the agent-authoring experience while closing several security boundaries and fixing 50+ bugs.

203 PRs from 5 contributors since v2026.8.30.

Autonomous Goal Execution & Goals System

Agents can now drive themselves through iterative tasks without human invocation. A goal defines what success looks like; LibreFang auto-spawns a disposable worker agent that runs the goal, optionally spawns a verifier that judges each iteration, and learns from tagged markers (GOAL_LEARNED: <text>) it encounters along the way.

New in this release:

  • librefang goal "<description>" CLI command with --loop-engineering mode for automated verification
  • Goals screen in the TUI with wizard-driven creation and live phase tracking
  • /goal slash command in Telegram and Slack
  • Dashboard Goals page with phase badges and outcome visibility
  • Per-goal evaluator_model to judge completion, plus auto-generated skills from captured learnings

Agent Types: Manifests as First-Class Citizens

Agent types (reusable manifests) moved from templates/ to the canonical agent-types/ directory and gained full CRUD support. Create, edit, and delete types from the dashboard Agent Types page instead of hand-editing TOML. Types can now be promoted directly to the public registry as a GitHub PR.

Related improvements:

  • Dashboard Agent Types page with card grid, Quick Run for ephemeral spawns
  • Shared Folders editor on agent type and instance details
  • librefang agent new discovers types in the flat canonical store
  • Registry sync resolves both legacy agents/ and new agent-types/ directories
  • Source template origin tracked on every agent spawned from a type

Channel Multi-Instance Support

A single channel adapter (Telegram, Slack, etc.) can now run as multiple named instances, each with its own configuration, secrets namespace, and assigned agent. Manage instances from the dashboard Channels screen or the TUI.

Key features:

  • Per-instance secret namespacing prevents credential sharing between bots
  • Collision detection rejects names that would map to the same namespace
  • Add/configure/delete UI on both dashboard and TUI
  • Instance name and per-instance agent binding in config forms

Per-Agent Reasoning Mode & Extended Thinking

DeepSeek V4 and OpenRouter-routed models now respect per-agent reasoning-mode settings. Agents can be configured to run with none, low, high, or max reasoning effort. The Anthropic driver now handles current Claude models (5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8+) which removed sampling parameters and moved extended thinking to a new schema.

What changed:

  • reasoning_mode settable per agent, globally, or per task
  • Provider-aware translation: DeepSeek gets thinking fields, OpenRouter gets nested reasoning, others get top-level reasoning_effort
  • Adaptive thinking on Claude (effort comes from reasoning_mode alone, no separate budget)
  • Fallback chain model = "default" now resolves correctly

Configuration, Credentials & Vaults

The operator experience for configuration just got significantly better. The dashboard gains a schema-driven config editor; the vault write API lets surfaces store credentials securely; and editing flows now validate and report failures instead of silently accepting bad input.

What's new:

  • Dashboard Config page with per-field editable rows derived from GET /api/config/schema
  • TUI Settings screen gains Configuration tab with real-time validation
  • Vault write API: GET /api/vault/keys, PUT /api/vault/keys/{key}, DELETE /api/vault/keys/{key}
  • Vault reads show effective source: environment, vault, or unset
  • Dashboard Channels settings are writable again

Model Management & Parameters

Every model parameter now uses the same control everywhere it appears. Context window, max output tokens, temperature, top-p, and the two penalties are now consistently editable with shared presets and bounds checking.

Improvements:

  • context_window and max_output_tokens are editable per agent from the API, CLI, TUI, and dashboard
  • Model parameter overrides survive registry syncs (schema v56)
  • Per-model limits show effective value vs. catalog figure
  • Unsupported parameters (e.g., reasoning_effort on a gateway that doesn't support it) are stripped and retried transparently

Memory System Hardening

Automatic memory scoping now closes three holes that let memories leak across boundaries:

  • capabilities.memory_read = [] now blocks substrate recall and context-engine injection (not just auto-retrieve)
  • capabilities.memory_write = [] blocks the per-turn writer, not just extraction
  • Per-turn writer stamps both chat_scope and session_scope so raw dialogue respects agent isolation
  • Full-text-index rebuilds on UPDATEs that cannot change indexed content (access-count bumps, decay sweeps)
  • Session and cron compaction run on the agent's own model chain, not the kernel default

Dashboard & TUI Enhancements

The UX got smoother everywhere. Failed operations now report what the daemon said instead of generic lines. The dashboard shows real values for configuration settings instead of cached placeholders. The TUI's goal detail panel, memory config editor, and every error message is now precise and actionable.

Highlights:

  • Dashboard login survives daemon restart (session tokens now restored correctly)
  • Agent detail drawer shows injected token footprint and last five LLM calls
  • Memory tab shows resolved extraction model and provenance
  • Workflow run detail shows step progress (current_step_index, total_steps, per-step variables)
  • Goals page shows autonomous run phase badges (finished, rate-limited, stopped, etc.)
  • Slider tick legends now position labels at their true values, not evenly spaced
  • Provider page shows real availability status, not a stale cached state
  • Add button re-enabled on Channels page after first instance is configured

Bug Fixes & Stability

50+ bugs fixed, including critical issues that affected real deployments:

  • Memory consolidation no longer merges memories across different peers, chats, or sessions
  • Tool loop guard now detects repeated identical results and refuses the call after three runs
  • Streaming replies with malformed tool-call markup are replaced with an honest sentence instead of sent raw to channels
  • Network byte quota now actually enforces [resources] max_network_bytes_per_hour (was accepted but ignored)
  • Docker sandbox container pooling now works (was created and destroyed per call)
  • Workflow step prompts expanded in single pass (order-independent, no iteration on substituted values)
  • Cron schedule editing no longer reverts to defaults when no changes made
  • Sidecar channel delete now removes every adapter instance, not guessed ones
  • Config reload correctly reports what actually took effect (not applied work it withheld)
  • Session streaming no longer wedges the daemon on message-history compaction
  • Approval routing now properly scoped to requesting agent's configured channels
  • Windows launcher (librefang.exe) no longer stack-overflows on startup

Security Fixes

  • Approval field payload injection blocked: config writes can no longer smuggle credential fields into tables
  • MCP server listing now requires Admin role (was exposing tokens in SSE/HTTP URLs)
  • API key revocation on POST /api/config/reload now applies to REST surface (was only effective on WebSocket)
  • Passkey login no longer accepts credentials filed under the wrong principal
  • Dashboard root path protected by auth (was unprotected even with password configured)
  • Dangerous-command gate no longer bypassed by quoted program names ("rm" -rf / now blocked)
  • Sidecar secrets no longer shared between sibling instances
  • Plugin [env] expansion can no longer reference reserved secrets
  • Chat WebSocket now verifies caller owns the agent (not just exists)
  • Rich HTML sanitization moved to structured parsing (no longer regex-based escaping that can be evaded)

Performance

  • Sidecar schema probes run concurrently (cold-start boot time reduced 10–30x on deployments with many adapters)
  • Per-adapter send backpressure prevents queuing under burst load
  • Memory index rebuilt only on content changes, not on every access-count bump or decay sweep
  • Reduced lock contention in concurrent retry scenarios

Migration Notes

  • Operator-visible behavior change: max_network_bytes_per_hour now enforces the 100 MB default if unset. Agents moving more traffic need an explicit larger value or 0 for unlimited.
  • Workflow approval gates now actually pause runs and wait for humans (previously ran unattended). Anything behind an approval gate will now require explicit approval to proceed.
  • Agent session isolation: agents running session_mode = "new" no longer recall raw dialogue from earlier invocations; set session_scoped_recall = false in agent.toml to restore prior behavior.
  • Configuration includes with unknown fields are now rejected when strict_config = true (was silently ignoring them).

Install / Upgrade 

# Binary
curl -fsSL https://get.librefang.ai | sh

# Rust SDK
cargo add librefang

# JavaScript SDK
npm install @librefang/sdk

# Python SDK
pip install librefang-sdk
