title: My fix was one line. Code review found two holes in it.
description:
The bug I fixed in Microsoft Agent Framework did not crash anything. That is what made it worth fixing.

When the framework called Gemini without streaming, the response knew which model had answered. When it made the same call with streaming, the model name could disappear on the way. The framework records its metrics through OpenTelemetry, and the model name is one of the dimensions those metrics are split by. On streamed calls, the token and duration histograms simply lost that dimension. Every request still succeeded. The per-model view of cost and latency just had a hole in it.

Why it happened

Each streamed chunk from Gemini may or may not carry a model_version. The streaming parser copied that field straight into the update, so a chunk without it produced an update without a model. The aggregator keeps the last non-empty value it sees, and there was nothing to catch up afterwards, so a stream whose chunks carried no version ended with no model at all.

The non-streaming parser, thirty-odd lines above, already handled this: it fell back to the configured model when the response did not name one. Two paths, same input type, different answers.

The one-line fix

So I proposed the obvious thing: apply the same fallback on the streaming path. One line, two tests, parity with the sibling.

It was wrong twice.

Hole one

I had raised this one myself, as an open question in the PR description: was the client's default model really the right fallback? The automated reviewer answered it. The fallback used the client's default model, not the model actually requested. A client configured for gemini-2.5-flash and called with gemini-2.5-pro for one request would label that request as Flash, metrics included. The model resolved for the request was already in scope where the stream was consumed, so the parser now takes it as an argument and falls back to that.

Hole two

Then the maintainer found the subtler one. Applying the fallback chunk by chunk could overwrite a version the server had already reported. If an early chunk said gemini-2.5-pro-002 and the final usage chunk carried no version, the aggregator, which keeps the last non-empty value, would replace the precise version with the requested alias gemini-2.5-pro.

The fix had to remember what the server said for the whole stream, not chunk by chunk:

fallback_model = model
async for chunk in response_stream:
    if chunk.model_version:
        fallback_model = chunk.model_version
    yield self._process_chunk(chunk, fallback_model)

and in the parser:

model=chunk.model_version or model,

What merged

Three iterations, four tests. One checks the version from a chunk is kept, one checks the fallback to the configured model, one the fallback to the requested model, and one replays the maintainer's exact case: an observed server version must survive a later chunk that omits it. The last one fails on the previous commit, which is the point of it.

What I take from it

My first version was not careless. It matched the sibling path exactly, it had tests, and it fixed the reported symptom. It was still wrong, twice. The first hole I had seen and left as a question. The second came from the maintainer.

That is the case for review in one PR. Not catching typos, but catching the second-order behaviour of a change: which value is in scope, what the aggregator does with it next, what a later chunk can undo. Observability bugs make this harder, because nothing fails. The only signal is a number that is quietly attached to the wrong thing, or to nothing.

If you run LLM calls behind OpenTelemetry, it is worth one test that compares a streamed call with a non-streamed one and checks every attribute, not just the status code.

The PR, with the full review thread: microsoft/agent-framework#9139

I am Ayoub Hammoudi, a backend and AI platforms engineer in Paris. More of my work is at github.com/Ayoubhm07.

title: The N+1 Query Problem — "It works locally, but is extremely slow in production"
description:
The scenario: Your API loads 100 users and their orders. It works locally — but becomes extremely slow in production. What could be causing it?

One of the most common (and sneaky) causes: the N+1 Query Problem. 🐢

What Is It?

Suppose the application needs to display 100 users along with their orders. You'd expect the database to fetch everything together in one efficient round-trip. But here's what often actually happens:

1️⃣ The application sends one query to fetch all 100 users.
2️⃣ It then sends one additional query per user to fetch that user's orders.

Result:

  • ✅ 1 query to fetch the users
  • ❌ 100 additional queries — one per user — to fetch their orders

That's 101 database queries for a single API request.

This is the textbook N+1 Query Problem:

1 query fetches the parent records, then N additional queries fetch the related records
individually — one per parent row.

With 100 users, this might go unnoticed in a local test with a fast local DB and no network latency. With 10,000 users, the same code path triggers 10,001 queries — and it becomes catastrophic in production, especially over a real network to a real database.

Why It Hurts

Every additional query introduces:

  • Network round-trip time (multiplied by N)
  • Database connection pool usage (queries competing for limited connections)
  • Query-processing/parsing overhead per call
  • More load on the database server
  • Significantly higher API response time — often the actual root cause of "works locally, slow in prod," since local dev DBs have near-zero latency per query while production round-trips add up fast.

Why Does It Happen?

Most commonly with an ORM using lazy loading. The application loads the users first (one query). Later, when code accesses user.getOrders() inside a loop, the ORM silently and transparently issues another database query per user at that exact point — invisible in the code (it just looks like a normal getter call), which is exactly why it's easy to miss in code review and easy to reproduce only under realistic data volumes.

How to Fix It

🔗 1. Fetch related data together (join fetch)

Use a join or fetch strategy that retrieves the parent (users) and the related child data (orders) together, in a single query, instead of triggering a separate query per parent row.

📦 2. Use batch fetching

Instead of loading orders one user at a time, retrieve the orders for multiple users in one batch query (e.g., WHERE user_id IN (1, 2, 3, ..., 100)). This can turn 100 queries into a small handful — often reducing hundreds of queries down to just a couple.

🎯 3. Fetch only the required fields (projections)

If the API only needs a user's name, order number, and status, don't load the complete User,Order, and every related entity graph. Project only the fields actually needed for the response — less data over the wire, less mapping overhead, and often avoids triggering lazy-loaded associations entirely. — less data over the wire, less mapping overhead, and often avoids triggering lazy-loaded associations entirely.

📄 4. Add pagination

Never load thousands of users (and their orders) in a single request. Retrieve a bounded page and only the data needed for that page — this caps the worst-case query count and payload size regardless of how large the underlying table grows.

How Do You Detect the N+1 Problem?

  • Enable database query logging (e.g., Hibernate's show-sql / format_sql, or the database's own slow-query log) and actually read what gets generated for a given endpoint.
  • Monitor the number of queries per API request — a sudden spike proportional to the result set size (e.g., queries scale linearly with the number of users returned) is the classic signature.
  • Use an APM tool (e.g., New Relic, Datadog, Elastic APM) — most surface a per-request query count and flag "N+1 detected" patterns automatically.
  • Look for repeated queries with different IDs in the log — the same SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE user_id = ? template repeated 100 times with different parameter values is the smoking gun.
  • Test using realistic data volumes — this bug is invisible with 3 test users locally and becomes an incident with 10,000 users in production; load/integration tests need production-like data sizes to catch it before release.

Spring Boot / JPA: Which Fix Should You Prefer?

A common follow-up question: "Which approach do you prefer in Spring Boot — fetch joins, entity graphs, batch fetching, or DTO projections?"

There isn't a single universally-correct answer — it depends on the access pattern — but here's how to reason about the trade-offs:

Approach How it works Best when Watch out for
Fetch Join (JOIN FETCH in JPQL) Single SQL query joins parent + child in one round-trip You always need the child collection alongside the parent for this query Fetching multiple collections with JOIN FETCH in one query causes a Cartesian product explosion (rows multiply); JPA restricts fetching more than one List-type collection this way
Entity Graph (@EntityGraph) Declaratively specifies which associations to eagerly fetch, per query/method, without changing the entity's default fetch type globally You want eager fetching for specific use cases but keep lazy loading as the sane default elsewhere Still one query per graph, but multiple collections in the same graph can hit the same Cartesian-product issue as fetch joins
Batch Fetching (@BatchSize, or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size) Lazy loading still triggers on access, but Hibernate batches the next N pending lazy loads into one IN (...) query instead of one-by-one You have unavoidable lazy access patterns (e.g., generic repository code used in many contexts) and want a broad, low-effort mitigation Doesn't eliminate extra queries entirely, just batches them — still more than a single join, though far better than true N+1
DTO Projections (JPQL constructor expressions, Spring Data interface projections, or a mapper) Query selects only the exact fields needed directly into a DTO — no entity graph traversal at all Read-only / API-response use cases where you don't need full entity objects or their lazy associations Loses JPA entity features (dirty checking, lazy nav) — but for a read API, you don't want those anyway

Default preference: start with DTO projections for read-heavy API endpoints — they sidestep the N+1 problem entirely because there's no entity graph to lazily traverse in the first place, and they also naturally satisfy "fetch only the required fields" (fix #3) at the same time. Reserve fetch joins / entity graphs for cases where you genuinely need full entity objects (e.g., you're about to modify and save them), and use batch fetching as a safety net for lazy-loaded associations you can't easily eliminate across a large, shared codebase.

🔗 Related

  • Designing APIs for Massive Datasets — takes pagination (fix #4) and field projection (fix #3) further for very large datasets: cursor-based pagination, sparse fields, DB-level filtering, caching, and compression.
  • Caching Strategies — caching read-heavy query results to avoid re-paying the query cost at all.

title: Dark Mode for Developers: Eye Strain, When You Need an Extension, and NightOwl vs Dark Reader
description:
Eye strain from bright screens is a real problem for developers who stare at browsers all day. Here's why dark mode matters beyond aesthetics, and when a dark mode extension is the right solution vs. OS-level dark mode.

Why Dark Mode Matters for Developer Health

Blue light and circadian rhythm: Screen blue light suppresses melatonin production, affecting sleep quality. Late-night coding with a bright screen delays your sleep onset — dark mode reduces blue light emission.

Eye strain in dim environments: When working in a dim room, high-contrast bright backgrounds cause the pupil to contract more (adjusting to the bright screen), then dilate when you look away. Repeated cycles cause eye fatigue.

Migraine triggers: Bright, high-contrast patterns are a known migraine trigger for susceptible people. Bright white backgrounds with black text on dark room walls create a stark contrast that some find triggering.

Note: Dark mode doesn't universally reduce eye strain — in bright room lighting, dark mode can actually cause more strain because pupils open wider for the darker screen. Dark mode is most beneficial in dim/dark environments.

OS Dark Mode: What It Covers and What It Misses

When you enable OS dark mode:

  • Your OS UI goes dark ✓
  • Firefox's own chrome (toolbar, menus) goes dark ✓
  • Sites that respect prefers-color-scheme: dark go dark ✓

Sites that respect prefers-color-scheme: GitHub, Dev.to, Stack Overflow, MDN, most modern developer tools.

What OS dark mode misses:

  • Legacy or unmaintained sites that ignore prefers-color-scheme
  • Sites with a dark mode toggle but that don't respond to OS settings
  • Custom web apps built without considering dark mode
  • PDF viewers opened in browser
  • Third-party embedded widgets on any page

For developers who work with a mix of modern and legacy tools, there will always be some bright pages.

When You Need a Dark Mode Extension

You need an extension when:

  1. You regularly use sites that don't support prefers-color-scheme: Legacy apps, internal tools, older documentation sites.
  2. You work at night and want consistent dark across all content: One bright tab breaking the dark environment defeats the purpose.
  3. You have visual sensitivity: Consistent low-brightness browsing matters for managing photosensitivity.

The extension applies dark CSS to pages regardless of whether the site supports dark mode natively.

NightOwl vs Dark Reader: Technical Comparison

Both extensions intercept page rendering and apply dark CSS. The key differences:

Dark Reader:

  • Three modes: Dynamic (analyzes colors), Filter (CSS inversion), Static (simple inversion)
  • Dynamic mode is the most accurate but heavier (analyzes DOM and computes color transformations)
  • Large community, extensive configuration options
  • Works well for most sites

NightOwl:

  • Smart inversion approach: analyzes existing colors and converts them
  • Lighter on CPU/memory than Dark Reader's Dynamic mode
  • Focused on doing one thing well (dark mode everywhere)
  • Simpler configuration

Filter mode comparison: Simple CSS filter inversion (filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg)) is fast but inverts images too. Both extensions have image preservation to avoid this.

Performance note: Dynamic mode in any dark mode extension adds some overhead per page load. On slow devices, this can be noticeable. Lightweight mode/NightOwl's approach is preferable.

Per-Site Control

Both extensions allow site-by-site control:

Disable for specific sites: If a site's native dark mode looks better than the forced dark mode, disable the extension for that domain.

Sites where native dark mode is usually better:

  • GitHub (their dark mode is well-designed)
  • Dev.to (native dark mode is excellent)
  • Twitter/X (their dark mode respects their UI patterns)

Sites where forced dark is often necessary:

  • Documentation sites built 5-10 years ago
  • Internal company tools
  • Stack Overflow (native dark is good but some may prefer consistent forced dark)
  • News sites with inconsistent dark support

The pattern: Use OS dark mode → browser respects it for prefers-color-scheme sites → extension covers the rest.

Installation

NightOwl: addons.mozilla.org → search "NightOwl" → Add to Firefox

After installation, NightOwl activates automatically. The extension icon lets you:

  • Toggle dark mode globally
  • Toggle for the current site
  • Access settings

About:config Approach (Without Extension)

Firefox has a built-in experimental forced dark mode:

In about:config:

layout.css.prefers-color-scheme.content-override = 1
  • 0 = force light
  • 1 = force dark
  • 2 = follow OS (default)

Important limitation: This setting only tells sites "you're in dark mode" via prefers-color-scheme. Sites that ignore prefers-color-scheme still show in light mode. Only sites that have dark mode CSS and respond to the media query will switch.

For true forced dark (even on sites with no dark mode), you still need an extension.

Reading Mode as an Alternative

For reading articles on bright sites: Firefox's Reading Mode (F9 or the book icon in address bar) removes everything except the article text and gives you a dark background option.

Reading Mode dark settings: click the Aa button → choose dark background.

Use case: Rather than forcing dark mode on an entire news site (which may affect navigation and menus), use Reading Mode for just the article. Clean, dark reading experience without the extension overhead for that specific use case.

Scheduled Dark Mode

The most ergonomic approach: automatic dark/light based on time of day.

OS-level scheduling:

  • Windows: Settings → Personalization → Colors → Custom → Schedule (sunrise/sunset or custom times)
  • macOS: System Preferences → General → Appearance → Auto (switches at sunset/sunrise)
  • Linux: gsettings schedule scripts or a GNOME extension for scheduled switching

When OS switches, Firefox's prefers-color-scheme changes, and dark mode extensions that watch this preference switch automatically.

Result: Bright mode during daytime work, dark mode in the evening and night — no manual toggling needed.

title: AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go is now generally available
description:
Today, AWS announces the general availability of the AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go, enabling Go developers to build resilient, long-running workflows using Lambda durable functions. With this SDK, developers can create multi-step applications like infrastructure automation, deployment rollouts with approval gates, and pipelines that call AI models and pause for human review directly in their Go code without implementing custom progress tracking.

Lambda durable functions extend Lambda's event-driven programming model with operations that checkpoint progress automatically and pause execution for up to an year when waiting on external events. The AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go provides a native Go experience for building with Lambda durable functions. It includes steps for progress tracking, callback integration for human and agent-in-the-loop workflows, durable invocation for reliable function chaining, and waits for efficient suspension.

The SDK works with the Go tools developers already use. Developers add it to a Go module with go get and deploy their function as a single static binary on the provided.al2023 runtime, like any other Go function on Lambda. Before deploying, they can locally test complete workflows on their own machine with the durabletest package, without requiring network access or AWS credentials, and use the durablelint analyzer to catch code that could break a workflow when it resumes.

To get started, see the Lambda durable functions developer guide and the AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go on GitHub. For Regional availability and pricing details for Lambda durable functions, see the AWS Capabilities by Region page and AWS Lambda Pricing.

title: AgentEval: Evidence-Bounded Assessment of Stateful Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21177v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Task completion alone does not determine whether a stateful agent satisfied its obligations, and a recorded judgment does not guarantee that its supporting evidence remains valid. We present AgentEval, a system that carries a contract-bound assessment record through tool execution, state and event capture, report qualification, and case maintenance. It separates what the agent did, what the evidence establishes, and whether the conclusion is supported for present use. On 32 tool-world administrations, independent checks agree on all 30 complete episodes, distinguishing satisfied, violated, and unresolved obligations; two interrupted administrations are retained. Controlled interventions on 48 evidence views expose 36 binding faults missed by hash-only checks without changing agent behavior. Scenario Studio connects reviewed cases to 12 two-turn reports with 24 independently checked answers. A separate public-benchmark study on 192 held-out executions reveals ten completed return subgoals within broader task failures and isolates the effect of missing evidence. These studies show how an executable assessment record makes scope, evidential support, and report reuse inspectable across an agent evaluation workflow.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for HPC Job Scheduling: A Statistical Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.21008v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers learned job selection for High-Performance Computing (HPC), but performance against heuristics alone does not establish value beyond action masking. Six DRL treatments are compared: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C), and Deep Q-Network (DQN), each with and without masking. Three heuristics and a seed-paired masked uniform random control provide baselines across ten seeds on two real Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) workload traces, one homogeneous and one heterogeneous, under a common non-parametric framework. All masked treatments complete evaluation, whereas unmasked treatments are truncated. On the homogeneous trace, no masked DRL treatment significantly improves average waiting time or average and maximum bounded slowdown over the control. On the heterogeneous trace, MaskablePPO improves all three metrics relative to the control. Its average waiting time is equivalent to that of the three heuristics within a 10% margin, and its maximum bounded slowdown is 22% lower than that of Last-Come, First-Served (LCFS). MaskablePPO has the leading average waiting-time rank among complete treatments on both traces, but Nemenyi comparisons detect no significant difference from MaskableA2C. Among masked variants, MaskablePPO has the lowest recorded mean training time, while MaskableDQN has the lowest mean decision latency. These findings distinguish completion from baseline-specific scheduling gains and support including a masked random control when assessing the value of learned selection.

title: Zero-Downtime Database Migrations: Lessons from GitLab's PostgreSQL Architecture
description:
Zero-Downtime Database Migrations: Lessons from GitLab's PostgreSQL Architecture

Running a standard schema migration on a small staging database is trivial: you run ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN bio text; and it finishes in 10 milliseconds.

However, when your PostgreSQL database holds billions of rows, multi-terabyte tables, and thousands of concurrent transactions per second (as GitLab.com does), a naive migration can trigger table-wide ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks. In seconds, transaction queues back up, connection pools exhaust, and your application goes down.

GitLab has pioneered some of the most rigorous, battle-tested patterns for zero-downtime database migrations in the open-source world.

In this guide, we will unpack GitLab’s database architecture rules and show you how to apply these enterprise patterns to your own production systems.

1. The PostgreSQL Locking Hierarchy: Understanding the Danger

Every schema alteration in PostgreSQL requests a lock. Understanding which locks conflict with standard reads (SELECT) and writes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) is essential:

Operation Lock Mode Acquired Blocks Concurrent Reads? Blocks Concurrent Writes?
SELECT AccessShareLock No No
UPDATE / DELETE RowExclusiveLock No No
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ShareUpdateExclusiveLock No No
ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN AccessExclusiveLock Yes Yes
CREATE INDEX (Standard) ShareLock No Yes

The Trap: Lock Queues

Even if an ALTER TABLE statement only takes 2 milliseconds to run, if it is forced to wait behind an active, long-running SELECT query, it waits in the lock queue.

While it waits, every single subsequent query behind it is blocked. Within 30 seconds, your entire application server runs out of database connections.

2. Rule 1: Always Use Low Lock Timeouts

In GitLab Core, migrations never wait indefinitely for locks. They configure strict lock timeouts and retry loops:

class AddStatusToDeployments < Gitlab::Database::Migration[2.2]
  # Limit waiting for the lock to 500ms
  SET_LOCK_TIMEOUT = 500

  def change
    # Set statement and lock timeouts for this transaction
    execute("SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '500ms';")
    execute("SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '5s';")

    add_column :deployments, :status, :smallint, default: 0, null: false
  end
end

If the migration cannot acquire the required lock within 500ms, it aborts cleanly, releasing the queue, and can be retried safely without taking down web traffic.

3. Rule 2: Never Create Indexes Synchronously

A standard CREATE INDEX locks the target table against writes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) for the entire duration of the index build. On a 100-million-row table, this can lock your database for 30 minutes!

The GitLab Pattern: add_concurrent_index

GitLab provides helper methods that disable DDL transactions and invoke PostgreSQL’s CONCURRENTLY engine:

class AddIndexToIssuesTitle < Gitlab::Database::Migration[2.2]
  disable_ddl_transaction! # Required for concurrent indexing

  def up
    add_concurrent_index :issues, :title, name: 'index_issues_on_title'
  end

  def down
    remove_concurrent_index_by_name :issues, 'index_issues_on_title'
  end
end

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds the index in the background using two table scans, allowing concurrent reads and writes to proceed uninhibited.

4. Rule 3: Safe Column Deletions (The 3-Phase Strategy)

Dropping a column directly from a live table (ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN phone;) instantly breaks existing application workers that are caching table columns in memory.

GitLab enforces a strict 3-phase deployment cycle across separate releases:

Release N (Phase 1):
  Ignore column phone in application models (ActiveRecord / ORM).
  New code no longer reads or writes the column.

Release N+1 (Phase 2):
  Mark column phone as ignored in DB schema.
  Remove column references from all background jobs.

Release N+2 (Phase 3):
  Safely execute: ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN phone;
  Zero application crashes.

In code, this is handled via ignore_column:

class User < ApplicationRecord
  # Inform the ORM to stop including this column in queries
  self.ignored_columns += %i[deprecated_token]
end

5. Rule 4: Batched Background Migrations (BBM)

What happens when you need to update 50,000,000 rows (e.g., populating a new UUID column)?

Running UPDATE users SET uuid = gen_random_uuid(); in a single transaction will blow up WAL logs, exhaust memory, and lock rows for hours.

GitLab solves this using Batched Background Migrations (BBM):

  1. Break the table down into discrete chunks (e.g., batches of 5,000 IDs).
  2. Execute the batch update asynchronously inside background worker jobs (Sidekiq).
  3. Throttle execution based on database replication lag: if replicas fall behind by more than 8 seconds, the background migration pauses automatically! 
class BackfillProjectTokens < Gitlab::Database::Migration[2.2]
  restrict_gitlab_migration gitlab_schema: :gitlab_main

  def up
    queue_batched_background_migration(
      job_class_name: 'BackfillProjectTokens',
      table_name: :projects,
      column_name: :id,
      job_arguments: [],
      batch_size: 5_000,
      sub_batch_size: 250,
      interval: 2.minutes
    )
  end
end

The migration runs smoothly over the course of several hours in the background while users experience 0.00ms of downtime or query slowdown.

6. Key Takeaways for High-Scale Applications

  1. Guard with Lock Timeouts: Never allow a migration to queue indefinitely; fail fast if locks conflict.
  2. Build Indexes Concurrently: Never run CREATE INDEX synchronously on live tables.
  3. Phase Destructive Operations: Delete columns and rename tables across at least two consecutive deployment cycles.
  4. Batch Data Updates: Throttle heavy data transformations against database replication lag.

Resources & Links

  • GitLab Database Documentation: docs.gitlab.com/ee/development/database/
  • GitLab Profile: gitlab.com/hrlpavan
  • GitLab Contributor Profile: contributors.gitlab.com/users/hrlpavan
  • GitHub: @hrlpavan

How does your team handle high-concurrency database migrations? Let’s talk database internals in the comments below!

title: StepSafe: Learning Timely Intervention with Context-Aware Safety Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.20960v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Safety in agentic systems is inherently sequential: whether an action is safe depends on prior actions, tool outputs, information disclosures, and interactions among agents. Recent work has shifted agent safety guardrails from post-hoc trajectory-level assessment toward step-level action diagnosis and proactive risk prediction, yet existing training objectives provide limited supervision for how step evidence accumulates over time and when it becomes sufficient to justify intervention. We propose \methodlong~(ASPO): a training framework for step-level timely intervention. Pre-fix level stage alignment allows crediting each decision at its own step: it compares each response with the other responses sampled at the same prefix and rewards the action that fits the stage, continuing before the risk is visible, asking while clarification can still avert harm, and stopping before harm is irreversible. Adaptive feedback self-distillation further credits the reasoning behind each decision, with the model itself as a teacher that sees the step annotations on intervention steps and rules mined from its own false alarms on safe steps. Its training data carry a violation taxonomy and an intervention window at every step and are extended through self-evolving multi-agent red-teaming. Finally we present \textsc{StepSafe}, a step-level reasoning guardrail with timely intervention, that achieves the state-of-the-art peformance among open-source guardrails across five agent-safety benchmarks on safety-utility pareto curve with Youden's $J$ of 53.0 (4B) against 46.2.

title: From Observation to Intervention: Distilling Self-Generated In-Context Demonstrations via Executable Causal Intervention
description:
arXiv:2610.21149v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-generated In-Context Learning (ICL) enables LLMs to synthesize their own few-shot demonstrations, often outperforming manual prompts. However, existing methods filter demonstrations by observation, assuming a rationale is high-quality if it leads to the correct output. We show such filtering suffers from \textit{observational equivalence}, whereby both faithful causal rationales and spurious post-hoc rationales can yield same outputs and are statistically indistinguishable from observation alone. Inspired by independent causal mechanisms, we argue that faithful rationales imply \textit{transfer invariance}, in which causal rationales should remain effective across logically similar samples. We instantiate this criterion as \textbf{E}xecutable \textbf{C}ausal \textbf{I}ntervention for \textbf{D}emonstrations \textbf{D}istillation (ECI2D), which abstracts language rationales into executable programs and applies the causal interventions ($do$-operator) on logically similar samples, retaining only those demonstrations that imply transfer invariance. Experiments on math, logical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ECI2D consistently outperforms observation-based ICL while retaining far fewer demonstrations, with gains exceeding 7 points as the test distribution shifts.

title: Orbia: Do Generated Videos Form a Consistent 3D World?
description:
arXiv:2610.20693v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video generators serve as interactive worlds for exploration and simulation, yet realistic and visually appealing frames do not necessarily depict a consistent 3D world. Existing benchmarks assess selected geometric properties or use vision-language models to judge memory and consistency, leaving systematic 3D evaluation underexplored. We introduce Orbia, the first benchmark dedicated to a systematic and comprehensive evaluation of 3D consistency in interactive world models. Through controlled exploration and revisit, we organize the evaluation into three dimensions: input preservation, generated-content persistence, and 3D self-consistency. For input preservation, registered RGB-D references and annotated anchors support appearance, geometry, and spatial stability measurements. For generated-content persistence, we compare revisits to regions absent from the input image with their first generated observations to test whether models preserve what they create. For 3D self-consistency, cross-view depth and feature correspondence, regional scale agreement, and held-out Gaussian rendering test whether generated views describe the same 3D scene. Minute-long exploration and revisits further test long-term consistency. Our construction and annotation pipeline brings together public datasets, self-captured scenes, and simulation, yielding 720 instances across indoor and outdoor environments and six exploration-and-revisit protocols. Evaluation spans 27 text-, action-, and camera-conditioned models through native-interface adapters. Our Orbia benchmark provides a systematic basis for diagnosing 3D inconsistency and developing more persistent video world models.

title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention
description:
arXiv:2610.20686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.

title: Spectral-Spatial Interpretation
description:
arXiv:2610.21114v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-hoc image explanations usually show where a model looks using spatial heatmaps or indicate which channels matter using global channel scores. These separate views are limiting for multispectral data because channel relevance is often spatially localized and physically meaningful. We introduce Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), a full-grid attribution method over position-channel players (g,c). For each spatial position, SSI fixes the observed surrounding context, defines a conditional game over the channels at that position, and applies the Shapley value to this local game. The result is a full spectral-spatial attribution matrix rather than a single heatmap or a global channel ranking. SSI has a clear local interpretation. It satisfies Shapley fairness within each position, and aggregating its channel attributions exactly recovers the position-level contextual contrast obtained by replacing that position with the baseline. SSI also differs from context-averaged Owen-style hierarchical accounting, which uses the same position-channel grouping but averages over external spatial coalitions. On HLS Burn Scar, SSI outperforms an MC-Owen estimator across retained attribution metrics while using only about 6% of its evaluation budget. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn Scar under both per-channel mean and zero baselines, SSI achieves the best joint deletion and insertion AUC over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines, yields the strongest spectral hit rates and channel deletion, and leads spatial localization on both annotated datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/AtheavenMa/Spectral-Spatial-Interpretation.

title: Vercel's AI Elements is being deprecated. Here are the alternatives for shadcn/ui AI chat UI
description:
If you built an AI chat with Vercel's AI Elements this year, the repository now carries a notice: the library will be deprecated at the end of November 2026, replaced by AI Elements from shadcn/ui.

This post covers what that means for your code, what the replacement is, and the other options if you are starting an AI chat UI with shadcn/ui in late 2026. I maintain one of those options, HextaUI, so I will say where it fits and where it does not.

First: your code keeps working

AI Elements was a shadcn-style registry. The components were copied into your project. There is no package to stop receiving updates, so nothing breaks on 1 December. The deprecation means no new components and no fixes from Vercel, and the docs will eventually point elsewhere.

You have time. Do not rush a migration this week.

What replaces it

In October 2026 shadcn/ui published its own AI Elements: 21 patterns for agentic interfaces built from shadcn/ui components. Chat, Prompt Input, Reasoning, Tool, Plan, Subagent and more. Each pattern page shows how to render it from AI SDK message parts. There is no package. You copy each pattern in.

They ship alongside two new components, Trace and Code Block, that work across Base UI, React Aria and Radix.

Migration from the Vercel library is meant to be low-friction. Export names and props are kept where the pattern was rebuilt, and each pattern page includes a migration prompt you can hand to an AI coding agent. Elements that were not rebuilt are not covered, so check the list against what you use.

The honest difference between pieces and screens

Every option below falls into one of two camps, and knowing which you want saves a week.

Pieces give you a Message, a Prompt Input, a Tool component. You design the screen and decide what happens when a reply fails, when a stream is stopped, when a tool needs approval, when an upload dies. Both versions of AI Elements, and prompt-kit, are pieces.

Screens give you the chat thread, composer, tool call list and settings pages with those decisions already made. You wire data in and restyle with your theme tokens. HextaUI's blocks and complete apps like Vercel's AI Chatbot template are screens.

Pieces are free and flexible. Screens are faster and opinionated. Neither is wrong.

Five options compared

1. AI Elements from shadcn/ui

Free, MIT, maintained by the shadcn team, built for Base UI, React Aria and Radix. Pieces, not screens. The natural default if you want to compose your own and stay on the most-used registry. New as of October 2026, so expect the pattern list to grow and the rough edges to be sanded over the next few months.

2. prompt-kit

Free, MIT, installs with the shadcn CLI. Prompt Input, Message, Reasoning, Chain of Thought, Tool, File Upload and example blocks including a chat app with a history sidebar. Pieces, with good examples. Built on Radix, so a Base UI project carries both primitive layers while you use it.

3. assistant-ui

Free, MIT, with an optional paid cloud for saved threads. This one is different in kind: it is a chat framework with its own runtime that manages the conversation, plus headless primitives and styled components that read from it. Adapters for the AI SDK, LangGraph, LangChain, AG-UI and others. Pick it if you want the runtime to own the chat state. Skip it if your state already lives in useChat or your own store and you do not want anything wrapping your app.

4. shadcn-chatbot-kit and the AI Chatbot template

Blazity's shadcn-chatbot-kit is a smaller set of chatbot components. Vercel's AI Chatbot is a complete Next.js app with sign-in and a database, which is the canonical reference if you want to see every piece wired. Both are useful to read even if you do not adopt them.

5. HextaUI blocks

Screens. A Chat Thread where failed replies offer Try again, stopped replies say so, and edits and retries become versions you can switch between. Tool Calls with every AI SDK tool state including approvals with a "do this instead" reason. Streaming and Markdown that never show half-typed syntax. A Prompt Input that is safe with Japanese and Chinese input, shows upload progress and retry, queues messages typed during a reply and keeps drafts across reloads. Plus the screens around a chat product: settings, models, API keys, billing, team, security.

The components underneath are free and MIT. The AI blocks are HextaUI Pro, a one-time payment with every later block included, and Prompt Input is free. Built on Base UI, reads AI SDK message parts without importing the SDK. Not for you if you want everything free, or if you want Radix.

At a glance

Camp Price Primitives AI SDK
AI Elements (shadcn/ui) Pieces Free Base UI, React Aria, Radix Used in examples
AI Elements (Vercel) Pieces Free Radix Required by setup
prompt-kit Pieces Free Radix Optional
assistant-ui Runtime Free, paid cloud Own Adapter
HextaUI Screens Components free, blocks paid once Base UI Optional, same parts shape

How to decide

  • You are starting fresh and want to compose your own: AI Elements from shadcn/ui.
  • You already have Vercel's AI Elements in your tree: keep it until you need something new, then move pattern by pattern using the migration prompts.
  • You want a runtime to manage threads, branching and persistence for you: assistant-ui.
  • You want the chat and the product screens around it done, with the failure states handled, and you are fine paying once: HextaUI.

All of these copy source into your project and use the shadcn/ui theme tokens, so you can mix them one screen at a time. The one caution is primitives: mixing a Radix-based kit into a Base UI project works, but you ship both.

I keep a more detailed comparison with the full piece-by-piece mapping at hextaui.com/compare/ai-elements, and a seven-way look at shadcn AI chat templates.

FAQ

When exactly is Vercel's AI Elements deprecated? The repository says the end of November 2026.

Will my existing AI Elements components break? No. They live in your repository. They stop receiving updates.

Is the new AI Elements a package? No. It is a set of patterns you copy in with the shadcn CLI, the same model as shadcn/ui itself.

Can I use HextaUI blocks without the Vercel AI SDK? Yes. They take messages as props in the AI SDK's parts shape, and do not import the SDK.

title: A million-tap linear-phase FIR in real time: 7 ms of plumbing, 650 ms of filter
description:
I'm building Sonir Bench, a macOS app that captures everything your Mac plays, runs it through a DSP chain you design, and sends it to your DAC. The first post in this series was the overview. This one goes deep on a single piece: long FIR convolution.

Here's the result up front. On an M6 Mac mini, I ran a 998,545-tap linear-phase FIR at 768 kHz in f64 for almost eight hours. Zero dropouts: no underruns, no overruns, no missed deadlines.

The round-trip latency was 657.43 ms. But 650.09 ms of that is the filter's own group delay. The machinery that moves the audio adds only 7.33 ms. It took me a few wrong turns to learn to keep those two numbers apart.

Direct convolution buys you about 1 ms

Bench upsamples everything to 705.6 kHz (the 44.1 kHz family) or 768 kHz (the 48 kHz family) before processing. The upsampling filter itself is user-designed: you pick the transition band and tap count.

The first thing I measured was direct convolution, one multiply-add per tap per sample. At 705.6 kHz stereo, one core tops out at 757 taps. That's about 1 ms of impulse response. Not enough for a steep resampling filter, let alone room correction.

So the convolver is a uniformly partitioned FFT convolution (overlap-save):

Split the IR into K partitions of length B → FFT each to 2B points, keep them

Every B samples:
  FFT the latest 2B input samples → push onto the frequency-domain delay line (FDL)
  Σ_k FDL[p−k] · IR_k → inverse FFT → the second half (B samples) is valid output

Here's one hop for one channel, lightly trimmed (error handling removed, comments translated):

// 1. FFT the latest 2B samples (forward FFT clobbers its input, so copy first)
for (dst, src) in self.time.iter_mut().zip(history) {
    *dst = T::from_bus(*src);
}
self.fft.process_with_scratch(&mut self.time, &mut self.spectrum, &mut self.fft_scratch)?;

// 2. Store it in the FDL
let slot = (ch * partitions + fdl_pos) * bins;
self.fdl[slot..slot + bins].copy_from_slice(&self.spectrum);

// 3. Σ_k FDL[pos−k] · IR_k
self.acc.fill(Self::zero());
for k in 0..partitions {
    let idx = (fdl_pos + partitions - k) % partitions;
    let x = (ch * partitions + idx) * bins;
    let h = k * bins;
    T::mul_add_mono(&mut self.acc, &self.fdl[x..x + bins], &self.ir_spectra[h..h + bins]);
}

// 4. Inverse FFT
self.spectrum.copy_from_slice(&self.acc);
self.ifft.process_with_scratch(&mut self.spectrum, &mut self.time, &mut self.ifft_scratch)?;

// 5. Overlap-save: only the second B samples are valid. realfft doesn't normalize, hence 1/2B
let norm = 1.0 / (2 * b) as f64;
for (dst, src) in out.iter_mut().zip(&self.time[b..]) {
    *dst = src.to_bus() * norm;
}

The FFT is realfft. The FFTs aren't where the time goes, though. Step 3 is: K complex multiply-accumulates over B + 1 bins, every hop. mul_add_mono is hand-written NEON, and in stereo the IR spectrum is loaded once and applied to both channels. For a million taps the IR spectrum is about 17 MB of f64 complex numbers, and every hop reads all of it, so halving the reads is a direct speedup.

Per-sample cost is roughly 12·N/B for N taps: linear in taps, divided by the partition length. Measured on an Apple M1, 705.6 kHz stereo, as a share of one core:

taps \ B 1,024 4,096 16,384 65,536
65,537 21.6% 7.6% 3.7% 2.4%
300,001 38.2% 10.9% 4.3% 2.7%
1,048,576 154.5% 33.9% 9.5% 4.0%

The same million taps doesn't fit in a core at B = 1,024 and costs 4% at B = 65,536. B matters more than the tap count.

Partitioning without adding latency

Textbooks say a partitioned convolver has a latency of B. That assumes the host's block size is smaller than B. Plugin hosts typically use 64 to 512 samples, so if you pick a large B for efficiency, you have to buffer input until you have B samples, and that buffering is the latency.

If the host's block size is a multiple of B, there's nothing to buffer. You convolve the block you were handed and return a block of the same length.

Bench's internal block length is the entry block length times the interpolation ratio. Take 256 frames at 48 kHz, upsample 16×, and you get 4,096 frames at 768 kHz. So B is set to the internal block length itself, and the convolver adds zero latency.

B is the largest power of two that divides the block length:

pub fn partition_for(block: usize) -> Option<usize> {
    if block == 0 {
        return None;
    }
    // Largest power of two dividing the block (= its lowest set bit).
    // If the block is a power of two, that's the block itself
    let b = block & block.wrapping_neg();
    (b >= MIN_PARTITION).then_some(b)
}

block & block.wrapping_neg() keeps only the lowest set bit in two's complement: 4,096 gives 4,096, and 6,144 gives 2,048.

A test pins this down. It builds the chain with a unit-impulse IR and checks the path latency is identical to an empty chain:

#[test]
fn a_default_partition_convolver_adds_no_latency_to_the_chain() {
    let empty = Chain::build(&spec_48(256), Vec::new(), config()).unwrap();
    let baseline = empty.report().latency_base_frames;

    // Unit impulse = pass-through IR. We only care about delay
    let mut ir = vec![0.0; DEFAULT_PARTITION * 128];
    ir[0] = 1.0;
    let conv = FirConvolver::new(ir, DEFAULT_PARTITION).unwrap();
    let chain = Chain::build(&spec_48(256), vec![Box::new(conv)], config()).unwrap();

    assert_eq!(chain.report().node_report.latency_frames(), 0);
    assert_eq!(
        chain.report().latency_base_frames,
        baseline,
        "adding the convolver increased path latency"
    );
}

Reporting zero latency and actually having zero latency are different claims, so a second test pushes a sine through the same chain and checks the output lines up with the input at the reported delay.

The latency hasn't vanished, though. A bigger B means a bigger entry block, and the round trip grows with it. B is an exchange rate between latency and CPU, and Bench lets you pick it in the UI (4,096 to 65,536).

Failure 1: 1.37 seconds of wrong output after every swap

Bench can swap the processing chain while audio is playing. You build two chains, A and B, and switch between them with a 5 to 10 ms crossfade to compare by ear.

The first version started each new convolver from empty. A partitioned convolver keeps the spectra of the last K input blocks in its FDL, so starting empty means wrong output until the FDL fills. With a long IR that took up to 1.37 seconds. No 10 ms crossfade hides that.

The fix came from noticing that the FDL holds spectra of the input. It doesn't depend on the IR at all. Hand the old convolver's FDL to the new one and the new one is correct from its first block. That's transfer_history:

pub fn transfer_history(&mut self, previous: &Self) -> bool {
    if self.partition != previous.partition
        || self.channels != previous.channels
        || self.bins != previous.bins
        || self.precision != previous.precision
        // ...
    {
        return false;
    }
    // Input-side state carries over as is
    self.history.copy_from_slice(&previous.history);
    self.stage.copy_from_slice(&previous.stage);
    self.fill = previous.fill;

    // Re-pack the FDL newest-first. K may differ, so positions are remapped
    // (a precision mismatch means a different FDL type; the guard above already bailed)
    let geo = self.geometry();
    let (channels, previous_partitions, previous_pos) =
        (self.channels, previous.partitions, previous.fdl_pos);
    let (Some(next), Some(old)) = (self.freq.as_mut(), previous.freq.as_ref()) else {
        return false;
    };
    match (next, old) {
        (FreqDomain::F64(next), FreqDomain::F64(old)) => {
            next.transfer_fdl(old, geo, channels, previous_partitions, previous_pos);
        }
        (FreqDomain::F32(next), FreqDomain::F32(old)) => {
            next.transfer_fdl(old, geo, channels, previous_partitions, previous_pos);
        }
        _ => return false,
    }

    // Don't carry the output side over. The old graph keeps emitting the same
    // blocks during the crossfade, so its pending output would play twice
    self.pending.fill(0.0);
    // ...
}

A new tap count means a new K, but re-packing newest-first handles that. If K grows, the oldest slots stay zero and only the tail of the new IR is missing for a few hops. That's orders of magnitude better than starting from nothing, so I accept it.

The output side is the other trap. During the crossfade the old chain is still producing the same blocks, so carrying its pending output over would play that audio twice. Only the input side transfers.

The transfer only works when B, the channel count and the precision all match. That implies a rule: never derive B, or the choice of implementation, from anything a swap can change, such as the tap count. I went on to break that rule twice.

One more thing: a longer crossfade isn't safer. Both chains run for its whole duration, which doubles the CPU load, and a longer fade means a longer stretch at double load. The crossfade is clamped to 5 to 10 ms.

Failure 2: 300k taps and a stuttering mess

One day a 300k-tap resampling filter turned the output into a string of clicks. Design-time validation had said the filter was fine.

The resampling stage turned out not to use the partitioned FFT convolver at all. It ran a direct polyphase filter. Polyphase saves you a factor of the interpolation ratio, 1/16 at 16×, and I'd assumed that made it cheap. Wrong comparison. Polyphase is still O(N) per sample against O(N/B) for the FFT path, and a constant factor of 1/16 can't beat a different complexity class. At 300k taps, stereo, 44.1 kHz in, it needed about 35 cores' worth of time, so it missed every single block.

The fix was one convolution engine. The FIR node in the graph and the resampling stages now share the same partitioned convolver.

My first version switched implementations by tap count: direct below a threshold, FFT above. A test then showed that a swap crossing the threshold changed the implementation, so transfer_history refused and the audio dropped out, all because you nudged a design parameter. Since FFT was cheaper even at the default 1,345 taps, I deleted the switch.

Failure 3: the limit wasn't the CPU

The next investigation started from this: "On an M1 Air, 300k taps looks like the real-time ceiling. The compute estimate is two orders of magnitude below what the machine can do. Is something other than raw compute the bottleneck?"

I went through thermal throttling, being scheduled on an E-core, allocation on the real-time thread, and memory bandwidth. None of them. The machine never got hot because the whole pipeline used one core out of eight.

The cause was one line:

// How B was chosen (at the time)
DEFAULT_PARTITION.min(block)

However long the internal block, B never went above 4,096. That cap came from a 20 ms round-trip latency budget, and the reason for that budget had already gone away (next section). When the premise died, nobody went back to revisit what had been built on it.

I made B follow the internal block length and removed the cap. That opened the hole next to it. If B is longer than the block, the convolver can't complete a hop and fills the output with silence, without any error. Nothing in the path looks wrong, and silence plays. B is now derived from the block length the device actually delivers, and blocks that couldn't be filled are counted and shown in the UI.

To count them, process now returns the number of frames it actually wrote:

/// Returns the number of frames that received convolution output. The rest is filled with silence.
pub fn process(&mut self, input: &[f64], output: &mut [f64]) -> usize {
    // ...
    // 1. Accumulate input; run one hop every time B samples are buffered
    let mut done = 0usize;
    while done < frames {
        let take = (b - self.fill).min(frames - done);
        // ... (copy into stage)
        self.fill += take;
        done += take;
        if self.fill == b {
            self.hop();
            self.fill = 0;
        }
    }

    // 2. Emit output. Silence if there isn't enough
    let emit = frames.min(self.available);
    // ... (copy from pending to output, zero-fill the rest)
    self.available -= emit;
    emit
}

When the block length equals B, each call runs exactly one hop and returns what it was given. That's the whole zero-latency trick from earlier. When B is longer than the block, calls before B samples have accumulated run no hop and emit is 0. The output buffer still has the right length, so nobody notices unless they check the return value.

The latency was the filter

This is the part I most wanted to write about.

Bench's round-trip latency target is 20 ms. Browser video and games go through it too, so lip sync puts the ceiling around there. Originally, designs that exceeded it couldn't be saved.

But a linear-phase FIR with N taps always has a group delay of (N−1)/2 samples. At 300k taps that's 212 ms of group delay alone, ten times the budget. Making the convolver add zero latency didn't matter when the filter itself carried an order of magnitude more.

The UI makes it obvious. Here's an upsampler designed at 500k taps, built for 48 kHz input. The latency panel (labels translated):

Segment ms
Input 5.33
IPC 1.00
Upsampler 354.60
Node chain 0.00
Decimator 0.00
DAC 1.00
Total 361.94

At 768 kHz the same transition band needs 8.8% more taps than at 705.6 kHz, so the upsampler was built with 544,673 taps. Its 354.60 ms is (544,673 − 1) / 2 = 272,336 samples at 768 kHz. Everything else (input 5.33, IPC 1.00, DAC 1.00) adds up to 7.33 ms. The DAC was fed 768 kHz directly, so there's no decimator and it shows 0.00 ms.

The odd tap count is deliberate. 272,336 is exactly 17,021 × 16, a multiple of the interpolation ratio. Otherwise the delay would be a fractional number of samples at the input rate, and the latency couldn't be reported as whole frames. For linear phase, the tap count gets bumped up slightly to make it line up:

/// Align a linear-phase tap count to the conversion ratio: grow it until the group
/// delay `(N−1)/2` is a whole number of frames at the lower rate
fn align_taps(requested: usize, phase: FirPhase, factor: usize) -> Option<(usize, u32)> {
    match phase {
        FirPhase::Linear => {
            let aligned = ((requested - 1) / 2).div_ceil(factor) * factor;
            let taps = aligned * 2 + 1;
            (taps <= MAX_TAPS).then(|| (taps, u32::try_from(aligned).unwrap_or(u32::MAX)))
        }
        FirPhase::Minimum => Some((requested, 0)),
    }
}

The extra taps aren't zero padding. They go inside the window and the filter is redesigned with them, because if you're paying the CPU anyway, it should buy filter performance. Minimum-phase filters don't have a (N−1)/2 group delay, so there's nothing to align.

Now roughly double the taps: 96 kHz input, a 998,545-tap upsampler, and an 18-node chain behind it. The upsampler alone is 650.09 ms (499,272 samples), for a total of 657.43 ms. Input, IPC and DAC are still 7.33 ms. At 96 kHz the interpolation ratio is 8×, so the entry block is 512 frames, which is still 5.33 ms. The 18 nodes add 0.00 ms.

Double the taps and the filter's delay roughly doubles. The plumbing stays where it was.

Stop refusing latency

Linear-phase group delay is a pure delay, constant across the band. It doesn't change the sound by a single bit. What it costs you is lip sync, and transport response (when you pause or skip, the delay's worth of audio is still in the pipe). Both are costs the user is entitled to decide to pay.

So Bench no longer refuses designs over the latency budget. It shows the current round-trip latency at all times instead. The bar isn't clipped at 20 ms; it extends to the actual value and keeps a line at the 20 ms mark. The condition is that nobody uses it without knowing, and the decision only stands as long as that display does.

CPU got the same treatment. For a while there was a gate that refused designs predicted to overload the CPU. But the prediction moves by 1.75× with thermal state alone, so passing the gate never guaranteed real-time performance. A gate that says yes reads as "this will be fine," which is exactly the wrong message. The gate became a forecast: the expected load at design time, then the measured load and dropout counts once it's playing.

Two CPU numbers

The status bar shows two numbers: "CPU load 46% (peak 77%)" and "CPU 46%".

There used to be one: callback wall-clock time divided by the block deadline. Then I noticed that changing the entry block from 256 to 512 frames, same design, made it jump from 7.0% to 22.2%. Still zero dropouts, and the forecast barely moved. The jump was a step, not a slope, so my theory was that longer callbacks were spanning scheduler quanta and the measurement was counting time spent preempted.

To test that, I measured the thread's own CPU time separately. Rust's standard library has no API for thread CPU time, so this is one line of unsafe:

/// CPU time consumed so far by the calling thread.
pub fn thread_cpu_time() -> Option<Duration> {
    let mut ts = libc::timespec { tv_sec: 0, tv_nsec: 0 };
    // SAFETY: `ts` is a valid `timespec` and `clock_gettime` only writes to it.
    let ok = unsafe { libc::clock_gettime(libc::CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID, &raw mut ts) } == 0;
    // ...
}

A call costs about 154 ns, twice per block. Against the 5.8 ms deadline of 256 frames at 44.1 kHz that's 0.005%, so measuring doesn't disturb what's being measured.

The result: wall clock and CPU time agreed to within 0.1 percentage points at every B. The jump wasn't preemption. The work really had grown, and my explanation was the thing that was wrong. I still haven't tracked down why the forecast misses it.

Splitting them was still worth it. I can only say the two agree because I measured them separately. With one number I'd never have gotten past "probably preemption." Both are shown now:

  • CPU load (wall clock ÷ deadline): are we making the deadline? Includes time spent waiting. At 100%, audio drops out.
  • CPU (thread CPU time ÷ deadline): pure compute. Used to check the forecast.

Over the eight-hour run, peak load was 77%, so even the worst block left about 20% headroom.

One caveat: this run had a single resampling stage. Output stayed at 768 kHz, so there was no stage bringing the rate back down. With a DAC that tops out at 192 kHz, a second filter runs on the way out, and you pay its CPU too.

These numbers are for f64 convolution. Bench also has a mode that runs only the frequency-domain part in f32, which is about 2× faster for the same design with error around −141 dBFS. You can't switch it while playing, though: the FDL type changes, so transfer_history can't carry state across.

Takeaways

  • Direct convolution at 705.6 kHz stereo caps out at 757 taps per core. Partitioned FFT convolution gets a million taps into real time.
  • If the internal block length equals the partition length B, the convolver adds zero samples of latency. The price is that a bigger B means a bigger entry block.
  • Never derive B or the implementation from anything a swap can change, like tap count. The FDL can't transfer, and a small design tweak becomes a dropout.
  • Almost all of the round-trip delay is the filter's group delay, not the plumbing: 650 ms for a million-tap linear-phase filter versus 7 ms to move the audio.
  • Neither latency nor CPU load is refused anymore. Both are shown: latency as the sum of each segment's reported value, CPU as a measurement.

Not done yet

  • The latency figures are the sum of what each segment reports. The group delay is exact by construction, but nothing here was measured with a loopback recording. The 1.00 ms IPC figure is an estimate, and since no audio actually crosses a process boundary, it's a segment with nothing behind it.
  • Convolution runs on one core. This stage is limited by memory traffic more than arithmetic, so more cores wouldn't scale linearly. I did the f32 frequency domain first (2.05×) and left parallelism for later.
  • Low latency and very long filters together would need non-uniform partitioning. Not implemented.

Try it

Sonir Bench is free during the beta. It runs on Apple Silicon Macs with macOS 13 or later.

title: A Jury, Not an Electorate: Label-Free Reliability Estimation for Ensembles of Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21085v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An ensemble of language models is a jury, not an electorate. The answers are testimony from witnesses of unknown reliability, and the question is not what the majority said but who is credible. Most ensemble methods assign each expert a fixed reputation, often learned from labels. We ask whether it can instead be inferred from the pattern of agreement and disagreement among the experts. We model the experts as a jury: each question has a latent true answer, each expert reports it with unknown reliability, and those reliabilities are estimated by Expectation Maximisation (EM) from unlabelled answer configurations alone. We show that its decision rule reduces to a log-odds weighted linear score over the experts' answer distributions. What changes is not how the jury votes, but how it learns whom to trust. On a 1560-question benchmark, the jury, with nine experts of up to 3B parameters, performs comparably to the same fusion rule with label-fitted weights, showing no statistically significant advantage from supervision. Instead, it outperforms the best single model with matched self-consistency and the strongest label-free alternative on the full benchmark.

title: Our Hysteria2 connections died after every upload speed test. The fix was 37 lines.
description:
We build Colitu, a VPN with open-source apps for Android, iOS, Windows, Linux and a browser extension. The apps carry traffic over several transports. Hysteria2 is a QUIC-based one that our apps prefer on many networks, because it holds up well on lossy mobile links.

The apps also check their own connection. Every 5 seconds they send a small request through the tunnel. If three checks in a row get no answer within 4 seconds, the transport is declared dead, and traffic moves to a TCP spare that is already connected. Users stay online. But a transport that keeps getting declared dead is a bug, even if nobody notices.

How we noticed

We were testing port hopping for Hysteria2 on an Android phone on home Wi-Fi. With port hopping, the client moves to a new UDP port every ~30 seconds, so networks that slow down long-running UDP flows have a harder time doing it.

Hopping itself worked. We saw five hops, and the server's replies arrived on every new port.

Then we ran a speed test. Hysteria2 carried traffic for about 50–60 seconds and then stopped for good. The health check gave up and traffic went to the spare. It happened every time.

We repeated the test on a server without port hopping and got the same result. So hopping was not the cause; it was just the test that showed the bug.

What the packets said

We captured traffic on the phone. After the stall:

  • the QUIC connection was alive: ACKs and small control packets went both ways;
  • UDP datagrams still flowed: DNS and the apps' own QUIC traffic, which Hysteria carries as datagrams;
  • the client sent no new TCP stream data at all, not even for brand-new requests;
  • the server logged nothing unusual.

A connection that is alive but will not send stream data points at flow control, not at the network.

What we ruled out first

We tested each of these instead of assuming:

Suspect How we tested it Result
ISP shaping UDP read the capture packets kept flowing both ways; the client stopped sending
Probe starvation under load watched after the load ended the stall lasted for minutes after the load was gone
Congestion control A/B build with Reno instead of BBR died the same way
Xray's "Chrome parrot" QUIC mode A/B build with it disabled died the same way
Stream limit counted streams ~90 open against a limit of 1,024
Many connections in general 1,400 short sequential connections all fine

One more thing we tried: a bigger flow-control window (64 MB per connection, 4 MB per stream). It did not fix anything. It only delayed the stall: with 6 parallel streams it failed in round 3, with 20 streams immediately. That was the strongest hint about where to look.

Reproducing it on one PC

To get rid of the network entirely, we built the official Hysteria server v2.11.0 from source and ran it on loopback with an Xray 26.10.10 client. A small Python harness opened parallel uploads through the client, aborted them with a TCP reset, and then checked whether new requests still worked.

The only thing we changed between runs was how the upload's destination behaved:

Target mode What the destination does Connection stalled?
fast reads everything no
slow reads 1 MB/s no
upclose closes the connection first no
stall stops reading but keeps the connection open yes: 0 of 5 new requests worked, no recovery in 30 s

An upload speed test behaves exactly like stall. The test server stops reading once it has measured enough, while the browser's upload request is still open.

The mechanism

QUIC limits how much unread data a peer may have in flight, per stream and for the whole connection. Hysteria's defaults are 8 MB per stream and 20 MB per connection. Received bytes count against both windows until the application actually reads them.

Here is what happens:

client (Xray)                 Hysteria server                 target
     |  upload on stream A  ->  |  io.Copy(target, stream A) -> |
     |                          |                               |  stops reading,
     |                          |  target's TCP buffer full     |  keeps conn open
     |                          |  write to target BLOCKS       |
     |                          |  -> server stops reading A    |
     |  A's unread bytes keep counting against the connection window
     |  (a few streams like A fill all 20 MB)
     |
     |  new request on stream B: blocked, no connection credit left
     |  writer for A: blocked on the same window, so the client
     |  never gets to cancel A either
     |
     |  UDP datagrams: not flow-controlled -> still flowing
  1. The client uploads through a Hysteria2 stream. The server dials the target over TCP and copies the stream into it.
  2. The target stops reading but does not close. Its receive buffer fills, the server's Write into the target blocks, and the server stops reading from the stream.
  3. The stream's unread upload data keeps occupying the connection-level receive window. A few such streams use up the whole window. From then on the client cannot send on any stream of the connection, including brand-new ones.
  4. The client never gives the stream up, because its own writer is blocked on the same window. On an instrumented server, the "stream given up" signal only arrived when we killed the client process.
  5. UDP datagrams are not covered by stream flow control, which is why DNS kept working and the connection looked healthy.

Interesting detail: we first suspected the server never calls CancelRead on dead streams. That was wrong. The stream's Close already does that. The real problem is that nothing ever reaches that Close, because the copy into the target is stuck in a blocking Write.

The fix

The server cannot tell a stalled target from a slow one by looking at the stream. It can tell by progress: a single write that makes no progress for a long time.

So the patch does two things:

  1. Every write into a TCP target gets a fresh 10-second budget. If one write makes no progress for 10 s, the target is closed. The normal cleanup then closes the stream, which releases its share of the connection window.
  2. When the client gives the stream up, the target is closed immediately, so both copy directions end even when the target is silent.

A slow target that keeps moving is never cut off, because every write starts a new timer. Only a target that has stopped accepting data is closed.

This is the version we sent upstream in PR #1703:

if h.config.TCPStallTimeout > 0 {
    guard := newStallGuardConn(tConn, h.config.TCPStallTimeout)
    tConn = guard
    stop := context.AfterFunc(stream.Context(), func() { _ = guard.Close() })
    defer stop()
}

// stallGuardConn closes the wrapped connection when a single Write makes no
// progress for timeout, and makes Close idempotent. Every Write gets a fresh
// timeout, so a slow target that keeps accepting data is never closed.
type stallGuardConn struct {
    net.Conn
    timeout   time.Duration
    timer     *time.Timer
    closeOnce sync.Once
    closeErr  error
}

func newStallGuardConn(conn net.Conn, timeout time.Duration) *stallGuardConn {
    c := &stallGuardConn{Conn: conn, timeout: timeout}
    c.timer = time.AfterFunc(timeout, func() { _ = c.Close() })
    c.timer.Stop()
    return c
}

func (c *stallGuardConn) Write(p []byte) (int, error) {
    c.timer.Reset(c.timeout)
    n, err := c.Conn.Write(p)
    c.timer.Stop()
    return n, err
}

func (c *stallGuardConn) Close() error {
    c.closeOnce.Do(func() { c.closeErr = c.Conn.Close() })
    return c.closeErr
}

Our production build (v2.11.0-colitu1) does the same thing with SetWriteDeadline before each write. For the upstream version we made three changes:

  • the check closes the connection from a timer, so it only needs Close and works with any net.Conn an outbound returns;
  • the timeout is configurable as server.Config.TCPStallTimeout (default 10 s, negative disables it);
  • Close is idempotent, because two paths can now close the target.

The PR also adds an integration test. Four streams upload into targets that never read (one end of a net.Pipe()), then a new request to an echo server must complete on the same connection. Without the fix it times out after 10 s. With it, it passes in about 3.5 s, with the stall timeout set to 2 s for the test.

One gotcha while writing that test: with one stalled stream it passed even without the fix. One stream can only fill its own 8 MB window, not the 20 MB connection window. It takes three or four.

Results

In the loopback lab:

Server Target Streams New requests work again after
official v2.11.0 stall 6 never (> 30 s)
patched stall 6 7.8 s
patched stall 20 7.8 s
patched fast / slow / upclose — 0.0 s (no regression)

On the phone, we ran four speed tests in a row over 160 seconds on a patched server in Berlin. Hysteria2 was never declared dead. Before the patch it died at ~60 s every time, both in Berlin and on a server in Vilnius.

Rollout without an app update

Because the bug was on the server, the fix did not need a new app release. Our node image now builds Hysteria from the official source tag with the patch applied. We rolled it out the same night, one server at a time. Each server's VPN service restarted for about 2 seconds. Android, iOS, Windows and Linux users all got the fix at once.

Upstream

The bug is in the open-source Hysteria server, and its client-side half is in Xray, so every service that runs them is affected, not only ours. We reported both:

  • HyNetworks/hysteria#1702: the bug, how to reproduce it, and everything we ruled out.
  • HyNetworks/hysteria#1703: the fix on the current development branch, with the configurable timeout and the integration test.
  • XTLS/Xray-core#7169: the client side. A client that cancels the write side of a stream it no longer needs (CancelWrite, i.e. RESET_STREAM) would release the window even on servers without the fix. A contributor has since traced it on Xray's main branch, reproduced the stall on loopback, and plans a CancelWrite-based fix.

Limitations

  • The lab runs on loopback: no packet loss, no added latency. It shows the mechanism and the effect of the patch, not real-world timings.
  • The device result is one phone on one network, four speed tests over 160 seconds. Encouraging, not a long-term measurement.
  • For up to 10 seconds before the timer fires, TCP over that connection can still pause. The patch makes the stall short; it does not make it zero. A client-side fix would complement it.

Takeaways

  • "Connected but silent" usually means flow control. If ACKs and datagrams flow but stream data doesn't, look at windows before you blame the network.
  • A bigger window that only delays a failure is a clue, not a fix.
  • Make the destination's behaviour a test variable. Four target modes (fast, slow, upclose, stall) narrowed this down faster than any amount of packet reading.
  • Write the test that fails first. Ours passed until we used enough streams to exhaust the connection window, which taught us something about the bug itself.

If you run Hysteria2 and your users see TCP die after big uploads while DNS keeps working, this is probably it. The PR is small and easy to apply to v2.11.0.

Full report with setup details: lab.colitu.com/research/hysteria2-stall-after-upload. Our apps are open source at github.com/colitu. Questions and corrections are welcome in the comments.

title: Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards
description:
arXiv:2610.20814v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often trains language models on responses generated by a different, possibly stale behavior policy. Correcting this mismatch with learner-to-behavior importance weights can introduce high variance for long responses. We introduce Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization (GGPO), which minimizes a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards among responses to the same prompt, without learner-to-behavior importance weights. We derive GGPO from KL-regularized policy optimization: on policy, its population loss is exactly the KL-regularized optimality gap, and under suitable coverage the learner's single-response expected reward is at least the behavior policy's best-of-$K$ reward, minus terms for the raw finite-group loss, regularization, and finite training data. We characterize reference refresh through exact Gibbs-target composition and a finite-data final-policy reward bound under local reference control and tokenwise behavior mismatch. This refresh is empirically important: in an ablation, fixed-reference GGPO scores $32.96$ on the five-benchmark problem-weighted average, versus $46.58$ with the default refresh schedule. Experiments on mathematical reasoning further show that GGPO outperforms GRPO and AGRO under training-inference mismatch and on fixed offline data, while maintaining its performance as controlled policy staleness grows.
