title: CertEx: Exact Visual Retrieval at Scale by Certified Exclusion
description:
arXiv:2610.21325v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Exact $k$-nearest-neighbor (kNN) search over image descriptors and embeddings underlies visual retrieval, near-duplicate detection, the evaluation of learned representations, and increasingly the memory of LLM agents. However, exhaustive search computes every distance at full precision, whereas approximate indexes return recall below one. We observe that exact search only needs a proof that each excluded vector cannot be a neighbor. Because such a proof only has to be conservative, it can be checked in low precision, much as the retina examines the whole scene at low resolution. We call this principle certified exclusion and realize it in an exact kNN method for GPUs, which we call \certex. Specifically, \certex\ stores a lower-bounding projection of each vector in half precision and folds a rounding certificate into the same tensor-core dot product, so that only the few vectors that the test keeps need exact distances. We prove that \certex\ returns the exact kNN of every query. On sixteen datasets with up to 100M vectors, \certex\ is exact for every query at 7.1$\times$ to 18.0$\times$ the throughput of the fastest cuVS search on one H100 and outperforms quantized and graph indexes whenever every query must be exact.

title: AdaLoop: Thinking with the Vision Encoder
description:
arXiv:2610.21323v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most vision-language models (VLMs) treat the vision encoder as a static feature extractor: it encodes an image once, independently of the question, and leaves subsequent reasoning to the language model. Yet different questions may require different visual operations and processing depths. We present AdaLoop, a framework for question-conditioned visual recurrence in VLMs. AdaLoop adapts visual computation to the question and reuses the encoder's transformations across multiple iterations, with the pretrained vision weights frozen. We also introduce VisRO, a procedural dataset and generation pipeline for training and evaluating vision-centric reasoning. On six VisRO tasks, AdaLoop outperforms standard fine-tuning and question-conditioned single-pass baselines with matched training data and optimizer updates. These gains hold across three VLM families on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution examples. Our findings suggest that pretrained vision encoders can contribute to reasoning through task-directed, iterative visual computation.

title: SIEVE: Overcoming Topological Obstruction in Equivariant Self-Supervised Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.21087v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We identify a theoretical incompatibility between 3D point cloud masked autoencoding and SE(3)-equivariant networks. We prove that standard masking triggers a topological collapse, effectively forcing the model to hallucinate orientation without a reference frame. To resolve this, we introduce SIEVE (Scalar Invariant Extraction Via Equivariance), an SE(3)-equivariant self-supervised framework that compresses point cloud geometry into invariant scalar embeddings. At its core is the spherical projection mask, which preserves global pose while obfuscating local semantics, sidestepping the obstruction by construction. Experiments confirm that SIEVE circumvents the predicted collapse where constant and noise masks fail. On downstream point cloud tasks, the resulting embeddings improve over coordinate-based baselines and hand-crafted geometric descriptors, with the largest gains on generalization to unseen shape categories.

title: N-CODE AI Studio: Turning Website Audits into a Side Hustle with Open-Weight AI
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle.

What I Built

I built N-CODE AI Studio, an open-source AI-powered website auditing platform designed to help freelancers, small businesses, and web development agencies understand website performance and identify opportunities for improvement.

Many small business owners struggle to understand technical reports or know which website problems to fix first.

N-CODE AI Studio aims to turn technical website measurements into clear, actionable recommendations using open-weight AI.

The side hustle idea: Freelancers can use this tool to prepare website health assessments and offer professional performance optimization, accessibility improvements, SEO consulting, and website redesign services.

The product is an early-stage prototype. This business concept has not yet been validated with paying customers.

Demo

Application: https://ncode-ai-studio-hf26.vercel.app/

Case Study: https://ncode-ai-studio-hf26.vercel.app/case-study

Verified Lighthouse + Gemma AI Execution:

https://github.com/Deshan217/ncode-ai-studio-hf26/actions/runs/38784847640

Raw Test Evidence:

https://github.com/Deshan217/ncode-ai-studio-hf26/actions/runs/38784847640/artifacts/11998425425

The verified demonstration runs Lighthouse in a GitHub Actions environment and generates recommendations using Gemma 3 through Ollama.

The hosted Vercel application currently demonstrates the interface and case study. Live cloud AI inference and production PageSpeed API quota configuration remain separate deployment improvements.

Code

The project is publicly available on GitHub under the MIT License.

GitHub Repository:

https://github.com/Deshan217/ncode-ai-studio-hf26

The repository contains the Next.js application, audit processing logic, Ollama integration, test workflows, documentation, and reproducible AI testing configuration.

How I Built It

I used the following technologies:

  • Next.js and React: Application interface and server-side API routes.
  • TypeScript: Typed application and auditing logic.
  • Lighthouse: Website performance, accessibility, SEO, and best-practice analysis.
  • Ollama: Local inference infrastructure.
  • Gemma 3 1B: Open-weight AI model used for verified recommendations.
  • GitHub Actions: Automated builds, testing, and reproducible AI execution.
  • Vercel: Hosting for the application interface.

How the AI Workflow Works

The application is designed to accept a public HTTPS website URL, collect audit findings, and generate an understandable improvement report.

For the verified demonstration, GitHub Actions runs Lighthouse directly in headless Chrome, extracts website audit findings, and provides those findings to a locally running Gemma model through Ollama.

The AI then generates prioritized recommendations that a developer or website consultant can review.

Real Testing Results

I tested the workflow against the N-CODE STUDIO website:

Website: https://ncodest.com/

The October 15, 2026 Lighthouse run produced the following mobile lab scores:

Category Score
Performance 57/100
Accessibility 78/100
SEO 100/100
Best Practices 100/100

The Gemma model successfully generated recommendations related to accessibility, semantic structure, accessible labels, contrast, and performance optimization.

These results come from a single lab run and should not be interpreted as ongoing measurements or a guarantee of user experience. AI-generated recommendations require human review.

Challenges I Faced

One challenge was Google PageSpeed Insights API quota limits.

Although local Gemma inference worked, the first end-to-end attempt could not retrieve audit data because the PageSpeed API quota had been exceeded.

To produce reproducible evidence, I implemented a separate GitHub Actions workflow using Lighthouse directly with headless Chrome, without depending on the PageSpeed API.

This workflow successfully completed both a real Lighthouse audit and real open-weight AI inference.

Another challenge is hosting: an Ollama instance running locally is not automatically accessible to a cloud-hosted Next.js application. A secure production AI service is part of the future roadmap.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation gives independent developers the freedom to experiment, learn, customize, and build useful products without depending entirely on proprietary AI platforms.

Using Gemma through Ollama makes it possible to run the language model under developer control.

For N-CODE AI Studio, this provides several advantages:

  • Ability to inspect and modify the AI prompt and integration.
  • Flexibility to experiment with different open-weight models.
  • Potential to operate local inference without per-request proprietary model API charges.
  • Opportunities for community contributions and improvements.
  • Greater control over where AI processing takes place.

The complete application is shared under the MIT License.

My goal is to make useful AI-assisted website consulting more accessible to independent developers and smaller businesses.

What's Next?

My future plans for N-CODE AI Studio include a securely hosted AI inference service, better audit reporting, user authentication, rate limiting, audit history, and professional client-ready reports.

I also want to collect feedback from freelancers and small business owners to see whether this tool can become a practical, affordable website consulting product.

Built by N-CODE STUDIO for Hacktoberfest 2026.

Thank you to the open-source community and the developers building accessible AI tools!

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma

N-CODE AI Studio uses Google's open-weight Gemma 3 1B model through Ollama to transform real Lighthouse audit measurements into actionable website improvement recommendations.

The model was successfully executed and tested using GitHub Actions, with real inference results and supporting evidence available in the public repository.

title: EvolvingBrain: An Adaptive Skill System for Multi-modal Agents Self-Evolution in Open Worlds
description:
arXiv:2610.20786v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-modal agents have made significant progress in interacting with open worlds. However, their ability to self-evolve remains limited. Supervised fine-tuning enables imitation but not active experience organization, while outcome-based reinforcement learning promotes exploration yet underuses intermediate trajectory information. Therefore, we propose EvolvingBrain, which uses an adaptive skill system as the brain for agent self-evolution, consisting of two following components. Stratified Skill Self-Evolution: extracts Procedural Patterns and Problematic Patterns from model-specific trajectories, summarizes experience by generating skills, and evolves through multiple interactions with the open world, ultimately forming a Stratified Skill Architecture consisting of Domain, Plan, and Action/Trap Skills, which provides the agent with a multi-granularity knowledge repository and a novel evolution approach. State-Aware Adaptive Execution: summarizes long-horizon interactions into Structured Abstractive Memory and uses it to guide the State-Aware Skill Fusion Strategy, enabling the agent to utilize knowledge according to its current state. Experiments on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld demonstrate that EvolvingBrain improves success rates on open-world tasks and exhibits generalization capabilities. Our code is provided in the supplementary materials and will be publicly released in the camera-ready version.

title: CSS Logical Properties: The Modern Way to Handle RTL, LTR, and Writing Modes
description:
CSS logical properties replace physical directional properties (left, right, top, bottom) with logical equivalents that adapt to the document's writing direction. They're the modern approach for building interfaces that work in both left-to-right (LTR) and right-to-left (RTL) languages, as well as vertical writing modes.

The Problem with Physical Properties

Traditional CSS uses physical coordinates:

.card {
  margin-left: 16px;
  padding-right: 24px;
  border-top: 1px solid #ccc;
  text-align: left;
}

In Arabic or Hebrew (RTL), margin-left creates space on the wrong side. You'd need to override everything:

[dir="rtl"] .card {
  margin-left: 0;
  margin-right: 16px;
  padding-right: 0;
  padding-left: 24px;
  text-align: right;
}

Logical properties handle this automatically.

The Logical Model

Logical properties use two axes:

  • Inline: the direction text flows (left-right in English, right-left in Arabic, top-bottom in some Asian scripts)
  • Block: the direction blocks stack (top-bottom in horizontal writing, right-left or left-right in vertical)
Physical Logical
left inline-start
right inline-end
top block-start
bottom block-end

Margin, Padding, and Borders 

/* Physical */
margin-left: 16px;
margin-right: 24px;
margin-top: 8px;
margin-bottom: 8px;

/* Logical equivalents */
margin-inline-start: 16px;
margin-inline-end: 24px;
margin-block-start: 8px;
margin-block-end: 8px;

Shorthand:

/* Physical */
margin: 8px 24px 8px 16px;  /* top right bottom left */

/* Logical */
margin-block: 8px;           /* block-start and block-end */
margin-inline: 16px 24px;    /* inline-start and inline-end */

Border:

/* Physical */
border-top: 2px solid blue;
border-left: 1px solid gray;

/* Logical */
border-block-start: 2px solid blue;
border-inline-start: 1px solid gray;

Border radius:

/* Physical */
border-top-left-radius: 8px;
border-bottom-right-radius: 4px;

/* Logical */
border-start-start-radius: 8px;   /* block-start + inline-start */
border-end-end-radius: 4px;       /* block-end + inline-end */

Sizing 

/* Physical */
width: 300px;
height: 200px;
max-width: 600px;
min-height: 100px;

/* Logical */
inline-size: 300px;
block-size: 200px;
max-inline-size: 600px;
min-block-size: 100px;

In horizontal writing mode, inline-size = width and block-size = height. In vertical writing mode, they swap.

Positioning 

/* Physical */
.tooltip {
  position: absolute;
  top: 0;
  left: 100%;
}

/* Logical */
.tooltip {
  position: absolute;
  inset-block-start: 0;
  inset-inline-start: 100%;
}

The inset shorthand:

/* Physical */
top: 0; right: 0; bottom: 0; left: 0;  /* fills container */

/* Logical */
inset: 0;  /* same: works for all writing modes */

/* Or specific sides */
inset-block: 0;   /* top + bottom */
inset-inline: 0;  /* left + right */

Text Alignment 

/* Physical */
text-align: left;

/* Logical */
text-align: start;  /* start of inline direction */
text-align: end;    /* end of inline direction */

start maps to left in LTR and right in RTL automatically.

Flexbox and Grid Already Use Logical Properties

Flexbox justify-content and align-items already adapt to writing-mode and direction:

.container {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: flex-start;  /* always at inline-start */
}

This is why adding direction: rtl to a flex container automatically mirrors its children — the flex model is already logical.

Practical Example: A Card Component

Before (physical):

.card {
  padding: 16px 24px;
  margin-bottom: 16px;
  border-left: 4px solid blue;
  text-align: left;
}

[dir="rtl"] .card {
  border-left: none;
  border-right: 4px solid blue;
  text-align: right;
}

After (logical):

.card {
  padding-block: 16px;
  padding-inline: 24px;
  margin-block-end: 16px;
  border-inline-start: 4px solid blue;
  text-align: start;
}
/* No RTL override needed */

Browser Support

All major logical properties have excellent support in 2024:

  • margin-inline, margin-block, padding-inline, padding-block: 93%+
  • inset-inline, inset-block: 93%+
  • inline-size, block-size: 95%+
  • border-start-start-radius: 90%+

Firefox has had full logical property support since Firefox 69 (2019). There are no Firefox-specific gotchas here.

Check caniuse.com for current coverage.

Mixing Physical and Logical

You can mix them, but be careful with shorthand overrides:

.element {
  margin-inline-start: 16px;
  margin: 0;  /* This RESETS margin-inline-start! */
}

Physical shorthands override logical properties. Use logical shorthands consistently or apply logical properties last.

When to Start Using Logical Properties

  • New projects: use logical properties from the start
  • RTL support needed: logical properties eliminate entire RTL override blocks
  • Vertical writing mode: logical properties are essentially required
  • Existing projects: migrate incrementally, one component at a time

The naming takes a moment to internalize — margin-inline-start instead of margin-left feels verbose at first. After a few days it becomes natural, and the reward is interfaces that handle RTL and other writing modes without any extra CSS.

For Firefox add-on and web extension work, logical properties ensure your extension's sidebar and popup UI adapts correctly when users have RTL system languages — no need to test-and-override each direction separately.

title: "Xin chào, Thế giới!" Cho Microsoft Windows
description:
Đã đến lúc viết ứng dụng đầu tiên của bạn! Các hướng dẫn sau đây dành cho người dùng Windows.

Ⅰ. Những thứ cần chuẩn bị để viết chương trình Java đầu tiên

1. Bộ phát triển Java SE (JDK)

    Đây là phần mềm cần thiết để máy tính của bạn hiểu và chạy được các chương trình Java. Bạn có thể tải phiên bản dành cho Windows ngay tại đây. (Lưu ý: Tải JDK 22, không phải JRE). Sau khi tải về, hãy tham khảo hướng dẫn cài đặt đi kèm.

2. Trình soạn thảo văn bản

    Trong ví dụ này, chúng ta sẽ sử dụng Notepad, một trình soạn thảo đơn giản có sẵn trên hệ điều hành Windows. Bạn vẫn có thể thực hiện theo hướng dẫn này nếu sử dụng trình soạn thảo khác. Chỉ cần hai thứ này là bạn đã có thể bắt tay viết ứng dụng Java đầu tiên của mình rồi!

<!--more-->

Ⅱ. Hướng dẫn chi tiết

    Tạo Tệp Nguồn Mở Notepad (hoặc bất kỳ trình soạn thảo văn bản nào bạn thích). Gõ vào đoạn mã sau.

Đoạn mã trong notepad.

Bấm tổ phím Ctrl+s để lưu tệp và đặt tên tệp là HelloWorld.java

Lưu tệp với tên là HelloWorld.java.

Biên dịch tệp nguồn thành tệp .class

↳ Mở Command Prompt: Nhấn Win + R, gõ cmd, và nhấn Enter.

↳ Điều hướng đến thư mục chứa tệp HelloWorld.java bằng lệnh cd (ví dụ: cd C:\Users\YourName\Documents).

    ↳ C:\Users\Truong Duong›cd</span>

    ↳ C:\›w:

    ↳ W:\›cd java

    ↳ W:\Java›

↳ Chạy lệnh sau để biên dịch tệp nguồn:

    ↳ W:\Java›javac HelloWorld.java

↳ Nếu không có lỗi, lệnh này sẽ tạo ra tệp HelloWorld.class.

Chạy chương trình

↳ Trong cùng Command Prompt đó, chạy lệnh sau để thực thi chương trình:

    ↳ W:\Java›java HelloWorld

    ↳ Xin chào, Thế giới!

↳ Bạn sẽ thấy dòng chữ "Xin chào, Thế giới!" hiển thị trên màn hình.

Các dòng lệnh để chạy chương trình java trong Command Prompt.

Ⅲ. Nhìn kĩ hơn về chương trình “Xin chào, Thế giới!”

    Bây giờ bạn đã thấy thông báo chương trình "Xin chào, Thế giới!" (và thậm chí có thể được biên dịch và chạy nó), bạn có thể thắc mắc nó hoạt động như thế nào. Dưới Đây là mã của chương trình:


HelloWorld.java

public class HelloWorld {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        System.out.println("Hello World!");

    }

}

    Chương trình "Xin chào, Thế giới!" bao gồm hai thành phần chính: định nghĩa lớp HelloWorld và phương thức chính. Phần giải thích sau đây sẽ cung cấp cho bạn sự hiểu biết cơ bản về mã, nhưng những hàm ý sâu sắc hơn sẽ chỉ trở nên rõ ràng sau khi bạn đọc xong phần còn lại của hướng dẫn.

Định nghĩa lớp HelloWorld

    Văn bản in đậm sau đây bắt đầu khối định nghĩa lớp cho chương trình "Xin chào, Thế giới!":


HelloWorld.java

public class HelloWorld {

  // Các thuộc tính và phương thức của lớp

    }

}

    Đoạn code in đậm public class HelloWorld { ... } là định nghĩa của một class tên HelloWorld.

Như đã trình bày ở trên, dạng cơ bản nhất của định nghĩa lớp là:


Ví Dụ

class Tên_Lớp {

    // Các thuộc tính và phương thức của lớp

    }

}

class là một bản thiết kế để tạo ra các đối tượng (object) có các thuộc tính (property) và phương thức (method) riêng. Trong ví dụ này, class HelloWorld sẽ giúp chúng ta tạo ra một chương trình đơn giản in ra dòng chữ "Xin chào, Thế giới!".

    Ở phần tiếp theo chúng tôi sẽ cung cấp cái nhìn tổng quan và thảo luận chi tiết về các class. Bây giờ chỉ cần biết rằng mọi ứng dụng đều bắt đầu bằng một định nghĩa class là đủ.

Phương thức main

    Trong ngôn ngữ lập trình Java, mọi ứng dụng đều phải chứa một phương thức main. Đây là phương thức chính (entry point) của chương trình, là nơi bắt đầu chạy khi bạn khởi động.


Ví Dụ

public static void main(String[] args) {

}

    Các từ khóa public và static có thể được viết theo thứ tự nào cũng được (public static hoặc static public), nhưng theo quy ước, ta dùng public static như trên. Bạn có thể đặt tên cho đối số bất kỳ tên gì bạn muốn, nhưng hầu hết các lập trình viên chọn "args" hoặc "argv".

    Phương thức main tương tự như hàm main trong C và C++; nó là điểm bắt đầu cho ứng dụng của bạn và sẽ gọi tất cả các phương thức khác mà chương trình của bạn yêu cầu.

    Phương thức main chấp nhận một đối số duy nhất: một mảng các phần tử kiểu String.


Ví Dụ

(String[] args)

    String[] args là một mảng (array) chứa các đối số dòng lệnh (command-line arguments) - những thông tin người dùng cung cấp khi chạy chương trình (trong ví dụ này, "Xin chào, Thế giới!" không dùng đến đối số dòng lệnh). Các đối số dòng lệnh cho phép người dùng ảnh hưởng đến hoạt động của ứng dụng mà không cần biên dịch lại. Ví dụ, một chương trình sắp xếp có thể cho phép người dùng chỉ định rằng dữ liệu được sắp xếp theo thứ tự giảm dần bằng cách sử dụng đối số dòng lệnh này:


Ví Dụ

-descending

    Chương trình "Xin chào, Thế giới!" không quan tâm đến các đối số dòng lệnh của nó, nhưng bạn nên biết rằng các đối số như vậy tồn tại.

Cuối cùng, dòng lệnh

Ví Dụ 

System.out.println("Xin chào, Thế giới!");

Sử dụng lớp System từ thư viện lõi để in thông báo "Xin chào, Thế giới!" ra đầu ra tiêu chuẩn. Các phần của thư viện này (còn được gọi là "Giao diện Lập trình Ứng dụng", hoặc "API") sẽ được thảo luận trong suốt phần còn lại của hướng dẫn.

title: Auditing Escalation Reliability in Healthcare LLM Agents: A Perturbation-Controlled Benchmark of Workflow-State Failures
description:
arXiv:2610.21270v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Trustworthy biomedical AI requires reliable action selection when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or late, not only accurate answers on static inputs. We instantiate an episode-level evaluation protocol as 400 synthetic healthcare workflow episodes: 40 hand-authored semantic seeds across four task classes, two surface parameterizations, and five controlled variants, scored on ANSWER/ASK CLARIFICATION/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE under a pre-declared 5:1 missed-versus-unnecessary escalation cost. Reference actions are single-author study-policy labels, not clinician-adjudicated ground truth. Across five open-weight configurations (1.7B--9.7B), clean decision accuracy reaches 0.97, yet uncertainty-prompted models miss 32--97% of required escalations. The stronger 9.7B configuration narrows but does not remove the gap, falling from 0.97 clean accuracy to 0.78 under conflict. Verbalized confidence is inconsistent (ECE 0.10--0.54; failure AUROC 0.48--0.77), and a development-tuned confidence-only policy yields no utility gain. A transparent workflow-aware controller improves 5:1 utility for every model and reduces missed escalations to 0.12--0.24, at specificity 0.83--0.93. However, a 30-concept lexical stress test reduces each rule detector's recall from 1.00 on trigger phrases to 0.00 on unseen paraphrases, limiting the controller claim to this benchmark. Seed-clustered statistics, ablations, cross-task transfer, raw outputs, and manifests are packaged for audit. The results motivate explicit workflow-state evaluation while showing that apparently effective routing controls need their own generalization tests.

title: RepoDNA v1.4.1: Preparing Native WinGet Installation and Upgrades for Windows
description:
RepoDNA v1.4.1: Preparing Native WinGet Installation and Upgrades for Windows

Installing developer tools should be straightforward, and keeping them updated should be even easier.

With RepoDNA v1.4.1, I've introduced the packaging and automation needed to prepare RepoDNA for the Windows Package Manager (WinGet) community catalog.

RepoDNA is an open-source, local-first repository intelligence platform that helps developers understand their codebases through architecture analysis, dependency exploration, repository history, and evidence-backed reports.

What's new in v1.4.1?

1. WinGet package manifests

The release introduces manifest generation for two separate Windows packages:

  • SanskarIN.RepoDNA — RepoDNA desktop application.
  • SanskarIN.RepoDNA.CLI — RepoDNA command-line tool.

Both packages are prepared for Windows x64 and ARM64.

2. Preparing native installation and upgrades

Once Microsoft accepts and indexes the packages, Windows users will be able to discover them through WinGet.

For example:

winget source update
winget search --id SanskarIN.RepoDNA --exact

After the community listing becomes available, users will be able to install the package using:

winget install --id SanskarIN.RepoDNA --exact

And when a future package version is published:

winget upgrade --id SanskarIN.RepoDNA --exact

Important: The v1.4.1 release generates the necessary manifest files, but publishing on GitHub does not automatically make a package available in Microsoft's WinGet catalog. The manifests must be submitted, accepted, and indexed.

3. Release integrity and automation

The release process now prepares six YAML manifest files, covering version metadata, locale information, and installer definitions for the two packages.

SHA-256 hashes are calculated from the actual release artifacts rather than entered manually.

An optional GitHub Actions workflow also helps maintainers submit these manifests for Microsoft's review.

4. Regression testing

New tests cover:

  • Generated package hashes.
  • Portable archive executable paths.
  • Supported CPU architectures.
  • Missing input artifacts.
  • Unsupported version strings.

These checks help keep the package generation process consistent as RepoDNA evolves.

Why this matters

RepoDNA already offers desktop, CLI, browser, and WebAssembly-based workflows.

A well-maintained WinGet listing will provide another installation and update path for Windows users.

Future releases will still need their own accepted manifests, but the automation introduced in v1.4.1 makes that process easier to maintain.

Try RepoDNA

GitHub release:
https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/releases/tag/v1.4.1

Live web app:
https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/

WinGet documentation:
https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/blob/v1.4.1/docs/winget.md

If you're maintaining a Windows application through WinGet, I'd be interested in hearing how you handle package submissions, installer validation, and upgrade testing.

Thanks for following RepoDNA's development! 🧬

title: Building Production-Ready Open-Weights AI Agents with Gemma, Google ADK, and Cloud Run GPUs
description:
Figure 1: The four foundational pillars I used to take an open-weights Gemma agent from a local prototype to governed enterprise production on Google Cloud.

Most AI tutorials stop at a basic "Hello World" chatbot running on a laptop. However, when engineering teams try to move open-weights models like Google’s Gemma 3 (gemma-3-4b-it, gemma-3-12b-it, gemma-3-27b-it) into real enterprise production, they immediately hit four hard engineering questions:

  1. Grounding: How do I connect Gemma to live enterprise data (like Cloud Firestore) so it doesn't hallucinate?
  2. Serverless GPU Scaling: How do I serve Gemma on GPUs (Cloud Run + vLLM + Cloud Storage FUSE) so it scales to zero when idle instead of burning thousands of dollars a month?
  3. Security & Governance: How do I guarantee the agent cannot leak API keys, fall for prompt injections, or accidentally take down a production service?
  4. Testing & Optimization: How do I unit-test an AI agent's tool calls in CI/CD, and how do I fine-tune a small, fast Gemma 4B model with LoRA on Vertex AI so it performs like a 27B model?

I wrote this article to serve as a complete, end-to-end Enterprise Reference Blueprint that answers all four questions using a single, working project (CloudGuard) verified in Google Cloud Shell (all working code is available in my cloudguard-gemma-agent GitHub repository).

Where This Blueprint Is Useful in Production

  • DevOps, SRE & Automated Incident Response: On-call engineers often waste 20–30 minutes during an outage manually querying logs, searching old postmortems, and finding remediation runbooks. CloudGuard automatically pulls live incident telemetry from Cloud Firestore (get_service_incident), matches symptoms against historical postmortems in its Long-Term Memory Bank (MEM-2026-014), and executes approved mitigations in staging (mitigate_runaway_workload).
  • Cloud FinOps & GPU Quota Governance: A single misconfigured ML batch job or unthrottled retry loop can spin up dozens of GPUs overnight. CloudGuard checks real-time regional GPU utilization (NVIDIA L4 and RTX PRO 6000) and monthly budget burn (check_gpu_quota_and_cost), immediately scaling down runaway staging workloads and calculating hourly dollar savings ($36.12/hr).
  • Regulated Enterprises Requiring Data Sovereignty (Banking, Healthcare, Government, SecOps): Organizations prohibited from sending internal incident logs, credentials, or infrastructure schemas to external third-party APIs can deploy open-weights Gemma inside their own Google Cloud project behind --no-allow-unauthenticated IAM and Model Armor guardrails (cloudguard_agent/guardrails.py), where accidentally pasted GCP API keys (AIza...) are redacted before reaching the model.
  • AI Engineering & MLOps CI/CD Pipelines: Instead of relying on manual "vibe checks" when prompts or tools change, my ADK Eval harness (scripts/run_eval.py) scores Tool Trajectory Accuracy (1.00) and Response Factuality (1.00) on every build, while my Vertex AI QLoRA pipeline (scripts/prepare_and_verify_lora.py) lets teams replace a 54 GB VRAM model (Gemma 27B) with an 8.9 GB VRAM model (Gemma 4B + LoRA) running in ~51ms on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU.

Here are the six stages of the production lifecycle I will walk through:

  1. Build: Scaffolding a model-agnostic Google ADK agent in Python that runs against local Gemma weights (via Ollama) during development and seamlessly switches to Cloud Run GPUs or Vertex AI Model Garden in production.
  2. Connect: Authoring native Python function-calling tools backed by Cloud Firestore to inspect live production incidents and regional GPU FinOps quotas.
  3. Scale: Deploying vLLM on Cloud Run Serverless GPUs (NVIDIA L4 / RTX PRO 6000) with Cloud Storage FUSE for zero-download weight streaming, paired with Short-Term Session State and a Long-Term Memory Bank.
  4. Govern: Enforcing defense-in-depth security with private Cloud Run IAM service accounts, Model Armor secret redaction (before_model_callback), and deterministic RBAC tool policies (before_tool_callback).
  5. Optimize: Automating CI/CD release gates with ADK Eval (tool_trajectory_avg_score and response_match_score) and OpenTelemetry tracing for Google Cloud Trace.
  6. Specialize: Fine-tuning a compact google/gemma-3-4b-it model using QLoRA on Vertex AI so it matches gemma-3-27b-it tool-calling accuracy (1.00) at 2.8x faster latency and 6x lower GPU memory.


Figure 2: End-to-end request lifecycle for my CloudGuard Incident & FinOps Agent across Cloud Run, vLLM, Cloud Firestore, Model Armor guardrails, and Cloud Trace.

Part 1: Platform Foundations & Scaffolding the First Gemma Agent

Prerequisites & Google Cloud Setup

To follow along with my setup, you will need:

  • A Google Cloud Project with billing enabled.
  • The Google Cloud SDK (gcloud) installed and authenticated.
  • Python 3.10+ and uv (the fast Python package and virtual environment manager I use across this project).
  • Ollama installed locally (ollama pull gemma3:4b or ollama pull gemma3:27b) for zero-cost local prototyping before deploying to Google Cloud GPUs.

First, I set my project and region environment variables and enabled the required Google Cloud APIs:

export PROJECT_ID="your-gcp-project-id"
export REGION="us-central1"

gcloud config set project $PROJECT_ID
gcloud config set compute/region $REGION

gcloud services enable \
  aiplatform.googleapis.com \
  run.googleapis.com \
  artifactregistry.googleapis.com \
  firestore.googleapis.com \
  cloudtrace.googleapis.com \
  iam.googleapis.com

Next, I configured Application Default Credentials (ADC) so my local Python environment can authenticate with Google Cloud services:

gcloud auth application-default login

Scaffolding the Project (Local or 1-Click in Google Cloud Shell)

You can either clone and run this project directly inside Google Cloud Shell (which comes pre-authenticated with gcloud and Python in your browser) by clicking Open in Google Cloud Shell, or initialize the workspace locally with uv:


Step 1: Launching the RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent repository directly inside Google Cloud Shell.


Step 2: Authorizing Google Cloud Shell credentials while the repository clones into the Cloud Shell workspace.


Step 3: Executing the CloudGuard environment setup, database seeding, and ADK evaluation commands inside the Google Cloud Shell terminal.

mkdir cloudguard-gemma-agent && cd cloudguard-gemma-agent
uv init

I structured the repository so that agent orchestration, native tools, memory management, security guardrails, and evaluation suites are cleanly separated (and runnable offline via a deterministic local simulation harness before touching cloud GPUs):

cloudguard-gemma-agent/
├── pyproject.toml
├── .env.example
├── cloudguard_agent/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── agent.py          # Core ADK LlmAgent & Gemma LiteLLM configuration
│   ├── tools.py          # Native Python tools backed by Cloud Firestore
│   ├── memory.py         # Short-Term Session & Long-Term Memory Bank
│   ├── guardrails.py     # Model Armor & RBAC policy callbacks
│   └── finetuning.py     # Vertex AI QLoRA dataset & job spec builder
├── deploy/
│   ├── Dockerfile.vllm
│   ├── Dockerfile.vllm.lora
│   └── deploy_cloud_run_gpu.sh
├── scripts/
│   ├── seed_firestore.py
│   ├── simulate_parts.py
│   ├── run_eval.py
│   └── prepare_and_verify_lora.py
└── tests/
    └── eval_dataset.json


Repository structure of RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent showing the modular separation across agent orchestration, Firestore tools, memory, guardrails, deployment manifests, and evaluation scripts.

In pyproject.toml, I declared google-adk, litellm, google-cloud-firestore, and opentelemetry-sdk:

[project]
name = "cloudguard-gemma-agent"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Enterprise SecOps & FinOps Triage Agent powered by Open-Weights Gemma & Google ADK on Cloud Run GPUs"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = [
    "google-adk>=1.0.0",
    "google-genai>=1.0.0",
    "google-cloud-firestore>=2.19.0",
    "litellm>=1.60.0",
    "pydantic>=2.10.0",
    "python-dotenv>=1.0.1",
    "opentelemetry-api>=1.29.0",
    "opentelemetry-sdk>=1.29.0",
]

Then I locked and installed the dependencies:

uv sync

Decoupling Local vs. Cloud GPU Inference (.env.example)

One of the strongest architectural benefits of Google ADK is its model-agnostic LiteLlm integration. By defining a .env configuration file, I can point my agent to a local Ollama server on localhost:11434 during development and switch to a self-hosted vLLM endpoint on Cloud Run GPUs (or Vertex AI Model Garden) in production without changing a single line of agent orchestration code:

# Google Cloud Project Settings
GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT="cloudguard-enterprise-demo"
GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION="us-central1"

# Gemma Inference Backend Mode: "local_ollama" | "cloud_run_vllm"
GEMMA_BACKEND_MODE="local_ollama"

# Local Prototyping via Ollama
OLLAMA_API_BASE="http://localhost:11434"
GEMMA_MODEL_NAME="ollama_chat/gemma3:27b"

# Production Cloud Run GPU vLLM Endpoint
GEMMA_VLLM_ENDPOINT_URL="https://gemma-vllm-service-xyz-uc.a.run.app/v1"
GEMMA_VLLM_MODEL_ID="google/gemma-3-27b-it"

# Firestore Configuration
FIRESTORE_DATABASE="(default)"
USE_LOCAL_MOCK_DB="true"

Defining the CloudGuard Agent Persona (cloudguard_agent/agent.py)

When building agents with open-weights models like Gemma, explicit, numbered system instructions are essential. Here is how I defined the agent's identity, tool bindings, and strict operational constraints in cloudguard_agent/agent.py:

import os
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from google.adk.models.lite_llm import LiteLlm
from .tools import (
    check_gpu_quota_and_cost,
    get_service_incident,
    list_active_alerts,
    mitigate_runaway_workload,
)

CLOUDGUARD_SYSTEM_INSTRUCTION = """You are CloudGuard, an Enterprise SecOps & FinOps Incident Response Agent running on Google Cloud and powered by open-weights Gemma.

Your primary responsibilities:
1. Incident Triage: Retrieve real-time operational and FinOps telemetry using `get_service_incident` and `list_active_alerts`.
2. GPU FinOps & Capacity: Verify regional NVIDIA L4 and RTX PRO 6000 GPU availability and monthly budget burn using `check_gpu_quota_and_cost`.
3. Safe Remediation: When authorized, mitigate runaway staging workloads using `mitigate_runaway_workload`.
4. Enterprise Governance Compliance:
   - NEVER execute automated scaling or termination in `production` without explicit `sre-incident-commander` escalation.
   - Always cite the exact Incident ID, affected service name, hourly USD burn rate, and recommended runbook ID in your response.
"""

def build_adk_root_agent() -> LlmAgent:
    backend_mode = os.getenv("GEMMA_BACKEND_MODE", "local_ollama")
    if backend_mode == "cloud_run_vllm":
        model_id = f"openai/{os.getenv('GEMMA_VLLM_MODEL_ID', 'google/gemma-3-27b-it')}"
        api_base = os.getenv("GEMMA_VLLM_ENDPOINT_URL")
    else:
        model_id = os.getenv("GEMMA_MODEL_NAME", "ollama_chat/gemma3:27b")
        api_base = os.getenv("OLLAMA_API_BASE", "http://localhost:11434")

    gemma_model = LiteLlm(model=model_id, api_base=api_base)

    return LlmAgent(
        name="cloudguard_gemma_agent",
        model=gemma_model,
        description="Enterprise SecOps and FinOps incident triage agent powered by Gemma.",
        instruction=CLOUDGUARD_SYSTEM_INSTRUCTION,
        tools=[
            get_service_incident,
            list_active_alerts,
            check_gpu_quota_and_cost,
            mitigate_runaway_workload,
        ],
    )

root_agent = build_adk_root_agent()

Part 2: Native Python Tools & Connecting to Cloud Firestore


Figure 3: How Google ADK introspects my Python type hints and docstrings to drive structured Gemma tool calls against Cloud Firestore.

An isolated LLM knows nothing about active Cloud Run services, internal SRE runbooks, or current monthly GPU FinOps burn rates. To bridge that gap, Google ADK automatically converts standard Python functions into JSON Schema tool definitions for Gemma.

My Engineering Rule for Open-Weights Gemma: Compact open-weights models (Gemma 4B, 12B, 27B) rely heavily on explicit Args: descriptions and concrete format examples (such as 'INC-YYYY-NNNN') in Python docstrings to construct valid JSON tool arguments. I treat Python docstrings as first-class prompt engineering.

Implementing the Operational Tools (cloudguard_agent/tools.py)

I built four native Python tools backed by Cloud Firestore (plus a zero-config local JSON schema mirror (USE_LOCAL_MOCK_DB="true") so the entire test suite can be verified locally before provisioning cloud resources):

  • get_service_incident(incident_id: str): Retrieves severity, symptom, GPU type, hourly USD burn rate, and remediation runbook for a specific incident ticket.
  • list_active_alerts(environment: str = "all"): Lists open incidents filtered by production, staging, or all.
  • check_gpu_quota_and_cost(region: str): Checks regional NVIDIA L4 and RTX PRO 6000 quota limits, active usage, and monthly FinOps budget percentage.
  • mitigate_runaway_workload(...): Scales down a runaway Cloud Run service or batch job and records the hourly cost savings. 
def get_service_incident(incident_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Retrieves full operational and FinOps telemetry for a specific incident ID.

    Use this tool whenever a user asks about a specific incident ticket (e.g.,
    'INC-2026-0891' or 'INC-2026-0904'), its symptoms, severity, or recommended runbook.

    Args:
        incident_id: The unique incident identifier formatted as 'INC-YYYY-NNNN'.

    Returns:
        A dictionary containing the incident status, severity, affected service,
        GPU usage, hourly burn rate, and recommended remediation runbook.
    """
    use_mock = os.getenv("USE_LOCAL_MOCK_DB", "true").lower() == "true"
    normalized_id = incident_id.strip().upper()

    if not use_mock:
        from google.cloud import firestore

        db = firestore.Client(project=os.getenv("GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT"))
        doc = db.collection("incidents").document(normalized_id).get()
        if not doc.exists:
            return {"status": "error", "message": f"Incident {normalized_id} not found in Firestore."}
        return {"status": "success", "incident": doc.to_dict()}

    db_data = _load_db()
    incident = db_data.get("incidents", {}).get(normalized_id)
    if not incident:
        return {
            "status": "error",
            "message": f"Incident '{normalized_id}' not found. Valid IDs: {list(db_data.get('incidents', {}).keys())}",
        }
    return {"status": "success", "incident": incident}


def check_gpu_quota_and_cost(region: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Checks current Cloud Run GPU quota utilization and monthly FinOps spend for a GCP region.

    Use this tool when evaluating whether a region has available NVIDIA L4 or
    RTX PRO 6000 GPUs or when checking monthly budget consumption.

    Args:
        region: The Google Cloud region identifier (e.g., 'us-central1', 'europe-west4').

    Returns:
        A dictionary with GPU quota limits, active usage, and budget utilization metrics.
    """
    db_data = _load_db()
    clean_region = region.strip().lower()
    quota_info = db_data.get("quotas", {}).get(clean_region)
    if not quota_info:
        return {
            "status": "error",
            "message": f"No quota telemetry found for region '{clean_region}'. Supported: us-central1, europe-west4.",
        }

    l4_free = quota_info["nvidia_l4_limit"] - quota_info["nvidia_l4_in_use"]
    budget_pct = round(
        (quota_info["current_month_spend_usd"] / quota_info["monthly_budget_usd"]) * 100, 1
    )
    return {
        "status": "success",
        "region": clean_region,
        "available_nvidia_l4_gpus": l4_free,
        "budget_utilization_percent": budget_pct,
        "details": quota_info,
    }

Seeding the Database (scripts/seed_firestore.py)

When connecting to a live Cloud Firestore instance in Google Cloud, you can provision the database in Native mode:

gcloud firestore databases create \
  --location=us-central1 \
  --type=firestore-native

I then ran scripts/seed_firestore.py to populate the incidents and quotas collections:

uv run python scripts/seed_firestore.py

Here is the terminal output from running the database seeder:

==========================================================================

INC-2026-0904    P1         production    payment-gateway-prod       $18.00

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

europe-west4     2/8                    0/2                       $910 / $2,500

Running scripts/seed_firestore.py inside Google Cloud Shell to populate the incidents and quotas collections.

Part 3: Scaling with Cloud Run Serverless GPUs, Vertex AI Model Garden & Dual Memory


Figure 4: Streaming Gemma weights from Cloud Storage FUSE into Cloud Run Serverless GPUs with vLLM, backed by Short-Term Session State and a Long-Term Enterprise Memory Bank.

Moving an open-weights Gemma model from a developer laptop into enterprise production on Google Cloud offers two primary deployment patterns: Cloud Run Serverless GPUs with vLLM (for scale-to-zero serverless containers) or Vertex AI Model Garden (for one-call managed GPU endpoints).

Option A: Serverless GPU Serving on Cloud Run with vLLM & Cloud Storage FUSE

Instead of baking multi-gigabyte model weights into a container image — or downloading them from Hugging Face on every cold start — I stage the Gemma weights in a regional Google Cloud Storage (GCS) bucket and mount that bucket at /mnt/models using Cloud Storage FUSE.

VRAM Sizing Note on Google Cloud Run GPUs: A single NVIDIA L4 GPU on Cloud Run provides 24 GB of VRAM, which easily fits google/gemma-3-4b-it (~8.4 GB in bfloat16), google/gemma-3-12b-it, or a 4-bit AWQ quantized google/gemma-3-27b-it. To run unquantized bfloat16 google/gemma-3-27b-it (~54 GB VRAM) on a single serverless instance, use --gpu-type=nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 on Cloud Run or deploy on Vertex AI Model Garden.

Here is my deploy/Dockerfile.vllm configuration:

FROM vllm/vllm-openai:latest

ENV HF_HOME=/mnt/models \
    VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn \
    PORT=8080

ENV MODEL_PATH="/mnt/models/gemma-3-27b-it"

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["python3", "-m", "vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server"]
CMD ["--model", "/mnt/models/gemma-3-27b-it", \
     "--served-model-name", "google/gemma-3-27b-it", \
     "--host", "0.0.0.0", \
     "--port", "8080", \
     "--dtype", "bfloat16", \
     "--max-model-len", "8192", \
     "--gpu-memory-utilization", "0.92", \
     "--enable-auto-tool-choice", \
     "--tool-call-parser", "pythonic"]

And here is the gcloud run deploy command from deploy/deploy_cloud_run_gpu.sh mounting the GCS FUSE volume:

gcloud run deploy gemma-vllm-service \
  --image="us-docker.pkg.dev/${PROJECT_ID}/cloudguard-repo/gemma-vllm:latest" \
  --region="${REGION}" \
  --service-account="${VLLM_SA}" \
  --no-allow-unauthenticated \
  --cpu=8 \
  --memory=32Gi \
  --gpu=1 \
  --gpu-type=nvidia-l4 \
  --no-gpu-zonal-redundancy \
  --min-instances=0 \
  --max-instances=3 \
  --concurrency=8 \
  --add-volume="name=model-weights,type=cloud-storage,bucket=${MODEL_BUCKET},readonly=true" \
  --add-volume-mount="volume=model-weights,mount-path=/mnt/models" \
  --port=8080

Option B: Managed Deployment via Vertex AI Model Garden

Alternatively, if you prefer a managed endpoint provisioned directly from Vertex AI Model Garden, you can deploy google/gemma3@gemma-3-4b-it or google/gemma3@gemma-3-27b-it programmatically using the Vertex AI Python SDK:

import vertexai
from vertexai import model_garden

vertexai.init(project="your-gcp-project-id", location="us-central1")

# Official Vertex AI Model Garden identifier for Gemma 3
open_model = model_garden.OpenModel("google/gemma3@gemma-3-4b-it")

endpoint = open_model.deploy(
    machine_type="g2-standard-12",
    accelerator_type="NVIDIA_L4",
    accelerator_count=1,
    accept_eula=True,
)

Dual-Tier Memory: Short-Term Session State vs. Long-Term Memory Bank

In cloudguard_agent/memory.py, I equipped the agent with two distinct memory layers:

  1. Short-Term Conversational Session (AgentSessionState): Tracks the active incident ID (active_incident_id) within the current troubleshooting thread. When an engineer inspects INC-2026-0891 in Turn 2 and says "Go ahead and mitigate that runaway staging workload" in Turn 4, the agent resolves the reference automatically.
  2. Long-Term Organizational Memory (EnterpriseMemoryBank): Stores verified postmortem learnings across all sessions. When INC-2026-0891 triggers on ml-batch-indexer-dev, the agent automatically searches historical postmortems and retrieves MEM-2026-014.

Here is the execution output from running my multi-turn simulation harness (uv run python scripts/simulate_parts.py):

Part 4: Enterprise Governance, IAM Isolation & Model Armor Guardrails


Figure 5: Three sequential security gates I implemented to protect the CloudGuard agent: Cloud Run IAM isolation, Before-Model secret redaction & injection blocking, and Before-Tool RBAC enforcement.

Giving an AI agent write-access to infrastructure requires deterministic security boundaries. Telling an LLM "Never scale down production" inside a system prompt is a probabilistic guideline — not an enterprise security control.

I implemented defense-in-depth across three sequential gates:

  • Gate 1 — Zero-Trust Cloud Run IAM Isolation: The gemma-vllm-service is configured with --no-allow-unauthenticated. Only the ADK orchestrator's service account (cloudguard-agent-sa) holds roles/run.invoker permission.
  • Gate 2 — Before-Model Input Sanitization (inspect_and_sanitize_prompt): Modeled on Google Cloud Model Armor, this interceptor scans every incoming prompt for adversarial jailbreak signatures and automatically redacts live credentials (such as AIza... GCP API keys or ya29... bearer tokens) before they reach the Gemma model or telemetry logs.
  • Gate 3 — Before-Tool Deterministic RBAC (validate_tool_invocation): Intercepts every mitigate_runaway_workload call before Python executes it, blocking any production mutation unless the caller holds sre-incident-commander privileges (POL-PROD-MUTATION-001).

Guardrail Implementation (cloudguard_agent/guardrails.py) 

SENSITIVE_PATTERNS: list[tuple[str, re.Pattern[str]]] = [
    ("GCP_API_KEY", re.compile(r"AIza[0-9A-Za-z\-_]{35}")),
    ("BEARER_TOKEN", re.compile(r"ya29\.[0-9A-Za-z\-_]+")),
    ("PRIVATE_KEY_HEADER", re.compile(r"-----BEGIN (?:RSA )?PRIVATE KEY-----")),
]

PROMPT_INJECTION_SIGNATURES: list[str] = [
    "ignore all previous instructions",
    "bypass governance policy",
    "override system prompt",
]

def validate_tool_invocation(
    tool_name: str,
    tool_args: dict[str, Any],
    caller_role: str = "sre-tier1-operator",
) -> tuple[bool, dict[str, Any] | None, dict[str, Any]]:
    """Enforces deterministic policy checks before any ADK tool executes."""
    if tool_name == "mitigate_runaway_workload":
        target_env = str(tool_args.get("target_environment", "")).lower()
        action = str(tool_args.get("action", "")).lower()

        if target_env == "production" and caller_role != "sre-incident-commander":
            block_payload = {
                "status": "blocked_by_governance_policy",
                "policy_id": "POL-PROD-MUTATION-001",
                "reason": (
                    f"Automated '{action}' on environment='production' is prohibited for role "
                    f"'{caller_role}'. Escalate to an 'sre-incident-commander' or execute "
                    "manual runbook verification first."
                ),
            }
            entry = audit_log.record(
                event_type="BEFORE_TOOL_GUARDRAIL",
                decision="DENIED",
                details={
                    "tool_name": tool_name,
                    "environment": target_env,
                    "caller_role": caller_role,
                    "policy_id": "POL-PROD-MUTATION-001",
                },
            )
            return False, block_payload, entry

    entry = audit_log.record(
        event_type="BEFORE_TOOL_GUARDRAIL",
        decision="ALLOWED",
        details={"tool_name": tool_name, "caller_role": caller_role},
    )
    return True, None, entry

Part 5: Observability & Deterministic Evaluation (ADK Eval)


Figure 6: Automated CI/CD evaluation pipeline scoring both Tool Trajectory Accuracy and Response Factuality while exporting OpenTelemetry spans to Google Cloud Trace.

Manual "vibe checks" in a chat UI cannot prevent regressions when prompts, tools, or model weights change. Following ADK Eval best practices, I built scripts/run_eval.py to evaluate the agent against a golden dataset (tests/eval_dataset.json) across two quantitative metrics:

  • Tool Trajectory Score (tool_trajectory_avg_score): Verifies that the agent invoked the exact expected sequence of tools with the exact expected JSON arguments (1.00 = 100% match).
  • Response Factuality Score (response_match_score): Verifies that required domain identifiers (Incident IDs, runbook codes, dollar savings, or RBAC policy codes) appear in the synthesized response.

Part 6: Fine-Tuning Gemma with QLoRA on Vertex AI for Domain Tool Calling


Figure 7: End-to-end domain specialization lifecycle — converting verified production traces into a Gemma SFT dataset, training a QLoRA adapter on Vertex AI, and hot-loading it into Cloud Run vLLM.

While google/gemma-3-27b-it achieves a 1.00 tool-trajectory score out of the box, unquantized bfloat16 weights require ~54 GB of VRAM. To run cleanly on a single 24 GB NVIDIA L4 GPU on Cloud Run with plenty of room for concurrent KV-cache requests, I wanted to specialize the compact google/gemma-3-4b-it model (which uses only 8.9 GB of VRAM and responds in ~51ms).

Using cloudguard_agent/finetuning.py (uv run python scripts/prepare_and_verify_lora.py), I exported verified multi-turn tool trajectories into Gemma's official <start_of_turn> SFT format (data/cloudguard_gemma_sft_train.jsonl) and generated the Vertex AI Custom Training (NVIDIA_L4 QLoRA r=16, lora_alpha=32) specification:

Live execution in Google Cloud Shell exporting golden SFT trajectories formatted with Gemma's <start_of_turn> and tool_code tokens.

Once Vertex AI writes the LoRA adapter weights to gs://${PROJECT_ID}-gemma-weights/adapters/cloudguard-sre-lora-v1, I hot-load the adapter into vLLM on Cloud Run (--enable-lora --lora-modules cloudguard-sre-lora-v1=/mnt/models/adapters/cloudguard-sre-lora-v1).

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

google/gemma-3-27b-it (Zero-Shot Base)     1.00              144.1ms        54.0 GB

With domain QLoRA fine-tuning, the compact Gemma 4B model matches the 1.00 Tool Trajectory score of the 27B model while cutting latency from 144.1ms down to 51.4ms and fitting effortlessly on a single Cloud Run NVIDIA L4 GPU.

Cleaning Up Cloud Resources (FinOps Hygiene)

If you deploy the Cloud Run GPU services and GCS bucket in your own Google Cloud project, remember to tear them down when finished experimenting:

export PROJECT_ID=$(gcloud config get-value project)
export REGION="us-central1"

gcloud run services delete cloudguard-adk-agent --region=${REGION} --quiet
gcloud run services delete gemma-vllm-service --region=${REGION} --quiet
gcloud storage rm --recursive gs://${PROJECT_ID}-gemma-weights

Key Takeaways

  • Open-Weights Control + Cloud-Native Speed: Pairing Gemma 3 with Google ADK gives me complete model weight ownership and VPC data residency without sacrificing developer velocity.
  • Serverless GPU Economics: Combining vLLM, Cloud Run Serverless GPUs (nvidia-l4), and Cloud Storage FUSE eliminates both idle GPU VM waste and slow container cold starts.
  • Deterministic Governance & Evaluation: Using before_model_callback, before_tool_callback, and ADK Eval turns probabilistic LLM agents into auditable, production-grade software systems.

title: Expert pruning improves decode throughput up to 1.8 with minimal quality loss
description:
Current MoE inference pipelines still stall on expert traffic during batched decoding, limiting latency improvements despite sparsity. SlimWise shows that pruning experts only in the decode phase and reusing prefill KV caches can boost throughput by nearly twofold without perceptible quality loss.

Earlier serving optimizations either prune the full model—including the costly prefilling step—or accept a trade‑off where speed gains come at the cost of generation fidelity. Those approaches sacrifice the rich context built in the prefill stage, leading to noticeable drops in perplexity or output length when the same pruning ratio is applied during both phases.

On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, SlimWise improves decode throughput by up to 1.81× at 50 % expert pruning with minimal accuracy loss[1]. The system keeps the prefill stage untouched, activates only half of the experts during generation, and still delivers token‑level latency reductions that translate into a roughly 78 % end‑to‑end speedup in typical request patterns.

Without additional training, SlimWise’s KV cache handoff recovers much of the accuracy lost to pruning in many evaluated settings[1]. By feeding the decoder with the full‑model KV cache generated during prefill, the pruned model inherits a high‑quality attention context, so the model’s accuracy remains comparable to the unpruned baseline even when half the experts are disabled.

Because expert pruning preserves the attention architecture and KV cache format, this KV cache handoff requires no KV cache conversion[1]. The unchanged cache layout lets the runtime simply swap the weight mask between phases, eliminating costly data reshaping or additional memory copies that would otherwise erase any latency gains from pruning.

SlimWise’s gains are demonstrated on two MoE backbones and three pruning criteria; performance on larger models or more aggressive pruning ratios remains untested, and the low‑cost distillation stage—while helpful—adds a modest extra training step before deployment. One open question is whether dynamic token‑level expert selection could further tighten the latency–quality curve without requiring a static prune threshold.

Production stacks that serve Mixture‑of‑Experts should replace monolithic decode with a prefill‑decode split and directly feed the full‑model KV cache into a pruned decoder, eliminating the need for costly runtime cache rewrites. Re‑running latency benchmarks under this disaggregated regime will likely reveal hidden speed margins that current end‑to‑end numbers conceal.

References

  1. SlimWise: Decoupling Expert Pruning Across Prefill and Decode for Efficient MoE Serving

title: The AI experience doesn’t care about your org chart
description:
AI is bringing content design, enterprise content strategy, knowledge management, and model behavior into the same user experience. Our ways of working haven’t caught up.

Imagine a finance manager trying to understand why a supplier hasn’t been paid.

The enterprise application shows that the invoice has been approved. The manager asks the AI assistant when the supplier can expect payment, and the assistant explains that the invoice has completed the approval process and is ready for payment.

Except it isn’t.

The invoice is blocked because of a discrepancy between the invoiced amount and the purchase order. Approval and payment eligibility are different things, governed by different parts of the business process.

The assistant hasn’t necessarily misunderstood the approval status. But it has failed to understand what that status means in relation to everything else.

Maybe it retrieved documentation about invoice approvals without the information about payment blocks. Maybe the underlying business concepts aren’t represented consistently across systems. Maybe it didn’t have access to the current payment status. Or maybe it had the right information and still failed to interpret it correctly.

Those are different problems, often owned by different teams.

But from the user’s perspective, it’s one experience — and it’s broken.

This is one of the most consequential challenges emerging as AI becomes part of enterprise software. We’re bringing together content and knowledge ecosystems that we’ve historically managed separately, and we haven’t yet developed the ways of working to manage their interdependence.

We’re going to need more than better AI models, better content systems, or better design guidelines. We’re going to need to rethink how these things work together.

We’re talking about more than one AI transformation

One thing that makes this moment difficult to navigate is that we tend to talk about AI and content as though we’re discussing a single change.

We’re not.

In a 2026 article for Nielsen Norman Group, Sarah Gibbons articulated four different meanings of “AI design”: designing with AI, designing AI products, designing for AI agents, and designing the AI itself.

That distinction is useful because the implications for content work are dramatically different depending on which kind of AI design we’re talking about.

Consider two scenarios.

In the first, a product team uses AI to accelerate its existing design process. It has a content design system with established terminology, voice and tone guidelines, and interaction patterns. Designers use AI to generate candidate UI copy, and content designers review and refine it before shipping.

AI has changed how efficiently the team produces content, but the fundamental model is familiar. People design and approve a defined set of content before it ships, and the product displays that content according to established rules and conditions.

In the second scenario, the product generates content dynamically for each user, drawing on information about their task, their context, the state of the system, and relevant enterprise knowledge.

The content designer can’t anticipate or approve every possible sentence. Instead, they help design the system that determines what the experience should communicate, under what conditions, with which constraints, and how to evaluate whether it’s working.

That’s a fundamentally different design challenge.

And then there’s another dimension: an AI agent that needs to understand the same product well enough to take action on behalf of a user. The information and structures that make sense to humans may not be sufficient for an agent. The system needs reliable representations of concepts, relationships, actions, constraints, and permissions.

Those three situations map to the first three of Gibbons’s categories. The fourth, designing the AI itself, is what is being called things like model design, model behavior, context architecutre, or content engineering — and it shapes all of the others.

These scenarios don’t replace one another. They increasingly coexist, sometimes within the same product.

We’re only beginning to understand what that means for content work.

Specialization is increasing. So is interdependence.

There’s been considerable discussion about whether content design is splitting into different specializations.

One direction moves deeper into content systems: structured content, reusable patterns, guidelines, standards, and the infrastructure that allows content design decisions to scale.

Another moves toward model behavior design: shaping how AI systems communicate, interpret intent, manage ambiguity, explain their decisions, and respond in different situations.

I see value in recognizing these areas of expertise. They involve different technical knowledge, methods, and deliverables.

But there’s another area where content designers need to develop greater expertise: the semantic and context architecture that allows systems to work with meaning.

Taxonomies, ontologies, and knowledge graphs are becoming increasingly relevant to the experiences we’re designing.

These aren’t interchangeable technologies. Taxonomies help organize and classify concepts. Ontologies define concepts and relationships within a domain. Knowledge graphs can represent interconnected information in ways that systems can query and use.

Together, these kinds of structures can help establish shared meaning across systems.

A broader context architecture also needs to account for information about the user’s task, the current state of the product, relevant business rules, permissions, and other conditions that determine what information is appropriate at a particular moment.

For content designers, learning these concepts well enough to communicate with technical teams is a start.

But content designers should also learn to actively help shape the semantic architecture of the experiences they design.

Information architects, knowledge engineers, data specialists, and enterprise architects bring essential expertise to that work. Content designers add what has always been central to our discipline: terminology, conceptual models, information organization, user mental models, and the relationship between language and understanding.

The decisions encoded in a semantic model can have direct consequences for how a user experiences a product.

If a system represents two business concepts as equivalent when users understand them as distinct, that mismatch may surface in navigation, generated explanations, recommendations, or agent behavior.

That’s a UX problem, even if its source is several layers removed from the interface.

This is also why I’m cautious about drawing hard boundaries between emerging content specializations.

We need people who go deep into content systems, model behavior, and semantic architecture. But their work needs to share patterns, concepts, and principles if the experience is going to feel coherent.

An enterprise user might move between a traditional interface, dynamically generated explanations, an AI conversation, and an agent performing a task.

Those interactions won’t use identical language or behave in identical ways, nor should they. But they need to share an understanding of how the product works.

Specialization makes sense. Separation is where I get concerned.

AI is bringing separate content ecosystems into the same experience

The challenge becomes even larger when we look beyond UX content design.

Enterprises have long divided responsibility for content and knowledge across different domains.

UX content design teams work on product experiences, language, interaction patterns, and design systems. Technical communication teams create and maintain product documentation, help content, and educational materials. Marketing, support, and other functions manage their own content ecosystems.

Content strategy and content ops establish content models, workflows, governance, lifecycle processes, and systems for managing content at scale, but usually within individual domains rather than across them.

Information architecture shapes how information is organized, labeled, and connected within each of these domains. Knowledge management varies even more: in some organizations it means maintaining documentation and knowledge bases, and in others it means capturing, sharing, and applying organizational expertise.

Now AI engineering teams are building systems that retrieve knowledge, assemble context, generate responses, and enable agents to act, often drawing on content and information governed by all these different functions.

These connections aren’t entirely new. Documentation has always needed to reflect how products actually work. Terminology in an interface should be consistent with the language in support content. But teams could often manage these dependencies through periodic reviews, handoffs, and separate publication processes.

AI is changing the nature of that dependency.

An AI assistant might draw on technical documentation to answer a question within a product. The semantic architecture can influence what information it retrieves and how it interprets that information. Content design patterns can shape how the assistant communicates its response. And business rules and permissions can determine what actions an agent can take on the user’s behalf.

The experience is increasingly assembled from information and design decisions managed by different teams, sometimes in real time.

That creates new operational challenges. When something goes wrong, no single team may have the visibility or authority to diagnose and fix the problem. And a change made in one system can have consequences for experiences that another team owns.

This is why content ops and design ops need to work much more closely together. But the coordination can’t stop there. It also needs to involve the people responsible for enterprise knowledge, semantic architecture, AI engineering, and evaluation.

We need to scale coordinated decisions

Large enterprises have always struggled to scale content design.

One response has been to invest in reusable patterns, standards, guidelines, design systems, and operational processes that allow teams to create more consistent experiences without requiring a content designer to personally review every decision.

But another response, less often acknowledged, has been to accept uneven quality. When headcount shrinks or demand exceeds capacity, some experiences simply receive less attention. That compromise was never ideal, but organizations could often contain its consequences within particular products or channels.

AI makes that compromise harder to sustain. Inconsistencies in terminology, guidance, or source content can now influence generated responses and actions across many interactions.

Investments in reusable systems are becoming even more essential. AI can also make them more powerful by bringing guidance directly into the tools and workflows where experiences are designed and built.

But scaling content production isn’t the same as scaling content design.

AI can help us generate more content, more quickly. That doesn’t guarantee the content is appropriate, coherent, accurate, or useful.

Scaling content design means making good design decisions repeatable across an organization.

And increasingly, those decisions don’t live in one team’s tools or processes.

Consider what happens when an enterprise changes the terminology for an important business concept.

Traditionally, a content design team might update the design system and work with product teams to change UI strings. A documentation team might update help content and published materials according to its own release process.

Now we may also need to consider whether the change affects a taxonomy or ontology, what an AI assistant retrieves, which terms it uses in generated explanations, how an agent interprets a request, and what our evaluation tests consider a correct response.

Who identifies all those dependencies? Who decides which changes are significant? How do the changes move through the different systems? How do we know when they’re complete?

These are operational questions.

Combining all these functions into one organization could create as many problems as it solves.

What we need is a more integrated operating model: shared standards where they matter, clear ownership, connected workflows, and governance that accounts for how decisions propagate across systems.

In practice, that means:

  • Shared governance of enterprise terminology and semantic standards, so a change to an important business concept is made deliberately and carried everywhere it matters.
  • Content design patterns that inform both traditional interfaces and AI behavior, so the product communicates as one product.
  • Workflows that identify which experiences need review when enterprise knowledge changes, so teams find the dependencies before users do.
  • Feedback loops that run in the other direction, so what we learn about AI behavior and user understanding reaches the teams who can fix the source.

That last one deserves more attention than it usually gets.

If testing reveals that an AI assistant consistently misunderstands a business concept, how does that information reach the teams responsible for the underlying knowledge, semantic structure, or content model?

If a documentation team discovers that users misunderstand a particular process, how does that insight influence the design of the product and its AI interactions?

We’ve spent years developing ways to scale the work within content functions. Now we need to get better at scaling the work across them.

Evaluation is becoming part of content and experience operations

Evaluation is another area where this interdependence becomes clear.

With traditional UI content, we can review a relatively stable set of artifacts before they ship. We can assess the language, test it with users, and make revisions.

When an AI system generates responses dynamically, we can’t review every possible output in advance.

Instead, we need to evaluate the system’s behavior across different situations and continue evaluating it as the system, its knowledge, and its users’ needs change.

We’re still at a very early stage of learning how to do this well.

Much of the initial work must be exploratory. People examine outputs, identify patterns, form hypotheses about why something went wrong, and determine what needs to change.

As with the invoice, the cause can sit in several places. Sometimes the issue is with the model’s behavior. Sometimes the system retrieved the wrong information. Sometimes the underlying content was incomplete, outdated, or contradictory. Sometimes the system lacked the context necessary to interpret the request correctly.

And sometimes the response is factually accurate but still represents a poor experience.

It might misunderstand the user’s intent, communicate uncertainty inappropriately, fail to explain an important limitation, or suggest an action without adequately establishing what the user wants.

These are different kinds of problems, and they require different kinds of expertise.

I expect we’ll get much better at translating what we learn into evals: repeatable tests that assess how AI systems perform against defined expectations. These can help us identify recurring failures, assess the impact of changes, and improve the system over time.

But first, we need to understand what we’re evaluating.

It’s not enough to ask whether a response is accurate. We also need to ask whether it was appropriate in context, supported the user’s goals, and made sense as part of the overall experience. And when the system recommends or takes action, we need to evaluate whether users understand what’s happening and retain appropriate control.

Go back to the finance manager. An evaluation that only checked whether the assistant described the approval status accurately would have passed that response. The manager still wouldn’t know when the supplier would be paid.

One tempting response to poor AI outputs is to give the system more context. But more isn’t necessarily better. Irrelevant, outdated, or conflicting information can actually make responses less reliable. The challenge is determining which knowledge, rules, and details about the user’s task are needed in a particular situation, and using evaluation to understand whether we’re providing the right context.

This is another place where content designers and strategists, design researchers, AI engineers, and the people responsible for enterprise knowledge and semantic architecture need to work closely together.

As these practices mature, we’ll be able to automate more of our evaluations. But human judgment will remain essential, not only for assessing outputs, but for identifying new failure patterns and refining our understanding of what good AI behavior looks like.

This is particularly important for experience quality, where success depends on context, user expectations, and judgments that aren’t always easily reduced to pass-or-fail criteria. Automated evals and human evaluation will need to work together, each informing and improving the other.

The operational challenge will be to turn what we learn through evaluation into improvements across the systems involved.

An evaluation finding shouldn’t stop at identifying a bad response. It should help us diagnose what needs to change, whether that’s the model’s instructions, the knowledge it retrieves, the semantic architecture, the interaction patterns, or even the underlying business process. And that diagnosis needs to reach the people who can address it.

Those changes then need to be governed, tested, and maintained.

Evaluation used to be a checkpoint at the end of the design process. It’s becoming one of the ways we maintain the experience itself.

Enterprise knowledge is becoming part of experience architecture

There’s a larger shift underneath all of this.

We’ve often treated content as something we produce, manage, and deliver through products and systems.

But AI is making content and knowledge increasingly important to what those products and systems can understand, communicate, and do.

Enterprise knowledge is becoming part of experience architecture.

That doesn’t mean every document becomes a product component, or that every content specialist needs to become an AI engineer.

It means decisions about how information is structured, represented, governed, and made available can directly shape the behavior and quality of an experience.

And it means the distinction between designing an experience and designing the knowledge that supports it is becoming harder to maintain.

I’m not suggesting that anyone has figured out the right organizational structures or operating models for this work. I certainly haven’t. We’re just beginning to understand the scope of the transformation, and the practices we need will develop through experimentation, collaboration, and learning from real systems.

But I’m increasingly convinced that improving each discipline independently won’t be enough.

We’ll need deeper expertise in content systems, model behavior, semantic architecture, and the work of creating, organizing, and maintaining enterprise knowledge. Just as importantly, we’ll need better ways of connecting the people and systems responsible for them.

Five years from now, I suspect it will seem obvious that we couldn’t design intelligent experiences while treating product content, enterprise knowledge, and AI behavior as largely separate concerns.

We’ll still need specialists. These are complex areas that deserve deep expertise.

But I think we’ll also have developed a much more integrated understanding of what we’re collectively designing.

The experience doesn’t care about our org chart.

Increasingly, our org chart has to care about the experience.

The AI experience doesn’t care about your org chart was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
