title: A Status Is Not Proof: The Laptop I Never Received, and the Job I Was Handed Anyway
description:
In October, an online marketplace asked me to return a laptop I never received.

A day later, after looking into it, they agreed I had never received it. Then they asked me to go and fetch it, and send it back myself.

I said no.

This is a small story compared with the ones I usually write about. But it shows, step by step, how one wrong record can travel through a system until a customer who did nothing wrong is first treated as the problem, and then asked to be the fix.

I write about this kind of thing because it is my work. I review how software behaves when something goes wrong, and my standard is called No Silent Failure. In this story, every failure stayed silent until it reached me.

What happened

In August, I ordered a refurbished laptop from a marketplace that sells devices from independent sellers. The order was set for delivery to my home.

It never arrived. Later that month, the order was refunded. As far as I was concerned, that was the end of it.

Two months later, in mid-October, I got an email from the marketplace's customer care team. It said the courier and the seller had both confirmed that the parcel was "successfully collected" from a service point, and that I therefore had both the laptop and the refund. It asked me to send the laptop back, and offered a 10% discount code once the seller confirmed it had arrived.

The same conversation also held a prepaid return label and a checklist for shipping the laptop back, including photographing it from every angle.

I had never been to a service point for this order. I had never asked anyone to collect it for me. I had never seen the laptop.

I wrote back the same day. I explained that the parcel never reached me, that I hadn't collected it or authorized anyone else to, and that under UK consumer law, goods remain the seller's responsibility until they are in the buyer's hands. I asked them to get the courier's proof of collection: the date and time, the service point's address, and the name, signature or ID given at the counter.

Later that day, a second agent replied. They apologized, opened an investigation, and promised an update within one business day.

The next day, the update came. The parcel had never been collected. It was still sitting at the service point.

And then: since the order had already been refunded, would I please go and collect it, and send it back to the seller with the prepaid label? As a goodwill gesture, here was a 10% discount code.

Where it went wrong

I have no view inside any of these systems, so I can only describe what they did from the outside. From the outside, I count six points where a check, a link or a handoff was missing.

1. The refund closed the money, not the parcel

When the order was refunded in August, the money side of the order was finished. The parcel side was not. By the marketplace's own account, the laptop sat at a service point for about two months after the refund, and nothing in the process asked where it was or brought it back to the seller.

A refund on an undelivered order is a moment when two records should agree: the payment and the parcel's location. Here, one record said "done", and the other was never asked.

What would work: when an order is refunded before delivery, the same step tells the courier to return the parcel to the seller, and the case stays open until the seller confirms it has arrived.

2. A status became a statement about me

Somewhere, a record said the parcel had been collected. Both the courier and the seller passed that on. My guess is that both were reading the same tracking entry, which would make two confirmations really one source repeated twice. But that is only a guess.

What I do know is what happened next. "Collected" became "you have the device and the refund". A line in a tracking system turned into a statement about a person, and was sent to that person, without anyone asking where the proof was.

What would work: before telling a customer they have something, attach the evidence: when, where, and who signed. If that evidence can't be found, ask the customer a question instead of telling them a fact.

3. The return started before anyone checked

The message asking me to return the laptop came with everything needed to do it: a prepaid label, a link to the return instructions, and advice on photographing the device. The process had already moved on to the next step, built on a claim nobody had looked at.

Automation is good at taking the next step quickly. That is exactly why steps that assume something about a person need a check in front of them.

What would work: when a return comes from a courier's status rather than from the customer's own request, ask the customer first. Create the label after they confirm, not before.

4. The message lived somewhere I wasn't looking

The email didn't appear on the order in my account. My first job was working out whether it was even real, because an unexpected email saying you have something you shouldn't, with a link and an attachment, is exactly the shape of a scam. Only later did I find the conversation under a separate messages section.

When a company tells someone they are holding something that isn't theirs, that message should be easy to verify and easy to answer. If it is hard to find, the person spends their effort proving the message is genuine before they can even reply to it.

What would work: attach every conversation about an order to that order, so the customer sees it in context and knows it's real.

5. The burden of proof landed on me

I was asked, in effect, to account for something I had never had. That is asking someone to prove a negative, and it is very hard to do. I can't photograph a parcel I never saw.

So I did the one thing I could: I asked for the proof that should have been there from the start. As soon as someone looked for it, the story changed. The parcel had never left the service point.

That is the part I keep coming back to. The truth was available all along. It took a customer asking for evidence before anyone checked.

What would work: the side making the claim holds the evidence. If a system says a customer has something, the system's own records should show it before the customer is ever contacted.

6. The cleanup was handed back to me

Once it was clear I had never had the laptop, the request changed from "send it back" to "go and get it, then send it back". The parcel was with the courier. The laptop belonged to the seller. The one person in the chain who had no part in what went wrong was the person asked to put it right.

It would have meant two trips, carrying a heavy laptop between them, for a parcel I never wanted to see again. It would also have meant signing for it, and that signature would have created exactly the record that started all this: proof that the parcel had been in my hands.

The discount code was offered as goodwill. But a discount on a future purchase isn't payment for work, and this was work that was never mine to do.

What would work: send the physical fix to the parties who have custody. The seller and the courier can return an uncollected parcel between themselves, and the customer only needs to hear that it's done.

What worked

I want to be fair here, because one part of this worked well.

The second agent read what I wrote, apologized, and opened an investigation the same day. They gave me a time frame and kept to it. When the facts came back, they told me plainly that the parcel had never been collected.

That is what a good handoff looks like: a person takes the customer's account seriously, checks it, and reports back. The investigation did its job. What came after it is where the process went wrong, because the system's answer to "the customer was right" was still "so the customer should fix it".

What I said

I said no, politely and in writing. I explained that I wouldn't collect the parcel or sign for it, and that returning it was a matter for the seller and the courier. I asked for three things: for them to arrange the return directly with the seller and the courier, for written confirmation that nothing more is needed from me, and for the note on my account saying I had collected the parcel to be corrected.

The shape of it

Put the six points together, and a familiar shape appears:

  1. A record is wrong.
  2. The system treats it as true and acts on it.
  3. The person on the other end has to show that it's wrong.
  4. When they do, the cost of fixing it still lands on them.

None of this needed anyone to be careless or unkind. Everyone I dealt with was polite. The trouble lives in the joins: between the payment and the parcel, between tracking and customer care, and between "the customer was right" and "who fixes it". Each join is a place where a check could sit, and in this story none did.

That is what I mean by No Silent Failure. A parcel sitting at a service point for two months is a silent failure. A wrong status is a silent failure. Neither made a sound until it reached me, and by then it arrived as an accusation.

My recommendations for businesses

If you run a business that ships things, or any process where a record can be wrong, here is what I'd recommend. None of it is expensive. Most of it is about where you place a check, and who you ask first.

  1. Keep the evidence with the status. A status like "collected" or "delivered" should carry its proof: when, where, and who signed or showed ID. If the proof is missing, the status is a lead to look into, not a fact to act on.

  2. Ask before you tell. When your records and your customer's experience might disagree, start with a question: "Our records show this parcel was collected on this date. Does that match what you saw?" A question invites the truth. A statement makes the customer defend themselves before they can help you.

  3. Give every refund a matching return. When you refund an order that never arrived, the same step should bring the goods back to the seller, and someone should confirm that they arrived. Money and goods should close together.

  4. Pause automation before it points at a person. Automate the routine steps freely. But when a step tells a customer they owe something, have something, or must do something, let a person or a clear rule confirm the facts first.

  5. Watch for things that sit still. A parcel waiting at a service point for two months is a record that stopped moving. Set a normal time for each stage, and flag anything that stays longer, so you notice it before your customer does.

  6. Keep the conversation where the customer looks. Put every message about an order on that order, in the customer's account. Then they can see at a glance that it's genuine, and answer it without first wondering whether it's a scam.

  7. Send the fix to whoever holds the problem. If the goods are with your courier or your seller, the fix belongs to them. The customer's part is simply to be told when it's done.

  8. Make the apology match the mistake. If a customer was told they had something they didn't, say so plainly, correct the record, and confirm it in writing. If you offer a goodwill gesture, make it a thank you for their patience, never a payment for more of their time.

Happy customers don't need a business that never makes mistakes. They need a business that notices its own mistakes first, owns them, and puts them right without handing the work back.

Here is a simple test: count what the customer had to do to fix your error. Every message they wrote, every proof they had to find and every trip they were asked to make shows how much of your process still rests on them. The goal is zero.

A status is not proof. A refund is not a return. And the customer is not the courier.

title: Sliced Wasserstein Sketches with Error Certificates
description:
arXiv:2610.20788v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compact representations that support geometrically meaningful comparisons are valuable for learning from probability distributions. We study optimal, free-weight $M$-atom quantization of one-dimensional probability measures in quadratic Wasserstein distance and extend it to higher dimensions via slicing. Using $L$ shared projections yields a sketch with $O(LM)$ comparison time. Our main result is an exact decomposition of squared distance error into residual and partition-mismatch terms, yielding computable certificates for arbitrary centroid sketches. For optimal sketches, a finite $(2+\delta)$ moment for some $\delta>0$ guarantees $O(M^{-1})$ error in the finite-direction sliced distance, while equal-mass sketches can converge more slowly. Each slice preserves its mean, while storing residual energies enables covariance recovery from sufficiently many generic directions. Experiments on document, point-cloud, and flow-cytometry benchmarks show that optimal sketches substantially reduce storage while preserving the classification performance of uncompressed sliced distances. They also improve generalization from few labelled subjects and support end-to-end learning as compact pooling layers.

title: A Quarantine Ledger for Agent Patches
description:
A CI suite runs 300 tests. Two of them fail on almost every diff. The failures land in files nobody touched.

Reviewers learn to scroll past red. An agent opens forty diffs a week. Each one looks green except the usual two. The suite stops being a gate and becomes wallpaper.

This post describes a workflow for that situation. It has three parts: a quarantine ledger with expiry dates, a property harness for agent patches, and a fixture budget that makes silent fixture edits visible. Every snippet below is runnable pytest against a small synthetic importer. The counts are illustrative, not measured.

The ledger

A ledger is one JSON file in the repo. Each entry names a test, an owner, a reason, and an expiry date.

{
  "tests": [
    {
      "id": "tests/test_billing.py::test_retry_after_webhook",
      "owner": "payments",
      "reason": "clock-dependent, fails ~3 of 20 runs on clean main",
      "opened_at": "2026-10-16",
      "expires_at": "2026-11-13"
    }
  ]
}

A conftest hook reads the ledger at collection time. Unexpired entries get skipped. Expired entries run again, which is the enforcement you want. The skip markers themselves are plain pytest, documented at https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/skipping.html.

# conftest.py
import json
import time
from pathlib import Path
import pytest

LEDGER = Path("quarantine.json")
RUN_LOG = Path("artifacts/quarantine-run.json")


def pytest_collection_modifyitems(config, items):
    entries = json.loads(LEDGER.read_text())["tests"] if LEDGER.exists() else []
    today = time.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    by_id = {e["id"]: e for e in entries}
    report = {"date": today, "skipped": [], "expired": [], "runnable": 0}

    for item in items:
        entry = by_id.get(item.nodeid)
        if entry and entry["expires_at"] > today:
            item.add_marker(pytest.mark.skip(reason=f"quarantined: {entry['reason']}"))
            report["skipped"].append(item.nodeid)
        else:
            if entry:
                report["expired"].append(item.nodeid)
            report["runnable"] += 1

    RUN_LOG.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    RUN_LOG.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2))

Expiry is the whole point. A skip without a date is a deletion in disguise. The run log also gives you one number to watch. The skipped count should fall over a quarter. If it rises, the suite is decaying faster than you repair it.

Properties instead of examples

Agent patches tend to preserve shapes and break rules. An example test asserts that row 42 credits ten dollars. A property test asserts that accepted plus rejected equals input, for any input.

Here is the code under test, small enough to reason about.

# app/importer.py
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class ImportResult:
    accepted: int
    rejected: int
    credited_sum: int
    checksum: int


class Importer:
    def __init__(self, conn):
        self.conn = conn

    def run(self, rows):
        accepted = rejected = credited = 0
        for row in rows:
            if row["amount"] == 0:
                rejected += 1
                continue
            cur = self.conn.execute(
                "insert or ignore into ledger_row (id, amount, currency) values (?, ?, ?)",
                (row["id"], row["amount"], row["currency"]),
            )
            if cur.rowcount == 1:
                accepted += 1
                credited += row["amount"]
        self.conn.commit()
        checksum = self.conn.execute(
            "select coalesce(sum(id), 0) from ledger_row"
        ).fetchone()[0]
        return ImportResult(accepted, rejected, credited, checksum)

And the fixtures, with an in-memory database and a seeded generator.

# tests/conftest.py
import random
import sqlite3
import pytest
from app.importer import Importer


class Snapshot:
    def __init__(self, conn):
        self.conn = conn

    def count(self, table):
        return self.conn.execute(f"select count(*) from {table}").fetchone()[0]

    def sum(self, table, column):
        return self.conn.execute(
            f"select coalesce(sum({column}), 0) from {table}"
        ).fetchone()[0]


@pytest.fixture
def snapshot():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    conn.execute(
        "create table ledger_row (id integer primary key, amount integer, currency text)"
    )
    yield Snapshot(conn)
    conn.close()


@pytest.fixture
def importer(snapshot):
    return Importer(snapshot.conn)


@pytest.fixture
def rows():
    def build(seed, n=40):
        rng = random.Random(seed)
        return [
            {
                "id": rng.randrange(10_000),
                "amount": rng.randrange(-500, 500),
                "currency": rng.choice(["USD", "EUR"]),
            }
            for _ in range(n)
        ]

    return build

Two properties carry most of the weight here: idempotency and conservation.

# tests/properties/test_import_properties.py
import pytest

pytestmark = pytest.mark.property

SEEDS = range(1, 26)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS)
def test_import_is_idempotent(seed, importer, snapshot, rows):
    batch = rows(seed)
    first = importer.run(batch)
    assert snapshot.count("ledger_row") == first.accepted

    second = importer.run(batch)
    assert second.accepted == 0
    assert snapshot.count("ledger_row") == first.accepted


@pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS)
def test_rejection_never_breaks_totals(seed, importer, snapshot, rows):
    batch = rows(seed)
    result = importer.run(batch)
    assert result.accepted + result.rejected == len(batch)
    assert snapshot.sum("ledger_row", "amount") == result.credited_sum

Twenty-five seeds across two properties is fifty cheap runs. That is a friendlier signal than one hand-written example. It also survives refactors better, because the invariant does not move when the row format does. When a property fails on seed 17, you keep seed 17 forever as a regression.

A fixture budget

Fixtures are shared state that agents can quietly rewrite. Pin a fingerprint and fail the build when the fixture set drifts.

# tests/test_fixture_budget.py
import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

PINNED = "9f2c41ab77de0013"  # update only in the same diff as a ledger entry


def fixture_fingerprint(root="tests/fixtures"):
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    for path in sorted(Path(root).rglob("*")):
        if path.is_file():
            digest.update(path.name.encode())
            digest.update(path.read_bytes())
    return digest.hexdigest()[:16]


def test_fixtures_did_not_drift():
    assert fixture_fingerprint() == PINNED, "fixture set changed; justify it in the diff"

This test is intentionally annoying. It forces the patch author to state why the fixture moved. Most agent diffs leave fixtures alone, so the cost is near zero. The benefit arrives the day a diff rewrites a fixture to match a bug.

Re-entry

Quarantine ends with evidence, not optimism. Run the test against clean main, twenty times, before you delete the entry.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/reentry.sh <nodeid>
set -euo pipefail
TEST_ID="$1"
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  pytest "$TEST_ID" -q || { echo "flake on run $i"; exit 1; }
done
python - "$TEST_ID" <<'PY'
import json, pathlib, sys
path = pathlib.Path("quarantine.json")
data = json.loads(path.read_text())
data["tests"] = [t for t in data["tests"] if t["id"] != sys.argv[1]]
path.write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2))
print("removed", sys.argv[1])
PY

Twenty passing runs on clean main is a weak guarantee, and you should say so out loud. It still beats deleting a skip because the log annoyed someone.

Deciding what to do

What you observe Ledger action Effect on the merge gate
Fails 2 of 10 runs on clean main Open entry with a 30-day expiry Excluded from the verdict, still recorded
Fails only on the agent diff No entry Merge blocked, treat as a real regression
Passes locally, fails in CI Freeze clock, timezone, locale New entry for the environment diff
Diff edits fixtures Fingerprint test fails Author must justify the change
Property fails on one seed Keep that seed as a regression Merge blocked until fixed

The rule behind the table is simple. Unknown failures lose their vote. Known failures keep it.

Where MonkeyCode fits

MonkeyCode is the operator's open-source project, and the fit here is narrow. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The operator states that free model access and a free server option are available, with a free allowance of 10 million tokens.

I have not verified quotas, hardware, or how long the offer lasts. Treat every limit as changeable and check the current terms before designing a nightly job around it. If the numbers hold for you, the free model access is where patch generation happens, and the free server option is where the repeated sweeps run. Fifty property runs per diff adds up quickly, and that repeated compute is exactly what a metered runner pushes you to skip.

Nothing above depends on MonkeyCode. Swap in any model and any runner, and the ledger, the properties, and the fingerprint test behave the same way.

Limits and who should skip this

A ledger without expiry becomes a graveyard. Review the skipped count monthly and treat growth as a bug. Property tests only work when you can state the invariant in one sentence. If you cannot, example tests are honest enough.

This approach fits three groups poorly. Teams with a deterministic suite should fix the flake and move on. Teams that need per-test evidence for compliance should not hide tests behind a skip marker. Teams without a named ledger owner should not start, because the file will rot within a quarter.

Start with one entry and one property. The ledger is not a place to hide failures. It is a record of what you do not know yet, with a date attached.

title: Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.20832v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Despite their extensive pretraining knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, large language models (LLMs) struggle to adaptively gather information in experimental design tasks. We study how to amortize sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) into an LLM by explicitly training the reasoning that guides action selection using information-gain rewards. Our approach specifies the experimental generative model independently of the LLM's own beliefs, allowing us to optimize expected information gain under a model of our choosing. We investigate the design choices for amortization, including alternative generative-model constructions, reward estimation, hypothesis-space specification, multi-step objectives, and computational costs relative to training- and inference-time BED baselines. On Twenty Questions, the resulting policies improve information acquisition and task performance, outperform inference- and training-time BED baselines at substantially lower computational cost, and generalize to unseen categories. We further demonstrate positive transfer from Twenty Questions training to Medi-Q, a real-world clinical dialogue benchmark. These results suggest that information gathering can be learned as a generalizable reasoning skill in LLMs.

title: The best workflow engine is a programming language
description:
The idea of orchestrating long-running, stateful logic on top of unreliable, stateless infrastructure isn't new. We've had message queues, job runners, microservice choreographies, and full-blown workflow engines for a long time. What we never had was a version of it that felt good to write.

I'd spent about six months working on a fork of Temporal, mostly on weekends, trying to turn it into a serverless answer with DX that felt more Vercel-native. Eventually it dawned on me that to ship that experience, I'd need to own the execution environment too. So I dropped the fork, joined Vercel, and started hacking on a new framework from scratch alongside Nathan Rajlich.

Code is already a DAG

A workflow is a DAG, a directed acyclic graph. Before Temporal (and Cadence before it), nearly every workflow framework made you draw that DAG by hand. Apache Airflow is the canonical example. You describe your pipeline as an explicit graph of tasks and dependencies, and your actual logic gets buried inside the nodes."

That always felt backwards to me. We already have a tool for expressing "do this, then that, and these in parallel, and branch here." It's called a programming language. An abstract syntax tree is a DAG. Software itself is a DAG.

I knew that in the abstract, but it didn't truly hit me until I saw Temporal, where you write what looks like normal sequential code and the engine makes it durable underneath. It was the dream all along.

What running Temporal taught me

Temporal is great once your infrastructure exists. I was starting from scratch, and setting it up meant:

  • Standing up Temporal Cloud (or self-hosting the server: Frontend, History, Matching, and Worker services, plus a Cassandra/Postgres/MySQL backend and sharding).

  • Running your own worker fleet: Temporal never executes your code. Your workers poll the server and run your workflows and activities. In practice that's a Kubernetes cluster you own.

  • Wiring it all together: task queues, activity registration, client config.

  • Managing the workers yourself: scaling, uptime, restarts, and the build-and-deploy pipeline for the worker processes.

  • Setting up encryption: workers talk to the control plane over the internet, so you're configuring mutual TLS and a data converter to encrypt payloads before they leave your environment.

Once all of that was in place, the workflow dream mostly became real. But I wanted something easy to start that could still scale as my project grew into production.

Versioning in-flight workflows

Beyond owning the worker build-and-deploy process myself, there was a harder problem. If I changed my workflow code while runs were still in flight, I was kind of stuck. There were no longer any workers running the old, correct version of that code. Replay would hit my new code with an old event history and break on a non-determinism error.

The official answer is the patching API (patched() / GetVersion). You branch your code on a change ID and march it through a multi-stage deprecate-then-remove lifecycle as old runs age out of retention. It works, but it means evolving workflow code very carefully. Over enough changes, the workflow code rots into a thicket of version flags.

I couldn't explain Temporal signals

Whenever I tried to show running Temporal demos to friends, signals / queries / updates turned into the single most confusing part. They're three separate primitives for getting data in and out of a running workflow, each with its own rules. Queries can't block, signals are fire-and-forget and get buffered, and you have to know when to reach for which. The concepts did land but it wasn't very intuitive. To me, that was a DX smell. If I can't explain the human-in-the-loop primitive without a whiteboard, it's too complicated. That's why Workflow SDK replaces all three with a single primitive, the hook.

What Workflow SDK looks like today

With Workflow SDK, you write one file of normal code. "use workflow" marks an orchestrator; "use step" marks a unit of side-effecting work. In between it's just await, try/catch, Promise.all, loops, and conditionals.

A few things fall out of that one file:

  • No DAG file: The compiler reads the directives and splits the code into workflow and client/step bundles. The graph is your control flow.

  • Retries: Uncaught errors retry by default. Throw new FatalError(...) to stop. Throw new RetryableError(..., { retryAfter }) for custom backoff. Set fn.maxRetries = n to tune.

  • Ad-hoc webhooks: const webhook = createWebhook() creates a real, callable URL inside a running workflow, in a single line. The run parks until someone hits it, with no route or handler.

  • Hooks: Webhooks are sugar over a more general primitive. Create a hook with createHook<T>(), await it, and the data someone sends is what comes back. This one concept replaces signals, queries and updates

Here's an ad-hoc webhook end to end. An approval that can pause for seconds or for weeks, with nothing extra to deploy.

A library, not a platform

Traditional engines make you bring infrastructure to the framework. Workflow SDK brings the framework to infrastructure you already have.

DBOS had the right idea

While I was working out how to actually build this, I studied every workflow engine I could find. The one that stood out was DBOS, an open-source durable execution library that runs almost entirely client-side. The only thing its server needs is Postgres.

Workflow SDK adopts that shape. There's no bespoke orchestrator to self-host or pay for, and no new stateful system to operate. The only infrastructure it needs is infrastructure you already run: your app, a database, a queue. All the heavy lifting happens in the library.

The backend is swappable

Workflow SDK pushes the idea past one database. The whole thing is a spec, a way of writing workflows, steps, and hooks that any infrastructure can back. You mix and match the substrate to fit your stack:

  • Redis / Kafka / etc. for your streams

  • Postgres / Cassandra / the file system / Turso / Durable Objects / etc. for durability

  • Vercel Queues / SQS / Cloudflare Queues / etc. for your queue

The runtime only ever talks to a single interface, the World, which covers storage, queuing, auth, and streaming. Swapping any layer never touches your workflow code.

In fact, we maintain a first-party Postgres world inspired by DBOS, using Postgres for durability, queueing, and streaming. And in every world, there's no worker fleet and no control plane. A framework integration exposes two plain HTTP endpoints that deploy like the rest of your app.

Even the Vercel backend is "just" a CRUD API

The Vercel Workflow Server, the thing that backs workflows on Vercel, is stateless and does no compute or orchestration at all. It's just like the Postgres world, but extended with Vercel's authentication and multi-tenancy. A CRUD API, nothing more. It even runs as a regular Vercel deployment. All the heavy lifting, all the actual workflow logic, lives in the open-source, Apache-licensed client-side library, which can be extended freely.

So the "managed" offering isn't a black box you're locked into. It's just another World, one implementation of a spec you can read, fork, and extend. The data format isn't bespoke either. You can swap out any piece of the stack.

Some patterns lean on the platform

I should be upfront. A few of Workflow SDK's design choices are shaped by how Vercel executes code. The clearest example is versioning, the same code-evolution problem that makes traditional engines so painful.

Our answer is to pin each run to the specific deployment that started it. The run keeps executing against the exact copy of the code it began on, so changing your workflow never breaks in-flight runs. It's a clean solution, but it was only easy to build because Vercel already keeps immutable deployments around for long periods. The official Postgres world doesn't track and route versions this way yet. Encouragingly, community worlds have already implemented the spec as intended. Platformatic's version-safe durable workflows on Kubernetes is a great example.

And I think that's exactly the right trade. Pinning moves the complexity of versioning off the developer writing workflows and onto the infrastructure. That burden lands on the world author, the infra provider, and us as the framework authors. If everyone using a framework hits the same hard problem and has to solve it themselves in the same painful ways, the framework has failed them. A good framework moves that complexity upstream.

Steps should be free

Performance is the next big problem for us to solve. Invoking a step isn't cheap. Each step involves networking and a trip over a queue to durably commit its result correctly. For correctness, that's the right thing to do. But it works against the pitch that distributed computing should feel like function calls.

When you write ordinary code, you don't think twice about the overhead of a function call. It's so fast it's effectively free. But if every step carried a heavy overhead, the abstraction leaks. You start rationing steps, reasoning about granularity, declining to turn a small function into a checkpoint because it's "not worth a step."

So the goal is blunt: steps should be free.

In the ideal version of this, you could take any function in an existing codebase, add "use step", and everything would just work, with no serialization constraints and no performance penalty.

That dream drives us.

What if any developer could turn a plain function into something with the performance, networking, observability, and availability of a standalone microservice, but using just two words: "use step"? That would change how we write code.

Workflow v5 (in beta at the time of writing) already delivers up to a 5x performance improvement with no change to the user-facing API, and v6 will push it further while making third-party worlds just as fast. We're sharing details as we go in this GitHub discussion, and you can start testing today with npm install workflow@beta.

I set out to build a durable framework that feels like writing ordinary code, runs on the infrastructure you already have, and is fast enough that you never think twice about reaching for a step. It's real today, and we're building the rest of it in the open.

Come build Workflow SDK with us

If designing durable systems under real-world constraints sounds like fun, the Workflow team at Vercel is hiring.

title: Environment variables now use Config and Secret types
description:
When you add or edit an environment variable in Vercel, you now choose Config or Secret instead of using the Sensitive toggle. Existing variables marked Sensitive are automatically treated as Secrets and continue to work without migration.

  • Config: The value remains readable after saving for members with access. Use Config for non-sensitive values you may need to inspect later, such as variables with a public framework prefix.

  • Secret: The value remains available to your deployments and can be replaced, but members cannot view or retrieve it after saving. Use Secret for passwords, API keys, and tokens.

You can select an environment or Preview branch for each value. The environment variable list in the dashboard shows each variable’s type and where it applies.

Team policy changes

The Enforce Sensitive Environment Variables team policy is deprecated with this update. When enabled, it required every environment variable created by a team member to be Sensitive, including non-sensitive configuration. With Config and Secret types, members can choose the appropriate type for each variable.

A new Separate Production Secret Values policy is available in your Security settings. When enabled, the Production value for a Secret must differ from the values used for the same key in Preview, Development, and custom environments.

If your team had the legacy policy enabled, confirm whether the Separate Production Secret Values policy should be enabled for your team. The deprecated policy is no longer enforced by the Vercel CLI.

Set variable types from the CLI

To choose whether an environment variable is a Config or Secret from the CLI, pass --visibility config or --visibility secret to vercel env add or vercel env update:

The existing flags continue to work. When --visibility is omitted, --no-sensitive maps to Config and --sensitive maps to Secret. After adding or updating a variable, the CLI output shows its type under Visibility.

Learn more in the Environment Variables documentation.

title: Sparse Attention for Video Generation Acceleration via Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search
description:
arXiv:2610.21129v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) dominate video generation but suffer from high inference cost due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Sparse attention mitigates this by skipping unnecessary computation in the attention matrix, but existing methods apply a fixed sparsity ratio throughout denoising and struggle to accurately determine which computations to skip. To address these limitations, we analyze attention dynamics through attention entropy and mean attention distance, and find that attention becomes increasingly concentrated across denoising steps. We further observe that blocks selected early continue to capture a large fraction of the total attention weight at later steps. These findings suggest two acceleration opportunities: the sparsity ratio should grow as denoising progresses, and earlier search results can be reused to reduce the search space. Based on these findings, we propose Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search (GSRS), a training-free framework that retains more computation early and progressively reduces it later, while restricting subsequent searches to an early candidate set to reduce search overhead. GSRS adopts Top-p selection for adaptive sparsity control, supported by a precise evaluation scheme that computes exact attention weights within the FlashAttention computation at negligible overhead. Experiments on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1 validate that GSRS achieves 1.55$\times$--2.21$\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality comparable to full attention.

title: PremiseCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of Human and AI Peer Reviews
description:
arXiv:2610.21046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.

title: Vercel Security Dashboard is now generally available
description:
The Vercel Security Dashboard is now generally available on all plans, giving you one place to see your security posture across every account and project.

You can access the Security Dashboard in the UI or run vercel security check in the Vercel CLI.

As teams grow and coding agents make it faster to spin up projects, small misconfigurations add up quietly. The Security Dashboard automatically flags issues like:

  • Team members without 2FA

  • Long-lived credentials that can be replaced with OIDC

  • Public preview deployments

  • Non-sensitive and stale environment variables

The Security Dashboard UI

Misconfigurations are ordered by risk with the most severe first, and each finding links to the settings that fix them.

Findings that are just noise for your team can also be muted, and all results can be exported to a CSV file for triage or reporting.

The Security Dashboard CLI

You can also run the same checks in your terminal through the new Vercel CLI vercel security check command, allowing your agents to work through the findings for you.

An agent using vercel security check --findings can read what failed, apply the fix and re-check to confirm. Fixes an agent can apply include:

  • Turning on Git fork protection

  • Marking an environment variable as sensitive

  • Replacing a static credential with OIDC federation

You can also scope the check to one project with --project when you want a narrow change set.

In CI or any other non-interactive environment, the command writes the report to stdout as JSON automatically, giving agents structured output without extra flags.

Get started by running your first scan from the Security Dashboard, and learn more in the Security Dashboard documentation.

title: Go Realtime Client After Logout: 3-Step Token Disconnect Recovery
description:
Short answer: treat logout as a two-part control-plane operation. Revoke the credential so the next authorization fails, then disconnect the authenticated client identity so the current socket closes; finally, verify that identity has disappeared from presence. Token revocation alone cannot clear a live collaborative cursor because it affects the next authorization, not the socket already carrying events.

The page that matters is not "revoke returned successfully." It is "logged-out learner still present in the support editor." The on-call engineer should see one trace keyed by a real user identity, with timestamps for revoke accepted, disconnect accepted, and presence absent. If the first two succeed but presence remains, recovery is incomplete.

This is an SLO problem before it is a vendor problem. Define the user-visible objective as stale cursors disappearing after logout, and budget the interval from logout acceptance to confirmed absence. Do not claim success at the first control-plane response.

Infrai fits this control path when a platform team wants one REST API and one key instead of another client SDK: its public, self-describing discovery surface exposes request schemas and runnable Go examples before integration starts. The trade-off is equally concrete: teams that need a specialist realtime client's native ecosystem should evaluate Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub first.

How can a realtime client stay connected after logout?

A live socket has already passed authorization. Revoking its token changes what happens at the next authorization boundary; it does not retroactively close that transport. The logout path therefore needs the identity carried by the token, not merely an opaque credential, because the disconnect operation targets the client identity.

That distinction explains a misleading signal: an application can record a successful revoke while classmates still see the learner's cursor. Both observations can be true. The wrong action was measured.

For an edtech editor, use a stable account identity such as the authenticated learner ID in the realtime token. Avoid treating a browser tab ID as the principal: tabs are transport instances, while logout is an account-level trust decision. Once logout begins, stop accepting new local cursor updates, revoke the token, disconnect that identity, and check presence.

Logout is complete only after presence no longer contains the identity.

Trace the alert back to the missing signal

A useful alert starts with the symptom and works backward. Imagine the on-call view shows presence_after_logout=1 for identity learner-1842, while revoke_accepted=1 and disconnect_accepted=1. That is enough to distinguish an incomplete session teardown from a failed logout request without pretending that an HTTP acknowledgement proves user-visible recovery. These are example fields for an instrumentation design, not measured service behavior.

Instrument three milestones under one logout operation ID:

  1. Record when token revocation is accepted. This protects the next authorization boundary.
  2. Record when identity disconnect is accepted. This targets the current connection.
  3. Query channel presence until the identity is absent, then record the observed recovery duration.

Keep retries bounded. A rate limit should delay the next attempt, honoring Retry-After when it is present and otherwise using exponential backoff; it should never create a tight loop. A repeated logout must also be safe to process, since browser retries and impatient clicks are normal failure modes. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window for capabilities marked idempotent, but check the public discovery record for the exact capability before depending on that behavior.

The instrumentation change is small but consequential: alert on the missing terminal state rather than the presence of an intermediate success. Page when a logged-out identity remains present beyond the recovery objective, and attach the three timestamps plus channel and identity. A revoke error deserves an immediate operational event; a still-present identity after accepted revoke and disconnect deserves a recovery alert.

Inspect the recovery surface with Go

Before implementing the state machine, inspect the live capability records instead of copying request fields from prose. This runnable Go program calls Infrai's public discovery endpoint, handles status and rate limits, and confirms that the three required operations are advertised. Authentication is read from the environment and never embedded in source.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Capability struct {
    Method string `json:"method"`
    Path   string `json:"path"`
}

type Discovery struct {
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

func getDiscovery(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key string) (Discovery, error) {
    var result Discovery
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return result, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return result, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return result, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return result, ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return result, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &result); err != nil {
            return result, err
        }
        return result, nil
    }
    return result, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    discovery, err := getDiscovery(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, key)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    wanted := map[string]string{
        "revoke token":       "token/revoke",
        "disconnect identity": "user/disconnect",
        "verify presence":     "presence/get/{channel}",
    }
    found := make(map[string]bool, len(wanted))
    for _, capability := range discovery.Capabilities {
        for operation, suffix := range wanted {
            if strings.HasSuffix(capability.Path, suffix) {
                found[operation] = true
            }
        }
    }
    for operation := range wanted {
        fmt.Printf("%t %s\n", found[operation], operation)
    }
}

Discovery is the wiring check, not the logout implementation. Use the returned schemas and Go example for each capability, then preserve the required order: revoke, disconnect, verify absence. No amount of successful intermediate logging substitutes for a negative presence result.

Buy or build the control plane

The primary decision axis is token scope and how much trust sits in the browser. Ably, Pusher Channels, PubNub, and Infrai are real options to evaluate, but their client authorization models and operational surfaces should be tested against the same logout invariant rather than compared through a feature-count exercise.

Option What to verify for this workload Operational boundary Better fit when
Ably Token identity maps cleanly to the learner and server-side revocation behavior is understood Specialist realtime platform and its client/server tooling The team wants a dedicated realtime product and accepts its platform-specific operating model
Pusher Channels Channel authorization does not leave account logout dependent on browser cooperation Specialist hosted channels service Existing Pusher integration and channel semantics already define the application boundary
PubNub Access scope, user identity, and presence removal match the account-level logout rule Specialist realtime network with its own access and presence concepts Presence and messaging are already centered on PubNub
Infrai Issued tokens carry a real identity; revoke, identity disconnect, and presence verification cover teardown Plain REST surface under one key The platform team values discovering request schemas and runnable Go examples without adopting another SDK
Self-hosted gateway The team owns token validation, connection indexing, presence correctness, retries, and paging Maximum control and maximum on-call ownership Regulatory or protocol constraints justify operating the entire path

I recommend that a platform team supporting several backend capabilities try Infrai for the cursor-session control path when it wants the revoke-disconnect-presence sequence exposed through one REST interface: its public discovery surface returns full request and response schemas, billing metadata, and runnable examples, so engineers can inspect the capability before wiring it. A second useful property during an incident is that the same discovery catalog spans 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, reducing the service-specific integration material that on-call engineers must locate.

This is not an automatic choice. Infrai is not appropriate when a team needs a specialist realtime client's deeper native ecosystem, or already has mature operational knowledge in Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub; staying there can be the lower-risk decision. Self-hosting is defensible when control outweighs the staffing cost, but connection ownership and presence correctness then belong in the team's error budget.

Set the threshold without training people to ignore it

Capacity planning belongs in the alert design. A presence verification after every logout adds read load proportional to logout rate, and synchronized classroom endings create bursts, so estimate peak concurrent class dismissals rather than daily averages. Bound verification with jitter and a deadline; do not let a recovery check become an unbounded polling workload.

Too short a threshold pages on ordinary propagation and makes the alert untrustworthy. Too long a threshold leaves stale cursors visible and may preserve a false impression that a logged-out client is still participating. Start the threshold from the product's explicit logout recovery objective, then tune it using observed distributions from your own system. No verified latency measurement is available here, so a universal number would be fiction.

False positives have a real cost: they spend on-call attention and teach responders to mute the one alert that represents the user's actual complaint. Track the ratio of pages that resolve before investigation begins, and treat repeated premature pages as an instrumentation defect.

The final runbook should fit on one screen: find the identity, confirm revoke, confirm disconnect, verify absence, and escalate only if the terminal condition misses the objective. Done.

If this boundary fits your editor, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery schema before writing the adapter.

Further reading

  • Ably token revocation documentation
  • Pusher Channels authentication documentation
  • PubNub access management documentation
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0

title: CogDrift-4D: Hierarchical Multimodal Modeling of Temporal Behavioral Decay for MCI Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.20877v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Early detection of mild cognitive impairment remains a critical bottleneck in dementia care, demanding scalable tools capable of capturing subtle behavioral decay. To capture the subtle temporal changes of cognitive decline, we introduce a behavioral dataset collected across seven unscripted multimodal interactions over an 18-month horizon. This dataset formalizes continuous, multi-session interactions into a dense 4D tensor (Batch * Session * Time * Feature) that explicitly preserves concurrent local dynamics alongside long-term changes. To effectively process these complex behavioral patterns, we propose CogDrift-4D: a novel, hierarchical 4D Transformer framework. To capture the complex trajectory of cognitive decline, CogDrift-4D implements a dual-level behavioral fatigue and drift modeling architecture. At the intra-session level, the model computes localized least-squares regression slopes to quantify the acute ``fading'' of frame-level facial action units and acoustic energy. At the inter-session level, a recursive cross-attention feedback encoder acts as a cumulative fatigue accumulator, mapping the patient's continuous behavioral drift across successive sessions. To mitigate environmental noise and track failures across sessions, a localized Quality Gate dynamically filters low-integrity features before final fusion, also an early fusion that integrates semantic insights with raw physical dynamics. Evaluated on structured verbal and linguistic interactions, our architecture successfully detects MCI with a classification accuracy of 0.733 +- 0.13 and an F1-score of 0.716 +- 0.14, outperforming advanced baselines. The framework provides a mathematically rigorous, scalable, and robust foundation for home-based, real-time dementia screening.

title: TRACER: Trajectory-Aware Tool Retrieval for LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21267v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern agents select tools from registries, but exposing entire registries incurs high token costs and can impair selection as they grow. We present TRACER, a retrieval front-end that indexes observed tool-call sequences in a trie and ranks continuations using a learned blend of empirical and contextual priors. On a mixed retail-and-telecom $\tau^2$ environment, TRACER improves GPT-5.4's tool-selection accuracy by 4.7 points while reducing input tokens per step by 80%, exposing just 5 of 128 tools. In autonomous full-turn execution, it matches GPT-5.4's full-registry task success with 61% fewer input tokens per step. Across six environments and four models, TRACER improves tool-selection accuracy over full-registry selection in 21 of 24 model-environment pairs, with average gains of 6 to 10 points; the three exceptions trail by at most 2.2. We analyze failures in both regimes to identify directions for future work.

title: Compute that takes any shape
description:
Workloads differ in how long they run, how much memory they take, and how much of the environment they control. That previously meant a different compute primitive for each job, so product iterations required provisioning infrastructure, not just working on a feature.

We built Vercel so that none of this has to be your problem. The compute layer is a single system with a simple job. Take any workload, assemble the machine it needs, swap configuration on the fly, and absorb burst capacity in real time.

We call this Fluid.

Builds ran on it first, then sandboxes, and now functions. If you've shipped on Vercel, you've been on Fluid without knowing it.

Fluid compute now runs over 15 million builds a day, 25 million sandboxes a week, and a trillion requests a month.

A history of compute

Changing a machine used to mean changing it by hand. You went down to the computer store, bought a hard drive or a stick of RAM, and swapped it in yourself.

Then you could rent bare metal when you needed it, and use it to serve a website, host a database, or send email.

Then the cloud let you request a machine in any configuration you wanted, choose its operating system, use it, and throw it away when you were done.

For agents, even the cloud is too slow. A standard VM can't provision fast enough to keep up with how they work, but this is where Fluid excels.

How a workload runs on Fluid

When a workload comes in, Fluid assembles a machine to fit its shape. If an agent needs to run code, Hive provides an isolated VM, usually one already warm, so it's ready instantly. Your own image boots on top as the environment. A Drive connects, and your files are right where you left them, because storage was never tied to the machine.

Each workload needs something different. A build is compute-bound, so it wants a beefy machine, heavy on CPU and memory. A function is IO-bound, loading specific code to run the instant a request lands, usually on a small VM. A sandbox is flexibility-bound, taking whatever configuration the work calls for with a Drive attached for user data.

Fluid compute is the execution model that all of this leans on. Many requests run on one instance, instead of each spinning up its own. Work starts immediately, and with Active CPU pricing, you pay for CPU only while your code is working, not while it waits on a database or a model.

Hive

Hive is the "hardware." We built it to control our own compute. It provisions the isolated machines every workload runs on. It picks the right machine for the job, keeps each one isolated in our multitenant environment, and does it at global scale. Hive gives every product one control-plane API, so our teams build on the same foundation instead of each maintaining their own.

Fluid images

Fluid images is the environment. Until now the OS was fixed. You ran the one the cloud gave you, not the one you chose. Now you push your own image to Vercel Container Registry, and run it across sandboxes and functions. In the background, Vercel converts images into a Fluid image in a format we call VHS (Vercel Hive Snapshot), the optimized boot format behind Dockerfile deploys and sandbox custom images, so it can resume rather than boot and a custom machine is ready in milliseconds. It uses the same technology behind Sandbox Snapshots, so optimizations in one product carry to the rest. v0 already uses it to build and run its own development environments.

Vercel Drives

Vercel Drives is the storage. Your files live in portable, durable storage that travels with the workload instead of being stranded on one machine's disk. Storage that outlives the compute attached to it is what makes the rest of the system work. Drives aren't bound to a single machine, you can swap the compute underneath it and pick up exactly where you left off in the next session. Drives attach to sandboxes today, in private beta, and extend to the rest of Fluid from there.

One system underneath

These are different shapes of the same system, not separate platforms. Because it's one compute layer underneath every product, a gain in boot time, isolation, scheduling, or caching lands across functions, sandboxes, and builds at once, instead of being rebuilt three times. New shapes of compute can be added without rebuilding the foundation. You don't end up with separate primitives that drift apart.

And it's real, not a diagram: Hive provisions a full VM in milliseconds and brings your filesystem state along with it, so you get isolation stronger than an isolate or a container, without paying for it in startup time.

The agent workload

For an agent to move fast, it needs the right machine, and it needs it immediately. The faster the machine assembles, the faster the agent works.

An agent runs untrusted code, so the machine needs a secure boundary. It brings its own tools, so the machine needs its own environment. And because an agent spins up and tears down constantly, its state has to outlive the compute. Fluid assembles that machine immediately, and then a fresh one for the next task.

For years, the machine was a fixed thing, and you fit your work to it.

In Fluid you describe the work, and the machine forms around it.

Read more
