title: Amazon SageMaker Studio simplifies getting started for new AI/ML builders with new sign-in options
description:
Amazon SageMaker Studio now lets new customers sign up with their Google, GitHub, or Apple credentials and land inside a fully configured Studio environment - no traditional AWS account setup and no console navigation required.

Previously, new customers who discovered a model on Hugging Face or an AWS product page had to complete a multi-step AWS account creation process, provide a credit card, navigate the AWS Console to find SageMaker AI, configure an environment, and set up IAM permissions before they could begin working. With earlier launches, we reduced environment setup to twenty seconds, pre-configured model customization permissions, and introduced deep links from Hugging Face and AWS product pages so customers could land directly inside Studio with a model pre-loaded. Now, with new sign-in options, customers complete a simplified sign-up using an existing identity, receive free credits as part of the AWS Free Tier with no credit card required in most cases, and arrive inside a ready-to-use SageMaker Studio environment where they can immediately fine-tune, evaluate, and deploy foundation models. Customers can invite team members by email, and collaborators sign in with their own email credentials to access the shared Studio environment, including shared models, notebooks, and endpoints without configuring IAM users or permissions. When a project grows beyond free credits, customers can upgrade to a paid plan and set a spend limit to stay within budget. Verified customers continue to receive default GPU access to G5, G6, G6e, and G4dn instances across endpoint deployments, training jobs, and notebooks without requesting quota increases.

This feature is available in all AWS Commercial Regions where Amazon SageMaker Studio is supported. To get started, visit any supported model on Hugging Face and select "Customize and Deploy on SageMaker AI" or "Deploy on SageMaker AI," or click Get Started from the SageMaker Studio page. To learn more, see the AWS sign-up documentation and SageMaker Studio setup guide.

title: Why a Deleted Linux File Can Still Consume Disk Space
description:
Your root partition is at 100%, you ran rm on a 50GB log file, and df still reports zero free bytes. Here is how inodes, unlinked file descriptors, and kernel references keep ghost data alive, and how to recover disk space without restarting production.

A critical disk alert fires on your phone.

A busy database node or API host just crossed 99% disk capacity on /var. Applications begin failing. MySQL refuses incoming transactions with disk-full errors. Docker containers start getting evicted by the kubelet. System loggers choke on write operations.

You SSH into the struggling server and run a quick scan to find the space hog:

ls -lhS /var/log/app/

-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser  52G Oct 16 19:40 debug.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser 1.2G Oct 16 00:00 access.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 appuser appuser 210M Oct 15 00:00 app.log.1

A rogue debug flag was left enabled in production, and debug.log has blown up to 52 gigabytes.

Relieved that you found the culprit so fast, you run the obvious command:

rm -f /var/log/app/debug.log

The shell prompt returns instantly. You run ls -lh /var/log/app/debug.log to make sure it is gone. The terminal confirms the file no longer exists:

ls: cannot access '/var/log/app/debug.log': No such file or directory

Problem solved, right? You run df -h to verify how much breathing room you just recovered:

df -h /var

Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda2        60G   60G     0 100% /var

The partition is still at 100% capacity. Available space is still 0 bytes.

Confused, you run du to inspect actual directory usage:

du -sh /var

4.8G    /var

du says /var is only consuming 4.8 gigabytes. df insists all 60 gigabytes are completely full.

Where did the other 55 gigabytes go? Did the filesystem corrupt itself? Is the storage hardware failing?

Neither. You just walked straight into one of the most common traps in Linux systems administration: the open unlinked file descriptor.

rm Does Not Delete Files

To understand where your disk space went, you have to unlearn what the rm command actually does.

On Linux, rm does not mean "delete file". It stands for remove, which invokes the unlink() or unlinkat() system call inside the Linux kernel.

Unix filesystems like ext4, XFS, and btrfs do not store file data inside filenames or directories. Storage architecture in Linux is split into three separate layers:

First, Directory Entries (dentries). A directory in Linux is simply a special structured file that maps human-readable names to numbers. When you look at /var/log/app/debug.log, the string debug.log is just a pointer sitting in a directory table. That pointer references an integer called an inode number.

Second, Inodes (Index Nodes). The inode is the actual metadata structure of the file. It stores file ownership (UID and GID), access permissions, file size, modification timestamps, and pointers to the physical data blocks or extents on the storage drive. Crucially, the inode also stores an internal counter named i_nlink (the hard link count). This tracks how many directory entries point to this specific inode.

Third, Data Blocks. These are the raw 4KB blocks on the physical drive where the file contents live.

When you execute rm -f /var/log/app/debug.log, the kernel only performs two specific actions:

// Simplified kernel logic during unlink()
unlink("/var/log/app/debug.log");
// 1. Remove the dentry "debug.log" from the directory
// 2. Decrement the inode link counter: inode->i_nlink--;

The directory entry is erased, so ls cannot find it. The i_nlink counter drops from 1 to 0.

However, the kernel will not free the allocated data blocks on disk back to the filesystem free block bitmap just because i_nlink reached zero.

The kernel tracks a second reference counter: the open file table references.

Whenever an active process opens a file with the open() system call, the kernel creates a struct file entry in its internal system-wide open file table and increments an in-memory reference counter (f_count).

The storage driver adheres to a strict rule:

Disk blocks and inode allocations are only released when both conditions are met:

  1. The hard link count reaches zero (i_nlink == 0).
  2. Every active process closes its file descriptor pointing to that inode (f_count == 0).

If an application (like your Node.js backend, a Java worker, Python daemon, or Nginx) opened /var/log/app/debug.log when it booted up and is still running, that process holds an active file descriptor pointing directly to the inode.

When you ran rm, you severed the directory entry. But the application still holds the open file handle.

The inode remains alive in kernel memory. The data blocks remain marked as active and allocated on your NVMe or SSD drive. The process keeps writing fresh bytes into those unlinked blocks.

You did not delete the file. You only removed its name from the phone book while the phone call was still active.

The Feud Between df and du

Now the conflicting numbers between df and du make complete sense.

These two utilities measure disk space from two completely different perspectives in the kernel.

du stands for Disk Usage. It is a directory tree crawler. When you run du -sh /var, the utility executes opendir("/var") and starts walking through every subdirectory with readdir(). For every filename it encounters, it calls the lstat() or stat() system call to ask the filesystem for the block count allocated to that path.

Because you ran rm, the directory entry for debug.log is gone. There is no filename for du to discover. It skips right past it. As far as du is concerned, those 52 gigabytes do not exist because they have no presence in the directory hierarchy.

df stands for Disk Free. It does not look at directories, filenames, or paths at all.

When you run df -h /var, df issues a single system call directly against the filesystem: statvfs() or statfs().

struct statvfs buf;
statvfs("/var", &buf);
// Reads total blocks, free blocks, and available blocks directly from the superblock

This system call queries the filesystem superblock and block group allocation bitmaps in kernel memory. The superblock tracks the real physical state of the storage partition:

  • Total block count on the partition
  • Total allocated blocks currently marked as "in use" in the allocation bitmap
  • Total free blocks available for new writes
  • Reserved blocks reserved strictly for the root user

Because your background daemon still has the file open, the filesystem driver continues to mark all 13 million 4KB blocks of that 52GB file as allocated. The superblock counters do not change.

df tells you the physical reality of your storage device. du tells you the visible contents of your directory tree.

When df and du disagree by gigabytes, it almost always means an active process is holding open a deleted file.

Tracking Down the Ghost Files

Finding these unlinked files does not require guessing which daemon is responsible. The Linux kernel exposes every open file handle in userspace.

There are two primary ways to track down these ghost files.

The fastest tool is lsof (List Open Files). You can instruct lsof to filter specifically for files whose hard link count is less than 1:

lsof +L1

The +L1 flag tells lsof to look for open files where link count < 1. If you want to restrict the search to a specific mount point like /var, add the filesystem path:

lsof +aL1 /var

Here is what the output looks like on a production host:

COMMAND     PID    USER   FD   TYPE DEVICE   SIZE/OFF NLINK      NODE NAME
node      24810 appuser   14w   REG    8,2 55834574848     0 144182931 /var/log/app/debug.log (deleted)

The columns lay out the exact crime scene. Under COMMAND and PID, you get the executable (node) and process ID (24810). The FD column shows descriptor 14w, meaning file descriptor 14 opened for writing. Most tellingly, NLINK shows 0, confirming the directory entry was unlinked from disk while SIZE/OFF reveals all 55.8GB sitting in limbo under /var/log/app/debug.log (deleted).

If lsof is not installed on a minimal container or hardened production bastion, you do not need to install anything. You can query the /proc virtual filesystem directly.

Every running process in Linux has a directory at /proc/<PID>/fd/. Inside this directory, the kernel creates symbolic links for every open file descriptor assigned to that process.

When a file is unlinked while still open, the kernel automatically appends the string (deleted) to the symlink target.

You can sweep the entire system in one command:

find /proc/*/fd -ls 2>/dev/null | grep '(deleted)'

144182931  54525952 -rw-r--r--   1 appuser appuser 55834574848 Oct 16 19:40 /proc/24810/fd/14 -> /var/log/app/debug.log\ (deleted)

The output reveals everything: Process ID 24810 holds file descriptor 14, which points to your unlinked 55GB log file.

To inspect what the process is currently doing with that descriptor, you can check its descriptor status in /proc:

cat /proc/24810/fdinfo/14

pos:    55834574848
flags:  0102001
mnt_id: 34
ino:    144182931

The pos field shows the current write offset in bytes. It is sitting at 55.8GB and steadily growing. The daemon is actively writing to a file that you thought you deleted twenty minutes ago.

Freeing the Space Without Killing the Process

Once engineers discover the PID holding the deleted file, their immediate reflex is to kill the process:

kill -9 24810

Do not do this unless you have no other choice.

Killing a production process drops active user websocket connections, terminates inflight database transactions, invalidates local cache pools, and can trigger cascading failure alerts in your monitoring stack. If the process is a core database or monolithic service, restarting it might take ten minutes of cache warm-up time.

There is a clean, zero-downtime way to reclaim every single byte immediately:

Truncate the open file descriptor directly through /proc.

Run this command as root or as the user owning the process:

> /proc/24810/fd/14

Alternatively, you can use the truncate utility:

truncate -s 0 /proc/24810/fd/14

Or redirect from /dev/null:

cat /dev/null > /proc/24810/fd/14

Why does this work?

/proc/<PID>/fd/14 is a magic symlink maintained by the Linux kernel. When you redirect output into this path using >, your shell opens the underlying inode referenced by descriptor 14 with the O_TRUNC flag.

The kernel receives the truncate request, bypasses the missing directory entry, and executes do_truncate() directly against the active inode.

The filesystem driver immediately deallocates the extents and data blocks mapped to that inode and writes them back into the free block bitmap. The file size resets to 0.

Now check df -h /var:

df -h /var

Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda2        60G  4.8G   53G    9% /var

Instantly, 53 gigabytes of storage return to the available pool. The disk-full alerts resolve. And best of all, the application never stopped running.

The O_APPEND Caveat

There is an important technical nuance you must understand before truncating a running file descriptor.

How the application behaves after truncation depends on how it originally opened the file.

Most production logging libraries, syslog daemons, and web servers open log files with the O_APPEND flag:

int fd = open("/var/log/app/debug.log", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_APPEND, 0644);

When a file descriptor has O_APPEND enabled, the Linux kernel guarantees that before every single write() call, the file offset is automatically reset to the current end of the file.

When you truncate the file to 0 bytes, the next write goes to offset 0. The file continues logging normally from byte zero.

However, if an unusual program opened the file without O_APPEND and maintains its own internal byte counter using lseek():

lseek(fd, current_offset, SEEK_SET);
write(fd, buffer, length);

If the internal offset was at 55GB, truncating the inode sets the length to 0, but the application's next write might seek forward to byte 55,000,000,000 and write 100 bytes there.

This creates a sparse file. On modern filesystems, sparse files do not consume physical disk space for unwritten zero-blocks, so your available disk space will still remain free. But reading the file will return gigabytes of null bytes (\0) before reaching the new log lines.

In practice, virtually all standard daemons (Nginx, Apache, Node.js Winston/Bunyan, Python logging handlers, Logstash) use append mode or standard streaming writes, making descriptor truncation completely safe.

Other Ways Linux Hides Deleted and Used Space

Open unlinked file descriptors account for roughly 90% of df vs du discrepancies. But when lsof +L1 returns completely empty and your disk is still full, one of three other subtle filesystem mechanisms is stealing your storage.

1. The Over-Mounted Directory Shadow

This is the sneakier cousin of the open file descriptor problem.

Suppose an automated backup script runs early during server initialization before external storage volumes are attached:

tar -czf /mnt/backups/system-backup.tar.gz /var/data

The backup script dumps 40 gigabytes into /mnt/backups/. At this moment, /mnt/backups/ is just a regular directory residing on your primary / root partition.

Twenty minutes later, a systemd automount unit or storage script mounts an external EBS volume, SAN LUN, or NFS share on top of that mount point:

mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/backups

What happened to the 40GB archive?

The mount operation did not delete it. It shadowed it.

When a filesystem is mounted on a directory, the kernel redirects all directory lookups to the root inode of the newly mounted device. The original directory contents on the underlying filesystem become completely invisible to ls, du, and find.

du /mnt/backups now measures the secondary disk /dev/sdb1.

Meanwhile, your root filesystem /dev/sda1 is still holding those 40 gigabytes of data blocks, and df -h / reports that root is almost full.

How do you check for shadowed files without unmounting active storage?

Use a bind mount to inspect the underlying root filesystem in an unmasked state:

mkdir -p /mnt/root_inspect
mount --bind / /mnt/root_inspect

A bind mount creates an alternate view of the root filesystem without re-triggering the mount points stacked on top of it.

Now you can inspect the shadowed directory directly:

ls -lh /mnt/root_inspect/mnt/backups/

There is your missing 40GB file. You can safely remove it from /mnt/root_inspect/mnt/backups/, and df on your root partition will instantly drop.

When you are done, clean up the inspection mount:

umount /mnt/root_inspect
rmdir /mnt/root_inspect

2. The Hard Link Survival Trap

Another common misconception is assuming rm frees disk blocks when a file has hard links.

If another engineer or an automated snapshot script created a hard link to your log or data file:

ln /var/log/app/debug.log /opt/archive/debug_backup.log

Both filenames point to the exact same inode number. You can verify this with ls -l or stat:

stat -c "Links: %h Inode: %i File: %n" /var/log/app/debug.log /opt/archive/debug_backup.log

Links: 2 Inode: 8912345 File: /var/log/app/debug.log
Links: 2 Inode: 8912345 File: /opt/archive/debug_backup.log

Notice the link count is 2.

When you run rm /var/log/app/debug.log, the kernel decrements the inode link count from 2 to 1.

Because i_nlink is still greater than zero, the inode is not marked for deletion. Not a single data block is freed. The 50GB file remains fully allocated on disk under the name /opt/archive/debug_backup.log.

If you run rm on a large file and space is not reclaimed even though no process holds it open, check if the file had multiple hard links before deletion:

find / -inum 8912345 2>/dev/null

3. Reserved Filesystem Blocks (The 5% Buffer)

Have you ever seen df -h show that a filesystem is 100% full, but the math does not add up?

Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1       100G   95G     0 100% /

Total size is 100G. Used space is 95G. Why is Available space sitting at 0 instead of 5G?

By default, the mke2fs utility reserves 5% of total filesystem blocks exclusively for the root user when creating ext2/ext3/ext4 partitions.

The reasoning dates back to early multi-user Unix systems:

  • It prevents unprivileged user processes from completely filling the disk, which would prevent system daemons (like sshd, syslog, or postfix) from writing state.
  • It mitigates filesystem fragmentation by ensuring the allocation engine always has contiguous blocks available.

On a 20GB disk created in 2005, a 5% reserve was only 1GB. On a modern 4TB NVMe drive, 5% is a staggering 200 gigabytes of wasted storage that regular service accounts cannot use.

When your application service account hits this 5% wall, its writes fail with ENOSPC: No space left on device, even though physical blocks are empty.

You can inspect and adjust this reserved percentage on a live, mounted ext4 filesystem with tune2fs:

tune2fs -l /dev/sda1 | grep "Reserved block count"

To reduce the reserve from 5% to 1% (or even 0% on a dedicated non-root data partition), run:

tune2fs -m 1 /dev/sda1

This immediately releases 4% of the partition's total capacity back to general users and background services without a reboot.

Exactly One Surprising Fact

The fact that unlink() keeps open files alive until process termination is not an accident, a bug, or an oversight of early filesystem design.

It was an intentional, foundational security and design pattern invented by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie in the early 1970s for Unix.

In Unix, programs frequently needed temporary scratchpad files for sorting, staging intermediate compiler output, or buffering pipeline streams. If a program crashed or was terminated with kill, temporary files littered /tmp and required manual cleanup scripts.

Thompson and Ritchie designed unlink() so that a program could create a file, immediately call unlink() on it, and continue reading and writing to its file descriptor in private memory.

Because the file had no directory entry, no other user on the shared multi-user mainframe could see the file, guess its name, or tamper with its data. And the microsecond the program finished or crashed, the kernel automatically cleaned up every single allocated disk block.

Modern Linux filesystems formalized this exact pattern in Linux kernel 3.11 with the O_TMPFILE flag passed to open():

int fd = open("/tmp", O_TMPFILE | O_RDWR, 0600);

This creates an anonymous, completely invisible inode that never exists in any directory tree from the moment of creation. It consumes disk blocks while open, and vanishes without a trace the moment the descriptor closes.

How to Prevent the Ghost File Trap in Production

Now that you understand the mechanics, here is how to make sure this never catches your team off guard again.

1. Never rm an Active Log File

If a service is currently running, never use rm on its active log files. Always truncate them instead:

# Good: Frees disk space immediately while keeping the file descriptor valid
> /var/log/app/debug.log

# Also good:
truncate -s 0 /var/log/app/debug.log

Truncation preserves the directory entry, resets the file length to zero, and forces the filesystem to reclaim the physical disk blocks instantly. The application continues logging without missing a write or needing a restart.

2. Configure logrotate Correctly

Most ghost file incidents occur because of misconfigured log rotation.

There are two primary paradigms in logrotate:

Approach A: Copy and Truncate (copytruncate)

/var/log/app/*.log {
    daily
    rotate 7
    compress
    missingok
    copytruncate
}

The copytruncate directive instructs logrotate to copy the live log file to a backup name (e.g., debug.log.1), and then truncate the original file in place to 0 bytes.

This is ideal for applications that do not support reloading log file handles (such as third-party binaries or proprietary Java apps). Because the original file is never unlinked, its descriptor remains intact.

Approach B: Move and Signal (create + reload signal)

/var/log/nginx/*.log {
    daily
    rotate 14
    missingok
    compress
    delaycompress
    sharedscripts
    postrotate
        [ -f /var/run/nginx.pid ] && kill -USR1 $(cat /var/run/nginx.pid)
    endscript
}

In this model, logrotate renames access.log to access.log.1 and creates a fresh empty access.log.

At this exact instant, Nginx is still writing to descriptor pointing to access.log.1.

The postrotate block sends the USR1 signal to Nginx. Nginx intercepts USR1, closes its existing file descriptors, and reopens /var/log/nginx/access.log.

If someone deletes the postrotate section or the signal fails because of an incorrect PID file path, the daemon will hold the rotated or unlinked file open forever.

3. Monitor Unlinked File Descriptors

Do not wait for a 100% disk outage to discover deleted files.

If you use Prometheus and the node_exporter, configure alerts on the divergence between filesystem size and available bytes:

# Alert when unlinked files or reserved blocks consume more than 15% of partition
(node_filesystem_size_bytes - node_filesystem_free_bytes) - (node_filesystem_size_bytes - node_filesystem_avail_bytes)

Alternatively, add a simple periodic cron check or Datadog custom metric that counts the volume of open unlinked files:

lsof +aL1 /var -F s | grep '^s' | cut -c 2- | awk '{s+=$1} END {print s/1024/1024 " MB"}'

The 60-Second Ghost File Triage Playbook

When df reports that a disk partition is full but du cannot find the files, follow this sequence:

First, identify all open files with zero directory links on the affected mount:

lsof +aL1 /mount_point

Second, if lsof is not available, sweep the process descriptors in /proc:

find /proc/*/fd -ls 2>/dev/null | grep '(deleted)' | sort -k7 -n

Third, note the Process ID (PID) and File Descriptor (FD) of the largest unlinked file.

Fourth, reclaim the disk space immediately without killing the process:

> /proc/<PID>/fd/<FD>

Fifth, verify that disk space has returned:

df -h /mount_point

Sixth, if the application supports signal reloading, notify it to close and reopen logs cleanly:

kill -HUP <PID>
# Or for Nginx:
kill -USR1 <PID>

Seventh, if lsof showed zero deleted files, check for shadowed files trapped under an active mount point:

mkdir -p /mnt/temp_root && mount --bind / /mnt/temp_root
du -sh /mnt/temp_root/* | sort -h
umount /mnt/temp_root && rmdir /mnt/temp_root

Wrapping Up

Storage in Linux is governed by reference counting, not desktop trash cans.

When you run rm, you are only removing a label from a directory index. As long as any running process keeps that file handle open, the Linux kernel protects those data blocks from being overwritten.

The next time df and du tell you two conflicting stories during a storage incident, do not reboot the server and do not reach for kill -9. Look at the file descriptors in /proc, truncate the open handle, and get your disk space back in seconds without taking your services down.

What is the largest ghost file you have ever chased down in production, and which daemon was stubbornly refusing to let it go?

If this breakdown saved you hours of debugging or gave you something practical to use in production, consider buying me a coffee. Your support directly fuels independent, zero-fluff Linux and DevOps technical guides.

title: Building a Go CLI Tool with Cobra and Configuration Management
description:
Most CLI tools in Go start the same way: a handful of flag.String calls and an os.Args slice you're hand-parsing two weeks later. It works until you need subcommands, persistent flags, or any real configuration — then it collapses. Cobra solves this, and Viper handles the configuration side, but combining them correctly takes a bit of setup you won't find in a single README.

Why Cobra (and Not Just flag)

The standard flag package is fine for simple tools, but it has no concept of subcommands. The moment your CLI needs myapp serve, myapp migrate, and myapp config set, you're implementing a command router by hand.

Cobra gives you:

  • Nested subcommands with inherited flags
  • Automatic --help generation
  • Shell completion (bash, zsh, fish, PowerShell)
  • Consistent error handling across commands

Get started:

go mod init myapp
go get github.com/spf13/cobra@latest
go get github.com/spf13/viper@latest

The canonical structure for a Cobra project:

myapp/
├── cmd/
│   ├── root.go
│   ├── serve.go
│   └── config.go
├── internal/
│   └── config/
│       └── config.go
└── main.go

main.go stays thin — just calls cmd.Execute().

// main.go
package main

import "myapp/cmd"

func main() {
    cmd.Execute()
}

Structuring Root and Subcommands

root.go defines the top-level command and persistent flags — flags available to every subcommand:

// cmd/root.go
package cmd

import (
    "fmt"
    "os"

    "github.com/spf13/cobra"
    "github.com/spf13/viper"
)

var cfgFile string

var rootCmd = &cobra.Command{
    Use:   "myapp",
    Short: "A production-ready CLI tool",
    Long:  `myapp is a CLI tool that demonstrates Cobra + Viper integration.`,
}

func Execute() {
    if err := rootCmd.Execute(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

func init() {
    cobra.OnInitialize(initConfig)
    rootCmd.PersistentFlags().StringVar(&cfgFile, "config", "", "config file (default: $HOME/.myapp.yaml)")
    rootCmd.PersistentFlags().String("log-level", "info", "log level: debug, info, warn, error")
    viper.BindPFlag("log_level", rootCmd.PersistentFlags().Lookup("log-level"))
}

func initConfig() {
    if cfgFile != "" {
        viper.SetConfigFile(cfgFile)
    } else {
        home, err := os.UserHomeDir()
        cobra.CheckErr(err)
        viper.AddConfigPath(home)
        viper.SetConfigType("yaml")
        viper.SetConfigName(".myapp")
    }

    viper.AutomaticEnv()
    viper.SetEnvPrefix("MYAPP")

    if err := viper.ReadInConfig(); err == nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "Using config file:", viper.ConfigFileUsed())
    }
}

A few things worth noting here:

  • cobra.OnInitialize runs initConfig before any command executes — this is how Viper gets loaded before your command logic runs.
  • viper.SetEnvPrefix("MYAPP") means MYAPP_LOG_LEVEL maps to log_level in Viper's key space.
  • viper.AutomaticEnv() enables environment variable lookup automatically.

Now add a subcommand:

// cmd/serve.go
package cmd

import (
    "fmt"

    "github.com/spf13/cobra"
    "github.com/spf13/viper"
)

var serveCmd = &cobra.Command{
    Use:   "serve",
    Short: "Start the HTTP server",
    RunE:  runServe,
}

func init() {
    rootCmd.AddCommand(serveCmd)
    serveCmd.Flags().Int("port", 8080, "port to listen on")
    serveCmd.Flags().String("host", "0.0.0.0", "host to bind")
    viper.BindPFlag("server.port", serveCmd.Flags().Lookup("port"))
    viper.BindPFlag("server.host", serveCmd.Flags().Lookup("host"))
}

func runServe(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
    port := viper.GetInt("server.port")
    host := viper.GetString("server.host")
    logLevel := viper.GetString("log_level")

    fmt.Printf("Starting server on %s:%d (log level: %s)\n", host, port, logLevel)
    // actual server startup here
    return nil
}

Note RunE instead of Run — RunE lets you return an error, which Cobra will print and exit non-zero. Use RunE everywhere; Run swallows errors silently.

Configuration Priority: Flags > Env > File > Defaults

One of Viper's biggest wins is its precedence chain. When you call viper.GetInt("server.port"), Viper checks:

  1. --port flag (if bound and set explicitly)
  2. MYAPP_SERVER_PORT environment variable
  3. server.port in the config file
  4. Default value from viper.SetDefault

You get this for free — no conditional logic in your command code. To set defaults explicitly:

func init() {
    viper.SetDefault("server.port", 8080)
    viper.SetDefault("server.host", "0.0.0.0")
    viper.SetDefault("log_level", "info")
}

A matching ~/.myapp.yaml config file:

log_level: debug

server:
  port: 9090
  host: 127.0.0.1

database:
  dsn: "postgres://user:pass@localhost/myapp"
  max_connections: 25

With this setup, MYAPP_SERVER_PORT=3000 myapp serve overrides the file's 9090, and myapp serve --port 4000 overrides the env var.

Validating Configuration at Startup

Don't defer config errors to runtime. Validate required values in PersistentPreRunE:

var rootCmd = &cobra.Command{
    Use:   "myapp",
    Short: "A production-ready CLI tool",
    PersistentPreRunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
        if viper.GetString("database.dsn") == "" {
            return fmt.Errorf("database.dsn is required (set via config file or MYAPP_DATABASE_DSN)")
        }
        return nil
    },
}

PersistentPreRunE runs before every subcommand and after initConfig, so Viper is already populated. This is the right place to check required values, initialize loggers, or connect to a database.

One caveat: if a subcommand also defines PreRunE, Cobra does not chain them by default. You need to call the parent's PersistentPreRunE explicitly, or use a helper:

func chainPreRunE(parent, child func(*cobra.Command, []string) error) func(*cobra.Command, []string) error {
    return func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
        if err := parent(cmd, args); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return child(cmd, args)
    }
}

This trips up a lot of Go CLI developers who expect automatic chaining — it isn't there by design.

Handling Sensitive Configuration Securely

Config files stored in home directories often end up in Git or shared filesystems. For credentials, you have two reasonable options:

Option 1: Accept secrets only via environment variables and document this clearly. Never write them to the YAML file.

Option 2: Integrate with a secrets backend. Viper supports remote config via viper.AddRemoteProvider (Consul, etcd). For Vault, fetch secrets at startup and inject them into Viper manually:

func loadVaultSecrets() {
    if dsn := os.Getenv("VAULT_INJECTED_DSN"); dsn != "" {
        viper.Set("database.dsn", dsn)
    }
}

If you're shipping CLI tools to production environments, reviewing your secrets handling against a security hardening checklist before deploying saves more time than it costs.

The Takeaway

The Cobra + Viper combination is the Go CLI stack worth learning. The flag precedence chain (flag > env > file > default) eliminates an entire class of config bugs. The main things to get right:

  • Use RunE, not Run
  • Call cobra.OnInitialize for config loading — order matters
  • Bind flags to Viper keys explicitly with BindPFlag
  • Handle PersistentPreRunE chaining manually when subcommands need it
  • Keep credentials out of YAML config files entirely

The structure above scales from a 200-line tool to a 20-command CLI without rewrites.

I run AYI NEDJIMI Consultants, a cybersecurity consulting firm. We publish free security hardening checklists — PDF and Excel.

title: Build a Spend Breaker Before You Ship AI
description:
Build a Spend Breaker Before You Ship AI

A solo founder ships one AI button on a Friday afternoon. The button turns a messy customer note into three tidy bullets. The demo lands, the weekend starts, and nobody watches the endpoint.

By Monday morning that endpoint has answered tens of thousands of calls. A worker retry loop kept hammering a timeout. The free allowance is gone, and every request now costs real money.

The numbers in that story are illustrative. The shape of the failure is not. A free tier never removes the budget; it changes the unit from dollars to tokens and CPU.

Arguments about AI fatigue keep circling the feed this week. The quieter question is who pays when a shipped AI feature misbehaves at three in the morning. For a solo build, the answer has to live in code, not in attention.

The loop that eats a free tier

Most first versions look like this.

// worker.mjs — the version that eats a weekend
async function summarize(note) {
  while (true) {
    try {
      return await callModel(note);
    } catch {
      // retry forever, because "free"
    }
  }
}

That loop has no governor. A timeout, a 429, or a slow backend turns one user action into thousands of billed calls. Providers are happy to keep answering until the quota runs out, then charge or refuse.

MonkeyCode is an open-source project that lists free model access and a free server option, both supplied by the operator. The free token allowance is currently advertised at 10 million tokens. Verify the project's current terms before you depend on any number, because allowances and limits change.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

A free allowance is still a budget. It just spends tokens instead of dollars, and it refills on someone else's schedule. So the breaker counts tokens first and money second. That order matters on day one of any indie build.

Three pieces: ledger, gate, settle

The breaker is small and deliberately boring. One append-only ledger, one gate before the call, one settle after it.

// spend.mjs
import { appendFileSync, readFileSync, existsSync } from "node:fs";

const LEDGER = process.env.LEDGER ?? "./spend.jsonl";
const TOKEN_BUDGET = Number(process.env.TOKEN_BUDGET ?? "200000");
const USD_BUDGET = Number(process.env.USD_BUDGET ?? "0");
const EST_OUT = Number(process.env.EST_OUT ?? "256");

export function estimateTokens(text) {
  // Rough heuristic: about four characters per token for English prose.
  // Treat this as a guess and settle with provider-reported usage.
  return Math.ceil(String(text).length / 4);
}

export function spendToday(now = new Date()) {
  const day = now.toISOString().slice(0, 10);
  const totals = { day, in: 0, out: 0, usd: 0, calls: 0 };
  if (!existsSync(LEDGER)) return totals;
  for (const line of readFileSync(LEDGER, "utf8").split("\n")) {
    if (!line.trim()) continue;
    let row;
    try { row = JSON.parse(line); } catch { continue; }
    if (!String(row.ts).startsWith(day)) continue;
    totals.in += row.in ?? 0;
    totals.out += row.out ?? 0;
    totals.usd += row.usd ?? 0;
    totals.calls += 1;
  }
  return totals;
}

export function gate(text, now = new Date()) {
  const estIn = estimateTokens(text);
  const s = spendToday(now);
  const projected = s.in + s.out + estIn + EST_OUT;
  if (projected >= TOKEN_BUDGET * 0.9) {
    return { ok: false, reason: "token-budget", estIn, ...s };
  }
  if (USD_BUDGET > 0 && s.usd >= USD_BUDGET) {
    return { ok: false, reason: "usd-budget", estIn, ...s };
  }
  return { ok: true, estIn, ...s };
}

export function settle(row, now = new Date()) {
  const record = { ts: now.toISOString(), ...row };
  appendFileSync(LEDGER, JSON.stringify(record) + "\n");
  return record;
}

The gate closes at ninety percent, not at one hundred. A closed gate still has to answer the user, so the wrapper ships a deterministic fallback instead of an error page.

// guard.mjs
import { gate, settle } from "./spend.mjs";

export function cheapFallback(note) {
  // No model call. Boring, instant, always available.
  const first = String(note).split(/[.!?]\s/)[0] ?? "";
  return first.slice(0, 120) || "Summary unavailable.";
}

export async function guardedSummarize(note, { callModel, now = new Date() }) {
  const verdict = gate(note, now);
  if (!verdict.ok) {
    settle({ route: "fallback", in: 0, out: 0, usd: 0, reason: verdict.reason }, now);
    return { text: cheapFallback(note), route: "fallback", reason: verdict.reason };
  }
  try {
    const res = await callModel(note);
    settle({
      route: "model",
      in: res.usage?.input_tokens ?? verdict.estIn,
      out: res.usage?.output_tokens ?? 0,
      usd: res.usage?.cost_usd ?? 0,
    }, now);
    return { text: res.text, route: "model" };
  } catch (err) {
    // Failed attempts usually still consume input tokens.
    settle({ route: "error", in: verdict.estIn, out: 0, usd: 0, error: String(err) }, now);
    throw err;
  }
}

The model call itself stays behind a thin adapter. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works, so the breaker never locks a solo build to one vendor.

// model.mjs — OpenAI-compatible adapter
export function makeCaller({ baseUrl, apiKey, model }) {
  return async function callModel(note) {
    const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/chat/completions`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "content-type": "application/json",
        authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        model,
        messages: [{ role: "user", content: `Summarize in 3 bullets:\n${note}` }],
        max_tokens: 256,
      }),
    });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${res.status} ${await res.text()}`);
    const json = await res.json();
    return {
      text: json.choices?.[0]?.message?.content ?? "",
      usage: {
        input_tokens: json.usage?.prompt_tokens ?? 0,
        output_tokens: json.usage?.completion_tokens ?? 0,
      },
    };
  };
}

Read baseUrl, apiKey, and model from environment variables filled in from the project's own setup page. Never hardcode a key into a repo that a free host will clone.

A test that proves the gate closes

The breaker is worth nothing if it is only read and never run. Here is a fully offline test with a stubbed model and an explicit clock.

// spend.test.mjs
import test from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { mkdtempSync } from "node:fs";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";

const dir = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "spend-"));
process.env.LEDGER = join(dir, "spend.jsonl");
process.env.TOKEN_BUDGET = "1000";
process.env.USD_BUDGET = "0";

const { guardedSummarize } = await import("./guard.mjs");
const { spendToday } = await import("./spend.mjs");

const callModel = async () => ({
  text: "ok",
  usage: { input_tokens: 40, output_tokens: 60 },
});

const note = "short note about a late invoice. ".repeat(4);

test("the gate closes before the budget is spent", async () => {
  const now = new Date("2026-10-16T09:00:00Z");
  const routes = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 40; i++) {
    const out = await guardedSummarize(note, { callModel, now });
    routes.push(out.route);
  }
  const modelCalls = routes.filter((r) => r === "model").length;
  const total = spendToday(now);
  assert.ok(modelCalls > 0, "at least one model call reached the endpoint");
  assert.ok(total.in + total.out < 1000, "stayed under the hard token budget");
  assert.equal(routes.at(-1), "fallback", "the gate closes and stays closed");
});

test("a new day reopens the gate", async () => {
  const day2 = new Date("2026-10-17T09:00:00Z");
  const out = await guardedSummarize(note, { callModel, now: day2 });
  assert.equal(out.route, "model");
});

Run it with the budget in the environment, so the numbers stay visible and easy to change.

LEDGER=/tmp/spend.jsonl TOKEN_BUDGET=1000 node --test spend.test.mjs

The first test loops forty times and still finishes in a few milliseconds. That is the point of an offline stub. The failure you fear took someone a weekend; here it takes a test run.

Where the free server fits

Run the worker and the ledger in the same process, on the same small host. The free server option is a reasonable place for exactly that shape: one Node process, one SQLite or JSONL file, one external model endpoint.

Keep the ledger path inside the app directory, not /tmp. A restart should not silently refund the day's spend. Limit the process to a single instance as well, because two workers writing the same file can double-count or lose rows.

Free hosts impose limits of their own. Read the current ones before you promise a customer anything, and decide what a cold or throttled start does to your fallback path.

A routing matrix for the first month

Situation Route Why
One user click, user is waiting Model call, gated Latency is acceptable, one call per action
Background job over many rows Batch with a per-run cap Runaway loops start in workers, not in UI
Gate already closed Deterministic fallback Ship a worse answer, not an outage
Provider returns 429 or 5xx Two retries, then fallback Unbounded retries multiply token spend
Accounting must be exact Neither route Use a billing system, not a JSONL file

Limitations and who should skip this

The ledger is per-process and file-based. Fine for one solo app, wrong for anything running multiple regions. The ninety percent threshold is a guess that you should tune against real traffic. The token estimate drifts from provider counts, so settle with reported usage whenever the endpoint returns it.

Above all, a breaker protects the allowance, not correctness. A bad prompt still returns bad summaries under budget. And free model access, like any free tier, is a moving target; check the current terms before you build a business rule on top of it.

Skip this approach if you already have provider-side quotas and a billing dashboard. Skip it for high-throughput services where a gateway belongs in front of every call. Skip it if you cannot read and re-read the provider's limits. A solo build with one AI button is the sweet spot, because a JSONL file and forty lines of Node buy you the one guarantee that matters: the weekend stays boring.

If you want to run this loop yourself, MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option are a cheap place to start. Bring the test file, not the feature.

title: Firefox 131+ UI Guide: Vertical Tabs, Tab Groups, Sidebar, and the Full Tab Workflow
description:
Firefox 131 introduced native vertical tabs and tab groups. Combined with existing features like the sidebar, these change the browsing experience meaningfully. Here's a practical guide to the new UI.

Vertical Tabs (Firefox 131+)

Enable: Settings → Tabs → "Enable vertical tab sidebar"

Or right-click on the tab bar → "Move Tab Bar to Sidebar"

The vertical tab bar appears on the left (or right, configurable) as a sidebar panel. Shows:

  • Tab favicon and title (not just favicon like the horizontal bar at scale)
  • Current tab highlighted
  • Drag to reorder tabs

Combining with hiding the horizontal bar:
The sidebar doesn't automatically hide the horizontal tab bar. To hide it:

  • Right-click horizontal tab bar → uncheck "Show horizontal tab bar" (Firefox 133+ may have this option)
  • Or via userChrome.css: #TabsToolbar { display: none !important; }

Vertical tabs with Tree Style Tab extension: Native vertical tabs don't have parent-child hierarchy (nested tabs). If you need hierarchical organization, Tree Style Tab still provides that. You can use it alongside native vertical tabs, though typically you'd pick one.

Tab Groups (Firefox 131+)

Create a tab group: right-click a tab → "New Tab Group" → name and color the group.

Or drag one tab onto another — a group creation prompt appears.

Collapsing groups: Click the group label to toggle collapse/expand. Collapsed groups show as a small colored indicator.

Managing groups: Right-click the group label → rename, change color, or ungroup.

Tab groups persist across Firefox restarts (unlike regular tab sessions which can be lost in some crash scenarios).

Use cases:

  • Group tabs by project: all "work-project-a" tabs together
  • Group research tabs: collapse when not reading
  • Group social/news tabs: keep separate from work

Tab groups complement Tab Manager & Session Saver: use tab groups within a session for organization, and Tab Manager sessions to save and restore different working contexts.

The Sidebar

Firefox has had a sidebar for years (bookmarks, history, synced tabs). It's been revamped:

Toggle: Click the sidebar toggle button in the toolbar (or View → Sidebar).

Sidebar contents:

  • Bookmarks
  • History
  • Synced Tabs (from other devices via Firefox Sync)
  • Vertical Tabs (new in 131)
  • Extensions can add sidebar panels (Tree Style Tab, Firefox View)

Multiple sidebars: Firefox lets you switch between sidebar panels. Vertical tabs, bookmarks, and history can all live in the sidebar space.

Firefox View

Firefox View is a new tab-like interface accessible via the Firefox logo at the top of the tab bar:

  • Recent Tabs: Tabs you've closed recently (like Ctrl+Shift+T but browseable)
  • Open Tabs: All tabs across all windows in current session
  • Synced Tabs: Tabs open on other devices (needs Firefox Sync)

This is useful for finding something you had open earlier without searching history.

The New Tab Page Customization

The default new tab page has:

  • Top Sites: Most visited sites (tiles)
  • Recent Activity: Recently visited pages
  • Sponsored stories (can be disabled)

Customize:
Settings → Home → Firefox Home Content → toggle each section

For minimal new tab: disable stories, disable sponsored, keep just the search bar.

Or: Settings → Home → "Homepage and new windows" → change to "Custom URLs" → set your own URL or use about:blank.

Search From the Address Bar

The address bar is a unified search and navigation bar. Configure it:

Settings → Search → Default Search Engine

Keyword searches: Set up one-click searches.
Settings → Search → One-Click Search Engines → Enable any engine.

Then in the address bar, type the engine keyword + space to activate it:

  • @g search term — Google
  • @w article name — Wikipedia
  • Any keyword you configure

Compact Toolbar

Firefox 89 removed the "compact" toolbar density. You can restore it:
Settings → Customize Toolbar → Density → "Compact"

If "Compact" isn't visible (some versions removed it):
about:config → browser.uidensity = 1 for compact

Tab Scrolling

With many tabs: Firefox scrolls the tab bar by default rather than shrinking tabs to unreadable sizes.

about:config → browser.tabs.tabClipWidth — minimum tab width before overflow scroll.

Or use the << and >> arrows at the ends of the tab bar to scroll.

See all tabs: Click the ⌄ dropdown at the right end of the tab bar to see a searchable list of all open tabs.

Pinned Tabs

Right-click a tab → "Pin Tab" — pins it to the left side, shows only favicon, can't be accidentally closed.

Useful for: always-open tools (calendar, communication apps, monitoring dashboards).

Pinned tabs persist across Firefox restarts.

Tab Multi-Select

Hold Ctrl while clicking tabs to select multiple. Then:

  • Right-click → "Close Tabs" — closes all selected
  • Right-click → "Bookmark Tabs" — saves all selected to a new folder
  • Drag to reorder as a group
  • Right-click → "Move to New Window" — detaches selected tabs into new window

Multi-select is useful for bulk tab management: select all the tabs from a finished project and close them at once.

Performance Impact of Features

Native vertical tabs: minimal performance impact (they're just CSS-repositioned existing tab UI).

Tab groups: minimal impact.

Sidebar: the sidebar panel loads its content lazily. Keeping it open to bookmarks doesn't significantly impact performance.

The most impactful change for performance is tab count — each tab uses memory regardless of UI organization.

The Full Modern Firefox Tab Workflow

With all features combined:

  1. Tab groups: Organize by context within a window
  2. Vertical tab bar: Better visibility of tab titles at scale
  3. Tab Manager sessions: Save/restore whole working contexts
  4. Firefox View: Find recently closed tabs
  5. Pinned tabs: Persistent tools that survive session changes

This layered approach handles everything from "I need to find that tab I had open" to "I need to save this whole working context for tomorrow."

title: QuasiLeak-Bench: Evaluating LLM-Based Privacy Detectors on Policy-Conditioned Quasi-Evidence Group Recovery
description:
arXiv:2610.21333v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Natural language messages often contain quasi-identifiers that are weak in isolation but can jointly reveal an individual's private attributes. We call such a jointly revealing set of cues a quasi-evidence group. Existing privacy benchmarks focus on explicit identifiers, attribute inference, or task-driven disclosures, leaving inference from quasi-evidence groups largely unmeasured. In practice, whether exposing such a quasi-evidence group violates privacy also depends on sender-specified disclosure policies. We introduce QuasiLeak-Bench, a benchmark for policy-conditioned quasi-evidence group recovery, which evaluates whether detectors recover complete quasi-evidence groups and flag the disclosures the given policy prohibits. To obtain reliable ground truth at scale, a reverse-construction pipeline first selects weak quasi-identifiers, composes them into quasi-evidence groups verified to jointly reveal a target attribute, and generates documents around this evidence, followed by automated quality control. Experiments show that existing privacy detectors transfer poorly to QuasiLeak-Bench, and locally deployable LLM-based detectors fall far behind proprietary models, mainly because they miss most quasi-evidence groups altogether. However, a 4B model fine-tuned on our training split surpasses the strongest prompted model on held-out documents, showing that the task is learnable.

title: On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20687v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Residual context is key to unlocking the speed-quality Pareto frontier of diffusion language models (DLMs) by carrying forward predictive distributions across denoising steps. Yet turning this seemingly simple mechanism into an effective learning paradigm is far from simple: there is no clear recipe for how residual context should be learned. We introduce ORL, a framework for on-policy residual learning in DLMs. Algorithmically, we identify that residual learning is inherently on-policy. ORL learns from model-induced residual trajectories on the fly and introduces an entropy-contraction objective that sharpens predictions as the model revisits its own predictions. System-wise, exact residual supervision requires capturing, retaining, and reprocessing many trajectory-dependent states. ORL co-designs the algorithm with asynchronous residual capture and transport, specialized block-diffusion attention, and packed compute-balanced training, making it practical at scale. On a 4B DLM converted from Qwen3-4B, ORL improves tokens per forward (TPF) by up to 6.2x and, with our dlmrt engine, end-to-end throughput by approximately 6.9x at comparable or better quality. In single-request serving on one H100, this mode achieves a stronger speed-quality Pareto frontier than autoregressive models with EAGLE3 and DFlash speculative decoding under both strict and relaxed verification, running 1.74x faster than DFlash at matched accuracy. ORL also transfers to existing DLMs: on LLaDA-2.1-mini, 36 H100-hours and 4.2M self-generated tokens, about 10x less data than prior LLaDA recipes, yield up to 1.5x higher TPF and up to 3x higher throughput at comparable quality, and on DiffusionGemma, ORL raises TPF by 1.1-1.2x. With dlmrt and NVFP4 quantization, ORL models decode a single request at up to 5,046 tokens/s on one B200, 7,708 on eight B200s, and 2,788 on a consumer RTX 5090, with comparable quality.

title: PRISM: PRIvileged Sibling-guided Multi-Agent Topology Design
description:
arXiv:2610.20628v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) based on large language models (LLMs) have become a powerful way to address complex problems, and their effectiveness depends critically on the collaboration topology that decides which agents participate and how they communicate. Recent work learns to generate this topology from the task query, fitting the generator to corpora of execution-verified graphs. The post-training method for such generators remains a limitation: a corpus lists the graphs that solved a query but never ranks them, leaving continued supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with no per-query preference to exploit. Without such a preference, the generator drifts toward the topologies the corpus contains most often rather than those that suit each query, so a gain on one task can come at a cost on another. We propose PRISM, which recovers per-query signal from the same corpus by learning with privileged information: a teacher reads, through a zero-initialized low-rank branch, a sibling graph that also solved the query and is unavailable at deployment, and the student matches its per-decision targets on trajectories the student samples itself. Across six diverse benchmarks PRISM improves over every topology-design baseline evaluated, and matched-teacher controls support the contribution of privileged query information. Code is available in this link.
