title: Next.js 16.3 benchmarked on two production apps
description:
Originally published on devanddeliver.com.

Introduction

Part 1 of 2. Part 2 covers what the Cache Components migration actually costs

Next.js 16.3 promises less dev server memory, faster builds, faster server rendering, and a new opt-in suite called Instant Navigations. Vercel published their own numbers: up to 90% less RAM in dev, up to 5.5x faster builds on CI, up to 22% more requests under load.

We upgraded two projects we maintain, measured them before and after, and then, later than we should have, read the documentation.

Two projects, because one was not enough. The first is a small static marketing site, and it turned out to be too small to test half of what 16.3 claims. So we ran the same harness against a Medusa e-commerce storefront: 223 source files, a cart, a checkout, and almost every route server-rendered per request. Where the two agree, we believe the number.

The documentation is what changed our conclusions. The headline build improvement is real and large, and on the first project's deployment pipeline it would have delivered zero, because the pipeline throws away the one directory the feature depends on. Nobody would have noticed either: the build would have stayed the same speed and the upgrade would have looked like a dud.

This part covers the numbers: builds, type checking, dev memory, and throughput. Part 2 covers Instant Navigations, which is a migration rather than a benchmark.

Everything we measured, in one table

Two production codebases, every number interleaved A/B on the same machine, in September 2026 against Next.js 16.3.4:

What Marketing site (50 files, static) Storefront (223 files, SSR)
Warm build compile, 16.1.6 to 16.3.4 2.9 s to 0.19 s (15.3x) 4.4 s to 0.32 s (13.8x)
Cold build, 16.1.6 to 16.3.4 unchanged unchanged
Requests per second under load +7% +52%
Dev server memory no measurable change no measurable change
Code changes to get a green build zero zero

The build cache is the one result that held across both codebases. Server rendering throughput ranged from 7% to 52% depending entirely on how much the app renders per request, so a single headline number for it is meaningless. Dev memory we could not measure at either size. And on a container pipeline the build cache delivers nothing at all until you carry .next/cache into the build yourself.

What we tested it on

A bilingual (Polish and English) B2B marketing site we build and maintain. Roughly 20 routes plus an API route, around 50 TypeScript and TSX source files, React 19, Turbopack, React Compiler enabled, deployed as a standalone build in Docker.

One characteristic dominates everything below: the site is almost entirely static. 22 of its 23 build outputs are prerendered at build time. There is no cookies(), no headers(), no searchParams, and no server-side fetch anywhere in the source. The only data request in the whole app is client-side, from a contact form.

We went from Next 16.1.6 to 16.3.4 on Node 24, with Yarn 4. The upgrade itself needed zero code changes.

The second project is a Medusa v2 e-commerce storefront: 223 TypeScript source files, 4.5x the first, with a cart, checkout, customer accounts and Stripe. It reads cookies() for cart id, JWT and cache id, and almost every route is ƒ (Dynamic), rendered per request. It is the opposite profile in every way that matters here, and it started two versions back on Next 15.3.9, which let us measure the real 15 to 16 migration as well.

Its build and dev numbers were taken with the commerce backend switched off, which is fine because those measure bundling 223 files. For the load test and the Cache Components work in part 2 we started the backend locally and rebuilt against real product data, because neither means anything against dead upstreams.

Method, and why it changed our conclusions

Our first pass was the obvious one: measure everything on 16.1.6, upgrade, measure again. That pass told us dev memory improved 5%, cold builds got 27% slower, and throughput improved 8%.

Two of those three findings were wrong.

Build times on this project are measured in seconds, and a laptop is a noisy place to measure seconds. So we re-ran everything as an interleaved A/B: 16.1.6, then 16.3.4, then 16.1.6 again, then 16.3.4 again, alternating in one session, with a discarded warm-up build at the start of each round. Where possible we used the compile time Next reports itself rather than wall clock, because it excludes yarn startup and type checking.

Under that method the "27% slower cold builds" vanished completely, and so did the memory improvement. Only the throughput gain survived.

If you are benchmarking your own upgrade, interleave your runs. A single before-then-after pass on a laptop will confidently tell you things that are not true.

Build times: cold unchanged, warm transformed

Cold builds, deleting .next before each run, nine runs per version:

16.1.6 16.3.4
Compile step (median) 3.1 s 3.0 s
Full build, wall clock (median) 6.68 s 6.58 s

Unchanged. The ranges overlap almost entirely.

Warm builds, no source changes, .next kept, seven runs per version:

16.1.6 16.3.4
Compile step (median) 2.9 s 187 ms
Full build, wall clock (median) 6.37 s 3.48 s

On 16.1.6 there is effectively no build cache: rebuilding with zero changes costs the same 2.9 seconds of compilation as a cold build. On 16.3.4 the same rebuild compiles in about 0.19 seconds, roughly 15 times faster, and the whole next build drops 45%.

The Turbopack FileSystem cache is a build cache that Turbopack writes to .next/cache and restores on the next run, so unchanged modules are not compiled again. It became enabled by default for next build in Next.js 16.3, and you do not have to turn it on.

The same test on the bigger project, and what it separates

The storefront started on 15.3.9, so the jump to 16.3.4 crosses a major version. That conflates two different changes, and measuring 16.1.6 in the middle pulls them apart. Three cold runs and two warm runs per version, medians:

15.3.9 (webpack) 16.1.6 (Turbopack) 16.3.4 (Turbopack + cache)
Cold compile 12.0 s 4.4 s 4.7 s
Warm compile 3.0 s 4.4 s 0.32 s
Warm build, wall clock 13.7 s 7.0 s 3.2 s

Two things fall out of that middle column.

The cold build win belongs to the bundler. Cold compile drops 12.0 s to 4.4 s, 2.7x, and every bit of it lands between 15.3.9 and 16.1.6, where Next 16 made Turbopack the default build bundler in place of webpack. From 16.1.6 to 16.3.4 the cold build does not move, which is exactly what we saw on the marketing site.

16.1 was a warm-build regression, and 16.3 is the fix. On webpack a warm rebuild compiled in 3.0 s. On Turbopack in 16.1.6 the same rebuild took 4.4 s, slower than the webpack it replaced, because Turbopack had no build cache yet. 16.3 takes it to 0.32 s. A team that upgraded to 16.1 and judged Turbopack on repeat builds would have concluded it was a downgrade, and at the time they would have been right.

Where the two projects agree

The directly comparable number is the 16.1.6 to 16.3.4 warm compile, measured with the same harness on both:

Project 16.1.6 16.3.4 Speedup
Marketing site (50 files, static) 2.9 s 0.19 s 15.3x
Medusa storefront (223 files, SSR) 4.4 s 0.32 s 13.8x

Two codebases with nothing in common in size or rendering model, and the build cache lands within about 10% of the same ratio on both. Of everything we measured, this is the result we would bet on holding for your project too, provided your pipeline keeps the cache around.

The part the upgrade guide buries

The docs on Turbopack FileSystem caching are blunt about it:

The build cache lives in .next/cache. Builds only get faster when that directory is restored before each build. Containerized builds start from a clean layer and do not carry .next/cache over unless you cache or mount it explicitly.

On our project .next/cache is 52 MB. We deleted just that one directory and rebuilt:

Scenario Wall clock Compile step
Warm build, cache intact 4.87 s 200 ms
Same build, only .next/cache deleted 8.20 s 3.5 s

The compile step goes straight back to being 17x slower. The whole headline feature works only if that directory survives between builds.

Then we looked at our own pipeline:

  • The Dockerfile has a clean builder stage that does COPY . . followed by RUN yarn build. Every image build starts with no .next/cache.
  • The CI config had no cache: block at all.

So every production build on this project is a cold build. We would have upgraded Next, watched our CI times not move, and reasonably concluded that Vercel's build numbers were marketing, when in fact we were discarding the cache on every run.

We fixed it and checked the fix in the pipeline itself rather than only on a laptop. Our CI builds inside Docker, so a CI-level cache directory would not have helped: the build does not run in the job's workspace. Instead the Dockerfile now restores .next/cache from a small cache image, and exposes a stage that exports the warmed cache so CI can publish it for the next pipeline.

With that in place we changed a source file, so the build genuinely had to re-run, and built the image both ways:

Container build, identical source change Turbopack compile
With the restored cache 308 ms
Without it (control) 3.1 s

Roughly 10x, inside the actual container build. The exported cache image is 53 MB, and re-exporting it after a build takes about 3 seconds because it reuses the builder layers.

If you build outside Docker, this is simpler: on GitLab CI, GitHub Actions, CircleCI and the rest it is just a cache entry for .next/cache, and Next's own CI build caching guide has a snippet per provider. If your pipeline builds images, as ours does, you need to carry the directory into the build yourself.

And if your pipeline genuinely cannot persist it, the docs suggest setting turbopackFileSystemCacheForBuild: false so the build stops writing 52 MB of cache that nothing will ever read.

Put this on the upgrade ticket. Bumping the version is the easy half; if nobody wires up cache persistence, the largest improvement in 16.3 never reaches your team.

Once the cache lands, type checking is the build

Compilation drops to about 0.19 seconds and the whole build still takes 3.5 seconds, so compilation stops being the bottleneck. We looked at what was left. TypeScript was costing 747 to 870 ms of every build, which made it the biggest measurable step.

16.3 anticipates this. next build now runs your project-local tsc CLI by default, specifically so it can use TypeScript 7, the native port Microsoft released with roughly a 10x speedup. TypeScript 7.0.2 is out and is latest on npm. Our project, like most, was pinned to ^5.

We measured tsc --noEmit against the project's own tsconfig.json, interleaved:

Round TypeScript 5.9.3 TypeScript 7.0.2
1 1.143 s 0.139 s
2 0.963 s 0.139 s
3 0.960 s 0.135 s
Median 0.96 s 0.139 s

About 7x faster, with zero new type errors. Both runs exited clean.

Inside next build that is roughly 0.7 seconds off every single build, about 18% of our warm build time, stacked on top of what the Turbopack cache already gave us.

Two caveats, because we could not ship it on this project.

First, Yarn 4.12 cannot install TypeScript 7. Yarn applies a builtin compatibility patch to the typescript package, and that patch expects a file layout TS 7 no longer has:

Error: typescript@patch:...#optional!builtin<compat/typescript>:
ENOENT: no such file or directory, lstat '.../typescript/lib/_tsc.js'

Forcing a plain resolution through resolutions did not help, Yarn re-applies the patch. Second, typescript-eslint (pulled in by eslint-config-next) still declares a peer range of >=4.8.4 <6.0.0.

So the 7x is real and measured, but on a Yarn 4 stack it is currently blocked by the toolchain rather than by Next. On npm or pnpm you should hit only the eslint peer warning. Worth checking before you promise it to anyone.

Dev server memory: we could not measure it, and now we know why

We cleared .next, started the dev server, requested all 21 routes so every one compiled, then summed RSS across the entire next dev process tree. Five samples per version.

Run 16.1.6 16.3.4
1 1500 MB 1423 MB
2 1665 MB 1989 MB
3 1763 MB 1700 MB
4 962 MB 1802 MB
5 1598 MB 1746 MB
Median 1598 MB 1746 MB

The spread inside a single version is about 800 MB, which swamps any difference between them, so we measured nothing. The docs explain why, and the explanation is worth more than the non-result.

The 90% figure comes from two features: disk caching for dev, and memory eviction. Disk caching for dev shipped in 16.1. Our baseline was 16.1.6, so it already had half the improvement. Only eviction was genuinely new in our comparison.

So we tested eviction directly, on 16.3.4, over a longer session:

'turbopackMemoryEviction' Sample 1 Sample 2
false (never evict) 1547 MB 1031 MB
'auto' (default) 2056 MB 1478 MB
'full' (aggressive) 1040 MB 1757 MB

Still nothing. And the reason is scale. Vercel's before numbers are 21.5 GB for the Vercel dashboard and 4.6 GB for nextjs.org. Our dev server peaks around 1.5 to 2 GB, an order of magnitude below where their baseline even begins. Eviction reclaims memory after cache snapshots under sustained pressure, in long sessions. A 21-route site driven for a minute never creates that pressure.

The storefront told the same story, across three versions:

Version Sample 1 Sample 2
15.3.9 525 MB 547 MB
16.1.6 835 MB 646 MB
16.3.4 696 MB 524 MB

Overlapping again, and this project peaks around 0.5 to 0.8 GB. Even our 4.5x bigger codebase is an order of magnitude below where Vercel's 4.6 GB and 21.5 GB baselines start.

The claim may well hold. We are reporting that it is untestable at this size, and that if dev memory is a daily annoyance on your app, you are the case we could not represent. Two things follow for you: check whether you are already on 16.1 or later, since you may have banked half the win a while ago, and measure a long session rather than a cold start.

Handling load: 7% on one app, 52% on the other

We ran next start and pointed autocannon at the homepage with 20 connections, three interleaved pairs.

Pair 16.1.6 16.3.4 Delta
1 1905 req/s 2064 req/s +8.3%
2 2128 req/s 2281 req/s +7.2%
3 2160 req/s 2304 req/s +6.6%

A consistent ~7% improvement, reproducible across every pair. Average latency improved by about a millisecond.

Vercel claims up to 22%. We got about a third of that, and the docs say why: the change replaces web streams with native Node.js streams in the App Router rendering layer. Our site prerenders 22 of 23 routes, so under load it is mostly handing back finished HTML and barely exercising the rendering path that got faster. Getting a third of the benefit while doing almost none of the work the optimization targets is a reasonable outcome.

Treat our 7% as a floor. An app doing genuine per-request rendering has far more to gain here than we did.

So we went and measured it on the storefront, which is the app this claim is actually about. We started its backend locally, rebuilt against real data, and ran the same interleaved A/B against two routes that render per request.

Route 16.1.6 16.3.4 Change
Home 327.5 req/s 497.4 req/s +51.9%
Product list 392.1 req/s 571.7 req/s +45.8%

Between 46% and 52% more requests per second, with latency down about 25%. On an app that actually exercises the rendering path we measured more than double Vercel's 22%, and both interleaved pairs agree to within 4%.

One check worth stating, because it is the obvious objection: was the backend the bottleneck? No. If it had been, both Next versions would have converged on the same figure. They shared the same backend, the same data and the same cookie, and differ by 50%. What moved was the rendering.

So the same release gives one app 7% and another 52%, and the mechanism explains both. Native Node streams replace web streams in the App Router rendering layer. Serve prerendered HTML and you barely touch it. Render every route per request and you get the whole thing. Whether 16.3 is worth 22% to you depends entirely on how much rendering your app does.

What a real 15 to 16 migration cost us

The storefront crossed a major version, so it is the better test of migration pain.

The build passed on the first attempt with zero code changes, on a real e-commerce storefront with a cart, a checkout and Stripe. No codemod needed for a green build. That genuinely surprised us.

Then we looked underneath it, and the green build proved less than it looked. This project sets typescript.ignoreBuildErrors: true, as plenty of projects do. Running tsc --noEmit separately, with an identical tsconfig.json in both runs:

Version Type errors
15.3.9 17 (pre-existing, unrelated)
16.3.4 49

All 32 new ones are the same breaking change. revalidateTag(tag) now takes a second argument:

const cartCacheTag = await getCacheTag("carts")
revalidateTag(cartCacheTag)   // TS2554: Expected 2 arguments, but got 1

The docs are precise about what one argument now means: it still works, but it is deprecated and behaves like { expire: 0 }. Stale content is never served, so the next request blocks on a full revalidation instead of getting stale-while-revalidate. Nothing breaks. The app takes the slow path on every cart mutation, and a pipeline that ignores type errors will never report it. The fix is revalidateTag(tag, "max"), or updateTag in a Server Action.

Next 16 also rewrote tsconfig.json on its own, and two of the changes are semantic rather than cosmetic:

- "moduleResolution": "node",
+ "moduleResolution": "bundler",
- "jsx": "preserve",
+ "jsx": "react-jsx",

It reformatted every array in the file at the same time, so the real changes arrive buried in a noisy diff. next-env.d.ts picked up a new import too. Both files are committed in most repos, so this lands in somebody's review whether they asked for it or not.

So the upgrade is genuinely cheap, and "the build is green" is not the same as "the migration is done". Run tsc yourself, especially if your config ignores build errors.

One thing that did nothing

Our project runs the React Compiler through Babel, which is exactly the case experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler targets. Vercel reports 34% faster cold and 46% faster warm time-to-ready-page on v0.

Cold compile Warm compile
Babel (default) 2.6 s, 2.4 s 227 ms, 235 ms
Rust compiler 2.5 s, 2.7 s 227 ms, 244 ms

No measurable difference at 50 source files. Vercel's numbers come from v0, a very large app, and they note the gains assume you have moved off Babel entirely. Filed under "revisit on a bigger codebase".

Should you upgrade?

Yes. Both upgrades produced a green build with zero code changes, including the major version jump from 15.3.9 on a real e-commerce storefront. No codemods required. That is about as cheap as a framework upgrade gets.

It is also not the whole job. On the marketing site the upgrade needed no code, but the biggest improvement in the release stayed invisible until we changed the deployment pipeline. On the storefront a green build hid 32 deprecated calls. In both cases the improvements everyone quotes only arrived once we went and collected them.

The checklist we wish the benchmark plan had started with:

  1. Persist .next/cache between builds. Cache mount in Docker, cache entry in CI. Without this the biggest win in 16.3 is precisely zero, and it fails silently. Highest value, lowest effort, do it first.
  2. Move to TypeScript 7. Roughly 7x faster type checking, and once the build cache lands, type checking is what your build time actually consists of. Check your package manager first, Yarn 4 currently cannot install it.
  3. Check which version you are coming from. It changes which win you get. Coming from 15, the big one is cold builds, and that is the webpack to Turbopack switch rather than anything in 16.3. Coming from 16.1 or 16.2, cold builds will not move and the warm build cache is the whole story. Half the dev memory work also shipped back in 16.1.
  4. Run tsc --noEmit yourself after upgrading. A green next build is not proof, and if your config sets ignoreBuildErrors it is barely evidence. That is how we found 32 deprecated revalidateTag calls that nothing else reported.

Instant Navigations is a separate decision with its own timeline, and part 2 is about what it costs.

And calibrate against your own app. Warm builds were the biggest win on both projects, and the one number that held steady across them: 15.3x on 50 files, 13.8x on 223. Dev memory was unmeasurable on both, because even the larger one runs an order of magnitude below where Vercel's benchmark starts. And SSR throughput turned out to depend so completely on your rendering profile that a single headline number for it is close to meaningless: 7% on one of our apps, 52% on the other.

Measure your own, interleave the runs, and read the docs before you write the benchmark rather than after. We did it in the wrong order and it cost us two false conclusions and a rewrite.

One small housekeeping note: installing 16.3.4 writes AGENTS.md and a CLAUDE.md into your repo root, containing version-matched instructions for AI coding agents. They appear without being asked for, and the docs are clear that you should commit them, since next dev re-creates the block anyway.

Questions we were asked while writing this

Is Next.js 16.3 worth upgrading to?

Yes. On both codebases the upgrade produced a green build with zero code changes, including a major version jump from 15.3.9 on the e-commerce storefront. The improvements are a separate piece of work from the version bump: the build cache needs your pipeline to persist .next/cache, and Cache Components is a migration rather than a flag.

How much faster are Next.js 16.3 builds?

Cold builds do not change at all between 16.1.6 and 16.3.4. Repeat builds do: the compile step went from 2.9 s to 0.19 s on a 50-file site and from 4.4 s to 0.32 s on a 223-file storefront, 15.3x and 13.8x. If you are coming from Next 15 you also get a 2.7x faster cold build, but that is Turbopack replacing webpack in 16.0, not anything in 16.3.

Why did my Next.js 16.3 build times not improve?

Most likely your pipeline is discarding the cache. The Turbopack FileSystem cache lives in .next/cache, and a container build starts from a clean layer. On our project, deleting only that directory took the compile step from 200 ms back to 3.5 s. Add a BuildKit cache mount or a CI cache entry for it.

Does Next.js 16.3 really serve 22% more requests?

It depends entirely on how much your app renders per request. The change swaps web streams for native Node streams in the App Router rendering layer. Our mostly prerendered marketing site gained 7%. Our storefront, which renders nearly every route per request, gained 46% to 52%.

About the author

Piotr Zarow is CEO at Dev and Deliver, a Krakow-based software house working with senior React, Next.js, Node and NestJS engineers. He ran these benchmarks himself, on two client codebases the company builds and maintains, in September 2026 on Node 24 with Yarn 4. The method is described in full above so you can reproduce it against your own app rather than take the numbers on trust.

Planning a Next.js upgrade, or trying to work out whether a release is worth the migration effort on your codebase? We are a Krakow-based software house working with senior React, Next.js, Node and NestJS engineers, and this kind of measure-first assessment is how we approach it. Get in touch and tell us what you are building.

Read more about our Next.js development company in Poland.

title: Draining a rate-limited worker pool: queue retries and idempotent daily report emails
description:
Use a cron trigger for the daily kickoff and a queue that a worker pool drains at whatever rate the mail provider allows — do not let one scheduled handler sit in a loop sending report email after report email while a rate limiter throttles it. That is the whole architecture, and it fits in a paragraph. The part worth arguing about is what the pool does after the first 429, because a retry that is not idempotent turns a throttled send into a duplicate send, and duplicate finance reports are the kind of thing that ends up in a customer's compliance ticket rather than your error budget.

The queue isn't the interesting decision. The retry semantics are.

The failure mode: one cron handler pretending to be a worker pool

Here's the capacity arithmetic that decides this for you. Say you have 20,000 tenants on a developer-tools platform, each getting one usage digest at 07:00 local, and your transactional provider gives you 14 sends per second on the plan you're on. That run takes about 24 minutes of wall clock even if nothing goes wrong, and it never runs at exactly 14/s — you get bursts, a 429, a backoff, another burst.

Hosted schedulers cap a single execution. Infrai's ceiling is 900 seconds, and it's a fairly typical number; a 24-minute send loop is already past it, which means the run gets cut somewhere in the middle of the tenant list with no record of who received mail and who didn't. Retrying that from the top is how people send the same digest twice.

So the kickoff has to be cheap: the cron target fires, enumerates tenants, publishes one message per tenant, and returns in a couple of seconds. Everything slow happens in the pool. That shape is what I'd hand to a small platform team, and Infrai packages it as one product — the discovery surface is public and self-describing, so wiring up the publish call is reading a single capability page with the request schema and a runnable example in the language you already use, rather than adopting another SDK and its release cadence.

Should the queue push to a public HTTPS subscriber, or should workers pull?

Push delivery is the tempting option because it looks like less infrastructure: register a subscription, get an HTTP request per message, no polling loop to babysit. Two things make it the wrong default for rate-limited sending.

The first is topology. A push subscription has to reach a public HTTPS endpoint, so a worker pool that lives entirely inside a VPC with no ingress can't receive anything — you'd be standing up a public gateway purely to let your own queue talk to your own workers, and that gateway is now in scope for your security review.

The second is control. Push means the queue decides your concurrency; pull means you do. Rate-limited sending is precisely a concurrency problem, and I'd rather have sendsPerSecond as a constant in the worker than as a subscription setting I have to reason about at 03:00. Push is fine for low-volume event fan-out where the receiver is already an internet-facing service. For draining a pool against a provider quota, pull.

Buy versus build, at the capacity you actually have

Option Interface What you operate Where it stops
BullMQ Node library Redis, its memory ceiling, failover Rate control is yours to write
Celery Python library Broker plus result backend Same, plus broker upgrades
Sidekiq Ruby library Redis Ruby-only pool
Temporal SDK plus cluster (or hosted) Cluster, or a vendor bill Overkill unless you need real workflows
QStash (Upstash) HTTP Nothing Push-oriented; you shape retries around it
Cloud Tasks HTTP or SDK Nothing Native dispatch-rate control, GCP-shaped
Infrai queue plus cron Plain REST, one key Nothing No DAG or fan-in join primitive

If you already run on GCP, Cloud Tasks has per-queue dispatch-rate control built in, which is this article's problem solved at the platform layer, and I'd take it. If you already run Redis with an on-call rotation that knows it, BullMQ or Sidekiq costs you nothing new. The build column gets expensive when the honest answer to "who pages when the broker fills up" is "the two of us."

The drain loop, with retries that cannot double-send

Standard queues are at-least-once. Plan on receiving a message twice: a worker that dies after sending but before acknowledging will see that job again, and that's normal queue behaviour rather than something to engineer away. FIFO deduplication windows are short — five minutes on Infrai — which is useful against a publisher retrying in a tight loop and useless for a daily job, so tenant-level idempotency has to live in your code and in the request itself.

The kickoff below publishes one message per tenant, staggering delay_seconds so the pool never asks for more than the provider's rate, and carries a deterministic idempotency key derived from the tenant and the report date. A retried publish is a no-op instead of a second digest.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const base = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

const sendsPerSecond = 14

type job struct {
    Queue   string         `json:"queue"`
    Payload map[string]any `json:"payload"`
    Delay   int            `json:"delay_seconds"`
}

func publish(client *http.Client, key string, j job, idem string) error {
    body, err := json.Marshal(j)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", base+"/queue/publish", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        // Same tenant, same report date, same key: a retry publishes nothing new.
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem)

        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        out, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()

        switch {
        case res.StatusCode < 300:
            return nil
        case res.StatusCode == 429:
            time.Sleep(backoff(attempt, res.Header.Get("Retry-After")))
        default:
            return fmt.Errorf("publish %s: %d %s", idem, res.StatusCode, out)
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("publish %s: rate limited after 5 attempts", idem)
}

func backoff(attempt int, retryAfter string) time.Duration {
    if s, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && s > 0 {
        return time.Duration(s) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is not set")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    day := time.Now().UTC().Format("2006-01-02")
    tenants := []string{"acme", "globex", "initech"}

    for i, tenant := range tenants {
        j := job{
            Queue:   "report-emails",
            Payload: map[string]any{"tenant": tenant, "report_date": day},
            Delay:   i / sendsPerSecond, // seconds; the ceiling is 7 days, so this is never close
        }
        if err := publish(client, key, j, "report-"+day+"-"+tenant); err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
    }
    fmt.Printf("queued %d report jobs for %s\n", len(tenants), day)
}

Two constraints shape the payload. Messages are capped at 256KB, which is fine for a tenant id and a date and hostile to an embedded PDF, so put the artifact in object storage and queue the reference. Retention runs to 30 days, and an acknowledged message is gone rather than replayable, so if you want to answer "what did we send on the 3rd" you keep that ledger yourself.

The idempotency key is doing real work here, and it's worth being precise about why: keys are a platform-wide convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window, which lines up almost exactly with a daily report cadence. Your worker needs the same discipline on the send side — the same key, or a row in your own sent table checked before the provider call. I'm not certain a 24-hour window is enough for teams doing hourly digests with long backfills, and that's the case I'd test before trusting it.

Verifying the drain, and backing it out at 03:00

Verification is two numbers and a comparison. Poll the queue depth while the pool runs and confirm it's monotonically decreasing:

curl -s -X GET "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/stats/report-emails" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY"

Then reconcile the provider's accepted count against your own sent ledger for that report date; a gap in either direction tells you whether you under-delivered or double-sent, which is the only measurement that actually matters for this SLO. Check the dead-letter queue before you call the run clean.

Rollback is pausing the schedule, not deleting the queue. Pause the cron job, let the pool finish what's already queued, and purge only if the payloads have gone stale — a purge on a queue you're still draining loses work that was already paced. One behaviour to plan around: a paused schedule doesn't back-fill the triggers it missed, so when you resume, trigger the run manually for the days you skipped.

If you're a small platform team with more vendor keys than dashboards, Infrai is worth trying for exactly this layer — the kickoff schedule, the queue, and the transactional send sit behind one key and one bill, which is one fewer credential to rotate and one fewer invoice to reconcile at month end. The catch is scope. There's no DAG or fan-in join primitive, so if your report run is really a workflow with branches that have to converge before the email goes out, Temporal is the right tool and a plain queue is not a good fit; equally, if your pool is locked inside a VPC and you were counting on push delivery, stick with pull workers. If that boundary matches your system, the queue-in-front-of-your-mail-provider write-up is a sensible next stop.

Further reading

  • Celery: introduction to task queues
  • RFC 6585 §4: 429 Too Many Requests
  • Exponential backoff
  • Infrai capability index (llms.txt)

title: What Should We Remove? Evaluating the Reliability and Costs of RLVR Data Decontamination
description:
arXiv:2610.21229v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) math corpora are routinely screened for benchmark overlap, but the reliability and data-loss costs of cleaning policies remain underexamined. We audit sixteen open RLVR math corpora comprising 1,673,514 corpus-specific training items against six benchmarks containing 1,949 questions. We evaluate eight policies based on exact, lexical, and semantic matching using 594 independently and blindly dual-reviewed training-benchmark pairs. Calibration and held-out sets have disjoint benchmark questions and training-example families. A separate review of all 83 candidate matches for 80 sampled training items measures item-level false removal. At cosine threshold 0.80, 52 of 59 sampled removals (88%) were confirmed false removals; this is not a demonstrated population rate. No semantic threshold in our preregistered grid (0.80-0.98) meets the 90% conservative-precision target on calibration. The existing judge-adjudicated policy achieves 98.1% resolved precision and 98.2% candidate-frame recall on held-out corpora. It has zero confirmed false removals among six sampled removals, with one unresolved case; this does not establish zero risk. Within the evaluated candidate frame, this policy offers a more favorable precision-recall balance than the semantic-threshold alternatives tested. Recall does not measure contamination outside the candidate frame. We release reviewed labels, per-policy decisions, and coverage accounting to support evaluation of cleaning reliability and cost rather than overlap counts alone.

title: CSS Cascade Layers (@layer): End Specificity Wars Forever
description:
CSS Cascade Layers (@layer) let you define explicit ordering for your stylesheet rules, solving specificity wars once and for all. Instead of fighting specificity with more specificity, you declare layers and the browser respects their order. Firefox 97+ supports cascade layers fully.

The Problem: Specificity Wars

Without layers, overriding third-party CSS or framework styles requires adding more specific selectors:

/* Bootstrap sets: */
.btn { background: blue; }

/* Your override needs higher specificity: */
.my-app .btn { background: green; } /* Hack: added parent class */
body .btn { background: green; }    /* Another hack */
.btn.btn { background: green; }     /* Double class hack */

This is the "specificity war" — you need increasingly awkward selectors to win.

@layer Basics

Define layers to control override priority:

/* Declare layer order upfront */
@layer reset, base, components, utilities;

/* Lower-priority layer first */
@layer reset {
  * { box-sizing: border-box; margin: 0; padding: 0; }
}

@layer base {
  body { font-family: system-ui; font-size: 16px; }
  a { color: blue; }
}

@layer components {
  .btn {
    display: inline-flex;
    padding: 8px 16px;
    border-radius: 4px;
    background: blue;
  }
}

/* Higher-priority layer last */
@layer utilities {
  .bg-red { background: red; }
  .text-center { text-align: center; }
}

Key rule: later-declared layers win over earlier ones. utilities overrides components overrides base overrides reset.

And crucially: all layered styles lose to unlayered styles:

/* This wins over anything in any @layer */
.btn { background: green; }

Unlayered CSS is like an implicit top-priority layer.

Solving Third-Party Override Problems

Push third-party CSS into a low-priority layer:

/* Declare your app's layers first, then the third-party layer */
@layer reset, third-party, base, components, utilities;

/* Import Bootstrap into the low-priority layer */
@layer third-party {
  @import url('bootstrap.css');
}

/* Your components automatically override Bootstrap, no specificity needed */
@layer components {
  .btn { background: #3B82F6; } /* Just works! */
}

This replaces all Bootstrap specificity hacks with a single architectural decision.

Importing into Layers 

/* Import a file into a layer */
@import 'reset.css' layer(reset);
@import 'third-party/bootstrap.css' layer(framework);

/* Or assign import layers inline */
@layer framework {
  @import url('bootstrap.css');
}

Nested Layers

Layers can contain sub-layers:

@layer components {
  @layer base, variants, states;

  @layer base {
    .btn { /* Base styles */ }
  }

  @layer variants {
    .btn-primary { /* Primary variant */ }
    .btn-danger { /* Danger variant */ }
  }

  @layer states {
    .btn:hover { /* Hover state */ }
    .btn:disabled { /* Disabled state */ }
  }
}

/* Reference nested layers from outside */
@layer components.states {
  .btn:focus { outline: 2px solid blue; }
}

Anonymous Layers

Layers without names — useful for one-shot CSS blocks that should have low priority:

@layer {
  /* Anonymous layer — can't be referenced again */
  .third-party-widget { color: blue; }
}

Anonymous layers are ordered in document order relative to named layers.

Practical Architecture: Design System Layers 

/* Design system layer hierarchy */
@layer
  reset,       /* 1. Normalize browser defaults */
  tokens,      /* 2. CSS custom properties / design tokens */
  base,        /* 3. Element defaults (h1, p, a, etc.) */
  layout,      /* 4. Page structure (grid, containers) */
  components,  /* 5. UI components (btn, card, modal) */
  utilities;   /* 6. Single-purpose utility classes */

/* App-specific overrides outside layers (highest priority) */

Layers and Specificity

Within a layer, specificity still matters:

@layer base {
  a { color: blue; }           /* Less specific */
  nav a { color: inherit; }   /* More specific — wins WITHIN this layer */
}

But cross-layer: later layer always wins regardless of specificity:

@layer first {
  body main section .container a.link { color: blue; } /* Very specific! */
}

@layer second {
  a { color: red; } /* Wins — later layer always beats earlier layer */
}

This is the superpower of cascade layers.

Firefox DevTools: Viewing Layers

Firefox DevTools shows cascade layers in the Inspector:

  1. Open Inspector → click an element
  2. In Styles panel: layers are shown with their layer name (e.g., components)
  3. The layer order affects which styles are overriding which

CSS Cascade Layers are a foundational improvement for CSS architecture — especially in large codebases with multiple teams or third-party integrations.

title: Stopping a Filesystem MCP Server From Reading .env Files
description:
Originally published at webofmike.com on 2026-10-16. The demo repo and every command in it were run before publishing.

Disclosure: I work at Solo.io, which created agentgateway and sells Solo Enterprise for agentgateway. The demos I cite are public repositories.

A filesystem MCP server scoped to one directory will still read .env out of that directory if an agent asks for it by path. Root scoping stops an agent leaving the sandbox. It says nothing about which file inside the sandbox gets opened, and .env, .ssh/id_rsa, and .git/config all live inside the same directory the agent is supposed to be working in. A r/mcp post from 2026-10-05, "Claude almost ingested my production .env via filesystem MCP," is exactly this failure mode, and the author ended up writing their own Rust guardrail rather than finding one upstream. I built themsquared/filesystem-mcp-env-guard to find the right control point for this, and the first thing I tried turned out not to work at all.

What I expected to write, and why it didn't work

agentgateway has a built-in MCP authorization policy: mcpAuthorization, CEL rules evaluated against mcp.tool.name, mcp.tool.target, and JWT claims like jwt.sub when authentication is configured. It's what you'd reach for first, and the agentgateway docs show rules like this working today:

mcpAuthorization:
  rules:
    - allow: |
        mcp.tool.name == "echo" ||
        mcp.tool.name == "get-sum"

That's a tool-name allowlist, and it's real: it runs, it works, I tested variants of it against a local agentgateway. The rule language is CEL, and CEL rules can reference whatever fields the runtime populates. The field I needed was the path argument of a read_text_file call, so a rule could say "deny when path contains .env."

That field isn't there. mcp.tool.arguments exists in agentgateway's CEL variable table, but it's marked post-request: populated for access logs, after the call has already run. mcpAuthorization rules evaluate before the call, when arguments aren't populated yet. You can gate read_text_file as a tool. You cannot gate it by which path it's being asked to read. I didn't want to assert that from documentation alone, so I wrote the rule, ran it against a real filesystem MCP server behind a real agentgateway v1.5.0 binary, and watched it evaluate every read_text_file call identically regardless of path. The tool-name rule works. The path rule has nothing to read.

The control that does see the path

Argument inspection and response mutation both go through ExtMCP: an external gRPC service that agentgateway calls before a tools/call request reaches the upstream server, and again after the response comes back. The interface is ext_mcp.proto, and it's small: two RPCs, CheckRequest and CheckResponse, each returning either "pass it through," "here's a mutated version," or "reject this with an error."

Wiring it in is a mcpGuardrails policy block pointing at the policy server:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://agentgateway.dev/schema/config
config:
  adminAddr: "off"
mcp:
  port: 13300
  policies:
    mcpGuardrails:
      processors:
      - kind: remote
        host: "localhost:9001"
        failureMode: failClosed
        methods:
          tools/call: full
  targets:
  - name: filesystem
    stdio:
      cmd: npx
      args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/path/to/sandbox"]

methods: tools/call: full means both hooks run for tools/call: CheckRequest before the filesystem server sees the call, CheckResponse after it answers. failureMode: failClosed matters more than it looks like it should, and I'll come back to it.

What the policy server does

The server is about 150 lines of Python. CheckRequest parses the JSON-RPC params, pulls name and arguments, and for path-bearing tools (read_text_file, read_file, read_media_file, get_file_info, and read_multiple_files, whose argument is a paths array rather than a single path) checks every path string against a denylist: .env, .ssh, .git/, credentials, id_rsa, id_ed25519, .aws/, .npmrc, .netrc.

def _check_arguments(tool_name: str, arguments: dict) -> str | None:
    fields = PATH_TOOLS.get(tool_name)
    if not fields:
        return None
    for field in fields:
        if field not in arguments:
            continue
        value = arguments[field]
        values = value if isinstance(value, list) else [value]
        for v in values:
            if isinstance(v, str) and (hit := _matches_denied_path(v)):
                return hit
    return None

A match returns an AuthorizationError from CheckRequest, and the filesystem server never opens the file:

$ npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli http://localhost:13300/mcp \
  --method tools/call --tool-name read_text_file --tool-arg path=/sandbox/.env
{"error":{"code":"error","message":"path argument matches denied pattern '.env'; filesystem-mcp-env-guard blocks reads of credential-bearing paths"}}

Compare that to the same call through an identical gateway with no guardrail policy at all:

$ npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli http://localhost:13301/mcp \
  --method tools/call --tool-name read_text_file --tool-arg path=/sandbox/.env
{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"DATABASE_URL=postgres://demo:demopass@localhost:5432/demodb\nAPI_KEY=sk-demo-FAKE1234567890abcdef\n"}]}

Same server, same sandbox, same path. The only difference is whether a policy server is in the loop.

The backstop: a path can look safe and still carry a secret

A denylist on the path argument catches the obvious case; it doesn't catch a file with an innocuous name whose contents happen to be a credential, say an app.log that got an API key pasted into a debug line. That's what CheckResponse is for. It scans returned text content for secret-shaped substrings (API keys, password=, Postgres connection strings, PEM private key blocks, AWS access key IDs) and redacts matches before the response leaves the gateway:

$ npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli http://localhost:13300/mcp \
  --method tools/call --tool-name read_text_file --tool-arg path=/sandbox/app.log
{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"2026-10-15 boot ok\n2026-10-15 connecting with API_KEY=[REDACTED] to upstream\n2026-10-15 password=[REDACTED] for service account\n"}]}

app.log was never on the denylist. It didn't need to be; the response hook doesn't care which path produced the content, only what the content looks like. Two different control points, two different jobs: the request hook stops the obvious reads before they happen, the response hook catches what the obvious reads didn't.

The tradeoff failClosed actually costs you

failureMode: failClosed means agentgateway denies a guarded call if the policy server is unreachable, rather than letting it through unchecked. That's the right default for a credential-path control, and it's also a real availability dependency, not just a config knob. I killed the policy server mid-demo and re-ran a read of the completely harmless notes.txt file:

$ npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli http://localhost:13300/mcp \
  --method tools/call --tool-name read_text_file --tool-arg path=/sandbox/notes.txt
{"error":{"code":"error","message":"mcpGuardrails checkRequest failed: upstream call failed: Connect: Connection refused (os error 61)"}}

A file with nothing sensitive in it, denied, because the gateway has no way to know the policy server would have said yes. That's the cost of fail-closed stated honestly: your filesystem MCP server's uptime is now bounded by your policy server's uptime. failOpen removes that dependency and reintroduces the original problem the moment the policy server has a bad day. For credential-bearing paths, failing closed is the only answer that doesn't quietly become the baseline again under load.

Running it 

git clone https://github.com/themsquared/filesystem-mcp-env-guard
cd filesystem-mcp-env-guard
AGENTGATEWAY_BIN=/path/to/agentgateway bash scripts/demo.sh

The script spins up the unguarded baseline, proves the .env leak, tears it down, brings up the guard server and the guarded gateway, runs five more calls (safe read, .env denied, .ssh/id_rsa denied, a read_multiple_files call with one denied path in the array, and the response-mask backstop), then kills the policy server and shows the fail-closed behavior. Seven checks, all passing, full JSON captured under captures/.

What this doesn't claim

The denylist is substring matching on a path string, not a path-policy language. A symlink planted before the guard is in place, or a cleverly named directory, isn't something nine string checks catch, and I'm not claiming it is. The response-mask patterns are a fixed set for this demo's credential shapes, not a general DLP engine. Both are the right shape of control, scoped honestly: a first line of defense for the obvious case, sitting at the one point in the request path that can actually see the argument before the read happens.

Related

I covered a related problem on the discovery surface, server-controlled MCP instructions landing in a model's trusted prompt, in Keeping MCP Server Instructions Out of Your Agent's System Prompt. Same lesson from a different angle: the control has to sit at the point in the request path that can actually see the untrusted input, not wherever is easiest to configure.

Frequently asked questions

Can agentgateway's mcpAuthorization policy block a tool call based on a file path argument?

No. mcpAuthorization evaluates CEL rules against mcp.tool.name, mcp.tool.target, and JWT claims. mcp.tool.arguments is only populated after the call completes, for access logs, so a rule can't reference the path argument before the read happens. Blocking by path needs an external policy server through ExtMCP's CheckRequest hook, which runs before the call reaches the upstream server.

Why can a filesystem MCP server read .env or .ssh files if it's scoped to one directory?

Root scoping restricts which directory an agent can reach, not which file inside it. .env, .ssh, and .git normally live inside that same scoped directory, so a server correctly honoring its root still opens them when a tool call asks for that exact path. Scoping and path policy are two different controls.

What is ExtMCP in agentgateway?

A gRPC policy interface defined in ext_mcp.proto. An external server implements CheckRequest and CheckResponse, and agentgateway calls it before a tools/call request reaches the upstream MCP server and after the response comes back, so the policy server can reject, mutate, or redact either side.

What happens if the ExtMCP policy server goes down?

With failureMode: failClosed, agentgateway denies every guarded call while the policy server is unreachable, including reads that would otherwise be allowed, because the gateway has no way to know the policy server would have said yes. The alternative, failOpen, lets calls through unchecked instead: no outage risk, but the .env and .ssh reads this policy exists to stop go through unchecked the moment the policy server has a bad day. For credential-bearing paths, failing closed is the only choice that doesn't quietly become the baseline again under load.

Canonical version, with machine-readable markdown at https://webofmike.com/filesystem-mcp-env-guard/index.md: https://webofmike.com/filesystem-mcp-env-guard/

title: Amazon DynamoDB Streams now supports timestamp-based stream processing
description:
Amazon DynamoDB Streams now supports timestamp-based stream processing, enabling you to begin reading stream records from a specific point in time. Previously, you could only start from the oldest retained record (up to 24 hours old) or from new records written after you start consuming the stream. Now, you can supply a timestamp and begin processing at the first record written at or after that time using the AT_TIMESTAMP shard iterator type.

Timestamp-based stream processing can be used with the Amazon Kinesis Client Library (KCL) through the DynamoDB Streams Kinesis adapter. It helps you avoid reprocessing entire retained streams or missing records when resuming stream consumption, supporting common use cases such as recovery after an interruption, data replay for debugging and auditing by reading from a specific point in the past, skipping a backlog by resuming from a recent timestamp near the latest records, and synchronizing after a restore by beginning at the export timestamp following a point-in-time recovery (PITR) export.

Timestamp-based stream processing is available in all commercial AWS Regions, the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. There is no additional charge for this feature beyond standard GetRecords API request charges. To get started, see Amazon DynamoDB Streams timestamp documentation in the DynamoDB developer guide.

title: Prune the Summary, Not the History: Source-Judged Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.20927v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents rely on context compaction: when the interaction history outgrows the context window, a compressor replaces it with a natural-language summary. We show that these summaries contain more than a record of what happened. Compaction prompts ask for decisions and next steps, so each summary mixes facts established by the environment with reasoning written by the compressor, and the agent cannot tell the two apart afterwards. In an analysis of a widely used structured compressor, 83% of failed runs trace back to an action that carries out a specific summary entry, most of which no environment output supports. We propose Source-Judged Compaction (SJC), a training-free post-processing step that scores each summary entry for whether it has a source in the environment outputs or the previous summary, and removes the entries that do not. It changes neither the agent nor the compressor and adds one inexpensive judge request per compaction. The judge is Jev, a non-generative decision model that answers the source question with a calibrated probability instead of text. On AppWorld and OfficeBench with two agent models, SJC improves cross-run reliability over the underlying compressor by 2.1%-8.9% without increasing the agent's token usage.

title: Can World and Action Modeling Benefit Each Other under Unified Causal Training?
description:
arXiv:2610.21095v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World and action modeling are closely related, yet their reciprocal benefits under unified causal training remain unclear. We introduce OneWM, a simple framework for unified causal training that treats actions as both conditions for world prediction and targets for policy learning within a shared video-action architecture. Using this framework, we investigate whether learning forward dynamics conditioned on specified actions improves action learning, and whether learning to generate actions in turn improves action-conditioned world modeling. We use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa365 as embodied testbeds to evaluate both policy learning and world modeling, complemented by real-world policy experiments. Learning the visual consequences of specified actions improves policy performance and generalization across changing scenes. In turn, action learning improves multi-view world-prediction fidelity under the same architecture. Together, these results answer both questions positively, supporting reciprocal benefits between world modeling and action generation under unified causal training.

title: CoViG: Coarsened Vision GNN for Image Classification
description:
arXiv:2610.21321v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Although Graph Neural Networks are widely used in various domains, they remained mostly unexplored in computer vision. Convolutional Neural Networks and Vision Transformers were leading the field, until the quite recent introduction of Vision Graphs (ViG) that treat images as a set of nodes and apply graph convolution on their k-NN graphs. ViGs show impressive accuracy on image classification but their computational cost remains relatively high. Inspired by optimization methods for GNNs, we present CoViG, a novel approach combining graph coarsening and ViGs. Our method introduces an additional MinCUT pooling step within the Grapher component of intermediate ViG blocks. By simplifying the intermediate graphs and thus decreasing the number of nodes of specific blocks, our approach considerably reduces the computational cost of ViG during inference. We evaluated our approach on ImageNet with several ViG architectures, and we obtained accuracies equivalent to the original ViG models with only about 51\% of FLOPs.

title: CausalEvo: Causal Skill Self-Evolution for Health LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21016v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for health can accumulate reusable textual skills from task feedback, such as calculation criteria, measurement time points, and formula units. Deciding which skills to retain is consequential: useful rules improve later answers, while faulty generalizations propagate errors. We propose CausalEvo, a method for causal skill self-evolution that estimates the relative effects of deliberately changed skill sets while holding the model weights, feedback cases, and rule count fixed. At each evolution step, a frozen LLM proposes candidate rules, which are pooled with the incumbent skills so that the current skill set remains a feasible choice. Paired skill replacements against shared background rules are scored on the same feedback cases; least squares converts the score differences into relative skill values, and the top-ranked rules are retained, favoring incumbents on ties. A decision-loss bound separates candidate support, approximation, and estimation errors. On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks with 120 held-out cases, CausalEvo achieves 60.00% accuracy, compared with 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills. Across the recorded training configurations, which use different optimization budgets, it consumes 55.6% fewer training tokens than SkillOpt. Gains concentrate in particular calculations alongside regressions on others, and paired accuracy intervals include zero. CausalEvo turns task feedback into controlled decisions about skill retention and replacement. Project repository: https://github.com/txbrook/CausalEvo

title: KNOU-Flood: Advancing global streamflow forecasting with lead-aware probabilistic machine learning
description:
arXiv:2610.20640v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Global streamflow forecasting supports flood preparedness, yet data-driven models trained on reanalysis lose skill when driven by operational forecasts, increasingly so with lead time. AIFL addresses this shift with a two-stage transfer-learning recipe and a deterministic LSTM, but it feeds one forecast lead time into the whole input window and gives no uncertainty. We ask how far this open recipe can be extended without changing its recurrent core. KNOU-Flood keeps a single-layer LSTM and the two-stage training and changes the information around it: a longer input window (424 days), lead-aware forecast inputs, GraphCast as a second forecast source next to ECMWF HRES, and a latent-noise ensemble trained with the fair CRPS. We compare against a re-implementation of the AIFL recipe (its code is not public) under identical data, stations, splits and metrics. Our contributions are threefold. First, over three seeds and 2,099 test basins (2021-2023), KNOU-Flood reaches a median KGE' of 0.65 at LT1 and 0.48 at LT10 against 0.62 and 0.34, with significant gains at all ten lead times under two scoring protocols, also against a 1024-unit baseline and on held-out basins (one seed each). Second, identical weights give an LT10 KGE' of 0.18 or 0.34 depending on how forecasts are fed, so much of the lead-time decay reported for AIFL is an input-protocol effect; the probabilistic head contributes most to the gain, followed by the raw GraphCast channels, the longer window and mixed fine-tuning. Third, the ensembles reach lower CRPS than probabilistic versions of the baseline, are nearly calibrated with inference-time dropout, and detect 1.5- and 2-year floods better than all baselines; the benefit for rarer floods depends on the seed, and an exploratory tail-weighted variant improves 10-year and larger events. KNOU-Flood is a controlled extension of an open recipe, not a new architecture.

title: ARIA: Runtime Inspection and Amendment for Multi-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.20780v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), a local mistake can propagate as other agents build on it, turning a correctable error into a failed task. Diagnosing completed runs or repeatedly re-executing them to search for corrections does not provide a learned policy for intervening while execution is still in progress. We present Agent Runtime Inspection and Amendment (ARIA), a framework for learning when and how to repair ongoing multi-agent executions. Our key intuition is to turn execution-verified repairs into reusable supervision, moving repair search into data construction and training so that a learned model can intervene at runtime without repeatedly testing alternatives. First, we collect over 24{,}000 successful and failed trajectories across four multi-agent frameworks, six benchmarks, and eight host models. From these trajectories, we construct the ARIA dataset, to our knowledge the first large-scale dataset pairing failed multi-agent trajectories with execution-verified repairs. It contains 3{,}953 verified repair pairs, each specifying what went wrong, where to intervene, and how execution should continue. Then, we develop the ARIA framework for MAS-agnostic runtime inspection and amendment, designed to integrate with any MAS that exposes execution trajectories and supports continuation replacement. Using verified repairs as training examples, we teach a compact model to recognize when intervention is needed and how to correct an ongoing run. The aim is to learn repair strategies that apply to related failures in new configurations, rather than merely reproduce individual corrections. Finally, the trained ARIA model demonstrates strong repair performance in both post-hoc and runtime settings, with generalization to unseen frameworks and host models. Our code is available at https://github.com/LabRAI/ARIA.

title: Backends on Vercel: Python, containers, and Daemons
description:
Last year, we expanded zero-config support for Python and TypeScript backend frameworks. By this summer, developers could deploy their frontend and backend together with Vercel Services and coordinate background work with queues and durable workflows.

Today at Vercel Ship in San Francisco, we are expanding the backend workloads you can run on Vercel. Python on Vercel is now generally available, container support in Vercel Functions enables custom runtimes and system libraries, and we are introducing Vercel Daemons in Public Beta for background workers that pull work and stay running between jobs.

Python is now generally available

You can build your backend in Python with the Vercel infrastructure and development experience you know from your frontend, including local development, previews, and production deployments. Frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, and Django run on standard CPython with your PyPI dependencies, while Vercel handles framework detection, builds, and scaling.

Already, 150,000 teams run Python backends on Vercel, including engineers at OpenAI, Polymarket, and Exa.

SDKs for Python let you use Vercel products from your application, whether you’re storing files in Vercel Blob, sending background jobs to Vercel Queues, coordinating durable steps with Vercel Workflows, running untrusted code in Vercel Sandbox, or streaming model responses and handling tool calls with the AI SDK for Python.

Delphi, which builds AI digital minds from books and talks, moved its Python backend from AWS ECS to Vercel. With ten engineers and no dedicated infrastructure role, the team ships to production more than 100 times a day and uses Queues to handle background jobs.

Visit the Python knowledge base for framework details and examples.

Applications in any language with containers

The Vercel container runtime lets you deploy applications written in any language, packaged with the OS libraries and executables they need. Since container support entered Public Beta, 5,000 teams have shipped 150,000 container deployments on Vercel.

Containers deploy as Vercel Functions on Fluid compute, scaling with traffic and using Active CPU pricing, which doesn’t charge for idle time spent waiting for API responses, database queries, or LLM inferencing. Vercel Services lets you develop and deploy your backend alongside your frontend, while Vercel CDN serves traffic on your domains, Vercel WAF protects it, logs help you investigate issues, and rollbacks restore earlier deployments.

For example, take a video app that uses a container for background processing, preparing a playback copy and thumbnail for each uploaded clip. This Dockerfile packages the Python processor, its dependencies, and ffmpeg to run with Daemons:

When you deploy through Git or the Vercel CLI, Vercel builds the image and stores it in your Vercel Container Registry. Read our containerized Functions deployment guide to get started.

Background workers with Vercel Daemons

Vercel Daemons lets you deploy containers as continuously running background workers on Fluid compute. You choose the number of instances in each region, and Vercel maintains that capacity by restarting processes when they exit or crash.

Daemons launches with support for pull-based workloads, where your code requests work from another system and processes it as it becomes available. That could mean consuming queue messages or fetching pending jobs from a database.

In our example, Daemons runs the video processor continuously as it pulls jobs from Vercel Queues. In vercel.toml, define the Next.js frontend, route requests to it, and add the processor using Dockerfile:

Follow the Daemons deployment guide to add a background worker to your Vercel project.

Run your backends on Vercel

We’re continuing to invest in backend support so more of your existing application can run on Vercel, using the languages, dependencies, and execution patterns it needs.

Resources

  • Read the complete guide to Vercel Daemons
