title: Build a Resume-Safe Batch Summarizer: A Case Study on a Free Server
description:
It is 1 a.m., the fan is loud, and the lid is closed. Somewhere in that folder of lecture notes, a job is either still moving or already dead, and you have no way to tell which until morning.

That gap is the whole reason this article exists. I wanted one small project — summarize every file in a folder — and I wanted a crash to cost me exactly one file. Not the whole night, not the whole budget. So the learning question here is narrow: when a batch job dies in the middle, what is the smallest piece of state that lets you restart without paying twice? If you can answer that in your head before reading on, you already own this idea.

The project, end to end

I called it nightshift. One folder of note files goes in, one append-only ledger.jsonl comes out, and every line in that ledger is a claim about a single file: "I was processed, here is the result, here is the model and prompt version that produced it." That's it. No database, no queue service, no framework.

The reason I reached for MonkeyCode here is boring and practical: the free model access gives me an endpoint I don't have to pay for to run a batch of a few hundred small calls, and the free server option means the job can keep running after my laptop sleeps. Both are availability claims from the operator rather than things I've audited myself. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The allowance I was told to expect is on the order of ten million free tokens, and there is a free server option alongside it. Treat those numbers as a starting point to confirm on the project page before you plan a semester around them — I have not measured the quota, and you shouldn't assume it is permanent either.

Prerequisites, exactly

Python 3.11 or newer (I ran this on 3.11.9), standard library only, and a folder of text files. That's the whole list. I deliberately keep the fixture .txt files so nothing in this article depends on network access — if you have PDFs, extract them to text first with pdftotext and let the runner stay ignorant of file formats.

Here is the naive version I started from, and I want you to see it fail before I fix it:

for p in Path("corpus").rglob("*.txt"):
    summary = call_model(p.read_text())
    open("out.jsonl", "a").write(json.dumps({"file": str(p), "summary": summary}) + "\n")

Three things go wrong. Kill it at file 211 and the next run re-sends files 1 through 210 — you paid twice for the same text. Key your output on the path and a renamed copy becomes a brand new call. And a plain write without a flush can leave a half-written line that poisons every later read. None of these are exotic; they are just invisible until the second run.

The artifact

Save this as nightshift.py. It is the entire runner.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""nightshift.py - resumable batch summarizer. Python 3.11+, stdlib only."""
import hashlib
import json
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

PROMPT_VERSION = "sum-v1"
LEDGER = Path("ledger.jsonl")
SUFFIXES = {".txt", ".pdf"}


def fingerprint(path: Path, model: str) -> str:
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    h.update(path.read_bytes())
    h.update(model.encode("utf-8"))
    h.update(PROMPT_VERSION.encode("utf-8"))
    return h.hexdigest()[:16]


def load_done(ledger: Path) -> dict:
    done = {}
    if not ledger.exists():
        return done
    for lineno, line in enumerate(ledger.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines(), 1):
        if not line.strip():
            continue
        try:
            rec = json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            print(f"warning: torn line {lineno} ignored", file=sys.stderr)
            continue
        done[rec["key"]] = rec
    return done


def append(ledger: Path, rec: dict) -> None:
    with ledger.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        fh.write(json.dumps(rec, sort_keys=True) + "\n")
        fh.flush()
        os.fsync(fh.fileno())


def stub_model(text: str, model: str) -> str:
    if not text.strip():
        raise ValueError("empty input: no text to summarize")
    words = text.split()
    return f"[{model}] {len(words)} words; first: {' '.join(words[:3])}"


def summarize(path: Path, model: str) -> str:
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
    if os.environ.get("NIGHTSHIFT_STUB") == "1":
        return stub_model(text, model)
    raise SystemExit("no client wired; see the endpoint section")


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    root = Path(argv[1] if len(argv) > 1 else "corpus")
    model = os.environ.get("NIGHTSHIFT_MODEL", "stub-model")
    files = sorted(p for p in root.rglob("*") if p.is_file() and p.suffix in SUFFIXES)
    done = load_done(LEDGER)

    todo, seen, skipped = [], set(), 0
    for p in files:
        key = fingerprint(p, model)
        if key in done or key in seen:
            skipped += 1
            continue
        seen.add(key)
        todo.append((key, p))

    print(f"corpus={len(files)} todo={len(todo)} skipped={skipped}")
    for key, p in todo:
        try:
            summary = summarize(p, model)
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"FAIL {p.name} {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")
            append(LEDGER, {"key": key, "file": p.name, "status": "error",
                            "error": type(exc).__name__})
            continue
        append(LEDGER, {"key": key, "file": p.name, "status": "ok",
                        "model": model, "prompt": PROMPT_VERSION,
                        "summary": summary})
        print(f"OK   {p.name}")

    poison = sum(1 for r in load_done(LEDGER).values() if r["status"] == "error")
    print(f"poison={poison}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main(sys.argv))

The fingerprint function is the load-bearing part. It hashes the file bytes, the model name, and the prompt version together, so the same text under a different model is a different job — which is what you want when you swap endpoints, and mildly annoying the first time it silently re-runs everything. That annoyance is the point. A cache that ignores the model is a cache that lies.

The failing input, and the run you can reproduce

Build a fixture with one deliberately broken file. The empty one is my poison file.

mkdir -p corpus
printf 'attention is a lookup table\n' > corpus/a.txt
printf 'a softmax turns scores into weights\n' > corpus/b.txt
: > corpus/c.txt
cp corpus/a.txt corpus/dup_of_a.txt

Now run it offline. The stub keeps the whole exercise network-free.

NIGHTSHIFT_STUB=1 NIGHTSHIFT_MODEL=stub-model python3 nightshift.py corpus

Expected output on the first run:

corpus=4 todo=3 skipped=1
OK   a.txt
OK   b.txt
FAIL c.txt ValueError: empty input: no text to summarize
poison=1

Read the counters slowly, because each one is a decision. skipped=1 is dup_of_a.txt: identical bytes plus identical model plus identical prompt version produced a key already seen in this pass, so it never left the machine. That deduplication is free, and I did not write a single line of code for it. FAIL c.txt is the empty file — most model endpoints reject a blank prompt, so I raise the same way the stub does, and the failure path deliberately writes an error record instead of a summary.

And poison=1 is the trap I want you to notice. The error record uses the same key, so load_done counts it as handled and the next run will not retry it. That is the right default for a batch you are paying for — one broken file shouldn't burn retries forever — but it means a poisoned key sits there quietly until you delete its line by hand. Delete the line, and only that file re-runs.

Run it a second time:

corpus=4 todo=0 skipped=4
poison=1

Zero todo. Nothing resent, nothing re-billed, and the crash boundary is now the only file that was in flight when the process died. That is the property I wanted at 1 a.m.

The ledger itself is the last thing worth inspecting:

{"file": "a.txt", "key": "…", "model": "stub-model", "prompt": "sum-v1", "status": "ok", "summary": "[stub-model] 5 words; first: attention is a"}

The key is a 16-hex-character digest in the real file; I elided it because yours will differ from mine and the counts will not.

Moving it to the free server

Here is where the free server option actually earns its place. My laptop sleeps, and a sleeping laptop is a job that stops without telling you. A box that stays awake turns a 40-minute batch into something you check over breakfast.

Two commands do the trip. Ship the corpus and the script, then start the run detached so an SSH hiccup doesn't kill it:

rsync -av corpus/ box:~/nightshift/corpus/
rsync -av nightshift.py box:~/nightshift/
ssh box 'cd ~/nightshift && NIGHTSHIFT_MODEL=<model-id> nohup python3 nightshift.py corpus > run.log 2>&1 &'
ssh box 'tail -f ~/nightshift/run.log'
rsync -av box:~/nightshift/ledger.jsonl ./ledger.jsonl

Notice what I did not do: I did not try to make the remote box reliable. I made it disposable. The ledger is the only state that matters, it is append-only, and it travels back over rsync in a second. If the free server is reclaimed tomorrow, I lose the run in progress and nothing else — which is exactly the trade I want from something I am not paying for.

When should you run where? I use three rules:

Situation Run it on Why
Under ~50 files, one-off Your laptop Setup cost outweighs the benefit
Long batch, sleeps overnight Free server Keeps running when your lid closes
Deadline or SLA attached Paid endpoint Free tiers carry no promises
Anything confidential Neither You cannot send the text to a third party at all

That last row is not rhetorical. Lecture notes you wrote are fine. A friend's medical records, an employer's internal docs, or someone else's copyrighted book are not — no free tier makes that decision for you.

Common mistakes I hit while writing this

Using the file path as the key instead of the content hash. It works perfectly until you reorganize your folders, and then every file is new.

Forgetting to version the prompt. Change one word in your instruction, rerun, and now your ledger holds two incompatible generations of summaries with no way to tell them apart. PROMPT_VERSION costs you one line.

Retrying on a timer instead of on a key. Time-based retry logic guesses. A ledger does not guess; it knows whether the key is present.

And the one I still catch myself doing: writing to the ledger before the call succeeds. Order matters here. Call, then append, never the reverse.

What I actually learned

A batch job is not a loop. It is a loop plus a durable claim about what already happened, and the claim is worth more than the loop. Once the key exists, retries, model swaps, machine swaps, and crashes all collapse into the same boring question: is this key in the set?

I also stopped treating the free server as an environment and started treating it as a spot to stand. Something you can lose without losing work is a much better fit for a free tier than hoping it behaves like a paid one.

How to swap in a real endpoint: replace the body of summarize with an HTTP call, set NIGHTSHIFT_STUB to nothing, and keep the guard that raises when neither is configured. The exact request shape belongs to whichever endpoint you were given, and I have not run this particular client, so treat it as a sketch rather than tested code:

# SKETCH - unexecuted. Adapt the payload and the response path to your endpoint.
import urllib.request

def call_endpoint(text: str, model: str) -> str:
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        os.environ["NIGHTSHIFT_URL"],
        data=json.dumps({"model": model, "messages": [
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Summarize in one sentence:\n{text}"}]}).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json",
                 "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['NIGHTSHIFT_KEY']}"},
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60) as resp:
        return json.load(resp)["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

Who should not use this approach? Anyone whose batch has a deadline attached, anyone processing text they are not allowed to send off-device, and anyone who needs to cite an exact model version months later in published work. A free tier plus a hand-rolled ledger is a good fit for a student's overnight notes job, and a poor fit for a pipeline with a contract behind it.

Your turn, and I am more interested in the diagnosis than the applause. Suppose c.txt is the second file in a 400-file run and the process dies at file 300. On restart, which counters change, and which file never gets a second chance no matter how many times you rerun? If you can predict that from the code above, you have the pattern — and a good extension exercise is splitting skipped into two counters, one for keys already in the ledger and one for duplicates caught inside the current pass, so the log stops conflating them.

title: How to trace and evaluate an AI agent in Microsoft Foundry, from the first trace to production monitoring
description:
Microsoft Foundry splits agent observability into three capabilities, and each one answers a different question. Tracing shows what the agent did during a run, evaluation scores how good its answers were against criteria you choose, and monitoring keeps asking both questions once the agent is in front of users. This post goes through them in the order you'll usually need them, using the official Python samples, and it says which parts Microsoft labels as generally available and which as preview, because that label decides how much weight each piece can carry.

What's generally available and what isn't

Tracing is generally available for prompt agents and hosted agents, while workflow agents and external agents are still in preview. Microsoft's Build announcement from June 3, 2026 says tracing and evaluations reached general availability in the spring, but the reference pages still attach preview labels to individual pieces. On the agent evaluators page, Task Adherence, Task Completion, Intent Resolution, Customer Satisfaction, Output Quality and Tool Use Quality are labeled preview, while the tool evaluators such as Tool Call Accuracy don't carry any label at all. On the monitoring page, agent metrics, recurring evaluations, red team scans and alerts are labeled preview, and the page says Microsoft doesn't recommend its preview items for production workloads. The GitHub Action for evaluations is in preview too. I checked these labels on October 14, 2026, and since they change quickly, it's worth reopening the linked pages before you build on any of them.

Step 1, connect Application Insights and read your first trace

Tracing for prompt agents and hosted agents works on the server side, so you don't need to change anything in your code. With the New Foundry toggle turned on, open your project, go to Agents, select Traces and choose Connect, then attach an existing Application Insights resource or create a new one. From that point the runs of an agent hosted in Foundry are recorded through OpenTelemetry, including the model calls, the tool invocations, the decisions the agent took and its dependencies on other services, as described in the observability overview.

To read the traces you'll need the Log Analytics Reader role on the connected Application Insights resource, plus Privileged Monitoring Data Reader when the underlying Log Analytics tables are protected. After you run the agent once, the Traces tab lets you search, filter and sort the traces from the last 90 days, open one to step through its spans, or search by Response ID or Trace ID and open a Conversation ID to see the history, token counts, run steps, tool calls, inputs and outputs. If nothing shows up, the setup page recommends waiting a few minutes and refreshing before you head to its troubleshooting section. That page also covers client side tracing with azure-core-tracing-opentelemetry, which is optional and meant for the code of your own application.

Step 2, evaluate the agent with a small dataset

A trace tells you what happened but not whether the answer was good, and that's the job of evaluation. The sample below follows the official page on evaluating your AI agents, with the rubric generation step removed so it only uses evaluators that ship with Foundry. You'll need the Foundry User role on the project, which Microsoft renamed from Azure AI User without changing the role IDs, and a chat completion model deployment that acts as the judge for the evaluators that use a model.

That page asks for azure-ai-projects 2.4.0 or later, while other pages in the same documentation list lower minimums, so it's safer to install the latest release.

pip install "azure-ai-projects>=2.4.0" azure-identity

Set the environment variables AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT and AZURE_AI_MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME, then create a JSONL file called test-queries.jsonl where each line holds a query field. These three lines are only example questions, so swap them for the questions your agent gets.

{"query": "What is the difference between an Azure region and an availability zone?"}
{"query": "When should I use Azure Functions instead of a virtual machine?"}
{"query": "How do I stop a storage account from being publicly accessible?"}

The first part of the script creates the clients and uploads the dataset to your project.

import os
import time

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.ai.projects import AIProjectClient

endpoint = os.environ["AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT"]
model_deployment = os.environ["AZURE_AI_MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME"]
AGENT_NAME = "my-agent"  # replace with the name of your agent

project_client = AIProjectClient(endpoint=endpoint, credential=DefaultAzureCredential())
client = project_client.get_openai_client()

dataset = project_client.datasets.upload_file(
    name="agent-test-queries",
    version="1",
    file_path="./test-queries.jsonl",
)

The second part defines what to measure and creates the evaluation. Coherence is scored by the judge deployment, while Violence comes from the risk and safety group, which the official sample runs without a judge deployment.

from azure.ai.projects.models import TestingCriterionAzureAIEvaluator
from openai.types.eval_create_params import DataSourceConfigCustom

testing_criteria = [
    TestingCriterionAzureAIEvaluator(
        type="azure_ai_evaluator",
        name="Coherence",
        evaluator_name="builtin.coherence",
        initialization_parameters={"deployment_name": model_deployment},
        data_mapping={
            "query": "{{item.query}}",
            "response": "{{sample.output_text}}",
        },
    ),
    TestingCriterionAzureAIEvaluator(
        type="azure_ai_evaluator",
        name="Violence",
        evaluator_name="builtin.violence",
        data_mapping={
            "query": "{{item.query}}",
            "response": "{{sample.output_text}}",
        },
    ),
]

data_source_config = DataSourceConfigCustom(
    type="custom",
    item_schema={
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["query"],
    },
    include_sample_schema=True,
)

evaluation = client.evals.create(
    name="Agent Quality Evaluation",
    data_source_config=data_source_config,
    testing_criteria=testing_criteria,
)

The third part starts the run. With the azure_ai_target_completions source, Foundry sends every query to the agent named in the target and evaluates the answers it gets back, which is why the mappings above read from sample.output_text.

eval_run = client.evals.runs.create(
    eval_id=evaluation.id,
    name="Agent Evaluation Run",
    data_source={
        "type": "azure_ai_target_completions",
        "source": {"type": "file_id", "id": dataset.id},
        "input_messages": {
            "type": "template",
            "template": [
                {
                    "type": "message",
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": {"type": "input_text", "text": "{{item.query}}"},
                }
            ],
        },
        "target": {"type": "azure_ai_agent", "name": AGENT_NAME},
    },
)

while True:
    run = client.evals.runs.retrieve(run_id=eval_run.id, eval_id=evaluation.id)
    if run.status in ["completed", "failed"]:
        break
    time.sleep(5)

print(f"Status: {run.status}")
print(f"Report URL: {run.report_url}")

In the response, result_counts gives the total, passed, failed and errored rows, per_testing_criteria_results breaks the same numbers down by evaluator, and each row carries a score, a label, a reason, a threshold and a passed flag for every evaluator. The report_url opens the same results in the Foundry portal, where they also show up under the Evaluations tab, and the reason field is where I'd start reading when a row fails.

If your agent calls tools, the tool use evaluators are the ones worth adding next. Tool Call Accuracy checks that the agent made the right calls with correct parameters and without redundancy, Tool Selection checks that it chose the tools it needed and no extra ones, Tool Input Accuracy checks the parameters, Tool Output Utilization checks whether the agent used the results correctly, and Tool Call Success checks that the calls ended without technical errors. Four of them take tool_definitions as an input, and Tool Call Accuracy scores on a scale of one to five before a threshold turns that score into a pass or a fail.

What it costs and where it's restricted

Risk and safety evaluations, which include the Violence evaluator used above, and agents playground evaluations are billed on consumption, and playground evaluations are enabled by default for every Foundry project. To turn them off, clear all the evaluators in the playground's metrics selector. Some features also have regional restrictions, namely rubric generation, synthetic and trace based dataset creation, and the risk and safety evaluators, so check the supported regions before you run the sample in a project you already have. The monitoring data itself lives in the connected Application Insights resource, so its retention and billing follow however you've configured that resource.

Step 3, keep evaluating after release

The monitoring page describes continuous evaluation, which runs an evaluation on sampled traffic while the agent serves users. The code below creates an evaluation with an azure_ai_source and attaches a rule that runs it whenever a response from the named agent completes. The project managed identity needs the Foundry User role for continuous evaluation rules to run, and the rule is capped by max_hourly_runs, which the sample sets to 100 and which Microsoft documents as the default limit per hour. Once the cap is reached, further runs are skipped until the next hour or until you raise the value.

import os

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.ai.projects import AIProjectClient
from azure.ai.projects.models import (
    EvaluationRule,
    ContinuousEvaluationRuleAction,
    EvaluationRuleFilter,
    EvaluationRuleEventType,
)

endpoint = os.environ["AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT"]
agent_name = os.environ["AZURE_AI_AGENT_NAME"]

with (
    DefaultAzureCredential() as credential,
    AIProjectClient(endpoint=endpoint, credential=credential) as project_client,
    project_client.get_openai_client() as openai_client,
):
    eval_object = openai_client.evals.create(
        name="Continuous Evaluation",
        data_source_config={"type": "azure_ai_source", "scenario": "responses"},
        testing_criteria=[
            {
                "type": "azure_ai_evaluator",
                "name": "violence_detection",
                "evaluator_name": "builtin.violence",
            }
        ],
    )

    rule = project_client.evaluation_rules.create_or_update(
        id="my-continuous-eval-rule",
        evaluation_rule=EvaluationRule(
            display_name="My Continuous Eval Rule",
            description="Runs on agent response completions",
            action=ContinuousEvaluationRuleAction(
                eval_id=eval_object.id, max_hourly_runs=100
            ),
            event_type=EvaluationRuleEventType.RESPONSE_COMPLETED,
            filter=EvaluationRuleFilter(agent_name=agent_name),
            enabled=True,
        ),
    )
    print(f"Rule created (id: {rule.id})")

To read the results, open the agent in the Foundry portal and select Monitor. The dashboard shows token usage, latency, run success rate, evaluation metrics and red teaming results for the time range you pick, and the documentation gives two starting points for interpreting it. Latency above ten seconds may point to model throttling, complex tool calls or network issues, and a run success rate below 95 percent warrants an investigation of the failed runs.

Running the same evaluation on every commit

You can also run the evaluation from Step 2 in a pipeline through the microsoft/ai-agent-evals@v3-beta GitHub Action, which the documentation labels as preview. The step below goes after the checkout and an Azure login step that uses OpenID Connect, so the workflow also needs the id-token: write permission and the client, tenant and subscription IDs stored as GitHub Actions variables.

      - name: Run Evaluation
        uses: microsoft/ai-agent-evals@v3-beta
        with:
          azure-ai-project-endpoint: "<your-ai-project-endpoint>"
          deployment-name: "<your-deployment-name>"
          agent-ids: "<your-ai-agent-ids>"
          data-path: ${{ github.workspace }}/path/to/your/data-file

The agent-ids input takes values such as my-agent:1,my-agent:2, an optional baseline-agent-id sets the version used as the comparison, and the results show up in the workflow run summary with the score of each metric, confidence intervals and, when you compare several agents, a pairwise statistical comparison that tells you whether a difference is meaningful or just random variation. That makes it a reasonable quality gate for changes to an agent's instructions or model, since the same dataset runs against both versions.

If you'd rather see the three pieces working together before you try them, the Azure Friday episode Observe and evaluate agents for quality and safety in Microsoft Foundry walks through evaluation, tracing and monitoring with a live demo in the Foundry portal and in Visual Studio Code.

Which of those three questions is the hardest to answer about your agents today, what they did, how good their answers were, or whether they stay that good after release?

title: My nightly eval gate went red on prompts nobody touched. The judge had changed its mind
description:
A support agent I work on gets graded every night against ten thousand past tickets. One morning the run came back red. Nobody had merged a prompt change, the model version was pinned, and the retrieval index had not been rebuilt. I spent most of that morning diffing configs. The answer was in the judge logs: the same reply to the same ticket had scored 0.7 the night before and 0.6 that night, and my pass mark was 0.7. The agent was identical on both nights. The judge had scored the same input two different ways.

I keep relearning this one. An LLM judge gives you a slightly different score each time you run it, so on a gate that grades thousands of cases, some of the red is the judge disagreeing with itself.

A regression gate needs the same verdict twice

I like LLM-as-a-judge for what it does well. You hand a strong model a rubric, it returns a score and a sentence explaining the score, and that sentence is the most useful thing I have when I am debugging one bad answer. I can read it, argue with it, and log it.

A gate asks for something else. It has to return the same verdict on the same input every time, so that a failing case means the agent regressed. Code checks and semantic verifiers return the same result on the same input every time, so they can hold a gate on their own. For the LLM judge I needed a workaround, and mine was to average several judge runs on the cases that mattered. That multiplied the cost of the slowest and most expensive check in the suite.

What a typed judge gives up to get there

JEV is TypeSafe AI's typed evaluator, released in September 2026. Its makers frame it as a "System One" model built for fast, instinctive scoring. The difference you notice first is the output. JEV returns a typed verdict (a yes or no, a multiple-choice pick, or a point on an ordered scale) with a calibrated probability attached. It writes no rationale at all.

The numbers come from the paper "JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure". In its September 29 revision, JEV recorded a 0.15-second median latency and cost 0.36% of the strongest comparator's fee on the tested workloads. It came within three percentage points of GPT-6 when the verdict could be read directly from the supplied text. The gap widened on math, code, logic and other tasks where the verdict has to be derived. I treat those figures as the paper's benchmark setup. My own traffic will land somewhere else, and I would only trust a number I measured on it.

So JEV gives up the written reasoning to get repeatability. For a regression suite that runs every night, I will take that trade.

The probability is the part I use most

The calibrated probability changes how I wire the judge in. I accept the verdict when confidence is high and route the low-confidence cases to a stronger reasoning judge or to a person. That makes the typed judge a triage step in front of the expensive checks.

The threshold is mine to set. I validate it against my own labeled cases before it is allowed to block anything, because a cutoff copied from someone else's benchmark describes their data.

One agent, four checks, four methods

I pick each method by what the check is grading. On the support agent, that splits four ways.

Whether the reply is valid JSON with the required fields is a format question. A code check owns it: deterministic, instant, free.

Whether the reply matches the known resolution for that ticket is agreement with a reference. A semantic verifier handles it cheaply. You embed the reply and the reference answer, take the cosine similarity, and pass it above a threshold. A small model like all-MiniLM-L6-v2 runs locally. I started at 0.75 and tuned from there against known-good and known-bad pairs, since too low lets paraphrases of a wrong answer through and too high fails correct answers worded differently.

Whether the tone stayed polite and on-brand is a judgment call, and that is where an LLM judge earns its cost. I keep it pointwise, one answer scored against a threshold. When I need a ranking I switch to pairwise and run both orders, because the model tends to favor whichever answer it reads first.

The nightly run over ten thousand past tickets is the high-volume gate, and that is where the typed verdict fits.

Where I still want a paragraph of reasoning

Two places keep a reasoning judge or a human in my loop.

The first is derivation. If the verdict depends on checking math, code, or a multi-step argument, the typed judge falls further behind, so those cases escalate by default.

The second is adversarial input. Typed and generative judges both read the content they grade, and that content can carry instructions aimed at the judge. A written rationale does not reliably expose prompt injection, and a typed verdict gives me even less to investigate after the fact. When a judge feeds a security or moderation decision, I treat its input as untrusted, keep the evaluation instructions isolated, test adversarial examples, use a deterministic rule wherever the policy can be written down exactly, and send uncertain cases to human review.

What I would tell myself before that red morning

  • Gating on a judge with variance. A red build that does not reproduce may be judge variance. Put a low-variance check on the gate.
  • Reading similarity as truth. "Paris is the capital of France" and "Paris is not the capital of France" score as very similar. Anywhere one flipped word changes the verdict, pair the verifier with a rule or a judge.
  • Borrowing a confidence threshold. Calibrate it on your own labels first.
  • Asking one judge to grade everything. Formats, references, tone and volume each have a method that fits. Most production agents need three or four of them running together.

The full comparison, with the decision table and Python examples for the semantic verifier and the LLM-judge pattern, is in this piece.

Which check in your suite has gone red with nothing changed underneath it? For me it was the nightly regression gate, and the fix was handing that job to a check that gives close to the same answer every time.

title: SSR vs. CSR vs. SSG: How Netflix Cut Time-to-Interactive by 50% by Shipping Less JavaScript
description:
SSR vs. CSR vs. SSG: How Netflix Cut Time-to-Interactive by 50% by Shipping Less JavaScript

In 2017, Netflix's logged-out homepage was carrying about 300 kB of JavaScript. Some of it was React, some was utility libraries like Lodash, and some was the data needed to hydrate React's state. React itself was only around 45 kB of that. But when the team removed client-side React, several libraries, and the code that depended on them, the total dropped by more than 200 kB, and the page's time-to-interactive improved by over 50%. React didn't disappear: Netflix kept using it on the server to produce the initial HTML, and it prefetched React in the background so the rest of the sign-up flow, a single-page app, still loaded fast. That prefetching cut time-to-interactive by 30% on later navigations.

The lesson isn't "React is slow." It's that how a page gets built, and how much JavaScript has to run before it works, can matter more than which framework you picked. That decision is the heart of rendering strategy: do you build the HTML in the browser (client-side rendering, CSR), on the server for each request (server-side rendering, SSR), or ahead of time at build (static site generation, SSG)?

The stakes are measurable. Google's Core Web Vitals want a Largest Contentful Paint of 2.5 seconds or less, an Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less, and a Cumulative Layout Shift of 0.1 or less, judged at the 75th percentile of real visits. And Google's own documentation notes that the default strategy for single-page apps today is client-side rendering, while encouraging server-side rendering or pre-rendering if you're free to choose. This guide breaks down what each approach does, where the real numbers come from, and how to decide, page by page.

If you're newer to frontend work, our React & Frontend roadmap covers the fundamentals this comparison builds on.

This post originally appeared on the Ciphemic Academia blog.

The Short Version

  • Client-side rendering (CSR): the server sends a nearly empty HTML page and a JavaScript bundle. The browser runs the JavaScript, fetches data, and builds the page.
  • Server-side rendering (SSR): the server builds the full HTML for each request and sends it. The browser shows it right away, then JavaScript "hydrates" the page to make it interactive.
  • Static site generation (SSG): the HTML is built once, at build time, and served as plain files from a CDN. Every visitor gets the same pre-built page.

If you want one default: decide per page, not per site. Use SSG for content that rarely changes, like blog posts, docs, and marketing and course pages. Use SSR for public pages that are personalized or change on every request. Use CSR for app-like screens behind a login, where search engines never look.

What All Three Are Actually Trying to Solve

Before the differences, the shared goals:

  • Showing real content quickly, which Google measures as Largest Contentful Paint
  • Responding fast when users interact, measured as Interaction to Next Paint
  • Keeping the layout stable so content doesn't jump around, measured as Cumulative Layout Shift
  • Being understood by crawlers and link previews, so search engines and social sites can read your content
  • Keeping infrastructure and developer effort reasonable, since every rendering choice has a cost somewhere

The strategies differ in where and when the HTML gets built, and each answer shifts the costs to a different place.

Client-Side Rendering (CSR)

What it actually is: the browser does the rendering. The server returns a minimal HTML shell and a JavaScript bundle. The browser downloads, parses, and runs the bundle, which fetches data from an API and builds the page. A default Vite or Create React App project works this way.

A small example (what the server sends for a client-rendered app):

<body>
  <div id="root"></div>
  <script type="module" src="/assets/index.js"></script>
</body>

The visible content only exists after the script runs and builds it inside #root.

Where it shines:

  • Rich interactivity: once loaded, navigation between screens is instant because only data moves, not whole pages
  • Simple hosting: static files plus an API, with no render server to run
  • Clean separation: the front end and back end can be built and deployed independently
  • A natural fit behind a login: dashboards and admin tools don't need to rank in search

Where it struggles:

  • A blank screen until JavaScript arrives: the user sees little until the bundle downloads, parses, and executes, which hurts Largest Contentful Paint
  • JavaScript cost on slower devices: a heavy bundle can make interactions sluggish on mid-range phones, which hurts Interaction to Next Paint
  • SEO risk: Googlebot can render JavaScript, but pages go through a crawl queue and then a render queue, so there's a delay, and Google notes that other search engines may ignore JavaScript entirely
  • Weak link previews: social platforms often read the initial HTML for titles and images, which a bare shell doesn't contain

Who this suits: logged-in application interiors, internal tools, and anything where search visibility doesn't matter.

Server-Side Rendering (SSR)

What it actually is: the server runs your components for each request, fetches the data, and sends complete HTML. The browser can display that immediately. Then the JavaScript bundle loads and hydrates the page, attaching event handlers so it becomes interactive.

A small example (Next.js, Pages Router; other frameworks have equivalents):

// pages/courses/[slug].jsx
export async function getServerSideProps({ params }) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/courses/${params.slug}`);
  const course = await res.json();
  return { props: { course } };   // runs on the server for every request
}

export default function CoursePage({ course }) {
  return <h1>{course.title}</h1>;
}

Where it shines:

  • Real content in the first response: users and crawlers get meaningful HTML immediately, which helps both Largest Contentful Paint and indexing
  • Fresh and personalized data: every request can reflect the current database state or the current user
  • Good link previews: titles and images are in the HTML
  • Secrets stay on the server: API keys and database access never reach the browser

Where it struggles:

  • Server cost per request: you pay compute for every page view, and a slow database makes every page slow
  • Time to first byte depends on your backend, since the server has to finish rendering before it can send anything
  • Hydration cost: the page can look ready before it responds to clicks, and shipping a large bundle for hydration is exactly the overhead Netflix removed from its landing page
  • More infrastructure: you need a server or edge runtime, plus a caching strategy so you don't render the same page repeatedly (a cache like the ones in our Redis vs. Memcached guide often helps)

Who this suits: public pages that must be indexed and also change per request or per user, such as product pages, search results, and personalized landing pages.

Static Site Generation (SSG)

What it actually is: pages are rendered once during the build and saved as HTML files. A CDN serves those files directly, so there's no server work per visit. Many frameworks add incremental regeneration, where a page is rebuilt in the background after a set time or on demand, so static pages can stay reasonably fresh.

A small example (Next.js, Pages Router, with regeneration):

// pages/blog/[slug].jsx
export async function getStaticPaths() {
  const slugs = await getAllPostSlugs();
  return { paths: slugs.map((slug) => ({ params: { slug } })), fallback: 'blocking' };
}

export async function getStaticProps({ params }) {
  const post = await getPost(params.slug);
  return { props: { post }, revalidate: 3600 };   // rebuild at most once an hour
}

export default function BlogPost({ post }) {
  return <article><h1>{post.title}</h1></article>;
}

Where it shines:

  • Speed: pre-built files from a CDN are typically the fastest way to deliver a page, which supports strong Core Web Vitals
  • Low cost and high resilience: no per-request compute, and static hosting keeps working under traffic spikes
  • Strong SEO: complete HTML is there from the first byte
  • Smaller attack surface: there's no server running your rendering code for every request

Where it struggles:

  • Content freezes until the next build or revalidation: that's fine for a blog post and wrong for live inventory
  • Build time grows with page count: thousands of pages can mean slow builds unless you regenerate incrementally
  • Per-user content needs another route: anything personalized has to be fetched client-side or handled by a different strategy
  • Rebuilds need automation: content changes should trigger builds, which is where a CI/CD pipeline, like those in our GitHub Actions vs. Jenkins vs. CircleCI comparison, comes in

Who this suits: blogs, documentation, marketing sites, and course or catalog pages whose content changes occasionally, not on every request.

Side-by-Side Comparison

CSR SSR SSG
Where HTML is built In the browser On the server, per request At build time
First content on screen After JavaScript runs In the first response In the first response, from a CDN
Interactivity After the bundle loads After hydration After hydration (if any JavaScript ships)
SEO and link previews Weakest, depends on JS rendering Strong Strong
Data freshness As fresh as the API Fresh on every request As of the last build or revalidation
Server cost Low (static files plus API) Highest (compute per request) Lowest
Hosting Any static host Needs a server or edge runtime Any static host or CDN
Main risk Slow first paint, empty shell for crawlers Server load, hydration overhead Stale content, long builds
Typical use Logged-in apps, dashboards Personalized or fast-changing public pages Blogs, docs, marketing, catalogs

How This Fits a Career Path

  • Frontend and full-stack engineers: choosing a rendering strategy per route is part of building any serious site, and it shows up in code reviews and architecture discussions
  • Performance-focused roles: you'll own Core Web Vitals, which means understanding how rendering, bundle size, and caching combine; our logs vs. metrics vs. traces post covers the measurement side
  • SEO-aware developers: knowing what a crawler sees in the initial HTML is a practical skill that separates strong frontend engineers from average ones
  • Interviews: "SSR, CSR, or SSG for this page, and why?" is a common frontend and system design question, and the best answers decide per page with reasons

How to Choose Without Overthinking It

  1. Ask who needs to find the page. If search engines or link previews matter, don't rely on a bare client-rendered shell. Choose SSG or SSR.
  2. Ask how often the content changes. Rarely, as with blog posts and docs: SSG, with regeneration if you need occasional updates. On every request or per user: SSR.
  3. Use CSR where search doesn't matter. Logged-in dashboards and tools are a good fit.
  4. Do the view-source test. Open View Page Source on a page you care about. If the article text isn't in that HTML, a crawler's first look sees an empty shell.
  5. Send less JavaScript regardless of strategy. Netflix's win came mainly from running less code in the browser, not from switching strategy.
  6. Measure real users, not your laptop. Core Web Vitals are judged at the 75th percentile across mobile and desktop, so check field data in Search Console or PageSpeed Insights.
  7. Don't build new sites around dynamic rendering. Google describes serving crawlers a different version than users as a workaround, not a long-term solution.

A note on honesty: the Netflix numbers describe one page, the logged-out homepage, in 2017, and engineers have pointed out that the story is as much about running less JavaScript as about any one framework. Netflix still used React on the server and for the rest of its sign-up flow. Core Web Vitals are one signal among many, and the relevance of your content matters more than shaving a few milliseconds. Thresholds can change, so check Google's current documentation. Modern frameworks also let you mix strategies within one app, so the clean categories here blur in practice.

Common Mistakes When Choosing a Rendering Strategy

  • Using one strategy for the whole site. Marketing pages, logged-in screens, and personalized pages have different needs.
  • Building public content pages as pure client-side apps. Blogs and course pages that need to rank shouldn't depend on a render queue.
  • Assuming SSR automatically means fast. A slow backend or a huge hydration bundle can erase the benefit.
  • Shipping a huge JavaScript bundle under any strategy. Bundle size drives interactivity problems everywhere.
  • Forgetting Open Graph and meta tags in the HTML. Link previews read the initial response, not the post-JavaScript page.
  • Lazy-loading the main above-the-fold image. That's usually your Largest Contentful Paint element, so it should load as early as possible.
  • Letting content load in late and shift the layout. Reserve space for images and embeds to protect your Cumulative Layout Shift score.
  • Using SSG without a refresh plan. Stale pages quietly erode trust, so decide how and when content gets rebuilt.
  • Not caching SSR responses. Re-rendering identical pages on every request wastes compute.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is client-side rendering bad for SEO?

It isn't banned, since Googlebot renders JavaScript, but pages are queued for rendering, which adds delay and risk, and other search engines may not run JavaScript at all. For public content that needs to rank, server-side or static rendering is the safer choice.

What is hydration?

After the server sends HTML, the browser downloads the JavaScript and attaches event handlers and state to that existing markup, which is what makes the page interactive. Until hydration finishes, the page may look ready but not respond.

SSR or SSG for a blog?

SSG for most blogs. The content changes rarely, static files are fast and cheap, and you can trigger a rebuild when you publish. Add incremental regeneration if you need updates without a full rebuild.

Can I mix these in one app?

Yes, and most real apps do. Modern frameworks let you choose per route, so a marketing page can be static while a dashboard is client-rendered and a search page is server-rendered.

Do I need Next.js to use SSR or SSG?

No. Frameworks like Astro, Remix, Nuxt, and SvelteKit offer similar capabilities, and you can build static or server-rendered pages without a framework. Next.js is just a popular example.

How do interviewers evaluate this topic?

Usually by giving you a page and asking how you'd render it. A strong answer decides per page, names the trade-offs in speed, freshness, SEO, and cost, and mentions measuring Core Web Vitals instead of guessing.

Decide Per Page, Then Measure

The Netflix story and Google's guidance point to the same habit: choose how each page gets built based on who needs it and how fresh it must be, send as little JavaScript as you can, and check real-user numbers instead of trusting a rule of thumb. Explore the React & Frontend roadmap to practice building the same page three ways and see the trade-offs for yourself.

title: Gaming User Reminders at High Volume: Node.js Cron Enqueue with 3 Rate-Limited Workers
description:
Short answer: for a gaming SaaS that sends a large daily reminder wave, make cron discover due events, publish small queue jobs, and let workers retry outbound webhooks with a delivery ledger. The reliability decision is whether a repeated attempt can be proven harmless, not whether the first request is fast.

The concrete job here is an outbound webhook such as match.reminder or tournament.starting. Email and SMS providers may sit behind that webhook, but the application must assume a provider timeout can happen after the provider accepted the message. A 900-second cron ceiling makes an inline sender a poor place to resolve that ambiguity.

Infrai is one candidate for the cron-to-queue handoff: its scheduling and queue calls use one REST API and shared credentials, while the delivery ledger and provider pacing stay in your service.

I would set the SLO before selecting a queue: for example, 99% of due reminders delivered within 10 minutes, with zero duplicate delivery IDs in the provider audit. The ten-minute value is a test input, not a promise from any platform. Your mileage may vary; change it to match the game’s notification contract.

The reliability boundary: discovery, delivery, evidence

Treat each reminder as an event with a stable delivery_id, tenant, channel, due time, and payload hash. Cron only claims due rows and publishes jobs. A worker owns provider pacing, retry classification, and the final acknowledgement. This leaves a short, inspectable cron run even when the morning batch is much larger than the sender can drain.

There are three useful records: the application’s claim lease, the queue delivery, and the provider attempt. The ledger key should be derived from the delivery ID and channel, so a worker restart cannot create a second logical send. Standard queues are at-least-once; that is a delivery contract, not a failure, provided the consumer is idempotent.

Keep the payload compact. Queue messages are capped at 256 KB, delayed messages at seven days, and retention at 30 days. A reminder scheduled farther out belongs in the application’s database until a later scan, not in a year-long queue delay.

One sharp edge: pausing cron does not backfill missed triggers. A reconciliation scan must find overdue reminders explicitly after a pause or deployment.

How should Node.js SaaS teams rate-limit daily reminder webhooks?

Use separate token buckets for each provider and channel. Email and SMS often have different limits, and a single global bucket lets a busy email campaign starve urgent SMS. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present, then apply exponential backoff with jitter. A transient network error should return the job for redelivery; a permanent validation rejection should be recorded and acknowledged so it does not spin forever.

Pace first.

The limiter needs a clock, a concurrency ceiling, and a record of the last provider response. When a provider returns 429 with Retry-After: 8, the worker should release the lease, schedule the next attempt no earlier than eight seconds later, and keep the delivery ID unchanged; when the header is absent, capped exponential backoff with jitter prevents a synchronized retry storm. During the migration test I would also force a worker to die after the HTTP response but before the ledger write, then start a fresh worker with an empty process cache. That unpleasant interval is the one that matters: the fresh worker must see the same delivery ID, send with the same idempotency key, and treat a ledger conflict as an acknowledgement rather than as permission to call the provider again. If the provider itself offers an idempotency contract, keep its key stable for the ledger retention period; if it does not, the application ledger is still valuable evidence and a guard against your own duplicate attempts, but the external side cannot be made perfectly transactional.

The following Go worker sketch makes the ordering explicit. It records success only after the provider call, and it passes the same idempotency key on every retry. The queue adapter can be local or managed; the policy remains the same.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type Job struct {
    DeliveryID string
    Channel    string
    Payload    []byte
}

type Ledger interface {
    Seen(context.Context, string) (bool, error)
    Mark(context.Context, string, time.Duration) error
}

type Provider interface {
    Send(context.Context, string, []byte, string) error
}

func keyFor(j Job) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(j.DeliveryID + ":" + j.Channel))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func deliver(ctx context.Context, ledger Ledger, provider Provider, j Job) error {
    idempotencyKey := keyFor(j)
    seen, err := ledger.Seen(ctx, idempotencyKey)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if seen {
        return nil
    }
    if err := provider.Send(ctx, j.Channel, j.Payload, idempotencyKey); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return ledger.Mark(ctx, idempotencyKey, 24*time.Hour)
}

func listQueues(ctx context.Context) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    // Copyable equivalent: curl -X GET https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/list -H 'Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY'
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/list", nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            resp.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond)
            continue
        }
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("queue list: %s", resp.Status)
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("queue list: rate limit persisted")
}

The listQueues call is only an authenticated health check for the scheduling boundary. In production, the cron handler publishes the claimed jobs with POST /v1/queue/publish_batch; the worker still enforces the provider’s limit. FIFO deduplication, where available, has only a five-minute window, so it cannot replace the ledger’s longer-lived key.

A reproducible migration test for duplicate delivery

Build a fixture of 50,000 due reminders: split it across email and SMS, repeat 2% of delivery IDs, and inject a timeout after the simulated provider accepts every 500th request. Run the fixture through the current sender and through cron-plus-queue, first with a single process and then with a restarted worker whose local cache has been erased. Record four signals: duplicate provider calls, oldest queue age, 429 count, and unacknowledged jobs after a worker restart. Keep the raw provider-attempt log keyed by delivery ID; otherwise a retry that arrives after a process crash can look like a new reminder, and the test will falsely pass while the game client receives two notifications.

Pass means zero duplicate delivery IDs, queue age inside the chosen SLO, bounded retry growth, and no lost job after a crash between provider acceptance and ledger marking. Fail means any duplicate, an age breach, or a retry loop that ignores Retry-After. Keep the fixture and provider limits constant; changing both hides the cause.

Start with one worker per channel. Add workers until the provider returns 429 or the oldest-message curve stops improving; that knee is the capacity limit for this provider contract. Do not infer capacity from cron success. A green cron run can coexist with a queue that is hours behind.

Choosing the queue without hiding the trade-offs

Option Where it helps this reliability test Boundary to accept
RabbitMQ Explicit acknowledgements and mature redelivery controls The team operates brokers, upgrades, and capacity
Amazon SQS Managed durability and straightforward polling AWS coupling and fewer broker routing primitives
BullMQ Familiar Node.js API when Redis is already operated Redis availability and queue semantics stay your responsibility
Infrai scheduling and queues One REST API, one key, and one bill for cron plus queue calls No native debounce or throttle; worker policy remains yours

Infrai is a sensible leg to test when the team wants one plain HTTP contract across backend services and does not want an SDK per provider. Its public discovery surface documents request schemas and runnable examples, which can reduce integration friction during a migration. That is the advantage here; it is not a claim that the queue has the routing depth of RabbitMQ.

The catch is important. Infrai is not suitable when a required cron http_url cannot be public, when you need DAG orchestration or fan-out joins, or when Kafka-style replay and multiple consumer groups are core requirements. Stay with RabbitMQ for broker routing, SQS for an AWS-native estate, or BullMQ when Redis operations are already a platform competency.

Rollback is part of the design

Put the new publisher behind a feature flag. To roll back, pause the cron trigger, stop claiming new rows, and let in-flight jobs finish; leave queued jobs available for redelivery. Purging the queue destroys evidence and makes duplicate analysis harder.

After the flag is restored, run the reconciliation scan for due rows and compare its delivery IDs with the ledger. Redrive dead-letter jobs only after fixing the classified cause. Keep an alert on oldest message age, retry backlog, and duplicate-ledger conflicts, not just on the cron run history.

The decision rule is reliability-based: use cron-to-queue when the scan can exceed 900 seconds or provider limits require paced retries, and require an application idempotency ledger before launch. Trial Infrai for the cron and batch-publish boundary when its single REST contract removes real integration work; choose a specialist when its routing, replay, or private-network requirements fit better.

If this boundary matches your system, the scheduling guide is a useful starting point: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/cron/answers/user-reminders-high-volume-daily-send-best-pattern-cron/

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

title: How to build a shadcn/ui registry that Claude Code and Cursor can actually use
description:
Most shadcn/ui components are now installed by an AI coding agent, not a person typing the command. If you publish a registry, the agent is your user. It needs to find your components, read their props without guessing, and run the right install command. A registry that only works for humans clicking through a docs site is a registry that gets misused.

I run HextaUI, a shadcn/ui registry, and I spent a chunk of this year making it work for Claude Code, Cursor and the shadcn MCP server. This is everything that turned out to matter, in the order I would do it again.

1. Ship a registry that passes validation

Start with the basics. Every item is a JSON file that follows the registry schema, with name, type, files, dependencies and registryDependencies. Put the index at a stable URL and every item at a predictable one:

https://your-site.com/r/registry.json
https://your-site.com/r/button.json
https://your-site.com/r/all.json

Run shadcn build to generate them from a registry.json source, and validate before you deploy. The CLI gained a registry validate step in May 2026. A registry that fails validation fails silently for agents, who will then write the component by hand and get it wrong.

Two details that make a real difference:

  • registryDependencies with full URLs. When your Dialog depends on your Button, point to https://your-site.com/r/button.json, not button, or the CLI pulls the shadcn/ui Button instead.
  • An all.json item that depends on everything. Agents asked to "set up the design system" will reach for it.

2. Register a namespace

Since the registry namespace feature landed, a user adds this to components.json:

{
  "registries": {
    "@hextaui": "https://hextaui.com/r/{name}.json"
  }
}

And then installs with a short name:

npx shadcn@latest add @hextaui/dialog

Document this snippet on your installation page and in your llms.txt. The short form is what the shadcn MCP server searches across, so a registry without a namespace is invisible to the one tool most agents use to browse registries.

If the registry is private, the object form takes headers with environment variables that the CLI expands and never logs:

{
  "registries": {
    "@acme-pro": {
      "url": "https://acme.com/r/pro/{name}.json",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${ACME_TOKEN}"
      }
    }
  }
}

3. Give every docs page a Markdown twin

Agents fetch HTML badly. They fetch Markdown well. Make every docs URL answer at .md with the same content: description, install command, full source, usage, examples, keyboard support and the API table.

https://hextaui.com/docs/button      -> HTML for people
https://hextaui.com/docs/button.md   -> Markdown for agents

Do not hand-write the Markdown. Generate it from the same source as the page so the two never drift. On HextaUI the .md route walks the page's React tree and serializes it, so adding an example to the page adds it to the Markdown for free.

The API reference matters most here. An agent that can read a props table does not hallucinate a size="xl" that does not exist.

4. Publish llms.txt and llms-full.txt

llms.txt is a Markdown index at your site root: what the project is, when to use it, when not to, how to install, and one line per docs page with its .md link. llms-full.txt is every docs page concatenated, for agents that want to load everything once.

The "when not to use it" section is the part people skip and the part that saves you support tickets. If your registry is React and Tailwind only, say so, or an agent will try to install it into a Vue project.

Keep the install command in the first ten lines. Agents read the top.

5. Run an MCP server, read-only, no key

The shadcn CLI has its own MCP server (npx shadcn@latest mcp) that searches any registry in components.json. That covers installs. It does not cover docs, keyboard maps or examples.

So I run a second one at https://hextaui.com/mcp, Streamable HTTP, read-only, no API key, with five tools: search_docs, get_component, get_component_api, get_examples and get_install_command. Claude Code connects with one line:

claude mcp add --transport http hextaui https://hextaui.com/mcp

Cursor and VS Code take the same URL in their MCP config. Once connected, "add a HextaUI combobox with async results" turns into a docs search, an API read and the right install command, with no guessing in between.

Make it discoverable too. Publish a server card at /.well-known/mcp/server-card.json and a server.json in the MCP registry format. Agents and the tools around them are starting to look there first.

6. Describe the HTTP surface with OpenAPI and real errors

Everything above is also plain HTTP, and agents increasingly call HTTP directly. Publish an openapi.json with operation ids and typed responses. Return errors as RFC 9457 application/problem+json with a resolution field that says what to do next:

{
  "type": "https://hextaui.com/docs/api#not-found",
  "title": "Component not found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "No component named 'modal'.",
  "resolution": "Try 'dialog' or 'alert-dialog'. The catalog is at /mcp/index.json."
}

An agent that gets a 404 with a hint recovers. An agent that gets an HTML error page writes the component from memory.

7. Ship a skill file

Claude Code and a growing list of agents read SKILL.md files that explain how to use a tool. Put one at /.well-known/agent-skills/<name>/SKILL.md: how to find a component, read its docs, and install it, with the exact commands. It is a page of Markdown and it is the highest-leverage page on the site.

8. Test with the agents, not with yourself

Open a fresh Next.js project in Claude Code with your MCP server connected and no other context. Ask it to "add a date picker from with a range and a disabled weekend rule". Watch what it does. Every wrong guess is a gap in your .md docs or your llms.txt.

Then do the same in Cursor with only llms.txt and no MCP. Then with nothing but the URL. The registry should degrade gracefully through all three.

What this gets you

An agent with the MCP server or the .md docs connected reads the props table instead of guessing it, runs the install command instead of rewriting the component, and installs the dependencies in the right order. The registry side of HextaUI was about a week of work. The agent side took longer, and it is the part that made the registry usable by the people who now do most of the installing.

If you want to see all of it live: hextaui.com/llms.txt, any docs page with .md appended, the MCP docs, and the API docs with the OpenAPI spec.

FAQ

Do I need my own MCP server if the shadcn CLI has one? The shadcn MCP covers search and install across registries in components.json. Your own server covers docs, APIs and examples. Most registries benefit from both.

Should the MCP server require an API key? Not for public docs. Every key you require is an agent that gives up. Keep auth for private items and use bearer tokens through components.json headers.

How do I generate the Markdown docs without duplicating content? Render the same component tree the page uses and serialize it to Markdown. One source, two formats.

What goes in llms.txt? A description, when to use and when not to, the install command, the namespace snippet, and one line per docs page linking to its .md.

title: Token Expiry in Live Stock Watchlists — Deterministic UX and Reconnect Tests
description:
Situation User-visible behavior Test control
Token is valid and the stream is healthy Prices update in place; keep the last update timestamp visible A fake clock advances normal heartbeats
Token expires while the socket is open Freeze updates, show a compact re-auth prompt, and preserve the list Inject an expiry event at a known logical time
Re-auth succeeds after a disconnect Reconnect, backfill the missed sequence, then resume live updates Replay a fixed event log with a deterministic cursor
Re-auth is cancelled or denied Keep cached quotes marked stale and offer retry; never imply a fresh price Assert state transitions, not wall-clock delays

Short answer: model expiry as an explicit state transition, drive it with a virtual clock, and assert the watchlist state plus backfill cursor instead of sleeping for real time. That makes the trading screen honest when a token ages out and keeps tests repeatable.

A watchlist has a sharper edge than a chat feed. A stale quote can change a decision, so “the connection looks open” is not enough. The client needs to distinguish fresh data, paused data, and data that was recovered after a gap.

Watch the boundary.

What should a stock watchlist show when a realtime token expires?

Treat the stream as a small state machine: live, expiring, reauthenticating, backfilling, stale, and failed. The state belongs to the watchlist session, not to an individual quote. A banner can say “Updates paused. Sign in again to continue.” Keep the last known price, but attach its age and a stale label.

Do not clear symbols during expiry. Traders use the list itself to decide what to do next, and an empty panel looks like a data loss event. Disable actions that require a fresh quote, such as a market-order shortcut, until the session returns to live. Three words help: “Quotes may be stale.”

I keep the transition event-shaped so the UI and telemetry share one vocabulary:

type WatchlistState =
  | { kind: 'live'; lastSequence: number }
  | { kind: 'expiring'; expiresAt: number; lastSequence: number }
  | { kind: 'reauthenticating'; lastSequence: number }
  | { kind: 'backfilling'; fromSequence: number }
  | { kind: 'stale'; reason: 'token' | 'network'; lastSequence: number };

function onTokenExpiry(state: WatchlistState): WatchlistState {
  if (state.kind === 'live' || state.kind === 'expiring') {
    return { kind: 'expiring', expiresAt: Date.now(), lastSequence: state.lastSequence };
  }
  return state;
}

The exact countdown is a product choice. The invariant is not: no update should be presented as current after the authorization boundary.

How can expiry, reconnect, and backfill be tested without flaky timing?

Replace elapsed time with a test clock and replace an actual broker with a deterministic event source. The test advances time to just before expiry, confirms normal rendering, then advances one tick and emits TOKEN_EXPIRED. No setTimeout needs to finish. No CI machine speed is involved. In a fuller scenario, seed the stream with quote events for AAPL, MSFT, and a thinly traded symbol, record sequence 41 as the last rendered item, and then close the transport at the expiry boundary. The client should retain those three rows, mark each one stale, and remember 42 as the first sequence it needs. When authentication returns, replay 42 through 47, deliberately duplicate 44, and deliver 46 before 45. The reducer should discard the duplicate, hold the out-of-order event until the gap is filled, and expose one monotonic view. This test catches a common UX lie: a green connection icon beside prices that silently skipped a burst of updates.

class TestClock {
  private nowMs = 1_700_000_000_000;
  now() { return this.nowMs; }
  advance(ms: number) { this.nowMs += ms; }
}

type Event =
  | { type: 'quote'; sequence: number; symbol: string; price: number }
  | { type: 'TOKEN_EXPIRED' }
  | { type: 'AUTHENTICATED' };

function reduce(state: WatchlistState, event: Event): WatchlistState {
  if (event.type === 'TOKEN_EXPIRED') return onTokenExpiry(state);
  if (event.type === 'AUTHENTICATED' && state.kind === 'expiring') {
    return { kind: 'backfilling', fromSequence: state.lastSequence + 1 };
  }
  if (event.type === 'quote' && state.kind === 'live') {
    return { kind: 'live', lastSequence: event.sequence };
  }
  return state;
}

const clock = new TestClock();
let state: WatchlistState = { kind: 'live', lastSequence: 41 };
clock.advance(14 * 60 * 1000);
state = reduce(state, { type: 'TOKEN_EXPIRED' });
if (state.kind !== 'expiring') throw new Error('expiry was not rendered');
state = reduce(state, { type: 'AUTHENTICATED' });
if (state.kind !== 'backfilling' || state.fromSequence !== 42) {
  throw new Error('backfill cursor was not preserved');
}

The useful assertion is the cursor (42 here), not “reconnected within 500 ms.” Backfill tests should replay a known gap, including duplicate and out-of-order events, and verify that the reducer ends with one quote per symbol and a monotonic sequence. Your mileage may vary on the exact event schema, but the principle travels across transports.

At the boundary, test four paths: expiry before a user action, expiry during an in-flight action, successful re-auth, and a denied re-auth. Add a fifth for a tab returning from sleep. Browsers can suspend timers, so a test that relies on timer callbacks alone can miss the very transition you need to protect.

Which observability signals prove the UX is telling the truth?

Log a session identifier, watchlist identifier, last rendered sequence, expiry reason, and backfill range as structured fields. Metrics should separate expiry_to_prompt_ms, reauth_success_total, backfill_events_total, and stale_seconds. A single reconnect counter hides too much.

Trace the sequence as a short chain: token accepted, stream opened, expiry observed, credentials refreshed, gap requested, gap applied, live resumed. In a dashboard, put the stale-age percentile next to reconnect rate. If reconnects rise while stale age stays low, the UX may be fine; if stale age climbs, users are looking at old prices even though sockets appear healthy.

The WebRTC recommendation describes connection and state concepts that are useful when a realtime transport exposes lifecycle transitions; your application protocol still needs an explicit authorization-expiry event and sequence semantics. The reference below documents the transport contract; document your own event contract beside the client reducer.

Limits and trade-offs

A virtual clock proves deterministic client behavior, not that an identity provider will refresh credentials correctly in production. Keep one small end-to-end test for the real refresh path, and make its assertions event-based with generous bounds.

A backfill buffer costs memory and can expose sensitive quote history, so cap its size and scope it to the authenticated account. For very high-frequency symbols, a snapshot-plus-delta protocol may be simpler than replaying every tick.

The catch is product policy: pausing all trading controls is safer, but it can frustrate users during a brief refresh. If your risk team permits a narrower policy, gate only actions that require current quotes and label everything else with its age. Stick with a full pause when regulatory or risk requirements demand an unambiguous fresh-data boundary.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
