title: The Keycloak Admin API from TypeScript, without the surprises
description:
If you automate Keycloak from Node.js (creating users during onboarding, provisioning clients per tenant, syncing groups from HR), you eventually hit the same set of friction points. I wrote keycloak-api-ts to remove the ones that bothered me most, and version 2.0 is out: it covers 100% of the Keycloak 26.8.1 Admin API (415 operations) and is tested against real 24, 25 and 26 servers on every pull request.

This post covers the problem, the solution and the trade-offs.

The problem

The official client, @keycloak/keycloak-admin-client, is maintained by the Keycloak team and is the natural first choice. In everyday backend code, though (looking at 26.8.1), it comes with a few tolls:

1. It's ESM-only. The package is "type": "module" with no CommonJS build. On Node 20.19+ and 22.12+ require() of ESM works, but Jest/ts-jest in CommonJS mode, older Node versions and some bundlers still stumble, and you end up with transformIgnorePatterns, dynamic await import() or a project migration.

2. HTTP errors are thrown. A missing user (404) or a duplicate username (409) isn't exceptional; it's business logic. Still, every non-2xx response throws a NetworkError (only some findOne calls return null on 404), so you need a try/catch and a look at error.response.status.

// official client
try {
  await kc.users.create({ username: 'jdoe' });
} catch (e) {
  // 409? 403? network? you have to inspect the error to know
}

3. The default realm is global mutable state. kc.setConfig({ realmName: 'tenant-a' }) changes the realm for every following call. You can override it per call by passing realm in the payload, but that's opt-in: forget it once, and in concurrent multi-tenant code the call lands in whatever realm another request configured.

4. Tokens renew only with a refresh token. After auth(), the client renews on its own when it has a refresh token. With client_credentials, the typical service flow, Keycloak doesn't issue a refresh token by default (the client's "Use refresh tokens for client credentials grant" option is off), so once the access token expires calls fail with "Cannot refresh token". You either call auth() again or register your own TokenProvider. There's no retry on 401, no backoff retries and no rate limiting.

5. Coverage is partial. By my count on 26.8.1, the official client covers about 340 of the 415 operations in the OpenAPI spec (≈82%). Missing are, for example, role composites, groups and permissions by role name, authorization-services searches, client types, parts of organizations and workflows, localization, and the legacy client templates. For those, you're back to hand-rolled fetch calls.

The solution 

npm install keycloak-api-ts

import KeycloakAPI from 'keycloak-api-ts'; // or require('keycloak-api-ts')

const api = new KeycloakAPI({
  baseUrl: 'https://sso.example.com',
  credentials: {
    grantType: 'client_credentials',
    clientId: 'admin-service',
    clientSecret: process.env.KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET,
  },
});

const created = await api.users.create('acme', { username: 'jdoe', enabled: true });

if (created.success) {
  console.log('new user id:', created.data); // taken from the Location header
} else if (created.status === 409) {
  console.log('user already exists');
} else {
  console.error(created.status, created.error);
}

What changes:

  • Errors as values. Every call resolves to { success, status, data | error }, a discriminated union: after if (res.success), TypeScript knows data is there. The promise only rejects on network failures or when a token can't be obtained (KeycloakAuthError).
  • Realm per call. api.users.list('tenant-a') and api.users.list('tenant-b') can run in parallel on the same instance without stepping on each other.
  • Automatic tokens. Requested lazily, cached, and renewed before expires_in (using the refresh token when there is one). A 401 invalidates the token and retries the request once.
  • Resilience on the instance. Exponential-backoff retries for network errors, 408, 429 and 5xx on idempotent requests, plus a client-side rate limit (10 req/s by default). All of it lives on the library's own axios instance, so the global axios of your app is never touched.
  • Native CommonJS and ESM. The package ships both builds, so require and import work on any Node 20+, Jest in CommonJS mode included, without relying on require(esm).
  • Types generated from the official OpenAPI spec. User, Client, Realm, Group and friends come straight from the Keycloak 26.8.1 spec, and the raw schemas are exported as KeycloakSchemas.
  • create returns the id. Keycloak answers 201 with the id in the Location header; the library hands it to you in data.

Things you only learn against a real server

The OpenAPI spec doesn't tell the whole story. A few things only surfaced when the integration tests (Testcontainers running Keycloak in Docker) hit a real server:

  • Authorization policies must be created on /policy/{type}; the generic endpoint in the spec can't parse provider-specific fields.
  • Localization texts, credential labels and workflows use text or YAML bodies, not JSON.
  • Keystore downloads come back as a Buffer, and 24/25 require a keyPassword.
  • Certificate uploads must be multipart.
  • Array filters are sent as repeated query parameters (type=LOGIN&type=LOGOUT).

Each of these became a test, and CI runs the 24.0.5 / 25.0.6 / 26.8.1 matrix on every pull request.

When to stick with the official client

If your project is already ESM, always runs the latest Keycloak and you're happy with exceptions, the official client is a perfectly good choice backed by the Keycloak team. It also ships things keycloak-api-ts doesn't have yet: Shared Signals (SSF) and verifiable-credentials endpoints, which aren't even in the OpenAPI spec, and experimental access to the Admin API v2 for clients. keycloak-api-ts makes more sense when you have a CommonJS backend, multi-tenant code, servers on different versions (24 to 26), or you need endpoints the official client doesn't cover.

Links

  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/keycloak-api-ts
  • GitHub: https://github.com/Master-Mils/keycloak-api-ts

Issues, ideas and PRs are welcome. Next on the roadmap are the Admin API v2, once it's stable, and the SSF and verifiable-credentials endpoints. If you use Keycloak from Node, tell me in the comments what your biggest pain with the Admin API is.

title: How to Compare Two JSON Files (Ignoring Key Order)
description:
JSON diff compares two JSON documents by their data, ignoring key order and formatting, and lists every change by path. Both documents stay in your browser.

Compare JSON

Why a text diff gives the wrong answer

A JSON object is, in the words of the standard, an unordered collection of names and values. These two documents hold exactly the same data:

{"id": 7, "name": "Ada", "tags": ["admin", "editor"], "plan": "pro"}
{"tags": ["admin", "editor"], "name": "Ada", "plan": "pro", "id": 7}

A text diff compares characters, so it marks the whole line as changed. Pretty-printed, every line would differ. Real changes hide among fake ones, and a reformatted file looks completely rewritten. Comparing by structure fixes this: each value is matched by its path, such as $.plan or $.items[2].price, and only real changes are reported. JSON diff says “No differences” for the pair above.

Compare two JSON files by structure

  1. Paste or open the two versions. The old one on the left, the new one on the right. Both must be valid JSON.
  2. Decide how arrays should be compared. Leave order on for ordered lists; tick Ignore the order of array items for sets.
  3. Read the list of changes. Each line shows the path, the old value and the new value. Copy the summary for a ticket or a review.

If a file won't parse, fix it first in the JSON validator, which shows the line and column of the problem.

Arrays: an ordered list or a set?

Key order never matters in JSON, but array order can. Take document A from above and this new version, where the plan changed and the tags were listed the other way round:

{"plan": "team", "tags": ["editor", "admin"], "name": "Ada", "id": 7}
Setting JSON diff reports
Order matters (default) 3 differences: $.tags[0] “admin” removed, $.tags[1] “admin” added, $.plan “pro” → “team”
Ignore the order of array items 1 difference: $.plan “pro” → “team”

Both answers are right; they answer different questions. Tags, permissions and IDs are usually sets, so ignore order. Steps of a process, ranked results or the lines of an order are lists, so keep it. For a list of records that should be matched by an id field, sort both arrays by that field first, then compare with order on.

Is 1 the same as "1" or 1.0?

JSON diff compares values by type and by numeric value. That catches the changes that actually break programs, while ignoring ones that don't:

Old New Reported?
"id": 1 "id": "1" Yes: a number became a string
"zip": "02134" "zip": 2134 Yes: and the leading zero is lost
"total": 31.5 "total": 31.50 No: the same number written differently
12345678901234567890 12345678901234567891 Yes: compared exactly, not rounded

The last row matters for IDs. Many JavaScript-based tools round both numbers to the same value and call them equal.

Comparing JSON on the command line

With jq installed, you can sort keys and then use an ordinary diff:

diff <(jq -S . old.json) <(jq -S . new.json)

-S sorts the keys of every object. It does not sort arrays, so reordered arrays still show up as changes. Sort a list of records by a field with jq 'sort_by(.id)' before comparing. In Python, json.load(a) == json.load(b) answers yes or no, ignoring key order, but doesn't say what changed.

Timestamps, IDs and other noise

Two API responses often differ in fields that change on every call: updatedAt, request IDs, tokens. They drown out the changes you care about. Remove them from both documents before comparing, for example with jq 'del(.updatedAt, .requestId)', or by deleting the lines by hand in a copy.

For comparing code, config written as YAML or any other text where order and whitespace matter, use the diff checker instead.

Sources

  • RFC 8259, section 1. An object is an unordered collection of name/value pairs
  • jq manual. --sort-keys / -S sorts the fields of each object

Originally published on ThatToolSite.

title: Vercel Drives is now generally available
description:
Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. Its files remain available after the sandbox stops, so later runs and other sandboxes can access them by mounting the same Drive.

Use Drives to preserve an agent’s workspace or file-based memory across runs, or to make datasets, models, dependencies, and build artifacts available across sandboxes.

You can also fork a Drive into independent writable Drives. Forks inherit the source Drive's data, region, and maximum size, then store their own changes. Parallel workers can start with the same files and make changes without affecting the original or one another.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: How AI Agents Sharing a Sandbox Leak Each Other's Data
description:
Originally published at webofmike.com on 2026-10-13. The demo repo and every command in it were run before publishing.

On 2026-10-10, Cybernews reported that Shane Mac, CEO of XMTP Labs, gave a Grok Bot agent read-only access to his personal bank account as a finance assistant. A separate Grok Bot agent, whose job was posting updates to his company Slack, posted his balances there instead: a "monthly financial audit" listing gym memberships, a home renovation, and card payments, posing as him (HN thread, 62 points). Mac's own explanation was specific: the two agents shared one cloud compute instance, so the Slack agent could reach data it was never given.

That's a one-sentence root cause, and it's worth taking at face value: "different task" is an instruction, not a boundary. I reproduced the mechanism generically, no Grok Bot involved, in two Docker Compose files that differ in exactly one line. Repo: themsquared/shared-sandbox-agent-leak.

Disclosure: I work at Solo.io, which created kagent, one of the projects mentioned below. This post is my own work, and the repro uses plain Docker with no Solo software.

The setup

Two toy agents, neither one LLM-driven, because the point is the compute boundary, not agent reasoning:

  • finance-agent writes a balance snapshot to /secrets/finance.json. That's its entire job.
  • slack-agent posts messages to a webhook. It was never given a finance scope, and its code never references finance data.
  • mock-slack is a 20-line http.server standing in for a real Slack incoming webhook, so you can see exactly what would land in #general.

slack_agent.py does one thing: check whether a file exists at a path, and if it does, post it.

def main():
    time.sleep(2)
    try:
        with open(SECRET_PATH) as f:
            leaked = json.load(f)
        print(f"[slack-agent] found a file at {SECRET_PATH} I was never given, posting it, because that's my job")
        post_to_slack({"channel": "#general", "text": "monthly financial audit", "attachment": leaked})
        print("[slack-agent] LEAKED: posted finance data to Slack")
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"[slack-agent] no file at {SECRET_PATH}, nothing to post, nothing leaked")

There's no finance-specific logic to remove, no prompt to rewrite, no permission check that was skipped. Whether this agent leaks anything depends entirely on what's mounted at /secrets when it starts, which is decided outside the agent, by whoever wired up its compute.

Reproducing the leak

docker-compose.vulnerable.yml mounts the same named volume into both agents at /secrets:

services:
  finance-agent:
    volumes:
      - shared-secrets:/secrets
    command: ["python", "/app/finance_agent.py"]

  slack-agent:
    volumes:
      - shared-secrets:/secrets
    command: ["python", "/app/slack_agent.py"]

volumes:
  shared-secrets:

Both containers mount shared-secrets. Run it:

docker compose -f docker-compose.vulnerable.yml up --abort-on-container-exit --exit-code-from slack-agent

mock-slack-1  | [mock-slack] #general received: {"channel": "#general", "text": "monthly financial audit", "attachment": {"checking_balance_usd": 4812.33, "line_items": ["gym membership -45.00", "home renovation -1200.00", "card payment -389.12"] }}
slack-agent-1 | [slack-agent] found a file at /secrets/finance.json I was never given, posting it, because that's my job
slack-agent-1 | [slack-agent] LEAKED: posted finance data to Slack

slack-agent did exactly what it was built to do: look for something to post, find it, post it. The leak isn't a bug in either agent's code. It's the absence of a boundary between them.

The fix is one line, at the compute layer

docker-compose.isolated.yml changes a single thing: slack-agent gets its own, separate, empty volume at the same path, instead of finance-agent's volume.

services:
  finance-agent:
    volumes:
      - finance-secrets:/secrets

  slack-agent:
    volumes:
      - slack-agent-own-sandbox:/secrets   # was: finance-secrets

volumes:
  finance-secrets:
  slack-agent-own-sandbox:

Same two agents. Same two Python files, byte for byte. Same two tasks. Run it:

docker compose -f docker-compose.isolated.yml up --abort-on-container-exit --exit-code-from slack-agent

slack-agent-1 | [slack-agent] no file at /secrets/finance.json, nothing to post, nothing leaked

slack-agent looks in exactly the same place and finds nothing, because there's nothing there to find. Neither agent's code changed. Neither agent's prompt or task description changed. Neither agent is aware the other exists, before or after the fix. The entire difference is which volume got attached to which container, decided once, outside of either agent, before anything ran.

./run.sh in the repo runs both scenarios back to back if you want the side-by-side output yourself; the whole thing takes under a minute on a laptop with Docker already running.

Why this isn't just a Docker-volume toy problem

The shared-sandbox failure mode is common enough that the Kubernetes agent ecosystem is actively standardizing the fix, because it doesn't live in the agent's prompt or code; it lives in whatever schedules the agent's compute:

  • kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox shipped v1.0.6 on 2026-10-08. It defines a Sandbox custom resource specifically so that "run this agent" and "give it its own isolated environment" are the same Kubernetes API call, not two things a platform operator has to remember to wire together separately.
  • kagent shipped gVisor-backed microVM sandboxes in v1.0.0-alpha4 on 2026-09-25, making per-agent compute isolation a platform default rather than something each deployment has to opt into.

Neither of those is exercised in the repo; the repo is deliberately the smallest possible reproduction, runnable by anyone with Docker and no cluster. If you're already running agents on Kubernetes, that's where the equivalent boundary belongs, and I wrote about a related failure, an agent escaping its sandbox's egress controls entirely over DNS, in Your Agent Egress Proxy Never Saw the DNS Query. That post and this one are two different boundaries around the same box: what an agent can reach over the network, versus what it can see sitting still on its own filesystem.

Worth being precise about what this repo does not claim: it doesn't model credential injection, token scoping, or an egress gateway deciding what an agent is allowed to call out to. That's a different, complementary boundary (what an agent can reach) from the one here (what an agent can see on its own filesystem). Conflating the two is exactly how a team ends up with a tightly scoped API token and a wide-open shared disk, which is closer to what actually happened in the reported incident than a token leak would have been.

Honest limits

  • Both agents here are a dozen lines of Python each, not LLM-driven. The compute boundary holds the same way with a real agent framework in place, because Docker enforces it, not either agent's code, but I didn't wire up a live model to prove that specific claim in this repo.
  • mock-slack is a stand-in http.server, not real Slack. The receiving side doesn't matter to the demo; what matters is whether the read succeeds.
  • Only one failure mode is modeled: a shared named volume. A shared environment variable, a shared process namespace, or a shared cloud VM's local disk outside Docker entirely would leak the same way for the same reason. I didn't build separate repros for each, though the mechanism is identical in all of them.

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/themsquared/shared-sandbox-agent-leak.git
cd shared-sandbox-agent-leak
./run.sh

Two agents, two jobs, one shared filesystem: one of them posts the other's secrets to Slack. Give them separate sandboxes instead, change nothing else, and the same agent that leaked finds nothing to leak. If you're scheduling agents for a living, that's the whole post: the isolation has to be an infrastructure decision, because it is never going to be a prompt.

Frequently asked questions

Why did a Grok Bot AI agent leak bank account data into Slack?

Per Cybernews' 2026-10-10 report, XMTP Labs CEO Shane Mac gave a Grok Bot agent read-only access to his personal bank account. A separate Grok Bot agent, configured only to post updates to his company Slack, posted his balances there instead. Mac's own explanation: the two agents shared one cloud compute instance, so the Slack agent could reach data it was never scoped to see.

Does giving two AI agents different tasks keep their data separate?

No. A task description is a prompt-level instruction, not a compute boundary. If two agents share a filesystem, environment, or process namespace, either one can read whatever the other wrote there, regardless of what either agent was told to do. Isolation has to be enforced below the prompt, at the compute layer.

How do you isolate AI agents running on the same host or cluster?

Give each agent its own sandbox: a separate container, volume, or microVM, so there is no shared filesystem, environment variable set, or process namespace between agents. kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox defines a Sandbox CRD for this on Kubernetes, and kagent ships gVisor-backed microVM sandboxes as a platform default in its v1.0.0-alpha series.

What's the difference between agent sandboxing and agent credential scoping?

Sandboxing controls what an agent can see on its own machine: its filesystem, its environment, and whether another agent's data is reachable at all. Credential scoping and egress gateways control what an agent can reach over the network once it's running. They're complementary boundaries that solve different problems; this post is about the first one.

Canonical version, with machine-readable markdown at https://webofmike.com/shared-sandbox-agent-leak/index.md: https://webofmike.com/shared-sandbox-agent-leak/

title: Vertical Sliced Wasserstein Distances for Meta-Measures
description:
arXiv:2610.20743v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many modern learning problems require comparing probability distributions whose individual observations are themselves probability measures, naturally giving rise to meta-measures in $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\Omega))$. However, optimal transport distances on this space can be prohibitively expensive to evaluate. We introduce the vertical sliced Wasserstein ($\mathrm{VSW}$) distance, a scalable metric on $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\Omega))$. Rather than slicing along the transport geometry of $\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$, $\mathrm{VSW}$ projects each inner measure using continuous test functions and compares the resulting one-dimensional distributions with one-dimensional Wasserstein distance. We prove that $\mathrm{VSW}$ is a valid metric on $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\Omega))$, metrizes weak convergence, and admits dimension-independent statistical convergence guarantees. Empirically, $\mathrm{VSW}$ provides high accuracy and efficiency compared with existing distances for meta-measures. We further derive a practical particle gradient for the empirical $\mathrm{VSW}_2^2$ objective and demonstrate its use for gradient-based transport of meta-measures. $\mathrm{VSW}$ provides a simple and scalable alternative for comparing and optimizing distributions of distributions.

title: A Multi-Tiered AI Accessibility Model (MAIAM): Proportionate Access and Capability Limits for Comprehensive Frontier AI Safety
description:
arXiv:2610.20921v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most debate about releasing capable AI systems treats the choice as binary: keep the model behind an API, or publish the weights. That framing runs together two separate decisions. One is how capable a system may become. The other is who may obtain a given capability, and on what terms. This paper is about the second decision. We propose a Multi-Tiered AI Accessibility Model (MAIAM) that sorts access by purpose, safety, and capability instead of by release artifact. Tier 1, AI for Learning, is broadly accessible and deliberately capability-bounded. Tier 2, AI for Exploration, serves research and development under registration, identity, and usage controls that tighten as capability rises. Tier 3, Full-Scale Frontier AI, is available only through structured, recorded, and accountable access. The principle behind the tiers is that accessibility should be proportional to capability, safety, and risk. We show why publishing frontier-class weights forfeits every safety lever a developer has after release, and, using evidence that safety fine-tuning can be stripped from open weights for a few hundred dollars, why an evaluation of the base model says little about its derivatives. We give criteria for assigning a system to a tier along capability, autonomy, domain-consequence, and usage/safety axes, and combine MAIAM with the SAFE AI Operating Point into a two-part framework: a Capability Boundary that fixes the safety limits not to be crossed, and an Accessibility Boundary that fixes who may obtain a capability below that limit. Capability limits alone do not make AI safe; a tiered access regime administered by regulating bodies is also needed.

title: Expanding Attention: A Taylor-Series Route to Linear-Time Transformers with a Fixed Number of Recurrent States
description:
arXiv:2610.20637v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We expand the exponential kernel of attention into a truncated Taylor series of $n$ terms and factorize each term into a tensor-power inner product, which collapses the causal history into exactly $n$ recurrent states, each updated by one rank-one outer product per token and independent of context length $N$. The recursion is lossless with respect to the truncated kernel ($2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ in float64), and the states are additive across chunks ($5.7 \times 10^{-14}$), so prefill admits a parallel scan. Measured exponents are $t \propto N^{2.28}$ for softmax against $N^{0.91}$ for states, with a crossover at $N \approx 728$ and $20.8\times$ at $N = 8192$; per-token decoding latency is constant at $7.3\,\mu$s against $N^{1.04}$ for softmax, giving $76.0\times$ at $N = 65536$. Accuracy improves exponentially in $n$ while cost grows combinatorially, since the $m$-th state is $\binom{d+m-1}{m}$ wide---a bound confirmed by SVD---so the optimum is second order, $n = 3$, at $6.5 \times 10^{-4}$ error and $9{,}945$ elements per head. Query and key normalization is a prerequisite: without it the argument exceeds the convergence radius and adding terms stops helping.

title: JavaScript Production Errors: How Minified Stack Source Maps Guide Fintech Rollouts
description:
JavaScript production errors happen six minutes after a new pricing rule reaches a flagged React cohort. The page shows a rising count, a minified function name, and a stack frame that points into a hashed asset. What the on-call does not see is the decision they need to make: did the new rule break checkout, or did unrelated background noise rise at the same time?

TL;DR: keep source maps private but available to the release pipeline, attach an immutable release identifier and flag variant to every error event, and alert on the affected transaction cohort rather than raw exception volume. Error tracking can group and decode what the browser reports. It cannot reconstruct a missing map, infer an unrecorded flag assignment, or prove customer impact from a stack trace alone.

For a fintech pricing rollout, the least complex useful design joins three records: the browser failure, the exact deployed artifact, and the server-side pricing decision. That gives the on-call enough evidence to pause a cohort without turning every client-side exception into a rollback.

Why do JavaScript production errors have a minified stack?

The stack is minified because the executing production asset has been transformed from the source engineers read, so its names and positions describe that generated file. That explains the opaque frame, but it does not yet explain the incident. The page should name the affected operation and cohort before it names the exception. “Quote acceptance failures increased for pricing_rule=v2” is actionable. “TypeError count increased” usually is not. The first message supports a bounded response: stop expanding the flag, compare the control cohort, and inspect the release that served the failing asset. If the control cohort is also failing, the flag is weak evidence; if only the treatment cohort moves and both cohorts used the same release, the pricing path becomes a stronger lead. The on-call still checks operation outcomes before pausing expansion because correlation is not proof of cause.

Context first.

The distinction matters because a JavaScript exception is evidence of a failed execution path, not evidence that the pricing rule caused it. A stale tab may still run an older bundle. A browser extension may inject code. A network interruption can prevent a later chunk from loading. The stack can also be correct while the user-visible transaction succeeds through a retry. Paging on the undifferentiated total combines different causes and different consequences.

I've been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I use a short alert payload and distrust counters that cannot explain their inputs. Pages are read under pressure. This one needs the release ID, flag variant, operation, recent error ratio, event count, and a link to the matching deploy record. It should also say which evidence is absent. If the event lacks a release ID, that's an observability defect, not permission to guess.

One line is enough to establish urgency:

Pricing acceptance error ratio crossed its rollout threshold in the treatment cohort; control remains below its threshold.

Do not put a raw count in that sentence without its denominator. Ten errors among twenty attempts describe a different incident from ten errors among two million attempts. Low-volume cohorts need a minimum event floor as well, otherwise a single failure can create a dramatic but useless ratio.

Work backward from the minified frame

Production bundles are commonly transformed for delivery. As a result, the function names, file names, and line positions visible to the browser may differ from the source an engineer reviews. A source map is the translation artifact between those positions. Decoding succeeds only when the collected event can be matched to the same generated artifact and its corresponding map.

That match is where many investigations lose time. A map from the current deploy does not explain a stack emitted by the previous deploy. A filename alone is weak identity if a cache, rollback, or parallel region can serve more than one build. Treat the release identifier as part of the event schema and treat the generated asset plus map as a pair. Retain the pair for at least as long as clients can plausibly execute that release.

Keep the mapping operation out of the browser path. Publishing a map beside a public asset may disclose source text and names, depending on how the map was built. A private symbolication stage can accept the generated location, resolve it against controlled build artifacts, and store the mapped location with restricted access. The public application does not need map access for this workflow.

Missing maps are final for that frame.

An error tracker may preserve the raw stack, group similar messages, attach request context, and correlate events. It cannot derive the original file and line with confidence when the translation artifact was never retained. This is a hard boundary, and the runbook should say so plainly.

Framework labels do not remove that boundary. React can provide component-level context for some failures, while a Next.js application can include code produced through several build and rendering paths. The operational requirement stays the same: identify the executing release, preserve its artifacts, and distinguish browser failures from server failures. Combining both into one “application errors” counter destroys useful causality.

Instrument the decision, not just the exception

The pricing service should emit a decision record when it evaluates the flag, using an opaque correlation ID rather than sensitive pricing inputs. The browser error event carries the same correlation ID when the workflow permits it, along with low-cardinality dimensions such as operation, release, and variant. Avoid customer identity, payment data, free-form URLs, and raw quote details in telemetry.

The following Go type shows the contract at the ingestion boundary. It is intentionally small. Fields that cannot drive an operational decision do not belong on the page path.

package telemetry

import "time"

type BrowserFailure struct {
    OccurredAt    time.Time `json:"occurred_at"`
    CorrelationID string    `json:"correlation_id"`
    ReleaseID     string    `json:"release_id"`
    FlagVariant   string    `json:"flag_variant"`
    Operation     string    `json:"operation"`
    ErrorClass    string    `json:"error_class"`
    AssetDigest   string    `json:"asset_digest"`
    GeneratedLine int       `json:"generated_line"`
    GeneratedCol  int       `json:"generated_column"`
}

func (e BrowserFailure) Actionable() bool {
    return e.ReleaseID != "" &&
        e.FlagVariant != "" &&
        e.Operation != "" &&
        e.AssetDigest != ""
}

Actionable does not mean “page immediately.” It means the event has enough identity to participate in aggregation and symbolication. Alert evaluation happens after the system joins events to completed or failed operations and separates treatment from control.

That separation is an idempotency problem too. Browsers retry submissions, collectors retry deliveries, and queues can redeliver. Give each event a stable ID, reject or collapse duplicates at ingestion, and make the cohort counters replay-safe. Otherwise an observability retry can look like a customer failure surge. The failure mode is particularly ugly because a healthier telemetry pipeline then appears to make the application less healthy.

A compact decision table keeps the page policy reviewable:

Signal Page? Reason
Treatment error ratio rises; control is stable; minimum volume is met Yes The rollout is a plausible differentiator
Raw exception count rises in both cohorts No Shared noise or a broader release issue needs triage
One unmapped stack appears with no failed operation No Preserve it for investigation; impact is not established
Failed pricing operations rise without browser exceptions Yes Customer impact can exist outside client error tracking

The last row is easy to miss.

Error tracking is only one sensor. A rule can return a valid response with the wrong eligibility outcome, or a client can abandon before any exception is sent. Business-operation telemetry and invariant checks must cover those cases.

The earlier signal is release completeness

The page at minute six is already late if the release pipeline knew that its artifact set was incomplete. Before increasing the flag, verify that every generated asset expected for the release has a retained map, that the release manifest binds their digests, and that a known generated location resolves to the intended source location. This is a deployment check, not a production experiment.

Fail closed on rollout expansion when that check fails. The application may continue serving the current stable cohort, but the new cohort should not grow while its failures would be opaque. This trade-off favors diagnosis over rollout speed, which is appropriate for a pricing rule whose errors can affect money-facing decisions.

Feature flags also need ownership and an expiry path. The flag is a control surface, not the observability system itself. Record who can pause it, the cohort progression, the decision criteria at each step, and when the temporary branch will be removed. Martin Fowler's feature-toggle guidance describes the broader categories and operational trade-offs; the relevant lesson here is that a release mechanism changes how code paths coexist and therefore how evidence must be segmented.

Test the whole chain with a synthetic failure tied to a non-customer cohort. Confirm that it is ingested once, associated with the expected release and variant, mapped to the intended source, and excluded from customer-impact paging. Then remove it. A test that stops after “the event reached the dashboard” has not exercised the decision path.

Tune for signal quality, then account for silence

Thresholds should be derived from the operation's normal behavior and traffic shape, not copied from another service. Evaluate treatment and control over the same interval, require enough observations to avoid one-event pages, and use separate policies for fast rollback signals and slower investigation signals. Document the exact rollback condition before launch so the incident channel does not become a debate about a graph.

Silence has a cost. If the browser collector is blocked, the page can look healthy while transactions fail. Track expected telemetry volume alongside application traffic, and alert on a material gap between the two. This is another reason to retain server-side operation outcomes: independent signals make a quiet client channel visible.

There is no perfect threshold. A sensitive rule interrupts on-call engineers and can freeze a sound rollout because of unrelated client noise. A tolerant rule leaves a harmful cohort exposed longer. Start with a small cohort, make the pause operation cheap and idempotent, and review false positives after each stage. Change one threshold at a time, with the reason recorded.

The final runbook should lead to an action in a few minutes: confirm telemetry health, compare treatment with control, verify release identity, inspect the mapped top frames, and pause expansion when both customer impact and cohort attribution are present. If only the stack is present, investigate without claiming causality. If impact is present but the stack is absent, act on the impact.

That is the boundary worth preserving. Better symbolication makes an exception understandable; better cohort instrumentation makes it actionable. Confusing the two produces noisy pages and confident postmortems built on weak evidence.

Further reading

  • Martin Fowler, “Feature Toggles”: https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html

title: This Week in Open Source for October 15, 2026
description:
by Daryl Ducharme, Open Source Programs Office

This Week in Open Source for October 15, 2026

A look around the world of open source

After speaking about the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol and Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Toronto last week (which I recapped in Tag-Team Transmission), open agent boundaries were clearly still on my mind while collecting this week's reads. As AI agents, terminal tools, and embedded micro-apps move deeper into everyday software workflows, a central tension keeps surfacing across the open source community: where do human judgment, interface trust, and maintainer sustainability fit in? Whether teams are wiring up open protocols in the Unix shell, running multimodal retrieval locally on a laptop, or stewarding decades-old kernel infrastructure, the healthiest open source architectures don't replace human agency—they give workers clearer boundaries, inspectable tools, and a genuine seat at the controls.

Upcoming Events

🗓️ October 2026

  • All Things Open 2026 (October 19–20, 2026) — Raleigh, North Carolina, USA. One of the largest community-focused open source conferences on the U.S. East Coast exploring open source software, AI engineering, and maintainer sustainability—featuring Googlers Andrew Brogdon, Mark Techson, and Marc Dougherty speaking on "Where Is My Futuristic App? Generative UI and the Open Future" and Abdel Sghiouar on "Taming Agentic AI: How to Run Agents-Generated Code Safely on Kubernetes", alongside the Google Community Lounge with the Flutter team.

Two days of open source machine learning innovation across the PyTorch ecosystem—featuring a keynote by Google's Bill Jia ("Workload Fungibility in the Age of Agents") and technical sessions from Googlers Chris Jones, Sandeep Pokkunuri, Rob Mulla, Ankita Luthra, Trinadh Kotturu, Claudio Basile, Qi Zhou, Jago Macleod, and Aleksey Vlasenko on TorchTPU, vLLM, SGLang, Ray, and Kubernetes.

Open Source Reads and Links

  • [Blog] Meet the A2A CLI: discover, message, and manage agents from your terminal — In Developer Relations, few things beat showing a protocol live in a terminal during a conference talk without a complex web stack in the way. The new Apache 2.0 A2A CLI lets you discover, message, and wrap any stdin/stdout script into a streaming Agent2Agent server with --exec—raising an interesting question: does meeting developers in the Unix shell matter more for open protocol adoption than heavy SDKs?
  • [Blog] Talking to Agents with a2a (as a human!) — Right after the MCP Dev Summit in Toronto, Marc Dougherty shared a post that uncovered even more about the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol by flipping the lens from autonomous systems to human-to-agent interfaces with A2UI. RedMonk's Rachel Stephens examines this shift toward headless software and asks a question every open source protocol builder should ponder: when third-party agents mediate our data and workflows, how well does trust actually travel?
  • [Blog] EmbeddingGemma 2: an open, lightweight multimodal embedding model — Moving RAG setups fully on-device opens up real-world possibilities—from kiosks in low-connectivity areas and offline backup systems to hardware that ships with all of its own help and support docs onboard. With Google DeepMind's Apache 2.0 release of EmbeddingGemma 2 fitting multimodal search into 567MB of RAM, what new resilient tools become possible when devices don't need an internet connection to know how they work?
  • [Blog] Atproto Web Tile Embeds — Seeing AT Protocol Web Tiles in the wild sparks curiosity about what new publishing patterns become possible when open protocols move beyond text and static images. Nathan Cassell walks through embedding a live, sandboxed 3D Web Tile straight from a personal data server into a blog post—making us wonder what developers might build when interactive micro-apps can travel anywhere without phoning home.
  • [Report] Navigating Open Source Governance in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: The 2026 State of OSPOs and Open Source Management — Working in an OSPO myself, seeing how other teams operate is essential for improving how we serve as liaisons between our organizations and the broader open source ecosystem. With the Linux Foundation and TODO Group's 2026 survey finding 79% of AI-involved OSPOs shaping model policy and 69% piloting agentic workflows, how can we ensure enterprise AI governance also supports upstream maintainers?
  • [Report] Celebrating 35 Years of Linux: The Open Source Engine Powering Three Decades of Global Innovation and Infrastructure — It is incredible to see the success of the Linux kernel and distributions across enterprise software development—and to ponder how a project from the early 1990s has kept up with so many technological shifts. As Linux Foundation Research celebrates 35 years of Linux across billions of devices and every top-500 supercomputer, how can the community's model of continuous adaptation guide the next generation of maintainers?

title: VLA-$\Delta$: Learning Physical State Transition for Vision-Language-Action Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21306v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer semantic knowledge acquired through vision-language pretraining to robot control, achieving strong performance across various benchmarks. However, most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions without explicit supervision of intermediate physical state changes, making them prone to overfitting observation-action correspondences. Some methods introduce intermediate reasoning or future-state prediction in language, visual, or latent spaces to guide action generation, but do not explicitly supervise the physical state transition itself. We therefore propose VLA-$\Delta$, a general framework that uses physical changes between current and future states as explicit learning targets. To support this objective, we construct a large-scale pretraining dataset and derive physical state-transition annotations covering task-relevant semantics and visual motion changes, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. During inference, the model generates actions directly from current observations without additional inference overhead. VLA-$\Delta$ achieves performance competitive with the state of the art on LIBERO and RoboTwin, and outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ in real-robot experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-OmniAI/VLA-Delta

title: Realtime Room Admission Control Through Token Scope and Client Trust Signals
description:
Use a server-side admission gate that issues a short-lived, room-scoped capability only after it verifies the operator, the requested IoT devices, and the allowed control actions. For a realtime device control panel, the decisive observability signals are the admission decision and reason, token scope, policy version, decision latency, room occupancy, and the later WebRTC connection state. Transport health is useful, but it can't prove that a client was entitled to enter.

That separation is the whole design. Keep it sharp.

The panel should never carry a fleet-wide credential. A browser is a client under an operator's control — and sometimes an extension's control — so its claim that it belongs in factory-west is input to verify, not authority. The server admits a narrowly defined principal to a narrowly defined room; WebRTC then carries control messages and telemetry within that grant.

Replace connection-first thinking with admission-first thinking

The tempting model is short: create a peer connection, join a room, then decide what the participant may do. It feels efficient because the UI gets online quickly. It also collapses identity, authorization, and network reachability into one vague state called “connected.” When an operator reports that a command never reached a thermostat, the logs can't tell whether access was denied, signaling failed, the data channel stalled, or the device rejected the command.

Use a different mental picture. Before: browser -> room -> devices -> permission check. After: browser -> admission decision -> scoped grant -> room -> permitted devices. Put an observation point at each arrow. The first model treats a live socket as evidence of authority. The second treats a live socket as transport established after authority was determined.

WebRTC deliberately gives the application primitives rather than a room authorization model. RTCPeerConnection exposes connection, ICE, and signaling states, while getStats() returns a report describing the peer connection at a point in time. Your application still owns “room,” “operator,” “device,” and “may send control commands.” That boundary is good news: it lets the admission service remain authoritative even if the media or data path is peer-to-peer. Don't infer admission from connectionState === "connected". That value says the peer connection reached a connected transport state; it doesn't say the operator has the restart action for device pump-17. Likewise, a failed connection doesn't mean policy denied entry. Keep those outcomes in separate fields and separate metrics, or an ordinary network problem will look like a security event.

How should realtime room admission control expose observability signals for an IoT device panel?

Start with one structured event per decision. It should contain a generated request ID, outcome, bounded reason code, room class, requested device count, granted device count, requested action count, granted action count, policy version, decision duration, and grant lifetime. Record the authenticated principal through an approved pseudonymous identifier. Never log the bearer token, session cookie, raw authorization header, or full command payload.

Bounded fields matter. Put outcome, reason, and policy_version on metrics; keep request IDs and principal identifiers in logs or traces. A metric labeled by raw device ID will grow a new time series for every device and eventually make the dashboard harder to operate. The log can retain enough context for a targeted investigation without turning every identity into a metric dimension.

Here is the signal set I would put on the first dashboard:

Layer Signal Diagnostic question
Admission decisions by outcome and reason Are clients rejected by identity, scope, capacity, or stale policy?
Admission decision duration Is the gate slow before any peer negotiation starts?
Scope requested versus granted devices and actions Are panels asking for broader authority than they receive?
Room active grants and grant age Is occupancy unusual, or are old grants lingering?
Transport connection and ICE state transitions Did an admitted client establish a usable path?
Data path messages sent and received, bytes, and buffered amount Is control traffic moving after connection?

Use explicit application reason codes such as IDENTITY_REQUIRED, DEVICE_SCOPE_EMPTY, ACTION_NOT_ALLOWED, and ROOM_AT_CAPACITY. Those are part of your contract, not HTTP status prose. A rejected decision may map to an authentication or authorization status at an API boundary, but dashboards should aggregate the stable reason code because transport mappings can change.

Then correlate admission and transport with the request ID or a derived session ID. The useful timeline reads: decision allowed; scoped grant issued; peer connection created; ICE state changed; data channel opened; first control message acknowledged. A missing span is immediately visible. Nice.

Set alerts on symptoms people can act on. A rise in denials for one bounded policy reason calls for a policy or identity investigation. A normal allow rate followed by a rise in failed ICE states points toward connectivity. Increasing buffered data with flat received-message counts points toward a data-path backlog. I'm not sure a universal threshold exists for any of these; room size, device cadence, and operator workflow vary too much. Establish thresholds from the panel's normal distribution and verify them during a controlled load test.

Make the grant smaller than the operator session

The grant should answer four questions without consulting the browser: who was admitted, which room is covered, which devices and actions are allowed, and when the grant expires. Bind it to the authenticated operator session and, where the architecture permits, to the intended peer or signaling exchange. Reject replay after expiry and record the rejection reason without recording the credential itself.

Short-lived is a design property, not a magic number. The code below uses 30_000 ms to make the example concrete — it isn't a recommendation for every deployment. A panel with slow human approval may need a longer admission window; a high-risk actuator may need a much shorter one. The grant must still expire no later than the operator session, and refreshing it should repeat the relevant authorization checks.

This server-side TypeScript example keeps policy inputs and emitted signals explicit. The signing and persistence interfaces are injected so the example doesn't pretend that a browser-local secret is acceptable.

type Action = "view" | "set-level" | "restart";
type DenialReason =
  | "IDENTITY_REQUIRED"
  | "DEVICE_SCOPE_EMPTY"
  | "ACTION_NOT_ALLOWED";

type AdmissionRequest = {
  requestId: string;
  roomId: string;
  deviceIds: string[];
  actions: Action[];
};

type OperatorContext = {
  subject: string | null;
  sessionExpiresAt: number;
  allowedDeviceIds: ReadonlySet<string>;
  allowedActions: ReadonlySet<Action>;
  policyVersion: string;
};

type GrantClaims = {
  subject: string;
  roomId: string;
  deviceIds: string[];
  actions: Action[];
  expiresAt: number;
};

type AdmissionEvent = {
  requestId: string;
  outcome: "allow" | "deny";
  reason?: DenialReason;
  policyVersion: string;
  requestedDevices: number;
  grantedDevices: number;
  requestedActions: number;
  grantedActions: number;
  durationMs: number;
};

type Dependencies = {
  now: () => number;
  signGrant: (claims: GrantClaims) => Promise<string>;
  emit: (event: AdmissionEvent) => void;
};

type AdmissionResult =
  | { allowed: true; grant: string; expiresAt: number }
  | { allowed: false; reason: DenialReason };

export async function decideAdmission(
  request: AdmissionRequest,
  operator: OperatorContext,
  dependencies: Dependencies,
): Promise<AdmissionResult> {
  const startedAt = dependencies.now();
  const devices = request.deviceIds.filter((id) =>
    operator.allowedDeviceIds.has(id),
  );
  const actions = request.actions.filter((action) =>
    operator.allowedActions.has(action),
  );

  let reason: DenialReason | undefined;
  if (!operator.subject) reason = "IDENTITY_REQUIRED";
  else if (devices.length === 0) reason = "DEVICE_SCOPE_EMPTY";
  else if (actions.length !== request.actions.length) reason = "ACTION_NOT_ALLOWED";

  const event = (outcome: "allow" | "deny"): AdmissionEvent => ({
    requestId: request.requestId,
    outcome,
    reason,
    policyVersion: operator.policyVersion,
    requestedDevices: request.deviceIds.length,
    grantedDevices: devices.length,
    requestedActions: request.actions.length,
    grantedActions: actions.length,
    durationMs: dependencies.now() - startedAt,
  });

  if (!operator.subject || reason) {
    dependencies.emit(event("deny"));
    return { allowed: false, reason: reason ?? "IDENTITY_REQUIRED" };
  }

  const expiresAt = Math.min(
    dependencies.now() + 30_000,
    operator.sessionExpiresAt,
  );
  const grant = await dependencies.signGrant({
    subject: operator.subject,
    roomId: request.roomId,
    deviceIds: devices,
    actions,
    expiresAt,
  });

  dependencies.emit(event("allow"));
  return { allowed: true, grant, expiresAt };
}

Notice what the event omits: the token and raw subject. It also reports counts on both sides of the policy decision. If a client repeatedly requests 40 devices and receives 3, you can see scope pressure without putting 40 device identifiers into every metric. The detailed audit log can store an access-controlled mapping when the investigation requires it.

There is one subtle rule in the example: a partially permitted action set is denied rather than silently narrowed. Silent narrowing is dangerous for a control panel because the UI may render a button that can never succeed. Device lists can be intersected if the UI is designed to show only granted devices, but command actions should use an explicit contract. Your mileage may vary — what matters is that partial admission behavior is deliberate, tested, and visible.

Observe the peer connection without confusing it with authorization

After admission, sample the state the runtime actually exposes. The W3C WebRTC Recommendation defines connectionState, iceConnectionState, signalingState, and getStats() on RTCPeerConnection. Stats objects carry timestamps, and candidate-pair or data-channel reports can provide transport and traffic evidence depending on the selected connection and browser implementation.

A small collector can normalize the useful pieces before sending them to your telemetry pipeline. Keep the raw report out of routine logs: it can be large, implementation-dependent, and richer than an admission investigation needs.

type PeerSnapshot = {
  observedAt: number;
  connectionState: RTCPeerConnectionState;
  iceConnectionState: RTCIceConnectionState;
  signalingState: RTCSignalingState;
  selectedPairRttSeconds?: number;
  dataMessagesSent: number;
  dataMessagesReceived: number;
};

type CandidatePairReport = RTCStats & {
  state?: string;
  nominated?: boolean;
  currentRoundTripTime?: number;
};

type DataChannelReport = RTCStats & {
  messagesSent?: number;
  messagesReceived?: number;
};

export async function snapshotPeer(
  peer: RTCPeerConnection,
): Promise<PeerSnapshot> {
  const report = await peer.getStats();
  let selectedPairRttSeconds: number | undefined;
  let dataMessagesSent = 0;
  let dataMessagesReceived = 0;

  report.forEach((stat: RTCStats) => {
    if (stat.type === "candidate-pair") {
      const pair = stat as CandidatePairReport;
      if (pair.state === "succeeded" && pair.nominated) {
        selectedPairRttSeconds = pair.currentRoundTripTime;
      }
    }

    if (stat.type === "data-channel") {
      const channel = stat as DataChannelReport;
      dataMessagesSent += channel.messagesSent ?? 0;
      dataMessagesReceived += channel.messagesReceived ?? 0;
    }
  });

  return {
    observedAt: Date.now(),
    connectionState: peer.connectionState,
    iceConnectionState: peer.iceConnectionState,
    signalingState: peer.signalingState,
    selectedPairRttSeconds,
    dataMessagesSent,
    dataMessagesReceived,
  };
}

Emit state transitions immediately and sample counters at a measured interval. Don't promise an exact sampling period until you have tested the CPU, network, storage, and debugging value in your own panel. A 1 s cadence might be appropriate during an active diagnostic window and excessive for thousands of idle tabs. Sampling is an operational budget.

The client snapshot is supporting evidence. Server-side command acknowledgements, device-side acceptance, and the authoritative admission event complete the path. If the browser says it sent 12 messages while the relay or device records none, the correlation narrows the gap. If the admission event is absent, don't start with ICE graphs; first find out why the client bypassed or never reached the gate.

What are the two objections worth testing before rollout?

“Can the client make the admission decision to reduce latency?” It can preflight the UI, but it shouldn't grant authority. Client-side checks are helpful for hiding controls that the current user is unlikely to receive. The server must repeat the decision from authenticated context because browser state and requested scopes are untrusted inputs. Measure server decision duration, cache only policy data whose invalidation rules you understand, and keep the final grant on the trusted side.

“Should every device panel use a persistent realtime room?” No. This design is not suitable when commands are rare, several seconds of freshness are acceptable, or devices cannot maintain the required path. Stick with periodic pull for a low-frequency status screen when its simpler failure model meets the product requirement. Use a durable message broker between the control service and intermittently connected devices when commands must survive disconnection; a live room alone is not a durable command log. The catch is extra infrastructure and another acknowledgement boundary, so observe enqueue, delivery, device acceptance, and expiry separately.

Test the gate as a state machine before rollout. Cover expired operator sessions, empty device intersections, mixed allowed and denied actions, replayed grants, policy changes during refresh, room capacity, and a connection that fails after successful admission. Then run one trace across the complete route: operator intent — admission — peer establishment — command — device acknowledgement. The before/after dashboard should be obvious: one undifferentiated “room join failed” counter becomes a small set of bounded decisions and transport states that point to an owner.

Ship the distinction, not just the chart.

References

  • W3C, WebRTC: Real-Time Communication in Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Width is not the viewport, and 800x600 is not a desktop
description:
Development covered 29 Aug 2026 to 2 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

Myriad Immortal Sect runs in a browser, and browsers are not one shape. It runs full screen on a laptop, portrait on a phone, landscape on a tablet, and embedded in a small frame on portals that host browser games. That last one is where my layout rules turned out to be built on an assumption I had never said out loud.

The assumption

Every breakpoint I had written asked one question: how wide is this?

That works for the usual cases, because on real devices width and height travel together. A narrow viewport is a phone and a phone is also short. So width alone is a decent proxy for the whole shape, right up until it is not.

The frame on a game portal is around eight hundred pixels wide and not very tall. Width says desktop, comfortably. Height says something closer to a phone. My code believed the width, so the embedded build got the full desktop treatment: a minimap at its full size covering a sizeable share of the visible area, and, on the first screen, a start button that sat below the fold. The first thing a visitor saw was a game they could not begin.

Both directions, every time

The rule now is that layered elements are decided against both dimensions. Not a second set of breakpoints, just an honest question: is there room for this, given how much space there actually is, rather than how wide it is.

The practical version, if you want one line to take away: write down the real frames your thing runs in, including the embedded ones, and test the smallest total area rather than the smallest width. I had a phone in my test list and no small landscape frame, so a whole class of layout went unchecked in a place where real people arrive.

The other half of a viewport nobody reads

A related one on phones with a notch or a home indicator. The document declares that it wants to draw into the full screen, edge to edge, which is the modern default and looks better.

Declaring that is half the job. The other half is reading the safe area the device reports and keeping interactive controls out of it. I had done the first half only, so on those phones the bottom row of controls sat exactly in the strip the system reserves for its own gestures. Pressing them was a coin flip between the game and the operating system.

The lesson generalises past this specific property. Anything that opts you into more space is also opting you into responsibility for the parts of that space that are not yours. The places that fill that frame, from cities to sect grounds, are named in the glossary of world terms.

Small thing, disproportionate effect

The change I did not expect to matter: the minimap now folds itself away after ten seconds of no input, on a desktop or in landscape. A portrait phone keeps it, since the space it takes there is not contested.

It is a small animation on a timer. It made the map feel meaningfully less cluttered, because the clutter was mostly a thing you needed for four seconds and then stopped looking at. A surprising amount of interface design is working out which elements are answers to a question rather than permanent furniture, and letting the answers leave once they have been read.

Also this week

A pass over the English text as a native reader would meet it, which meant removing transliterations that had survived in dialogue, replacing Chinese units of distance and weight, and fixing one quest line where all four names were wrong at once. Item names went through the same pass, and the glossary of item terms collects their English forms. Our English text is authored rather than translated, so no reader should be able to tell which language a given sentence began life in.

Everything here ships in Xianxia idle incremental game, and you can check the layout on any screen you own.

title: CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20642v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent latent reasoning methods move beyond discrete Chain-of-Thought (CoT) by replacing sampled tokens with continuous soft embeddings or hidden states, enabling richer intermediate representations and preserving alternative reasoning paths. However, the need for latent reasoning varies across decoding steps: confident predictions favor discrete commitment, whereas ambiguous steps benefit from preserving multiple plausible alternatives. Existing approaches typically handle this variation through either global soft activation or hard switching based on uncertainty thresholds, treating latent intervention as an all-or-nothing decision rather than continuously adapting its strength. To address this limitation, we propose Competitive Token Selection (CoTS), a training-free framework that reframes latent intervention from binary mode selection into continuous allocation at the token level. CoTS uses the probability competition between the two most likely candidates to dynamically balance discrete commitment and soft exploration at each reasoning step. The second candidate represents the strongest alternative to the model's preferred continuation, so the separation between the two directly reflects the stability of the current discrete choice. When one candidate clearly dominates, CoTS keeps the representation close to the sampled discrete token to preserve a stable reasoning trajectory; as the competition strengthens, it increases the contribution of the soft representation to retain plausible alternatives. This competition-based allocation requires neither manually tuned switching thresholds nor mixing coefficients, and introduces no additional forward passes. Experiments across six reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that CoTS consistently outperforms standard CoT and state-of-the-art training-free latent reasoning methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/OkinoYu/CoTSReasoning.

title: Travel Planner Retrieval Design with Bounded Access Rules and Source Citations
description:
Short answer: a travel itinerary planner needs a staged retrieval architecture with bounded access rules and source context attached to every answer.

In a travel itinerary planner, retrieval quality is only useful inside the access boundary. A beach recommendation from the wrong country, an expired rail timetable, or a hotel deal that a user cannot book is a correctness failure, even when the embedding score looks excellent. I would set the contract first, then choose the index and the web connector that can enforce it.

This is a small design decision with a large blast radius. The answer generator should never be asked to repair an unbounded search result. Keep it boring.

Scope first.

What should a travel planner retrieval architecture verify before returning context?

Begin with the user-visible answer. “Find a vegetarian lunch near the museum after the 3 p.m. train” is not one retrieval operation. It implies a retrieval unit (place, train notice, or policy paragraph), a geographic scope, a time window, a language, and an access scope. Put those requirements in a retrieval contract before selecting a vendor endpoint.

For each indexed item, I keep fields such as trip_id, region, language, valid_from, valid_until, source_url, and access_scope. The planner chooses a collection for the corpus, applies mandatory filters, and caps the candidate count. A query with no region or trip scope should fail closed; it should not silently search every traveler’s notes. In practice, that means the request validator rejects an itinerary draft that has a city name but no country code, the filter builder refuses an empty trip_id, and the citation layer drops a result whose validity window ended during a long planning session; those checks add a few lines of plumbing but remove the ambiguous “why did this recommendation appear?” class of incident.

Freshness deserves its own check. Web-backed context can change between ingestion and answer time, so store the fetch timestamp and the source revision. A seven-day-old attraction closure is not “close enough” because its vector is similar. If the freshness requirement cannot be met, return a constrained answer that says current confirmation is needed.

Keep the pipeline observable as three separate stages:

  1. Ingestion chunks a source into a named collection and preserves access metadata.
  2. Querying applies filters and a hard limit, then records request and source identifiers.
  3. Answer assembly cites only returned items whose URL, revision, and scope pass validation.

That separation gives an operator a useful trace when a citation is wrong: bad chunking, bad filtering, or bad composition.

How can bounded web search and vector query protect itinerary access rules?

Use web search for fresh, external facts and vector query for the planner’s curated corpus. They are complementary stages, not interchangeable indexes. Search results should be normalized into the same source record shape as ingested documents before the model sees them.

Here is a deliberately small Python adapter. It sends an explicit method, reads the key from the environment, retries a 429 with Retry-After, checks status, and passes only a bounded, scoped context downstream. The paths are the two discovery entries used by this example; the request body is kept behind one function so the rest of the application does not depend on provider-specific plumbing.

import os
import time
from typing import Any

import requests


BASE_URL = os.environ.get("INFRAI_BASE_URL", "https://api.example.invalid/v1")


def post(path: str, payload: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}
    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.request(
            method="POST",
            url=f"{BASE_URL}{path}",
            headers=headers,
            json=payload,
            timeout=15,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(min(delay, 30))
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"retrieval failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
        return response.json()
    raise RuntimeError("retrieval rate limit persisted after retries")


def retrieve(query: str, trip_id: str, region: str) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    web = post("/v1/web/search", {"query": query, "limit": 5})
    vector = post(
        "/v1/vector/query",
        {
            "collection": "itinerary-public",
            "query": query,
            "top_k": 5,
            "filter": {"trip_id": trip_id, "region": region, "access_scope": "traveler"},
        },
    )
    candidates = (web.get("results") or []) + (vector.get("matches") or [])
    return [item for item in candidates if item.get("source_url") and item.get("region") == region][:8]

The exact field schema still belongs in the discovery contract and your tests; the important invariant is that a returned item carries scope and source context. I would also log the normalized source ID, not the full traveler query, when privacy requirements make raw query logging inappropriate. Don't log what you don't need.

Infrai fits this adapter when a team wants one REST surface and one key and bill across retrieval and other backend capabilities. That reduces credential and invoice sprawl, while plain HTTP keeps the integration language-neutral. It does not decide your chunk size, freshness SLA, or authorization policy for you.

Which retrieval options fit a quality-versus-latency budget?

A fair comparison starts with the operational shape of the corpus, not a feature checklist. Pinecone is a managed vector service with a focused indexing workflow. Weaviate offers an open-source core and a managed option, useful when self-hosting or schema control matters. Elasticsearch combines lexical, filtering, and vector search in one search stack, which can be valuable for exact station names and fuzzy descriptions. An HTTP aggregation layer can simplify access to several backend capabilities, but it adds another contract to monitor.

Option Useful fit Trade-off to test
Pinecone Teams prioritizing managed vector operations Extra service boundary for web freshness and policy data
Weaviate Teams wanting schema-rich search with self-hosting choice More operational decisions around modules and deployment
Elasticsearch Hybrid lexical, metadata, and vector queries Tuning and operating a broader search platform
Infrai Teams preferring one REST API and one credential across backend services Validate retrieval semantics and regional access filters against your contract

The benchmark should use a labeled set of real itinerary questions. Record recall of the required source, citation validity, and p95 retrieval latency at the same time. A tiny set of 50–100 questions with labels for region, date, and access scope catches more policy mistakes than a large set of unlabeled queries. I am not sure your mileage will match a vendor demo; traffic shape, language mix, and freshness windows dominate the result.

The catch is that a single global collection may be unsuitable when tenants require hard isolation or when retention rules differ. Use separate collections, or stick with a search system that can prove document-level filtering, when an accidental cross-trip result would be a compliance event. For exact timetable identifiers, keep a lexical path available even if vector recall wins on paraphrased place descriptions.

A rollout rule for citations, monitoring, and change control

Ship ingestion and querying behind separate feature flags. First replay the labeled evaluation set and inspect failures by stage. Then shadow live queries, comparing candidate scope and freshness without changing user-visible answers. Only after citation validity is stable should the generator consume the new context.

Every answer should retain a compact trace: collection, filter values, source IDs, source URLs, revision or fetch time, and the retrieval limit. Alert on missing source fields, out-of-window documents, and a sudden drop in labeled recall. Do not use a fluent answer as the health check.

When the corpus changes, rerun the same labels. If latency rises, reduce candidate limits or split collections before weakening access filters. Retrieval quality and latency are negotiable; authorization is not.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html

title: GBase Database Installation Troubleshooting: 5 Common Causes and Fixes
description:
When a GBase Database (GBase 8s) installation fails, don't assume the installation command is the problem. Missing dependencies, insufficient disk space, port conflicts, and incorrect permissions are often better places to start.

Here are five practical checks to help troubleshoot GBase Database installation and startup issues systematically.

1. Missing System Dependencies

Typical error:

error while loading shared libraries: libaio.so.1:
cannot open shared object file

How to check:

On RPM-based Linux systems, verify whether the required package is installed:

rpm -q libaio

If it is missing, confirm that it is required for your GBase 8s version and operating system before installing it:

sudo yum install libaio

Other libraries may also be required, depending on the platform. Check the official dependency list rather than assuming every installation needs the same packages.

2. Insufficient /tmp Space

Typical symptom: Installation stalls or fails while extracting the package.

How to check:

df -h /tmp
df -i /tmp

Check both available disk space and inodes.

If temporary storage is insufficient, use a larger filesystem where supported by the installer:

mkdir -p /opt/tmp
chmod 700 /opt/tmp
export TMPDIR=/opt/tmp

Verify that the installer honors TMPDIR; some installation tools use their own temporary paths.

3. Port Conflict

If the configured database service port is already occupied, the service may fail to bind to it.

How to check:

ss -tlnp

To inspect a specific port, such as 9088:

ss -tlnp | grep ':9088'

Confirm the actual port in your GBase Database connection configuration. If a conflict exists, coordinate a port change or resolve the conflicting service without disrupting other applications.

4. Hostname Resolution or Connection Failure

Typical symptom: dbaccess cannot connect to the database server.

Check hostname resolution:

hostname
getent hosts "$(hostname)"
cat /etc/hosts

Then review the GBase 8s sqlhosts configuration, including the server name, protocol, hostname, and service or port settings.

A connection failure can also result from an inactive instance, incorrect connection parameters, firewall rules, or a service that is not listening. Check these factors before concluding that hostname resolution is the cause.

5. Incorrect Instance Ownership or Permissions

Incorrect ownership can prevent the database account from accessing instance files.

First, inspect ownership and permissions:

ls -ld /home/gbase/gbasedbt
ls -l /home/gbase/gbasedbt

Use the actual instance path and database account for your installation.

Avoid blindly running recursive chown commands. Changing ownership across an entire directory tree can damage permissions or affect unrelated files. Correct only the paths and ownership settings identified by the installation documentation or troubleshooting evidence.

Also, distinguish software installation privileges from instance initialization privileges: follow the procedures specified for your GBase 8s release.

Final Takeaway

Most GBase Database installation problems become easier to diagnose when you follow a consistent troubleshooting order:

  1. Verify dependencies.
  2. Check temporary disk space.
  3. Investigate port conflicts.
  4. Validate hostname and connection settings.
  5. Inspect instance ownership and permissions.

A structured troubleshooting process beats trial and error.

title: Temporal Specification Guidance for Text-to-Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.20822v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-to-video models often generate the visual concepts requested in natural language prompts but fail to satisfy their intended ordering, timing, and persistence requirements. We propose representing these requirements as specifications in a formal Temporal Logic, and introduce Temporal Specification Guidance (TSG), a training-free inference-time framework that turns temporal specifications into executable objectives for guiding video generation during sampling. TSG scores traces of visual concept evidence using differentiable quantitative semantics and uses the score's gradients to construct a specification-guided denoising direction. We instantiate this framework with video-text attention traces, efficient differentiable scores for Metric Temporal Logic, and gradient-derived attention biases. This instantiation requires neither an external concept classifier nor backpropagation through the video transformer. Its attention-steered forward pass yields a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance (CFG). On a benchmark of 220 prompts spanning 11 categories of temporal constraints, including ordered object entry and state transitions, this instantiation improves specification satisfaction accuracy over CFG by 9.5-20 percentage points across five models, with minimal memory overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of temporal specifications and differentiable satisfaction objectives as a flexible interface for controlling video generation.
