title: LEV: Thinking Fast and Deep with Looped Decision Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20951v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decision models answer typed questions about an input with one probability per option, computed in a single forward pass without generating text. Like the fast System 1 of dual-process theory, they answer at once, but their depth is fixed at training time, so they spend the same computation on easy and hard questions. Models that reason in generated text can think longer, but they pay for every extra step in decoded tokens. We present LEV, a decision model that thinks deeper by rerunning its layers in a loop instead of generating tokens. LEV builds on a language model pretrained as a loop, reads the options after every loop step and trains all steps jointly, so one checkpoint can answer at any depth. On three looped backbones, accuracy rises with depth on the same weights, mostly on hard questions, and a 2.6B LEV goes from 63.2% at depth one to 76.2% at depth four on JevBench. On-demand depth, set per question by a small stopper with a threshold fitted on unlabelled requests, saves 15% to 24% of the computation at a cost of under one accuracy point, level with or slightly above a fixed mix of depths. On a locked test set, the 1.4B and 3B models are 5.4 to 8.8 points more accurate than dense (non-looped) models and cascades of the same latency below 50 ms.

title: Probing Negation Understanding in Vision-Language Models With Object Attention
description:
arXiv:2610.20852v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Negation is a fundamental aspect of language understanding and it is important vision-language models (VLMs) are able to process it effectively. We investigate how VLMs process negation by analysing attention patterns of different models. We draw comparisons between human gaze and attention in models when processing affirmative vs negated statements. We compare object level model attention to human eye-fixations in both binary and multary settings, evaluating with both synthetic and realistic datasets. We find models generally do not follow human-like attention patterns when resolving negation, suggesting they rely on mechanisms outside of attention. While layerwise analysis shows that PaliGemma2-3B shifts object attention to the alternative under negation, our headwise ablations suggest this is a byproduct rather than a negation processing mechanism. Additionally, we find that LLaVA-1.5-7B displays a spatial bias towards left-side objects. Our evaluation of models on downstream tasks shows that all models have a discrepancy between affirmative and negated questions highlighting the need to better understand the underlying processing of negation to close this performance gap. Code available at https://github.com/otmive/negation_attention

title: A Self-Improving Agent that Grows its Own DSL: Oracle-Free Operator Induction for Exact Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2610.20809v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A self-improving agent has to decide which new skills to keep, and in practice it keeps whatever earns a high reward, convinces a judge model, or compresses its library, even when the skill is wrong. That is fine until the answers have to be exactly right: over a table of transactions, a total is either right or wrong. We ask a harder question: can an agent grow what it can compute with no reward, no judge, and no answer key, and still be exactly right? A single frozen model runs two nested loops over a small, exact domain-specific language (DSL). The inner loop answers new questions only when two independently written expressions agree on every record. The outer loop discovers its own missing capability and authors an operator for it, admitted only when an independent second implementation agrees and the result obeys a conservation law, all without ground truth. The inner loop roughly triples the answerable-question set, and the outer loop self-extends on disjoint starting sets, inventing operators outside the starting closure; a no-induction control answers none of the new questions. The admission rule is empirically sound: it rejects 138 of 138 buggy operator variants under an independent reference, even one written by a different model family, where the admit-if-it-runs, self-consistency, and compression signals the field relies on admit most of them. Unmodified, the same mechanism self-extends on two further domains with unrelated schemas, business-ledger and clinical-encounter question answering, growing their answerable sets more than tenfold and nearly twentyfold. The loop transfers across model families too: run with further proposers, the gate stays sound and independent families self-extend comparably, with only the induction yield tracking each proposer's DSL fluency.

title: Selection-Safe Conformal Early Exit: Distribution-Free Coverage under Adaptive Depth
description:
arXiv:2610.20773v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Calibrating a conformal prediction set at each early exit does not preserve coverage once a data-dependent exit is selected. We construct one terminal path score from prefix maxima, calibrate a single split-conformal quantile, and return nested prefix sets that all contain the valid terminal set. The guarantee is selection-safe without an alpha/L correction and holds simultaneously for every post-calibration label-free stopping policy that preserves terminal-set containment. We also bound the efficiency cost of the path maximum by the empirical tail of the early-over-terminal score excess. Across eight encoder task-backbone cells, pathwise selection attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814 for naive layerwise selection, with average set size 1.41 and latency fraction 0.71. On CIFAR-100 with a 24-exit ViT-L/16 (n_cal=500), first-eligible stopping at budget b=4 attains coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57, and the same calibration supports deployment-time budget changes without refitting. In a joint exit-count/calibration-size sweep at n=100, pathwise set size moves only from 3.02 to 3.11 as exits increase from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni degenerates to the full label space for 12 or more exits. Paired comparison against MinSE valid selection at (n,L)=(100,24) gives a set-size difference of 0.80 [0.47, 1.13]. Full-vocabulary decoder experiments remain a negative boundary, with sets of 7,162-9,620 tokens. Pathwise calibration is most useful when candidate exits are many relative to calibration size, when budgets change after calibration, and when shallow heads return actionable sets.

title: Hermes Agent: A Practical Beginner's Guide to Doing Real Things With It (2026)
description:
Hermes Agent: A Practical Beginner's Guide to Doing Real Things With It (2026)

Hermes Agent is an open-source AI agent framework by Nous Research that runs in your terminal, your messaging apps, and your IDE. Most of the time "AI agent" means a chatbot with some extra steps. Hermes is different: it ships with the actual building blocks that make an agent useful — persistent memory, scheduled jobs, subagents that run in parallel, and a plugin system you can extend without forking the code.

This guide is the version I wish existed when I started. It skips the marketing and focuses on: what Hermes can actually do for you, how to get running in about two minutes, and the four features that separate it from a plain chat assistant.

What Hermes Agent is (in one paragraph)

It's a self-hosted agent that keeps a persistent model of you and your environment. It can run terminal commands, edit files, browse the web, search its own past conversations, schedule itself to do jobs on a timer, and spawn parallel subagents. The same agent can answer you in the terminal, on Telegram, on Discord, in Slack, or over email — and it uses the same memory and tools on every platform.

That last part is the big deal. Most chat tools start from zero every conversation. Hermes remembers your preferences, your projects, and what it has learned.

Getting started (about two minutes)

On Linux, macOS, or WSL:

curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash
source ~/.bashrc
hermes

On native Windows (PowerShell):

iex (irm https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.ps1)
hermes

That drops you into an interactive chat. A few commands matter:

  • hermes model — pick your LLM provider and model
  • hermes setup — the full setup wizard (config, tools, messaging)
  • hermes doctor — diagnose install or config problems
  • hermes update — pull the latest version

If you want the desktop app after a CLI-only install, just run hermes desktop.

The four features that actually matter

1. Persistent memory

Hermes keeps a curated memory file that carries across every session. Tell it your preferences once ("I use a Mac and deploy with Cloudflare") and it doesn't forget. It also can search its own past sessions — ask it to recall something you discussed weeks ago and it can find it. This is what turns a tool you re-brief every day into something that builds up context over time.

2. Skills (its self-improvement loop)

Skills are small documents that encode a procedure — "how I do X in this environment" — that the agent loads when a matching task comes up. The important bit: when Hermes works out a non-trivial workflow, it can save that as a skill so it reuses the approach next time. It's a genuine learning loop: it gets better at your specific recurring tasks the more you use it.

3. Cron / scheduled jobs

You can schedule the agent to run on a timer — "every morning at 6, check these things and send me a summary to Telegram." Jobs can be agent-driven (it figures out what to do) or just plain scripts (run this and only wake me if the output changed). This is how people turn Hermes into an overnight worker rather than something you have to sit in front of.

4. Subagent delegation

For a big task, Hermes can spawn isolated child agents that each get their own context and tools and run in parallel, then report back. Three at a time by default. It's how you get a team of workers instead of one slow conversation: one researches, one drafts, one reviews — and you only see the results.

Where people actually use it

  • Personal automation — a morning briefing, a nightly backup, a "watch this price and tell me when it drops" job.
  • Self-hosted assistants — the same agent reachable from your phone over Telegram or WhatsApp.
  • Developer workflows — it reads your code, runs your tests, opens pull requests, and remembers your repo's conventions.
  • Multi-agent setups — a team of agents with isolated profiles and shared skills for a bigger project.

A note on running it seriously

Hermes is free and open source, but you still need a place for it to live if you want it running 24/7 — a always-on machine, a VPS, or a container. For a personal setup most people keep it on a home machine; for a team setup it runs on a small server. If you're building a project site or dashboard around an agent, cheap VPS hosting covers it — you can start a Hostinger VPS for a few dollars a month: Hostinger (referral code OVDAMRMASPIM).

Keep one rule: the memory and skill files are yours and live on your machine, so back them up. They're the part of Hermes that is actually irreplaceable.

Bottom line

If you want a chatbot, Hermes is more than that. If you want an agent that does things — runs your commands, schedules itself, remembers you, and learns your workflows — this is one of the most complete open-source options available. Start with the two-minute install, point it at a real recurring task, and let the skills and memory accumulate. That's where it goes from "a tool" to "something that actually works for you."

This guide is part of the how-to collection on HermesGuide — 90+ guides on installing, configuring, automating, and extending Hermes Agent. Hosting your agent deployments? Grab a cheap VPS via Hostinger referral OVDAMRMASPIM.

title: CSS Container Queries: Truly Reusable Components That Adapt to Their Container
description:
Container Queries are one of the most significant additions to CSS in years. Instead of styling components based on the viewport (media queries), you style them based on their container's size. This makes truly reusable components possible — a card component looks right whether it's in a narrow sidebar or a wide main column.

The Problem with Media Queries for Components

With media queries:

/* Works fine in the main column */
.card { font-size: 16px; }

@media (max-width: 768px) {
  .card { font-size: 14px; } /* Assumes small viewport = narrow card */
}

But what if the card is in a sidebar on a wide viewport? The sidebar might be 300px wide even on a 1440px screen — the media query doesn't trigger, so the card looks wrong.

Container queries solve this: the card responds to its container's size, not the viewport.

Basic Container Query 

/* Step 1: Define a containment context */
.sidebar {
  container-type: inline-size; /* Enable inline-size queries */
  container-name: sidebar;     /* Optional: name for targeting */
}

/* Or shorthand */
.sidebar {
  container: sidebar / inline-size;
}

/* Step 2: Style children based on container size */
@container (min-width: 400px) {
  .card {
    display: flex;
    flex-direction: row;
  }
}

@container (max-width: 399px) {
  .card {
    display: block;
  }
}

Named Containers

Target a specific ancestor:

.main-layout {
  container: main / inline-size;
}

.sidebar-layout {
  container: sidebar / inline-size;
}

/* Only applies when card is inside .sidebar-layout < 300px */
@container sidebar (max-width: 300px) {
  .card { padding: 8px; }
}

/* Only applies when card is inside .main-layout > 600px */
@container main (min-width: 600px) {
  .card { padding: 24px; }
}

Container Query Units

Container queries introduce new units relative to the container:

.card {
  /* cqi: container query inline (horizontal) */
  font-size: max(14px, 2.5cqi); /* At least 14px, grows with container */

  /* cqw: container query width */
  width: 50cqw; /* 50% of container width */

  /* cqh: container query height */
  max-height: 80cqh; /* 80% of container height */

  /* cqb: container query block (vertical) */
  /* cqmin, cqmax: min/max of cqi/cqb */
}

Practical Examples

Card Component 

.card-container {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.card {
  padding: 16px;
}

.card-image {
  width: 100%;
  aspect-ratio: 16/9;
}

/* Wide container: horizontal layout */
@container (min-width: 480px) {
  .card {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;
    gap: 16px;
  }

  .card-image {
    width: 200px;
    aspect-ratio: 1;
  }
}

Navigation 

.nav-container {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

nav { display: flex; gap: 8px; }

@container (max-width: 600px) {
  nav {
    flex-direction: column;
    align-items: stretch;
  }
}

Product Grid 

.products-container {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.product-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr; /* Single column by default */
  gap: 16px;
}

@container (min-width: 400px) {
  .product-grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); }
}

@container (min-width: 700px) {
  .product-grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); }
}

@container (min-width: 1000px) {
  .product-grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr); }
}

The grid adapts to its container, not the viewport. Put this product grid in a modal, a sidebar, or a full-width section — it always shows the right number of columns for the available space.

Container Query + CSS Grid Combination 

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: minmax(200px, 300px) 1fr;
}

.sidebar { container-type: inline-size; }
.main { container-type: inline-size; }

/* Sidebar cards are narrow — stack layout */
@container (max-width: 250px) {
  .card { flex-direction: column; }
}

/* Main cards are wider — side-by-side layout */
@container (min-width: 500px) {
  .card { flex-direction: row; }
}

Browser Support

Firefox 110+ supports container queries. All modern browsers support them as of 2023.

Check support:

@supports (container-type: inline-size) {
  /* Use container queries */
}

Container Queries vs. Media Queries

Container queries don't replace media queries:

  • Media queries: global layout decisions (sidebar visible at >= 768px)
  • Container queries: component-level decisions (card layout when container >= 400px)

Use both together:

/* Media query: sidebar visible/hidden */
@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .sidebar { display: block; }
}

/* Container query: card layout inside sidebar vs. main */
@container (min-width: 400px) {
  .card { flex-direction: row; }
}

title: TurboMamba: Faster Inference, Faster Training, and Better Prediction with Lexical Memory
description:
arXiv:2610.20682v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce TurboMamba, a language-model architecture for faster inference, faster training, and better token prediction. A global Mamba-3 model runs once per completed token block. A small Transformer uses this global context and earlier tokens within the block to predict the next token. Three lightweight additions improve local predictions: direct access to the previous block's last token, a small correction to next-token scores, and a learned mixture with recent-token frequencies. We compare twelve small-scale implementations on public FineWeb-Edu, with comparable parameter counts and shared training-budget caps. The baselines include Transformer, Mamba-3, Jamba, and Zamba. The Jamba and Zamba versions use Mamba-3 in place of their original Mamba modules. TurboMamba achieves the lowest mean test prediction loss (negative log-likelihood, NLL) among all twelve models. Its mean NLL is 9.4% lower than that of Mamba-3, 7.3% lower than that of the Jamba version, and 18.3% lower than that of the Zamba version. End-to-end training throughput is 2.60x that of Mamba-3, 2.81x that of the Jamba version, and 4.82x that of the Zamba version. We measure end-to-end batch latency for a batch of 32 sequences, each with a 256-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. On this workload, TurboMamba achieves a 3.12x speedup over Mamba-3, a 3.53x speedup over the Jamba version, and a 6.21x speedup over the Zamba version.

title: Why I Built Total Connect: A Modern Open-Source FileZilla & Total Commander Alternative in Go
description:
For decades, FileZilla and Total Commander have been staples for sysadmins, developers, and power users. But let’s be honest:

  • FileZilla paywalls essential cloud protocols (S3, Google Drive, OneDrive) behind a commercial Pro license.
  • Managing files on remote headless servers or mobile devices without X11/GUI forwarding is still a headache.
  • Security and plaintext password storage have historically plagued legacy FTP clients.

To solve this, I built Total Connect — a modern, unified, open-source file manager and transfer ecosystem written in Go, powered natively by rclone.

🌟 What makes Total Connect different?

  1. Tri-Interface Architecture (TUI + Web + CLI):

    • Interactive Terminal UI: Powered by Charmbracelet (bubbletea, lipgloss) featuring classic dual-pane navigation, Total Commander shortcuts (F5, F6, F8), and multi-file selection.
    • Headless Web Daemon: An embedded, responsive web interface that runs on any remote machine, VPS, or Google Colab, featuring a modern Fluent design and touch tabs for mobile browsers.
    • Scriptable CLI: For quick headless operations.

  2. 50+ Cloud Providers via Rclone:
    Rather than wrapping rclone via subprocesses, Total Connect imports rclone directly as internal Go modules. This enables true atomic operations, password obfuscation, and zero-overhead transfers.

  3. No Setup Friction:

    • Single static binary for Linux, macOS, and Windows (Intel & ARM).
    • In-app "+ Add Connection" wizard for FTP, SFTP, WebDAV, S3, Mega, and Google Drive without editing config files.

title: When Judges Agree and Are Wrong: Consistency-Accuracy Dissociation as a Blind Spot for Label-Free Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.21128v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Label-free evaluation methods, such as self-consistency filtering, majority-vote aggregation, and agreement-based reliability scoring, rely on an implicit assumption that consistency can serve as a proxy for correctness when ground-truth labels are unavailable or expensive to obtain. In this paper, we test this assumption directly. Using four financial QA datasets (multiple-choice and free-form), ten consistency dimensions, and two frontier model families, we measure the joint distribution of consistency and accuracy at the level of individual examples rather than in aggregate. We find that 60% of all incorrect answers fall in the high-consistency region (consistency $\geq$ 0.8), and that 77.7% of these show complete answer collapse, i.e. identical wrong answers across all perturbation variants. This high-consistency/incorrect quadrant cannot be detected by any evaluation signal that is built on agreement alone, as the model appears maximally reliable while being wrong. We show that the phenomenon is robust to the choice of consistency threshold t (it persists from t=0.50 to t=1.00), is shared across model families, and is concentrated in specific intersections of perturbation dimension and domain. We map where this quadrant occurs, analyze its stability properties, and discuss the implications for evaluation pipelines that use agreement-based signals in place of human labels.

title: Exa joins the Vercel AI Gateway and Agent Marketplace
description:
Exa is now available on the Vercel AI Gateway and Agent Marketplace as a native integration. Exa's neural search engine grounds models in current information.

  • Exa search is now a built-in tool on AI Gateway, which runs the search for you without an Exa account of your own.

  • You can also add Exa to a Vercel project from the Agent Marketplace to power search or a research agent, with a single API key that works across every Exa product and billing through your Vercel account.

Exa search on AI Gateway

Every model on AI Gateway can search with Exa through a built-in tool, with no Exa account or key of your own required. Pass gateway.tools.exaSearch() alongside your prompt and the gateway runs the search, hands the results back to the model, and keeps going until the model stops searching. You get one finished response with a synthesized answer rather than raw results to stream back yourself.

The tool takes the same controls as the Exa API, so you can set how many results come back, focus a search on a category such as news or research papers, restrict it to a country, and include or exclude domains.

title: The Unclickable Hamburger Button: Three Wrong Fixes Before I Found the CSS Bundle Order Bug
description:
The report

QA filed this against our internal business web app (React + Vite):

The three-line icon next to the date can't be clicked

One screenshot attached. No device, no screen width, no description of what actually happened on click. From that single line, I fixed the wrong thing three times in a row — and the real culprit turned out to be the order of rules inside the production CSS bundle. Here's the whole detour, as it happened.

Context: there are two hamburger buttons

The sidebar behaves differently depending on viewport width:

  • Desktop (>900px): the sidebar is always visible. A "≡" button in the sidebar header collapses it into a 60px icon rail (the state is persisted in localStorage)
  • Narrow (≤900px): the sidebar becomes a drawer, and a "≡" appears in the app bar (next to the date) to open it

So there are two "≡" buttons, and the app-bar one is hidden on desktop via CSS:

.sidebar-toggle-mobile { display: none; }

@media (max-width: 900px) {
  .sidebar-toggle-mobile { display: inline-flex; }
}

The "three-line icon next to the date" in the report is the app-bar button. I immediately assumed the reporter was on a phone. That assumption was mistake number one.

Wrong fix #1: the collapsed state in localStorage

At 375px locally, everything worked. But when I set "collapsed=true" in localStorage, I could reproduce a state where the drawer opened only as a 60px rail — which does look like "nothing happens."

Convinced I'd found it, I shipped a fix that ignores the collapsed flag at narrow widths. The reporter's reply: "Same as before."

Wrong fix #2: the collapse button inside the drawer

Next I noticed the drawer still contained the desktop collapse "≡", which either shrank the drawer to a rail or did nothing. I replaced it with an "×" (close) button and hid the app-bar "≡" while the drawer was open. Second deploy.

The reporter answered:

I don't understand why there's a ≡ here at all

That one sentence was the decisive clue: they were seeing a "≡" outside drawer mode. And then came the detail that cracked it open:

I'm looking at this on a 16-inch MacBook

Desktop width. The button that display: none was supposed to hide was visible on a wide screen.

The real cause: rule order in the bundle

I downloaded the deployed production CSS bundle and located the two rules by byte offset:

.sidebar-toggle-mobile{display:none}   → at byte 8,975
.icon-btn{display:inline-flex}         → at byte 72,008

.icon-btn is a shared icon-button class, and this "≡" has it too. Both selectors are a single class, so their specificity is identical — and on a tie, the later rule wins. display: inline-flex was overriding display: none.

Why only in production? The sidebar.css imported by the component ended up earlier in the bundle than the entry point's index.css. An order that was harmless on the dev server flipped in the production build.

Suddenly every observation lined up. On desktop, the "≡" is visible. Clicking it does update state — but the drawer and the backdrop are both disabled by CSS at desktop width, so nothing on screen changes. "It can't be clicked" was a perfectly accurate observation.

The fix: a selector that doesn't depend on bundle order

The fix is one line — add a parent class to raise specificity:

.app-bar .sidebar-toggle-mobile { display: none; }

@media (max-width: 900px) {
  .app-bar .sidebar-toggle-mobile { display: inline-flex; }
}

Two classes beat one, wherever the rule lands in the bundle.

Verification was done against production-like builds: I served a local production build and confirmed the computed display was none at 1400px and flex at 375px. After deploying, I downloaded the actually-served CSS bundle again and grepped it to confirm the new rule was in.

Takeaways

  • Dev builds and production bundles can order CSS differently. When something is "only broken in production," look at the deployed bundle itself
  • Don't fill in the reporter's assumptions yourself. "It's a hamburger icon, so it must be a phone" is where the detour started. Ask for device, viewport width, and what exactly appeared on click — first
  • "Correct" fixes are the most dangerous ones. Each of my three fixes was a legitimate improvement in isolation. None of them fixed the reported problem

The decisive clue came from conversation, not code. The three questions to ask before attempting to reproduce: which device, which viewport width, and what exactly did you see when you clicked? Next time, I'm asking those first.

title: Architecting Policy-Enforced Smart Contracts for Autonomous AI Agents on Stellar Soroban
description:
By Kenneth Okenwa (@symplyKen | GitHub: @anekenonso)

1. The Autonomous Agent Dilemma

As autonomous AI agents transition from read-only assistants to execution-capable economic actors, a critical engineering hurdle emerges: The Authority-Safety Paradox.

If you hand an autonomous agent an unrestricted private key or raw wallet signing authority, you have introduced an unbounded blast radius. A single hallucinated function call, poisoned context window, or rogue reasoning loop can liquidate your entire treasury in a single transaction. Conversely, if you force human approval for every micro-operation, you eliminate the autonomy that made the agent valuable in the first place.

The solution cannot live solely off-chain in Python or TypeScript guardrails. Off-chain heuristics can be bypassed, intercepted, or desynchronized. Authority enforcement must be mathematically and cryptographically locked directly on-chain within smart contract logic.

In this technical breakdown, we analyze how to architect, implement, and formally test policy-enforced smart contracts using Rust on Stellar Soroban, drawing from production patterns implemented in AgentVault.

2. Why Soroban Outclasses EVM for Autonomous Systems

Developers migrating from Solidity and EVM architectures often misunderstand Soroban's paradigm. Soroban is not an EVM derivative; it is a high-performance WebAssembly (WASM) execution runtime with distinct architectural advantages:

Dimension EVM (Solidity) Stellar Soroban (Rust)
Execution Sandbox Bespoke 256-bit bytecode Standard WebAssembly (WASM)
Type Safety Dynamic casting, integer quirks Compile-time Rust strict typing (soroban-sdk)
Re-entrancy Ubiquitous attack vector Architecturally impossible (state updates are isolated)
Fee Predictability Volatile, auction-based gas spikes Metered CPU/Memory with explicit footprint declarations
State Lifecycles Permanent, bloating storage Explicit storage tiers: Instance, Persistent, Temporary
Auth Model Fragile msg.sender Granular multi-party auth (require_auth())

For autonomous agents, predictable execution footprints and native multi-authorization are game-changers.

3. Core Architecture: The Policy-Enforced Vault

In AgentVault, an agent is granted granular spending delegation under strict, deterministic invariants:

  1. Per-Transaction Cap: An agent cannot spend more than $X$ units in a single call.
  2. Epoch Window Rate Limits: An agent cannot exceed $Y$ cumulative volume within a sliding or bucketed block window.
  3. Recipient Whitelisting: Outflows are constrained to approved counterparties or vendor contracts.
  4. Emergency Tripline: The vault owner can freeze or revoke permissions atomically.

Storage Architecture on Soroban

Soroban introduces three explicit storage tiers:

  • Instance: Storage tied to the contract instance (ideal for global vault settings, admin keys, and global paused flags).
  • Persistent: High-durability storage preserved indefinitely as long as rent is refreshed (ideal for agent policy definitions).
  • Temporary: Ephemeral storage automatically pruned when expired (ideal for rate-limiting epoch counters and replay nonces). 
// contracts/vault/src/types.rs
use soroban_sdk::{contracttype, Address, String};

#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub struct AgentPolicy {
    pub agent: Address,
    pub token: Address,
    pub max_per_tx: i128,
    pub epoch_limit: i128,
    pub epoch_window_ledgers: u32,
    pub active: bool,
}

#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub struct EpochState {
    pub window_start_ledger: u32,
    pub spent_in_window: i128,
}

#[contracttype]
pub enum DataKey {
    Admin,
    Paused,
    Policy(Address),    // Maps Agent Address -> AgentPolicy
    Epoch(Address),     // Maps Agent Address -> EpochState
}

4. Contract Implementation: Multi-Auth and Invariant Checks

Below is the core Soroban contract execution loop demonstrating how Rust idiomatic error handling and Soroban authentication primitives enforce agent boundaries:

// contracts/vault/src/lib.rs
#![no_std]
use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, token, Address, Env, IntoVal};

mod types;
use types::{AgentPolicy, DataKey, EpochState};

#[contract]
pub struct AgentVaultContract;

#[contractimpl]
impl AgentVaultContract {
    /// Initialize the vault with an administrative owner
    pub fn initialize(env: Env, admin: Address) {
        if env.storage().instance().has(&DataKey::Admin) {
            panic!("Vault already initialized");
        }
        env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Admin, &admin);
        env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Paused, &false);
    }

    /// Owner defines or updates an on-chain policy for an autonomous agent
    pub fn set_agent_policy(env: Env, policy: AgentPolicy) {
        let admin: Address = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Admin).expect("Uninitialized");
        admin.require_auth(); // Cryptographically verifies signature of Vault Owner

        env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Policy(policy.agent.clone()), &policy);
    }

    /// Autonomous Agent executes a payment within its policy envelope
    pub fn spend(env: Env, agent: Address, recipient: Address, amount: i128) {
        // 1. Verify agent authorization
        agent.require_auth();

        // 2. Verify vault is not paused
        let is_paused: bool = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Paused).unwrap_or(false);
        if is_paused {
            panic!("Vault operations are paused");
        }

        // 3. Load agent policy from Persistent storage
        let policy: AgentPolicy = env
            .storage()
            .persistent()
            .get(&DataKey::Policy(agent.clone()))
            .expect("No policy configured for this agent");

        if !policy.active {
            panic!("Agent policy is inactive");
        }

        // 4. Invariant Check: Per-Transaction Ceiling
        if amount > policy.max_per_tx {
            panic!("Amount exceeds single-transaction cap");
        }

        // 5. Invariant Check: Sliding Window Epoch Cap
        let current_ledger = env.ledger().sequence();
        let mut epoch: EpochState = env
            .storage()
            .temporary()
            .get(&DataKey::Epoch(agent.clone()))
            .unwrap_or(EpochState {
                window_start_ledger: current_ledger,
                spent_in_window: 0,
            });

        // Reset epoch if window expired
        if current_ledger - epoch.window_start_ledger >= policy.epoch_window_ledgers {
            epoch.window_start_ledger = current_ledger;
            epoch.spent_in_window = 0;
        }

        if epoch.spent_in_window + amount > policy.epoch_limit {
            panic!("Amount exceeds epoch spending limit");
        }

        // Update state
        epoch.spent_in_window += amount;
        env.storage().temporary().set(&DataKey::Epoch(agent.clone()), &epoch);

        // 6. Execute token transfer via Soroban Token Client
        let token_client = token::Client::new(&env, &policy.token);
        token_client.transfer(&env.current_contract_address(), &recipient, &amount);
    }
}

5. Testing the Boundaries: Soroban SDK Environment

Soroban's test suite allows executing full end-to-end unit and property tests in pure Rust without deploying a local node or RPC mock. Everything runs natively in memory:

// contracts/vault/src/test.rs
#[cfg(test)]
mod test {
    use super::*;
    use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env};

    #[test]
    fn test_agent_spending_enforcement() {
        let env = Env::default();
        env.mock_all_auths(); // Mocks cryptographic signatures for simulation

        let admin = Address::generate(&env);
        let agent = Address::generate(&env);
        let recipient = Address::generate(&env);
        let token_contract = env.register_stellar_asset_contract_v2(admin.clone());

        let vault_id = env.register(AgentVaultContract, ());
        let client = AgentVaultContractClient::new(&env, &vault_id);

        client.initialize(&admin);

        // Configure policy: Max 50 per TX, Max 100 per 100 ledgers
        let policy = AgentPolicy {
            agent: agent.clone(),
            token: token_contract.address(),
            max_per_tx: 50,
            epoch_limit: 100,
            epoch_window_ledgers: 100,
            active: true,
        };
        client.set_agent_policy(&policy);

        // Step 1: Valid spend should succeed
        client.spend(&agent, &recipient, &40);

        // Step 2: Single TX exceeding cap should panic
        // client.spend(&agent, &recipient, &60) -> Panics: "Amount exceeds single-transaction cap"
    }
}

6. Key Takeaways for Web3 & Agent Developers

  1. Move Boundaries to Code: Do not trust agent prompts to self-police token balances. An agent with unrestricted private keys is an inevitable loss incident.
  2. Leverage Storage Semantics: Use Soroban's Temporary storage for rate-limiting sliding windows. It prevents state bloat and saves rent costs.
  3. Multi-Auth Architecture: Soroban's require_auth() pattern ensures that only authorized delegate keys can invoke protected methods, without requiring brittle custom signatures.

Full open-source implementation and property tests available in the AgentVault GitHub Repository.

title: When Reasoning Traces Conflict with Evidence: How Answer Configuration Shapes Evidence Following
description:
arXiv:2610.20805v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A reasoning trace retained at answer time plays two roles: it can raise accuracy, and it can compete with the current evidence when the two disagree. We disentangle these roles by crossing verified evidence versions with the traces generated from each and answering from the same traces and evidence under two configurations: continuation of the model's own thinking and a separate answer call. Across three model families (gpt-oss, Gemma4, Qwen3) on HotpotQA and MuSiQue, the separate call raises evidence-following over continuation by 29.9 to 60.6 points. On the same pairs, removing the trace lowers accuracy by similar amounts under both configurations. Yet continuation repeats the stale conclusion in most conflicts, and the separate call follows the current evidence far more often. Benefiting from a trace and deferring to it are therefore distinct properties. Further analyses show that the final line of a trace carries most of its value, gold evidence helps most before the trace is written, distractors weaken correction under a separate call, and renewed reasoning, unlike a verification instruction, follows the current evidence in most conflicts. Because trace deletion alone cannot reveal which source an answer follows, evaluations should report both properties together with the answer configuration.

title: Accumulating Empty Video Rooms: Cleanup by Lease Generation and Reconciliation
description:
Do not destroy a video room on the last leave event. Mark it empty, wait through a bounded grace period, and then require a second, authoritative occupancy check before teardown. For a fintech support call that also exposes typing indicators and read receipts, this rule keeps presence accurate during reconnects while ensuring abandoned sessions cannot accumulate forever.

TL;DR: Treat room deletion as a state transition, not an event callback. A leave signal starts suspicion; a later observation proves absence. Make teardown idempotent, retain a periodic reconciler as the repair path, and measure how long rooms remain empty rather than counting successful callbacks.

That distinction matters because WebRTC describes peer connections, not the application-level membership of a room. The W3C API exposes connection state and a way to close an RTCPeerConnection, but it does not appoint the browser, signaling node, or media layer as the owner of a shared room record. The application has to define that ownership boundary.

Why does the last participant keep leaving a room behind?

The usual bug begins with a reasonable shortcut: decrement an in-memory counter when a socket disconnects, and delete the room when the counter reaches zero. That counter is only a local projection. A tab can reconnect to another process, two disconnect notifications can be delivered in an awkward order, a process can stop before its cleanup callback runs, or a delayed heartbeat can make an absent participant look current. None of those observations alone is a durable statement about room occupancy.

Read receipts and typing indicators make the trap easier to see. They are ephemeral signals associated with a participant, but they have different expiry rules. A typing flag should disappear quickly; a read position may need to remain as business data; a WebRTC peer connection can be closed while the authenticated support session remains eligible to reconnect. Folding all three into one boolean named online creates a cleanup system whose result depends on whichever signal happened to arrive last.

So separate them. Maintain durable membership identity, expiring presence leases, and disposable connection records. Derive occupied from unexpired leases stored in the authoritative presence system, not from the number of connections known to one signaling process. This is the capacity-planning reflex worth keeping: if the correctness of cleanup changes when the service grows from one node to two, the state was in the wrong place.

No proof, no deletion.

Use a monotonic empty-room state machine

The safe path has four useful states: active, suspected empty, confirmed empty, and deleted. A participant departure may move a room from active to suspected empty and record a generation plus a deadline. Any valid presence renewal returns it to active and advances the generation. Once the deadline passes, a worker reads current leases; only zero live leases for the same generation permits deletion.

Short callbacks help. The request or socket handler should record intent and return, because media cleanup, transcript finalization, and audit retention do not belong on its latency path.

The following Go sketch deliberately uses interfaces rather than a database-specific transaction API. The important constraints are the compare-and-set generation check and an idempotent delete operation.

package cleanup

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var ErrStateChanged = errors.New("room state changed")

type Room struct {
    ID            string
    Generation    uint64
    CleanupAfter  time.Time
    State         string
}

type Store interface {
    MarkSuspectedEmpty(ctx context.Context, roomID string, now, cleanupAfter time.Time) (Room, error)
    CountLiveLeases(ctx context.Context, roomID string, at time.Time) (int, error)
    DeleteIfUnchanged(ctx context.Context, roomID string, generation uint64) error
}

type Cleaner struct {
    Store Store
    Grace time.Duration
}

func (c Cleaner) OnLastObservedDeparture(ctx context.Context, roomID string, now time.Time) error {
    _, err := c.Store.MarkSuspectedEmpty(ctx, roomID, now, now.Add(c.Grace))
    return err
}

func (c Cleaner) ConfirmAndDelete(ctx context.Context, room Room, now time.Time) error {
    if room.State != "suspected_empty" || now.Before(room.CleanupAfter) {
        return ErrStateChanged
    }

    live, err := c.Store.CountLiveLeases(ctx, room.ID, now)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if live != 0 {
        return ErrStateChanged
    }

    return c.Store.DeleteIfUnchanged(ctx, room.ID, room.Generation)
}

The generation is doing real work. Suppose a cleanup job reads generation 41, then a support agent reconnects and advances the room to generation 42. The stale job has already passed its deadline check, and it may even have read zero live leases a moment before the renewal committed; without one final conditional write, it can delete the room that the agent has just rejoined. The compare-and-set makes that race lose safely because generation 41 is no longer current. Retrying the same job must also be harmless: an already deleted room is success, while a changed generation is a no-op rather than an error that wakes the on-call engineer. This is the concrete pitfall behind the design, and a mutex inside one process cannot fix it because the reconnect and the cleanup may run on different nodes.

Do not guess the grace interval from taste. Set it from the reconnect behavior the product promises, the presence lease duration, and the cleanup-lag SLO. If clients may legitimately renew a lease until its expiry, the confirmation read has to occur after that evidence can be evaluated. A fixed number copied from another system is not evidence.

Make reconciliation part of the normal path

Event-driven cleanup lowers delay, but it cannot be the only route to correctness. A periodic reconciler should scan rooms whose cleanup deadline has passed, claim a bounded batch, and execute the same confirmation function. This is not a second deletion policy. It is another trigger for the same transition.

Keep the scan bounded by both rows and time so a backlog does not monopolize the datastore. Persist a cursor or use an indexed deadline range, limit worker concurrency, and apply backoff when the authoritative presence store is unavailable. Failure to confirm absence must preserve the room. Fail closed.

That choice has a cost.

Capacity planning starts with arrival and service rates. Track the number of rooms entering suspected-empty state per minute, the rate at which workers confirm them, and the age of the oldest eligible room. If arrivals exceed completions for a sustained window, more callbacks will not rescue the queue; either worker capacity, datastore capacity, or the confirmation dependency is saturated. The oldest age is the user-relevant symptom.

For a first operating envelope, define two explicit objectives rather than hiding behind an average:

  • No active lease is removed by automated teardown.
  • A chosen high percentile of rooms with zero live leases is deleted within the cleanup-lag target.

The first is a safety invariant. The second is a timeliness SLO whose threshold must come from retention, capacity, and product requirements. They need separate alerts because the mitigations point in opposite directions: aggressive deletion improves lag and increases safety risk, while conservative deletion protects reconnects and consumes more resources.

Verify the race, not merely the happy path

A unit test that calls leave and observes delete proves very little. Drive the state machine with a controllable clock and exercise reordered operations: renewal before the deadline, renewal between confirmation and deletion, duplicate departure, duplicate cleanup, worker restart, and an unavailable presence store. The expected outcome is boring: active generations survive, stale jobs do nothing, and eligible empty generations eventually disappear.

Then test across two signaling processes. One process should observe the apparent last departure while the other accepts a reconnect. If the room vanishes, the implementation still relies on local knowledge somewhere. This single test catches a surprising amount of accidental in-memory authority.

Instrument transitions, not participant identifiers. Useful low-cardinality dimensions include transition result, worker shard, and failure class. Useful values include suspected-room count, eligible-room count, cleanup lag, generation-conflict count, lease-check failures, and idempotent-delete outcomes. Room IDs belong in sampled logs or traces under the organization's data-handling rules; they do not belong in metric labels.

Avoid using WebRTC's connectionState as the deletion oracle. Per the specification, it is an aggregate state of an individual RTCPeerConnection. It can help diagnose transport progress for that peer, and calling close() terminates that peer connection, but neither action proves that no other participant lease exists for the application room.

Buy or build the control plane?

This decision is narrower than the usual platform debate. Managed signaling, a hosted presence service, or a self-hosted stack can all support correct cleanup if they expose authoritative membership, conditional state changes, expiry semantics, and enough observability to verify the SLO. Evaluate the control-plane contract, not the logo.

Decision surface Managed service Self-hosted control plane Acceptance test
Presence authority Contract and limits are externally defined Team owns storage and lease semantics Two-node reconnect cannot be deleted by a stale job
Conditional deletion May be an API primitive or require application state Can be implemented in the chosen datastore Old generation cannot delete a renewed room
Reconciliation May be built in, observable, or application-owned Team schedules and operates workers Missed departure is repaired within the SLO
On-call load Less infrastructure, but dependency behavior remains More control and more failure modes to cover Dependency loss preserves active rooms and raises a useful alert
Portability Depends on event and state-model coupling Depends on internal schema and operations Cleanup logic runs behind a small generic interface

I would reject either option if it only promises a departure webhook without a read-after-delay occupancy check. I would also reject a design whose delete cannot be conditioned on version or generation. Those two gaps turn ordinary delivery races into data-loss decisions.

The limitation of this method is delayed reclamation: the grace period intentionally retains an empty room for longer, and the reconciler adds datastore reads plus an operated queue. It is not appropriate for a purely local, single-user preview whose entire state can disappear with the process, because there is no shared room to protect; direct teardown is simpler there. At the other extreme, if regulation requires a durable call record after media ends, delete only ephemeral transport and presence state, then hand the retained record to the separately governed retention workflow. The trade-off is explicit: a longer grace period tolerates more reconnect delay but increases temporary room inventory, while a shorter one reclaims capacity sooner but demands tighter lease timing.

Roll out with a kill switch and a drain plan

Start in observation mode: compute which rooms would be deleted, record the generation and evidence, but do not execute teardown. Compare those candidates with live lease data and with later reconnects. Only after the false-positive count is demonstrably zero over a representative operating window should automated deletion begin, first for a small deterministic slice of rooms.

Rollback must be immediate. A runtime kill switch should stop new destructive actions without stopping lease expiry, candidate marking, or reconciliation telemetry. If the safety invariant is threatened, disable deletion and retain evidence for analysis; do not attempt to recreate a removed live session from logs.

The runbook needs three concrete branches: rising cleanup lag with healthy lease reads, failed lease reads, and generation conflicts. The first calls for inspecting worker and datastore capacity. The second pauses deletion because absence cannot be proven. The third may be normal reconnect activity, but a sharp change warrants checking client retry behavior and event ordering before increasing capacity.

The final decision rule stays small: suspect on an event, prove from current state, delete conditionally, and reconcile until the lag objective is met. Empty rooms then become a measurable lifecycle, while typing indicators, read receipts, and reconnecting calls retain the distinct semantics they require.

References

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: Real-Time Communication Between Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Managing the Relationship with Service Providers: How Easy Is It?
description:
Managing the Relationship with Service Providers: How Easy Is It?

Most engineering organizations depend on service providers more than they admit. Cloud platforms, payment processors, SaaS tools, managed support teams, outsourced development partners, and staffing firms now sit inside the critical path of many products. When those relationships work, nobody notices them. When they fail, the failure shows up as an outage, a missed audit, a surprise invoice, or a team that cannot ship.

The uncomfortable question is simple: how easy is it to manage these relationships well? For most teams the honest answer is "not very easy". Contracts are signed by procurement, technical contacts change, service levels are written but never measured, and the provider's account manager becomes the only person who knows what was promised. This article looks at why provider management is hard, what makes it easier, and how engineering leaders can build a practical system around it. Java examples are included where automation makes the process more reliable.

Why provider relationships are harder than they look

Service providers differ from internal teams in three important ways. First, their incentives are partly outside your control. A provider wants renewals, expansion, and a healthy margin. Your interests are uptime, predictable cost, and the ability to leave if needed. Those goals overlap, but they are not identical.

Second, information is asymmetric. The provider knows its architecture, its staffing, its roadmap, and its internal incidents. You usually see only what it chooses to show you, through status pages, quarterly reviews, and the reports you remember to request.

Third, the relationship is spread across people. Procurement negotiated the contract. Finance pays the invoices. Engineering consumes the service. Security reviews the data processing terms. Nobody owns the whole picture, so problems fall into gaps between these groups.

These three factors explain why provider management often feels reactive. A dispute surfaces, someone searches for the contract, and the team discovers that the notice period for cancellation was missed last quarter.

Step 1: Know what you actually depend on

You cannot manage what you have not listed. Start with an inventory of every external service your systems or teams rely on. For each entry, record:

  • Service and purpose: what it does for you and which products depend on it.
  • Criticality: what happens if it is unavailable for one hour, one day, or one week.
  • Data involved: whether personal, financial, or confidential data flows through it.
  • Owner: an internal person accountable for the relationship, not just the contract.
  • Contract terms that matter: renewal date, notice period, price escalation, service levels, and exit obligations.

The inventory should live somewhere searchable and kept current, not in a spreadsheet that one person updates once a year. A simple structure in code can make it queryable and testable. The sketch below models a provider record and flags relationships that are overdue for review or approaching a notice deadline:

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.List;

public enum Criticality { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL }

public record ServiceProvider(
        String name,
        String purpose,
        Criticality criticality,
        boolean handlesPersonalData,
        String internalOwner,
        LocalDate contractRenewal,
        int noticeDays,
        LocalDate lastReview) {

    public LocalDate noticeDeadline() {
        return contractRenewal.minusDays(noticeDays);
    }
}

public final class ProviderReviewPolicy {

    private static final int MAX_DAYS_BETWEEN_REVIEWS = 90;

    public List<String> findAttentionItems(List<ServiceProvider> providers, LocalDate today) {
        return providers.stream()
                .filter(p -> p.criticality() == Criticality.HIGH || p.criticality() == Criticality.CRITICAL)
                .flatMap(p -> {
                    java.util.List<String> items = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
                    if (p.lastReview() == null
                            || p.lastReview().plusDays(MAX_DAYS_BETWEEN_REVIEWS).isBefore(today)) {
                        items.add(p.name() + ": business review overdue");
                    }
                    if (!today.isBefore(p.noticeDeadline()) && today.isBefore(p.contractRenewal())) {
                        items.add(p.name() + ": notice period is running, decide renew or exit");
                    }
                    return items.stream();
                })
                .toList();
    }
}

The value here is not the code itself. It is the habit of asking the same questions for every provider and getting a list of items that need attention before the deadline arrives.

Step 2: Make service levels measurable

Many provider contracts contain service level agreements that look reassuring on paper. An uptime target of 99.9 percent sounds strong until you calculate that it allows roughly 43 minutes of downtime per month. Before signing or renewing, translate every commitment into a number you can observe, and decide how you will observe it.

Three questions help. What exactly is measured, and by whom? How is downtime defined, and does a degraded but working service count? What credit or remedy applies, and is it meaningful compared to the cost of the outage?

Measurement should not depend only on the provider's own reports. Where possible, monitor the service from your side: synthetic checks, error rates on your integration points, latency from your regions, and the number of support tickets your team opens. When the provider's report and your measurements disagree, you have a concrete basis for a conversation.

Some teams wrap provider calls in a small client that records latency and failures, so the data exists even when nobody asks for it. A minimal example with a timeout and a circuit breaker shows the idea:

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

public final class ProviderClient {

    private final String providerName;
    private final MetricsRecorder metrics;
    private int consecutiveFailures = 0;
    private long openUntilMillis = 0;

    private static final int FAILURE_THRESHOLD = 5;
    private static final Duration OPEN_DURATION = Duration.ofSeconds(30);

    public ProviderClient(String providerName, MetricsRecorder metrics) {
        this.providerName = providerName;
        this.metrics = metrics;
    }

    public synchronized <T> T call(Supplier<T> request, T fallback) {
        if (System.currentTimeMillis() < openUntilMillis) {
            metrics.record(providerName, "short_circuited");
            return fallback;
        }
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            T result = request.get();
            consecutiveFailures = 0;
            metrics.record(providerName, "success", System.nanoTime() - start);
            return result;
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            consecutiveFailures++;
            metrics.record(providerName, "failure", System.nanoTime() - start);
            if (consecutiveFailures >= FAILURE_THRESHOLD) {
                openUntilMillis = System.currentTimeMillis() + OPEN_DURATION.toMillis();
                consecutiveFailures = 0;
            }
            return fallback;
        }
    }

    public interface MetricsRecorder {
        void record(String provider, String outcome);
        void record(String provider, String outcome, long durationNanos);
    }
}

This pattern does two things. It protects your system when the provider degrades, and it produces evidence. A quarterly report built from these metrics is far more persuasive than a memory of "it felt slow last month".

Step 3: Assign one accountable owner per relationship

Every provider needs an internal owner who is accountable for the relationship as a whole. That person does not have to do all the work, but they should know the contract's key dates, the current service performance, the open issues, and the escalation path.

The owner's job includes a short recurring review. For critical providers, a monthly operational check covers incidents, support responsiveness, and upcoming changes. A quarterly business review covers cost, roadmap alignment, and whether the relationship still fits your needs. Annual reviews cover the market: is there a better option, and what would switching cost?

A common failure is treating the provider's account manager as the owner. That person works for the provider. Their job is to renew the contract, and they are good at it. Your owner's job is to protect your interests, which sometimes means pushing back on them.

Step 4: Plan for exit before you need it

Ease of managing a provider depends heavily on how easy it would be to leave. Teams often discover too late that their data cannot be exported in a usable format, that a proprietary API has no equivalent elsewhere, or that the contract requires a twelve-month notice for termination.

Exit planning does not require building an identical replacement for every service. It requires knowing the answers to a few questions: Can we export our data, in what format, and how long would it take? Which parts of our code depend on provider-specific features, and how isolated are they? Is there a realistic alternative, and what would migration cost in time and money?

Architectural isolation helps here. Wrapping a provider behind an internal interface, as in the client above, confines vendor-specific details to one place. The interface does not need to be perfectly portable. It only needs to make the cost of change visible and bounded.

Step 5: Govern changes and risk together

Providers change things constantly: pricing, terms, subprocessors, data locations, supported versions, and features. Each change can affect your risk profile, and many arrive as an email nobody reads. A lightweight intake process helps. Route provider notices to a shared channel that the owner monitors. For each notice, decide whether it requires action, an update to the inventory, or a review with security or legal.

Security and compliance deserve their own checkpoints. Before onboarding a provider that handles personal or financial data, confirm the data processing terms, the certifications the provider holds, where data is stored, and how access is revoked when your contract ends. Revisit these at each renewal, because the provider's answers can change without much notice.

Step 6: Measure the relationship, not just the invoices

A useful scorecard for each critical provider includes a small number of measures reviewed consistently:

  • Availability and incident count measured from your side, with the provider's reported figures alongside.
  • Response and resolution time for the support requests you open, compared to the contract.
  • Total cost of ownership, including the internal time spent managing the provider, not only the invoice.
  • Change frequency and surprise rate, meaning how often the provider changes something that affects you without enough notice.
  • Owner's confidence rating, a simple score from one to five, updated monthly. A declining score often predicts problems before the metrics show them.

The point is to see trends. A provider that is slightly slower each quarter is a different conversation from one that had a single bad week.

Common mistakes

  • Signing without reading the exit terms. Notice periods and data return clauses matter more than the discount.
  • Letting the provider define success. Their dashboard shows what they choose to measure.
  • Spreading ownership across departments. When everyone is responsible, nobody is.
  • Ignoring the cost of management. A cheap provider that consumes a senior engineer's time every week is not cheap.
  • Waiting for a crisis to start the review. The best time to discuss service levels is before the outage.

A practical ninety-day plan

Days 1 to 30: Build the inventory of external services, with owners and contract dates. Identify the five providers whose failure would hurt most, and mark their notice deadlines in the team calendar.

Days 31 to 60: For those critical providers, translate service levels into measurable targets, add monitoring from your side, and schedule the first monthly operational review. Document the exit path for the most critical one.

Days 61 to 90: Introduce the scorecard, start the quarterly business review, and set up a shared intake for provider notices. Review the inventory with procurement, finance, and security so the owners know who to call for what.

Key takeaways

  • Provider relationships are hard to manage because incentives, information, and responsibility are spread across the organization.
  • Start with an inventory that records criticality, data, owners, and contract deadlines.
  • Turn service level promises into numbers you can observe yourself, and keep evidence.
  • Give every critical relationship one accountable internal owner who is not the provider's account manager.
  • Plan your exit before you need it, and isolate provider-specific code behind your own interfaces.
  • Track a scorecard over time, because trends reveal problems that single incidents hide.

So, how easy is it to manage service providers? It can be easy enough, once the relationship is visible, measured, and owned. The effort is modest compared to the cost of discovering a missed notice deadline or an unmeasured outage in the middle of a critical launch.

title: Making every stage of medical device document assessment with large language models deterministic
description:
arXiv:2610.21300v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: To show that a medical device complies with regulation, experts judge whether documents and records meet each requirement and record the judgment for others to verify. For each assessment item that experts define, large language models could prepare a preliminary assessment: a label such as Satisfied or Not satisfied, a reason and quoted evidence. We sent fourteen commercial deployments of such models (seven models from three providers, through six routes) the same request repeatedly, with the deterministic sampling settings each accepted; every deployment returned differing assessments for at least one request, and in twelve the label changed. Reducing reasoning where the interface allows it did not reduce the variation, and prompts of retrieved passages removed it only for the smallest models. The same open-weight model was reproducible or not depending only on how it was served. A pipeline we built to be deterministic at every stage -- text extraction and optical character recognition (OCR), chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval and inference -- returned byte-identical output at each stage across reruns, interruptions, edits, machines of one graphics processing unit (GPU) model and days, for blood glucose meter and infusion pump documents. OCR, embedding and approximate retrieval varied when their own serving was not made invariant, and outputs changed with the GPU model and with the inference engine's scheduling settings, which therefore belong in the recorded configuration. End-to-end determinism is achievable and gives a testable basis for audit and change control.

title: Semantic Latent Alignment for Flow Matching with Invertible Bi-Lipschitz Adapters
description:
arXiv:2610.21332v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pretrained latent spaces trade compression, reconstruction, and the learnability of the coordinates a downstream generator has to work in, which complicates adapting these spaces to different domains or tasks: continued training is expensive, and without a new alignment objective it often fails to improve downstream generation. We instead leave the encoder and decoder fixed and change only the coordinates between them, using an invertible bi-Lipschitz adapter aligned offline to a semantic teacher and frozen during class-conditional flow matching. Invertibility preserves compatibility with the pretrained autoencoder, while the bi-Lipschitz constraint limits how far alignment can distort its latent geometry. This provides a simple way to improve semantic organization while retaining the compression and reconstruction properties of the original latent space. On two medical imaging datasets, constrained latent adaptation improves feature metrics, seed stability and counterfactual edit strength, while remaining competitive on downstream classification. In contrast, unconstrained adaptation can become highly anisotropic and sensitive despite remaining invertible, highlighting the importance of controlling geometric distortion. Our results suggest that carefully constrained post-hoc adaptation offers a parameter-efficient and tuning-free alternative to jointly modifying the representation during generative training.
