title: Introducing Vercel for Slack
description:
Vercel Agent now works in Slack. Mention it the way you'd pull a teammate into a thread, and it reads the discussion, answers with the context of the platform running your app, and turns the team's decisions into changes you approve. Vercel for Slack is available today in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

Work starts in conversation. An alert gets noticed in a channel, a fix gets agreed on in a thread, and then someone leaves Slack to do the work. With Vercel Agent, you can tag it in for answers about your infrastructure or hand it the work, all without leaving the conversation.

What is Vercel Agent?

When we introduced Vercel Agent, we called it an AI teammate for your development workflow. Today it's the first responder for your production apps. When something changes, it investigates your logs, metrics, and deployments, finds the root cause, and proposes a fix, often before anyone's opened a laptop. Give it a PR and it flags the regressions and risky changes that a passing CI run won't show.

In Slack, that agent joins the conversation itself. It is a core part of Vercel, so your deployments, build statuses, logs, metrics, code reviews, and PRs are in front of it before you've typed anything. Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM, and it answers like a teammate with every tab already open. And answering is only half of it, because once you know what's wrong, the agent can go fix it:

  • Diagnose issues: Investigate incidents, trace errors to the deploy that caused them, explain a cost spike, and answer questions about your codebase.

  • Code alongside your team: Fix failing builds and CI, review PRs with knowledge of how the code runs in production, and turn a thread's decision into a tested pull request.

  • Operate your projects: Roll back deployments, update configuration, manage feature flags, and resolve unusual usage before it becomes a bill.

The agent is read-only by default, and anything that changes code or configuration goes through a plan that you approve. Vercel for Slack brings that whole loop into the threads where you and your team are already discussing work.

Accelerating development with a conversation

Teams form decisions through collaboration. Incidents get triaged in a channel, code reviews are hashed out in threads, and features get scoped between standups. But once a thread settles on what needs to be done, the actions still need to be translated into tickets, terminal commands, and PR descriptions. Every handoff drops context, and the conversation that held the full picture becomes the thing everyone summarizes from memory. Vercel for Slack gives the agent the full context of the original conversation for every turn.

Answers in one place speed up the whole team

A deployment goes out at 1:42pm. By 1:51, checkout error rates are climbing and an alert lands in the platform engineering channel.

What used to happen next was a scatter. One responder opens logs to see how bad it is, another asks their coding agent to line up the anomaly up against the deploy timeline, a third starts reading the diff of the suspect PR. Each person investigates alone, in their own view of the same system, and the thread is where they reconcile by pasting screenshots, summarizing agent findings, and correcting each other as they establish the actual state of the situation. The minutes that matter get spent assembling the picture before anyone can act on it.

With Vercel for Slack, the first question goes to the agent, right in the thread.

"@Vercel, checkout errors spiked after the 1:42 deploy. What's going on?"

It sizes the blast radius, correlates the spike with the deployment, identifies the PR that shipped in it, and explains which change, in which file, caused which behavior. The answer arrives in the channel, where the whole team reads the same diagnosis at the same time.

Nobody has to re-run a teammate's investigation or wait for the recap, because everyone is looking at the same report. The engineer who knows the checkout code speaks to the change itself, the on-call weighs how many users are hit against how long a fix would take, and what's left for the thread is the decision, whether to roll back or fix forward.

Vercel Agent understands how your team already talks

The thread, channel, or DM is the beginning of the prompt itself. You don't have to re-explain anything that was already said, or pass in any context from your app or codebase. Bring it into a conversation like any other team member and it reads the room, picks up what the team has been discussing, and can act on it when asked.

One example of this was our iteration on Vercel Agent's plan card, the message it posts in Slack to request approval for the work it wants to do. The first version we tested internally was a wall of text, but when one of our engineers noticed that people were often approving actions without reading all of the details, we had a redesign thread that ran 47 replies deep on what a person needs to see before confirming an action on the group's behalf. Tagging Vercel Agent in at the end of that thread is what resulted in the card you see today.

By the time a PR from a conversation like this lands in a thread, the tests have already run and the preview deployment is live, so the team can start reviewing it in the conversation that kicked off the feature in the first place.

Vercel Agent reviews pull requests in the thread

Ask Vercel Agent for a review in the thread where the PR is being discussed, and the conversation is passed along with the request. What your team has been raising becomes context for what Vercel Agent checks, and its findings land back in the same thread, so discussing them, deciding, and fixing them is one loop instead of a trip to another tool.

One example from one of our own PR discussions was a review someone requested mid-thread. The agent came back with a bug sitting just outside the diff, the same title rendered twice in the UI.

A finding doesn't have to end as a comment. If the team agrees it should be fixed, the agent can patch the PR itself, and that change arrives the same way everything else does, as a proposal waiting on an approval.

Changes always go through a plan your team approves

When a thread lands on a change, Vercel Agent replies with a plan that says what will happen, in which project, and at what scope. Decisions in a channel form in fragments, across people and hours, and nobody types "DECISION:", so the plan is where all of that becomes one explicit thing to say yes to. Once approved, the agent does the work under its own identity, and the audit trail shows who asked, who approved, and what ran.

One example from our own threads was a cached page showing stale data after we shipped an update. Someone called for a cache purge scoped to just the specific pages, since it was peak hours, and asked the agent to set it up. The plan that came back matched the ask exactly, a purge of the specific path and its sub-paths with the rest of the site's cache left warm, and nothing ran until someone approved it.

Whether a thread ends in a diagnosis, a pull request, or a cache purge, the last step belongs to a person.

Getting started

The easiest way to get started is to simply ask Vercel Agent questions. Ask about the error you're chasing or the build that just failed, see what comes back, and let your team decide over time how much of the work the agent takes on. Until someone approves a plan, it's only ever reading.

Vercel for Slack is available in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. To start using Vercel Agent in Slack:

  • Open the Slack app in the Vercel Marketplace and click Connect Account.

  • Choose the Slack workspace to connect, then click Allow.

  • Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM.

  • Sign in to your Vercel account when it prompts you the first time.

See the Vercel for Slack docs for setup and permissions.

title: CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF
description:
arXiv:2610.21138v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feedback noise is pervasive in preference data, arising from subjective human judgments, annotation mistakes, and imperfect LLM judges. Standard reward modeling trained on such feedback yields a biased estimate of the clean risk. Although classical denoising methods are directly applicable to noisy feedback learning, they generally assume a uniform noise ratio across samples. However, this assumption fails for feedback data, where noise is intrinsically sample-wise. To address this challenge, we propose CleanRM, which uses a few clean feedback to calibrate sample-wise noise ratios via optimal transport. Specifically, CleanRM aligns the joint distribution of preferences reverted from noisy feedback with that of clean feedback and then trains the reward model using a noise-corrected surrogate loss. Theoretically, we prove that the resulting objective is unbiased with respect to the clean risk. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CleanRM outperforms state-of-the-art denoising baselines and yields more effective downstream RLHF alignment.

title: Do VLAs Really Follow Instructions? Diagnosing How-Level Instruction Following in Vision-Language-Action Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21251v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are expected to follow instructions like their language backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-level instructions that specify the task rather than How-level instructions that specify how to carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find that How-level instructions do not help current VLAs and lower task success. We hypothesize that pairing each training episode with a single instruction limits How-level instruction following, and show that training with segment-level enriched instructions makes actions respond to such instructions without consistently raising task success. To measure How-level instruction following beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success requires conditions given only in the instruction. It shows that the gained responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge.

title: Reference-Guided Turn-Taking Style Transfer for Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20763v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Full-duplex spoken language models decide at every frame whether to take the floor, defining a conversational personality -- yet each set of weights encodes exactly one, which human speakers bracket rather than share. Existing controls mostly act from outside; none identifies the quantity that sets how much the model speaks. We identify it: a single late-layer residual-stream direction, the initiative vector, extracted from the model's own conversations without training or annotation. The same direction reads the decision, anticipating onsets up to 800 ms ahead, and shifts it: scaled during generation, it moves speech ratio from 6-12% to 42-61% (no steering: 21-30%), consistently across conversations, weights, and corpora. A short reference recording suffices to transfer a speaker's turn-taking style to the model, and the transfer is reference-specific: swapping in another speaker's reference worsens the match in 93-98% of cases, whereas the best uniform dose is indistinguishable from no steering. Turn-taking style is not frozen into the weights but a direction that can be read, shifted, and calibrated per person. Audio examples are available at https://elpsykongloo.github.io/initiative-vector/.

title: Twitter Added id_str in 2010 Because JavaScript Can't Hold a Java long
description:
• Book: Kotlin and Java to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

On October 18, 2010, Twitter told every developer on its API that tweet IDs were about to change shape. A new generator called Snowflake would produce 64-bit IDs, and TechCrunch's write-up of the notice put the date plainly: "on November 26, these IDs will go longer than 53 bits." The fix Twitter shipped was blunt. Starting October 22, every ID in a JSON response would come back twice, once as a number and once as a string. In the words of developer advocate Matt Harris, quoted in the same article: "To allow javascript and JSON parsers to read the IDs we need to include a string version of any ID."

That string field is id_str, and it is still in the API. The current X developer docs tell v1.1 clients to "always use id_str", and v2 skipped the number entirely: IDs come back as strings by default.

Sixteen years later, the same bug still ships. A Spring Boot or Ktor service returns a Long ID, a TypeScript client calls JSON.parse, and the last few digits change. No exception. No warning in the console. The client then sends the wrong ID back to the server, and you get a 404 on a record that exists, or a hit on a different record whose ID happens to be the rounded value.

Why Twitter needed 64 bits in the first place

Snowflake was built for Twitter's move from MySQL to Cassandra. The original README is direct about the motive: "there is no sequential id generation facility in Cassandra, nor should there be." The requirements were uncoordinated generation across machines, rough time ordering, and IDs that stay under 64 bits.

The layout it settled on:

  • 41 bits of millisecond timestamp against a custom epoch ("gives us 69 years")
  • 10 bits of machine ID, for up to 1024 machines
  • 12 bits of sequence number, rolling over every 4096 IDs per machine

That is 63 bits of payload, which fits a signed 64-bit integer: a Java long, a Kotlin Long, a Scala Long. The Java Language Specification gives long the range -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807. Every JVM backend can hold a Snowflake ID without thinking about it. The trouble starts when the ID leaves the JVM.


A JVM long has 64 bits to spend. A JavaScript number has 53 for the integer part.

53 bits of mantissa versus 64 bits of long

A JavaScript number is an IEEE 754 double. MDN's page on Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER spells out the consequence: a double "only has 52 bits to represent the mantissa," plus one implicit leading bit, so it can only safely represent integers between -(2^53 - 1) and 2^53 - 1. That ceiling is 9007199254740991.

Past it, a double still exists for every power of two, but not for every integer. Just above 2^53 the gap between neighbouring doubles is 2. Just above 2^60 it is 2^(60-52), which is 256. Modern Snowflake IDs live up there, so a parsed ID snaps to the nearest representable double, and two real IDs generated a moment apart can land on the same one.

You can see it in four lines:

const body = '{"id": 9007199254740993}';
const order = JSON.parse(body) as { id: number };

console.log(order.id);                       // 9007199254740992
console.log(Number.isSafeInteger(order.id)); // false

MDN shows the same collapse from the arithmetic side: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 === Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2 evaluates to true. The X docs use 10765432100123456789, which is past even a Java long's ceiling, and show it printing back as 10765432100123458000.

None of this breaks the JSON spec. RFC 8259, section 6 "allows implementations to set limits on the range and precision of numbers accepted," and names only the integers in [-(2^53)+1, (2^53)-1] as the range where implementations "will agree exactly on their numeric values." Jackson writing 9007199254740993 is valid JSON. JSON.parse rounding it is also valid. The contract between them is the bug.

TypeScript does not help here. JSON.parse returns any, your as { id: number } is a promise you made to the compiler, and the value already satisfies number. The type system checks the shape, and the shape is fine.

Why BigInt doesn't fix JSON.parse

The natural reaction from a JVM developer is: JavaScript has arbitrary-precision integers now, so parse into BigInt. Two things get in the way.

First, JSON.parse never produces a BigInt. Numbers become doubles during parsing, before your code sees anything. The MDN JSON.parse page is explicit that the reviver "is run after the value is parsed," so numbers "will have already been converted to JavaScript numbers, and may lose precision in the process." Writing BigInt(value) inside a classic two-argument reviver gives you an exact BigInt of the wrong number.

Second, the trip back is closed by default. Per MDN's BigInt page, calling JSON.stringify() on any value containing a BigInt throws a TypeError unless you supply a toJSON or a replacer.

So BigInt is a fine type to hold an ID once you have the exact digits. It cannot recover digits the parser already threw away. The digits have to survive the parse, which means either they arrive as a string, or the parser hands you the source text.


Above 2^53, distinct IDs can parse to the same JavaScript number.

Fix it on the JVM side: make the ID a string in the contract

The fix Twitter chose, and the one Discord documents for its own Snowflake IDs ("they are always returned as strings in the HTTP API"), is to put the ID on the wire as a JSON string. Keep Long in the database and in your domain model. Change only the serialized form.

With Jackson, a per-field annotation does it:

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonFormat;

public record OrderDto(
    @JsonFormat(shape = JsonFormat.Shape.STRING)
    long id,
    long totalCents
) {}

In Jackson 2, the number serializers return ToStringSerializer.instance when the shape is STRING, so id goes out as "9007199254740993" with the quotes. The annotation lives in jackson-annotations, which the Spring team notes kept its package unchanged when Spring Boot 4 moved to Jackson 3 under tools.jackson, so the same line works across that upgrade.

If every Long in your API is an identifier, you can register the serializer by type instead. On Spring Boot 3 with Jackson 2:

@Bean
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer longsAsStrings() {
    return b -> b
        .serializerByType(Long.class, ToStringSerializer.instance)
        .serializerByType(Long.TYPE, ToStringSerializer.instance);
}

Be careful with that one. It also quotes counts, cents and timestamps that never needed it. Jackson's blunter switch, JsonWriteFeature.WRITE_NUMBERS_AS_STRINGS (off by default), "forces all regular number values to be written as JSON Strings," doubles included. Per field is usually the honest scope.

On Ktor with kotlinx.serialization, the library ships a serializer for exactly this case. The LongAsStringSerializer docs describe it as "intended to be used for interoperability with external clients (mainly JavaScript ones)":

import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable
import kotlinx.serialization.builtins.LongAsStringSerializer

@Serializable
data class OrderDto(
    @Serializable(with = LongAsStringSerializer::class)
    val id: Long,
    val totalCents: Long,
)

Then write it down. If you publish an OpenAPI spec, the ID is type: string, not type: integer, format: int64, so generated TypeScript clients get string too.

Fix it in the TypeScript client

On the client, type the ID as what it is on the wire: a string. A branded type keeps it from mixing with other strings:

type OrderId = string & { readonly __brand: "OrderId" };

interface Order {
  id: OrderId;
  totalCents: number;
}

You compare it, put it in URLs and send it back. You almost never do arithmetic on an ID, so a string loses nothing. If you need ordering or math, convert with BigInt(order.id) at that moment, from exact digits.

Sometimes you don't own the server and it still sends bare numbers. For that case, TC39 added source text access to JSON.parse; the proposal is at stage 4. For primitive values, the reviver gets a third context argument whose source property is "the original JSON string representing this value" (MDN). MDN's compatibility data lists it in Chrome 114, Firefox 135, Safari 18.4, Node.js 21, Deno 1.33 and Bun 1.1.43.

type Ctx = { source?: string };

function idsAsStrings(key: string, value: unknown, ctx?: Ctx) {
  if (key !== "id" || typeof value !== "number") return value;
  if (ctx?.source === undefined) {
    throw new Error("JSON.parse source access not supported");
  }
  return ctx.source; // the exact digits, before rounding
}

const order = JSON.parse(text, idsAsStrings) as Order;

The reviver throws when the runtime doesn't pass context, because falling back to String(value) would hand you the rounded digits as a string, which is the original bug wearing a disguise. And you need the raw text to call it: Response.json() takes no reviver, so read the body with await res.text() and parse it yourself.

The same proposal added JSON.rawJSON for the outbound direction. A replacer like typeof v === "bigint" ? JSON.rawJSON(v.toString()) : v lets JSON.stringify emit a BigInt as a bare JSON number without precision loss, when a server insists on numeric IDs in request bodies.

If you own the server, the one-line @JsonFormat change is the whole fix, and it costs less to ship before your ID generator crosses 2^53 than after the first 404 on a record that exists.

If this was useful

This bug lives exactly on the seam between the JVM and TypeScript: a Long that is perfectly safe on one side and quietly lossy on the other. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript is the book I wrote for that seam, mapping what you already know from Java and Kotlin (variance, null safety, sealed hierarchies, coroutines) onto how TypeScript does the same jobs.

It's part of The TypeScript Library, five books with a clear path through them. Books 1 and 2 are the core path. If you come from the JVM, book 3 stands in for book 1. If you ship TypeScript at work, book 5 is the production layer:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

title: 5 Next.js Server Action API Logging Rules for Redacted Logistics JSON
description:
Short answer: Centralize structured logs from Next.js server actions, API routes, cron handlers, and authentication events, but remove personal data before transmission and preserve stable request and deployment identifiers; the winning system is the one that can reconstruct a delayed shipment without turning the log store into a second customer database.

That trade-off matters more than another dashboard. For a logistics application, the useful postmortem question is concrete: which request accepted the address change, which deployment handled it, and did the label-generation cron observe the same safe shipment identifier? A bright chart can show a spike. It can't supply evidence that was never recorded.

Below are five rules I would use to draw that boundary. The scenario is bounded but realistic: a customer reports that shipment shp_7F3A was sent to the old depot, and the team needs to correlate a server action, an API route, and a cron run without retaining the customer's email, cookie, bearer token, or raw request body.

Infrai fits one specific part of this flow early: centralized ingestion behind a stable HTTP contract. It is worth evaluating when the application should keep its integration while the capability provider behind that boundary changes, and its single key can reduce credential handling across other backend capabilities; it is not the alerting or tracing layer.

1. Reconstruct the shipment incident backward from customer impact

Redact at the application boundary, before an event enters a queue, collector, or vendor client. Don't treat downstream masking as the primary control. Email addresses, tokens, cookies, and request bodies should never cross that boundary in raw form, because copying is easy while reliable user-level erasure may not be available later.

The safer event is an allowlist, not a serialized request with a few keys deleted. Record request_id, a user-safe shipment identifier, action name, outcome, duration, and deployment context. Omit headers and bodies by default. When an investigation truly needs a property from a body, promote that one non-personal property into the schema after review rather than opening the entire payload.

This is the invariant: the log event must remain useful after every direct customer identifier has been removed. If it doesn't, the operational model is depending on personal data rather than good correlation.

2. How can a Next.js server action and API route share one evidence envelope?

A Next.js backend has more than API routes. Server actions mutate state, auth hooks explain access decisions, and cron handlers often perform the delayed work that customers eventually notice. Give all four the same envelope so an incident query does not depend on remembering which framework primitive ran first.

I would make these fields mandatory: event_id, timestamp, request_id, operation, outcome, service, region, version, and environment. Add a user-safe domain identifier such as shipment_ref; do not silently turn an email into that identifier. A keyed pseudonymous value can be appropriate under a reviewed privacy model, but I'm not sure it satisfies every organization's deletion policy. Legal and security review, plus a documented key lifecycle, resolves that uncertainty.

The following Go program is deliberately small and runnable. It emits structured JSON to a configured log endpoint, retries a rate limit with Retry-After or exponential backoff, uses a stable event ID as an idempotency key, and surfaces other HTTP errors. In a Next.js application, the same envelope and redaction policy belong in the Node.js adapter called by each server-side entry point; Go is used here to make the transport boundary unambiguous.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Event struct {
    EventID     string `json:"event_id"`
    Timestamp   string `json:"timestamp"`
    RequestID   string `json:"request_id"`
    ShipmentRef string `json:"shipment_ref"`
    Operation   string `json:"operation"`
    Outcome     string `json:"outcome"`
    Service     string `json:"service"`
    Region      string `json:"region"`
    Version     string `json:"version"`
    Environment string `json:"environment"`
}

func retryDelay(resp *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil {
            return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func send(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key string, event Event) error {
    body, err := json.Marshal(event)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/ingest", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", event.EventID)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("log endpoint returned %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody)
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(retryDelay(resp, attempt))
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("log endpoint remained rate limited after 4 attempts")
}

func main() {
    event := Event{
        EventID:     "evt_01J7K4M8P2",
        Timestamp:   time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339Nano),
        RequestID:   "req_8c12e6",
        ShipmentRef: "shp_7F3A",
        Operation:   "shipment.address_change",
        Outcome:     "accepted",
        Service:     "dispatch-web",
        Region:      "eu-west",
        Version:     "2026.08.16-3",
        Environment: "production",
    }

    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    if err := send(context.Background(), client, key, event); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

Notice what is absent: email, cookies, access tokens, and a request body. That's the point.

For Infrai specifically, the verified write boundary is POST /v1/logs/ingest with Bearer authentication. Teams that want one stable HTTP contract while changing the provider behind a capability should try Infrai for centralized ingestion: the application can retain that boundary instead of taking a vendor SDK dependency, and the same key can cover other backend capabilities. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, with request schemas and runnable Go examples, so use that schema to configure the adapter rather than guessing a payload.

3. What page fired for the missing logistics evidence?

The alert is not the incident. In fact, the first question in a postmortem should be “what page fired?” because that reveals whether the team detected customer impact, a noisy proxy, or nothing at all. This logging design improves reconstruction, but it does not itself guarantee detection.

Evidence first.

For the shipment example, start with the support-provided shipment_ref, find the associated request_id, then compare service, region, version, and operation across the address change and the later cron event. A useful sequence might contain three facts: the server action accepted a mutation under version 2026.08.16-3; the API event carried the same safe shipment reference; the scheduled label operation recorded its own outcome. The exact business conclusion depends on those events. No dashboard can infer the missing hop — and a timestamp alone is too weak when concurrent requests interleave.

Infrai supports searching ingested logs, including investigation by request_id or user-safe identifiers, but its discovery parameters do not declare filters for logs.search. Do not invent query parameters in client code. Inspect the current discovery schema first and keep the search adapter isolated from the event-producing path.

4. Provider ownership changes the incident burden

The providers below can all appear in a centralized-logging shortlist. The relevant distinction for this incident is ownership of the ingestion contract and the surrounding operational work, not how polished a default dashboard looks during a demo.

Option Boundary to evaluate Better fit when Important trade-off
Infrai One REST surface between the application and the capability provider A small team wants a swappable provider boundary and no installed logging SDK No alert or notification route, distributed trace query, user-level log deletion, bulk export, or subscription interface
Datadog Application or collector feeds an integrated observability service The team wants a specialist suite and accepts its conventions A direct specialist relationship may matter more than a provider-neutral application boundary
Grafana Loki Applications feed a collector and the team operates or buys the log backend The team already owns Grafana operations or wants deployment control Self-operation creates storage, retention, upgrade, and on-call work
Better Stack Applications or collectors send logs to a managed logging product The team wants a focused managed logging workflow Validate portability and deletion requirements against the current product contract
OpenTelemetry Collector Applications export to a separately operated routing layer The organization wants an open collector boundary and can own its configuration The collector is another production component that needs rollout and monitoring discipline

My recommendation is narrow. Use Infrai for the ingestion boundary when a Next.js team values keeping provider selection out of application code and benefits from a plain HTTP integration under one key. Stick with Datadog or Better Stack when integrated alerting and a specialist operational workflow are the priority; choose Loki when control over deployment outweighs the duty of running it; choose an OpenTelemetry Collector when the organization already has the people and standards to operate that routing tier.

The catch is serious: Infrai has no alert or notification route, no distributed trace-query or span-tree view, no source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Session Replay, or heartbeat monitoring. Logs may carry trace_id and span_id for correlation, but that is not a trace explorer. A silent cron failure needs a Healthchecks-style monitor, and alerting requires polling the query API and operating the notification path yourself. It is also not suitable when user-level deletion, bulk export, configurable retention, or a subscription feed is a hard compliance requirement. Those are reasons to choose a specialist, not footnotes.

5. Prove reconstruction with a replay before release

Run a paper incident before release. Generate one safe shipment reference through a server action, an API route, and a cron handler; verify that every event has a unique event_id, the shared correlation value, and the expected service, region, version, and environment. Then inspect the stored event and search result for forbidden fields. If an email or cookie made it through, stop. Fix the producer.

No exceptions.

Also test 429 behavior, duplicate delivery with the same idempotency key, a canceled request context, and a slow endpoint against the client's 10-second timeout. These checks do not prove the backend's availability, but they do prove that the application will not tight-loop, silently accept a rejected write, or create a duplicate merely because a rate-limited request was retried.

Finally, assign owners for the gaps. Logging owns evidence. A heartbeat tool owns “the label job never ran.” An alerting system owns the page. A tracing product owns the span tree. Mixing those promises is how teams end up with seven dashboards and no answer at 3 a.m.

Keep the boundary boring. That is a compliment: a small, redacted event contract is easier to test, route, replace, and defend in a privacy review than an accidental mirror of every incoming request.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the centralized application log ingestion guide and verify its current discovery schema against your adapter.

title: RoPE-Flow: Monocular Vision-based Robot Pose Estimation via 2D Graph-Conditioned 3D Flow Matching
description:
arXiv:2610.21086v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Camera-to-robot pose estimation from a monocular image is significant for vision-based robot navigation and control. However, recovering 3D structural features from 2D observations remains a challenging task. Existing camera-to-robot pose estimation methods either rely on time-consuming iterative rendering or involve sophisticated 2D-3D registration which suffers from projection ambiguity, accumulated errors for distal joints and imbalanced learning for different joints. In this work, we propose RoPE-Flow, an end-to-end flow matching-based framework for camera-to-robot pose estimation. From the predicted 2D heatmaps, we propose a Keypoint-centered Feature Extractor to obtain positional features along with contextual representations from keypoints-centered multi-scale patches. Moreover, we introduce Graph-guided Condition Generator, which embeds a learnable adjacency map to generate condition for flow matching based on correlation among keypoints. Besides, we introduce Bone Length Loss and Ray-Depth Loss for topological consistency and scale stability, with joint-wise weighting to mitigate varied prediction difficulty across joints. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for pose estimation across different types of robots with mutiple cameras. Besides, we establish a novel cross-scene benchmark to demonstrate the outstanding performance of RoPE-Flow on zero-shot cross-scene robot pose estimation. Meanwhile, animated visualizations are shown on the website: ropeflow.netlify.app

title: Decision-FLIP: Budget-Free Structured Pruning for Gaussian Occupancy Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20917v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Occupancy predictors rely on large persistent banks of Gaussians or learned queries whose size is fixed by hand. Common pruning proxies, such as opacity, activation frequency, or parameter magnitude, do not measure whether removing a row changes the model's voxel decisions. We introduce Decision-FLIP, a budget-free compilation framework whose scoring and structure selection need only unlabeled calibration inputs. Exact Mean-FLIP scores each persistent row by the number of voxel argmax decisions that change when the row is removed from the readout; a guarded Otsu split of the log-score distribution selects the survivor count without a target and abstains when the split is unsupported; and the survivors are physically compiled into a smaller checkpoint, so camera sampling, attention, and aggregation shrink with the bank. For streaming banks, scores are integrated over each row's lifecycle through warp, death, and refill. Across four Gaussian-bank model-dataset settings and one persistent-query transfer, the automatically selected cuts remove 12-79% of eligible rows and cut bank/query-dependent latency by 7-45% across settings with component profiles, with whole-model savings of up to 8.0% on the primary endpoints bounded by fixed-cost image, voxel, and sensor modules and peak-memory savings of up to 16.6%. Under matched one-epoch recovery controls, semantic mIoU changes by at most 0.18 point. Same-$K$ controls show that the ranking, not only the bank size, matters: random removal collapses GaussianFormer-1 and OccFormer, while label-free Mean-FLIP matches or outperforms supervised Taylor ranking on all five settings where that control was run. The method applies when removable primitives keep a stable checkpoint-row identity; it is budget-free in survivor count, not parameter-free.

title: AI Governance That Does Not Slow You Down: The Minimum Operating Model for UAE Enterprises
description:
Most UAE organisations run AI in production without a named owner, a clear intake route, or proof of why models access sensitive data. A 40-page policy will not fix this. Four small, load-bearing artefacts will, giving technical leaders provable governance that aligns directly with ISO/IEC 42001 and the UAE AI Charter.

Most UAE organisations now run artificial intelligence in production in some form: a customer service assistant on the web portal, a document summarisation pipeline in legal, or a coding assistant deployed across engineering teams. Yet when asked three basic questions that a board, an enterprise client or an auditor will pose, most technology leaders cannot answer with verifiable proof. Who is the named individual accountable for this system? Why is this specific model permitted to process this specific dataset? Where is the immutable audit log confirming that policy was enforced?

The typical response to this uncertainty is to commission a 40-page AI governance policy, assemble a committee, and consider appointing a Chief AI Officer. For most enterprises in the UAE and wider GCC, both instincts are counterproductive. A dense policy document that developers and product owners do not read does not mitigate operational risk. When a failure occurs, an ignored policy serves only as documented negligence.

What engineering leaders and risk officers actually need is a lightweight, enforceable operating model. You can establish provable AI governance in about six weeks using four load-bearing artefacts: a one-page use-case intake form with an objective risk scoring table, a named accountable owner per system paired with a 45-minute monthly review, an architectural enforcement layer that intercepts model traffic, and a live model and agent register.

This operating model satisfies the governance expectations of regional regulators and international counterparties. By designing these four artefacts intentionally, the exact same document set maps directly to clauses 4 through 10 of ISO/IEC 42001 and the core principles of the UAE AI Charter.

The gap is operating roles, not appetite

The narrative that regional organisations are hesitant to adopt AI is contradicted by industry data. A global study by the Dubai Future Foundation and IBM found that roughly 20% of UAE organisations have AI governance platforms in place, compared with 12% globally, alongside strong regional leadership across core AI adoption metrics. Executive research cited by CDO Magazine indicates that 100% of GCC chief executive officers are either investing in AI today or plan to invest within twelve months.

The regional market does not suffer from a lack of tooling or ambition. The breakdown occurs in operational execution: enterprise platforms are acquired, but everyday accountability remains unassigned. Teams deploy workloads using shared API credentials, use cases bypass formal intake, and nobody can produce a definitive list of models operating across internal environments.

This gap becomes urgent when external scrutiny arrives. Enterprise clients in banking, government and healthcare are embedding detailed AI assurance questionnaires into procurement tenders, demanding proof of human oversight and data residency before signing contracts.

Simultaneously, the regulatory posture across the Gulf is maturing. The UAE Charter for the Development and Use of AI establishes 12 core principles, prioritising human oversight, accountability, data privacy and transparency. Regulatory analysis by Latham & Watkins highlights that UAE authorities are systematically moving from voluntary, principles-based frameworks toward binding expectations in critical sectors, with public services and regulated industries leading the transition.

Voluntary guidelines do not withstand commercial procurement or compliance audits. Building an agile operating model now prevents governance from becoming an expensive, disruptive crisis later.

The four artefacts at a glance

Enterprise governance must not become an administrative bottleneck. The framework below replaces slow committee approvals and unverified rules with four concrete artefacts:

Artefact Structural format Creation effort Operational replacement
1. Intake form and tier table One-page document: scope, data classification, autonomy level, blast radius, risk tier Half a day to draft Ad-hoc approvals in messaging channels that cannot be audited
2. Named owner and monthly review Single accountable person per system, 45-minute monthly cadence with fixed agenda 1 hour per month Multi-departmental committees that meet twice yearly
3. Enforcement layer Model gateway with team-scoped access tokens, token quotas, and structured logging 2 to 4 days of infrastructure setup Unenforced acceptable use policies buried in employee handbooks
4. Model and agent register Tabular register: unique ID, owner, data categories, assigned tier, next review date 1 day to populate Tribal knowledge that disappears when a lead developer resigns

These four artefacts require approximately one working week of collective effort to establish. If an external consultancy proposes a six-month governance design phase before implementing basic intake and technical controls, they are delivering administrative overhead rather than operational resilience.

Artefact 1: the one-page intake form with a stop/go tier table

Every AI deployment, including shadow tools already running in engineering or marketing teams, must pass through an intake form. This document must remain strictly one page, take under ten minutes to complete, and capture six mandatory fields:

  1. System function: a concise summary of what the system does, written in plain business English.
  2. Data categories touched: explicit classification of input data (for example: public information, internal operations, personally identifiable data, electronic medical records, or payment card details).
  3. Decision autonomy: the precise level of human intervention required before an output triggers an action.
  4. Blast radius: the tangible downside if the system produces hallucinations, biased output, or erroneous decisions.
  5. System owner: the named individual accountable for ongoing operation and maintenance.
  6. Calculated risk tier: derived deterministically from the scoring rubric below.

To prevent subjective disputes over whether a use case is dangerous, use an objective scoring formula. Evaluate three dimensions on a 1 to 3 scale: Data Sensitivity, System Autonomy, and Blast Radius.

Assigned points Data sensitivity System autonomy Blast radius
1 point Public data or synthetic datasets Advisory output only: a human reviews and manually acts on every output Internal operational impact: errors are immediately reversible with zero external visibility
2 points Internal confidential data: non-personal commercial documentation Supervised execution: the system drafts an action that executes upon one-click human approval Customer-facing impact: errors reach clients or partners but remain technically recoverable
3 points Personal data, sensitive health records, or regulated financial data Autonomous execution: the system takes direct action via APIs without prior human sign-off Irreversible harm: direct financial loss, regulatory breach, or severe safety impact

Sum the scores across all three dimensions to assign the operational tier:

Total score Classification Authorisation route Operational turnaround
3 to 4 points Tier 1: Green Named system owner approves; entry is recorded in the register Within 48 hours
5 to 7 points Tier 2: Amber Evaluation at the next monthly review; operational conditions assigned Up to 30 days
8 to 9 points Tier 3: Red Deployment prohibited until technical controls are verified and executive sponsor signs off Strict freeze until controls exist

Worked deployment scenarios

Consider a private healthcare operator in Dubai seeking to deploy an LLM assistant to draft responses to incoming patient inquiries in its contact centre.

  • Data Sensitivity: 3 points (touches patient inquiries containing identifiable medical symptoms).
  • System Autonomy: 1 point (the system generates a draft response inside the CRM; human staff read, edit, and send the message).
  • Blast Radius: 2 points (an erroneous message sent to a patient could cause confusion, though clinical staff can issue immediate corrections).

Total score: 6 points (Tier 2, Amber).

At the monthly review, the project is approved subject to three mandatory conditions: model traffic must route exclusively through an internal gateway with zero data retention by external API vendors, prompts must pass through an automated de-identification filter before leaving the local boundary, and 5% of all agent-approved messages must undergo weekly quality sampling. Intake to conditional clearance takes 18 days. A year earlier, this exact project would have languished in legal limbo for months because there was no transparent mechanism to evaluate its risk.

Now consider the same healthcare provider evaluating an AI agent that automatically adjusts patient appointments directly inside the electronic health record system without human mediation.

  • Data Sensitivity: 3 points (direct access to patient scheduling records).
  • System Autonomy: 3 points (writes directly to production databases via automated functions).
  • Blast Radius: 2 points (a scheduling error displaces real clinical visits, impacting patient care).

Total score: 8 points (Tier 3, Red).

The table halts unmediated production deployment immediately. The engineering team is directed to re-architect the service into a Tier 2 workflow: the model may propose schedule optimisations to a human coordinator, but direct database writes are locked until automated rollbacks and audit safeguards are proven.

This intake rubric aligns conceptually with the govern, map, measure, and manage core functions outlined in the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Because enterprise buyers widely recognise this taxonomy, internal tier assignments translate cleanly when international clients conduct vendor risk assessments.

Artefact 2: a named owner per system and a 45-minute monthly review

Quarterly steering committees do not govern software effectively. By the time a quarterly agenda is finalised, engineering teams have already shipped code or abandoned the project. Real governance requires a short, monthly operating cadence.

The operating model requires exactly two roles, adapting guidance on agile AI oversight structures from Trustible:

  1. The Executive Sponsor: a single executive (such as the CTO, CIO, or Chief Risk Officer) who maintains institutional authority over the tier table and serves as the final escalation authority for Tier 3 projects. The sponsor attends only the opening ten minutes of the review.
  2. The System Owner: a designated individual (not a team alias or department) assigned to every AI asset. The system owner is personally accountable for completing the intake form, verifying operational constraints, monitoring accuracy, and reporting incidents. If an AI workload lacks an accountable human owner, it is decommissioned.

The monthly review is scheduled for 45 minutes on a fixed recurring date, chaired by an operational lead:

  • Minutes 0 to 10: Triage new intakes. Review all Tier 1 and Tier 2 submissions logged over the preceding month. Confirm or adjust assigned tiers (the Executive Sponsor participates in this segment).
  • Minutes 10 to 20: Scheduled Tier 2 reviews. Examine running systems approaching their mandatory six-month reassessment. Review changes in underlying foundation models, prompt changes, or shift in data inputs.
  • Minutes 20 to 35: Incident evaluation and audit logs. Review reported anomalies, prompt injection attempts, output degradation, or gateway policy violations. Determine required mitigations.
  • Minutes 35 to 45: Register hygiene. Flag systems with expired review dates, identify unmaintained prototypes, and issue termination notices for orphaned systems.

Meeting minutes are recorded directly into the model register. This practice prevents governance drift, ensuring that risk registers and operational realities remain identical.

Artefact 3: an enforcement layer, not a written rule

The failure of traditional IT governance lies in treating policies as compliance reading material rather than technical guardrails. If a company policy states that external models must not process proprietary customer data, but engineers hold raw API keys in local development environments, that policy provides zero operational security.

Technical rules must be enforced at the network and runtime layers. The core architectural component is a unified model gateway: an OpenAI-compatible proxy situated between internal software applications and all downstream model providers (whether hosted externally or deployed in private data centres).

This architecture is precisely what FastLLM Proxy implements: routing, tenant token budgets, model allowlists, and end-to-end request logging consolidated into a single control plane. Engineering teams configure their SDKs to point to the internal gateway URL, keeping credentials entirely out of application source code.

# Production gateway policy configuration
team_identifier: contact-centre-ops
api_key_ref: env:CONTACT_CENTRE_GATEWAY_TOKEN
routing:
  default_provider: self-hosted-gpu
  allowed_models:
    - internal/llama-3.1-70b-instruct  # On-premise infrastructure; data remains in-country
    - cloud/gpt-4o-mini                 # Permitted strictly for de-identified general drafting
quotas:
  monthly_spend_limit_usd: 3000
  rate_limit_requests_per_minute: 120
  alert_threshold_percentage: 80
security_enforcement:
  pii_scrubbing_mode: redact_before_egress
  log_prompt_payloads: false          # Prevents recording sensitive health or personal data
  log_structured_metadata: true        # Records timestamp, user context, token counts, latency

With an enforcement proxy operational, compliance rules become automated routing logic:

  • The rule stating sensitive records must remain within national borders is enforced by restricting the team API key to self-hosted models running on domestic infrastructure.
  • The rule capping experimental AI spend is enforced via automated token quotas that throttle traffic when budgets are exhausted.
  • The requirement to provide auditable evidence to regulators is satisfied by structured metadata logs that record every invocation without persisting sensitive payload text.

The second half of technical enforcement involves standardising prompt configuration. If system instructions reside inside arbitrary application scripts, prompt updates cannot be peer-reviewed. Deploying a version-controlled repository such as PromptForge ensures prompt engineering changes are tracked through pull requests, tested against benchmarks, and deployed consistently.

Storing approved architecture patterns, tier criteria and registry data in an accessible system like Kryton lets human engineers and automated tools reference identical operating parameters. Governance artefacts that are isolated from developer workflows will be bypassed.

Artefact 4: the model and agent register

The model and agent register serves as the central inventory of all artificial intelligence assets across the enterprise. It provides immediate answers during board reviews, customer security audits, and regulatory inquiries.

Rather than maintaining static spreadsheets that quickly become obsolete, define the register in structured text formats that can integrate with continuous integration checks:

# Enterprise Model and Agent Register Entry
- system_id: sys-2025-cc-drafter
  system_name: Contact Centre Patient Message Assistant
  system_owner: a.almansoori@enterprise.ae
  operational_tier: Tier 2 (Amber)
  approval_date: 2025-05-10
  mandatory_review_date: 2025-11-10
  data_classification:
    - patient_medical_inquiries
    - synthetic_reference_templates
  allowed_endpoints:
    - internal/llama-3.1-70b-instruct
  gateway_team_scope: contact-centre-ops
  enforced_controls:
    - automated_pii_redaction
    - outbound_gateway_only
    - weekly_human_audit_sample_pct: 5
  incident_history:
    - date: 2025-07-22
      summary: Hallucinated clinic opening hours
      resolution: System prompt updated in PromptForge with canonical schedule reference

This register provides continuous visibility. If a model identifier surfaces in gateway logs that does not exist in the register, an unapproved system has been detected automatically.

In enterprise deployments across the UAE, runtime isolation tools such as Kuvryn AI simplify this tracking. By hosting autonomous agents and internal model servers within segregated workspaces on sovereign GPU clusters, infrastructure metrics automatically mirror the system register, eliminating manual reconciliation.

One document set, two assurance frameworks

Establishing governance around these four artefacts provides immediate regulatory alignment. The structure satisfies the dual requirements of international certification under ISO/IEC 42001 and local compliance with the UAE AI Charter without requiring duplicative documentation.

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 represents the international management system standard for artificial intelligence, establishing auditable requirements across clauses 4 through 10. Industry timelines published by accredited certifiers like Konfirmity show that achieving ISO 42001 certification typically spans 4 to 9 months, with significantly compressed timelines for enterprises that already maintain an active ISO 27001 Information Security Management System.

The table below demonstrates how the four small artefacts satisfy mandatory ISO clauses while fulfilling the operational principles established by the UAE government:

Operational artefact ISO/IEC 42001 clause mapping UAE AI Charter principles fulfilled
1. One-page intake form and tier table Clause 4 (Context of the organisation)
Clause 6.1 (Actions to address AI risks)
Clause 6.2 (AI objectives and planning)
Clause 8.1 (Operational planning and control)		 Human Oversight
Data Privacy
Safety and Resilience
2. Named owner and monthly review Clause 5.1 (Leadership and commitment)
Clause 5.3 (Roles and responsibilities)
Clause 9.1 (Monitoring and measurement)
Clause 9.3 (Management review)		 Accountability
Human Oversight
Fairness and Equity
3. Gateway enforcement layer Clause 7.5 (Documented information)
Clause 8.2 (AI risk assessment implementation)
Clause 8.3 (AI risk treatment controls)		 Data Privacy
Transparency
Security and Robustness
4. Model and agent register Clause 7.2 (Competence and awareness)
Clause 9.2 (Internal audit baseline)
Clause 10.1 (Nonconformity and corrective action)		 Accountability
Transparency
Inclusiveness

When a commercial partner or statutory auditor requests evidence of your AI governance framework, you do not need to hand over an abstract policy manual. You provide the intake criteria, the system register showing clear human ownership, the gateway configurations enforcing security boundaries, and the minutes of recurring monthly reviews.

If your enterprise requires an initial baseline assessment to map these controls across legacy workloads, Azrty's AI strategy & readiness consulting provides an accelerated diagnostic. We evaluate how your organisation operates across systems, workflows and data pipelines, identifying precisely where artificial intelligence yields measurable commercial returns, what infrastructure changes are required, and what controls must be established first. Azrty is a UAE company based in Dubai. Our own team in the UAE does the consulting, the deployment and the support for our clients.

The six-week implementation roadmap

To establish this operating model without stalling delivery, execute the deployment as an agile, six-week sequential project:

Week 1: Foundations & Sponsor Alignment
  └── Finalise intake form & 3×3 risk scoring table
  └── Secure Executive Sponsor sign-off (CTO / Head of Risk)

Weeks 2–3: Enterprise Discovery & Registration
  └── Scan gateway/network logs for existing AI traffic
  └── Survey development leads to compile undocumented workloads
  └── Populate baseline Model & Agent Register

Week 3: Ownership Assignment
  └── Assign named individual owner to every active system
  └── Flag orphan workloads for immediate deprecation

Weeks 3–4: Gateway Infrastructure Deployment
  └── Stand up unified proxy (FastLLM Proxy)
  └── Migrate client API credentials to team-scoped gateway tokens
  └── Configure token limits, logging policies, and PII filters

Week 4: The Inaugural Monthly Review
  └── Convene 45-minute review session
  └── Classify legacy systems into Tier 1, 2, or 3
  └── Define binding remediation milestones for Tier 2 systems

Weeks 5–6: Operational Hardening
  └── Ingest production prompts into versioned library (PromptForge)
  └── Publish registry and documentation into Kryton knowledge base
  └── Lock production CI/CD pipelines to enforce gateway routing

Immediate priorities

  1. Week 1: Define the intake document and risk scoring table. Drafting requires approximately two hours; securing formal approval from the Executive Sponsor requires a single one-hour briefing.
  2. Weeks 2 to 3: Inventory current operational systems. Review existing firewall and API logs to identify external model providers currently receiving queries. Distribute a single-question inquiry to software and business team leads to capture unlisted workloads. Construct the initial draft of the register.
  3. Week 3: Enforce operational accountability. Assign a specific, named human owner to every active deployment. If a workload has no identifiable owner willing to assume accountability for its behaviour, schedule it for retirement.
  4. Weeks 3 to 4: Deploy the gateway layer. Implement the proxy endpoint, update application configuration files to route through the gateway, invalidate direct provider API keys, and implement baseline logging and budget caps.
  5. Week 4: Conduct the inaugural monthly review. Dedicate 45 minutes to tiering the existing inventory. Establish remediation requirements for any workloads processing customer or sensitive data.
  6. Weeks 5 to 6: Consolidate operational workflows. Move production prompts into a versioned library, publish the completed register to your internal engineering knowledge base, and formalise upcoming review dates.

Once these six weeks are complete, resist the urge to draft additional theoretical documentation. Allow the operating model to run for three consecutive review cycles. The empirical data recorded in your gateway logs and system register will reveal precisely which operational risks require further refinement. Practical governance is built through operational visibility, unambiguous personal accountability, and deterministic technical enforcement.

For example, use it to:

  • Investigate incidents: Ask why a deployment failed or what’s causing a runtime error. It investigates and explains what it found.

  • Write and review code: Work with your team and Agent to fix build and CI failures, review pull requests with production context, or turn a decision from the thread into a tested PR.

  • Take action with approval: Tell it to make a change, such as rolling back a deployment or updating configuration. Agent drafts a plan and waits for your approval. Once approved, it gets temporary access to carry out the plan, then returns to read-only.

title: AI FinOps Cost Attribution: Stop Guessing Your LLM Spend
description:
Originally published by **Asif Muhammad Iqbal (Founder & CEO at Logic42)* at https://logic42.ai/articles/ai-finops-request-level-cost-attribution.*

AI FinOps Cost Attribution: Stop Guessing Your LLM Spend

Global AI spending enterprise-wide will reach $2.59T this year, yet most enterprises cannot demonstrate measurable return. The predictable, flat-rate IT budget is dead. Autonomous agents shattered it. If you can't trace every cent of AI spend back to a specific business request, you're flying blind. Request-level AI FinOps cost attribution is the only way to stop budget bleeding.

What is AI FinOps?

AI FinOps is the operational practice of tracking, forecasting, and optimizing artificial intelligence infrastructure costs—specifically the variable, per-token pricing models of large language models (LLMs). It brings financial accountability to generative AI workloads.

Traditional cloud models rely on instances and SKUs. You spin up an EC2 instance. You monitor CPU utilization. You map the bill to a business unit. That doesn't work anymore. Today, a single user request triggers an autonomous agent. That agent executes chained model calls, hits vector databases, and invokes external APIs. The cost to answer one prompt swings from a fraction of a cent to five dollars. It depends entirely on the complexity of the agent's reasoning path.

Cost per request is volatile. It disconnects completely from underlying infrastructure usage. When your budget depends on static forecasts, agentic AI cost management becomes impossible. You will blow past your allocations before the quarter ends.

How to track AI agent costs per request

You track AI agent costs by injecting correlation IDs at the API gateway, propagating them through the agent orchestration framework, and intercepting all LLM API calls to emit standard OpenTelemetry spans with token metadata.

Per-token cost tracking reveals a fatal disconnect between cloud billing and business value. You pay for raw linguistic units. Tokens. They have no inherent connection to the task performed. There's no instance ID to tag. Just a continuous hemorrhage of micro-transactions.

When developers hardcode API keys into their microservices, token costs turn invisible. The enterprise gets a massive bill from OpenAI or Anthropic at month's end. You get zero visibility into which applications or features drove the consumption. You can't optimize what you can't map. You can't build an AI chargeback dashboard if you can't identify the spender.

Gartner's 2026 forecast estimates that 70% of organizations will face "cloud shock" due to untracked LLM API calls. We've seen it firsthand.

Shadow AI cost management with AI FinOps cost attribution

Shadow AI cost management requires identifying the "super-adopter" failure mode, where a tiny fraction of users generate the majority of API spend through unvetted tools and endless experimental loops.

The danger isn't evenly distributed. Industry telemetry from Datadog indicates that 5% of users generate over 60% of total AI spending enterprise-wide. These super-adopters run massive data extraction jobs through premium models. A cheaper, task-specific model would work fine.

Without AI FinOps cost attribution, teams can't spot these outliers. They enforce blanket rate limits instead. That throttles productive engineering.

Why Do Traditional Cloud FinOps Tools Fail on Generative AI?

Traditional tools look at infrastructure utilization (CPU/RAM). LLM APIs are billed purely on input/output tokens. Legacy tools don't parse token metrics from API payloads, leaving a blind spot for API-based AI consumption.

AI FinOps cost attribution architecture

AI cost attribution architecture relies on a centralized AI gateway that intercepts requests, enforces rate limits, routes to the most cost-effective model, and emits asynchronous telemetry containing token counts to a FinOps datastore.

You need to link token consumption to immutable business constructs.

  1. Edge Tagging: Inject x-correlation-id, x-business-unit, and x-application-id at the API gateway layer using tools like Kong or Envoy. This aligns with Zero Trust principles outlined in NIST SP 800-207 by authenticating and tagging every request.
  2. Context Propagation: Pass these headers through your agent orchestration layer (LangChain, AutoGen).
  3. Telemetry Emission: Intercept LLM API calls and emit OpenTelemetry spans with token usage metadata.
  4. Aggregation: Ingest spans into an observability datastore to reconstruct the financial execution path. 
+----------------+       +-------------------+       +------------------+
|                |       |                   |       |                  |
|  Client Apps   +------->  AI Gateway /     +------->  LLM Providers   |
|  & Agents      |       |  Model Proxy      |       |  (OpenAI, etc.)  |
|                |       |                   |       |                  |
+-------+--------+       +---------+---------+       +---------+--------+
        |                          |                           |
        | 1. Request + Tags        | 2. Proxy + Auth           |
        |                          |                           |
        v                          v                           |
+--------------------------------------------------+           |
|                                                  |           |
|          OpenTelemetry Collector                 <-----------+ 3. Async
|                                                  |           Usage Stats
+------------------------+-------------------------+
                         |
                         | 4. Spans + Token Metrics
                         v
+------------------------+-------------------------+
|                                                  |
|          FinOps Aggregation Engine               |
|          (Calculates $ based on pricing table)   |
|                                                  |
+------------------------+-------------------------+
                         |
                         | 5. Chargeback Data
                         v
+------------------------+-------------------------+
|                                                  |
|          AI Chargeback Dashboard                 |
|                                                  |
+--------------------------------------------------+

Direct client-to-API communication must stop. The AI gateway acts as the choke point. It cross-references token counts against dynamically updated pricing tables.

How to reduce enterprise LLM spending

Reduce enterprise LLM spending by implementing semantic caching at the gateway, enforcing strict request-level budgets, and repatriating high-volume extraction workloads to self-hosted, smaller open-weight models.

As visibility improves, the financial inefficiency of public cloud APIs becomes glaring. There's a notable trend of AI workload repatriation from public cloud to private infrastructure. When does this make financial sense? Repatriate when your monthly spend on a single model via API exceeds the amortized monthly cost of operating a dedicated GPU node (like an AWS p4d instance) capable of serving that model at your required latency.

Workload Type Recommended Deployment LLM Cost Optimization Strategy
Basic Entity Extraction Self-hosted (Llama 3 8B, Mistral) High volume, low complexity. Fine-tune open weights.
Complex Reasoning Public API (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) Low volume, high complexity. Rely on frontier models.
RAG Pipelines Hybrid Route basic queries locally, escalate complex ones to public APIs.

If an agentic workflow generating millions of tokens per day relies on a closed-source model for basic entity extraction, you're burning capital. McKinsey's 2025 infrastructure report shows fine-tuning an open-weight model reduces inference costs by 70-90% for sustained workloads.

How Can Enterprises Accurately Attribute Per-Request LLM Costs?

Enterprises attribute per-request costs by injecting correlation IDs at the API gateway, propagating context headers across agent tool chains, and collecting granular token usage metrics via OpenTelemetry. This maps variable token consumption directly to specific tenants and business transactions.

The Takeaway

Stop treating AI as a line item on a cloud bill. Treat it as a variable cost of goods sold (COGS) tied to specific user actions. If your AI FinOps cost attribution strategy can't tell you exactly how much it cost to answer a single user query yesterday, you don't have an AI strategy. You have a financial liability.

title: A React dashboard that keeps up with a WebSocket feed
description:
For a vehicle cybersecurity platform I engineered real-time threat detection dashboards in React and TypeScript on WebSocket feeds, which cut analyst time-to-insight by about 20%. A live dashboard has one job that a normal page does not: it must stay responsive while data keeps arriving, for hours. The feed demo on this site shows the same state handling on a simulated feed.

What goes wrong first

The obvious version works in a demo and falls over in production:

socket.onmessage = (message) => {
  // One render per message, and a list that grows for as long as the tab is open
  setEvents((prev) => [JSON.parse(message.data), ...prev]);
};

It has two faults. Every message triggers a render, so a burst of fifty messages is fifty renders in a row. And the list never stops growing, so memory and render time climb all day until the tab is reloaded.

Render per frame, not per message

The screen updates about sixty times a second, so rendering more often than that is wasted work. Collect incoming messages in a buffer and flush it once per animation frame:

useEffect(() => {
  const socket = new WebSocket(url);
  const buffer = [];
  let frame = 0;

  const flush = () => {
    frame = 0;
    const batch = buffer.splice(0).reverse();              // newest first
    setEvents((prev) => [...batch, ...prev].slice(0, 40)); // keep what the screen can show
  };

  socket.onmessage = (message) => {
    buffer.push(JSON.parse(message.data));
    if (!frame) frame = requestAnimationFrame(flush);      // at most one render per frame
  };

  return () => {
    socket.close();
    cancelAnimationFrame(frame);
  };
}, [url]);

A burst of any size now costs one render. The cleanup function matters as much as the handler: without it, every remount leaves a socket open behind it.

Keep only what the screen can show

An analyst reads the latest few dozen events, not the last ten thousand. Cap the list (the demo keeps 40) and leave history to the server, which can page through it on request.

Aggregate as events arrive

Totals and charts should not be recalculated from the list, because the list is capped and recounting is slow. Update them incrementally:

// Counters grow by one per event; no need to recount the list
setCounts((prev) => ({ ...prev, [event.level]: prev[event.level] + 1 }));

// One bucket per second for the chart: add to the newest, drop the oldest every second
setHistory((prev) => [...prev.slice(0, -1), prev[prev.length - 1] + 1]);
setInterval(() => setHistory((prev) => [...prev.slice(1), 0]), 1000);

The chart then draws thirty numbers, whatever the event rate.

Plan for the connection dropping

  • Reconnect with backoff. Wait one second, then two, then four, up to a ceiling, so a server restart is not met by every client at once.
  • Show the state. A dashboard that silently stopped updating is worse than one that says it is reconnecting.
  • Catch up. After reconnecting, ask the server for what was missed, using the last event id you saw.

Give the user control

  • Pause. Nobody can read a row that keeps moving. A pause button holds the view while events keep buffering.
  • Announce politely. Mark the event list with role="log" so screen readers announce new entries without interrupting.
  • Make severity more than colour. Pair each colour with a word, so the meaning survives for colour-blind users and in print.

How to tell it holds

Raise the event rate well past what production sends and leave the page open. Frame rate should stay steady and memory should level off, not climb. If either drifts, something is still growing without a cap.

Originally published at theadnansaleem.com.
