title: Learning Topology-Aware Representations for Mechanics-Relevant TPMS Metamaterials
description:
arXiv:2610.20684v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning informative representations of mechanical Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) metamaterials is important for mechanics analysis and structural design, yet existing methods have rarely explicitly supervised learned representations with information about global structural connectivity that is relevant to mechanical response. We propose a topology-aware representation learning framework that integrates persistent homology into a DMAE backbone to explicitly encode global structural connectivity. A persistence-guided masking strategy prioritizes patches associated with persistent topological features, while an auxiliary persistent-homology decoder encourages the latent representation to retain information about topological feature counts across connected components, tunnels, and voids. We evaluate the learned representations on two complementary TPMS datasets using family classification, mechanical-property classification, unsupervised clustering, and regression. Across the two datasets, our method demonstrates strong performance in both structural family and mechanical-property classification, improving family classification by up to 3.9% while achieving the best linear-probe performance. More notably, unsupervised property-clustering performance improves by up to 26.7% and 51.5% across the two datasets, while strong regression performance is retained with $R^2=0.993$. These results establish persistent topology as an effective inductive bias for representation learning of complex three-dimensional mechanical metamaterials.

title: Gemini API 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: why your limit is 0
description:
The error:

{
  "error": {
    "code": 429,
    "message": "You exceeded your current quota, please check your plan and billing details. ...
* Quota exceeded for metric: generativelanguage.googleapis.com/generate_content_free_tier_requests, limit: 0, model: gemini-3.1-pro
Please retry in 10h17m5.723541104s.",
    "status": "RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED"
  }
}

Tested on: @google/genai: 2.27.0 · API tier: Free (AI Studio key) · Node / OS: 24.14.0 / Windows 11 Pro · Date: October 7, 2026

Every Gemini quota error looks the same at first: HTTP 429, "status": "RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED", "You exceeded your current quota". The part that matters is one line further down, in the * Quota exceeded for metric lines: the limit number and the model. With a free AI Studio key I hit three different ones on purpose, and each one needs a different fix:

The message says What it means Retry delay it gave me
limit: 0, model: gemini-3.1-pro Your tier has no quota for this model 10h17m (waiting doesn't help)
limit: 5, model: gemini-3.5-flash Requests per minute used up 46s
limit: 20, model: gemini-3.5-flash Requests per day used up 9h54m, until 00:00 UTC

The details array names the quota exactly. The per-minute one was GenerateRequestsPerMinutePerProjectPerModel-FreeTier, the daily one GenerateRequestsPerDayPerProjectPerModel-FreeTier.

limit: 0: the model isn't in your tier

This was the first call I made with the key. It wasn't a burst: a single request to gemini-3.1-pro-preview came back 429 straight away. Same for gemini-pro-latest. On the free tier these models have a quota of zero. The error still says "Please retry in 10h17m", but that only marks when the daily counters reset. Retrying at that time gets the same limit: 0.

Use a model that your tier has quota for. With this free key, gemini-3.5-flash, gemini-3.5-flash-lite and gemini-flash-latest answered normally:

const res = await ai.models.generateContent({
  model: 'gemini-3.5-flash',
  contents: 'hi',
});

If you need the Pro model specifically, that means a paid tier (billing turned on for the Google Cloud project behind the key). I didn't test that: it costs money, and it's the only way past a limit: 0.

Per-minute limit: wait the time it gives you

Sending one tiny request after another to gemini-3.5-flash, calls 1 to 7 succeeded, and call 8 failed 8.4 seconds in:

* Quota exceeded for metric: generativelanguage.googleapis.com/generate_content_free_tier_requests, limit: 5, model: gemini-3.5-flash
Please retry in 46.130728812s.

The limit says 5, but seven got through first, so don't use the number to pace yourself exactly. The @google/genai SDK (2.27.0) threw this straight to my code: it didn't retry on its own.

Wait the retryDelay from the error's RetryInfo detail, then retry. But cap the wait, because a daily limit sends a delay of hours:

import { GoogleGenAI, ApiError } from '@google/genai';
const ai = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY });

async function generateWithRetry(params, maxWaits = 4) {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await ai.models.generateContent(params);
    } catch (err) {
      if (!(err instanceof ApiError) || attempt >= maxWaits) throw err;
      if (err.status === 503) { // "high demand": back off and try again
        await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2000 * 2 ** attempt));
        continue;
      }
      if (err.status !== 429) throw err;
      const body = JSON.parse(err.message).error;
      if (/limit: 0\b/.test(body.message)) throw err; // no quota for this model at all
      const delay = body.details?.find((d) => d['@type']?.endsWith('RetryInfo'))?.retryDelay ?? '10s';
      const ms = Math.ceil(parseFloat(delay) * 1000) + 500;
      if (ms > 120_000) throw err; // a daily quota: the delay runs to midnight UTC
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
    }
  }
}

✅ After the per-minute 429, waiting 50 seconds and calling again succeeded. With the helper, a limit: 0 model and a used-up daily quota both failed at once instead of hanging, which is what you want: neither one recovers by waiting a minute.

⚠️ The SDK's retryOptions won't cover this @google/genai has httpOptions.retryOptions (attempts, backoff starting at 1 second, up to 60). Exponential backoff guesses at the wait. The error already tells you the exact delay, and for a daily limit no amount of backoff is long enough.

Daily limit: it resets at midnight UTC, not Pacific time

My test calls used up gemini-3.5-flash's free daily quota (limit: 20). The retry delay pointed at 2026-10-08 00:00:13 UTC. That's 8 PM in New York and 5 PM in San Francisco, not midnight Pacific as a lot of older answers say.

Switch to a different model until the reset. Each model has its own counters: right after gemini-3.5-flash hit its daily limit, nine calls in a row to gemini-3.5-flash-lite all succeeded.

💡 The quota IDs end in PerProjectPerModel: the counters belong to the Google Cloud project behind the key, and to one model. From that wording, a second key in the same project would share them. I didn't create one to check.

Not a 429: "This model is currently experiencing high demand"

While I was testing, gemini-3.8-flash (the newest Flash) returned this on every call, and later gemini-3.5-flash did too, for a few calls:

{
  "error": {
    "code": 503,
    "message": "This model is currently experiencing high demand. Spikes in demand are usually temporary. Please try again later.",
    "status": "UNAVAILABLE"
  }
}

This is Google being overloaded, not your quota. There's no retry delay in it, and other models kept working at the same moment. Calls that did go through during that period were slow, too: one took 56 seconds.

Back off and retry, or use another model for a while. The helper above waits 2, 4, then 8 seconds. In my run the 503s stopped after those three waits (the next answer was the daily-limit 429, because by then my test calls had used up the day's quota).

What didn't work

❌ Waiting out the "retry in 10h" on a limit: 0 model. That delay only points to the daily reset. The quota for that model on the free tier is zero, so it's zero again after the reset.

❌ Trusting the limit number to pace requests. With limit: 5 per minute, seven requests got through before the 429. Pace from the 429 and its delay, not from the number.

❌ Retrying a daily limit with backoff. My first helper honoured the delay with no cap and went to sleep for 36,030 seconds. If a delay is longer than a couple of minutes, it's a daily quota: stop and switch model.

💡 Gemini says the model is gone? With a new key, gemini-2.5-flash and gemini-2.5-pro didn't return a 429 at all. They returned 404 "no longer available to new users". That's a different fix (the model name), not your quota.

How this was tested

A free Google AI Studio API key on October 7, 2026, with @google/genai 2.27.0 on Node 24.14.0 (Windows 11). Every request was one word with maxOutputTokens: 1, sent one after another, never in parallel. Limits were reached on purpose: a Pro model for limit: 0, a fast loop for the per-minute limit, and the day's test calls for the daily one. The limits shown are the free tier's on that day. Google changes them, so read the numbers in your own error message. I didn't test paid tiers, Vertex AI, or the Gemini CLI, whose 429s come from a different quota.

The code for every case above is public, so you can run it yourself: gemini-429 in nk-repro.

Originally published, with updates as new versions ship, at nilaykabariya.blog. Written with AI assistance; every error and fix was reproduced on a real machine before it was written up.

title: GBase Database Pre-Deployment Checklist: 4 Essential Environment Checks
description:
Before installing GBase Database (GBase 8s), take a few minutes to validate the target Linux environment. Missing dependencies, insufficient disk space, network configuration issues, and incorrect locale settings can all complicate database deployment.

A structured GBase Database pre-installation checklist helps identify these issues before they become troubleshooting sessions.

1. Check Network and Security Settings

Start by checking the firewall, SELinux status, and hostname resolution:

# Check firewall status
systemctl status firewalld

# Check SELinux mode
getenforce

# Review hostname and hosts configuration
hostname
cat /etc/hosts
getent hosts "$(hostname)"

Verify that the required database ports are accessible and hostname resolution works correctly.

Don't automatically disable the firewall or SELinux. Configure the necessary network rules and security policies according to your GBase 8s version and deployment requirements. If troubleshooting requires a temporary security-policy change, follow your organization's security procedures.

2. Verify System Resources

Insufficient temporary disk space or memory can interrupt installation or complicate instance initialization.

# Check temporary directory space
df -h /tmp

# Check available memory
free -h

# Check CPU architecture and core count
uname -m
nproc

# Check available inodes
df -i /tmp

Compare the results against the hardware and operating system requirements for your target GBase Database release. Don't rely on a single resource threshold for every deployment.

3. Validate System Dependencies

Check required libraries and packages before running the installer.

On RPM-based Linux systems, rpm -q can verify whether a specified package is installed. Use the dependency list documented for your particular GBase 8s version and operating system.

Remember that package names vary across Linux distributions, and package presence alone doesn't guarantee library compatibility.

4. Confirm Character Set and Locale

Character-set planning is especially important when migrating existing applications or data.

Check the current locale:

locale
locale -a

Confirm the required database and client locale settings before initialization. Values such as zh_CN.utf8 and en_US.utf8 are examples; select settings supported by the target operating system and compatible with your application requirements.

Changing character-set-related settings after deployment may require substantial migration or reconfiguration work, depending on what needs to change.

Final Takeaway

A reliable GBase Database deployment starts with four checks: network and security, system resources, dependencies, and character-set planning.

For teams working on Xinchuang (China's IT application innovation) migrations, incorporating these checks into deployment documentation helps improve consistency, traceability, and installation readiness.

Do you use a standardized pre-deployment checklist for every GBase Database installation?

title: The Vercel Sandbox CLI is now more agent-friendly
description:
The Sandbox CLI version 4.0.1 ships four output and error improvements:

  • New sandboxes point users towards how to connect into them.

  • A sandbox not found error shows where to look for existing sandboxes.

  • Common mistakes, like typing a command after sh, redirect to the command that was intended.

  • Outdated installs show an update notice when they create a new sandbox.

Each of these messages now carries the action to take next instead of leaving you to work it out.

New sandboxes tell you how to connect

create and fork output now ends with a connect hint, so a fresh sandbox never leaves you wondering what to type next.

Not found errors point you to your sandboxes

When a command references a sandbox that does not exist, the error is quiet and actionable instead of a raw API dump. Setting DEBUG=sandbox:errors restores the request detail for debugging.

A misused command explains the right one

sh opens a plain interactive shell, so it takes no command of its own. The CLI can now return precise answers that rewrite the attempt into the command that does what you meant, whatever the command is.

Outdated installs warn you at creation time

create, sh, and run check for a newer published CLI and print an update notice when the install is behind. The check is cached to a file and refreshed at most once per hour; when a lookup does run it happens concurrently with the creation request, so it adds no latency. Creation defaults, such as the base image, are chosen client side, so an outdated global install silently keeps old defaults. Prerelease versions skip the check, and SANDBOX_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 disables it.

Learn more in the Sandbox CLI documentation.

title: Exploring Freecine APK: A Practical Guide for Developers and Technology Enthusiasts
description:
Mobile entertainment has changed significantly over the past few years. People now expect video applications to offer convenient navigation, responsive playback, and a consistent experience across different screen sizes. For developers, these expectations create interesting opportunities to explore how media applications are designed and built. Freecine APK is one example worth examining when discussing Android media apps, playlist management, and digital entertainment software.

This guide explores the Freecine APK concept from a technical perspective, explains the main considerations when evaluating a media application, and introduces useful development techniques for anyone interested in building their own video player.

Understanding Freecine APK

An APK, short for Android Package Kit, is the file format Android uses to distribute and install applications. Freecine APK generally refers to an Android installation package associated with an application using the Freecine name.

It is important to recognize that different websites may use the same or similar app names. Their versions, publishers, and advertised features may not be identical. Developers should therefore verify the source of an application before treating its functionality or technical implementation as confirmed.

One publicly listed application called Freecine describes itself as a media playlist organizer and player. Its Google Play listing mentions support for user-configured media sources, categorized content, favorites, and a continue-watching feature. These details apply to that particular listing and should not automatically be attributed to every Freecine-branded APK.

For developers, the broader lesson is that understanding an application begins with identifying its publisher, distribution channel, intended purpose, and supported features.

Features Worth Examining in a Media Application

When evaluating a media player, it helps to look beyond its appearance and consider how individual features contribute to usability and performance.

  1. Simple Navigation and Interface Design

A well-designed media application should help users find content without navigating through unnecessary menus. Clear categories, readable labels, recognizable icons, and consistent layouts can make a significant difference.

Android developers can achieve this using Jetpack Compose or traditional Android layouts. The most appropriate approach depends on the project requirements, existing codebase, and target devices.

  1. Media Organization

Organizing media into categories can improve the experience when users have extensive playlists or collections. Search, favorites, and recently played items can also reduce the time required to find previously viewed content.

From a development perspective, these features introduce useful topics such as data modeling, local storage, filtering, and efficient list rendering.

For example, a developer might store a user's favorite media identifiers locally and use them to retrieve the corresponding items whenever the application opens.

  1. Video Playback

Playback is one of the most important components of any video application. Users expect play and pause controls, seeking, appropriate buffering behavior, and reliable handling of interruptions.

Android developers can explore Media3 ExoPlayer, Google's modern media playback library, to implement these capabilities. It supports common playback workflows and provides tools for handling media sources, playback states, and player events.

Actual playback performance depends on the media format, device hardware, network conditions, and implementation quality.

  1. Compatibility With Different Screens

A media application designed for a mobile phone may need a different layout when used on a tablet or Android TV. Television interfaces generally require larger controls, clear focus indicators, and navigation that works with a remote control.

Developers should test different screen sizes, aspect ratios, and input methods instead of assuming that one layout will work equally well everywhere.

How Developers Can Build a Basic Android Media Player

Studying media applications can provide inspiration, but building a small working project is a practical way to understand the underlying technology.

Step 1: Configure the Development Environment

Start with Android Studio and create a new Android project. Choose a suitable minimum Android version and configure the dependencies required by your application.

For modern Android development, consider AndroidX Media3 ExoPlayer rather than starting with older playback APIs.

Step 2: Add the Media3 Dependency

In your app-level Gradle file, add the Media3 ExoPlayer library. Keep the library versions consistent across related Media3 dependencies.

For example:

dependencies {
implementation("androidx.media3:media3-exoplayer:")
implementation("androidx.media3:media3-ui:")
}

Replace with the current stable version appropriate for your project.

Step 3: Create a Player Interface

A basic video screen usually includes a playback view and controls. Media3 provides a PlayerView component that can display video and expose standard playback controls.

Your interface should also communicate useful states, such as loading, playback errors, and the end of a video.

Step 4: Connect a Test Media Source

During development, use a sample video that you own or have permission to access. For example, a player can be configured with a test media URL:

val mediaItem = MediaItem.fromUri(
sample-video.mp4
)

player.setMediaItem(mediaItem)
player.prepare()
player.play()

This snippet illustrates the basic workflow. The player must be initialized correctly, connected to the appropriate UI, and released when it is no longer needed. The example URL is a placeholder, not a working video source.

Step 5: Handle Errors and Lifecycle Events

A reliable player should account for network interruptions, unavailable media, unsupported formats, and playback failures.

Developers should also manage the player lifecycle carefully to avoid unnecessary resource consumption. Depending on the application's architecture, this may involve lifecycle-aware components and explicit cleanup when playback is finished or the screen is closed.

Improving Playback Performance

Smooth playback requires more than a play button. Several technical factors influence the final experience.

Buffering: Network delays can interrupt streaming. Appropriate buffering strategies and informative loading indicators help manage these situations.

Video resolution: High-resolution content can require more bandwidth and processing power. Applications should account for device capabilities and connection quality.

Memory management: Large media collections and unnecessary background tasks can affect responsiveness. Developers should avoid retaining unused player instances or loading excessive data into memory.

Testing: Test on physical devices as well as emulators when possible. Different processors, Android versions, and network conditions can produce different results.

These principles are useful when developing any Android media player, regardless of whether Freecine or another application inspired the project.

Security and Privacy Considerations

Security deserves particular attention when installing or evaluating an APK obtained outside a trusted app store.

Before installing an unfamiliar package, consider the following precautions:

Verify the publisher and download source wherever possible.

Scan downloaded files with reputable security tools, while remembering that a clean scan cannot guarantee safety.

Review requested permissions and question access that appears unrelated to the application's purpose.

Avoid entering sensitive credentials into an application whose identity and privacy practices cannot be verified.

Keep Android and other installed software updated.

Confirm that media sources are authorized to distribute the content they provide.

Developers building their own applications should also use secure network connections, protect sensitive information, handle errors without exposing private data, and publish a clear privacy policy.

A media player and the content sources it accesses are separate components. Evaluating one does not automatically establish that the other is safe, reliable, or legally authorized.

Legal and Responsible Media Access

Media technology makes it easier to organize and play digital content, but access to a file does not necessarily mean that its distribution is authorized.

When developing or testing a media application, use original content, appropriately licensed sample files, or sources that explicitly permit the intended use. If an application supports user-configured playlists, its documentation should explain that users are responsible for selecting lawful sources where applicable.

This approach helps developers build useful software while respecting copyright and the requirements that apply in their jurisdiction.

Why Media Applications Are Useful Learning Projects

A video player provides an opportunity to explore several important software engineering concepts in one project.

Developers can practice asynchronous programming, interface design, network communication, state management, application lifecycle handling, testing, and performance optimization. More advanced projects can introduce subtitle rendering, accessibility support, casting, and adaptive streaming.

Rather than attempting to reproduce an entire commercial application immediately, start with a small player and add features gradually. This makes problems easier to isolate and provides a clearer understanding of how each component works.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Freecine APK?

Freecine APK is a term used for Android installation packages associated with applications branded as Freecine. Because different sources may distribute different versions, verify the exact application and publisher before installing it.

Can developers use Freecine as a learning resource?

Developers can examine publicly available documentation, app listings, and observable user-interface behavior for general design ideas. They should not assume that an application's internal code is publicly available or copy proprietary assets without permission.

Which Android library is suitable for building a media player?

AndroidX Media3 ExoPlayer is a strong starting point for modern Android playback projects. The appropriate library and architecture depend on the application's specific requirements.

Does every Freecine APK offer the same features?

No such assumption should be made. Features and compatibility claims may differ between packages and distribution sources. Check the details for the specific version being evaluated.

Is an APK automatically safe because it installs successfully?

No. Successful installation only shows that Android accepted the package for installation. It does not prove that the application is trustworthy, free from malicious behavior, or compliant with relevant content licensing rules.

title: Semurg: local persistent memory for AI agents over MCP
description:
Agents forget everything when a session ends. Semurg is a memory for them: a knowledge graph, vectors and graph retrieval on one
engine, written from scratch, running on your own machine. Your agent connects over the Model Context Protocol, stores what it learns,
and finds it again in the next session, with every answer cited to where it came from. The node sends nothing to a hosted service. It
runs on Intel and AMD (x86_64) machines: on Ubuntu 24.04 directly, on Windows through WSL2 with Ubuntu 24.04, or in Docker on an x86_64
host. One node is free, with no licence key.

Today your agent remembers a piece of text together with the facts it found in it, and your node stores both once, in one scope on your own disk; in a later session your agent asks that scope a question and gets the facts back, each cited to the passage it came from.

What your agent gets

Seven memory tools over MCP, and the same seven calls over plain HTTP: memory_status, memory_remember, memory_recall,
memory_relate, memory_forget, memory_context and memory_document.

  • A knowledge graph with no schema to write. Entities, their types and the relationships between them. The classes and relations are recorded from what is stored, and one call reads them back so the next agent reuses them; keeping their spelling consistent is still the writer's job on this release, and the ontology post says exactly what is and is not automatic. A relationship may name an entity stored by an earlier call; one that names an entity neither listed in the call nor stored is refused by name, and nothing from that call is stored.
  • Questions, not only names. memory_context starts from every stored name in a question, walks the relationships around them and returns the facts and the passages that mention them.
  • Every answer is cited. Each item carries a citation: the document it came from and when that was stored, and for a passage or a fact read from text, the sentence it quotes, checked against the stored text before it is served. When a quote cannot be checked, the span is left empty and the reply says why, rather than showing an unchecked quote. A fact your agent sent without text is marked as asserted, so it is never shown as a quote.
  • Search by meaning, locally. With the node's embedding model installed, a question finds stored passages that match what was meant, not only the words. The model runs on your node.
  • Separate memories. Every call names a scope. Agents that share a scope share what they learn; a different scope stays private. One app can give each of its end users a memory of their own with user_id, and an X-Semurg-User header pins a connection to one of them, over MCP and HTTP alike: a call that names another user is refused. That keeps one app's users apart; between apps or teams, use separate API tokens.
  • Forget works at once. Forgetting an entity hides it, its facts and every passage linked to it, over MCP and every other API, from the moment the call answers. A passage that contains the name but was never linked to it stays, and the reply counts it in passages_retained, so you can forget that text too.
  • Answers that say when they are empty. When nothing stored matches, the reply says nothing_stored. Recall finds a stored name by its exact spelling, its letter case, a close spelling, or one whole word of a longer name ("Priya" finds Priya Raman), and says how it matched.
  • Answers that say how well they are supported. A stored name can share one word with a question it does not answer, so every context reply carries a grounding state: grounded when one cited item covers every content word of the question, grounded_by_meaning when a passage found by meaning answers a reworded question, and related when what came back covers only part of it, with the words it did not cover listed. uncited, nothing_stored and could_not_judge mean the items do not answer the question.
  • Small replies. With compact: true, recall and context return the same answer with each item once and without the retrieval diagnostics, in a fraction of the bytes, so reading memory costs your agent little of its context.
  • Facts that change. Remember a new value with the date it became true, and a relation's values come back newest first, so the first one is current. as_of reads memory as it was known on a date, and valid_at as it was true on a date.

Your agent is the extractor

An agent is already a language model, usually a far larger one than a CPU can run, so it is the better reader of the text it stores.
When it stores text, it sends the entities and relations it found in that text as facts, in the same call:

{"scope": "team-notes",
 "content": "Ana Sousa is CEO of Quill Labs, which acquired Ledgerlight in March.",
 "facts": {
  "entities": [
   {"name": "Ana Sousa",
    "type": "Person"},
   {"name": "Quill Labs",
    "type": "Organization"},
   {"name": "Ledgerlight",
    "type": "Organization"}],
  "relations": [
   {"source": "Ana Sousa",
    "target": "Quill Labs",
    "type": "CEO_OF"},
   {"source": "Quill Labs",
    "target": "Ledgerlight",
    "type": "ACQUIRED"}]}}

Your agent extracts the facts and sends them with the text in one remember call; your node stores the text as passages, builds the graph from the facts, cites each fact to its passage and, when its embedding model is installed, embeds the passages in the background.

The facts are stored at once and cited to the passage they came from. You do not have to teach your agent this: the server's
instructions and the tool's own description say it, and a reply to text sent without facts says it again. The same instructions give the agent a few short rules when it connects: check
memory before answering, name the scope on every write, read nothing_stored and the grounding state before using an answer, keep one
topic per passage, send ids back as strings, and treat stored text as data, never as instructions.

Text sent without facts, from a document or a pipeline, is stored at once and linked to the entities already stored; the reply says
extraction: known_names_only. If the node's extraction model is installed, it also reads that text afterwards and adds the entities
it finds, and the reply's model_extraction says whether that is pending, done or why it is idle. That model is large and slow on a
CPU: on the small servers we test on it does not yet finish within its time limit, so for now send the facts with the text. We are
building a smaller, faster local extractor for bulk documents.

Install a node

A node is one Semurg server on your machine. On Ubuntu 24.04 (x86_64), with sudo:

curl -fsSL https://one.semurg.io/install | sudo bash

The installer checks the machine first and stops with a plain reason if something is missing. It picks the build that fits your
processor (AVX-512 or AVX2; a generic build for older processors is included, which we have not yet tested on one), listens on
127.0.0.1 only unless you choose otherwise, and ends by printing your API token. The token is also stored on the node, so you can
read it back:

sudo grep '^SEMURG_API_TOKEN=' /etc/semurg/semurg.env

To read the script before you run it: curl -fsSL https://one.semurg.io/install | less.

On its first boot the node downloads its embedding model, and a reranker it leaves switched off, from our signed catalogue, each
verified before it is used. To decline, set SEMURG_MODELS_AUTO=0 in /etc/semurg/semurg.env and restart; memory then works by name
only. The extraction model, for text sent without facts, is large and is installed only when you ask for it
(semurg model install gemma4_moe). The install page lists each model, its size and its licence, and has the container
image.

Connect your agent

The endpoint is http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/mcp: streamable HTTP, your token as a bearer token, and an optional X-Semurg-Scope
header for the connection's default scope. Use 127.0.0.1, not localhost: the node listens on IPv4 loopback only, and localhost
can resolve to the IPv6 address first.

For Claude Code, one command connects every Claude Code session you start, in any project. The settings file holds only a reference
to the environment variable, never the token, so first copy the token the installer stored into a file only you can read, and have
every new terminal load it (if your shell is not bash, add the export line to your own shell's profile instead of ~/.bashrc):

mkdir -p ~/.config/semurg
(umask 077; sudo grep '^SEMURG_API_TOKEN=' /etc/semurg/semurg.env | cut -d= -f2- > ~/.config/semurg/token)
echo 'export SEMURG_API_TOKEN="$(cat ~/.config/semurg/token)"' >> ~/.bashrc
export SEMURG_API_TOKEN="$(cat ~/.config/semurg/token)"

Then add the node once, for your user:

claude mcp remove semurg -s user 2>/dev/null
claude mcp add-json --scope user semurg '{
  "type": "http",
  "url": "http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/mcp",
  "headers": {
    "Authorization": "Bearer ${SEMURG_API_TOKEN}",
    "X-Semurg-Scope": "default"
  }
}'
claude mcp list

claude mcp list should show semurg as connected. In a new session, tell the agent something worth keeping, then open another
session and ask about it. Persistent memory for Claude Code gives each repository its own scope
in six lines of CLAUDE.md.

To change the token later, sudo semurg admin api-token rotate <new-token> swaps it on the running node: the old one stops working
at once, with no restart. Then write the new token into ~/.config/semurg/token and open a new terminal, or every client that reads
that file is refused.

The agents page has the configuration for Claude Desktop, Cursor, the OpenAI Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Hermes Agent and
OpenClaw. It also has a complete program for each framework we test:

  • LangChain and LangGraph, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, the Microsoft Agent Framework and the OpenAI Agents SDK;
  • Google ADK, Pydantic AI, Mastra and the Vercel AI SDK;
  • LangChain for Elixir and Jido.

Each program stores facts and reads them back, and the page names the release it last ran on in our tests.

Guides

  • Give your agent persistent memory with MCP in five minutes: install, check the memory over plain HTTP, connect your agent, and watch a fact cross from one client to another.
  • Connecting to Semurg over MCP: the endpoint at the level a client author needs, the protocol versions it speaks, the tools, and how a refusal comes back.
  • One memory per end user: one app, many users, none of them meeting.
  • The develop page: the memory routes over HTTP, the limits each call refuses by name, and a rules file you can drop into your repository as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md so a coding agent uses the memory well. Every route and parameter is listed in llms.txt.

What it does not do yet

Said plainly, so you can plan around it:

  • No Mac and no ARM build: it runs on x86_64 only, on Ubuntu 24.04 directly, on Windows through WSL2 with Ubuntu 24.04, or in Docker on an x86_64 host. The installer refuses other Linux distributions for now, and Apple Silicon cannot run it, natively or emulated.
  • Without an embedding model, memory works by name only, and recall, context and text replies say so (meaning: not_armed).
  • Search by meaning covers stored passages. Entity names and facts stored without a passage are found by name, not by meaning. Meaning search is exact up to 10,000 passages per scope; above that, it answers could_not_judge with the count, never a partial list, until the per-scope index ships.
  • The node's own extraction of text sent without facts does not yet finish within its time limit on the small servers we test on. Facts your agent sends are stored at once.
  • We have not published a benchmark against other agent memory products yet. When we do, it will name the release it ran on.
  • Forgotten data is unreachable at once, but it is not yet erased from the disk: its bytes stay until space reclaim ships, and anyone with access to the node's disk or a backup of it can still read them. If your obligations require physical erasure, this release does not meet them yet.
  • A stopped or killed node loses nothing it acknowledged. A power cut or operating-system crash can lose the last few seconds of acknowledged writes, because the filesystem records a file's new length a few seconds after the write.
  • There is no export or backup command yet.

Tell us what breaks

Install it, connect your agent, and tell us where it falls short. When a call fails, the reply names the limit it hit and what to
change, so the reply is your bug report: paste it to us on the contact page.

Every behaviour this post describes was checked on 2026-10-15 against the tool descriptions, the refusal catalogue and the
installer of the release that publishes this text.

title: EigDiff: Eigensample Diffusion - or how to significantly reduce training dataset size with marginal performance variation?
description:
arXiv:2610.20999v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models are notoriously expensive to train, requiring large-scale datasets to learn how to gradually reverse the noise from images over multiple small denoising steps. Current approaches focus on distilling the number of diffusion steps, neglecting potential redundancies of the training data. In this paper, we explore the potential of harnessing eigensamples to train diffusion models on significantly smaller datasets, while preserving model performance. To mitigate the sensitivity to affine transformations of eigenimages, we harness the latent space of a pre-trained CLIP model. We next compute latent eigenvectors by performing principal component analysis (PCA) in CLIP space. Further, we employ eigenvectors as reference points to guide the selection of a representative training set comprising comprising both exemplars (images whose embeddings are closest to eigenvectors) and diverse images. Our comprehensive experiments with different diffusion models applied on multiple datasets indicate that our approach (EigDiff) can reduce training data by up to 14x and accelerate subset selection by up to 1607x, with marginal performance differences.

title: SHIP: Structured and Hierarchical Insight with Privacy
description:
arXiv:2610.21048v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Extracting insights from textual data while protecting user privacy is increasingly important. Existing methods produce private insights in diverse forms for different analytical purposes, making their utility difficult to assess and compare. In this work, we formulate differentially private (DP) insights as reusable representations for answering analytical queries, providing a common basis for utility assessment. Answering these queries, however, requires fine-grained details and cross-attribute statistics that existing representations may omit. To capture this information, we introduce Structured and Hierarchical Insight with Privacy (SHIP), which automatically maps queries to attributes, builds a hierarchical hybrid taxonomy, and releases a DP synthetic table for further analysis. We also develop an evaluation protocol based primarily on QA performance and structured fidelity. Our experiments demonstrate SHIP's strong performance on both measures relative to existing private insight baselines, while identifying queries that remain challenging for structured representations.

title: Planning Commitment of LLM under Partial Observability
description:
arXiv:2610.21108v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based planning agents commit to plans of different lengths before interacting with a partially observable environment. Some aggressively commit to a long plan based on assumptions about unobserved states, while others conservatively plan only over what they have observed. Both behaviors emerge implicitly in pre-trained models, whether the LLM outputs a plan directly or generates a PDDL formulation for a classical solver. Aggressive commitment risks costly failures, while conservative commitment risks excessive LLM calls. This choice pits safety against efficiency, a trade-off that has been neither characterized systematically nor made controllable. We investigate aggressive and conservative LLM planners and formalizers on two partially observable domains, where priors are provided as either explicit statistics or common-sense knowledge. Across three LLMs, both strategies reach similar accuracy. Conservative methods achieve fewer failed attempts (safety) at the cost of more API calls (efficiency). Aggressive methods fail more often but replan efficiently only when priors are informative. Interestingly, analysis shows that LLMs treat the provided priors nearly as facts, which risks failure when priors are unreliable. We also explore hybrid strategies with tunable hyperparameters that adjust the balance between safety and efficiency.
