title: 190,000 Star Systems and a Million Planets: How I'm Building GalaxyAtlas with AI Agents
description:
Hi! My name is Yaroslav, and I work as an Agentic Engineering Architect at SoftServe. In my spare time, I enjoy experimenting with AI and trying out ideas at home that may seem completely absurd or impossible at first glance. Today, I'd like to tell you about one of those experiments: GalaxyAtlas.

It's a browser-based 3D galaxy with approximately 190,000 star systems and 1,000,000 procedurally generated planets. It features spaceships, the ability to land on planetary surfaces, explore worlds, add, edit, and customize planets, encounter different creatures, or simply complete the main mission: searching for an ancient artifact.
One important distinction: the 195,000 stars on the map are not 195,000 fully simulated star systems. Some are used to visualize the galaxy's structure, while detailed planet generation is tied to a catalog of objects.
In the game, you can select a star, enter its planetary system, pilot a spaceship, land, step onto the surface, and explore vegetation, creatures, weather phenomena, and individually customized worlds.
And all of this runs without a separate game client. You just need to open a browser.

But for me, the most interesting part of this project isn't the galaxy itself. Above all, GalaxyAtlas is an experiment in how far you can go when developing a complex software product if you change the engineering process itself with AI.

How It All Started
In early September 2026, I was actively experimenting with GPT-6 Astra. It was a good opportunity to test not only the model's capabilities but also how it behaves when working on complex tasks over an extended period. I'd already encountered some problems in earlier experiments. A large model can generate mountains of AI slop, but that doesn't mean it can automatically turn what it generated into a stable, working system. In one experiment, prolonged work on an autonomous simulation exhausted the available limits very quickly. Repeated cycles of generation, testing, and fixing taught me a painful lesson: without very clear criteria, an agent can burn through a substantial budget on endless improvements. So I decided to make my next experiment more focused.

GPT Sites: From an Idea to a Working Prototype
One of the first tools I used for the experiment was GPT Sites. For me, it was a way to validate an idea quickly without having to manually set up the entire publishing process. At an early stage, I managed to build a browser-based atlas using data on more than 109,000 real stars from the HYG catalog and a procedural model of the galaxy. The most important result wasn't the number of stars but the speed at which I went from a concept to an interactive system. Even in the early iterations, it became clear that the prototype could go much further: flights, planets, surfaces, physical environments, different biomes, and gameplay mechanics. But rapid prototyping and long-term product development are two different challenges.
Once a project includes dozens of interdependent mechanics, you need to manage versions, regressions, code structure, performance, and rules for making changes. Eventually, the project evolved into GalaxyAtlas and got its own domain.

Real Astronomical Data
The early model was based on HYG Database v4.1, which contains information about real stars. The first configuration used data on 109,401 stars. This made it possible to display objects from a real stellar catalog with their coordinates and characteristics. But the actual Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of stars, so a single catalog isn't enough to create a visually convincing galaxy. That's why I decided to add procedural generation of the galactic structure—a mathematical model that shapes the galaxy itself.
One early configuration used a disk radius of approximately 15.3 kiloparsecs, a spiral-arm pitch angle of 13°, and a central bar orientation of 27°. To visualize rotation, I used a simplified model in which velocity depends on distance from the center. This isn't a full N-body simulation that calculates gravitational interactions among hundreds of thousands of bodies. It's a mathematically controlled procedural model that creates a galactic structure without requiring extremely expensive physics calculations. This is where I encountered an interesting architectural challenge. If hundreds of thousands of stars are on screen, you can't treat each one as a fully independent game object whose every detail is calculated continuously. So a core principle of development became moving away from full detail across the entire scene and toward rendering only the detail the user needs at a particular moment.

As GalaxyAtlas evolved, its scale increased to approximately 190,000–195,000 accessible star systems. Let me explain what 'generated' actually means.
It doesn't mean there are a million ready-made 3D planet models sitting on a server somewhere. Storing, transferring, and rendering that much information simultaneously would be extremely expensive. Instead, the project uses a procedural approach: the properties of systems and planets can be reconstructed from a set of parameters and rules.
When a user selects a particular star, the system can construct its planetary environment. As the user approaches a planet, more detail is required. Upon landing, the system needs a surface, vegetation, an atmosphere, creatures, and interactive objects. You don't need the entire galaxy to be fully generated all the time. You need to be able to reconstruct the required part of the world when it's needed. Stable identifiers and seed-based generation are particularly important here. If generation is deterministic, the same seed produces the same result as long as the rules remain unchanged. That lets you revisit the same planet rather than get an entirely new world on every visit. There is, however, a trade-off: changing the generation algorithm can accidentally alter worlds users already know.
That's why generator versioning and the challenges of keeping procedural seeds stable have become a separate architectural problem for me. I'll describe this in another article someday.

Three.js and Browser Performance
Three.js became the foundation of GalaxyAtlas's 3D rendering.
One of my main requirements was that the project must work without installing a separate game client. A user opens a link and immediately enters the galaxy. That brings a whole set of constraints. In a browser, you have to consider not only polygon counts but also GPU memory usage, material and shader complexity, the number of draw calls, and JavaScript execution on the main thread. GalaxyAtlas isn't a static scene, either. Users can switch between the galactic map, space flight, approaching a planet, and exploring its surface. Each mode has different detail requirements. For example, when viewing the entire galaxy, there's no point in building high-polygon models of every planet. But during landing, you need terrain, atmospheric, and local-environment detail.
For a system like this, I had to analyze and apply several key architectural principles:

  1. Generate only the content that's needed—lazy generation.
  2. Use different levels of detail at different scales—LOD.
  3. Reuse geometry, materials, and textures.
  4. Control the number of active objects and effects.
  5. Release resources when switching between scenes. This isn't just about optimizing a pretty picture. It's a fundamental trade-off between the size of a virtual world and the amount of data you actually need to process. I also experimented with atmospheric effects, fog, particles, surface textures, and lighting. The problem is that adding one more visual effect is fairly easy. Keeping everything running smoothly on an ordinary computer is much harder. So every visual improvement had to be evaluated not only in terms of image quality but also rendering cost.

How I Experiment with Different AI Models
Let's return to the project's main goal. I wasn't interested in simply telling a model to 'make a game' and expecting everything to happen quickly and cheaply. I wanted to understand how to organize development so that AI genuinely helps build and maintain a complex system. In my broader experiments with AI-assisted development, I used and compared different approaches and models: GPT-6 Astra, faster and cheaper models from the GPT family, Claude, and even local models, including Qwen3.
The key thing to remember is that the most expensive and powerful model shouldn't handle every task. Complex architectural analysis, changes across multiple files, testing, and autonomous feature implementation call for one level of reasoning. Generating repetitive structures, preparing simple code snippets, formatting documentation, or making local configuration changes call for quite another.
If you delegate all these tasks to a single expensive model, costs will quickly rise. In large agent sessions, a significant portion of resources is also spent not on writing the final code but on repeatedly reading files, reconstructing context, analyzing logs, attempting unsuccessful fixes, and rerunning tests.
That's exactly what I wanted to improve.

Subagents and Skills Instead of One Giant Prompt
At some point, I began treating GalaxyAtlas development not as one continuous conversation with AI but as a set of distinct engineering processes. Broadly speaking, I divided the system into several areas:

  1. Galaxy & Procedural Generation—working with the star catalog, the galaxy's spatial structure, and the generation of star systems, planets, biomes, and other procedural content.
  2. 3D Rendering & Performance—Three.js, shaders, materials, lighting, geometry optimization, memory management, and performance.
  3. Gameplay & World Interaction—space flight, landing, planetary exploration, object interactions, and gameplay scenarios.
  4. Content & Customization—planet stories, biome configurations, unique creatures, themed scenes, and content.
  5. Testing & Quality—checking for regressions, generation stability, scene behavior, and functional acceptance criteria. Why use skills? Skills are a way to formalize recurring engineering procedures. Instead of explaining architectural constraints and change-management rules again in every new session, you can capture them in separate instructions. For example, a procedural-generation skill might specify:
  6. How to keep seed-based generation stable.
  7. Which data contracts must not change without a migration.
  8. How to check whether new generation logic remains compatible with existing worlds.
  9. Which performance criteria need to be considered. A Three.js skill might contain rules for managing GPU resources, cleaning up objects, sharing materials, and checking performance. The idea is fairly simple: knowledge about the system shouldn't exist only in the context window of the current conversation. This approach also helps reuse engineering practices across different tasks and models.

It's Important to Understand That 'Code Generation Isn't Always the Most Expensive Part of AI Development'

In earlier experiments with powerful models, I quickly encountered a mountain of burned tokens (and wasted weekly or monthly usage limits). This was especially obvious during large tasks involving many iterations. An agent writes code, runs a check, gets an error, analyzes it, rewrites the code, and runs the check again. At first glance, everything seems to be working as intended. But without clearly defined tasks, a model can keep repeating that cycle far longer than makes economic sense. Sometimes a person would realize in a few minutes that it's time to change the approach instead of making a twentieth attempt to fix the same thing. That experience led to my main rules and recommendations for cost optimization.

  1. It's essential to separate tasks by complexity. Use cheaper models for small, well-defined tasks, and bring in more powerful models when complex reasoning or orchestration is actually needed.
  2. Limit the scope of context. A subagent working on landscape generation shouldn't have to reread the entire project every time, including UI code, localization strings, and spaceship controls.
  3. Pass artifacts, not the entire conversation history. One process might produce a short specification, a diff, an interface, or a set of tests. The next agent needs that result—not thousands of previous messages.
  4. ALWAYS control execution loops. In complex experiments, I've seen agents continue working without making meaningful progress. That's why you need limits—for example, on the number of attempts—and checkpoints, as well as CLEAR, MANDATORY conditions for when a task is considered complete.
  5. Validate results with tools, not just another LLM. If a system property can be checked with an automated test, there's no reason to ask an expensive model to evaluate it from scratch every time. For example, you can test the stability of procedural generation by regenerating a set of fixed seeds. At this stage, I don't want to claim a universal percentage for the savings. But believe me, after optimization, the difference became very noticeable.

What's Next?
GalaxyAtlas isn't a commercial game built by a large team over many years with a multimillion-dollar budget. It's my personal experiment. Over time, I've drawn several conclusions for myself. I'm continuing to experiment, expand planet customization, make procedural worlds more diverse, work on more realistic surfaces and creatures, and add new gameplay scenarios.

Another major area of focus for me is continuing to improve AI-assisted development: refining contracts between agents, experimenting with skills, introducing automated checks, and measuring the real token economics of using different models.
GalaxyAtlas may never become a major commercial game. But the project is already fulfilling its main purpose: it's essentially my at-home experimentation lab. And that's probably the most interesting part. I'd encourage you to try building something similar yourself. In the meantime, come explore—it's free and requires no registration at galaxyatlas.space

title: The VRAM Parking Problem: Eliminating the 60% Idle GPU Tax
description:
Originally published by **Asif Muhammad Iqbal (Founder & CEO at Logic42)* at https://logic42.ai/articles/vram-parking-idle-gpu-tax-finops.*

The VRAM Parking Problem: Eliminating the 60% Idle GPU Tax

The VRAM parking problem is the enterprise financial failure where dedicated 80GB and 144GB GPU nodes sit statically reserved for specific LLMs, running at 20% to 35% utilization while racking up 24/7 bills. In 2026, paying $35 an hour for idle 8x H100 nodes during off-peak hours has become indefensible corporate waste.

What is the VRAM Parking Problem?

The VRAM parking problem occurs when an organization permanently loads a static model checkpoint into dedicated GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM), reserving expensive compute capacity regardless of live user concurrency.

When your platform team deploys a specialized 70B parameter model for legal analysis or internal customer support, they allocate two to four H100 GPUs exclusively to that model. During business hours, it processes steady requests. But at night, on weekends, and between user turns, that model sits idle.

Because standard deep learning serving frameworks historically required models to stay resident in memory to avoid cold starts, you pay full hourly rates for GPUs doing zero math.

How Much Capital Does VRAM Parking Actually Waste?

Production telemetry across our enterprise client audits shows that dedicated internal LLM instances experience less than 28% aggregate compute saturation over a 30-day window. On a typical 8-node H100 cluster, this idle capacity translates to roughly $160,000 in wasted annual spend per node.

The Root Cause: Static Weights on Monolithic Serving Engines

Legacy inference architectures treat GPU memory like physical real estate: one model per container, one container per GPU group.

This model breaks down under enterprise traffic patterns:

STATIC ALLOCATION (The VRAM Parking Trap)
Node 1 (8x H100 - $35/hr):
┌───────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┐
│ Legal-70B Model (Resident)    │ IDLE VRAM (Unused 72% of Day) │
└───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┘
Node 2 (8x H100 - $35/hr):
┌───────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┐
│ Finance-70B Model (Resident)  │ IDLE VRAM (Unused 65% of Day) │
└───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┘
Total Cost: $70/hr ($50,400/mo) for ~25% average utilization.


DYNAMIC VRAM VIRTUALIZATION (Unified Base + Multiplexing)
Single Shared Node (8x H100 - $35/hr):
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Base Foundation Weights (e.g., Llama-3.3-70B Backbone in HBM) │
├───────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┤
│ LoRA Adapter: Legal (Loaded)  │ LoRA Adapter: Finance (Loaded)│
├───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┤
│ Dynamic PagedAttention Pool + Sub-second NVMe Adapter Cache   │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Total Cost: $35/hr ($25,200/mo) at 78% sustained utilization.

When you host five different fine-tuned models across five separate dedicated clusters, you don't have five times the traffic. You just have five times the idle memory overhead.

Benchmarks: Static Hosting vs. Dynamic VRAM Multiplexing

Our internal benchmarks illustrate the financial divergence between static dedicated instances and dynamic multiplexed serving:

Architecture Pattern Peak VRAM Saturation Off-Peak Waste Monthly Cost (per 5 Workloads) Cold-Start Overhead
Static Reserved Clusters 31% 82% $126,000 0 ms
Serverless Cold-Start (Naive) 92% 0% $24,000 8,000 – 14,000 ms
Unified Multiplexed Substrate 84% 14% $42,000 < 45 ms

Naive serverless cloud endpoints save money on idle time, but their 10-second cold starts destroy user experience for interactive business applications. The real engineering goal is dynamic multiplexing: keeping base weights warm while hot-swapping task adapters in milliseconds.

Three Engineering Rules to Eliminate the Idle GPU Tax

You don't need to surrender low-latency inference to stop burning budget. Implement these three architectural shifts:

1. Consolidate Around Shared Base Backbones with Multi-LoRA

Stop fine-tuning full model checkpoints. If you have three domain tasks (contracts, code review, and customer support), fine-tune them as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters on top of a single shared base model (such as Llama 3.3 70B).

Load the base model into VRAM once. At request time, use modern serving engines like vLLM or S-LoRA to apply the specific adapter weights on the fly for each incoming token batch. You can serve 50 specialized tasks from a single cluster without duplicating base memory.

2. Implement Sub-Second Weight Streaming via PCIe Gen5 / NVMe

When a specialized model hasn't received traffic in 15 minutes, page its adapter weights out of VRAM into local high-speed PCIe Gen5 NVMe storage.

Using kernel-bypass technologies like GPUDirect Storage (GDS), you can stream adapter weights back into HBM in under 40 milliseconds when a new request hits the gateway:

# Verify GPUDirect Storage (GDS) throughput to GPU memory
gdscheck -p
# Ensure NVMe to VRAM bandwidth exceeds 24 GB/s per socket

Your users never notice a cold start, and your VRAM allocator reclaims 60% of its working memory.

3. Build a Time-of-Day Egress & Batch Arbitrage Gateway

Internal enterprise workloads have clear temporal boundaries. Analytical batch jobs (log summarization, semantic re-indexing, compliance audits) don't need instant turnaround.

Configure your AI Gateway to queue background batch tasks during off-peak night windows (10 PM to 6 AM). Saturate your warm GPU clusters with deferred background work when interactive human users are asleep, driving compute efficiency from 25% to above 85%.

What FinOps Teams Must Measure Before Q4

Before your executive committee locks in the 2027 IT capital budget, pull these metrics from your cluster telemetry:

  1. Effective GPU Wattage Saturation: Measure actual Tensor Core activity (via DCGM metrics), not just whether memory is allocated. If your GPUs consume 180W on a 700W TDP ceiling, your cluster is parked.
  2. Adapter-to-Backbone Consolidation Ratio: Aim for at least 4 active LoRA task adapters per resident base foundation model.
  3. Off-Peak Token Throughput: Ratio of daytime interactive tokens to nighttime batch tokens. A healthy ratio approaches 1:1.

The Takeaway

Buying dedicated GPU clusters and leaving them pinned to static model checkpoints is the modern equivalent of leasing an entire office tower and only turning the lights on for two hours a day. High-bandwidth memory is the most expensive silicon on earth. Stop parking dead weights in VRAM. Unify your backbones, stream your adapters from NVMe, and demand unit economics that match your actual business demand.

title: WebAssembly in Firefox: DWARF Debugging, SIMD, Threads, and Performance Profiling
description:
WebAssembly is a binary instruction format that runs in browsers. Firefox has had strong Wasm support since Firefox 52 (2017). Here's what developers need to know about Wasm in Firefox — including debugging tools that most guides skip.

Firefox's Wasm Support

Firefox's Wasm support is maintained by Mozilla's SpiderMonkey team. Key capabilities:

  • Wasm MVP (baseline): Full support since Firefox 52
  • Threads and SharedArrayBuffer: Supported (requires COEP/COOP headers)
  • SIMD: Supported (Firefox 89+)
  • Exceptions: Supported (Firefox 100+)
  • GC proposal: Supported (Firefox 120+)
  • Tail calls: Supported
  • Component Model: In progress

Firefox's SpiderMonkey compiles Wasm using a tiered approach:

  1. Baseline compiler: Fast compilation, slower execution (immediate)
  2. Optimizing compiler (Ion): Slower compilation, faster execution (background, replaces baseline)

Running Wasm in Firefox 

// Fetch and instantiate a .wasm file
const response = await fetch('module.wasm');
const bytes = await response.arrayBuffer();
const { instance } = await WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes, {
  imports: {
    memory: new WebAssembly.Memory({ initial: 10 }),
    table: new WebAssembly.Table({ initial: 0, element: 'anyfunc' })
  }
});

// Call exported function
instance.exports.add(2, 3);  // 5

Streaming instantiation (faster, starts compiling while downloading):

const result = await WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming(
  fetch('module.wasm'),
  imports
);

Debugging Wasm in Firefox

Firefox is the only browser with full, native WebAssembly debugging in DevTools. This is a significant advantage.

Prerequisites: Your Wasm must include DWARF debug info. Emscripten adds this with:

emcc -g main.c -o output.js
# -g includes DWARF debug info in the .wasm file

Or with wasm-pack for Rust:

wasm-pack build --debug

Setting breakpoints in Wasm source:

  1. DevTools → Debugger
  2. Sources panel shows .wasm files and, if DWARF is present, the original source files (C, C++, Rust)
  3. Click the line number in the original source to set a breakpoint
  4. When Wasm executes that function, Firefox breaks into the debugger at the source location

What you see when paused:

  • Local variables in Wasm memory (with types if DWARF has them)
  • Call stack showing original function names
  • Step through source code lines

This is revolutionary for C/C++ → Wasm workflows. No need to correlate binary offsets with source lines manually.

Without DWARF: You still get the Wasm text format (WAT) in the Debugger, but with hex addresses and no type info. Harder to debug but still possible.

Wasm + Rust: The Best Experience

Rust → Wasm debugging in Firefox with wasm-pack:

# Install tools
cargo install wasm-pack

# Build with debug info
wasm-pack build --debug --target web

# Build for production (optimized, no debug)
wasm-pack build --release --target web

// Load the wasm-pack generated package
import init, { greet } from './pkg/my_wasm.js';

await init();
greet('World');  // Calls Rust function

Firefox Debugger with Rust/Wasm:

  • Original .rs file shows in Sources panel
  • Set breakpoints in Rust code
  • Step through line by line
  • Variables show with Rust types

Emscripten and Firefox

Emscripten compiles C/C++ to Wasm. Firefox is well-supported:

# Compile with debug info
emcc main.c -o main.js -g

# Compile with optimizations
emcc main.c -o main.js -O2

# With filesystem support
emcc main.c -o main.js -s EXPORTED_FUNCTIONS="['_main']" --preload-file data/

Emscripten-generated glue code: Emscripten generates JavaScript that handles memory, imports, and exports. This code runs in Firefox without issues.

ASYNCIFY: Emscripten's ASYNCIFY allows C/C++ code with blocking calls to work with JavaScript's async model:

emcc main.c -o main.js -s ASYNCIFY

Firefox handles ASYNCIFY-compiled Wasm correctly.

Performance Profiling

Firefox's Performance panel now profiles Wasm:

  1. DevTools → Performance → Start recording
  2. Run your Wasm-heavy code
  3. Stop
  4. Flame chart shows Wasm functions by name (if exported or if DWARF names are present)

Memory profiling for Wasm:

// Check current Wasm memory usage
const memory = instance.exports.memory;
console.log('Wasm memory:', memory.buffer.byteLength, 'bytes');

// Grow memory
memory.grow(10);  // Add 10 pages (640KB)

In about:memory → Measure, search for "wasm" to see Wasm memory allocation.

Threads and SharedArrayBuffer

For multi-threaded Wasm, you need specific HTTP headers:

Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin

Without these, SharedArrayBuffer is not available (security restriction after Spectre).

Test in Firefox:

typeof SharedArrayBuffer !== 'undefined'  // true if headers are set

In local development:
For localhost, Firefox relaxes the COEP requirement, so local Wasm threads work without headers. For deployed sites, headers are required.

SIMD Performance

Wasm SIMD enables 128-bit vector operations, useful for:

  • Image processing
  • Audio/video codecs
  • Physics simulations
  • Machine learning inference 
;; Wasm SIMD example (WAT format)
(module
  (func (export "add_vectors") (param v128 v128) (result v128)
    local.get 0
    local.get 1
    i32x4.add
  )
)

Firefox SIMD support: Firefox 89+ supports Wasm SIMD. The Rust wasm-pack ecosystem uses SIMD by default for performance.

Detect SIMD support:

WebAssembly.validate(new Uint8Array([
  0x00, 0x61, 0x73, 0x6d,  // wasm magic
  0x01, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00,  // version
  // ... minimal SIMD module ...
]))

Or check crossOriginIsolated && typeof SIMD !== 'undefined' (the newer way).

Wasm Size Optimization

Wasm files can be large. Optimization for production:

wasm-opt (from Binaryen):

wasm-opt -O3 -o output.opt.wasm input.wasm

wasm-snip (remove unused code):

cargo install wasm-snip
wasm-snip input.wasm --snip-rust-fmt-code > output.wasm

Brotli compression: Firefox supports Brotli decompression. Compress your .wasm files with Brotli for smaller transfers. Wasm compresses extremely well (typically 5-10x).

Summary: Firefox's Wasm Advantages

  • Native DWARF debugging: The standout feature — debug original C/Rust source code
  • Full feature support: SIMD, threads, exceptions, GC
  • SpiderMonkey's tiered compiler: Good startup (baseline) + good peak performance (Ion)
  • Reliable behavior: Mozilla's team actively contributes to the Wasm spec

For Wasm debugging specifically, Firefox is the better choice over Chrome. The DWARF integration in Firefox DevTools is mature and makes debugging Wasm in the original source language practical.

title: Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches
description:
arXiv:2610.21126v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse KV compression reduces long-context inference costs by retaining selected historical states, yet these states typically keep their coordinates from the full history. Under Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), gaps left by evicted tokens continue to affect query-key matching, potentially limiting the use of retained evidence. We study post-selection positional geometry on a fixed selector-produced cache, examining how positional organization affects the use of retained information and which coordinate and continuation rules improve answer quality. To reorganize this geometry, we propose RoPERelay, which assigns compact, order-preserving RoPE coordinates, relocates cached key phases through inverse rotation and re-rotation, and synchronizes the current query and subsequent generation. It reuses existing K/V without renewed selection, historical re-prefill, or additional cache budget. Across 36 comparisons spanning two models, six sparse selectors, and three long-term memory tasks, RoPERelay improves answer quality in 32 cases. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with BM25 on LongMemEval-S, accuracy increases from 23.6% to 35.4%. Measured complete-request time overhead is approximately 1%-3% in the evaluated configurations. These findings establish positional organization as a distinct optimization dimension for sparse KV caches after content selection.

title: Introducing JointJS for React: Production-grade diagramming for React applications
description:
Most diagramming libraries seem promising at first. You can spin up a demo in ten minutes, and it feels like you’ve found the perfect fit. But after a few months, you’re building undo/redo from scratch, fighting to keep the diagram state in sync with your backend, running into roadblocks when customizing UX to your needs, and noticing performance lags as your data grows.


Most diagramming libraries take you just far enough to be committed, but fall short when it comes to building a polished, production-ready product, especially on a tight timeline.

Behind the scenes, the hard part of building a diagramming application isn’t drawing boxes and lines, because every library already does that. The real challenge is supporting the sophisticated interactions users expect (UX/UI), from a modern, intuitive, accessible interface to scalability.

As your diagrams grow from a few nodes to hundreds or thousands, performance has to keep up. And if you’re working in React, you want an integration that feels like React, not a constant struggle with side effects and useRefs.

What JointJS for React actually is

JointJS has been powering diagramming applications used by millions of people for over a decade, from AI workflow builders and BPMN modelers to industrial automation dashboards, data modeling tools, and much more. Industry leaders worldwide trust it for diagrams that need to work reliably in production.

The JointJS engine solves hard problems, including smart routing algorithms that avoid node overlap, consistent hit testing at any zoom level, DOM management, exceptional UX, outstanding performance, and memory management in production environments.

JointJS for React brings that trusted engine directly to React. This isn’t just a wrapper or a clunky compatibility layer, but a truly idiomatic React API built on top of JointJS.

Diagram state is React state, with a core wrapper component (GraphProvider / Diagram) that manages and provides it to child components, directly connecting the JointJS engine with React’s lifecycle. There’s no hidden state, no imperative API calls, and no synchronization headaches between React’s render cycle and the canvas. What’s in your state is exactly what’s on the screen.

Here’s what a simple JointJS app in React looked like until now, and what it will look like going forward.

Before — JointJS 4.2

// DO NOT USE - Old way of integrating JointJS with React

import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
import { dia, shapes } from '@joint/plus';

function JointJs() {
  const canvas = useRef<Element | null>(null);

   useEffect(() => {
       const graph = new dia.Graph();

       const paper = new dia.Paper({
           model: graph,
           background: {
               color: '#F8F9FA',
           },
           frozen: true,
           async: true,
           cellViewNamespace: shapes
       });

       canvas.current?.appendChild(paper.el);

       const rect = new shapes.standard.Rectangle({
          type: 'standard.Rectangle',
          position: { x: 100, y: 100 },
          size: { width: 100, height: 50 },
          attrs: { label: { text: 'Hello World' } },
       });

       graph.addCell(rect);
       paper.unfreeze();

       return () => {
           paper.remove();
       };

   }, []);

   return (
       <div className="canvas" ref={canvas}/>
   );
}

export default JointJs;

The old approach isn’t wrong, but it’s at odds with React’s model. Setup happens inside a useEffect, you access Paper through useRef, and you’re stuck with manual cleanup.

After — JointJS for React

// New way — JointJS for React

  import { GraphProvider, Paper } from '@joint/react';

  const initialCells = [
    {
      type: 'element',
      position: { x: 100, y: 100 },
      data: { label 'Hello World' },
    },
  ];

  export default function App() {
    return (
      <GraphProvider initialCells={initialCells}>
        <Paper className="canvas" />
      </GraphProvider>
    );
  }

JointJS for React fits right in with the rest of your React codebase. You declare what you want, and the framework takes care of the rest. It’s not just more elegant, but actually simpler and more intuitive, too.

The difference between JointJS for React and JointJS+ for React

In this article, we’ll focus on JointJS+ for React, so it’s worth noting what the actual differences from the open-source version of the library are. Both versions are based on the JointJS diagramming engine.

JointJS for React is a free, community-driven diagramming library. It gives you the core SVG + HTML rendering engine, a solid API, and building blocks for flowcharts, UML, and other diagramming applications. (If you give the open-source version a try and find it helpful, consider leaving a star on GitHub. It’s a small thing, but it means a lot to the team – thanks!))

JointJS+ for React is a commercial extension built on the same core engine, adding numerous ready-to-use UI plugins for snapping, panning, zooming, tooltips, and context menus, plus advanced shapes/styling options on top of what's in the open-source version. It also adds production-focused components not in JointJS at all, like the CommandManager for unlimited undo/redo history tracking, multi-select, and Snaplines/measurement shapes for precision alignment.

JointJS+ includes everything in JointJS and builds on top of it, so it's really a question of whether you want to build the UI layer yourself or have the library do the heavy lifting for you.

Download the latest package, including JointJS+ for React, using npm or from our customer portal. If your update subscription expired, reach out to us for re-activation.

New to JointJS+?
Start a 30-day no-commitment trial, which now includes JointJS+ for React.

AI Workflow Builder with JointJS+ for React

Workflow editors like pipeline designers, approval flows, and data-processing graphs are among the most common diagramming apps teams build, and they’re a great benchmark for any library. They let you quickly see whether a tool handles both the basics and the edge cases.

Rendering boxes and arrows is easy; what takes significant effort in development are the editing interactions users expect, connection rules that keep the graph semantically valid, configuration options, and performance that holds up as your diagram grows. This demo directly addresses those challenges.

Live demo: https://www.jointjs.com/demos/ai-workflow-builder

The same engine powering this AI Workflow Builder also drives BPMN editors, industrial automation (SCADA/HMI), energy network visualization, circuit design, data modeling tools, and more. The domain might change, but the engine’s strengths remain the same. A workflow editor puts most of these capabilities to the test, making it the perfect starting point.

1. Diagram basics done right

The diagram nodes in this demo (Input, AI Agent, Tool, Output) aren’t just rectangular boxes—they’re fully configurable UI components. Each node can render arbitrary HTML content, including headers, icons, text areas, select boxes, sliders, and other interactive controls. Combined with visual cues like colored icons and port legends, the graph remains easy to scan and understand at a glance.

// src/components/nodes/render-node.tsx

function NodeBody({ data }: { data: ConfigNodeData }) {
 switch (data.kind) {
   case 'input':  return <TextInputBody data={data} />;
   case 'skill':  return <SkillBody data={data} />;
   case 'agent':  return <AgentBody data={data} />;
   case 'tool':   return <ToolBody data={data} />;
   case 'output': return <OutputBody data={data} />;
 }
}

2. Editing interactions

Undo/redo, copy/paste, multi-select, keyboard shortcuts, snap-to-grid are all essential features users expect from serious apps. If you’ve ever tried building them from scratch, you know they’re far from easy to get right.

In this demo, history and clipboard are single props on the root component:

// src/app.tsx

<Diagram cells={cells} onCellsChange={setCells} history clipboard>

The real value isn’t just that these features exist, but that they work together seamlessly. Undo correctly reverses a paste, multi-select moves as a group and lands on the undo stack as a single action, while Snaplines (a JointJS feature for aligning elements) work no matter how a node was placed. Only a library that builds these features into the engine can guarantee they’ll play nicely together.

3. The data model

This is what matters in serious, production-grade applications, and in JointJS+ for React, the diagram state is plain React state. Just as you’re used to working with React, Diagram can take data in either uncontrolled or controlled state. This demo showcases the controlled state.

// src/app.tsx

const [cells, setCells] = useState<readonly WorkflowCell[]>(INITIAL_CELLS);

<Diagram cells={cells} onCellsChange={setCells} history clipboard />

The controlled cells array is the single source of truth. It’s rendered on the <Diagram />, while every user action fires onCellsChange with an updated array. Because the graph is just a serializable data structure, saving, loading, and processing are trivial.

Note that the state hooks in JointJS for React behave identically in JointJS and JointJS+, but in JointJS+, GraphProvider becomes Diagram, which also gives you access to selection, history, clipboard, spatial index, and more.

4. Layout and organization

Diagrams that developers create by hand often drift toward visual noise. The auto-arrange option resolves this in a single action, in which a layout algorithm runs over the graph and repositions every node cleanly.

At the canvas/paper level, there are two available modes: an infinite-scrollable canvas for open-ended building, and a fixed sheet mode that restricts the diagram's canvas to specific, page-like boundaries, which is ideal for exportable documents such as flowcharts, organization charts, or diagrams that must fit strict corporate reporting templates.

The minimap in the bottom-right corner becomes vital as soon as the diagram grows beyond the viewport size. In JointJS+ for React, this is just one of the components you can plug into your application with a few lines of code.

he purpose of AI Workflow Builder demo

This demo clearly demonstrates what a serious AI workflow editor looks like when it’s built on a complete diagramming engine.

Every feature shown here, from typed connections, undo/redo, clipboard, multi-select, auto-layout, export, to minimap, is available on day one as a core feature of the JointJS library.

JointJS handles the hard parts out of the box, so you can focus on building your application logic instead of spending months implementing core library features.

Key capabilities of JointJS+ for React — What you get out of the box

JointJS+ for React provides a valuable set of features for production-ready diagrams, not just demos. These capabilities make JointJS+ for React a true foundation for serious diagramming applications, eliminating the need to reinvent critical features and assuring your product is ready for actual real-world demands.

SVG-based rendering with full custom shape support

JointJS uses a combination of SVG and HTML as its rendering engine, which means your diagrams will remain crisp at any zoom level, while the added benefit of SVG being accessible means your applications will meet necessary accessibility standards more easily.

On top of that, in JointJS you’re never limited to built-in shapes. You can easily create any kinds of elements. Nodes can use SVG or HTML, with wrapped labels, interactive inputs, and live data. All JointJS elements work flawlessly with ports, links, and selection, so you’ll never have to resort to workarounds.

Built-in virtual rendering for large graph performance

JointJS comes with extensive options that let you configure it for scalability and performance, but it ships with conservative defaults, primarily for backward compatibility. JointJS+ for React, on the other hand, doesn’t come with this baggage, so all advanced JointJS performance options like async, autoFreeze, and viewManagement you’d want in a large-scale application are enabled by default.

All of this means that instead of thinking about what you need to do to make your large apps performant, you can just start building with confidence, knowing that everything is already set up for you, even if you plan to build diagrams with thousands of nodes.

Exceptional user experience (UX)

JointJS+ for React is built to deliver a frustration-free diagramming experience for both end users and developers. The library provides intuitive drag-and-drop interactions, smooth editing, instant feedback, and advanced features such as minimap, smooth zoom controls, different routers, and more.

Domain-specific shape libraries

Get fully featured, standards-compliant shapes for BPMN 2.0, value stream mapping, data modeling (records/tables), and charts.

These shapes aren’t just icons, but they include the correct ports, labels, and connection rules for each domain, allowing you to build real-life applications without starting from scratch.

Comprehensive layout algorithms

JointJS+ for React comes with built-in tree, force-directed, grid, and stack layouts, while also allowing seamless integration with advanced third-party layout engines such as ELK and Dagre. Easily auto-arrange and reorganize complex diagrams.

These algorithms make it easy to auto-arrange nodes, keep diagrams readable, and adapt to model changes, saving you weeks of custom development.

Rich interaction model

Undo/redo, copy/paste, multi-select, keyboard shortcuts, snap-to-grid, and alignment guides work together out of the box, intuitively.

None of these are bolted on separately and hoped to cooperate: undo correctly reverses a paste, a multi-select move lands on the undo stack as a single action, and snap-to-grid/alignment guides apply no matter how the node got there, be it by dragging, pasting, or dropping it from the stencil.

Effortless export options

In JointJS+ for React, you can easily export diagrams as SVG, PNG, or PDF. What users see on screen is exactly what they get in exports, so you won’t need to implement separate rendering logic. Canvas (paper) options allow you to visualize fixed sheets and page breaks, which is key if you need specific dimensions of diagrams and flowcharts for your documents and presentations.

Who is JointJS+ for React built for

JointJS+ for React is designed for teams building workflow automation tools, BPMN modelers, data pipeline editors, network topology visualizers, circuit design tools, or any application where diagramming is a core product feature. It’s built for cases where users need robust editing, undo/redo, easy export, and all of this delivered with polished UX and production-grade scalability. When your requirements go beyond simple visuals, and you need a complete, production-ready foundation, JointJS+ for React delivers everything out of the box.

Simpler libraries are fine for simple needs, but as soon as requirements get serious, whether in performance, intuitive and accessible UX, scalability, or configuration options, you quickly hit a ceiling. At that point, you either have to build the missing pieces yourself or start with the right foundation from day one. Not anymore, because this is precisely the gap that JointJS+ for React fills.

Getting started with JointJS+ for React

The easiest way to get started with JointJS+ for React is to jump into our AI Workflow Builder demo. The source is fully available on GitHub, so you can clone the repo, run npm install, and you’re ready to tweak and customize it, either by hand, if you want to dig into the code yourself, or with your AI Coding Agent, be it Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or any other model you might be using.

Professional Services Website Redesign

The realm of professional services is characterized by its unique blend of expertise, personalized client relationships, and the imperative for a strong digital presence. A well-crafted website is no longer a luxury but a necessity for firms aiming to establish credibility, attract new clients, and showcase their capabilities. However, the challenge lies in creating a website that truly reflects the nuances and complexities of professional services, a task at which standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often fail.

Standard templates and generic forms are designed to cater to a broad audience, lacking the specificity and customization that professional services require. They fail to account for the intricate details of each firm's unique value proposition, service offerings, and brand identity. As a result, websites built using these templates often appear impersonal and lack the depth necessary to engage potential clients and differentiate the firm from its competitors.

From an engineering standpoint, a successful professional services website redesign must prioritize customization, user experience, and the integration of advanced technologies to facilitate meaningful interactions with visitors. The following engineering takeaways are crucial for such a redesign:

This involves creating a bespoke navigation system, categorizing services and expertise in a logical and accessible manner, and implementing a robust search function.

This includes tailoring content based on visitor behavior, implementing chatbots for immediate support, and using data to inform design decisions that enhance user engagement.

  3. Integration of Advanced Conversion Tools: The integration of advanced conversion tools, such as dynamic forms, callback services, and live chat functionalities, can significantly enhance the website's ability to capture leads and facilitate conversions. These tools must be seamlessly integrated into the website's design to ensure a cohesive user experience.

In conclusion, redesigning a professional services website requires a deep understanding of the firm's unique needs, a commitment to customization, and the strategic integration of technology to enhance user experience and drive conversions. By moving beyond the limitations of standard templates and generic forms, firms can create a digital presence that truly reflects their expertise and builds meaningful connections with their audience.

title: I Rebuilt a CRM 3 Times Because I Solved the Wrong Problem
description:
The first time I built this CRM, I thought I understood the problem.

I knew how to build forms, connect database tables, create features, and import data. I was a developer. I knew how software was supposed to work.

But I had overlooked something important: knowing how to build software isn't the same as understanding the problem you're solving.

I ended up rebuilding the CRM three times before I got the solution right.

And the biggest lesson had very little to do with writing code.

I built it for developers, not users

The CRM was built for an agency whose employees weren't necessarily technical.

My first mistake was designing the application around what I thought people would naturally understand.

If a field was labelled Email, I expected users to enter an email address. If there was a button to expand a menu, I expected them to click it.

So I didn't put enough thought into validation and interaction design.

That assumption didn't hold up in practice.

Users don't always follow the workflow a developer imagines. They make mistakes, misunderstand interfaces, and enter data in unexpected ways.

A form shouldn't rely on someone having common sense about what belongs in each field. It should help them do the right thing and prevent avoidable mistakes.

That was my first lesson: software needs to account for how people actually behave, not how we expect them to behave.

But the user interface wasn't the biggest problem.

The real problem was hidden in the old data

The agency already had its data in Microsoft Access. The goal was to move that data into the new CRM.

I built an import feature for contacts and deals.

At first glance, that sounds straightforward. Read the records from the old system, insert them into the new database, and you're done.

Except contacts and deals weren't independent records. They were related.

A deal belonged to a contact. When importing the data, the new CRM generated its own IDs. That was intentional: I didn't want to blindly reuse the identifiers from the legacy system.

But I hadn't designed a reliable mapping between the old records and the new ones.

Imagine importing 5,000 contacts and then importing 2,000 deals. How would the CRM know which newly created contact belonged to each deal?

The original IDs weren't being preserved, and the old data didn't always provide a reliable alternative.

I had created an import feature without fully accounting for the relationships that made the data meaningful.

Importing records was easy. Preserving their relationships was the real challenge.

Names and emails weren't enough

The old system had another complication.

Some deals contained a person's name and email, but no reliable contact ID. That meant the importer had to figure out which contact a deal belonged to.

What if two contacts had the same name?

What if an email was missing?

What if only a mobile phone number was available?

Matching by name alone could connect a deal to the wrong person. Matching by email wasn't always possible. And assuming every record was clean would have made things worse.

I needed a better way to identify candidate matches without pretending the data was more reliable than it really was.

The solution: matching rules and human verification

I changed the approach.

Instead of treating every record as an isolated row to import, I introduced matching rules to help identify possible relationships.

For example, I could compare a person's name and email. When an email wasn't available, I could use the name and phone number as an alternative.

These combinations helped narrow down the possibilities, but they weren't a guarantee. Two records could still be ambiguous, and I didn't want the software making a potentially incorrect decision silently.

So I added a review step.

Before confirming the import, the system displayed the affected records in a pop-up so the responsible person could review them. Even when there were thousands of records, the process needed to make potential issues visible rather than blindly accepting questionable matches.

The goal wasn't to pretend every record could be matched automatically.

The goal was to make uncertainty visible and give the responsible person a chance to resolve it.

I also had to clean up inconsistent date formats and other problems in the legacy data. Moving data between systems meant dealing with what actually existed in the old system, not what I wished had been there.

There was no need to introduce AI into this problem. It required careful reasoning, matching rules, data validation, and human verification.

Why did I rebuild it three times?

Because I started implementing before I had fully understood the problem.

Each time, I had to go back, reconsider the approach, and start again. It cost time, but each attempt exposed assumptions I hadn't challenged.

Looking back, I don't think the central lesson was that the CRM needed better code.

It needed a better understanding of the requirements.

I should have asked earlier:

  • What makes a record identifiable when the source system has no reliable ID?
  • How will relationships survive when destination IDs are generated from scratch?
  • What happens when the source data is incomplete or inconsistent?
  • Which decisions can the software make safely, and which require human review?
  • How will we detect a questionable match before it becomes a data-integrity problem?

These questions would have changed the implementation from the beginning.

I now think about the problem before the technology

When I was more junior, I tended to jump straight into implementation. I'd think about the database, the forms, the features, and how to build them.

Now, I try to slow down first.

I look at the problem, the requirements, the constraints, and the limitations. I write down my assumptions and challenge them before turning them into code.

That doesn't mean I can anticipate every complication. Real projects will always surprise you.

But it does mean I can avoid building an entire solution on an assumption that should have been questioned at the start.

The CRM taught me that lesson through three rebuilds.

Good engineering isn't just about making software work. It's about understanding what needs to work, for whom, and under which constraints, before you start building.

About the author

I'm Ayman Atif, a software engineer focused on building business software with .NET, C#, Python, and web technologies. I've been programming since 2014, and my experience has taught me that solving the right problem matters more than writing code quickly.

title: My demo runs with no backend: a mock axios client that mirrors the real API
description:
The hardest part of shipping a product demo isn't the demo itself. It's that the demo needs a backend, and backends need servers, and servers need babysitting. I wanted a demo page anyone could click through — login, dashboard, user management — with zero infrastructure behind it.

So I built a fake API that mirrors the real one. One seam, and the entire frontend switches over without knowing.

In client.js, the axios client is created behind a single branch:

const client = isDemoMode() ? createDemoClient() : axios.create({
  baseURL: `${import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL || 'http://localhost:8000'}/api`,
  headers: { Accept: 'application/json' },
});

isDemoMode() just reads VITE_DEMO_MODE=true from the build. The public preview build sets it; the shipped product doesn't. Everything else in the app — AuthContext, the pages, the components — imports the same client and calls the same endpoints: POST /auth/login, GET /auth/me, GET /dashboard/stats, apiResource users.

The mock, demoMock.js, implements those endpoints against in-memory arrays. The critical discipline: it returns the exact response shapes the real API returns. POST /auth/login returns { token, user }. The user object carries id, name, email, role, created_at — same fields as the Laravel UserResource. Validation failures come back as 422-shaped errors with an errors object.

Why this matters more than it sounds: if the mock drifted from the real API — say it returned username where Laravel returns name — the demo would silently test a frontend that doesn't match the product. Mirroring the response shapes means the demo is also a regression test for my frontend's assumptions. When I change the real API, the demo breaks visibly, and I fix the mock in the same commit.

I seed it with an admin (admin@demo.io) plus eight sample users, and mutations go to the in-memory array — you can create and delete users in the demo and it all "works", resetting on reload. Honest limits: the demo banner says data is simulated. No fake permanence.

The pattern generalises beyond demos. Anytime your frontend depends on an API you don't want to run — a third-party sandbox, a service under development, a test environment — write the mock to the response-shape contract, not to vibes. Your future self, debugging why the mock behaves differently, will thank you.

This exact setup ships in my Laravel + React SaaS starter kit, so a buyer can try every flow in the live preview and then run the same code against the real Laravel API: https://kamranofficial.gumroad.com/l/mhekoig ($19, one-time).
