arXiv:2610.21006v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: To use language models to help us make decisions we would like to understand the rationale behind the language model's outputs. In principle, the language model provides its rationale as part of its text output. However, the sheer volume of text makes this hard to use in practice. In this paper, we are interested in extracting the cruxes that lead a model to recommend one action over another. We take a crux to be a sub-question that a model's rollouts disagree on, where changing its value may have altered the conclusion. A crux is therefore a property of the distribution of a model's rollouts, not of any one rollout. We consider three strategies of increasing computational cost. First, we just ask a model to identify, a priori, what the cruxes of a decision will be. Second, we have the model actually go through the process of generating a response and then extract the cruxes that arose in its reasoning. Finally, we generate many responses and extract the cruxes by comparing the reasoning across the rollouts. We make this last procedure computationally tractable with cheap calls to a reranker, an estimated 86 times less compute than a judge. We then conduct an extensive empirical evaluation to assess whether the computationally inexpensive options are sufficient. They are not. Across domains and models, we find that a model's a priori assessment of the cruxes has little relation to the factors that are actually identified as important a posteriori. Using a single rollout helps, but is still inadequate for identifying the full set of cruxes. Accordingly, for high-stakes decisions (and to understand the space of language model decision making) the many rollout procedure is unavoidable.

title: Same Context, Different Agents: A Behavioral Study of Semantic Layers, Orchestration and Compaction in Data Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.20959v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Answering questions over heterogeneous data means combining evidence from files, databases, documents and the web. Data agents automate this, but their success depends on context. Three context-engineering techniques (CETs) help by shaping it: semantic layers describe the data, orchestration splits work among agents, and compaction condenses interaction history. Existing studies validate each CET alone, leaving open how agent behavior shapes its effect. We present a comprehensive analysis of the three CETs, alone and combined, with seven large language models (LLMs) on 1,514 long-horizon tasks from five benchmarks, covering behavior, accuracy and cost. We find that data agents without CETs form three behavior groups: investigators, premature answerers that answer without inspecting data, and early stoppers that give up. Each CET delivers its known benefit, from more investigation to smaller prompts, but only the behavior group it matches turns that benefit into accuracy, such as premature answerers under orchestration. For investigators, the same CETs can hurt: the semantic layer stops them from looking, orchestration makes them overconfident, costing 5 percentage points, and compaction makes them repeat steps. Combining CETs yields smaller gains and losses than their sum. We derive guidance for choosing CETs by agent behavior, task demands and accuracy-cost trade-offs.

title: Two-Plane Observability on Google Cloud: Signal Contracts, Alert Policies and a Hexagonal Dispatcher
description:
We stopped learning about production failures from other teams by splitting observability into two planes: telemetry that's always on, and notification that's deliberate and rare. This is how we built it: the contracts, the config and the sharp edges we hit along the way.

Our services happen to be written in Go, so the code samples are Go. The architecture isn't: every boundary is OpenTelemetry, Cloud Monitoring or JSON on Pub/Sub, so a workload in any language can plug in.

Context in 60 seconds

  • The fleet: a GKE cluster of Go services plus more than a dozen Cloud Run jobs, across three environments (dev, preprod, prod), each in its own GCP project.
  • Before: every component instrumented differently, logs as the only real signal, and one Teams channel per service.
  • The trigger: a sub-step in a Cloud Run job failed; the job swallowed the error and exited 0. No alert fired. A downstream team noticed hours later.
  • The goal: any failure that needs a human reaches one within minutes, through one predictable channel. Everything else stays quiet, but visible.

Architecture at a glance

Component Role Runs on
Instrumentation library One way to emit metrics, traces and logs; owns the signal contract every workload (ours: Go)
Cloud Monitoring alert policies Decide when a human should hear about something (most alerts) Google Cloud
App events The rare alert a metric can't express, published from code every workload
Pub/Sub topic Single entry point for alerts, one per environment Google Cloud
Dispatcher Normalizes, dedupes and routes alerts; channels behind a port one per environment
Postgres schema Delivery claims, per incident and channel an instance we already ran
Teams Workflows Post alerts into the blockers and warnings channels Microsoft Teams / Power Automate

What's language-specific, and what isn't

The only code that has to exist per language is the instrumentation library. Everything downstream depends on what lands in Google Cloud, not on how it was produced:

Boundary The contract Language-specific?
Telemetry OpenTelemetry signals with fixed names, units and labels; Cloud Logging field names Only the library that emits them
Alert decisions Cloud Monitoring alert policies, in Terraform No
App events A JSON message on a Pub/Sub topic Only a small publish helper
Dispatcher, dedupe, routing Consumes Pub/Sub, reads config No: it's one service, in whatever language you like

A Python, Java or Node.js service joins the platform by emitting the same signals and publishing the same JSON. The policies, dashboards and dispatcher don't change.

Two planes that never mix

The telemetry plane is always on. Every workload emits the same signals, all the time, straight to Google Cloud Observability. Dashboards and Error Reporting read Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging directly. Nothing in this path goes through a service of ours.

The notification plane is deliberate and rare. Nothing reaches a person unless someone decided, on purpose, that it's worth interrupting someone for. Most of the time that decision is a Cloud Monitoring alert policy on the shared signals. Occasionally it lives in code, for app-level events that can't be expressed as a metric.

Pub/Sub carries alerts, never telemetry. It's tempting to send metrics through the same bus, but then a service of ours would have to aggregate time series, store history and evaluate alert conditions, all things Cloud Monitoring already does. It would also sit in the path of every signal: if it went down, we'd lose visibility exactly when we needed it.

One instrumentation library per language

If every team instruments differently, you can't build anything on top. So each language gets exactly one small library, and it's the only sanctioned way to wire up telemetry. Our fleet is Go, so we have one. This is what using it looks like in a Cloud Run job:

ocfg := obs.Config{
    GCPProject:     cfg.Project, // empty = telemetry off (local runs)
    ServiceName:    "report-syncer",
    ServiceVersion: buildSHA,
    Environment:    cfg.Env, // dev | preprod | prod
    ComponentType:  obs.ComponentJob, // or obs.ComponentService
}
shutdown, err := obs.InitOTel(ctx, ocfg)
if err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("init otel: %w", err)
}
defer func() {
    // Fresh context: the caller's ctx may already be canceled,
    // and this flush carries the run's final result.
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(
        context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := shutdown(ctx); err != nil {
        slog.Error("otel shutdown", "err", err)
    }
}()
slog.SetDefault(slog.New(obs.NewCloudLoggingHandler(ocfg)))

// Root span + run.duration + run.result{status}, same everywhere.
return obs.RunJob(ctx, doWork)

The decisions behind that call apply in any language:

  • ComponentType picks the export path. Cloud Run jobs use the in-process Google Cloud exporters: no collector, flush on shutdown. GKE services export OTLP to an in-cluster OpenTelemetry Collector. A service configured without a Collector address fails at startup instead of silently exporting to localhost and dropping everything. Both paths must land on the same metric types, or every template further down breaks; check that first when you add a Collector.
  • Sampling follows the workload. Jobs sample every run, because volume is low and every run matters. Services use ParentBased(TraceIDRatioBased(0.1)), so a distributed trace stays complete across hops.
  • There's an activation gate. With no GCP project set, or in local mode, the library installs nothing and returns a no-op shutdown, so local runs need no credentials. The W3C tracecontext + baggage propagator is installed either way, so context still flows through a process that isn't exporting.
  • A wrapper emits the job contract for you. RunJob opens the root span, times the run, records the outcome and marks the span as errored on failure. Teams can't get the contract wrong because they don't write it.
  • The shutdown flush gets its own deadline. For a job, the final flush is the run result. Flush under an already-canceled context (or skip the flush on exit) and you silently drop the one data point every alert depends on.

Porting it to another language

A library in Python, Java or Node.js has the same six jobs. If it does these, the rest of the platform can't tell the difference:

  1. Initialize the OpenTelemetry SDK with the Google Cloud exporters for jobs, or OTLP to the Collector for services.
  2. Name instruments <service>.<suffix>, with exactly the suffixes, units and label values in the contract below.
  3. Wrap the unit of work (a job run, a request) so the contract signals are emitted automatically.
  4. Map log fields to what Cloud Logging expects (next section).
  5. Flush on shutdown with its own timeout.
  6. Publish app events as the JSON shape described in the alert event contract.

The conformance test is simple: run a sample job and check the metric types and labels that appear in Cloud Monitoring. If they match, the dashboards and policies work unchanged.

The logging gotcha that broke Error Reporting

Cloud Logging reads a field called severity, but most JSON loggers write level by default: Go's slog, Python's common JSON formatters, Node's pino, Logback's JSON encoders. Ship that as-is and every line lands at default severity: severity filters, log-based metrics and Error Reporting all quietly misclassify everything.

The library's log handler fixes that in one place:

Typical logger default What Cloud Logging expects
level severity with Cloud Logging values (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL)
msg message
no trace link logging.googleapis.com/trace as projects/<PROJECT_ID>/traces/<TRACE_ID>, plus logging.googleapis.com/spanId and logging.googleapis.com/trace_sampled
no error context serviceContext (service, version) and a stack_trace on error-level records

Two details matter. The trace field needs the full resource name, not a bare trace ID, or the log-to-trace link never appears. And the stack trace is captured at the log call site, written in the language's native stack format (Go's goroutine … [running]: layout for us) so Error Reporting can parse it, with the logging library's own frames dropped. Leave those frames in and Error Reporting groups every error under the logger instead of the code that failed.

That was the cheapest win of the whole project. Once error logs are shaped correctly, Error Reporting groups them fleet-wide with zero configuration. You get "all the problems in one place" on day one, before a single dashboard exists.

The signal contract

A small, fixed vocabulary that every workload emits:

Signal Labels Emitted by Meaning
<service>.run.duration none RunJob histogram (ms): how long a job run took
<service>.run.result status: success or failure RunJob counter: one increment per run
<service>.errors error_kind obs.Errors counter: something went wrong, by cause
<service>.self_heal outcome: transient_recovered or remediated obs.Count counter: a failure the workload fixed on its own

The first three are built into the library. self_heal is a naming convention on top of the generic obs.Count helper, so the library doesn't enforce its label values; code review does.

GKE services emit errors and self_heal too, and get request rate, errors and latency from OpenTelemetry's standard HTTP and gRPC instrumentation (otelhttp / otelgrpc in Go; every language has an equivalent) instead of inventing their own. Pod health comes from GKE system metrics and Managed Service for Prometheus at the platform level, not from the app.

Why the service name is in the metric name

Every instrument is named <service_in_snake_case>.<suffix>, so report-syncer emits report_syncer.run.result, which lands in Cloud Monitoring as workload.googleapis.com/report_syncer.run.result. That's on purpose: the Google Cloud metric type comes from the instrument name, so a prefix guarantees two services can never collide on a metric with a different meaning or shape.

The trade-off is that there's no single run_result metric to query across the fleet. One component's run outcomes look like this:

sum by (status) (
  increase(workload_googleapis_com:report_syncer_run_result[1h])
)

What makes it scale anyway is that the suffixes and labels are identical everywhere. The fleet dashboard, the per-component dashboards and the baseline alert policies are all Terraform templates that loop over the list of components and stamp out the same query for each one. Adding a component means adding a name to a list.

Baseline alert policies

Every component gets two policies by default, so none can be silent:

  • Failure: run.result{status="failure"} greater than zero → severity=critical.
  • Heartbeat: no run.duration sample within the expected interval (metric absence).

The heartbeat has three edges worth knowing before you rely on it:

  1. A metric-absence condition only fires after the metric has existed. A brand-new component that has never written a point can't trip it. Make "first successful run in each environment" part of onboarding.
  2. The absence window maxes out at 23.5 hours. That's fine for jobs that run hourly. For a once-a-day job, the schedule plus normal start-time jitter doesn't fit, so write its heartbeat as a PromQL condition over a longer range instead.
  3. Every execution is a new time series. The library sets service.instance.id to the Cloud Run execution and task index, so each run writes its own series. Absence is evaluated per series, so aggregate across executions (sum by service) first. Otherwise every finished run's series looks "absent" and the heartbeat fires constantly.

Labels: bounded, and no owners

Service identity travels as resource attributes (service.name, service.namespace, service.version, deployment.environment, service.instance.id and a custom component_type), set once by the library alongside what the GCP resource detector finds. There are deliberately no team or owner labels: routing is by severity, triage context is by service, and ownership metadata goes stale faster than anything else in a label set.

The other hard rule: metric labels stay bounded. status, error_kind, outcome and a few other fixed enums. Never object paths, URIs, run IDs or user IDs: those belong on spans and logs.

Alert policies into Pub/Sub

Most alerts start as Cloud Monitoring policies. Cloud Monitoring already does evaluation, incident lifecycle and its own dedup well, so we let it, and give each policy a Pub/Sub notification channel pointing at the environment's alerts topic.

The setup details that cost us time:

  • IAM. Monitoring publishes as its notification service agent, service-<PROJECT_NUMBER>@gcp-sa-monitoring-notification.iam.gserviceaccount.com. It needs roles/pubsub.publisher on the topic. Without it, incidents open in the console and nothing ever arrives.
  • User labels carry routing. Every policy sets severity, service and component_type as user labels; the Terraform template sets them, so nobody forgets. They arrive in the incident payload (policy_user_labels), and the dispatcher's Pub/Sub adapter maps them onto the same event shape app code publishes.
  • Incidents open and close. The payload carries state: open | closed. Carry that through as a resolved notification for the same incident, not as a new alert, or every recovery looks like a second incident.

The alert event contract

Whether an alert comes from a policy or from code, the dispatcher works with one shape. The contract is the JSON on the wire, not a type in any one language. Our library ships a Go struct for producers, but the dispatcher doesn't import it: the two sides share only the documented schema, so either can evolve on its own as long as the JSON holds. In a polyglot fleet, publish that schema as JSON Schema and generate the types per language:

type Event struct {
    // critical | warning | info
    Severity string `json:"severity"`
    // component name, as in the metric prefix
    Service string `json:"service"`
    // job | service
    ComponentType string `json:"component_type"`
    // one human-readable line
    Summary string `json:"summary"`
    // rare routing override; usually empty
    Channel string `json:"channel,omitempty"`
    // dashboard, trace, logs
    Links map[string]string `json:"links,omitempty"`
    // dedupe key: <service>/<kind>
    Fingerprint string `json:"fingerprint,omitempty"`
    // extra context, never secrets
    Attributes map[string]string `json:"attributes,omitempty"`
}

Two fields do the heavy lifting:

  • Severity expresses how much this matters.
  • Fingerprint expresses what this is, for example report-syncer/run-blocked, so repeated occurrences collapse into one incident instead of a hundred messages.

There's no environment in the event or the fingerprint, and that's deliberate. Each environment has its own project, topic and dispatcher, so a fingerprint is unambiguous inside the pipeline that receives it.

The producer declares intent, not delivery. It says how severe something is; it doesn't pick a Teams channel, decide whether to email or open a ticket. Routing falls out of severity:

func (e Event) ResolveChannel() string {
    if e.Channel != "" {
        return e.Channel // explicit override, used rarely
    }
    switch e.Severity {
    case SeverityCritical:
        return ChannelBlocker
    case SeverityWarning:
        return ChannelWarn
    default: // unknown severity: never dropped, never pages
        return ChannelDigest
    }
}

The default branch is a small decision we're happy with: a typo in a severity lands in the quietest bucket. The event isn't lost, and nobody gets woken up by a mislabeled one.

ResolveChannel is the producer-side reference for the primary channel. The dispatcher applies the same mapping, and its routing config can add mirrors on top, such as email for criticals.

One hard rule is baked into the contract: the payload never carries sensitive data. No request bodies, no payment fields, no customer identifiers in Summary or Attributes. Alerts travel through Pub/Sub and land in chat tools, which is the wrong place for anything you wouldn't put on a whiteboard.

Pub/Sub in the middle

The topic between producers and the dispatcher is there on purpose:

  • Decoupling. Producers don't know or care how many channels exist, or whether the dispatcher is up. They publish and move on.
  • One door for two sources. Alert policies and app events arrive the same way, so the dispatcher has one input.
  • Fan-out. One event can drive several subscribers: the dispatcher now, an archive or a ticket integration later.

One sharp edge, stated plainly because it bit us in planning: by default, a topic doesn't keep messages; subscriptions do. Only subscriptions that exist at publish time receive a message. Create the topic today and the dispatcher's subscription tomorrow, and everything published in between is gone.

Two ways around it: create the subscription in the same Terraform apply as the topic, or enable topic message retention, which lets a subscription created later seek back to a timestamp and pick up what it missed.

The dispatcher: ports and adapters

The dispatcher turns an incoming event into the right notification: a blockers message, a warnings message, an email or a digest entry, or nothing at all if it's a duplicate. It uses a ports-and-adapters (hexagonal) architecture, so adding a new way to notify never touches the core.

Four boundaries, only three of them ports

Boundary Kind In our dispatcher
Dispatch(ctx, Event) error driving port: the use case the core offers Called by the Pub/Sub adapter, once per message
Notifier driven port One instance per configured channel: Teams blockers, Teams warnings, email, …
DeliveryLog driven port Dedupe claims, in Postgres
Routes plain value, not a port Routing config, read once at startup

Three decisions hide in that table:

  • The core doesn't read from Pub/Sub; Pub/Sub calls the core. The core offers one function, Dispatch(ctx, event) error. The Pub/Sub adapter receives each message, calls it, and turns the result into an ack or a nack. The core never sees a subscription, so it's trivial to test and doesn't care how events arrive.
  • Normalizing payloads is the adapter's job. Two very different JSON shapes arrive on the topic: Cloud Monitoring incidents and app events. Translating both into one Event is technology-specific parsing, so it lives in the Pub/Sub adapter. The core never sees a Cloud Monitoring payload.
  • Static config doesn't need a port. Routing is data that's loaded once, so it's a constructor argument. It would only earn a port if it had to reload at runtime.

The outbound port 

package dispatch // the core: no Teams, no SMTP, no URLs

// ChannelID names a configured destination, e.g. "blocker" or
// "oncall_email". It comes from routing config; the core never
// sees URLs or channel types.
type ChannelID string

// State follows the incident: Cloud Monitoring reports open and close.
type State string

const (
    StateOpened   State = "opened"
    StateResolved State = "resolved"
)

// Notification is what the core asks a channel to deliver: what
// happened, not how it looks. Each adapter renders it (Adaptive
// Card, email, ticket).
type Notification struct {
    Key           string // idempotency key: fingerprint + state
    State         State
    Severity      Severity
    Service       string
    ComponentType string
    Summary       string
    Links         map[string]string // dashboard, trace, logs
    Occurrences   int               // repeats folded into this incident
    FirstSeen     time.Time
}

// ErrPermanent marks failures a retry can't fix:
// rejected payload, deleted workflow, revoked credentials.
var ErrPermanent = errors.New("permanent notification failure")

// Notifier is the outbound port. One instance per configured channel.
//
// Contract:
//   - nil means the channel ACCEPTED the notification. Delivery may
//     still be asynchronous (Teams Workflows answers 202 first).
//   - Wrap ErrPermanent when a retry can't help; any other error
//     is transient.
//   - Respect ctx: the core sets a deadline per send.
//   - May be called more than once with the same Key (at-least-once).
//     Adapters that can dedupe on Key should.
type Notifier interface {
    Notify(ctx context.Context, n Notification) error
}

Most of the design lives in the comment, not the signature. What nil means, which errors are worth retrying and whether a duplicate call is safe are exactly the questions Pub/Sub acks and dedupe depend on.

The core, end to end 

type DeliveryLog interface {
    // Claim reports whether key should go to ch now: not already
    // sent there within window. Safe under concurrent redeliveries.
    Claim(ctx context.Context, key string, ch ChannelID,
        window time.Duration) (bool, error)
    // Release undoes a claim after a transient failure,
    // so a redelivery retries it.
    Release(ctx context.Context, key string, ch ChannelID) error
}

type Service struct {
    routes   Routes                 // severity → []ChannelID, from config
    channels map[ChannelID]Notifier // wired in main, validated at startup
    log      DeliveryLog
    window   time.Duration
}

// Dispatch is the inbound port.
//   nil           → ack
//   ErrPermanent  → ack and log loudly
//   anything else → nack; the redelivery retries only failed channels
func (s *Service) Dispatch(ctx context.Context, ev Event) error {
    key := ev.Fingerprint + "#" + string(ev.State)
    var transient, permanent []error
    // ev.Channel override, or severity → channels
    for _, ch := range s.routes.For(ev) {
        ok, err := s.log.Claim(ctx, key, ch, s.window)
        if err != nil {
            transient = append(transient, err)
            continue
        }
        if !ok {
            continue // already sent to this channel within the window
        }
        sendCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 10*time.Second)
        err = s.channels[ch].Notify(sendCtx, s.notification(ev, key))
        cancel()
        switch {
        case err == nil:
        case errors.Is(err, ErrPermanent):
            permanent = append(permanent, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", ch, err))
        default:
            _ = s.log.Release(ctx, key, ch)
            transient = append(transient, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", ch, err))
        }
    }
    if len(transient) > 0 {
        return errors.Join(transient...)
    }
    if len(permanent) > 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("%w: %v",
            ErrPermanent, errors.Join(permanent...))
    }
    return nil
}

Three details carry the weight:

  • Claims are per (key, channel), not per fingerprint. A critical goes to both blocker and oncall_email. If Teams succeeds and email fails, the redelivery retries only email. With a single claim per fingerprint you'd either post to Teams twice or lose the email.
  • The claim key includes the state. Otherwise a close that arrives inside the window would be swallowed as a duplicate of the open it resolves.
  • Errors map onto Pub/Sub. Transient failures nack, so Pub/Sub redelivers. Permanent ones ack, because retrying a rejected payload forever helps nobody. A dead-letter topic with a max-delivery-attempts limit on the subscription is the backstop for anything stuck in between.

The Teams adapter

MS Teams is the first adapter. It posts through Teams Workflows (Power Automate): one workflow per channel, built on the "When a Teams webhook request is received" trigger, which posts the card into that channel.

The trigger expects an Adaptive Card wrapped in a message attachment, and the adapter is also where HTTP status codes become the port's error classes:

// adapters/teams: the only package that knows about Workflows.
type Workflow struct {
    url  string // from Secret Manager, injected in main
    http *http.Client
}

func (w *Workflow) Notify(
    ctx context.Context, n dispatch.Notification,
) error {
    body := message{
        Type: "message",
        Attachments: []attachment{{
            ContentType: "application/vnd.microsoft.card.adaptive",
            Content:     adaptiveCard(n), // opened or resolved layout
        }},
    }
    resp, err := postJSON(ctx, w.http, w.url, body)
    if err != nil {
        return err // network or timeout: transient
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    switch {
    case resp.StatusCode == 400, resp.StatusCode == 401,
        resp.StatusCode == 403, resp.StatusCode == 404:
        return fmt.Errorf("%w: teams workflow returned %d",
            dispatch.ErrPermanent, resp.StatusCode)
    case resp.StatusCode >= 300: // 429, 5xx: transient
        return fmt.Errorf("teams workflow returned %d", resp.StatusCode)
    }
    return nil // 202: accepted, not necessarily posted
}

Three things about Workflows shape the adapter:

  • 202 Accepted means queued, not posted. The flow runs asynchronously, so a bad card or a broken flow fails in the flow's run history, not in your HTTP response. That's why the port says nil means accepted. Turn on failure notifications for the flow, and keep the email mirror for criticals so one broken flow can't silence the blockers channel.
  • A workflow belongs to a person, not a channel. If its owner leaves and nobody else owns it, the flow stops, and you've rebuilt the silent failure this platform exists to prevent. Add co-owners, and run the flow's connections under a shared or service account.
  • The trigger URL is a credential. It carries a signature (sig=) that works like a password, so it lives in Secret Manager, never in config or code.

The other adapters

  • Email is a second Notifier, configured as the oncall_email channel: a durable record for criticals that outlives a chat scroll.
  • Digest (planned) is a Notifier too. Instead of sending anything, it records the notification for the daily digest job, so info-severity events have a home before the digest exists.
  • Tickets (planned) fit the same port, because the contract is incident-shaped: the same Key means the same incident, so the adapter can create a ticket the first time and comment on it after that. It would need its own port only if the core needed something back, for example a ticket URL to put into the Teams card before sending it.

Dedupe: a claim, a window, three kinds of duplicate

Pub/Sub delivers at least once, so the dispatcher will occasionally receive the same event twice. For an alert dispatcher that means a duplicate Teams message at best, and two people jumping on one problem at worst.

It's the same redelivery problem as on the consumer side of any message pipeline (I wrote about it in The Redelivery Trap), and the same family of fix works: claim a key before acting, and skip anything already claimed. Here the claim is per (key, channel), and the state lives in a dedicated schema on a Postgres instance we already ran.

The difference is lifetime. A billing inbox remembers a message forever, because charging twice is never acceptable. An alert dispatcher should remember a claim only for a window:

  • Inside the window, a repeat is folded into the existing incident: bump a counter, update "last seen", send nothing.
  • After the window, a repeat is news again. A failure that recurs tomorrow should alert tomorrow.

The Postgres side of DeliveryLog.Claim is one upsert:

-- $1 = key (fingerprint#state), $2 = channel,
-- $3 = dedupe window, e.g. '1 hour'
-- PRIMARY KEY (key, channel)
INSERT INTO alert_delivery AS d (key, channel, last_sent_at, repeat_count)
VALUES ($1, $2, now(), 0)
ON CONFLICT (key, channel) DO UPDATE
   SET repeat_count = d.repeat_count + 1,
       last_sent_at = CASE WHEN d.last_sent_at < now() - $3::interval
                           THEN now() ELSE d.last_sent_at END
RETURNING (last_sent_at = now()) AS claimed;

The row lock taken by ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE makes concurrent redeliveries safe: the second one waits, sees a fresh last_sent_at and gets claimed = false. Release sets last_sent_at to '-infinity' for that one channel, so the redelivery claims it again instead of treating it as a duplicate.

That store absorbs three kinds of duplicate: Pub/Sub redeliveries of the same event, a workload reporting the same problem on every run, and the retry after a partial fan-out failure.

One more needs a decision up front: the same failure reported by both sources. If a job publishes its own critical event and the failure policy on run.result fires for the same run, two different payloads describe one problem. Either make them produce the same fingerprint (give the failure policy a kind: run-blocked user label, so both sources produce report-syncer/run-blocked), or decide per condition which source owns it.

Routing and configuration

Delivery is a function of severity and config. The routing table lives in Terraform next to the rest of each environment's infrastructure, not in code and not scattered across per-service channel integrations. The dispatcher reads it once at startup and fails fast if a route names a channel that isn't configured:

# illustrative routing config (one per environment, rendered by Terraform)
channels:
  blocker:      { type: teams_workflow, url_secret: teams-blocker-url }
  warn:         { type: teams_workflow, url_secret: teams-warn-url }
  oncall_email: { type: email, enabled: false } # mirror for criticals
  digest:       { type: digest }                # for the daily digest

dedupe:
  window: 1h   # repeats inside this fold into one incident

routing:
  critical: [blocker, oncall_email]   # act now
  warning:  [warn]                    # checked once a day
  info:     [digest]                  # no real-time ping

Each channels entry becomes one Notifier instance in main; the core only ever sees the keys. Workflow trigger URLs live in Secret Manager and the config only names the secret, so the routing file is safe to review in a pull request.

Severity Where it goes Example
critical blockers channel, immediately (+ email if enabled) someone has to act now: data a downstream consumer depends on is missing, wrong or late
warning warnings channel, checked daily needs attention, but nothing breaks today: an optional source failed, or the next run will pick it up
info digest channel, no real-time ping noteworthy but benign: a source was skipped on purpose

Severity describes impact, not how much of a run failed. One failed unit can be critical if it's the billing export; half the units failing can be a warning if they're optional or retried on the next run. Only the producer knows which, so the producer decides.

To be precise about the last row: that's info-severity alert events, not info log lines. Logs never pass through the dispatcher.

Because routing lives in config, "stop mailing on criticals in dev" or "add a channel for one noisy component" are config changes, not code changes.

Dashboards: three tiers, all templates

With a uniform signal contract, dashboards become Terraform modules instead of hand-built one-offs. Three tiers let people zoom from "is anything on fire?" to "what exactly broke?":

  • Tier 1: Fleet health. The default screen. Rollups and top-N only: open incidents by severity, jobs with no successful run or with failures, service error rate and p95, errors by service, self-heals by outcome.
  • Tier 2: By workload class. One for GKE services, one for Cloud Run jobs, grouped by component. For the platform layer we reuse Google's built-in GKE dashboards and the run.googleapis.com/job/* metrics.
  • Tier 3: Per component. One deep dashboard per service or job, created from a reusable module when that component adopts the library.

Every Tier 1 or Tier 2 tile links into the relevant Tier 3 dashboard, and every Teams card links to the same places, so an alert, a dashboard and a trace are always one click apart.

Self-healing in code

Once there's a clean "this failed" signal, the tempting move is to wire every failure to an alert. We did, briefly, and promptly rebuilt the noise problem. So workloads now try to recover before anything is reported. The pattern is plain control flow, so it translates to any language:

func (s *Syncer) process(ctx context.Context, unit WorkUnit) Outcome {
    err := s.attempt(ctx, unit)
    if err == nil {
        return Outcome{Status: statusSuccess}
    }

    // 1) Transient? Retry with backoff.
    if isTransient(err) {
        if err2 := s.retryWithBackoff(ctx, unit); err2 == nil {
            obs.Count(ctx, "self_heal", 1,
                attribute.String("outcome", "transient_recovered"))
            return Outcome{Status: statusSuccess}
        }
    }

    // 2) Not transient, or the retry failed: is there a different remedy?
    //    e.g. reload a manifest, reprocess a single file, fall back to an
    //    alternate source. Self-heal doesn't always mean "try again".
    if fix := s.remediation(err); fix != nil && fix(ctx, unit) == nil {
        obs.Count(ctx, "self_heal", 1,
            attribute.String("outcome", "remediated"))
        return Outcome{Status: statusSuccess}
    }

    // 3) Recovery failed: now it's worth a human.
    obs.Errors(ctx, errorKind(err))
    return Outcome{Status: statusFailure, Err: err}
}

Two things to notice. Recovery is failure-specific: a retry for a network blip, a locked row or a cold dependency; a different action for a bad manifest or one corrupt file. The workload knows which remedy fits which failure. And every recovery is counted, so self-healing shows up on a dashboard instead of disappearing. A rising self_heal rate is an early warning in its own right.

Then the run aggregates its outcomes and notifies once, at a severity that reflects the impact of what failed, not the share of units that failed:

fp := func(kind string) string { return svc + "/" + kind }
failed := failedUnits(outcomes)

var ev *alert.Event
switch {
case len(outcomes) == 0:
    // nothing to process: not a failure; the heartbeat policy
    // still catches a job that stops running altogether

case len(failed) == 0:
    // full success: telemetry records it, nobody is interrupted

case s.blocking(failed):
    // downstream data is missing or wrong: interrupt someone
    ev = &alert.Event{
        Severity:    alert.SeverityCritical,
        Fingerprint: fp("run-blocked"),
        Summary: fmt.Sprintf("sync run blocked: %d of %d units failed",
            len(failed), len(outcomes)),
    }

default:
    // failures that can wait: warn, don't page
    ev = &alert.Event{
        Severity:    alert.SeverityWarning,
        Fingerprint: fp("run-degraded"),
        Summary: fmt.Sprintf("sync run degraded: %d of %d units failed",
            len(failed), len(outcomes)),
    }
}

if ev != nil {
    ev.Service, ev.ComponentType = svc, "job"
    ev.Links = runLinks(ctx) // dashboard, trace, logs; never payloads
    if err := s.alerts.Notify(ctx, *ev); err != nil {
        slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "notify failed", "err", err)
    }
}

The impact rule lives in the job, because only the job knows which of its units matter:

// blocking decides by impact, not by ratio: one failed required
// unit (say, the billing export) is critical; a few failed
// optional ones are not.
func (s *Syncer) blocking(failed []Outcome) bool {
    for _, o := range failed {
        if o.Unit.Required {
            return true
        }
    }
    return len(failed) > s.maxOptionalFailures
}

The same rule decides what the run returns: a blocked run returns an error, so run.result records a failure and the baseline policy fires too; a degraded run returns nil and reports only the warning. Otherwise the policy would page for runs the job itself rated as able to wait.

The empty-run case is spelled out because "nothing to do" and "nothing worked" must never look the same. Ignoring an empty run is safe here only because the heartbeat policy covers a job that stops running.

The Notify error is logged, not fatal. The failure policy on run.result is the second, independent path to the blockers channel, which is exactly why the both-sources dedupe case above matters.

What's next

  • A daily digest. A scheduled Cloud Run job that assembles the last 24 hours (active incidents, failures and missed runs, service errors and latency, top Error Reporting groups, self-heal counts, GKE restarts) and emails it delta-first: what's new since yesterday comes before what's still true. "Nothing to report" is a good digest.
  • Tickets. The ticket adapter described above, switched on per environment from a configurable severity.
  • AI-assisted triage, longer term. We're exploring plugging Aura Tracker GCP, an open-source GCP investigation tool I maintain, into the pipeline: analyzing incidents against live cloud state and writing a likely cause and recommended fix into the ticket. Applying fixes, if ever, only behind a preview-and-approve step.

Design decisions and trade-offs

Decision Why What it costs
Telemetry and notification as separate planes Telemetry can be cheap and always on; notification stays rare Two systems to understand instead of one
One library per language, contract emitted by a wrapper Teams can't get the contract wrong Every workload depends on it; each new language means one more library to keep in step
Service name in the metric name No cross-service collisions on metric type No single fleet-wide metric; Terraform templates do the looping
Alert policies first, app events second Cloud Monitoring already does evaluation and incident lifecycle Policy payloads need mapping onto the event shape
Producer declares severity, config decides delivery Routing changes without touching any service One more config file per environment
Pub/Sub between producers and dispatcher Decoupling, one input, fan-out later At-least-once delivery, so dedupe is mandatory
Windowed claims per (incident, channel) in Postgres Folds redeliveries and repeats into one incident; a partial fan-out retries only what failed Window length is a judgment call per environment
Channels behind an incident-shaped Notifier port, identity from config New channels never touch the core; adapters own rendering and error classification A little more structure than a direct HTTP call
Payload normalization in the inbound adapter The core never sees Cloud Monitoring JSON Two translators to keep in step with their sources
Self-heal before notify, and count every heal Most "incidents" were transient Remediation code to write and maintain per failure mode

If you're building something similar

Start in this order; each step is useful on its own:

  1. Fix log shape first. severity, message, full trace resource name, stack_trace on errors. Error Reporting alone will show you more on day one than most dashboards.
  2. Define the signal contract and emit it from a wrapper, not by hand.
  3. Add the two baseline policies per component: failure and heartbeat, with the 23.5-hour limit in mind.
  4. Point policies at a Pub/Sub topic, grant the Monitoring service agent publisher on it, and put routing in user labels.
  5. Build the dispatcher last, with per-channel dedupe and a clear transient vs. permanent error contract from the first commit.
  6. Then teach workloads to heal themselves, and count every time they do.

The dispatcher, the routing and the self-healing all get easier once "telemetry" and "notification" stop being the same word.

title: Intersection Observer API: Lazy Loading, Infinite Scroll, Scroll Animations, and TOC Active Links
description:
The Intersection Observer API lets you detect when elements enter or leave the viewport — without polling, without scroll event listeners, and without expensive getBoundingClientRect() calls. It's the modern solution for lazy loading, infinite scroll, animation triggers, and ad viewability measurement. Firefox has full support.

Why Intersection Observer

The old approach to detecting element visibility:

// BAD: forces synchronous layout on every scroll event
window.addEventListener('scroll', () => {
  const rect = element.getBoundingClientRect();
  if (rect.top < window.innerHeight) {
    loadImage();
  }
});

Problems:

  • getBoundingClientRect() forces a synchronous layout (expensive)
  • Scroll events fire rapidly (60+ times/second on smooth scroll)
  • Main thread blocking causes jank

Intersection Observer:

  • Runs asynchronously, not on the main thread
  • Callbacks only fire when intersection changes (not on every scroll)
  • Batches observations
  • ~10-100x less CPU usage

Basic Intersection Observer 

const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  entries.forEach(entry => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
      // Element entered viewport
      loadContent(entry.target);
      observer.unobserve(entry.target); // Stop watching after first load
    }
  });
});

// Start observing elements
document.querySelectorAll('.lazy-image').forEach(img => {
  observer.observe(img);
});

Options: threshold and rootMargin 

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(callback, {
  // threshold: percentage visible that triggers callback
  threshold: 0,        // trigger when any pixel is visible (default)
  threshold: 0.5,      // trigger when 50% is visible
  threshold: 1.0,      // trigger only when fully visible
  threshold: [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0], // trigger at each percentage

  // rootMargin: expand/contract the observation area
  rootMargin: '0px',           // default (exactly viewport)
  rootMargin: '200px',         // start loading 200px before entering viewport
  rootMargin: '-20px',         // only trigger when element is 20px inside viewport
  rootMargin: '0px 0px -100px 0px', // top right bottom left

  // root: default is the viewport
  root: document.getElementById('scroll-container'), // or any scrollable element
});

Lazy Loading Images 

<img data-src="/photo.jpg" class="lazy" alt="Photo" loading="lazy">

// IntersectionObserver approach (works everywhere, more control)
const imageObserver = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  entries.forEach(entry => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
      const img = entry.target;
      img.src = img.dataset.src;
      img.classList.remove('lazy');
      imageObserver.unobserve(img);
    }
  });
}, { rootMargin: '300px' }); // Start loading 300px before viewport

document.querySelectorAll('img.lazy').forEach(img => imageObserver.observe(img));

Alternative: the loading="lazy" HTML attribute is simpler for images and <iframe> elements. Firefox supports it natively. The IntersectionObserver approach gives you more control (custom loading indicator, threshold, etc.).

Infinite Scroll 

// Add a sentinel element at the bottom of the list
const sentinel = document.getElementById('list-sentinel');

const sentinelObserver = new IntersectionObserver(async (entries) => {
  if (entries[0].isIntersecting) {
    await loadMoreItems();
  }
}, { rootMargin: '100px' }); // Load 100px before reaching the bottom

sentinelObserver.observe(sentinel);

async function loadMoreItems() {
  const newItems = await fetchNextPage();
  renderItems(newItems);
  // sentinel is still being observed — will trigger again when it comes back into view
}

Scroll-Triggered Animations 

const animationObserver = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  entries.forEach(entry => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
      entry.target.classList.add('animate-in');
    }
    // Optionally remove class to re-animate on scroll up:
    // else { entry.target.classList.remove('animate-in'); }
  });
}, { threshold: 0.15 }); // Trigger when 15% visible

document.querySelectorAll('.animate-on-scroll').forEach(el => {
  animationObserver.observe(el);
});

.animate-on-scroll {
  opacity: 0;
  transform: translateY(30px);
  transition: opacity 0.5s, transform 0.5s;
}

.animate-on-scroll.animate-in {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: translateY(0);
}

Reading Progress Indicator 

const article = document.getElementById('article');
const progressBar = document.getElementById('progress-bar');

const progressObserver = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  const articleRect = article.getBoundingClientRect();
  const progress = Math.min(
    1,
    Math.max(0, (window.innerHeight - articleRect.top) / articleRect.height)
  );
  progressBar.style.width = (progress * 100) + '%';
}, { threshold: Array.from({ length: 101 }, (_, i) => i / 100) }); // 100 thresholds

progressObserver.observe(article);

Table of Contents Active Link 

const headings = document.querySelectorAll('h2, h3');
const tocLinks = document.querySelectorAll('.toc a');

const headingObserver = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  entries.forEach(entry => {
    const id = entry.target.id;
    const tocLink = document.querySelector(`.toc a[href="#${id}"]`);

    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
      tocLinks.forEach(l => l.classList.remove('active'));
      tocLink?.classList.add('active');
    }
  });
}, { rootMargin: '-100px 0px -66% 0px' }); // Focus on top third of viewport

headings.forEach(h => headingObserver.observe(h));

IntersectionObserverEntry Properties

In the callback, each entry has:

entry.isIntersecting         // boolean: visible now?
entry.intersectionRatio      // 0-1: how much is visible
entry.boundingClientRect     // element's position
entry.intersectionRect       // visible portion's position
entry.rootBounds             // viewport/root bounds
entry.target                 // the DOM element
entry.time                   // DOMHighResTimeStamp when the change was detected

Cleanup

Always disconnect when no longer needed:

// Stop observing a specific element
observer.unobserve(element);

// Disconnect all observations (clean up when component unmounts)
observer.disconnect();

In React:

useEffect(() => {
  const observer = new IntersectionObserver(callback);
  observer.observe(elementRef.current);
  return () => observer.disconnect(); // cleanup
}, []);

Firefox DevTools Visualization

There's no dedicated Intersection Observer panel in DevTools, but you can debug it:

  1. Add console.log(entry) in the callback
  2. Open DevTools Console
  3. Scroll the page — you'll see entries logged with full IntersectionObserverEntry data

Check entry.intersectionRatio and entry.rootBounds to verify your thresholds are triggering correctly.

title: PVS-Studio 8.01: OWASP Benchmark, JDK 25 and Go 1.27 support, and much more
description:
PVS-Studio 8.01 has been released. This version features expanded support for OWASP, JDK 25 and Go 1.27 support, and much more.

OWASP Benchmark for Java

In this release, we checked the Java analyzer SAST rules against the OWASP Benchmark for Java.

Evaluating the quality of security-related diagnostic rules on real-world projects can be quite challenging. We can't predict how many vulnerabilities the code will contain, so we can't determine which defects the analyzer has overlooked.

We used the benchmark to address gaps in the Java analyzer SAST capabilities, which made the tool more effective at detecting security defects.

New versions of Java and Go

With the release of PVS-Studio 8.01, we've added support for the latest platform versions. The Java analyzer now supports JDK 25, and the Go analyzer supports Go 1.27.

This enables teams to analyze projects using the latest language versions and standard libraries without delaying updates due to limitations in their analysis tools.

JDK 25 is also an LTS release, making its support particularly important for teams migrating to a new long-term support version.

Reports with analysis configuration details

The PVS-Studio_Cmd.exe utility for analyzing MSBuild projects now includes in JSON reports the project configurations used during analysis. This makes it easier to fix warnings that occur on specific platforms.

In addition, the fullhtml report generated by PlogConverter.exe now groups warnings by analysis configuration.

Expanded configuration options

This release expands the configuration options for our analyzers and utilities, making them easier to tailor to specific project requirements and environments.

The JavaScript and TypeScript analyzer now supports the max-old-space-size setting. You can find it in the pvs-settings.toml configuration file and the pvs-js.exe command-line utility. This setting enables you to specify how much memory the analyzer's Node.js server can use.

In PVS-Studio_Cmd.exe, you can now specify dependency cache paths relative to the .pvsconfig configuration file.

The C and C++ analyzer now offers more options for configuring diagnostic rules. Now, you can specify custom types as "cheap-to-copy," and configure the analyzer behavior based on the target platform.

The V719 diagnostic rule now supports additional configuration options: ignoring default branches and small enum types, specifying individual values to ignore, and setting the maximum number of constants that can be ignored.

Extended warning filtering

The Plog Converter utility for converting and filtering reports now allows you to filter diagnostic rules by CWE codes and SAST identifiers.

Breaking Change

This release includes a change that breaks backward compatibility with previous versions of the analyzer. You may need to adjust how you use the analyzer due to these changes.

The PVS-Studio installer for Windows now returns exit code 100 if Visual Studio plugin installation fails. We also added the skipVSIXInstallErrorCode flag to disable the non-zero exit code in this case.

New diagnostic rules

Java

  • V5341. OWASP. A cookie was created without enabling the 'Secure' attribute. This may lead to the exposure of sensitive data.
  • V5342. OWASP. Potentially tainted data is stored in an object that can be used as a source of trusted data.
  • V5343. OWASP. A cryptographically weak random number is used for sensitive data.

Articles

Here's the traditional roundup of posts from our blog! Over the past two months, we've published articles where we looked for bugs in the popular C# ORMs, RepoDB and SqlSugar, reviewed VSCode source code, explored the new features of Java 27, found bugs in the Create mode, and much more. The full list is below:

C and C++

  • The worst programming language of all time /s

Csharp

  • What popular ORMs for C# hide: Let's check RepoDB and SqlSugar

Java

  • What's new in Java 27
  • I found some bugs in Create mod and checked them in Minecraft

JavaScript and TypeScript

  • We checked the source code of VS Code

Go

  • PVS-Studio for Go: Quick overview of new diagnostic rules

Security

  • Avoid adding new library to project: 10-year retrospective

Other

  • Why do we integrate PVS-Studio analyzer with so many tools?

Webinars

Let's make a programming language. Variables

We continue building our own programming language from scratch. In this video, we'll take the next step by adding variables to the language.

So far, our programs have consisted of a single expression built from smaller language constructs. Now it's time to evolve the language. Instead of parsing a single expression, we'll introduce a list of declarations, allowing our language to support variable declarations and laying the groundwork for more complex programs.

During the video, Yuri will walk through the implementation step by step, showing how variables are represented and processed in our language, and how to add this functionality to your language in C++.

This video is designed for developers who want to understand how programming languages work under the hood—not just how to use them.

Go-Go-Gadg...Error? A closer look at the mistakes Go developers make!

Mistakes happen in Go code just like in any other language: typos, duplicates, broken condition checks, and so on.

But why do they still slip through? After all, many teams use tools like go vet, which catches all of this perfectly well... right?

In this webinar we covered:

  • Common mistakes in Go code, straight from well-known projects;
  • Errors that standard tools and approaches fail to catch, and how to handle them.

Let's make a programming language. Functions

We continue building our own programming language from scratch.

In the previous session, we introduced variables—they could be declared, reference one another, and were resolved through a global hash table. Now it's time to add one of the core building blocks of any language: functions. Implementing functions is really a story about scopes and name resolution. We'll explore how identifiers are looked up across different scope levels: the global scope, function scopes with their own variables, and nested local scopes inside function bodies. What happens when the same variable name exists in multiple scopes? How does the compiler determine which one to use?

In this video, we will walk through the implementation step by step, demonstrating how functions, scopes, and symbol lookup are built in code using C++. Along the way, you'll gain a deeper understanding of one of the fundamental mechanisms behind modern programming languages.

Let's make a programming language. Evaluator

We're reaching the final stage of our journey of building a programming language in C++!

So far, we've created a lexer, a parser, and an AST. Now it's time to make our language do what it was designed to do—evaluate expressions.

In this webinar, we'll explore how to represent the results of computations in our language and learn how to evaluate expressions step by step. By the end of the session, we'll bring all the pieces together and complete our own programming language.

Go vet can't go: How to create your own Go analyzer?

A static analyzer is a powerful dev tool, and any Go developer who has worked with go vet knows it. But what if its capabilities aren't enough? Would you look for a new tool, or... build your own?

In this live talk, PVS-Studio's Developer Advocate walks through Go's built-in tools and code-parsing capabilities, explains the basics of static analysis, unpacks what a semantic model is, shows how to build a syntax tree, and much more.

The end goal? Build your own static analyzer, tailored to catch what matters most in your projects.

Bugbusters

This is the first episode of our new podcast, Bugbusters. Our guest is Nathan Baggs, a content creator and YouTuber. We discussed whether it's worth learning C++ in 2026, how the language is evolving, what it's used for, and what its drawbacks are. We hope you enjoy this episode! We look forward to your comments!

Conclusion

If you would like to receive news about PVS-Studio releases, subscribe to our newsletter here.

If you haven't checked your project using PVS-Studio yet, start with a trial license.

title: O que fazer quando seu banco de dados não aguenta mais? Uma introdução ao Sharding
description:
Empresas como Notion, Slack e Discord passaram por isso e usaram a mesma técnica: o sharding. Estudei sobre o assunto e quero compartilhar com vocês de forma simples, afinal a melhor forma de aprender é ensinando.

O cenário: o banco não aguenta mais

Seu sistema cresceu, o banco ficou lento e as escritas começam a engasgar. O primeiro reflexo é comprar uma máquina maior, com mais CPU, mais memória e disco mais rápido. Isso se chama escala vertical, ou seja, crescer "para cima".

Porém, nem tudo são flores. A escala vertical tem um teto: em algum momento não existe máquina maior para comprar. Além disso, fica cada vez mais caro, e se essa única máquina cair, cai tudo junto. É o famoso ponto único de falha.

"Mas e as réplicas?"

Réplicas são cópias do banco e ajudam muito na leitura, porque espalham as consultas. Porém, toda escrita continua indo para um único banco principal. Se o gargalo é escrita ou volume de dados, réplica não resolve.

O que é sharding

Em vez de uma máquina maior, você usa várias máquinas, e cada uma guarda só uma parte dos dados. Cada parte é chamada de shard. Todas têm as mesmas tabelas, mas linhas diferentes. Ou seja, escala horizontal.

Por exemplo, um app com 3 milhões de usuários. A shard key (já explico o que é) é o id do usuário: ids de 1 a 1 milhão vão para o shard 1, de 1 a 2 milhões para o shard 2 e de 2 a 3 milhões para o shard 3.

É como uma biblioteca que lotou e abriu unidades: autores de A a M na unidade 1, de N a Z na unidade 2. Achar um livro pelo autor é fácil. Mas achar "todos os livros de 2020" obriga a visitar todas as unidades. Guarda essa ideia, porque ela é o coração dos problemas do sharding.

Sharding, particionamento e replicação

Três termos que confundem muito:

  • Particionamento: dividir uma tabela em pedaços, geralmente no mesmo servidor. Por exemplo, o partitioning nativo do PostgreSQL.
  • Sharding: dividir os dados entre servidores diferentes.
  • Replicação: fazer cópias iguais dos dados em vários servidores.

Ou seja, sharding ajuda a escalar escrita e volume, e replicação ajuda a escalar leitura e disponibilidade. E eles andam juntos: na prática, cada shard costuma ter as suas próprias réplicas. Um não substitui o outro.

Como o sistema sabe onde está cada dado?

Se os dados estão espalhados, alguém precisa encaminhar a consulta para o shard certo. Isso pode ficar:

  • No código da aplicação, que calcula o shard.
  • Num intermediário, como o Vitess, que nasceu no YouTube e é usado pelo Slack.
  • No próprio banco, como o sharding nativo do MongoDB ou o Citus no Postgres.

No MongoDB, por exemplo, a aplicação fala com o roteador mongos, que consulta os metadados nos config servers e manda a query para o shard certo.

A shard key: a decisão mais importante

A shard key é a coluna que decide em qual shard cada linha vai morar. Uma boa chave tem muitos valores diferentes, distribui os dados por igual e aparece em quase toda consulta. Por exemplo, o id do usuário.

Por faixa (range)

Ids de 1 a 1 milhão no shard A, de 1 a 2 milhões no shard B. É ótima para buscar intervalos. Mas se a chave for a data, toda escrita de hoje cai no mesmo shard, que fica sobrecarregado.

Por hash

O sistema passa a chave por uma função matemática (algo como hash(user_id) % N) que espalha os dados por igual entre os shards. Distribui muito bem. Porém, buscar um intervalo vira perguntar para todos os shards e juntar a resposta.

Por região ou por cliente

Também dá para separar por região, deixando os dados perto do usuário, ou por cliente. Por exemplo, o Notion dividiu o banco pelo id do workspace. Assim, os dados de uma mesma empresa ficam juntos e quase toda consulta vai para um shard só.

Dica: shards lógicos

Uma dica que o Notion usou: crie muito mais shards "lógicos" do que máquinas. Eles começaram com 480 shards em 32 bancos. É como uma mudança: você empacota tudo em 480 caixas. Se trocar 32 armários por 64, move caixas inteiras, sem desempacotar livro por livro.

Os problemas

Lembra das unidades da biblioteca? Consultas que cruzam shards, como JOINs e relatórios gerais, precisam perguntar para todos e juntar o resultado na aplicação. E transações envolvendo vários shards ficam caras e complicadas.

Outros problemas:

  • Ids: o auto-incremento de cada shard pode repetir o mesmo número.
  • Shard "quente": um cliente muito ativo concentra a carga. O Discord conta isso no post sobre como guarda trilhões de mensagens.
  • Resharding: mudar os dados de shard com o sistema no ar é a parte mais arriscada.

Então quando usar?

Só depois de tentar o mais simples: melhorar queries e índices, colocar cache, réplicas de leitura e uma máquina maior. E quando o problema é escrita ou volume que não cabe mais num servidor. Sharding cedo demais é complexidade de graça.

Ou seja, sharding resolve o limite de um banco só, mas cobra em complexidade para sempre, na aplicação e na operação. E sempre que possível, prefira ferramentas que já fazem isso por você (Vitess, Citus, MongoDB) em vez de reinventar.

Conclusão

Apresentei apenas algo introdutório, recomendo se aprofundarem! Se você já é experiente, complementa nos comentários. Obrigado por ler até aqui!

  • Slack Engineering: Scaling datastores at Slack with Vitess
  • Notion: Sharding Postgres at Notion
  • Discord: How Discord stores trillions of messages
  • Bases de datos distribuidas: sharding
  • Sharding vs. Partitioning

title: Provenance gate: no AI agent memory write without a source
description:
By Mikhail Oskola, founder of Retailbox Automation.

A provenance gate is a rule that sits in front of an AI agent's memory: an agent can propose a fact, but it can't become memory until it names where the fact came from. No source, no write. We built one for a hackathon project called FleetMemory, then attacked it ourselves. The first version let a whole class of lies through, 6 out of 6 tries. The fixed version blocked 30 out of 30.

What a provenance gate actually checks

Most agent memory systems trust whatever the agent writes. That's the failure mode: an agent infers a number, states it with confidence, and the system files it next to facts a customer actually said. Read it back in a month and there's no way to tell which is which.

A provenance gate adds one deterministic check before any write commits: does this fact trace to a source? A customer saying "our budget is now $14,000" is sourced, and it supersedes the old value. An agent inferring a budget from context, with nothing a person actually said behind it, is not sourced. That claim quarantines instead of writing straight to memory.

In the FleetMemory demo, a rogue agent asserts a budget of $1,800 through the exact same write path everything else uses. The gate can't tell that number is false; it isn't comparing values, it's checking for a citation. It quarantines the claim with a gold "held for review" stamp, and an adversarial verifier reads the case and rejects it, right above the real fact it contradicts: $18,000, sourced to an actual customer message.


The demo mid-attack: the rogue $1,800 budget is held for review, directly above the $18,000 fact Alex learned from the customer. Maria, the second agent, still answers from $18,000.

  • Junk and duplicate checks: malformed or already-known writes drop before they cost a verifier call.
  • Contradiction checks: a new value that conflicts with an existing fact gets flagged, not silently overwritten.
  • Confidence floor: a guess below a minimum confidence never reaches memory.
  • Provenance check: a claim with no customer utterance behind it quarantines, no matter how confident the agent sounds.

The red-team run that found the hole

A gate is only as good as what you throw at it. We ran 30 adversarial writes across 5 attack classes against the real gate and verifier, not a mock. The script and full results ship in the public repo.

The first run caught a real gap: unsourced novel claims, facts that don't contradict anything already in memory because there's nothing to contradict, sailed past the deterministic gate 6 out of 6 times. A brand-new, confident, entirely made-up fact walked straight into the fleet's shared memory.

The fix was a rule we call needs_provenance: a claim with no customer utterance behind it quarantines and faces the verifier, and claimed confidence alone can no longer auto-supersede a fact that already has a source. We re-ran the same 30 attacks. This time all 30 were blocked, including junk, oversized payloads, absurd-confidence guesses, unsourced contradictions, and the unsourced novel claims that got through the first time.

The gate still let through 9 of 10 legitimate customer-confirmed updates, not 10 of 10. The one it missed is a disclosed race condition: a value looping back to what it originally was while an intermediate update sat unresolved. It's traced in the decision journal, not hidden or tuned away. Median gate latency across the run: 293 milliseconds.


Where that trace lives: the decision journal is an ordinary CockroachDB table. This view is the demo customer, not the red-team run: seven facts still active, six clean accepts, and two contradicting writes quarantined, then rejected by the verifier.

Why the verifier defaults to reject

A quarantined claim doesn't just sit there. An adversarial LLM verifier reads it and rules on it, and its default is reject, not accept. If the verifier call itself fails for any reason, that also counts as a rejection.

The verifier's job is to weigh provenance specifically: a direct customer statement supersedes an old fact; an unsourced value gets rejected, even if it sounds plausible, even if the agent stating it sounds confident. Every verdict, with a one-sentence reason, gets written back onto the same decision-journal row as the original write attempt.

Corrections don't delete anything either. A fact that gets superseded keeps its old row, marked invalid and pointed at whatever replaced it. Ask the system what it believed on any past date and it can tell you, including beliefs it has since abandoned.


The verifier's ruling on that claim: refused, struck through, with its one-sentence reason on the card. The $1,800 had no customer statement behind it; the $18,000 did.

The strongest kind of proof: someone else validating it

Anyone can claim their own system works. While building this we found LangChain's AsyncPostgresSaver checkpointer failing against CockroachDB, and filed it upstream with a standalone repro and a proposed fix direction (langchain-ai/langgraph#8620).

A community contributor picked it up, built a complete fix along that direction, and verified it independently against both PostgreSQL 17.5 and CockroachDB v26.2.4. It's pending maintainer review as of this writing. Nobody on our team wrote that fix or ran that verification, which is a stronger signal than any benchmark we'd publish about ourselves.

Where to see it running

FleetMemory is our own entry in the CockroachDB x AWS "Build with Agentic Memory" hackathon, not a paid client project. It's public and MIT-licensed so anyone can read the gate logic or rerun the red team.


How the pieces fit: every agent write goes through the gate, quarantined claims go to the verifier, and facts plus the decision journal live in CockroachDB. AWS runs session state (AgentCore Memory), the models (Bedrock) and the public demo (Lambda).

  • Live demo, no login required: talk to agent Alex, come back as agent Maria, then hit "hallucinate a fact" and watch the gate catch it. https://pskmxv5sm4k3fj2rjoh2aoijka0ofgob.lambda-url.us-east-1.on.aws/
  • Public repo (MIT license): the gate, the verifier, the red-team script, and the eval results. https://github.com/retailbox-automation/fleetmemory
  • 1:15 demo video walking through the quarantine-and-reject moment. https://youtu.be/SDFpU-z9h2w
  • The upstream issue: a fix verified by a third-party contributor, pending maintainer review. https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/issues/8620

FAQ

What is a provenance gate in AI agent memory?

A provenance gate is a check that runs before any fact commits to an agent's memory. It asks whether the fact traces to a named source, like a direct customer statement, rather than trusting the agent's own confidence. A claim without a source quarantines instead of writing straight to memory.

Isn't a confidence score enough to filter out bad facts?

No, and that's the exact gap our red team found. An agent can state a brand-new, unsourced fact with high confidence, and if nothing already in memory contradicts it, a confidence-only filter has nothing to compare it against. It sailed through our first gate 6 out of 6 times. The fix checks for a source, not a confidence number.

What happens to a fact the gate rejects?

It doesn't disappear. It's written to a decision journal with the reason for the rejection, so anyone can query what was attempted, when, and why it didn't pass. Accepted facts that later get corrected aren't deleted either. The old value is marked invalid and kept, so the system can answer what it used to believe.

Is this the same as citing sources in a RAG answer?

Related, but earlier in the pipeline. RAG citations tell a user where an answer's text came from. A provenance gate decides whether a claim is even allowed to become a durable fact in memory in the first place, before any agent ever retrieves and repeats it.

Can I run the red team myself?

Yes. The repo is MIT-licensed and includes the red-team script and the eval results cited here. Point it at your own CockroachDB cluster and it reruns the same 30 attacks.

Originally published at https://retailbox-automation.com/blog/ai-agent-provenance-gate. The pattern behind it, agents that write to shared memory only through a verification gate, is one we can build into an agent project for a client: AI Agent Development Company.

title: Layanan Rumah Tools
Kolab: Benchmarking Human-Agent Collaboration in Long-Horizon Workflows
description:
arXiv:2610.21109v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When humans collaborate with AI agents on long-horizon tasks, what happens to the agents' contributions? For solving long-horizon tasks, humans place greater importance on ongoing interaction with AI agents (e.g., revising plans) than on an agent's ability to complete the task in a single attempt. However, most agentic benchmarks have focused more on automation. Strong performance on such benchmarks does not imply effective real-world collaboration. Professional workflows offer a useful setting, as they often involve interdependent steps. To address this gap, we introduce Kolab, a new dataset of 115+ hours of screen recordings of 50 professionals from 40 occupations collaborating with agents on realistic, long-horizon problems. Kolab also contains participants' collaboration and output quality judgments. Our analysis reveals diverse collaboration patterns, highlighting the importance of when and how professionals coordinate with agents. A collaborative agent must do two things that automation benchmarks never test: anticipate whether experts will adopt, modify, or reject its contribution once it leaves the chat window to guide its next steps, and assess collaboration quality from the unfolding workflow without constant expert feedback. Our benchmark operationalizes both: (1) forecasting how professionals use agent contributions at diverse workflows, and (2) verifying their judgments of collaboration satisfaction and output quality. Findings show that frontier models, both agentic and non-agentic, overestimate collaboration with experts and struggle to distinguish between high- and low-quality collaboration. Longer workflow context does not consistently improve these predictions. As frontier agents cannot yet understand long-horizon collaboration with experts, we position Kolab as a valuable dataset for studying human-agent collaboration grounded in real professional workflows.

title: Introducing Run SDK: secure eval for your agents
description:
Agents increasingly write TypeScript programs to coordinate tools and process their results. Once those programs touch real applications, some steps require authentication, while others need human approval.

Executing that code with eval gives it the same access as the application around it, including its secrets and internal services, and leaves no durable way to pause at those boundaries.

Today, we're releasing the Run SDK, a package for executing untrusted JavaScript and TypeScript without giving it direct access to your application or system. Applications expose narrow host functions and can interrupt execution for authentication or human-in-the-loop approval. The program resumes after a decision without repeating completed work.

A small interface to the host

The Run SDK evaluates JavaScript or type-stripped TypeScript in a fresh QuickJS context inside a worker thread, with no direct route to Node.js or the network.

The application exposes selected operations through hostFunctions. These are regular functions that become callable globals inside the sandbox:

Here, the generated program knows about store.listOrders(). The database client and its credentials remain in the application.

Calls cross the sandbox boundary through serialization. A host function may return a promise, so existing service clients can sit behind this interface without being passed into the sandbox.

You can try this in the playground. Code you run there can only reach the host functions on the page.

Code mode in practice

The Run SDK is the internal module powering code mode tool execution in the AI SDK. Giving an agent a program changes the unit of work. One model response can describe the calls and the logic connecting them:

The two requests happen concurrently, and invoice filtering stays local to the program. Only the useful result returns to the application.

This is a good fit for agents that work across several internal services. A research agent can combine search results before answering. A support agent can inspect an account without putting an entire billing response back into its context.

The same package can power a code interpreter or a product feature that accepts customer-defined transformations. In both cases, the application chooses the available data and operations.

Host functions work best when they map to actions in your product, like refunding an order. Exposing orders.refund(id) gives the application a clear place to check the user and the order. A generic request function would make that authority much harder to reason about.

Native support for human-in-the-loop and auth

Reading invoices is different from issuing a refund. When generated code reaches a sensitive operation, the host function can interrupt execution:

When the run is interrupted, the result includes a signed token the application can save with an approval request and use to resume the run when a decision arrives.

Resuming replays the program, but settled host function calls use their recorded results. Host function work completed before the interruption does not run again. The interrupted function receives the approval and continues from there.

This mechanism also works when a workflow must wait for authentication. The application owns the waiting period; the worker does not need to remain alive.

Running within limits

A sandbox still needs to account for code that loops forever or produces an oversized result. createRunner() sets shared limits:

Limits can also be set per run. The defaults cover the QuickJS heap and the values crossing the host boundary; applications can tighten them for their workload.

Each invocation receives a new QuickJS context. Dynamic evaluation is disabled and built-in prototypes are hardened. This boundary applies to the generated program, while host functions remain trusted application code and must perform their normal authorization checks.

The Run SDK is intended for JavaScript computation inside an application. Workloads that require an operating system, package installation, or process-level isolation should use Vercel Sandbox instead.

Extracting the execution layer

The first version of this runtime lived inside just-bash as js-exec, backed by QuickJS. It let agents write TypeScript against the shell's virtual filesystem and command set.

We extracted that layer into the Run SDK and replaced the Node-shaped environment with application-defined host functions. We tested the underlying mechanism in eve, using it to run agent-generated TypeScript against real tools. It now powers code mode in the AI SDK where existing AI SDK tools are mapped to host functions, while the Run SDK handles their sandboxed execution.

Getting started

The Run SDK supports Node.js 22.13+ and Bun. You will need pnpm or another package manager installed on your local development machine.

Check out the documentation and API reference.
