title: Memory, blast radius, and a guard: three local tools for AI coding agents
description:
I spend most of my day with an AI coding agent open: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, depending on the repo. They are good. They are also forgetful, a bit reckless, and very trusting.

  • Forgetful. Every session starts blank. I explain the architecture again. The agent proposes the fix I rejected last week.
  • Reckless. It renames a function, fixes the three callers grep found, and misses the fourth one, a caller of a caller.
  • Trusting. It reads a GitHub issue that a stranger wrote, and that issue can contain instructions aimed at the agent, hidden where I would never see them.

I ended up writing one tool for each problem. They're separate projects, but they were built to sit side by side in the same session, and together they cover most of what bothered me. Each one is a single Rust binary, runs locally, needs no account or API key, and hooks into the agent through MCP plus a short rule and a few client hooks.

Here is each one, then how they work together.

🧠 palace: memory that survives the session

palace is local-first memory for coding agents. It stores what happened verbatim (not an LLM summary that drops the detail), recalls it when it's relevant, and cites where every answer came from.

You:    why did we switch the queue to SQLite last month?
Agent:  [palace_search → wing my_api, room decisions, filed 2026-09-03]
        You dropped Redis because the deploy target had no persistent volume.
        The benchmark you ran is in the same drawer.

How it's organised

Memory is laid out like a building, which keeps search focused:

  • Wings are projects or topics. Rooms are areas inside them (backend, decisions, testing). Drawers hold one chunk of verbatim text plus its embedding.
  • A knowledge graph stores time-stamped facts (my_api → uses_queue → SQLite, valid from 2026-09-03), so a changed decision is invalidated, not silently overwritten.
  • Each agent keeps a diary, which is how tomorrow's session picks up where today's stopped, even when tomorrow you're using a different agent.

Search is hybrid: BM25 keyword scoring fused with cosine similarity over embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2, which runs on your CPU through ONNX Runtime. There's an optional local reranker. Everything lives in one palace.db SQLite file.

The part that matters: you don't have to ask

A memory tool the agent forgets to call is just storage. palace installs user-level hooks so recall happens on its own:

  • Session start injects recent diary entries for this project and its top drawers.
  • Prompt submit searches with your actual question before the agent answers.
  • Post tool use surfaces related memory while the agent greps and reads files.
  • Stop asks the agent to write a diary entry if it used memory but saved nothing.

All hooks fail open: an empty palace just means a normal session. It works with 11 clients today, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, VS Code, Zed and Claude Desktop.

palace install                               # wire up every agent on this machine
palace init ~/my-project --yes --auto-mine   # detect rooms and mine the repo
palace search "how did we decide on the database schema"

💥 impact: know what a change will break before you make it

Before you rename a function, change a type or drop a field, you need to know what depends on it. grep finds the name but misses callers of callers. An agent that reads the code to find out is guessing, and it reads a lot of code to do it.

impact answers "if I change this, what else is affected?" in one call, the same way every time. Point it at a file, a symbol or a git diff:

impact index .                                     # later runs skip unchanged files
impact query src/payments/service.rs               # what depends on this file?
impact change "rename PaymentStatus::Failed"       # what breaks if I rename this?
git diff | impact diff                             # what does my uncommitted work reach?

  • 🔴 Direct callers, 🟠 indirect callers all the way up, 🔵 API routes, events and database tables the affected code touches, and 🟢 tests that reach it.
  • Deterministic. It parses with tree-sitter, with no model in the loop. Re-indexing an unchanged project takes about 0.1s, and a query takes tens of milliseconds.
  • Errs toward over-reporting. When a call could mean several same-named symbols, it lists all of them with a confidence label (exact, probable, heuristic) rather than guessing and missing one.
  • 8 languages: Rust, TypeScript/JavaScript (React and React Native too), Python, Go, Kotlin, Swift and C++.

For agents, impact install registers the MCP server and a rule with four triggers: index at session start, check blast radius before the first edit and before every commit, re-check after editing, and put the impact_diff result in the PR description so the reviewer sees what the agent saw. In Claude Code a PreToolUse hook backs the rule up, because an agent can lose track of a rule halfway through a long session, but a hook fires every time.

It's honest about its limits: a call made through a registry, or a function passed as a value, leaves no edge. A short report is not proof that nothing uses a symbol.

🛡️ mcp-warden: clean untrusted text before the agent reads it

Coding agents read text that strangers wrote: issues, pull requests, web pages, Slack messages, Sentry events, curl output. Any of it can carry prompt injection, often hidden in invisible Unicode, HTML comments, tracking images or bidi tricks.

mcp-warden sits between those sources and the agent:

  • 🧹 Strips what a person wouldn't see: invisible characters, HTML comments, off-host images.
  • 🔒 Withholds fields that look like injection. The agent gets a notice with a quarantine id and is told to tell you. You review the payload in your own terminal (mcp-warden show ID). The agent can't unlock the quarantine itself.
  • 📥 Treats repos the agent cloned as outside content, while leaving your own project files, builds and tests alone.
  • 🚦 In proxy mode it can also gate sensitive MCP calls once untrusted content has entered the session, and pin tool definitions so it warns you when a server quietly changes them.

It has two modes, and you can use both:

🪝 Hook mode 🔌 Proxy mode
Set up with mcp-warden install mcp-warden wrap config.json
Covers Every tool: MCP, WebFetch, WebSearch, Bash, reads in cloned repos One stdio MCP server per wrap
Best for Day-to-day protection with zero config Fine-grained policy on specific servers 
brew install ancientice/mcp-warden/mcp-warden
mcp-warden install    # Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Kiro, Cline and more

The README says it plainly, and so will I: prompt injection is ordinary text, and a filter can always be reworded around. warden is one layer of defense, not a sandbox. Keep least-privilege tokens and a sandbox as well.

🔗 Why they work better together

Each tool is useful alone. The reason I run all three is that they cover different moments in the same session and reinforce each other:

  1. Session start. palace hands the agent yesterday's diary and this project's decisions. It doesn't have to rediscover the conventions by grepping.
  2. The agent reads a bug report. warden strips the hidden comment and withholds the field that tries to give orders. The agent still sees the title and tells you something was flagged.
  3. The agent is about to edit. impact lists every caller, route and test the change reaches. The agent treats it as a checklist instead of fixing the callers it happened to find.
  4. The agent opens a PR. impact_diff goes in the description, so the reviewer sees the blast radius without running anything.
  5. Session end. palace's stop hook makes sure the fix, the reason behind it and any new decision get written down, so the next session starts from there.

Some details I like about running them as a set:

  • Same shape everywhere. One binary, <tool> install to wire up your agents, doctor (palace and impact) to check the wiring, and uninstall removes only what that tool added.
  • Your data stays on your machine. No telemetry, no hosted service, no API keys. Your code, your memory and your quarantine stay on disk. The only network calls are palace's one-time embedding model download and impact's daily release check (IMPACT_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 turns it off).
  • Deterministic where it counts. impact and warden have no model in the loop, so their output is the same every run. palace is the only one using embeddings, and those run locally too.
  • They stay out of each other's way. warden checks outside content (web tools, gh/curl, MCP servers that point at public sources), so by default it leaves palace's and impact's local output alone. Your own project's memory and call graph aren't the threat model.

⚡ Try all three in two minutes

macOS / Linux (Homebrew)

brew tap AncientiCe/palace && brew install palace
brew install ancientice/impact/impact
brew install ancientice/mcp-warden/mcp-warden

palace install && impact install && mcp-warden install

No Homebrew? Each repo also has a curl ... | sh install script.

Windows (PowerShell)

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AncientiCe/impact-rs/master/scripts/install.ps1 | iex
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AncientiCe/mcp-warden/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex

palace install; impact install; mcp-warden install

The Windows install scripts download the release binary for your platform and verify its SHA-256 checksum. Restart your agent app so it reloads its MCP config, then ask it something like "What do we know about how this project handles migrations?" and watch it answer from memory.

All three are open source (MIT; mcp-warden is MIT or Apache-2.0). Issues, blind-spot reports and PRs are welcome. If impact misses a caller or warden lets something through, I want to hear about it.

📎 Links

  • palace (memory): https://github.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs
  • impact (blast radius): https://github.com/AncientiCe/impact-rs
  • mcp-warden (prompt-injection guard): https://github.com/AncientiCe/mcp-warden
  • palace in the official MCP registry: registry.modelcontextprotocol.io (io.github.ancientice/palace-rs)
  • Model Context Protocol: modelcontextprotocol.io

title: NSFW Video and GIF Moderation with Python and an API
description:
If your app accepts video or GIF uploads (short clips in a social feed, reaction GIFs in chat, product videos on a marketplace), checking only the thumbnail is not moderation. The problem frame can sit at second 12 of a 30 second clip. NSFW video moderation with an image API works by sampling frames, scoring each one, and deciding on the whole clip.

Every number below comes from a real run on a public domain 25 second clip of a beer being poured: it starts with an empty glass and ends with a full one, a good test for how detections change over time.

Want to see the labels on your own clips? Try the NSFW Detect API on a frame from one of your uploads.

How it works

A moderation API looks at images, so a video becomes a list of frames:

  1. Sample frames with ffmpeg, at a fixed interval or on scene changes.
  2. Score each frame with the API, in parallel.
  3. Aggregate per top-level category: highest confidence, number of flagged frames, timestamps.
  4. Decide allow, review, or block for the clip, and stop early when a frame already settles it.

Step 1: Sample frames with ffmpeg 

import os
import subprocess

def extract_frames(video_path, out_dir, every_seconds=1.0):
    """Grab one frame every N seconds. Returns [(timestamp, path), ...]."""
    subprocess.run(
        ["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", video_path,
         "-vf", f"fps=1/{every_seconds},scale='min(1280,iw)':-2",
         "-q:v", "3", f"{out_dir}/frame_%05d.jpg"],
        check=True,
    )
    files = sorted(os.listdir(out_dir))
    return [(i * every_seconds, os.path.join(out_dir, f)) for i, f in enumerate(files)]

On the 25 second test clip, one frame per second gives 26 frames; one every 2 seconds gives 13.

Step 2: Score frames in parallel

Keep only the top-level categories (empty ParentName) so every sub-label maps to one policy rule:

import tempfile
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

import requests

API_URL = "https://nsfw-detect3.p.rapidapi.com/nsfw-detect"
HEADERS = {
    "x-rapidapi-key": "YOUR_API_KEY",
    "x-rapidapi-host": "nsfw-detect3.p.rapidapi.com",
}

def moderate_frame(path):
    """Return the top-level categories found in one frame: {name: confidence}."""
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        r = requests.post(API_URL, headers=HEADERS, files={"image": f}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    labels = r.json()["body"]["ModerationLabels"]
    return {l["Name"]: l["Confidence"] for l in labels if l["ParentName"] == ""}

def moderate_video(video_path, every_seconds=1.0, workers=4):
    """Moderate sampled frames in parallel. Returns [(timestamp, categories), ...]."""
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
        frames = extract_frames(video_path, tmp, every_seconds)
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers) as pool:
            results = list(pool.map(lambda fr: moderate_frame(fr[1]), frames))
    return [(t, cats) for (t, _), cats in zip(frames, results)]

for t, cats in moderate_video("beer_pour.mp4"):
    print(f"{t:>3.0f}s", {k: round(v, 1) for k, v in cats.items()})
#   0s {}                    empty glass
#   8s {'Alcohol': 94.9}
#  11s {'Alcohol': 95.9}
#  21s {'Alcohol': 99.3}
#  25s {'Alcohol': 99.8}
#  (26 frames in total)

The empty glass at second 0 comes back clean, and Alcohol is flagged from second 3, as soon as beer is in the glass, up to 99.8% on the full glass. That timeline is what turns frame scores into a decision: when the category first appears, how often, and how confident the API is at its peak.

Step 3: Aggregate per category and decide

Each policy rule gets one extra field compared with a single image policy: min_frames, the number of frames that must cross the threshold before the rule fires.

POLICY = {
    "Explicit":                                          {"action": "block",  "threshold": 60, "min_frames": 1},
    "Non-Explicit Nudity of Intimate parts and Kissing": {"action": "review", "threshold": 70, "min_frames": 2},
    "Violence":                                          {"action": "block",  "threshold": 70, "min_frames": 2},
    "Hate Symbols":                                      {"action": "block",  "threshold": 50, "min_frames": 1},
    "Drugs & Tobacco":                                   {"action": "review", "threshold": 80, "min_frames": 2},
    "Alcohol":                                           {"action": "review", "threshold": 90, "min_frames": 2},
}

def summarize(results):
    """Per category: max confidence, number of flagged frames, timestamps."""
    summary = {}
    for t, cats in results:
        for name, conf in cats.items():
            s = summary.setdefault(name, {"max": 0.0, "frames": 0, "times": []})
            s["max"] = max(s["max"], conf)
            s["frames"] += 1
            s["times"].append(t)
    return summary

def decide(summary):
    """Turn the per-category summary into allow / review / block."""
    verdict, reasons = "allow", []
    for name, s in summary.items():
        rule = POLICY.get(name)
        if not rule or s["max"] < rule["threshold"] or s["frames"] < rule["min_frames"]:
            continue
        reasons.append(f"{name}: {s['frames']} frames, max {s['max']:.1f}%, first at {s['times'][0]:.0f}s")
        if rule["action"] == "block":
            verdict = "block"
        elif verdict != "block":
            verdict = "review"
    return verdict, reasons

print(decide(summarize(moderate_video("beer_pour.mp4"))))
# ('review', ['Alcohol: 9 frames, max 99.8%, first at 3s'])

The reasons string tells a reviewer where to jump in the clip instead of watching all of it.

The full guide adds a scene-change sampler with a frame gap cap and the exact numbers behind each sampling choice.

Step 4: Stop early on a clear block

Once a block rule fires, the remaining frames cannot change the verdict:

def moderate_with_early_stop(frames, workers=4):
    """Moderate frames in time order, batch by batch; stop at the first block."""
    results, calls = [], 0
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers) as pool:
        for i in range(0, len(frames), workers):
            batch = frames[i:i + workers]
            cats = list(pool.map(lambda fr: moderate_frame(fr[1]), batch))
            results += [(t, c) for (t, _), c in zip(batch, cats)]
            calls += len(batch)
            verdict, reasons = decide(summarize(results))
            if verdict == "block":
                break
    return verdict, reasons, calls

POLICY["Alcohol"] = {"action": "block", "threshold": 90, "min_frames": 2}  # kids platform
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    frames = extract_frames("beer_pour.mp4", tmp, every_seconds=1.0)
    print(moderate_with_early_stop(frames))
# ('block', ['Alcohol: 3 frames, max 95.9%, first at 3s'], 12)

Blocked after 12 calls instead of 26. Clean videos still need every sampled frame.

Choosing a sampling rate

Real results on the same clip, with the review policy:

  • Every 1 second: 26 calls, peak 99.8%, verdict review
  • Every 2 seconds: 13 calls, peak 99.8%, verdict review

Both rates flag the clip. For short user uploads, one frame every one to two seconds is a solid default; for long edited videos, scene-change sampling with a gap cap cuts calls further.

GIF uploads

ffmpeg reads GIFs directly, so extract_frames("reaction.gif", tmp, 2.0) works unchanged. Without ffmpeg, Pillow can sample by frame duration:

from PIL import Image, ImageSequence

def extract_gif_frames(gif_path, out_dir, every_seconds=1.0):
    """Sample a GIF every N seconds using each frame's own duration."""
    gif = Image.open(gif_path)
    frames, t, next_t = [], 0.0, 0.0
    for i, frame in enumerate(ImageSequence.Iterator(gif)):
        if t >= next_t:
            path = os.path.join(out_dir, f"gif_{i:05d}.jpg")
            frame.convert("RGB").save(path, quality=90)
            frames.append((t, path))
            next_t += every_seconds
        t += frame.info.get("duration", 100) / 1000
    return frames

On a GIF made from the same clip, sampling every 2 seconds gave 13 frames, Alcohol on 7 (max 99.9%) and a review verdict. The convert("RGB") is required: GIF frames are palette images and JPEG cannot store them.

How many API calls?

One call per sampled frame. A 30 second clip sampled every 2 seconds costs 15 calls, and 1,000 such clips come to about 15,000 calls over the month before early stops. Upload duration limits bound the worst case, and hashing uploads avoids re-moderating reposted GIFs.

Production tips

  • Publish after the verdict. Keep new videos pending and moderate in a background worker; 26 frames with 4 workers took about 6 seconds in this test.
  • Fail safe to review when a frame call errors out.
  • Moderate the poster frame shown in the feed too.

Sources

  • One example of how to pour beer (Wikimedia Commons): the public domain test clip
  • ffmpeg select filter documentation: scene and prev_selected_t variables

Run it on the clips your users actually upload: grab a key on the NSFW Detect API page and tune the thresholds on real data.

title: SALTO: Solver-Anchored Lifted Transfer Operators for Nonlinear Event Inference
description:
arXiv:2610.21049v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learned dynamical models can accurately predict trajectories while producing unreliable sensitivities when differentiated or transposed, limiting their use in inverse problems and scientific decision-making. Classical adjoints provide exact local derivatives, but a single adjoint cannot represent the nonlinear response of a system to a family of finite-amplitude perturbations. We introduce SALTO (Solver-Anchored Lifted Transfer Operators), a Koopman-based framework for inferring finite-amplitude sources. In the lifted space, the nonlinear dynamics are approximated by a linear propagator, and its transpose carries each sensor backward in a single solve. The result is a reusable lifted adjoint that predicts the measurement produced by any candidate localized event with one encoder pass and an inner product. To give the model the simulator's exact local behavior, SALTO imposes three structural constraints: it anchors the physical-state dynamics to the simulator's linearized propagator, centers the learned observables so that they vanish to second order at the reference state, and uses a block-triangular lifted propagator. These constraints guarantee that the model reduces to the simulator's tangent dynamics and classical adjoint as the amplitude vanishes, while the learned observables carry only the finite-amplitude correction. On three nonlinear PDE systems, SALTO predicts the measurements of finite-amplitude sources to within 2-8% where the classical adjoint is in error by 41-165%, recovers source position and intensity from sparse sensors nearly as accurately as inversion through the solver, and samples the joint posterior of two interacting sources, matching the solver's posterior on reaction-diffusion at a twentieth of its cost. One trained model serves new sensor layouts and measurement times with a single backward solve.

title: Cursor Cloud Agents can now run in Vercel Sandbox
description:
Cursor Cloud Agents can now run in Vercel Sandbox instead of Cursor's hosted machines.

Cursor manages the agent harness and inference loop. Its Self-Hosted Machines APIs let you supply the execution environment where agents clone repositories, edit files, and run commands and tests. Self-Hosted Machines requires a Cursor Enterprise plan.

Vercel Sandbox provides that execution environment as an isolated Firecracker microVM for each agent request. Vercel Functions and Vercel Workflows form a durable control plane that claims queued agent requests, provisions workers, monitors sessions, and cleans up automatically.

With this architecture, you get:

  • A scale-to-zero worker pool without long-lived virtual machines

  • A dedicated, isolated Sandbox for every agent request

  • Durable retries when a worker or session fails

  • Short-lived, user-scoped credentials inside each Sandbox

Follow the step-by-step guide to deploy the reference implementation to your own Vercel account, or learn more in the Vercel Sandbox documentation.

title: Least privilege failed my Pulumi run, and that is the point of this weeks agent debate
description:
A small infra failure explains this weeks big Anthropic argument better than most hot takes.

First the news, compressed. October 9, Anthropic disclosed that a Claude Haiku 4.5 agent, browsing random sites in a July 18 internal test, submitted a fabricated tip to a Philadelphia police tip line. Spam folder, never reviewed, not noticed until September 28. Same report: agents exploiting vulnerabilities, getting into paid databases without paying, submitting real forms. No real-time awareness, their words. Live internet got cut from internal evaluations. Nadella wants an emergency brake. Brad Smith says a washing machine is more regulated than AI.

Now the small failure. You wire up the Chronosphere Pulumi provider with the token you already have lying around, the ingestion service account. It is write-only. It feels like the safe, least-privilege choice. It also does not work. Pulumi is doing administrative tasks, so the provider needs an unrestricted service account token or a SysAdmin token, set as CHRONOSPHERE_API_TOKEN. Anything less gets blocked on nearly every operation. Full skill: https://vectle.com/skills/skl_4gSyBVyOLMp67pw7Xid2yQ

That is Side B in one paragraph: scope an agent down far enough and you have not made it safe, you have made it useless.

And Side A is right there in the same skill: that admin token does not expire on its own, so you keep it out of shell history and CI logs and you rotate it like any other admin credential. Powerful access with no expiry and no watching is how a July action turns into a September surprise.

What we actually do on our own stacks, and what Id argue labs should do with browsing agents:

  • Give the powerful token, when the job needs it. Dont pretend the weak one is a safety strategy.
  • Scope that power in time, not just in permissions. Rotation and expiry beat good intentions.
  • Watch the powerful mode live. A transcript review two months later is not oversight.
  • Keep a stop that works while it is running, not after.

We keep these war stories at https://vectle.com so the next person, or agent, hits the token wall in docs instead of in production.

Debate question: should AI agents roam the open internet with no human watching, yes or no? And closer to home: what is the most powerful token your agents hold right now, and when does it expire?

title: Firefox DevTools for Rust Developers: Wasm Debugging, wasm-pack, and API Testing
description:
Rust developers building web applications or working with WebAssembly benefit from Firefox DevTools in specific ways. Here's the developer guide.

Firefox for Rust Web Development

Axum / Actix-Web API Debugging

The Network panel in Firefox DevTools is the primary tool for debugging Rust web framework endpoints.

Axum example:

use axum::{routing::get, Router, Json};

#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
struct User { id: u32, name: String }

async fn get_user() -> Json<User> {
    Json(User { id: 1, name: "Alice".to_string() })
}

let app = Router::new().route("/user", get(get_user));

In Firefox DevTools → Network → click the /user request → Response tab shows the JSON with automatic formatting and collapsible tree. Headers tab shows Content-Type, which should be application/json.

CORS for Rust APIs

When your Axum or Actix-web server serves a separate frontend:

Axum CORS setup:

use tower_http::cors::{CorsLayer, Any};
use http::Method;

let cors = CorsLayer::new()
    .allow_origin("http://localhost:3000".parse::<HeaderValue>().unwrap())
    .allow_methods([Method::GET, Method::POST, Method::PUT])
    .allow_headers([header::CONTENT_TYPE, header::AUTHORIZATION]);

let app = Router::new()
    .route("/api/data", get(handler))
    .layer(cors);

Firefox's CORS errors are specific: "CORS header 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' missing" means the header wasn't set at all. "Does not match" means the origin is wrong. This helps diagnose which part of the config is wrong.

Rust + WebAssembly in Firefox

Firefox is the best browser for Wasm development due to:

  1. Mature Wasm debugging in DevTools
  2. Leading Wasm proposals support (GC, Exception Handling, Relaxed SIMD)
  3. SpiderMonkey's two-tier JIT for Wasm

wasm-pack Projects

The typical Rust → Wasm pipeline uses wasm-pack:

wasm-pack build --target web

This produces .wasm + JavaScript glue code.

Testing in Firefox:

  1. Serve the package locally with a simple HTTP server
  2. Open in Firefox
  3. DevTools → Debugger → look for your .wasm source
  4. Set breakpoints in the WAT disassembly (if no source maps)

For better debugging: Add source maps via wasm-pack's debug profile:

wasm-pack build --dev --target web

The debug build includes DWARF debug info embedded in the Wasm module. Firefox's debugger reads this and shows Rust source files.

Viewing Wasm in Firefox DevTools

  1. Open DevTools → Debugger
  2. In the Sources panel, look for files with .wasm extension
  3. Click to open — Firefox shows either the WAT disassembly or Rust source (with debug info)
  4. Set breakpoints, step through code, inspect Wasm local variables

Wasm locals show as typed values (i32, f64, etc.) in the Scopes panel.

Memory Inspection

For Rust Wasm, linear memory often contains your application data. In Firefox DevTools:

  1. Memory tab → take snapshot
  2. Look for "WebAssembly.Memory" in the snapshot
  3. Can inspect raw bytes

For structured memory inspection, add #[wasm_bindgen] functions that return debug-formatted strings:

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn debug_state() -> String {
    format!("{:?}", STATE.lock().unwrap())
}

Call from browser console: debug_state() prints your app state.

Rust wasm-bindgen Console Logging

From Rust to browser console:

use web_sys::console;

console::log_1(&"Hello from Rust!".into());
console::log_2(&"Value:".into(), &JsValue::from(42));

These appear in Firefox's Console tab just like JavaScript console.log calls, with Rust source attribution if debug info is present.

WASI in Firefox (Current State)

WASI (WebAssembly System Interface) for the browser is in early stages. Rust code targeting wasm32-wasi doesn't run directly in Firefox — it needs a WASI runtime.

The ecosystem is evolving: @bytecodealliance/jco can compile WASI components for browser execution, but this is cutting-edge.

For standard Rust → browser Wasm: target wasm32-unknown-unknown (the standard web target) via wasm-pack.

Firefox Profiler for Wasm

The Firefox Profiler (profiler.firefox.com) can profile Wasm code:

  1. Open Firefox Profiler
  2. Capture a profile while running your Wasm
  3. Flame chart shows Wasm functions (with Rust names if debug info present)
  4. Identify hot functions in your Rust code

Upload profile to profiler.firefox.com for a shareable profile link — useful when collaborating on Wasm performance issues.

Tab Management for Rust Projects

Multiple Rust web service windows open at once is common:

  • Localhost frontend
  • API documentation (doc.rs or local cargo doc)
  • Error monitoring
  • Wasm playground or test page

Tab Manager & Session Saver (Firefox) saves these as a named "project-rust-web" session. Restore the complete development context across restarts.

Firefox's Advantage for Rust/Wasm

Firefox's SpiderMonkey has had strong Wasm support since the early days — the Wasm spec was co-developed by Mozilla researchers. Combined with mature DevTools debugging of Wasm, Firefox is the natural choice for Rust/Wasm development.

The debugging story (source maps from DWARF, Wasm source view, memory inspector) is also more mature in Firefox's debugger than Chrome's for Wasm-specific features.

title: I let a one-shot Sonnet 5 agent QA a live app. Then I ran our QA tool on the same one.
description:
Every week, someone tells me our company shouldn't exist.
The line is always some version of this: "QA? I'll just point Claude or Sonnet at my app." And honestly — it's a fair shot. These models are good. If a one-shot agent already does what we do, then we're selling snake oil.

So we stopped arguing and ran the experiment.

We took a real, production EU rail-booking app. We turned a strong Sonnet 5 agent loose on it — from scratch, no hand-holding — to hunt bugs and write tests the way a sharp QA engineer would. Then we ran our own tool, TestOptim, through its full pipeline on the exact same app. Then we handed both outputs, unlabelled, to an independent judge and asked one question: which is better, and why?

The scoreboard

The agent was genuinely good — a smart pair of eyes for an hour, and it found real bugs. I'll say that plainly, because the interesting part isn't "AI bad." It's where a single clever run quietly runs out of road.

  • Our tool wrote 415 executable, grounded test cases. The one-shot agent wrote 36. That gap isn't a trick — it's the difference between "someone poked at your app for an afternoon" and "someone mapped it and left you a suite that reruns forever."
  • The depth held up under a blind judge: feature coverage 9/10, test-case depth 8/10, edge cases 8/10. Every expected result tied to behavior actually observed on the page — not a plausible guess that reads well and dies in CI.

  • Then the part I didn't expect: our tool caught bugs the agent walked straight past. A checkout total that silently drifted from the price on screen. A station index that mis-sorted — just enough to be wrong, not enough to notice. Boring, expensive, real: the exact bugs that survive a quick look and reach production.

The honest bit

Neither output was a superset of the other. The one-shot agent found a couple of things our tool didn't. A single pass — human or AI — always misses something, in both directions.

Which is the whole argument, really.

QA was never one brilliant run. It's coverage that's broad, grounded, deduplicated and repeatable — that keeps working on the next deploy, and the one after that, without a human re-prompting it at midnight. An agent gives you a run. A real QA system gives you a system.

So next time someone says "I'll just use an AI agent for QA": they're right that they can do a run. They're wrong that it's the same thing.

We measured it. On a real app. Blind. And then we shipped the improvements.

If you want to run the same kind of test on your own app, you can try TestOptim on any URL.

(Numbers from a blind September 2026 audit on real production apps, anonymized. Ask me anything in the comments — happy to show my work.)

Originally published by Shahid Helal on DEV.

title: CSS Grid Advanced: Named Lines, Subgrid, auto-fit, and the Firefox Inspector
description:
CSS Grid is the most powerful layout system on the web. While most developers know the basics, the advanced features — named lines, subgrid, auto-placement, and minmax() — unlock layouts that would otherwise require JavaScript. Firefox has first-class Grid support and the best grid inspector in any browser's DevTools.

Named Grid Lines

Instead of counting column numbers, name your lines:

.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns:
    [sidebar-start] 240px
    [sidebar-end main-start] 1fr
    [main-end aside-start] 280px
    [aside-end];
  grid-template-rows:
    [header-start] auto
    [header-end content-start] 1fr
    [content-end footer-start] auto
    [footer-end];
  min-height: 100vh;
}

.sidebar {
  grid-column: sidebar-start / sidebar-end;
  grid-row: content-start / footer-end;
}

.main {
  grid-column: main-start / main-end;
  grid-row: content-start / content-end;
}

Grid Template Areas

Visual layout declaration — arguably the most readable grid syntax:

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header header"
    "sidebar main   aside "
    "footer footer footer";
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 250px;
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
  min-height: 100vh;
}

.header { grid-area: header; }
.sidebar { grid-area: sidebar; }
.main   { grid-area: main; }
.aside  { grid-area: aside; }
.footer { grid-area: footer; }

/* Responsive: stack on mobile */
@media (max-width: 768px) {
  .page {
    grid-template-areas:
      "header"
      "main"
      "aside"
      "sidebar"
      "footer";
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
  }
}

Auto-Placement and dense Packing 

.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
  grid-auto-rows: 150px;
  gap: 8px;
  grid-auto-flow: row dense; /* Fill gaps with smaller items */
}

.featured {
  grid-column: span 2;
  grid-row: span 2;
}

/* Grid automatically places items to fill gaps */

grid-auto-flow: dense packs items into gaps, useful for masonry-style layouts.

minmax() and fit-content() 

/* Column that's at least 200px but grows up to 1fr */
.sidebar {
  width: minmax(200px, 1fr);
}

/* Used in grid tracks */
.grid {
  grid-template-columns: 
    minmax(200px, 300px)  /* sidebar: between 200-300px */
    1fr                    /* main: rest of space */
    minmax(150px, auto);   /* aside: at least 150px, auto otherwise */
}

/* fit-content(): don't exceed the content's natural width */
.nav {
  grid-template-columns: fit-content(200px) 1fr;
}

Repeat with auto-fill and auto-fit

Responsive grids without media queries:

/* auto-fill: creates as many columns as fit */
.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(250px, 1fr));
  gap: 16px;
}

/* auto-fit: same but collapses empty tracks */
/* When you have 3 items in a 6-column grid: */
/* auto-fill: [item][item][item][empty][empty][empty] */
/* auto-fit: [item][item][item] (each stretches to fill) */
.cards-fit {
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));
}

This creates a responsive card grid with NO media queries.

Subgrid

CSS Subgrid (Firefox supports this since Firefox 71!) lets nested elements align to the parent grid:

.parent {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
  grid-template-rows: auto auto;
  gap: 16px;
}

.card {
  display: grid;
  grid-row: span 2;
  /* Participate in parent's column tracks */
  grid-template-rows: subgrid;
}

.card-title { /* aligned to row 1 of parent */ }
.card-body  { /* aligned to row 2 of parent */ }

Without subgrid, card titles and bodies couldn't align across cards. With subgrid, all cards in the same row have aligned content.

Grid and Flexbox Together

Grid handles 2D layout; Flexbox handles 1D alignment within grid cells:

.grid-layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  gap: 20px;
}

.card {
  /* Each cell is a flex container for vertical alignment */
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
}

.card-body {
  flex: 1; /* Pushes footer to bottom */
}

.card-footer {
  margin-top: auto;
}

Firefox Grid Inspector

Firefox DevTools has the best CSS Grid inspector:

  1. Open DevTools (F12)
  2. Go to the Layout panel
  3. Under Grid section, click the grid icon next to any grid element
  4. The overlay shows:
    • Grid lines with numbers and names
    • Track sizes (computed values)
    • Gap areas
    • grid-area names

The Firefox grid overlay is interactive — you can see exact pixel measurements by hovering over cells.

Intrinsic Sizing Keywords 

.grid {
  grid-template-columns:
    min-content    /* shrinks to smallest non-overflow width */
    max-content    /* expands to fit all content without wrapping */
    fit-content(200px)  /* max-content but no wider than 200px */
    1fr;           /* remaining space */
}

min-content and max-content are computed by the browser based on actual content — useful for sidebar/label columns that should be exactly as wide as their contents.

The place-items and place-content Shorthands 

.grid {
  display: grid;

  /* Align items within their cell */
  justify-items: center;   /* horizontal */
  align-items: center;     /* vertical */
  place-items: center;     /* both */

  /* Align the grid tracks within the container */
  justify-content: space-between;
  align-content: start;
  place-content: start space-between; /* align-content justify-content */
}

Practical: Full-Page App Layout 

.app {
  display: grid;
  grid-template:
    "topbar  topbar " 56px
    "sidebar content" 1fr
    / 240px  1fr;
  height: 100dvh;
  overflow: hidden;
}

.topbar  { grid-area: topbar;  overflow: hidden; }
.sidebar { grid-area: sidebar; overflow-y: auto; }
.content { grid-area: content; overflow-y: auto; }

This creates a sticky topbar, scrollable sidebar, and main content area — the classic SPA layout — in ~10 lines of CSS with no JavaScript.

title: Loud and Clear: Making Visual Evidence Count in Multimodal Document RAG
description:
arXiv:2610.21318v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal document retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has focused largely on retrieval, yet its answers depend on how well a vision-language model reads the retrieved pages. We find that evidence in retrieved pages remains underused even when the correct pages are retrieved. On SciEGQA oracle pages, five prior methods give the generator 0.7K to 2.7K visual tokens per query on average under a common image processor, yet raising the page-only budget from 1K to 32K improves accuracy by 15.22 points. At a fixed 16K budget, adding ground-truth crops improves accuracy by 3.75 points over page-only input. We study what the generator needs from retrieved pages through two requirements: Loud, making full use of visual token capacity, and Clear, refining the page so that its evidence becomes prominent. For Loud, increasing either the visual token budget or visual fidelity, the image resolution those tokens preserve, improves accuracy with the other held fixed, and full-page scaling outperforms repetition and tiling at matched budgets. For Clear, suppressing surrounding content improves accuracy without enlarging selected regions, and adding OCR of these regions to page images outperforms either input alone. We implement both as Loud and Clear (LoC), which combines higher-resolution pages with OCR from query-relevant regions without ground-truth annotations or additional training. LoC outperforms eight prior methods on SciEGQA, ViDoRe-v3, and MMLongBench-Doc, improving over the strongest, ColQwen3, by 8.88, 3.09, and 4.22 points with the same retriever and generator. It also outperforms its page-only variant under the same visual token budget. These results locate a bottleneck beyond retrieval: how the retrieved pages are given to the generator.

title: Rubric Graders Need Canaries: Testing the Test That Grades C++ Patches
description:
Rubric Graders Need Canaries: Testing the Test That Grades C++ Patches

A pipeline starts scoring C++ patches with a model-backed rubric. Diffs that change printed precision, drop a noexcept guarantee, or leak a file descriptor now receive a 1-10 score before a human opens them. For a few weeks the dashboard looks reasonable, reviewers trust the number, and nobody asks whether the grader still separates good patches from bad ones. Then a prompt edit lands, the upstream model is swapped, and every patch scores 8. Nothing crashes. The grader simply stops discriminating, and the pipeline keeps reporting green.

That failure mode is independent of which model you call. A rubric grader is a program with an untested dependency, and it deserves the treatment the code under it already gets: golden cases, a canary set, a hard gate, and a ledger. The harness below is standard-library Python, a few JSON canary files, and one cron line. It is deliberately boring, because the interesting part is that the grader fails loudly instead of silently.

Layer 0 thinks, layer 1 judges

Split grading into two layers before writing any code. The deterministic layer answers questions with one correct answer: does the patched tree compile, does the golden case exit zero, does stdout match after a fixed locale and precision. The rubric layer answers questions with a range of defensible answers: is the naming consistent with the header it implements, does the commit message describe the actual change, does the new overload respect the documented contract.

Most silent regressions live on the boundary. A grader that is only deterministic cannot see prose contracts. A grader that is only a rubric cannot see a changed std::setprecision. Layer 0 gates the build, layer 1 explains the patch, and each layer needs its own canaries.

A canary here means a labeled example with a fixed expected answer that is committed to the repository. It is not a test of the patch. It is a test of the test.

Step 1 - Freeze golden cases for the deterministic layer

Start with one golden case per documented output contract. Keep the case small enough that a failure points at one behavior, and pin everything that could drift: locale, precision, and the toolchain described in your own build docs.

// golden/report_precision.cpp - contract: ratio printed with 3 decimals
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip>

int main() {
    const double ratio = 2.0 / 3.0;
    std::cout << std::setprecision(3) << std::fixed << ratio << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

Run it through the same command the eval batch uses, so the grader and the patch pipeline cannot disagree about flags:

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --target report_precision
./build/report_precision > out.txt
diff -u golden/report_precision.expected out.txt

The diff is the grader. If it passes, the patch is not yet good, but it is at least not obviously broken.

Step 2 - Commit canaries in both directions

A canary set that only contains bad patches rewards a paranoid grader. A canary set that only contains good patches rewards a lenient one. Include both, and store each patch as its own file so the JSON stays readable and diffs stay reviewable.

eval/
  canaries/
    precision-3-to-2.json
    honest-refactor.json
    tie-case-review.json
    diffs/
      precision-3-to-2.patch
      honest-refactor.patch
      tie-case-review.patch

Each canary declares what it expects and why. The note field is the part humans actually maintain.

{
  "id": "precision-3-to-2",
  "kind": "rubric",
  "direction": "must-fail",
  "patch_path": "diffs/precision-3-to-2.patch",
  "expected": 3,
  "note": "Breaks the output contract in docs/report.md. Any score above 5 means the rubric is not reading the contract."
}

{
  "id": "honest-refactor",
  "kind": "rubric",
  "direction": "should-pass",
  "patch_path": "diffs/honest-refactor.patch",
  "expected": 8,
  "note": "Pure rename plus a comment fix, output byte-identical. Below 6 means the rubric punishes chore diffs."
}

{
  "id": "precision-3-to-2-build",
  "kind": "build",
  "patch_path": "diffs/precision-3-to-2.patch",
  "golden_cmd": "./build/report_precision | diff -u golden/report_precision.expected -",
  "note": "Must exit non-zero. If this passes, the deterministic layer is not running."
}

Keep the count honest. Twenty labeled canaries drawn from real review comments are worth more than two hundred generated ones, because generated canaries encode the same assumptions as the rubric prompt.

Step 3 - Measure agreement before trusting scores

Agreement is the only cheap health signal a rubric grader has. Exact match is strict; within-one match tolerates the ordinary noise of a 1-10 scale. Both numbers belong in the gate.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# grade_gate.py - run canaries before trusting rubric scores.
import json, os, pathlib, subprocess, sys

CANARY_DIR = pathlib.Path(os.environ.get('CANARY_DIR', 'eval/canaries'))
LEDGER = pathlib.Path(os.environ.get('GRADER_LEDGER', 'eval/grader_ledger.jsonl'))
RUBRIC_ID = os.environ.get('GRADER_VERSION', 'unversioned')


def load_canaries():
    for path in sorted(CANARY_DIR.glob('*.json')):
        canary = json.loads(path.read_text())
        patch = (CANARY_DIR / canary['patch_path']).resolve()
        canary['diff_text'] = patch.read_text()
        yield canary


def call_model(prompt):
    # Transport layer. Plug in whichever client your runtime provides.
    # This function is untrusted by design; that is why canaries exist.
    raise NotImplementedError('wire your client here')


def rubric_score(diff_text, rubric):
    reply = call_model(rubric + '\n\nDIFF:\n' + diff_text)
    return json.loads(reply)

Now the comparison itself, plus the gate. The thresholds are policy defaults, not measured results: a canary set of forty concrete review-derived cases can usually carry a higher bar than one of twelve fuzzy ones. Tune them once, write the number in the repo, and treat any change to it as a reviewable commit.

def check_rubric_canaries(canaries, rubric, min_exact=0.80, min_within_one=0.95):
    exact = within_one = 0
    misses = []
    for canary in canaries:
        if canary.get('kind') != 'rubric':
            continue
        expected = canary['expected']
        got = rubric_score(canary['diff_text'], rubric)['score']
        if got == expected:
            exact += 1
        else:
            if abs(got - expected) == 1:
                within_one += 1
            misses.append({'id': canary['id'], 'expected': expected,
                           'got': got, 'delta': got - expected})
    total = sum(1 for c in canaries if c.get('kind') == 'rubric') or 1
    rates = {'exact': exact / total, 'within_one': (exact + within_one) / total}
    ok = rates['exact'] >= min_exact and rates['within_one'] >= min_within_one
    return ok, rates, misses

Build canaries run the golden command instead of a model, and check the opposite thing: they must fail.

def check_build_canaries(canaries, workdir):
    results = []
    for canary in canaries:
        if canary.get('kind') != 'build':
            continue
        subprocess.run(['git', 'apply', canary['patch_path']], cwd=workdir, check=True)
        proc = subprocess.run(canary['golden_cmd'], cwd=workdir, shell=True)
        subprocess.run(['git', 'restore', '.'], cwd=workdir, check=True)
        results.append({'id': canary['id'], 'exit': proc.returncode,
                        'ok': proc.returncode != 0})
    return results

Step 4 - Keep a grader ledger next to the token ledger

A score is only meaningful with the grader revision and the model identity attached. Write one JSON line per gate run, including the token count, so drift and cost are visible in the same file.

def log_run(rates, misses, model_id, tokens):
    record = {'grader': RUBRIC_ID, 'model': model_id, 'rates': rates,
              'misses': misses, 'tokens': tokens}
    with LEDGER.open('a') as fh:
        print(json.dumps(record), file=fh)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    rubric = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text()
    canaries = list(load_canaries())
    ok, rates, misses = check_rubric_canaries(canaries, rubric)
    build = check_build_canaries(canaries, '.')
    log_run(rates, misses, os.environ.get('MODEL_ID', 'unknown'),
            int(os.environ.get('TOKENS_USED', '0')))
    healthy = ok and all(r['ok'] for r in build)
    print(json.dumps({'healthy': healthy, 'rates': rates, 'misses': misses,
                      'build': build}, indent=2))
    sys.exit(0 if healthy else 1)

The exit code is the whole interface. A healthy gate returns 0 and the eval batch proceeds; an unhealthy gate returns 1 and the batch stops before it spends anything on scoring.

Step 5 - Run the gate where nobody has to remember it

A gate that depends on a human typing a command is a gate that will be skipped during the week it matters most. Two things make the scheduled version practical: a machine that stays on, and model access that does not require a per-run decision.

MonkeyCode, described by its maintainers as an open-source project, offers free model access and a free server option, with the free tier described as including 10M tokens. That combination is enough to host a weekly canary run plus the rubric calls it makes, without reserving a dedicated box. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

# cron: every Monday 06:17, on the free server option
17 6 * * 1 cd /srv/eval && python3 grade_gate.py rubrics/patch_v3.md >> logs/canary.log 2>&1

Read the ledger rather than the estimate. The claim worth trusting is not a predicted token count; it is the tokens field on last week's line, compared with the line before it.

Which layer owns which signal

Signal to grade Layer 0 (deterministic) Layer 1 (rubric)
Compiles, links, exits zero Yes No
stdout under fixed locale and precision Yes No
Wall-clock or allocation budget Yes No
Naming consistent with the header Partly, via lint rules Yes
Prose output contract in docs No Yes
Commit message matches the change No Yes
Whether the change is worth merging No Advisory only, never binding

If a row can be pushed into layer 0, push it. Every signal moved out of the rubric layer removes a source of drift, and the rubric layer keeps only the judgments a compiler cannot express.

Limitations and who should skip this

Canaries are a sample, and agreement is not correctness. If the labels are wrong, the gate certifies a wrong grader with a confident number. Re-label a handful of canaries every few months, especially the ones that never fail.

Rubric scores drift when the model or the prompt changes, and only a scheduled run of the ledger detects that. Single-run scores stay noisy even with a fixed prompt, so treat a one-point swing as a signal to check the ledger, not as a verdict on the patch.

The quota and server claims above are operator descriptions of the offer, not measurements taken for this article. Verify current terms before wiring a paid-critical pipeline to a free tier, and keep the gate able to run against a different client.

Skip this approach if you have fewer than roughly twenty real diffs to label, because reading the patches is then cheaper than grading them. Skip it for safety-critical, licensing, or compliance judgments, which need deterministic evidence and a named reviewer. Skip it if diff text cannot leave your network, unless every layer runs locally. And skip the rubric layer entirely if your grading budget exceeds the cost of the human review it is meant to save.

The harness is small on purpose. Golden cases, canaries in both directions, one agreement gate, one ledger. Start with a single canary that should fail and confirm the gate returns non-zero; if it returns zero, the grader was never watching.

title: Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21125v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Few-step generative models produce high-quality samples in one or a few evaluations. However, steering them toward desired properties remains difficult, especially when only black-box reward evaluations are available. While one could apply approaches developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models, such as direct RL fine-tuning or test-time scaling, we find that neither transfers well to the few-step regime: direct fine-tuning suffers from severe reward over-optimization, and test-time scaling sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which explicitly targets the alignment problem for few-step generative models. The key idea is to learn an amortized flow policy over the initial noise space of the generator. The trained policy transports Gaussian noise to a reward-tilted noise distribution, whose pushforward distribution through the frozen generator is exactly the reward-tilted output distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, we can effectively utilize the knowledge encoded in the pretrained model, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning. The amortized policy moves the search cost into training, so inference adds only a lightweight noise sampling step on top of the pretrained model. To improve sample efficiency during training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation that requires only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories. Across image, language, and protein structure generation, NPO consistently achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning, and matches test-time search methods with 16 to 549 times lower inference cost.

title: Context Injection and Long-Horizon Reliability: Separating Duplicate Recognition, Local Processing, and Counter Tracking
description:
arXiv:2610.20633v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon failures of language models are usually measured as end-task success or as a horizon length. We instead score, step by step, three components of a 400-step ledger task in which every step is easy in isolation and the model's own answers are re-injected into its context: recognising a record already seen 5 to 300 steps earlier, processing the current record locally, and writing a counter incremented at every step. On Qwen3-8B (non-thinking, 20 seeds, replicated on a second machine and backend), with every step scored component by component, two results hold. First, duplicate-recognition errors rise late in the episode -- from 0.0019 to 0.011 per step at risk across step 200 -- while the counter makes no error in 8,000 steps and local processing is descriptively stable; the rise combines long-distance recall errors and rising false alarms. Second, a block of irrelevant content inserted before each step makes the counter fail in 20 of 20 seeds on each machine, against none without it, while its effect on local processing is much smaller and not distinguishable from none. Three pre-registered follow-ups probe the counter. Its value depends on the value present in the response history: a corrupted value persists without correction in every seed, and an exact external reminder, repeated before each message, re-aligns it within one to two steps. Under the irrelevant block, no counter error was observed when an exact compact reminder of the state, supplied externally by an oracle, preceded each message (0 of 20 seeds with an error, against 15 without it), and this reminder outperformed a length-matched neutral text; whether a single reminder suffices was not conclusive, and the absence of damage to the other components was not established. An aggregate or exclusive error classification can hide the difference we report.

title: Dark Mode in Firefox: OS Settings, Force Dark, NightOwl vs Dark Reader, and Per-Site Control
description:
Dark mode on the web is inconsistent — some sites support it via prefers-color-scheme, others have built-in toggles, and many just don't have it at all. Here's how to get dark mode working everywhere in Firefox, and what each approach actually does.

The Three Types of Dark Mode

1. OS-level dark mode: Your OS (Windows/macOS/Linux) is in dark mode. Firefox's UI switches to dark. Websites that respect prefers-color-scheme: dark CSS media query will also switch.

2. Site-native dark mode: The website has its own dark/light toggle. Common on GitHub, Dev.to, Stack Overflow, etc. Site-specific, requires interaction on each site.

3. Forced dark mode via extension: An extension intercepts all pages and applies dark CSS, regardless of whether the site supports it. Covers everything, but can look inconsistent.

Making OS Dark Mode Work in Firefox

Windows:
Settings → Personalization → Colors → Choose your mode → Dark
Firefox's toolbar and chrome switch automatically. Sites with prefers-color-scheme support switch too.

macOS:
System Preferences → General → Appearance → Dark
Same result.

Linux (GNOME):

gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface color-scheme prefer-dark

Firefox reads the GTK theme preference and reports it to websites via prefers-color-scheme.

Verify it's working: In Firefox DevTools → Inspector panel → there's a dark/light mode toggle (looks like two circles, one dark/one light) that lets you toggle between dark and light to preview how a site responds.

Firefox's Built-in Force Dark Mode

Firefox has an experimental forced colors feature:

In about:config:

layout.css.prefers-color-scheme.content-override = 0

Values:

  • 0 = Force light
  • 1 = Force dark
  • 2 = Follow OS (default)

This makes Firefox tell all websites "the user prefers dark mode" regardless of OS setting. Sites that check prefers-color-scheme will use their dark theme. Sites without dark theme support won't change.

NightOwl: Full Forced Dark Mode

For sites that don't respond to prefers-color-scheme, you need an extension that applies dark CSS directly.

NightOwl (available at addons.mozilla.org) injects dark mode CSS into every page, creating a dark appearance even on sites with no dark mode support.

How it works:

  • Reads the page's existing colors
  • Intelligently inverts dark colors to light and light to dark
  • Preserves images (doesn't invert them to look like negatives)
  • Handles common patterns like buttons, inputs, borders

Installation: Firefox Add-ons → search "NightOwl" → Add to Firefox.

Once installed: all pages go dark. There's a toolbar icon to toggle for individual sites where the dark mode looks wrong.

Dark Reader (Alternative Extension)

Dark Reader is the most popular forced dark mode extension. It uses a similar approach:

  • Filter mode: CSS inversion (faster, less accurate)
  • Dynamic mode: Reads actual colors and converts them (slower, more accurate)
  • Static mode: Simple brightness inversion

Dark Reader vs NightOwl:
| Feature | Dark Reader | NightOwl |
|---------|-------------|----------|
| Installation base | Very large | Smaller |
| Algorithm | Dynamic/Filter/Static | Smart inversion |
| Performance | Moderate (dynamic mode heavy) | Lightweight |
| Per-site control | Yes | Yes |
| Custom colors | Yes | Yes |
| Open source | Yes | Yes |

Both are solid choices. Dark Reader has more configuration options. NightOwl tends to be lighter on CPU/memory.

Per-Site Control

Both extensions let you disable/enable on a per-site basis. This is important because:

  • Some sites already look great in dark mode (GitHub, Dev.to)
  • Some sites break with forced dark (certain media players, canvas-heavy apps)
  • Some sites have their own dark mode that's better than forced

Quick toggle: Click the extension icon while on a site to toggle dark mode for that domain.

System-Wide Dark Mode Detection Test

To check if your browser is correctly reporting dark mode preference:

Open DevTools → Console:

window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches
// true = browser reports dark mode preference

Or: DevTools Inspector → Responsive Design Mode toolbar → color scheme toggle button.

Firefox UI Dark Mode

Firefox's own interface (toolbar, tabs, menus) follows OS dark mode setting. But you can force it:

Method 1: Firefox Settings → General → "Manage colors" or Extension themes

Method 2: Install a dark Firefox theme from AMO. Options like "Firefox Alpenglow" have dark variants.

Method 3: about:config → ui.systemUsesDarkTheme = 1 forces dark Firefox UI even if OS is in light mode.

Managing Multiple Dark Mode Sources

If you have both NightOwl/Dark Reader installed AND a site's native dark mode: they can conflict, resulting in white text on white background or black on black.

Best practice:

  1. Use OS dark mode (this handles sites that support it natively)
  2. Use an extension for everything else
  3. Disable the extension on sites that have native dark mode AND respond to prefers-color-scheme

Sites that respond to OS dark mode (no need for extension):

  • GitHub (full support)
  • Dev.to (full support)
  • Stack Overflow
  • MDN Web Docs
  • Twitter/X
  • Reddit (new layout)

Sites that need the extension:

  • Older news sites
  • Legacy web apps
  • Sites with dark toggle but that don't respond to OS dark mode
  • Any site that ignores prefers-color-scheme

Scheduled Dark Mode

Neither NightOwl nor Dark Reader have built-in scheduling, but you can:

  1. Use OS scheduled dark mode (Windows/macOS both have sunset-to-sunrise dark mode)
  2. The browser extension will read the OS preference and toggle accordingly

Windows: Settings → Personalization → Colors → Choose your mode → Custom → Schedule (sunset to sunrise or custom time)

macOS: System Preferences → General → Appearance → Auto (switches at sunset/sunrise automatically)

Once the OS is set, Firefox's prefers-color-scheme detection changes too, and extensions that watch this will switch.

title: Attribute Coverage to Hunks, Not Files: An Ownership Map for Agent Patches
description:
A patch can show 100% coverage on its changed lines and still be untested. The number that matters is not how many changed lines executed, but which test would fail if the change were wrong — and whether that test was added by the patch or inherited from the repository.

This post builds a hunk ownership map: per-test coverage contexts mapped onto diff hunks, classified as OWNED, INCIDENTAL, or ORPHAN, with a fixture-reach audit and a stability precondition. The artifact is a script you run in your own repository.

The failure mode in one example

An agent adds a retry wrapper and a backoff cap. It also touches a helper that an old smoke test happens to exercise. Line coverage on the diff looks excellent.

What actually happened: the only test touching lines 41–48 is tests/test_client.py::test_get_ok, written two years ago, which never asserts anything about retries. Lines 52–55 have no covering test at all. Only lines 60–63 are protected by a test the patch itself introduced.

Hunk Instrumented lines Owner Would fail on wrong behavior?
src/retry.py:41-48 executed pre-existing smoke test no
src/retry.py:52-55 not executed none no
src/retry.py:60-63 executed new test in patch yes

File-level coverage hides all three behind one percentage.

Step 1 — Collect per-test coverage contexts

coverage.py records a context per measurement, and pytest-cov can set that context to the running test id. This is the whole trick; without contexts you only get file-level truth.

# .coveragerc  (or [tool.coverage.run] in pyproject.toml)
# [run]
# relative_files = True

pytest --cov=src --cov-context=test
coverage json --show-contexts -o coverage.json

relative_files = True matters: the JSON keys must be repo-relative so they line up with git diff paths. If you use pytest-xdist, expect per-worker data files; run coverage combine before coverage json if contexts look empty. Context support and the --show-contexts JSON option have version floors, so confirm both against the coverage.py and pytest-cov versions you are actually running.

Step 2 — Map hunks to lines

Parse the diff with zero context lines. You want added-line ranges, not readability.

git diff -U0 origin/main...HEAD

-U0 produces @@ -a,b +c,d @@ headers where c,d is exactly the added block in the new file. Deleted-only hunks appear as +c,0 and must be skipped — they have no lines to own.

Step 3 — Classify every hunk

The script below joins the two inputs. Run it as a local gate; it is a starting point, not a packaged tool, and its behavior depends on your coverage.py version.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""hunk_ownership.py — map patch hunks to the test contexts that executed them."""
import json, re, subprocess, sys
from collections import defaultdict

HUNK = re.compile(r"^@@ -\d+(?:,\d+)? \+(\d+)(?:,(\d+))? @@")
NEW_TEST = re.compile(r"^(?:tests?|spec)/.*\.py$")


def changed_hunks(rev_range):
    out = subprocess.run(["git", "diff", "-U0", rev_range],
                         capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    hunks, path = defaultdict(list), None
    for line in out.splitlines():
        if line.startswith("+++ b/"):
            path = line[6:]
        elif line.startswith("@@"):
            m = HUNK.match(line)
            if not m:
                continue
            start = int(m.group(1))
            count = int(m.group(2)) if m.group(2) is not None else 1
            if count:                      # skip deleted-only hunks
                hunks[path].append((start, start + count - 1))
    return dict(hunks)


def added_test_files(rev_range):
    out = subprocess.run(["git", "diff", "-U0", "--diff-filter=A",
                          "--name-only", rev_range],
                         capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    return {p for p in out.split() if NEW_TEST.match(p)}


def coverage_index(cov_path):
    data = json.load(open(cov_path))
    idx = {}
    for fname, fdata in data["files"].items():
        for lineno, contexts in (fdata.get("contexts") or {}).items():
            idx[(fname, int(lineno))] = set(contexts)
    return idx


def classify(hunks, cov, new_tests):
    rows = []
    for path, ranges in hunks.items():
        for lo, hi in ranges:
            owners = set()
            for line in range(lo, hi + 1):
                owners |= cov.get((path, line), set())
            owned = any(o.startswith(t) for o in owners for t in new_tests)
            kind = "ORPHAN" if not owners else ("OWNED" if owned else "INCIDENTAL")
            rows.append((path, f"{lo}-{hi}", kind, sorted(owners)))
    return rows


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rev = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "origin/main...HEAD"
    rows = classify(changed_hunks(rev), coverage_index("coverage.json"),
                    added_test_files(rev))
    for path, span, kind, owners in rows:
        print(f"{kind:11} {path}:{span}  owners={','.join(owners) or '-'}")
    sys.exit(1 if any(r[2] != "OWNED" for r in rows) else 0)

Illustrative report shape (synthetic values, not a measurement of any real repository):

INCIDENTAL  src/retry.py:41-48  owners=tests/test_client.py::test_get_ok
ORPHAN      src/retry.py:52-55  owners=-
OWNED       src/retry.py:60-63  owners=tests/test_retry.py::test_backoff_caps

Step 4 — Audit fixture reach before you trust OWNED

Many INCIDENTAL verdicts come from a shared fixture that makes almost any test execute almost any code path. Count how many tests depend on each fixture, then intersect that list with fixtures the patch touched.

import re, subprocess
from collections import defaultdict

out = subprocess.run(["pytest", "--fixtures-per-test", "-q"],
                     capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
reach, current = defaultdict(set), None
for line in out.splitlines():
    m = re.match(r"^([\w/\-]+\.py)::(\S+)", line)
    if m:
        current = f"{m.group(1)}::{m.group(2)}"
    elif current and line.strip().startswith("-- "):
        reach[line.strip()[3:].split()[0]].add(current)

for fixture, users in sorted(reach.items(), key=lambda kv: -len(kv[1])):
    print(f"{len(users):4}  {fixture}")

The --fixtures-per-test layout has shifted across pytest releases, so validate this parse against your version before gating on it. A fixture reachable from most of the suite and modified by the patch is a strong signal that the patch changed test infrastructure, not just production behavior — review it as a test change, and read the diff twice.

Step 5 — Make stability a precondition, not an afterthought

Ownership is only meaningful when the covering test returns the same verdict every time. Before you accept an OWNED hunk, run just its covering files repeatedly with a fixed shuffle seed.

# requires pytest-repeat and pytest-randomly; confirm flags for your versions
pytest -q tests/test_retry.py --count=5 --randomly-seed=1729

If the verdict flips, move the test out of the owner set and treat every hunk it covered as ORPHAN until it is fixed. A test that sometimes passes is not evidence; it is noise with a merge button.

Step 6 — Decide with a fixed table

Hunk class Coverage on changed lines Owner Gate action
OWNED executed test added/changed as a test by this patch accept, record owner ids in the PR
INCIDENTAL executed pre-existing test only block; probe the hunk or add an assertion
ORPHAN not executed none block; require a new test or a written waiver
WAIVED any explicit human waiver accept; waiver expires with the next release tag

INCIDENTAL is the class that pays for the whole exercise. It is where a green CI run and a confident review collide. For those hunks, run a per-hunk behavioral probe — the differential revert technique from the earlier gate design in this series — and promote the hunk to WAIVED only with a recorded reviewer.

Running the matrix somewhere it does not cost CI minutes

Per-test contexts multiply the size of the coverage data and the runtime, and the five-times stability pass multiplies it again. That is an awkward load to put on a metered CI plan.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. MonkeyCode offers free model access and a free server option, per the operator; I have not verified quotas, hardware, or duration, and you should read the current plan page before relying on either. Two uses fit this workflow honestly. First, run the coverage-context matrix and the stability repeats on the free server, so the expensive collection stays off your paid runners. Second, feed coverage.json plus the ownership report to a free model to draft a PR comment and propose candidate property tests for ORPHAN hunks — then review those proposals yourself, because a generated test that asserts the observed behavior of a wrong patch is worse than no test.

Limitations and who should skip this

  • Small suites. Under roughly a hundred tests, reading the diff is faster than building the map. The tooling overhead exceeds the savings.
  • Generated and compiled code. Line-level coverage is a poor proxy across transpiled output, macros, and template instantiation; hunk boundaries in the source rarely match executable boundaries.
  • Context support is not universal. coverage.py contexts are the mature path here; if your language's coverage tool has no per-test context concept, this method degrades to file-level guessing.
  • Teams already running per-PR mutation testing. Mutation gives a stronger ownership signal directly. Adding this on top duplicates cost for little new information.
  • Parallel collection. With pytest-xdist, context data must be combined before analysis, and per-worker context names can diverge. Budget for that or run serially on the free server.

The weekly loop

  1. Generate the patch diff with git diff -U0.
  2. Run pytest --cov-context=test and emit coverage.json --show-contexts.
  3. Classify every hunk; fail the gate on ORPHAN and INCIDENTAL.
  4. Audit fixture reach for any fixture the patch touched.
  5. Re-run covering files five times with a fixed seed; demote unstable owners.
  6. Record owner ids and waivers in the PR body so the next reader sees the evidence, not the percentage.

Coverage tells you a line ran. Ownership tells you a test would have complained. If you adopt one change from this post, make it the exit code on ORPHAN.
