title: How to Build a Production-Ready SaaS with Spring Boot 3, React 18 & Stripe in 2026
description:
When building a new B2B SaaS, 90% of the boilerplates and tutorials out there focus exclusively on the JavaScript ecosystem (Next.js, Node, Remix).

But if you want the type safety, multithreading performance (Virtual Threads in Java 21), and enterprise reliability of Spring Boot 3 combined with a fast React 18 frontend, you usually end up spending 3 to 4 weeks configuring the exact same plumbing from scratch:

  • Stateless JWT Authentication & Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
  • PostgreSQL persistence with Flyway database migrations
  • Stripe Checkout & asynchronous Webhook signature verification
  • CORS, security filters, and production deployment configs

In this guide, we’ll walk through the exact production architecture for a Spring Boot 3 (Java 21) + React 18 SaaS in 2026—and look at the core code patterns that hold it all together.

💡 Want to skip the 40+ hours of setup? I packaged this entire production-ready architecture (with full source code, Stripe webhooks, JWT Auth, Flyway migrations, and AI modules) into SaaSKit — The Spring Boot 3 & React 18 SaaS Boilerplate. Check out the live demo and documentation!

1. High-Level Architecture Overview

A modern, decoupled B2B SaaS architecture needs to be stateless, easy to scale horizontally, and strictly typed across boundaries:

  • Backend: Java 21 + Spring Boot 3.x (Spring Security 6, Spring Data JPA)
  • Database & Migrations: PostgreSQL + Flyway (versioned SQL schemas)
  • Frontend: React 18 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS (hosted on Vercel)
  • Payments: Stripe Checkout Sessions + Webhook Event Handler

Let's break down the three hardest parts of the implementation: Database Migrations, Stateless JWT Security, and Stripe Subscription Webhooks.

2. Database Schema & Flyway Migrations (V1__init.sql)

Never use spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update in production. One accidental entity change can corrupt customer data or break constraints. Instead, set ddl-auto=validate and let Flyway manage your PostgreSQL schema deterministically.

Place your initial migration inside src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__init_schema.sql:

CREATE TABLE users (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    role VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ROLE_USER',
    stripe_customer_id VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE,
    subscription_status VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'FREE',
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_stripe_customer ON users(stripe_customer_id);

This guarantees that every environment—from your local Docker container to staging and production—runs the exact same schema version.

3. Stateless JWT Security in Spring Boot 3 (Spring Security 6)

With Spring Security 6, the configuration uses the functional Lambda DSL. Since our React 18 frontend is hosted separately (e.g., on Vercel) and communicates via REST APIs, we disable CSRF for stateless endpoints, configure strict CORS policies, and inject a custom JwtAuthenticationFilter.

Here is the clean SecurityConfig.java pattern:

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class SecurityConfig {

    private final JwtAuthenticationFilter jwtAuthFilter;
    private final AuthenticationProvider authenticationProvider;

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
            .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .sessionManagement(session -> 
                session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS)
            )
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers(
                    "/api/v1/auth/**",
                    "/api/v1/stripe/webhook",
                    "/v3/api-docs/**",
                    "/swagger-ui/**"
                ).permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            )
            .authenticationProvider(authenticationProvider)
            .addFilterBefore(jwtAuthFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class);

        return http.build();
    }
}

Notice how /api/v1/stripe/webhook is explicitly whitelisted in permitAll(). Why? Because Stripe servers don't have a user JWT token—they authenticate via cryptographic webhook signatures instead.

4. Handling Stripe Subscriptions & Webhooks Reliably

The biggest mistake developers make when integrating Stripe with React and Spring Boot is updating the user's subscription status on the frontend redirect (?success=true). Users close their browser tabs, lose connectivity, or spoof URLs.

The only source of truth for SaaS billing is the Stripe Webhook.

Here is how to securely verify the Stripe-Signature header and provision access in Spring Boot 3:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/stripe")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
@Slf4j
public class StripeWebhookController {

    @Value("${stripe.webhook.secret}")
    private String endpointSecret;

    private final SubscriptionService subscriptionService;

    @PostMapping("/webhook")
    public ResponseEntity<String> handleStripeWebhook(
            @RequestBody String payload,
            @RequestHeader("Stripe-Signature") String sigHeader) {

        Event event;
        try {
            event = Webhook.constructEvent(payload, sigHeader, endpointSecret);
        } catch (SignatureVerificationException e) {
            log.warn("Invalid Stripe webhook signature!");
            return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST).body("Invalid signature");
        }

        switch (event.getType()) {
            case "checkout.session.completed" -> {
                Session session = (Session) event.getDataObjectDeserializer().getObject().orElseThrow();
                subscriptionService.activateSubscription(
                    session.getClientReferenceId(),
                    session.getCustomer(),
                    session.getSubscription()
                );
            }
            case "customer.subscription.deleted" -> {
                Subscription sub = (Subscription) event.getDataObjectDeserializer().getObject().orElseThrow();
                subscriptionService.cancelSubscription(sub.getCustomer());
            }
            default -> log.debug("Unhandled Stripe event type: {}", event.getType());
        }

        return ResponseEntity.ok("Webhook processed");
    }
}

When a user clicks "Upgrade to Pro" in your React 18 dashboard:

  1. React calls POST /api/v1/billing/checkout-session with the user's JWT.
  2. Spring Boot creates a Stripe Checkout Session passing the user's UUID in client_reference_id.
  3. Once payment succeeds, Stripe fires checkout.session.completed to your backend, and Flyway-backed PostgreSQL updates subscription_status = 'PRO'.

5. Connecting React 18 with Axios Interceptors

On the React 18 side, you can centralize token handling and automatic 401 redirects using an Axios instance:

import axios from 'axios';

export const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,
});

api.interceptors.request.use((config) => {
  const token = localStorage.getItem('access_token');
  if (token) {
    config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
  }
  return config;
});

🚀 Skip the Boilerplate & Launch Your SaaS in Days

Building authentication, password resets, Stripe webhook retries, database migrations, responsive UI dashboards, and legal pages from scratch takes weeks away from validating your actual business idea.

If you want this entire stack ready to deploy today, check out SaaSKit:

👉 Explore SaaSKit — Spring Boot 3 & React 18 SaaS Boilerplate

What you get out of the box:

  • ✅ Full-Stack Production Code: Java 21, Spring Boot 3, and React 18 (Dark Mode UI)
  • ✅ Complete Security: JWT Authentication, Role-Based Access Control & Protected Routes
  • ✅ Stripe Billing Ready: Pre-built Checkout, Customer Portal & Webhook handlers
  • ✅ Database & Migrations: PostgreSQL + Flyway pre-configured
  • ✅ Step-by-Step Guide: Includes the full SaaSKit-Documentation-Guide.pdf for quickstart and cloud deployment

title: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research
description:
arXiv:2610.21055v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.

title: Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, and CLS — What They Measure and How to Fix Them
description:
Core Web Vitals are Google's set of performance metrics that directly affect search ranking. More importantly, they measure real user experience: whether your page loads visibly fast, responds quickly to interaction, and stays stable as it renders.

The three metrics, what they measure, and how to improve them.

The Three Core Web Vitals

LCP — Largest Contentful Paint

Measures when the largest visible element (hero image, h1, article body) finishes rendering. The goal is under 2.5 seconds.

LCP is the "does the page look done?" metric. It's what users notice when they're waiting — the blank space before the main content appears.

What hurts LCP:

  • Large, unoptimized hero images
  • Server response time (TTFB)
  • Render-blocking scripts and stylesheets
  • Client-side rendering (JS renders the content)

How to improve LCP:

Optimize the LCP element itself:

<!-- Preload the LCP image -->
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.webp" fetchpriority="high">

<!-- Use modern formats -->
<picture>
  <source srcset="/hero.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="/hero.webp" type="image/webp">
  <img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Hero" width="1200" height="600">
</picture>

Remove render-blocking resources:

<!-- Non-critical CSS: load async -->
<link rel="preload" href="/styles/non-critical.css" as="style"
      onload="this.onload=null;this.rel='stylesheet'">

<!-- Defer non-critical scripts -->
<script src="/analytics.js" defer></script>

INP — Interaction to Next Paint (replaced FID in 2024)

Measures the latency between user interaction (click, tap, keypress) and the next visual update. Goal: under 200ms.

INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) in March 2024. FID only measured the first interaction; INP measures all interactions throughout the page lifecycle.

What hurts INP:

  • Long JavaScript tasks blocking the main thread
  • Heavy event handlers
  • Synchronous layout reads during interaction (layout thrashing)

How to improve INP:

Break up long tasks:

// Bad: one long synchronous task
function processLargeList(items) {
  items.forEach(item => heavyOperation(item));
}

// Better: yield to the browser between chunks
async function processLargeList(items) {
  const CHUNK_SIZE = 50;
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i += CHUNK_SIZE) {
    const chunk = items.slice(i, i + CHUNK_SIZE);
    chunk.forEach(item => heavyOperation(item));
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0));  // yield
  }
}

Use scheduler.yield() when available (Chrome 115+, proposal stage for others):

async function handleClick() {
  doUrgentWork();
  await scheduler.yield();  // let browser render first
  doNonUrgentWork();
}

Avoid layout thrashing:

// Bad: alternating read/write forces multiple layout recalculations
elements.forEach(el => {
  const height = el.offsetHeight;  // read
  el.style.height = height + 10 + 'px';  // write → forces layout
});

// Good: batch reads, then batch writes
const heights = elements.map(el => el.offsetHeight);  // all reads
elements.forEach((el, i) => {
  el.style.height = heights[i] + 10 + 'px';  // all writes
});

CLS — Cumulative Layout Shift

Measures unexpected visual shifts — elements jumping around as the page loads. Goal: under 0.1.

CLS is the "why did the button move when I was about to click it?" metric.

What causes CLS:

  • Images without dimensions
  • Ads, embeds, iframes without reserved space
  • Dynamically injected content above existing content
  • Web fonts causing FOIT/FOUT

How to fix CLS:

Always set image dimensions:

<!-- Reserve space before image loads -->
<img src="photo.jpg" width="800" height="450" alt="...">

<!-- Or use CSS aspect-ratio -->
<style>
.image-wrapper {
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  width: 100%;
}
</style>

Reserve space for ads and embeds:

.ad-slot {
  min-height: 250px;  /* reserve before ad loads */
}

Prevent font-swap layout shift:

@font-face {
  font-family: 'MyFont';
  src: url('myfont.woff2') format('woff2');
  font-display: optional;  /* don't show fallback if font loads quickly */
}

Or use size-adjust to match fallback font metrics:

@font-face {
  font-family: 'FallbackFont';
  src: local('Arial');
  size-adjust: 103%;  /* scale fallback to match custom font */
  ascent-override: 90%;
}

Measuring Core Web Vitals

In Firefox DevTools

Firefox's Performance profiler doesn't show CWV directly, but you can measure:

  • LCP: Watch the timeline for when the largest paint fires
  • CLS: Check Layout panel for unexpected reflows
  • INP: Performance recording shows main thread blocking during interaction

For accurate field measurements, use PageSpeed Insights (which uses real Chrome User Experience data) or install the Web Vitals extension.

In Code (JavaScript) 

import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS } from 'web-vitals';

onLCP(metric => {
  console.log('LCP:', metric.value, metric.rating);  // 'good', 'needs-improvement', 'poor'
});

onINP(metric => {
  console.log('INP:', metric.value);
});

onCLS(metric => {
  console.log('CLS:', metric.value);
});

The web-vitals library (from Google) is the reference implementation.

Lighthouse

Run from Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse tab, or via CLI:

npx lighthouse https://yoursite.com --output=html --view

Lighthouse scores are lab measurements (controlled environment). They don't match field data (real users on varied connections). Both matter — lab for reproducible testing, field for actual impact.

Priority Order for Fixes

  1. LCP first — it's the most visible to users and usually has the biggest impact
  2. CLS second — easy to fix (add image dimensions) and directly affects usability
  3. INP last — hardest to fix, requires JS profiling, but matters for interactive apps

Quick LCP Checklist

  • [ ] LCP element is an image? Preload it with fetchpriority="high"
  • [ ] Image in WebP or AVIF format?
  • [ ] Image properly sized (not 4000px wide for a 800px slot)?
  • [ ] Server response under 800ms? (Check TTFB in Network panel)
  • [ ] No render-blocking scripts before the LCP element?
  • [ ] CDN serving static assets?

Quick CLS Checklist

  • [ ] All images have width and height attributes?
  • [ ] Ad slots have min-height reserved?
  • [ ] No content injected above the fold after initial render?
  • [ ] Font font-display: optional or swap with size-adjust?

Core Web Vitals scores are now a Google search ranking factor — not the dominant one, but measurable. More importantly, improving them correlates with higher conversion rates: Google's data shows that sites meeting "Good" thresholds for all three metrics have significantly lower bounce rates than those that don't.

title: Mutable retry state inside authenticated encrypted DTN mailboxes
description:
Mutable retry state inside authenticated encrypted DTN mailboxes

Most mesh people talk about routing first. I spend more time worrying about what happens when a message never gets delivered at all.

GhostWire is a Rust mesh-protocol experiment: libp2p, XChaCha20-Poly1305, Kademlia-backed offline mailboxes, and DTN store-carry-forward routing. The mailbox layer has one awkward requirement:

  • sender seals a message for the recipient’s public key
  • recipient is offline
  • one or more peers stores the sealed envelope
  • retries happen without re-sealing the payload

That seemingly small requirement forces a design decision that I became uncomfortable with and want to put in front of people who understand AEAD better than I do.

The envelope 

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct MailboxEnvelope {
    pub recipient_id: String,
    pub ephemeral_pub: String,
    pub ciphertext: Vec<u8>,
    pub nonce: String,
    pub created_at: u64,
    pub message_id: String,
    pub attempts: u32, // deliberately excluded from AAD
}

impl Drop for MailboxEnvelope {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        self.ciphertext.zeroize();
    }
}

The encrypted mailbox AAD is bound to immutable metadata:

  • recipient identity
  • ephemeral key
  • nonce
  • message ID
  • creation timestamp

attempts is intentionally not in the AAD.

Tradeoff A: include retry state in AAD

This is the clean cryptographic posture. The authenticator describes everything about the record, including mutable control state.

The practical problem: if retry state changes, the previous authenticator is invalidated. That means either:

  1. re-seal every time under the same recipient key, destroying a useful property
  2. predefine every possible retry counter, which is absurd
  3. let recipients reject or duplicate records every time a signer’s local counter changes

A strict AEAD model collides with retry policy changes.

Tradeoff B: exclude mutable retry state from AAD

The record authorizes what matters:

  • who gets it
  • who sealed it
  • when it was created
  • which message identifier it carries

Retries are a local delivery/cost concern layered above the sealed payload. AAT in this case is concerned with authenticity of intent, not anti-replay accounting for every delivery attempt.

I chose B because the alternative re-creates a seal for every attempt.

What I do not like: a future reader could miss that state at a glance. I need better documentation and possibly a separate signed receipt so retry behavior is non-cryptographically attested.

Retry state should become a proven promise

Instead of dropping attempts into AAD, the more honest pattern seems to be:

  • keep ciphertext immutable and bound to the original AD
  • keep retry-state metadata outside it
  • expose an API boundary that returns a signed envelope descriptor only when attempts are changed
  • audit every state mutation separately from payload readability

This treats the cryptographic envelope as an evidence object and the delivery system as a policy object. That is better than pretending one signature can mean both things.

The more serious concern: accidental ciphertext copies

MailboxEnvelope derives Clone, and this type can travel through serde serializations.

Drop zeroization only affects the dropped allocation. If:

  • a cloned mailbox copy is held elsewhere
  • a temporary serialization buffer is allocated
  • transport middleware buffers bytes

then “the original object was zeroed” is not the same as “all copies disappeared.” Production Rust code has libraries specifically for this: secrecy, zeroize-on-drop patterns, and more explicit small-source handling.

I am not yet sure this level of copy-safety is necessary for ciphertext that is, by design, something one recipient is supposed to decrypt. It may still matter against heap snapshots, debug traces, or process forensics, but the right point is an operational requirement, not an automatic obvious gate.

If you work in Rust cryptography, I want one concrete answer

When ciphertext is being handled by protocols at multiple layers, what is the least effortful and still correct handling model?

  1. Manual Drop plus short-lived scope?
  2. secrecy::Expose and CryptographicBuffer wrapper everywhere?
  3. Accept temporary copies but only allow canonical object copies to remain live for bounded durations?

I am especially interested in patterns that are realistic at 100+ messages/second, not “never instantiate temporary slices.”

What stayed out of this post

GhostWire’s roadmap includes post-quantum key exchange, mix routing, and AI-assisted pathing, but none of that improves the trust model if mailbox confidentiality is sloppy. The mailbox layer is intentionally primitive because it is where subtle assumptions become failures.

If you have experience implementing this kind of encrypted storage in the Rust ecosystem, the comments here are the part I want most.

title: Building and Optimizing a Competitive AI Coding Agent
description:
I developed an autonomous coding agent designed to solve challenging programming tasks in a competitive environment. Rather than relying on an LLM to generate code in a single pass, I built a complete workflow combining repository analysis, planning, implementation, execution, testing, and iterative refinement.

The agent’s workflow:

Task → Analyze → Plan → Implement → Execute → Test → Diagnose → Refine → Retest → Submit

The feedback loop is where the real improvement happens. When a test fails, the agent analyzes the error, identifies the likely cause, updates the code, and reruns the relevant tests. This helps catch logic errors and edge cases before submission instead of accepting the first plausible-looking solution.

Performance comparison

I evaluate the agent with and without iterative feedback using the same benchmark tasks and execution limits:

Task success rate: [baseline]% → [optimized]%

Tests passed per task: [baseline] → [optimized]

Average completion time: [baseline] → [optimized]

Compute cost per successful task: [baseline] → [optimized]

These measurements help show whether each optimization improves correctness and reliability without introducing excessive latency or compute overhead.

Beyond the feedback loop, I optimize model selection, prompt design, repository context, tool usage, inference settings, and failure recovery. The goal is to build an agent that doesn't just generate code, but uses execution results as evidence to improve its solutions systematically.

title: CLAD: Keypoint Matching Using Global Line Correspondences
description:
arXiv:2610.21409v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Traditional keypoint descriptors, such as SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) and ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF), are computed from local image patches. They may be unreliable in scenes with repetitive patterns or weak textures, where patches at different locations can look similar. We propose the Contextual Line-Assisted Descriptor (CLAD), a keypoint matching method that addresses this problem by using global geometric context from line correspondences. CLAD represents each keypoint with a vector whose elements indicate its proximity to matched lines. It can therefore use the keypoint's spatial relationships to the lines in the scene. We use HOME (Hough-space One-dimensional Matching of Extrema) to detect both clear and weak linear structures and to establish enough line-to-keypoint associations to represent this context. Evaluations on the TUM RGB-D SLAM dataset and outdoor video sequences show that CLAD provides geometrically consistent matches that complement those obtained with traditional local descriptors. In repetitive scenes, where local descriptors may not distinguish similar patches, CLAD uses global structure to improve matching reliability. The method is computationally lightweight and practical to implement.

title: PRISM: Transfer and Limits of Activation Interventions in Tool-Calling Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent literature shows that unsafe tool calls can often accompany textual refusals in language models. To investigate this hidden vulnerability, we introduce PRISM, a framework for evaluating the transfer of activation interventions across precision, languages, and scales. Our findings demonstrate that leveraging lower-resource settings (specifically quantized NF4 labels and cross-lingual transfer) offers a robust pathway to expose and improve model alignment. Notably, using behavioral labels from an NF4 copy enables stable intervention estimation even with very few scenarios. Furthermore, these alignment improvements transfer effectively across languages: five-language NF4-supervised directions successfully transfer to held-out Arabic, reducing unsafe violations in Llama-3.1-8B by 21.95 percentage points without target-language tuning. By mapping paired benign activations, we also successfully transfer these safety interventions to much larger models (up to 70B parameters). Ultimately, PRISM highlights how auxiliary supervision from compressed models and multilingual data can uncover and mitigate hazardous tool-calling behaviors across different model families. We release all experimental code and supporting artifacts at https://github.com/GiKerche/prism, alongside an interactive explorer of recorded model responses and experimental results at https://gikerche.github.io/prism/.

title: Go Production Debugging: 3 Checks When Published Events Are Never Seen
description:
TL;DR: When a published device-status event never reaches an e-commerce support room and neither side reports an error, compare the event name with the provider's supported type list first. A typo is a contract mismatch: nothing subscribes, nothing fails loudly, and retries faithfully repeat the wrong publish. Fetch the type list during Go service startup, validate every event constant from one module, and refuse readiness when any constant is unknown.

The page arrives as "video support room live, device status absent." The room may be healthy, its scoped client token may be valid, and other traffic may still flow. The immediate action is narrow: stop retrying the suspect event, inspect the exact emitted name, and test it against supported types. This is an SLO problem because successful publish attempts are an input metric, while visible status transitions are the user outcome.

How should you debug published events that are never seen?

Silent non-delivery is the signature. Suppose checkout support opens a video room so an agent can help diagnose a customer's payment terminal. The backend intends to emit device.status.changed, but the publisher contains a one-character misspelling. No subscriber matches it, and no error has to appear. A dashboard built around HTTP success can remain green while the customer and agent stare at stale state.

The first useful signal should have fired before that page: an invariant check during deployment or process startup. Count attempted publishes for capacity planning, but do not confuse that count with delivery. The operational objective is closer to "a valid device transition becomes observable by the authorized room client"; the event-name contract is one dependency of that objective, alongside token scope, connection state, and the client handler.

This distinction also keeps token debugging disciplined. A scoped token should grant only the room and actions the client needs. Broadening client trust to make a missing event appear is the wrong experiment when the name itself is invalid. Validate the server-side event vocabulary first, then inspect token scope if a known type still does not arrive.

Names first.

Make the vocabulary a startup dependency

Keep event constants in one Go package. Exhaustiveness matters more than cleverness: scattered literals make it impossible to know whether startup validation covered every publisher. This program reads the API base from configuration, calls the verified event-type route, accepts JSON without assuming an undocumented field name, and exits before readiness if a configured name is absent. The discovery call is public, so the program does not send a credential.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

var applicationEvents = []string{
    "device.status.changed",
    "support.room.joined",
}

func collectStrings(v any, out map[string]struct{}) {
    switch x := v.(type) {
    case string:
        out[x] = struct{}{}
    case []any:
        for _, item := range x {
            collectStrings(item, out)
        }
    case map[string]any:
        for _, item := range x {
            collectStrings(item, out)
        }
    }
}

func supportedTypes(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, baseURL string) (map[string]struct{}, error) {
    url := strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/") + "/realtime/event/types"
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("event type discovery returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
    }

    var document any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &document); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("decode event types: %w", err)
    }
    types := make(map[string]struct{})
    collectStrings(document, types)
    if len(types) == 0 {
        return nil, errors.New("event type discovery returned no strings")
    }
    return types, nil
}

func main() {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    types, err := supportedTypes(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 6 * time.Second}, baseURL)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    var unknown []string
    for _, name := range applicationEvents {
        if _, ok := types[name]; !ok {
            unknown = append(unknown, name)
        }
    }
    if len(unknown) != 0 {
        sort.Strings(unknown)
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "unsupported realtime event constants: %v\n", unknown)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The parser deliberately treats discovery as a set-membership source instead of binding the application to an unverified response field. In production I would cap startup retries and leave the instance unready, because accepting traffic with an unchecked vocabulary exchanges a visible deployment failure for silent customer impact. Five seconds is an example timeout, not a latency claim or universal setting; set it from the deployment budget and measurements in your environment.

One trap deserves emphasis. Do not "fix" a failed assertion by deleting the constant from applicationEvents. The list must be the single source imported by every publisher, otherwise the check becomes theater. A code-generation step can enforce that relationship in a large repository, but a plain Go package is enough for a small service.

Fail closed.

Trace the alert backward, then change the signal

Start at the page and walk toward the earliest discriminating observation. The on-call sees a live video room, an authorized client, and a missing device update. A publish-success counter says only that a request was accepted; it cannot prove that a subscriber registered the same string. The next check is the emitted name against the supported set. If the name is absent, stop there. The instrumentation change has two layers: startup validation blocks new bad binaries, while runtime telemetry compares accepted device transitions with client-observed transitions over the service's chosen window, partitioned by event type but not by unbounded room or customer identifiers. Alert on sustained outcome loss, and keep the raw startup mismatch as a deployment event that points directly to the bad constant. This catches both vocabulary mistakes and later delivery failures without pretending they share a cause. Capacity planning enters sooner than teams expect because event type is a bounded label and room ID is not; a per-room metric can turn one incident into a monitoring-cardinality incident, raising query cost and weakening the alert needed during a peak support period. Keep room-level correlation in structured logs keyed by a request identifier, and reserve metrics for bounded dimensions. This is a deliberate trade-off: metrics answer whether the SLO is at risk, while logs answer which room needs inspection.

The useful page names the failed outcome and the event type, not merely the publish operation. It should send the responder to the contract diff first. Only after the type is known should the investigation fan out to room membership, scoped-token authorization, client connection state, and handler registration.

Where should offline delivery meet the video room?

A live socket is not durable storage. If the customer briefly loses connectivity while the device changes state, publishing once and hoping the browser is present turns a recoverable disconnect into stale support data. A queue should hold the notification until a worker can attempt delivery; the video-room client receives only the scoped realtime event it is authorized to see. Consumer-side idempotency remains mandatory for an at-least-once standard queue, so the business transition needs a stable identifier even when transport attempts repeat.

Infrai is one plausible combined choice because realtime/RTC and jobs/queues sit behind one REST API, one key, and one bill; fewer credential rotations and invoices are useful to a small platform team, while public self-describing discovery supports the startup assertion above. The trade-off is concentration: one vendor becomes the trust and billing boundary for both durable handoff and live delivery. It is not a good fit when policy requires separate providers or the team wants to replace queue and realtime layers independently.

The platform discovery surface reports 295 routes across 20 modules. That breadth can reduce credential sprawl, but it makes provider review more consequential, not less.

The verified route set used here does not specify a queue enqueue operation or its request schema, so a queue-to-socket request sample would require invented fields. The safe implementation boundary is a durable worker that reads the business transition, checks its idempotency key, and publishes a supported realtime type; generate its exact queue path and payload from live discovery before shipping.

With Pusher plus Amazon SQS, the equivalent stack requires two service signups, two credential sets, two billing relationships, and glue mapping an SQS delivery to a Pusher channel event while handling retries and deduplication. That separation can be desirable: IAM can be narrower, and either side can be replaced without migrating the other. It also increases on-call load.

Option Token scope and client trust Durable handoff Best fit Main limitation
Infrai realtime/RTC plus jobs/queues Backend issues scoped client access; one backend key spans both groups Combined service surface; consumers still need idempotency Small platform teams accepting a unified boundary Provider concentration
Pusher Channels plus Amazon SQS Pusher channel authorization is separate from AWS IAM SQS buffers; application glue delivers AWS teams wanting replaceable components Two signups, credential sets, and bills
Ably plus an external queue Token capabilities constrain client operations Separate queue and worker required Teams prioritizing realtime-specific controls Integration remains yours
PubNub plus an external queue PubNub access controls govern messaging clients Separate queue and worker required Teams wanting a managed pub/sub product Durable workflow spans products
Socket.IO plus a managed queue Application owns authentication and authorization Chosen queue feeds an application worker Teams wanting protocol and hosting control Highest build and on-call ownership

These products are not interchangeable merely because each can appear in the same diagram. Pusher, Ably, and PubNub center managed realtime messaging; Socket.IO gives more application control; the AWS pairing gives explicit infrastructure components. Choose according to the trust boundary the team can explain during review and the systems it can operate at 03:00, not the shortest initial setup.

Pick the boundary deliberately.

Set the threshold with the false-positive budget in view

The final risk is an alert that fires whenever one client disconnects normally. A zero-tolerance ratio over a tiny window will page on ordinary mobile churn; a wide aggregate window may conceal a typo affecting one event type. Segment by the bounded event vocabulary, require enough traffic to make the comparison meaningful, and page only when the sustained gap threatens the customer-facing SLO. Record lower-volume mismatches for investigation without waking someone.

There is no universal number in the available evidence. Derive the window and threshold from observed event volume, reconnect behavior, and the error budget for the support workflow. Then test the alert by introducing an unsupported constant in a non-production contract test: startup should fail, no customer token should be broadened, and no live publish should be necessary.

That closes the trace. The page becomes actionable because the earlier signal identifies a vocabulary mismatch, the startup gate prevents recurrence, and the runtime outcome metric remains available for failures that are not spelling mistakes. The cost of setting the threshold too low is alert fatigue and wasted on-call capacity; the cost of setting it too high is a customer discovering stale status first. Treat both as reliability costs.

References

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • Pusher Channels, authenticating users: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/server_api/authenticating-users/
  • Amazon SQS, delivery semantics: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues-at-least-once-delivery.html
  • Ably, token authentication: https://ably.com/docs/auth/token
  • PubNub, access manager: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/security/access-control
  • Socket.IO, delivery guarantees: https://socket.io/docs/v4/delivery-guarantees

title: Clinically Interpretable Biological Age Estimation Using CatBoost and SHAP with Continuous and Categorical Features from NHANES
description:
arXiv:2610.20868v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Biological age (BA) captures inter-individual variation in physiological aging beyond chronological age (CA). Although machine-learning models have advanced BA estimation, many rely primarily on continuous laboratory biomarkers, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) dependence plots are typically interpreted visually. We developed a clinically interpretable machine-learning framework for BA estimation using heterogeneous clinical data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES 2011-March 2020, N = 24,983 adults aged >= 18). A CatBoost regression model incorporated 44 demographic, laboratory, physical examination, and lifestyle predictors to estimate CA, defining model-estimated age as BA. SHAP provided multi-level interpretability. Crucially, building on standard visual inspection, we implemented a prespecified automated procedure directly on SHAP dependence plots to quantify feature-value ranges associated with lowest and highest BA contributions, corresponding adjustment magnitudes, and zero-crossing thresholds. Model-estimated BA strongly correlated with CA in held-out testing data (Pearson r = 0.798, P < 0.001). Population-level SHAP identified blood urea nitrogen, serum glucose, vigorous recreational activity, red cell distribution width, and alanine aminotransferase among the leading predictors, with three categorical variables ranking among the top 25. Automated quantitative SHAP analysis mapped predictor-specific ranges, effect sizes, and inflection points, while waterfall plots enabled individual explanations. By extending qualitative visual interpretation to reproducible quantitative metrics across heterogeneous clinical data, this framework enhances transparency and provides a scalable methodological foundation for biological aging research and precision health.

title: Long-Context Drafting Does Not Require Long-Context Drafters
description:
arXiv:2610.20865v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding pairs a cheap drafter with parallel verification against the target. At ultra-long context it stops paying, because a drafter that attends over the full prefix inherits the target's context-dependent cost, so the speedup it was meant to provide first erodes and then reverses. The standard response is to build a long-context drafter, by training or fine-tuning one, or by using a multi-token-prediction head shipped inside the target checkpoint. We argue this is unnecessary, because the drafters in use are target-conditioned, reading hidden states the target computed over the entire prefix, so distant context already reaches them without their own attention, and verification corrects what they miss. We therefore freeze released short-context drafters and run them far past their training length under two inference-time mechanisms, one bounding the attention cache they see, which fixes their cost, and one re-basing their rotary position indices into the trained range. No weight is touched and the only tunable saturates early, so one vLLM-side configuration spans 4k to two million tokens, costing at most 0.16x of speedup at short length. We prove when a common index shift leaves the drafter's computation exactly unchanged, and decompose acceptance into two measurable gaps with sharp bounds. Whatever speedup a frozen drafter delivers at short context, it retains out to two million tokens, across three target-drafter pairs and five corpora. The claim concerns the flatness rather than the multiple, and removing either mechanism eliminates it. The gain is conditional on the speculative cost per emitted token staying below the matched target-only cost.

title: Hybrid Generative-Tagging Decoding for Efficient Product Attribute-Value Extraction
description:
arXiv:2610.21329v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attribute-value extraction is important for building high-quality product catalogs in e-commerce. Existing systems either rely on generative or tagging strategies for extracting the attribute names and their corresponding values. Tagging models directly label spans in the source, making them fast and grounded, but they cannot produce values that require reformatting or generate rare attribute names outside their label space. Generative models avoid these drawbacks by generating both attribute names and values token by token, but this auto-regressive nature makes them slow and limits attribute coverage. We introduce hybrid generative-tagging decoding, a novel model architecture that combines tagging source spans and open-ended generation. For frequent attributes whose values are copyable, a tagging head extracts values directly from the source. This lets the generative head focus on the remainder - rare attributes outside the tagger's label space and non-copyable values, including implicit or normalized values. Integrated into vLLM inference, the hybrid decoder raises attribute coverage by 10% and extracts 63% more correct attribute-value pairs at no precision cost, while reducing latency by 44%.

title: AutoOnboarder: Autonomously Onboarding LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21218v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic large language models have been documented to lose reasoning capability when placed inside a harness, the software that mediates their observations and actions. To reconcile these losses, we introduce AutoOnboarder, an autonomous system that adapts an agent to a task the way a trainer onboards a new employee. It places the agent under the supervision of an intelligent ``Onboarder'' coding agent, which iteratively tailors its foundation model, prompt, and harness source code to simultaneously improve performance and decrease cost. Like a real onboarding process, the Onboarder is only given tens of examples, and all evaluation data is isolated on a separate virtual machine to prevent leakage. We report the lessons learned from building and testing AutoOnboarder on genomic-sequencing prior authorization form submission. Autonomously onboarded agents are able to match or exceed the performance of a Gemini 3.5 Flash baseline at up to 29$\times$ lower costs. However, these agents remain imperfect, and the Onboarding process varies greatly in terms of final performance. We conclude that future Onboarding systems require a robust environment for the Onboarder, including a structured thought interface, (controlled) internet access, and a wide model search space.

title: CCIL Test Studio source 07: README.md
description:
# CCIL Test Studio

A complete interactive frontend built with React, plain JavaScript, CSS, and custom SVG icons. React and React DOM are the only runtime dependencies. Vite is the only development dependency, used for the local server and production build.

## Run locally

```powershell
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:5175/. MCM is the default team and includes populated synthetic sample data.

Select a team and enter its shared password. Sample teams use `team-demo` for User access or `admin-demo` for Administrator access, through the same sign-in form. There are no individual role accounts. Administrators can add teams with their own team and administrator passwords.

All team users can create System Baselines and workspaces, upload documents, resolve source-backed questions, and generate/edit test suites. Only adding a team and approving System Baseline updates require Administrator access. Initial baseline creation has no approval step.

System Baseline and CR creation both require at least one document from **Business**, **Technical**, or **Functional / Bug Information**. Any one category is sufficient; all three are never compulsory.

MCM means Membership and Collateral Management. Membership is an alias of MCM; it is not a separate team. Existing Membership-owned records retain their IDs and source references when migrated to MCM.

```powershell
npm run build
npm run preview
npm test
```

The production build is in `dist/`. Tests use Node's built-in test runner and Vite's existing loader; no test framework is installed.

## Included pages and workflows

1. Sign-in and team selection using a shared team password and two access levels.
2. Overview and workspaces: live counts, attention queue, searchable/paginated lists, create/copy wizard, shared team access.
3. System Baselines: reusable library, three document categories, a one-document minimum, initial creation without approval, knowledge manifest, and version history.
4. CR evidence: exactly Technical, Functional / Bug Information, and Business categories; combined documents; CR creation; local routing review; manual source-linked requirements; and activity.
5. Knowledge versions: baseline/CR selection, ADD/REPLACE/REMOVE diff, prerequisites, conflicts, incorporated-CR protection, and shared contracts.
6. Workspace chat: persistent version-specific conversations, cited local evidence lookup, attachments, historic threads, typed clarification answers, and immediate source-backed answer resolution.
7. Generation readiness: concrete blockers, final/provisional gates, template selection, persistent local run stages, cancellation, interruption handling, and retry.
8. Test suites: scenario search, editing and revisions, team reviews, citations, coverage/gaps, historic version identity, and CSV export.
9. Templates: manual fields and ordering, immutable versions, selection, CSV example import with header/source-row review, and separate example suites.
10. Baseline approvals: requests, precise diffs, exact manifest SHA-256, checklist, Administrator-only approval, decision history, and new immutable local baseline versions.
11. Dependency graph: custom SVG, directed relationships, source inspector, unresolved references, pan, zoom, search, type filters, and bounded hops/nodes.
12. Administration: shared team access, source-sharing grants/revocation, local connection configuration, audit history, metadata backup/import, and demo reset.

Light/dark themes, mobile navigation, keyboard focus, command search (Ctrl+K), accessible dialogs, empty/error states, and reduced-motion support are included. Hover motion uses short CSS transitions. The optional DM Sans stylesheet falls back to system fonts offline.

## Storage and integration boundaries

All seeded business content is synthetic. Backend services and agents are deferred.

- Application records use localStorage under `ccil-studio-demo-v1`.
- Original uploads use browser IndexedDB (`ccil-local-files`). Files receive type/size checks and SHA-256 checksums. Plain text, Markdown, and SQL have local previews. PDFs and DOCX are retained for original download. Nothing is sent to a server.
- Local source review does not claim classification, extraction, indexing, or authoritative validation.
- Chat uses a visible deterministic keyword lookup over eligible readable sources. It abstains when matching text is absent. This is not a model integration.
- Generation creates local demo fixtures from selected rules and reviewed answers. Provisional suites retain unresolved expected outcomes. These fixtures do not establish complete test coverage.
- CSV import/export is implemented locally. XLSX parsing/export and PDF/DOCX extraction await backend integration.
- Knowledge changes reset clarification readiness and create a fresh chat context. Historic chats and suites retain their original version.
- Baseline approval creates a new local immutable version. Existing workspaces keep their selected baseline. Real approval enforcement belongs on the backend.
- Connection settings store endpoint/model identifiers with an explicit disconnected state. No API keys are accepted or stored.
- JSON backups include records, conversations, and readable source text, but not original file bytes. Storage is per browser/device and is not a server database.
- Shared password verification and access checks are a browser-local prototype, not server-side authentication. Password digests are stored locally; plaintext passwords are not persisted. Backend authentication is deferred.

## Source layout

```text
src/
  access.js        # Shared team login, upload validation, and migration
  AppShell.jsx       Navigation, themes, search, local run progression
  store.jsx          React state, persistence, version/readiness checks, CSV helpers
  seed.js            Synthetic fixtures
  generation.js      Deterministic source-linked demo suites
  files.js           Native browser file checks, checksums, IndexedDB
  ui.jsx             Shared controls, dialogs, source/file components
  pages/             One module per application area
  styles.css         Approved visual foundation
  studio.css         Full layouts, responsive behavior, lightweight hover states
tests/
  frontend.test.mjs  Page rendering and version/readiness/CSV invariants
```

No UI kit, routing package, state-management package, graph/chart package, animation library, TypeScript compiler, or backend framework is added.

title: Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
description:
Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-Silva

When Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded.

This post is about that search for the needle.

The Four hours before a fix

Consider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it?

As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner.

The MELT Layer

“What caused the issue?”

Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to.

The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer:

The timeline of an investigation

So how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again?

In our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover.

The disagreement underneath

The instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow.

It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle.

Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas, our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found.

The difficulty is that they do not agree on what they are talking about. A thing that is an application in one system is a service in a second and a cluster in a third, with names differing by a suffix, a casing convention, or a rename only a couple of people remember (SMEs, ring a bell?). Joining across them requires a human carrying the mapping in their head, and that person becomes the bottleneck in such cross-domain investigations. The hard part of end-to-end observability is probably better understood as a data modelling problem.

What we lacked was an explicit, machine-readable agreement about the entities in our operational world.

The Ontology

This agreement has a name: an ontology. Ontology is a formal specification of types, the properties they carry, and the relationships they may have. Its unit is the triple, one fact expressed as subject, predicate, object. Consider the following example triples.

api-gateway   rdf:type       ops:Application .
api-gateway   ops:ownedBy    "Team Bedrock" .
api-gateway   ops:deployedIn "us-east-1" .

INC-5377      rdf:type       ops:Incident .
INC-5377      ops:affects    api-gateway .
INC-5377      ops:severity   "SEV 2" .

In the example here, we have already encoded six facts, and can answer in one query, a question that used to span three tools.

“Which incidents affected applications owned by Team Bedrock in us-east-1?” is a single query in place of looking up incidents, Spinnaker and Radar.

We call our ontology layer, The Observability Ontology. It acts as the schema, rule set and shared agreement that standardizes how different systems understand entities like applications, services, incidents, deployments, etc.

We built it on the W3C stack for this: RDF for the data model, OWL for the ontology, SHACL for validation, and SPARQL for querying. These standards are well specified and widely implemented, which keeps the model portable across graph stores.

The data from the ontology itself, is stored as a knowledge graph, persisted to QuipuDB, our homegrown RDF graph database, a distributed quad store based on redb, a Rust-based embedded key value db. Data here is generated by parsing raw telemetry, logs, and incident discussions into triples (subject-predicate-object facts).

Every harvest also produces a full Turtle serialization for archival, making it human-readable and diff-friendly, which has proven more useful for debugging than we expected.

Our ontology is organized into twelve namespaces, each owning one operational domain:

There are two decisions about this ontology that mattered while we built it, so they’re worth sharing.

The first is that we refused a generic Service type. “Service” means four different things across our tooling, so applications resolve to exactly one type, ops:Application, and every one of them is validated against our software catalog of roughly 49,000 entries before the entity is created. Unvalidated strings like usernames, team names, dependency names scraped from network topology, never become applications. We also cap dependency edges in both directions, because one popular service can carry thousands of reverse dependencies and would otherwise dominate the graph.

The second decision concerns what we chose to model. Incident chat carries the reasoning behind an incident. The hypotheses tried and discarded, the mitigation that worked, who knew why, is all context in the incident’s Slack channel and that knowledge evaporates when the channel goes quiet. So a 200-message, 50-person, 15-service incident channel becomes a structure, converting the operational chaos of an incident into ordered triples:

Creating determinism from non-determinism

Building this graph means using tools that are inherently stochastic. LLMs summarize discussions. Fuzzy matching resolves service names. A probabilistic engine proposes causal chains. None of these produce the same output twice with certainty, but what comes out at the end of our system is a deterministic graph that answers a SPARQL query the same way every time.

The ontology is the mechanism that creates this determinism through its pipelined approach. We think of the pipeline as a ladder that drives entropy down, where entropy means the proportion of information still trapped in unstructured form. For example, at the start of this pipeline, an LLM could say anything, but it cannot emit a triple that violates the type system. We constrain the output space tightly enough and a stochastic process yields a deterministic contract:

# The model may produce any prose. Its output MUST fit these predicates:
category  IN ["incident", "question", "discussion", "decision"]
sentiment IN ["positive", "neutral", "negative", "urgent"]

# Result — a deterministic triple:
thread:123  slack:category          "incident" .
thread:123  slack:isIncidentRelated "true"^^xsd:boolean .

There are five layers that get us down this ladder. Any single step of this ladder is non-deterministic. But in aggregate, the chain becomes deterministic. That inversion is the whole trick. We describe them below:

Enrichers: Agents as entropy reducers

We use what we call, enrichers, to reduce entropy across the knowledge graph. Dozens of enrichers run over the graph. Each one of them takes noisy input and emits typed triples, and each reads what earlier enrichers wrote. The contract for an Enricher is deliberately narrow:

class Enricher:
    async def _enrich_async(self, ...):
        raw    = await self.fetch(...)      # 1. read noisy input
        result = self.analyze(raw)          # 2. process (may be stochastic)
        graph.add((uri, RDF.type, OPS.X))   # 3. emit TYPED triples
        graph.add((uri, OPS.pred, Literal(result.value)))
        return EnrichmentResult(success=True, triples_added=count)

Three invariants that are standard across the enrichers:

  • every entity carries an rdf:type,
  • every URI follows a single naming scheme, and
  • the catalog gates every ops:Application.

Two operational choices are worth naming here, as well. The enrichment pipeline runs sequentially — load the graph, add triples, and save.

This sequencing removes an entire category of race conditions at a cost in wall-clock time we are happy to pay. And calls out to external systems like metrics, logs, events and the rest could be best-effort, so a slow downstream API doesn’t block the graph harvest, albeit some degradation. To that end, we are also working to translate these separate systems into the ontology, such as the Metrics Ontology and the Alerts Ontology, so everything could be queried from the Ontology itself.

The Correlation Engine: finding the correlation chains

The correlation engine assimilates the vast number of signals from diverse input sources and condenses them into causal or correlatory chains of events. Today, the engine reads thirteen signal types, including log errors, metric anomalies, slow and failed traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, config changes, experiments, autoscaling, commits, end-to-end bottlenecks, and error patterns. It then searches for paths among them. Some ordered pairs are known to be causal and carry a high prior weight. For example, deployment before log error, config change before metric anomaly, failed trace before incident, and so on. Others, which show high correlation are considered correlation chains. Such chains are scored on temporal proximity and severity, inside a ten-minute window, with anything under 0.6 confidence getting discarded.

The role of the engine here is to propose with evidence, not to make conclusions. Hence, the engine stores its chains along with the graph records that were used to create them.

A 0.87 chain in the above example, is a strong hypothesis for a human or an agent to check, and the graph records the confidence alongside the claim so that consumers can understand why a chain is what it is and weigh their options to make decisions.

The knowledge flywheel

Each harvest cycle turns the same four steps, and each rotation leaves the graph richer for the next. This is the Knowledge Flywheel, leading to continuous enrichment and improvement of the context about our system, stored in the knowledge graph.

Observe collects the signals. Enrich adds typed triples. Infer finds patterns invisible in the raw data. Adapt feeds knowledge back, so that established patterns become detection rules. The compounding result of the four phases leads to a self-improving system. A causal chain discovered in one incident becomes a known pattern for the next, and the ontology gradually stops being a schema and starts being a memory.

Consider the example above. When we first see an incident in api-gateway caused due to a timeout and resolve it, we convert this knowledge into entries to the ontology. This becomes encoded knowledge. As we go through multiple cycles of this encoding, the graph starts learning patterns. After N cycles, patterns become wisdom — “api-gateway deploys cause 40% of SEV-2s” and “30% of deployment issues in api-gateway come from Connection Timeouts”. Surface this as an insight and we proactively start reducing incidents, not just react quickly to new ones.

Putting the graph to work

On top of the graph sits AutoRCA, our internal agentic AI solution, built with a set of specialist agents coordinated around one question. Walking the home page regression from the top of this post, the agentic system’s reasoning chain might look something like this:

Each specialization to the inputs is built by people who understand their respective domain deeply. That division of labour only works if the specialists can pass findings to one another without having to agree on the terms of communication or even have knowledge of each other. The ontology acts as the interface. Each specialist learns one vocabulary — the graph’s. A team writing specialized use cases for how they use traces record their findings as triples about an ops:Application, the logs specialization reads triples about that same ops:Application, and neither needs to know the other exists. A new specialist learns the same vocabulary once and can immediately read everything the other six have written.

Set against the investigation we opened with, the change is narrower than it might sound. The alert still fires at 3:30pm, an engineer still has to weigh the evidence, and the fix still has to be written by someone who understands the code. The hour or two that used to go into assembling context — finding the owning team, reconstructing what shipped, correlating information from different parts of the system, recalling that something similar happened last quarter — all that work is the part the ontology and the graph absorbs. We are early enough that the ranked hypotheses are sometimes wrong, which is why each one carries the evidence that produced it. But when the engineer now starts the investigation, they are already holding the picture that used to take half an afternoon to assemble.

If you want to build one of these

A fair amount of what we have built, we learned by getting it wrong first. Based on this experience, these are the principles we would carry into a second attempt.

  • Model identity before anything else. Choose one authoritative catalog per entity kind and validate against it before creating an entity.
  • Treat the ontology as code. Version it, review it, test it, and let changes arrive as pull requests. Treating the ontology as code lends itself to agentic development and lets teams scale and contribute to it.
  • Separate concepts from instances. Concepts change on a human timescale and instances change continuously, conflating them makes both harder to evolve.
  • Build on open standards. RDF, OWL, SHACL and SPARQL are specified, implemented many times over, and portable. A bespoke graph model ties a future consumer to one implementation.
  • Constrain stochastic tools with a type system. This is the principle we would defend hardest. Models are useful precisely where determinism is impossible, and a sufficiently narrow output contract converts their output into something a query engine can trust.
  • Make enrichment best-effort and ordered. A slow dependency should utmost degrade the graph, never block it. And ordering enrichers so each builds on the last buys more accuracy and that’s worth the tradeoff with parallelism that buys speed.
  • Model human reasoning alongside machine telemetry. The most valuable edges in our graph came from discussion. Telemetry records what the system did, discussion records what people understood and interpreted. The reasoning is more valuable to store and serve as wisdom when we need it.
  • Keep humans as the approvers. Let agents propose fixes, enrichers, and ontology changes, and route every proposal through a review process with humans in the loop.

What comes next

The graph makes three things possible. First, automatic root cause analysis, where a regression arrives with a ranked set of graph-backed hypotheses attached. Next, automated remediation, where a sufficiently confident diagnosis carries a proposed action like a targeted rollback, a traffic shift, a code change. And eventually infrastructure that heals itself, acting on a predicted failure before members feel it.

Alongside this, we plan to integrate the Observability Ontology with Upper, the domain-modeling language at the heart of Netflix’s Unified Data Architecture (UDA). Upper lets teams describe business and system domains as interconnected, machine-readable models and preserve their meaning and constraints as those models are projected into concrete schemas and systems. This integration would connect operational concepts such as applications, alerts, deployments, and incidents to the broader set of domains modeled across Netflix, giving engineers and agents a shared semantic layer for querying, validation, and reasoning. We will begin with a proof of concept that models incidents in Upper and use what we learn to determine where the two systems should converge.

Acknowledgements

None of this would exist without the teams who share their data, expertise, and patience with an early system. We want to specially acknowledge the efforts of our own team members who made this possible from very early on in this lifecycle, Kaela Marsheck and Aditya Gaur. We are also especially grateful to our collaborators in Netflix’s ontology working group, Peter Royal, Alex Hutter, and to Alexandre Bertails and members of the Unified Data Architecture (UDA)/Knowledge Foundations team for sharing Upper and their domain-modeling expertise, and for helping us explore how the Observability Ontology can become part of a broader semantic foundation at Netflix.

Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Microsoft
description:
Vercel Connect now includes a managed connector for Microsoft, so your apps and agents can access all Microsoft products such as Teams, OneDrive and more.

As a Vercel Managed Connector, Vercel registers the Entra application and configures federated credentials for it, so you don't have to create an app registration or manage client secrets yourself. Authorize the app for your Microsoft tenant once, then attach the connector to the projects and environments it needs.

Create a connector from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI:

With the connector attached, your code requests a token only when it needs one. The @vercel/connect SDK authenticates with your deployment's OIDC identity and returns a short-lived token for the app itself, using the application permissions your admin granted:

Each token is scoped to what you request and refreshed automatically, so there's nothing to leak or rotate. To act as a specific person instead, pass that user as the subject and the token carries their delegated permissions:

Read the Vercel Connect docs and create a Microsoft connector to get started.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python is now a first-class language and runtime on Vercel. Build APIs, full-stack applications, and AI agents with native Python SDKs and a shared development and deployment workflow for your Python backend and JavaScript frontend.

Python framework and runtime support

Vercel handles the infrastructure so you can focus on your application:

  • Automatic framework support: FastAPI, Flask, and Django applications are automatically recognized and configured, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the Vercel CDN.

  • Native Python runtime and tooling: Vercel runs CPython on Linux and supports uv and pyproject.toml for dependency management.

  • Compute for APIs and workers: Scale request-driven applications with Fluid compute and run long-running pull-based workloads with Vercel Daemons.

Native Python SDKs

Within your application, Python SDKs let you build agents, run untrusted code, and orchestrate durable workflows.

  • Sandbox: Give your application or agent an isolated Linux VM on demand.

  • AI SDK for Python (Beta): Generate or stream model responses and call tools. Get started with uv add ai.

  • Workflow SDK for Python (Beta): Persist execution state and retry failed workflow steps.

  • Queues (Beta): Send and receive messages for background work.

  • Connect: Obtain credentials for calling external APIs.

  • Blob: Upload and retrieve files in object storage.

Use the SDKs individually or combine them in the same Python application.

Your frontend and backend, together

For full-stack applications, Vercel Services allows you to deploy your frontend and backends together in one project, with shared previews and atomic deployments and rollbacks. Within that project, you can view logs by service and connect backends privately through service bindings.

For a frontend in frontend/ and a FastAPI app defined in backend/main.py, add this vercel.toml at the repository root.

Requests under /api/ reach matching FastAPI routes with the path unchanged, while other requests reach the frontend. Run both services locally with vercel dev, then deploy them together from the same repository.

Read the Python documentation to get started.
