title: CCIL Test Studio source 16: src/pages/Admin.jsx
description:
import React, { useRef, useState } from 'react';
import Icon from '../Icon.jsx';
import { canonicalTeamName, teamNames, upgradeDemoState } from '../seed.js';
import { addTeam, hashPassword } from '../access.js';
import { useStudio, canApprove, uid, log, download } from '../store.jsx';
import { Badge, Button, Empty, Field, Heading, Modal, Note, Tabs } from '../ui.jsx';

export default function Admin({ navigate }) {
  const { state: s, mutate, notify, reset } = useStudio();
  const [tab, setTab] = useState('Teams & access'), [team, setTeam] = useState('');
  const [teamPassword, setTeamPassword] = useState(''), [adminPassword, setAdminPassword] = useState(''), [busy, setBusy] = useState(false);
  const [source, setSource] = useState(''), [consumer, setConsumer] = useState(s.teams.find(t => t !== s.session.team) || '');
  const [settings, setSettings] = useState({ ...s.settings }), [dialog, setDialog] = useState(''), [error, setError] = useState('');
  const file = useRef(null), administrator = canApprove(s);
  async function createTeam(event) {
    event.preventDefault(); if (!administrator || busy) return;
    setError(''); setBusy(true);
    try {
      if (teamPassword.length < 6 || adminPassword.length < 6) throw new Error('Use at least six characters for each password.');
      const teamName = canonicalTeamName(team);
      const [userHash, administratorHash] = await Promise.all([hashPassword(teamPassword), hashPassword(adminPassword)]);
      if (!teamName || s.teams.some(t => t.toLowerCase() === teamName.toLowerCase())) throw new Error('This team already exists.');
      if (userHash === administratorHash) throw new Error('Team and administrator passwords must be different.');
      mutate(d => { addTeam(d, teamName, userHash, administratorHash); log(d, `Added team ${teamName}`); });
      setTeam(''); setTeamPassword(''); setAdminPassword(''); notify('Team created. Its shared password can now be used on the sign-in screen.');
    } catch (failure) { setError(failure.message); } finally { setBusy(false); }
  }
  async function importBackup(event) {
    const uploaded = event.target.files?.[0]; event.target.value = ''; if (!uploaded) return;
    try {
      if (uploaded.size > 10 * 1024 * 1024) throw new Error('Use a backup under 10 MB.');
      const parsed = JSON.parse(await uploaded.text());
      const keys = ['teams', 'workspaces', 'baselines', 'documents', 'crs', 'questions', 'suites', 'templates', 'candidates', 'shares', 'audit', 'jobs'];
      if (parsed.schema !== 1 || keys.some(key => !Array.isArray(parsed[key])) || !parsed.session || !parsed.teams.includes(parsed.session.team) || !parsed.threads || !parsed.settings) throw new Error('This file is not a compatible backup.');
      const restored = upgradeDemoState(parsed);
      mutate(d => { for (const key of Object.keys(d)) delete d[key]; Object.assign(d, restored); d.jobs = d.jobs.map(j => j.status === 'running' ? { ...j, status: 'Interrupted', stage: 'Imported run. Retry to continue.' } : j); });
      notify('Backup restored.'); setError('');
    } catch (failure) { setError(failure.message); }
  }
  return <><Heading eyebrow={`${s.session.team} · SHARED STUDIO`} title="Administration" description="Team access, source sharing, and connection settings."/>
    <Tabs value={tab} onChange={setTab} items={['Teams & access', 'Knowledge sharing', 'Connections', 'Data & audit']}/>
    {tab === 'Teams & access' ? <div className="detail-grid"><section className="card padded"><h2>Configured teams</h2>
      {s.teams.map(t => <div className="history-row" key={t}><span className="team-avatar">{t[0]}</span><span><strong>{t}</strong>{teamNames[t] && <small>{teamNames[t]}</small>}<small>{s.workspaces.filter(w => w.team === t).length} workspaces · {s.baselines.filter(b => b.team === t).length} System Baselines</small></span><Badge tone="green">Active</Badge></div>)}
      <h3 className="form-section-label">Add a team</h3>
      {administrator ? <form onSubmit={createTeam}><Field label="New team name"><input required maxLength={40} value={team} onChange={e => setTeam(e.target.value)} placeholder="Team name"/></Field><Field label="Shared team password"><input type="password" autoComplete="new-password" required minLength={6} value={teamPassword} onChange={e => setTeamPassword(e.target.value)}/></Field><Field label="Administrator password"><input type="password" autoComplete="new-password" required minLength={6} value={adminPassword} onChange={e => setAdminPassword(e.target.value)}/></Field><p className="supporting-copy">Use different passwords. Both access levels sign in through the same team login.</p>{error && <p className="form-error" role="alert">{error}</p>}<div className="modal-actions"><Button variant="primary" type="submit" icon="plus" disabled={busy}>{busy ? 'Adding…' : 'Add team'}</Button></div></form> : <Note>Only an Administrator can add a new team. All existing teams use shared team sign-in.</Note>}
    </section><section className="card padded"><h2>Two access levels</h2><div className="role-row"><Icon name="users" size={19}/><div><strong>User</strong><p>Create System Baselines and workspaces, upload documents, resolve questions, generate and edit tests, manage templates, and request baseline updates.</p></div></div><div className="role-row"><Icon name="shield" size={19}/><div><strong>Administrator</strong><p>Everything a User can do, plus add teams and approve or reject System Baseline updates.</p></div></div><Note>Everyone signed in to a team shares the same working capabilities. Only System Baseline updates need approval.</Note><Button onClick={() => { mutate(d => { d.session.authenticated = false; }); navigate('login'); }}>Sign out / change access</Button></section></div>
    : tab === 'Knowledge sharing' ? <section className="card padded"><h2>Explicit source sharing</h2><p className="supporting-copy">Share a source with another team while preserving its ownership and provenance.</p><div className="table-scroll"><table><thead><tr><th>SOURCE</th><th>OWNER</th><th>CONSUMER</th><th>STATUS</th><th>ACTION</th></tr></thead><tbody>{s.shares.map(g => <tr key={g.id}><td>{s.documents.find(d => d.id === g.sourceId)?.name || g.sourceId}</td><td>{g.owner}</td><td>{g.consumer}</td><td><Badge tone={g.status === 'Active' ? 'green' : 'neutral'}>{g.status}</Badge></td><td><Button onClick={() => { mutate(d => { d.shares.find(item => item.id === g.id).status = g.status === 'Active' ? 'Revoked' : 'Active'; log(d, `Updated sharing for ${g.sourceId}`); }); notify('Sharing updated.'); }}>{g.status === 'Active' ? 'Revoke' : 'Restore'}</Button></td></tr>)}</tbody></table></div><form className="sharing-form margin-top" onSubmit={e => { e.preventDefault(); if (!source || !consumer) return; mutate(d => { d.shares.push({ id: uid('share'), sourceId: source, owner: s.session.team, consumer, status: 'Active' }); log(d, `Shared source with ${consumer}`); }); setSource(''); notify('Sharing grant saved.'); }}><Field label="Source owned by current team"><select required value={source} onChange={e => setSource(e.target.value)}><option value="">Choose a source</option>{s.documents.filter(d => d.team === s.session.team).map(d => <option key={d.id} value={d.id}>{d.name}</option>)}</select></Field><Field label="Consuming team"><select value={consumer} onChange={e => setConsumer(e.target.value)}>{s.teams.filter(t => t !== s.session.team).map(t => <option key={t}>{t}</option>)}</select></Field><Button type="submit" variant="primary" disabled={!source || s.shares.some(g => g.sourceId === source && g.consumer === consumer)}>Save sharing grant</Button></form></section>
    : tab === 'Connections' ? <section className="card padded settings-card"><div className="section-heading inset"><h2>Model connection configuration</h2></div><form onSubmit={e => { e.preventDefault(); mutate(d => { d.settings = settings; log(d, 'Saved connection settings'); }); notify('Connection settings saved.'); }}>{[['Model gateway URL', 'gateway', 'https://your-internal-gateway'], ['Generation / reasoning model ID', 'reasoningModel', 'Configured endpoint model identifier'], ['Classification / extraction model ID', 'extractionModel', 'Configured endpoint model identifier'], ['Embedding model ID', 'embeddingModel', 'Pinned embedding profile identifier']].map(([label, key, placeholder]) => <Field label={label} key={key}><input type={key === 'gateway' ? 'url' : 'text'} value={settings[key]} onChange={e => setSettings(v => ({ ...v, [key]: e.target.value }))} placeholder={placeholder}/></Field>)}<Field label="Bounded retry limit"><input type="number" min={0} max={5} value={settings.retryLimit} onChange={e => setSettings(v => ({ ...v, retryLimit: Number(e.target.value) }))}/></Field><div className="modal-actions"><Button type="submit" variant="primary">Save connection settings</Button></div></form></section>
    : <><section className="card padded"><h2>Team workspace</h2><p className="supporting-copy">Back up your workspace records and review activity.</p><div className="row-actions margin-top"><Button icon="external" onClick={() => download('ccil-studio-backup.json', JSON.stringify(s, null, 2), 'application/json')}>Export metadata backup</Button><Button icon="upload" onClick={() => file.current.click()}>Import metadata backup</Button><Button onClick={() => setDialog('reset')}>Reset application records</Button><input ref={file} className="sr-only" type="file" accept=".json" onChange={importBackup}/></div>{error && <p className="form-error" role="alert">{error}</p>}<Note>Metadata backups include source text and conversations. Original file bytes are not included.</Note></section><section className="card margin-top"><div className="section-heading"><h2>Audit trail</h2><span className="count-pill">{s.audit.length}</span></div>{s.audit.slice(0, 40).map(a => <div className="activity-row" key={a.id}><Icon name="clock" size={17}/><div><strong>{a.action.replace(/Team Baseline/g, 'System Baseline').replace(/local demo/gi, 'studio')}</strong><p>{a.actor === 'Demo fixture' ? 'System' : a.actor} · {a.team || 'System'}</p></div><small>{new Date(a.at).toLocaleString('en-IN')}</small></div>)}</section></>}
    {dialog === 'reset' && <Modal title="Reset application records?" close={() => setDialog('')}><p className="modal-intro">This replaces application records with synthetic samples. Export a metadata backup first to retain your changes.</p><Note>Original uploaded files are retained in browser storage.</Note><div className="modal-actions"><Button onClick={() => setDialog('')}>Cancel</Button><Button variant="primary" onClick={() => { reset(); setDialog(''); navigate('login'); }}>Reset application records</Button></div></Modal>}
  </>;
}

title: L2GSSL: Label-Efficient Local-to-Global Self-Supervised Learning for Volumetric Healthcare Data
description:
arXiv:2610.21356v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Healthcare institutions routinely accumulate high-dimensional computed tomography (CT) volumes, but only a fraction can be annotated by experts. We present L2GSSL, a local-to-global self-supervised learning framework that leverages unlabeled volumes by decomposing pretraining into intra-slice and inter-slice representation spaces. A slice encoder learns view-invariant local features, and a global encoder aggregates the resulting tokens to model volumetric context. The stop-gradient isolates the local space from the global objective, while slice-wise execution and a three-phase schedule support training under constrained GPU memory. On LIDC-IDRI lung nodule malignancy classification, L2GSSL reaches $0.9229$ AUROC with only $10\%$ of the labels and $0.9377$ with $25\%$, exceeding the volume-level VICReg by $0.0229$ and $0.0294$, respectively. With all labels, the strongest supervised baseline exceeds L2GSSL by only $0.0044$ AUROC, consistent with self-supervised pretraining providing its greatest value when annotations are limited. Without adaptation to the external LNDb cohort, a model fine-tuned on $25\%$ of LIDC-IDRI obtains $0.8138$ AUROC and $0.7589$ AUPRC, improving over the strongest evaluated self-supervised baseline by $0.1130$ and $0.0954$. Experiments across data sources, thoracic and abdominal anatomy, downstream tasks, and two backbones examine healthcare-data variety, while lesion-slice masking shows that the predictions depend on lesion-bearing content.

title: Understanding Parameters and EventCallbacks in Blazor
description:
Understanding Parameters and EventCallbacks in Blazor

In Blazor, a component can receive information from its parent through parameters. Parameters are declared with the [Parameter] attribute, allowing a parent component to provide values such as text, numbers, dates, or Boolean values.

Blazor also supports EventCallback, which lets a child component notify its parent when a user performs an action. For example, a child can raise a callback after a button is clicked, while the parent decides what should happen next. This keeps reusable components focused on displaying information and reporting user actions.

The following two Razor components are provided separately. The code blocks are kept together without explanatory text between them.

@page "/parameters-demo"

<h3>Parent Component</h3>

<p>Message received: @receivedMessage</p>

<ChildComponent Name="Ayush"
                OnMessageSent="HandleMessage" />

@code {
    private string receivedMessage = "No message received yet.";

    private void HandleMessage(string message)
    {
        receivedMessage = message;
    }
}

// GymCard.razor    
<div class="card gym-card h-100 shadow-sm">
    <div class="card-body d-flex flex-column">
        <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-start gap-2 mb-3">
            <h5 class="fw-bold mb-0">@GymName</h5>
            <span class="badge @(Status == "Active" ? "bg-success" : "bg-secondary")">
                @Status
            </span>
        </div>

        <p class="gym-detail">
            <i class="bi bi-geo-alt me-2"></i>@Address, @CityName
        </p>

        <p class="gym-detail">
            <i class="bi bi-telephone me-2"></i>@Phone
        </p>

        <p class="gym-detail">
            <i class="bi bi-envelope me-2"></i>@Email
        </p>

        <p class="gym-detail">
            <i class="bi bi-clock me-2"></i>
            @OpeningTime.ToString(@"hh\:mm") - @ClosingTime.ToString(@"hh\:mm")
        </p>

        <p class="gym-detail">
            <i class="bi bi-people me-2"></i>
            Class capacity: @TotalClassCapacity
        </p>

        <div class="d-flex flex-wrap gap-2 mb-3">
            <span class="facility-badge">
                Locker: @(LockerFacility ? "Yes" : "No")
            </span>
            <span class="facility-badge">
                Parking: @(ParkingAvailable ? "Yes" : "No")
            </span>
        </div>

        <div class="d-flex gap-2 mt-auto">
            <button type="button"
                    class="btn btn-outline-primary btn-sm flex-fill"
                    @onclick="EditGym">
                <i class="bi bi-pencil me-1"></i>Edit
            </button>

            <button type="button"
                    class="btn btn-outline-danger btn-sm flex-fill"
                    @onclick="DeleteGym">
                <i class="bi bi-trash me-1"></i>Delete
            </button>
        </div>
    </div>
</div>

@code {
    [Parameter] public Guid Id { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public string GymName { get; set; } = string.Empty;
    [Parameter] public string Address { get; set; } = string.Empty;

    [Parameter] public TimeSpan OpeningTime { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public TimeSpan ClosingTime { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public int TotalClassCapacity { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public bool LockerFacility { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public bool ParkingAvailable { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public string Status { get; set; } = "Active";

    [Parameter] public EventCallback<Guid> OnEdit { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public EventCallback<Guid> OnDelete { get; set; }

    private Task EditGym() => OnEdit.InvokeAsync(Id);
    private Task DeleteGym() => OnDelete.InvokeAsync(Id);

@page "/admin/gyms"
@attribute [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]

@using System.Net.Http.Json
@using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations
@using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Forms
@using GymManagement.Client.Components.Admin

@inject HttpClient Http
@inject IJSRuntime JS

<PageTitle>Manage Gyms</PageTitle>

<div class="container-fluid py-4">
    <div class="d-flex flex-wrap justify-content-between align-items-center gap-3 mb-4">
        <div>
            <h2 class="fw-bold mb-1">Manage Gyms</h2>
            <p class="text-secondary mb-0">Add, update, search, and manage gyms.</p>
        </div>

        <button class="btn btn-primary" @onclick="OpenAddForm">
            <i class="bi bi-plus-circle me-1"></i>Add Gym
        </button>
    </div>

    <div class="card shadow-sm border-0 mb-4">
        <div class="card-body">
            <div class="row g-3">
                <div class="col-12 col-md-8">
                    <label class="form-label">Search gyms</label>
                    <input class="form-control"
                           @bind="searchText"
                           @bind:event="oninput"
                           placeholder="Search name, city, phone, or email..." />
                </div>

                <div class="col-12 col-md-4">
                    <label class="form-label">Sort by</label>
                    <select class="form-select" @bind="sortBy">
                        <option value="name">Gym name</option>
                        <option value="city">City</option>
                        <option value="status">Status</option>
                    </select>
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>
    </div>

    @if (isLoading)
    {
        <div class="text-center py-5">
            <div class="spinner-border text-primary"></div>
            <p class="text-secondary mt-2">Loading gyms...</p>
        </div>
    }
    else if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(errorMessage))
    {
        <div class="alert alert-danger">
            @errorMessage
            <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger ms-2"
                    @onclick="LoadGymsAsync">Retry</button>
        </div>
    }
    else if (FilteredGyms.Count == 0)
    {
        <div class="alert alert-info">No matching gyms found.</div>
    }
    else
    {
        <div class="row g-4">
            @foreach (var gym in FilteredGyms)
            {
                <div class="col-12 col-md-6 col-xl-4" @key="gym.Id">
                    <GymCard Id="@gym.Id"
                             GymName="@gym.GymName"
                             Address="@gym.Address"
                             CityName="@gym.CityName"
                             Phone="@gym.Phone"
                             Email="@gym.Email"
                             OpeningTime="@gym.OpeningTime"
                             ClosingTime="@gym.ClosingTime"
                             TotalClassCapacity="@gym.TotalClassCapacity"
                             LockerFacility="@gym.LockerFacility"
                             ParkingAvailable="@gym.ParkingAvailable"
                             Status="@gym.Status"
                             OnEdit="OpenEditForm"
                             OnDelete="DeleteGymAsync" />
                </div>
            }
        </div>
    }
</div>

@if (showForm)
{
    <div class="modal-backdrop-custom">
        <div class="card modal-card shadow-lg">
            <div class="card-header bg-white d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center">
                <h5 class="mb-0">@(isEditMode ? "Edit Gym" : "Add Gym")</h5>
                <button class="btn-close" @onclick="CloseForm"></button>
            </div>

            <div class="card-body">
                <EditForm Model="@formModel" OnValidSubmit="SaveGymAsync">
                    <DataAnnotationsValidator />
                    <ValidationSummary />

                    <div class="row g-3">
                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Gym name</label>
                            <InputText class="form-control" @bind-Value="formModel.GymName" />
                            <ValidationMessage For="@(() => formModel.GymName)" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">City</label>
                            <InputText class="form-control" @bind-Value="formModel.CityName" />
                            <ValidationMessage For="@(() => formModel.CityName)" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-12">
                            <label class="form-label">Address</label>
                            <InputText class="form-control" @bind-Value="formModel.Address" />
                            <ValidationMessage For="@(() => formModel.Address)" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Phone</label>
                            <InputText class="form-control" @bind-Value="formModel.Phone" />
                            <ValidationMessage For="@(() => formModel.Phone)" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Email</label>
                            <InputText class="form-control" @bind-Value="formModel.Email" />
                            <ValidationMessage For="@(() => formModel.Email)" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Opening time</label>
                            <InputText type="time" class="form-control"
                                       @bind-Value="formModel.OpeningTime" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Closing time</label>
                            <InputText type="time" class="form-control"
                                       @bind-Value="formModel.ClosingTime" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Total class capacity</label>
                            <InputNumber class="form-control"
                                         @bind-Value="formModel.TotalClassCapacity" />
                            <ValidationMessage For="@(() => formModel.TotalClassCapacity)" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Status</label>
                            <InputSelect class="form-select" @bind-Value="formModel.Status">
                                <option value="Active">Active</option>
                                <option value="Inactive">Inactive</option>
                            </InputSelect>
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6 form-check ms-2">
                            <InputCheckbox class="form-check-input"
                                           @bind-Value="formModel.LockerFacility" />
                            <label class="form-check-label">Locker facility</label>
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6 form-check ms-2">
                            <InputCheckbox class="form-check-input"
                                           @bind-Value="formModel.ParkingAvailable" />
                            <label class="form-check-label">Parking available</label>
                        </div>
                    </div>

                    <div class="d-flex justify-content-end gap-2 mt-4">
                        <button type="button" class="btn btn-outline-secondary"
                                @onclick="CloseForm" disabled="@isSaving">
                            Cancel
                        </button>
                        <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary" disabled="@isSaving">
                            @(isSaving ? "Saving..." : isEditMode ? "Update Gym" : "Save Gym")
                        </button>
                    </div>
                </EditForm>
            </div>
        </div>
    </div>
}

@code {
    public class GymCardModel
    {
        public Guid Id { get; set; }
        public string GymName { get; set; } = "";
        public string Address { get; set; } = "";
        public string CityName { get; set; } = "";
        public string Phone { get; set; } = "";
        public string Email { get; set; } = "";
        public TimeSpan OpeningTime { get; set; }
        public TimeSpan ClosingTime { get; set; }
        public int TotalClassCapacity { get; set; }
        public bool LockerFacility { get; set; }
        public bool ParkingAvailable { get; set; }
        public string Status { get; set; } = "Active";
    }

    public class GymFormModel
    {
        public Guid Id { get; set; }

        [Required, StringLength(100)]
        public string GymName { get; set; } = "";

        [Required, StringLength(250)]
        public string Address { get; set; } = "";

        [Required, StringLength(100)]
        public string CityName { get; set; } = "";

        [Required]
        public string Phone { get; set; } = "";

        [Required, EmailAddress]
        public string Email { get; set; } = "";

        [Required]
        public string OpeningTime { get; set; } = "06:00";

        [Required]
        public string ClosingTime { get; set; } = "22:00";

        [Range(1, 100000)]
        public int TotalClassCapacity { get; set; } = 20;

        public bool LockerFacility { get; set; }
        public bool ParkingAvailable { get; set; }
        public string Status { get; set; } = "Active";
    }

    public class OperationResponse
    {
        public bool Success { get; set; }
        public string Message { get; set; } = "";
    }

    private List<GymCardModel> gyms = new();
    private GymFormModel formModel = new();
    private bool isLoading;
    private bool isSaving;
    private bool showForm;
    private bool isEditMode;
    private string searchText = "";
    private string sortBy = "name";
    private string errorMessage = "";

    private List<GymCardModel> FilteredGyms =>
        gyms.Where(g =>
                string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(searchText) ||
                g.GymName.Contains(searchText, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                g.CityName.Contains(searchText, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                g.Phone.Contains(searchText, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                g.Email.Contains(searchText, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
            .OrderBy(g => sortBy switch
            {
                "city" => g.CityName,
                "status" => g.Status,
                _ => g.GymName
            })
            .ToList();

    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync() => await LoadGymsAsync();

    private async Task LoadGymsAsync()
    {
        isLoading = true;
        errorMessage = "";

        try
        {
            var result = await Http.GetFromJsonAsync<List<GymCardModel>>("api/GymCenter");
            gyms = result ?? new();
        }
        catch
        {
            errorMessage = "Unable to load gyms. Check the API URL and connection.";
        }
        finally
        {
            isLoading = false;
        }
    }

    private void OpenAddForm()
    {
        formModel = new GymFormModel();
        isEditMode = false;
        showForm = true;
    }

    private void OpenEditForm(Guid id)
    {
        var gym = gyms.FirstOrDefault(g => g.Id == id);
        if (gym is null) return;

        formModel = new GymFormModel
        {
            Id = gym.Id,
            GymName = gym.GymName,
            Address = gym.Address,
            CityName = gym.CityName,
            Phone = gym.Phone,
            Email = gym.Email,
            OpeningTime = gym.OpeningTime.ToString(@"hh\:mm"),
            ClosingTime = gym.ClosingTime.ToString(@"hh\:mm"),
            TotalClassCapacity = gym.TotalClassCapacity,
            LockerFacility = gym.LockerFacility,
            ParkingAvailable = gym.ParkingAvailable,
            Status = gym.Status
        };

        isEditMode = true;
        showForm = true;
    }

    private async Task SaveGymAsync()
    {
        if (!TimeSpan.TryParse(formModel.OpeningTime, out var opening) ||
            !TimeSpan.TryParse(formModel.ClosingTime, out var closing) ||
            closing <= opening)
        {
            await ShowMessageAsync("Invalid hours",
                "Closing time must be later than opening time.", false);
            return;
        }

        isSaving = true;

        try
        {
            var payload = new
            {
                formModel.Id,
                formModel.GymName,
                formModel.Address,
                formModel.CityName,
                formModel.Phone,
                formModel.Email,
                OpeningTime = opening,
                ClosingTime = closing,
                formModel.TotalClassCapacity,
                formModel.LockerFacility,
                formModel.ParkingAvailable,
                formModel.Status
            };

            HttpResponseMessage response = isEditMode
                ? await Http.PutAsJsonAsync($"api/GymCenter/{formModel.Id}", payload)
                : await Http.PostAsJsonAsync("api/GymCenter", payload);

            var result = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<OperationResponse>();

            if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode || result?.Success != true)
            {
                await ShowMessageAsync("Unable to save gym",
                    result?.Message ?? "The API could not save the gym.", false);
                return;
            }

            showForm = false;
            await LoadGymsAsync();
            await ShowMessageAsync("Success", result.Message, true);
        }
        catch
        {
            await ShowMessageAsync("Error", "An error occurred while saving the gym.", false);
        }
        finally
        {
            isSaving = false;
        }
    }

    private async Task DeleteGymAsync(Guid id)
    {
        var confirmed = await JS.InvokeAsync<bool>(
            "gymUi.confirmDelete", "Delete gym?", "The gym will be soft-deleted if allowed.");

        if (!confirmed) return;

        try
        {
            var response = await Http.DeleteAsync($"api/GymCenter/{id}");
            var result = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<OperationResponse>();

            if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode || result?.Success != true)
            {
                await ShowMessageAsync("Unable to delete",
                    result?.Message ?? "The gym could not be deleted.", false);
                return;
            }

            await LoadGymsAsync();
            await ShowMessageAsync("Success", result.Message, true);
        }
        catch
        {
            await ShowMessageAsync("Error", "An error occurred while deleting the gym.", false);
        }
    }

    private void CloseForm()
    {
        if (!isSaving) showForm = false;
    }

    private Task ShowMessageAsync(string title, string message, bool success) =>
        JS.InvokeVoidAsync("gymUi.showMessage", title, message, success).AsTask();
}

@page "/login"

                    <button class="btn border" type="button" @onclick="() => IsPasswordVisible = !IsPasswordVisible">
                        <i class="bi @(IsPasswordVisible ? "bi-eye-slash" : "bi-eye")">  </i>
                    </button>
                </div>
                <ValidationMessage For="@(() => user.Password)" />
            </div>

    public User user = new User();

        if (response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
        {
            Console.WriteLine(response.Content.ToString());
            var token = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<TokenResponse>();
            await localStorage.SetItemAsync("accessToken", token.AccessToken);
            await localStorage.SetItemAsync("refreshToken", token.RefreshToken);

        public string Password { get; set; } = "";
    }
}

title: Firefox Accessibility Features: Screen Readers, Zoom, Caret Browsing, and Reading Mode
description:
Firefox includes more accessibility features than most users realize. Whether you have permanent accessibility needs, temporary disabilities, or just want to reduce eye strain and improve usability, Firefox's built-in tools are worth knowing.

Screen Reader Support

Firefox has strong support for screen readers on all platforms:

Windows: NVDA (free, open source) and JAWS both work well with Firefox. Mozilla actively tests Firefox with NVDA and funds accessibility work.

macOS: VoiceOver works with Firefox. Safari historically had better VoiceOver integration, but Firefox has improved significantly.

Linux: Orca screen reader (GNOME's screen reader) integrates with Firefox via AT-SPI2, the Linux accessibility stack.

To enable a screen reader, you typically don't configure Firefox directly — you enable the screen reader in your OS, and Firefox responds to it via accessibility APIs.

Developer tip: Use Firefox's Accessibility Panel (DevTools → Accessibility tab) to inspect the accessibility tree of any page. This shows how screen readers see the page.

Keyboard Navigation

Firefox is fully keyboard-navigable without a screen reader:

Tab: Move focus through interactive elements (links, buttons, forms)
Shift+Tab: Move backwards
Enter/Space: Activate focused element
Arrow keys: Navigate within components (menus, selects, radio groups)

Tab focus on all elements (including non-interactive elements like divs):
In Settings → General, there's a "Use cursor keys to navigate within pages" option, or use:

  • F7: Toggle Caret Browsing mode — puts a text cursor on the page so you can navigate with arrow keys like a text editor

This is particularly useful for users with motor impairments who find mouse targeting difficult.

Caret Browsing

Caret Browsing deserves more attention. Press F7 to toggle it.

In Caret Browsing mode:

  • A text cursor appears on the page
  • You navigate with arrow keys, Page Up/Down, Home/End
  • Shift + arrow keys selects text
  • Works like a document editor

This makes it much easier to read and navigate long pages without a mouse. It's also useful for precise text selection on complex pages.

Zoom Controls

Firefox has two zoom systems:

Page Zoom (Ctrl+/Ctrl-): Scales everything on the page — text, images, layout.

  • Default zoom: Settings → General → Zoom
  • Remember zoom per site: enabled by default
  • Reset: Ctrl+0

Text-only zoom: View menu → Zoom → Zoom Text Only

  • Only enlarges text, not images or layout
  • Useful when the layout zoom breaks page structure

Minimum font size: Settings → General → Fonts → Advanced → Minimum font size

  • Forces all text to be at least N pixels, even if the page specifies smaller
  • Good for pages that use tiny text that resists zoom

Color and Contrast

Override page colors: Settings → General → Colors

  • Firefox can force its own text and background colors on all pages
  • Useful for high-contrast mode
  • Options: Use system colors, always use Firefox colors

High contrast mode: If Windows/macOS high contrast mode is enabled, Firefox respects it by default. Pages can be forced into high contrast via the color override settings above.

Forced colors: Firefox 107+ respects CSS forced-colors media query, allowing websites to detect high-contrast mode and adapt their styles.

Reduced Motion

Firefox respects prefers-reduced-motion CSS media query automatically if you have reduced motion enabled in your OS:

  • Windows: Settings → Ease of Access → Display → Show animations
  • macOS: System Preferences → Accessibility → Display → Reduce Motion
  • Linux (GNOME): Accessibility settings or gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface enable-animations false

When reduced motion is set, animations on websites that respect it will be minimized or eliminated. This helps users with vestibular disorders, migraines, or attention disorders.

You can also force this in about:config:

ui.prefersReducedMotion = 1

Reading Mode

Firefox's Reading Mode strips away navigation, ads, and sidebars from articles, showing just the content.

To activate: Click the book icon in the address bar (appears on article-type pages), or press F9.

In reading mode:

  • Adjust font size (Aa button in toolbar)
  • Choose serif or sans-serif font
  • Select background color: white, sepia, dark
  • Adjust line spacing and column width
  • Listen to the article with text-to-speech (TTS)

Text-to-speech in Reading Mode:
The headphone icon in Reading Mode controls starts reading aloud. This uses the OS TTS engine, so voice quality depends on your system. Speed and voice can be adjusted.

Firefox Accessibility DevTools Panel

For developers and QA testers, the Accessibility panel is invaluable:

Open DevTools (F12) → Accessibility tab

Features:

  • Accessibility tree: Visual tree showing how screen readers see the page
  • Properties: Accessibility properties of selected element (role, name, description, states)
  • Check for accessibility issues: Automated scan for common issues (missing labels, poor contrast)
  • Simulate: Simulate various visual impairments (protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia, achromatopsia, contrast loss, blurred vision)

The color simulation feature is particularly useful for designers — switch to "Protanopia" view to see how your page looks to users with red-green color blindness.

Mouse and Pointer Settings

For motor accessibility:

Cursor size: Controlled by OS settings, but Firefox respects system cursor.

Click-lock: Enable in Windows Ease of Access — allows dragging without holding the mouse button.

Mouse dwell click: Third-party tools like Gnome-Mousetrap allow clicking by hovering — Firefox works fine with these.

Extensions for Accessibility

Voice Control: Dragon NaturallySpeaking / Voice Control on macOS works with Firefox.

Accessibility extensions:

  • Zoom Page WE: Finer-grained zoom control, per-element zoom
  • Dark Reader: High-contrast dark mode for all sites (also helps with migraines/photosensitivity)
  • Open Dyslexic: OpenDyslexic font injection for users with dyslexia
  • Bionic Reading: Bolded word beginnings for faster, easier reading

Summary

Feature How to access
Caret Browsing F7
Page Zoom Ctrl+/Ctrl-
Text Zoom View → Zoom → Text Only
Reading Mode F9 or address bar icon
TTS in Reading Mode Headphone icon in Reading Mode toolbar
Force colors Settings → General → Colors
Min font size Settings → General → Fonts → Advanced
Accessibility DevTools F12 → Accessibility tab
Reduced motion OS setting or ui.prefersReducedMotion in about:config

Firefox doesn't advertise these features as loudly as some competitors, but the underlying accessibility support is strong and kept up-to-date.

title: Learning When to Withdraw: Curriculum Coverage and Rule-Specific Failures in Fine-Tuned Language Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21045v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using language agents must revise prepared actions when evidence changes or authority is revoked. Selective withdrawal means suspending affected actions, preserving supported work, and resuming only after sufficient repair. We study supervised fine-tuning in NAQD-Env, a synthetic environment with explicit dependencies and a deterministic reference policy. Four LoRA checkpoints of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct compare an original curriculum with an enriched one, the latter under three system-prompt framings with identical views and targets. Three instruction-tuned baselines and all four checkpoints are evaluated under three inference prompts on fresh validation cases, held-out dependency families, and held-out structural combinations. Under the naqd prompt, SFT checkpoints reach decision agreement of 0.77-0.92 and withdrawal recall of 0.46-0.86, versus 0.45-0.63 and at most 0.06 for the baselines. Rule-level diagnostics qualify these gains. The original-curriculum checkpoint wrongly withdraws 26 of 34 actions with surviving alternative support; enriched checkpoints withdraw 0-1. Conversely, all SFT checkpoints narrow prohibited combinations less often than the 7B and 8B baselines, a case absent from both curricula. Delegation results show more withdrawal but poorer preservation of independently authorized actions, and all four checkpoints omit valid event reports. Framing contrasts vary across metrics and splits and do not establish a reproducible advantage or equivalence. One training run per arm, jointly changed curriculum properties, prior evaluation exposure, and baseline-SFT quantization differences limit causal attribution. The contribution is a method for detecting rule-specific regressions that aggregate accuracy can conceal, not evidence that fine-tuning alone ensures agent safety.

title: How I Passed AWS Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03) in 4 Weeks
description:
I'm a DevOps/Platform Engineer from Sri Lanka, and I passed the AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate exam after 4 weeks of preparation. In this post I'll share the exact plan I followed, so you can skip the confusion I had at the start.

Exam at a glance

Item Details
Exam code SAA-C03
Questions 65 (multiple choice / multiple response)
Time 130 minutes
Passing score 720 / 1000
Cost 150 USD
Validity 3 years

The 4 domains:

  1. Design Secure Architectures – 30%
  2. Design Resilient Architectures – 26%
  3. Design High-Performing Architectures – 24%
  4. Design Cost-Optimized Architectures – 20%

Notice that security is the biggest chunk. Don't skip IAM.

Step 1: Read the official exam guide (30 minutes)

Download the exam guide from the AWS Certification page. Highlight the in-scope services. This is your syllabus; anything outside it, don't stress about.

Step 2: Create a free-tier account and set a budget alert FIRST

Before touching any service, protect yourself from surprise bills:

  1. Go to Billing → Budgets → Create budget
  2. Choose Zero spend budget
  3. Add your email

Also enable MFA on the root user and create an IAM user for daily work.

Step 3: Learn the core services (2–3 weeks)

Focus your time here, in this order:

  • IAM – users, roles, policies, least privilege
  • VPC – subnets, route tables, IGW, NAT Gateway, security groups vs NACLs
  • EC2 – instance types, pricing models (On-Demand, Reserved, Spot, Savings Plans)
  • ELB + Auto Scaling – ALB vs NLB, scaling policies
  • S3 – storage classes, lifecycle rules, versioning, encryption
  • RDS & Aurora – Multi-AZ vs Read Replicas (this comes up a LOT)
  • DynamoDB – when to pick NoSQL
  • Route 53 – routing policies
  • CloudFront – caching and edge
  • SQS, SNS, EventBridge – decoupling
  • Lambda & API Gateway – serverless basics
  • CloudWatch, CloudTrail – monitoring vs auditing

Step 4: Get hands-on (don't skip this!)

Reading alone won't stick. Build these mini labs:

  1. Launch a web server in a custom VPC

    • Create a VPC with 2 public and 2 private subnets
    • Launch EC2 in a public subnet, install nginx
    • Put an ALB in front with an Auto Scaling group

  2. Host a static website on S3 + CloudFront

  3. Create an RDS database in a private subnet and connect from EC2

  4. Build a serverless API: API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB

Delete everything after each lab. Watch out for NAT Gateways and RDS; they cost money even when idle.

Step 5: Learn the "keywords" pattern

SAA questions are scenario-based. The keyword usually tells you the answer:

If the question says... Think...
"Most cost-effective" S3 lifecycle, Spot, right-sizing
"Highly available" Multi-AZ
"Read-heavy workload" Read Replicas, ElastiCache
"Decouple components" SQS
"Least operational overhead" Managed / serverless services
"Disaster recovery across regions" Cross-region replication, Aurora Global
"Static content, global users" CloudFront
"Temporary credentials" IAM Roles, STS

Step 6: Practice exams (1–2 weeks)

  • Do at least 4–6 full-length practice exams
  • Aim for 80%+ consistently before booking
  • Review EVERY wrong answer, and the right ones you guessed
  • Keep a "mistakes notebook" sorted by domain

Step 7: Exam day tips

  • Book via Pearson VUE (online or test center)
  • If taking it online, clear your desk completely and check your webcam the day before
  • Use flag for review; don't get stuck on one question
  • Eliminate obviously wrong answers first; usually 2 options are clearly out
  • There's no penalty for wrong answers, so never leave a question blank

My biggest lessons

1.Networking was my weakest area until I built a VPC by hand

  1. Hands-on practice beats watching videos at 2x speed
  2. Understand why an answer is right, not just memorizing it

Final thoughts

SAA isn't about memorizing every service; it's about thinking like an architect: secure, resilient, fast and cost-effective. Follow these steps, stay consistent, and you'll get there.

If you're preparing right now, drop a comment with your exam date. Happy to answer questions! 🚀

I'm Ajith, a DevOps/Platform Engineer and visiting lecturer. I share DevOps and cloud content

Connect with me on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/ajithkumara-madialagan/

title: From One Prompt to Every Screen: Claude Code's Editable Design Canvas
description:
Every new product or feature starts the same way. Before anyone can discuss the idea, someone has to draw the obvious: login, home, a list, a detail page, a profile. Then the states nobody draws in the first version: empty, loading, error, success.

It's necessary work, but it's not where design adds the most value. The valuable part comes after: flow, hierarchy, interactions and product decisions.

A recent Claude Code feature goes straight at that bottleneck. You can ask, in plain language, for every screen of your app, and you get back a design canvas where each screen is a live, editable artboard. Not a screenshot. Not a static mockup.

This post covers what it is, what happens under the hood, how to ask for it, and the tips that make the difference between a generic result and a useful first draft.

What it is

The result is an infinite canvas with live artboards. Each screen becomes a frame on the canvas, at real device size, organized by flow, with titles and notes.

It isn't limited to mobile apps. The same canvas works for web pages, landing pages, and even social media posts.

The canvas is published as a private page on claude.ai. You see the screens appear as they're drawn, and you decide whether and when to share it with your team.

How to ask

There's no special command or syntax. You just ask. It works anywhere Claude Code runs: the terminal, the desktop app or the web.

A good first request looks like this:

Create a design canvas with every screen of the app in this repo:
onboarding, login, home, calendar, detail and profile.
Mobile 390×844. Include empty, loading and error states.
Use our design system.

The most useful detail: run it inside your repository. Claude Code reads the code to find the screens that actually exist (routes, pages, components), so the canvas reflects your real app instead of a generic template.

What happens after you hit Enter

Roughly four steps:

  1. It understands the request. It reads the repo, its routes and components, to learn which screens exist and how they connect.
  2. It picks the look. If your account or organization has a default design system, it uses it. If not, it defines a coherent visual identity and tells you which decisions it made.
  3. It draws screen by screen. Each artboard is an independent HTML component at real device size, which is why everything stays editable.
  4. It hands you the link. A private canvas on claude.ai, where you watch the screens appear and decide what to do next.

The part that won me over: everything is editable

This is what separates it from "AI generated a picture of an app".

Because every screen is a live component, you can:

  • Tweak it directly. Change copy, colors and spacing in a properties panel, and see the screen update right away.
  • Comment on a screen. Leave a comment like "make the card bigger and swap the icon", and Claude makes the change on that screen.
  • Keep iterating in conversation. Ask for a new variation, a new state or a new flow without starting over.
  • Take it further. Link screens into a clickable prototype, or share the canvas with your team for feedback.

Five tips for a great canvas on the first try

The quality of the canvas depends a lot on the quality of the request. These are the things that matter most.

1. Name the screens and flows

"Design my app" gets you something generic. Name each screen and group them into flows: onboarding (welcome, sign up, permissions), auth (login, password reset), main (home, list, detail, profile, settings).

2. Set the format

Say what you're designing for: mobile at 390×844, web at 1440px, a landing page, a social post. Otherwise you'll get a reasonable guess, which may not be your guess.

3. Ask for the states

Empty, loading, error and success. This is where most of the time savings are, because these are the screens nobody wants to draw by hand, and the ones most often forgotten until development.

4. Point to the brand

Your design system, colors, fonts, or simply the repository. Without a reference, it will create a coherent identity, but it won't be yours.

5. Iterate in small steps

"On the login screen, change the CTA to 'Continue with email'" works much better than asking it to redo everything. Small, specific requests keep what's already good and change only what you asked for.

A full prompt you can copy

Putting the tips together, this is a prompt I'd use as a starting point:

Create a design canvas with every screen of the app in this repo.

Flows:
- Onboarding: welcome, sign up, permissions
- Auth: login, password reset
- Main: home, list, detail, profile, settings

Mobile 390×844, one artboard per screen, grouped by flow with a title for each.
For each main screen, also include the empty, loading, error and success states.

Use our design system. If there isn't one, propose a simple identity
and tell me which decisions you made.

Use real copy from the app's domain, no lorem ipsum.

The last line matters more than it looks. Real copy makes layout problems visible early: long names, button labels that don't fit, empty states that need an explanation.

What it doesn't do

It's worth being clear about the limits, so expectations stay realistic:

  • It doesn't replace designers. It gives you a starting point. Decisions about hierarchy, interaction, accessibility and the product itself are still human work, and they're the ones that matter most.
  • Vague requests give generic results. If you don't name screens, formats and states, you get a plausible but bland app.
  • It reflects what it can read. If the repo is half-built or the screens are only in someone's head, describe them in the prompt.
  • Review it like any first draft. Check contrast, touch target sizes and edge cases before treating anything as final.

Who it's for

  • Designers skip the rough draft and start at refinement: hierarchy, interactions and product calls.
  • Engineers see the screen before coding, and can discuss layout and states with something concrete instead of a description in a ticket.
  • Product managers validate a flow early, bringing real screens into the conversation before the sprint starts.

The way I see it: designers keep making the calls. Claude delivers the starting point.

Wrapping up

The time between "we have an idea" and "we have screens to discuss" used to be measured in days. With an editable canvas generated from your own repository, it can be minutes, and what you get is something you can keep working on, not a picture you have to redraw.

If you try it, start small: one flow, one format, all the states. Then iterate.

Have you tried it yet? I'm curious how designers feel about starting from a generated first draft instead of a blank canvas.

title: MARS - A foundational map auto-regressor
description:
arXiv:2610.20843v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Map generation tasks feature extensive non-structural vectorized data (e.g., points, polylines, and polygons) and thus pose significant challenges to common pixel-wise generative models. Conventional approaches use multiple stages, first segmenting these features at the pixel level and then performing vectorized post-processing, with errors and complexity compounding at each stage. Motivated by the recent success of auto-regressive language modeling, we propose the first map foundation model, named Map Auto-Regressor (MARS), that is capable of generating both multi-polyline road networks and polygon buildings in a unified manner. For training MARS, we collected to our knowledge the largest multi-class map extraction dataset totaling 3.4M examples, which we call MAP-3M. Across four road and building datasets, MARS outperforms or matches the performance of multistage baselines. Additionally, we develop a "Chat with MARS" capability that enables interactive human-in-the-loop map generation and correction, supported by the auto-regressive nature of our end-to-end approach. We release our MAP-3M dataset and project demo page at (1) https://huggingface.co/datasets/bag-lab/MAP-3M and (2) https://huggingface.co/spaces/bag-lab/MARS, respectively.

title: How AI Coding Tools Leak Your API Keys, And What I Built to Stop It
description:
Last week I watched Claude Code read my .env file, extract my OpenAI API key, and paste it into a curl command in a shell script it was writing for me. The key worked. The script worked. And my sk-proj- key was now sitting in a file on disk, in Claude's session history, and in Anthropic's API logs.

I didn't ask Claude to use the key. It just... did what a helpful agent does. It saw the environment, understood the task, and wired things up. That's the whole point of AI coding tools. It's also the problem.

The threat is not hypothetical

GitGuardian's State of Secrets Sprawl 2026
reports 28.65 million new hardcoded secrets in public GitHub commits in 2025, a
34% year-over-year increase. AI-service secrets separately increased 81% year
over year; that category-specific figure does not apply to all secrets.

Here is one common high-risk pattern when an AI coding tool has dotenv access:

  1. You have a .env file with OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-abc123...
  2. The AI agent reads that file to understand your project
  3. Your real API key is now inside the LLM's context window

Once a secret enters the context window, several downstream systems can become exposure paths:

  • Session logs. Most AI tools persist conversation history. Your key is sitting in a JSON file in ~/.claude/ or ~/.cursor/, probably unencrypted.
  • Prompt injection. A malicious README, dependency, or code comment can instruct the LLM to exfiltrate environment variables. This isn't theoretical — Check Point Research demonstrated it with CVEs against both Cursor and Claude Code: crafted prompts that trick the agent into sending secrets to attacker-controlled servers.
  • Malicious MCP servers. The Model Context Protocol lets AI tools call external services. A compromised MCP server can request environment context and receive your real keys.
  • Accidental commits. The AI writes code that hardcodes a key, or generates a test fixture with real credentials. You review it quickly, approve, and push.

The standard advice — "just don't put secrets in .env" — ignores reality. Developers need secrets in their environment to build software. The question isn't whether AI will read your .env. It's what it finds when it does.

Phantom tokens: keep real credentials out of the AI boundary

I built Phantom to reduce that exposure at the architecture
level. The core idea: replace heuristically detected, Phantom-managed dotenv
secrets with phantom tokens — cryptographically random placeholders that
are not accepted as credentials by the upstream provider.

Here's what your .env looks like before and after running phantom init:

# Before
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-abc123def456ghi789...
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_51HG7a9s8d7f6g5h4j3k2l1...
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-api03-example...
NODE_ENV=development
PORT=3000

# After
OPENAI_API_KEY=phm_a7f3b9e2d1c4f8a6b3e7d2c5f9a1b4e8...
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=phm_c3d7f2a9e1b5d8c4a7f3b6e2d9c1a5f8...
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=phm_e8b2d5a9c3f7e1b4d8a2c6f3e7b1d5a9...
NODE_ENV=development
PORT=3000

Those phm_ tokens use 256 bits of CSPRNG output. They are not provider
credentials and cannot be redeemed directly against OpenAI, Anthropic, or
Stripe. They are still mappings worth protecting. Client headers and bodies
never resolve them, but a stolen live proxy bearer can authorize exact routes
that inject their own credentials. Rotate an exposed project token. Non-secret config values such as NODE_ENV and PORT
are normally left untouched by the detection heuristics.

Your real secrets are stored through the platform credential backend (macOS
Keychain, the Linux kernel keyring, or Windows Credential Manager), with an
encrypted-file fallback when its passphrase can be persisted and verified.
Linux kernel-keyring entries do not survive a reboot.

The reverse proxy: route-owned authentication

When you run phantom exec -- claude, Phantom starts a local HTTP reverse proxy on 127.0.0.1 and rewrites the base URLs in your environment:

OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/openai
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/anthropic
STRIPE_API_BASE=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/stripe

Here's the full request lifecycle:

Your code / AI agent
     |
     |  POST http://127.0.0.1:PORT/openai/v1/chat/completions
     |  Client request (no credential substitution)
     v
Phantom Proxy (localhost)
     |
     |  1. Authenticate session and match exact route
     |  2. Inject route-owned key into fixed auth header
     |  3. Forward client headers/body without token resolution
     |  4. Forward over TLS to api.openai.com
     |  5. Drop request buffers; the session lookup copy remains until proxy exit
     v
OpenAI API (real endpoint, HTTPS)
     |
     |  Response returns through content-aware scrubbing
     v
Your code / AI agent

This is not a MITM proxy. It does not inject CA certificates or break TLS. Your code sends plaintext HTTP to localhost; the proxy initiates a fresh TLS connection to the upstream API. This is a standard reverse proxy pattern — the same architecture as nginx sitting in front of an application server.

Key design decisions:

  • Reviewed routes. Agentic proxy sessions accept Phantom's exact built-in service definitions and reject repository-authored proxy destinations. This constrains injection, but endpoint integrity, DNS/TLS, the local account, and the configured provider remain in the threat model.
  • Localhost only. The proxy binds to 127.0.0.1, never 0.0.0.0. It is not reachable from the network.
  • Ephemeral ports. Each session gets a random high port, reducing the window for local process abuse.
  • Session-scoped proxy authentication. phantom exec gives the child process fresh phm_ placeholders and a fresh proxy bearer. Client placeholders never resolve; the bearer becomes invalid when that proxy exits. Project tokens stored in dotenv are different values and persist until phantom rotate.

Supported SDKs that honor Phantom's implemented base-URL overrides can work
without source changes. This is not a claim for every HTTP client or protocol.
Protected database connection strings currently make phantom exec fail
closed; Phantom does not inject them into the child environment.

Real usage: three commands 

# 1. After installing the reviewed v0.7.9 GitHub release, initialize the project
$ phantom init
-> Found .env with 5 entries
-> Detected 3 secret(s): OPENAI_API_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
-> Skipped 2 non-secret(s): NODE_ENV, PORT
-> Stored real values in OS keychain
-> Rewrote .env with phantom tokens
ok Project initialized. Run `phantom exec -- <cmd>` to start coding.

# 2. Work with AI — supported SDK routes use the proxy
$ phantom exec -- claude
-> Proxy listening on an ephemeral 127.0.0.1 port
-> Proxying: OPENAI_API_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
-> Starting: claude

# The app loads phm_ tokens; Claude uses value-blind MCP metadata.
# The SDK hits localhost; the matched route injects its fixed auth header and forwards to the real API.
# Supported SDK calls use the reviewed local proxy route; MCP stays value-blind.

# 3. Deploy — push real secrets to your platform
$ phantom sync --platform vercel
-> Synced 3 secrets to Vercel (real values, not phantom tokens)

MCP server for AI-native secret management

Phantom also ships an MCP server so Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and Codex can manage secrets natively — listing, adding, rotating — without ever seeing a real value:

$ phantom setup --client claude

The release-schema-verified catalog currently contains 54 unique tools covering
vault status, init, safe interactive secret entry, checks, diagnostics, cloud
sync, audit, validation, rotation, expiry, compliance, and team vaults. The
deprecated plaintext add tool refuses secret values through MCP, so real
credentials stay out of the agent context. Runtime tools/list is canonical.

Architecture: modular Rust workspace 

phantom-core     Config, .env parsing, token generation (256-bit CSPRNG, phm_ prefix)
phantom-vault    VaultBackend trait: OS keychain + encrypted file fallback
phantom-proxy    HTTP reverse proxy (hyper), token replacement, TLS forwarding (reqwest)
phantom-cli      clap-based CLI with agent readiness, proxy, sync, audit, teams
phantom-mcp      MCP server (rmcp SDK), stdio transport, schema-verified catalog
workspace/kernel Value-blind setup plus fail-closed governed-execution foundations

The vault uses ChaCha20-Poly1305 for encryption with Argon2id key derivation
(for the encrypted file fallback). Major vault retrieval, serialization, and
decrypted-file buffers use targeted zeroization, while some proxy lookup copies
remain ordinary strings. Zeroization is defense in depth, not a complete
memory-erasure guarantee. CI runs the Rust test suite and clippy before release.

The cloud client can encrypt a vault payload before upload so the vault API
stores ciphertext rather than decrypted secret values. That property does not
remove the client, account, endpoint, or deployed-service trust boundaries.

Why not existing tools?

I looked at the landscape before building this.

1Password / HashiCorp Vault — Enterprise secret-management systems with
different runtime models. Environment-injection workflows such as op run can
still expose a value to an agent that can inspect that process environment;
their current product capabilities should be evaluated independently.

Doppler / Infisical — Centralized secret-management systems that can inject
real values at runtime. If an agent can inspect the target environment, that
specific integration pattern may cross the agent context boundary.

dotenvx — Encrypts .env files at rest, which is useful. But at runtime, secrets are decrypted into real environment variables. The AI sees them.

The design gap Phantom targets is narrower: agent workflows where readable
dotenv values or real process-environment credentials can enter model context,
transcripts, generated files, or tool calls.

Get started 

phantom init

Install the checksum-verified v0.7.9 GitHub release binaries using the
current platform instructions before running
this command. Three commands establish the local boundary for supported API routes. Keep
dotenv reads denied, review the generated config, and use the documented
recovery and CI controls for the rest of the system.

Phantom's local CLI and proxy are MIT-licensed Rust software and do not require
the hosted service for local protection. Hosted packaging and future pricing
are separate from the open-source license.

  • Website: phm.dev
  • GitHub: github.com/ashlrai/phantom-secrets
  • Docs: phm.dev/docs/getting-started

If you've ever pasted an API key into an AI coding tool and felt a twinge of guilt — you were right to. But you don't have to stop using AI to fix it.

title: Sample Runs, Not Spans: Shrink Agent Traces Without Losing Failures
description:
At 09:12 the on-call page fired. A checkout agent returned HTTP 500 for forty minutes.

We opened the trace store and found two weeks of spans. The failing run was not in it.

Our sampler had dropped the interesting spans. It kept the boring ones. That is the classic sampling bug, and it is a retention problem, not a tracing problem.

Why span-level sampling fails

Most teams sample at the span level. A coin flip decides each span independently.

That breaks causality. A tool call survives; its parent LLM call does not. You cannot replay a run with holes in it.

Worse, failures are rare and correlated. A 5% span sample catches roughly 5% of a broken run, and the interesting leaf spans are exactly the ones your status filter already flags.

So you pay 5% of the storage and lose 95% of the debuggability. The incident you care about is the one you stored least.

Change the unit of sampling

Sample runs, not spans. A run is either fully recorded or fully summarized. No partial runs, no orphan spans.

Three storage modes are enough:

  1. Full — every span, every payload, exact bytes, sequence numbers intact.
  2. Summary — one lossy record per span: id, kind, status, duration, token counts, byte counts. No payloads.
  3. Anomaly-pinned — the same as full, but exempt from sampling forever, because the run already proved it can break.

Then add one rule that overrides chance. Any run that touches a known anomaly keeps full detail, regardless of the sample rate.

A decision table you can argue about

Span or run class Decision Retention Why
run has any error span full 30 days root-cause evidence
any span has status = retry full 30 days retry storms hide real bugs
span has a truncation flag full 14 days the payload was already cut
span exceeds the latency p99 budget full 14 days regression evidence
clean run, hash-selected full 7 days baseline for diffing
clean run, not selected summary 90 days trend lines and cost accounting
health-check span neither 0 pure noise

Two things stand out. Clean runs are kept longest in summary form, because they are cheap and they answer trend questions. Broken runs are kept shortest in full form, because the fix arrives fast.

The sampler, in about forty lines

This is a proposal, not a benchmarked result in your environment. Run it against archived traces before you put it in front of production traffic.

# sampler.py — proposal; measure it on your own archive first
import hashlib
import os

SALT = os.environ.get("TRACE_SAMPLE_SALT", "change-me")
ANOMALY_STATUSES = {"error", "retry", "truncated", "budget_exceeded"}

def is_anomalous_span(span: dict) -> bool:
    if span.get("status") in ANOMALY_STATUSES:
        return True
    return bool(span.get("truncated"))

def run_is_pinned(run: dict) -> bool:
    return run.get("anomaly_count", 0) > 0

def selected_for_full(run_id: str, success_sample_rate: float = 0.05) -> bool:
    """Deterministic, stable per run_id. Sample whole runs, never spans."""
    digest = hashlib.sha256((SALT + run_id).encode()).hexdigest()
    bucket = int(digest[:8], 16) % 10_000
    return (bucket / 10_000.0) < success_sample_rate

def store_mode(run: dict) -> str:
    if run_is_pinned(run):
        return "full"
    if selected_for_full(run["run_id"]):
        return "full"
    return "summary"

Two design choices matter here.

  • Hashing on run_id, not a random draw. The same run gets the same verdict in every process, on every retry, and after a restart. Random draws make your retention policy non-reproducible.
  • A SALT from the environment. Without it, anyone can compute which runs you kept. With it, selection is stable but not guessable.

The one test that matters

A single invariant protects the whole policy: an anomalous run is never summarized away.

# test_retention.py — proposal; wire into CI
def test_anomalous_runs_are_never_summarized():
    for status in ("error", "retry", "truncated", "budget_exceeded"):
        run = {"run_id": "r-1", "anomaly_count": 1, "status": status}
        assert store_mode(run) == "full"

def test_selection_is_stable_across_calls():
    a = [selected_for_full("r-42") for _ in range(100)]
    assert len(set(a)) == 1

def test_selection_is_not_all_or_nothing():
    kept = sum(selected_for_full(f"r-{i}") for i in range(10_000))
    assert 300 < kept < 700  # ~5% with sane variance

The third test is the subtle one. A salt or modulus bug can silently push your sample rate to 0% or 100%, and nobody notices until an incident review.

Where the pipeline runs

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The collector and summarizer are small, periodic, and CPU-bound. That is a good fit for a free server option, because you are not paying for idle capacity between jobs.

MonkeyCode is an open-source project with free model access, and the operator lists a 10M-token free allowance alongside the free server option. Treat both as claims to verify against the current terms before you depend on them.

The model access has a genuine role here. Full payloads are expensive to keep; one-line run digests are not. So generate a digest for every run, not just the sampled ones, and store it permanently next to the summary records. Something like:

Input: 40 summary records for run r-8891
Output: one sentence — what the run attempted, what changed, what failed

That digest is what an on-call engineer reads first at 09:12. It costs a few hundred tokens per run, which is why a free allowance changes what you can afford to keep.

Two cautions. Never put payload contents you cannot share into a third-party model call, and never treat a free tier as a system of record. Check the current limits and retention terms yourself.

Measure before you trust the policy

Do not adopt this on vibes. Compute the ratio on one day of archived traces.

# total bytes and runs
wc -c < traces.jsonl
wc -l < traces.jsonl

# bytes owned by anomalous runs (approximation: runs with an error line)
jq -c 'select(.status == "error") | .run_id' traces.jsonl \
  | sort -u > pinned.txt
rg -F -f pinned.txt traces.jsonl | wc -c

Then report two numbers: pinned_runs / total_runs and kept_bytes / total_bytes.

Acceptance criteria I would use, and you should replace with your own:

  • pinned_runs / total_runs under 2% in steady state.
  • kept_bytes / total_bytes under 15% after summarization.
  • Zero runs missing a stored digest.

If pinned_runs is much higher than your error rate, your anomaly rules are too broad. Fix the rules before you lower the storage bill.

Limitations

  • Summaries cannot answer unanticipated questions. If you did not record a field, you cannot query it later. Add fields to the summary schema only when you can justify the bytes.
  • Sampling breaks exact replay for unselected runs. Keep the sample rate high enough that a baseline exists for diffing.
  • Hash sampling can correlate with your id scheme. If run_id starts with a tenant prefix, some tenants get sampled more than others. Salt alone does not fix that; hash the full id or re-bucket.
  • Latency budgets need a warm baseline. On a sleeping free server, the first request after idle inflates duration. Exclude cold-start spans or your p99 rule pins everything.
  • Not for audit or legal hold. A sampling policy is an engineering choice, not a compliance record.

Who should skip this

If you run fewer than a few thousand agent runs per day, storage is cheap and full-fidelity tracing is simpler. Skip the sampler.

If you operate under retention obligations, keep everything and solve cost elsewhere. Skip the sampler.

If your failures are exactly the class you would sample away, for example silent wrong answers with clean statuses, pin on an outcome signal instead of a status code.

Start with one day of traffic

Sample runs, not spans. Pin anomalies unconditionally. Store a model-written digest for every run.

Take one archived day of traces. Run the sampler over it. Report the two ratios and the three invariants.

If the numbers hold, you have shrunk the store without losing the one run you will need at 09:12.

title: Pixels to Tokens: Token Space Efficient Active Learning for Low-Budget Semantic Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.20881v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While foundation models and vision transformers (ViTs) have redefined visual representations, current active learning (AL) strategies for these backbones largely operate at the patch or region level, where annotation requirements remain high due to extensive pixel labeling. Extending ViT-based AL to the pixel-level, low-budget regime is uniquely challenging: with as little as one pixel query per image, a method must simultaneously identify the most informative locations and train a reliable decoder head from an extremely sparse signal. We introduce TEAL (Token-space Efficient Active Learning), the first pixel-level AL framework built around ViT representations. TEAL uses a frozen ViT backbone and performs diversity-based selection directly on its native token lattice, avoiding the artifacts introduced by interpolating token embeddings to dense pixel resolutions. Our framework applies a two-level MaxHerding strategy over multi-layer token descriptors to select representative candidates, followed by margin-based uncertainty refinement on a finer decoder grid. Across CamVid, Cityscapes, ADE20K, and Pascal Context, TEAL consistently outperforms previous baselines under extreme label scarcity, improving over the strongest baseline by up to +24.36 mIoU with a single labeled pixel (px) per image, and reaching up to 97% of fully supervised performance with just 10 px. To rigorously establish the source of the gains, we further show that the improvements persist when all baselines are equipped with the same DINOv3 backbone, demonstrating that coupling token-space selection with uncertainty refinement on the decoder grid makes ViT token geometry an effective foundation for extremely low-budget active segmentation.

title: All-in-One Memory: Process-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Memory Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21147v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on external memory to answer queries grounded in long-horizon histories such as multi-session dialogues and lengthy documents. However, existing memory methods often optimize retrieval and memory construction separately, without a shared reward space for evaluating search, writing, and stopping decisions. To address this, we propose All-in-One Memory (AiO-Mem), which organizes these operations as transitions over a shared evidence state and directly evaluates the semantic quality of each action in a unified reward space. AiO-Mem compiles heterogeneous histories into source-traceable multi-view events, providing a shared substrate for retrieval and memory writing. A unified memory policy actor then rolls out complete interaction trajectories over this shared evidence state. A separate trajectory-conditioned process reward model is trained through evidence-grounded supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level DPO to assign process scores to the collected trajectories. These scores are aggregated into an action-balanced trajectory reward and used by Process-Aligned DAPO (PA-DAPO) to optimize the memory policy. Across long-context memory benchmarks, AiO-Mem consistently improves answer accuracy over both static memory systems and RL-trained memory agents.
