title: The end of credential sprawl for agents
description:
Every useful agent reaches beyond your codebase. It posts to Slack, opens pull requests, queries Snowflake, or calls an internal API. That reach is what makes it valuable, and it's also where the risk lives, because for years, granting it meant provisioning a long-lived token and hoping it never leaked.

Vercel Connect replaces long-lived tokens with ones your code requests at runtime, scoped to the task and expiring on their own.

During the public beta, we've grown the ecosystem past 100 connectors, unified how they work, and added the governance capabilities teams need in production.

Today, Vercel Connect is generally available.

Vaults don't fix long-lived tokens

Managing credentials has become its own workload. Teams write rotation scripts, copy secrets across environments, and share tokens between users. Putting a token in a vault made it harder to steal, but no less dangerous once stolen. It never expires, and no vault limits what a leaked credential can do.

Agents compounded the problem by touching more systems with greater autonomy, more often. Yet the tools to contain a secret haven't changed.

With Vercel Connect, your app never stores credentials. It requests one:

  • You register a connector once for a provider like Slack, GitHub, Snowflake, Shopify, or your own OAuth service

  • You attach it to the projects and environments that need it

  • Your code requests a token at runtime, and it refreshes automatically

  • Your app has no provider secret to commit by accident

Requesting a token doesn't require another secret. Every deployment on Vercel carries an OIDC identity, and the SDK uses it to prove who's asking.

What changes when access becomes a request

The difference shows up in the properties of the credential:

Property

Stored token

Vercel Connect

Lifetime

Never expires

Short-lived, refreshed automatically

Reach

Everything the agent could need

Scoped to the task in the request

Identity

One shared bot for every user

App or a specific named user

Rotation

Mint, update copies, redeploy

None to perform

Revocation

Rotate and redeploy

One command, per user or all tokens

Credentials that used to sit in environments long after the work finished now expire on their own. Nothing lingers for an attacker to find.

Scoping happens per request. One step of an agent might read a repository, the next opens an issue, and each asks for only that.

How fine-grained a token can be depends on the service, and GitHub is the clearest example. Requests can restrict a token to a single repository with read-only permissions, rather than trusting a standing grant organization-wide.

The open-source GitHub Tools SDK puts this into practice. Choose a preset like code-review, and it mints tokens with only the required scopes.

Identity is per request as well. Tokens act as the app by default, but pass a named user as the subject and the token acts on their behalf, scoped to what they authorized during a one-time consent flow.

Connectors for the services you already use

Vercel Connect now ships with 100+ preset connectors for developer tools and SaaS providers like Notion, Shopify, and Workday, as well as managed connectors for Slack, GitHub, Linear, Salesforce, and more.

Your own services follow the same model via custom OAuth and API Key authentication, and any OAuth-capable MCP server can serve as a connector.

Finding and creating them is faster, too. Browse the full catalog on the Vercel website, create a connector in fewer steps, and manage everything from the dashboard, CLI, or API.

Governance that scales with your team

Teams adopting Vercel Connect need more than scoped tokens. They need to control who manages connectors and to track how access is used.

GA adds three capabilities:

  • Fine-grained RBAC controls who can create and manage connectors

  • Audit logs record authorization and connector activity

  • Token and trigger observability shows usage across projects

Together with per-environment attachment and one-command revocation, access becomes something you can inspect and prove.

When an auditor asks who had access to a system and when, the answer is a query against the audit log, not an investigation across projects and Slack threads.

Wherever your agents run

Vercel Connect is available wherever you and your users are:

  • Custom Environments are supported, so a qa environment gets its own connector alongside production, preview, and development

  • eve supports Connect out of the box, with connections declared per agent

  • Chat SDK support brings the same model to conversational apps

Build connected apps in v0

Apps and agents built in v0 use the same model.

Tell v0 which service your app needs, and it sets up the connector during the build. Slack, GitHub, and other managed connectors need nothing on the provider's side, and since tokens are minted at runtime, the generated app has no secret to keep.

The KERNEL team shipped a voice-driven browser agent this way:

Events flow in, without a secret either

Requesting tokens is half the picture. Your agent also needs to hear about events.

Triggers handle this without putting a secret back in your app. When a user posts in Slack, the provider sends the event to Vercel Connect. It verifies the signature server-side, re-attests the event with an OIDC identity, and forwards it to your project. Forwarded events arrive even with Deployment Protection enabled.

Your app has no bot token to act with and no signing secret to verify webhooks, yet the full loop still runs.

Moonpig Group runs its internal legal agent on this loop in production:

Built around a single call

Underneath everything is getToken from the Vercel Connect SDK.

Whether your agent is built on eve or the AI SDK, runs as a background job in Vercel Workflows, or is a loop you wrote yourself, it asks for a credential the same way.

Around that call, adapters handle the wiring:

  • @vercel/connect/eve supplies the credentials behind an agent's connections

  • @vercel/connect/chat hooks Connect into Chat SDK adapters

  • @vercel/connect/betterauth and @vercel/connect/authjs produce provider configs for Better Auth and Auth.js

  • @vercel/connect/ai-sdk and @vercel/connect/mcp do the same for AI SDK tools and MCP clients, whether your agent calls tools directly or through a server

For eve agents and Chat SDK applications, the two secrets a Slack integration usually keeps in your environment, SLACK_BOT_TOKEN and SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET, are gone from your app entirely.

Pricing and availability

Vercel Connect is available on all plans, with pricing based on token requests and trigger events. The Hobby plan includes 500 token requests and 1,000 triggers per month at no additional cost. Pro plans are billed at $3 per 1,000 token requests and $0.95 per 1,000 triggers, with custom pricing on Enterprise.

If you used Vercel Connect during the beta, your current billing terms stay unchanged until September 25, 2026, when the updated pricing takes effect.

  • Follow the complete guide in the knowledge base or read the changelog

  • Hand the prompt below to your coding agent to set up Vercel Connect:

title: Mine, Sample, Render: Test-Time Diversity Alignment Of Generative Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21185v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern generative models produce high-quality individual outputs but struggle to sample diversely, even when explicitly instructed to do so. We introduce MINE-SAMPLE-RENDER (MSR), a test-time approach that externalizes the diversity into an explicit, corpus-derived sampling procedure. Our pipeline (i) mines an interpretable categorical schema from a corpus of real artifacts and supplies statistics for sampling; (ii) samples attribute configurations from the corpus-derived statistics; (iii) uses a generative model purely as a conditional renderer of a sampled configuration. Across weather report generation, user simulation, webpage design, text-to-image generation, and agent-generated 3D assets, we evaluate the diversity and output quality of MSR-guided generation and show that MSR improves alignment with corpus distributions and diversity of generated outputs.

title: When native cloud schedulers are enough, and when not
description:
Every cloud platform ships with a scheduler. For work that stays inside that platform it is usually the right tool, and adding an orchestrator on top buys you a hop, a credential and a failure mode.

The trouble starts at the boundary, where one platform's scheduler has to wait on another platform's work and no single graph covers the run. Here are five checks for working out which side of that line you are on, and three ways across it if you are on the wrong side.

The five checks

You are still comfortably inside one platform when:

  • every step is a first-class job in the same platform, not an HTTP call;
  • a single dependency graph covers the whole run;
  • monitoring shows the whole run, not one platform's slice of it;
  • retries and idempotency are handled inside the platform;
  • adding a step does not mean inventing a new integration pattern.

You are past the edge when:

  • steps are chained with storage events, webhooks or polling timers;
  • a step is a service call rather than a job the scheduler understands;
  • "did the other platform's job finish?" is answered by a person, or by a table someone maintains;
  • lineage and run history stop at the platform boundary;
  • adding the next platform means building another bespoke bridge.

All five hold and the native scheduler is enough. Any one fails and you are about to start building glue. That is worth saying plainly: a scheduler that ships with the platform is not a compromise. There is nothing extra to run, retries happen where the failures happen, and the platform's own team keeps it working.

What glue actually looks like

Glue is not a product. It is the work that exists because one platform has to wait on another: a storage event that fires a function, a webhook that calls the next platform's API, a polling timer that asks whether the other job finished, or a lookup table somebody keeps current by hand.

Two properties matter before you build more of it:

  • Glue has no graph. The dependency lives in the event subscription or the timer, not in something anyone can draw.
  • Glue makes the run invisible at the edges. Each platform sees only its own slice, so retries, lineage and error handling end at the boundary, and it breaks quietly.

Scenario 1: one platform does the whole job

Picture a pipeline where every stage lives in Databricks. Data is ingested from cloud storage and message buses by the platform's declarative pipelines, transformations run in the same pipelines, and unstructured documents are parsed with an AI function:

SELECT ai_parse_document(content) FROM documents

The parsed output is indexed for search with Databricks AI Search, and analysts read the result in AI/BI dashboards. Lakeflow Jobs schedules the lot with one dependency graph, and the platform's monitoring shows every task in one place.

Run the five checks: all five hold. In this shape an external orchestrator removes nothing.

Scenario 2: the same pipeline, two platforms

Now mirror it. Ingestion in Azure Data Factory, document extraction on Azure Document Intelligence, transformation on Databricks, the search index in Azure AI Search, dashboards in Power BI.

Logically identical. Physically it crosses three or four boundaries. Data Factory can invoke a Databricks job directly and has a connector that writes to an Azure AI Search index, so those hops are expressible inside the platform. Document extraction has no first-class activity, so it becomes a Web call, a place where the dependency no longer resolves on its own. The Databricks job schedules its own tasks on its own clock, and Power BI refreshes on a third.

Run the five checks again. The graph no longer covers the run. Monitoring is split across four consoles. None of this is a defect in any one product. It is what a boundary does.

Three ways across, and when each is right

  1. Event glue. Storage events, webhooks or a polling timer pick up where the last platform left off. Cheapest to start, and the cost shows up later as silent gaps and manual reconciliation.
  2. A scheduler of schedulers. One job whose only task is to start other schedulers and wait. It works, but each platform still sees only its own slice, and the outer graph is a script one person owns.
  3. A control plane that spans the platforms. Each platform stays the executor; a separate layer holds the dependency graph across them, maps parameters between tasks and keeps one run history.

A simple test settles it: try to answer, for one run, what ran, in what order, and what waited on what. If the honest answer needs four browser tabs, the boundary is costing more than an orchestrator would.

Where Polysync fits

Polysync is a control plane rather than a replacement for the platforms you already run. It treats pipelines, jobs and functions across Azure, Databricks, Fabric, AWS and Google Cloud as first-class nodes in one dependency graph, and decides what runs, when, and what waits. It does not move your data and does not change how any platform executes its work.

The article this is based on is the canonical home for this piece, with the figures: https://www.polysync.com.au/articles/native-cloud-schedulers?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=articles&utm_content=native-cloud-schedulers

title: a desktop app that shows what your Linux server is really doing, over plain SSH, with nothing installed on the server
description:
Lightminedust / Kubo

See and manage your Linux server over SSH — visually. Nothing installed on the server, nothing leaves your machine.

Kubo

Manage your Linux server from a window, not just a terminal.

Kubo is a free desktop app for Windows and Linux. It connects to your own Linux server over SSH and shows you what is going on: files, open ports, firewall, websites, services, Docker, Redis, packages.

Nothing is installed on your server. Nothing is sent anywhere else.

⬇ Download for Windows  ·  ⬇ Download for Linux  ·  Website  ·  Java included  ·  ~75 MB

Who it's for

You rented a VPS, set up a Raspberry Pi, or run a small server for a website, a bot or a game. You can use the terminal, but you don't want to remember twenty commands just to answer simple questions:

  • Which ports are open, and which ones can the internet actually reach?
  • Why isn't my website answering?
  • Who keeps trying to get into my server?

title: Myth FAQ: Your Lockfile Is Not a Reproduction
description:
Your CI is green. Your lockfile is committed. So your build reproduces, right?

That is the claim I hear most often. It also breaks loudest at 2 a.m., on a machine you have never touched.

This is a myth-busting FAQ. Claims first, evidence second, corrected mental model last.

Myth 1: "The lockfile pins everything."

A lockfile pins what your resolver selected. It does not pin what your environment will install.

Watch the gaps:

  • Extras and optional dependencies. requests[socks] and requests resolve differently.
  • Environment markers. PEP 508 markers like sys_platform == "win32" evaluate at install time.
  • Optional platform binaries. Node packages ship per-arch optional deps for things like bundlers.
  • Features and build tags. Cargo.lock pins versions, not the feature set or target triple.

Corrected model: a lockfile describes a set of constraints. Your platform, extras, and flags pick the actual subset.

Myth 2: "The same lockfile gives the same tree."

Same inputs, same outputs. Sounds obvious. It is not true across environments.

Two boxes, one lockfile, different results:

  • A wheel exists for linux/amd64 but not linux/arm64.
  • One falls back to a source build, the other does not.
  • A post-install script fetches a prebuilt binary from a CDN.

The resolved versions match. The installed artifacts do not.

Corrected model: reproducibility is a property of an environment pair, not of a file.

Myth 3: "Hashes prove the dependency set."

Hashes prove artifact identity. They do not prove set completeness.

pip install --require-hashes will refuse to install anything unpinned. That is strong. It still says nothing about a package fetched inside a build hook.

npm records integrity hashes in the lockfile. Great for the tarball. Useless for what a lifecycle script downloads afterward.

So ask the sharper question: can anything enter this environment that the lockfile never named?

Myth 4: "Green CI proves reproducibility."

CI is a warm room. That is the whole problem.

  • Docker layer caches keep an old wheel alive.
  • Runners preinstall toolchains, compilers, and system libs.
  • Reused virtualenvs carry leftover packages.

Your pipeline may be deterministic and misleading. Both at once.

Corrected model: reproducibility evidence comes from a cold environment. Caches are a performance feature, not proof.

Myth 5: "A pinned version is immutable code."

Version strings are labels. Registries vary in whether labels are permanent.

  • Some registries allow re-upload or yank-and-republish behaviors.
  • Git dependencies without a full commit SHA can move under you.
  • Mirrors and proxies may serve different bytes than upstream.

Check your registry's policy instead of assuming. Where the option exists, prefer commit SHAs and verified hashes over friendly version numbers.

The artifact: a two-environment fingerprint

The fix is cheap. Install on two machines that share nothing, then compare a normalized fingerprint.

Here is a template. I have not executed it against your repository, so adapt paths and read it before you run it.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# fingerprint.sh — write a sorted, normalized view of an installed Python env
set -euo pipefail

OUT="${1:-env-fingerprint.txt}"

python - <<'PY' > "$OUT"
import importlib.metadata as md
import platform, sys

pkgs = []
for dist in md.distributions():
    name = dist.metadata["Name"]
    if not name:
        continue
    pkgs.append(f"{name.lower().replace('_', '-')}=={dist.version}")

pkgs.sort()
print("# interpreter:", platform.python_version(), platform.python_implementation())
print("# platform:", sys.platform, platform.machine())
for line in pkgs:
    print(line)
PY

sha256sum "$OUT" | awk '{print "fingerprint_sha256=" $1}'

Step 1 — cold install, box A 

python -m venv /tmp/venv-a
/tmp/venv-a/bin/pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.lock
./fingerprint.sh fp-a.txt

Step 2 — cold install, box B

Box B must never have seen this project. Different architecture if you can get one.

python -m venv /tmp/venv-b
/tmp/venv-b/bin/pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.lock
./fingerprint.sh fp-b.txt

Step 3 — diff, then explain every line 

diff <(grep -v '^#' fp-a.txt) <(grep -v '^#' fp-b.txt) || true

Three outcomes, three meanings:

  1. Identical package lines. Your dependency set is stable across platforms. Good.
  2. Different versions of the same package. A marker or resolver branch fired. Investigate.
  3. Packages present on one side only. Something installed outside the lockfile. This is the failure you wanted to find.

Record the interpreter version and platform in the fingerprint. Otherwise your diff is noise.

Node and Rust equivalents 

# Node: install strictly from the lockfile
npm ci --ignore-scripts   # then compare `npm ls --all --json` output

# Rust: lockfile plus target triple plus features
cargo metadata --format-version 1 > meta-a.json

--ignore-scripts is diagnostic, not a default. It tells you whether lifecycle scripts are part of the picture.

Decision table: when is the lockfile enough?

Scenario Lockfile alone enough? Extra evidence to collect
Pure-Python deps, one platform, no extras Often yes Fingerprint from one cold box
Native extensions or platform wheels No Fingerprint per OS/arch pair
Optional extras installed No Record which extras were enabled
Any post-install or lifecycle script No Mirror or vendor what the script fetches
Container base image drift No Pin and log the base image digest
Git dependency without full SHA No Replace refs with commit SHAs
Build tags or feature flags No Log the exact flags beside the fingerprint

Print this table's answers into your build log. A fingerprint nobody recorded is a fingerprint nobody can compare.

Limitations, and who should skip this

Be honest about the cost before you adopt it.

  • Two cold installs are slow. Do them on release branches, not every commit.
  • Fingerprints are environment-specific. They compare like with like, not across everything.
  • This catches drift, not correctness. A stable wrong tree is still wrong.
  • Solo prototypes do not need this. If you rebuild weekly from scratch, you already have the signal.
  • Regulated builds need more. Signed artifacts, provenance attestation, audit trails. This is a floor, not a ceiling.

Skip the whole exercise if your deployment target is a single long-lived machine. You have one environment, so you have one truth.

Where an ephemeral box fits

The hard part is box B. It must be cold, and it must not be your laptop.

That is the honest use case for a throwaway server. Spin one up, run step 2, copy the fingerprint, destroy it. MonkeyCode's free server option is one place to do this, and its free model access is handy for turning a raw diff into a short explanation list. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Do not trust a vendor for the result, though. Your fingerprint is your evidence.

What to remember

A lockfile is a constraint set, not a receipt. Hashes prove identity, not completeness. Green CI proves your cache is warm.

So here is the question I keep coming back to: when your build last passed, which machine had actually never seen it before?

If you cannot answer that, you do not have reproducibility yet. You have a habit that usually works.

title: 48-Hour Field Notes: My Diff Blamed the Model; My Stream Logger Was Splitting UTF-8
description:
Two hosts, one prompt, ten runs each, and three diffs that should not exist. I spent most of two days trying to explain why the same request produced different answers, and the explanation turned out to be embarrassingly local. Nothing about the model or the network was inconsistent. My own logging layer was corrupting the text before the diff ever saw it.

This is a field note, not a tutorial: what I tried, what broke, and what I would keep. It ends with a test you can run in under a second with no network access at all.

The setup: ten identical requests, two places they ran

My working assumption was that comparing outputs across environments is mostly about controlling the request. So I froze everything I could:

  1. One prompt, stored as a file, hashed with SHA-256 and printed at the top of every run.
  2. One request body, serialized once with sort_keys=True so key order could not drift.
  3. Ten sequential calls per host, no retries, no concurrency, a two-second sleep between calls.
  4. Raw response bytes written to disk before any parsing happened.

I ran half the calls from my laptop and half from a small remote box, so the harness would survive me closing the lid. That box was MonkeyCode's free server option, and the endpoint I pointed it at was MonkeyCode's free model access; both are operator-supplied availability claims, not measurements I made. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Their relevance to the story is narrow: a 48-hour loop was cheap enough to leave running, and a second host existed at all.

The comparison itself was dumb on purpose. Decode both raw logs, normalize whitespace, diff the text.

Hour 4-12: the diffs looked real, so I blamed sampling

Three of twenty responses differed. All three differences were small - a word here, a punctuation mark there - which is exactly what a stochastic model looks like when you compare two samples. So I did the obvious thing: bumped the sample size to fifty runs, forced a zero-temperature setting where it was supported, and expected the diffs to collapse.

They did not collapse. They clustered. That is the detail I should have stopped on twelve hours earlier.

Every differing response contained a non-ASCII character somewhere: an em dash, a curly quote, a box-drawing character in a generated table. Responses that were pure ASCII matched byte for byte across both hosts. That is not a distribution you get from sampling noise. That is a distribution you get from a codec.

Hour 12-30: I grepped my own logs for the replacement character

The raw byte logs were large, so I searched instead of reading them.

# Count corruption markers in each raw log
for f in logs/*.raw; do
  printf '%s\t%s\n' "$(grep -c $'\xef\xbf\xbd' "$f")" "$f"
done | sort -rn | head

Output, trimmed:

1412    logs/free-server/run-07.raw
1108    logs/free-server/run-03.raw
 906    logs/laptop/run-02.raw
  17    logs/laptop/run-09.raw

U+FFFD, sitting inside the log I was treating as ground truth. Not in the model's response. In my log.

Then I read my own reader, which I had written specifically so I could keep raw bytes around:

# The buggy reader. Fine on ASCII, mangles everything else.
def read_sse(byte_chunks):
    for chunk in byte_chunks:
        # Each chunk is decoded on its own, so a UTF-8 sequence
        # split across a chunk boundary becomes U+FFFD.
        text = chunk.decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        for line in text.split("\n"):
            if line.startswith("data:"):
                yield line[5:].strip()

That is the entire failure. A response chunk is a transport artifact, not a character boundary. When a three-byte character straddles two chunks, errors="replace" silently invents a replacement character instead of crashing; the log stays readable, and the diff downstream reports a difference that does not exist in the upstream bytes.

The three "different" responses were the three responses whose non-ASCII characters happened to land on a chunk boundary. My instrumentation had corrupted the thing it was measuring.

Hour 30-40: reproducing it without a network

I did not want to debug this against a live endpoint, so I reduced it to a fake byte stream. Two files, standard library only.

sse_lines.py:

import codecs
from typing import Iterable, Iterator


def lines(byte_chunks: Iterable[bytes]) -> Iterator[str]:
    """Split a byte stream into lines without assuming chunk == character."""
    decoder = codecs.getincrementaldecoder("utf-8")("strict")
    buffer = ""
    for chunk in byte_chunks:
        buffer += decoder.decode(chunk)        # holds a partial tail internally
        while "\n" in buffer:
            line, buffer = buffer.split("\n", 1)
            yield line.rstrip("\r")
    buffer += decoder.decode(b"", final=True)  # raises if the stream was truncated
    if buffer:
        yield buffer.rstrip("\r")


def data_payloads(line_iter: Iterable[str]) -> Iterator[str]:
    parts = []
    for line in line_iter:
        if line == "":
            if parts:
                yield "\n".join(parts)
                parts = []
        elif line.startswith("data:"):
            parts.append(line[5:].lstrip(" "))
    if parts:
        yield "\n".join(parts)

test_sse_lines.py:

from sse_lines import lines, data_payloads

# "cafe with an accent": the e-acute (0xC3 0xA9) is split across two chunks,
# and the event's terminating newline lands in a third chunk.
CHUNKS = [b'data: {"text": "caf', b'\xc3', b'\xa9 late"}\n\n']


def test_multibyte_split_across_chunks():
    payloads = list(data_payloads(lines(CHUNKS)))
    assert payloads == ['{"text": "caf\u00e9 late"}']
    assert "\ufffd" not in payloads[0]


def test_naive_per_chunk_decode_is_lossy():
    naive = [c.decode("utf-8", errors="replace") for c in CHUNKS]
    assert "\ufffd" in "".join(naive)   # the bug, asserted on purpose

Run it:

python -m pytest test_sse_lines.py -q
# 2 passed in 0.01s

The second test is the important one. It pins the failure mode in place, so nobody "fixes" the reader by going back to per-chunk decoding and quietly gets a green suite again.

Hour 40-48: re-running the comparison

With the reader fixed, I re-ran both hosts. Where the raw byte streams were identical, the decoded text was now identical too, and the diff count went to zero. Where the byte streams genuinely differed, the diffs stayed, and for the first time I could trust them.

Here is the table I wish I had on hour four:

Symptom Likely cause First check
Diffs only in outputs containing non-ASCII chunk-boundary decode count U+FFFD in the raw log
Diffs on every run, including pure ASCII genuine sampling, or a request that changed compare hashes of the request body
Diffs only from one host client library version, proxy buffering, compression print library versions and Content-Encoding
Diffs vanish when logging is disabled the logger transforms the stream log bytes, not strings

What I would repeat, and what I would change

Keep:

  • Hashing the request body per run and printing the hash. It removes a whole class of doubt before you start.
  • Writing raw bytes first and decoding later. Storage is cheap; re-running a 48-hour comparison is not.
  • Reducing a live failure to a fake input. The network version cost hours; the fixture version cost a second.

Change:

  • Grep the raw log for U+FFFD before blaming the model. It is a one-line check, and it would have saved a day.
  • Treat every layer that touches the stream as suspect, including your own logging. The instrument is part of the measurement.

Limitations and who should not do this

This workflow answers one narrow question: given identical request bytes, did the response bytes differ? It cannot tell you whether either response is correct, and a clean diff is not an eval. If you need pass/fail judgments about output quality, you need a graded dataset rather than string equality, and you need to decide the grading criteria before the run starts.

Do not use a shared free box for latency numbers or capacity planning. A shared host is the wrong instrument for timing, and free tiers are not a promise about availability or permanence. If your team needs pinned model versions, fixed hardware, or an SLA, run your harness somewhere you control and pay for. Also, if your outputs are guaranteed ASCII by construction, most of this article is about a bug you will never hit, and your time is better spent on request pinning.

If you want to reproduce any of it, the artifact above needs nothing but the Python standard library. Pin your HTTP client version, log bytes before strings, and if you need somewhere for a long comparison to keep running, my second host is still the free server option on MonkeyCode.

title: Node.js Scheduled Data Cleanup: BullMQ, RabbitMQ, or Hosted Queue for Small SaaS
description:
Short answer: for a small edtech SaaS sending scheduled shipment updates, start with a hosted queue plus cron, and choose BullMQ or RabbitMQ only when you are ready to own their delivery machinery.

Keep it boring.

Measure twice.

A shipment update is a deceptively small feature. A teacher changes a delivery window, and thousands of learners may need the same notice. The real decision is delivery guarantee: can a message be delivered at least once, can a duplicate be harmless, and can an operator see a stuck job before support does?

The field guide: pick a queue by the failure you can operate

Option Pick this when Delivery shape Operational catch
BullMQ with Redis Your team already runs Redis and wants a Node.js-native job API At-least-once workers with retries You own Redis persistence, upgrades, and worker supervision
RabbitMQ You need broker-level routing and have messaging operations experience Explicit acknowledgements and redelivery Topology, monitoring, and capacity become part of the product
Hosted queue You want cron-triggered dispatch with minimal platform work At-least-once delivery; make consumers idempotent You accept one provider's limits and outage surface
Inngest You want managed event steps and retries Provider-managed workflow delivery Its workflow model can exceed a single queue need

For a small SaaS, the hosted row is usually the least expensive in human time and the easiest to explain during an incident. That is a judgment about operations, not a promise about a vendor invoice.

How should a small SaaS choose BullMQ, RabbitMQ, or a hosted queue for scheduled cleanup and fan-out?

Start with the work unit. A cron trigger should enqueue a compact record range or cursor, then a worker loads the rows and sends updates. Do not put a deletion manifest or a full subscriber list into one message: the queue message limit is 256KB. A cursor such as {\"shipmentId\":\"shp_4821\",\"page\":7} is easier to retry and audit.

Delivery is at-least-once. I once treated a retry as a rare edge case and let the handler append a notification row before checking its idempotency key; a timeout after the insert produced duplicate mail on the next attempt. The fix was boring and effective: derive a stable job key from shipment ID plus page, then make the database write conditional. Five minutes later, the retry was harmless.

Here is the small handoff I use for a Node.js worker. It publishes a batch and reports a failed item through the same base URL and key. The response body is retained as evidence for the run; a real service would also persist the request ID beside its job key. Infrai offers one key, one bill, and one plain REST API for both dispatch and captured errors keeps the contract stable when the backend provider changes. No SDK install is required.

const baseUrl = "https://api.example.invalid/v1";
const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const headers = {
  Authorization: `Bearer ${key}`,
  "Content-Type": "application/json",
};

async function publishShipmentPage(shipmentId: string, page: number) {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/queue/publish_batch`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers,
    body: JSON.stringify({
      messages: [{
        idempotency_key: `shipment:${shipmentId}:page:${page}`,
        payload: { shipmentId, page },
      }],
    }),
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`queue publish failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }

  const result = await response.json();
  if (result.failed?.length) {
    await fetch(`${baseUrl}/errors/capture`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers,
      body: JSON.stringify({
        message: "shipment fan-out publish reported a failed item",
        context: { shipmentId, page, result },
      }),
    });
  }

  return result;
}

publishShipmentPage("shp_4821", 7).catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

The important detail is the handoff: queue output and captured errors are visible under one key, so a dead-letter spike can be investigated beside application errors. Infrai's differentiator here is the contract: swapping the backend behind a capability does not force a code rewrite, and the same plain REST surface covers dispatch and observability. An SQS plus Sentry setup can do the same job, but it means two sign-ups, two credential sets, and glue code to correlate message IDs with error events.

Retries need backoff, and a standard queue has no Kafka-style replay or multi-consumer-group history. Keep the queue for work dispatch, not as your audit log. If a cleanup job runs longer than 900 seconds, let cron enqueue it and have a worker consume pages; do not make cron host the long task.

What each serious option looks like in production

BullMQ is a sensible pick when Redis is already a staffed dependency and every service is TypeScript. Its familiar worker model makes local development pleasant. The catch is that Redis operations are now coupled to shipment reliability; persistence settings and failover are your responsibility.

RabbitMQ fits teams that need routing keys, exchanges, or established AMQP tooling. It is a strong broker, but it asks for more topology and monitoring discipline than a single cleanup pipeline usually justifies. Stick with it when those routing semantics are a requirement, not because the name sounds more durable.

A hosted queue fits the small-SaaS boundary when one queue, a cron trigger, and idempotent workers cover the workflow. Amazon SQS is the obvious comparison for teams already deep in AWS. The trade is concentration: one provider, one bill, and one outage surface. That is acceptable only if your runbook includes provider status checks, bounded retries, and a way to pause fan-out.

Limits that should change your design

The queue does not provide DAG orchestration, a join primitive, native debounce, or throttle. Delayed messages top out at seven days, retention at 30 days, and FIFO deduplication at five minutes. Cron does not replay triggers missed while paused, and its run output keeps only the first 4KB. Push targets must be publicly reachable HTTPS endpoints.

Those boundaries are design inputs. In a busy enrollment week, a page can fan out to 10,000 subscribers while the cleanup cursor remains a few dozen bytes; that asymmetry is why I separate scheduling, dispatch, and durable audit state instead of forcing one tool to do all three. Store the durable audit record in Postgres, claim pages with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, and enqueue IDs or cursors. If your requirement is a replayable event stream or a multi-stage workflow, choose a system built for that job instead.

References

  • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron
  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html

title: The top-up nobody knows went through
description:
A customer asks for a prepaid airtime top-up at a corner store. The system debits the store's balance and sends the request to the carrier. The carrier does not answer.

Did the top-up reach the phone? At that moment nobody knows. And with the carrier, nobody can ask: the answer arrives tomorrow, in the reconciliation.

For years I worked on an electronic top-up platform. Requests came in from terminals, apps and points of sale, and reached the carrier after two, three and up to four hops, each with its own protocol and its own timeout. Everything happened: double top-ups, charges with no top-up. This note is about why, and about the state almost no system designs in from the start.

The figures in the examples are illustrative: calculated to show the mechanism. They are not that platform's numbers.

There are three answers, not two

A system that moves money is usually thought of with two outcomes: the operation went through, or it did not. On a network there is a third: unknown. The request went out and the answer never came back. The request may have been lost, and the top-up does not exist. Or the answer may have been lost, and the top-up is already on the phone.

From this side of the wire, the two cases look identical.

Every hop is one more place where an answer can get lost. If each one loses one in two thousand, with a hundred thousand top-ups a day, one hop leaves 50 in doubt; four hops, 200. Every day. It is not a bug you fix once: it is a probability you manage forever.

And the hardest case is at the end of the chain: the carrier does not answer, or its answer gets lost, but the internal system has already debited.

Everyone decides what to do with "unknown"

When the screen hangs, somebody decides, and every decision is a bet with someone else's money:

  • The cashier presses the button again. If the first one did go through, the customer gets two top-ups and the store pays for two.
  • The terminal retries on its own. Same thing, without anyone noticing.
  • The platform retries toward the carrier. Same thing, one hop deeper.
  • The platform marks the operation as failed and refunds the store. If the carrier did apply it, the platform gave away a top-up.
  • The platform marks it as good. If the carrier did not apply it, the customer paid and got nothing, and is going to complain.

None of them is right. They are all bets as long as nobody knows what happened.

An ID that travels end to end

The first defense is for every top-up to have a unique identifier from the moment it is born, in the terminal or the app, and for that same identifier to travel through every hop. We called it the externalID.

With it, a retry stops being a new top-up. If a request arrives with an externalID that was already processed, the system does not run it again: it answers with the result of the first one. The cashier can press ten times and the store pays once.

And it makes it possible to ask. Backwards, from the platform toward the points of sale, you could: the terminal could ask what happened to its externalID instead of sending another top-up.

What you cannot ask

With the carriers, you could not. There was no status query. The only thing was batch reconciliation: a file every 24 hours with what the carrier says it applied, against what the platform says it sent.

That means a top-up in doubt stays in doubt until the end of the day, or until the next day. Meanwhile, the store's balance has already been debited, the customer may be complaining, and the platform has nothing to tell them.

And reconciliation, when it comes, is torture: cross-matching files, finding the differences, deciding each one, and sometimes resolving them by hand.

Why not reverse

The way out that looks obvious is the reversal: when in doubt, cancel the operation with the carrier and return the money. In this business reversals are not desirable: they kill the business.

The margin on a top-up is very small. Every reversal costs work, time and arguments with the carrier, and eats the profit of many sales. And if you reverse something that did go through, the loss is total.

What I would do from the start

Design "unknown" as a real state. In the database, on the cashier's screen and in the reports: in progress, not failed or successful. A screen that says "in progress, do not repeat it" is worth more than any later validation.

The externalID from the origin, mandatory, and honored at every hop. A request with no identifier does not get in. A repeated identifier returns the stored result and never runs again.

No human retries blindly. The retry button checks the status first. If there is no answer, it shows that the operation is in progress; it does not send another.

Staggered timeouts. Each hop has to wait longer than the next one. If the terminal gives up before the platform does, the terminal retries while the first request is still alive inside.

Automatic reconciliation from day one. Not as a spreadsheet someone puts together once there are problems, but as part of the system: the carrier's file comes in, gets matched on its own, and a person only gets the differences.

Measure the doubts. How many top-ups stay in progress, per carrier, per hour and per hop. When that number goes up, something broke, and it is better to know today than in tomorrow's reconciliation.

To see what each way of deciding costs with your own numbers (top-ups a day, hops, timeouts), there is the top-up simulator: it runs in the browser and counts the doubled, given-away and charged-without-top-up operations of each policy, and what waits for reconciliation with an externalID.

None of these measures eliminates "unknown". What they do is stop it from being a bet: the money sits in a state everyone can see, nobody duplicates it out of desperation, and reconciliation only has to resolve what truly could not be known. Mitigating it was a lot of programming and infrastructure work. There was no shortcut.

Israel Negrete Lepe is an electronics engineer. Twenty-five years building systems that make it to production: telemetry, vehicle tracking, municipal video surveillance, RFID asset control and transactional platforms.

title: Connect v0 apps to Slack, Google, and 100+ other services
description:
Apps and agents built in v0 can now securely connect to more than 100 services, including Slack, Google, Notion, GitHub, and Salesforce, through Vercel Connect.

Ask v0 to connect your app to a service. It opens the connector setup and guides you through it.

You set up each connector once for your team, then reuse it across apps.

For managed connectors like Slack and GitHub, Vercel handles app registration, so you don’t need to create or configure an app with the provider. For other services, you can provide your own credentials. In both cases, Vercel Connect issues short-lived tokens at runtime, so your application doesn’t need to store or rotate long-lived secrets.

Using v0 and Vercel Connect, Danny from KERNEL built a voice-controlled browser agent that generates Playwright code to operate a real browser. We built a personal dashboard that brings Slack messages, Gmail, and Linear issues into one view and summarizes what needs attention.

title: 14,399 Backtest Events Gave Me t = 8.20. Equal-Weighting Days Gave 1.66
description:
A crypto-perpetual breakout simulation produced 14,399 events across 15 symbols from September 2025 to September 2026. Mean net return was +25.98 bps per event, with a naive event-level t-statistic of +8.20.

But the result depended heavily on how observations were weighted. Returns were concentrated in a small number of market sessions, something the aggregate statistic did not reveal.

Same events, different unit of analysis

I grouped events by calendar day, computed one mean event return per day, then ran a one-sample t-test on those 365 daily means:

event-level:  t = mean(event returns) / (sd / √N)
               = +25.98 / (380.2 / √14,399)  =  +8.20

day-level:    t = mean(daily means)   / (sd / √N)
               = −4.67  / (53.82 / √365)     =  −1.66

These are different estimands. The first weights every event equally; the second weights every trading day equally. The sign reversal does not prove the naive SE was wrong — it shows that the result is sensitive to the weighting choice, which is reason enough to report both. The second is a diagnostic, not a replacement for clustered standard errors or a block bootstrap. For any strategy that fires multiple times a day on correlated moves, it's a useful sanity check.

The day behind the result

October 10, 2025 accounted for most of the positive event-level return. DOTUSDT traded between $0.94 and $4.29 during a market-wide flash crash. ATOMUSDT also experienced extreme price dislocations. Whether the simulated trades could have been executed at those prices is unclear. The simulation's 434 events that day averaged +981 bps. Remove that one day and the event-level mean changes from +25.98 to −3.69 bps.

The median event lost −16.2 bps. Win rate was 34%. The maximum event return was +8,756 bps. The top 1% of events were enough to flip the mean. Only one day made it positive.

October 10, 2025 contributed 434 of 14,399 events, but those events averaged +981 bps. Removing that one day changes the event-level mean from +25.98 to −3.69 bps.

Statistic Unit / N Mean net t-stat Note
Naive t-test 14,399 events +25.98 bps +8.20 Assumes independent events
Daily diagnostic 365 days −4.67 bps −1.66 Two-sided p ≈ 0.098
Sensitivity: without Oct 10 364 days −7.37 bps −9.42 Post-hoc; exposes concentration

The sensitivity row is not a confirmatory result. Removing an outlier and calling the rerun clean is p-hacking. It is there to show how much of the claim rests on one day.

The diagnostic 

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

def day_block_t(returns_bps: np.ndarray, timestamps: pd.Series) -> dict:
    """Equal-weighted daily diagnostic for event returns.

    Groups events by calendar day, computes the mean return per day,
    and tests whether the distribution of daily means differs from zero.

    This changes the unit of analysis from event to trading day.
    It is NOT a cluster-robust standard error for the event-level mean.
    """
    returns_bps = np.asarray(returns_bps, dtype=float)
    days = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(timestamps), utc=True).dt.floor("D").to_numpy()
    if len(returns_bps) != len(days):
        raise ValueError("returns_bps and timestamps must have equal length")
    if not np.isfinite(returns_bps).all():
        raise ValueError("returns_bps must be finite")
    frame = pd.DataFrame({"return_bps": returns_bps, "day": days})
    daily = frame.groupby("day")["return_bps"].mean()
    if len(daily) < 2:
        raise ValueError("at least two trading days are required")
    t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_1samp(daily, popmean=0)

    return {
        "n_events": len(frame),
        "n_days": len(daily),
        "daily_mean_bps": round(daily.mean(), 2),  # input already in bps
        "t_stat": round(float(t_stat), 4),
        "p_value": round(float(p_value), 4),
        "daily": daily,   # keep the series — inspect it, don't trust the summary
    }

# Usage
result = day_block_t(event_returns_bps, event_timestamps)
print(f"Event-level t = {event_returns_bps.mean() / (event_returns_bps.std(ddof=1) / len(event_returns_bps)**0.5):.2f}")
print(f"Day-level   t = {result['t_stat']}  (N={result['n_days']} days)")
# Event-level t = +8.20
# Day-level   t = -1.6579  (N=365 days)

Keep the daily series in the result. A t-statistic is one number; the series shows where the result is coming from.

Inspecting the concentration 

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

daily = result["daily"]  # already in bps

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3))
colors = ["#ef4444" if v > 200 else ("#4ade80" if v > 0 else "#f87171")
          for v in daily]
ax.bar(range(len(daily)), daily.values, color=colors, alpha=0.7, width=1)
ax.axhline(0, color="#6b7280", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel("Trading day")
ax.set_ylabel("Daily mean return (bps)")
ax.set_title(f"Daily mean return — {result['n_days']} days, t = {result['t_stat']:.2f}")

# Flag days > 3σ
mean, std = daily.mean(), daily.std()
outliers = daily[(daily - mean).abs() > 3 * std]
for idx, val in outliers.items():
    ax.annotate(f"{val:.0f} bps", xy=(daily.index.get_loc(idx), val),
                xytext=(0, 8), textcoords="offset points",
                ha="center", fontsize=8, color="#ef4444")
plt.tight_layout()

Limits

There is no single correct return series. If capital is allocated to a portfolio, construct portfolio returns. If the estimand is per-event alpha, preserve that estimand and use an estimator that accounts for dependence: clustered standard errors, a block bootstrap, or HAC/Newey–West where it applies.

Nor is deleting October 10 a valid way to obtain a clean p-value. The primary result keeps every day. The removal is explicitly a post-hoc sensitivity analysis: it tells us how fragile the claim is, not what a pre-specified experiment would have concluded.

The daily t-test still assumes independence across days. It does not automatically account for serial correlation, which is another reason it is a diagnostic rather than the final inference procedure.

The 14,399 events weren't 14,399 independent observations. Most of the positive return came from 434 events on a single day. The naive t-stat didn't reveal that concentration. The daily breakdown did.

Part of the HFM Research methodology series — six things we found when we audited our own backtest results.

title: How to Add, Read, Edit, and Delete Excel Comments in Java
description:
When working with Excel spreadsheets, you may need to add information that doesn't belong directly in a cell, such as the reason for a price change, an explanation of an unusual value, or a reminder to verify certain data.

Excel comments let you attach these notes to individual cells without changing their values. You can also use Java to add, read, update, or remove them programmatically.

This article covers these four operations with complete Java examples.

1. Add the Maven Dependency

To get started, add an Excel processing library to your Java project. If you're using Maven, include the following repository and dependency in your pom.xml file:

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>com.e-iceblue</id>
        <name>e-iceblue</name>
        <url>https://repo.e-iceblue.com/nexus/content/groups/public/</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>e-iceblue</groupId>
        <artifactId>spire.xls.free</artifactId>
        <version>16.3.1</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

2. Add Comments to Excel Cells in Java

To add a comment to an Excel cell, use the CellRange.addComment() method. It returns an ExcelComment object, which you can use to set the comment text and adjust its appearance.

For the examples below, we'll use a workbook named sales.xlsx, with the following data on its first worksheet:

Product Quantity Unit Price Amount
Product A 20 49 980
Product B 15 60 900

The table occupies cells A1:D3. We'll add a note explaining the price in C2 and another reminding us to verify the amount in D3:

import com.spire.xls.*;

public class AddExcelComments {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();

        try {
            // Load the Excel file
            workbook.loadFromFile("sales.xlsx");

            // Get the first worksheet
            Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);

            // Add a comment to cell C2
            ExcelComment comment1 =
                    sheet.getCellRange("C2").addComment();

            comment1.setText(
                    "The unit price was updated this month.");

            // Set the comment box size
            comment1.setWidth(220);
            comment1.setHeight(60);

            // Keep the comment box hidden by default
            comment1.setVisible(false);

            // Add a comment to cell D3
            ExcelComment comment2 =
                    sheet.getCellRange("D3").addComment();

            comment2.setText(
                    "Please verify this amount.");
            comment2.setAutoSize(true);

            // Save the modified workbook
            workbook.saveToFile(
                    "sales-with-comments.xlsx",
                    ExcelVersion.Version2016);

        } finally {
            workbook.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The program creates sales-with-comments.xlsx, with a comment attached to each of the two cells.

Besides setting the text, you can control how a comment appears:

  • setWidth() and setHeight() specify the comment box dimensions.

  • setAutoSize(true) adjusts the box size to fit its text.

  • setVisible(false) keeps the comment box from being displayed continuously.

Setting a comment's visibility to false doesn't remove it. The comment remains attached to the cell and can still be viewed in Excel.

3. Read Comments from an Excel Worksheet

You may also need to inspect comments already stored in a workbook, such as when checking notes left during a review.

The Worksheet.getComments() method provides access to the comments collection for a worksheet. You can iterate through it and retrieve each comment's text and location.

The following example reads all comments from the workbook created in the previous section:

import com.spire.xls.*;

public class ReadExcelComments {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();

        try {
            // Load the Excel file
            workbook.loadFromFile(
                    "sales-with-comments.xlsx");

            // Get the first worksheet
            Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);

            // Get the number of comments
            int count = sheet.getComments().getCount();

            System.out.println("Total comments: " + count);

            // Read each comment
            for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {

                ExcelComment comment =
                        sheet.getComments().get(i);

                System.out.println("Comment " + (i + 1));
                System.out.println("Row: " + comment.getRow());
                System.out.println("Column: " + comment.getColumn());
                System.out.println("Text: " + comment.getText());
                System.out.println("----------------");
            }

        } finally {
            workbook.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The program prints the number of comments and the row, column, and text of each one.

If you already know which cell contains the comment, there's no need to loop through the entire collection. You can retrieve it directly using getComment():

ExcelComment comment =
        sheet.getCellRange("C2").getComment();

if (comment != null) {
    System.out.println(comment.getText());
}

The null check matters because not every cell has a comment. It prevents a NullPointerException when the requested cell has none.

4. Edit an Existing Excel Comment

Comments sometimes need to be updated as the information in a spreadsheet changes.

For example, suppose the unit price in C2 has now been verified. We can replace the original comment with "The current unit price has been verified."

There's no need to remove the existing comment and create a new one. Simply retrieve it with getComment() and update its text using setText().

import com.spire.xls.*;

public class EditExcelComment {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();

        try {
            // Load the workbook containing comments
            workbook.loadFromFile(
                    "sales-with-comments.xlsx");

            // Get the first worksheet
            Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);

            // Get the existing comment in C2
            ExcelComment comment =
                    sheet.getCellRange("C2").getComment();

            // Update the comment
            if (comment != null) {

                comment.setText(
                        "The current unit price has been verified.");

                // Resize the comment box to fit the text
                comment.setAutoSize(true);
            }

            // Save the updated workbook
            workbook.saveToFile(
                    "sales-edited-comments.xlsx",
                    ExcelVersion.Version2016);

        } finally {
            workbook.dispose();
        }
    }
}

After running the code, open sales-edited-comments.xlsx to see the updated comment in C2.

Only the comment text and its box sizing are changed. The cell's value remains the same.

You can also modify other comment properties, such as its dimensions, visibility, and text formatting, without recreating the comment.

5. Delete Comments from Excel Cells

Once a note is no longer needed, you can remove it from the worksheet.

Suppose the amount in D3 has been checked, and the reminder to verify it is no longer relevant.

Use getComment() to retrieve the comment, then call remove() to delete it.

import com.spire.xls.*;

public class DeleteExcelComment {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();

        try {
            // Load the workbook containing comments
            workbook.loadFromFile(
                    "sales-with-comments.xlsx");

            // Get the first worksheet
            Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);

            // Get the comment in cell D3
            ExcelComment comment =
                    sheet.getCellRange("D3").getComment();

            // Remove the comment if it exists
            if (comment != null) {
                comment.remove();
            }

            // Save the modified workbook
            workbook.saveToFile(
                    "sales-removed-comment.xlsx",
                    ExcelVersion.Version2016);

        } finally {
            workbook.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The resulting file, sales-removed-comment.xlsx, no longer contains the comment in D3. The value stored in that cell is preserved, as are the comments in other cells.

If you need to remove comments from several known cells, you can repeat the same operation for each one.

6. A Few Things to Keep in Mind

Traditional Comments vs. Threaded Comments

The examples in this article work with traditional Excel cell comments, which are called Notes in newer versions of Microsoft Excel.

These are different from modern threaded comments, which support replies and @mentions. The APIs shown here should not be assumed to work with threaded comments.

Check Whether a Comment Already Exists

Before adding a comment to a cell, consider whether it already has one.

If your goal is to update an existing note, use getComment() followed by setText() rather than creating another comment.

Save Changes to the Workbook

Adding, editing, or deleting a comment changes the workbook in memory. To write those changes to an Excel file, you must call workbook.saveToFile().

The examples save their results to new files so that the original workbook remains unchanged. If you need to overwrite an existing file, it's worth keeping a backup.

title: HideProxy Review: Real-world pros and cons of a new residential proxy service
description:
When using GoLogin to manage multiple accounts, choosing the right type of proxy is crucial for the stability and longevity of your profiles. Beginners often find themselves weighing the differences between Residential, Datacenter, Mobile, and ISP proxies.
Residential proxies are currently the top choice. Because they use real IP addresses from individual user devices, they appear more natural and are harder for platforms like Facebook, Google, or TikTok to detect. When paired with GoLogin, residential proxies significantly reduce the risk of triggering security checkpoints. Services like HideProxy fall into this category, offering stable "sticky sessions" and flexible country-based targeting.
Datacenter proxies offer the advantages of high speed and low cost. However, since these IPs originate from data centers, they are easier to identify. This type is best suited for low-risk tasks, such as quick checks or running automated tools that do not require a high level of trust.
Mobile proxies provide the highest level of reliability because the IPs come from mobile network carriers. Many social platforms consider mobile proxy IPs to be very "clean." The downsides are their higher cost and the fact that their speeds can sometimes be less consistent than those of residential proxies.
ISP proxies occupy a middle ground. They offer speeds comparable to datacenter proxies while possessing the characteristics of residential proxies, making them a great fit for users who need long-term stability.
In reality, no single proxy type is perfect for every scenario. The key is to align the proxy type with your specific use case and the platform you are targeting. Many GoLogin users have found that switching to high-quality residential proxies—such as those provided by HideProxy—noticeably reduces the rate of profile errors.
Which type of proxy do you use most frequently with GoLogin? What has your experience been like comparing residential proxies to mobile or ISP proxies? Share your insights so we can all learn and discuss together!

title: The "Onion Rule" of Frontend Architecture: Why Your Interceptor Order Is Secretly Breaking Your UX
description:
Recently, while designing the core network layer for a production Angular application, we encountered a subtle bug. When a user opened a page that fired three parallel API calls (forkJoin) while their short-lived access token was expired, the application did something strange:

  1. It successfully refreshed the token in the background.
  2. Yet it still popped up three error dialogs on the screen.

Fixing it didn't require rewriting a single line of RxJS inside our services or components. It required swapping two words in app.config.ts:

// Before
withInterceptors([authInterceptor, errorInterceptor])
// After
withInterceptors([errorInterceptor, authInterceptor])

1. What Is an Interceptor—and Why Do Enterprise Apps Need Them?
In a small prototype, a component calls http.get('/api/data'), passes a header, and writes a catchError block to show a toast message.

Now scale that to an enterprise platform with 80 components, 150 endpoints, role-based access control (RBAC), silent token rotation, and retry policies. If every service or component handles its own authentication, retries, and error popups:

  • You violate DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): Boilerplate error-handling code is duplicated hundreds of times.
  • You violate SRP (Single Responsibility Principle): Feature services now care about token expiration and modal dialogs instead of business data.
  • You create race conditions: When 4 parallel requests fail at the same millisecond, 4 independent error handlers fight over the UI.

An HTTP Interceptor solves this by sitting in the middle of the HTTP client pipeline. It intercepts every outbound HttpRequest before it touches the browser's network stack and inspects every inbound HttpResponse (or HttpErrorResponse) before your services ever receive it.

2. The Mental Trap: Linear vs. Onion Execution
The most common misconception in frontend engineering is that an array of interceptors [A, B, C] executes linearly from A -> B -> C for both requests and responses.

It does not.

Every modern interceptor pipeline—whether in Angular, Axios, or backend middleware the Onion Model (also known as the Russian Doll pattern). Each interceptor wraps the next() handler inside its own observable stream.


Notice the two directions:

  • Outbound (The Request Phase): Flows Left-to-Right (Index 0 -> Index 1 -> Network).
  • Inbound (The Response/Error Phase): Flows Right-to-Left (Network -> Index 1 -> Index 0).The last interceptor to touch the request on the way out is the first interceptor to touch the response on the way back.

3. Anatomy of a Production Bug: [auth, error] vs. [error, auth]
Let’s trace what happens when a component fires three parallel catalog requests (geos, flows, payment-types) using forkJoin, and the user's JWT cookie has expired (401 Unauthorized).

Scenario A: The Wrong Order ([authInterceptor, errorInterceptor])
Here, errorInterceptor is at Index 1 meaning it is the innermost ring closest to the network.

  1. All 3 requests hit the backend and return 401 Unauthorized.
  2. Because errorInterceptor is closest to the network, it catches the 401 first.
  3. It reads the custom fallback error context for each of the 3 endpoints and immediately opens 3 error modals on the screen.
  4. It rethrows the error outward to authInterceptor (Index 0), which then refreshes the token—way too late to save the user experience.

Scenario B: The Architect's Order ([errorInterceptor, authInterceptor])
Now we swap them. authInterceptor is at Index 1 the innermost ring guarding the network boundary.

  1. All 3 requests return 401 Unauthorized from the network.
  2. authInterceptor catches them first. The UI layer (errorInterceptor) has no idea anything went wrong.
  3. authInterceptor pauses the failed requests, calls /auth/refresh once, gets a 200 OK with fresh credentials, and seamlessly replays the 3 requests.
  4. The replayed requests return 200 OK and pass straight through errorInterceptor to the component. Zero popups. Zero user friction.
  5. What if the user's account is genuinely deactivated and /refresh (or the retry) still fails? Only then does authInterceptor throw the unrecoverable error outward to errorInterceptor, which deduplicates the identical error signature in a Map and shows one clean modal.

4. When & How to Bypass the Onion (HttpContext Tokens)
A rigid global pipeline is dangerous if individual endpoints cannot opt out. For example:

  • What happens when the /login endpoint itself returns 401 because the user typed the wrong password? You don't want authInterceptor trying to refresh a token on /login, and you don't want errorInterceptor launching a global system crash modal for a simple typo.
  • What happens when uploading a binary file directly to an S3 presigned URL? Attaching your internal Authorization header will cause S3 to reject the request.

In modern Angular, never hardcode URL string checks (if (req.url.includes('/login'))) inside interceptors. Instead, use strongly-typed HttpContextToken flags:

This respects the Open/Closed Principle (SOLID). Your interceptors remain generic, while specific service calls can selectively disable layers of the onion:

5. The Frontend Architect's Checklist for Interceptor Design
Whenever you are setting up or auditing the HTTP layer of an enterprise application, apply these four rules:

1. Order from UI-Inward to Network-Outward:
Place UI-facing interceptors (Global Error Modals, Loading Spinners) at the beginning of the array (Index 0), and network-recovery interceptors (Auth, Token Refresh, Retry) at the end of the array (Index N).

2. Deduplicate UI Error Modals by Signature:
When forkJoin fires parallel requests and the network drops, multiple streams will fail at the same millisecond. Track active error modals in a Map keyed by ${title}||${message} so the user is never spammed with duplicate popups.

3. Use HttpContext Instead of URL Matching:
Let the calling service declare its intent via HttpContextToken rather than polluting interceptors with fragile regex or .includes() checks.

4. Never Mutate Requests Directly:
Always use req.clone() to maintain immutability across retries. If an interceptor retries a request 2 times, each retry should operate on a clean, predictable request state.

Architecture isn't about making code look complicated. It's about putting boundaries in the exact right order so complex failures look effortless to the user.

title: Sci$\Pi$vot: Benchmarking Principal-Investigator Judgment at Pivotal Moments of Scientific AutoResearch Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21082v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. We construct Sci$\Pi$vot, a 248-case benchmark of scientific judgment based on human corrections. The benchmark draws on records from six months of research in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six scientific fields and repeatedly intervened to correct the agents' research judgments. In each case, an agent chooses between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative, using only the project record available before the correction as context. We compare LLM and human performance and examine the effects of reasoning effort, access to the project record, and reconsideration. At medium reasoning effort with the project record, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan over the human-corrected alternative. Four of five frontier models perform below chance on the selected cases. The highest accuracy in the project condition across the tested models and reasoning effort settings is 63.5%, compared with 73.4% for fresh researchers. At medium effort, every model achieves lower accuracy with the project record than without it, and reconsideration does not consistently improve overall accuracy. Even with a human-corrected alternative available, frontier models struggle with the selected research decisions, while Sci$\Pi$vot supports systematic evaluation of scientific judgment for LLM agents.
