title: PEDBench: Can Speech Models Detect Phonetic Errors?
description:
arXiv:2610.20830v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Phonetic error detection (PED) aims to identify phoneme-level substitutions, deletions, and insertions and is essential for educational and clinical speech assessment and intervention. Despite recent advances in speech models for phoneme recognition, their ability to reliably detect fine-grained phonetic errors remains unclear because of a lack of high-quality evaluation data. To address this gap, we introduce PEDBench, the first PED benchmark spanning a continuum from natural to controlled speech. It comprises real-world recordings of spoken errors made by children (N=334), scripted error productions by human actors (N=1,188), and synthetic error productions generated using phone-conditioned text-to-speech (N=1,083). All phonetic annotations were transcribed and verified by two phonetically trained annotators. Our evaluation of 13 state-of-the-art speech models shows that they fail to reliably detect phonetic errors, even under controlled conditions with acted and synthetic speech, where acoustic variability is reduced. The models also exhibit low precision, frequently misclassifying correctly pronounced phonemes as errors. Our speech-language models, fine-tuned on synthetic data, outperform commercial and open-source baselines on word-level PED, although a sim-to-real domain gap remains. We plan to publicly release our code and recipes, along with our acted and synthetic datasets, to support the development of more accurate PED systems.

title: Rubric First, Box Second: A Bootcamp Lab Where the Setup Is the Deliverable
description:
The short version: in a bootcamp lab, the environment is part of the answer. If a classmate can't rebuild your box from your repo and get the same bytes back, then your clever prompt never mattered. So this lab grades setup, checkpoints, and a rubric — before it grades the agent at all.

Why flip the order?

Most AI labs hand students a working sandbox and a problem. The sandbox is invisible, so the lesson students actually absorb is "the sandbox was just there." That's a bad lesson to carry into a job.

Free tiers make it worse. A free model sitting behind a shared queue is not guaranteed to be the same model tomorrow. A free server is not the same machine next week. Neither of those is a defect — it is the honest shape of free infrastructure. But it means the reproducible part of your work has to be the contract: what you pinned, what you recorded, and what you can rebuild from scratch.

Hence the flip. Deliverable one is a shell script. Deliverable four is a rubric. The agent run sits in the middle, where it belongs.

The lab contract

Four artifacts, one repo:

  1. bootstrap.sh — rebuilds the box from nothing.
  2. manifest.json — pins inputs, model identity, and budget.
  3. checkpoints/ — three named checks a stranger can run.
  4. rubric.json — the scoring rules, written by the student.

Nothing here is exotic. That's the point. If it feels boring, you're doing it right.

Artifact 1: a bootstrap that assumes amnesia 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
# lab/bootstrap.sh — rebuild from an empty box. Bash 5+, Debian-ish target.
LAB_ROOT="${LAB_ROOT:-$HOME/lab}"
python3 -m venv "$LAB_ROOT/.venv"
"$LAB_ROOT/.venv/bin/pip" install --quiet -r "$LAB_ROOT/requirements.txt"
mkdir -p "$LAB_ROOT/runs"
git -C "$LAB_ROOT" rev-parse --short HEAD > "$LAB_ROOT/runs/git-sha.txt"
date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ        > "$LAB_ROOT/runs/built-at.txt"
echo "built $(cat "$LAB_ROOT/runs/git-sha.txt") at $(cat "$LAB_ROOT/runs/built-at.txt")"

Two rules for students:

  • It must run on a box where $LAB_ROOT does not exist yet.
  • It must print a build stamp. No stamp, no credit.

Why so strict? Because "it works on my machine" is a sentence, not evidence.

Artifact 2: pin the model, don't assume it

This is where free access actually changes the design. The project this lab is built around — the open-source coding agent from MonkeyCode — is described by its operator as offering free model access and a free server option.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

I am deliberately not quoting a token quota or a machine spec here. Those numbers move, and a bootcamp that hard-codes them teaches students to trust a stale README. Check the project's own page the morning you run the lab, and write down what you found. That check is itself worth a point.

What you do pin is which model actually answered:

{
  "schema": 1,
  "runtime": "python3.11",
  "model": { "alias": "student-default", "recorded_id": "fill-me-in", "fallback": "fill-me-in" },
  "inputs": { "fixture": "fixtures/issue-0007.md", "sha256": "fill-me-in" },
  "budget": { "max_calls": 40, "max_wall_clock_s": 900 },
  "rebuild": { "script": "bootstrap.sh", "verified_at": null }
}

rebuild.verified_at stays null until the student has run bootstrap.sh twice, on two fresh boxes. That one field kills more hand-waving than any rubric line I've ever written.

Artifact 3: three checkpoints

Not one checkpoint. Three, and each must be cheap enough to run on a whim.

  1. Cold — bootstrap.sh on an empty box, then print the build stamp.
  2. Frozen — re-run the agent with the fixture hash unchanged; assert the output hash equals run one's output hash.
  3. Fenced — assert the diff touches only paths listed in allowed_paths.

A checkpoint is a command, not a paragraph:

$ ./checkpoints/frozen.sh
frozen: output hash 3f9c...  == run-001   OK

If a checkpoint needs three sentences of explanation to run, it isn't a checkpoint. It's a wish.

Artifact 4: stretch goals

Stretch goals are where the lab stops being a tutorial and starts being work:

  • Swap the model alias and keep the same score.
  • Cut wall clock by a third without losing a single checkpoint.
  • Add one rubric criterion that would catch a specific cheat, then explain who it punishes unfairly by accident.

That third one is the best hour of the week. Students grumble, then quietly rewrite the criterion twice.

The fair rubric

A rubric is only fair if two people applying it in the same room land on the same number. Otherwise you're not grading work, you're grading mood.

{
  "criteria": [
    {"id": "R1", "name": "rebuild", "weight": 3, "pass": "bootstrap.sh runs on an empty box and prints a build stamp"},
    {"id": "R2", "name": "repro",   "weight": 3, "pass": "two runs from the same manifest produce identical output bytes"},
    {"id": "R3", "name": "log",     "weight": 2, "pass": "runs/latest.json names model id, fixture hash, and call count"},
    {"id": "R4", "name": "scope",   "weight": 2, "pass": "no edits outside allowed_paths"}
  ],
  "disagreement_rule": "if two graders differ on any criterion, neither score counts until both re-read the manifest"
}

And a twenty-line grader, so the rubric is executable instead of decorative:

import json, sys

def grade(rubric_path, run_path):
    rubric = json.load(open(rubric_path))
    run    = json.load(open(run_path))
    earned = 0
    for c in rubric["criteria"]:
        ok = bool(run.get("checks", {}).get(c["id"]))
        print(f"{c['id']:>3}  {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {c['name']}")
        earned += c["weight"] if ok else 0
    total = sum(c["weight"] for c in rubric["criteria"])
    return earned, total

if __name__ == "__main__":
    earned, total = grade(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])
    print(f"score {earned}/{total}")
    sys.exit(0 if earned == total else 1)

Then the drill that makes it real: two students grade the same run file, separately, no talking. Different score? The rubric is broken, not the run. Fix the wording of the criterion and try again. That loop — not the agent output — is the skill being taught.

Limitations, honestly

  • Free infrastructure recycles. A box can vanish between checkpoint two and three. That is the lesson, but it also eats lab time.
  • Shared queues make wall clock noisy. So don't grade speed. Grade recorded call counts.
  • The grader reads logs, not code. Pair it with a human read, or students optimize for the log format.
  • bootstrap.sh assumes network access and a Debian-ish base. Porting it elsewhere is part of the assignment, not a footnote.
  • These scripts are a skeleton. I haven't validated them across a distro matrix — adapt, then stamp your own manifest.

Who should not use this

  • Teams that need one fixed production model with compliance paperwork. Pin something stable instead.
  • Courses where the environment isn't the lesson. A pure algorithms unit gets overhead and nothing back.
  • Anyone who can't tolerate a free tier that changes shape mid-semester. Grade the contract, or pay for predictable hardware.

Try it, then break it

Run the lab once with a classmate grading you blind. Then ask the only question that survives contact with a deadline: could a stranger rebuild this from your repo on a Tuesday you didn't plan for?

If you'd rather not provision anything yourself just to find out, the free server option and the free model access are the cheapest way to start — check the project page for what's actually available today.

title: Ready to Make Your Web App Speak? No External TTS API Required
description:
Your browser does more than run your app. It can give it a voice, too.

Adding TTS (text-to-speech) capability to your web app doesn't necessarily require a separately hosted text-to-speech solution, audio file generation, or the addition of any external dependencies to your application.

I initially thought I'd need an external TTS service to make sentences playable in my app. But while looking into it, I found out that my browser could already do the job with just a few lines of JavaScript. No extra service, no audio files. I hadn't expected it to be that simple.

How It Works

The Web Speech API is, indeed, an interface providing speech synthesis.

It exposes methods and properties which provide access to the speech synthesis capabilities of the browser.

It turns out that creating a SpeechSynthesisUtterance instance and calling speak on it simply queues up the speech request for synthesis by the implementation which powers the API.

The quality of the synthesized speech, the voices available for selection, and even the specific speaker voice used will vary depending on the browser, the operating system, and the speech synthesis implementation in use.

That also means your application does not need to generate an audio file or send any text to some server in order to use this API.

The general flow looks like this:

application → Web Speech API → speech synthesis implementation → audio output.

How do you get started?

In other words, your application doesn't necessarily have direct access to the speaker voice. That will always be a part of whatever system the application is running on. The same code, therefore, can produce somewhat different results on different devices.

The Web Speech API provides the JavaScript interfaces for working with speech: recognition and synthesis. We only need the latter (synthesis) for the purposes of this article.

Here's a minimal, safe helper:

function speak(text) {
  if (
    !("speechSynthesis" in window) ||
    !("SpeechSynthesisUtterance" in window)
  ) {
    console.warn("Speech synthesis is not supported.");
    return;
  }

  window.speechSynthesis.cancel();

  const utterance = new SpeechSynthesisUtterance(text);
  utterance.lang = "en-US";

  window.speechSynthesis.speak(utterance);
}

Calling cancel() stops the current speech and clears queued utterances. This is useful when a new message should replace the current one, but not when you want queued messages to play in order.

That's enough to queue a speech request. You can also tweak values like speaking rate or pitch and select from available voices.

But how does this work behind the scenes? What are the limits to this approach? And what should you know before adding this to your application?

What the Native Speech Synthesis Does Not Offer

It's worth noting that the Web Speech API is generally convenient to use, but is still limited in some ways.

These limitations become more apparent when you go to production.

1. Voices and Their Qualities Can Vary

It can be challenging to select the right voice for the right purpose if you can't audition voices or test how they sound on target devices.

Setting the language with utterance.lang = "en-US"; only tells the speech synthesizer which language to use. It doesn't specify an accent, a speaker, or any particular quality of the voice.

For language learning applications (or other uses), voice quality and accent can be critically important.

There is also a common gotcha: in some browsers, speechSynthesis.getVoices() returns an empty list on the first call. The voices load asynchronously, and the browser fires a voiceschanged event when they are ready. So it's safer to wait for them:

function loadVoices() {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const voices = window.speechSynthesis.getVoices();
    if (voices.length) return resolve(voices);

    window.speechSynthesis.addEventListener(
      "voiceschanged",
      () => resolve(window.speechSynthesis.getVoices()),
      { once: true }
    );
  });
}

Once the voices are available, you can pick the closest match and fall back gracefully:

async function pickVoice(lang = "en-US") {
  const voices = await loadVoices();

  return (
    voices.find((v) => v.lang === lang) ??  // exact match
    voices.find((v) => v.lang.startsWith(lang.split("-")[0])) ?? // same language
    null   // browser default
  );
}

const utterance = new SpeechSynthesisUtterance("Hello! How are you today?");
utterance.lang = "en-US";

const voice = await pickVoice("en-US");
if (voice) utterance.voice = voice;

window.speechSynthesis.speak(utterance);

If no suitable voice is found, leaving utterance.voice unset lets the browser use its default voice for the given language.

What to do:

Wait for the voice list before selecting a voice. Pick the closest match for your target language and provide a fallback. Make sure the voices you rely on exist on your target devices and operating systems. Test with text, numbers, and punctuation on those devices.

2. Playback Is Asynchronous and Platform-Dependent

SpeechSynthesisUtterance simply queues up speech for playback.

It has no effect on whether or when the speech actually plays.

There may be other queued utterances which cause yours to start later than expected.

You can listen for events, such as 'start', 'end', or 'error'.

The Web Speech API is generally consistent across browsers, but variations between operating systems still affect how speech is handled.

Mobile is generally a bigger concern for differences in voices and overall speech behavior.

What to do:

Use and manage the utterance queue explicitly.

Make sure to call speechSynthesis.cancel() when removing queued items. Check that the necessary interfaces are available at run time rather than assuming they will always be there. Pay attention to the behaviors and quirks of the particular browsers and mobile platforms you support.

3. It Isn't Always Totally Offline

Your application may not need to handle a TTS API hosted elsewhere, but that doesn't mean that the speech synthesis implementation doesn't require a network connection to operate.

This is especially true on mobile, where network connections are generally less reliable.

A hosted TTS service may offer more consistent performance than some native implementations.

What to do:

If your application makes essential use of text-to-speech and requires offline or low-network support, test with the actual implementation to make sure that it satisfies your requirements.

When Should You Use Native Speech Synthesis?

Use native speech synthesis for quick, simple implementations where voice consistency isn't essential. Choose a hosted TTS service when you need greater control over voice quality and output.

Neither is universally better. It depends on your application's needs.

Speech synthesis can support accessibility, language learning, and reading apps. The key is knowing what the browser can do and where its limits lie.

And Speech Is Just the Beginning

Browsers already come with a growing collection of APIs that let us do more with less infrastructure.

For example:

  • Clipboard API: Copy text to the clipboard without relying on an extra library.
  • Web Share API: Open the device's native sharing interface to share links, text, or files.
  • Web Audio API: Generate sounds, build audio effects, and process audio directly in the browser.
  • Geolocation API: Access a user's location with their permission.
  • Vibration API: Trigger vibration patterns on supported devices.
  • Web Crypto API: Perform cryptographic operations using built-in browser capabilities.

They're worth knowing about before adding another dependency to a project.

I used to think about the files and services I needed to add. Now, I find it just as useful to ask a different question first:

What can the browser already do?

And that might be the beginning of another article.

Sometimes, we're so busy looking for something new that we forget to look at what we already have.

See you in the next article!

title: SATOR: Backpropagation-Free 3D Test-Time Adaptation via Sample-Adaptive Token Routing
description:
arXiv:2610.21367v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) mitigates the performance degradation of source-pretrained models on unlabeled test data under distribution shifts. Recent backpropagation-free token-purging methods address 3D point cloud distribution shifts by filtering unreliable tokens. However, their reliance on predefined purge-size candidates requires multiple forward passes per sample and increases inference cost. We propose SATOR (Sample-Adaptive TOken Routing), a source-free and backpropagation-free 3D TTA framework that eliminates this search by deriving both the partitioning threshold and routing decision directly from each sample. SATOR computes token abnormality scores from complementary attention and geometric relation graphs. It then derives a sample-specific partition into retained and pruned tokens via Otsu-based separability, without evaluating candidate sizes. Keep-ratio-calibrated routing then selects the pruned prediction only when its entropy, penalized by the keep ratio, is lower than that of the original prediction. Experiments on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C demonstrate that SATOR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on three 3D corruption benchmarks.

title: Bring your agent to Notion with Chat SDK
description:
Your team already works in Notion. Now your agent can too.

With the new Notion adapter for Chat SDK, the same agent you run on Slack, Discord, GitHub, Teams, or WhatsApp can join comment discussions on your Notion pages, no separate codebase required.

Each Notion page maps to a channel and each comment thread to a thread, so replies stay threaded automatically.

The adapter supports mentions, message editing, conversation history, and up to three file attachments. By default, your bot replies when @-mentioned and where mentions aren't available in a workspace, it can trigger on a keyword or on all comments instead.

Notion doesn't support buttons, modals, or reactions, and cards render as markdown. Discussions can start at the page or block level, but not on inline text ranges. History fetches return only open comments.

Read the documentation to get started, browse the directory, or build your own.

title: ZoomCap: Evidence-Routed Visual Zooming for Recoverable Visual Information Transfer
description:
arXiv:2610.21320v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Detailed captions transfer visual information into vision-language model supervision, but quality is easily conflated with length: long single-pass outputs still miss small objects, text, and spatial relations or promote uncertain observations into confident claims. We formulate fine-grained captioning as recoverable visual information transfer, in which a teacher acquires missing evidence under a finite observation budget and converts it into reusable supervision. ZoomCap uses a draft caption to route conditional knowledge retrieval, OCR-sensitive reading, coverage-gap recovery, and adaptive visual zooming, allocating deeper crops only to the most complex eligible region, deriving spatial relations from grounded geometry, and fusing non-duplicate evidence. We also introduce FactCycle, which scores caption-derived atomic claims on two blind anchors--source image (truthfulness) and reconstruction (realizability)--separating fabrication from generator loss claim by claim; human and multi-judge comparisons complement this fact-level view. Against Qwen3.5-397B-A17B captions, ZoomCap achieves an 81.9% human tie-adjusted preference score with a teacher over 10x smaller, and FactCycle counts 52.4 transferred claims per image vs. 31.5 for ScaleCap. The evidence also transfers: in continual pre-training, ZoomCap-450K improves the 11-benchmark average by 1.31-2.38 points over the strongest competing corpus and Ling-Tiny-VL-v3 gains 1.4 points on a production document/OCR monitor suite (1.5 on perception) at 60B tokens; in medical pre-training, 2.64M ZoomCap-captioned images improve five VQA benchmarks by 3.04 points (vs. 1.76 for same-image Gemini-3.1-Pro captions).

title: The AI Automation Billing Trap Nobody Explains (Zapier vs Make vs n8n)
description:
If you are building AI workflows for your business or clients, you are probably choosing between the big three: Zapier, Make, and n8n.
Most people just look at the starting price tier (like "$20/month"), enter their credit card details, and hit subscribe.
That is a massive mistake. Here is why.
The real trap isn't the monthly base fee; it's how these platforms count your usage when AI gets involved. A single AI loop that processes incoming leads, filters them, runs a prompt, and updates a database can cost you $30 on one platform and explode to $400+ on another within a single week.
Here is the quick breakdown of how they quietly drain your budget:
• Zapier (The Task Trap): Zapier charges per completed "Task". It sounds fair, but if your workflow uses filters, paths, or webhooks, those tasks vanish instantly. It has the best UI and integrations, but scaling high-volume AI loops here will break the bank.
• Make (The Operation Explosion): Make charges per "Operation". Every single bubble or module that touches data counts as an execution. If an AI module processes 10 items in a bundle, that counts as 10 separate operations. It is much cheaper than Zapier for bulk data, but a poorly optimized workflow can eat through your monthly limit in 48 hours.
• n8n (The Fair Competitor): n8n is built heavily for advanced workflows and developers. Their cloud version is priced fairly, but their real superpower is the Open-Source Community Edition. If you know how to self-host it on a basic $5 VPS or your own machine, your execution costs drop to literally zero.

📊 The Hand-Checked Cost Comparison Table

We got tired of the marketing hype and affiliate sales pitches. So, we opened the pricing pages, read all the small print, and calculated the exact multi-tier billing math by hand.
If you want to see the exact numbers, hidden caps, and which platform fits your specific monthly volume so you don't get trapped by a surprise bill:
👉 Click here to see the full Zapier vs Make vs n8n breakdown on VOXA

title: Perception or Reasoning? Diagnosing and Tackling Reinforcement Learning Bottlenecks in VLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.21380v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning has brought strong gains to language model reasoning, but its improvements on visual tasks remain less consistent. One difficulty is that visual task failures can arise from different sources: the same benchmark may be limited by perception for one model and by reasoning for another. We introduce Perception and Reasoning Attribution (PARA), which measures the remaining perceptual and reasoning headroom of each model--benchmark pair by comparing how many current errors are recovered with more accurate visual information versus a stronger reasoner. Across 4 vision-language models and 17 multimodal benchmarks, PARA broadly agrees with the expected characteristics of existing benchmarks while revealing substantial model-specific variation. More importantly, it shows that RL gains become smaller as perceptual headroom increases, but larger when reasoning explains more of the recoverable errors, suggesting that current RL exploits reasoning headroom more effectively than perceptual headroom. Motivated by this gap, we analyze how existing RL objectives affect visual perception and find that reward- and token-level signals influence visual attention only indirectly. We therefore propose GRAD, a group-relative attention distillation objective that uses the best rollout in each group to directly guide the visual attention of weaker rollouts. GRAD consistently improves performance across two model scales and seven benchmarks, and further complements existing RL methods.

title: Claude Fable 5.1 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Claude Fable 5.1 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway.

Fable 5.1 improvements compared to previous Claude models are concentrated in long, multi-stage work like agentic coding, knowledge work, and research that takes several rounds of searching and following up.

Anthropic ships Fable 5.1 with cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Finding vulnerabilities in source code is allowed, but some routine coding and debugging may still be refused. To ensure requests are still serviced when the safety classifiers are triggered, use model fallbacks.

Add a models array to providerOptions.gateway listing the models to try. AI Gateway sends the request to Fable 5.1 first, and if Anthropic refuses it, works down the array in order and returns the response from the first model that succeeds:

This request falls back to Opus 5, then Sonnet 5, if a safety classifier is triggered. The same models option works on every AI Gateway API format, including Chat Completions, Messages, and OpenAI Responses.

Try Fable 5.1 in the model playground.

title: Purify Before You Align: Improving Representation Alignment for Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20761v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Representation alignment improves and accelerates diffusion training by encouraging intermediate features to match a pretrained visual encoder. However, standard alignment matches pretrained representations without distinguishing what information may be more useful for generation. We introduce local appearance purification (LAP), which improves generation quality and makes encoders such as MAE more effective alignment targets by removing locally predictable content and aligning to the residual. LAP modifies only the alignment target, and requires no changes to diffusion training or inference. Through controlled interventions within a fixed encoder, we show that effective alignment depends on what information the target emphasizes, not simply how much image information it contains. Our theory gives a variational interpretation of standard alignment and, for fixed local predictors, a sum of token-wise information bounds conditioned on local appearance. To understand why purification benefits some encoders more than others, we derive an exact constant-readout test that measures how well the target can be matched without using the diffusion model's hidden state. LAP improves generation quality across five pretrained representations (MAE, AIMv2, CLIP, DINOv2, DINOv3), with the largest gain for MAE: on ImageNet-256 with SiT-B/2, it reduces FID from $53.1$ to $42.3$. Its gains persist with stronger alignment recipes and tokenizers. Computed before diffusion training, the constant-readout score predicts the benefit of purification (Spearman $\rho=0.94$ across 13 encoders).

title: Giving an Open-Weight Language Model the Vote in Among Us Meetings
description:
Meetings are the part of Among Us that a language model looks made for. The crew is trying to find the few hidden impostors among them. When a body is found, everyone talks, states where they were, accuses someone and votes, and whoever gets the most votes is thrown off the ship. My simulator's bots normally vote with small recurrent networks trained on thousands of meetings, which read who saw whom and who accused whom and output a suspicion score for each player. I expected that handing the meeting to a real language model, one that could argue, ask questions and catch lies, would make the crew better at finding impostors. Across six setups it never did.

The setup

The model is gpt-oss:20b, an open-weight model from OpenAI, running locally through Ollama. In a meeting every surviving player, crewmate or impostor, is a separate prompt to the same model, and its reply is that player's speech and vote. A crewmate's prompt contains only what that player could know: where it walked, who it saw and when, any kill or vent it witnessed, and the table of where everyone claims to have been. An impostor's prompt also contains its real movements, marked secret, and permission to lie. Movement, tasks and kills between meetings stay with the trained bots; only the meetings change.

There were three meeting formats. In the first, players speak in rounds and may ask each other structured questions ("where were you 20 seconds ago?"). In the second, each crewmate's prompt also includes the voting network's guesses as an "instinct" (described below). In the third, players hold a free conversation in turns, again with the instinct.

The comparison is the same bots in the same lobby with the trained networks doing all the voting, crew and impostors alike, over 300 games. So the language model replaces both sides' votes at once, and a worse result for the crew could come from worse crew votes or from better impostor talk; the runs below cannot tell those apart. I measured the baselines after the language-model runs, on the current version of the simulator. Five of the six language-model runs used an earlier version, which I mark. The bots come from different leagues (training runs), and each league trained its own voting network.

Eight players, two impostors

These used the bots from my second league. The network baseline did not record wrongly ejected crewmates.

who votes games crew wins impostors ejected per game crewmates ejected per game
the trained networks (current version) 300 52.0% 0.99 not recorded
gpt-oss, rounds and questions (earlier version) 16 2 (12.5%) 0.06 0.94
gpt-oss, rounds and questions plus the instinct (earlier version) 16 8 (50%) 1.00 0.63
gpt-oss, conversation plus the instinct (earlier version) 16 6 (37.5%) 0.81 0.69

On its own the language model did much worse than the networks. The crew ejected an impostor once in sixteen games and an innocent crewmate almost every game, and won 2 games of 16 where the networks' crew wins about half. That gap is well beyond chance (one-sided Fisher exact test, p = 0.0017), with the caveat that the simulator version differed.

The "instinct" put the voting network's numbers into each crewmate's prompt as a line of text. It opens "Your instinct (a trained model reading everything YOU saw, plus the accusations so far; it picks the right impostor about 70% of the time, so weigh it with the facts):" and then gives each other player's percentage chance of being an impostor. The 70% in that line was my rough estimate when I wrote the prompt, not a measurement. With the instinct and the rounds format, the crew won 8 of 16, indistinguishable from the networks (p = 0.54). If the model mostly voted the way the instinct line pointed, that is the result you would expect; I did not measure how often it did.

Fifteen players, three impostors

In these lobbies the crew wins more often under both kinds of voting, and the ordering held. All three runs use the conversation format with the instinct.

bots networks voting (300 games, current version) gpt-oss, conversation plus the instinct
league 2 89.7% 10 of 12 (83%), earlier version
league 4 84.7% 11 of 20 (55%), earlier version
league 6 93.3% 16 of 20 (80%), current version

The league 6 row is the only like-for-like comparison: same bots, same simulator version, same settings, run on the same day. Sixteen of 20 against 280 of 300 is a one-sided Fisher exact p of 0.052, and the 95% interval on 16 of 20 is 58% to 92%. On its own, that row is suggestive rather than settled. The league 4 gap is far larger (p = 0.0025), but between that run and its baseline I changed how meetings treat a running sabotage and what impostors know when they shut doors, so I would not lean on it.

Counting across all six setups: in one the language model was clearly worse than the networks (eight players, no instinct). In the five with the instinct it matched the networks once and fell short four times, by margins that are individually too small or too confounded to be conclusive. I have no setup in which it did better.

What it costs

A 15-player game with gpt-oss meetings took 524 seconds of wall-clock time on average in the league 6 run. Nearly all of that was about 4 meetings' worth of turns, at one model call per player per turn. The networks' votes need no model calls at all. That would be a fair price for better votes, and the votes were not better.

Why I think it happens

This part is my reading rather than a measurement. The networks have an unfair advantage that is also the point: they were trained on the outcomes of thousands of meetings in this simulator, so their suspicion scores are calibrated against who actually turned out to be an impostor here. The language model brings general knowledge of how deception sounds. An impostor here does not sound like anything; it names a room, and the only way to catch the lie is to check that claim against who could have seen that room. The prompts contain what each player saw. Nothing in the results suggests the model made that check reliably, and with the network's numbers in the prompt it did no better than the network.

An earlier benchmark of mine, which ranked language models on spotting liars in Mafia, found first-day accusations at chance. There, on the first day, nothing about the liars is knowable yet. Here the evidence is in each crewmate's prompt, which makes falling short of a small network harder to excuse.

The simulator, the meeting prompts and the measurement scripts were written by Claude Code at my direction. The code is not public. Every figure above comes from the result files the runs wrote, and the significance tests are recomputed from those counts.

title: Failed Job Retry Explained: Managed Queues, Idempotency, and Dead Letters
description:
Short answer: for production failed-job retries, choose a managed queue when reducing Redis maintenance and getting a built-in dead-letter pattern matter more than keeping scheduling inside the application; whichever queue you choose, assume at-least-once delivery and make the consumer idempotent before it acknowledges work.

For a property manager's renewal reminder, the business deadline is the invariant. A retry system is successful when one reminder takes effect by that deadline, even if the same message reaches a worker twice. It is not successful merely because a dashboard says that a job ran.

That distinction drives the runbook below.

What should Node.js teams compare in BullMQ, SQS, managed queue retries, and DLQs?

Start with delivery guarantees, then count the operational work required to preserve them. BullMQ is fast to introduce in a Node.js application, but it also introduces Redis operations that a small team may not want for a basic retry path. A managed queue decouples retry traffic from the web process and lets workers consume independently. Neither choice removes the need for application-level idempotency when delivery is at least once.

“Easiest” depends on which burden the team can carry. Embedded scheduling makes the first commit small; the capacity plan still has to include Redis availability, queue depth, worker saturation, retry storms, and the person paged for each. A managed service moves part of that burden outside the team, though it creates a provider contract and migration question. Cheapest has the same ambiguity: an invoice comparison that omits engineering time and on-call load is incomplete, while an operations comparison that ignores usage charges is also incomplete. I’m not sure which side wins for a given portfolio without its arrival rate, deadline distribution, and staffing model.

Here is the buy-versus-build cut I would use before approving the design:

Option Operations owner Delivery posture for this design Prefer it when Avoid it when
BullMQ Your team operates the Redis-backed path Consumer idempotency remains part of the application The team already operates Redis and wants a Node.js-embedded job library The point of the project is to remove Redis maintenance
Amazon SQS Managed service Design the worker for at-least-once handling and a DLQ pattern AWS is already the accepted provider boundary A cloud-specific contract is unacceptable
Google Cloud Pub/Sub Managed service Keep the business effect idempotent before acknowledgment GCP is already the accepted provider boundary The application must remain independent of that provider contract
RabbitMQ Your team or a chosen host operates the broker Define retry and dead-letter behavior as part of broker operations The team deliberately wants broker control A small team does not want another stateful service on call
Infrai Managed service behind one REST contract Standard queues are at least once, so the same idempotency rule applies The team wants to swap the provider behind the capability without changing application code; one REST API works from any runtime without installing an SDK The workload needs workflow DAGs, fan-out/join, or Kafka-style replay

The last row is a strong portability option, not a universal winner. For Infrai, the concrete advantage is one REST API for the entire backend: it is pure HTTP, requires no SDK installation, and works from any language or runtime. Its contract stays put while the provider behind the capability moves. The catch is that abstraction trades some provider-specific control for a stable application boundary, and it is not suitable for a workflow engine: use Temporal or Airflow when the job is a DAG, and keep RabbitMQ when broker-level control is the actual requirement.

Define the failure signal before choosing the retry mechanism

The renewal service needs an SLO stated in business terms, such as “accepted renewal reminders produce one recorded send effect by the business deadline.” The exact target and error budget belong to the product and platform teams; inventing a percentage here would hide the decision rather than clarify it. Measure queue age against time remaining until the deadline, not just aggregate throughput. A queue with low average latency can still strand the oldest reminder.

Watch three signals: age of the oldest eligible message, the ratio of retry attempts to first attempts, and dead-letter growth. Queue depth alone is weak. Ten thousand reminders due next week can be healthy, while twenty reminders due in two minutes can already exhaust the available worker capacity.

Capacity planning should use the deadline window. If 12,000 reminders become eligible across a 20-minute window and a worker safely completes 10 per second, the arithmetic says 1,200 seconds of single-worker service time before retry overhead. That is the entire window, so one worker has no failure margin. Those figures are an illustrative calculation, not a benchmark; substitute measured service time, the real due-time distribution, and a retry amplification factor from production observations.

Push delivery deserves one early check. It is available only when the consumer is a public HTTPS endpoint. An internal-only worker cannot receive a push subscription, so use pull consumption instead. This is a topology decision, not a late deployment toggle.

Make the worker idempotent before enabling retries

The safe order is receive, claim the business operation using an idempotency key in the application database, apply the effect, record completion, and only then acknowledge the queue message. If another delivery finds the same completed key, it acknowledges without repeating the effect. If two workers race, a unique constraint decides which one owns the claim.

Do this first.

The following runnable Go program publishes through the real queue route and then models the consumer-side contract. Export INFRAI_API_ORIGIN using the API origin shown in the account documentation, export INFRAI_API_KEY, set INFRAI_QUEUE_PUBLISH_BODY to a JSON file produced from the public queue.publish discovery schema, and run it with go run main.go. Reading that discovered body rather than printing guessed fields here keeps the example aligned with the live request schema. The local store stands in for the database transaction boundary, and the duplicate delivery demonstrates the required behavior. In production, make ClaimAndApply a database transaction whose unique key is stable business data such as the lease ID plus renewal date; a random key generated by each retry cannot deduplicate anything.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Reminder struct {
    IdempotencyKey string
    LeaseID        string
    RenewalDate    string
}

type Store struct {
    mu        sync.Mutex
    completed map[string]struct{}
}

func (s *Store) ClaimAndApply(_ context.Context, r Reminder) (bool, error) {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()

    if _, exists := s.completed[r.IdempotencyKey]; exists {
        return false, nil
    }

    // Replace this print with the reminder effect inside the same transaction.
    fmt.Printf("record reminder for lease=%s renewal=%s\n", r.LeaseID, r.RenewalDate)
    s.completed[r.IdempotencyKey] = struct{}{}
    return true, nil
}

func handle(ctx context.Context, store *Store, r Reminder) error {
    applied, err := store.ClaimAndApply(ctx, r)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("claim reminder: %w", err)
    }
    if !applied {
        fmt.Printf("duplicate suppressed: %s\n", r.IdempotencyKey)
    }
    // A real consumer acknowledges only after this function succeeds.
    return nil
}

func publish(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, origin string, body []byte, key string) error {
    endpoint := strings.TrimRight(origin, "/") + "/v1/queue/publish"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("build publish request: %w", err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "lease-4182:renewal:2026-11-01")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("publish reminder: %w", err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("read publish response: %w", readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Printf("publish accepted: %s\n", responseBody)
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("publish status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody)
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("publish remained rate limited after 5 attempts")
}

func main() {
    origin := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_ORIGIN")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    bodyPath := os.Getenv("INFRAI_QUEUE_PUBLISH_BODY")
    if origin == "" || key == "" || bodyPath == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_ORIGIN, INFRAI_API_KEY, and INFRAI_QUEUE_PUBLISH_BODY")
    }
    body, err := os.ReadFile(bodyPath)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := publish(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}, origin, body, key); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    store := &Store{completed: make(map[string]struct{})}
    r := Reminder{
        IdempotencyKey: "lease-4182:renewal:2026-11-01",
        LeaseID:        "lease-4182",
        RenewalDate:    "2026-11-01",
    }

    for delivery := 1; delivery <= 2; delivery++ {
        if err := handle(ctx, store, r); err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
    }
}

The example deliberately does not couple the business handler to BullMQ, SQS, or another transport. Put the vendor adapter outside handle. That boundary makes migration testable and stops queue receipt IDs, SDK exceptions, and acknowledgment tokens from leaking into the renewal domain.

For a remote publish operation, treat HTTP 429 as backpressure: honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff. A write retry also needs a stable client-supplied idempotency key. Don't tight-loop. A retry storm arriving just before the deadline is exactly when an unbounded loop does the most damage.

Verify delivery, dead letters, and the business deadline

Verification starts with duplicates, not the happy path. Publish the same logical reminder twice under one idempotency key and confirm that the business table contains one completed effect. Then force the worker's application operation to fail, leave the message unacknowledged or negatively acknowledge it according to the chosen adapter, and confirm that retry state is visible without recording completion.

Next, exhaust the configured retry policy in a test environment and verify that the message reaches the dead-letter path with enough identity to investigate it. Redriving a dead letter must preserve the original business idempotency key; changing that key turns redrive into a second effect. Alert on sustained dead-letter growth and on oldest-message age consuming the remaining business-deadline budget. A raw DLQ count without a time window or deadline context will page the team at the wrong times.

There are hard boundaries to include in the test plan for the portable managed option: delayed delivery is limited to 7 days, a message is limited to 256 KB, retention is at most 30 days, and acknowledged messages are deleted. FIFO deduplication covers only a 5-minute window. Those limits reinforce the same architecture: store renewal state in the application database, place a compact reference on the queue, and never treat the queue as the system of record or a replay log.

Be skeptical of green dashboards. The acceptance check is the recorded business effect, joined to the intended deadline, with duplicates suppressed.

Roll back without losing the retry state

Rollback should stop new publishes to the new adapter before it stops consumers, because draining known work is safer than creating two active ingress paths. Keep the previous adapter deployable, compare outstanding queue age and application completion records, then switch the publisher back. Do not “fix” uncertainty by replaying every reminder: reconcile by idempotency key and republish only missing business operations.

If the deadline can be more than 7 days away, retain the future reminder in the application database and enqueue it only when it enters the supported delay window. For long-running work, a scheduler should trigger enqueueing and a worker should consume the job; an individual cron execution is capped at 900 seconds. Paused cron schedules do not backfill missed triggers, so rollback and resume procedures must reconcile missed deadlines from the database.

The final decision rule is narrow: use BullMQ when existing Redis ownership makes the embedded path genuinely cheap; use SQS or Pub/Sub when the corresponding cloud boundary is already intentional; use RabbitMQ when broker control is worth operating it; consider a stable multi-provider REST contract when portability and credential simplicity dominate. In every case, the application database owns the idempotency decision. The queue only delivers attempts.

References

  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/dlx
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429
  • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_backoff

title: Wrong Votes, Right Gradients: Why Majority-Vote Rewards Track Verifiable RL
description:
arXiv:2610.20898v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with self-generated labels, such as majority vote over a model's own samples, often recovers most of the gain of training with verifiable rewards. This is puzzling from the usual prompt-level view, in which majority vote only returns a model's modal answer and cannot add information about correctness. We argue that the relevant unit is the batch-level update. Because parameters are shared, a prompt's own gradient accounts for less than 1\% of the change in that prompt's output at practical batch sizes, so a wrong label matters only to the extent that label errors share a direction across prompts. We decompose the majority-vote update into shrinkage and misdirection relative to the gold update, and show that misdirection vanishes with batch size whenever errors are incoherent across prompts, however often the labels are wrong. Measuring per-response gradients on five models, we find that majority-vote errors are as incoherent as a random-reward null, that the majority-vote update agrees with the gold update as closely as two independent gold updates agree with each other, and that its noise-corrected cosine with the gold update is 1 within error. Randomly flipping up to 30\% of gold labels leaves the update direction intact, while the same fraction flipped by a shared rule destroys it, and rewards that favor a kind of response on every prompt, such as a learned reward model, fall measurably short. The equivalence holds at every checkpoint we examine but is local: gold-reward training still ends ahead on held-out majority accuracy. Error coherence, not error rate, determines when self-generated labels can stand in for verification.

title: TIL: Troubleshooting SELinux Issues During GBase Database Installation
description:
Today I learned an important lesson while troubleshooting GBase Database (GBase 8s) installation: SELinux configuration can affect database startup, file access, and network connectivity on Linux systems.

SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) enforces security policies that restrict what processes can access. If a policy blocks an operation required by GBase Database, the result may be a startup failure or unexpected permission error.

1. Check the SELinux Status

Before installing GBase Database, check the current SELinux mode:

getenforce
sestatus

The output will typically indicate one of three modes:

  • Enforcing: SELinux actively enforces security policies.
  • Permissive: Policy violations are logged but not blocked.
  • Disabled: SELinux is turned off.

2. Temporarily Switch to Permissive Mode

For troubleshooting, you can temporarily switch SELinux to permissive mode:

sudo setenforce 0
getenforce

The expected output is:

Permissive

This change lasts until the system reboots or the mode is changed again. It does not disable SELinux completely.

Important: Permissive mode is a diagnostic measure, not a universal installation requirement. Review security audit logs and follow the requirements for your specific GBase 8s version before changing production security settings.

3. Check SELinux Alongside Other Environment Settings

When troubleshooting GBase Database installation or startup issues, check these areas together:

  • SELinux: Review audit logs for policy denials.
  • Firewall: Verify that required database ports are accessible.
  • File permissions: Confirm that the database account can access required directories.
  • System configuration: Validate hostname resolution in /etc/hosts.
  • Dependencies: Check required system libraries and packages.

For example, search recent SELinux audit events with:

sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts recent

This can help identify access denials that may explain the problem.

Final Takeaway

Successful GBase Database deployment starts with a properly prepared Linux environment. Understanding SELinux, firewall rules, file permissions, and system dependencies can help reduce installation failures and simplify troubleshooting.

Rather than automatically disabling security controls, identify the actual cause and apply the appropriate configuration.

How do you troubleshoot SELinux-related issues during Linux database deployment?
