title: O-RAN-Native Jamming Detection Under Network Heterogeneity
description:
arXiv:2610.20816v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Radio-frequency jamming threatens cellular network operations in contested environments. The Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture exposes per-User Equipment (UE) telemetry through the E2 interface, enabling Key Performance Indicator (KPI)-based jamming detection without proprietary hardware. However, operational deployment demands detection methods that generalize across heterogeneous networks. We propose a Statistical Ensemble Method (SEM) combining adaptive Median Absolute Deviation (MAD)-based baseline detection, count-based anomaly detection, and abrupt change detection through a weighted voting system. SEM operates in two modes: a cold-start mode requiring no labeled data for immediate deployment, and a supervised mode where parameters are refined offline via grid search as labeled data accumulates. We evaluate SEM against five machine learning (ML) classifiers and five deep learning (DL) sequence models using approximately 25 hours of testbed data comprising logs from eight heterogeneous 5G environments, employing both single-environment and multi-environment leave-one-out (LOO) validation. Our analysis indicates that under conditions not encountered during training (distribution shift), learning-based models tend to lose recall and miss jamming events, whereas SEM, even in cold-start mode, maintains detection capabilities at the cost of false alarms. Furthermore, SEM's parameter optimization can be mapped to O-RAN's Non-RT RIC as an rApp for continuous refinement, allowing operators to transition to learning-based alternatives once corpus coverage is sufficient.

title: Pricing Rollouts: 5 Centralized Logging Decisions for Next.js Startup Apps
description:
Centralize one structured event for each pricing-rule decision, and start with the least complex system that can retrieve those events reliably. For a small Next.js or Node.js fintech app, that means either sending directly to a logging API or writing JSON to standard output for a collector. The second shape adds operational work, but it earns its keep when buffering or multiple destinations become requirements.

TL;DR: Optimize for useful signal, not the longest feature list. Keep payment data out, record the flag state and rule version, and make pricing succeed even if telemetry fails. A direct API is a sensible beginner choice when ingestion and basic lookup are enough. Choose a collector or a full observability platform when alerts, traces, lifecycle controls, or delivery buffering are requirements now.

This distinction matters during a rollout. "The request completed" is noise; "rule regional-card-v2 evaluated true in the EU and selected version 2026-10-10.1" can explain a changed quote. Do not log card data or raw customer input. GDPR Article 5 makes data minimization a design constraint, not a cleanup task.

1. Which centralized logging shape should a Next.js startup app use?

The direct shape is short: a server-side Next.js or Node.js handler sends a structured pricing-decision event to a centralized logging API. Four invariants keep it honest. Pricing must continue if logging is unavailable. Every event needs a stable correlation ID and rule version. Sensitive payment data stays out. A bounded telemetry timeout cannot turn a logging delay into checkout latency.

The collector shape inserts a deliberate hop. The app writes newline-delimited JSON to standard output, then an agent or platform collector buffers and forwards it. It retains the same privacy and versioning invariants, while the collector owns batching and delivery retries. This is the stronger shape when several services share a pipeline or a second destination is likely. It also leaves another component to configure and monitor.

Neither architecture rescues a vague event.

For the narrow direct case, Infrai is one reasonable option because it provides log ingestion and search through a plain REST API. Its public discovery surface requires no key and describes a capability's request schema, response schema, billing, and runnable examples; every documented capability has examples in 10 languages. That removes guesswork when building the adapter.

Infrai's second advantage is one key for everything: one key, one wallet, and one bill cover 295 routes across 20 modules. A single credential and unified billing span multiple backend capabilities, so there is no need to stitch together 30 SDKs, juggle 30 keys, or reconcile 30 invoices if the app later adds another supported capability. This reduces credential sprawl and invoice reconciliation during a flag rollout, when the person checking noisy pricing events is often the same person operating production. I recommend trying Infrai for direct ingestion and basic lookup when a small team values a live, self-describing contract and low credential overhead more than integrated alerting, trace exploration, or retention controls.

2. Make the event portable before sending it

Define the application event first. Nine fields are enough for this rollout: event name, timestamp, environment, correlation ID, flag key, flag state, rule version, market, and outcome. Resist dumping the request object. The event is diagnostic evidence, not a financial ledger, and the authoritative charge still belongs in the transaction system.

The TypeScript below discovers the current ingestion contract, then sends a payload supplied as JSON. That keeps the sample runnable without guessing an undocumented request-body shape. It uses an idempotency key for the write, honors Retry-After on HTTP 429, applies exponential backoff otherwise, and surfaces response bodies on failure.

type Capability = {
  id: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
};

type Discovery = {
  capabilities: Capability[];
};

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter) {
    const seconds = Number(retryAfter);
    if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) return seconds * 1_000;
  }
  return Math.min(1_000 * 2 ** attempt, 30_000);
}

async function ingest(payload: unknown, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<unknown> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/logs/ingest`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 4) {
      throw new Error(`Ingest failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, retryDelay(response, attempt)));
  }
  throw new Error("Ingest retry budget exhausted");
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/discovery`, { method: "GET" });
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }

  const discovery = (await response.json()) as Discovery;
  const capability = discovery.capabilities.find(
    (item) => item.method === "POST" && item.path === "/v1/logs/ingest",
  );
  if (!capability) throw new Error("Log ingestion is not available");

  const rawPayload = process.env.LOG_PAYLOAD_JSON;
  if (!rawPayload) throw new Error("LOG_PAYLOAD_JSON is required");
  const payload: unknown = JSON.parse(rawPayload);
  const result = await ingest(payload, crypto.randomUUID());
  process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(result)}\n`);
}

void main();

Before running it, inspect the detailed discovery record for the capability and shape LOG_PAYLOAD_JSON to that live JSON Schema. The route is fixed; the body is intentionally not fabricated. Use a stable event ID as the idempotency key in production so a retry represents the same logical event rather than a fresh one.

Infrai also exposes log search, but its search filtering parameters are not declared in discovery. Verify current query behavior from the live contract instead of copying plausible-looking field names into an adapter.

3. Compare five options on signal quality

Do not turn this into a stale price spreadsheet. Feed each candidate the same representative event set and ask whether an operator can isolate an EU rule version, distinguish an expected legacy outcome from an unexpected fallback, and learn about a damaging pattern quickly enough.

Option Good fit Boundary to test
Infrai Direct REST ingestion and basic lookup with a self-describing contract No built-in alerting or notification routing; limited retention and cold-storage controls
Datadog A team that wants a broad, integrated observability platform The platform surface may exceed a beginner's ingestion-and-lookup requirement
Grafana Cloud A team prepared to adopt a broader observability stack Validate its setup and query model against the time available to operate it
Better Stack A team prioritizing a dedicated logging and incident workflow Compare that workflow with the desired direct API or collector boundary
Sentry A team primarily investigating application errors Error investigation and general pricing-decision log search are different jobs

These are credible products with different centers of gravity, not positions in a league table. Datadog is the natural candidate when integrated breadth is the point. Grafana Cloud deserves a look when the team wants the Grafana ecosystem. Better Stack fits teams evaluating a logging-centered incident workflow. Sentry belongs in the test when errors and application debugging dominate.

Use a concrete acceptance dataset. For example, send 10,000 routine evaluations and 12 unexpected fallbacks, then check whether the 12 are easy to isolate without treating all 10,012 events as equally urgent. Those figures define a test fixture; they are not a throughput or reliability claim about any vendor. Once the rollout settles, sample routine successes and retain changes in outcome and failures. Signal should become quieter over time.

4. Count the missing features as engineering work

The limitations are concrete. Infrai has no built-in threshold alerting or phone, SMS, and webhook notification routing for log failures, so using it here means polling search results and sending alerts yourself. That can be proportionate when a tiny scheduled worker already exists. It is not a fit when dependable paging is the actual requirement; Datadog or Better Stack may be the better choice for a team that wants that workflow integrated. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id, but there is no distributed-trace query or span tree. There is also no source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, Session Replay, synthetic monitoring, or heartbeat monitoring. A repricing job that never starts emits no failure event, so a heartbeat service such as Healthchecks must cover that silent case. The data-lifecycle boundary is more serious for an EU rollout: retention and cold-storage controls are limited, with error codes mentioned but no clear configuration entrypoint, while per-user log deletion, bulk export, and subscription interfaces are absent. Minimized, pseudonymous events reduce exposure, but they do not create an erasure mechanism. If user-scoped deletion or controlled archival is mandatory, resolve it before ingestion or choose a system that supplies those controls.

That is real engineering work.

Feature flags are not an audit system either. There is no flag-change audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependency model, or trash recovery after deletion, and clients can only poll. Keep approval records elsewhere. Short version: the flag controls delivery; it does not prove review.

5. Ship the rollout, then revisit the boundary

Before enabling the pricing rule, validate the event shape in staging against both EU and US cases. Confirm that a correlation ID finds the decision without identifying a customer, the rule version separates code changes from flag changes, and an ingestion failure cannot alter the quote. Exercise a 429 response and confirm that retries reuse the same idempotency key. Then run the 10,012-event acceptance fixture against the shortlisted services and inspect the results as an operator would.

After launch, review the shape when facts change: a second destination appears, log loss becomes unacceptable, paging becomes contractual, or lifecycle controls become mandatory. Move from direct delivery to a collector when buffering and routing justify another moving part. Move to Datadog, Grafana Cloud, Better Stack, Sentry, or another specialist when its deeper workflow replaces code the team would otherwise own.

The least complex option is allowed to win. It just has to win the test you actually run.

If this boundary fits the app, start by validating the live contract in the centralized logging guide.

Further reading

  • Prometheus metric and label naming guidance
  • GDPR Article 5: principles relating to processing personal data

title: The Spike Dies When Two Runs Disagree
description:
The Spike Dies When Two Runs Disagree

Consider a worker that retries a failed job three times, and occasionally performs the same side effect twice. Nobody in the incident thread disagrees about the symptom, but everyone disagrees about the cause, and the argument has already outlasted the fix it is about. Someone proposes asking an AI coding assistant to patch it, and the thread splits a second time: half the team wants the diff now, the other half refuses to trust a patch nobody can reproduce.

That split is not a debate about model quality, and no amount of opinion will settle it. What settles it is evidence narrow enough to be produced inside one meeting block: two attempts, one hypothesis, and a kill rule written down before either attempt starts. A spike is not a smaller project; it is a bet with a deadline, and a bet that cannot lose is not a bet.

Write the hypothesis before the clock starts

The spike begins with a single sentence that predicts a specific, falsifiable outcome. Vague goals such as "evaluate the assistant on our codebase" produce hours of pleasant activity and no verdict, because nothing in them can be contradicted. The card below is the correct size for the exercise, and it is short enough to be read aloud before anyone types a prompt.

Hypothesis: the failing test retries_spec::replays_side_effect_once fails because
            the retry wrapper re-enqueues before the first attempt is acknowledged.
Prediction: a patch that acknowledges before re-enqueue makes the test pass twice
            on HEAD <sha>, touching the retry wrapper and nothing else.
Kill criteria: baseline test already green, two runs disagree on outcome, the two
            diffs share no file, or 90 minutes elapse.
Out of scope: production config, performance, security review.

Three properties make this useful. The base revision is pinned, so a moving branch cannot contaminate the comparison. The prediction names an observable result instead of an intention, so "it feels better" is never an outcome. And the kill criteria are checkable by a script, which matters because the person running the spike is the person most motivated to keep it alive.

One passing run is mostly a coincidence

A single attempt that turns a red test green tells you that something worked once. It does not tell you whether the assistant found the cause or merely found a way past the assertion, and those two futures look identical in a terminal. Cheap sampling makes both futures visible: run the same unmodified prompt twice, on the same revision, in two disposable worktrees, then compare outcomes and diffs side by side.

Two runs do not prove correctness, and the protocol never claims they do. They bound how much confidence a 90-minute budget can honestly buy, and they convert a matter of taste into a pair of files on disk. When two runs disagree, the disagreement itself is the finding: the prompt, the test, or the model is unstable, and none of those three should be shipped over.

The discipline that makes this work is refusing to coach the second run. If the first attempt fails and the operator rewrites the prompt, pastes the stack trace, or points at the guilty file, the two runs are no longer samples of the same process. The second run then demonstrates the operator's understanding, which was never the open question.

A harness that shares one ninety-minute clock

The script below creates the worktrees, records the base revision, checks that the target test actually fails before the assistant touches anything, and saves each attempt's patch, diff stat, and test result. One deadline is computed at the start and shared by both runs, so no run receives a private 90 minutes.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# spike.sh - two-run, time-boxed spike harness. Illustrative: adapt the paths and commands.
set -euo pipefail

TEST_CMD=${TEST_CMD:-"npm test -- --runInBand"}
ASSISTANT_CMD=${ASSISTANT_CMD:-"./scripts/ask-assistant.sh"}  # your client, your model
PROMPT=${PROMPT:-"spike/hypothesis.md"}
BUDGET=${BUDGET:-5400}              # 90 minutes of wall clock for the whole spike
RUNS=${RUNS:-2}

OUT="spike/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
mkdir -p "$OUT"
deadline=$(( $(date +%s) + BUDGET ))
left() { echo $(( deadline - $(date +%s) )); }

for n in $(seq 1 "$RUNS"); do
  wt="$OUT/wt$n"
  git worktree add --detach "$wt" HEAD >/dev/null 2>&1      # docs: git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree
  git -C "$wt" rev-parse HEAD > "$OUT/run$n.base"

  # 1. Baseline must fail, or the hypothesis is rejected before any model call.
  if timeout "$(left)"s bash -c "cd '$wt' && $TEST_CMD" > "$OUT/run$n.before" 2>&1; then
    echo "run$n: baseline already green - hypothesis rejected" > "$OUT/verdict.txt"
    exit 2
  fi

  # 2. Exactly one attempt per run, with the prompt piped in unchanged.
  timeout "$(left)"s bash -c "cd '$wt' && $ASSISTANT_CMD < '$PROMPT'" > "$OUT/run$n.answer" 2>&1 || true

  # 3. Evidence: what changed, and whether the test passes now.
  git -C "$wt" diff      > "$OUT/run$n.patch"
  git -C "$wt" diff --stat > "$OUT/run$n.stat"
  if timeout "$(left)"s bash -c "cd '$wt' && $TEST_CMD" > "$OUT/run$n.after" 2>&1; then
    echo pass > "$OUT/run$n.result"
  else
    echo fail > "$OUT/run$n.result"
  fi
done

python3 spike/verdict.py "$OUT"

Two details are easy to get wrong. timeout measures wall clock, so a run that hangs on a prompt cannot borrow time from the next one; the semantics are documented in the coreutils manual. And the worktrees are detached at HEAD, which means the spike never touches the branch a human is working on, while git worktree remove --force and git worktree prune clean up afterwards.

Two transcripts, four possible verdicts

The reduction step is deliberately blunt. It reads the two result files, the two base revisions, and the file lists from the diff stats, then emits exactly one verdict without weighting anything and without asking for a summary.

# spike/verdict.py - reduce two spike runs to one verdict.
import json, pathlib, sys

out = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
runs = {}
for result_file in sorted(out.glob("run[0-9]*.result")):
    name = result_file.name.split(".")[0]
    runs[name] = {
        "result": result_file.read_text().strip(),
        "base": (out / f"{name}.base").read_text().strip()[:12],
        "touched": sorted((out / f"{name}.stat").read_text().splitlines()),
    }

outcomes = [run["result"] for run in runs.values()]
bases = {run["base"] for run in runs.values()}
overlap = set.intersection(*(set(run["touched"]) for run in runs.values())) if runs else set()

if len(runs) < 2:
    verdict, why = "kill", "the spike did not finish both runs inside the budget"
elif len(bases) > 1:
    verdict, why = "kill", "runs started from different revisions"
elif outcomes == ["pass", "pass"] and overlap:
    verdict, why = "ship-to-review", "both runs passed and touched at least one identical file"
elif outcomes == ["pass", "pass"]:
    verdict, why = "kill", "two passes with disjoint diffs; the cause was not identified"
else:
    verdict, why = "kill", "runs disagree on outcome"

(out / "verdict.json").write_text(json.dumps({"verdict": verdict, "why": why, "runs": runs}, indent=2))
print(verdict, "-", why)
Run 1 Run 2 Diffs share a file Verdict
pass pass yes ship to review
pass pass no kill
pass fail either kill
fail fail either kill, and rewrite the hypothesis
any unfinished - kill, with no partial credit

The harshness is the point. A spike that ends with a patch, two transcripts, and a written reason for killing it has produced real value, because the next person will not spend another afternoon on the same argument. "Ship to review" is not "ship": the patch still goes through normal review, and the reviewer still asks the questions a two-run protocol cannot answer.

Where free model access changes the arithmetic

The protocol above doubles the number of attempts and test executions, which is exactly the kind of cost that pushes teams toward sampling once and calling it evidence. MonkeyCode, the open-source project behind this outreach, currently offers free model access and a free server option, which removes the per-attempt price argument from the decision and lets the second run happen as a matter of routine rather than as a favor.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Two honest qualifications belong here. The free tier, including any token allowance, is defined by the project and changes over time, so read the current terms on the project page instead of planning around a number quoted in a blog post. And the assistant invocation in the harness is a placeholder on purpose: the interface for talking to a hosted model is a project detail, so check the repository for its current client shape rather than assuming a command-line tool that may not exist.

Where the free server option genuinely participates is the clock. If the harness runs on a machine that is not the developer's laptop, a slow test suite no longer competes with an editor, and the 90 minutes are spent where the work actually happens. A long run can be detached and its log followed, but the deadline must stay attached to the process.

# Illustrative: detach the spike so the 90-minute clock outlives the terminal session.
cd ~/repo && PROMPT=spike/hypothesis.md nohup ./spike.sh > spike.log 2>&1 &
tail -f spike.log

Limits, and who should skip this entirely

The protocol measures agreement between two samples, and nothing else. It cannot separate a flaky test from a flaky model, so a suite that already fails intermittently will generate kills for the wrong reason; stabilize the flake first or the spike is just noise. It says nothing about performance, security, or behavior under production load, and it never justifies skipping review.

Some teams should not use it at all. Anyone who needs the fix today should fix it today, because a spike is the wrong instrument for an outage. Teams in regulated environments that require auditable tooling and data handling agreements should confirm those constraints before sending code to any hosted assistant. And anyone evaluating a model rather than a bug should choose a different design, because two runs on one test is far too small a sample for that question.

The useful version of this workflow ends with a small directory of evidence: two patches, two base revisions, two test logs, and one verdict with a reason attached. If a spike that costs nothing to repeat is the interesting part, the free model access and free server option are the cheapest way to find out whether your hypothesis survives its first honest disagreement.

title: Open weight takes 71.5% of tokens and 23% of spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — October 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from July, August, and September.

October 2026 summary

  • Open-weight models now process more than seven in ten gateway tokens and account for nearly one in four dollars. Their share of spend has more than quadrupled since June.

  • September’s gateway spend was about 13 times December’s, while the average price per token was 47% lower. Almost one in three teams changed their most-used lab in September, an index record.

  • Nearly 70% of September’s gateway spend on Chinese models went through US-based providers, up from less than 10% in December.

  • Jev was the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history, reaching 35% of paid teams in its first two weeks, but it accounted for just 0.27% of gateway spend over that same period. Opus 5.5 took more than one in ten gateway dollars in its own first two weeks, the largest spend share of any September model launch.

Frontier spend up 900%, spend share down 22%

In August, open-weight models processed the majority of AI Gateway token volume for the first time. The money is now following. Open weight’s share of spend has more than quadrupled over the last three months, from one in twenty gateway dollars in June to nearly one in four in September.

Open weight's growth is coming from both ends of its price range, and it mirrors the wider gateway. The cheapest models drive token growth, while the expensive models drive spend.

Led by Kimi K3, models priced at least four times the open-weight average cost per token accounted for about two-thirds of the increase in open-weight spend.

In contrast, DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash alone processed nearly half of all September tokens but took just 2.6% of spend. Its price per token was about a fifth of the open-weight average.

Customers are increasing budgets on both sides of the market. Since December, spend on frontier models has grown tenfold; spend on open-weight models has grown more than seventyfold.

In September, 68% of teams that put more money into open-weight models did the same for closed-weight models. And more than two in five teams already paying for frontier models spent more on them than in August, the highest share this year.

Spending on the frontier is still growing, but spending on alternatives is growing faster. A company can spend more with a frontier lab while relying on it for fewer workloads, so the lab gets more money, but a smaller part of the customer’s business.

AI spend increases 13x while the cost per token halves

Market share is changing hands inside a market that is getting much bigger and cheaper.

September's gateway spend was about 13 times December's, an increase of 1,180%, while the average price per token fell 47%. The median paid customer active in both December and September more than doubled its spend.

Teams are spending more, but labs have to keep winning their business. In September, nearly one in two teams changed their most-used model. And almost one in three changed their most-used lab, an index record.

Even teams with lower token volumes use a wide mix of models. Since December, teams that processed at least 10 million tokens over that period used an average of 15 different models. The average rose to 26 for teams processing at least 100 million tokens, and 42 for those processing at least a billion.

The model is becoming a replaceable part of a much larger investment. Companies can continuously improve their AI products and workflows while changing which models power them. They can spend more on AI without becoming more dependent on any one lab.

Chinese models are big business for American providers

More than two-thirds of September’s gateway spend on Chinese-origin models went to US-based providers, up from less than a tenth in December. The Chinese lab builds the model; the American provider runs it and sells access.

DeepSeek’s models processed 58% of all gateway tokens for 6.6% of spend. More than four in five of those tokens were served by DeepSeek itself, yet two in five dollars spent on its models went through US-based providers.

Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based lab behind Kimi, accounted for 3.6% of gateway tokens and 13.2% of spend in September. US-based providers served nine in ten of those tokens.

Z.ai, also based in Beijing and the creator of GLM, accounted for 7.2% of all tokens and 4.5% of spend. US-based providers served seven in ten.

Customers can use Chinese models through access sold by American providers. For teams that put more money into Chinese models in September, an average of 53% of their spending on those models went through US-based providers and 41% through China-based ones.

The same Chinese model can compete with US-based models while generating revenue for US-based providers.

September model launch scorecard: Jev, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6

Whether a model launch is successful depends on what you measure: how broadly it’s tried, how much usage and spend it receives, or what share of its initial users return. We ranked every model launch in September with at least two weeks of data by these metrics; the tables show the top ten for each. The full scorecard is at the end of the report.

Jev is the most-adopted and most-called model

In its first two weeks, Jev reached more than a third of paid teams, nearly double the reach of Sonnet 5.5 in second place. This is the fastest adoption of any model in AI Gateway history.

Jev also received the most requests of any model in September, even though it launched halfway through the month. Of the teams that tried Jev in week one, 55.6% returned in week two, the fifth-highest retention rate.

Jev is a decision model. Compared with typical language-model requests, a Jev request is faster, cheaper and uses a fraction of the tokens. So although its adoption was fast and broad, it accounted for just 1% of the month’s tokens and 0.15% of spend.

In September, Jev quickly became a popular model for production while remaining a tiny part of the inference bill.

Opus 5.5 takes more than one in ten gateway dollars

The launch that received the most dollars was Opus 5.5, with more than twice the share of any other September launch, followed by GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash.

Opus 5.5 caught on quickly, with almost nine in ten dollars coming from teams already using Opus 5. Existing customers were trying the new release while the wider Opus family was losing market share.

Across all versions, Opus accounted for almost a third of gateway dollars in September, down from one in two in August. Anthropic’s overall share fell below half of total gateway spend for the first time, dropping from 63.7% to 43.9%.

Luna brought users back; Astra brought spend

GPT-6 Luna reached nearly three out of every twenty paid teams in its first two weeks, in third place behind Jev and Sonnet 5.5. But its return rate was the highest of the month; almost two-thirds of the teams that tried it in its first week came back in the second.

GPT-6 Astra reached a smaller audience but took more budget. In its first two weeks, it accounted for about one in twenty gateway dollars; Luna accounted for less than one in a hundred. Luna reached almost three times as many teams while Astra captured more than five times the share of spend.

OpenAI is attracting more customers with Luna, but capturing far more money with Astra, even though fewer teams use it.

Full September scorecard

Previous AI Gateway Production Index reports

  • May 2026

  • June 2026

  • July 2026

  • August 2026

  • September 2026

About this report

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through September 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Token volume includes input, output, reasoning, cached-input and cache-creation tokens.

  • Spending is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ. Average price per token is estimated spending divided by token volume.

  • Open-weight classifications follow the current AI Gateway model list, a broader definition than in earlier reports.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million paid tokens in both months. “Most-used” is measured by paid tokens.

  • Provider location means company headquarters.

  • Launch metrics cover external paid teams during each model’s first 14 days. Reach uses paid teams active from the start of the launch month through the data cutoff. Spend share uses total paid gateway spending during the model’s window. Return rate is the share of first-week teams that used it again in week two.

  • Model counts cover December–September, with each version counted separately. Team-size thresholds use total input and output tokens over that period.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

Read more about our methodology, and explore or download the public data.

title: I Hid 40 Bugs in an Online Store and Let an AI Play QA Tester
description:
Every team I've worked with has shipped something that passed its automated checks but still confused people. The button did its job, but nobody could find it. The form submitted, but only after you'd typed your phone number three different ways. Automated tests only catch what someone thought to write an assertion for. A good human QA tester is the one who notices what nobody wrote down, and says "this is annoying."

So I wanted to know: can an AI agent do that part of the job? Not "does the page load," but "would a real person get confused here?"

And if it can, how much does it depend on how you ask?

A coffee shop with 40 problems hidden in it

To test a tester, you need to know the right answers in advance. A real website doesn't give you that. If the agent reports five issues, you can't tell whether it missed ten or there were only five.

So I made a fake one: Ponto Coffee Roasters, a small online store with a shop page, product pages, a basket, a two-step checkout and a sign-up form. There is no real server behind it. A small piece of code pretends to be one, with random delays and an order that always fails on the first attempt, because how an app behaves while waiting and failing is a big part of user experience.

Then it got filled with problems, from two sources. Claude built the store and planted the first 20 bugs. I then asked Codex, a different AI, to introduce 20 more, and kept that request and the new bug list outside anything Claude could see. Claude was also the model doing the testing, so I didn't want all the bugs to come from the same model that would be hunting them.

The 40 bugs cover a wide range. There's pale grey text you can barely read, an "Add to bag" button that gives no sign it worked, and a review step that says shipping is "Free" while the total quietly includes €6.90. The basket's minus button actually adds coffee, the logo takes you to the basket, and on a phone the checkout spills off the screen. Some are quiet: the search box clears itself when you click away, and the surname field stops accepting letters after eight characters.

Three ways of asking

The experiment changed only one thing: the prompt.

Level 1 was the one-liner most people would type first:

You are a QA engineer. Test the website and look for UX errors.

Level 2 gave the agent a role (a senior QA tester who cares about user experience), some context about the store, a way of working (main journey first, then mistakes and small screens) and a report format.

Level 3 was level 2 plus a full checklist, built on Jakob Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics (a classic list of what makes interfaces easy to use) and the basics of WCAG, the web accessibility guidelines. It also told the agent to test in passes: desktop, mistakes, waiting and failure, phone size, keyboard only.

The checklist was written before any bug existed. Otherwise it might have described the answers without me noticing.

Keeping it fair

Every run used the same agent and model: Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent, running Claude Sonnet 5.5. It drove a fresh browser through Playwright, a tool that lets an AI click, type and look at web pages. The browser was its only tool. It couldn't read files or use a terminal, so it couldn't peek at the source code or the answer key. It could only use the site the way a visitor does. Each level ran three times, because AI output varies from run to run.

Every report was scored against the answer key: a full point if a bug was clearly described, half a point if it was only touched on, nothing if it was missed. I'll call the result a weighted detection score. To reduce scoring subjectivity, a separate AI agent scored all nine reports against the answer key and scoring rules, without seeing my scores. Its numbers came within half a point of mine on every report.

The results

Prompt Runs Average score Percentage Time per run Cost per run
Level 1: one-liner 24, 25, 25 24.7 / 40 62% 1.7 min $0.51
Level 2: role + context 21, 22, 23.5 22.2 / 40 55% 1.9 min $0.51
Level 3: full checklist 27.5, 31.5, 32 30.3 / 40 76% 3.5 min $0.81

The first surprise is right there in the middle row.

Surprise one: the "better" prompt did worse

I expected each level to beat the one before. Level 2 lost to the one-liner.

Level 2 produced longer, more polished entries, with a title, location, impact and severity for every issue, and it scored lower. The one-liner runs wrote quick, dense lists. The reporting format may have contributed, but these runs don't isolate its effect from differences in how each agent explored the site. It's a pattern worth testing, not a conclusion.

Surprise two: a checklist changes behaviour, not just wording

Level 3 didn't only describe things better. It did different things.

It was the only level that ever pressed the Tab key. That's how you test a site for people who don't use a mouse, and it's how all three level 3 runs noticed there was no visible keyboard focus. None of the six other runs caught it.

Every single run, at every level, shrank the window to phone width at some point. But only level 3 caught the checkout overflowing on a phone, in two of its three runs. None of the level 1 or 2 runs reported it, and one of them stated there was "no horizontal scroll at 375px."

The checklist worked like a test plan. It didn't make the agent smarter. It made it go to places it otherwise skipped.

Surprise three: a checklist also narrows attention

The opposite happened too. The newsletter box in the footer has a spinner that never stops. One of the one-liner runs clearly reported it, and the other two got partial credit. None of the six runs with detailed instructions got any credit. They followed the journey they were given, and the footer wasn't on it.

I've seen this in people before. Give a tester a checklist and they'll cover the checklist. Freedom finds odd things, and structure finds thorough things.

The bugs nobody found

Five bugs were missed by all nine runs. Four came from Codex's set:

  • the search box only accepts 12 characters
  • the search clears itself when you click away
  • the surname field stops at 8 characters
  • the Huila Sunrise card on the shop page shows another coffee's picture

The fifth was one of Claude's: double-clicking "Add to bag" adds the item twice.

Most of these have one thing in common. They don't produce an obvious error message or broken layout. Finding them requires trying a boundary value or comparing behaviour across interactions. None of the reports identified the image mismatch between the shop and product pages.

The double-click bug is a messier case, and it taught me something about the experiment itself. Codex's set also made a single click add two items, so a double click added four. Because one click already added two items, the repeated-click issue was harder to distinguish. Planted bugs can hide each other.

The bugs everyone found

On the other hand, every run reported the logo leading to the basket and the password shown in plain text. The same went for the "Free" shipping that wasn't, the basket row that ignored quantity and the price that changed between pages: all nine runs caught these numerical inconsistencies, including the one-liner runs.

The scorer flagged at most one false alarm per run, mostly complaints about slow loading caused by my test environment rather than the app. Every run also found real problems nobody planted, like form fields with no autocomplete hints, error messages that screen readers wouldn't announce, and a header that still said "Create account" after you'd made one.

What I'd be careful about

This is a small experiment. Nine runs with one model is a hint, not proof, and another model could shift the numbers. The tests ran in a cloud sandbox that blocked web fonts, which isn't quite a real visitor's experience. All 40 bugs came from AIs, two different ones, so a human would probably plant different problems. And some planted bugs interacted: the clipped product description partly hid the wall-of-text problem, and the doubled "Add to bag" muddied the double-click bug. That changes how visible some bugs were, and it means the five universal misses don't all point to a single weakness in the agent.

What I'd try next: a checklist that learns

I haven't tested the workflow below yet. It's what I'd try next.

The checklist made the agent thorough, and the one-liner's freedom made it curious. So I'd run two complementary passes before each release: a checklist run, and a free-form run told to explore and report anything odd. The free run's job isn't to find more bugs. Looking back at my saved scores, I combined runs in pairs, giving each bug the best credit either run earned. One free-form run plus one checklist run averaged 31.6 out of 40, and two checklist runs averaged 32.3. That's a retrospective calculation, not a separately tested workflow, but it suggests a free run won't raise the score. Its job is to find the bugs that aren't on the checklist yet.

Those discoveries, along with what human testers find and what real users complain about, feed the checklist. Some become general habits, like "type an unusually long value into every field," and stay there because they need judgment.

Others are specific regressions, like "the newsletter spinner must stop." For those, the checklist is a cheap placeholder. Adding a line takes seconds. An end-to-end test (a script that clicks through the site the same way each time, written with a tool like Cypress) takes real attention to write. So the line goes on the checklist first. Later, when there's time or the list gets long, it graduates into a Cypress test and leaves the list.

Neither half is a guarantee. My own newsletter results show that an instruction in a prompt doesn't ensure the agent follows it, and scripted tests can be flaky too. But the split puts judgment where AI helps and repetition where scripts are cheaper.

So, can an AI be your QA tester?

In this small experiment, a browser-driven AI found many of the planted functional and usability problems, quickly and cheaply. The best setup scored 76% for under a dollar a run. A checklist improved coverage, but several quiet bugs went unnoticed in every run. I'd use it as a first pass before a release, not as a replacement for a person who types a long name, clicks away by accident and thinks "wait, didn't this look different a second ago?"

The thing I'll take away is about prompting. A prompt for an AI tester works a lot like a test plan. What you put in it tends to get covered carefully. What you leave out may never be visited. And like any good test plan, it should never be finished: every bug the agent misses today is a candidate line for tomorrow's checklist.

The whole experiment is open: the store, the 40 bugs, the three prompts, every agent's report and the scores. You're welcome to run your own prompt against it and see how many you can catch. github.com/rodrinobrega/agent-qa-experiment

Have you tried using AI agents for QA or UX reviews? I'd love to hear what they caught for you, and what they walked right past.

title: DLOSAC: Joint Spatial-Geometric Image Estimation via Delaunay-Guided Local Optimization RANSAC
description:
arXiv:2610.21215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable image geometric estimation from noisy matching points is typically addressed using RANSAC, often combined with local optimization to refine inliers and model parameters. However, existing paradigms are predominantly residual-centric; even heuristic attempts to enforce spatial uniformity suffer from a sequential, two-stage nature that inherently decouples distribution optimization from geometric refinement, preventing an effective trade-off. In this paper, we propose DLOSAC, a local optimization framework that jointly incorporates both geometric consistency and spatial distribution information. We begin by constructing a Delaunay triangulation over candidate inliers to explicitly encode neighborhood topology. The geometric module introduces an edge-based consistency metric to evaluate geometric errors, while the spatial module derives distribution descriptors from triangle areas and edge attributes to quantify the clustering of inliers. Finally, we combine edge-based geometric constraints, spatial distribution regularization, and traditional point-level geometric constraints to improve the quality of geometric parameters. Extensive experiments on six publicly available real-world datasets, covering three types of geometric estimation tasks, achieve state-of-the-art performance.

title: UltraDiff: Transferring High-Fidelity Priors to Compressed Latent Spaces for High-Resolution Image Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.21202v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-resolution synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) faces a fundamental trade-off between computational cost and generative fidelity. This trade off is largely governed by the latent compression factor f (e.g. f8 denotes f=8 and f32 f=32). While aggressive compression (f32) significantly improves efficiency, it suffers from severe information loss and ambiguity compared to standard f8 models. We propose UltraDiff, a framework that reformulates this challenge as joint latent diffusion learning followed by marginal score distillation. We introduce MixTeacher, a dual branch DiT that models the joint f8-f32 distribution, utilizing shared attention to resolve the ambiguity of the compressed space with high fidelity f8 priors. Crucially, we propose vector field distillation in the native f32 space. Theoretically, this compels the student to learn the conditional expectation of the teacher trajectory, effectively filtering out compression artifacts. Across the evaluated 1K to 4K settings, UltraDiff approaches f8 level quality while preserving f32 efficiency. With 20 sampling steps on a single A100 GPU, it generates a 2K image in 6.2 seconds over 40 times faster than our f8 baseline.

title: Kubernetes Pod Churn & Node Thrashing: Ephemeral Storage Exhaustion and Eviction Cascades
description:
When background worker pods continuously write temporary scratch files, un-rotated log buffers, or dynamic assets directly to container filesystems without explicit ephemeral storage limits, worker nodes quietly enter local disk pressure states. The kubelet then triggers aggressive pod evictions, sparking cluster-wide pod churn, Karpenter/Cluster Autoscaler thrashing, and AWS bill inflation. Here is an architectural deep dive into diagnosing local disk exhaustion and configuring resilient kubelet eviction boundaries.

In high-throughput B2B SaaS platforms running containerized microservices, background processing workloads (e.g., generating PDF reports, processing video/image assets, compiling code, or handling CSV batch imports) frequently rely on local container file systems for temporary scratch space. Under heavy traffic, un-capped ephemeral storage usage creates an invisible cluster-level failure mode: Cascading Node Eviction and Auto-Scaler Thrashing.

1. The Mechanics of OverlayFS and Ephemeral Storage Eviction

By default, when a container writes files to its own filesystem (outside of explicitly mounted Persistent Volumes), those writes land on the node's local disk through the container runtime's writable layer, typically the OverlayFS storage driver. Disk-backed emptyDir volumes and container logs consume the same node disk. If a pod uses significant local disk space without ephemeral storage requests and limits in its manifest, it triggers a chain reaction across the host node.

The Anatomy of a Node Eviction Cascade

  • Unbounded Disk Growth: A burst of PDF generation worker tasks writes 15GB of temporary files to /tmp inside the container overlay filesystem.
  • Kubelet Disk Pressure Breach: The node's disk crosses a kubelet hard eviction threshold (by default, nodefs.available below 10% or imagefs.available below 15%). The kubelet marks the node DiskPressure = True, the node is tainted, and the scheduler stops placing new pods on it.
  • Aggressive Pod Eviction: The kubelet first garbage-collects dead containers and unused images, then starts evicting pods. It ranks pods by whether their disk usage exceeds their ephemeral storage request, then by pod priority, then by usage. With no requests set, every pod counts as over its request, so priority dominates, and lower-priority core services can be evicted before the high-priority worker that is actually filling the disk.
  • Auto-Scaler Thrashing (Karpenter / Cluster Autoscaler): Rescheduled evicted pods flood neighboring nodes, pushing those nodes into disk pressure as well. The autoscaler provisions new EC2 instances for pending pods while consolidation removes others, so nodes churn continuously and compute spend can multiply for the duration of the incident.

2. Diagnosing Ephemeral Storage Bloat in Production

Pod objects do not report disk usage, so kubectl get pods cannot show it. The kubelet's stats summary endpoint does. Run the following diagnostic commands to find which pods are consuming node disk and driving instability (requires jq):

# Top 20 pods by ephemeral storage usage (MiB) across all nodes
for node in $(kubectl get nodes -o name | cut -d/ -f2); do
  kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$node/proxy/stats/summary" \
    | jq -r --arg node "$node" '.pods[]
        | [$node, .podRef.namespace, .podRef.name,
           ((.["ephemeral-storage"].usedBytes // 0) / 1048576 | floor)]
        | @tsv'
done | sort -t$'\t' -k4 -rn | head -20

# Inspect recent eviction events
kubectl get events --all-namespaces --field-selector reason=Evicted | grep -i "ephemeral"

# Detailed check of Node Disk Pressure conditions
kubectl describe node <node-name> | grep -A 8 "Conditions:"

A pod status displaying Evicted with the message The node was low on resource: ephemeral-storage confirms your cluster is actively suffering from un-capped container write exhaustion.

3. Production-Ready Remediation: Strict Resource Limits & In-Memory emptyDir

Step 1: Enforce Ephemeral Storage Requests and Limits

Every Kubernetes manifest deployed to production must explicitly define ephemeral-storage resource boundaries alongside CPU and memory parameters. This lets the scheduler place pods according to available disk, and when a container exceeds its storage limit, the kubelet evicts only that pod instead of letting the whole node reach disk pressure.

# PRODUCTION-GRADE DEPLOYMENT MANIFEST WITH EPHEMERAL LIMITS
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: pdf-generator-worker
  namespace: production
spec:
  replicas: 8
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: pdf-generator-worker
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: pdf-generator-worker
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: registry.internal.net/pdf-worker:v2.1.0
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "2Gi"
            ephemeral-storage: "1Gi" # Scheduler reserves this much node disk
          limits:
            cpu: "2000m"
            memory: "4Gi"            # Includes up to 2Gi of tmpfs scratch below
            ephemeral-storage: "4Gi" # Hard ceiling: kubelet evicts this pod if exceeded
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /tmp/scratch
          name: scratch-volume
      volumes:
      - name: scratch-volume
        emptyDir:
          medium: Memory # Back temporary writes with RAM (tmpfs)
          sizeLimit: 2Gi # Cap scratch space so it cannot consume all memory

Step 2: Redirect High-Frequency Scratch Writes to In-Memory tmpfs

For workloads requiring ultra-fast, short-lived file creation (e.g., image resizing or PDF rendering), mount an emptyDir volume backed by RAM (medium: Memory). Writes to this volume bypass the node disk entirely, removing them as a source of disk pressure and speeding up file I/O. One catch: files in a memory-backed emptyDir count toward the container's memory limit, not its ephemeral storage limit. Size the memory limit to cover the application plus the scratch volume, as in the manifest above, or a full scratch directory will get the pod OOM-killed.

4. Tuning Kubelet Eviction Thresholds and Karpenter Node Consolidation

Reduce premature evictions by tuning kubelet eviction settings in your node configuration (for example, the kubelet config in your EKS node group launch template or Karpenter EC2NodeClass user data):

# Kubelet Eviction Configuration Parameters (kubelet-config.json)
{
  "evictionHard": {
    "memory.available": "5%",
    "nodefs.available": "10%",
    "nodefs.inodesFree": "5%",
    "imagefs.available": "15%"
  },
  "evictionSoft": {
    "nodefs.available": "15%"
  },
  "evictionSoftGracePeriod": {
    "nodefs.available": "2m"
  },
  "evictionMaxPodGracePeriod": 60
}

Then slow down Karpenter's consolidation so short traffic spikes don't cause node churn (Karpenter v1 API):

# Karpenter v1 NodePool with churn guardrails
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
      expireAfter: 720h # Rotate nodes every 30 days for patching
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    consolidateAfter: 5m # Wait before consolidating so spikes can settle
    budgets:
      - nodes: "10%"     # Never disrupt more than 10% of nodes at once
  • Soft Eviction Grace Periods: With a soft threshold, the kubelet only evicts if disk stays below 15% free for a full 2 minutes. Short spikes that clear on their own (a batch job finishing, logs rotating, image garbage collection) no longer trigger evictions. The hard threshold at 10% still protects the node.
  • Karpenter Consolidation Guardrails: consolidateAfter delays consolidation so nodes are not removed the moment utilization dips, and disruption budgets cap how many nodes Karpenter can replace at once. expireAfter handles routine node rotation; it is not a churn control on its own.

5. Executive Summary & Systems Rules

  • Always Specify ephemeral-storage Requests and Limits: Unbounded container writes will fill host node disks and trigger cascading evictions across unrelated pods.
  • Use RAM-Backed emptyDir for Transient Files: Mount temporary scratch directories with medium: Memory to keep high-frequency file I/O off node disks, and raise the memory limit to cover the scratch size.
  • Set Soft Kubelet Eviction Windows: Configure grace periods on nodes so brief disk spikes can clear before the kubelet evicts pods, and add consolidation delays and disruption budgets to your autoscaler.

title: The permission you can't prompt away
description:
Enforcing agent safety in the tool layer, not the system prompt.

Drawn from a personal agentic system ("Vantage") I built and run daily.

Most agent "guardrails" are sentences. Somewhere in a system prompt there is a line like "Never delete files without asking" or "Do not send email on the user's behalf." The line is polite, it is well-intentioned, and it is not a control. It is a request addressed to a probabilistic text generator, evaluated anew on every turn, competing with everything else in the context window. The day it loses that competition is the day you find out your safety model was a suggestion.

I want to argue a narrower and more useful position than "prompts are unreliable," which everyone already knows. The position is: the boundary between what an agent may suggest and what it may do should be enforced by the shape of the tools you give it — ideally by the tools you withhold — and that enforcement belongs in a service you can test without a model in the loop. A prompt is a request. A missing tool is a guarantee.

I'll make the case with a system I actually run.

The setup

Vantage is a personal agentic system. The agent (Claude Code, today — the substrate is meant to be replaceable) connects over MCP to a Spring Boot service that owns everything durable: an append-only event log in MySQL, a set of read collectors, and a small number of write tools. The service is plain Java, tested with JUnit, with no LLM anywhere in its tests. That split is the whole design — the model is the controller, the service is the service layer — and the safety model falls directly out of it.

The founding rule is three sentences long:

Read, summarise and draft are autonomous. Send, spend, delete, or anything publicly visible requires explicit confirmation. This is enforced in the service, not in a prompt.

The interesting word is the last one, and the interesting mistakes are in how you honour it.

"Write" is the wrong category

The first thing the tiering gets right is that it does not tier on read versus write. It tiers on effect in the world.

That distinction matters because the obvious implementation — "reads are free, writes need approval" — immediately strangles the system. The agent's most useful autonomous act is to record things: file an idea, note an observation, draft a proposal. Those are writes. They are also completely safe, because they touch only the system's own metadata — nothing is sent, nothing is spent, nothing is deleted, nothing becomes visible to anyone but the user. We call that tier zero: a write whose blast radius is zero stays autonomous.

So the question a new tool has to answer is not "does this write?" but "can the effect of this be seen or felt outside the system, and can it be undone?" Draft an email: tier zero. Send it: gated. The category that needs a human is irreversible or outward-facing effect, and conflating it with "write" is how you end up with an agent that needs permission to take a note and no permission to wire money.

The gate that is a hole

Here is the part I find most worth stealing.

The system's one tool that speaks first — that produces output nobody asked for — lets the agent file a proposal: a suggested next action on a project, for the user to accept or reject. The agent can file one. It cannot accept one. Not because a prompt tells it not to, but because there is no tool that accepts a proposal. The accept path exists only in the user-facing console, behind a human click.

The comment in the source is the entire security argument:

/**
 * There is no accept_proposal and there must not be. Vantage suggests and Jason decides.
 * The service enforces the budget, but nothing except the absence of this tool stops an
 * agent accepting its own suggestion into Jason's declared next actions -- which would make
 * the accept/reject history a record of Vantage agreeing with itself, and that history is
 * the only feedback signal this feature has.
 */

Read that last clause carefully, because it is the general principle hiding inside a specific feature. An agent that can both propose and approve is not an assistant with oversight; it is an agent with a logbook it writes itself. The approval record becomes a record of the system agreeing with itself, which is worse than no record, because it looks like oversight. The only way to keep the human judgment real is to make it structurally impossible for the agent to forge — and the cheapest structural impossibility is a function that was never written.

This generalises cleanly. Every time you are tempted to write "the agent should not do X on its own" into a prompt, ask whether X corresponds to a tool the agent is holding. If it does, you have not built a guardrail; you have built a label on a loaded tool. The fix is usually to split the tool: one that proposes X, one that commits X, and the second one lives somewhere the agent cannot reach.

Bounding the human, not the agent

The same proposal tool shows a second lesson, which is that even a perfectly safe action has a cost, and the cost is the human's attention.

The first design was a per-run budget: an agent reviewing a project may file at most three proposals. It is the obvious cap and it does not work. Two runs produce six proposals; five runs produce fifteen; each run is individually within budget, and the review pane floods anyway, just more slowly. The flood you have to fear is the second review — the one nobody is watching for.

The cap that works counts what is open, not what was filed per run: at most three undecided proposals may stand against any one project at a time. This looks like a cosmetic change and is a categorical one. A per-run cap bounds the generator's enthusiasm. An open-items cap bounds the human's backlog — the system cannot offer a fourth decision until you have made one of the first three. The limit is denominated in the scarce resource, which is not the agent's output but the user's willingness to keep reading it. A guardrail that caps the wrong quantity gives you the comfortable feeling of a limit and none of the protection.

And because the limit lives in the service, the tool's own description can tell the model the reason — "every proposal costs a decision the user did not ask to make, and one that wasn't worth it trains him to dismiss the next one" — so the model files one strong proposal instead of three mediocre ones to fill the quota. The prompt-level instruction is still there. It is just no longer load-bearing. If the model ignores it, the service refuses the fourth proposal regardless. Belt from the service; suspenders from the prompt — never the other way around.

Make the judgment measurable

Two smaller decisions round out the pattern, both about keeping the human's judgment legible after the fact.

Accepting is editing. When the user accepts a proposal, they can accept it as reworded. The system stores both the original text and what was actually accepted, so the gap between what the agent suggested and what the human was willing to endorse stays measurable. A system that overwrites the suggestion the instant it's accepted throws away its only signal about how good its suggestions were.

Decisions are append-only. A decided proposal cannot be re-decided. If the answer changes, you file a new one; two dated rows disagreeing is the history. The approval log is a judgment record, and a judgment record you can quietly edit is not a record. This is the same instinct as the event log underneath the whole system: you append, you never rewrite, and you can therefore replay and audit the system's entire life at 3am when you need to know exactly what it did and when.

What this costs, honestly

This approach is not free, and it is not always right.

It pushes work out of the prompt and into typed service code, which is slower to change — you ship a Java method and a migration, not a sentence. For a throwaway agent, that overhead is not worth it; a prompt-level "please don't" is a fine control for a toy. The structural approach earns its keep exactly when the cost of the agent being wrong is real and the system is going to live for a while — which is to say, in production, in a company, on anything that can send, spend, or be seen.

It also demands that you actually enumerate your dangerous actions and give each one a home in the tiering. That is work, and it is the work — "which of our tools have outward-facing effect, and which of those is the agent currently holding?" is a question most teams shipping an agent have not written down the answer to. The value of the tool-layer approach is that it forces you to write it down, because a tool either exists or it doesn't.

The one line to keep

If you take a single thing from this: your agent's real permissions are the set of tools it can call, not the set of instructions you've written for it. Audit the first list. The second one is documentation of your intentions, and your intentions are not a security boundary.

This is one of a set of write-ups drawn from real systems. If your team is putting agents into an environment where a wrong action has consequences — enterprise, regulated, on-prem — the same structural approach applies, and I do advisory work on exactly that: MCP tool design, tiered permission gating, and auditable agent runtimes in Java/Spring environments.

title: FocusOPD: Structure-Guided On-Policy Distillation for Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21250v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation enables rectified-flow models with diffusion-transformer architectures to combine task-specific capabilities within a single student. However, matching model outputs does not guarantee that their internal representations are aligned, and it remains unclear where and when additional feature supervision is most useful. We analyze the teacher-student feature mismatch across Transformer blocks and denoising timesteps, and find that the mismatch is concentrated in deeper Transformer blocks during early denoising and persists after OPD distillation, indicating ineffective distillation. Motivated by this observation, we introduce FocusOPD, which augments the base OPD objective with token-wise directional feature alignment restricted to deep layers and early denoising steps. Across two rectified-flow backbones and multiple OPD objectives, FocusOPD improves capability transfer in compositional generation, text rendering, and preference-based evaluation. On the primary benchmark, it improves over DiffusionOPD from 0.953 to 0.967 on GenEval, from 23.797 to 23.944 on PickScore, and from 6.052 to 6.199 on LAION-Aesthetic. Ablations show that selective deep and early supervision is more effective and efficient than alignment over the full network and trajectory.

title: Introducing Flat Rate CDN
description:
Over the past year, we have improved Vercel’s Pro pricing to better reflect how teams build, with expanded user roles, flexible credits, access to enterprise features, and more. But one area our customers continued to give us feedback on was CDN pricing.

CDN costs should be predictable, but viral launches, traffic bursts, or misconfigured routes sometimes turned an otherwise normal month into an unexpected bill. For teams building on Vercel, that uncertainty made growth feel like a problem at exactly the moment it should feel exciting.

Today, we are introducing Flat Rate CDN for Pro teams: a new way to pay for CDN usage with a predictable monthly bill, built-in spike protection, and service tiers designed for different traffic profiles.

What is Flat Rate CDN?

Flat Rate CDN is an alternative to usage-based CDN billing that provides you with a predictable monthly bill.

The model is designed around a simple idea: teams should be able to choose the CDN capacity that corresponds to their typical usage profile, pay a known amount monthly, and avoid surprise overages from temporary spikes.

Flat Rate CDN has several advantages over usage-based billing:

  • Fixed monthly price: Pay a fixed amount for Vercel CDN each month.

  • Covers traffic spikes: CDN Requests, Fast Data Transfer, and other resources are no longer billed directly, so spikes don't result in surprise bills.

  • No overages: Your bill will never increase because of temporary usage spikes.

Importantly, predictable pricing does not mean lower-quality bandwidth. Every request still runs on Vercel’s premium network, including private fiber that routes around congestion on the public internet, which can improve performance by up to 60%. Comparable routing is often sold as a premium add-on, but Vercel includes it by default for Pro teams, and performance isn't degraded during traffic spikes.

How it works

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default, and existing Pro teams can opt in. Usage is tracked at the team level and covers all projects, so you no longer need to manage capacity for them individually.

What’s included

On Flat Rate CDN, one fixed monthly fee covers:

  • CDN Requests

  • Fast Data Transfer

  • Blob Data Transfer

  • Observability events generated by CDN requests

The default tier is included with Pro. You can upgrade to a higher tier for increased request and data transfer capacity.

Your tier is fixed throughout any given billing period, so you never have to worry about charges from temporary traffic spikes.

What happens during a spike

The following team had a relatively normal usage profile that would fit comfortably in our $20/month Flat Rate CDN tier:

Only days after the above period, they experienced a viral product launch that generated a significant surge in traffic:

If the team had been on usage-based pricing, their CDN bill would have reached tens of thousands of dollars. On Flat Rate CDN, it stayed at $20 for the month.

No caps and no performance hit

Flat rate pricing from other infrastructure providers often places caps on usage when you reach your capacity, resulting in rapid performance degradation and request rejection. Flat Rate CDN is different in two ways:

  1. We recognize usage spikes and remove them when evaluating your CDN usage against capacity.

  2. We rightsize your Flat Rate CDN tier every month based on sustained usage.

This means we’ll never bring down your site when you’re going viral, and you don’t have to actively manage your tier when you’re growing quickly.

You can still monitor every covered resource on the Usage page or in the CLI, including traffic spikes absorbed by Vercel:

What we heard from customers during beta

Even though surprise bills are rare across our entire customer base, we’ve seen numerous stories from Pro customers about unexpected bills, many of which famously blew up on X. One team we interviewed was running hundreds of client sites and told us that CDN costs were “by far our largest line item, and the hardest to forecast,” especially when traffic spiked “from a client’s listing going viral, seasonal traffic, or bot traffic.”

In May, we released Flat Rate CDN to a small set of teams in limited beta. Over the last several months, it has changed how they operate on Vercel.

They worried less:

Flat Rate CDN eased our billing anxiety. With the recent increase in AI crawler traffic, we used to frequently check bot activity through Observability and monitor which bots were generating traffic. We now spend much less time doing that.

They built more:

Knowing that CDN usage is predictable makes us more willing to adopt caching-oriented approaches. We're now considering broader use of Cache Components and other caching strategies in our Next.js architecture, whereas previously we had to think more carefully about the potential cost impact of additional cache traffic.

This is exactly what we built Flat Rate CDN to do. No surprise bills, predictable pricing, and peace of mind to ship the next project.

Get started

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default. Existing Pro teams can opt in to the new plan:

  1. Select Billing in the navigation.

  2. Browse to Flat Rate CDN and toggle the setting to on.

  3. Choose a capacity tier that corresponds to your typical usage.

  4. Review your selection, which will show subscription costs if you chose a paid Flat Rate CDN tier.

  5. Select Enable to apply.

Learn more about Flat Rate CDN pricing in the documentation.
