title: A 429 at 02:00: Postmortem for a Quota Outage
description:
A 429 at 02:00: Postmortem for a Quota Outage

Your phone buzzes at 02:07 with a failed staging job, which on its own is survivable, and then four minutes later the production summarizer starts emitting truncated output for real users. You check the model provider's status page and it is a wall of green, so you conclude the model is fine and start hunting through your own prompts instead. That instinct costs you twenty minutes, because the outage was never a model problem — it was a credential and retry problem that the model was merely the first to notice.

A boundary before we go further: this is a teaching postmortem, reconstructed from a well-documented failure class rather than a report on one named company's incident. The timeline is a plausible sequence, the code below is runnable against a fake provider, and the only numbers you should trust are the ones you print on your own machine. That distinction matters, because postmortems copied verbatim from someone else's outage teach you nothing about your own blast radius.

Timeline

Time Observation
02:00 Nightly staging suite begins; it imports the same client library and the same API credential as production.
02:03 Staging's summarization fixtures exhaust the shared quota; the provider starts returning 429.
02:07 Production requests begin returning 429 as well, and the client treats them as generic errors.
02:11 Retry amplification peaks: every in-flight worker retries on the same fixed one-second boundary.
02:19 On-call inspects prompts and model selection, because error dashboards only count 5xx responses.
02:34 A per-environment key rotation in staging stops the bleeding; production recovers without a deploy.
03:10 First honest summary: the feature degraded because our retry policy converted a soft limit into a hard outage.

Contributing factors, in order of leverage

The first factor is shared credentials across environments, which turns a test suite into a production dependency without anyone deciding that on purpose. Nobody wrote a ticket saying “let staging rate-limit production,” but that is precisely what the shared key encoded, and it stayed invisible because both environments succeeded for months. When you cannot attribute a request to an environment, you also cannot revoke or budget it independently.

The second factor is retry without jitter, which is the classic way to convert a temporary throttle into a sustained stampede. Fixed delays look harmless in a single-threaded test and become a synchronized heartbeat in production, where dozens of workers wake at the same millisecond and fire again. Exponential backoff helps only when you also randomize the interval and cap the number of attempts; otherwise you have made each individual client polite while making the fleet as rude as before.

The third factor is alerting that keyed on 5xx only, which meant a 429 looked like success to the dashboard and like failure to the user. Quota pressure is a leading indicator, so if your error-rate panel ignores status 429 you will always learn about exhaustion from the customers instead of the graph. The uncomfortable lesson is that our observability was tuned for crashes, not for throttling.

The fix you can rehearse

The durable fix has four parts, and only the first is infrastructure: environment-scoped keys, a client-side token budget with a hard ceiling, jittered retries with a small attempt cap, and a circuit breaker that fails fast once throttling is sustained. The script below models the difference between a naive client and a jittered client behind a breaker, using a deterministic fake provider so the result is reproducible on any laptop.

"""quota_sim.py — rehearse a retry storm against a capped fake provider.
Run: python quota_sim.py
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
import random


@dataclass
class CappedProvider:
    """Accepts a fixed number of call-units, then returns 429 forever."""
    capacity: int = 100
    cost_per_call: int = 12
    seen: int = field(default=0)
    accepted: int = field(default=0)

    def complete(self) -> int:
        self.seen += 1
        self.capacity -= self.cost_per_call
        if self.capacity < 0:
            return 429
        self.accepted += 1
        return 200


class Breaker:
    """Opens after `threshold` consecutive throttles, stays open for the run."""

    def __init__(self, threshold: int = 4) -> None:
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.failures = 0
        self.open = False

    def record(self, status: int) -> None:
        if status == 429:
            self.failures += 1
            if self.failures >= self.threshold:
                self.open = True
        else:
            self.failures = 0


def naive_client(provider: CappedProvider, rng: random.Random) -> int:
    """Fixed one-second retry, no jitter: every worker resumes together."""
    for _ in range(6):
        status = provider.complete()
        if status == 200:
            return status
        # time.sleep(1.0) — identical across all workers
    return 429


def jittered_client(provider: CappedProvider, rng: random.Random) -> int:
    """Full jitter, three attempts, then a breaker that fails fast."""
    breaker = Breaker()
    for attempt in range(3):
        if breaker.open:
            return 429
        status = provider.complete()
        breaker.record(status)
        if status == 200:
            return status
        base = 0.2 * (2 ** attempt)
        delay = min(2.0, base) * rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5)  # time.sleep(delay)
        _ = delay
    return 429


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for name, fn in (("naive", naive_client), ("jitter+breaker", jittered_client)):
        provider = CappedProvider()
        rng = random.Random(11)
        codes = [fn(provider, rng) for _ in range(40)]
        amplification = provider.seen / max(provider.accepted, 1)
        print(
            f"{name:>15}: requests={provider.seen:>4} "
            f"ok={provider.accepted:>3} failed={codes.count(429):>3} "
            f"amplification={amplification:.2f}"
        )

The invariant worth asserting in CI is directional rather than numeric: the jittered client behind a breaker should issue strictly fewer requests per successful call than the naive client, and it should stop issuing requests entirely once the breaker opens. Your absolute amplification depends on capacity, worker count, and cost per call, so treat the printed table as a knob you tune rather than a benchmark to quote. Add a test that fails when amplification for the naive strategy drops below the jittered one, and you have encoded the lesson instead of just writing it down.

Where a free tier belongs in this workflow

Here is the part that is genuinely useful: you want to rehearse this failure class regularly, and rehearsal that spends real money is rehearsal that quietly stops happening. MonkeyCode offers free model access and a free server option that the project documents on its own pages, which makes it a reasonable place to run disaster drills like the one above without treating production budget as the test fixture. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. I have not measured its quotas, hardware, or long-term availability, and free-tier terms change, so read the current allocation on the project site rather than trusting any number quoted in a blog post, including this one.

Workload Sensible home Reasoning
Retry-storm drills, breaker tests Free tier Failure is the point; nothing of value is lost when the drill trips a limit.
Nightly staging suites Free tier, separate credentials Isolates test load from anything a customer can feel.
Prompt-regression evals on synthetic data Free tier Cheap, repeatable, and easy to throw away when the schema changes.
User-facing generation with an SLO Paid, environment-scoped keys Throttling here is an outage, not a signal.
Anything bound by a data-processing agreement Whatever your legal review approved Free hosting does not change your obligations.

Limitations and who should not do this

A circuit breaker is a blunt instrument that can mask a genuine provider-side regression, because once it opens you stop collecting the evidence you would need to tell throttling apart from a broken deploy. If your team has nobody who owns the shared client library, adding a token budget and breaker to it will produce three divergent copies within a quarter, and the drift will be worse than the original bug. Per-environment keys also add rotation chores, so a two-person team should weigh whether a shared key plus a hard client-side ceiling is enough for now.

You should not adopt this pattern if you need guaranteed throughput, if your latency budget cannot absorb a fail-fast response, or if your prompts carry data your agreements forbid sending to a third-party endpoint of any price. Free model access is excellent for rehearsal and poor for contractual guarantees, and pretending otherwise is how you end up writing a second postmortem about the same night. For everyone else, the sequence is unglamorous: scope the credentials, budget the tokens, jitter the retries, break the circuit, and alert on 429 before your users do.

The 02:00 page was never about which model you picked, and the fix that survived review was fourteen lines in a client library that nobody had looked at in six months. If you want to rehearse that night without spending anything, the free tier is a reasonable place to start, and you can keep the simulation in your repository as the artifact that proves you learned it.

title: Mind the Tail: Data Selection Through Sparse Concepts
description:
arXiv:2610.21007v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data selection reallocates training support across visual concepts, including objects, attributes, color, texture, and backgrounds. Different allocation strategies may produce varied downstream model behavior, especially for tail concepts supported by only a few samples. Discarding them can hurt test-time robustness, while overemphasizing samples lying on category boundaries may introduce unstable training signals. This work explicitly investigates this relationship across fine-grained, spurious-correlation, and general image classification, as well as multimodal pretraining. Specifically, we use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract concept activations from individual images. During selection, we accumulate the dataset-level concept support for each added sample. Applying diminishing returns to this distribution down-weights well-represented concepts and shifts the focus to the distribution tail. We then incorporate local support to find samples that reliably strengthen under-supported concepts. Empirical results show consistent improvements over strong data selection baselines across all benchmarks. We also reveal the connection between concepts our method enhances and the induced behavioral changes, including improved robustness against out-of-distribution and spurious contexts. This work establishes concept support, beyond individual sample importance, as a useful principle for data-efficient and robust learning.

title: Price Free AI Capacity in Deadline Slack, Not in Tokens
description:
It is 02:14. Your nightly batch window closes at 02:30. The free lane is still running, and the token meter reads zero.

Last week that felt like a win. Tonight the window is gone. Which operational action follows from that evidence?

Not delete the free lane. Price it.

Two numbers, one decision

Most teams measure the wrong number.

  1. Token spend. Cheap, often zero on a free tier.
  2. Deadline slack. Seconds you can spend before an SLO breaks.

Free capacity converts the first into the second. That conversion has a rate. Measure the rate, not the sticker price.

Define slack use per job class:

slack_used = free_p95_duration * (1 + retry_ratio) - paid_p50_duration

Three terms matter. The free lane p95 per attempt. The extra attempts per completed job. The paid baseline you gave up.

What the retry tax actually costs

A retry is not a retry. It is wall-clock time plus a new queue position plus a fresh attempt.

  • Preemption returns the worker mid-attempt. The partial work is gone.
  • Throttling returns a rate-limit signal. The partial work is gone.
  • Worker loss returns nothing at all. You wait for a timeout to notice.

Each event resets the attempt clock. Each event consumes slack, not tokens. That is how a free lane stays cheap and still blows the window.

If your provider returns 429, stop and back off. Do not retry around the limit.

The artifact: a break-even router

Here is a small script. It reads measured job-class statistics from one fixed window and prints a routing decision.

It does not call a model. It prices time.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# breakeven.py - route batch job classes by deadline slack, not list price.
import json
import sys
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class ClassStats:
    name: str
    attempts: int          # free-lane attempt starts in the window
    completed: int         # jobs that finished inside the class deadline
    free_wall_p50: float   # seconds per attempt, free lane
    free_wall_p95: float   # seconds per attempt, free lane
    paid_wall_p50: float   # seconds per job, reserved lane
    paid_cost: float       # currency units per completed job, reserved lane
    slack_budget: float    # seconds of negative slack this class may spend
    miss_penalty: float    # currency units charged when the deadline slips


def retry_ratio(s):
    if s.completed == 0:
        return None
    return max(s.attempts - s.completed, 0) / s.completed


def free_duration_p95(s):
    r = retry_ratio(s)
    return None if r is None else s.free_wall_p95 * (1.0 + r)


def slack_used(s):
    d = free_duration_p95(s)
    return None if d is None else d - s.paid_wall_p50


def miss_proxy(s):
    # Crude upper-bound proxy, not a fitted probability model.
    used = slack_used(s)
    if used is None:
        return 1.0
    if used <= s.slack_budget:
        return 0.0
    return min(1.0, (used - s.slack_budget) / max(used, 1e-9))


def route(s):
    used = slack_used(s)
    if used is None:
        return 'hold', 'no completed jobs in window'
    if used > s.slack_budget:
        return 'reserved', 'p95 slack use exceeds budget'
    risk = miss_proxy(s) * s.miss_penalty
    if risk >= s.paid_cost:
        return 'reserved', 'risk-adjusted free cost >= paid cost'
    return 'free', 'slack within budget and risk below paid cost'


def main(path):
    with open(path) as fh:
        rows = [ClassStats(**json.loads(l)) for l in fh if l.strip()]
    print('class             slack_used  budget  miss_p  free_risk  decision')
    for s in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r.name):
        used = slack_used(s)
        decision, why = route(s)
        risk = miss_proxy(s) * s.miss_penalty
        used_s = 'n/a' if used is None else '%ds' % used
        print('%-17s %9s %6ds %7.2f %10.2f  %s' % (
            s.name, used_s, s.slack_budget, miss_proxy(s), risk, decision))
        print('%-17s reason: %s' % ('', why))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 'jobs.jsonl')

Declared workload for the sample fixture

State the conditions before you quote any result.

  • Two job classes, 1,000 and 900 completed jobs in one 24h window.
  • Free lane: one worker pool, no reserved capacity, timing measured per attempt.
  • Paid baseline: p50 per job from the previous week on reserved capacity.
  • No model-quality comparison. This drill prices time, not accuracy.

Run it locally in under a minute

Create the fixture. These are sample values, not published measurements.

{"name":"nightly-embed","attempts":1180,"completed":1000,"free_wall_p50":38.0,"free_wall_p95":96.0,"paid_wall_p50":41.0,"paid_cost":0.42,"slack_budget":120.0,"miss_penalty":180.0}
{"name":"ocr-backfill","attempts":960,"completed":900,"free_wall_p50":22.0,"free_wall_p95":150.0,"paid_wall_p50":24.0,"paid_cost":0.11,"slack_budget":60.0,"miss_penalty":40.0}

Run the router:

python3 breakeven.py jobs.jsonl

Expected output on the fixture above. Label it expected until your own window reproduces it.

class             slack_used  budget  miss_p  free_risk  decision
nightly-embed            72s    120s    0.00       0.00  free
                  reason: slack within budget and risk below paid cost
ocr-backfill            136s     60s    0.56      22.36  reserved
                  reason: p95 slack use exceeds budget

The second class is the interesting one. Its per-attempt p95 is slower, and its retry ratio adds about 7 percent. Slack use lands at 136 seconds against a 60 second budget.

Free is the expensive lane here, and tokens never entered the calculation.

Failure injection: prove the ledger counts

A routing rule you never broke is a guess. Break the lane first.

# worker.py is a throwaway harness, not a model client.
python3 worker.py --class ocr-backfill --concurrency 4 &
WPID=$!
for i in 1 2 3; do
  sleep 60
  pkill -f 'worker.py --class ocr-backfill' -n
  sleep 5
  python3 worker.py --class ocr-backfill --concurrency 4 &
  WPID=$!
done
kill $WPID
python3 breakeven.py jobs.jsonl

Watch one thing: does a killed attempt show up as attempt=fail or does it vanish?

If it vanishes, your attempts counter is wrong. Your retry ratio is then wrong. Your routing decision is then wrong.

A minimal harness so the smoke test runs:

# worker.py - throwaway harness for the ledger drill only.
import argparse, random, time

p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument('--class', dest='cls', required=True)
p.add_argument('--concurrency', type=int, default=1)
p.add_argument('--attempt-seconds', type=float, default=30.0)
p.add_argument('--fail-rate', type=float, default=0.15)
a = p.parse_args()

while True:
    time.sleep(a.attempt_seconds)
    ok = random.random() > a.fail_rate
    print('%s attempt=%s' % (a.cls, 'ok' if ok else 'fail'), flush=True)

This harness proves your ledger counts. It proves nothing about any model. Swap in your real worker for that.

Telemetry you must emit

Without these fields the ledger is unreadable a week later.

  • job_class and route at admission time
  • attempt_index per job, starting at 0
  • attempt_started_at, attempt_ended_at
  • attempt_outcome: ok, preempted, timeout, throttled, worker_lost
  • deadline_at and slack_remaining_s at completion
  • tokens_in, tokens_out, even on a free tier
  • worker_id, so a bad host is visible

Keep tokens_in on free runs. You need it later to compute the exchange rate between free capacity and reserved capacity.

Decision table and threshold rationale

Evidence in the window Route Why
p95 slack use under 50 percent of budget free headroom absorbs the retry tax
p95 slack use between 50 and 100 percent free, alert at 70 percent one bad hour breaks it
p95 slack use over budget reserved measured breach, not a guess
risk-adjusted free cost at or above paid cost reserved free is the expensive lane
zero completed jobs hold no data, no route

Why 50 percent as a default? Because retry ratio is usually noisier than wall time. If your retry ratio p95 moves more than your duration p95, tighten the threshold.

If the miss penalty is contractual, do not run the free lane at any threshold. Slack budgets are for engineering tradeoffs, not for contracts.

Cleanup and rollback

Run these in order. Write them down before the drill, not after.

  1. Drain the class. Set free-lane route weight to 0.
  2. Wait for in-flight attempts, or cancel them and record worker_lost explicitly.
  3. Restore the reserved weight from your config store, never from memory.
  4. Keep the window JSONL file. It is the evidence for the next review.
  5. Revert alert thresholds only after two clean windows.

Step 3 matters most. A rollback typed by hand at 02:20 is a second incident.

Where free capacity fits in this drill

The drill needs a free lane before you can price one. MonkeyCode is an open-source project with free model access; the operator states 10M free tokens and a free server option.

I treat both availability claims as operator-supplied. Limits and terms change, so confirm them on the project page before you plan around them.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

In this workflow the free tier is exactly the lane whose retry ratio you are measuring. Point the harness at one small class, run one window, read the ledger. Start with one class and one window on the free tier, then decide.

Limitations and who should not use this

Be honest about the edges.

  • Not for synchronous user traffic with a hard p99. Free lanes are variable by nature.
  • Not for classes where a single miss is contractually unacceptable. Keep those reserved.
  • Not reliable under about 200 completed jobs per window. The p95 is noise below that; widen the window.
  • miss_proxy is a proxy, not a fitted model. Replace it with your own estimator if you have one.
  • Do not use this to justify free capacity against a regulated deadline without a named risk owner.

The threshold question

Every number here is a threshold with a rationale, and yours will differ. The useful question is not whether free capacity is cheap.

It is: how many seconds of slack does a retry buy, and who pays when the budget runs out?

Answer that with a measured window, and routing stops being a mood.

title: E-commerce Node.js Backend: Feature Flags Disable Noisy Alerts Quickly
description:
TL;DR: In an e-commerce Node.js backend, continue measuring every AI agent loop, but put the final notification decision behind a feature flag evaluated by the backend. This separates evidence collection from a noisy alert rule, permits suppression without redeployment, and keeps rollback confined to a narrow adapter. Polling still imposes a stale interval, so record the flag value used for each decision and make notification delivery idempotent.

The storage bill is made from two unlike terms. Compact accounting facts such as request identity, vendor, latency, cache status, and cost grow mainly with call count; full prompts, model responses, tool arguments, and repeatedly indexed logs grow with both call count and payload size. For an agent that may invoke a model and several commerce tools per customer request, payload retention can therefore dominate even though the small decision ledger is the part needed for reconciliation.

Retain the compact record for every loop. Sample or expire bulky content under an explicit data-lifecycle policy, then gate only the notification branch. This change moves the dominant byte count without making a muted rule look like a healthy system.

There is a price. After a transcript expires, an immutable request ID may establish that an expensive or slow turn occurred while no longer explaining the model's exact choice. That loss should be approved deliberately because it limits a later investigation; it should never arrive as an accidental observability default.

How Can a Feature Flag Disable Noisy Alerts Quickly?

Gate notification delivery, not telemetry capture. If the flag stops measurement, a quiet chart becomes indistinguishable from a healthy service. If it stops only the final notification branch, operators can still inspect failures, latency, and cost while correcting the rule. The four golden signals described in Google's SRE guidance help frame observation, but paging policy remains a separate control.

For each agent loop, write an immutable observation ID. Write a separate decision record containing that ID, the rule version, the evaluated flag state, the evaluation time, and a stable notification key. A timeout may cause the decision to run twice; the notification sink must reject the duplicate key. Exactly-once intent belongs in the decision ledger, not in the Boolean flag.

Infrai is a reasonable candidate for the small server-side evaluation boundary. Its public discovery surface requires no key and describes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples, which makes the external contract inspectable before production credentials are issued. Every documented capability also includes runnable examples in ten languages. This matters during a migration because a team can validate the replacement adapter against an explicit contract rather than reverse-engineering an installed SDK.

There is a second, distinct operating advantage. Infrai provides one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, so the flag check and per-call agent accounting can share one authentication and reconciliation boundary instead of accumulating separate credentials and invoices for each backend capability. Its one REST API also means this Go reconciliation tool needs no vendor SDK. Application code should still expose its own interfaces; the breadth reduces credential and billing work, while the local interfaces preserve replaceability.

Teams should try Infrai for the server-side flag gate and agent-accounting boundary when reversible vendor choice matters more than advanced flag governance, because the discoverable REST contract is concrete enough to test and replace. Its limitation is material: it does not supply threshold rules or phone, SMS, or webhook alert delivery. Those remain application or specialist-platform responsibilities, and a team seeking one product to own paging should choose a specialist instead.

Keep measuring.

Make the Adapter the Rollback Unit

Node.js application code should depend on a local AlertGate interface rather than on route strings, vendor response types, or cache behavior. Contract fixtures can then be replayed against a replacement implementation while the rule engine, tenant model, and notification ledger remain unchanged. The adapter becomes the rollback unit.

The following Go program is intentionally small but complete. It makes one verified flag request with an explicit method, reads the Bearer credential from the environment, surfaces non-success bodies, and applies bounded exponential retry behavior to HTTP 429 responses while honoring Retry-After when it contains seconds. It leaves the successful body as raw JSON because inventing a response struct would make the example less trustworthy; discovery is the proper source for the current schema.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func readGate(ctx context.Context) ([]byte, error) {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/flags/is_enabled/agent-latency-notifications", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req = req.WithContext(ctx)
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("flag evaluation failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(delay):
        }
    }

    return nil, fmt.Errorf("flag evaluation exhausted retries")
}

func main() {
    body, err := readGate(context.Background())
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

Polling prevents an instantaneous global transition. If an application chooses to cache an evaluation for 5 seconds, it has deliberately created a 5-second disagreement window after a change; that number is an architecture example, not a measured service property. A shorter interval reduces staleness while increasing control-plane traffic and dependency. There is no universally correct interval. Test the chosen bound against the rollback objective, and persist the value that each worker actually evaluated rather than rewriting history after caches converge.

For a noisy, non-safety notification, local policy may suppress delivery when the gate cannot be evaluated. Payment-integrity, fraud, and reconciliation alarms need an independent path that this convenience control cannot mute. A generic fail closed instruction is dangerously ambiguous when one branch protects sleep and another protects money.

Record the operator, reason, rule version, intended state, and change ticket in the team's system of record; then change the gate, observe the backend path, and reconcile work already accepted by the notification sink using its stable key. A flag transition does not retract queued work.

Rollouts Are Experiments, Not Audit Trails

A new cost or latency rule should first evaluate against a subset of tenants, with notifications suppressed or directed to review. Rollout controls can stage that exposure before all tenants receive the rule. Compare the same immutable observations under the same rule version, or a shift in shopping-agent traffic may be mistaken for a better threshold.

Keep the graph shallow. Infrai flags have no parent-child dependency, evaluation statistics, change audit log, or trash-and-restore behavior for deleted flags. One notification rule, one gate, and one documented owner is easier to reverse than a master switch with implicit children. Clients only poll, which is why a critical mute decision belongs in the server-side notification path instead of a browser or long-lived shopper session.

Compliance limits narrow the choice further. A control subject to separation of duties, approval chains, or durable proof of who changed what needs an external system of record or a specialist flag product that verifiably supplies those controls. An evaluation response proves neither authorization nor approval. The logging boundary also needs separate review: there is no per-user deletion interface, no bulk export or subscription interface, and no exposed configuration entry point for retention or cold storage. Searchable logs alone do not establish support for a GDPR erasure workflow.

Stop before deleting.

Deletion deserves special care. With no trash or restore operation for a deleted flag, disabling a gate is safer than deleting it during an incident. The former is a reversible state transition; the latter changes the recovery procedure. Consider a rollout in which tenant A has already produced a notification decision while tenant B has not yet evaluated the new value: deleting the control at that moment does not reconcile either decision, and recreating a similarly named flag does not establish historical continuity. The ledger must preserve both evaluated states, the rollout cohort, and each delivery key until the reconciliation job proves that accepted work was either delivered once or deliberately suppressed.

Compare the Boundary, Not the Logo

An e-commerce agent backend needs telemetry analysis, flag control, and notification delivery. No product below should be treated as an interchangeable bundle, and the rollback objective is served better when each responsibility is explicit.

Option Strong reason to evaluate it Boundary to verify
LaunchDarkly A specialist flag platform fits teams whose main requirement is flag operations and governance. Verify server-side freshness, approval evidence, audit retention, and rollout semantics against the rollback objective.
Unleash It is a candidate when a team wants feature management assessed independently from telemetry. Verify polling behavior, deployment ownership, deletion recovery, and compliance evidence.
Datadog Its log ingestion and indexing model fits a broader specialist observability procurement. Model ingestion and indexed retention separately, then verify alert delivery and governance.
Sentry It merits evaluation when grouped application errors and investigation are the primary operational job. Verify the required flag integration, notification path, privacy controls, and retention.
Grafana It fits teams that want dashboards and alert evaluation composed with telemetry stores they already operate. Account for collectors, stores, notification components, and retention controls.
Infrai Its discoverable REST contract keeps a flag check and per-call agent metadata behind a narrow adapter. Supply notification delivery and flag-change audit evidence elsewhere; polling freshness remains explicit.

A dedicated flag product is the stronger choice when durable change history, approval workflows, and organizational flag governance are mandatory; LaunchDarkly or Unleash should be evaluated for that case. This is the central trade-off. Datadog, Sentry, or Grafana deserves evaluation when a specialist observability workflow is the actual procurement boundary. Infrai does not fit requirements for distributed trace queries or span trees, source-map symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, Session Replay, or heartbeat monitoring; logs may carry trace and span identifiers for correlation, but those identifiers do not create a trace-query system. A Healthchecks-style service addresses the separate question of whether a scheduled task ran at all.

Datadog's published pricing structure illustrates why retention requires architectural treatment: log ingestion and indexed retention are separate dimensions. Current unit prices are unnecessary for this decision. The important arithmetic is the amount of high-volume content retained and indexed, followed by the evidence deliberately discarded when that term is reduced.

A Rollback Decision Rule

Choose the boundary by writing the failure test first. If a vendor becomes unavailable or unsuitable, can the application swap one adapter while preserving observation IDs, rule versions, notification keys, and the audit record? If yes, the dependency is acceptably narrow. If business logic imports vendor types or treats a dashboard as the ledger, migration will be a data and correctness project rather than an adapter change.

For this agent loop, retain compact latency and cost facts for every call, sample sensitive or bulky transcripts according to policy, evaluate the suppression gate on the backend, and deduplicate the final delivery. Roll out a new rule to a subset before broad exposure. Keep financial-integrity alarms outside the mutable convenience gate.

The design is reversible only when the evidence survives the suppression mechanism. A fast mute that erases measurements is not rollback safety; it is loss of visibility at the moment visibility matters most.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the feature-flag incident-response guide and verify the live discovery contract before implementing the adapter.

Further reading

References

  • Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems
  • Datadog pricing and log billing model
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Grafana Alerting documentation
  • Infrai discovery: metrics.report fields and billing
  • Infrai discovery: flags.rollout fields

title: A large-scale climate-aware satellite image dataset for domain adaptive land-cover semantic segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.21238v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A few well-annotated datasets for land-cover semantic segmentation have recently been introduced to advance the field of earth observation technologies. However, these datasets overlook the significant diversity among geographic areas with different climates, which can greatly impact and diversify land cover. Consequently, this leads to a domain gap in remote sensing images and severe performance degradation of the segmentation models. To enhance land-cover semantic segmentation with improved generalization ability, we conducted the first investigation into the impact of climate on this task. In this paper, we present a unique large-scale Climate-Aware Satellite Images Dataset (CASID) specifically designed for domain adaptive land-cover semantic segmentation. It consists of 980 satellite images with a size of 5000 x 5000 pixels, collected from 30 different regions around Asia, covering over 24,500 square kilometers. These images are gathered from four distinct climate zones, namely temperate monsoon, subtropical monsoon, tropical monsoon, and tropical rainforest. It includes four sub-datasets/domains, each representing one of the aforementioned climate zones. This characteristic makes CASID the first climate-aware land-cover semantic segmentation dataset with multiple domains. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the samples from the four climate zones, emphasizing differences in global image features, image texture, category distribution, spectral value, and object shape. These analyses offer valuable insights for subsequent research in this field. Moreover, we conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the latest semantic segmentation and unsupervised domain adaptation methods on the CASID dataset. These results serve as a robust baseline for future research endeavors. Our dataset will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Linwei-Chen/CASID.

title: Rate Limiting Like Gandalf: Building a Distributed Cache with Redis
description:
The Quest Begins (The "Why")

Ever had your API melt down because a sudden traffic spike hammered every endpoint at once? I remember a late‑night deploy where our “simple” in‑process counter crashed under a flash sale, and the pager started singing like a busted karaoke machine. We needed a way to throttle requests without turning every service into a bottleneck or rewriting the whole stack.

The problem boiled down to: how do we share a counter across many instances, keep it fast, and survive node failures?

A naïve approach—each service keeps its own local counter—fails the moment you scale beyond one node. A centralized DB works but adds latency that kills throughput. Enter Redis: an in‑memory key‑value store that can be replicated, clustered, and accessed with sub‑millisecond latency. It felt like discovering a hidden armory in a dungeon—suddenly we had the right tool for the job.

The Revelation (The Insight)

The magic insight is decoupling the rate‑limit decision from the storage mechanism by using a token bucket algorithm implemented with a single Redis key per client (or IP, or API key).

Here’s why this beats the usual alternatives:

Approach Pros Cons
Local in‑memory counter Zero network latency No shared state → limits are per‑instance, easy to bypass
Central SQL/NoSQL DB Strong consistency Higher latency, more operational overhead
Redis + Lua script Atomic increment & expiry, O(1) time, built‑in TTL for auto‑cleanup Requires Redis cluster, but that’s a solved problem for most teams

The critical insight is that we can let Redis do the heavy lifting atomically with a Lua script, so we never read‑modify‑write in two steps (which would invite race conditions). The script returns the current token count and, if allowed, decrements it—all in one round trip.

ASCII diagram of the flow 

+----------------+      Lua Script (EVAL)      +----------------+
|  Service A     |  --------------------->    |   Redis Cluster  |
|  (or B, C…)   |  <--------------------     |   (key: bucket) |
+----------------+      (INCR + EXPIRE)       +----------------+
        |                                               |
        |  Decision: allow/deny based on tokens       |
        v                                               v
+----------------+                               +----------------+
|  HTTP Response |                               |  TTL refresh   |
+----------------+                               +----------------+

The bucket key holds two fields: tokens (remaining permits) and timestamp (last refill). On each request we:

  1. Refill tokens based on elapsed time (now - last_refill).
  2. Cap at the max bucket size.
  3. If tokens >= 1, consume one and reply 200.
  4. Else reply 429 Too Many Requests.

All of this happens inside Redis, guaranteeing that two concurrent requests can’t both see the same token count and both slip through.

Wielding the Power (Code & Examples)

The Struggle (Before) 

# Bad: naive per‑process counter (race condition city)
import time
from flask import Flask, request, abort

app = Flask(__name__)
counter = 0          # ← only one process sees this
LIMIT = 100          # requests per minute
WINDOW = 60          # seconds

@app.before_request
def limit():
    global counter
    now = time.time()
    if not hasattr(limit, "reset"):
        limit.reset = now
        counter = 0
    if now - limit.reset > WINDOW:
        limit.reset = now
        counter = 0
    if counter >= LIMIT:
        abort(429)
    counter += 1

What’s wrong? If you run three Gunicorn workers, each gets its own counter. Three workers × 100 = 300 effective limit—your rate limit is basically useless. Plus, the global variable isn’t safe across threads or processes.

The Victory (After)

We’ll use the redis-py client and a Lua script that does the token‑bucket math atomically.

import time
import redis
from flask import Flask, request, abort

app = Flask(__name__)
r = redis.Redis(host='redis-cluster', port=6379, decode_responses=True)

# Lua script stored as a string; we'll load it once at startup
LUASCRIPT = """
local key = KEYS[1]
local limit = tonumber(ARGV[1])   -- max tokens
local refill_rate = tonumber(ARGV[2])  -- tokens per second
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])

local bucket = rcall('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'timestamp')
local tokens = tonumber(bucket[1]) or limit
local last = tonumber(bucket[2]) or now

-- refill
local delta = math.max(0, now - last)
tokens = math.min(limit, tokens + delta * refill_rate)

local allowed = 0
if tokens >= 1 then
    tokens = tokens - 1
    allowed = 1
end

rcall('HMSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'timestamp', now)
rcall('EXPIRE', key, math.ceil(limit / refill_rate) + 5)  -- auto‑clean
return allowed
"""

# Register the script (returns a SHA we can call with EVALSHA)
SCRIPT_SHA = r.script_load(LUASCRIPT)

def allow_request(client_id: str, limit: int = 100, per_seconds: int = 60) -> bool:
    """Return True if request is allowed, False otherwise."""
    key = f"rate_limit:{client_id}"
    now = time.time()
    refill_rate = limit / per_seconds  # tokens per second
    # EVALSHA returns 1 (allowed) or 0 (denied)
    result = r.evalsha(SCRIPT_SHA, 1, key, limit, refill_rate, now)
    return bool(result)

@app.before_request
def enforce_limit():
    # Use IP or API key as the client identifier
    client_id = request.remote_addr  # or request.headers.get('X-API-Key')
    if not allow_request(client_id, limit=100, per_seconds=60):
        abort(429)

@app.route('/api/hello')
def hello():
    return {"msg": "Hello, traveler!"}

What changed?

  • We moved state to Redis, so every service instance sees the same bucket.
  • The Lua script guarantees the read‑modify‑write cycle is atomic—no race conditions even under thousands of concurrent requests.
  • Keys auto‑expire (EXPIRE) after a bit of idle time, keeping memory usage bounded.

Common Traps to Avoid

  1. Using GET/SET separately – If you fetch the token count, then decrement it in a second command, two threads can interleave and both think they have a token. Always wrap the logic in a Lua script (or use Redis’ INCRBY with a custom TTL trick, but Lua is clearer).
  2. Forgetting to set an expiration – Without EXPIRE, idle clients will linger forever, wasting memory. A short TTL (a few multiples of the refill interval) lets Redis reclaim keys automatically.

Why This New Power Matters

Now you can drop this snippet into any service—Flask, FastAPI, Node.js, Go—and instantly get a globally consistent rate limiter that scales horizontally with your Redis cluster. No more per‑instance guesswork, no more surprise 429s during a flash sale, and no extra latency that makes users feel like they’re stuck in a loading screen.

You’ve turned a flimsy, local counter into a resilient, shared guardrail—think of it as giving your API a magical shield that only lets through the worthy adventurers.

Your Turn

Grab a Redis instance (even a free tier on Redis Cloud works), copy the Lua script above, and try limiting a public endpoint with a different algorithm—maybe a fixed‑window counter or a sliding‑window log. Compare latency, memory usage, and ease of tuning. Share your findings in the comments; I’d love to hear what quest you embark on next!

Happy coding, and may your rate limits always be just right. 🚀

title: Value-Informed Schedule Trimming for Accelerated Sequential Monte Carlo Guidance in Discrete Diffusion
description:
arXiv:2610.20669v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reward-guided discrete diffusion enables test-time alignment with downstream objectives, but applying Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) guidance at every denoising step is computationally expensive. Active guidance steps require additional reward evaluations and, for gradient-based proposals, value-gradient computations. Sparse guidance reduces this cost by guiding only a subset of timesteps, but commonly used schedules are fixed heuristics whose effectiveness can vary substantially across tasks. We propose VISTA, a training-free method that automatically selects guided timesteps under a fixed budget. VISTA formulates sparse guidance as approximation of the ideal full-guidance probability path and derives an estimable upper bound on \(\ell_1\) path deviation. Using value statistics collected from a small number of full-guidance warmup generations, VISTA optimizes the resulting empirical surrogate exactly via dynamic programming. The warmup generations can be retained as model outputs, and after schedule selection VISTA has the same per-generation guidance complexity as other sparse schedules with the same budget. Across text, biological sequence, and image generation tasks, VISTA discovers task-dependent schedules and outperforms hand-designed sparse schedules in most tested settings, while approaching or exceeding full-guidance performance on several task metrics. In toxic-text generation, for example, VISTA attains a 0.99 unique-toxic ratio compared with 1.00 for full guidance while reducing post-selection per-generation latency from 204.23 s to 38.16 s, a 5.35$\times$ speedup.

title: Rubric Judgments Lack Uncertainty: Conformal Weighting for LLM Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.21214v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rubric-based evaluation is widely used to assess large language model (LLM) outputs by decomposing quality into multiple criteria and assigning each a binary judgment from an LLM verifier. However, judgment certainty varies substantially across criteria. Existing methods uniformly aggregate these judgments into a final score, implicitly treating every criterion as equally certain and overlooking this heterogeneity. As a result, uncertain judgments remain incorporated into reward estimation without distinction, potentially yielding misleading training signals for downstream reinforcement learning (RL). To address this limitation, we propose Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW), a training-free framework that quantifies criterion-level judgment uncertainty via conformal calibration. Specifically, URW elicits a soft uncertainty signal from a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates and converts it into a per-criterion weight using split-conformal $p$-values with provable coverage guarantees. Extensive experiments demonstrate that URW consistently improves pairwise preference accuracy and delivers stronger downstream RL alignment.

title: Halve-Then-Greedy: Adaptive Sampling for Posterior Success with Near-Optimal Instance Dependence
description:
arXiv:2610.20997v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study fixed-budget adaptive experimentation aimed at maximizing the probability of obtaining sufficient posterior evidence that a recommended design's mean performance exceeds a target. Unlike best-arm identification, this objective does not require finding the best design. For Gaussian bandits with a Gaussian prior, we propose \emph{Halve-Then-Greedy} (HTG), which combines a large initial balanced allocation, successive halving, and posterior-greedy sampling. We prove instance-dependent, finite-budget exponential bounds on posterior-failure probability that capture both separation from unfavorable arms and the presence of multiple favorable arms. On one-positive-arm families, we establish an asymptotic sample-complexity lower bound that HTG matches up to a logarithmic factor. We further analyze uniform sampling and sequential halving, revealing regimes where they require more samples than HTG by linear and logarithmic factors, respectively. Simulations illustrate HTG's sample-efficiency advantages and their dependence on instance structure.

title: One Bias Score, Two Factors: How Mitigations Affect Option Bias in Multiple-Choice Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.20993v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reordering multiple-choice options can change a model's answer, an effect studied as selection bias (a preference for certain option letters) and as order sensitivity (changes in answers across option orderings). We connect these perspectives through the pooled selection-rate standard deviation (pooled SD), which measures how unevenly option letters are selected across questions and orderings. When every option of each question appears equally often at each position, the pooled SD is exactly the product of two label-free factors: the flip rate and the positional skew. The flip rate is the fraction of questions whose chosen option changes across orderings; the positional skew is the standard deviation of option-letter selection rates among those questions. Across 41 checkpoints and 12 benchmarks, the flip rate tracks accuracy and output uncertainty, while the positional skew tracks the estimated option-symbol prior. Prior correction for selection bias mainly reduces the positional skew. Aggregating each ordering with its reversal, a mitigation for order sensitivity, mainly reduces the flip rate. Both reduce the range of accuracy across correct-answer letters by similar amounts, but aggregation leaves fewer model-rank reversals. Applying prior correction before aggregation reduces both factors and further narrows this accuracy range. However, aggregation lowers the flip rate partly by settling questions on the same wrong option. We therefore recommend reporting both factors to distinguish mitigation effects, alongside accuracy to distinguish stability from correctness.

title: Sidebery: Vertical Tab Sidebar for Firefox with Tree Structure and Session Snapshots
description:
If you work with many tabs, Firefox's default tab bar is a horizontal row that eventually becomes unusable. Sidebery moves your tabs to a vertical sidebar with tree structure, groups, and session management — transforming how you organize browser sessions.

Why a Vertical Tab Sidebar

The problem with horizontal tabs:

  • At 15+ tabs, tabs shrink to icons with no visible titles
  • You can't see what's open at a glance
  • Navigation requires clicking through tabs or using Ctrl+Tab cycling
  • No visual grouping of related tabs

Sidebery puts tabs in a vertical panel. Benefits:

  • Tab titles are always readable (you have all vertical screen space)
  • Tree structure: child tabs indent under parent (open a link from a tab = its child)
  • Collapsible groups for organizing related tabs
  • Pinned tabs stay pinned but separate
  • Search box to find any open tab

Installing Sidebery

addons.mozilla.org → search "Sidebery" → Add to Firefox.

After installing:

  1. A sidebar icon appears in your toolbar
  2. Click it to open the Sidebery sidebar
  3. By default, it appears on the left side
  4. Optionally: hide the original horizontal tab bar (via Sidebery settings + userChrome.css)

Hiding the Horizontal Tab Bar

To get a clean UI with only the Sidebery sidebar:

  1. Create a userChrome.css file:

Find your profile folder: about:support → Profile Folder → Open Folder

Create chrome/userChrome.css:

/* Hide horizontal tab bar */
#TabsToolbar {
  visibility: collapse !important;
}

/* Optionally: make the sidebar wider */
#sidebar-box {
  min-width: 200px;
  max-width: 400px;
}
  1. Enable userChrome.css:
    • about:config → toolkit.legacyUserProfileCustomizations.stylesheets = true
    • Restart Firefox

Now Firefox shows the Sidebery sidebar without the horizontal tab bar. Clean, vertical-only tab management.

Tree Structure: How It Works

When you Ctrl+click a link (or right-click → Open in New Tab from a context menu), the new tab is a child of the current tab.

In Sidebery:

  • Parent tab shows with an arrow/indent indicator
  • Child tabs appear below, indented
  • Collapsing the parent hides all children
  • Closing the parent can optionally close all children (configurable)

Practical example:

  1. Search Google
  2. Open 5 results in new tabs
  3. Those 5 tabs are children of the Google search tab
  4. Collapse the Google tab → all 5 results hidden
  5. Expand when you want to compare them

This is much more useful than the flat tab list.

Tab Groups

Sidebery supports explicit tab groups (independent of the tree):

  1. Right-click in the Sidebery sidebar → Create Group
  2. Drag tabs into the group
  3. Collapse/expand the group
  4. Name the group

Groups are good for manually organizing tabs that don't have a natural parent-child relationship.

Searching Open Tabs

In the Sidebery panel, there's a search icon (or press Ctrl+Space by default in some Sidebery versions). Type to filter tabs by title or URL.

This replaces the awkward Ctrl+Tab cycling for finding a specific tab by name.

Session Management with Sidebery

Sidebery can save and restore sessions of tabs:

Snapshots: Sidebery automatically takes snapshots of your tabs periodically. Access via: Sidebery icon → Menu (gear icon) → Snapshots

Creating a named snapshot:

  1. Sidebery menu → Create Snapshot
  2. Give it a name
  3. Saved snapshots can be restored later

This is similar to a session manager extension, but integrated with the tab tree structure. A restored snapshot brings back the full tree, not just a flat list of URLs.

Combination with Tab Manager & Session Saver extension: For cross-device session sync, use Firefox Sync for "open tabs" and a dedicated session manager. Sidebery's snapshots are local-only; they don't sync across devices. If you want sessions accessible on multiple machines, export from Sidebery and use a separate sync method.

Sidebery Settings Worth Knowing

Access via: Sidebery icon → gear icon → Settings

Tab behavior:

  • "Create child tab on middle-click": links opened by middle-click become tree children
  • "Activate parent after close": when closing a child, activates parent
  • "Move child tabs to parent if parent closed": reorganizes tree on tab close

UI:

  • Colorize tabs by container (if using Multi-Account Containers)
  • Show close button: always / on hover
  • Tab height: compact / normal / wide

Sidebar position: Settings → Sidebar → Position (left or right)

Using Sidebery with Multi-Account Containers

If you use Firefox Multi-Account Containers, Sidebery colors the tabs by container. Each container gets a border color, making it visually obvious which tabs belong to which context (Work, Personal, Shopping, etc.).

This is genuinely useful visual differentiation — you can see at a glance which tab is in which container without reading the label.

Keyboard Shortcuts in Sidebery

Sidebery adds some new keyboard actions:

  • Ctrl+.: Focus the Sidebery sidebar (navigate with arrow keys)
  • Ctrl+Shift+C: Create a new container tab

Configure more in Sidebery settings → Keybindings.

Sidebery vs Tree Style Tab

The other major vertical tab extension for Firefox:

Feature Sidebery Tree Style Tab
Active development Yes Yes
Container coloring Yes Yes
Session snapshots Yes Limited
Groups Yes Limited
Customization Very deep Deep
Performance Good Good
Complexity More Less

Tree Style Tab is the long-established option; Sidebery is the newer, more feature-rich option. Both are good. Sidebery has more built-in features; Tree Style Tab is simpler.

Performance Note

With 200+ tabs, Sidebery's rendering can slow down slightly (it's rendering a large virtual list). For extreme tab counts (500+), consider whether session management is a better solution than keeping all tabs open simultaneously.

The Tab Manager & Session Saver extension pairs well with Sidebery: save current sessions to disk, close the tabs, and use Sidebery's tree for the tabs you're actively working on.
