title: Prompt Cache Control puts a live countdown on Claude Code’s 5 minute cache
description:
Claude Code already caches your prompt prefix. What it does not tell you is how much of the last request the cache actually served, or how many seconds you have left before that cache lapses and you pay to write the whole thing again.

That number matters most exactly when you are not looking at it. You read a long file, Claude answers, you go think for six minutes, you come back and type one line, and that one line costs you a full rewrite of a 150k token prefix.

// Detect dark theme var iframe = document.getElementById('tweet-2106455605925822967-193'); if (document.body.className.includes('dark-theme')) { iframe.src = "https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=2106455605925822967&theme=dark" }

What the band shows

One row above the prompt, redrawn every second:

cache 98% read 80k · wrote 1k · new 300 · 3:41 · 5m · warm: keep going
cache  0% read 0 · wrote 52k · new 300 · 4:58 · 5m · cache missed: model changed
cache 98% read 150k · wrote 1k · new 300 · 0:00 · 5m · expired: the next message rewrites 151k tokens

Three numbers per request, which is how the API reports a prompt: what the cache served, what this request wrote into it, and what went past it uncached. Then a countdown, the lifetime in force, and a verdict.

The verdict is the part that earns its row. “Keep going” means a reply now is a cache read. “Expired” with a large prefix means the next message is a cache write at 1.25x base input, and the Mod says /compact instead, or /clear if you are done with the task anyway.

When it misses, it names why: the model changed, the entry lapsed, or the prefix changed. A prefix change is anything the request is built on top of, so switching model or effort, changing your tool set, or editing CLAUDE.md all land in that bucket.

/cache, and the toasts

// Detect dark theme var iframe = document.getElementById('tweet-2106455608090099799-415'); if (document.body.className.includes('dark-theme')) { iframe.src = "https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=2106455608090099799&theme=dark" }

/cache opens a pane with the time left as a bar that shrinks, green down to yellow below 40% of the lifetime and red from the warning threshold, a stacked read / wrote / new bar for the last request, and a colour coded table with one row per turn. That table is the part I actually read after a long session, because it shows where the misses were.

The toasts fire once per cache entry: at the warning threshold, which is 60 seconds by default, and then again at 10, 3, 2 and 1 seconds. Only for prompts of 20k tokens or more, so a short session never nags you.

Every request that reads the cache refreshes it at no extra cost. That is Anthropic’s rule, not the Mod’s, and it is why the toast says what it says: any message keeps the 5 minute window alive, and the Mod is only telling you the window is closing.

Installing it 

npx claude-code-templates@latest --mod observability/prompt-cache-control

It lands in .claude/skills/prompt-cache-control/ and loads as prompt-cache-control@skills-dir. Then /reload-plugins and you have the band.

Mods need Claude Code v2.1.287 or later and are on by default from that version. If you still export CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 from the early access period, drop it, because v2.1.287 and later ignores it. The component page still carries the old 2.1.259 line, and that is on me to fix.

The options worth changing 

{
  "pluginConfigs": {
    "prompt-cache-control@skills-dir": {
      "options": { "warnSeconds": 120, "compactAtTokens": 60000, "status": true }
    }
  }
}
  • ttl: auto, 5m or 1h. Leave it on auto unless you know better than the inference.
  • warnSeconds: when the band turns yellow and the first toast fires. Default 60.
  • compactAtTokens: the prefix size from which an expired cache suggests /compact. Default 100000.
  • band, status, toast: the three surfaces. Band on, status line entry off, toasts on, by default.

One caveat on that 100k default: it is a judgement call, not a figure from Anthropic’s documentation. If your model’s cache writes hurt, lower it.

pluginConfigs is read from user or managed settings only. Project and local entries are ignored, so putting this in a repository's .claude/settings.json does nothing.

How it works out your lifetime

// Detect dark theme var iframe = document.getElementById('tweet-2106474300785996075-391'); if (document.body.className.includes('dark-theme')) { iframe.src = "https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=2106474300785996075&theme=dark" }

The cache is 5 minutes by default and 1 hour when asked for, and which one you get depends on your account and your environment. The Mod walks the same precedence chain Claude Code does: its own ttl option, then FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M, CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL, the promptCacheTtl setting, ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H, and finally the account, which is 1 hour on a subscription inside its plan usage and 5 minutes on usage credits, an API key or a cloud provider.

Then it watches the traffic, which overrules all of that. A cache hit more than 5 minutes after the previous request proves the 1 hour lifetime. A miss between 5 and 60 minutes later, with the same model and a prompt that did not shrink, says the entry lapsed, so 5 minutes. That covers what a Mod cannot read: managed settings, a gateway rewriting the TTL, or a subscription that ran out of plan usage mid session.

The reason it has to infer at all is a gap in the surface. The API names the TTL of each write, and Claude Code’s status line exposes it as prompt_cache.ttl, but the Mod API hands over only the four token counts. If you want the ground truth, run claude -p "hello" --output-format json and read usage.cache_creation.

Where the Mods live

  • The component: Prompt Cache Control on aitmpl.com
  • Context Timeline, the other way to watch a session: Context Timeline
  • Every Mod in the catalog: the Mods index
  • Everything else: aitmpl.com

title: Malformed Metrics Query JSON: Implementing Defensive Alert Worker Boundaries
description:
TL;DR: Treat a malformed metrics-query response as an explicit unknown result, never as zero failures. For a marketplace's nightly data pipeline, attach tenant, pipeline stage, and run identifiers before logs enter shared storage; measure stored bytes by those dimensions; retain compact audit records for every query; and alert separately when the monitoring response cannot be proved valid. The least complex implementation is a strict Go decoder at the worker boundary plus a small, bounded quarantine record containing a digest and a truncated payload.

This ordering matters because the monitoring bill is usually discussed after the parser breaks, although the bill determines what evidence will still exist when it does. The useful quantity is not an advertised unit price. It is attributable stored volume:

daily bytes = sum(encoded event bytes × copies × retention path)

Measure that term first. A worker that silently converts a bad response into an empty result can suppress the failure alert and also assign the query's retrieval cost to an unclassified bucket. That is a correctness defect with an accounting symptom.

What is the bill actually made of?

For this workload, separate ingestion, retained storage, query scanning, and duplicated copies. CloudWatch's public pricing page, for example, describes log ingestion in per-GB terms; the durable lesson is that bytes crossing the ingestion boundary are a cost driver, while the exact commercial rate is deliberately outside this design. Compression, indexing, regional replication, and query execution may add different meters in a particular system, so exporting one total invoice number into a dashboard does not create cost attribution.

Start with an inventory measured from the encoded records, not from an estimate of source rows. The following program accepts an illustrative nightly volume, average encoded size, copy count, and retention days. The sample inputs are an arithmetic demonstration, not a benchmark: 8,000,000 records, 420 bytes each, two retained copies, and 14 days.

package main

import "fmt"

func gib(bytes uint64) float64 {
    return float64(bytes) / (1024 * 1024 * 1024)
}

func main() {
    const records uint64 = 8_000_000
    const encodedBytes uint64 = 420
    const retainedCopies uint64 = 2
    const retentionDays uint64 = 14

    daily := records * encodedBytes * retainedCopies
    retained := daily * retentionDays
    fmt.Printf("daily_ingested_gib=%.2f retained_gib_days=%.2f\n", gib(daily), gib(retained))
}

The multiplication exposes the dominant term without pretending every backend bills identically. Run it again with measurements from each pipeline stage. If catalog_export emits ten times the bytes of settlement_reconcile, optimize the former first even when the latter has the more alarming event count.

Cost attribution must be present at emission time. A useful minimum is marketplace_account, pipeline_stage, run_id, event_class, and outcome. Keep bounded values; a raw error message or order identifier used as a label can create an uncontrolled number of index terms. The high-cardinality detail belongs in the log body, while the stable dimensions belong in the fields used for allocation and filtering.

Do not infer ownership later from free-form text. It fails audit review because the mapping can change after the charge was incurred.

How should an alert worker defensively parse a malformed metrics query JSON response?

The response boundary needs three distinct checks: syntactic JSON validity, the expected envelope shape, and semantic validity of the values used by the alert. HTTP success alone proves none of them. A body containing valid JSON such as {"status":"ok"} is still unusable if the worker's contract requires a numeric failure count and a query identifier.

Model the outcome as valid, invalid, or transport_error. Two states are insufficient. In particular, do not use a zero value as the fallback for a missing number: zero means the pipeline was observed and no failures matched, whereas invalid means the observation could not be completed.

This complete program uses only the Go standard library. UseNumber delays numeric conversion, DisallowUnknownFields detects contract drift rather than ignoring it, the second decode rejects trailing JSON values, and validation refuses blank identifiers, negative counts, or a run mismatch.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
)

type QueryResult struct {
    QueryID     string      `json:"query_id"`
    RunID       string      `json:"run_id"`
    FailureCount json.Number `json:"failure_count"`
}

func parseResult(body []byte, expectedRun string) (QueryResult, error) {
    var result QueryResult
    decoder := json.NewDecoder(bytes.NewReader(body))
    decoder.UseNumber()
    decoder.DisallowUnknownFields()

    if err := decoder.Decode(&result); err != nil {
        return result, fmt.Errorf("decode response: %w", err)
    }
    if err := decoder.Decode(&struct{}{}); !errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
        if err == nil {
            return result, errors.New("response contains a trailing JSON value")
        }
        return result, fmt.Errorf("inspect response suffix: %w", err)
    }
    if result.QueryID == "" || result.RunID == "" || result.FailureCount == "" {
        return result, errors.New("response omits a required field")
    }
    if result.RunID != expectedRun {
        return result, errors.New("response run_id does not match the requested run")
    }
    count, err := result.FailureCount.Int64()
    if err != nil || count < 0 {
        return result, errors.New("failure_count must be a non-negative integer")
    }
    return result, nil
}

func main() {
    tests := [][]byte{
        []byte(`{"query_id":"q-41","run_id":"run-2026-10-08","failure_count":3}`),
        []byte(`{"query_id":"q-42","run_id":"run-2026-10-08","failure_count":`),
        []byte(`{"query_id":"q-43","run_id":"run-2026-10-08"}`),
        []byte(`{"query_id":"q-44","run_id":"wrong-run","failure_count":0}`),
    }
    for _, body := range tests {
        result, err := parseResult(body, "run-2026-10-08")
        fmt.Printf("query=%q count=%q valid=%t error=%v\n",
            result.QueryID, result.FailureCount, err == nil, err)
    }
}

Strict unknown-field rejection is a conscious trade-off. It turns an additive upstream field into a visible compatibility event, which is appropriate when this narrow envelope is an internal contract and deployment is coordinated. For a public or independently evolving API, decode a versioned envelope and tolerate documented additive fields instead. The invariant is narrower: the worker must prove the fields that drive the alert, bind them to the requested run, and reject ambiguous values.

Preserve evidence without retaining every successful payload

Parsing is only half the incident record. For every attempt, write an immutable audit event with the request ID, run ID, pipeline stage, account allocation key, response class, byte length, content digest, parser version, and final decision. Store the raw body only in a bounded quarantine path when the class is invalid; cap its length before persistence and apply access controls appropriate to the data it may contain.

The digest answers a narrow but important question: did two workers receive the same bytes? It does not establish what the remote system intended to send, and it must not be used as a substitute for the response body during diagnosis. Likewise, retries must reuse an idempotency key derived from the logical query and pipeline run, while each attempt receives its own attempt number. The logical decision record is written once; attempt records remain append-only.

That is the exactly-once mindset in practical form. Network delivery is allowed to repeat. The alert decision is not.

A parser failure should open a monitoring-integrity alert whose fingerprint is based on stable dimensions such as operation, schema version, and parser error class, rather than the raw body or request ID. Sentry documents how event grouping and custom fingerprints influence which events become one issue; the general lesson applies without requiring a particular incident tool. Stable grouping prevents every nightly run from becoming a separate incident while retaining run IDs in the event details for reconstruction.

Make the alert state machine explicit

After parsing, the decision table is small enough to review with both operations and finance:

Observation Pipeline alert Integrity alert Cost allocation
Valid count is zero Closed Closed Requested account and stage
Valid count is positive Open Closed Requested account and stage
JSON or schema is invalid Unknown, never closed Open Requested account and stage plus invalid_response
Transport fails after retry budget Unknown, never closed Open Requested account and stage plus transport_error

The distinction between open and unknown is operationally useful. Reusing the pipeline-failure alert for parser defects obscures whether the marketplace job failed or its observer failed. Closing an existing failure alert on unknown evidence is worse: it converts loss of visibility into apparent recovery.

Deploy the contract parser behind recorded fixtures for truncated input, HTML accidentally returned as a body, valid JSON with missing fields, decimal counts, negative counts, duplicate logical responses, and a mismatched run ID. The HTML fixture should fail at decoding; no special content sniffing is required for correctness. Also test the retry boundary with a fake transport so that two deliveries produce two attempt records but one logical decision.

These tests serve auditability as much as reliability. A reviewer can trace the decision from requested run, through exact response classification, to the alert transition and its allocation key.

Retention is a decision about future evidence

The change that moves the dominant storage term is usually selective retention, not parser micro-optimization. Keep compact audit events for all queries, full invalid responses for a short and explicitly governed quarantine period, and aggregated counts for trend analysis. Stop keeping full successful query payloads once the audit event and verified aggregate have been committed.

This deliberately removes the ability to replay an old successful response byte for byte after its retention window. If a later parser defect is discovered, the team can reconstruct which parser version made the decision and compare the stored count and digest, but it cannot reinterpret a body that no longer exists. That loss should be accepted in a retention review, with compliance and incident-reconstruction requirements setting the window; it should not emerge accidentally from a storage cleanup.

The final control is reconciliation. Compare the count of scheduled pipeline runs with valid decisions, invalid decisions, and exhausted transports for the same allocation period. Those categories must account for every run exactly once. Any remainder is a missing observation, and any excess is a duplicate logical decision, even if every individual worker log line looks healthy.

Further reading

  • https://docs.sentry.io/concepts/data-management/event-grouping/

title: PiCo: Physics-Informed Concept Probing for Geo-Foundation Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20973v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geo-foundation models (GFMs) are typically evaluated by downstream task predictive performance, revealing little about which physical features they are sensitive to or use in prediction. This limits developers' ability to test hypotheses about model behaviour and users' ability to select models for new tasks. We propose Physics-Informed Concept Probing (PiCo), a post-hoc framework for explaining GFM predictions. PiCo identifies concept vectors in a GFM's embedding space by generating synthetic multispectral satellite observations from a 3D radiative transfer model coupled with a game engine. These vectors reveal physical sensitivities that inform domain-based hypotheses about downstream performance. Projecting embeddings onto these concept vectors produces low-dimensional representations for quantifying concept importance in making predictions. We evaluate PiCo on three GFMs with different input modalities using seven physical concepts covering forest leaf optics and canopy structure. In ground-cover estimation, RGB restriction reduces dry-matter sensitivity and disproportionately degrades predictions for dry vegetation and bare ground, supporting a hypothesis derived from sensitivity analysis. For hierarchical forest type and tree species classification, concept representations retain 70.0-93.8% of full-embedding accuracy. Models capture similar physical contrasts between classes, such as structural differences between broadleaf forest and cleared ground and leaf-water-content differences between oak and beech, yet differ in the strength of these contrasts and the concepts driving classification. PiCo thus provides a physical basis for hypothesis testing and model assessment, with potential applicability beyond Earth observation wherever forward models enable controlled simulation and pretrained embeddings are accessible for probing.

title: GRADS: Graph-Regulated Agentic Data Synthesis with Controllable Difficulty
description:
arXiv:2610.21167v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep research agents are increasingly deployed to retrieve precise information from large corpora, yet multi-hop, long-horizon tasks remain challenging. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a scalable solution, with existing pipelines typically expanding seed tasks to increase their apparent depth and breadth. However, this expansion does not reliably translate into necessary reasoning: newly introduced evidence may be only weakly coupled to the answer, creating a mismatch between intended and empirical difficulty. To address this problem, we introduce GRADS, a graph-guided agentic data synthesis framework with explicit difficulty control. GRADS runs a closed loop of seed selection, evidence expansion, question--answer construction, and verification while maintaining a graph of the evidence and inference dependencies required to derive each answer. At each step, it conditions generation on a relevant subgraph, preserving indispensable inference without accumulating irrelevant context. Experiments across security, software-engineering, and scientific-document domains show that GRADS consistently generates verified tasks with empirically separated difficulty distributions, as measured by independent solvers. Moreover, under matched training budgets, post-training on this data delivers consistent gains at every level: SFT raises the solution-termination rate to over 95% while cutting tool calls and turns by up to 75%, RL trims tool use by up to a further 19.5%, and on our held-out, domain-specific benchmarks, the resulting 4B model matches Sonnet~4 on software engineering and surpasses it on the scientific and security domains.

title: Failure Is the Mother of Success: Recovering Supervision with Grounding Hindsight
description:
arXiv:2610.21018v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When every rollout for a problem fails, GRPO receives neither a successful exemplar nor a nonzero group-relative advantage, so it learns nothing from exactly the problems it most needs to learn. The failed reasoning can nevertheless suggest what to try next. We present Replay-Selected Hindsight Distillation (RSHD), which turns failed attempts into an additional, tested source of supervision during GRPO training. The policy writes a corrective note about each failed attempt without seeing a reference answer or solution, then re-solves the problem with the note in context. A note is admitted only if its replays succeed more often than the original group did, after screening for notes that state the answer, and an admitted replay is distilled into the plain-prompt policy. Because admission is decided by fresh successes rather than by the failed rollout itself, the procedure can recover supervision from groups in which every attempt failed, and it applies equally to failures in mixed groups. Only the policy is trained, the only judge is the outcome verifier, and deployment requires no notes or extra inference. Across model families and sizes and two training domains, RSHD consistently improves over GRPO on in-domain benchmarks, and the gains carry over to out-of-domain evaluation sets.

title: Web Accessibility: Semantic HTML, ARIA, Keyboard Navigation, and Testing
description:
Web accessibility (a11y) is about building interfaces that work for everyone — including people who use screen readers, keyboard navigation, switch controls, or have cognitive disabilities. It's also increasingly a legal requirement in many jurisdictions.

The good news: accessible HTML is mostly just correct HTML. Most accessibility mistakes come from using the wrong element for a job, or overriding browser defaults that were already correct.

Semantic HTML First

The single most impactful accessibility improvement is using semantic HTML:

<!-- Wrong: everything is a div -->
<div class="button" onclick="submit()">Submit</div>
<div class="header"><div class="nav">...</div></div>

<!-- Right: semantic elements -->
<button type="button" onclick="submit()">Submit</button>
<header><nav>...</nav></header>

Semantic elements come with built-in accessibility: <button> is keyboard-focusable, activatable with Enter/Space, and announced as "button" by screen readers. A <div> is none of these things without significant ARIA work.

Key Semantic Elements 

<main>        <!-- primary page content, one per page -->
<header>      <!-- page or section header -->
<nav>         <!-- navigation links -->
<aside>       <!-- secondary content (sidebar, related links) -->
<footer>      <!-- page or section footer -->
<article>     <!-- self-contained content (blog post, comment) -->
<section>     <!-- thematic grouping with a heading -->
<h1> - <h6>   <!-- headings: use in order, don't skip levels -->
<ul>, <ol>    <!-- lists: screen readers announce item count -->
<table>       <!-- tabular data: NOT for layout -->
<figure>      <!-- image with caption -->
<figcaption>  <!-- caption for figure -->

Images

Every image needs an alt attribute:

<!-- Informative image: describe what the image shows -->
<img src="chart.png" alt="Bar chart showing 40% increase in Firefox users Q3 2024">

<!-- Decorative image: empty alt, screen readers skip it -->
<img src="decorative-line.svg" alt="">

<!-- Icon button: describe the action, not the icon -->
<button>
  <img src="delete.svg" alt="Delete item">
</button>

<!-- Complex image: use a figcaption for detail -->
<figure>
  <img src="architecture-diagram.png" alt="System architecture diagram showing three services">
  <figcaption>The data pipeline connects the ingestion service to the processing queue and storage layer.</figcaption>
</figure>

SVG icons inline in buttons need a title or aria-label:

<button aria-label="Close dialog">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><!-- icon --></svg>
</button>

Forms 

<form>
  <!-- Every input needs a label -->
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required
         autocomplete="email"
         aria-describedby="email-hint">
  <p id="email-hint">We'll never share your email.</p>

  <!-- Error messages -->
  <input type="text" id="username"
         aria-invalid="true"
         aria-describedby="username-error">
  <p id="username-error" role="alert">Username already taken</p>

  <!-- Group related inputs -->
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Notification preferences</legend>
    <label>
      <input type="checkbox" name="email-notifs"> Email notifications
    </label>
    <label>
      <input type="checkbox" name="sms-notifs"> SMS notifications
    </label>
  </fieldset>
</form>

aria-describedby links the input to its hint/error message. Screen readers announce the description after the input label.

role="alert" announces content immediately when it's added to the DOM — good for validation errors.

Keyboard Navigation

All interactive elements must be keyboard-accessible:

// Keyboard event handler (don't rely only on click)
element.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') {
    e.preventDefault();
    activate();
  }
});

Tab order: Users navigate with Tab (forward) and Shift+Tab (backward). The default order follows DOM order — don't use tabindex values > 0 (they mess up natural order):

<!-- tabindex=0: include in tab order at natural position -->
<div role="button" tabindex="0">Custom button</div>

<!-- tabindex=-1: focusable programmatically, not via Tab -->
<div id="modal" tabindex="-1">Modal content</div>

<!-- tabindex=1+: avoid — overrides natural tab order -->
<input tabindex="3"> <!-- don't do this -->

Skip navigation: Let keyboard users skip to main content:

<a href="#main-content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a>
<main id="main-content">...</main>

.skip-link {
  position: absolute;
  top: -100%;
}
.skip-link:focus {
  top: 0;  /* appears when focused */
}

ARIA Roles and Labels

ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) supplements HTML semantics. Use it when native HTML can't express the role:

<!-- Custom toggle button -->
<button aria-pressed="false" id="dark-mode-toggle">Dark mode</button>

<script>
  const btn = document.getElementById('dark-mode-toggle');
  btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
    const pressed = btn.getAttribute('aria-pressed') === 'true';
    btn.setAttribute('aria-pressed', !pressed);
  });
</script>

<!-- Expanded/collapsed state -->
<button aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="menu">Menu</button>
<ul id="menu" hidden>...</ul>

<!-- Live regions: announce dynamic updates -->
<div aria-live="polite" id="status-message"></div>
<!-- Polite: announces after current speech ends -->
<!-- Assertive: interrupts immediately (use sparingly) -->

ARIA first rule: If a native HTML element has the semantics you need, use it. ARIA is for custom widgets only.

Color and Contrast

WCAG 2.1 requires a contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text (18pt+ or 14pt+ bold).

Check with browser DevTools:

  • Firefox: Inspector → pick element → Accessibility panel → contrast ratio
  • Or use WebAIM Contrast Checker

Never convey information through color alone:

<!-- Wrong: only color distinguishes the error -->
<span style="color: red">Required field</span>

<!-- Right: color + text/icon -->
<span style="color: red" aria-label="Required">
  ⚠ Required field
</span>

Focus Styles

Never just remove focus outlines — keyboard users rely on them:

/* Don't do this */
*:focus { outline: none; }

/* Better: custom focus style */
:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid #2563eb;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

:focus-visible only shows the outline when using keyboard navigation, not on mouse clicks. This is the modern approach — no need to suppress focus rings for mouse users.

Modal Dialogs

Modals have specific accessibility requirements:

// When modal opens:
// 1. Move focus into the modal
// 2. Trap focus inside
// 3. Return focus to trigger when closed

function openModal(modal, trigger) {
  modal.removeAttribute('hidden');
  modal.querySelector('[autofocus], button, [href], input').focus();

  // Trap focus
  modal.addEventListener('keydown', trapFocus);

  // Close on Escape
  modal.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
    if (e.key === 'Escape') closeModal(modal, trigger);
  });
}

function closeModal(modal, trigger) {
  modal.setAttribute('hidden', '');
  trigger.focus();  // return focus
  modal.removeEventListener('keydown', trapFocus);
}

Native <dialog> handles all of this automatically — use it:

<dialog id="my-modal">
  <h2>Dialog title</h2>
  <p>Content</p>
  <button autofocus>Close</button>
</dialog>

document.getElementById('my-modal').showModal();

Firefox has supported native <dialog> since Firefox 98 (2022).

Testing Accessibility

Manual testing:

  1. Navigate the page with Tab only — can you reach everything?
  2. Test with Firefox Reader View — does the content make sense?
  3. Use Firefox Accessibility Inspector (DevTools → Accessibility tab)

Screen reader testing:

  • macOS: VoiceOver (Cmd+F5)
  • Windows: NVDA (free) or JAWS
  • iOS: VoiceOver
  • Android: TalkBack

Automated audits:

  • Firefox DevTools: Accessibility panel → check for warnings
  • Lighthouse: npx lighthouse --categories=accessibility https://yoursite.com
  • axe browser extension

Automated tools catch about 30-40% of accessibility issues. Manual testing and real user testing are required for the rest.

The most important shift: think of accessibility not as a checklist to pass but as correct implementation. Semantic HTML, proper labels, and keyboard support aren't extras — they're how the web is supposed to work.

title: When Should a Low-Light Pipeline Generate? Auditable Risk Control for Selective Generative Enhancement
description:
arXiv:2610.21335v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative low-light enhancers recover plausible texture but may hallucinate structure; restoration networks preserve structure but can leave regions under-enhanced, and neither advantage is spatially uniform. Therefore, we formulate selective generative enhancement as a decision problem: determine where overriding a frozen base expert is beneficial and refuse to switch when the evidence is insufficient. We propose VetoNet, an auditable regional routing framework centered on a certified veto. It first measures the complementary strengths and routing direction of a frozen restoration generative pair, then predicts the utility of regional overrides from deployment-available signals alone and admits an override only when a distribution-free harm-budget certificate says the perceptual (LPIPS) risk budget allows it. Experiments across multiple expert pairs and domains show that VetoNet adapts its routing behavior to the strength and reliability of the available evidence. When expert complementarity is sufficiently predictable, it achieves statistically significant certified gains; when the relative strengths of the experts change, it correspondingly reverses the routing direction; and when routing evidence is weak or affected by cross-domain shift, it conservatively vetoes switching.

title: Founders Today vs Indie Hackers for SaaS Founders
description:
If you build a SaaS product, you have probably posted on Indie Hackers or thought about it. Founders Today is a newer community that overlaps with it in some ways and differs in others. The short version: Indie Hackers is better for long, open stories about building a business, and Founders Today is better for a launch page that stays listed and for quick feedback in a feed. Most SaaS founders get more from using both, for different jobs, than from picking one.

This guide compares them on what SaaS founders actually need: useful feedback, a launch, access to buyers, and a post that does not vanish in a day. It also says where each one falls short, including Founders Today, which is younger and smaller. If you landed here looking for an Indie Hackers alternative, start with what is actually missing for you. The answer changes which platform helps.

Founders Today vs Indie Hackers at a glance

Indie Hackers Founders Today
Format Forum threads, groups, interviews, and a podcast A feed of launches, discussions, and opportunities
Strongest at Open revenue stories and long build logs Launch pages that stay listed, and fast builder-to-builder talk
Product pages Product pages with milestones and updates Launch pages with media
Launch day No ranked launch day: you post and engage A launch system, currently in beta
Extra reach Podcast and newsletter Publisher widgets and a weekly newsletter feature
Track record Running since 2016, bought by Stripe in 2017, independent again since Newer, still early
Cost to join Free Free

The Indie Hackers column comes from its own product pages, podcast, and press coverage. The Founders Today column comes from Founders Today's own pages. Both sites change, so check them for anything new before you decide.

What Indie Hackers is best at

Indie Hackers started in 2016 as a place where founders share real revenue numbers and explain how they got there. Stripe bought it in 2017, as TechCrunch reported at the time, and it later returned to independence. Today it is a mix of forum threads, topic groups, interviews, a podcast, and product pages where you can post milestones and updates.

For a SaaS founder the strongest part is the culture of showing numbers. A post that says you went from 12 to 40 paying customers and shows what changed fits the site better than a polished announcement. If you can share your MRR, your churn, a pricing test that failed, or an acquisition channel that cost more than it returned, you are speaking the local language, and people tend to reply in kind.

The archive is the other asset. Years of interviews and build logs mean you can research how someone in your niche reached their first thousand dollars a month before you write a word of your own. Few communities have that depth.

The limits are mostly about format. It is a forum, so a thread gets most of its attention in the first day or two. If you cannot share revenue yet, you have less to talk about. And a bare link with no story or question attached gets ignored.

What Founders Today is best at, and where it is still early

Founders Today is a feed with launches, discussions, opportunities, and toolkits, plus a member directory where you can follow people and message them. For a SaaS founder the useful pieces are the launch page, which stays listed instead of rotating off a one-day leaderboard, and the discussion feed, where a short question can get answers without a long essay first.

It also runs distribution outside the feed. The publisher program places product widgets on partner blogs, and a weekly tools list goes out through newsletter partners. Treat those as channels to measure, not guarantees. Put a tracking link on your launch page and see what actually arrives.

It is fair to say what is not there yet. Founders Today is younger and smaller than Indie Hackers. The launch system is in beta, and push notification partnerships are still being built. There is no deep archive of revenue case studies like the one Indie Hackers has built over years. If archive depth and brand recognition are what you want, that is a real gap, and you should weigh it honestly.

Founders Today vs Indie Hackers on what SaaS founders care about

Getting useful feedback

Feedback quality depends more on how you ask than on where you ask. Both communities respond to specific questions: is this pricing page clear, which step of onboarding lost you, would you pay this much for this. The difference is format. Indie Hackers threads suit longer replies from people who have run a business, so a detailed critique usually comes from there. A feed suits quick reactions, so five fast opinions on a landing page are easy to collect on Founders Today.

Whichever you use, ask one question per post and say what you plan to change based on the answers. People reply more when they can see their reply will matter.

Launching a product

Indie Hackers gives you a product page and a post. There is no ranked launch day, so your launch is whatever you make of the post and the conversation under it. That suits founders who like to tell a story and stay in the comments for a couple of days.

Founders Today gives you a dedicated launch page with images and media that stays listed after launch week, plus the distribution described above. That suits founders who want a page to point people to long after the post has aged.

Either way, prepare assets first: a one-line description, three screenshots, a short demo, and one clear call to action. If you are comparing launch options more widely, the Product Hunt alternative page and the list of free startup launch platforms with active communities cover the rest of the field.

Reaching buyers, not just builders

Be honest about who is reading. Both audiences are mostly builders. If you sell to developers, indie founders, or other SaaS teams, you are posting in front of possible buyers, and either platform can send real signups. If you sell to dentists, recruiters, or HR managers, these communities will give you feedback, credibility, and links, but your buyers are somewhere else.

In that case use founder communities to sharpen the product and the pitch, then spend your selling time where your buyers gather. The best SaaS founder communities list and the SaaS community page can help you find those other rooms.

Founders Today's publisher widgets are the one feature aimed at readers outside the founder crowd, since they sit on third-party blogs. Whether that reaches your buyers depends on which blogs carry them, so ask which ones before you count on it.

How long your work stays visible

Every feed and forum pushes old posts down. On Indie Hackers a thread is live for a day or two, then lives on mostly through search and your product page. On Founders Today the launch page stays listed, but a feed post ages the same way. Plan a follow-up update a week or two later instead of relying on one post.

Credibility and track record

Indie Hackers has history. People know the name, the press has covered it, and a profile there carries weight with some audiences. Founders Today is newer, so its name means less outside its own members. For a SaaS founder, credibility mostly comes from what you show anyway: a clear product, real numbers, and steady updates over months.

Community culture and tone

Indie Hackers leans toward long, personal, number-heavy posts, and a lot of members share what they earn. Founders Today leans toward shorter posts, quick questions, launches, and discussion threads about tools and news. Neither tone is better, but copying the wrong one costs you replies. A three-paragraph business update with figures reads as normal on Indie Hackers and a little heavy in a feed, while a one-line question can look thin on a forum. Read ten recent posts that got plenty of replies on each platform before you write yours, and match the length and the level of detail.

Time cost

Both are free to join, so the real cost is your time. Fifteen minutes a day of useful replies on one platform beats a big post on two. If you have to choose, pick the one where your likely users already spend time.

Which one fits your stage

Idea stage. You need to know if the problem is real. Post a question about the problem, not a pitch for your solution. Ask how people handle it today and what they pay for. Both communities work for this only if the people answering could be your users.

Pre-launch. You need a handful of people who will try the product on day one. Spend a few weeks commenting on other people's posts before you post your own. People check profiles, and a profile with nothing but your own link looks like an ad.

Launch week. You need a page to point to and some people who see it. This is where the two differ most: Indie Hackers for the story, Founders Today for a page that stays listed. Doing both in the same week is fine as long as the posts are different.

First 100 users. Feedback matters more than traffic here. Ask specific questions, like which onboarding step confused someone, and answer every reply. Write down what you hear and what you changed.

B2B pipeline. Use both for credibility and early adopters if your buyers are founders or developers. If they are not, treat both as places to learn, not places to sell.

Three examples of how this plays out

These are made-up scenarios to show the decision, not case studies.

A developer tool. Say you built an API monitoring tool. Your buyers are developers, so both communities sit close to your audience. Post a build log with real numbers on Indie Hackers, then launch on Founders Today so you have a page that keeps listing. Either one can send trial signups, and you can compare them with separate tracking links.

Vertical software for non-founders. Say you built scheduling software for physiotherapy clinics. Founder communities will critique your pricing and onboarding well, but clinic owners are not reading them. Take the feedback, then bring the product to clinic groups, professional associations, and local forums where the buyers are.

A small solo micro-SaaS. Say you make a few hundred dollars a month. Indie Hackers still welcomes small numbers if you are specific about how you got them, and a launch page gives you something to link from your profile everywhere else. You do not need big revenue to be useful in either place. You need a clear story and the patience to reply to people.

How to tell if it is working

Pick three numbers and check them every Friday for a month: signups from each tracking link, replies that included a specific suggestion, and visits to your product or launch page. Replies like 'nice work' feel good but do not change your product. Replies that name a problem do. If a platform gives you suggestions you act on, it is working, even when signups are small. If it gives you neither signups nor suggestions after a month of steady posting, change the format of your posts before you leave.

A four-week plan for using both

Week 1. Set up your profile and product page on both. Write one plain sentence on what you do and who it is for. Spend about 15 minutes a day replying to other people's posts.

Week 2. Share one specific lesson from your build, with a number in it. For example, what you changed after a user interview and what happened next.

Week 3. Ask one pointed question you really need answered, such as whether your pricing page is clear. Reply to every answer, even short ones.

Week 4. Launch. Put the full launch page on Founders Today. On Indie Hackers, tell the story of the launch as a post and link to your product page instead of pitching.

Two rules for all four weeks. Never paste the same post in both places, because the formats reward different things. And use a separate tracking link for each community, so after 30 days you can see which one sent signups and not just visits.

Mistakes that waste a post

  • Posting a link with no story or question attached.
  • Asking for upvotes instead of asking for feedback.
  • Posting once and disappearing, instead of staying in the comments while the post is live.
  • Making claims without numbers, like 'growing fast' with no figure behind it.
  • Treating a founder audience as your buyers when your product is for someone else.
  • Judging a platform after a single post. Give each one a month of steady replies first.

Which one should you start with?

  • You can share revenue and want long-form credibility: start with Indie Hackers.
  • You are about to launch and want a page that keeps listing: start with Founders Today.
  • You sell to non-founders: use both for feedback, then put your selling effort where your buyers are. The list of free places to promote your startup is a good next step.
  • You have no product yet: neither. Talk to ten people who have the problem first. The guide to networking platforms for new founders can help you find them.

For a direct side-by-side with feature rows, see the Founders Today vs Indie Hackers comparison page.

FAQ

Is Founders Today an Indie Hackers alternative or a replacement? Neither, exactly. They do different jobs. Indie Hackers is stronger for long-form transparency and has a much deeper archive. Founders Today is built around launches and a feed. Many founders will want both.

Can I post the same thing on both? You can, but it works badly. Rewrite it for each format. A long build log suits a forum thread. A short update with a link to your launch page suits a feed.

Which is better for B2B SaaS? Neither is a buyer channel by default. If your buyers are founders or developers, both can send signups. If they are not, use both for feedback and credibility and sell elsewhere.

Do links from either community help SEO? Check the link attributes yourself before counting on it. Even where a link is followed, a community post is worth more as a place to get feedback and early users.

How long before I see results? Give each platform a month of steady replies and one launch post, and track signups per link. One post is not enough to judge either.

Is it free? Both are free to join as of writing. Check each site for current plans.

Pick one thing you want feedback on this week, write it as a question with one number in it, and post it where your users spend time. If you have a SaaS ready to show people, you can submit your launch on Founders Today for free.

title: Recursive Offline Distillation via Entropy Gain Sampling and Answer Mixing
description:
arXiv:2610.20914v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Distillation of reasoning chains from Large Language Models (LLMs) into their smaller siblings is a standard training approach. Frequently, researchers do not have full access to a teacher model and its internal representations, which limits the resulting performance. We propose a recursive offline distillation method combining two components: entropy-based sampling for selective distillation and answer mixing. Specifically, for three open models (3-4B), at each epoch, we sample reasoning chains weighted by entropy difference with an auxiliary medium model (70-72B) and, next, supplement thinking traces with single-token ground truth answers. Our approach consistently outperforms naive distillation with comparable data budgets ($57.15 \pm 1.01$ vs 51.61 on average) and offers a much steeper learning curve. Additionally, we present a comparative analysis of methods to generate and normalize distillation traces.

title: Reviewing NestJS collections, provider lifetimes and runtime behavior
description:
Replacing repeated find calls with a Map can change which duplicate wins. Start with that contract, then check provider identity, resource readiness and cache behavior before making performance claims.

Example scope: NestJS 11.2.7, TypeScript 5.9.3, Node.js 20+; local checks used Node.js 24.11.0. Nest examples assume reflect-metadata, experimentalDecorators and emitDecoratorMetadata. Controllers, authentication and persistence are omitted unless shown. The article snippets were compiled and checked locally; they are teaching examples, not production benchmarks.

Preserve the collection contract

The response must keep request order, repeated IDs and the first matching catalog row.

Before: search the catalog for every ID 

// collections.ts
export type Card = { id: string; title: string };

export function selectCardsBefore(
  rows: readonly Card[], ids: readonly string[],
): Card[] {
  const result: Card[] = [];
  for (const id of ids) {
    const row = rows.find(candidate => candidate.id === id);
    if (row) result.push({ id: row.id, title: row.title });
  }
  return result;
}

After: build one request-local index 

// collections.ts, continued
export function selectCardsIndexed(
  rows: readonly Card[], ids: readonly string[],
): Card[] {
  const firstById = new Map<string, Card>();
  for (const row of rows) {
    if (!firstById.has(row.id)) firstById.set(row.id, row);
  }

  const result: Card[] = [];
  for (const id of ids) {
    const row = firstById.get(id);
    if (row) result.push({ id: row.id, title: row.title });
  }
  return result;
}

The has check preserves the first duplicate. Iterating over ids preserves order and repetitions. Explicit { id, title } projection returns fresh public objects and excludes extra fields.

Test those details before accepting the refactor:

// collections.test.ts
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { selectCardsBefore, selectCardsIndexed } from './collections';

const rows = Object.freeze([
  Object.freeze({ id: 'a', title: 'First', internalToken: 'private' }),
  Object.freeze({ id: 'a', title: 'Later', internalToken: 'private' }),
]);
const ids = Object.freeze(['missing', 'a', 'a']);
const expected = [{ id: 'a', title: 'First' }, { id: 'a', title: 'First' }];

for (const select of [selectCardsBefore, selectCardsIndexed]) {
  const result = select(rows, ids);
  assert.deepEqual(result, expected);
  assert.notStrictEqual(result[0], rows[0]);
  assert.notStrictEqual(result[0], result[1]);
}
Need Starting point Tradeoff
One lookup in a small array find No index setup
A yes/no answer some Stops at the first match
Repeated lookups Map Setup work and extra memory
Repeated membership checks Set of stable IDs Object equality still uses identity

A Set can filter IDs while keeping their order and repetitions. Authorization must supply the allowed IDs from a trusted server-side policy:

// collections.ts, continued
export function permittedIds(ids: readonly string[], allowedIds: readonly string[]) {
  const allowed = new Set(allowedIds);
  return ids.filter(id => allowed.has(id));
}

These selectors assume validated, bounded inputs. Local push does not mutate caller-owned arrays; repeatedly spreading a growing accumulator can create quadratic copying. Measure index construction and realistic hit rates before claiming a speed improvement.

Bound the resource at its boundary

Bound request bytes, input items, database reads and output separately.

  • JSON parser: a 4 KiB request body.

  • Input validation: at most 32 IDs, each 1–40 characters.

  • Data adapter: filtering, projection and a query limit.

  • Output construction: an integer limit from 1 to 32.

Validate JSON as unknown

This standalone parser rejects extra fields and malformed values. Use the project's existing validation tools when available; TypeScript types alone do not validate JSON.

// selection.ts
import { BadRequestException } from '@nestjs/common';

export function parseSelection(value: unknown): { ids: string[]; limit: number } {
  if (!value || typeof value !== 'object' || Array.isArray(value)) {
    throw new BadRequestException('Invalid selection');
  }
  const input = value as Record<string, unknown>;
  const { ids, limit } = input;
  if (Object.keys(input).some(key => key !== 'ids' && key !== 'limit') ||
      !Array.isArray(ids) || ids.length > 32 ||
      !ids.every(id => typeof id === 'string' && id.length >= 1 && id.length <= 40) ||
      typeof limit !== 'number' || !Number.isInteger(limit) || limit < 1 || limit > 32) {
    throw new BadRequestException('Invalid selection');
  }
  return { ids: [...ids], limit };
}

Apply the byte bound before JSON parsing completes. This factory accepts your existing root module and initializes an Express application without opening a listening port:

// http-app.ts
import { Type } from '@nestjs/common';
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';

export async function createHttpApp(root: Type<unknown>) {
  const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(root, {
    bodyParser: false, logger: false,
  });
  app.useBodyParser('json', { limit: '4kb' });
  await app.init();
  return app;
}

logger: false keeps this teaching harness quiet. Configure application logging separately. See Nest's body-parser guidance and validation pipeline.

The bounded collection reference also checks output limits inside the selector, so direct service calls cannot bypass them. An early break limits result construction; it cannot undo a full catalog load or index build.

Make DI identity and lifetime visible

Inject a narrow port with a shared runtime token

An interface disappears at runtime. Nest resolves the shared Symbol; useExisting aliases the registered adapter.

// stock.ts
import { Inject, Injectable, Module } from '@nestjs/common';

export interface StockReader { available(sku: string): Promise<number> }
export const STOCK_READER = Symbol('inventory.stock-reader');

@Injectable()
export class LocalStock implements StockReader {
  async available(sku: string): Promise<number> {
    return sku === 'book' ? 3 : 0; // Teaching adapter; no database.
  }
}

@Injectable()
export class CanReserve {
  constructor(@Inject(STOCK_READER) private readonly stock: StockReader) {}

  async execute(sku: string, quantity: number): Promise<boolean> {
    if (!sku || !Number.isSafeInteger(quantity) || quantity <= 0) {
      throw new Error('Invalid reservation');
    }
    const count = await this.stock.available(sku);
    if (!Number.isSafeInteger(count) || count < 0) throw new Error('Invalid stock');
    return count >= quantity;
  }
}

@Module({
  providers: [LocalStock, { provide: STOCK_READER, useExisting: LocalStock }, CanReserve],
  exports: [STOCK_READER, CanReserve],
})
export class StockModule {}

Import the same token everywhere: another Symbol('inventory.stock-reader') has a different identity. A separate useClass registration can create another adapter instance. See custom providers.

CanReserve only checks availability; it does not reserve stock atomically. A substitute adapter must preserve errors and valid counts. Converting a dependency failure to zero changes behavior despite a matching TypeScript signature.

Choose the instance owner

Scope Instance ownership
Default singleton Shared across consumers of that provider registration
Transient Separate per consumer instance; repeated method calls reuse it
Request Per request context; scope can propagate to consumers

Request isolation adds construction work. Test sharing with Nest's real container and explicit context IDs; a tenant-shaped object alone proves no authorization. The versioned scope tests demonstrate these boundaries.

Treat startup, shutdown and logs as contracts

Reject invalid configuration before readiness

A factory can validate configuration during provider construction:

// settings.ts
export function parsePort(raw = '3000'): number {
  if (!/^[0-9]+$/.test(raw)) throw new Error('Invalid PORT');
  const port = Number(raw);
  if (!Number.isInteger(port) || port < 1 || port > 65535) throw new Error('Invalid PORT');
  return port;
}

export const SETTINGS = Symbol('settings');
export const settingsProvider = {
  provide: SETTINGS,
  useFactory: () => Object.freeze({ port: parsePort(process.env.PORT) }),
};

Register settingsProvider in your module. Prefer the existing ConfigModule where installed; this factory omits secret loading and configuration precedence.

Await connection and cleanup

Register ManagedResource and provide RESOURCE with your adapter:

// resource.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

export interface Resource { connect(): Promise<void>; close(): Promise<void> }
export const RESOURCE = Symbol('resource');

@Injectable()
export class ManagedResource {
  ready = false;
  constructor(@Inject(RESOURCE) private readonly resource: Resource) {}

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> {
    await this.resource.connect();
  }
  onApplicationBootstrap(): void { this.ready = true; }
  onModuleDestroy(): void { this.ready = false; }
  async onApplicationShutdown(): Promise<void> {
    await this.resource.close();
  }
}

Cleanup runs in onApplicationShutdown, after Nest closes its connections. Nest recognizes these method names without lifecycle interfaces; the interfaces can add compile-time checks. Lifecycle documentation describes the order.

Production boundary: adapters need deadlines, cancellation and partial-connection cleanup. Coordinate readiness, ingress removal and bounded draining in the deployment. app.close() tests do not prove OS signal handling or live-request draining. Enable shutdown hooks for the deployment's signals; an immediate process.exit() can interrupt cleanup.

Project log fields explicitly

Type annotations do not strip extra properties. Build the event you intend to emit:

// completion.ts
export function completionEvent(input: {
  requestId: string; status: number; durationMs: number;
}): string {
  if (typeof input.requestId !== 'string' || !/^[a-zA-Z0-9-]{1,64}$/.test(input.requestId) ||
      !Number.isInteger(input.status) || input.status < 100 || input.status > 599 ||
      !Number.isFinite(input.durationMs) || input.durationMs < 0) {
    throw new Error('Invalid completion event');
  }
  return JSON.stringify({
    event: 'request.completed', requestId: input.requestId,
    status: input.status, durationMs: input.durationMs,
  });
}

This prevents extra authorization/body fields from reaching the event. The sink still needs backpressure, failure and retention policies. This helper does not configure or test Nest's bootstrap logger.

Measure the cost an optimization moves

Share pending cache loads and define expiry

This cache holds one public immutable string, at most 1024 UTF-8 bytes, for one second. Injecting the clock makes expiry tests deterministic.

// summary-cache.ts
export class PublicSummaryCache {
  private cached?: { value: string; expiresAt: number };
  private pending?: Promise<string>;

  constructor(
    private readonly load: () => Promise<string>,
    private readonly now: () => number = Date.now,
  ) {}

  read(): Promise<string> {
    if (this.cached && this.now() < this.cached.expiresAt) {
      return Promise.resolve(this.cached.value);
    }
    if (this.pending) return this.pending;

    this.pending = Promise.resolve().then(() => this.load()).then(value => {
      if (typeof value !== 'string' || Buffer.byteLength(value, 'utf8') > 1024) {
        throw new Error('Invalid summary');
      }
      this.cached = { value, expiresAt: this.now() + 1000 };
      return value;
    }).finally(() => { this.pending = undefined; });
    return this.pending;
  }
}

Empty strings are valid hits. Failed or oversized loads are not cached, and pending callers share the same promise. Coalescing does not cancel a hung origin request. Enforce origin deadlines; size checks occur after the value is allocated. This process-local cache omits invalidation and authorization-aware keys needed for private data. Nest cache-manager/store TTL rules must be checked against their own versions.

Carry bounds to the data adapter

Validate the page request, then pass filtering, ordering, projection and the limit to persistence:

// titles.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

export interface TitleRow { id: number; title: string }
export interface PageQuery {
  fetch(request: {
    tenant: string; afterId: number; limit: number;
    select: readonly ['id', 'title']; order: 'id-asc';
  }): Promise<TitleRow[]>;
}
export const PAGE_QUERY = Symbol('page-query');

@Injectable()
export class ListTitles {
  constructor(@Inject(PAGE_QUERY) private readonly query: PageQuery) {}

  async execute(tenant: string, afterId: number, limit: number): Promise<TitleRow[]> {
    if (!/^[a-z0-9-]{1,32}$/.test(tenant) ||
        !Number.isSafeInteger(afterId) || afterId < 0 ||
        !Number.isSafeInteger(limit) || limit < 1 || limit > 50) {
      throw new Error('Invalid page');
    }
    const rows = await this.query.fetch({
      tenant, afterId, limit, select: ['id', 'title'], order: 'id-asc',
    });
    if (rows.length > limit) throw new Error('Adapter exceeded page limit');
    let previous = afterId;
    return rows.map(row => {
      if (!Number.isSafeInteger(row.id) || row.id <= previous ||
          typeof row.title !== 'string' || row.title.length > 200) {
        throw new Error('Invalid page response');
      }
      previous = row.id;
      return { id: row.id, title: row.title };
    });
  }
}

The caller supplies a trusted tenant identity. A fake adapter proves the requested contract and public-field projection. The real adapter must enforce authorization, parameterize inputs and apply these bounds in the database. Query plans and representative data establish the database cost.

Include first-use cost in lazy-loading decisions

Lazy loading defers provider construction to the first caller, including its cost and failure. A module in the same file still has its JavaScript evaluated eagerly. Nest also does not invoke lifecycle hooks in lazy-loaded modules/providers.

Compare startup, first use and steady state. An async method still runs its synchronous CPU work on Node's event loop. Neither a shorter function nor an async signature establishes a performance gain.

Apply these checks with NestJS Skills

NestJS Skills v2.5.0 adds 15 collection checks and 17 operations, DI and performance checks. A compatible coding agent can use the guidance to inspect these patterns, propose a bounded change and add regression tests.

Skill Practical review focus
nestjs-architecture-principles Provider identity, DI and module boundaries
nestjs-features-performance Runtime contracts and performance evidence
nestjs-professional-software-engineering Focused implementation and verification

Install from your project:

npx skills add amirtaherkhani/nestjs-skills

Give the agent a concrete contract:

Review this endpoint with NestJS Skills. Check repeated lookups, input
bounds, public output and provider lifetimes. Explain the tradeoffs.
Preserve ordering, duplicates and errors. Add regression tests for the
agreed change. Measure performance claims against the same workload.

From a checkout of the skills repository, with Node.js 20 or newer:

npm ci
npm run test:fixtures
npm run test:runtime

These run the collection and runtime reference suites. They do not run your application's tests or the additional article-snippet checks. The documentation explains how to apply the skills. Local checks establish teaching behavior; production latency, database plans, broker behavior and live shutdown need evidence from your application.

title: SpaceCache: Intermediate Feature Reuse for Efficient Semantic Segmentation on Point Cloud Streams
description:
arXiv:2610.21207v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Point-cloud streams are central to autonomous driving and robotics, yet existing segmentation networks process every frame from scratch, although consecutive frames largely overlap. We observe that the intermediate features of point-cloud transformers remain semantically consistent across frames for the same spatial region, especially in deep stages. Building on this, we present SpaceCache, a training-free feature cache that reuses these features across frames. Tokens of previously observed regions skip a sequence of transformer blocks and take their cached features, only the remaining tokens are computed, and the full token layout is restored for dense prediction. Lightweight cache management keeps reused features reliable by limiting each entry's age and evicting low-confidence entries. Unlike token merging, SpaceCache selects tokens at negligible cost and runs its cache operations once per encoder stage. On both outdoor and indoor benchmarks, such as nuScenes, Waymo, and ScanNet, with two transformer backbones of Utonia and LitePT-B, SpaceCache achieves up to 1.65x speedup with less than 1-point mIoU drop and consistently outperforms token-merging methods.

title: Object Storage Backups: Private Access, Retention, and S3-Compatible Delivery
description:
When a game backend writes a nightly database dump, the important constraint is not finding a public URL. It is keeping the bytes private while making a restore download boring and dependable. Short answer: choose private object storage with signed links when day-level retention is enough; choose a dedicated backup system when you need immutable versioned copies.

That decision also determines whether the application has to proxy a 4 GB export. A worker can upload directly to an object store, record the object key in the ledger, and hand an operator a time-limited download link later. The app moves metadata, not the file.

A restore is the first acceptance test

For app data backups, “cheapest” is a three-part number: stored bytes, bytes downloaded during a restore, and request volume. A storage service that looks inexpensive per gigabyte can still be a poor fit if restore traffic is unpredictable or if its tooling forces a custom client. S3-compatible commands and libraries keep a scheduled dump script small, which is useful when the script must be audited six months after it was written.

The backup object should be private by default. Name it with fields you can filter by prefix, such as prod/us-east/db/2026-08-19T02-00Z.sql.gz; server-side metadata search is limited, so the object key becomes part of the index. Keep a database row with the exact key, checksum, creation time, and retention deadline. That row is your audit trail when someone asks which dump was restored, and it gives a reconciliation job enough data to distinguish a missing object from a stale manifest, a distinction that matters when an operator is deciding whether to retry a restore or page the backup owner.

A signed download is an authorization decision, not a new copy. The API creates a URL that expires; the restore service streams from storage to the operator or restore job. There is no permanent public-read ACL in this model, so it is unsuitable for a game launcher that needs an eternal asset URL, a static site, or an image host.

Keep it private.

Short-lived links are easier to reason about. I use a 15-minute window for an interactive restore and log the request ID beside the restore ticket. Your mileage may vary: an overnight transfer over a constrained link may justify a longer window, but that is a policy choice that belongs in configuration, not in a hard-coded URL.

What should private S3-compatible storage provide for app data backups?

The minimum useful contract is deliberately plain:

  1. A private bucket and an object write operation.
  2. A signed read operation for an operator or restore worker.
  3. Lifecycle expiration with a day-level boundary.
  4. Predictable listing by key prefix.
  5. A client-side checksum and an idempotent write record.

The day-level boundary matters. Lifecycle can expire old backups, but it cannot express “delete this at 02:15,” and multipart fragments do not get an automatic cleanup rule. Set the retention deadline in your own job, then let lifecycle provide a second, coarse safety net.

There is a harder boundary: no object versioning and no object lock (WORM) means an overwrite is not recoverable from the bucket. A ransomware-style credential leak can replace yesterday’s dump with a valid-looking object. For financial or regulatory records that must not change, use a backup platform or an external immutable repository; object storage alone is the wrong control.

Strict compare-and-swap writes are another gap. Without an If-Match condition, two workers can race to the same key. Generate unique keys, serialize promotion in a database or queue, and treat the object checksum as evidence. Exactly-once is a mindset here: retries must be harmless even when the network response is lost.

The upload path should be small and repeatable

The following sketch keeps the application out of the byte path. It uses the documented storage routes for writing an object and creating a signed URL, reads the key from the environment, and makes retries explicit. The request body in a real backup worker would be the dump stream; this small example uses a byte slice so the control flow is visible.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func call(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, path string, body []byte, idem string) ([]byte, error) {
    base := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if base == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    url := base + path
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, url, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/octet-stream")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("storage request failed (%s): %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit retries exhausted")
}

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 60 * time.Second}
    bucket := "backup-prod"
    key := "prod/us-east/db/2026-08-19T02-00Z.sql.gz"
    putPath := strings.NewReplacer("{bucket}", bucket, "{key}", key).Replace("/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}")
    if _, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodPut, putPath, []byte("backup bytes"), "backup-2026-08-19T02-00Z"); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    presignPath := strings.NewReplacer("{bucket}", bucket, "{key}", key).Replace("/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}")
    link, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodPost, presignPath, nil, "sign-2026-08-19T02-00Z")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(link))
}

The idempotency key is stable for the logical backup, not for each network attempt. In production I would also persist the checksum before publishing the database row, then verify the downloaded bytes during a restore. That ordering gives reconciliation something concrete to compare.

Where each storage option fits

The alternatives are not interchangeable once retention and access policy enter the design. AWS S3 is the reference point for S3 tooling and is the natural choice when your organization already depends on its broader backup controls. Cloudflare R2 and Backblaze B2 are credible candidates to price and test for the same private-object workflow. A unified API such as Infrai is useful when the application already has several backend dependencies and one key and one bill reduce credential and invoice reconciliation; its discovery surface and consistent HTTP conventions also keep a small Go worker portable.

Option Private signed downloads Retention and recovery question Good fit
AWS S3 Yes, through the established S3 ecosystem Validate versioning and object-lock policy for your account Teams needing the broadest surrounding AWS controls
Cloudflare R2 Evaluate with the same private-bucket and signed-link test Confirm lifecycle and restore behavior for your regions Workloads already close to Cloudflare delivery
Backblaze B2 Evaluate S3-compatible tooling and private access Confirm retention, replication, and restore operations Teams optimizing a simple backup store
Unified REST storage API Private bucket plus signed access, with one key and bill across backend services Day-level lifecycle; no object versioning or WORM in this model App teams that value one control plane and can add immutable storage separately

Do not turn that table into a benchmark it cannot be. Run a representative dump, a restore, and a failed retry in the regions you actually serve. Record storage, egress, request counts, latency, and the operator steps required to prove which object was restored.

The catch is compliance. If an auditor requires an unalterable seven-year record, the unified object store is not suitable by itself; stick with a dedicated backup platform or add an immutable external target. It is also a poor fit for browser-direct uploads that require self-service CORS configuration, because that workflow needs a separately managed CORS policy. For permanent public links, choose a public asset service instead.

A rollout that preserves the audit trail

Start with one non-production game shard. Create a private bucket, write keys with an environment and timestamp prefix, and set a one-day-or-longer lifecycle rule that matches the retention policy. Keep the manifest in your database, including checksum and restore owner. Then execute three tests: a normal scheduled dump, a duplicate retry with the same idempotency key, and a restore through an expired signed link followed by a newly issued link.

Promote only after the reconciliation report is boring. If the report cannot explain a missing object, pause and fix the manifest or the retention rule before adding more shards. That discipline is more valuable than shaving a fraction from a storage quote.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html

title: Probe-and-Resume: When and How to Evaluate Agent Execution
description:
arXiv:2610.21088v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time search can improve agent performance by exploring alternative actions and using a critic to select promising branches. We study this approach in terminal-based computer-use environments, which expose only a partial view of a large underlying state, and find that the Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) configuration we evaluate does not significantly improve task success. We identify two sources of poor critic performance: the agent's observations omit environment state needed for evaluation, and intermediate states offer limited evidence of whether a trajectory will succeed. At intermediate states, critics rank continuations only modestly better than chance, and environment access improves this little. We study when to invoke a critic and what access to give it to evaluate a node. Our findings motivate a policy that invokes the critic only at nodes the agent believes are final, rather than during partial progress. Further, the policy gives the critic read, write, and execute access to a fork of the computer's current and initial state, allowing it to probe and perform potentially destructive actions to surface any hidden state the trajectory omits. We call the resulting design Probe-and-Resume: when the agent claims to be done, the critic probes a fork of its state, and a rejected agent resumes where it stopped. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, this raises success by 8.4 percentage points over MCTS with conventional critics, and approaches the success rate of the Codex CLI agent with the same underlying model at less than half its cost.

title: Docker Stop Signals Reach PID 1, Not Every Process in the Container
description:
A common misconception says that docker stop sends SIGTERM to every process inside a container. It does not. The signal is sent to the container’s main process: PID 1 in the container’s PID namespace.

This distinction matters when PID 1 is not the application that needs to shut down gracefully. Consider an image with this instruction:

ENTRYPOINT service --listen

This is Dockerfile shell form. Docker normally starts it through a shell equivalent to:

/bin/sh -c 'service --listen'

The shell becomes PID 1, while service runs as its child. When the container is stopped, the runtime signals the shell. Whether the application receives that signal now depends on the shell’s behavior. A non-interactive shell may not forward SIGTERM to its child. The service can therefore miss its opportunity to stop accepting work, flush buffers, close connections, or persist state.

After the configured grace period expires, Docker sends SIGKILL to the container. SIGKILL cannot be caught or handled, so the application is terminated immediately.

Exec form removes this unnecessary intermediary:

ENTRYPOINT ["service", "--listen"]

Here, service itself becomes PID 1 and directly receives the stop signal. A wrapper script can also work, but it should replace itself with the application by using exec:

#!/bin/sh
prepare_environment
exec service --listen

Without exec, the wrapper remains PID 1 and must explicitly forward signals.

PID 1 also has a special process-management responsibility. Orphaned descendants are reparented to it, and it must reap exited children to prevent zombie processes. Applications that spawn subprocesses but do not handle this role well may benefit from a small init process such as Docker’s --init option. That init process can forward signals and reap children while remaining PID 1.

The precise rule is simple: stopping a container signals its designated main process, not every process in the container. Graceful shutdown depends on ensuring that PID 1 either is the application or correctly forwards signals to it.
