title: Your Server Action Error Messages Vanish in Production, and Throwing Is the Wrong Tool
description:
Here is a bug report you will eventually get: "The signup form told me what was wrong on your machine, but on the live site it just says something went wrong."

Nothing is broken. Next.js is doing this on purpose. But the code that triggers it looks completely normal, and it is in a lot of Server Actions tutorials, including a version in my own earlier post on replacing API routes.

The Code That Works Locally 

// actions/signup.ts
'use server';

export async function signup(formData: FormData) {
  const email = formData.get('email') as string;

  const existing = await User.findOne({ email });
  if (existing) {
    throw new Error('That email is already registered');
  }

  await User.create({ email });
}

// components/SignupForm.tsx
'use client';

export function SignupForm() {
  const [error, setError] = useState('');

  async function handleSubmit(formData: FormData) {
    try {
      await signup(formData);
    } catch (e) {
      setError((e as Error).message);
    }
  }

  return (
    <form action={handleSubmit}>
      <input name="email" type="email" />
      <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
      {error && <p>{error}</p>}
    </form>
  );
}

In development, a duplicate email shows "That email is already registered". After next build and next start, or on Vercel, the same submission shows a generic message about an error occurring on the server, with a short digest string instead of your text.

Why Next.js Hides It

An error thrown on the server can carry anything: a database connection string inside a driver message, a file path, a query, a stack trace. If Next.js forwarded every thrown message to the browser, a single unexpected failure could leak internal details to anyone watching the network tab.

So in production builds, Next.js replaces the message of a thrown error with a generic one and attaches a digest, a short hash you can search for in your server logs. In development it shows you the real message because you are the only one looking.

That is the correct default. The mistake is using throw for something that is not an unexpected failure.

Two Kinds of Errors, Two Different Tools

Expected errors are things that will happen during normal use: a duplicate email, a wrong password, a failed validation, a card that was declined. The user should see a specific message and fix it.

Unexpected errors are things that should not happen: the database is down, a bug, a null that should not be null. The user should see a safe generic message and you should see the details in your logs.

throw is the right tool for the second kind. It is the wrong tool for the first, because the framework treats every thrown error as potentially sensitive and strips it.

The Fix: Return Expected Errors as Data 

// actions/signup.ts
'use server';

import { z } from 'zod';

const SignupSchema = z.object({
  email: z.string().email('Enter a valid email'),
});

export type SignupState = {
  success: boolean;
  message?: string;
  fieldErrors?: Record<string, string[]>;
};

export async function signup(
  prevState: SignupState | null,
  formData: FormData
): Promise<SignupState> {
  const parsed = SignupSchema.safeParse({
    email: formData.get('email'),
  });

  if (!parsed.success) {
    return {
      success: false,
      fieldErrors: parsed.error.flatten().fieldErrors,
    };
  }

  const existing = await User.findOne({ email: parsed.data.email });
  if (existing) {
    return { success: false, message: 'That email is already registered' };
  }

  await User.create({ email: parsed.data.email });
  return { success: true, message: 'Account created' };
}

// components/SignupForm.tsx
'use client';

import { useActionState } from 'react';
import { signup } from '@/actions/signup';

export function SignupForm() {
  const [state, action, isPending] = useActionState(signup, null);

  return (
    <form action={action}>
      <input name="email" type="email" />
      {state?.fieldErrors?.email && <p>{state.fieldErrors.email[0]}</p>}
      <button type="submit" disabled={isPending}>
        {isPending ? 'Creating account...' : 'Sign up'}
      </button>
      {state?.message && <p>{state.message}</p>}
    </form>
  );
}

A returned value is just data. Next.js does not treat it as sensitive, so the exact same message reaches the user in development and in production. You also get useActionState handling pending state and the previous result for free, with no try/catch in the component.

Keep throw for the Real Failures 

export async function signup(prevState, formData) {
  // ...expected errors returned as data above...

  try {
    await User.create({ email: parsed.data.email });
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('signup failed', error); // full details stay in your logs
    throw error; // user gets the safe generic message
  }

  return { success: true, message: 'Account created' };
}

When this throws in production, the user sees the generic message and an error boundary can take over. You search your logs for the digest and find the real error. Nothing sensitive reaches the browser.

Why This Survives Testing

Every manual test happens in next dev, where thrown messages are shown in full. The code looks perfect right up until the first production build, which is usually when real users start signing up.

The Rule

Return expected errors as data, throw only for unexpected failures. If a message is meant for the user to read, it should travel as a returned value. If it is meant for you to debug, it should go to your logs and surface to the user as something generic.

I use this return-a-state pattern in the forms and dashboard actions across my Next.js templates, so validation messages behave identically in development and on the live site.

Get the templates: https://pixelanas.gumroad.com

Search your own codebase for throw new Error inside files marked 'use server'. For each one, ask whether a user is supposed to read that message. If yes, it is probably already invisible in production. Drop what you find in the comments.

Anas, full-stack Next.js developer building SaaS products and premium templates. X: @ASheikh69751

title: Managed Metrics API vs Self-Hosted Dashboard — Choose Attributable Incident Evidence
description:
Choice Best fit Main burden Cost attribution
Managed metrics API One person shipping weekly, with no appetite for operating the metrics path Provider evaluation, retention policy, and export testing Strong only if tenant and region labels survive ingestion and billing can be reconciled to usage
Self-hosted collector and dashboard Teams that need control over storage, query behavior, or deployment boundaries Capacity, upgrades, backups, alert delivery, and the telemetry system itself Direct infrastructure costs, plus engineering time that must be counted separately

A managed metrics API is my default choice for a solo fintech SaaS, but only when it preserves the labels needed to reconstruct a customer incident and attribute ingestion by tenant and region. Otherwise, I would self-host the metrics path. The deciding boundary is evidence ownership, not dashboard polish.

TL;DR: send a deliberately small metric set through a standards-based client, attach bounded identifiers such as region and operation, and keep high-cardinality customer evidence in logs or traces. Test export and deletion before committing. This gives a small startup a useful dashboard without pretending that a time-series database is an incident ledger.

What should a startup demand from an alternative metrics dashboard?

A chart that says error rate rose is useful during detection. It is insufficient for reconstruction. In fintech, the harder question arrives later: which operation failed, in which processing region, during which deployment, and what evidence connects the symptom to a customer-visible outcome?

That distinction changes the selection exercise. I care about two jobs. The first is fast operational feedback: rates, latency distributions, saturation, and a few business-process counters. The second is durable evidence. Metrics handle the first job well. Logs, traces, and application records usually carry the individual event detail needed for the second.

That is the boundary.

Do not force both jobs into metric labels. Prometheus instrumentation guidance warns that every unique label combination creates a new time series and specifically cautions against high-cardinality dimensions such as user IDs and email addresses. A customer_id label looks convenient on day one. As customers and operations multiply, it turns a bounded dashboard into an open-ended storage and query problem.

Keep the join explicit instead. A metric can identify region, operation, result, and release, provided each value comes from a controlled set. The detailed record can carry an opaque correlation ID. During an incident, the chart narrows the time window and failure class; the correlated records reconstruct individual outcomes.

Consider a release followed by a rise in failed captures in the EU processing region. The dashboard should narrow the search using 4 bounded dimensions: region, operation, result, and release. It should not answer by exposing a customer identifier as a metric label. An operator takes the affected time window and release value to the structured records, follows correlation IDs to the application events, and separates declined payments from processing errors. The metric detects and scopes; the records establish what happened to each operation. This exercise also exposes a selection failure early: if an API drops the region label, obscures timestamps during export, or can't return the values used by the runbook, its attractive dashboard doesn't preserve enough evidence for this job.

Criterion one: can usage be attributed without cardinality debt?

Cost attribution needs a stable unit. For this system, I would start with bytes or accepted data points by service, region, and environment, then reconcile those figures against the provider invoice or the self-hosted storage bill. Tenant-level allocation belongs in the design only if the tenant population is tightly bounded. For an expanding SaaS, tenant IDs in every series are the wrong default.

The practical compromise is a small number of commercial cohorts. A startup might distinguish plan=standard and plan=regulated, for example, if those values drive different retention or support obligations. It should not encode a free-form account name. Cardinality needs a budget just like memory does.

I use three checks before accepting a label:

  1. Is the value drawn from a documented, bounded set?
  2. Will the label help make an operational decision during an incident?
  3. Can finance or engineering reconcile its usage without adding a customer identifier?

If any answer is no, the field moves to structured logs, traces, or the application database. This is a real trade-off: aggregate allocation becomes less exact, but the metric pipeline remains predictable. For a one-person company, predictable wins because every hour spent tuning telemetry storage is an hour not spent shipping the weekly release.

There is another trap. Infrastructure spend alone is not total cost. A self-hosted system exposes compute and storage clearly, while maintenance time hides in a calendar. A managed endpoint reverses the visibility: the invoice is obvious, but uncontrolled labels can silently drive usage. Compare both approaches using the same ledger: ingestion, retention, data transfer, on-call investigation, upgrades, and restore tests. Do not reduce the decision to a headline unit price.

Count the hours.

Criterion two: can evidence cross regions without losing meaning?

Europe and the United States are deployment facts, not decorative dashboard filters. Region should appear in the telemetry schema from the first release. Use a short controlled value, document what it means, and test that aggregation never drops it. The useful question is not merely whether a service accepts traffic in two places. It is whether an operator can isolate one region, compare equivalent operations, and export the underlying evidence in a usable form.

Two regions are still one schema.

Retention deserves the same precision. Define how far back incident reconstruction must reach, then verify that metrics, logs, and application records cover that window according to their separate roles. The required duration comes from the business and its obligations; it should not be invented by the observability tool.

A managed service must also pass an exit test. Can the team export representative data with timestamps, labels, and values intact? Can it document deletion behavior? Can it explain where data is processed and stored? Those answers are contract and architecture inputs. If they are missing, the apparent convenience is borrowed time.

Self-hosting offers direct control over placement and retention, but control creates work. Someone still owns upgrades, capacity, backups, restore verification, and access policy. In a solo operation, that someone is also shipping product and answering customers. Control is valuable only when its operational cost buys a requirement the managed route cannot meet.

A bounded TypeScript instrumentation example

The application boundary should not know which dashboard renders the result. It should emit a narrow record through an interface that can be adapted to a standards-based metrics client or another backend. More importantly, the type system can keep dangerous dimensions out of the metric path.

const regions = ["eu", "us"] as const;
const operations = ["authorize", "capture", "refund"] as const;
const results = ["accepted", "declined", "error"] as const;

type MetricLabels = {
  region: (typeof regions)[number];
  operation: (typeof operations)[number];
  result: (typeof results)[number];
  release: string;
};

type IncidentRecord = MetricLabels & {
  correlationId: string;
  occurredAt: string;
  tenantRef: string;
};

interface MetricsSink {
  increment(name: "payment_operations_total", labels: MetricLabels): void;
}

export function recordPaymentOutcome(
  sink: MetricsSink,
  event: IncidentRecord,
): void {
  const { region, operation, result, release } = event;
  sink.increment("payment_operations_total", {
    region,
    operation,
    result,
    release,
  });
}

tenantRef and correlationId remain available to the incident record, but they cannot enter the counter through this interface. The compiler is doing useful policy enforcement. It does not prove that release is bounded, so the deployment pipeline must normalize that value, and a test should reject unexpected labels before release.

This example is intentionally small. Histograms for latency and gauges for current resource state may be appropriate, but each instrument needs an operational question. Instrumentation without a decision behind it becomes inventory.

The deployment check is equally plain: emit one known event per region in a non-production environment, verify its counter and detailed record, then query the same dimensions used by the incident runbook. After deployment, compare the release dimension against the prior release. If telemetry disappears, the release is not observable enough to trust.

When the self-hosted runner-up is the better choice

Choose the self-hosted path when deployment boundaries prohibit the managed route, when required retention or export semantics cannot be contracted, or when the team already has the operational capacity to own collection and storage. It can also be rational when query control is a product requirement rather than an internal convenience.

Be honest about the boundary. Running a collector and drawing a dashboard is the easy demonstration. Production ownership includes upgrades, storage growth, authentication, authorization, backups, restore drills, alert delivery, and observability for the observability system. Those tasks can be worthwhile. They are still tasks.

My decision rule is compact: pick the managed API if a proof-of-concept preserves bounded dimensions, passes regional and export checks, and produces usage that can be reconciled. Pick self-hosting if any non-negotiable evidence requirement fails and you can fund the ongoing ownership. Revisit the result after the label set, incident requirements, or staffing changes.

For a solo fintech SaaS, the first option usually leaves more revenue-producing hours for product work. The exception matters more than the default: never outsource evidence you cannot retrieve, interpret, and connect to the customer event.

Sources

  • https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/metrics/
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/common/

title: Multimodal AI Detection for Math-Heavy Scientific Text
description:
arXiv:2610.21062v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As large language models become increasingly capable of generating, and assisting with, scientific writing, there is a need for greater transparency and disclosure around the use of AI in research. Consequently, a veritable subfield of research and a number of commercial services aim to flag AI-generated content automatically. However, existing detectors which rely only on text extracted from PDFs fail to benefit from the rich visual information contained in the formatting of math-heavy scientific content. To study this, we select human-written proof and prose passages from pre-2022 arXiv LaTeX sources and re-generate them using 15 modern LLMs within the context of the same paper. This leaves us with coupled human and AI outputs in three different representations: the LaTeX source, a rendered image of the PDF, and the text extracted from the PDF. We find that the accuracy of the state-of-the-art Pangram 4 drops significantly as the mathematical content in a passage increases, especially when evaluated on text as opposed to LaTeX. However, this is not an inherent limitation of detecting AI-generated math: finetuning Qwen-3.5-27B based detectors on this domain recovers the gap, with LaTeX inputs performing significantly better than text since they preserve more formatting information. Since LaTeX sources are rarely available in practice, we also train SnapJudge: an image-based detector operating on screenshots of both prose and proofs from papers. At 0.1% false positive rate, SnapJudge achieves a detection rate of 92% on proofs and 93% on prose generated by frontier models, substantially outperforming both Pangram 4 and our text-based detector. We release our data, models and code at https://nlplab.cs.duke.edu/snapjudge.

title: Testing Python-to-Java Parity in a Graph Retrieval Library
description:
What does it take to port a graph-retrieval library from Python to Java without relying on API similarity alone?

For RagLeap Graph Java v0.2.0, the answer was a combination of parity tests, deliberate mutations, database integration tests, and validation of the actual published artifact.

Release: RagLeap Graph Java v0.2.0

Features in this release

The Java library now includes:

  • Optional LLM-based entity and relation extraction.
  • Configurable extraction and entity deduplication.
  • Cross-chunk relation handling.
  • Hybrid vector + graph retrieval and graph-only retrieval.
  • Chunk and graph-path citations.
  • Pluggable graph and vector search interfaces.
  • Backfill utilities and a schema migration runner.

Regex-based extraction remains the default. LLM integration is optional.

How we approached parity testing

We compared the Java implementation against the Python ragleap-graph v0.9.0 implementation.

Rather than comparing method names, we exercised behavior using recorded calls, parameters, outputs, and scripted model responses.

The test scenarios covered:

  • 422 string-similarity pairs.
  • 25 extraction-configuration cases.
  • Entity and relation extraction.
  • Graph upserts, including Cypher statements and parameters.
  • Backfills and migration behavior.
  • Retrieval scenarios and retrieval configurations.

We also ran 27 deliberate mutations across the new functionality. Every injected break was caught by the parity tests.

This is evidence for the tested cases, not a mathematical guarantee of complete equivalence.

Why mutation testing matters

A passing test suite can still miss bugs if its assertions are too weak.

Mutation testing deliberately changes behavior to check whether the tests notice. For this release, the 27 deliberate breaks were caught by the parity tests.

That gave us additional confidence that the tests were checking behavior rather than merely executing code paths.

Testing the real release

The full local run used generated parity fixtures and a live Neo4j 5.26.29 Community instance:

  • 129 tests
  • 0 failures
  • 0 skipped tests

After publishing, we resolved the Maven artifact in a clean project and exercised health checks, upserts, backfills, and graph-only retrieval against live Neo4j.

Maven coordinates:

io.github.antonyrag:ragleap-graph:0.2.0\

What still needs testing?

LLM extraction hasn't been verified against a real model provider. Compatibility with other Neo4j deployments also needs more testing, and the optional vector-search adapter hasn't been tested against a live RagLeap facade.

The PostgreSQL audit writer hasn't been ported yet.

Documenting these limitations is part of making a library easier to evaluate responsibly.

Try it and share feedback

Source and release notes:

https://github.com/antonyrag/ragleap-core/releases/tag/ragleap-graph-java-v0.2.0

RagLeap is fully open-source and self-hosted, with a wider ecosystem of retrieval, graph, and AI tooling libraries.

If you work with Java or Neo4j, I'd appreciate feedback on the API, compatibility, test coverage, and integration experience.

What integration test would you add before using this library in production?

title: Renting Out One T4 to Three Customers: Gemma 4, vLLM Multi-LoRA and a Rust Gateway
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

This article provides a step by step guide to renting out one NVIDIA T4 on a Google Cloud VM to several small customers at once, with Gemma 4 E2B served by vLLM and a small Rust gateway in front. Every log, script and number is committed.

https://github.com/xbill9/t4-timeshare

One customer sending 4,000-token prompts pushes everyone else's first token from 0.28 s to 29.90 s on a shared T4. vLLM's priority scheduling brings that back to 6.52 s. The gateway adds what turns a shared GPU into a business: keys, a fine-tune per customer that no one else can call, a prefix cache per customer, and a ledger that matched vLLM's own token counters exactly. Billed by GPU time, the long-prompt customer pays 27.2% of the VM for 22.0% of the tokens.

What I Built

A small AI job costs too much either way. A GPU of your own sits idle most of the day. A per-token API bill grows with every customer you add, and every prompt leaves your building.

The side hustle is the middle: one person rents one T4, and sells shares of it to a few small businesses at a flat monthly price. Each customer gets:

  • an API key that works with any OpenAI client
  • its own fine-tuned adapter on the shared base model, callable by that customer only
  • a prefix cache that other customers cannot read through response timing
  • a bill computed from metered tokens, weighted by what each token costs the GPU

The operator gets one config file and a ledger.

The three demo tenants are picked so each one loads the T4 differently:

Tenant Job Shape
A Summarise long daily logs Few requests, 4,096-token prompts
B Triage short support emails One 512-token request every 2 s
C Tag product rows, with its own adapter One 512-token request every 2 s

Demo

The gateway listens on port 8080 and speaks the OpenAI chat API. day3/demo.sh, run with bash -v:

curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer demo-key-B" \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Label this email: my parcel arrived broken"}],"max_tokens":20}' \
  | jq -c '{model, usage: .usage.total_tokens}'
{"model":"xbill9/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-w4a16-ct-text-emb4","usage":37}
curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer demo-key-C" \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Label this email: my parcel arrived broken"}],"max_tokens":20}' \
  | jq -c '{model, usage: .usage.total_tokens}'
{"model":"rand","usage":26}
curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer demo-key-B" \
  -d '{"model":"rand","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}' -w ' %{http_code}\n'
{"error":"adapter belongs to another tenant"} 403
curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}' -w ' %{http_code}\n'
{"error":"missing or unknown key"} 401
tail -4 ledger.jsonl
{"completion_tokens":20,"model":"xbill9/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-w4a16-ct-text-emb4","prompt_tokens":17,"queue_ms":0.0006799999999999999,"status":200,"tenant":"B","total_ms":355.14126200000004,"ts":1792165075.2638927}
{"completion_tokens":9,"model":"rand","prompt_tokens":17,"queue_ms":0.000778,"status":200,"tenant":"C","total_ms":498.805413,"ts":1792165075.7809048}
{"refused":"adapter belongs to another tenant","status":403,"tenant":"B","ts":1792165075.7979941}
{"refused":"missing or unknown key","status":401,"tenant":null,"ts":1792165075.8125255}

The same request from B and C reaches two different models: B gets the base model, C gets its adapter without naming it. B asking for C's adapter is refused, and so is a request with no key. Every one of the four lands in the ledger.

Code

https://github.com/xbill9/t4-timeshare

Path What
gateway/src/main.rs The gateway, 245 lines of Rust (axum, reqwest, tokio)
gateway/tenants.toml Keys, adapters, priorities and in-flight caps
day1/ Checks on the T4 before building: LoRA, cache salt, streamed usage, priority, prefill cost
day2/ The noisy-neighbour test straight to vLLM
day3/ The same test through the gateway, isolation checks, the bill and VM pricing

How I Built It

At This Point You Should Have…

  • A Google Cloud VM with one NVIDIA T4. This one is an n1-standard-2 in us-west2-b
  • vLLM 0.29.0 serving xbill9/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-w4a16-ct-text-emb4, Gemma 4 E2B with Google's quantization-aware 4-bit weights, fp16, at most 8 sequences at once
  • Rust, for the gateway
  • A clone: git clone https://github.com/xbill9/t4-timeshare

Step 1 — Check the Engine Can Do Multi-Tenant Work

Four features decide whether one vLLM can serve several paying customers. Each was checked on the T4 before any gateway code was written (day1/RESULTS.md):

Check Result
LoRA adapters on the 4-bit weights, Turing GPU 🟢 A zero adapter returns the base model's output, 40 of 40 tokens. A random adapter differs from token 1. 6 of 6 requests in one mixed batch match their solo output.
Per-request prefix-cache salt 🟢 Same salt, repeat: 1,216 of 1,217 tokens from cache. Different salt: 0.
Token usage on streamed responses 🟢 Present with stream_options.include_usage, absent without it. The gateway sets it.
Priority scheduling 🟢 With --scheduling-policy priority, a high-priority request queued last finished first.

The 6 of 6 is what makes per-customer fine-tunes cheap: requests for different adapters share one batch on one GPU, and each still gets its own model's answer.

Step 2 — Measure What Hurts on a T4

A customer's request costs the GPU in two parts: reading the prompt (prefill) and writing the answer (decode). day1/prefill_cost.py times prefill alone, one request at a time, 5 per length, with the prefix cache unable to help:

prompt ~  256: median    106.9 ms  min    103.4  max    108.7
prompt ~  512: median    262.0 ms  min    258.9  max    267.9
prompt ~ 1024: median    730.8 ms  min    717.0  max    737.4
prompt ~ 2048: median   2180.8 ms  min   2149.6  max   2223.6
prompt ~ 4096: median   7122.4 ms  min   7050.4  max   7363.7
prompt ~ 8192: median  25364.0 ms  min  25261.6  max  25697.8
prefill fit over 30 requests: -12.8 ms + 374.32 us x n + 336.9989 ns x n^2; worst error 2.1%
decode: median 9.34 ms per output token over 5 pairs (256 tokens minus 1 token, same length prompt)

Prefill grows with the square of the prompt. One 4,096-token prompt costs as much GPU time as 767.8 output tokens. On a T4 the customer who hurts the others is the one with long prompts, more than the one with many requests.

Step 3 — Watch One Customer Stall the Others

day2/m1_direct.py runs the three tenants straight against vLLM. B and C each send one 512-token request every 2 seconds and stream 64 tokens back. For 180 seconds, A keeps four 4,096-token summaries in flight. Every prompt starts with a random tag, so nothing comes from cache.

First come, first served, every request in the same queue:

[quiet] B: 90/90 ok  first token median    0.29 s  95th    0.29 s  max    0.34 s | total median    0.98 s  95th    0.99 s
[flood] A: 16/16 ok  first token median   30.82 s  95th   45.37 s  max   46.12 s | total median   50.08 s  95th   54.03 s
[flood] B: 90/90 ok  first token median   29.78 s  95th   44.47 s  max   47.81 s | total median   35.07 s  95th   48.91 s

A support-email triage that answered in a third of a second now waits half a minute for its first word. B pays for A's prompts.

Step 4 — Put the Gateway in Front

gateway/src/main.rs does six things per request, in order:

  1. Key to tenant. Authorization: Bearer <key> looks the tenant up in tenants.toml. No key or an unknown one: 401.
  2. Model check. The tenant gets its own adapter by default, or the base model on request. Another tenant's adapter: 403.
  3. Priority. The tenant's priority goes into the request body, overwriting whatever the client sent.
  4. Cache salt. cache_salt is set to the tenant's name, so cached prompts are shared within a tenant and never across tenants.
  5. In-flight cap. The request waits for one of the tenant's slots, a tokio semaphore per tenant.
  6. Ledger. When the response ends, or the client disconnects, one JSON line is written with the tenant, the model, the status, vLLM's own prompt and output token counts, the time spent waiting for a slot and the total time.

The demo tenants:

[[tenant]]
name = "A"
key = "demo-key-A"
max_inflight = 1
priority = 10

[[tenant]]
name = "C"
key = "demo-key-C"
adapter = "rand"
max_inflight = 8
priority = 0

A has one slot and runs last. B and C have 8 slots each, the most vLLM runs at once. C's rand adapter is a random rank-8 LoRA from day1/make_adapters.py, standing in for a customer's fine-tune.

Streaming responses pass straight through. The gateway watches the stream for the one chunk that carries usage and records it when the stream ends. A request that dies halfway is still in the ledger, and its slot is released at that moment.

Step 5 — Check Isolation 

python3 day3/isolation.py

PASS  no key: 401
PASS  unknown key: 401
PASS  B asks for C's adapter: 403
PASS  B asks for a model that is not served: 404
PASS  B gets the base model: xbill9/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-w4a16-ct-text-emb4
PASS  C gets its own adapter by default: rand
PASS  C's answer differs from the base model's: 'Here are a few examples of how a spare G' vs 'Here are three common uses for a spare G'
PASS  B's repeat is served from B's cache: 2400 hit tokens (first send 0)
PASS  A sending B's prompt gets none of B's cache: 0 hit tokens
9 of 9 pass

The last two lines are the privacy check. When B sends a long prompt twice, the second send is served from cache. A sends the identical prompt and gets nothing from B's cache, so A cannot tell from response time whether B ever sent it. The hit counts come from vLLM's /metrics, not from timing.

Step 6 — Rerun the Noisy Neighbour Through the Gateway 

day3/run_m1.sh
python3 day3/compare.py

run                                   B+C first token median    95th     max  B+C done  A done
quiet, no A (direct)                                  0.28 s  0.29 s  0.37 s       180       0
direct, first come first served                      29.90 s 44.49 s 47.81 s       180      16
direct, A at low priority                             6.52 s 14.71 s 16.31 s       180      16
gateway: priority + A capped at 1                     7.06 s 12.11 s 13.55 s       180       7

Priority does most of the work: B and C's median wait falls from 29.90 s to 6.52 s. Capping A at one request shortens the worst waits, from 14.71 s to 12.11 s at the 95th percentile. A pays for it, finishing 7 summaries in the window against 16.

B and C still wait about 7 s, close to one 4,096-token prefill (7.1 s in Step 2). A request that arrives while A's prompt is being read waits for that read to finish.

🔎 Tip: size the cap above what the tenant needs. B sends a request every 2 seconds and each one spends about 12 seconds on the GPU under load, so B needs about 6 slots. With B capped at 4, the same run gave B a median time inside vLLM of 11.61 s and a median wait for a gateway slot of 37.77 s (day3/cap4/). A cap is for the customer you want to slow down.

Step 7 — Check the Ledger Against vLLM

A bill is only as good as its meter. day3/bill.py adds up the ledger and compares it with vLLM's own prompt_tokens_total and generation_tokens_total counters, read before and after the run:

ledger vs vLLM counters: prompt 122,442 vs 122,442, output 12,416 vs 12,416; match: True

Every token vLLM processed in the run is attributed to a tenant, and no tenant is charged for a token vLLM did not process.

Step 8 — Send the Bill

The VM's on-demand price comes from the Cloud Billing Catalog API, fetched during the build (day3/pricing.us-west2.txt):

T4 0.410000 + 2 vCPU x 0.037970 + 7.5 GiB x 0.005089 = 0.5241 USD/hour
x 730 hours = 382.60 USD/month

bill.py prices each request in GPU seconds, using the prefill fit from Step 2 plus 9.34 ms per output token, and splits the month by each tenant's share. Over the gateway run:

tenant   requests refused  prompt tok  output tok token share     GPU s GPU share  bill USD
A               7       0      28,718         896       22.0%      58.7     27.2%    104.22
B              90       0      46,803       5,760       39.0%      78.4     36.4%    139.11
C              90       0      46,921       5,760       39.1%      78.5     36.4%    139.26

A sent 22.0% of the tokens and used 27.2% of the GPU. A flat price per token would undercharge the long-prompt customer and pass the difference on to the other two. Weighting prompt tokens by their measured prefill cost puts it back.

Compare and Contrast

Straight to vLLM vLLM with priority Through the gateway
B and C, median first token under load 29.90 s 🥈 6.52 s 🥇 7.06 s
B and C, 95th percentile 44.49 s 🥈 14.71 s 🥇 12.11 s
Keys per customer ❌ no ❌ no 🟢 yes
Adapter only its owner can call ❌ no ❌ no 🟢 yes
Prefix cache per customer ❌ no ❌ no 🟢 yes
Per-customer bill, checked against vLLM ❌ no ❌ no 🟢 yes

So, Which One?

Turn on --scheduling-policy priority for any shared vLLM: on these runs it is the single biggest change, and it costs one flag. Selling the GPU takes the gateway, because priority alone still lets any client claim any priority, call any adapter and read any cache. The gateway sets all three from the key.

Prior Work

  • The T4 rig: the VM, vLLM 0.29.0 install, Turing patch and the vllm-t4 script come from my earlier gemma4-dev T4 serving work.
  • gemma-rust: reqwest client patterns for the OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
  • dev-hacktoberfest (Week 1): every result checked by code that did not produce it.
  • Open source used: vLLM (Apache 2.0), Gemma 4 E2B (Gemma terms), axum, reqwest, tokio.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Every part of this business needs the weights.

  • The model runs on hardware the operator controls. That is possible only with downloadable weights, and it is what lets the operator promise a customer that its emails never reach a model vendor.
  • One base model, one small adapter per customer. Per-customer fine-tunes that share one GPU and one batch need the weights and an engine that serves adapters side by side. vLLM's multi-LoRA does that on a 2018-era T4.
  • The cost is flat. The operator pays 382.60 USD a month whatever the customers send. A heavy customer costs the others waiting time, which the scheduler controls, and costs the operator nothing extra.
  • Everything can be checked. Engine, gateway and model are open, so the cache isolation and the bill are tested against vLLM's own counters, and a customer can read the code that bills them.

Prize Categories

Gemma: Gemma 4 E2B, served locally on a T4 with vLLM, with per-customer LoRA adapters on Google's quantization-aware 4-bit weights.

Summary

The goal of this project was to sell shares of one T4 to several small customers without one customer ruining the service for the others. The key to the solution was vLLM's priority scheduling, adapters and cache salt, controlled per customer by a gateway that holds the keys. The results were:

  • 🟢 A long-prompt customer pushed other customers' first token from 0.28 s to 29.90 s. Priority brought it to 6.52 s; the gateway's cap on that customer brought the 95th percentile from 14.71 s to 12.11 s.
  • 🟢 9 of 9 isolation checks pass: keys, adapter ownership and a prefix cache per customer.
  • 🟢 The ledger matched vLLM's token counters exactly: 122,442 prompt and 12,416 output tokens.
  • 🟢 A per-adapter customer runs in the same batch as base-model customers, at about the same speed.
  • ⚠️ B and C still wait about one long prefill, around 7 s, while A is active. Chunking long prompts further, or giving A its own hours, are the next steps.
  • ❌ A's throughput falls from 16 summaries to 7 in the window. That is the price A pays for a cheaper share.

Scope: one T4 on one Google Cloud VM, vLLM 0.29.0, one 180-second run per configuration. The two direct runs and the gateway run used separate server starts with the same flags; in the direct runs C used the base model, through the gateway it used its adapter. The token bucket, the per-customer fair queue and a tenant-count sweep from SPEC.md are not built. The VM price excludes disk and network.

The strategy for renting out one T4 to several customers with Gemma 4 and vLLM was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

References

  • Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 2
  • t4-timeshare on GitHub
  • vLLM
  • Gemma 4 E2B, 4-bit build used here
  • Google Cloud GPU pricing

title: An AI Agent Is Running a Real Microbusiness Solo. Here's the Function Split Worth Studying.
description:
In mid-October, Alex Finn posted that his Grok Bot — the same class of consumer agent most people use to draft emails — had built a use-case website on its own, decided to monetize it with sponsors, kept shipping updates without being asked, and closed its first sponsor. Finn's remaining job: running the social media accounts. Everything else ran agent-side.

Label this honestly: it's one source, from the person with every incentive to promote it, and the revenue is real-but-small — first sponsor money, not a payroll. Treat it as anecdote, not proof.

But it's the first plausible report of a consumer agent operating a real (if tiny) business end-to-end, and it makes a question concrete that most owners only ask abstractly: if you had an agent like that, which functions of your business could it actually own?

Most coverage of "AI runs a business" runs it through hype or threat. Both skip the exercise an owner can do in twenty minutes. That exercise — function allocation — is the part worth stealing.

Task Delegation Is Not Function Ownership

There's an important distinction hiding here, because "delegate to AI" already has a playbook — the junior agent drafts, a human reviews every output before it ships. That's task delegation. It's the right pattern for most work, and it's not what happened in this case.

Function ownership is different: the agent runs the entire loop, the output goes to real people without a human looking at it first, and the human only audits results — weekly, not per-output.

  • A task delegate drafts your follow-up emails. You read each one and send.
  • A function owner maintains your website, publishes updates, answers the inbound, invoices the customer. You review traffic and revenue on Friday.

The test is brutal and simple: does the work leave the building without a human in the loop? If yes, the agent owns the function. If a human signs off on each output, you've delegated a task — which is fine, and much safer, but it's a different bet.

The Agent-First Seats

Look at what held up as agent-owned in the reported case, and why each survived:

  • The website. Built and maintained by the agent. Bad output is immediately visible to anyone who visits.
  • Continuous updates. The agent shipped improvements unprompted. A dud update shows up in the numbers within days.
  • Inbound negotiation. The agent handled sponsor inquiries through to a closed deal — inside authority limits someone set up front.
  • The records. Tracking what shipped, what earned, what's owed. Bookkeeping-ish work with a paper trail.

There's a shared property: the feedback loop is external and fast. A weak update surfaces as traffic loss in days. A misjudged reply bounces back as an email. The work self-corrects before small errors compound into big ones. Fast, visible, cheap-to-fix feedback is what makes a function ownable.

The Human-Kept Seats

Notice where the human stayed in the same case: the public-facing voice. Social media ran through Finn — because the brand's face is an asset that an agent can degrade faster than any dashboard can measure.

For your business, the human-kept seats are the ones that fail that external-fast-feedback test:

  • Your name in public. Reputation damage is slow to surface and expensive to repair — the opposite of a fast feedback loop.
  • Key client relationships. An agent can draft; the relationship compounds because a specific human answers.
  • Judgment calls with compounding downside. Pricing strategy, hiring, which market to enter. Wrong answers take months to show up, and by then the cost is sunk.
  • Anything where being wrong is invisible until it's expensive. If you can't check the output cheaply on a weekly cadence, you can't own-by-audit.

Calibrate the Expectation Before You Run It

The payday in this case is a first sponsor on a niche website — dollars, not millions. If the pattern works at all, it frees the owner's time and adds small revenue streams, not a payroll.

The reason to pay attention isn't the money. It's that the boundary of "ownable" just moved — the same way website builders moved it and Zapier moved it. Each shift lets a smaller business cover one more seat without a hire. The allocation exercise is how you catch that shift early instead of paying for software and people who duplicate it.

Run the Allocation Exercise on Your Business Tonight

This takes twenty minutes and one page:

  1. List your functions. Marketing, sales, fulfillment, support, records, admin. Six rows.
  2. Apply the ownership test to each row. Three questions: Can output leave without human review? Is the feedback loop fast and external? Is being wrong cheap and visible?
  3. Score it. Three yeses → pilot it as function ownership. Two → task delegation (drafts plus review). One or zero → human seat, and stop feeling guilty about it.
  4. Start with exactly one function. Give the agent the seat, set its authority limits in writing, and audit weekly — results only, not outputs. If the audit passes four weeks in a row, hand it the next function.

The mistake to avoid is confusing the two modes. An agent that drafts well isn't ready to own the function; an agent that owns the inbox shouldn't also get the brand. Most failed AI rollouts in small businesses happen when a task delegate gets promoted to function owner without the feedback loop to support it.

Want the full framework? The AI Agent Owner's Playbook covers function allocation, authority limits, and the weekly audit format in one walkthrough — $49 CAD, instant download.

SMB Scale Up helps small businesses build AI agent systems that actually work — without the enterprise price tag.

title: Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements
description:
arXiv:2610.20782v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The closed world asks AI for specialized competence and lets it manufacture the iid data its theory assumes: a fixed criterion licenses collecting examples until the task is covered. The open world asks for versatility --- taking up tasks a machine was not built for, from few examples and with little prior from a human designer --- and offers data that is grouped, not shuffled. Its tasks are not known in advance, so a machine must do inference-time learning (1st requirement). Modeling tasks as sharing latent factors and decomposing the training objective, we derive two more: a *rich representation*, retaining more than iid generalization requires, and a predictive disentanglement that aligns inputs and outputs into matched low-dimensional groups. The analysis further predicts the need for a consistent inner learner, and the benefit of long contexts spanning related tasks. We test these claims on language models up to 8B, asking whether a model has a property (qualitative) rather than how much it wins (quantitative). Models that meet the requirements improve as data from related tasks accumulates; the rest degrade, and neither scale nor layer-type interleaving repairs this.

title: WeightWatch: Detección Black-Box de Backdoors en LLMs Fine-Tuneados
description:
La cadena de suministro de modelos de IA representa un vector de ataque emergente y crítico. Los modelos open-weight fine-tuneados pueden contener puertas traseras (backdoors) latentes que solo se activan ante triggers específicos, siendo indetectables mediante inspección superficial.

Presentamos WeightWatch (github.com/amurlaniakea/weightwatch), una herramienta de auditoría de seguridad diseñada para escanear modelos de lenguaje antes de su despliegue.

Características técnicas principales:

Análisis Black-Box: No requiere acceso a los datos de entrenamiento originales ni a un modelo base de referencia limpio.

Detección Híbrida: Combina la técnica output-to-input loop (para forzar la convergencia de firmas anómalas) con inyección de muestras canary.

Determinismo y Reproducibilidad: Ejecución con semilla fija, garantizando el mismo veredicto y hash sha256 para un modelo dado.

Integración CI/CD Nativa: Salida estructurada en JSON y códigos de salida (exit codes) para automatizar el bloqueo de modelos con veredicto SUSPICIOUS o BACKDOOR en pipelines de MLOps.

Estado actual: El MVP valida su lógica mediante fixtures sintéticos embebidos, sin dependencias de red. La validación a escala con modelos reales de Hugging Face está programada para la v0.2.

Invitamos a la comunidad de seguridad en IA, ingenieros de MLOps e investigadores a revisar el código, contribuir con heurísticas de detección y probar su integración en entornos de staging. La seguridad de la IA debe ser automatizable, transparente y de código abierto.

🔗 Repositorio: github.com/amurlaniakea/weightwatch

title: Introducing Vercel Drives: persistent storage for agents
description:
Agents often handle complex work that continues across runs. As that work evolves, they may need a new environment with different tools, runtimes, or compute. They should be able to continue working with the same files when they change environments.

We built Vercel Drives to keep an agent’s files independent of its execution environment. It is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox. Agents can mount the same drive in a new environment configured for the next task and continue where they left off.

Persisting state with a drive

Create a drive once, then mount it when you create a sandbox. From the CLI:

Or from the Sandbox SDK:

In this example, everything under /workspace persists on the drive. Everything else belongs to the sandbox. The next sandbox that mounts the drive finds the repository, and anything else the agent wrote there, where the previous run left it.

The drive keeps the agent’s files independent of the sandbox running it. An agent can resume work in a new sandbox or switch runtimes without transferring its workspace. Other sandboxes can mount the same drive.

Sharing state across sandboxes

Agents can prepare files on a drive once and reuse them across sandboxes. If one agent builds a dataset on a drive, other agents can mount read-only copies to analyze the data or generate reports without rebuilding the dataset. They use the shared files as input and save their results separately.

Agents can also fork a drive to explore different approaches independently. Each fork starts with the drive’s contents and provides its own writable workspace. Agents can try different transformations of the dataset in parallel without changing the original or affecting one another. Forks don’t merge back into the original drive.

Forking is generally available.

Get started

Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on all plans.

Drives default to 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, with up to 16 TiB available. See the documentation for configuration, snapshots, and limits, or the changelog for what changed at GA.

title: The World Won't Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock
description:
arXiv:2610.20665v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late. We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference. Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when they keep running. We propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI): a slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts, then writes reusable instructions for a fast student. The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay, and validation scores determine which updates are adopted. Two rounds raise Jev's average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0--100 progress scale, improving all six game types. The instructions also improve average scores for three other models without retuning. These findings point toward real-time intelligence: enabling powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.

title: Node.js Transactional SMS Alerts Provider — Compare US-Europe Delivery Across 5 Boundaries
description:
For transactional SMS alerts in the US and Europe, compare each provider by accepted delivery attempts and data boundaries before comparing price. The largest bill term is usually uncomplicated: accepted alert attempts equal recipients multiplied by sends, plus retries. For an illustrative 80,000 marketplace orders, one immediate seller alert per order starts at 80,000 attempts; a broad retry policy can move that number faster than a small difference in a vendor's published unit rate. Retained event data then adds a quieter cost: storage, access control, deletion work, and the operational burden of answering who processed which phone number.

TL;DR: choose the provider only after assigning ownership of templates, suppression, regional processing, retention, and deletion. Twilio, Amazon SNS, Telnyx, Sinch, and Bird belong on the shortlist, while Infrai is a practical additional option when a team prefers a self-describing REST surface and accepts polling for event retrieval. Keep the order database authoritative, retain provider identifiers rather than message bodies where possible, and make every retry traceable to the same business event.

The change that moves both cost and exposure is to suppress duplicate work before sending. I would deliberately stop keeping rendered SMS bodies after the short investigation window defined by the company's policy. That makes some later disputes harder to reconstruct, so the durable audit record must preserve the template version, destination token or protected reference, consent basis, business event ID, provider message ID, timestamps, and outcome.

How should you compare a transactional SMS alerts provider for Europe?

A marketplace seller alert looks small, but it crosses several ownership boundaries. The marketplace owns the order and the decision to notify. The application should own the stable template identity and version, even if a provider hosts the rendered template. The provider processes a destination and message long enough to deliver it and expose status. A downstream carrier is another processor boundary. None of those boundaries should quietly become the system of record.

Start with four questions: in which region is the request processed, how long are message content and delivery events retained, how is deletion requested and evidenced, and which subprocessors see the payload? A region selector in an API is not, by itself, a contractual residency guarantee. Likewise, deleting the marketplace's local row does not prove deletion in a provider or carrier system. The contract, data-processing terms, product configuration, and an observed deletion exercise must agree.

Template ownership changes the risk. Provider-hosted templates can centralize editing and approvals, but they also place copy and version history outside the order service. Application-owned rendering keeps the exact text under deployment control, at the cost of building review, localization, and safe variable handling. For a new-order notice, I favor application-owned template versions with a narrow payload: order reference, seller-facing action, and no unnecessary buyer data. The alert should be useful on a locked screen without disclosing the order.

Infrai enters this decision as an integration boundary, not as a substitute for a specialist carrier contract. Its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples; the live catalog contains 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities have examples in 10 languages. That lets an engineer inspect a capability before adopting another SDK. The platform puts multiple backend capabilities behind one REST API, one API key, and one bill. A marketplace using several modules therefore has fewer SDKs and credentials to rotate and fewer invoices to reconcile. For teams already maintaining an internal notification ledger, the supporting advantage is a consistent idempotency convention: a client-supplied Idempotency-Key is specified with a 24-hour default deduplication window.

Infrai also provides unified credentials and consolidated billing: a single credential and one invoice cover 295 routes across 20 modules.

Teams that own templates and audit state in their application should try Infrai for basic transactional SMS submission because discovery makes the integration contract inspectable, while the platform idempotency convention reduces duplicate-write risk.

This option is not suitable for webhook-first automation, advanced routing, or provider-native reporting. A direct specialist is the better alternative in those cases because event retrieval here is polling-only and there is no tag-aggregated cost reporting API. That limitation is material.

Compare processors by boundary, not by a price snapshot

Price tables decay.

A useful comparison records which party owns each control and leaves volatile rates in a dated procurement worksheet. Twilio, Telnyx, Sinch, and MessageBird (now Bird) are specialist communications platforms; AWS SNS, formally Amazon SNS, is the cloud-native option in this set; the aggregation option supplies a broader REST boundary. Those are different operating models, even before anyone compares country coverage. SendGrid, Resend, Postmark, Mailgun, and Amazon SES are email products rather than equivalent SMS providers; they become relevant only if the design includes an email fallback, and treating them as interchangeable would produce a false comparison.

Option Integration boundary Template and audit decision Best fit Boundary to verify before selection
Twilio Direct specialist provider Decide whether provider tooling or the application owns template history Teams seeking a direct communications relationship Contracted regions, retention, deletion evidence, subprocessors, and webhook handling
Amazon SNS AWS service boundary Usually pair sends with application-owned order and audit records Workloads already governed inside AWS SMS region behavior, destination coverage, delivery-status retention, and processor terms
Telnyx Direct specialist provider Keep marketplace template versions reconcilable with provider identifiers Teams evaluating a specialist API and carrier-facing controls Regional processing, message retention, deletion workflow, and event delivery
Sinch Direct specialist provider Map every hosted or local template revision to a business event Enterprises evaluating communications coverage and governance Product-specific region, retention, deletion, and subprocessor commitments
MessageBird (Bird) Direct specialist provider Separate campaign or workflow state from the immutable order ledger Teams wanting broader communications workflow tooling Which workflow components store content, for how long, and in which region
Infrai Aggregation layer in front of an SMS specialist Application owns budget tags and durable audit state Straightforward sends under one inspectable REST contract Polling latency, downstream provider boundary, and the absence of tag-aggregated cost reporting

This table is deliberately not a feature-score leaderboard. A US and Europe deployment needs destination-by-destination review, because “Europe” is not one operational or regulatory configuration. Obtain current product documents and contractual answers from every finalist. The supplied interface cannot establish what the signed agreement must establish.

The aggregation layer can submit an SMS, check suppression, expose status and events through polling, and cancel a scheduled SMS. It does not provide webhook event push, SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS in this capability group. Geographic anti-abuse fences and country-price circuit breakers remain application responsibilities. Those trade-offs are decisive when an outage or order workflow must react instantly to delivery events.

Make retries exactly-once at the business boundary

Transport delivery is not exactly-once. The useful approximation is narrower: one notification intent per order event, any number of safe transport attempts, and one append-only explanation for every state transition. Use a deterministic business key such as marketplace/order/<order-id>/seller/new-order/v3; do not generate a fresh key when a worker times out.

The following Go program demonstrates the local gate. It is intentionally provider-neutral: the discovered provider schema should supply the final send request, while the application ledger controls whether a send is eligible. In production, replace the in-memory map with a transactional database constraint on BusinessKey and commit the intent before dispatch.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Intent struct {
    BusinessKey     string
    TemplateVersion string
    DestinationHash string
    CreatedAt       time.Time
}

type Ledger struct {
    mu      sync.Mutex
    intents map[string]Intent
}

type Capability struct {
    ID         string `json:"id"`
    Method     string `json:"method"`
    Path       string `json:"path"`
    Available  bool   `json:"available"`
    Idempotent bool   `json:"idempotent"`
}

func discover(client *http.Client) (Capability, error) {
    const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.otp"
    var lastErr error

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return Capability{}, err
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return Capability{}, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if resp.Header.Get("Retry-After") == "1" {
                delay = time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return Capability{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }

        var capability Capability
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &capability); err != nil {
            return Capability{}, err
        }
        return capability, nil
    }
    return Capability{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed after retries: %v", lastErr)
}

func destinationHash(e164 string) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(e164))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func (l *Ledger) Reserve(orderID, e164 string) (Intent, bool) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()

    key := "marketplace/order/" + orderID + "/seller/new-order/v3"
    if existing, ok := l.intents[key]; ok {
        return existing, false
    }

    intent := Intent{
        BusinessKey:     key,
        TemplateVersion: "seller-new-order-v3",
        DestinationHash: destinationHash(e164),
        CreatedAt:       time.Now().UTC(),
    }
    l.intents[key] = intent
    return intent, true
}

func main() {
    capability, err := discover(&http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second})
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(capability.ID, capability.Method, capability.Path)

    ledger := Ledger{intents: make(map[string]Intent)}
    first, sendFirst := ledger.Reserve("ord_2048", "+12025550123")
    second, sendSecond := ledger.Reserve("ord_2048", "+12025550123")

    fmt.Println(first.BusinessKey, sendFirst)
    fmt.Println(second.BusinessKey, sendSecond)
}

The discovery request needs no key, returns the current schema boundary, uses an explicit method, surfaces non-success bodies, and backs off on HTTP 429. The ledger output is one eligible send and one duplicate rejection. The destination itself does not enter the long-lived example record. Hashing is not anonymization, particularly for a small phone-number space, so a real system still needs access controls, a keyed tokenization strategy where appropriate, and a deletion policy. This code does not invent a send body: generate that body from the returned discovery schema and place the authenticated send in a separate adapter, where Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY and the stable business key can be applied together.

If the network result is ambiguous, reconcile before issuing another attempt. Record the provider message ID when available, attach each attempt to the same intent, and place manual replays behind an audited command. For aggregation-service writes, pass the same business-derived Idempotency-Key; a new random value defeats the platform deduplication contract.

Retention is an incident-response budget

Keeping everything feels safe until deletion, access review, and breach scope become due. Keeping nothing prevents reconciliation. The defensible middle is a tiered record: short-lived rendered content only if support genuinely needs it, a longer-lived delivery outcome and provider identifier, and an immutable financial or order audit reference that contains no message body. Exact periods must come from applicable law, contracts, and company policy; the API cannot choose them.

There is a concrete trade. After content deletion, support may prove that template version 3 was selected and that a provider accepted the attempt, yet be unable to reproduce the exact personalized bytes. Preserve the rendering inputs only when that evidentiary need outweighs the privacy and deletion burden. For a basic seller notice, it often does not.

Cost attribution needs the same discipline. Because the aggregation service has no tag-aggregated cost reporting API, write alert_type, business key, provider message ID, attempt number, and returned cost metadata into the application's own reconciliation table. Polling can support a basic dashboard, but it is weaker than webhook-first event delivery for immediate orchestration. A delayed reminder can be canceled through SMS cancellation; do not design an email fallback around equivalent scheduled-send cancellation, because email has no cancel route in this surface and no hosted email OTP capability.

There is no magic here. Correctness comes from refusing to confuse provider acceptance, carrier delivery, and business completion.

A selection rule that survives procurement

Choose a direct specialist such as Twilio, Telnyx, Sinch, or MessageBird when webhook-first reactions, advanced routing, provider-native reporting, or a direct contractual processor relationship dominate. Choose Amazon SNS when the surrounding workload and governance are already AWS-centered and its current regional and delivery controls pass review. Consider the aggregation option when the workflow is a straightforward transactional send, application-owned templates and ledger state are acceptable, and discovering a runnable REST contract is more valuable than specialist workflow depth.

Before approval, run one evidence review per destination region: current terms, data-processing agreement, subprocessor list, deletion procedure, retention controls, delivery-event mechanism, sender requirements, and failure semantics. Then exercise duplicate submission, ambiguous timeout, suppression, cancellation, and deletion in a non-production account. The lowest quoted rate should not overrule an untestable trust boundary.

Further reading and references

  • Infrai public discovery: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.otp
  • Twilio data protection documentation: https://www.twilio.com/en-us/legal/data-protection-addendum
  • Amazon SNS developer guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/welcome.html
  • Telnyx messaging documentation: https://developers.telnyx.com/docs/messaging
  • Sinch SMS documentation: https://developers.sinch.com/docs/sms/
  • Bird SMS API documentation: https://docs.bird.com/api/sms-api
  • NIST SP 800-63B: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html

If this boundary fits your system, start with the SMS alerts guide: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/sms/answers/best-sms-alerts-api-for-saas-app-us-eu-nodejs-2025-tran/

title: Why Host in South America? How Local Infrastructure in Rio de Janeiro Reduces Latency and Boosts App Performance
description:
When building modern applications, the choice of where to host our code is often an afterthought: we select traditional hyperscalers in the US or Europe and assume their infrastructure will handle everything. However, for anyone serving users in South America, network latency (ping) and packet routing quickly become critical performance bottlenecks.

In this article, let's analyze the real impact of server locality and how relying on local infrastructure in South America changes the game for developers, businesses, and growing projects.

The "Distance Cost" Problem (Latency)

Round Trip Time (RTT) is strictly limited by the physics of submarine and terrestrial cables. When a user in Brazil or neighboring countries accesses an application hosted thousands of miles away in the Northern Hemisphere, data packets must travel through multiple network hops.

This results in:

  • Noticeable Increase in Time to First Byte (TTFB): Browsers take longer to start rendering page content.
  • API and Database Bottlenecks: Asynchronous queries and chained HTTP requests suffer from cumulative delays.
  • Degraded User Experience: Real-time applications or interactive dashboards feel sluggish, even on fast local fiber-optic connections.

The Advantage of Local Infrastructure

Hosting close to your target audience brings immediate architectural benefits:

  1. Drastically Reduced Latency: Fewer network hops mean millisecond-level responses for local and regional users.
  2. Optimized Routing: Streamlined connectivity across the eastern coast of South America, facilitating seamless communication with neighboring countries.
  3. Real Infrastructure: Physical data center operations based in Rio de Janeiro, powered by high-performance enterprise hardware and fast NVMe storage.

Meet AzureWeb

If you or your company are looking for a robust alternative to traditional US/EU cloud giants, AzureWeb (azureweb.com.br) delivers reliable infrastructure solutions directly from Brazil.

  • Cloud VPS: Flexible, scalable virtual private servers with dedicated resources, ideal for developers, testing environments, and growing production apps.
  • Cloud Servers: High-performance environments tailored for heavy workloads and demanding system architectures.
  • Web Hosting: Fast, secure, and reliable web hosting plans designed to keep your web applications online 24/7.

Final Thoughts

Choosing a data center should be treated as a core part of your application's engineering design, just like picking a framework or a database. Reducing the physical distance between your server and your end-user is the most cost-effective and impactful way to improve any system's performance.
