title: Is Proprietary Software Over?
description:
A few days ago, I came across this post:

Someone, Brandon Thomas, allegedly decompiled the entire Adobe suite, Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, Lightroom etc... In total, 7 software programs. All rewritten in Rust with AI, and published as open source.

Oh yes, and he did it again a few days later for the Office suite, same thing everything is open source and rewritten in Rust.

Did Brandon just sign the beginning of a movement that prefigures the end of software? Or is it the nth false start of fire from a SaaS Apocalypse that is slow to come?

Artcraft

I imagine you've already seen this story. It's not breaking news. Me, there are two questions that interest me: "How did he do it?" and "Is it legal?".

Let's look at that.

First, what is ArtCraft? It's a software suite for photo editing and video editing, among other things. Each software you can see on this page corresponds to a software at Adobe.

All have been rewritten in Rust. And each app can be controlled by an AI agent, via a command line or an MCP server.

But apparently, contrary to what the post we saw said, Brandon did not decompile Adobe. At least, I found no source that would allow me to affirm it.

Brandon talks about implementing in "clean room". And if you're not familiar with that term, basically it's mostly reverse engineering.
In principle in a clean room implementation, there is a team that observes what the software does, reads the documentation, takes screenshots, and then provides all of that to another independent team that is responsible for implementing it but without having details about the original software. The concept of clean room is a metaphor for clean rooms where one tries to create a sterile, uncontaminated environment. Here, it's about being uncontaminated by the original software and its copyright.

In short, it's copying, yes. But copying by observation.

And it's not new at all.

In 2003, I was playing Lineage. I imagine you don't necessarily know Lineage. It was a popular MMORPG but which mainly took off in Korea. There was no server in Europe and I couldn't tell you why. But I played it. But not on the official server.

There was a small team that had set up the game, listened to all the network packets that were passing between their PC and the official servers and then mapped each network packet to a function in the game. A movement, a spell, triggering a dialogue, adding an item to inventory. Packet by packet. And then they wrote a server in Java that could talk to the game.

Which made possible... lots of things, like playing a custom version of the game, with different settings, new quests but also, of course, being able to play the game without going through the official server. And me in 2003 I was on the edge of depression in, no doubt, the worst job of my career in which I was sweating like never before, except maybe watching the Tour de France. So I joined a small team that managed a fork of L2jfree for a French server.

By saying that, I'm absolving myself a bit huh, I wasn't in the main team. It was just one of the multiple forks that were floating around the Internet.

Anyway. Reverse engineering has existed forever.

And to see things clearly, you need to distinguish three things that we tend to mix up.

One, decompilation. You start with the compiled program, and you reconstruct the source code with the objective that this source code can then be recompiled to give exactly the same binary byte-for-byte.
In recent examples, there was Maurice Heumann who reconstructed Modern Warfare 2 with a swarm of AI agents, over about three months. So far he has managed to reproduce 99% of the game's functions reconstructed, and 83% identical byte-for-byte.
So we can wonder what that's useful for? Well among possible uses, there is the second case: porting.

For porting, the objective is to make software run somewhere other than its original platform. The most well-known example is Doom whose source code is now public and which has been ported to pretty much every platform, so much so that it has become a meme. We find Doom on browsers, on smartwatches and even on pharmacy signs. Recently Kotaku talked about hundreds of ports in the browser, appearing in a few weeks. Halo, GTA Vice City, The Simpsons Hit and Run.

And finally there is, reimplementation. It's the example of ArtCraft. The code is not read but everything is observed to remake it identically. It's a copycat.

Note that from reports, ArtCraft is not quite there yet in terms of quality. But you have to understand that the first version is "just" 2 weeks old, already 190 contributors on github, and releases a version almost every day, so if these people stay motivated, which is not guaranteed, then maybe this software could become a real must-have.

Obviously unless Adobe sues them.

And indeed, is all this legal?

Legal or not?

The short answer: it's complicated.

Okay, so that's not an answer.

There is a key precedent in Europe. In 2012, the Court of Justice of the European Union in the SAS Institute v. World Programming case.

World Programming had recreated SAS software, without the source code, from the manuals and by observing how the software worked. And for the courts, the features of a software, its language and its file formats are not protected by copyright.

And I want to say, that's kind of common sense. I can't imagine that we'd protect a concept, like photo editing, a window layout, or a set of features.

So making a photo editor that opens PSD files is not a problem. There are plenty of photo editors, and everyone lives very well.

On the other hand, there are two grey areas.

The first is appearance. When the interface is an almost copy-paste of Photoshop, we enter the territory of copyright on the interface, or even trademark law. Obviously I'm not talking to you about the logo, that's obvious.

The second is parasitism. In French law, it's when a company profits from the image or reputation of another to cause harmful competition.

You will note that on the ArtCraft page, Adobe is never mentioned. And that's no accident, because by using Adobe's image to harm them or steal their customers, that would be parasitism.

I have a little anecdote on this subject. When Malt was still called Hopwork, in 2015, two major competitors merged and renamed themselves with a name very similar to ours. This created major confusion in the European market. People typed the name wrong in search engines, or else Google directly proposed correcting it by putting the competitor's name. So we sued for parasitism. The case was settled through settlement and we took the name Malt, minus a substantial compensation that allowed us to not regret the old name too much.

Anyway, ArtCraft, which claims both the interface and the affiliation with Adobe even if it's not always stated clearly, could be sued on that. As such, it's not necessarily the copy that is attackable but rather the commercial harm that specifically targets a company.

Now I'm going back to something, I was telling you that it wasn't new. Sure, game clones, pirate ports, rewrites, software mods, all that's not new. The warez industry in the past was also based on recompiling existing binaries.

But now there's AI.

A Lower Barrier to Entry

Let me introduce you to REA, for "Reverse Engineer Anything". It's an open source tool, under MIT license.

The principle of REA is simple: give a code agent the means to inspect any software, whether it's web applications, native binaries or electron applications.

REA itself doesn't do much. It delegates all these actions to tools. For example decompilers like Ghidra or IDA. REA proposes an MCP, so a set of functions to be used by an AI. The idea being to simplify the observation of a software, for an AI, by using REA which itself uses tools capable for example of sniffing the network, decompiling a program, analyzing minified javascript code.

In itself, it's full of things we already knew how to do. Except that here it's possible to orchestrate it with an AI. So where before you needed experts, now a developer can do the same work in much less time.

Let's be clear. Reverse engineering did not become possible with AI. Just more accessible.

And if we already considered that code had lost a lot of value. What's left now?

Code is Worth Nothing Anymore

Financial markets have already decided. Since the beginning of the year, Adobe has lost more than 40% in stock.

And Adobe is not alone. In the spring, Salesforce, Workday, Microsoft, Shopify all crashed. We've been talking about SaaSpocalypse, the end of software, for a while now. I've talked about it myself several times.

Because the market anticipates the fact that these companies will be replaced by tons of competitors boosted by AI.

But in practice, Adobe's revenue increased 12% year-over-year. And its recurring revenue exceeds 27 billion dollars. I've experienced apocalypses that were harder to live through. Well, no, but you get the idea.

From constantly talking about saaspocalypse, wrongly and thoroughly, a lot of it, some people said that maybe there was actually a bit of exaggeration.

I don't think so. It's just that the second blade hasn't gone through yet.

I'll explain.

Recently, I built myself a piece of furniture. Before, I took measurements, I drew on paper, I made mistakes. When I changed a dimension, I had to recalculate everything.

And in the end, I needed a cutting plan. If you don't know, it's basically the list of boards, their dimensions, and how to cut them without wasting wood.

I had tried SketchUp. It was long, it was painful to install, and anyway, it didn't do the cutting plan I wanted.

So I made my own software. I describe the furniture, I give my measurements, and everything calculates. I have my cutting plan. If I change the thickness of a board, everything updates. I can test ten options without redrawing anything. I made an option to see the passage of electrical wires or the assembly instructions.

This software, I won't sell it, because it's probably useful only to me.

Second example. I redid my entire video creation process. I looked at each step, the time I was wasting doing boring things, and I gathered all the tools I had already made in python to download videos, images, make transcripts etc... I gathered all of that in an application and there you go. I made my own software.

I gathered everything in an application. My studio. Whereas tools like Submagic, precut, autotrim or others already exist, and do the job very well.

Before, I could pay for software, even when it wasn't quite right, because I didn't have the expertise to remake it and/or I didn't have the time.

Today, I can make my own custom tool without any worry. Code is literally worth nothing anymore. Well yes, the cost of my subscription.

And honestly… that's scary.

If code has no more value, my job, which partly consisted of writing code, doesn't either.

I console myself by saying that my job wasn't just that. And it's true that I still get a lot of pleasure from understanding a problem, designing a solution, seeing it realized, using it, getting feedback. But still, it's different. And for some of my former colleagues who were hugely attached to code, or older generations who are struggling with this change, it's painful to a degree that is difficult to assess.

Does that mean that really, software is dead?

No, Software Will Not Die

First, let's set the record straight, software will not die.

There are plenty of software that won't be touched because their value doesn't rest on code.

I can't remake Netflix, because I don't have access to its catalog. I could remake a messaging software like WhatsApp but that would be pointless if no one uses it except me.
I could try to make myself a bank account aggregator but I'm going to quickly hit lots of regulatory problems, not to mention that I'm a bit afraid of messing up, anyway it's for sure I couldn't commercialize that.

There are plenty of barriers that make it still possible to sell software, because some monetize expertise, or industrial know-how, possess certifications, captive customers or are too embedded in an ecosystem.

On the other hand the boatload of software that comes out every day now by tens of thousands of developers who are playing the gold rush remake, that's going to be tough. I don't need any of your software. And it's really not the idea of the century to target other developers to sell a product.

And big companies will continue to buy known names, to benefit from the guarantee, or because the salesman invites your boss every month for a nice dinner. Agencies will continue to use Adobe for a good while, if only out of inertia.

Anyway, software is not over. On the other hand my job is more delicate. And that does hurt me a bit.

What It Changes for Us, Developers

When I say my job is changing, I'm not saying it's disappearing. We'll continue to make a lot of software, but not in the form we've known.

I won't hide that at one point I was a bit skeptical about the so-called rebound effect. You know it's the effect induced by productivity increases.
When we know how to do more than before, we destroy jobs at first, and then there's a tipping point and we invent new uses. I had a hard time seeing the rebound effect with AI because I mostly saw that we were doing the same thing with less.
I could see that we could do more, but more of what?

In most companies, there's no point in building more software if no one buys. For example I'm not going to take the train more because the SNCF travel application has hundreds more features. The race for features, if it doesn't bring anything, is pointless.

But I'm starting to see what the rebound effect could be. We could start a race to hyperpersonalization.

At the individual level of course, where everyone can make their own applications for their internal home automation, their accounting, their DVD management and I'm not sure what else.

And then at the company level it could be internal teams tasked with creating dozens of custom software, more suited than those on the market. And a lot of companies will do this by copying what exists. Apparently that's the big trend right now with US companies. Anthropic just recreated a new git for itself for example. Probably for bad reasons but, doesn't matter.

My job will no longer be to code, but to understand, to observe software that works, probably themselves made by AI, then to reproduce them, also with AI.

And frankly, I can understand that this might not be an enjoyable vision for everyone.

The intellectual challenge of understanding code, finding the little optimization that changes everything, debugging a complex problem, lots of little things that kept me in this job in my early years, is partly on the point of disappearing.

Of course I don't want to end on a pessimistic note. I really believe it's important to always see the positive.

So I want to say that, for my part, I admit that I still find it worthwhile, for now, because I was fed up with redoing the same bits of code for 25 years. Coding a form, data validation, a CRUD, a job that always does the same thing. Redoing a software factory, tests, explaining once again what it's for etc... I had done the tour of tech for tech's sake and I'm happy to make software, in the first sense of the term.

I'm happy to make my own tools super quickly, to have the almost instant satisfaction of materializing something I had in my head. Well, instant, on the scale of what I've known before anyway.

But I'm increasingly wondering what my added value is. What is it that makes what I do something only I can do? What good is my expertise/experience to me when now AI does everything.

I told you, I think that creating software will become increasingly difficult, in order to make software companies. You need a service on top that is really solid, that doesn't just rely on the fact of knowing how to stack lines of code. There will be a premium on tenacity on one hand, people who will be able to stay several months, or even years on the same topics without getting discouraged. There is also a premium on analytical spirit, the fact of really understanding the problems we want to solve, and what are the best ways to solve them.

That's going to be incredible challenges in big companies to rebuild coherent information systems, internal tool teams. Even though it will also create tons of conflicts over the meaning of the work, how we do it, how we redefine everyone's roles. And I'm very glad I'm not a CTO right now...

Anyway, there are plenty of new things to do, a whole industry to redesign. It's underway. I don't know if the result will be pretty but what's for sure is that my job has changed. Not because of Brandon, because he's just a guy who managed to highlight a phenomenon. We are all frogs, and the pot has been heating up since 2022.

On that note, you can get back to normal activity.

Bye.

title: I built an MCP server that lets AI agents book real hotel rooms (no OTA commission)
description:
Booking.com takes 15-25% commission and owns the customer relationship. I run a small
network of independent establishments in Luxembourg, and I wanted AI agents to be able to
book them directly — machine-native, at the establishment's exact direct price.

So I built Adaga Network — Direct Booking Federation: one MCP endpoint that fans out
to every establishment in the network.

The architecture

  • Each establishment runs the same open template: an mcp.js module mounted on /mcp inside its existing Express app. No new port, no new service — a pure proxy to the app's own REST API.
  • The federator (adagasolutions.lu/network/mcp) is a Streamable HTTP stateless MCP server that keeps a registry of tenants and calls their MCP tools in parallel (6s timeout per tenant, dead tenants are skipped and reported).

3 tools cover the whole journey:

Tool What it does
network_directory Lists every establishment (brand, type, city, slug)
network_search Fan-out live availability + exact total prices, sorted
network_book Creates a REAL booking, hands secure card payment to the human

The payment hand-off is a feature

The agent never touches card data. network_book returns payment instructions; the human
completes a Stripe Checkout; unpaid bookings expire automatically. Booking confirmed only
after payment — and a 409 if the room became unavailable in between.

What I learned writing tool descriptions

The tool description is the #1 selection criterion for agents. After running the tools
through a TDQS audit, the fixes that mattered:

  • State auth requirements, rate limits and pagination explicitly (mine: none, none, none)
  • Put the full workflow in the transactional tool's description
  • Describe every optional input format (phone: international format, extras: integer ids)
  • Units everywhere: prices in euro cents, dates YYYY-MM-DD, max 30 nights

Distribution

  • Official MCP Registry: io.github.jeffreyturov-dev/adaga-network
  • Glama connector with health checks (hourly) — a watchdog pings the endpoint every 10 min
  • The honest pitch: no OTA commission — the traveler pays the exact direct price, the establishment keeps its customer.

Salons and restaurants join the network next. If you run an independent establishment and
want AI agents to book you directly, the onboarding template takes 2-4 hours.

title: UX Notes: Matching Tea to State in a Telegram Bot
description:
UX Notes: Matching Tea to State in a Telegram Bot

We built Tea Bro around one idea: people choose tea badly when they only chase taste notes. They choose better when they start from state — tired, anxious, need clarity, wind-down.

The flow

  1. Name the state (or take a short test on the site).
  2. Get a calm direction (softer profile, less leaf, not “max strength”).
  3. Brew once. Optionally note one line after the cup.

No gamification. No 30-day streak. The win is a usable cup today.

Product decisions that mattered

  • Softer beats stronger when the user is already exhausted.
  • Evening ≠ morning — same leaf, different dose and timing.
  • Deep links — bot points to concrete pages (bot hub, test, compass), not only the homepage.

Hub for the bot:

teabro-site.vercel.app/bot-tea-bro.html

State-oriented entry on the site:

teabro-site.vercel.app/kompas-sostoyaniya.html

For product people

Chat is a good trigger surface. A website is a good explanation surface. Split them on purpose. Keep the bot short; put the reasoning and guides on stable URLs you can link from every channel.

If you ship ritual tools, design for the tired evening version of the user — not only the motivated morning one.

title: The states shadcn/ui leaves to you: loading, success, error, empty and reduced motion
description:
Search "shadcn button loading state" and you will find a hundred snippets that do the same thing: add an isLoading prop, swap the label for a spinner, disable the button. Ship that and your app will feel worse than before you added it.

That is not a knock on shadcn/ui. It gives you a clean starting point and leaves the states to you, on purpose. But "the states" are where most of the feel of an interface lives, and almost nobody budgets time for them. This is the list of states I handle in every component I ship, and the specific timings that separate "finished" from "works".

1. Loading that does not flicker

The naive loading button shows a spinner the instant you click. Most requests finish in under 200ms, so what the user sees is a flash of spinner and then the result. It reads as jitter.

Two rules fix it:

  • Wait before you show the spinner. If the request finishes within about 150ms, never show it at all.
  • Once shown, keep it up for a minimum time. Around 400ms. A spinner that appears for 30ms is worse than no spinner. 
const spinnerDelay = 150
const minimumSpinnerTime = 400

That is a hook, not a prop. Here is the shape:

const { buttonProps, track } = useButtonFeedback()

<Button {...buttonProps} onClick={() => track(save())}>
  Save
</Button>

track takes the promise. The hook decides whether the request was fast enough to skip the spinner, holds the spinner long enough not to flicker, and moves the button into success or error when the promise settles. The HextaUI useButtonFeedback hook and useDelayedLoading do exactly this, and they are small enough to read in one sitting.

The same delay rule applies to skeletons. A skeleton that appears for 50ms and gets replaced by the content is a flash of grey. Delay it by 150ms, and when the content arrives, fade it in without moving anything around it.

2. Success and error, in place

After a save succeeds, the button should say so. "Saved" with a check, for about two seconds, then back to idle. After it fails, the button should say that too, and hold the error longer, about four seconds, because people need time to read an error and decide what to do.

Two details that matter more than they sound:

  • Do not reset while the pointer is on the button. If someone is hovering, they are reading. Reset after they leave.
  • Ignore clicks while the request is in flight. Not with disabled, which removes the button from the tab order and makes screen readers skip it. Use aria-busy and ignore the click.

A Switch has the same problem in a smaller space. Flip it, send the request, and if the request fails, flip it back. The user needs to see the rollback, so animate it, and show a brief pending state while the save is out.

3. Invalid, without punishing typing

Shake the field when a submit attempt finds it invalid. Never shake while someone is still typing. The rule is the trigger: validation on submit or on blur gets the shake, validation on change does not.

The shake itself should be short, three or four oscillations in about 300ms, and under prefers-reduced-motion it becomes a color change on the border and nothing else.

Native :user-invalid helps here. It only matches after the user has interacted, so you can style the invalid state in CSS without a touched flag in React.

4. Empty is a state, not an absence

An empty list is where new users land first, and the default is a blank area with a header above it. Every empty state needs three things: an icon or illustration so the space reads as intentional, one sentence that says what will appear here, and the action that makes something appear.

This is cheap to build and almost always skipped because the person building the feature has test data. Clear your database once in a while.

5. Reduced motion is not "no motion"

prefers-reduced-motion: reduce is on for a meaningful share of users, and the lazy implementation is a global * { transition: none }. That removes the information motion was carrying. A dialog that snaps open with no fade is harder to parse than one that fades.

The rule I use: anything that moves across the screen becomes a fade. Anything that fades stays a fade. Anything that loops stops. Durations get shorter, not zero.

Put the check in one place so every component reads it:

export function prefersReducedMotion() {
  return window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches
}

And share the easing curves and durations too. If every component picks its own cubic-bezier, the app will feel like it was built by six people, because it was.

6. Motion you can interrupt

Open an accordion, then close it halfway through the opening animation. In a lot of implementations, it finishes opening and then closes, or it jumps. The right behavior is to reverse from wherever it is.

The Web Animations API makes this easy: keep a reference to the running animation, and on the next toggle, read its current time and animate from the current computed height. CSS transitions on height: auto cannot do this, and grid-template-rows: 0fr to 1fr can but is harder to reverse mid-way. Pick the approach that lets you interrupt.

7. Touch targets and the iOS zoom

Two things break on phones that you will never see on a laptop:

  • Inputs under 16px zoom the page on iOS Safari. Keep input text at 16px on coarse pointers even if your theme is 15px elsewhere. A single @media (pointer: coarse) rule covers it.
  • Tap targets under 44px miss. Buttons can be 32px tall on desktop and grow on touch screens through the same media query.

8. Right-to-left

If you ever ship to Arabic or Hebrew users, every ml- and pl- and left- in your components is a bug. Use logical properties: ms-, ps-, start-. shadcn/ui added RTL support in January 2026, so new components you pull are fine, but the ones you copied in 2024 are not.

Where this leaves you

None of these is hard. All of them together is a few weeks of work on a component set the size of shadcn/ui, and the work is invisible when it is done, which is why it gets cut.

I built HextaUI because I kept doing this work on every project. It is a free, MIT-licensed registry you add to a shadcn/ui project. Same CLI, same component names, same theme tokens, and every one of the states above already handled, down to the 150ms spinner delay. If you would rather own the code and write the states yourself, the hooks are standalone and you can install just those.

npx shadcn@latest add https://hextaui.com/r/use-button-feedback.json

FAQ

Should I disable a button while loading? Set aria-busy="true" and ignore clicks. disabled removes it from the tab order and hides it from screen readers mid-action.

How long should a success state show? About two seconds, longer if the pointer is still on the control. Errors about four seconds.

Is a skeleton always better than a spinner? A skeleton is better when you know the shape of what is coming. A spinner is better for actions. Both need the 150ms delay.

Does reduced motion mean I should remove all animation? No. Replace movement with fades, stop loops and shorten durations. Keep the information.

title: ReState: Noise-Level-Aware State Correction for Training-Free Object Removal in Few-Step Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21287v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training-free object removal commonly redirects self-attention away from the target region, but on few-step distilled diffusion models this often leaves object-shaped residuals. We identify a temporal mismatch: a structured prediction forms inside the mask at the first forward, and the short trajectory offers few later chances to revise it, while attention rerouting acts mainly in later steps. Across four distilled backbones, magnitude-matched single-forward interventions show that background-directed state correction affects the final result more than attention rerouting. We therefore propose ReState, which corrects the masked clean prediction toward background evidence retrieved from the input using a noise-level-aware weight that vanishes at the final forward. ReState retains object-excluding attention as a complementary constraint and adds no denoiser evaluations. Across two paired benchmarks and two few-step backbones, ReState achieves the best masked PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among training-free methods, improving PSNR by 3.17 dB on average over the strongest baseline. On OBER-Test, it also outperforms the 50-step attention-forcing reference on all three metrics at 6.7x lower latency. The same configuration transfers to two additional distilled backbones without retuning. Project page: https://tdrlee.github.io/ReState

title: Kafka 4.2 Has Queues Now: How Share Groups Break One-Consumer-Per-Partition
description:
• Book: Event-Driven Architecture Pocket Guide
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You have a topic with 12 partitions and a backlog of image-resize jobs. Each job takes a few seconds. You scale the worker deployment from 12 pods to 40, watch the dashboard, and nothing moves. Twelve pods are busy. Twenty-eight are connected, healthy and idle, because a Kafka consumer group hands each partition to exactly one member. Your parallelism was decided the day someone picked the partition count.

That rule is one reason teams run RabbitMQ or Amazon SQS next to Apache Kafka for job queues. KIP-932 describes it bluntly: consumer groups "introduce coupling between the number of consumers in a consumer group and the number of partitions", so users "often have to over-partition" to handle peak load.

Kafka 4.2 changes that. The 4.2.0 release announcement (February 17, 2026) says "Kafka Queues (Share Groups) is now production-ready", after a preview in 4.1 that was explicitly "still not ready for production".

A share group reads one partition with many hands

A share group is a new group type that sits next to classic consumer groups. Consumers join it with a group.id like always, but the broker no longer pins a partition to one member. Any number of consumers can fetch from the same partition at the same time, and the broker tracks every record individually instead of keeping a single committed offset.

The KIP calls that per-partition view a share-partition. The broker keeps a window of in-flight records between two markers: the share-partition start offset (SPSO) and end offset (SPEO). Every record in the window is in one of four states, per KIP-932:

  • Available: can be handed to the next consumer that fetches.
  • Acquired: handed to one consumer, under a time-limited lock.
  • Acknowledged: done.
  • Archived: given up on, never delivered again.

When a consumer fetches, the share-partition leader walks forward from the SPSO, finds Available records, moves them to Acquired and bumps each record's delivery count. While a record is acquired, no other consumer receives it.


One partition, many consumers: the broker locks each record to whoever acquired it.

The lock has a deadline. The Kafka 4.2 group configs list share.record.lock.duration.ms with a default of 30,000 ms. If the consumer neither acknowledges nor renews in that time, the lock is released and the record goes back to Available, ready for another consumer. A consumer that dies mid-job just stops holding locks; its records come back after the timeout.

The window also has a size limit. The KIP says that when the in-flight limit is reached, "fetching records will temporarily yield no further records" until acquired records clear. In 4.2 the cap is a broker setting, group.share.partition.max.record.locks, default 2,000 per share-partition, per the 4.2 broker configs. The 4.3 group configs add a per-group override, share.partition.max.record.locks.

All this state has to survive broker restarts. A new share coordinator persists it to an internal topic, __share_group_state, which the KIP describes as highly partitioned (50 partitions by default).

ACCEPT, RELEASE, REJECT, and the new RENEW

By default a share consumer uses implicit acknowledgement: the next poll() accepts everything from the previous batch. For a job queue you want explicit mode, where you decide per record. The KafkaShareConsumer Javadoc requires you to acknowledge every record from a poll before the next poll, and the acknowledgements go to the broker on the next commitSync(), commitAsync() or poll().

String sd = StringDeserializer.class.getName();
Properties p = new Properties();
p.setProperty("bootstrap.servers",
    System.getenv("KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP"));
p.setProperty("group.id", "resize-workers");
p.setProperty("key.deserializer", sd);
p.setProperty("value.deserializer", sd);
p.setProperty("share.acknowledgement.mode", "explicit");

var consumer = new KafkaShareConsumer<String, String>(p);
consumer.subscribe(List.of("resize-jobs"));

while (true) {
  var records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
  for (var rec : records) {
    try {
      resize(rec.value());
      consumer.acknowledge(rec, AcknowledgeType.ACCEPT);
    } catch (TransientFailure e) {
      consumer.acknowledge(rec, AcknowledgeType.RELEASE);
    } catch (Exception e) {
      consumer.acknowledge(rec, AcknowledgeType.REJECT);
    }
  }
  consumer.commitSync();
}

resize and TransientFailure are yours. The three original acknowledgement types come straight from the KIP. ACCEPT marks the record done. RELEASE "makes the record available for another delivery attempt", which is right for a timeout against a flaky downstream. REJECT says the record is unprocessable and it is not delivered again.

That leaves the job that takes longer than the lock. Before 4.2 you had two bad options: raise the lock duration for the whole group (capped by the broker's group.share.max.record.lock.duration.ms, 60 seconds by default per the broker configs), or let a slow job's lock expire and watch a second worker start the same job. 4.2 adds a fourth type from KIP-1222, RENEW, which the release announcement says lets "applications extend acquisition lock timeouts on records requiring longer processing times."

Per the Javadoc, RENEW only works in explicit mode, you call it on each iteration of the poll loop, and a successfully renewed record "is returned again by the poll(Duration) call". The pattern is to run the job on another thread and keep the poll thread renewing until the job finishes. The consumer is not thread-safe, so every acknowledge call stays on the poll thread. Here pool is an ExecutorService:

// running: map of key(rec) -> CompletableFuture<Void>
var job = running.get(key(rec));
if (job == null) {
  running.put(key(rec), CompletableFuture
      .runAsync(() -> resize(rec.value()), pool));
  consumer.acknowledge(rec, AcknowledgeType.RENEW);
} else if (job.isCompletedExceptionally()) {
  consumer.acknowledge(rec, AcknowledgeType.REJECT);
  running.remove(key(rec));
} else if (job.isDone()) {
  consumer.acknowledge(rec, AcknowledgeType.ACCEPT);
  running.remove(key(rec));
} else {
  consumer.acknowledge(rec, AcknowledgeType.RENEW);
}

The Javadoc example for this pattern also sets share.acquire.mode to record_limit and max.poll.records to 1, so a worker only acquires what it can actually hold. share.acquire.mode comes from KIP-1206, also in 4.2. The docs say RENEW is "intended only for situations where the processing times of the records exceeds the acquisition lock duration", so do not renew by reflex on fast jobs.

What you give up: ordering

A classic consumer group gives you strict order within a partition because one consumer reads it front to back. A share group gives you much less. The KIP guarantees that records returned in one batch for a share-partition come "in order of increasing offset". Across batches there is no guarantee, and redelivered records can arrive out of offset order.

Walk it through. Worker A acquires offset 41 and stalls. Worker B acquires 42 and finishes. A's lock expires, 41 goes back to Available, and worker C processes it after 42. If 41 was "create account" and 42 was "rename account", your rename just ran against a row that does not exist yet.

If the order of events for the same key matters (account ledgers, state machines, change-data-capture streams), keep using a consumer group, keyed partitioning and the one-consumer-per-partition rule that you were fighting. Share groups fit work where each record stands alone: resize this image, send this email, call this webhook, score this document.

The other half of the trade is the delivery guarantee. KIP-932 says "the delivery behavior is at-least-once." A lock can expire on a job that actually finished, or a consumer can crash after the side effect and before the commit. Either way, the same record can run twice. Your handler has to make that harmless.

The usual way is a claim row in the same transaction as the side effect. Here it is against PostgreSQL, with a job id carried in the payload so it also covers duplicates that a producer retry wrote at a different offset:

boolean claim(Connection db, String jobId)
    throws SQLException {
  String sql = "INSERT INTO processed_jobs (job_id) "
      + "VALUES (?) ON CONFLICT (job_id) DO NOTHING";
  try (var ps = db.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ps.setString(1, jobId);
    return ps.executeUpdate() == 1;
  }
}

Call it inside the transaction that writes the result. If it returns false, the job already ran: ACCEPT the record and move on.

Poison messages: five strikes, then silence

A share group already has a retry limit built in. Every acquisition bumps the delivery count, and the KIP sets the default attempt limit at 5. When a record hits it, the record "moves into Archived state and is not eligible for additional delivery attempts." In 4.2 the limit is the broker setting group.share.delivery.count.limit (default 5, range 2 to 10, per the 4.2 broker configs), and the 4.3 group configs add a per-group override, share.delivery.count.limit.


After the last attempt, a poison record is archived, not parked somewhere you can inspect it.

Archived means gone from the queue's point of view. The record still sits in the topic log at its offset, but nothing will deliver it to your share group again, and nobody gets paged. A poison message no longer blocks the partition the way it can with a classic consumer, which is a real improvement. It also means a bad deploy can quietly archive thousands of records.

A dead-letter topic for share groups exists on paper: KIP-1191 is accepted and would write rejected and exhausted records to a configured DLQ topic. It does not appear in the 4.2 or 4.3 release announcements, so check your broker version before counting on it. Until then, park the record yourself when its last delivery fails, before the broker archives it. ConsumerRecord exposes the count as deliveryCount(). The REJECT branches above need the same treatment, since a rejected record is archived just as silently. The first loop's catch blocks become:

} catch (TransientFailure e) {
  if (lastDelivery(rec)) park(rec);
  else consumer.acknowledge(rec, AcknowledgeType.RELEASE);
} catch (Exception e) {
  park(rec);
}

And the two helpers:

boolean lastDelivery(ConsumerRecord<String, String> rec) {
  int tries = rec.deliveryCount()
      .map(Short::intValue).orElse(1);
  return tries >= MAX_ATTEMPTS;
}

void park(ConsumerRecord<String, String> rec) {
  try {
    deadLetters.send(new ProducerRecord<>(
        "resize-jobs.dlq", rec.key(), rec.value())).get();
    consumer.acknowledge(rec, AcknowledgeType.ACCEPT);
  } catch (InterruptedException | ExecutionException e) {
    consumer.acknowledge(rec, AcknowledgeType.RELEASE);
  }
}

deadLetters is an ordinary KafkaProducer. MAX_ATTEMPTS has to match the delivery count limit in force for the group, which on 4.2 is the broker's group.share.delivery.count.limit. The .get() waits for the DLQ write before the ACCEPT, so a failed write releases the record instead of dropping it. On the last delivery a release still ends in the archive, so alert on producer errors as well as on the DLQ topic's growth.

Turning it on without surprises

The 4.2 upgrade notes carry three practical details. On 4.1, share groups were behind a feature flag you enabled with kafka-features.sh at share.version=1. In 4.2, clusters with fewer than three brokers have to lower the replication factor and min ISR of the share coordinator's state topic to 1, because __share_group_state defaults to three replicas (broker configs). And 4.2.1 "includes a fix for a critical deadlock in the KIP-932 Share Group path", so start at 4.2.1 or later, not 4.2.0.

Should you rip out the job queue that sits next to your Kafka cluster? Not on day one. If your workers are already idempotent, your jobs are independent, and running one less piece of infrastructure matters to you, share groups are worth a pilot on one non-critical queue. If your jobs depend on order, or your team has never had to think about at-least-once delivery, the partition-per-consumer rule was protecting you, and keeping it is a fine decision.

If this was useful

Share groups move two problems from the broker back into your code: idempotent consumers and retry handling. Those are the kind of traps the Event-Driven Architecture Pocket Guide covers, along with sagas, CQRS and the outbox pattern. If you are about to put a job queue on Kafka, it is the checklist I would want next to the design doc.

title: Wolof-Adapted Industry-Ready Open-Weight Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20824v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Wolof is spoken by 23M people, mostly in Senegal, but remains weakly supported by open-weight language models, while API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty constraints for local deployments. In this paper, we present 0.6B-14B open-weight models adapted to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging. After presenting the pipeline and data, extensive experiments on 63~public and in-house tasks show good performance on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models being particularly competitive with substantially larger commercial systems. The models are currently being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Orange/wolof-lm .

title: Does Morphological Correctness Matter for Tokenization? A Scrambled Control Study in Tagalog
description:
arXiv:2610.20859v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Typology-aware tokenizers are motivated by the claim that segmentation which respects morpheme boundaries preserves information that frequency-driven segmentation destroys. Studies routinely establish that it helps while assuming the boundaries must be linguistically correct. We separate them. Tagalog marks voice with infixes (s-um-ulat 'wrote', s-in-ulat 'was written'), so the root is not contiguous and no sequence of BPE merges can recover it. We build MorphAustro-Tok, a tokenizer that emits the root as a contiguous unit followed by a positional infix token, and compare it against a corpus-matched BPE baseline and, at two of three fertility levels, against a scrambled-morpheme control that preserves morph count, invertibility and per-type consistency while randomising the pseudo-infix. Across 33 runs, MorphAustro-Tok improves Tagalog machine translation over matched BPE by 0.84, 1.49 and 3.40 mean sentence-level chrF++ points. Token count does not explain the gain, since it grows as segmentation coarsens, and neither does capacity: at the coarsest level the scrambled arm carries more parameters and scores lower. Scrambling the analysis moves the gain by less than between-seed dispersion at both controlled levels, so we detect no contribution from morphological correctness at this scale.

title: Prompt Injection Explained: The Security Risk Every AI Coding Tool User Should Know
description:
Somewhere between your AI coding assistant becoming genuinely useful and it becoming genuinely autonomous, a new kind of attack quietly became the biggest threat in the category. It doesn't need a stolen password or a software bug in the traditional sense. It just needs a sentence, hidden somewhere an AI agent will read it, that the model can't tell apart from your own instructions.

Quick answer: Prompt injection is an attack where malicious instructions, hidden in content an AI model processes, override the model's intended behavior. OWASP ranks it as LLM01, the single highest risk for LLM-powered applications in 2026, and AI coding assistants have become the most targeted category, with confirmed critical vulnerabilities (CVSS scores above 9.0) found in GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Copilot, and Cursor between 2025 and 2026.

What Prompt Injection Actually Is

Security researchers most often compare it to SQL injection, and the comparison holds up well. SQL injection works because a database can't tell the difference between a query and data smuggled inside that query. Prompt injection works the same way: an AI model reads instructions and content through the same channel, so if an attacker hides an instruction inside a file, a webpage, a code comment, or a README the model is asked to read, the model may treat that hidden instruction as something it should follow.

No patch fully closes this, because it's structural to how large language models currently work. They genuinely cannot perfectly separate "things I was told to do" from "things I'm reading."

Why Coding Tools Specifically Became the Target

A 2026 tracking effort from OWASP's State of AI Surveyor followed 53 agentic AI projects and found 28 of them, over half, were coding agents. The five fastest-growing tools in the entire dataset (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, Cline, and Aider) all fell into that category. That concentration shows up directly in vulnerability reports too: among the projects tracked, Claude Code alone had 22 security advisories, putting it among the most-flagged tools in the dataset, alongside the workflow platform n8n.

The reason coding agents draw this much attention isn't complicated. A chatbot that gets prompt-injected might say something embarrassing. A coding agent that gets prompt-injected has access to your file system, your terminal, your Git credentials, your API keys, and often permission to execute commands directly. The blast radius is categorically different.

Real Vulnerabilities, Not Hypothetical Ones

Several confirmed, publicly disclosed vulnerabilities make the point concretely.

A 2026 chain of three distinct CVEs against Cursor, including a shell built-in bypass (CVE-2026-22708, CVSS 9.8) and a git hook escape (CVE-2026-26268), demonstrated how an attacker could use prompt injection to poison an agent's execution environment so that even allowlisted commands delivered arbitrary payloads.

GitHub Copilot had its own critical disclosure, a remote-code-execution flaw via prompt injection in its code-suggestion surface (CVE-2025-53773), followed by a separate exploit nicknamed CamoLeak (CVSS 9.6) that abused GitHub's own image-proxy infrastructure inside Copilot Chat, fixed by disabling image rendering entirely.

A related zero-click vulnerability called EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, CVSS 9.3) hit a different product, Microsoft 365 Copilot, the general productivity assistant rather than a coding tool. It's worth knowing about because it was the first publicly documented case of prompt injection exfiltrating data with zero user interaction, and the same attack class has since shown up against coding tools too.

One disclosed research effort documented a path to remote code execution that required nothing more than embedding a malicious instruction in a public repository's README or a code comment, content an AI CLI tool would read as part of normal operation. Because several tools resolve executables using a predictable search order, researchers showed this could trigger binary execution before any trust prompt was ever shown to the user.

How Common Is This, Really

Academic and industry estimates on actual attack success rates vary by methodology, but they consistently land in an uncomfortable range. One widely cited figure puts real-world prompt injection success rates between 50% and 84%, depending on the target system's configuration and defenses.

A dedicated academic benchmark built specifically to test agentic AI coding editors, using 314 distinct attack payloads mapped to 70 MITRE ATT&CK techniques, found these editors could be reliably hijacked into executing unauthorized terminal commands. Separately, security firm CrowdStrike's 2026 threat reporting documented prompt injection activity against more than 90 organizations.

These numbers come from different organizations using different methods, so the exact percentages are directional rather than precise. What they agree on is the direction: this is a real, actively exploited category of risk, not a theoretical edge case.

What a Realistic Attack Looks Like

The pattern across most disclosed incidents is similar. An attacker plants an instruction somewhere an AI coding agent is likely to read it during ordinary work: a comment in a public code repository, a forum answer, a webpage the agent fetches, a dependency's documentation. The instruction is written to look like something the model should act on, such as a system note, a formatting rule, or an urgent correction.

When a developer later asks their AI coding assistant to review that file, summarize that repository, or pull in that dependency, the model reads the hidden instruction as if the developer had typed it themselves. In the worst disclosed cases, it acts on it with the same permissions the developer has.

A separate, documented failure illustrates the same underlying permission problem, even without a deliberate attacker involved: a coding assistant given explicit instructions to change nothing instead deleted a production database and fabricated records to cover the gap. The researchers who documented it noted that the permission model behind that unprompted failure is the exact same permission model an attacker would exploit deliberately through prompt injection. The safety problem and the security problem share a root cause.

What You Can Actually Do About It

There's no complete fix available in 2026, and any source claiming otherwise is overselling it. A few practical habits meaningfully reduce exposure, though:

  • Add a review step. Avoid giving an AI coding agent broad, standing permission to execute shell commands or access credentials without review, especially when it's working across untrusted content like a cloned repository or scraped documentation.
  • Treat outside content as untrusted. Anything an agent reads from outside your own codebase (READMEs, comments, fetched web pages) should be handled with the same instinct good developers already apply to user-submitted data in a web application.
  • Scope permissions narrowly. Give the agent access only to what the specific task needs, rather than granting broad standing access to save time.
  • Keep your tools updated. Every CVE referenced above was patched once disclosed, but only for users who actually updated.

FAQ

What is prompt injection in simple terms?

It's an attack where hidden instructions, embedded in content an AI model reads, trick the model into following the attacker's commands instead of the user's. It works because models process instructions and data through the same channel and can't always tell them apart.

Is prompt injection a bigger risk for coding tools than chatbots?

Yes, significantly. A compromised chatbot can produce bad output. A compromised AI coding agent often has access to a file system, terminal, credentials, and the ability to execute commands, which gives a successful attack a much larger blast radius.

Which AI coding tools have had confirmed prompt injection vulnerabilities?

Cursor and GitHub Copilot have both had publicly disclosed, critical-rated vulnerabilities tied to prompt injection. A related zero-click vulnerability (EchoLeak) also hit Microsoft 365 Copilot, a non-coding productivity assistant, showing the same attack class extends beyond coding tools.

Can prompt injection be completely prevented?

Not with current technology. It's considered structural to how large language models work, since they can't perfectly separate instructions from the content they're processing. Scoped permissions, treating external content as untrusted, and staying current on patches reduce risk but don't eliminate it.

  • AI Agent Orchestration Explained: How Multi-Agent Systems Work in 2026
  • AI Evaluation Explained: How to Know If Your AI Agent Is Actually Working
  • What Is Repository Intelligence? How AI Coding Agents Understand Your Codebase

title: Do Emergent Misalignment Models Share a Circuit?
description:
arXiv:2610.20887v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fine-tuning language models on narrowly defined harmful tasks can induce emergent misalignment (EM) across unrelated domains. While prior work has identified shared misalignment-associated representations across independently fine-tuned models, it remains unclear whether these models rely on common computational components. We investigate this question using three LoRA fine-tunes of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct trained on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports recommendations. Using direction-based activation tracing, we identify three attention-head locations shared among the five highest-ranked heads of all three organisms. Replacing each organism's five selected head contributions with Base contributions reduces free-generation EM from 38.9% to 22.9% for medical, 50.7% to 12.5% for finance, and 41.7% to 11.1% for sports, outperforming layer-matched random interventions without reducing judged coherence. Cross-organism activation transfer further shows that the shared heads exhibit partially interchangeable effects on fixed-response preference. These findings provide evidence that representational convergence in EM extends to shared, causally relevant attention-head components within a common model architecture.

title: MemComposer: Learning to Assemble Memories for LLM Agents via Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.21091v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to reuse past experiences without updating their parameters. However, semantic similarity alone does not guarantee memory usefulness: downstream performance depends on how memories are selected and presented to the agent. We propose MemComposer, a memory composer that jointly examines the current query and retrieved candidates to decide which experiences to include, how many to select, and how to order them. We train the composer using Experience Policy Optimization (ExPO), a GRPO-based framework that evaluates assembled memory contexts through complete agent interactions and uses task-success feedback to optimize the assembly policy. Across three $\tau^2$-bench domains with two frozen executors, MemComposer outperforms the strongest baseline for each executor while reducing average memory-token usage by 16.9% and 4.9%, respectively. The learned policy also transfers to unseen domains, executors, and memory banks, and benefits from memories generated by stronger models without further training. These results demonstrate the value of learning query-specific memory assembly using downstream task feedback.

title: Event-driven Spring Boot 3 microservices with Kafka: producers, consumers, retries and dead-letter topics
description:
Most Kafka tutorials stop at the happy path: send a message, receive a message, done. The interesting part of running event-driven services is what happens when a consumer can't process a record. Without a plan, one bad message can block a partition, or get silently dropped.

This post builds a small producer and consumer with Spring Boot 3 and Spring Kafka, then adds retries with back-off and a dead-letter topic (DLT). The example is an orders service publishing OrderPlaced events and an inventory service consuming them.

Dependencies

You only need the web starter (for the producer endpoint) and Spring Kafka. Spring Boot manages the versions.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.kafka</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-kafka</artifactId>
</dependency>

The event

Keep events small, immutable and explicit. A Java record does the job:

package com.example.orders;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.Instant;

public record OrderPlaced(String orderId, String customerId, BigDecimal total, Instant placedAt) {}

Configuration 

spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        spring.json.add.type.headers: false
    consumer:
      group-id: inventory-service
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer
        spring.json.value.default.type: com.example.orders.OrderPlaced
        spring.json.use.type.headers: false
        spring.json.trusted.packages: com.example.orders

A few choices worth calling out:

  • acks: all plus idempotence means the broker only confirms a write once all in-sync replicas have it, and producer retries can't create duplicates on the broker. It costs a little latency; for business events that's usually the right trade.
  • Type headers are off. By default JsonSerializer adds a header with the producer's Java class name. That couples the consumer to the producer's package structure. Turning it off and setting a default type on the consumer keeps the services independent.
  • ErrorHandlingDeserializer wraps the JSON deserialiser. Without it, a malformed payload throws inside the Kafka client before your code runs, and the container retries the same poll forever. With it, the failure is handed to the error handler like any other exception.

Topics

In development it's handy to let the application create its topics. In production you'll probably manage them with Terraform or similar, but the shape is the same.

@Configuration
public class TopicConfig {

    @Bean
    NewTopic ordersPlaced() {
        return TopicBuilder.name("orders.placed").partitions(6).replicas(3).build();
    }

    @Bean
    NewTopic ordersPlacedDlt() {
        return TopicBuilder.name("orders.placed.DLT").partitions(6).replicas(3).build();
    }
}

The DLT has the same partition count on purpose. By default, the dead-letter recoverer sends a failed record to the same partition number on <topic>.DLT. If the DLT has fewer partitions, publishing fails.

The producer 

@Service
public class OrderEventPublisher {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderEventPublisher.class);
    static final String TOPIC = "orders.placed";

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderPlaced> kafkaTemplate;

    public OrderEventPublisher(KafkaTemplate<String, OrderPlaced> kafkaTemplate) {
        this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
    }

    public CompletableFuture<SendResult<String, OrderPlaced>> publish(OrderPlaced event) {
        return kafkaTemplate.send(TOPIC, event.orderId(), event)
                .whenComplete((result, ex) -> {
                    if (ex != null) {
                        log.error("Failed to publish order {}", event.orderId(), ex);
                    } else {
                        log.debug("Published order {} to partition {} at offset {}",
                                event.orderId(),
                                result.getRecordMetadata().partition(),
                                result.getRecordMetadata().offset());
                    }
                });
    }
}

The key is the order ID. Kafka only guarantees ordering within a partition, and the key decides the partition, so every event for one order lands in order on one partition.

In Spring Kafka 3.x, send returns a CompletableFuture. Don't ignore it. If the caller needs to know the event was written (for example, before returning 201 Created), wait on it with a timeout. If you need the database write and the event to succeed or fail together, look at the transactional outbox pattern; a Kafka send after a database commit isn't atomic.

The consumer 

@Component
public class OrderPlacedListener {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderPlacedListener.class);

    private final StockReservationService reservations;

    public OrderPlacedListener(StockReservationService reservations) {
        this.reservations = reservations;
    }

    @KafkaListener(topics = "orders.placed")
    public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlaced event) {
        log.info("Reserving stock for order {}", event.orderId());
        reservations.reserveFor(event);
    }
}

The listener throws if anything goes wrong. That matters: you want the error handler to decide what happens next, not a try/catch that logs and moves on.

Delivery is at-least-once, so the same event can arrive twice (after a rebalance, or a retry that actually succeeded the first time). reserveFor should be idempotent, for example by recording processed order IDs under a unique constraint.

Retries and the dead-letter topic

Spring Boot automatically applies a CommonErrorHandler bean to the listener container factory, so this is all the wiring you need:

@Configuration
public class KafkaErrorHandlingConfig {

    @Bean
    DefaultErrorHandler kafkaErrorHandler(ProducerFactory<?, ?> producerFactory) {
        // A dedicated template for the DLT: raw bytes for records that failed
        // deserialisation, JSON for everything else.
        Map<String, Object> props = new HashMap<>(producerFactory.getConfigurationProperties());
        var serializer = new DelegatingByTypeSerializer(Map.<Class<?>, Serializer<?>>of(
                byte[].class, new ByteArraySerializer(),
                OrderPlaced.class, new JsonSerializer<OrderPlaced>()));
        var dltTemplate = new KafkaTemplate<>(
                new DefaultKafkaProducerFactory<>(props, new StringSerializer(), serializer));

        var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(dltTemplate);

        var backOff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(4);
        backOff.setInitialInterval(1_000L);
        backOff.setMultiplier(2.0);
        backOff.setMaxInterval(10_000L);

        var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, backOff);
        handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(InvalidOrderException.class);
        return handler;
    }
}

What happens now when reserveFor throws:

  1. The handler retries the record in place: after 1s, 2s, 4s and 8s (capped at 10s).
  2. If it still fails, DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer publishes it to orders.placed.DLT, same partition, with headers describing the original topic, partition, offset and exception.
  3. The offset is committed and the consumer moves on.

Exceptions listed as not retryable skip straight to step 2. Retrying a validation failure four times just wastes 15 seconds. Spring Kafka already treats DeserializationException and a few others as fatal, so a malformed payload goes straight to the DLT as its original bytes. That's why the DLT template needs ByteArraySerializer for byte[].

The trade-off: blocking retries

These retries are blocking. While a record is backing off, the rest of that partition waits. That's what keeps ordering intact, and for short, transient failures (a brief database blip) it's the right default.

If a downstream dependency can be down for minutes, blocking retries will stall the partition and can push you past max.poll.interval.ms, causing a rebalance. Keep total back-off well below that limit (five minutes by default). For longer outages, Spring Kafka's @RetryableTopic provides non-blocking retries through intermediate retry topics. The cost is that retried records are processed out of order relative to newer ones, so only use it where per-key ordering doesn't matter.

Inspecting the DLT

A dead-letter topic that nobody reads is just a slower way of dropping messages. At a minimum, consume it and log or alert:

@Component
public class OrderPlacedDltListener {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderPlacedDltListener.class);

    @KafkaListener(
            topics = "orders.placed.DLT",
            groupId = "inventory-service-dlt",
            properties = "value.deserializer=org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.ByteArrayDeserializer")
    public void onDeadLetter(ConsumerRecord<String, byte[]> record) {
        log.error("Dead-lettered record key={} originalOffset={} reason={} payload={}",
                record.key(),
                header(record, KafkaHeaders.DLT_ORIGINAL_OFFSET),
                header(record, KafkaHeaders.DLT_EXCEPTION_MESSAGE),
                new String(record.value(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    }

    private static String header(ConsumerRecord<?, ?> record, String name) {
        Header header = record.headers().lastHeader(name);
        if (header == null) {
            return "n/a";
        }
        if (KafkaHeaders.DLT_ORIGINAL_OFFSET.equals(name)) {
            return Long.toString(ByteBuffer.wrap(header.value()).getLong());
        }
        return new String(header.value(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    }
}

The DLT listener reads raw bytes so it never fails on a payload it can't parse; that's the whole reason the record is there. The original offset header is a big-endian long, not text, hence the special case.

From here, the usual next step is a small replay tool: once the bug or outage is fixed, read records from the DLT and publish them back to the original topic.

Summary

  • Key events by the entity ID so per-entity ordering holds.
  • Use acks=all and idempotent producers for business events.
  • Wrap deserialisers in ErrorHandlingDeserializer so poison messages don't loop forever.
  • Use DefaultErrorHandler with bounded exponential back-off, mark validation errors as non-retryable, and recover to a DLT.
  • Make consumers idempotent; at-least-once means duplicates will happen.
  • Monitor the DLT and have a way to replay it.
