title: React vs Vue vs Svelte vs Solid in 2024: Performance, Bundle Size, and When to Choose Each
description:
React, Vue, Svelte, and Solid are all choices for building reactive web UIs in 2024. They share concepts — reactivity, components, props — but differ significantly in architecture and approach. This guide compares them with Firefox DevTools integration in mind.

The Problem They Solve

Without a framework, updating the DOM in response to state changes requires manual work:

let count = 0;

document.getElementById('btn').addEventListener('click', () => {
  count++;
  document.getElementById('counter').textContent = count; // Manual sync
});

Frameworks automate the "update the DOM when state changes" part.

React: The Incumbent

React uses a virtual DOM — changes are diffed against a virtual tree and only necessary DOM updates happen.

import { useState } from 'react';

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <div>
      <p>Count: {count}</p>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Increment</button>
    </div>
  );
}

Key concepts:

  • useState, useEffect, useMemo, useCallback hooks
  • Virtual DOM diffing
  • One-way data flow (props down, events up)
  • Server components (React 19+)

Performance in Firefox:
React renders can be profiled in the Firefox Performance tab. Long tasks (>50ms) show in the flame graph. React DevTools extension provides component-level timing.

Vue: The Progressive Framework

Vue is more prescriptive with a clear structure. Its Composition API (Vue 3) is similar to React hooks:

<template>
  <div>
    <p>Count: {{ count }}</p>
    <button @click="count++">Increment</button>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue';
const count = ref(0);
</script>

<style scoped>
button { padding: 8px 16px; }
</style>

Key concepts:

  • Single-file components (template + script + style)
  • Reactivity via ref() and reactive()
  • Directives: v-if, v-for, v-bind, v-model
  • Built-in transition system

Performance: Vue uses a compiler to optimize templates at build time — fewer runtime comparisons than React.

Svelte: Compile-Time Reactivity

Svelte has no virtual DOM. It compiles components to vanilla JavaScript that directly manipulates the DOM:

<script>
  let count = 0;
</script>

<p>Count: {count}</p>
<button on:click={() => count++}>Increment</button>

That's it — no imports needed. Svelte compiles this to DOM manipulation code.

Key concepts:

  • Reactive assignments: count++ automatically updates the DOM
  • $: reactive statements (runs when dependencies change)
  • Stores for shared state
  • Zero runtime in the browser (no framework to download)

Bundle size: A Svelte app ships ~2KB of runtime vs React's ~45KB. For performance-critical apps, this matters.

Solid: React-like but Faster

Solid looks like React but compiles to direct DOM updates (like Svelte):

import { createSignal } from 'solid-js';

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = createSignal(0);

  return (
    <div>
      <p>Count: {count()}</p>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count() + 1)}>Increment</button>
    </div>
  );
}

Key concepts:

  • Signals: fine-grained reactivity (only updates what changed)
  • No virtual DOM — direct DOM updates
  • JSX compiled to DOM operations
  • createSignal, createEffect, createMemo (similar to React's hooks)

Performance Comparison

In Firefox DevTools:

  • Open Performance tab → Record
  • Click through your app
  • Stop recording
  • Analyze the flame graph

What to look for:

  • React: "React" frames in the flame graph, batch updates
  • Vue: compiled getter/setter calls, virtual DOM patches
  • Svelte: direct DOM updates with no framework overhead visible
  • Solid: signal subscriptions and fine-grained updates

Measured render performance (rough order, fastest first):

  1. Solid (fine-grained reactivity, no VDOM)
  2. Svelte (compiled to direct DOM ops)
  3. Vue (optimized compilation)
  4. React (VDOM diffing, though React 19 improves this)

For most apps, these differences don't matter. They matter for: many DOM nodes updating simultaneously, 60fps animations driven by state changes, large data tables.

Choosing in 2024

Choose React if:

  • Largest ecosystem and job market
  • Need React Native for mobile
  • Your team already knows it

Choose Vue if:

  • Want an opinionated structure
  • Building moderately complex apps
  • Like single-file components

Choose Svelte if:

  • Bundle size matters (content sites, embedded widgets)
  • Want the simplest syntax
  • SvelteKit is your preferred meta-framework

Choose Solid if:

  • Maximum performance is critical
  • React API familiar but need faster rendering
  • Building very reactive, data-heavy UIs

Firefox Extensions and Framework Choice

Firefox WebExtensions can use any framework for popup/options UIs. Svelte is popular for extensions because of its minimal bundle size — popup UIs that ship 45KB of React feels heavyweight.

A Svelte popup UI might ship as 3-5KB of JavaScript. A React equivalent might be 50-60KB (though still fast — just larger download).

For Tab Manager & Session Saver, the session management UI benefits from reactive frameworks — displaying dozens of tabs, updating state as tabs open/close.

title: JavaScript Array Methods: map, filter, reduce, flatMap, and the ES2023 Immutable Ones
description:
JavaScript array methods are one of the best investments in your day-to-day productivity. Once you internalize map, filter, reduce, and their siblings, most data transformations become a few readable lines instead of nested for loops.

The Core Three

map — Transform Each Element

map returns a new array with each element transformed:

const prices = [10, 25, 8, 42];
const withTax = prices.map(price => price * 1.1);
// [11, 27.5, 8.8, 46.2]

const users = [{ name: 'Alice', age: 30 }, { name: 'Bob', age: 25 }];
const names = users.map(user => user.name);
// ['Alice', 'Bob']

// Extract and rename
const simplified = users.map(({ name, age }) => ({ label: name, value: age }));

filter — Keep Elements Matching a Condition

filter returns a new array with only the elements where the callback returns true:

const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
const evens = numbers.filter(n => n % 2 === 0);
// [2, 4, 6]

const users = [
  { name: 'Alice', active: true },
  { name: 'Bob', active: false },
  { name: 'Carol', active: true }
];
const active = users.filter(u => u.active);
// [{ name: 'Alice' ... }, { name: 'Carol' ... }]

reduce — Accumulate to a Single Value

reduce is the most versatile — it can implement any transformation, but it's most useful when you need to collapse an array into a single value:

const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
const sum = numbers.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0);
// 15

// Count occurrences
const fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'apple', 'cherry', 'banana', 'apple'];
const counts = fruits.reduce((acc, fruit) => {
  acc[fruit] = (acc[fruit] || 0) + 1;
  return acc;
}, {});
// { apple: 3, banana: 2, cherry: 1 }

// Group by property
const events = [
  { type: 'click', x: 10 },
  { type: 'scroll', y: 50 },
  { type: 'click', x: 30 }
];
const grouped = events.reduce((acc, event) => {
  (acc[event.type] = acc[event.type] || []).push(event);
  return acc;
}, {});
// { click: [...], scroll: [...] }

Finding Elements

find and findIndex 

const users = [
  { id: 1, name: 'Alice' },
  { id: 2, name: 'Bob' },
  { id: 3, name: 'Carol' }
];

const bob = users.find(u => u.id === 2);
// { id: 2, name: 'Bob' }

const bobIndex = users.findIndex(u => u.id === 2);
// 1

// Returns undefined (not -1) if not found
const nobody = users.find(u => u.id === 99);
// undefined

some and every 

const scores = [85, 92, 78, 95, 88];

const allPassing = scores.every(s => s >= 70);  // true
const anyPerfect = scores.some(s => s === 100);  // false
const anyFailing = scores.some(s => s < 70);     // false

Flattening and Combining

flat and flatMap 

const nested = [1, [2, 3], [4, [5, 6]]];
nested.flat();    // [1, 2, 3, 4, [5, 6]]
nested.flat(2);   // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]  — depth 2
nested.flat(Infinity);  // flatten any depth

// flatMap = map + flat(1)
const sentences = ['hello world', 'foo bar'];
const words = sentences.flatMap(s => s.split(' '));
// ['hello', 'world', 'foo', 'bar']

// Useful for expanding items conditionally
const items = [{ type: 'product', qty: 2 }, { type: 'gift' }];
const lines = items.flatMap(item =>
  item.qty > 1
    ? Array.from({ length: item.qty }, () => item)
    : [item]
);

Sorting

sort mutates the array. Use a copy for immutability:

const numbers = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6];

// Wrong: sort() without comparator sorts lexicographically
numbers.sort();  // [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9] — works here by accident

// Right: always use a comparator for numbers
numbers.sort((a, b) => a - b);  // ascending
numbers.sort((a, b) => b - a);  // descending

// Strings
const words = ['banana', 'apple', 'cherry'];
words.sort();  // alphabetical: ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
words.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b));  // locale-aware

// Objects
const users = [{ name: 'Charlie' }, { name: 'Alice' }, { name: 'Bob' }];
users.sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name));

// Immutable sort (ES2023)
const sorted = numbers.toSorted((a, b) => a - b);  // returns new array

Checking and Searching 

const arr = [1, 2, 3, NaN];

arr.includes(2);          // true
arr.includes(5);          // false
arr.includes(NaN);        // true  ← unlike indexOf

arr.indexOf(2);           // 1
arr.indexOf(5);           // -1
arr.indexOf(NaN);         // -1  ← NaN !== NaN

arr.lastIndexOf(2);       // 1 (searches from end)

Array Construction 

// Create array of length n
Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => i);  // [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
Array.from({ length: 5 }, () => 0);      // [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]

// From iterable
Array.from('hello');           // ['h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o']
Array.from(new Set([1, 2, 2])); // [1, 2]  — deduplicate
Array.from(nodeList);          // NodeList to array

// Array.of
Array.of(1, 2, 3);  // [1, 2, 3]

Mutation Methods (use carefully) 

const arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

arr.push(6);       // add to end, returns new length
arr.pop();         // remove from end, returns removed element
arr.unshift(0);    // add to start, returns new length
arr.shift();       // remove from start, returns removed element
arr.splice(1, 2);  // remove 2 elements at index 1, returns removed
arr.reverse();     // reverses in place

// Immutable alternatives (ES2023)
arr.toReversed();  // reversed copy
arr.toSpliced(1, 2);  // spliced copy
arr.with(2, 99);   // copy with arr[2] = 99

Chaining

Methods chain naturally since most return arrays:

const data = [
  { name: 'Alice', score: 92, active: true },
  { name: 'Bob', score: 65, active: false },
  { name: 'Carol', score: 88, active: true },
  { name: 'Dave', score: 45, active: true }
];

const result = data
  .filter(u => u.active)        // only active users
  .filter(u => u.score >= 70)   // only passing scores
  .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score)  // sort by score descending
  .map(u => `${u.name}: ${u.score}`)  // format
  .join(', ');
// "Alice: 92, Carol: 88"

Performance Note

For very large arrays (millions of items), for...of loops are faster than chained array methods because they avoid creating intermediate arrays. For typical application data (hundreds to thousands of items), the readability benefit of array methods outweighs any performance difference.

The immutable methods (map, filter, reduce) are also better for React state management — they return new references, which is what React's reconciler checks to detect changes.

title: $1 million hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox
description:
Agents need to run untrusted code, and the microVM has become the standard way to do it: a dedicated guest kernel per workload, isolated from the host and from every other workload on the same machine.

But recent security research and real-world incidents have revealed that agents running untrusted code do not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment; they only need one network path the security model failed to account for, which we explained in our post A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox.

Isolation only holds if both sides of it hold: the Firecracker microVM and the host-side network controls. Recently our CTO pointed an open-weight model with no safeguards at Vercel Sandbox. It did not escape, but it mapped the guest kernel, built a VM to reproduce its ideas, and wrote a fuzzer.

Defenders have first-mover advantage, but it won't last forever, and the choice is when to test the boundaries (we strongly encourage building a scanning program, which you can do on any budget with an open-source tool like deepsec and AI Gateway).

We are proactively choosing to test Vercel Sandbox on our own schedule, not an attacker's, and we are doing it in the open, with the best researchers in the world.

So for two weeks, we are paying up to $1,000,000 USD to the researchers who can escape a Vercel Sandbox.

The challenge

Starting today, Vercel is running a two-week public HackerOne program focused on Vercel Sandbox isolation.

  • Program: Public HackerOne program, open to all eligible researchers

  • Window: Tuesday, August 18 to Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the reward pool is exhausted

  • Max per report: $50,000 USD, for a vulnerability that lets a threat actor read or modify another Vercel tenant's data

  • Total pool: Up to $1,000,000 USD in total payouts

Bounties are paid per report, scoped to a single root cause, and assigned by Vercel triage based on the maximum demonstrable impact. The full bounty table, detailed scope, and the list of known-duplicate classes are on the HackerOne program page.

How Vercel Sandbox is built

Vercel Sandbox runs on bare-metal EC2 hosts. Each sandbox gets its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and inside that microVM a Linux container runs the operator's code. The microVM, not the container, is the security boundary, so operator-supplied code runs two layers removed from the host. We assume that code is fully hostile: root inside the container, full kernel access inside the microVM, and motivated to reach the host or another tenant.

The network side of the boundary is enforced on the host, outside the microVM, where code inside the sandbox cannot modify or disable it. The sandbox firewall intercepts outbound TCP and DNS, checks each connection against the operator's domain and CIDR policies, and can inject credentials at the boundary so they never enter the microVM.

What we're looking for

In short: anything that breaks the sandbox boundary.

  • Compute boundary: Escaping the Firecracker microVM to the EC2 host, or reaching another tenant's sandbox through the compute layer (reading, modifying, or executing code in it), or crashing another tenant's sandbox from within another sandbox

  • Network boundary: Defeating the sandbox firewall without crossing the microVM: reaching destinations the operator did not authorize, exfiltrating data, or retrieving brokered credentials

Container namespace escapes that only reach the Firecracker guest OS are not in scope. Namespaces are a developer-experience feature, not the security boundary.

Bounties

Severity

Bounty

Critical

$25,000 – $50,000

High

$10,000 – $25,000

Medium

$5,000 – $10,000

Low

$1,000 – $5,000

The full bounty table, with example vulnerability classes for each tier, is on the HackerOne program page.

How to participate

The program is open now and closes on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the $1,000,000 USD reward pool is exhausted. Reports go through the HackerOne program page.

To reproduce a finding, boot a sandbox with the @vercel/sandbox SDK and demonstrate the impact with a live proof of concept. The default sandbox OS is enough for most reports; bring a custom image from the Vercel Container Registry only if your PoC needs extra tooling. We will not reward static-analysis-only findings; to issue a payout, we need to see the boundary break.

Full rules, eligibility, the complete scope and bounty table, and the submission process are on the HackerOne program page.

Results and payouts

We will triage reports from the day the program opens through one month after it closes. As findings are confirmed, we will pay bounties, ship fixes, and credit every researcher whose report holds up. The techniques discovered during this program will become permanent additions to the sandbox boundary, protecting every workload on Vercel long after the challenge ends. After the program closes, we will publish a follow-up writeup of the techniques and the fixes we shipped.

Thanks to HackerOne for standing up the program, and to the researchers who will spend the next two weeks trying to break what we built.

title: CSS Animations and Transitions: What to Animate, prefers-reduced-motion, and Performance
description:
CSS animations and transitions are the tools for making interfaces feel responsive and polished without JavaScript. They're hardware-accelerated, performant, and declarative. Knowing when to use transitions vs animations — and how to make them not annoy users — is the practical skill.

Transitions

Transitions animate property changes between two states. They require a trigger (hover, focus, class change):

.button {
  background: #2563eb;
  transform: scale(1);
  transition: background 200ms ease, transform 150ms ease;
}

.button:hover {
  background: #1d4ed8;
  transform: scale(1.03);
}

The transition shorthand: property duration easing delay.

Multiple Properties 

/* Animate specific properties */
transition: opacity 200ms ease, transform 300ms ease-out;

/* Animate all changed properties — use sparingly */
transition: all 200ms ease;

Avoid all — it can catch unexpected property changes and create weird visual artifacts.

Timing Functions

The easing function controls the pace of the animation:

transition-timing-function: ease;           /* slow start, fast middle, slow end */
transition-timing-function: ease-in;        /* slow start, fast end */
transition-timing-function: ease-out;       /* fast start, slow end */
transition-timing-function: ease-in-out;    /* slow start and end */
transition-timing-function: linear;         /* constant speed */
transition-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1);  /* custom bounce */

For UI elements: ease-out feels most natural (fast response, gradual settle). ease-in feels sluggish for user-initiated actions.

Animations

Animations play automatically (no trigger needed), can loop, and can animate through multiple keyframes:

@keyframes fade-in {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(-8px); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
}

.notification {
  animation: fade-in 250ms ease-out;
}

Multiple keyframes:

@keyframes pulse {
  0%   { transform: scale(1); }
  50%  { transform: scale(1.05); }
  100% { transform: scale(1); }
}

.badge {
  animation: pulse 2s ease-in-out infinite;
}

Animation shorthand: name duration easing delay iteration-count direction fill-mode.

.spinner {
  animation: spin 1s linear infinite;
}

.toast {
  animation: slide-in 200ms ease-out forwards;
  /* 'forwards' keeps the final state after animation completes */
}

What to Animate (and What Not To)

Performant — animate these:

  • transform: translate, scale, rotate
  • opacity

These are composited by the browser — handled on the GPU without triggering layout or paint. Smooth on most devices.

Avoid animating:

  • width, height, top, left, margin, padding
  • border-width, font-size
  • Any property that triggers layout recalculation

These cause layout thrashing on every frame. Use transform: translate() instead of animating top/left.

/* Slow: triggers layout every frame */
.moving {
  transition: left 300ms ease;
}
.moving:hover { left: 100px; }

/* Fast: GPU-composited */
.moving {
  transition: transform 300ms ease;
}
.moving:hover { transform: translateX(100px); }

will-change

Hint to the browser that an element will be animated:

.card {
  will-change: transform;
}

This tells the browser to promote the element to its own compositor layer in advance. Use sparingly — every will-change consumes GPU memory. Apply it only to elements you know will animate, not as a blanket optimization.

Respecting User Preferences

Some users disable animations for accessibility or motion sensitivity. Always respect prefers-reduced-motion:

.notification {
  animation: slide-in 250ms ease-out;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .notification {
    animation: none;
    /* Or use a simple fade instead */
  }
}

Or set animations to zero by default and only enable them when preferred:

/* Disable all animations globally unless user accepts motion */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}

Firefox respects the system's prefers-reduced-motion setting. Test with it enabled.

State-Based Animations with CSS Custom Properties

CSS custom properties let you drive animations dynamically from JavaScript:

.progress {
  width: 0%;
  transition: width 500ms ease-out;
}

document.querySelector('.progress').style.width = '75%';
// CSS transition handles the animation

Or with a custom property:

.bar {
  transform: scaleX(var(--progress, 0));
  transform-origin: left;
  transition: transform 500ms ease-out;
}

document.querySelector('.bar').style.setProperty('--progress', 0.75);

Staggered Animations

Animate a list of items in sequence using animation-delay:

.list-item {
  opacity: 0;
  animation: fade-in 200ms ease-out forwards;
}

.list-item:nth-child(1) { animation-delay: 0ms; }
.list-item:nth-child(2) { animation-delay: 50ms; }
.list-item:nth-child(3) { animation-delay: 100ms; }
.list-item:nth-child(4) { animation-delay: 150ms; }

Or dynamically with CSS custom properties:

<li style="--delay: 100ms">Item</li>

.list-item {
  animation: fade-in 200ms ease-out var(--delay, 0ms) forwards;
}

Loading Skeletons

Skeleton loading states are a good use case for CSS animations:

.skeleton {
  background: linear-gradient(
    90deg,
    #e5e7eb 0%,
    #f3f4f6 50%,
    #e5e7eb 100%
  );
  background-size: 200% 100%;
  animation: shimmer 1.5s ease-in-out infinite;
  border-radius: 4px;
}

@keyframes shimmer {
  0%   { background-position: -200% 0; }
  100% { background-position:  200% 0; }
}

Dark Mode Transitions

Avoid jarring color mode switches with a transition on color changes:

:root {
  --bg: #ffffff;
  --text: #111827;
}

:root.dark {
  --bg: #111827;
  --text: #f9fafb;
}

body {
  background: var(--bg);
  color: var(--text);
  transition: background 200ms ease, color 200ms ease;
}

Performance Checklist

  • [ ] Only animating transform and opacity?
  • [ ] prefers-reduced-motion handled?
  • [ ] Using ease-out for user-initiated animations?
  • [ ] will-change applied only where needed?
  • [ ] Animation duration under 300ms for UI feedback (hover, click)?
  • [ ] Looping animations (spinners) using linear timing?
  • [ ] Not using transition: all?

The most common mistake is animating layout-triggering properties instead of transforms. Switch any width/height/top/left animation to an equivalent transform, and you'll immediately see smoother performance on lower-end devices.

title: Designing a Film Journal Export You Can Actually Reuse
description:
A film journal can look correct on screen and still produce an unusable export. Two viewings of the same film might collapse into one row. A missing rating might become zero. A note containing a comma might shift the remaining values into the wrong columns.

The design problem is not merely adding a Download CSV button. It is defining what the exported data means and checking that another tool can preserve it. The following is a proposed export contract for a personal film journal, not a description of a deployed feature.

Start with the viewing event

Use one row per viewing event. A film identifier describes the work; an event identifier describes this particular viewing. Rewatching the same film produces another event, even when the title, edition, and rating happen to match.

Keep the work identifier and edition details in separate fields. The edition can be unknown. An export should not infer it from the film title, and an importer should not merge events just because those titles match.

A small contract might include schema_version, event_id, work_id, title, release_year, viewed_on, date_precision, viewing_status, edition_note, rating_value, rating_scale, and notes. Each column needs a documented meaning. Some values will legitimately be empty.

Preserve what the user knows about time

A date-only viewing entry should remain a date. Turning it into midnight UTC invents a time and can display as the previous day when another tool applies a local timezone.

If the product allows approximate dates, export that precision explicitly. A user who remembers October but not the day should not acquire an invented October 1 entry. Define whether viewed_on accepts a year, a year-month, or a full date, and use date_precision to make the interpretation unambiguous.

If actual timestamps are also supported, define their offset handling separately. Do not silently make a date-only field serve both jobs.

Give empty values a meaning

For this contract, an empty rating_value means “not rated,” not zero. A real zero is a value only if the declared rating scale allows it. Preserve rating_scale so a three on a five-point scale is not reinterpreted as three out of ten.

CSV does not supply those semantics for you. Document them in the export format description. If the product needs to distinguish “unknown,” “not applicable,” and “intentionally left blank,” add an explicit status field instead of pretending one empty cell carries all three meanings.

Likewise, viewing_status should distinguish completed and unfinished entries. Having a row in the journal is not sufficient evidence that someone finished the film.

Quote text correctly, then test a real round trip

RFC 4180 describes a common CSV format in which fields containing commas, double quotes, or line breaks are enclosed in double quotes. A double quote inside a quoted field is represented by two double quotes. That is why splitting every physical line on commas is not a safe parser for free-form film notes.

Use a CSV writer and parser that handle those rules. Choose and document UTF-8 for this export so accented titles and notes have an explicit encoding contract; that is a design choice here, not a claim that RFC 4180 mandates UTF-8.

Round-trip test a note with a comma, a quoted phrase, and a paragraph break. Compare the restored value with the original string, rather than judging success from whether a spreadsheet opens. Include a title with accents and an unrated event in the same test set.

Preview imports before changing the journal

An import preview should show row counts, a few representative entries, and errors tied to the affected record and field. Unknown columns can be reported without silently discarding them. Missing required columns should produce an actionable message before records are written.

Use stable event identifiers to make a second import of the same file recognizable. Define a conflict policy: skip identical records, and present changed records for a deliberate update decision. Do not silently append duplicates or overwrite newer notes.

If an identifier is meaningful only within one journal, include that journal’s namespace in the identity contract. “Event 12” from two separate collections is not automatically the same event.

Keep catalog discovery outside the viewing record

A catalog link can help someone find a film, but it does not establish that they watched it. In a journal associated with DVDWholesaleShop’s catalog, browsing or saving a product should therefore remain separate from creating a viewing event.

That separation also keeps an export useful when product pages change. The journal should retain the user’s title, date, edition note, and response without requiring a live commercial URL to explain every row.

Acceptance means preserved meaning

Before calling the export ready, import it into an empty test journal and check repeated viewings, approximate dates, missing editions, unrated entries, and multiline notes. Import the same file again and verify the documented conflict behavior.

Opening the file is a format check. Recovering the same events and the same uncertainty is the more useful acceptance criterion.

title: Vercel Daemons is now in public beta
description:
Vercel Daemons is now in public beta, allowing you to run long-running processes that pull and execute work from Vercel Queues, databases, or third-party systems without requiring an HTTP server:

  • Consumers using Vercel Queues poll mode, Celery, BullMQ, RabbitMQ, or Kafka.

  • Temporal or Cadence workers that long-poll their task queues.

  • Self-hosted CI runners for GitHub Actions, GitLab, or CircleCI that poll for jobs without requiring inbound connections.

Daemons run containers on Fluid compute and deploy alongside your app in the same project. Vercel builds your image and maintains the instance count you configure in each region, restarting instances that exit or crash.

Get started by packaging your application and dependencies in a Dockerfile or Containerfile, then adding a daemons entry to one configuration file at your project root. This example uses worker/Dockerfile to run one Celery worker in iad1 (Washington, D.C.):

Set any connection details your worker needs in your project's production environment variables, then deploy to production. Vercel starts the configured instances, and their output appears in your project's Logs. CPU and memory metrics are available with Observability Plus.

Learn more in the Vercel Daemons documentation.

title: Entertain, then Cancel: How Thinking Makes Reasoning Models Read Some and Or Literally
description:
arXiv:2610.21204v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a speaker says ``some students passed'', listeners infer that not all of them did. Reasoning models now let users decide how long a model thinks before it answers, but we do not know what extra thinking does to such everyday inferences. We study this directly: we keep a model's weights fixed, change only how much it thinks, and record which reading it chooses. A second tool cuts the model's own reasoning at successive points and asks for an answer, showing where the reading changes. Thinking makes models read logical words as logic: it cancels the implicatures of \emph{some} (\emph{not all}) and \emph{or} (\emph{not both}) in most tested open reasoning models and in GPT-5, while context-driven inferences such as indirect answers improve. The trace shows why: models first entertain the enriched reading and cancel it later. Answering from that early reading, an exploratory inference-time remedy, recovers these implicatures without losing literal accuracy. Evaluations of reasoning models should measure how they interpret, not only how accurate they are.

title: TRACER: A Multimodal Harness for Patient Care in Hospitals
description:
arXiv:2610.21266v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continuous video and clinical records provide complementary information for understanding how patient behavior evolves over a hospital stay. A central challenge is how to represent behavior across the entire stay while preserving access to fine-grained visual and clinical evidence. We introduce TRACER, a training-free multimodal harness that constructs minute-level action records from video and combines them with clinical records into hourly reports. The harness equips an LLM agent with tools to query this hierarchy, inspect relevant video, and retrieve clinical records. To evaluate TRACER, we construct two benchmarks. The first contains 397 annotated one-minute clips spanning 15 atomic actions; the second poses 144 clinician-informed multiple-choice questions, grounded in 264 hours of video and clinical records from two ICU patients. TRACER achieves up to 84.8% accuracy for action detection and 61.0% QA accuracy versus 49.3% for the strongest baseline using the same backbone. Across 280 patients spanning approximately 60,000 camera-hours, TRACER identifies significantly less purposeful activity in patients with a positive delirium assessment during their stay than in those without (p < 0.0001). Our results show that combining continuous video with clinical records can support understanding of patient behavior over time and across patient cohorts without training on protected health data.

title: Node.js Marketplace Failures: Error Grouping Through Fingerprinted Stack Traces and Releases
description:
The least complex useful error-tracking setup for a marketplace pipeline is a structured error event with a stable fingerprint, a normalized stack trace, a release, an environment, and cost-attribution fields. Page on failed business outcomes, not raw exception counts. Keep exception events searchable so the on-call can move from an alert to one failure group, one owner, and one rerun decision.

TL;DR: Group errors by the part of the failure that engineers can act on. For a nightly catalog pipeline, that usually means exception type plus normalized application frames and a low-cardinality job stage. Attach release, deployment.environment.name, marketplace, pipeline_stage, and run_id as separate fields. Never put tenant IDs, offer IDs, or timestamps into the fingerprint. Those belong in searchable context.

At 02:17, the page should say that the nightly offer-index publication missed its completion objective for three marketplaces. It should not say that 18,421 errors occurred. The first message identifies impact and scope; the second may represent one poison record retried thousands of times. An on-call needs the failed stages, affected marketplaces, current release, last successful checkpoint, and a query that opens the relevant error groups.

This is the beginner's mental model: an event is one occurrence, a group collects occurrences that probably share a fix, and a fingerprint is the grouping key. A stack trace supplies evidence. Release and environment show where the change happened. None of those fields, alone, proves root cause.

How should a SaaS app use error grouping and fingerprinting?

Work backward from the missed publication. The late page is a lagging signal: completed_marketplaces < scheduled_marketplaces after the deadline. Useful, but late. Earlier warnings come from control flow: a stage has stopped advancing, retry age exceeds its budget, the dead-letter count is rising, or the oldest unprocessed partition is getting older while workers remain nominally healthy.

Error tracking and alerting answer different questions. Error events help explain why work failed. Progress and freshness metrics establish whether the marketplace outcome is at risk. Paging on every captured exception mixes transient failures, handled validation errors, and terminal failures into one noisy number. Paging only on a business deadline burns recovery time. A good runbook joins the two.

That separation is the first trade-off.

For this pipeline, make the page key on publication freshness and terminal stage failure. A warning can fire earlier on stalled progress, provided it has a sustained window long enough to ignore normal partition skew. The error group is supporting evidence attached to the alert, not the alert condition itself.

Retries create many events without necessarily creating many incidents. If attempts 1, 2, and 3 have the same actionable cause, they should normally land in one group. Record the attempt number, but leave it out of the fingerprint.

One record. One incident.

Treat grouping as an operational API

Automatic grouping commonly starts from exception type, message, and stack trace. Messages often contain unstable data. offer 884921 missing seller 731 and offer 992104 missing seller 518 should probably be one group if the same validation path and fix apply. Conversely, context deadline exceeded from fetch and publish stages may need different owners even when their messages match.

A practical key is exception class + normalized in-app frames + pipeline stage + failure class. Normalize away line numbers, generated wrapper frames, temporary paths, request IDs, record IDs, and retry counters. Keep enough application frames to distinguish call sites. A fingerprint should change when the likely remediation or owning team changes, not whenever the input changes.

That rule has a cost consequence. Excessively specific fingerprints produce thousands of tiny groups, increasing storage, indexing, and human triage work. Overly broad fingerprints collapse unrelated failures, hiding which marketplace or stage consumes the error budget. Cost attribution therefore stays in dimensions adjacent to the fingerprint: marketplace, team, pipeline_stage, and a bounded workload class. Aggregate ingestion and retained bytes by those dimensions. Do not create a group per payer.

The limitation is unavoidable: no static fingerprint can know whether two failures share a root cause. Imagine a parser release that changes generated frames while a malformed supplier feed begins arriving in the same run. Grouping only by frames may split one feed defect across releases; grouping only by exception class may merge the feed defect with a code regression. Keep raw context, sample several events, and let responders merge or split their incident view without rewriting history. The extra review costs time, but silent collisions cost more because they send the wrong team toward the wrong fix.

Cardinality needs a budget. pipeline_stage might have six known values; deployment.environment.name might have three. run_id is unique per execution and belongs in event context, where it enables reconstruction, not in metric labels or group keys. Seller and offer identifiers deserve the same treatment and may require redaction or hashing under the system's data-handling policy.

Add structure at the capture boundary

Instrumentation should create one terminal error event after retry policy is exhausted, while preserving attempt-level diagnostics only when they are useful. This Go type models an event that a Node.js worker could emit through a language-neutral telemetry boundary:

package pipeline

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "io"
    "time"
)

type ErrorEvent struct {
    Timestamp   time.Time `json:"timestamp"`
    Severity    string    `json:"severity_text"`
    Message     string    `json:"body"`
    Type        string    `json:"exception.type"`
    Stacktrace  string    `json:"exception.stacktrace"`
    Fingerprint string    `json:"error.fingerprint"`
    Release     string    `json:"service.version"`
    Environment string    `json:"deployment.environment.name"`
    Marketplace string    `json:"marketplace"`
    Stage       string    `json:"pipeline_stage"`
    RunID       string    `json:"run_id"`
    Attempt     int       `json:"attempt"`
}

func StableFingerprint(exceptionType, stage, failureClass string, frames []string) string {
    h := sha256.New()
    io.WriteString(h, exceptionType+"\x00"+stage+"\x00"+failureClass)
    for _, frame := range frames {
        io.WriteString(h, "\x00"+frame)
    }
    return hex.EncodeToString(h.Sum(nil)[:16])
}

Derive frames from parsed stack frames rather than slicing rendered text. Preserve the original trace. Source maps are part of the release artifact for transpiled or bundled Node.js code; without the matching map, a trace may point at generated JavaScript instead of authored source. Access to maps should follow source-code controls because they can reveal source.

OpenTelemetry's log data model defines exception attributes including exception.type, exception.message, and exception.stacktrace. Its semantic conventions define service.version and deployment.environment.name. These established names reduce translation work, though a backend may represent fingerprints differently. That mapping is an adapter, not application logic.

Release means a deployed build identity, not merely a branch such as main. Environment identifies the deployment context, such as production or staging. Together they answer two fast questions: did this group first appear after a deployment, and is it confined to one environment? Keep the values consistent across logs, traces, and deployment records.

Names drift. Prevent it.

Reconstruct one run before changing the alert

Start with scope. Confirm the completion objective, affected marketplaces, and stage. Filter terminal events by run_id, inspect the largest actionable groups, and compare their first-seen release with the last successful run. Read several events from the leading group. A fingerprint is a hypothesis, and sampling catches accidental collisions.

Then check the retry ledger and checkpoint. A rerun must be idempotent. For index publication, that may mean writing a versioned index and switching it only after validation rather than mutating the live index record by record. The datastore changes the mechanism, but the invariant remains: replaying the same run must not duplicate offers or expose a partial publication. Error tracking cannot supply that guarantee.

Before deploying a grouping change:

  1. Replay fixed stack-trace fixtures and verify that record IDs and line-number changes do not split a group.
  2. Inject failures at two stages and verify that different owners do not collapse into one group.
  3. Compare group counts and top-group event shares on a bounded historical sample, while ensuring raw events remain recoverable.

Deploy the change like a schema migration. Version the algorithm, emit old and new fingerprints during a short validation window when feasible, and record the cutover release. Otherwise regrouping can resemble a new incident or make a real regression appear resolved.

Thresholds spend attention

The earlier signal is only better if someone can act on it. A stall threshold shorter than ordinary marketplace skew will page on healthy runs. A threshold longer than the recovery window merely restates the missed deadline. Set it from the observed distribution of stage durations and remaining recovery budget, then review it after schedule, data volume, or concurrency changes.

Cost attribution needs two ledgers. The compute ledger assigns worker time, retries, and transferred bytes to a marketplace and stage. The observability ledger assigns emitted events, indexed attributes, retention, and query load to the same bounded dimensions. Joining them through run_id explains a costly run, but the unique ID should not become a long-lived metric label.

Do not optimize ingestion by deleting the only evidence. First reduce duplicate attempt events, cap oversized payloads, sample known high-volume nonterminal classes under an explicit policy, and shorten retention for verbose diagnostics while retaining terminal summaries. Verify that the retained record still supports ownership, replay safety, and release comparison. The cheap event that cannot answer an incident question is waste.

False positives carry a concrete operational cost: they train responders to distrust early warnings and consume attention needed for real deadline risk. After each page, classify whether action was required, whether the signal arrived with enough recovery time, and whether its attached group led to the correct owner. Tune sustained windows and stage-specific budgets from that evidence. Keep the final completion alert. It is the backstop when an earlier model is wrong.

Further reading

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/exceptions/exceptions-logs/
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/resource/deployment-environment/
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/resource/service/
  • https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/

title: Migrate VPAID interactivity to SIMID when your delivery partners can support it.
description:
Originally published on VASTLint. This article is part of the Migrate video standards with evidence series.

An interactive video campaign becomes expensive to operate when every destination needs a different creative package. The sales team sells one experience, the studio builds several implementations, and operations discovers the exceptions near launch. A migration should reduce that repeated work while preserving the experience the advertiser bought.

SIMID is a useful destination for interactive video, but a migration decision needs more than a newer acronym. Start with the placements you can actually serve, the interactions those placements support, and the evidence required to call the campaign ready. A format that passes a document check can still encounter an unsupported player.

Separate the interactive experience from video playback.

IAB Tech Lab describes SIMID as the interactivity component of the move away from VPAID. The interactive layer communicates with the player through defined messages while the media remains separate. The player controls playback and handles requests from the creative. Measurement belongs in the Open Measurement path.

That separation gives a migration team a concrete engineering objective. The video should play through the destination's normal media pipeline. The interaction should add the approved behavior without taking ownership of the whole playback implementation. The test plan can then distinguish a media failure from an interaction failure.

Treat any claimed commercial benefit as a hypothesis to measure. If one reusable package replaces several destination-specific builds, record the builds avoided and the remaining exceptions. If the same engineering work merely moves into a new adapter, the operating cost may not have improved yet.

Start with one interaction you can sell and test.

Choose a narrow experience, such as a product information panel with an approved destination link. Write down the required user actions, the allowed player responses and the behavior when the interaction cannot run. Avoid making the first release depend on every feature of an existing VPAID creative.

Ask each publisher or platform to confirm support for that exact experience on the intended app, device and delivery method. A general statement that a platform supports VAST or interactive video does not answer whether the proposed SIMID package will execute there. Save the tested player and SDK versions with the acceptance record.

Specify the business fallback too. If the interactive feature was an optional enhancement, ordinary video may be acceptable. If the advertiser bought a particular interaction, losing that feature can change the delivered product. Operations should not silently count the fallback as equivalent fulfillment.

Keep verification on its own migration track.

Inventory everything the old creative does. Some VPAID packages combine an interaction, a measurement vendor integration and media handling. Replacing only the interaction does not demonstrate that the verification requirement has been met.

Create a separate acceptance record for measurement. Identify the destination integration, the verification resource and the provider that must receive usable signals. Require a runtime test in addition to checking the VAST declaration. A successful interaction is evidence about the interaction, not about the provider's measurement report.

Keep this distinction in the handoff to commercial teams. An experience can be visually correct while failing a buyer's verification requirement. Conversely, a properly measured video may lack the interactive feature that the campaign proposal promised.

Run a small pilot with an explicit failure path.

First, save the current creative, VAST response and expected behavior. Build the SIMID version against the published interface specification, then validate its document with VASTLint. Retain the findings and corrected document so the next reviewer can see what changed.

Next, run the package in each approved destination. Test normal playback, the intended interaction, a blocked interaction resource and a slow response. Record what the user sees, whether the video continues as agreed and which events reach the relevant reporting systems. Include an ordinary non-interactive video as a control.

Release only to the destinations that passed those checks. Keep a routing rule and a tested rollback package. A practical pilot produces a list of approved environments with evidence, rather than a global switch labeled migrated.

Measure the work saved before projecting revenue.

Compare the pilot with a similar recent campaign. Count creative packages produced, review rounds, destination-specific fixes and support time. Record the campaign scope so a small two-placement pilot is not compared directly with a large multi-market launch.

Suppose, as an illustration, a team normally spends six hours adapting one experience and spends four hours on the new route. The observed result would be two hours less work for that comparison. It would not establish a universal reduction, additional impressions or increased sales. Include any extra player integration work before claiming net savings.

For an advertiser, the commercially relevant question may be whether the requested interactive product can reach the booked placements. For a publisher, it may be whether the feature can be accepted without custom creative execution. Those are specific outcomes that a pilot can document.

Expand from an approved delivery contract.

Write the accepted media requirements, interaction behavior, verification requirements and fallback policy into the creative brief for the next campaign. Give the studio and trafficker the same test record. Require an explicit review when a new device or delivery path is added.

Use VASTLint to repeat the document checks at each handoff. Keep player execution and provider reporting as separate acceptance steps. The migration earns its place when a second campaign can reuse the approved route with less uncertainty and a clear explanation of its remaining limits.

title: A Cache Key Bug in an Agent PR: Cross-Tenant Leakage, Tested
description:
The pull request arrived at 02:14 with a green checkmark and three files changed. Its claim was modest: skip duplicate model calls, cut latency on repeated prompts. The reviewer's first instinct was to trust the test suite.

The tests only covered the happy path. That is exactly where a caching change is least likely to break.

Note: the diff below is a minimal reconstruction for teaching, not a verbatim vendor pull request.

The Diff Under Review 

import hashlib

CACHE = {}

def complete(prompt, tenant_id, model="default"):
    key = hashlib.sha256(prompt.encode()).hexdigest()
    if key in CACHE:
        return CACHE[key]
    resp = call_model(model, prompt)   # network call, can raise
    CACHE[key] = resp
    return resp

Three things stand out on the first read. The tenant_id argument is accepted and never used. Nothing checks whether the response is usable before storing it. The dictionary has no size bound, no TTL, and no eviction path.

The diff passes review because it is small and readable. Small and readable is not the same as correct.

Why the Happy Path Passes

The accompanying test calls complete twice with one prompt and one tenant. It asserts that the model client was invoked once.

That assertion is true. It also stays true after every defect below is fixed, which is why the suite gives reviewers no signal at all.

Three Defects the Existing Tests Never Touch

1. The Cache Key Ignores Tenant Identity

The key is a hash of the prompt text alone. Two tenants that send an identical string share one cache entry.

For a prompt like "Summarize the incident report." the collision is not theoretical. Support tooling, templates, and system prompts repeat across accounts all day long.

2. Blank and Failed Results Get Cached

If call_model returns None or an empty string on a transient upstream failure, that value becomes the stored answer. Every later caller reads the failure until the process restarts.

Negative caching converts a one-second blip into a multi-hour outage. The diff never distinguishes a good answer from a bad one.

3. The Cache Is Process-Local and Unbounded

Four workers mean four separate dictionaries and four independent hit rates. Memory grows with the number of unique prompts and never shrinks.

The diff looks like a shared cache. It behaves like a per-worker notebook with no eraser.

What to Trust, What to Revert, What to Test

  1. Trust the pure helper. hashlib.sha256 is a reasonable key primitive.
  2. Keep the tenant_id parameter and thread it into the key.
  3. Revert the module-level mutable dictionary.
  4. Revert any write of an empty, failed, or partial response.
  5. Replace the single happy-path test with isolation, failure, and concurrency tests.

A Reproduction Plan You Can Run in Ten Minutes

Step 1: Write the isolation test first 

import pytest

calls = []

def fake_call_model(model, prompt, tenant_id):
    calls.append(tenant_id)
    return f"{tenant_id}-answer"

def test_cache_does_not_leak_between_tenants():
    calls.clear()
    a = complete("Summarize the incident report.", tenant_id="acme")
    b = complete("Summarize the incident report.", tenant_id="globex")
    assert calls == ["acme", "globex"]
    assert a != b

Run pytest -k tenant -x. It fails against the diff. That failure is the evidence, not an opinion.

Step 2: Patch the key and rerun 

def cache_key(tenant_id, model, prompt):
    parts = [tenant_id, model, prompt]
    return hashlib.sha256("\x00".join(parts).encode()).hexdigest()

The null-byte separator prevents ambiguous concatenation. The same test should now pass unchanged.

Step 3: Prove failures are not cached 

def test_failures_are_not_cached(monkeypatch):
    calls.clear()
    def boom(*args, **kwargs):
        calls.append("attempt")
        raise TimeoutError("upstream")
    monkeypatch.setattr("app.model.call_model", boom)
    for _ in range(2):
        with pytest.raises(TimeoutError):
            complete("boom", tenant_id="acme")
    assert len(calls) == 2

Two attempts, two upstream calls. A cached exception would produce one.

Step 4: Measure the cross-worker hit rate 

for i in $(seq 1 40); do
  curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/complete \
    -H 'content-type: application/json' \
    -d '{"prompt":"ping","tenant_id":"acme"}' > /dev/null
done
grep -c 'model_call' /var/log/app.log

Forty requests with one unique prompt should log far fewer than forty model calls. If the count stays near forty, the cache is not shared across workers.

Decision Table

Change Verdict Reason
cache_key helper Keep small, pure, easy to test
tenant_id in the key Keep and require blocks cross-tenant reads
module-level CACHE dict Revert process-local, unbounded, no TTL
caching of empty or failed results Revert turns a blip into a lasting outage
single happy-path test Replace never exercises isolation or failure

Reusing This Review Loop on a Free Server

The agent that produced the diff ran against MonkeyCode's free model access. The repro suite above ran on the project's free server option, which is enough for a few hundred test calls in one sitting.

The operator states the free tier also includes a promotional token allowance, currently advertised at 10 million tokens. Confirm the current terms in the repository before planning around any number. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The model is not the interesting part here. The loop is: generate, reproduce, revert, retest.

Limitations and Who Should Skip This

  • Teams with strict data residency rules should not send prompts to any hosted endpoint, free or paid.
  • Multi-tenant products need cache keys derived from tenant, model, and prompt version together.
  • A process-local dictionary is acceptable for a single-worker prototype and wrong in every other deployment.
  • If hit rate matters at scale, use a shared store with TTL, eviction, and a size cap.
  • This review does not attempt to validate model output quality. It only checks whether one tenant can read another tenant's answer.

Closing Note

An agent PR is a draft, not a decision. Trust the pure functions, revert the shared mutable state, and test the tenant boundary before anything else.

title: Build a Crash-Resistant AI Podcast Production Pipeline on Telnyx Edge
description:
Podcast post-production is rarely one operation. Before an episode can be published, someone must transcribe the recording, identify chapters, write show notes, create promotional copy, and produce a trailer. Each step depends on the one before it, which makes the workflow vulnerable to interruptions.

If processing fails after transcription, should the application transcribe the entire recording again?

I built Show Wrap Desk to explore a more durable approach.

It is a TypeScript application running on Telnyx Edge Compute that turns one podcast recording into:

  • A speaker-labeled transcript
  • Timestamped chapters
  • AI-generated show notes
  • A short trailer script
  • An MP3 trailer generated with Text-to-Speech

The workflow is owned by one Stateful Actor per show, so completed stages remain recorded when later work fails.

The pipeline

A producer starts the workflow with one request:

curl -X POST https://<your-worker>/wrap \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "show": "engineering-notes",
    "audioUrl": "https://example.com/episode.mp3"
  }'

The endpoint immediately returns an episode ID and a 202 Accepted response while the actor continues processing:

transcribing → chapterizing → notes → wrapped

You can inspect progress at any time:

curl "https://<your-worker>/wrapstatus/<episodeId>?show=engineering-notes"

One Stateful Actor per show

The worker derives a deterministic actor name from the show:

const desk = env.DESKS.idFromName(`show:${show}`);
const result = await desk.onWrap(show, audioUrl);

Every episode submitted for the same show reaches the same WrapDesk actor.

The actor stores its workflow data in embedded SQL tables:

  • episodes tracks status, errors, and completion times.
  • chapters stores titles and timestamps.
  • assets stores transcripts, show notes, and trailer audio.

This gives the workflow a durable ledger without requiring a separate orchestration database.

Stable tasks prevent duplicate pipelines

Each episode is processed by a scheduled task with a stable ID:

await this.schedule(
  0,
  "wrapTick",
  { episodeId },
  { id: `wrap:${episodeId}` }
);

Scheduling the same ID again replaces the pending task instead of creating another copy.

After each successful stage, the actor updates the episode status and re-arms that task for the next stage. If the same audio URL is submitted again while processing is incomplete, the actor finds the existing episode and resumes it.

The individual stages also check for persisted output before doing work. A stored transcript is not transcribed again, existing chapters are preserved, and generated notes or trailer audio are reused.

A failure can repeat the currently executing external operation if it occurred before the result was saved. However, completed and persisted stages are not restarted.

Speaker-labeled transcription

The first stage downloads the recording and submits it to the Telnyx Speech-to-Text API using Deepgram Nova-3:

const form = new FormData();

form.append("file", blob, "episode.mp3");
form.append("model", "deepgram/nova-3");
form.append("response_format", "verbose_json");
form.append(
  "model_config",
  JSON.stringify({
    diarize: true,
    smart_format: true,
    punctuate: true,
  })
);

The response includes word-level timestamps and speaker labels. The actor normalizes those words and stores them as the transcript asset before advancing the episode.

Creating chapters

The application groups consecutive words from the same speaker into turns. A silence longer than 60 seconds begins a new chapter:

const turns = buildTurns(words);
const chapters = splitIntoChapters(turns, 60);

Boundary detection happens locally, so the application does not need an AI request to determine every timestamp.

Telnyx AI Inference then receives short summaries of the resulting sections and returns chapter titles. The sample uses zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash through the Edge Compute TELNYX binding.

Writing show notes

The next inference request creates Markdown show notes containing:

  • A summary of the episode
  • Key takeaways
  • A pull quote
  • The generated chapter list

The transcript sent to the model is bounded to keep the example inside a manageable context window. A production implementation should introduce chunking or hierarchical summarization for long recordings.

Generating the trailer

The model selects a promising chapter and writes a trailer script capped at 400 characters.

That script is sent to the Telnyx Text-to-Speech WebSocket:

socket.send(JSON.stringify({ text: " " }));
socket.send(JSON.stringify({ text: script }));
socket.send(JSON.stringify({ text: "" }));

The actor collects base64 audio frames until the service sends:

{ "isFinal": true }

The sample defaults to azure.en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural, but HOST_VOICE can be changed to another supported voice.

The project does not automatically clone the podcast host’s voice from the submitted recording. A custom or cloned voice must be configured separately.

Running the example 

git clone https://github.com/team-telnyx/telnyx-code-examples.git
cd telnyx-code-examples/show-wrap-desk

npm install
cp .env.example .env

Add your Telnyx API key, then generate the bindings and deploy:

npm run types
npm run deploy

Set the generated worker URL as DEPLOY_URL and run:

npm run bootstrap

The included demo uses a public-domain LibriVox recording.

Taking the pattern further

Before using this architecture in production, add authentication, audio-size limits, URL validation, retention controls, workflow telemetry, and human review for generated promotional content.

Large transcripts and audio files should also move to durable object storage instead of being kept directly in actor SQL.

The reusable idea is bigger than podcasting:

  1. Assign each workload a durable actor.
  2. Store the output of every stage.
  3. Track progress with explicit statuses.
  4. Schedule work using stable IDs.
  5. Make each stage safe to attempt again.
  6. Expose status through the same durable ledger.

That pattern can support transcription batches, media processing, document enrichment, report generation, and other long-running AI workflows.

The full source is available here:

https://github.com/team-telnyx/telnyx-code-examples/tree/main/show-wrap-desk

title: Towards automatic digital garment assembly
description:
arXiv:2610.20651v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Creating digital garments from existing two-dimensional patterns remains a time-consuming process. Although patterns are widely available in digital form, their assembly in garment CAD software involves manual definition of sewing operations and arrangement of the pattern panels for drape simulation. We present two learning-based approaches that automate both tasks using the 2D vector pattern as their sole input. Our automatic sewing model operates at the segment level, leveraging a Transformer encoder with multiple prediction heads. Our novel architecture supports many-to-many, ordered segment correspondences, as well as hems, overlapping seams needed for multilayer garments, and construction properties such as seam allowances and stitch types, required for the finished virtual garment but neglected by previous methods. A complementary panel-level model predicts body-region assignments, layers, and placement coordinates to initialize the drape simulation. We evaluate both models on a curated dataset of 4,035 professionally assembled garment instances. The sewing model exactly recovers all seam and hem topologies of 63.3\% of test garments, while the arrangement model meets the specified placement criteria for all panels in 66.2\% of test garments. We also integrate both methods into garment CAD software, demonstrating automatic assembly of successfully predicted garments.

title: React Query Best Practices: Build Faster and More Reliable React Apps
description:
Managing server state in React becomes challenging as applications grow. Fetching data, handling loading states, synchronizing updates, preventing duplicate requests, and keeping cached information fresh can quickly make components difficult to maintain.

TanStack Query, formerly known as React Query, simplifies these challenges by providing caching, background refetching, request deduplication, and mutation management out of the box. Instead of manually coordinating API calls with useEffect and useState, developers can focus on building reliable user experiences.

However, using React Query effectively requires more than wrapping an API request in useQuery. Understanding query keys, cache configuration, error handling, mutations, and invalidation strategies helps prevent subtle bugs and improves application performance.

8 React Query Best Practices Every Developer Should Follow

1. Create a Shared QueryClient

Initialize QueryClient once at the application level and provide it through QueryClientProvider. Creating a new client during every render can reset caches and undermine the benefits of server-state management. Configure sensible defaults centrally while allowing individual queries to override them when necessary.

2. Use Consistent and Predictable Query Keys

Query keys identify cached data and determine which queries should be updated or invalidated. Use arrays containing meaningful identifiers and filters, such as ["users", userId] or ["products", { category, page }]. Keep a consistent naming convention so related queries can be invalidated together without accidentally refreshing unrelated data.

3. Separate API Logic from Components

Keep HTTP requests in reusable API functions instead of embedding fetch logic inside every component. This makes request handling easier to test, reuse, and maintain. Your query functions should return parsed data and throw meaningful errors when the response is unsuccessful, because React Query relies on rejected promises to identify failed requests.

4. Configure staleTime and gcTime Intentionally

staleTime determines how long cached data is considered fresh, while gcTime controls how long inactive cached queries remain in memory. A longer staleTime can reduce unnecessary requests for data that rarely changes. Use shorter freshness windows for frequently changing information, and remember that stale data can remain visible while a background refetch occurs.

5. Use Mutations and Invalidation for Updates

Use useMutation for operations that create, update, or delete server-side data. After a successful mutation, invalidate the relevant query keys so affected screens can refresh their data. For interactions that require immediate feedback, consider optimistic updates, but implement rollback and cache reconciliation carefully.

6. Handle Loading, Empty, and Error States

A reliable interface distinguishes between initial loading, background fetching, empty results, and failed requests. Use isPending for the initial pending state, isFetching to identify ongoing fetch activity, and isError to render an appropriate error message. This makes the application easier to understand and prevents a failed request from being mistaken for an empty result.

7. Avoid Unnecessary Refetching

TanStack Query can refetch data when a component mounts, a window regains focus, or a network connection is restored. These behaviors are useful for keeping data fresh, but they should match your application's requirements. Configure refetchOnWindowFocus, retry, and other options deliberately instead of disabling every automatic behavior globally.

8. Keep Queries Independent and Testable

Build custom hooks around recurring data-access patterns, such as useUsers or useProducts. Keep query keys and API functions easy to locate, and test success, failure, and invalidation behavior. For dependent requests, use the enabled option when a required identifier is not yet available rather than executing an incomplete request.

import React from "react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import {
  QueryClient,
  QueryClientProvider,
  useQuery,
  useMutation,
  useQueryClient,
} from "@tanstack/react-query";

// Step 1: Create a shared client outside the React component tree.
const queryClient = new QueryClient({
  defaultOptions: {
    queries: {
      staleTime: 60_000, // Keep successful data fresh for one minute.
      gcTime: 5 * 60_000, // Retain inactive cache entries for five minutes.
      retry: 1, // Retry a failed query once.
      refetchOnWindowFocus: false,
    },
  },
});

// Step 2: Define stable query keys in one place.
const userKeys = {
  all: ["users"],
  lists: () => [...userKeys.all, "list"],
};

// Step 3: Keep API requests separate from UI components.
async function fetchUsers() {
  console.log("Step 3: Requesting users from the API...");
  const response = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users");

  // fetch does not reject automatically for HTTP 4xx or 5xx responses.
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Unable to fetch users: HTTP ${response.status}`);
  }

  const users = await response.json();
  console.log(`Received ${users.length} users successfully.`);
  return users;
}

// Step 4: Create a reusable hook for server-state access.
function useUsers() {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: userKeys.lists(),
    queryFn: fetchUsers,
  });
}

// Step 5: Define a mutation and invalidate affected cached queries.
async function createUser(newUser) {
  console.log("Step 5: Sending a create-user request...");
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users",
    {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify(newUser),
    }
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Unable to create user: HTTP ${response.status}`);
  }

  return response.json();
}

function UsersPage() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();
  const { data: users, isPending, isError, error, isFetching } = useUsers();

  const mutation = useMutation({
    mutationFn: createUser,
    onSuccess: async () => {
      console.log("Step 6: Mutation succeeded; invalidating user lists.");
      await queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: userKeys.all });
      console.log("User list cache has been marked stale and refreshed when active.");
    },
    onError: (mutationError) => {
      console.error("Create-user mutation failed:", mutationError.message);
    },
  });

  // Step 7: Render an explicit initial loading state.
  if (isPending) {
    return <p>Loading users...</p>;
  }

  // Step 8: Keep errors distinct from successful empty results.
  if (isError) {
    return <p role="alert">Could not load users: {error.message}</p>;
  }

  function handleCreateUser() {
    console.log("Step 9: Preparing a sample user mutation.");
    mutation.mutate({
      name: `Demo User ${Date.now()}`,
      username: `demo${Date.now()}`,
      email: `demo${Date.now()}@example.com`,
    });
  }

  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Users</h1>
      {isFetching && <p>Refreshing users in the background...</p>}
      {users.length === 0 ? (
        <p>No users found.</p>
      ) : (
        <ul>
          {users.map((user) => (
            <li key={user.id}>
              {user.name} — {user.email}
            </li>
          ))}
        </ul>
      )}
      <button onClick={handleCreateUser} disabled={mutation.isPending}>
        {mutation.isPending ? "Creating user..." : "Create sample user"}
      </button>
      {mutation.isError && (
        <p role="alert">Creation failed: {mutation.error.message}</p>
      )}
      {mutation.isSuccess && <p>User creation request completed.</p>}
    </main>
  );
}

// Step 10: Provide the same QueryClient to the entire application.
function App() {
  return (
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <UsersPage />
    </QueryClientProvider>
  );
}

// Step 11: Mount the application in the browser.
const rootElement = document.getElementById("root");
if (!rootElement) {
  throw new Error("Missing #root element in index.html");
}

console.log("Starting the React Query best-practices demo...");
createRoot(rootElement).render(
  <React.StrictMode>
    <App />
  </React.StrictMode>
);

// Note: This example requires React, React DOM, and @tanstack/react-query.
// The JSONPlaceholder POST endpoint simulates creation; it does not persist users.

Conclusion

React Query works best when server-state management follows a clear and consistent architecture. Shared query keys, reusable API functions, intentional cache settings, and mutation-driven invalidation make applications easier to maintain while reducing unnecessary network requests.

Start with a shared QueryClient and a small set of custom query hooks, then introduce more advanced techniques such as optimistic updates, pagination, and dependent queries as your application grows. Avoid adding configuration simply because it exists; every cache and refetch option should serve a specific requirement.

Most importantly, treat loading states, errors, and cache consistency as core parts of the user experience rather than implementation details. When these practices are applied consistently, TanStack Query becomes a dependable foundation for building responsive, scalable React applications.

title: Designing Fee Engines for Different Payment Rails
description:
Making fees transparent when providers calculate and collect them differently.

Fees seem simple until a product supports several payment rails.

One provider may deduct a fixed fee from the recipient amount. Another may charge the platform separately. A bank transfer may use a percentage with a minimum, while a wire transfer uses a flat charge. Some fees may be waived above a transaction threshold or after sufficient monthly activity.

A single fee field cannot explain all of these outcomes.

Separate the amounts in the quote

A payment quote should distinguish:

send amount
customer fee
total sender debit
provider request amount
provider fee
recipient amount
fee currency

These values may be expressed in different currencies. A fee charged in the receiving currency should not be subtracted blindly from the sending wallet.

Model who absorbs the provider fee

Suppose the recipient should receive exactly 1,000 units and the provider deducts 50.

If the platform sends 1,000, the recipient receives 950. If the product promises an exact recipient amount and the platform covers the provider fee, the provider request may need to be 1,050 while the customer quote still shows a recipient amount of 1,000.

That policy should be explicit:

provider_amount = recipient_amount
if fee_policy == "platform_covers_recipient_fee":
    provider_amount += quoted_provider_fee

Do not hide this adjustment in an adapter without recording the quoted and submitted values.

Configure fee rules as data

Fee rules change more frequently than transaction code. Store configurable values such as:

  • percentage;
  • flat amount;
  • minimum fee;
  • maximum cap;
  • transaction waiver threshold;
  • monthly activity threshold; and
  • rail-specific overrides.

Only one applicable active configuration should exist for a given scope. Changes should be auditable.

Record fee outcomes in the ledger

When a fee is charged, create a financial record. When it is waived, preserve the waiver reason and threshold used.

For monthly maintenance, use a deterministic account-and-period reference so concurrent workers cannot charge the same month twice.

Return concise fee information to clients

The API should provide the values the interface needs without forcing it to recreate fee logic. If a fee or cap is zero, the client can omit it. If a fee is waived, the API can return the effective fee as zero along with short eligibility information.

The backend remains authoritative for calculation; the frontend remains responsible for clear presentation.

The design principle

A fee engine translates commercial policy and provider behavior into explicit financial amounts.

The quote, sender debit, provider submission, recipient credit, and recorded fee must reconcile. If those values are not separately represented, the customer experience and financial reporting will eventually disagree.

LinkedIn post 12A

“Fee” is not one number in a cross-currency payment.

You may need to distinguish:

• customer fee

• total sender debit

• provider fee

• provider request amount

• recipient amount

• fee currency

When the provider deducts a fee from delivery, sending the quoted recipient amount may underpay the recipient.

PaymentFees #Fintech #ProductEngineering #Accounting

title: DefoliationCAM: An Edge-AI System for Real-Time Insect Defoliation Severity Assessment in Grapevines
description:
arXiv:2610.20879v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Insect-induced defoliation threatens grapevine health and yield, yet severity assessment relies on subjective manual scouting. We developed DefoliationCAM (D-CAM), a solar-powered edge AI system that estimates canopy defoliation and transmits results via LoRa to a web dashboard. The pipeline uses YOLOX-Nano to localize grapevine cordons in 4K images and a MobileNet-based classifier with lightweight channel attention to classify 320 x 320 pixel patches. The 29,674 field-collected patches were labeled as background or one of four damage levels: no to negligible, mild, moderate, and severe. Merging moderate and severe classes reduced the class imbalance ratio from approximately 40:1 to 8.8:1. Synthetic augmentation increased macro-F1 from 0.768 to 0.838. The classifier outperformed ResNet-50 in macro-F1 with fewer parameters (1.08 M versus 23.52 M). Patch predictions were aggregated into a canopy-level Non-linear Global Defoliation Severity (NGDS) score and validated against an entomologist's ratings of 86 held-out canopy images. Quadratic discriminant analysis identified boundaries of 9% and 29% separating negligible damage, mild damage requiring monitoring, and action-level damage warranting on-site scouting and insecticide treatment consideration. The 29% boundary aligned with the 25%-30% action threshold range for Japanese beetle management in grapevine. Using TensorRT FP16 on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, the pipeline processed each 4K image in approximately 1.5 s, with a complete operating cycle of 57-60 s. A five-week deployment of two field units demonstrated the feasibility of autonomous solar-powered operation, LoRa communication, and remote defoliation monitoring. D-CAM supports frequent, objective canopy damage assessment for targeted scouting and timely pest-management decisions.
