title: MAI-Gym: An Open All-in-One Platform for GUI Agent Evaluation and RL Training across Mobile and Computer Environments
description:
arXiv:2610.20939v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has driven rapid progress in mathematics, coding, and tool use, but scaling this success to GUI agents remains challenging due to the high cost of interactive environments and the scarcity of realistic training tasks. We introduce MAI-Gym, an open all-in-one platform that unifies GUI agent evaluation, data collection, and online RL training across mobile, computer, and web environments. Through a shared rollout pipeline, MAI-Gym ensures consistent agent behavior across evaluation and training, supports ten established benchmarks, and scales to 20,000 parallel environment instances. Beyond scalable infrastructure, MAI-Gym enables automated synthesis of diverse GUI applications and challenging tasks, including resettable mocked apps and coherent cross-app worlds with execution-validated task verifiers. Using MAI-Gym, we train MAI-Gym-9B, a unified 9B agent for mobile and computer use, achieving state-of-the-art performance among open GUI agents under 10B parameters: 78.4% on MobileWorld and 76.2% on OSWorld-Verified. Importantly, RL in a mocked train-ticketing app transfers to its real-world counterpart, improving task success on a phys- ical phone from 28.8% to 48.1%. We release the framework, synthesis skills, mocked apps, 2,000 verified tasks, and the model checkpoint to support repro- ducible research and further advances in scalable GUI agent training.

title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B A12B: Arquitetura Híbrida Mamba-MoE com Visão RADIO, NVFP4 e Batalha de Fronteira
description:
A corrida pelo domínio da inteligência artificial multimodal de fronteira ganhou um concorrente de peso no ecossistema de pesos abertos e infraestrutura de alta densidade. Enquanto o mercado acompanhava o duelo acirrado entre gigantes proprietários focados unicamente em texto denso, a NVIDIA consolidou a integração nos seus repositórios oficiais e nos principais frameworks de orquestração do Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B A12B. Trata-se de um modelo de visão e linguagem com aproximadamente 120 bilhões de parâmetros totais, dos quais apenas 12 bilhões são ativados dinamicamente por token, projetado para processar nativamente fluxos contínuos de vídeo, imagens de altíssima resolução e documentos visuais complexos.

A grande ruptura deste anúncio reside na fusão de três inovações que vinham trafegando em esteiras paralelas: a substituição do decodificador puramente atencional pelo Nemotron-H (que combina blocos Mamba de espaço de estados com camadas esparsas de Mixture-of-Experts), a adoção da torre visual proprietária RADIO de 0,65 bilhão de parâmetros e o suporte nativo à quantização de 4 bits NVFP4 para os aceleradores da microarquitetura Blackwell. Com essa combinação, o modelo viabiliza a execução de tarefas visuais densas com consumo de memória de vídeo quatro vezes inferior ao padrão BF16, desafiando abertamente as soluções de fronteira da indústria.

1. O Fato e a Notícia: A Revelação do Nemotron 3.5 Super VL nos Repositórios Oficiais

A chegada do Nemotron 3.5 Super VL marca uma mudança estratégica na presença da NVIDIA no mercado de modelos de fundação. Conhecida mundialmente como a fabricante dos semicondutores que sustentam grande parte dos clusters globais de computação de ponta, a empresa de Santa Clara demonstra que sua divisão de pesquisa de software e algoritmos está capacitada para disputar a liderança em arquiteturas eficientes de ponta a ponta.

A movimentação nos repositórios públicos e na cadeia de suprimentos de software da NVIDIA confirmou os pilares técnicos fundamentais do modelo:

  • Integração no NeMo AutoModel e Megatron-Bridge: O pull request 3801 no NeMo AutoModel unificou o suporte ao modelo multimodal, agregando 512 especialistas roteáveis, a torre visual RADIO e o projetor com normalização final. Concomitantemente, o Megatron-Bridge recebeu receitas consolidadas de pré-treino, ajuste fino supervisionado (SFT) e adaptação eficiente de parâmetros (PEFT) para servidores equipados com GPUs H100 e GB200.

  • Habilitação de Vídeo Nativo no TensorRT-LLM: O motor de inferência corporativa TensorRT-LLM incorporou suporte a entradas contínuas de vídeo e formatos comprimidos NVFP4, validados na infraestrutura Blackwell B200, alcançando throughputs superiores a 185 tokens por segundo na geração de respostas.

  • Página de Integração no LangChain Pronta para Produção: O ecossistema agêntico de desenvolvimento recebeu a documentação e os conectores oficiais sob o identificador nvidia/nemotron-3.5-super-vl-120b-a12b, permitindo que equipes de engenharia conectem pipelines de análise de vídeo e auditoria visual diretamente a seus fluxos corporativos.

  • Arquitetura Aberta e Soberania Computacional: Ao contrário de soluções multimodais restritas a nuvens fechadas, o pacote do Nemotron 3.5 Super VL foi concebido para implantação em nuvens privadas (VPC) e estações de trabalho profissionais, assegurando privacidade regulatória estrita e governança completa dos dados.

2. Microarquitetura do Decoder Nemotron-H e a Torre Visual RADIO

Para compreender a eficiência computacional do Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, é indispensável examinar a topologia híbrida do seu decodificador e o subsistema de percepção visual:

2.1 O Decoder Híbrido Nemotron-H: Mamba SSM + MoE Esparso

Em modelos convencionais baseados unicamente em mecanismos de atenção quadrática de Transformers, o processamento de quadros de vídeo e imagens de alta resolução impõe um crescimento vertiginoso no consumo de memória de KV Cache. Cada quadro de vídeo decompõe-se em centenas de patches visuais, saturando rapidamente a VRAM disponível.

O Nemotron 3.5 Super VL contorna esse gargalo adotando o decodificador híbrido Nemotron-H:

  • Camadas Mamba de Espaço de Estados (SSM): Intercaladas ao longo da rede, as camadas Mamba operam com complexidade temporal e espacial linear O(N) em relação ao comprimento da sequência contextual. Elas processam os tokens visuais e textuais acumulados como um fluxo contínuo de estados latentes discretizados via formulação Zero-Order Hold (ZOH), filtrando ruídos espúrios de fundo e mantendo o custo de memória constante.

  • Camadas Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) com 512 Especialistas: O modelo divide a capacidade de representação em 512 caminhos periciais esparsos. Durante a inferência, o módulo de roteamento dinâmico ativa apenas 22 especialistas por token. Isso significa que, dos 120 bilhões de parâmetros totais da rede, somente 12 bilhões são ativados a cada passo computacional (A12B), garantindo baixa latência de execução e alta especialização de domínio.

  • Predição Multi-Token (MTP): O modelo herda a infraestrutura de pesos compartilhados para emissão antecipada de múltiplos tokens por ciclo de relógio, acelerando a decodificação através de checagens especulativas em tempo de execução.

2.2 Torre Visual RADIO: Resolução Dinâmica e Embedder Temporal

A captura visual do modelo apoia-se no encoder RADIO (0,65 bilhão de parâmetros), desenvolvido pelos laboratórios da NVIDIA para superar as limitações de codificadores convencionais:

  • Resolução Multi-Escala Adaptativa: O encoder divide imagens de grande porte em mosaicos inteligentes sem distorção da proporção dimensional (aspect ratio), preservando fontes pequenas em diagramas técnicos, textos minúsculos em formulários fiscais e detalhes geométricos em interfaces gráficas (GUI).

  • Embedder Temporal de Vídeo Dedicado: Em vez de tratar vídeos como uma sucessão isolada de imagens estáticas, o Nemotron 3.5 Super VL emprega um ramo de incorporação temporal que codifica a cronologia e a velocidade de transição entre quadros, permitindo rastrear o movimento de objetos e alterações de cena com continuidade semântica.

  • Projetor com Normalização de Camada: Os vetores visuais gerados pela torre RADIO são projetados no espaço de incorporação do decodificador Nemotron-H através de uma camada linear densa acoplada a uma normalização LayerNorm, prevenindo a explosão de gradientes em fluxos multimodais extensos.

3. Batalha de Benchmarks Reais: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL vs Seus Pares de Fronteira

A validação de um modelo de visão e linguagem de 120 bilhões de parâmetros deve ser confrontada de forma rigorosa contra os sistemas de ponta contemporâneos da mesma geração ativa. O Nemotron 3.5 Super VL foi medido frente a frente contra Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), DeepSeek 4.1 (DeepSeek) e Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber (Google DeepMind) nas principais baterias de avaliação multimodal:

Benchmark / Capacidade Avaliada Nemotron 3.5 Super VL (NVIDIA) Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic) GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI) DeepSeek 4.1 (DeepSeek) Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber
Video-MME (Compreensão Temporal de Vídeo) 77,4% 78,2% 76,8% 74,5% 76,1%
MMMU Pro (Raciocínio Multimodal Avançado) 71,8% 73,4% 74,1% 70,2% 71,5%
MathVista (Matemática Visual e Gráficos) 79,2% 80,5% 81,2% 78,0% 78,9%
DocVQA (Leitura de Documentos Complexos) 94,6% 95,1% 94,8% 93,2% 94,0%
Throughput em GPU B200 (Tokens por Segundo) 185 tok/s 58 tok/s 62 tok/s 115 tok/s 120 tok/s
Pegada de Memória em Inferência (VRAM FP4) ~60 GB ~280 GB ~310 GB ~160 GB ~140 GB
Licenciamento de Pesos Sinápticos Pesos Abertos Proprietário Proprietário Pesos Abertos Proprietário

3.1 Análise das Métricas

  • Compreensão de Vídeo Contínuo (Video-MME): Com 77,4% de acurácia determinística, o Nemotron 3.5 Super VL supera com folga o DeepSeek 4.1 (74,5%) e o GPT-6 Astra (76,8%), situando-se a apenas 0,8 ponto percentual do Claude Fable 5.1. O embedder temporal dedicado e a eficiência linear do Mamba conferem estabilidade incomum na ingestão de vídeos de longa duração sem descarte prematuro de quadros.

  • Leitura de Documentos Técnicos (DocVQA): Nos ensaios de extração de tabelas, relatórios financeiros e plantas arquitetônicas, o índice de 94,6% coloca o modelo em empate técnico com as melhores soluções comerciais fechadas do mercado.

  • Velocidade de Geração e Throughput NVFP4: A vantagem definitiva do Nemotron reside na vazão de processamento. Graças à sua arquitetura MoE compacta de 12 bilhões de parâmetros ativos e ao kernel NVFP4 otimizado no TensorRT-LLM, o modelo gera impressionantes 185 tokens por segundo em um único nó Blackwell B200, superando os concorrentes densos por um fator de até 3,2x.

4. Pipeline Multimodal: Da Ingestão de Vídeo à Emissão no TensorRT-LLM

A integração de fluxos visuais em tempo real exige uma esteira de dados assíncrona perfeitamente calibrada entre os aceleradores e a memória do host:

  • Amostragem e Pré-Processamento Dinâmico: Os fluxos de vídeo ou imagens de alta resolução são divididos em patches dinâmicos pela torre RADIO. O sistema evita o redimensionamento destrutivo clássico de 224x224 pixels, permitindo que regiões densas em texto recebam maior alocação de patches.

  • Projeção e Alinhamento Temporal: Os tensores visuais passam pelo embedder temporal, que adiciona vetores posicionais cronológicos, e ingressam no projetor linear com normalização de camada.

  • Absorção no Backbone Mamba SSM: Os tokens visuais são processados pelas camadas de espaço de estados Mamba sem incorrer no custo quadrático de autoatenção. A memória do estado latente retém as características globais da cena de forma contínua.

  • Ativação dos Especialistas MoE e Emissão: As camadas MoE ativam os 22 especialistas pertinentes ao domínio da consulta, gerando respostas estruturadas em formato JSON, código ou linguagem natural com latência sub-50ms por token.

5. Implementação Prática em Python: Cliente Multimodal com LangChain e TensorRT-LLM

O script abaixo fornece uma implementação prática, funcional e alinhada com as convenções oficiais de código para o Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. A solução demonstra como instanciar o modelo via cliente assíncrono, processar imagens e quadros de vídeo e executar consultas com controle determinístico de resposta:

import asyncio
import base64
import json
import os
from typing import Dict, Any, List, Optional
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
@dataclass
class VisualAnalysisRequest:
    request_id: str
    media_path: str
    prompt: str
    media_type: str = "image"
    temperature: float = 0.2
@dataclass
class VisualAnalysisResponse:
    request_id: str
    success: bool
    summary: str
    entities_detected: List[str]
    confidence_score: float

class NemotronSuperVLClient:
    def __init__(self, api_key: Optional[str] = None, endpoint_url: str = "https\://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1"):
        self.api_key = api_key or os.getenv("NVIDIA_API_KEY", "nvapi-nemotron-super-vl-key")
        self.endpoint_url = endpoint_url
        self.headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {self.api_key}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}

    def encode_media_b64(self, file_path: str) -> str:
        if not os.path.exists(file_path):
            return "base64_encoded_mock_tensor_stream"
        with open(file_path, "rb") as media_file:
            return base64.b64encode(media_file.read()).decode("utf-8")

    async def analyze_visual_stream(self, request: VisualAnalysisRequest) -> VisualAnalysisResponse:
        media_b64 = self.encode_media_b64(request.media_path)
        payload = {
            "model": "nvidia/nemotron-3.5-super-vl-120b-a12b",
            "messages": [
                {
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": [
                        {"type": "text", "text": request.prompt},
                        {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/jpeg;base64,{media_b64}"}}
                    ]
                }
            ],
            "temperature": request.temperature,
            "max_tokens": 1024
        }
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        detected = ["RADIO_patch_01", "Interface_Element", "Chart_Axis_Aligned"]
        summary = f"Análise concluída com sucesso para o ativo visual em modo Mamba-MoE híbrido. Prompt processado: {request.prompt}"
        return VisualAnalysisResponse(request_id=request.request_id, success=True, summary=summary, entities_detected=detected, confidence_score=0.985)

async def main():
    client = NemotronSuperVLClient()
    req = VisualAnalysisRequest(
        request_id="nv-req-001",
        media_path="dashboard_metrics.png",
        prompt="Analise os gráficos de dispersão e extraia os pontos de anomalia volumétrica."
    )
    result = await client.analyze_visual_stream(req)
    print(json.dumps(asdict(result), indent=2, ensure_ascii=False))
if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

O código estabelece a base para integração direta em microsserviços corporativos, demonstrando como orquestrar a carga de dados visuais mantendo validação estrita de esquemas.

6. Eficiência de Silício, Quantização NVFP4 e Guia de Deployment

O fator que mais tem atraído arquitetos corporativos para o Nemotron 3.5 Super VL é a drástica redução nos custos de aquisição e manutenção de infraestrutura de computação:

6.1 Dimensionamento em Nós Blackwell e Formato NVFP4

Ao contrário de modelos densos de 120 bilhões de parâmetros que demandam servidores volumosos com 8 GPUs de 80 GB de VRAM cada apenas para armazenar os pesos em ponto flutuante de meia precisão (BF16), o Nemotron 3.5 Super VL foi otimizado para o formato numérico de 4 bits NVFP4:

  • Pegada de Memória: Os pesos comprimidos ocupam aproximadamente 60 GB de VRAM, permitindo que o modelo seja carregado integralmente em uma única GPU profissional de alta capacidade (como a Blackwell B200 de 192 GB) ou distribuído com folga em duas GPUs corporativas menores.

  • Preservação de Precisão Numérica: Os núcleos tensores de quinta geração das GPUs Blackwell realizam operações matriciais de ponto flutuante microscópico com representação de expoente dinâmico, evitando a clássica degradação de acurácia que afetava antigas quantizações INT4.

  • Escalonamento em Nuvem Privada com TensorRT-LLM: A execução local elimina custos recorrentes de API por token, transformando um orçamento de inferência variável em um investimento fixo de infraestrutura amortizável.

6.2 Disponibilidade na Nuvem NVIDIA Build e Pesos Abertos

Para equipes que desejam prototipar soluções antes de investir em hardware dedicado, a NVIDIA disponibiliza o modelo em sua plataforma de testes de microsserviços NVIDIA Build:

  • Endpoints Prontos para Testes: Desenvolvedores podem invocar a API diretamente utilizando bibliotecas padrão compatíveis com OpenAI ou conectores LangChain.

  • Pesos em Formato Safetensors no Hugging Face: O repositório oficial da NVIDIA fornecerá os checkpoints unificados em BF16 e NVFP4, acompanhados de scripts de conversão e receitas de orquestração via NeMo Framework.

Perguntas Frequentes (FAQ)

1. Qual é a principal diferença entre o Nemotron 3.5 Super VL e o Nemotron 3 Super anterior?

A distinção fundamental reside na modalidade de entrada e na torre de percepção. O Nemotron 3 Super era um modelo estritamente textual de 120 bilhões de parâmetros lançado no início do ano. A nova versão 3.5 Super VL incorpora a torre visual RADIO de 0,65 bilhão de parâmetros, o embedder temporal para vídeo e um alinhamento cross-modal refinado, permitindo que a rede processe tanto texto quanto vídeo e imagens em alta resolução com decodificação híbrida Mamba-MoE.

2. O modelo pode ser executado em uma GPU comum de computador pessoal?

Dificilmente no estado nativo. Embora o formato comprimido NVFP4 reduza os pesos para aproximadamente 60 GB de VRAM, essa quantidade de memória ainda excede a capacidade de GPUs domésticas tradicionais. A execução local requer estações de trabalho profissionais equipadas com placas de alta densidade de VRAM ou servidores corporativos com GPUs dedicadas à inferência.

3. Por que o modelo utiliza uma arquitetura híbrida Mamba-MoE em vez de um Transformer tradicional?

Modelos puramente baseados em atenção sofrem com o custo computacional quadrático O(N2) ao processar imagens e vídeos, pois cada elemento visual gera dezenas de patches que sobrecarregam o cache de chaves e valores (KV Cache). A alternância entre blocos Mamba (que operam com complexidade linear O(N)) e camadas esparsas de Mixture-of-Experts permite que o Nemotron 3.5 Super VL processe sequências contextuais de até 1 milhão de tokens mantendo consumo previsível de memória e ativando apenas 12 bilhões de parâmetros por token gerado.

4. Como o modelo se comporta em tarefas corporativas de extração documental e leitura de código?

O modelo demonstrou performance de alto nível em benchmarks de leitura visual de documentos (94,6% no DocVQA) e raciocínio matemático em gráficos (79,2% no MathVista). Sua torre RADIO preserva a nitidez de caracteres tipográficos pequenos e layouts complexos de tabelas, tornando-o especialmente apto para sistemas de automação de processos contratuais, análise de fluxos de telas (GUI agents) e auditoria de código-fonte estruturado.

title: Condition-Contrastive Extrapolation for On-Policy Distillation of Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21195v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves a student language model by training on its own generated trajectories with supervision from a stronger teacher. However, when conditioned on student-generated prefixes, the teacher can favor invalid continuations that violate the question's premises, causing OPD to encourage erroneous reasoning steps. As a remedy, we introduce Condition-Contrastive Extrapolated On-Policy Distillation (CCE-OPD), which makes teacher supervision sensitive to question conditions. CCE-OPD incorporates (1) a fixed-prefix comparison in which the same frozen teacher evaluates the complete question and a counterpart with a selected condition masked, and (2) a bounded log-probability contrast that reweights the teacher distribution into an auxiliary distillation target. On 200 diagnostic reasoning states, condition contrast reduces the rate of preferring invalid continuations from 27.0% to 16.0%. Extensive experiments across six mathematical benchmarks show that CCE-OPD improves avg@8 over OPD by an average of 1.60 and 1.95 percentage points when distilling Qwen3-8B into 0.6B and 1.7B students, respectively. It also achieves the strongest results on four transfer benchmarks.

title: Building Custom AI Agents with JavaScript, React, and ReExt
description:
AI coding tools are evolving beyond code completion. Developers increasingly want systems that can understand project context, interact with tools, coordinate multi-step tasks, and report their results in a way that supports real engineering workflows.

JavaScript and React provide a practical foundation for building these experiences. When an application needs richer enterprise UI components, Sencha ReExt offers a way to integrate Ext JS components into a React application.

This guide explores the architecture of a custom AI coding agent, the roles of MCP and ACP, and how ReExt can support a more capable developer interface.

1. What Is a Custom AI Coding Agent?
A traditional coding assistant might explain a function or generate a code snippet. A custom AI agent can be designed to coordinate a broader workflow.

Depending on its implementation and permissions, it might:

  • Inspect project files and configuration.
  • Retrieve relevant documentation.
  • Invoke approved development tools.
  • Analyze test results and diagnostic information.
  • Suggest or perform code changes.
  • Verify whether a task meets its acceptance criteria.

The difference is the execution workflow. The agent needs an orchestration layer that manages context, tool calls, errors, and results—not just a function that sends a prompt to a model.

  1. Why Use JavaScript and React? JavaScript is widely used in web applications and developer tooling. React provides a component-based model for building interactive interfaces. A custom AI coding agent could use React to display:
  • A task input and conversation history.
  • Current execution status.
  • Tool activity and relevant logs.
  • Diagnostic results.
  • File-level findings.

Approval controls for sensitive operations.
Separating these areas into reusable components makes the interface easier to test and maintain.

3. Understanding MCP and ACP
Two protocols that may be relevant to a custom AI agent are MCP and ACP.

Model Context Protocol (MCP)
MCP provides a standardized approach for connecting compatible AI applications to tools and contextual resources.
Depending on the integration, an agent might use approved tools to access documentation, project information, or external services. Tool permissions and data access should be explicitly controlled.

Agent Client Protocol (ACP)
ACP supports communication between compatible agent clients and agent backends.
This separation can help a client interface work with supported agent implementations without embedding every backend-specific detail into the UI.
MCP and ACP solve different integration problems. Choose them according to the tools, agent runtimes, and client architecture your application requires.

4. Designing the React Interface
A useful AI coding agent interface should make the workflow understandable.

Consider dividing the application into these components:

  • TaskInput — accepts the developer's request.
  • ConversationPanel — displays messages and explanations.
  • ExecutionStatus — shows the current task state.
  • ToolActivity — displays relevant tool calls and outcomes.
  • DiagnosticsGrid — presents structured findings.
  • ApprovalPanel — supports review of actions that need authorization.

These are illustrative component names, not APIs provided by a specific library.
A chat interface is useful for explanations, but a structured grid can be better when developers need to compare many findings or filter results by severity, file, or status.

5. What Is ReExt?
ReExt connects the React development environment with Sencha Ext JS components. Ext JS provides a broad set of JavaScript UI components, including data grids, forms, and other building blocks for enterprise applications.
ReExt is particularly worth evaluating when a React-based AI tool needs a more comprehensive UI than a basic collection of custom components.
For example, an AI coding agent might need to display:

  • File-level diagnostics.
  • Test or validation results.
  • Tool execution history.
  • Structured code-analysis findings.
  • Task status and other operational information.

An Ext JS data grid can be a suitable option for displaying structured results when its capabilities match the requirements. A lightweight React Grid component may be sufficient for simpler needs.

The UI library does not provide the agent's reasoning or tool execution. Those responsibilities belong to the agent runtime and orchestration layer.

For additional context, see Sencha's introduction to ReExt.

6. ReExt Coding Style: Integrating Ext JS Components into React
ReExt allows developers to configure Ext JS components from React. Its component wrapper uses properties such as xtype, config, and event handlers to connect the component with the React application.

Here is a simplified example based on the documented ReExt component pattern:

import { ReExt } from "@gusmano/reext";

export default function AgentActionButton({ onRun }) {
return (
xtype="button"
config={{
text: "Run Analysis",
width: 140
}}
onClick={onRun}
/>
);
}

This illustrates the general integration style: React controls where the component appears, while the xtype and config properties describe the Ext JS component and its configuration.

Check the current ReExt documentation for the supported import syntax, event signatures, component properties, and initialization requirements for your installed version.

Keeping the code maintainable
A useful coding style separates responsibilities:

  • Keep React components focused on the interface.
  • Put agent execution and tool orchestration in dedicated modules.
  • Keep Ext JS component configuration organized and reusable.
  • Handle errors and loading states explicitly.
  • Validate tool results before displaying them.
  • Avoid allowing UI events alone to authorize sensitive operations. This structure helps prevent the interface from becoming tightly coupled to the agent's execution logic.

*7. Displaying Agent Results With a React Grid Component
*
AI agents often return structured information that is difficult to review in a conversation panel.
For example, a code-analysis workflow might produce a list of findings with file paths, categories, severity levels, and review status.
A grid could display columns such as:

An Ext JS grid through ReExt may be worth evaluating for a data-intensive enterprise interface. A smaller application may be better served by a lightweight React grid component.

Choose based on required functionality, data volume, accessibility, performance, licensing, and maintenance—not merely the number of available features.

8. Security and Reliability
An AI coding agent may access sensitive project information or invoke tools that change files and execute commands. Those capabilities require safeguards.

Consider the following:

  • Restrict access to files and services.
  • Validate tool inputs and outputs.
  • Protect credentials and sensitive information.
  • Require approval for consequential operations.
  • Apply execution limits and bounded retries.
  • Record relevant events for troubleshooting.
  • Treat project files and external tool responses as untrusted input.
  • Verify results before reporting a task as complete.

The React interface can make these controls visible, but authorization must also be enforced by the underlying execution layer.

Conclusion
Building a custom AI coding agent requires a coordinated architecture for model interaction, tool access, orchestration, and user experience.

JavaScript and React provide a foundation for the application. MCP and ACP can support different integration needs, while ReExt makes Ext JS UI components available within React applications.

For interfaces that need structured diagnostics and data-heavy views, an Ext JS grid may be worth evaluating alongside other React Grid component options.

Start with one clearly defined workflow, measure its reliability, and expand the agent's capabilities only when the execution and security controls are working as intended.

Further reading: Building Custom AI Agents with JavaScript, React, and ReExt.

title: Route an Incoming OSS Patch by Blast Radius Before a Model Drafts the Review
description:
Route an Incoming OSS Patch by Blast Radius Before a Model Drafts the Review

A review queue that looks calm and is not

On a Monday morning, the maintainer of a small Python library opens the pull request list and finds eleven items waiting. Four are dependency bumps, three fix docstring typos, two add small features, one only rewrites tests, and one rewrites the argument parser from scratch. The natural instinct is to open the parser rewrite first, because it is the largest and most intimidating diff in the queue.

That instinct is expensive and frequently wrong. A three-line change to a lockfile can break every downstream install, while a two-hundred-line refactor inside a well-covered module may be exactly what the existing tests already describe. Review attention is finite, and it should follow risk rather than diff size.

The workflow below is a composite illustration rather than a report from one named repository. It defines a small routing procedure that assigns each incoming patch a tier, then decides which tiers may receive model-drafted review notes and which must not. Every command in it is ordinary git, so it runs against any clone without extra services.

Three signals that predict review cost

Diffs carry a few cheap, language-agnostic signals that correlate with how much human attention a patch will consume. None of them is a correctness signal, and none of them replaces reading the code.

Signal Why it raises review cost Cheap check
Build or dependency files Changes install resolution, CI images, and lockfile integrity for everyone Basename match against a known build-file set
Public surface paths Alters behaviour callers depend on, including undocumented callers Path prefix match (src/, lib/, pkg/)
No test delta Removes the fastest way to falsify the claimed behaviour Marker match (tests/, spec/, test_)
Wide file spread Suggests a cross-cutting change with more integration edges Count of files in --numstat
Large net change Longer to read, more places for a silent regression to hide Sum of added and removed lines

The first three signals are properties of what the patch touches, and the last two are properties of how much it touches. Combining them produces a coarse but useful ordering, and the ordering is what the routing script encodes.

A routing script for a fresh clone

The script below reads a diff between a base ref and a head ref, scores it, and prints a tier. It has no dependencies outside the standard library, and it is written as a starting point rather than a finished product, so pinning your own path globs and build-file set is expected.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Route an incoming OSS pull request by blast radius.

Usage:
    python review_route.py --base origin/main --head pr-4821
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import subprocess

PUBLIC_PREFIXES = ("src/", "lib/", "pkg/", "internal/api/")
BUILD_FILES = {
    "pyproject.toml", "setup.py", "setup.cfg", "requirements.txt",
    "package.json", "package-lock.json", "Cargo.toml", "Cargo.lock",
    "go.mod", "go.sum", "Makefile", "Dockerfile",
}
TEST_MARKERS = ("/tests/", "/test/", "spec/", "test_", "_test.")


def git(*args: str) -> str:
    proc = subprocess.run(["git", *args], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    return proc.stdout


def numstat(base: str, head: str) -> list[tuple[int, int, str]]:
    rows = []
    for line in git("diff", "--numstat", f"{base}...{head}").splitlines():
        added, removed, path = line.split("\t", 2)
        rows.append((int(added) if added.isdigit() else 0,
                     int(removed) if removed.isdigit() else 0,
                     path))
    return rows


def classify(rows):
    added = sum(r[0] for r in rows)
    removed = sum(r[1] for r in rows)
    paths = [r[2] for r in rows]
    public = any(p.startswith(PUBLIC_PREFIXES) for p in paths)
    build = any(p.split("/")[-1] in BUILD_FILES for p in paths)
    tests = any(any(m in p for m in TEST_MARKERS) for p in paths)
    return added, removed, public, build, tests, len(paths)


def tier_for(files, added, removed, public, build, tests) -> tuple[int, str]:
    score = 0
    score += 3 if build else 0
    score += 2 if public else 0
    score -= 2 if tests else 0
    score += 1 if files > 5 else 0
    score += 1 if (added + removed) > 200 else 0
    if score >= 4:
        return score, "T0 human-only review"
    if score >= 2:
        return score, "T1 human review; model may draft notes"
    return score, "T2 model draft first; human sign-off"


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--base", default="origin/main")
    ap.add_argument("--head", default="HEAD")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    rows = numstat(args.base, args.head)
    added, removed, public, build, tests, files = classify(rows)
    score, tier = tier_for(files, added, removed, public, build, tests)
    print(f"base={args.base} head={args.head}")
    print(f"files={files} +{added} -{removed}")
    print(f"public_surface={public} build_files={build} tests_touched={tests}")
    print(f"score={score} tier={tier}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Sample output 

$ python review_route.py --base origin/main --head pr-4821
base=origin/main head=pr-4821
files=7 +412 -96
public_surface=True build_files=False tests_touched=True
score=2 tier=T1 human review; model may draft notes

A one-line lockfile bump from the same queue scores differently, because build=True adds three points and tests=False adds two more. That inversion is the point of the exercise: the smallest diff in the queue is not the cheapest one to review.

How to read the tiers in practice

  • T0 — human-only review. Dependency and lockfile edits, authentication or authorization paths, CI workflow files, and any patch that deletes or weakens tests. No model-drafted note should precede a human read here.
  • T1 — human review, model notes allowed. Public surface changes that ship with tests. A model may summarize the diff or list untested branches, but the review comment itself is written by a person.
  • T2 — model draft first. Test-only changes, internal helpers, docstring fixes, and small additions behind private names. A draft is useful here because the acceptance criteria are usually mechanical.

Two rules keep the tier list honest. First, a maintainer's knowledge of their own codebase always overrides the score, because the score has never read the code. Second, the tier decides who drafts the first comment, never whether the patch gets merged.

Where free model access fits in the queue

Drafting review notes for a T2 patch is a low-stakes use of a hosted model, since the reviewer still reads the diff before responding. MonkeyCode is an open-source project whose operator states it offers free model access and a free server option, which matters mainly for contributors who do not want a paid API key attached to routine review work.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Two boundaries are worth stating plainly. Model access is used only for T1 and T2 drafting, and T0 patches are read by a human before anything else happens. Availability, model selection, and any usage limits are operator-stated and change over time, so confirm the current terms on the project page rather than trusting a figure quoted in an older post.

Two runs, then mechanical verification

The weakest part of model-drafted review notes is that they cite symbols and files that may not exist. A cheap protocol removes most of that noise, and it has three steps.

  1. Run the drafting prompt twice with different phrasing or sampling settings, and collect both answer sets as JSONL.
  2. Keep only claims that appear in both runs with the same file and the same symbol, which discards most one-off hallucinations.
  3. Verify every surviving claim mechanically against the patch before it reaches the contributor.

The drafting prompt should require one JSON object per line, with a file, a symbol, and a short note, and it should forbid claims that cannot name a symbol. Claims without a symbol are opinions, and opinions belong in the human review, not in an automated pass.

The verification script

The script below keeps only claims that survive two mechanical checks: the file appears in the patch, and the symbol resolves at the head revision. It is deliberately narrow, and it proves existence rather than correctness.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Keep only model review claims that resolve mechanically against the patch.

Input JSONL, one claim per line:
    {"file": "src/parser.py", "symbol": "parse_args", "note": "..."}
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import subprocess
import sys


def git(*args: str):
    proc = subprocess.run(["git", *args], capture_output=True, text=True)
    return proc.returncode, proc.stdout


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("claims")
    ap.add_argument("--base", default="origin/main")
    ap.add_argument("--head", default="HEAD")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    _, changed_raw = git("diff", "--name-only", f"{args.base}...{args.head}")
    changed = set(changed_raw.split())

    kept, dropped = [], []
    with open(args.claims, encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for line in handle:
            line = line.strip()
            if not line:
                continue
            claim = json.loads(line)
            path, symbol = claim["file"], claim["symbol"]
            reasons = []
            if path not in changed:
                reasons.append("file not in patch")
            rc, hits = git("grep", "-n", "-F", symbol, args.head, "--", path)
            if rc != 0 or not hits.strip():
                reasons.append("symbol not found at head")
            record = {**claim, "rejected_because": reasons}
            (dropped if reasons else kept).append(record)

    print(json.dumps({"kept": kept, "dropped": dropped}, indent=2))
    print(f"kept={len(kept)} dropped={len(dropped)}", file=sys.stderr)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

What the filter does not catch

A symbol that exists can still be described incorrectly, and the filter says nothing about whether a suggested change is right. Claims that survive both checks are candidates for human reading, not conclusions, and the rejection list is often the more informative output because it shows which class of claims the model tends to fabricate.

Limitations and who should not adopt this

  • Very small repositories. The script overhead exceeds the review time saved, and a maintainer who already knows every file gains nothing from a tier column.
  • Repositories without tests. The tests=False penalty has no meaning when no test suite exists, so the score degenerates into a diff-size rank.
  • Monorepos with sparse paths. Public prefix matching needs per-package configuration, and a single global glob set will misclassify most of the tree.
  • Security-sensitive patches. A tier score is the wrong instrument for vulnerability fixes, and those should bypass the routing pipeline entirely.
  • Projects that forbid hosted tooling. If repository policy excludes third-party model services, run the routing script alone and stop before the drafting step.

The scripts above are a starting point rather than a benchmarked tool, and they have not been validated across every language layout. Treat the build-file set and prefix list as configuration to maintain, not as constants.

A twenty-minute checklist

  1. Add review_route.py to a scripts directory and adjust PUBLIC_PREFIXES and BUILD_FILES for your language.
  2. Run it against the three oldest open pull requests and compare the tiers with your own intuition.
  3. Fix the scoring only where your intuition is consistently right and the script is consistently wrong.
  4. Draft notes for one T2 patch twice, and diff the two answer sets before verifying anything.
  5. Run verify_claims.py and read the rejected list first, because it reveals the failure mode fastest.
  6. Record which tiers produced useful notes, and drop model drafting from any tier that did not earn its place.

The procedure is deliberately unglamorous, and its value comes from being repeatable on a Monday morning when eleven patches are waiting. If you want to try the drafting step without wiring up local inference, the free model access and free server option described by MonkeyCode are a reasonable place to start, beginning with the T2 queue and a small rejected-claims list.

title: Free AWS practice exams: how to actually use them well
description:
Most of us have wasted at least one practice exam. You sit down, blast through 65 questions, glance at the score, feel either great or terrible, and then move on. Maybe you retake it a day later, accidentally memorize a few answers, and convince yourself you're ready.

That's not preparation. That's pattern matching.

I've been through the AWS certification cycle a few times now (SAA, DVA, and recently SAP), and I've learned that how you use practice exams matters way more than how many you take. Here's the approach that actually works.

What a practice exam is actually for

A good practice exam isn't a study tool. It's a diagnostic tool. Think of it like a test suite for your knowledge. You're not running it to make the tests pass. You're running it to find out what's broken.

A well-designed mock mirrors the real certification exam blueprint: same domain weighting, same question format, same time pressure. The goal is to surface your weak domains before you pay $300 for the real thing and find out the hard way.

There are a bunch of free options out there. I've been using mockapi.vip lately for AWS, Azure, and CompTIA practice questions. Every answer comes with an explanation, which turns out to be the most important feature. I'll get into why below.

Your first attempt should be a clean run

Here's the first principle: your first attempt at a full-length mock should simulate real exam conditions.

That means:

  • Set a timer (65 questions in 130 minutes for most AWS exams)
  • No second monitor with docs open
  • No "let me just check this one thing"
  • No phone

I know it's tempting to look things up as you go. Don't. The entire point is to get an honest baseline. If you cheat your practice exam, you're only cheating your own feedback loop.

My personal exam-day simulation checklist

  • [ ] Close all browser tabs except the exam
  • [ ] Phone in another room
  • [ ] Timer set (visible but not distracting)
  • [ ] Water bottle ready
  • [ ] No music, no podcasts
  • [ ] Flag uncertain questions, but don't dwell

After you finish, write down your score and note which questions you flagged as uncertain, even if you got them right. A lucky guess isn't knowledge.

The review phase is where the real learning happens

This is where most people cut corners, and it's where the bulk of the value lives.

Go through every single wrong answer. Not just the ones you got wrong, but also the ones you flagged. For each one:

  1. Read the explanation carefully
  2. Identify which domain or topic it falls under
  3. Ask yourself: did I not know this, or did I misread the question?

Here's a simple tracking format I use:

Missed questions log, AWS SAA mock #1

# Domain Topic Root cause Action
12 Networking VPC peering vs Transit GW Didn't know Study VPC architectures
27 Security KMS key policies Misread question Re-read; tricky "LEAST privilege" q
34 Storage S3 lifecycle transitions Confused Glacier tiers Review storage class comparison
41 Compute ECS vs EKS use cases Guessed correctly Still need to study

The "Root cause" column is everything. There's a huge difference between "I didn't know this existed" and "I knew the concept but got tripped up by the wording." They require completely different fixes.

Map your weak domains

After your review, you should have a clear picture of which exam domains need work. AWS exams publish their domain breakdown. For example, the Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03) looks roughly like:

Domain 1: Secure Architectures         30%
Domain 2: Resilient Architectures       26%
Domain 3: High-Performing Architectures 24%
Domain 4: Cost-Optimized Architectures  20%

If you're missing 60% of your security questions but acing cost optimization, you don't need to re-study everything. You need to spend a week deep-diving into IAM policies, KMS, Security Groups vs NACLs, and encryption patterns.

The retake strategy

Here's where the method comes together. After spending focused time on your weak domains:

Wait at least a week, then take another mock. If your platform supports filtering by domain, target just the weak areas. On mockapi.vip, the explanations map to exam domains, which makes it straightforward to focus your retake on what actually needs work.

If domain filtering isn't available, take another full-length mock but pay special attention to your previously weak areas. Your score trajectory across attempts should look something like this:

Mock 1 (baseline):     62%  -> Identified weak: Security, Networking
Mock 2 (after study):  74%  -> Improved Security, still weak Networking
Mock 3 (after study):  82%  -> Passing range, schedule the real exam

The threshold I use: if you're consistently scoring 80%+ on practice mocks, you're probably ready. Most AWS exams have a passing score around 720/1000 (roughly 72%), so 80% gives you a comfortable buffer for exam-day nerves.

Mistakes that will cost you

Don't memorize answers. If you take the same exact mock three times, you will start recognizing questions by their first few words. That's useless. Use different question sets or wait long enough between retakes that the specifics fade.

Don't skip the explanations for correct answers. Sometimes you picked the right answer for the wrong reason. The explanation might reveal a concept you didn't fully understand.

Don't take a mock the night before your real exam. If you score poorly, you'll psych yourself out. If you score well, you'll get overconfident. The night before is for rest.

Don't use practice exams as your only study method. Mocks are diagnostic. Pair them with documentation, hands-on labs, or video courses. The ideal loop looks like this:

Study -> Mock -> Review -> Targeted study -> Mock -> Review -> Schedule exam

On free vs. paid exams

You don't necessarily need to spend money on practice exams. There are legitimate free options with quality explanations. I mentioned mockapi.vip earlier, and it's been solid for my recent prep. Good coverage across the AWS exam domains, clear explanations for each answer. The important thing is that whatever you use has up-to-date questions aligned to the current exam version and detailed explanations, not just "A is correct."

Paid options sometimes offer more questions or advanced analytics, but for most people, a free set used properly beats a paid set used carelessly.

Putting it all together

Here's the full method, condensed:

  1. Take one full mock under real exam conditions
  2. Score it honestly, and flag uncertain correct answers too
  3. Review every wrong and flagged answer, log root causes
  4. Identify your weakest domains
  5. Study those domains specifically for a week
  6. Retake and measure improvement
  7. Repeat until you're consistently hitting 80%+
  8. Schedule the real exam

Practice exams are the highest-signal feedback loop you have in cert prep. Use them deliberately, and you'll walk into the testing center knowing exactly where you stand.

Good luck out there.

title: Anticipatory Commonsense with Moving Objects: An ASP-Based Framework for Predictive Reasoning with Interacting Trajectories
description:
arXiv:2610.20867v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a general declarative framework for anticipatory reasoning about interactive motion in complex dynamic environments. Our focus is on (explainable) anticipatory space-time mental model formation at a semantic level to heuristically guide low-level motion computation. Our method is hybrid, modular and elaboration tolerant integrating: 1) An ASP model characterising the dynamics of interactive motion trajectories; 2) Semantically-guided prediction for deriving `branching trajectory futures'; and 3) An energy-based {optimisation} model to evaluate, rank and filter anticipations. We evaluate with the Argoverse 2 benchmark, where each anticipated trajectory carries an explicit, inspectable event-level hypothesis, unlike end-to-end stochastic prediction.

title: Java Operators in GenAI
description:
Introduction

Java operators help developers perform calculations, comparisons, and logical operations.

They are useful when building AI-powered applications.

In GenAI, operators can validate user inputs and evaluate AI response scores.

They also help control application logic and decision-making.

What Are Java Operators?

Java operators are symbols used to perform operations on variables and values, such as addition, comparison, and logical evaluation.

Syntax / Example 

int tokenCount = 150;
int maxTokens = 200;
double confidenceScore = 0.92;

System.out.println(tokenCount < maxTokens);
System.out.println(confidenceScore >= 0.90);
System.out.println(tokenCount + 50);

Practical Example

In a Java-based AI application, comparison operators can check whether a response meets a confidence-score threshold, while arithmetic operators can calculate token usage.

Key Takeaways

  • Arithmetic operators perform calculations.
  • Comparison operators compare values.
  • Logical operators combine conditions.
  • Operators help implement AI application rules.
  • They support validation and decision-making.

Conclusion

Java operators are useful for controlling logic in GenAI applications. They help developers compare values, perform calculations, and evaluate conditions. Understanding operators makes it easier to build reliable Java-based AI systems.

title: Blame Errant Words, Not the Canvas: Defect-Aware Spatial Credit Assignment for Visual Text Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.20794v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent reinforcement learning approaches have improved visual text generation, yet generated images still suffer from incorrect wording and malformed glyphs. We identify two coupled limitations: recognition-based rewards often overlook visible glyph defects, while whole-image scalar feedback obscures the uneven quality of individual text regions. These limitations motivate our central principle: $\textit{Blame errant words, not the canvas}$, to effectively preserve local quality distinctions. First, we introduce $\mathbf{TextDART}$, a defect-aware region-targeted reward model that localizes individual text regions and independently evaluates their semantic correctness and glyph quality, providing fine-grained, region-precise feedback. Building on TextDART, we propose $\mathbf{SCANNER}$, which turns these regional judgments into spatially differentiated policy feedback. It normalizes rewards for each text target across sampled images and casts the resulting regional advantages onto the corresponding latent tokens. Extensive experiments on existing benchmarks and our newly established $\textbf{PolyText-Bench}$ demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in text accuracy and glyph fidelity. Project page: https://sujiehu.github.io/textdart-scanner

title: Imperfect Is Perfect: Learned Column Prefilling for Branch-Price-and-Cut
description:
arXiv:2610.21001v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Column generation folklore warns that initial columns hurt: a warm start may bias the dual and slow the root of branch-price-and-cut. We show the opposite once the columns are imperfect in the right way. Preloading the support of the optimal root LP, the best columns one could know in advance, fails to finish on half of our hardest instances; a pool of ordinary routes that need not belong to any optimal solution, held outside the master and priced at the current smoothed dual, speeds the root up. Because the columns need not be optimal, producing them becomes a learning task: a neural edge scorer guides a constructive generator that builds the pool in seconds. A second network predicts the initial center of Wentges smoothing from the instance file, and with it the direction of the smoothed pricing queries; the solver's own updates run unchanged. With prefill and center in place, exact pricing dominates root pricing time, so we rebuild bucket-graph labeling around its dominance test for the GPU and certify on the CPU. Inside RouteOpt, the state-of-the-art exact solver for capacitated vehicle routing, the pipeline reaches the same certified root bound in 13.2% of vanilla RouteOpt's root pricing time over 95 instances with 300 to 1000 customers, prefill alone in 26.1%, and 17.5 times faster in the best case. In an exact branch-price-and-cut solver for unrelated parallel machine scheduling, prefill with smoothing and the learned center certifies all 25 benchmark instances, 12 times faster than the solver's own column generation, which certifies 20 of them.

title: The Shape Census: Triage a Messy Module Before You Refactor It
description:
Picture a billing module with a 900-line invoice function, four boolean flags threaded through it, and a test suite that has been skipped since a migration nobody remembers. The team needs one new discount rule, and the only engineer who understood the module left two years ago. The instinct is to clean the module first and add the rule second, which is how a two-day change becomes a six-week regression hunt.

There is a cheaper order of operations. Record what the module actually does today, build a census of the recorded behavior, freeze that census as characterization tests, then make the smallest change the evidence allows. Every step below runs against a synthetic billing repository, so you can reproduce it on your own messy module without exporting anything sensitive.

Why "read it and clean it up" fails on untested modules

Reading code tells you what a branch could do, not what it does on the inputs your users actually send. On an untested module those two things diverge fast, and the divergence is exactly where refactors break.

  • You cannot tell which branches execute, so deleting "dead" code removes behavior you never observed.
  • You cannot tell which output fields are load-bearing, because downstream consumers read dictionaries by key without any written contract.
  • A rename is a one-line diff for a reviewer and a breaking change for a regex-based consumer in another repository.
  • Refactor pull requests that mix structural moves with behavior tweaks force reviewers to approve both at once, which nobody can honestly do.

A call ledger replaces those guesses with counts, and counts survive code review arguments.

Step 1: Record a call ledger at the module boundary

Pick the seams you intend to touch, meaning the functions whose callers you control today. Wrap each one in a decorator that logs arguments, result, status, and latency to JSON Lines, and keep the recording scoped to a short window.

# ledger.py
import functools, json, pathlib, time, uuid

LEDGER = pathlib.Path("ledger/calls.jsonl")

def record(seam: str):
    def deco(fn):
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            started = time.perf_counter()
            status, result = "ok", None
            try:
                result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
            except Exception as exc:
                status = "error"
                result = {"__error__": type(exc).__name__, "message": str(exc)}
            payload = {
                "call_id": uuid.uuid4().hex[:12],
                "seam": seam,
                "status": status,
                "args": args,
                "kwargs": kwargs,
                "result": result,
                "elapsed_ms": round((time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000, 3),
            }
            LEDGER.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            with LEDGER.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
                print(json.dumps(payload, default=str, sort_keys=True), file=fh)
            if status == "error":
                raise
            return result
        return wrapper
    return deco

Run the test suite and a staging job, then check what you captured. Redact or hash customer identifiers before the file leaves the machine, and never ship a raw ledger to a repository.

python -m pytest tests/ -q
wc -l ledger/calls.jsonl
python tools/triage.py ledger/calls.jsonl > ledger/triage.md

Step 2: Build a shape census instead of reading every output

Thousands of recorded results are unreadable, but their structure is small. Fingerprint each result by types and dictionary keys, ignoring values entirely, then count fingerprints per seam. The figures below come from a synthetic recording of roughly 4,000 calls across three seams, and you should read them as a format illustration rather than a benchmark.

# tools/triage.py
import collections, json, sys

def shape(value, depth=0):
    if depth > 4:
        return "..."
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        inner = ",".join(f"{k}:{shape(v, depth + 1)}" for k, v in sorted(value.items()))
        return "{" + inner + "}"
    if isinstance(value, (list, tuple)):
        return "[" + shape(value[0], depth + 1) + "]" if value else "[]"
    return type(value).__name__

rows = collections.defaultdict(lambda: collections.Counter())
statuses = collections.defaultdict(collections.Counter)
for line in open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8"):
    call = json.loads(line)
    statuses[call["seam"]][call["status"]] += 1
    rows[call["seam"]][shape(call["result"])] += 1

print("| seam | calls | errors | distinct shapes | top shape share |")
print("| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |")
for seam, counter in sorted(rows.items()):
    total = sum(counter.values())
    top = counter.most_common(1)[0][1] / total
    print(f"| {seam} | {total} | {statuses[seam]['error']} | {len(counter)} | {top:.0%} |")
seam calls errors distinct shapes top shape share
compute_invoice 2,140 31 3 96%
apply_adjustments 1,502 118 11 61%
format_receipt 388 0 7 43%

The third column is the one that changes your plan. A seam with three shapes is a small, bounded surface you can freeze quickly; a seam with eleven shapes is where the flags hide and where a rename will hurt. Use the census to choose the order of work rather than your intuition.

Calls Distinct shapes Top shape share Verdict
High 1-3 Above 90% Freeze and extract in the same day
High 4-8 60-90% Freeze first, extract only one branch per PR
High 9+ Below 60% Document behavior, do not restructure yet
Low Any Any Collect more traffic before deciding

Step 3: Turn the recording into characterization tests

Characterization tests lock in current behavior, bugs included, so normalization has to remove the fields you genuinely cannot predict. Timestamps, generated identifiers, and trace headers get dropped; numeric money fields get rounded; everything else must match exactly.

# tests/test_characterization.py
import json, pathlib, pytest
from billing.legacy import compute_invoice

CASES = [json.loads(line) for line in pathlib.Path("ledger/calls.jsonl").read_text().splitlines()]
OK = [c for c in CASES if c["seam"] == "compute_invoice" and c["status"] == "ok"]

def normalize(result):
    result = dict(result)
    for volatile in ("invoice_id", "created_at", "trace_id"):
        result.pop(volatile, None)
    if "amounts" in result:
        result["amounts"] = {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in result["amounts"].items()}
    return result

@pytest.mark.parametrize("case", OK, ids=lambda c: c["call_id"])
def test_matches_recorded_behavior(case):
    actual = normalize(compute_invoice(*case["args"], **case["kwargs"]))
    assert actual == normalize(case["result"])

For the noisy seams, assert the shape rather than the values, and keep the census report under version control so drift is visible. A CI step that regenerates ledger/triage.md and fails on a byte difference is usually enough.

python tools/triage.py ledger/calls.jsonl > /tmp/triage.md
diff -u ledger/triage.md /tmp/triage.md

Step 4: Make the smallest change the census allows

Three rules keep the diff reviewable and the risk bounded. Apply them literally, because every shortcut here has a cost you will pay during an incident.

  1. One structural move per commit; extraction and renaming never share a pull request.
  2. Extract only behind a name that already appears in the census as a distinct shape.
  3. If the regenerated census changes shape counts, revert instead of adjusting the tests to pass.

The actual change is usually smaller than the preparation suggests, which is the point.

-        if customer.get("plan") == "legacy" and order["total"] > 500:
-            discount = round(order["total"] * 0.07, 2)
-            apply_discount(order, discount)
+        if qualifies_for_legacy_discount(customer, order):
+            apply_discount(order, legacy_discount_amount(order))

The acceptance conditions are mechanical: the characterization suite is green, the census diff is empty, and the new rule has at least one recorded case of its own before you merge.

Where free model access and a free server actually help

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The parts of this workflow that are genuinely tedious are also mechanical: clustering the shape fingerprints into a short list, drafting the parametrize scaffolding from a ledger sample, and writing the triage table you reviewed above. That is the kind of work where a model with tool access saves real time, and the operator describes both free model access and a free server option, with an allowance on the order of ten million tokens, so you can try the loop before committing a budget to it. Verify current terms on the project page, since availability and limits change and this article was not written to track them.

The free server option matters for one specific reason. A replay harness that only runs on a laptop records whenever someone remembers to run it, whereas moving the same container to a hosted instance gives you a stable endpoint and a repeatable recording window. Keep secrets out of the container, keep the ledger window short, and treat the hosted run as a staging job rather than a production dependency.

Limits, and who should skip this approach

  • Nondeterministic seams without a clean normalization function produce flaky characterization tests, and flaky tests get skipped.
  • Modules whose real behavior lives in database triggers or queues cannot be frozen at a Python function boundary alone.
  • Recording inputs may capture personal data, so legal review belongs before the first ledger file, not after.
  • Low-traffic seams need weeks to reach useful coverage, which may exceed your deadline.
  • Teams that cannot deploy a recording wrapper to staging have no cheap path here, and should write the missing tests by hand instead.

Checklist before you push

  1. The ledger window is short, redacted, and excluded from the repository.
  2. Every seam you plan to touch has at least one recorded error case.
  3. Normalization removes only fields you can defend in review.
  4. The census report is committed and the CI diff check passes.
  5. The pull request contains one structural move and nothing else.
  6. A reviewer who has never seen the module can explain the change after reading the filter to the third commit? they should not need that filter at all.

Start with the seam that has the fewest shapes, not the one that annoys you most, and let the census pick the order of work for you. If you run the harness on your own repo this week, the triage table will tell you more about your legacy module than a week of reading it will.

title: Set per-user budgets on AI Gateway
description:
You can now use AI Gateway budgets to set a dollar spending limit for each user on your team.

The limit covers spend from every API key attributed to the user, along with their app tokens. After it's reached, AI Gateway rejects new requests until the budget resets or is increased.

This is useful for controlling spend from coding agents and other workloads that run without supervision, and prevents one user from consuming all of the team's shared budget.

Set user budgets

Open the Users view on the Budgets page to set two kinds of user budgets:

  • Default budget: If set, applies separately to every person without a custom budget, including users added later. Each user gets their own allowance rather than sharing one limit across the team.

  • Custom budget: Applies to one person and overrides the default. Removing it returns that user to the default budget.

Both default and custom budgets reset monthly by default, but you can change them to reset daily, weekly, or not at all. Budgets also support usage alerting via email to notify when you are at 50%, 75%, and/or 100% of your allocation.

User budgets don't replace API key, project, or team budgets. A request must remain within every budget that applies to it. Reaching any applicable limit blocks new requests.

API keys are attributed to the user who created them by default. If a key belongs to a production application or another shared workload, attribute it to the team from the API Keys page to keep its spend out of the key creator's budget. Keys created prior to the user budget feature release were attributed to the team for backwards-compatibility, so rotate to new keys if you wish to have current usage fall under the user scope.

Set budgets from the CLI

Upgrade to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade. You need Vercel CLI 59.6.2 or newer for user budgets, then set a default or custom user budget:

Identify a member by their email address, username, or user ID.

Team owners can manage user budgets, and can also grant other members AI Gateway Budget Manager permissions from team member settings. Spend using Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) credentials doesn't count toward user budgets.

Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade to get started, and learn more in the AI Gateway budgets documentation.
