title: ControlFlow3D: Distilling Multi-View Knowledge into Latent Flow Matching for Point Cloud Upsampling
description:
arXiv:2610.21190v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Point cloud upsampling is essential for 3D applications but remains challenging due to sparse, under-constrained observations. Multi-view images can resolve geometric ambiguity, but existing multi-modal methods do not fully exploit visual cues. We propose ControlFlow3D, a framework that distills knowledge from pretrained foundation models into a lightweight generation network during training, enabling strong performance without multi-view images available at test time. Specifically, our method performs conditional flow matching in a structured latent space defined by a frozen 3D encoder. Multi-view image tokens and 3D latent tokens are jointly clustered into shared prototypes via unsupervised soft KMeans; the resulting prototypes guide the flow trajectory through velocity control and are aligned by a consistency loss that progressively transfers image knowledge into the base network. A Mamba-based geometry decoder then maps latent features to dense coordinates with linear complexity. We also construct ShapeNetPU, a 35K-object multi-modal benchmark that is 31 times larger than prior datasets. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and its strong generalization capability.

title: CoSTA: Compressed Speech Token Adaptation for Efficient Spoken Dialogue Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21143v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spoken Dialogue Models (SDMs) typically share a speech-token space for generation and synthesis, leading to long autoregressive sequences and costly inference. Lower-rate speech tokenizers shorten sequences but may introduce compression-quality trade-offs and costly replacement without breaking this coupling. To address this limitation, we propose CoSTA, a compatibility-preserving post-hoc framework that decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder. CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations via mean-initialized vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, followed by deterministic expansion back to the original speech-token space before synthesis. On bilingual speech-dialogue benchmarks, CoSTA achieves approximately $1.7\times$ expanded speech-token generation speed, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput while preserving response quality. Analyses show more sustained interaction under limited budgets and a practical trade-off among compression, decoding efficiency, and quality. Further experiments demonstrate cross-architecture transfer and complementarity to low-rate tokenization.

title: MCP Explained: The 10-Minute Guide to Connecting AI Agents to Real Tools (2026)
description:
MCP Explained: The 10-Minute Guide to Connecting AI Agents to Real Tools (2026)

Every AI agent demo eventually hits the same wall: the model can reason brilliantly, but it can't touch anything — not your database, not your files, not your CRM. MCP (the Model Context Protocol) is the fix that became the de facto standard in 2026. This is the plain-language guide I wish existed when I first hit the term.

What MCP actually is

MCP is an open, standard protocol that defines how an AI application (the "client") connects to external tools and data (the "server") in a consistent way.

The one idea to grab: it's a plug-in standard for AI tools. Before MCP, every tool integration was a bespoke, one-off API hookup. With MCP, any tool exposes itself once as an MCP server, and any MCP-aware assistant can use it. Think of it as USB-C for AI capabilities.

The three pieces (this is 80% of the guide)

  1. MCP Client — the AI app that uses tools: Claude Desktop, Cursor, your OpenClaw or Hermes agent, or your own agent code.
  2. MCP Server — the program that exposes a capability: "read a Postgres database," "search the web," "control a Home Assistant device." A server is just a small program implementing the MCP spec.
  3. The tools/resources it exposes — a server advertits a set of named tools (e.g. query_database, get_weather), each with a JSON-schema description of what it takes and returns. The client hands that description to the model; the model picks a tool; the client runs the server; the result comes back.

That's the whole loop: describe → pick → execute → return.

Why it changed the game

Before MCP, wiring one tool into one agent was a project. Now:

  • Reuse: one MCP server for Slack works across Claude, Cursor, your OpenClaw, and n8n — no rework.
  • Composability: your agent gets more capabilities by adding servers, not by forking the agent.
  • The ecosystem exploded: within months there were hundreds of community MCP servers (databases, browsers, file systems, GitHub, Stripe, Home Assistant...) — most of them free.

The standard effect is real: MCP stopped being "a protocol" and became the way agent-tool integration is described.

Setting up an MCP server (the realistic path)

You rarely write your own MCP server from scratch — you usually install one and point your client at it.

1. Pick a server

Start with one that solves a real problem in your workflow:

  • Filesystem — let the agent read/write files in a folder
  • Postgres / SQLite — query your data
  • GitHub / Stripe / Notion — act on SaaS you already use
  • Browser (playwright) — let the agent drive a webpage

2. Configure the client

MCP clients hold a small config listing each server and how to launch it. The pattern is always the same — a server name, a command (or a URL for remote servers), and optional env vars:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "postgres": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres", "postgresql://localhost/app_db"],
      "env": { "DATABASE_URL": "postgresql://..." }
    },
    "filesystem": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/home/you/projects"]
    }
  }
}

Restart (or reconfigure) the client, and the tools show up. That's it.

3. Run remote servers on a VPS

Here's where self-hosting earns its keep. Many MCP servers do useful but heavy work (web scraping, database access, home-automation control). You can host the server on a cheap always-on VPS and point any client at it over a remote/HTTP transport. For the box itself, a low-cost VPS is all you need — e.g. Hostinger (referral code OVDAMRMASPIM).

Writing your own MCP server (15 lines of the idea)

When no existing server fits, you write one. A server is just a program that, on request, returns the tool list and executes a chosen tool. In TypeScript (MCP's official SDK), the shape is:

import { McpServer } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js";
const server = new McpServer({ name: "weather", version: "1.0.0" });

server.tool("get_weather", "Get the weather for a city.",
  { city: "string" },
  async ({ city }) => { /* call your API */ return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "18°C" }] }; }
);

// start over stdio (local) or http (remote)

The discipline that matters: describe tools precisely. The model chooses tools by reading their names + descriptions + schemas. Vague descriptions = the agent picks the wrong tool or hallucinates an argument. Treat the tool description like you'd write a function's docstring for a junior dev.

The part everyone skips: security

An MCP server is code your agent can run with your credentials. That's powerful and dangerous. Three rules:

  1. Least privilege. Give each server only the credentials it needs (a read-only DB user, not a superuser). Scope a filesystem server to one folder, not the whole disk.
  2. Audit what your agent can do. List the tools each server exposes and ask: "if the model is wrong, what's the worst it can do?" A read-only tool has a boring worst case; a write tool with your AWS key does not.
  3. Don't expose servers publicly. Keep local servers on stdio (they run in-process, never on a port). If a server must be remote, put it behind auth + a firewall — never an open port with a global database key in the env.

For team or production use, add logging + rate limits on every remote server, and treat MCP config the same as any secrets file.

MCP + n8n: the no-code path

If you'd rather not write config, n8n (the visual automation tool) has native MCP integration: you point an AI agent node at an MCP server and build your automation visually instead of in JSON. That's how non-developers get the same capability — "when X happens, have my AI agent look up Y via MCP, then do Z." If you're self-hosting n8n for that, it's another small VPS — cheap on Hostinger OVDAMRMASPIM.

The honest bottom line

MCP is the piece that turned AI agents from "they can chat" into "they can do." If you're building anything agentic in 2026, MCP is not optional — it's how your agent connects to the real world. Start by installing one server your agent actually needs (filesystem or your database are the best first picks), keep its permissions tight, and scale up from there.

This guide is part of the MCP & AI-agent collection on AgentStack — 75+ pages on MCP, n8n, and building agents. Hosting your MCP servers or n8n instance? A cheap always-on VPS via Hostinger OVDAMRMASPIM covers it.

title: Integration testing Spring Boot with Testcontainers, PostgreSQL, Kafka and JUnit 5
description:
Mocks are great for unit tests, but they can't tell you whether your SQL works on PostgreSQL, whether your JSON survives a round trip through Kafka, or whether your listener is wired to the right topic. H2 and embedded Kafka get closer, but they aren't the things you run in production.

Testcontainers starts real dependencies in Docker for the duration of a test run. Since Spring Boot 3.1, @ServiceConnection wires them into your application automatically, so the setup is now a handful of lines.

This post tests a small service that consumes OrderPlaced events from Kafka and stores them in PostgreSQL. The examples use Spring Boot 3.5 and the Testcontainers 1.x version it manages. You'll need Docker (or a compatible runtime) available wherever the tests run.

Dependencies 

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-testcontainers</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
    <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
    <artifactId>kafka</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

Boot's dependency management covers all of these, plus Awaitility (pulled in by spring-boot-starter-test), which we'll use for asynchronous assertions.

The code under test

An event, an entity, a repository and a listener:

public record OrderPlaced(String orderId, String customerId, BigDecimal total, Instant placedAt) {}

@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class Order {

    @Id
    private String id;
    private String customerId;
    private BigDecimal total;
    private Instant placedAt;

    protected Order() {}

    public Order(String id, String customerId, BigDecimal total, Instant placedAt) {
        this.id = id;
        this.customerId = customerId;
        this.total = total;
        this.placedAt = placedAt;
    }

    public String getId() { return id; }
    public String getCustomerId() { return customerId; }
    public BigDecimal getTotal() { return total; }
    public Instant getPlacedAt() { return placedAt; }
}

public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, String> {

    List<Order> findByCustomerIdOrderByPlacedAtDesc(String customerId);
}

@Component
public class OrderPlacedListener {

    private final OrderRepository orders;

    public OrderPlacedListener(OrderRepository orders) {
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    @KafkaListener(topics = "orders.placed", groupId = "order-projection")
    public void on(OrderPlaced event) {
        if (orders.existsById(event.orderId())) {
            return; // at-least-once delivery: ignore duplicates
        }
        orders.save(new Order(event.orderId(), event.customerId(), event.total(), event.placedAt()));
    }
}

The Kafka settings in application.yml are the usual JSON serialiser and deserialiser, with auto-offset-reset: earliest so the listener sees messages sent before its partitions were assigned. Notice there's no bootstrap-servers or datasource URL in the test setup below; that's what @ServiceConnection replaces.

Option 1: containers in the test class

The most direct approach declares containers as static fields:

@SpringBootTest(properties = "spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop")
@Testcontainers
class OrderPlacedListenerIT {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static KafkaContainer kafka = new KafkaContainer("apache/kafka:3.8.0");

    @Autowired
    KafkaTemplate<String, OrderPlaced> kafkaTemplate;

    @Autowired
    OrderRepository orders;

    @Test
    void storesOrderWhenEventArrives() {
        var event = new OrderPlaced("ord-1", "cust-42", new BigDecimal("19.99"),
                Instant.parse("2026-01-15T10:00:00Z"));

        kafkaTemplate.send("orders.placed", event.orderId(), event);

        await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(15)).untilAsserted(() ->
                assertThat(orders.findById("ord-1"))
                        .hasValueSatisfying(order -> {
                            assertThat(order.getCustomerId()).isEqualTo("cust-42");
                            assertThat(order.getTotal()).isEqualByComparingTo("19.99");
                        }));
    }
}

KafkaContainer here is org.testcontainers.kafka.KafkaContainer, which runs the official apache/kafka image in KRaft mode (no ZooKeeper). Spring Boot 3.4 and later support it with @ServiceConnection; on older Boot versions, use the Confluent-based org.testcontainers.containers.KafkaContainer instead.

How the pieces fit:

  • @Testcontainers and @Container hand lifecycle to the JUnit 5 extension. Static fields mean the containers start once for the class, not once per test.
  • @ServiceConnection tells Boot to derive spring.datasource.* and spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers from the running containers. Previously you'd write a @DynamicPropertySource method for this; that still works, and you'll need it for containers Boot doesn't recognise.
  • Awaitility handles the asynchrony. The listener runs on a different thread, so asserting immediately after send would be flaky. untilAsserted retries the AssertJ block until it passes or the timeout expires. Avoid Thread.sleep; it's both slower and less reliable.

ddl-auto=create-drop keeps the example short. If you use Flyway or Liquibase, drop that property and let migrations run against the container. Testing your real migrations on real PostgreSQL is one of the best reasons to use Testcontainers at all.

Option 2: a shared test configuration

Option 1 starts fresh containers for every test class. Once you have a dozen integration test classes, that adds up. The approach Spring Initializr generates is to declare containers as beans:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class TestcontainersConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgresContainer() {
        return new PostgreSQLContainer<>(DockerImageName.parse("postgres:16-alpine"));
    }

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    KafkaContainer kafkaContainer() {
        return new KafkaContainer(DockerImageName.parse("apache/kafka:3.8.0"));
    }
}

Test classes then import it:

@SpringBootTest(properties = "spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop")
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration.class)
class OrderQueriesIT {

    @Autowired
    OrderRepository orders;

    @Test
    void returnsCustomerOrdersNewestFirst() {
        orders.save(new Order("q-1", "cust-7", new BigDecimal("5.00"), Instant.parse("2026-01-01T09:00:00Z")));
        orders.save(new Order("q-2", "cust-7", new BigDecimal("8.00"), Instant.parse("2026-01-02T09:00:00Z")));

        assertThat(orders.findByCustomerIdOrderByPlacedAtDesc("cust-7"))
                .extracting(Order::getId)
                .containsExactly("q-2", "q-1");
    }
}

Spring starts the containers with the application context and stops them when the context closes. Because Spring's test framework caches contexts, every class with the same configuration reuses the same context and the same containers.

The trade-off is that shared containers mean shared state. Tests must not depend on an empty database or topic. The habits that keep this manageable:

  • Use unique IDs per test (as above: q-1, ord-1, or random UUIDs) and assert on those, not on table counts.
  • Clean up explicitly where needed, for example with @Sql scripts or a @BeforeEach that deletes rows the test owns.
  • Keep context configuration identical across classes. A stray @MockitoBean or different properties creates a new context, and with it new containers.

Bonus: the same containers for local development

The shared configuration can also run the application locally against throwaway containers. Add a main class under src/test/java:

public class TestOrderServiceApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.from(OrderServiceApplication::main)
                .with(TestcontainersConfiguration.class)
                .run(args);
    }
}

Run it from your IDE (or ./mvnw spring-boot:test-run) and you get PostgreSQL and Kafka without a separate docker-compose.yml to keep in sync.

Things to watch

  • Pin image versions. postgres:latest will change under you. Match the major version you run in production.
  • CI needs Docker. Most hosted runners have it. Some locked-down environments don't, so check before you commit to this approach.
  • Start-up time is real. Expect several seconds for Kafka and PostgreSQL to start. Shared containers keep that a one-off cost per run rather than per class.
  • Keep unit tests as unit tests. Integration tests are slower and should cover wiring, SQL, serialisation and configuration, not every branch of your business logic.

Summary

  • @ServiceConnection removes the property plumbing: declare a container and Boot connects to it.
  • Use Awaitility for anything asynchronous, such as Kafka listeners.
  • Move containers into a shared @TestConfiguration once you have more than a couple of test classes, and write tests that tolerate shared state.
  • Test against the same database engine and migrations you run in production.

title: Tracking Payment Liquidity with FIFO Funding Lots
description:
Moving beyond aggregate balances to understand the real cost of every payout.

A payout account may show enough money to complete a transfer, but that balance alone cannot explain what the transfer costs.

Liquidity is often acquired in separate batches. Each batch may have a different exchange rate, funding date, provider cost, or settlement source. When a payout consumes that liquidity, finance teams need to know which funds were used and what margin remained.

An aggregate balance answers “how much is available?” A funding-lot ledger answers “where did it come from, what did it cost, and which transactions consumed it?”

Represent liquidity as inventory

A funding lot can contain:

reference
funding date
original amount
remaining amount
acquisition rate
status
source metadata

The remaining amount changes as payouts consume the lot, while the original amount and acquisition rate remain part of the audit history.

Allocate oldest liquidity first

FIFO allocation is easy to describe and subtle to implement. One payout may consume the remainder of one lot and continue into the next.

with database_transaction():
    lots = lock_open_lots().order_by("funded_at", "created_at")
    remaining = payout_amount

    for lot in lots:
        if remaining <= 0:
            break

        used = min(remaining, lot.remaining_amount)
        create_allocation(lot=lot, reference=reference, amount=used)
        lot.remaining_amount -= used
        lot.save()
        remaining -= used

Row locks prevent two payouts from consuming the same remaining liquidity concurrently.

Make allocation retry-safe

Before allocating, calculate how much has already been assigned to the transaction reference. A retried task should allocate only the difference.

The database should also prevent the same transaction-lot relationship from being inserted twice accidentally.

Distribute financial values across lots

If one payout spans multiple lots, its revenue and provider fee must be distributed proportionally. Assigning the full revenue or fee to each allocation overstates the transaction.

For each allocation, calculate:

  • share of the total payout;
  • attributed customer revenue;
  • provider-fee share;
  • cost at the lot’s acquisition rate;
  • payout cost excluding provider fee; and
  • resulting FX margin.

The final allocation should absorb rounding differences so the parts equal the original transaction totals exactly.

Reconcile derived values

Financial rules evolve. A reconciliation service should be able to rebuild remaining lot balances and derived allocation values from authoritative transactions without deleting valid live history.

Manual overrides must be explicit and traceable. A corrected revenue value should be marked as an override rather than becoming indistinguishable from a calculated value.

The design principle

Liquidity is financial inventory. Funding lots and immutable allocations make its movement explainable.

This structure supports treasury visibility, transaction-level cost attribution, controlled reconciliation, and reliable margin analysis without relying on today’s aggregate balance to reconstruct yesterday’s economics.

title: Event-Driven Architecture in Java: Designing Systems That React to What Happened
description:
Event-Driven Architecture in Java: Designing Systems That React to What Happened

Most business systems are built around requests. A customer clicks "place order", the frontend calls the order service, the order service calls payment, then inventory, then shipping, and the caller waits for everything to finish. This synchronous chain is easy to understand and easy to debug at small scale. It also creates tight coupling: every service must know about every other service that cares about an order, and a slow or failing dependency blocks the whole flow.

Event-driven architecture (EDA) offers a different model. Instead of asking other services to do things, a service announces that something happened: OrderPlaced, PaymentCaptured, InventoryReserved. Interested services subscribe to those facts and react on their own schedule. The producer does not need to know who is listening, and the system can grow new reactions without changing the code that emitted the original event.

This article explains the core ideas, the patterns that matter most in practice, and how to implement them in Java with Spring Boot and Apache Kafka. It also covers the trade-offs that teams often discover too late: eventual consistency, duplicate delivery, and the difficulty of debugging flows that no single service owns.

Events, commands, and queries

The vocabulary matters because mixing these concepts causes design mistakes.

  • An event is a fact about the past, named in the past tense: OrderPlaced. It is immutable and can have many consumers.
  • A command is a request for an action in the future, named as an imperative: ReserveInventory. It has one intended handler.
  • A query asks for information and changes nothing.

Event-driven systems are built mostly from events, with commands used sparingly inside a bounded context. When a team publishes ReserveInventory on a shared topic and then waits for a reply, they have rebuilt synchronous coupling with extra latency. A useful test: if the producer would be surprised by a new consumer, the message is probably an event. If the producer expects a specific reaction, it is probably a command, and it should go directly to its owner.

Core patterns

Three patterns cover most real designs.

Event notification is the lightest form. An event carries only an identifier and perhaps a few fields, and consumers call back to the source if they need more detail. This keeps messages small and avoids copying data, but it increases coupling at runtime, because consumers depend on the source being available.

Event-carried state transfer puts the relevant data into the event itself. A CustomerAddressChanged event carries the new address, so downstream services can maintain their own copies. This improves autonomy, at the cost of larger messages and the need to manage schema evolution carefully.

Event sourcing stores the sequence of events as the source of truth, and derives current state by replaying them. It provides a complete audit trail and makes it easy to rebuild projections, but it is a significant commitment. Use it where history matters, such as financial ledgers, and avoid it as a default.

Most teams start with event notification or event-carried state transfer, and reserve event sourcing for the few aggregates that truly need it.

Modeling an event

Events should be explicit, versioned, and small enough to be useful without being a dumping ground for the database row. A Java record is a good fit:

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.UUID;

public record OrderPlaced(
        UUID eventId,
        int schemaVersion,
        Instant occurredAt,
        UUID orderId,
        UUID customerId,
        BigDecimal totalAmount,
        String currency) {

    public static OrderPlaced of(UUID orderId, UUID customerId, BigDecimal total, String currency) {
        return new OrderPlaced(UUID.randomUUID(), 1, Instant.now(), orderId, customerId, total, currency);
    }
}

The eventId is essential. Message brokers usually guarantee at-least-once delivery, which means consumers will sometimes see the same event twice. A stable identifier lets consumers detect and ignore duplicates. The schemaVersion field makes it possible to evolve the payload without breaking older consumers, and occurredAt records when the fact happened, which is often different from when it was processed.

Publishing reliably: the outbox pattern

A common bug looks like this: the service saves an order to its database, then publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka. If the process crashes between the two steps, the order exists but nobody knows about it. Reversing the order has the opposite problem: an event announces an order that was never saved.

The transactional outbox pattern solves this. The service writes the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the state change. A separate relay process reads unpublished rows and sends them to the broker, marking them as published afterward. Because the state change and the outbox row commit together, the system never loses or invents events.

import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.JdbcTemplate;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final ObjectMapper json;

    public OrderService(JdbcTemplate jdbc, ObjectMapper json) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.json = json;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void placeOrder(UUID orderId, UUID customerId, java.math.BigDecimal total) throws Exception {
        jdbc.update("INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total, status) VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'PLACED')",
                orderId, customerId, total);

        OrderPlaced event = OrderPlaced.of(orderId, customerId, total, "USD");
        jdbc.update("""
                INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregate_type, aggregate_id, event_type, payload, created_at)
                VALUES (?, 'Order', ?, 'OrderPlaced', ?::jsonb, now())
                """,
                event.eventId(), orderId, json.writeValueAsString(event));
    }
}

The relay is a scheduled job or a change-data-capture connector such as Debezium. A simple polling relay looks like this:

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.KafkaTemplate;
import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.Scheduled;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.JdbcTemplate;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class OutboxRelay {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;

    public OutboxRelay(JdbcTemplate jdbc, KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.kafka = kafka;
    }

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)
    public void publishPending() {
        List<Map<String, Object>> rows = jdbc.queryForList("""
                SELECT id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload
                FROM outbox
                WHERE published_at IS NULL
                ORDER BY created_at
                LIMIT 100
                """);

        for (Map<String, Object> row : rows) {
            String key = row.get("aggregate_id").toString();
            String payload = row.get("payload").toString();
            String topic = "orders." + row.get("event_type").toString().toLowerCase();
            kafka.send(topic, key, payload).join();
            jdbc.update("UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = ?", row.get("id"));
        }
    }
}

Two details matter. The message key is the aggregate ID, which keeps events for the same order in one partition and therefore in order. And the relay may publish an event and crash before marking it, so it will publish again after restart. That is acceptable because consumers are designed to handle duplicates.

Consuming safely: idempotency

Every consumer must assume it will receive the same event more than once, and possibly out of order across different aggregates. The standard defense is to record processed event IDs in the same transaction as the side effect.

import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.JdbcTemplate;
import org.springframework.kafka.annotation.KafkaListener;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

@Component
public class InventoryConsumer {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final ObjectMapper json;

    public InventoryConsumer(JdbcTemplate jdbc, ObjectMapper json) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.json = json;
    }

    @KafkaListener(topics = "orders.orderplaced", groupId = "inventory-service")
    @Transactional
    public void onOrderPlaced(String payload) throws Exception {
        OrderPlaced event = json.readValue(payload, OrderPlaced.class);

        int inserted = jdbc.update(
                "INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES (?) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING",
                event.eventId());
        if (inserted == 0) {
            return; // already processed, ignore the duplicate
        }

        reserveStockFor(event.orderId());
    }

    private void reserveStockFor(UUID orderId) {
        // Business logic: reserve items, update stock, emit InventoryReserved via the outbox
    }
}

The insert into processed_events and the business update share a transaction, so either both happen or neither does. A duplicate delivery finds the event ID already present and exits quietly. Keep the processed-event table pruned after a retention window that exceeds your maximum redelivery time.

Failure handling

Consumers fail. A database is unavailable, a downstream API times out, or a message contains data that cannot be processed. Three mechanisms help:

  • Retries with backoff for transient failures. Spring Kafka's retry topics or a DefaultErrorHandler with exponential backoff handle this well.
  • Dead-letter topics for messages that keep failing. Route them somewhere visible, with the original payload and the error, and assign an owner to inspect them.
  • Replay from the broker. Because Kafka retains events for a configured period, a fixed consumer can reprocess history. This only works if consumers are idempotent, which is why idempotency comes first.

Do not let a poison message block an entire partition indefinitely. A consumer stuck on one bad event is a silent outage for everything behind it.

Observability for flows nobody owns

The hardest operational problem in event-driven systems is understanding a business flow that spans five services and three topics. No single log shows the full story. Teams mitigate this in three ways.

First, propagate a correlation identifier in every event header, and log it everywhere. A search on one order ID should reveal every event, every consumer, and every failure.

Second, measure consumer lag. A growing lag means a consumer cannot keep up, and it is often the earliest warning of an incident. Alert on lag trends, not only on errors.

Third, keep a catalog of events: who publishes each one, who consumes it, what schema version is in use, and who to contact. Without this, changing a field becomes guesswork.

Trade-offs to accept deliberately

Event-driven architecture is not free. It trades immediate consistency for autonomy and resilience. A customer may see an order as "placed" before inventory is reserved, and the system must handle the case where reservation fails afterward, typically with a compensating event such as OrderCancelled or a saga. Users need interfaces that show pending states honestly rather than pretending everything is instant.

Testing becomes harder, because behavior emerges from the interaction of many consumers. Invest in contract tests for event schemas, and in integration tests that run the real broker for critical flows. Keep a small number of well-understood end-to-end scenarios, rather than trying to test every combination.

Finally, avoid the temptation to make everything an event. Synchronous calls are the right choice when a caller needs an answer now, such as validating a payment card before showing a confirmation screen. Choose the style per interaction, not per architecture diagram.

A practical adoption roadmap

Weeks 1 to 2: Pick one business flow with clear value, such as order processing, and map its current synchronous calls. Identify which ones are notifications masquerading as requests.

Weeks 3 to 4: Introduce the outbox table and a relay in the producing service. Publish events for the flow while keeping the existing calls, so you can compare behavior.

Weeks 5 to 6: Add one consumer with idempotency, retries, and a dead-letter topic. Migrate one downstream responsibility to it, and monitor lag and error rates.

Weeks 7 and beyond: Create the event catalog, add correlation identifiers across services, and gradually retire the synchronous calls that no longer need to be synchronous.

Key takeaways

  • Events describe facts in the past tense; commands request future actions and should have a single owner.
  • Use the transactional outbox so state changes and events are never out of step.
  • Assume at-least-once delivery, and make every consumer idempotent with a processed-events record.
  • Key messages by aggregate ID to preserve ordering where it matters.
  • Plan for failures with retries, dead-letter topics, and replay, and keep poison messages from blocking partitions.
  • Make business flows observable with correlation IDs, consumer lag monitoring, and an event catalog.
  • Choose synchronous or asynchronous interaction deliberately, per use case.

Event-driven architecture rewards teams that treat events as contracts and take the operational discipline seriously. Start with one flow, get the publishing and consuming patterns right, and let the rest of the system follow when the benefits are proven.

title: Plan, Prioritize, and Manage IT Support and Maintenance Activities
description:
Plan, Prioritize, and Manage IT Support and Maintenance Activities

IT support and maintenance rarely make it onto a product roadmap. They are the work that keeps systems running while everyone else builds new features. Yet this work consumes a large share of most engineering and operations teams: patching servers, responding to incidents, renewing certificates, upgrading dependencies, answering tickets, and reviewing backups. When it is unplanned, it becomes a constant interruption. When it is planned well, it becomes predictable, measurable, and far less disruptive to the business.

This article describes a practical approach to planning, prioritizing, and managing IT support and maintenance activities. It covers how to classify work, how to set a priority model that people trust, how to schedule maintenance without surprising the business, and how to measure whether the system is actually improving. Java examples are included where automation or tooling helps.

The problem: reactive work crowds out everything else

Most support teams start in reactive mode. A request arrives, someone handles it, and the next one arrives. Over time three problems emerge:

  • Priorities are implicit. Whoever shouts loudest gets served first, and urgent-looking work displaces important work.
  • Maintenance is deferred indefinitely. Patches, certificate renewals, and dependency upgrades are always "next sprint", until an outage forces them through under pressure.
  • Knowledge stays in people's heads. Recurring problems are solved from scratch each time because nobody recorded the fix.

The cure is not heroic effort. It is a small set of explicit practices: a shared intake, a priority model everyone understands, a maintenance calendar that is treated as seriously as a release calendar, and a feedback loop based on data.

Step 1: Put all work in one place

You cannot prioritize what you cannot see. Support requests arrive through email, chat, phone calls, monitoring alerts, and hallway conversations. The first practice is to route all of them into a single queue, whether that is Jira Service Management, ServiceNow, or a well-configured shared board.

Each item should capture a minimum set of fields:

  • Category: incident, service request, problem, or maintenance task.
  • Affected service or system.
  • Business impact: how many users are affected and what they cannot do.
  • Requester and owner.
  • Creation time and target time.

Keeping the vocabulary consistent matters more than the tool. An incident is an unplanned interruption or degradation of a service. A service request is a standard, low-risk request such as access or a license. A problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents. Maintenance is planned work that reduces future risk. When these categories blur, every queue becomes a mix of everything, and prioritization becomes guesswork.

Step 2: Prioritize with impact and urgency, not volume

A widely used model combines two dimensions: impact, which is how much damage the issue causes, and urgency, which is how quickly the damage grows or how soon a deadline hits. A simple matrix turns these into a priority:

Low urgency Medium urgency High urgency
High impact P2 P1 P1
Medium impact P3 P2 P1
Low impact P4 P3 P2

The matrix itself is less important than the rules behind it. Write them down. For example, "High impact means a customer-facing service is down or a regulated process is blocked. Medium impact means a team cannot complete its work but a workaround exists. Low impact means cosmetic or single-user issues." When everyone can see these definitions, disagreements become discussions about classification rather than arguments about who is more important.

Maintenance work needs its own treatment. Patching a vulnerability that is being actively exploited is urgent. Upgrading a library that nobody has complained about may be low priority. A reasonable approach is to score maintenance items on three factors: risk reduction (how much exposure the work removes), effort, and deadline (end-of-support dates, certificate expiry, audit requirements). Items with a hard deadline move up regardless of their score.

Step 3: Make the priority score explicit in code

Teams often start with a spreadsheet and graduate to automation. A small Java model is enough to make the rules transparent and testable. The following example scores work items so the queue can be sorted consistently:

public enum Impact { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH }
public enum Urgency { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH }

public record WorkItem(
        String id,
        String title,
        String category,       // INCIDENT, SERVICE_REQUEST, PROBLEM, MAINTENANCE
        Impact impact,
        Urgency urgency,
        int riskReduction,     // 1-5, used for maintenance items
        int effortDays,        // estimated effort
        java.time.LocalDate deadline // nullable
) {}

public final class PriorityCalculator {

    public String priorityOf(WorkItem item) {
        // Incidents and classic impact/urgency matrix
        if (!"MAINTENANCE".equals(item.category())) {
            return matrixPriority(item.impact(), item.urgency());
        }
        // Hard deadlines override scoring
        if (item.deadline() != null
                && item.deadline().isBefore(java.time.LocalDate.now().plusDays(14))) {
            return "P1";
        }
        // Score maintenance by risk reduction per unit of effort
        double score = item.riskReduction() / Math.max(1.0, item.effortDays());
        if (score >= 1.0) return "P2";
        if (score >= 0.3) return "P3";
        return "P4";
    }

    private String matrixPriority(Impact impact, Urgency urgency) {
        int i = impact.ordinal();   // 0 = LOW, 2 = HIGH
        int u = urgency.ordinal();
        int level = i + u;          // 0..4
        if (level >= 3) return "P1";
        if (level == 2) return "P2";
        if (level == 1) return "P3";
        return "P4";
    }
}

The point of this code is not the exact thresholds. It is that the rules are written down, reviewed in pull requests, and covered by tests. A few unit tests that encode the policy prevent quiet drift: when someone changes a threshold, the test fails and the change becomes a conscious decision.

Step 4: Plan maintenance as a calendar, not a backlog

Maintenance that lives only in a backlog gets postponed. Maintenance that lives on a calendar gets scheduled. Treat recurring work as a set of commitments with clear cadences:

  • Weekly: review the incident queue for patterns, check backup job results, review failed jobs and alerts.
  • Monthly: apply security patches to non-critical systems, rotate service accounts, review access lists for leavers.
  • Quarterly: test disaster recovery procedures, review capacity trends, review vendor support end dates.
  • Annually: renew certificates and licenses in advance, run a full access review, verify business continuity plans.

Two details make this work. First, schedule maintenance windows with the business, not around it. Publish the windows, explain the expected impact, and agree on rollback criteria before the work starts. Second, reserve capacity explicitly. A common rule is to allocate about 20 percent of the team's time to planned maintenance and small improvements. If the reserved capacity is always consumed by urgent incidents, that is a signal that the problem backlog needs attention, not that maintenance can be dropped.

Change management deserves a light but real process. For standard changes, such as a routine patch that has been done many times, a pre-approved template is enough. For non-standard changes, a short change record should state the purpose, the systems affected, the test evidence, the rollback plan, and the owner. The goal is not bureaucracy. It is making sure that the person on call at 2 a.m. knows what was changed and how to undo it.

Step 5: Turn recurring incidents into problems

One of the highest-leverage practices is problem management. When the same incident happens three times, it is no longer an incident. It is a problem with a root cause that is not yet fixed. Each recurring pattern should open a problem record, assigned to an owner with a target date for a permanent fix or a documented workaround.

A simple trigger works well: any incident category that appears more than three times in a month opens a problem review. The review answers four questions: what keeps happening, what is the root cause, what permanent fix is feasible, and what is the cost of not fixing it. Often the answer to the last question justifies the fix immediately.

Automation can help detect these patterns. The following sketch groups incidents by a normalized signature and flags clusters:

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public record Incident(String id, String service, String errorSignature, java.time.Instant openedAt) {}

public final class ProblemDetector {

    private static final int THRESHOLD = 3;

    public Map<String, List<Incident>> recurringPatterns(List<Incident> incidents) {
        return incidents.stream()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(i -> i.service() + "|" + normalize(i.errorSignature())))
                .entrySet().stream()
                .filter(e -> e.getValue().size() >= THRESHOLD)
                .collect(Collectors.toMap(Map.Entry::getKey, Map.Entry::getValue));
    }

    // Strip volatile parts such as IDs, timestamps, and numbers so similar errors group together
    private String normalize(String signature) {
        return signature
                .replaceAll("\\b[0-9a-fA-F-]{8,}\\b", "<id>")
                .replaceAll("\\d+", "<n>")
                .toLowerCase()
                .trim();
    }
}

Normalization is the part that needs care. Two errors that differ only by a request ID are the same problem. Two errors that differ by the failing dependency are not. Review the grouping output periodically, because over-grouping hides distinct causes and under-grouping hides patterns.

Step 6: Measure what matters

Teams that cannot measure their support work cannot improve it. A small set of metrics is enough to guide decisions:

  • Mean time to acknowledge and mean time to resolve, broken down by priority. Averages hide problems, so look at the distribution, especially the slowest 10 percent.
  • Reopen rate: the share of tickets closed and then reopened. A high rate usually means fixes are superficial.
  • Ratio of planned to unplanned work. If unplanned work dominates, the team is in firefighting mode regardless of how fast it responds.
  • Maintenance completion rate against the calendar. Missed maintenance is a leading indicator of future incidents.
  • Recurring problem count and how many have a permanent fix in place.

Review these monthly with the people who do the work and the people who depend on it. The conversation should focus on trends and decisions, such as "we need to shift 10 percent of capacity to fixing the authentication failures", rather than on blaming individuals for individual tickets.

Step 7: Communicate proactively

Support teams are often judged by how they communicate during disruption. Three habits make a large difference. First, publish a status update at a predictable interval during any priority one incident, even if the update is only "still investigating, next update in 30 minutes". Second, after every significant incident, publish a short review that states what happened, what was done, and what will change. Third, tell the business about planned maintenance early and in plain language. People accept interruptions they understand far more readily than surprises.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating every request as urgent. If everything is P1, nothing is. Enforce the definitions.
  • Maintaining a backlog that nobody reviews. Items older than a set period should be closed, reprioritized, or explicitly accepted as risk.
  • Skipping rollback plans. A maintenance task without a rollback is a gamble.
  • Measuring only speed. Fast closure of tickets that reopen is not progress.
  • Automating before defining. A script that prioritizes according to unclear rules just makes confusion faster.

A roadmap for the first ninety days

Days 1 to 30: Consolidate intake into one queue. Define the category, impact, and urgency vocabulary and publish it. Start tracking time to acknowledge and resolve.

Days 31 to 60: Introduce the priority matrix and the maintenance calendar. Agree maintenance windows with the business. Open problem records for every recurring incident pattern you can identify manually.

Days 61 to 90: Automate the priority calculation and recurring pattern detection. Set up the monthly metrics review. Reserve a fixed share of capacity for planned maintenance and start reporting against it.

By the end of the ninety days, most teams can answer three questions they could not answer before: what is the team working on and why, what is coming next, and whether the system is getting more reliable over time.

Key takeaways

  • Consolidate all incoming work into one queue with a shared vocabulary of categories.
  • Prioritize using impact and urgency with written definitions, and treat maintenance with its own scoring that includes deadlines.
  • Encode priority rules in code and test them, so policy changes are deliberate.
  • Plan maintenance on a calendar, reserve capacity for it, and coordinate windows with the business.
  • Turn recurring incidents into problems with owners and target dates.
  • Measure distribution, reopen rates, and the balance between planned and unplanned work, and review trends monthly.

Reliable IT services are rarely the result of one heroic fix. They come from a steady system of planning, prioritization, and follow-through, and that system is worth building deliberately.

title: Threads Are Not Connections: A Spring Boot Concurrency Incident
description:
Description:

A Spring Boot service slowed down under load because API calls and database calls shared one thread pool. How the team found it, fixed it, and why virtual threads would not have helped.

Load went up, and the service slowed down with it. p99 latency climbed from 400 ms to 18 s. CPU sat around 20%. Connection timeout errors started showing up in the logs.

A slow service usually has something working too hard. This one did not. Requests were piling up, yet very little real work was getting done. Most of the time was going to waiting, and the engineers had to find out what for.

What the service was doing

Each unit of work was a short chain of blocking calls. Some went to external APIs. Some went to the database. A single unit could touch both, more than once, one after another.

The service ran many units at the same time with CompletableFuture. Every stage of every unit ran on one shared thread pool of 100 threads. Database access went through a Hikari connection pool with 20 connections.

Both kinds of calls block the thread that makes them. A thread that sends an HTTP request sits idle until the response comes back. A thread that needs the database first asks Hikari for a connection. If none is free, it waits. Then it waits again for the query. While a thread waits, it does no useful work. It is also unavailable for anything else.

So the 100 threads were one shared budget for two different kinds of waiting. When the APIs were fast and connections were free, the budget was enough. When either side slowed down, it spent the budget for both.

That design was the team's own choice, and it was easy to set up. The problem was that 100 did not describe any real limit in the system. It was just a number.

Finding the cause

The team took thread dumps during the slowdown and lined them up with Hikari's metrics. Nearly every pool thread was blocked. Some were waiting on HTTP responses. Many more were parked inside getConnection. Hikari showed all 20 connections in use and up to 60 threads waiting for one.

A thread could get stuck in two ways, and each made the other worse.

The first was slow API calls. Under load, external calls took longer and held their threads longer. That left fewer threads for every other stage, including database work, which sat in the executor's queue.

The second was the database. With 100 threads and only 20 connections, most of the pool could end up waiting inside Hikari. A thread waiting for a connection is just as unavailable as one waiting on HTTP. API stages then queued behind them.

Because both kinds of work drew from the same threads, slowness on one side became delay on the other. Every unit of work waited in the same queue, whatever resource it needed next.

The root cause was a mismatch between thread demand and available connections. The thread pool and the connection pool had been sized as two separate settings. They should have been one decision. This also explained the low CPU. Blocked threads use almost none.

Transaction scope made it worse. One code path opened a transaction, called an external API, and wrote the result before committing. The connection stayed checked out for the whole API call. In that path, every slow response took a connection out of the pool while no query was running.

The fix: one executor per resource

The team split the shared pool into two executors. One runs database work. The other runs external API calls. Each stage now runs on the executor for the resource it blocks on.

@Configuration
class ExecutorConfig {
    // 18 = Hikari maximum-pool-size (20) minus 2 for request-path queries
    @Bean ThreadPoolTaskExecutor dbExecutor()  { return pool("db-", 18); }
    // 80 = ~200 calls/s x 0.3 s p95 latency = 60, plus headroom
    @Bean ThreadPoolTaskExecutor apiExecutor() { return pool("api-", 80); }

    private static ThreadPoolTaskExecutor pool(String prefix, int size) {
        var ex = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        ex.setCorePoolSize(size);
        ex.setMaxPoolSize(size);
        ex.setThreadNamePrefix(prefix);
        return ex;
    }
}

The DB executor was resized to align with the Hikari pool. A database thread without a connection can only wait, so threads beyond the connection count add waiting and nothing else. With the sizes aligned, extra database work waits in the executor queue, where it holds no thread and no connection. The executor got 18 threads rather than 20, because a few request-path queries use the same Hikari pool outside the executor.

The API executor needed a different method, and Little's Law gives it. In plain words, the calls in flight equal the calls started per second multiplied by the seconds each call takes. At peak, the service handled about 100 units of work per second, each making two API calls. That is about 200 calls per second. The API's p95 latency under load was around 300 ms, so about 60 calls are in flight at any moment. The team added headroom and set the executor to 80 threads.

The total thread count barely changed, from 100 to 98. What changed was which work could use which threads.

Latency is a live input here. If the API gets twice as slow, the same throughput needs twice as many threads. A call with no timeout breaks the math completely, because it can hold a thread for as long as the remote side likes.

The stages then hop between executors explicitly. A simplified version:

CompletableFuture<Void> process(Job job) {
    return CompletableFuture
        .supplyAsync(() -> externalApi.fetch(job), apiExecutor)
        .thenApplyAsync(data -> repository.save(job, data), dbExecutor)
        .thenApplyAsync(saved -> externalApi.confirm(saved), apiExecutor)
        .thenAcceptAsync(reply -> repository.markDone(job, reply), dbExecutor);
}

The Async variants matter. Plain thenApply can run the next stage on whatever thread completed the previous one. In this chain, that would quietly put database work back on an API thread.

The split also assumes each stage touches one resource. The transactional path broke that rule, so the team moved its API call out of the transaction. The transaction now covers only the writes. They also added dashboards and alerts on pending connections and on each executor's queue depth.

After the fix, p99 at peak load settled around 450 ms. Connection timeout errors stopped. Peak throughput went from about 70 units per second during the incident back to the expected 100.

It worked because the two kinds of waiting stopped sharing a budget. A slow API can fill its own executor, but it cannot take threads from database work. A busy database cannot stall API stages. A slow API still lowers overall throughput, since every unit needs both. It just no longer drags the database side down with it.

Would virtual threads have prevented this?

Java 21 made virtual threads a standard feature. They are cheap, and a service can run a very large number of them. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, it usually releases the platform thread underneath it. Spring Boot 3.2 added a spring.threads.virtual.enabled property that moves several of its own components onto virtual threads on Java 21 or later.

The incident was a story about blocked threads, so the question is fair. The answer is no. Virtual threads make threads cheap. They do nothing about connections, and there would still be only 20 of those.

Picture the same service with one virtual thread per task, using Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). The 100-thread limit is gone, and every unit starts

title: SHRED: Self-Play for Heterogeneous Road-Users without Expert Demonstrations
description:
arXiv:2610.20866v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Realistic traffic simulation and autonomous planning both depend on modeling interactions among heterogeneous road users whose dynamics, constraints, and behaviors differ fundamentally. Existing approaches predominantly learn realistic interaction behavior from large-scale human driving demonstrations. In this work, we ask whether such behavior can instead emerge purely through self-play. We present SHRED, a framework that jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. SHRED combines type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, allowing diverse behaviors to emerge through closed-loop interaction. On the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC), SHRED jointly controls all three road-user types and outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that use demonstration-trained reference policies. Policies trained only on nuPlan map geometry retain comparable realism under zero-shot evaluation on Waymo. For planning, SHRED outperforms all compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark. Controlled ablations show that heterogeneity in self-play improves both traffic realism and planning performance, with particularly large planning gains in interaction-heavy scenarios. Together, these results establish heterogeneous procedural self-play as a scalable, demonstration-free paradigm for learning realistic and interactive traffic behavior.

title: What a Hexagonal Port Costs in Go: itabs, Escape Analysis and a Postgres Round Trip
description:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You put a UserRepository interface between your domain and Postgres. The review comes back with one line: "Interfaces are slow in Go. Just pass the pool."

That objection is half right, and the half that is right is not the one people argue about. The dispatch itself is a pointer load and an indirect call. What costs you is that the compiler cannot see through the interface, so it stops inlining and starts sending values to the heap. That second part is a known, open compiler limitation: golang/go#36964 has tracked it since February 2020.

You can check all of this yourself with one benchmark file and -gcflags=-m.

What your domain holds: two words and an itab

An interface with methods is two machine words. The current layout lives in internal/abi/iface.go:

type NonEmptyInterface struct {
    ITab *ITab
    Data unsafe.Pointer
}

type ITab struct {
    Inter *InterfaceType
    Type  *Type
    Hash  uint32     // copy of Type.Hash
    Fun   [1]uintptr // variable sized
}

Data points at your adapter, say a *pgRepo. ITab points at a table pairing the interface type with the concrete type, followed by one function pointer per method. The source comment says itabs are allocated in non-garbage-collected memory, and runtime/iface.go keeps them in a global table it reads without locks on the common path. They are built once, not per call.

The call repo.Save(ctx, u) then does what Russ Cox described back in Go Data Structures: Interfaces (2009): the equivalent of tab->fun[0](data). Load the itab pointer, load the function pointer, call it with the data word as the receiver.


An interface value is two words: an itab pointer and a data pointer.

Vicent Martí spelled out what that indirection costs in PlanetScale's 2022 generics deep dive: a call through an interface prevents inlining. Lose inlining and you also lose the optimizations it would have opened up. (Devirtualization, below, is the exception.)

Where it costs you: escape analysis gives up at the interface

Escape analysis decides whether a value can live on the stack. To decide, it has to see every function the pointer is handed to. Through an interface, it can't: the callee is whatever sits in the itab at runtime.

In #36964, a Go compiler contributor explains the bind: at the moment you allocate the value, the compiler may not know which interface methods it will be passed to. So it assumes the worst. A pointer argument to an interface method escapes, even when every implementation you ship only reads it.

The receiver side has its own open issue. #62653, "avoid always escaping the receivers in interface method calls", is milestoned for Go 1.28 after moving from 1.27 in June 2026. A March 2026 report, #78336, shows a non-pointer value stored in an interface being heap-allocated through runtime.convT64 because a method is called on it.

That is the second allocation source to know about. Since Go 1.4, interface values always hold a pointer, so storing a non-pointer value in an interface means boxing it. The runtime skips the allocation for integers under 256 (staticuint64s) and for empty strings, and allocates otherwise. A logging decorator that passes u.ID into a ...any argument pays that on every call once your IDs pass 255.

A benchmark you can run: direct, port, decorated port

Run go mod init portcost in an empty directory and save what follows as port_test.go. One file, no dependencies. The first part is the domain type, the port, an in-memory adapter and a decorator:

package portcost

import (
    "context"
    "sync/atomic"
    "testing"
)

type User struct {
    ID    int64
    Name  string
    Email string
}

type UserRepository interface {
    Save(ctx context.Context, u *User) error
}

type memRepo struct{ last int64 }

func (r *memRepo) Save(ctx context.Context, u *User) error {
    r.last = u.ID
    return nil
}

// A decorator, the way metrics or logging wraps a port.
type counting struct {
    next  UserRepository
    calls atomic.Int64
}

func (r *counting) Save(ctx context.Context, u *User) error {
    r.calls.Add(1)
    return r.next.Save(ctx, u)
}

Below it, in the same file, go two services that are identical except for the field type, and a benchmark for each setup. The //go:noinline on both Rename methods is deliberate: it keeps the outer call identical, so the only difference is what happens inside.

type Direct struct{ repo *memRepo }

//go:noinline
func (s *Direct) Rename(ctx context.Context, id int64) error {
    u := User{ID: id, Name: "renamed"}
    return s.repo.Save(ctx, &u)
}

type Ported struct{ repo UserRepository }

//go:noinline
func (s *Ported) Rename(ctx context.Context, id int64) error {
    u := User{ID: id, Name: "renamed"}
    return s.repo.Save(ctx, &u)
}

var bg = context.Background()

func BenchmarkDirect(b *testing.B) {
    s := &Direct{repo: &memRepo{}}
    for b.Loop() {
        _ = s.Rename(bg, 42)
    }
}

func BenchmarkPort(b *testing.B) {
    s := &Ported{repo: &memRepo{}}
    for b.Loop() {
        _ = s.Rename(bg, 42)
    }
}

func BenchmarkPortDecorated(b *testing.B) {
    s := &Ported{repo: &counting{next: &memRepo{}}}
    for b.Loop() {
        _ = s.Rename(bg, 42)
    }
}

b.Loop needs Go 1.24 or newer. Before Go 1.26 it also blocked inlining in the loop body, which is one more reason for the //go:noinline pins: the outer call stays the same on every version. Run the benchmarks with allocation counts, and ask the compiler what it decided:

go test -bench . -benchmem -count 5
go test -run '^$' -bench . -gcflags=-m 2>&1 \
  | grep -E 'heap|devirt|inlin'

I haven't run this myself, so there are no numbers here; yours are the ones that count anyway. In the -m output, Direct.Rename should show inlining call to (*memRepo).Save and no heap line for u. Ported.Rename is where you'd expect moved to heap: u, because &u goes into an interface method the compiler can't see. Those message formats come straight from the compiler's inliner, escape and devirtualize passes.

In the benchmark output, compare the allocs/op column before you look at ns/op. The decorated version adds a second indirect call plus an atomic add, which is about what a metrics decorator costs in production.

If -m prints nothing, the build came from cache. Touch the file and run it again.

When the compiler deletes the port for you

The devirtualize package runs two passes. The static one rewrites an interface call into a direct call when the concrete type is known at compile time, and -m reports it as devirtualizing ... to .... This is the classic benchmark trap: write var r UserRepository = &memRepo{} and call r.Save in the same function, and you are timing a direct call while thinking you're timing a port. If a devirtualizing line points at the line inside Ported.Rename, your port benchmark isn't measuring a port.

The second pass is profile-guided. Go 1.21 made PGO ready for general use and added devirtualization of interface calls to the most common callee. Go 1.22 widened it and interleaved devirtualization with inlining. The rewrite is a guarded direct call with the original call as fallback, shaped like this in the compiler's own doc comment:

if c, ok := i.(Concrete); ok {
    c.Foo()
} else {
    i.Foo()
}

Two details from the source matter for ports. The pass skips callees it knows won't inline, because inlining is the whole point. And -pgo=auto only picks up default.pgo for main packages, per the go command docs, so in a test you pass the profile yourself:

go test -run '^$' -bench PortDecorated -cpuprofile cpu.pprof
go test -run '^$' -bench . -benchmem -pgo=cpu.pprof \
  -gcflags=-m 2>&1 | grep -i 'pgo devirtualizing'

Notice that the fallback branch is still an ordinary interface call. My reading is that &u still flows into an unknown method there, so check whether moved to heap: u survives in the PGO build before you count on the allocation going away. For whole programs, the PGO guide reports 2 to 14% runtime gains across a representative set of Go programs as of Go 1.22.

Put it next to one Postgres round trip

Add a second file, pg_test.go, in the same directory. It uses pgx through database/sql (run go get github.com/jackc/pgx/v5 first) and skips itself unless you point it at a database.

package portcost

import (
    "database/sql"
    "os"
    "testing"

    _ "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib"
)

func BenchmarkPostgresRoundTrip(b *testing.B) {
    dsn := os.Getenv("PG_DSN")
    if dsn == "" {
        b.Skip("set PG_DSN to run")
    }
    db, err := sql.Open("pgx", dsn)
    if err != nil {
        b.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer db.Close()
    if err := db.PingContext(bg); err != nil {
        b.Fatal(err)
    }
    var one int
    for b.Loop() {
        row := db.QueryRowContext(bg, "SELECT 1")
        if err := row.Scan(&one); err != nil {
            b.Fatal(err)
        }
    }
}

Run it against the database your service actually talks to, not a laptop container, and divide. For a rough anchor before you have your own numbers, the latency table attributed to Jeff Dean puts a round trip within one datacenter at 500,000 ns and a branch mispredict at 5 ns. The table is old and your network is not Google's, but the ratio is the point: even if every port call cost as much as a mispredicted branch, one query would pay for about 100,000 of them, before the server does any work.


Dispatch and one database round trip are not on the same scale.

The allocation is the part worth watching. One small heap object per call is cheap on its own, and Go 1.27 made some allocations under 80 bytes up to 30% cheaper. It adds up when a port sits inside a loop that runs per row or per item: a PriceRule interface called 100,000 times per request is a design problem. A UserRepository called twice per request, each time followed by a network trip, is not.

So keep ports where hexagonal architecture puts them anyway, at the I/O boundary. Pass batches across them, not single items in a tight loop. And when a reviewer says interfaces are slow, send them the -benchmem output and the SELECT 1 number side by side.

If this was useful

The benchmark tells you what a port costs. Where it belongs is the question Hexagonal Architecture in Go is built around: which interfaces the domain owns, how persistence adapters plug in, and how to lay out the packages so the boundary stays at the I/O edge. If you want the architecture side of what you just measured, start with the book here. It's half of the Thinking in Go series.
