title: Building Modular Monoliths With Kotlin and Spring
description:
Over a decade ago, Netflix became one of the early adopters of microservice architecture, showcasing its potential at a large scale. Since then, many companies have jumped on the microservices bandwagon, building their backends this way from day one. While microservices offer isolation and independent scaling, their distributed nature requires managing multiple deployments, monitoring interservice communication, and handling network failures across service boundaries.

As teams have gained real-world experience with this complexity, there's been a shift back toward monoliths, but not the tightly coupled monoliths of the past. Instead, developers are embracing modular monoliths: an architectural pattern where single deployable applications are organized into well-defined modules based on logical boundaries or business domains. Think of an e-commerce platform where users, products, and orders live in separate modules that interact through clear contracts, such as APIs for synchronous calls and events for async communication. This separation lets teams work in parallel for faster development and better maintainability, while single-unit deployment keeps releases simple and avoids microservice operational complexity.

In this guide, we explore how modular monoliths differ from traditional monoliths, why they're gaining traction, and how to build them using Spring Modulith and Kotlin.

The Need for Modular Monoliths

The growing modular monolith countertrend makes more sense when viewed against the shortcomings of traditional approaches.

Traditional monoliths bundle the entire backend into a single codebase with tight coupling between user interfaces, business logic, and data access patterns. In an e-commerce platform, for example, the product catalog, checkout, payments, and order history services are in a single codebase and are deployed together. A monolith uses function calls for internal communication, and often, the call patterns and interdependencies become messy or difficult to maintain.

Microservices emerged to solve these maintainability challenges by splitting backends into loosely coupled services, each handling a specific domain. A cab-hailing platform may separate users, drivers, ride matching, payments, and notifications into independent services. However, this introduces distributed system challenges, including complex service discovery, coordinating deployments across dependent services, and debugging interservice communication issues. Without proper expertise, tooling, and observability, this can slow down development.

Modular monoliths strike a balance by keeping everything in a single codebase and deploying it as one artifact, while structuring the application into logical modules with well-defined interfaces. This addresses the challenges of distributed systems while maintaining the structural benefits of well-defined interfaces and independent development workflows. Some benefits of a modular monolith include:

  • Simplified deployment: A single deployment artifact simplifies the release process because you don't need to coordinate multiple service rollouts, manage service meshes, or handle distributed database migrations and rollbacks.
  • Reliable testing: As modules in a monolith communicate in-process rather than over a network, integration tests are faster and more stable. You can use mocks where needed, avoid brittle network dependencies, and run end-to-end (E2E) and performance tests in a controlled environment.
  • Stronger domain modeling: Modular monoliths group related business logic into modules, with clear ownership and communication boundaries between modules. It enforces communication only through well-defined interfaces and enables domain objects to be shared directly without serialization or cross-service APIs. This makes the system easier to maintain and improves development velocity.
  • In-process communication: Since modules communicate through direct method invocations instead of network calls, it reduces latency and points of failure.

Designing a Modular Monolith

When you're building a modular monolith, you first identify the business domains and split the application into multiple loosely coupled modules with clear boundaries and dependencies. Unlike the tightly interwoven code of a traditional monolith, the modular design ensures that the modules can be developed and maintained independently while still being deployed as a single unit. For example, you can break down an e-commerce platform into separate modules such as users, product catalog, shopping cart, payments, and orders:

Each module encapsulates a specific entity or capability. A product catalog module would manage product details and categories, and an order processing module would handle order and payment entities. Unlike traditional monoliths, where internal calls often use ad hoc dependencies, in a modular monolith, the interactions with other modules are performed using explicit interfaces and well-defined contracts. This ensures that the intermodule dependencies remain clear and intentional. The communication between the modules uses in-process function calls, so it's faster and less error-prone compared to network-based interservice calls in microservices.

The modular structure allows logical separation between the modules and enforces fixed boundaries, increasing development speed, improving maintainability, and making testing more reliable. Each module defines its user interface, business logic, and data access layers separately:

These boundaries also lay the groundwork for extracting a particular module as a microservice based on the scaling requirements.

Integrate Spring Modulith

Spring Modulith is a Spring Boot framework that's based on modular monolith architectural principles. It helps identify, structure, and enforce application modules. It also includes tools for verifying module boundaries and observing their behavior, along with module-level testing capabilities, making Spring Boot applications easier to build and maintain.

Here's how to integrate Spring Modulith into a Kotlin-based Spring Boot application.

All the code samples are drawn from a fully working Kotlin example, which you can find in this GitHub repository.

Quick Start Kotlin Example

Spring Modulith can be added to any Spring Boot application by including its dependencies in the project's build.gradle.kts:

// build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter")
    implementation("org.springframework.modulith:spring-modulith-starter-core:1.4.3")
}

Note: If your project uses Maven, you can add these dependencies to the pom.xml file.

To define the modules, you need to add relevant package directories to the src directory. This code snippet illustrates order and product packages added to the application, each handling its own business logic, data, and services:

SpringModulithExample
└── src/main/java
    ├── example
    │   └── SpringmonolithApplication.kt
    └── example.order
        └── …
    └── example.product
        └── …
    └── example.payment
        └── …

Within each of the modules, you can define the business logic, service, and data access layers based on your application's requirements. The following code snippet shows a ProductService within the example.product package that returns a static greeting message:

package com.example.springmonolith.product

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service

@Service
class ProductService {

    fun getGreeting(): String {
        return "Hello from Product Module!"
    }
}

Similarly, define an OrderService within the example.order package that invokes ProductService::getGreeting() and returns a combined greeting message:

package com.example.springmonolith.order

import com.example.springmonolith.product.ProductService
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service

@Service
class OrderService(
    private val productService: ProductService
) {

    fun getGreeting(): String {
        return "Hello from Order Module!"
    }

    fun getCombinedGreeting(): String {
        return "Hello from Order Module and: ${productService.getGreeting()}"
    }
}

After adding similar business logic for each of the modules (eg ProductService, PaymentService), you also need to add the @Modulithic annotation to the Spring Boot Application class to mark it as modular. The annotation tells Spring Modulith to automatically detect modules based on package structure and enable the tooling for verification, testing, and observability:

package com.example.springmonolith

import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication
import org.springframework.boot.runApplication
import org.springframework.modulith.Modulithic

// add this annotation to the application
@Modulithic
@SpringBootApplication
class SpringmonolithApplication

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    runApplication<SpringmonolithApplication>(*args)
}

Next, you can update the package info file for each of the modules to define the allowed module dependencies. Since the order module depends on the methods defined in the product module, you'll need to add the following annotation in the order/package-info.java file:

// add this annotation
@org.springframework.modulith.ApplicationModule(allowedDependencies = {"product"})
@org.springframework.lang.NonNullApi
package com.example.springmonolith.order;

Finally, you can update the product/package-info.java file to set an empty dependency list for the product module:

// add this annotation
@org.springframework.modulith.ApplicationModule(allowedDependencies = {})
@org.springframework.lang.NonNullApi
package com.example.springmonolith.product;

The above annotation ensures that if a class or object defined in the product module tries to invoke a method defined outside the module, Spring Modulith verification tests will flag the violation. You will see an example of this scenario in later sections.

Spring Modulith Features

Spring Modulith supports various tools for working with modules, including module verification, documentation, and runtime observability. With @Modulithic, the application automatically recognizes its modules (based on package structure) and enables the modulith tooling. Let's look at how these work.

Modular Structure Checks

Spring Modulith provides built-in tooling to verify that the module boundaries adhere to the constraints. It checks for cyclic dependencies, validates that modules access other modules only through their public API packages (not internal code), and enforces explicit dependency rules. In your tests, you can use the ApplicationModules.verify() to verify the modular structure:

ApplicationModules.of(Application::class.java).verify()

Refer to the source code on GitHub for a complete example of the ModularityTest. With the above test configured, if the ProductService tries to invoke an order module method, the module verification test will fail. You can test the behavior by extending the ProductService to call getGreeting as shown below:

// add import
import com.example.springmonolith.order.OrderService

@Service
class ProductService(
    private val orderService: OrderService
) {

    // add this after getGreeting()
    fun getCombinedGreeting(): String {
        return "Hello from Product Module and: ${orderService.getGreeting()}"
    }
}

Since product module is configured to disallow all intermodule dependencies, when you run unit tests (./gradlew test), you would get a module violation error as shown below:

— TRUNCATED OUTPUT —
ModularityTests > verifiesModularStructure() FAILED
    org.springframework.modulith.core.Violations at ModularityTests.kt:20

You can replace direct intermodule calls with application events that let one module publish a domain event and another module listens to it. This preserves boundaries and avoids compile-time coupling between modules. For example, the order module can publish an event when an order is created, as shown below:

// order module
import org.springframework.context.ApplicationEventPublisher

@Service
class OrderService(private val events: ApplicationEventPublisher) {

    fun completeOrder(orderId: String) {
        events.publishEvent(OrderCompleted(orderId))
    }
}

data class OrderCompleted(val orderId: String)

Notice that the completeOrder method publishes the OrderCompleted event, and other modules (eg, InventoryPolicy) could react to the event using @ApplicationModuleListener, as shown below:

// product module
import org.springframework.modulith.events.ApplicationModuleListener
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component

@Component
class InventoryPolicy {

    @ApplicationModuleListener
    fun on(event: OrderCompleted) {
        println("Updating inventory for order: ${event.orderId}")
    }
}

Notice that the InventoryPolicy component has a listener configured for the OrderCompleted event that prints the order ID when it receives the event. Refer to the refactor branch on GitHub for a complete example on domain events.

Modular Level Testing

Modulith supports writing integration tests scoped to a single module. You can annotate a test class with @ApplicationModuleTest to test the module and its dependencies in isolation. This avoids the need to spin up the entire application, reducing setup overhead and making tests more reliable. For example, this code snippet shows a bare-bones integration test for the product module:

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
import org.springframework.modulith.test.ApplicationModuleTest

@ApplicationModuleTest
class ProductModuleTests {

    @Test
    fun testProductServiceGreeting() {
        val greeting = productService.getGreeting()
        assertTrue(greeting.contains("Product Module"))
    }
}

For the OrderService test, since it depends on the product module, you need to set the extraIncludes parameter in the @ApplicationModuleTest annotation to include it as shown below:

package com.example.springmonolith.order

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired
import org.springframework.modulith.test.ApplicationModuleTest
import org.springframework.test.context.junit.jupiter.SpringJUnitConfig
import kotlin.test.assertTrue

@ApplicationModuleTest(extraIncludes = ["product"])
@SpringJUnitConfig
class OrderModuleTests {

    @Autowired
    private lateinit var orderService: OrderService

    @Test
    fun testOrderServiceGreeting() {
        val greeting = orderService.getGreeting()
        assertTrue(greeting.contains("Order Module"))
    }
}

Observability into Module Interactions

Spring Modulith helps generate developer documentation using the Documenter abstraction. This tool can generate Unified Modeling Language (UML) component diagrams describing the relationship between modules and can also generate a tabular view of the key elements of a module. This code snippet generates an application module component diagram using Documenter:

class DocumentationTests {
    private val modules = ApplicationModules.of(SpringmonolithApplication::class.java)

    @Test
    fun writeDocumentationSnippets() {
        Documenter(modules)
            .writeModulesAsPlantUml()
            .writeIndividualModulesAsPlantUml()
    }
}

Spring Modulith also integrates with Micrometer to capture spans for module interactions. These spans can be sent to tracing tools such as Zipkin to generate runtime visualizations, making it easier to inspect which modules depend on each other, see how events flow across modules, and monitor interactions in production.

Deciding When to Use a Modular Monolith

Although a modular monolith can be the ideal balance between simplicity and structure in many cases, it isn't universally the right choice.

A modular monolith makes sense for:

  • Early-stage development or limited resources: In the early stages of a product or when working with small teams, a modular monolith reduces operational overhead. Developers can focus on delivering features quickly without the complexity of distributed systems. The modular design still enforces boundaries between business capabilities, so if the system grows, you can gradually migrate high-demand modules into separate microservices.
    • Example: A food delivery platform can start with modules for restaurants, menu, and orders inside a single deployable unit, but it can later extract and deploy one of the modules as a microservice.
  • Complex business domains: Applications that involve complex business logic, workflows, or dependencies can benefit from a modular structure. By encapsulating each business capability in its own module, the system becomes easier to develop, test, and maintain.
    • Example: An insurance platform can split policy management, claims processing, and customer support into separate modules to avoid creating interdependencies that can become difficult to maintain.

But a modular monolith may not be the right choice for:

  • Systems with independent scaling needs: Some systems have uneven load patterns where certain components handle millions of requests daily, while others are rarely used. Because modular monoliths deploy as one unit, you can't scale individual parts independently. A microservice-based approach can more easily scale components that expect a higher load than others.
    • Example: In an e-commerce platform, the product catalog or recommendation services may experience higher request volumes than order or payment services.
  • Systems that use diverse tech stacks: In some organizations, different teams rely on different programming languages, runtimes, or specialized infrastructure for different parts of the system. A modular monolith requires the entire application to use the same stack, which can limit flexibility. In these cases, a microservice-based architecture can provide the isolation needed to mix and match technologies.
    • Example: Machine learning or analytics teams may want to use Python or Go for their services, while client-facing or internal services can be based on Kotlin or Java.

Conclusion

Modular monolith architecture allows you to split the application logic into isolated modules with their own business logic, while still being deployed as a single artifact. It combines the benefits of a modular design while maintaining the development and release-related benefits of a monolithic architecture. Additionally, modern programming languages such as Kotlin provide tools that can help you achieve monolith stability without giving up the productivity that draws people to microservices.

Spring Modulith and Kotlin provide the tools to design and enforce clear module boundaries, test modules independently, and monitor their interactions. Try out Spring Modulith to build modular Kotlin applications, while keeping the flexibility to evolve into microservices if your scaling needs change.

title: The Power of Names: What Taborlin the Great Teaches Us About AI Prompting
description:
In The Kingkiller Chronicle, Taborlin the Great was a legendary wizard whose power was quite simple. He knew the names of things, and in knowing their true names, he commanded power over them. He could call the name of stone and demand it split in two. He could step off a tall tower and call the name of the wind, and the wind would carry him to safety.

While AI sometimes feels like a superpower in itself, it can also be incredibly frustrating. An image that seems clear and simple to describe in your head comes out looking like an artistic war crime when the model tries to interpret your prompt. The feature that seems straightforward in your application does not function at all as expected after implementation.

Furthermore, it can often be hard to even describe what makes the first implementation seem so off. I find this similar to how I feel at a wine tasting. While an aficionado can tell you all about the balanced, layered complexity of the wine, I simply know, "yes, I like this," and struggle to say why.

I believe this is why different people have such different experiences with AI and why the term "vibe coding" has become so overloaded. To some, it means blindly prompting off pure vibes with zero engineering rigor. To others, it just means directing an AI in natural language instead of typing every line of syntax yourself. In engineering work, I commonly hear, "The architecture of the code it generates is garbage," which comes from confusing the two.

Sure, it takes the path of least resistance. If you tell it, "implement code that gets data from Service A, transforms it, and loads it into our data warehouse", you're likely going to get entirely imperative-style code that does those steps in a giant, 500-line single god-method that would horrify the Chandrian themselves. No abstraction. Direct inline calls to the DB. It will not track historical changes or trends over time.

If instead you tell it to isolate side effects behind DAOs and service client classes, utilize IoC and DI for testability, and structure the warehouse around a medallion data model using Type 2 SCDs to track change over time, you'll get drastically improved, more maintainable results without significantly more effort. This comes simply by knowing the names of these basic patterns and knowing when to use them.

This doesn’t apply just to code. If you can picture an art style but don’t know what it’s called, you might ask for something like "old-timey storybook" and hope the model interprets that the same way you do. Learning that the look you’re after is Art Nouveau gives you a much more specific starting point. Technical documentation stops sounding like it was written with the flourish of the Edema Ruh when specifying that it should be written in Simplified Technical English instead of a more vague prompt like "keep it concise and unambiguous."

What I find about my own AI usage is that I’m now spending more time understanding these sorts of fundamentals in areas I'm not very familiar with. I’m studying art styles in order to better generate images. I’m studying writing styles in order to better generate prose fit to purpose. AI guides that study to help me learn the basic names, as I can now simply drop an image in and ask questions about the artistic style in a way I could never do before.

Taborlin the Great became a legend by learning the names of things to wield their power. AI gives us this superpower for far less effort. Although I'm still searching for the true name of Book 3. "Write 'The Doors of Stone.' Make no mistakes." unfortunately did not work very well.

If you're looking for a starting point, check out Semantic Anchors, a cool project that attempts to capture the names of many patterns, styles, and concepts that are useful in your prompting.

title: Help Your Coding Assistant Find the Right Code in Large Repos
description:
Get the starter: sdahal1/repo-search-workshop on GitHub. The reproduction, searches, tests, and typecheck were rehearsed locally on October 16, 2026, with Node.js 24.10.0, npm 11.6.0, ripgrep 15.2.0, and ast-grep 0.51.0. The published repository was cloned and its starter revision verified. The supplied local folder and Git bundle also work for this guide.

Author: Saurabh Rob Dahal, Developer Advocate, AWS

Description: Investigate a TypeScript retry bug using repository mapping, ripgrep, ast-grep, symbol navigation, and an evidence note you can use with different coding assistants.

Level: Beginner · Time: 60 minutes with a facilitator, after setup

A coding assistant can suggest a plausible fix before it understands a repository. A useful investigation makes its reasoning checkable: where does the behavior live, what evidence explains it, and which checks would distinguish a correct fix from a partial one?

In this workshop, you will investigate one prepared bug. A client configured with maxRetries: 0 still makes three requests when its transport fails. You will follow that setting across files, ask an assistant for a supported explanation, and make a small change.

The bug is deliberately small. The practice is learning how to approach unfamiliar code without reading every file or accepting the first plausible explanation. The same approach is useful when an application setting behaves unexpectedly, a wrapper changes an argument, or an error originates in another package.

Each step answers a different question. If the evidence is incomplete, return to a focused lookup before editing.

You can follow along with Kiro, Codex, Claude Code, or another assistant that can read your project, run shell commands, and edit files. Choose a coding model supported by your tool. The exercise uses ordinary commands and a Markdown note, so it does not depend on a particular model, context window, or project-memory format.

Your editor supplies definition and reference navigation. No AWS account, credentials, or cloud deployment is required. If you are working independently, pause at the evaluation prompts and take the time you need.

Before the workshop

You need Git, Node.js 24 with npm, ripgrep, and an editor with TypeScript definition and reference navigation. You should be comfortable opening a terminal and editing a text file. Complete your chosen assistant's sign-in before the session.

The commands use a Bash-compatible shell: Terminal on macOS, a Linux terminal, or WSL on Windows. Run commands from the repository root unless a step says otherwise. Copy the contents of a command block without adding a leading $ prompt.

Install ripgrep using the official installation instructions. On a Mac with Homebrew:

brew install ripgrep

Use a fresh checkout. Choose one of these routes, then run the shared setup below. Clone the workshop starter repository:

git clone https://github.com/sdahal1/repo-search-workshop.git repo-search-workshop
cd repo-search-workshop

If you already have the supplied local folder, skip cloning and enter it:

cd repo-search-workshop

If you have repo-search-workshop.bundle in your current directory, create a checkout from that local Git bundle instead:

git clone --branch starter ./repo-search-workshop.bundle repo-search-workshop
cd repo-search-workshop

From the repository root, pin the workshop's starter revision and install its dependencies:

git checkout --detach 5280be1e6659942e2335b10bde88b1fccdf9b76d
git switch -c workshop/my-investigation
node --version
npm --version
rg --version
npm ci
npx --no-install ast-grep --version
git status --short

The checkout puts everyone on the same source revision. The new branch gives you a place to keep your work. The starter pins @ast-grep/cli to 0.51.0 as a development dependency. npm ci installs dependencies from the committed lockfile without updating it. npm ci documentation

Check your setup: Node should report version 24, ast-grep should report 0.51.0, and git status --short should produce no output in this fresh checkout. Open the entire repository folder in your editor so it can find the TypeScript project configuration.

The npx commands use the installed project executable. If npm offers to download a package, stop and check that installation succeeded and that you are in the repository root.

The starter provides a fake transport, a failing regression test, an investigation template, and a saved AST rule. A transport is the component that performs the underlying request. Here, a small local function stands in for it, records calls, and fails predictably. No real service is involved.

You may type each command yourself or ask the assistant to run the exact command. For the first pass, run the searches yourself so you can connect their inputs to their results. Later, delegate those same steps with an explicit scope.

1 Show the failure

Time: 0–4 minutes

Concept: A reproduction turns a report into an observable difference between expected and actual behavior. It also gives you a check to run after editing.

The report says: “I set maxRetries to zero, but the client still retries.” Before investigating, define what counts as a retry. In this project, it is an additional attempt after the initial request. Therefore:

total attempts when every request fails = 1 + allowed retries
zero retries = one initial attempt

Count transport calls, including the initial request. The symptom does not yet tell us which function is responsible.

Task: Run the demo, then the focused test:

npm run demo
npm run test:repro

Expected result before the fix: The demo records three transport calls for maxRetries: 0. The focused test fails because it expects one call and observes three. A failing assertion is intentional here; a missing-module or command-not-found error is a setup problem.

The local rehearsal confirmed this failure. The full starter suite ran 11 tests: 10 passed, and only the zero-retries reproduction failed. Typechecking passed before the fix, showing that this behavioral bug is not a type error.

Evaluate: Open packages/client/test/client.test.ts. Find where the test supplies zero to the public client API, where the fake transport increments its counter, and where the test checks the final count. Confirm that the test observes behavior through the public API rather than directly testing a helper expression.

Write the reproduction command, expected count, and actual count in workshop/INVESTIGATION.md. Do not change an assertion to match the current behavior.

Teaching moment: “The transport ran three times” is evidence. “The retry loop is off by one” is a hypothesis. Other explanations are possible: the option might be dropped, defaulted incorrectly, or interpreted differently. Keep those possibilities open until you trace the value.

2 Map the repository

Time: 4–12 minutes

Concept: A repository map identifies responsibilities and boundaries. It helps you choose where to look before spending time on implementation details.

Task: Run:

git ls-files
git ls-files 'README*' '*package.json' '*tsconfig*.json'
git ls-files 'packages/client/*'

The first command shows tracked paths. The next commands narrow that inventory to project descriptions, manifests, TypeScript configuration, and the client package. Quoting the patterns passes them to Git instead of asking the shell to expand them. git ls-files documentation

Open README.md, the root package.json, packages/client/package.json, and docs/client-options.md. Find the test scripts and the meaning of maxRetries. A manifest describes a package's dependencies, scripts, and entry points; it helps connect a folder to what the project runs.

Use the map to choose a starting area. The relationships must still be confirmed in source and tests.

Ask your assistant:

Map this repository using its tracked file paths, README, package
manifests, and docs/client-options.md. Do not edit files.

Identify the package most likely to own the reported retry behavior.
Explain your choice using paths and documented responsibilities.
Do not read every implementation file yet.

Expected result: packages/client is the likely owner. Its src directory contains implementation and its test directory contains the reproduction. The option documentation establishes that zero is valid.

Evaluate: Write one sentence explaining why the client package is relevant. “It has client in its name” is a starting clue. A documented responsibility and a reproduction that imports the package are stronger support.

Also identify the package's test command before editing. That prevents the assistant from guessing how the project is verified.

Teaching moment: A map is a working hypothesis about ownership. Expand your scope if imports lead elsewhere. git ls-files is an inventory of tracked files; it does not include every untracked file on disk, and it does not describe runtime behavior.

3 Search by text

Time: 12–18 minutes

Concept: Text search is useful when you know a name, error, or literal value. It finds mentions in code, tests, comments, and documentation.

Task: Search the owning package and option documentation:

rg -n -F 'maxRetries' packages/client docs/client-options.md
rg -n -C 3 -F 'maxRetries' packages/client/src

rg runs ripgrep. -n displays line numbers, -F treats the query as literal text, and -C 3 includes three surrounding lines. The final arguments select where to search. ripgrep guide

Expected result: Matches lead to the option type, request path, retry implementation, and regression test. Read a result as a location to inspect, not a complete explanation. Open the enclosing function when three surrounding lines are insufficient.

Choose the search that matches your question. These tools complement one another throughout an investigation.

Evaluate: Classify useful matches by their role:

Kind of match What to learn from it
Option definition Which values the API accepts
Caller or wrapper Whether the value is forwarded or transformed
Implementation How the value affects behavior
Test Which behavior is asserted
Documentation What behavior is promised

Add useful paths and symbols to your investigation note. Record actual line numbers from your checkout; the article does not prescribe fixed line numbers.

If the search returns nothing, first check spelling, case, and your directory. A zero-result search means no matching text was found in the searched scope. It does not prove the behavior is absent from the program.

Teaching moment: A matching name does not establish a call relationship. Two modules may declare independent variables with the same spelling. Text search finds candidates; symbol navigation will help you distinguish them.

4 Search by structure

Time: 18–23 minutes

Concept: An abstract syntax tree, or AST, represents code through syntax nodes and their relationships. An expression such as left || right has an operator and two operands. Structural search asks for that arrangement while allowing selected parts to vary. ast-grep core concepts

You already know the option's name. Now ask a second question: where does the code use an OR expression that might supply a fallback? This is useful when the same structure appears under different variable names or across multiple lines.

Task: Start with the operator as literal text:

rg -n -F '||' packages/client/src

Keep -F: the pipe character has special meaning in regular expressions. Then run the prepared structural query:

npx --no-install ast-grep run --lang ts \
  --pattern '$VALUE || $FALLBACK' packages/client/src

Here, run performs a one-time search, --lang ts selects TypeScript, and --pattern supplies the code shape. There is no rewrite argument, so this command does not modify code. ast-grep run reference

Understand the placeholders

$VALUE and $FALLBACK are metavariables that match syntax nodes. Leave those names in the command. Keep the single quotes so the shell passes the dollar signs unchanged instead of expanding shell variables. ast-grep quick start

For this candidate:

options.maxRetries || DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES

the left capture is options.maxRetries and the right capture is DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES. The names VALUE and FALLBACK are labels we chose; they do not tell ast-grep what the author intended.

The simplified tree shows what stays fixed—the OR operator—and what the metavariables can capture.

Compare matches and counterexamples

Consider these illustrative snippets. They explain the pattern; they are not claimed to be exact starter files.

const a = options.maxRetries || DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES;

const b = options.timeoutMs
  ||
  5000;

const allowed = isAdmin || isOwner;

// options.maxRetries || DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES
const explanation = "options.maxRetries || DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES";

const enabled = isReady && hasPermission;

The broad pattern matches the OR expressions assigned to a, b, and allowed. The multiline expression still has the requested shape. The comment and string are not executable OR expressions, and the final expression uses a different operator. ast-grep pattern syntax

isAdmin || isOwner is a valuable counterexample: it matches, but the boolean logic may be entirely correct. A syntax match is not a bug diagnosis. The tool does not know whether zero is meaningful to this particular API.

Narrow and save the query

Require the property name while leaving the object and right-hand expression variable:

npx --no-install ast-grep run --lang ts \
  --pattern '$OPTIONS.maxRetries || $FALLBACK' packages/client/src

Expected result: The candidate in packages/client/src/retry.ts remains. The object name can vary, so config.maxRetries || 2 also matches. However, this narrower pattern would miss options['maxRetries'] || 2 or a property read first assigned to a local variable. That is a reason to inspect the surrounding code, not a reason to search every possible expression at once.

The starter's workshop/defaulting.yml saves the broad query:

id: find-or-expressions
language: TypeScript
rule:
  pattern: $VALUE || $FALLBACK

Run it with:

npx --no-install ast-grep scan \
  --rule workshop/defaulting.yml packages/client/src

The rule gives the query a name and language so someone else can repeat it. ast-grep rule essentials

In the pinned starter, the broad query returns four candidates: the multiline request-label expression, the trace expression, the retry-input validation condition, and the retry-setting expression. The first three implement intentional behavior. The narrowed query returns only the candidate in retry.ts. Compare these results with the literal text search, which also finds mentions inside a comment and a string.

Evaluate: Explain why each relevant match deserves inspection. Compare what text search found with what the structural query found. Save the candidate and its enclosing symbol in your note.

Teaching moment: Structural search reduces ambiguity about code shape. It does not establish runtime values, symbol identity, or business intent. Those need different evidence.

5 Follow the symbols

Time: 23–28 minutes

Concept: Symbol navigation resolves an identifier to its declaration and finds uses of that declaration. It helps answer which function is actually involved when names repeat or imports are renamed.

For example, a module could import withRetry as runWithRetries. Searching only for the original name might find the import but miss calls written with the alias. Definition navigation can connect those uses through the project language service.

Task: In your editor:

  1. Open the reproduction test and use Go to Definition on createClient.
  2. In packages/client/src/client.ts, locate the request path and the call to withRetry.
  3. Use Go to Definition on withRetry to reach packages/client/src/retry.ts.
  4. Use Find References on its definition to inspect the callers.
  5. Inspect ClientOptions in packages/client/src/types.ts and compare it with the documented contract.

Use the editor's context menu or command palette to find these actions. The names and shortcuts can differ; for one concrete implementation, see TypeScript navigation in Visual Studio Code.

Confirm the arrows by navigating definitions and inspecting callers. The picture illustrates the starter's relationships; it is not a screenshot or a generated runtime trace.

Expected result: You can follow the option from the public client API to the retry implementation. Check whether the wrapper forwards zero unchanged before interpreting the defaulting expression.

Evaluate: Record the caller and callee paths and symbols. A reference result may be a declaration, import, or call. Read it before recording a call relationship. Navigation also does not prove that a branch executed during the reproduction; combine it with the test and implementation.

Teaching moment: Language Server Protocol, or LSP, standardizes communication for code intelligence. Editors can also provide TypeScript navigation through their own language-service integrations. The shared requirement here is working definition/reference navigation. There is no universal lsp terminal command, and your assistant does not need direct LSP access. LSP specification

6 Gather evidence before asking for a fix

Time: 28–36 minutes

Concept: A short investigation note separates observations from interpretations and makes your context portable. Another assistant or teammate can inspect the same evidence without reconstructing a long conversation.

Keep the evidence compact enough to review, but specific enough to reproduce and challenge.

Task: Complete workshop/INVESTIGATION.md:

# Investigation

## Observed behavior
Reproduction command:
Expected behavior:
Actual behavior:

## Repository area
Owning package and evidence:

## Relevant code
Paths, symbols, actual line numbers, and caller relationships:

## Constraints
Preserve the public API and omitted-option behavior.
Keep the fake transport and meaningful assertions.

## Root cause hypothesis
Leave blank until the next step.

## Proposed modification points
Leave blank until the next step.

## Verification
npm run test:repro
npm test
npm run typecheck
git status --short
git diff
git diff --check

An evidence entry might say, “The reproduction passes zero at the public API and observes three transport calls.” Attach the actual test location. A hypothesis would say, “A defaulting expression may replace zero before the loop runs.” Keeping these in different sections makes it easier to notice what remains unproven.

Include a short reason beside each source location. “This wrapper forwards the option” is more useful than a list of six paths with no explanation. Leave out unrelated search results and large copied files; the assistant can open the referenced code.

Evaluate: Could someone who missed the walkthrough reproduce the failure and locate the relevant expressions from your note? Could they tell which claims you observed and which still require checking?

Teaching moment: Good context is selected evidence with an explicit purpose. Paths and symbols help someone relocate it; line numbers identify positions in this checkout and may move after edits.

7 Explain the root cause before editing

Time: 36–43 minutes

Concept: A supported hypothesis connects the input, the transformation, and the observed output. Evaluate that connection before changing code.

Task: In a fresh or existing assistant conversation in the same checkout, paste:

Read workshop/INVESTIGATION.md. Do not edit files.

Inspect the referenced code and explain the failing behavior.
If evidence is missing, identify the next focused lookup needed.

Return:
- Your root-cause hypothesis.
- Supporting paths, symbols, and actual line numbers.
- Any uncertainty or competing explanation.
- The smallest proposed change and expected modified files.
- Tests that distinguish a correct fix from a partial fix.

Stop before editing.

You may use a plan or read-only mode if your tool provides one. The explicit instruction is still useful because it tells the assistant what deliverable you want at this stage.

Expected explanation: 0 || DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES selects the default because zero is falsy. With a default of two retries, the always-failing transport receives one initial call plus two retries. The ?? operator uses its fallback only for null or undefined, preserving zero. TypeScript nullish coalescing documentation

The operator table explains language behavior. Its null, false, and empty-string examples do not expand the client's numeric input contract.

For a text version of the diagram:

| Left value (x) | x \|\| 2 | x ?? 2 | API meaning here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 2 | 0 | Valid: disable retries |
| undefined | 2 | 2 | Omitted option: use the default |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | Valid: allow one retry |
| null | 2 | 2 | Language example, outside the option type |
| false | 2 | false | Language example, outside the option type |
| '' | 2 | '' | Language example, outside the option type |

Neither operator validates input. The proposed change corrects defaulting for values already allowed by the API.

Evaluate: Check three links in the explanation:

  1. The public contract allows zero, and the wrapper delivers it unchanged.
  2. The identified expression replaces zero with the documented default of two.
  3. The retry loop interprets two as additional attempts, producing three total calls.

If one link is missing, perform the next focused lookup. An answer that simply recommends ?? has not yet explained the whole symptom. A proposed loop change also needs evidence that the loop itself is wrong.

Optional self-check in your terminal:

node -e 'console.log({ or: 0 || 2, nullish: 0 ?? 2 })'

The expected values are or: 2 and nullish: 0. This checks language behavior in isolation; it does not prove the repository's value follows that path. The earlier evidence establishes that connection.

Update the hypothesis and proposed modification sections of your note. Do not broaden the API to accept null, strings, or booleans just because the operator table includes them.

Teaching moment: Different models may phrase the explanation differently. Judge the evidence and predicted behavior. A useful hypothesis also tells you what you should observe after the fix.

8 Make the narrow change and verify it

Time: 43–56 minutes

Concept: A fix must correct the reported behavior and preserve the surrounding contract. Test results and diff review provide different parts of that evidence.

Task: After checking the explanation, tell the assistant:

Apply the smallest change supported by our investigation.
Preserve the public API and default retry behavior.
Keep the reproduction's original assertion intact.
Add focused regression coverage only where it is missing.
Do not refactor unrelated code or update dependencies.
Do not stage or commit the changes.
Run the verification commands in workshop/INVESTIGATION.md.
Report the modified files and actual results, including failures.

The expected production change is:

- const retries = options.maxRetries || DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES;
+ const retries = options.maxRetries ?? DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES;

If you are editing manually, make the same justified change in the editor. Avoid a global replacement of ||: other matches may intentionally use boolean logic or falsy-value defaults.

Run the checks yourself if the assistant has not run them:

npm run test:repro
npm test
npm run typecheck
npm run demo
git status --short
git diff
git diff --check

Evaluate the behavior

A useful test matrix checks the repaired boundary and nearby behavior that should remain valid.

With the fake transport failing on every attempt, verify:

Input Expected total transport calls after the fix Why check it
maxRetries: 0 1 Reproduces the reported boundary
Option omitted, default of 2 3 Preserves the default
maxRetries: 1 2 Preserves explicit positive values

Also preserve immediate success: when the first request succeeds, there should be one call, regardless of a larger retry allowance. A retry budget allows extra attempts after failure; it does not require them after success.

The rehearsed solution passed the reproduction, all 11 tests, and typechecking; its demo showed one call for zero retries. Those are the expected results for your fix. Read the test output rather than accepting a summary that says “looks good.” Check which command ran and whether it completed successfully.

Evaluate the change

Inspect every changed file. The investigation note is expected to change. Production edits should be limited to the justified implementation; test edits should strengthen coverage while preserving the reproduction's original assertion.

Ask why any dependency lockfile, public type, unrelated helper, or large formatting block changed. Such edits need their own justification. Also inspect untracked files reported by git status, because a normal diff does not display their contents.

git diff shows unstaged tracked changes. If you staged anything, also run git diff --cached. git diff --check checks whitespace errors; silence does not establish behavioral correctness. git diff documentation

Teaching moment: The reproduction checks the bug. Nearby tests check preserved behavior. Typechecking checks type compatibility. Diff review checks the scope and meaning of edits. A passing check cannot answer all four questions.

Finish with a reusable investigation

Time: 56–60 minutes

Explain the bug to a partner in three sentences: what failed, where the value changed meaning, and how you verified the fix. Point to evidence for each sentence.

Then name the question each tool answered. Text search found mentions. AST search found a code shape. Symbol navigation connected definitions and uses. Tests observed behavior. Your investigation note connected those findings into an explanation someone else could review.

On your next unfamiliar repository, start with a reproducible symptom and a small map. Choose searches according to the question you need answered. Expand the scope when the evidence requires it, and give your assistant a clear boundary between investigating and editing.

If a step behaves differently

Symptom Next check
rg is not found Install ripgrep, reopen the terminal, and run rg --version.
ast-grep is missing or the version differs Return to the repository root; confirm npm ci succeeded with development dependencies installed.
AST search has no matches Check the directory, TypeScript language flag, and single quotes. Confirm you still have the unfixed starter.
Definition navigation fails Open the repository root, install dependencies, and confirm the editor recognizes the TypeScript project. Follow imports manually while fixing navigation.
The reproduction already passes Inspect the checkout and existing diff. You may have the solution or a previous edit. Preserve your work and use a fresh starter checkout.
A test reports a setup error Resolve that error before interpreting it as evidence of the retry bug.
The assistant edits during investigation Inspect the diff before continuing. Preserve your note and use a fresh starter checkout if needed.
The fix passes one test but breaks another Compare the failing case with the documented contract; revisit the hypothesis instead of weakening an assertion.

No cloud resources are created by this exercise, so there is no AWS cleanup step. Keep your checkout to reuse the investigation note and commands.

title: Replicable Dueling Bandits
description:
arXiv:2610.20908v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dueling bandits choose each comparison based on earlier noisy outcomes, so two runs on the same preferences can compare different pairs. We study replicable dueling bandits, where two executions with shared internal randomness and independent comparison outcomes must select the same ordered pair in every round with probability at least $1-\rho$. Building on Beat-the-Mean, whose scores change as arms are eliminated and need not rank the best arm highest, we design the first such algorithms with sublinear regret. Under relaxed stochastic transitivity with parameter $\gamma\ge 1$ and the stochastic triangle inequality, we design an algorithm that achieves expected regret $\widetilde{O}(\gamma^8 K^4 H_{\mathrm{p}}/\rho^2)$, where $H_{\mathrm{p}}=\sum_{i=2}^{K}(P_{1i}-1/2)^{-1}$. Under strong stochastic transitivity, we design an algorithm based on simultaneous elimination that improves the dependence on $K$ and achieves $\widetilde{O}(K^2 H_{\mathrm{p}}/\rho^2)$ regret. For linear dueling bandits, we design an algorithm that achieves regret $\widetilde{O}(d^3\sqrt{T}/(c_\mu\rho))$. Experiments on synthetic and language-model preferences show replicability, with sublinear regret.

title: AlphaDiana: A Measurement System for Agents in Verifiable Reasoning Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.20675v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents pair reasoning models with harnesses that organize model calls, execute tools, load skill instructions, and retain history in memory. Understanding agent performance requires linking execution conditions to outcomes, behavior, and resource use. We introduce AlphaDiana, a measurement system with modular interfaces for datasets, agents, environments, and scorers. It preserves harness-native control loops while controlling file reuse and memory retention separately. AlphaDiana supports macro analyses of complete agents and micro interventions on agent components such as tools, skills, and memory under matched conditions. We study three open-source models and three open-source harnesses on five answer-based benchmarks, with two models also tested on two interactive benchmarks. We find that harnesses do not consistently improve the accuracy of reasoning: gains on questions unsolved by the model alone can be outweighed by losses on questions it answers correctly without tools. This inconsistency extends to component interventions: neither skill guidance nor retained history reliably improves accuracy. Behavior and output-token use must be assessed with correctness: low token entropy can accompany wrong answers, and less output per execution can mean more output tokens per correct answer when accuracy falls. AlphaDiana links answer correctness and execution status to traces and resource records for comparing agents and diagnosing failures under shared task and resource policies.

title: Who May Release an Agent's Promise? Standing over Commitments in Multi-Party Chat
description:
arXiv:2610.21203v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When an assistant serving a team makes a promise to Alice, who may cancel it? We call this standing: only the creditor (the person owed) or someone the creditor or operator policy authorizes may release a commitment, regardless of rank. In a controlled chat environment we vary who cancels and separate two errors: unauthorized release (obeying someone without standing) and override (executing a released promise). Across six models, smaller open ones override the creditor (Qwen3.5-9B: 69%); larger ones drop promises on a peer's direct word (Qwen3.8-27B: 89%; gpt-6.1-sol: 83%); nearly all act on a bystander's "go ahead after all". Oracles dissociate the errors: stating the rule or the creditor curbs unauthorized release but not override, which the latter even raises in three of four models; among them, only knowing whether the promise is still owed cuts override. Enabling thinking moves smaller models the way scale does. A self-kept commitment ledger stops override in four of five models; with a one-paragraph release policy it matches or beats the best oracle store, raising gpt-6-luna's strict accuracy from 49% (policy alone) to 83%. Code, prompts, outputs and labels are released.

title: WebSockets vs Server-Sent Events vs Polling: When to Use Which
description:
Real-time features — chat, live notifications, collaborative editing, live dashboards — all require the server to push data to the client. There are three main approaches: WebSockets, Server-Sent Events (SSE), and polling. Picking the wrong one leads to either unnecessary complexity or something that doesn't scale.

Polling

The simplest approach: the client asks the server for updates on a schedule.

// Client
setInterval(async () => {
  const response = await fetch('/api/notifications/new?since=' + lastCheck);
  const data = await response.json();
  if (data.notifications.length > 0) {
    updateUI(data.notifications);
    lastCheck = Date.now();
  }
}, 3000);  // check every 3 seconds

Pros:

  • Works with any HTTP server
  • Simple to implement and debug
  • No special infrastructure
  • Works behind all proxies and firewalls

Cons:

  • Latency = polling interval (up to 3 seconds in the example above)
  • Wasteful: most polls return nothing
  • Generates constant load even when idle

Long polling reduces waste by holding the connection open until data is available:

async function longPoll() {
  while (true) {
    try {
      const response = await fetch('/api/events/wait');  // server holds 30s
      const data = await response.json();
      handleEvent(data);
    } catch {
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 5000));  // retry after error
    }
  }
}

// Server (Express)
app.get('/api/events/wait', async (req, res) => {
  const event = await waitForEvent(req.user.id, { timeout: 30000 });
  if (event) {
    res.json(event);
  } else {
    res.json({ type: 'timeout' });
  }
});

Long polling is a reasonable choice when you need real-time but can't use WebSockets (corporate proxies, simple infrastructure).

Server-Sent Events (SSE)

SSE is a simple protocol for one-way server-to-client streaming over HTTP. The browser keeps a persistent HTTP connection open; the server sends events as text:

// Client
const source = new EventSource('/api/stream');

source.addEventListener('message', (e) => {
  const data = JSON.parse(e.data);
  updateUI(data);
});

source.addEventListener('notification', (e) => {
  showNotification(JSON.parse(e.data));
});

source.addEventListener('error', () => {
  console.log('Connection lost, will auto-reconnect');
});

// EventSource automatically reconnects on disconnect
source.close();  // explicit close

// Server (Express)
app.get('/api/stream', (req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, {
    'Content-Type': 'text/event-stream',
    'Cache-Control': 'no-cache',
    'Connection': 'keep-alive',
    'X-Accel-Buffering': 'no'  // disable nginx buffering
  });

  const send = (event, data) => {
    res.write(`event: ${event}\n`);
    res.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify(data)}\n\n`);
  };

  // Send initial data
  send('message', { type: 'connected', userId: req.user.id });

  // Subscribe to updates
  const unsubscribe = notificationBus.subscribe(req.user.id, (event) => {
    send('notification', event);
  });

  // Cleanup on disconnect
  req.on('close', () => {
    unsubscribe();
  });
});

Pros:

  • Simpler than WebSockets (standard HTTP, easy to debug in Network panel)
  • Automatic reconnection built into the browser
  • Works with HTTP/2 multiplexing
  • Works behind most proxies (it's just HTTP)

Cons:

  • One-way only (server → client)
  • HTTP/1.1 limited to 6 connections per domain (HTTP/2 removes this)
  • Not supported in older IE (but 97%+ browser support now)

Best for: Notifications, live feeds, progress updates, AI streaming responses (ChatGPT-style).

WebSockets

WebSockets provide full-duplex, persistent connections between client and server. Both sides can send messages at any time.

// Client
const ws = new WebSocket('wss://api.example.com/ws');

ws.addEventListener('open', () => {
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'subscribe', channel: 'room-42' }));
});

ws.addEventListener('message', (e) => {
  const data = JSON.parse(e.data);
  handleMessage(data);
});

ws.addEventListener('close', (e) => {
  console.log('Closed:', e.code, e.reason);
  // Implement reconnection logic
});

ws.addEventListener('error', () => {
  console.error('WebSocket error');
});

// Send a message
ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'chat', text: 'Hello!' }));

// Server (Node.js with 'ws' library)
const WebSocket = require('ws');
const wss = new WebSocket.Server({ port: 8080 });

const rooms = new Map();

wss.on('connection', (ws, req) => {
  ws.userId = authenticate(req);  // extract from cookie/token
  let currentRoom = null;

  ws.on('message', (message) => {
    const data = JSON.parse(message);

    if (data.type === 'subscribe') {
      currentRoom = data.channel;
      if (!rooms.has(currentRoom)) rooms.set(currentRoom, new Set());
      rooms.get(currentRoom).add(ws);
    }

    if (data.type === 'chat') {
      const room = rooms.get(currentRoom);
      if (room) {
        room.forEach(client => {
          if (client.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) {
            client.send(JSON.stringify({
              type: 'chat',
              userId: ws.userId,
              text: data.text
            }));
          }
        });
      }
    }
  });

  ws.on('close', () => {
    if (currentRoom && rooms.has(currentRoom)) {
      rooms.get(currentRoom).delete(ws);
    }
  });
});

Pros:

  • Full duplex (both sides can send)
  • Low latency (no HTTP overhead per message)
  • Ideal for high-frequency bidirectional communication

Cons:

  • More complex than SSE
  • Some proxies/firewalls block WebSocket upgrades
  • Stateful connection — harder to load balance
  • Reconnection logic must be implemented manually

Libraries that simplify WebSocket complexity:

// Socket.io handles reconnection, rooms, namespaces, fallbacks
const io = require('socket.io')(server);

io.on('connection', (socket) => {
  socket.on('join-room', (room) => {
    socket.join(room);
  });

  socket.on('send-message', ({ room, text }) => {
    io.to(room).emit('message', { text, from: socket.id });
  });
});

Decision Guide

Polling SSE WebSockets
Direction Client → Server (periodically) Server → Client Both
Protocol HTTP HTTP WS/WSS
Reconnect Manual Automatic Manual
Proxy friendly Yes Usually Sometimes
Complexity Low Medium High
Load balancing Easy Easy Needs sticky sessions

Use polling when:

  • Infrequent updates (> 30 second intervals acceptable)
  • Simple infrastructure, can't add WebSocket support
  • Low traffic, simplicity matters more than efficiency

Use SSE when:

  • Server pushes data to many clients (notifications, feeds, live updates)
  • One-way communication is sufficient
  • You want simplicity with better performance than polling
  • AI text streaming (ChatGPT, Claude streaming responses use SSE)

Use WebSockets when:

  • Bidirectional, low-latency communication (chat, collaborative editing, games)
  • High-frequency data exchange (trading, live sports, multiplayer)
  • Client needs to send data frequently, not just receive

For most web apps, SSE covers 80% of real-time needs at much lower complexity than WebSockets. Reserve WebSockets for genuinely bidirectional, latency-sensitive use cases.

title: Interpreting Language Model Parameters
description:
arXiv:2610.20748v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover how neural networks use their parameters to implement their impressive neural algorithms. Although previous work has uncovered substantial structure in the intermediate representations that networks use, little progress has been made to understand how the parameters and nonlinearities of networks perform computations on those representations. In this work, we present a method that brings us closer to this understanding by decomposing a language model's parameters into subcomponents that each implement only a small part of the model's learned algorithm, while simultaneously requiring only a small fraction of those subcomponents to account for the network's behavior on any input. The method, adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD), optimizes for decompositions of neural network parameters into simple subcomponents that preserve the network's input-output behavior even when many subcomponents are ablated, including under ablations that are adversarially selected to destroy behavior. This encourages learning subcomponents that provide short, mechanistically faithful descriptions of the network's behavior that should aggregate appropriately into more global descriptions of the network's learned algorithm. We study how sequences of interactions between these parameter subcomponents produce the network's output on particular inputs, enabling a new kind of 'circuit' analysis. While more work remains to be done to deepen our understanding of how neural networks use their parameters to compute their behavior, our work suggests an approach to identify a small set of simple, mechanistically faithful subcomponents on which further mechanistic analysis can be based.

title: StochLOB: Heavy-Tailed Score Matching for Robust Limit Order Book Trend Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.21081v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Score-based diffusion methods usually perturb data with Brownian Gaussian noise, corresponding to a light-tailed forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). For market time series this SDE can be a poor abstraction: limit order book (LOB) order flow is heavy-tailed, bursty, and occasionally jump-like. We study STOCHLOB, a training-only score-matching framework that changes the forward diffusion corruption law while leaving the deployed predictor deterministic. Instead of Brownian-only Gaussian corruption, the noising process uses two non-Gaussian SDE-inspired alternatives: jump-L\'evy noise through a compound-Poisson variance mixture, and clipped $\alpha$-stable noise through a positive-stable Gaussian scale mixture. These corruptions inject finite jumps and heavy-tailed residuals into training without requiring reverse-time diffusion sampling at inference. The resulting score target has a useful interpretation: its radial factor $h_t(r)$ is the posterior expected corruption precision, so large residuals are weighted according to the latent corruption scale that most plausibly generated them. On chronologically held-out Coinbase LOB data, the proposed variants remain competitive on uncorrupted BTC and altcoin test horizons and improve several realized tail-window stress diagnostics. An exploratory Feishu A-share transfer study further tests whether the probability outputs remain usable under transaction costs and trading-rule constraints. Code and configuration files are available at https://github.com/ArshiAbolghasemi/Penny.

title: Defining and Generating Compositional Structure
description:
arXiv:2610.20922v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compositional structure is pervasive in nature and across scales: atoms combine into molecules, molecules into cells, and cells into organisms, while further compositional hierarchies appear within each level. More broadly, compositionality, the reuse and recombination of parts into novel structures, is a fundamental source of interesting complexity in both natural and artificial systems. Yet despite its importance, and despite our apparent ease in recognizing it, mathematical accounts capturing what we intuitively mean by compositional structure remain limited. Here, we fill this gap by formalizing a simple idea: compositional structure emerges when parts, considered together, reveal shared structure that is not captured when those parts are modeled separately. We express this idea using algorithmic information theory, the mathematics of information and compression, which provides a natural way to identify structure in arbitrary data without specifying in advance what that structure must look like. Applied across scales, our definition informs where and how compositional structure emerges within an object. Using tractable approximations, we then invert the framework to generate compositional objects: we specify the desired form of their compositional structure without prescribing their particular content, and optimize directly over strings and images. The resulting objects exhibit readily recognizable hierarchical reuse and part-whole organization, suggesting that the definition captures compositional structure rather than merely complexity, regularity, or shared information. Finally, we discuss implications for machine learning, including a new perspective on depth in neural architectures and principles for constructing compositional data curricula capable of supporting open-ended learning.

title: Quantile-Guided Diffusion for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2610.20739v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantile forecasts summarize uncertainty at each future time step, while diffusion forecasters represent it through sampled future trajectories. We study how predicted quantiles can serve as distributional controls for diffusion forecasting. Specifically, we investigate how the mechanism of quantile integration affects its effectiveness in guiding a pretrained diffusion forecaster. We find that residual control throughout the denoising network yields the most consistent improvements. We instantiate this approach as Control-TS, which learns a quantile-control pathway while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. Across eight benchmarks, Control-TS consistently improves the backbone's CRPS, achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art forecasting models, and retains its gains in capacity-matched comparisons. Further analyses examine how these gains depend on quantile granularity, predictor choice, and forecast quality. Finally, we introduce the Conditional Linear Predictive Score (CLPS), which complements distributional metrics by evaluating the downstream forecasting utility of generated futures. Together, these findings support predicted quantiles as an effective interface between explicit uncertainty estimates and diffusion-based trajectory generation.
