title: How our agents build on-brand pages with design.md
description:
Across Vercel, we use coding agents to design and build pages that have to look and feel like Vercel. The typography, color, and composition all need to carry the same judgment that we put into the pages we already ship ourselves.

We recently wrote about product-design, our skill that teaches agents how we design when they work in our codebases. The skill lives in each repository alongside the code that it governs, explaining how agents can find and understand our design system as well as product guidelines for whatever they are building.

This works great when agents are working in our codebases, where everything the skill needs is right there. But what about reports, proposals, and the one-off pages that still have to look like Vercel but get made in tools that can't read any of those files? For us, the answer was design.md, one public file any agent can load.

How we approached building design.md

What made product-design work well was that the design system and product guidelines were sitting right there in the repository for agents to read. We needed a way for agents and tools outside that environment to reach the same knowledge, so that the pages coming out the other end would still look like something we designed ourselves. That set two requirements:

  • A single public URL that anyone can point their agents at, regardless of the environment they run in.

  • Guidance covering everything that made product-design useful in the first place, from brand, layout, and copywriting to the design system, responsiveness, and information architecture.

The naive approach we tried first was to simply port product-design into a public prompt, collapsing the skill's reference files into one file any agent could read from a URL. The problem we found was that while the prompt described our visual language just fine, every model reading it interpreted that description differently, generating vastly different pages from the same guidance.

Part of this comes from the fact that design language is subjective. Phrases like "keep the layout clean" can really mean anything. What is "clean"? Beyond that, the bigger problem was everything else the prompt left behind. Inside our codebases, an agent reads product-design surrounded by real components and shipped examples of the things it describes. But a public prompt includes none of that, leaving every model to rebuild our style from just words alone.

So what we needed to do was distill what that environment provided into a single file, and the only way to know whether we were getting closer was to look at the pages coming out. We set the port aside and started writing a new file from scratch, this time testing every change against a repeatable set of eval prompts.

We wrote seven of them, pulled from real use cases and paired with mock inputs:

  • Usage and performance report

  • Renewal proposal

  • Benchmark report

  • Interactive planning page

  • Build-versus-buy brief

  • Security governance brief

  • Presentation deck

The prompts stayed fixed while the file changed, so any difference in the output traced back to the guidance.

The first comparison

These evals gave us a way to measure both what the file was actually doing and how it was being interpreted by different agents. For our first test, we wanted to know whether design.md would actually change what a model produced at all. We ran the renewal proposal eval twice in the same environment with the same model, once without design.md and once with it loaded, keeping the prompt, data, and viewport identical in both runs.

Without design.md, the model generated a generic SaaS dashboard. But with it, the page led with the renewal recommendation itself, pulled the commercial evidence into one grid, put peer values on a single scale so they could actually be compared, and kept supporting detail available without letting it compete with the summary. This allowed us to conclude that the file changed the page’s structure and hierarchy as well, not just the styling like we originally found, giving us enough signal to keep building the guidance like this, one rule at a time.

The three parts that make the system work

As we tested and rebuilt design.md, the scope evolved into a three-part system that made the entire thing work:

  • design.md supplies guidance that shows agents how to frame the reader's job, structure evidence, and choose a composition.

  • A public stylesheet that defines a bounded, documented vocabulary of classes and tokens.

  • An evaluation loop turns repeated human feedback into better guidance and deterministic checks.

Each of these layers covers a different slice of the work that creates a high-quality, on-brand Vercel page. The judgment that gets encoded in design.md gives agents guidance on:

  • Shaping a page for both a quick executive read and a detailed audit.

  • Writing copy with concrete claims and honest caveats.

  • Composing hierarchy, typography, and color so that evidence and prose support each other.

  • How to publish as Vercel, down to the asset rules for our wordmark and the triangle logo.

design.md also names the recurring generated-design patterns that we never want to see, allowing agents to recognize and avoid them far more reliably by giving the patterns names.

We created a stylesheet because agents kept inventing their own typography, spacing, and layout, so we took those decisions away from the model entirely. The stylesheet packages our design system's primitives, such as headers, tables, stat strips, and chart styles, as CSS that any page can use via a public URL. Then design.md documents the class names and tokens that the stylesheet provides, allowing the agent to build the page with those names in the HTML instead of reinventing them.

Another benefit to this is that the agent never actually reads the stylesheet itself. The stylesheet loads when the page renders in your browser, so none of the code enters the model's context, saving more room for design guidance instead.

Last, the evaluation loop is what helps make the other two pieces work. Deterministic checks are used to help catch mechanical failures, such as a table that ignores the width available to it, while people judge the subjective parts that can't be automated, like hierarchy, composition, and whether the page actually gives the reader what they came for.

How guidance made it into the file

Every line of guidance in design.md earned its place through the eval loop. We generated pages from fixed scenarios, reviewed what came back, encoded the corrections we accepted, and reran the scenarios to see whether each change stuck, since a change that helped one artifact could quietly hurt another. Nothing got in any other way.

Scenarios and rounds

Each of the seven prompts becomes a scenario, meaning the prompt is frozen together with its mock inputs and render settings. The renewal proposal, for example, always runs with the same fake customer data with the same viewport settings, keeping design.md as the only thing that changes between runs. A round means generating a fresh page from every scenario against the current version of the file. Full rounds cover all seven scenarios on both Claude Opus 4.8 and Codex with GPT-5.5.

If we want to investigate something specific, such as a rule change that only affects tables, we can rerun the affected scenarios or a single model, keeping iteration loops tight.

Generating all seven pages together also made them easy to compare side by side, and what stood out was that design.md wasn't pushing every page toward one template. The interactive planning page put its controls front and center, because someone opens a planning page to change the numbers and see what happens. The renewal proposal instead led with the recommendation and the commercial comparison behind it, because its reader is deciding whether to renew. Every page used the same Vercel typography, color, and spacing, but each one was structured around what its reader came to do.

Reviewing every run

To review the pages each round produced, we built a local app that displays full-page renders and runs blind A/B comparisons. This app eventually became our eval harness, running each scenario and storing the results. Each stored run keeps the prompt, inputs, model configuration, the version of design.md it used, the screenshots, and whatever feedback the reviewer left about it. Reviewers record every correction against the exact run that produced it.

Turning corrections into rules and checks

Each correction a reviewer records gets landed in the narrowest place that can consistently enforce it. Judgment changes go into design.md as prose, reusable mechanics go into the stylesheet, and anything that we can check mechanically becomes a deterministic check in code. Problems with the harness itself stay in the harness, and when a single model fails in a way the others don't, we keep it out of the rules until it repeats.

Take one of the early renewal proposals. Its commercial terms table came back squeezed to the same width as the prose, even though the page had room for the table to be twice as wide.

During review, we flagged that evidence tables should use the full width available to them. But when looking through previous outputs, we found this same failure everywhere. So this correction ended up going into two places:

  • A rule in design.md stating the intended behavior.

  • A deterministic check in code that catches the same layout failure the next time it appears.

Once this landed, later renewal proposal prompts resulted in pages with correct full-width tables. To verify changes like this one, we reran the affected scenarios after encoding them. At milestones we went further, running blind A/B rounds that put the updated design.md against an earlier version of the file to decide whether to keep, revise, or revert each change.

Measuring whether it worked

Building the file had taken well over 200 runs, counting full rounds, targeted checks, dry runs, and all of the dead ends. Alongside the human reviewers, a model judge wrote critiques for each round, and every round's feedback went into improving the next run.

After all of those runs, we wanted to know whether the corrections we had encoded were actually preventing the failures they were written for. So we picked three desktop scenarios, and for each one we had Codex with GPT-5.5 generate the page twice, once with design.md loaded and once without. We kept the first attempt from every generation, with no re-rolls. Then we ran our deterministic checks over all six pages and counted how many times a known failure, like a table that ignores its available width, showed up in each set. The pages generated with design.md had 39 of those failures. The pages generated without it had 91, which works out to 57% fewer in this test.

Those numbers come with two caveats. The checks can only catch failures we have already seen and written down, so this test says nothing about whether a page is well designed overall. Six pages is also far too small a sample to make claims about quality or reliability, and every one of them, with or without the file, still had at least one failure serious enough to block shipping. But what the test does well is tell us that once we name a failure and encode it, that failure tends to stay gone.

How design.md stays current

The eval loop got the file shipped, but what keeps it current is real usage. Inside our Slack, that usage comes through @design-agent, an agent built on eve that we use for anything from design critiques and copy alternatives to icon recommendations and report sites built from pasted data. Instead of setting up a prompt or hunting down source files, you just mention the agent in a thread. For website requests, it loads the current design.md, builds the page against the published stylesheet, and posts a full-page screenshot and deployment URL back to the thread. Unlike our fixed scenarios, each of these threads captures a real request, a real output, and whatever feedback or steering followed, showing us how the guidance performs out in the wild.

Every week, we gather all of that feedback in one place, the Slack threads along with comments from GitHub reviews and Figma. Automation groups the comments that keep repeating, and each repeated complaint becomes a proposed change. A person then reviews each proposal, checks whether the system already handles it, and decides where the accepted fix belongs, whether that is @design-agent, the product-design skill, design.md, the stylesheet, or a deterministic check. And if people start asking for a kind of page we have never tested, that request becomes a new eval scenario.

To know whether any of this is working, we count how often each kind of complaint shows up in similar work over time. Once we encode a fix, that count should start falling. When it does not, something about the fix is wrong. The rule might be unclear, it might not be loading when it is needed, the stylesheet might not have a primitive that can express it, or it might need a deterministic check instead of prose.

Build your own

You can build the same loop yourself, starting with one recurring artifact and one manual comparison.

1. Pick one repeated artifact

Use a recent task with a real reader and real inputs, like a proposal, performance report, benchmark, or microsite. Avoid broad goals such as "make it on-brand." Before generating anything, write down a short rubric. A good one checks that the supplied facts survived, that the reader's decision is clear, and that the correction you keep making by hand actually got resolved.

2. Save the baseline first

Generate the page once without any new design context, and save the prompt, inputs, configuration, and a screenshot. Keep that first output even if it looks rough, unless the harness itself failed. You cannot tell whether new context helped without a before.

3. Start from your last ten corrections

Collect the feedback you keep giving in design reviews, pull requests, or Slack, and rewrite each correction as something observable. That means writing Let evidence tables use the full available width instead of Make the table feel less cramped, since only one of those can be checked.

Put the decisions in one file with sections for scope, reader and task, observable decisions, and available primitives. That file is your first design.md.

4. Constrain repeatable mechanics

If your outputs keep inventing their own typography, spacing, or layout, publish a stylesheet and document the exact classes and tokens the agent may use. Keep your judgment in prose, and push the repeatable mechanics into CSS or deterministic checks.

5. Run one matched comparison

Generate the page one more time with the same input, model, and viewport, but now with your file loaded. Shuffle it with the baseline and score both against your rubric without knowing which is which.

You do not need a runner or a model judge to start, a single trial can reveal the large, obvious failures. To measure reliability, run multiple independent first-attempt trials (Anthropic's guide to evals for agents) and report how often the result holds.

6. Encode the correction

Review the output alongside whatever follow-up prompts you have to send, and then ask:

  • What did the user have to repeat or steer manually?

  • Is a rule missing or unclear?

  • Can the stylesheet express the correction?

  • Is the failure mechanical enough to check in code?

  • Does the correction generalize beyond this output?

Update the guidance instead of hand-tuning the generated page. Your next comparison tells you whether first attempts actually improved.

Add tooling after the manual loop starts paying off:

  • Include scenarios where the guidance should and should not apply.

  • Keep a small holdout hidden while editing.

  • Record model and guidance versions.

  • Automate mechanical checks.

  • Use multiple blind reviewers.

However far you take the automation, keep final changes human-reviewed.

Then keep the loop running. Collect feedback on a cadence, and watch whether each kind of complaint actually becomes less common after you change the guidance. A passing evaluation matters less if people keep correcting the same mistake in production.

And if you want working examples, ours are public. We load design.md into tools like v0, Codex, and Claude every day to make artifacts that feel like Vercel, and the eve design agent template will get you a Slack design agent like the one we run.

title: Do As I Do, Not As I Say: On-Policy Distillation Inherits the Teacher in Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20989v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Improving the reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) often relies on post-training with supervision from stronger models. Two common strategies are supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which trains on teacher-generated demonstrations, and on-policy distillation (OPD), which provides teacher feedback on trajectories generated by the student itself. While OPD can be more data-efficient by supervising student-generated trajectories, it is unclear how the teacher's supervision at each state affects the student's learned behavior. To study this question, we conduct a controlled comparison of OPD and filtered SFT across data budgets and tasks where the teacher exhibits different levels of reliability, and analyze how these differences shape student accuracy and completion behavior. Across the two tasks, we find that OPD is effective only when the teacher remains reliable on student-generated trajectories. On ChartQA, where the teacher completes 99% of its solutions, OPD trained on only 10% of the data comes within 1.4 accuracy points of full-data SFT. In contrast, on Geometry3K, where the teacher fails to complete 22% of its solutions, OPD underperforms SFT by 7.9 points, with most of the gap explained by incomplete responses. More strikingly, starting OPD from an SFT student reduces its completion rate from 76% to 62%, effectively erasing the completion behavior learned through SFT. Filtering teacher demonstrations for completeness alone recovers much of SFT's advantage. These results show that on-policy supervision can transfer not only teacher knowledge but also persistent failure modes on student-visited states. Code is available at https://github.com/ffy208/opd-inherits-teacher-vlm.

title: How to Extract Text from PowerPoint in Java: All Slides, Specific Slides, and Tables
description:
PowerPoint presentations often contain text that needs to be reused in reports, documentation, or other files. Instead of copying it slide by slide, you can use Java to extract the text and save it to a separate file.

This article covers three scenarios: extracting text from an entire presentation, reading text from a specific slide, and extracting text from PowerPoint tables.

1. Add the Maven Dependency

First, add a PowerPoint processing library to your Java project. If you're using Maven, include the following repository and dependency in your pom.xml file:

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>com.e-iceblue</id>
        <name>e-iceblue</name>
        <url>https://repo.e-iceblue.com/nexus/content/groups/public/</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>e-iceblue</groupId>
        <artifactId>spire.presentation</artifactId>
        <version>11.9.10</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

For the examples below, we'll use a presentation named report.pptx containing slide titles, body text, project updates, and tables.

Each example is a standalone Java program that saves the extracted content to a UTF-8 text file.

2. Extract Text from All PowerPoint Slides

To extract text from an entire presentation, you can loop through its slides and examine the shapes on each one.

In PowerPoint, titles, text boxes, and many shapes containing text can be accessed through the IAutoShape interface. Each text frame contains paragraphs, and their text can be retrieved using ParagraphEx.getText().

Here's the complete code:

import com.spire.presentation.*;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Paths;

public class ExtractAllPPTText {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        Presentation presentation = new Presentation();

        try {
            // Load the PowerPoint presentation
            presentation.loadFromFile("report.pptx");

            StringBuilder result = new StringBuilder();

            // Loop through all slides
            for (int i = 0;
                 i < presentation.getSlides().getCount();
                 i++) {

                ISlide slide = presentation.getSlides().get(i);

                // Add the slide number
                result.append("Slide ")
                      .append(i + 1)
                      .append(System.lineSeparator());

                // Loop through shapes on the slide
                for (Object shape : slide.getShapes()) {

                    if (shape instanceof IAutoShape) {

                        IAutoShape autoShape = (IAutoShape) shape;

                        // Read text from each paragraph
                        for (Object item :
                                autoShape.getTextFrame()
                                         .getParagraphs()) {

                            ParagraphEx paragraph =
                                    (ParagraphEx) item;

                            String text = paragraph.getText();

                            if (text != null &&
                                    !text.trim().isEmpty()) {
                                result.append(text)
                                      .append(System.lineSeparator());
                            }
                        }
                    }
                }

                result.append(System.lineSeparator());
            }

            // Save the extracted text as UTF-8
            Files.write(
                    Paths.get("ppt-all-text.txt"),
                    result.toString()
                          .getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));

            System.out.println("Text extraction completed.");

        } finally {
            presentation.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The program creates ppt-all-text.txt, with the extracted text grouped by slide number.

The main methods are:

  • getSlides() retrieves the slides in the presentation.

  • getShapes() provides access to the shapes on each slide.

  • getTextFrame().getParagraphs() retrieves the paragraphs inside a text-containing shape.

  • ParagraphEx.getText() returns the text of each paragraph.

The code skips empty paragraphs and adds a slide number before each group of text.

One limitation is worth noting: this example extracts text from IAutoShape objects, not every type of content in a PowerPoint file. Text in tables, speaker notes, images, and some other objects requires separate handling.

Also, the extracted text follows the order of shapes in the slide's collection, which may differ from their visual reading order.

3. Extract Text from a Specific PowerPoint Slide

Sometimes you only need the text from one slide. For example, you might want to extract a project summary from slide 3 without processing the rest of the presentation.

You can access a particular slide using presentation.getSlides().get(index) and then read the text from its shapes.

The following example extracts text from the third slide:

import com.spire.presentation.*;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Paths;

public class ExtractSingleSlideText {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        Presentation presentation = new Presentation();

        try {
            // Load the PowerPoint presentation
            presentation.loadFromFile("report.pptx");

            // Specify the slide number
            int slideNumber = 3;

            // Check whether the slide exists
            if (slideNumber < 1 ||
                    slideNumber > presentation.getSlides().getCount()) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                        "The specified slide does not exist.");
            }

            // Get the specified slide
            ISlide slide = presentation.getSlides()
                    .get(slideNumber - 1);

            StringBuilder result = new StringBuilder();

            // Loop through shapes on the slide
            for (Object shape : slide.getShapes()) {

                if (shape instanceof IAutoShape) {

                    IAutoShape autoShape = (IAutoShape) shape;

                    // Extract text from each paragraph
                    for (Object item :
                            autoShape.getTextFrame()
                                     .getParagraphs()) {

                        ParagraphEx paragraph =
                                (ParagraphEx) item;

                        String text = paragraph.getText();

                        if (text != null &&
                                !text.trim().isEmpty()) {
                            result.append(text)
                                  .append(System.lineSeparator());
                        }
                    }
                }
            }

            // Save the extracted text
            Files.write(
                    Paths.get("slide-3-text.txt"),
                    result.toString()
                          .getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));

            System.out.println("Slide 3 text extracted.");

        } finally {
            presentation.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The program saves the text from the third slide to slide-3-text.txt.

Keep in mind that slide indexes start at zero:

  • get(0) accesses slide 1.

  • get(1) accesses slide 2.

  • get(2) accesses slide 3.

That's why the code uses slideNumber - 1 to convert the slide number into a collection index.

It also checks whether the requested slide exists before trying to access it.

If you need text from several selected slides, you can use an array of slide numbers and process only those slides.

4. Extract Text from Tables in PowerPoint

PowerPoint presentations may also contain tables, such as project schedules, budget summaries, or comparison data.

Unlike ordinary text boxes, tables store their text in individual cells. To read that content, you can locate ITable objects, loop through their rows and columns, and extract the text from each cell.

The following example searches all slides for tables and saves their contents as tab-separated text.

import com.spire.presentation.*;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Paths;

public class ExtractPPTTableText {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        Presentation presentation = new Presentation();

        try {
            // Load the PowerPoint presentation
            presentation.loadFromFile("report.pptx");

            StringBuilder result = new StringBuilder();

            // Loop through all slides
            for (int i = 0;
                 i < presentation.getSlides().getCount();
                 i++) {

                ISlide slide = presentation.getSlides().get(i);

                // Find tables on the slide
                for (Object shape : slide.getShapes()) {

                    if (shape instanceof ITable) {

                        ITable table = (ITable) shape;

                        result.append("Table on Slide ")
                              .append(i + 1)
                              .append(System.lineSeparator());

                        // Get the number of rows and columns
                        int rowCount =
                                table.getTableRows().getCount();

                        int columnCount =
                                table.getColumnsList().getCount();

                        // Loop through table cells
                        for (int row = 0; row < rowCount; row++) {

                            for (int col = 0;
                                 col < columnCount;
                                 col++) {

                                // Read text from the cell
                                String text = table.get(col, row)
                                        .getTextFrame()
                                        .getText();

                                if (text != null) {
                                    // Replace line breaks and tabs
                                    text = text.replace("\r", " ")
                                               .replace("\n", " ")
                                               .replace("\t", " ");

                                    result.append(text);
                                }

                                // Separate columns with tabs
                                if (col < columnCount - 1) {
                                    result.append("\t");
                                }
                            }

                            result.append(System.lineSeparator());
                        }

                        result.append(System.lineSeparator());
                    }
                }
            }

            // Save the extracted table text
            Files.write(
                    Paths.get("ppt-table-text.txt"),
                    result.toString()
                          .getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));

            System.out.println("Table text extraction completed.");

        } finally {
            presentation.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The code uses three methods to access table content:

  • getTableRows().getCount() returns the number of rows.

  • getColumnsList().getCount() returns the number of columns.

  • table.get(col, row) retrieves a cell using its column and row indexes.

Notice that table.get() takes the column index first, followed by the row index. Both indexes start at zero.

Once a cell is retrieved, getTextFrame().getText() returns its text.

For example, suppose a slide contains this table:

Task Owner Status
Module A Alex Completed
Module B Emma In Progress

The extracted text would look approximately like this:

Table on Slide 2
Task    Owner   Status
Module A    Alex    Completed
Module B    Emma    In Progress

Columns are separated by tabs, while rows are separated by line breaks. This makes the output easier to read or import into another application.

The example also replaces line breaks and tabs inside individual cells with spaces to keep each table row on one line.

For tables with merged cells, a straightforward row-and-column loop may produce empty or repeated positions. Those cases may require additional handling based on the table structure.

5. Things to Keep in Mind

Text Inside Images Requires OCR

If a slide contains text as part of an image, such as a screenshot or scanned document, it cannot be extracted using ordinary text frame methods.

You would need optical character recognition (OCR) to identify the text in those images.

Not All PowerPoint Text Is Stored in Regular Shapes

Slide titles and text boxes can typically be accessed through IAutoShape, while table content is accessed through ITable.

Speaker notes, chart labels, text inside grouped objects, and other elements may require different handling.

If you need to extract all available text from a presentation, check which object types are present instead of assuming a single loop will capture everything.

Plain Text Does Not Preserve Formatting

Saving extracted content as TXT removes the original PowerPoint formatting, including font styles, colors, positions, and slide layouts.

If you need to preserve information such as heading levels or table structures, consider adding markers during extraction or using a structured output format instead.

Use UTF-8 for Text Files

All three examples use StandardCharsets.UTF_8 when writing the output files.

This helps preserve non-ASCII characters, including Chinese, Japanese, and other multilingual text, across different operating systems.

6. Conclusion

Extracting text from PowerPoint in Java depends on where the text is stored.

Before processing a presentation, it's worth checking whether its content consists of regular text, tables, images, or other objects. This helps you choose the appropriate extraction method and avoid missing content.

title: How to Train Your Little Dragon: Teaching a Small Language Model to Construct and Refine GPU Optimization Scripts
description:
arXiv:2610.20980v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compiler transformations interact, making GPU kernel optimization a search for combinations that preserve the computation while improving performance. We introduce HOW TO TRAIN YOUR LITTLE DRAGON, a training method that teaches a small language model both to construct complete optimization scripts and to improve existing ones. Instead of ranking candidates or generating kernel code, our model generates optimization scripts. We devise a compact, lossless representation whose deterministic decoding reconstructs the exact compiler trace, preserving its transformation parameters and dependencies. We use a compiler framework TVM MetaSchedule to build training data on 54,116 distinct workloads, and construct 108,594 examples in two training sets: 60,236 teach the model to generate an optimized script from an unoptimized kernel, while 48,358 teach it to produce a better script given the kernel and a somewhat optimized script. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to construct and improve optimization scripts from these search-derived examples. We then add reinforcement learning with a shaped reward that combines correctness with measured performance, awarding a latency-based bonus only to numerically correct kernels. We apply this training method to a model with 8 billion parameters. After supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, the model achieves per-attempt correctness of 91.27% for construction and 92.01% for refinement, while reinforcement learning produces faster kernels than supervised training on 88 of 102 construction tasks and 145 of 170 refinement prompts. With only 8B parameters, our LITTLE DRAGON achieves higher per-attempt correctness and better kernel performance than six frontier LLMs: GPT-6 Astra, Opus 5, Kimi-K3, and GLM-5.3 among them, each with hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters, for which task-specific training is unavailable or expensive.

title: MeddeX: A Retrieval-Augmented LLaMA-3 System with Gemini Vision for Evidence-Backed Medical Report Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.20632v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern healthcare generates increasingly complex medical reports that challenge clinical professionals in terms of time and interpretive burden. Manual review processes are slow, error-prone, and difficult to scale. This paper presents MeddeX, a Medical Report Analyzer that combines a QLoRA fine-tuned LLaMA-3 (8B) model with Retrieval-Augmented Gen eration (RAG) and a multimodal Gemini Vision layer to deliver accurate, concise, and evidence-backed summaries of medical documents. The system handles text-native PDFs, scanned image based PDFs, and direct radiological images through an intelligent hybrid extraction pipeline that includes a novel garbage-text detection mechanism for corrupted and UTF-16-encoded doc uments. Beyond single-report Q&A, MeddeX introduces report scoped retrieval for precise contextual grounding, an automated longitudinal report comparison engine, and a self-healing backfill pipeline that lazily processes legacy documents on demand. A FastAPI backend, Supabase vector store, and Next.js fron tend complete the end-to-end architecture. Evaluation against the base LLaMA3-Med42-8B model demonstrates consistent improvements across ROUGE-1 (+9.2%), ROUGE-2 (+10.0%), ROUGE-L (+11.8%), BLEU (+71.4%), and BERTScore (+0.8%), validating the benefit of domain-specific fine-tuning. MeddeX represents a practical and robust step toward AI-assisted clinical decision support.

title: DeSpatial: The devil of Agentic Spatial Reasoning Lies in 3D Itself
description:
arXiv:2610.20990v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial agents have access to reconstruction and segmentation tools, yet inconsistent predictions and fragmented object identities can prevent their outputs from becoming reliable 3D scene information. A simple oracle experiment exposes this perception bottleneck: replacing tool-predicted perception with ground-truth 3D bounding boxes raises an agent to nearly full score across five object-centric VSI-Bench tasks, while retaining the same reasoning tools. Motivated by this finding, we believe the devil of spatial reasoning lies in 3D itself, and introduce DeSpatial(Devil of Spatial), which explicitly decomposes spatial understanding into perception and reasoning. DeSpatial has a shared 3D perception tool to reconcile independent perception outputs into a unified, metric, gravity-aligned 3D scene. This perception tool has two core components: a) a joint segmentation--depth co-refinement module that consolidates masks of the same object and removes projection artifacts caused by inconsistent segmentation and depth within a single frame; b) a cross-view instance fusion module that consolidate voxel-overlapping instances but not allowed to merge same-frame instances. This fusion module additionally fuses spatially disjoint fragments caused by insufficient multi-view observations, by checking their 3D structure and source mask appearance. After receiving the complete and unified 3D scene information, the agent chooses reasoning or computational tools to solve the spatial problem. DeSpatial achieves leading performance on VSI-Bench, MindCube-Tiny, and ViewSpatial, with additional long-video results on VSI-SUPER, revealing the bottleneck of spatial understanding lies in a precise 3D perception itself.

title: Test your Node.js fetcher for SSRF in GitHub Actions
description:
A request throwing an error does not tell you whether it reached an internal
service first. If your link-preview service, URL importer or webhook sender
accepts a user-supplied destination, that difference matters.

I built ssrf-lab to make that difference
observable. This walkthrough connects a Node.js fetch function to an isolated
fixture, proves that an unprotected client reaches it, and turns the result
into a pull-request check.

The starter covers seven direct-address cases and two redirects. It does
not test DNS rebinding or TLS, and a passing result is not a complete security
assessment.

What the check measures

The fixture has an entry service and a separate internal service. The internal
service counts requests independently of the client. If it received a request,
a later exception cannot change that result into a successful block.

The CI check also requires two kinds of controls:

  • The application's allowed request must return the real entry response. A fetcher that rejects everything cannot pass.
  • Native fetch must reach the internal service directly and through a redirect. A fixture that nobody can reach cannot produce a false green.

Each attack case then needs an explicit address-policy refusal and zero
contradictory internal hits. DNS errors, connection failures and timeouts do
not establish that the address policy worked.

1. Run the working example

Use Node.js 22.19 or newer. From a disposable development environment:

git clone https://github.com/roshan-amble/ssrf-lab.git
cd ssrf-lab
git checkout ac0d4906592a5c41c27785b7a4327d449bc10da9
npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm run build
node examples/custom-fetcher/check.mjs

The included application module calls pinned guarded-fetch@0.1.5. This local
smoke test covers the seven direct-address cases. Expect explicit refusals,
zero internal hits from the tested client, and exit 0. Local address behavior
can vary by operating system; the isolated CI run below is the reproducible
nine-case check.

Now deliberately remove the protection:

node examples/custom-fetcher/check.mjs --unsafe

This uses native fetch as a control. Expect internal reach and exit 1. An
unsafe client is supposed to fail the gate.

Watch the recorded isolated execution.
The recording uses the nine-case CI fixture; it includes real command output
and intentional reading pauses. The raw JSON and timed terminal transcript
are linked from the recording evidence.

2. Connect the fetcher your application actually uses

Create test/ssrf-fetcher.mjs in your application. The harness needs a module
that exports fetchUrl(url, { signal, timeoutMs }) and returns a real
fetch-compatible Response.

For the working guarded-fetch example, the core looks like this:

import {
  createGuardedDispatcher,
  guardedFetch,
  GuardedFetchError,
} from 'guarded-fetch'

const dispatcher = createGuardedDispatcher()

export function fetchUrl(url, { signal, timeoutMs }) {
  return guardedFetch(url, {
    signal, timeoutMs, dispatcher, opaqueErrors: true,
  })
}

export function classifyRefusal(error) {
  if (!(error instanceof GuardedFetchError)) return undefined
  if (['hostname_unsafe', 'host_not_allowed', 'redirect_to_unsafe_host']
    .includes(error.code)) {
    return 'forbidden-address'
  }
}

export async function close() {
  await dispatcher.destroy()
}

For your application, replace the implementation with an import of its
existing fetch function and configuration. Map only its genuine address-policy
error. Do not put a new blocker into the adapter just to make the test pass.
The goal is to test the code you ship.

If your public helper returns parsed data, use its lower-level HTTP function
that returns a Response. Preserve redirect handling and honor cancellation
or a finite timeout. See the full module contract.

3. Add the pull-request check

After committing that module, add this workflow to your application as
.github/workflows/ssrf.yml:

name: SSRF regression check
on: [pull_request, push]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  ssrf:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: '24'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build --if-present
      - name: Check the application's fetcher
        id: ssrf
        uses: roshan-amble/ssrf-lab@ac0d4906592a5c41c27785b7a4327d449bc10da9
        with:
          fetcher-module: test/ssrf-fetcher.mjs
      - name: Save the report, including failed checks
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: ssrf-report
          path: |
            ${{ steps.ssrf.outputs.report-path }}
            ${{ steps.ssrf.outputs.errors-path }}
          if-no-files-found: warn

Adjust the application install/build steps to match your project. For a
monorepo, set the Action's working-directory input to the application folder;
fetcher-module is resolved relative to that directory.

The Action installs its own pinned harness, creates a Linux network namespace
with only loopback enabled, and runs the check there. The fixture's entry
address, 93.184.216.34, is assigned to loopback inside that namespace. It does
not send the test to an external service at that address.

The check verifies isolation before importing the application module. Use the
provided GitHub-hosted Ubuntu setup. Network isolation contains the traffic;
it is not a sandbox for untrusted application code.

4. Read failures correctly

Exit code Meaning Next step
0 Every selected attack case produced an explicit address refusal, with no internal reach. Keep the regression check in CI.
1 At least one attack request reached the internal fixture. Inspect the per-probe report and the application's policy.
2 Setup/control failure or inconclusive coverage. Fix the setup or explain the result before claiming protection.

The artifact contains per-probe verdicts, entry/internal request counts,
runtime information and controls. Report paths are produced even when the
check fails; dependency installation failures occur before a report exists.

If your application requires HTTPS, a specific hostname allowlist, or network
access during initialization, this fixture may fail its allowed-entry control.
Keep the production policy intact and adapt the fixture deliberately.

What this establishes

This gives you a repeatable test for a defined set of address and redirect
cases. It does not cover DNS rebinding, TLS, cross-origin credentials,
arbitrary private-network addresses or response-body limits.

Try the working example
and connect one real fetcher. If the fixture does not fit, an issue with your
fetcher type, expected policy and the failing case is useful feedback.

If the project is useful, a GitHub star helps you find it again and follow new
coverage: roshan-amble/ssrf-lab.

Disclosure: Codex assisted with the implementation, test execution, recording
and writing. Results are linked to the captured CI output.

title: Velocity vs Capacity
description:
When sprint planning rolls around, two numbers often get tangled: velocity and capacity. They look alike, but they serve opposite purposes—one looks backward, the other forward. Understanding the distinction helps teams set realistic commitments and keep stakeholders honest.

Velocity

  • Historical output – Velocity is the average story points your team has completed over the last few sprints.
  • A trailing indicator – It tells you what actually happened, not what will happen. Because it’s derived from past performance, it’s useful as a baseline but not a guarantee for the next sprint.

Capacity

  • Available time this sprint – Capacity measures the total person‑hours or story points the team can realistically spend, after accounting for vacations, holidays, on‑call duties, and other non‑project work.
  • A forward‑looking input – Use capacity to sanity‑check the amount of work you plan to pull in. If the team has less time than usual, the commitment should shrink accordingly.

How They Interact

  • Velocity sets the baseline – Start with your average velocity as a rough guide for how much work you could handle.
  • Capacity adjusts it – If the upcoming sprint has reduced capacity (e.g., two developers are on leave), plan below the average velocity. Conversely, a sprint with extra headcount can allow you to stretch a bit beyond the historical average, but only within a reasonable range.

Common Mistake

  • Committing to average velocity always – Ignoring that this sprint has three people on leave leads to over‑commitment and spillover.
  • Chasing a velocity target – Inflating estimates or adding hidden work just to hit a number turns velocity into a performance metric rather than a planning tool.

Do / Avoid

Do

  • Adjust commitment down for known capacity dips.
  • Use velocity as a range, not a fixed target.
  • Track both velocity and capacity separately on the sprint dashboard.

Avoid

  • Don’t commit to full average velocity during a low‑capacity sprint.
  • Don’t use velocity as a performance metric for individuals.
  • Don’t let stakeholders treat velocity as a promise.

Keep velocity as the historical compass and capacity as the current weather report; together they guide the team to realistic, sustainable sprint commitments.

title: OLED Monitors and Dark Mode: Why CSS Inversion Often Beats Your OS Settings
description:
OLED Monitors and Dark Mode: Why CSS Inversion Often Beats Your OS Settings

If you have an OLED monitor or OLED laptop screen, you've probably noticed that "true black" matters. OLED pixels that display pure black are literally off — no backlight, zero power, perfect contrast. This is why dark mode on OLED feels so different from LCD.

But there's a problem: OS-level dark mode doesn't actually control websites.

The Gap Between OS Dark Mode and Web Dark Mode

When you enable dark mode on macOS or Windows, you're changing the OS theme. Apps that respect your preference (VS Code, Slack, etc.) switch to dark. Your browser's chrome (the toolbar, tabs, sidebar) also goes dark.

But websites? They're in charge of their own styling. A site only goes dark if:

  1. The site explicitly supports prefers-color-scheme: dark in its CSS, OR
  2. Something forces it to

Most sites don't support it well. Some support it partially. Some ignore it completely.

How Browser-Level Dark Mode Forcing Works

A Firefox extension like NightOwl uses CSS inversion to force dark mode on any page regardless of whether the site implemented it:

html {
  filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg);
}

img, video, canvas, svg {
  filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg);
}

The invert(1) flips all colors. The hue-rotate(180deg) corrects the hue shift so that reds stay red and blues stay blue — just inverted in brightness. The second rule re-inverts images and videos so they still look correct.

This is crude but effective. Every white background becomes dark gray/black. Every dark text becomes light.

Why This Matters Specifically for OLED

On an LCD screen, the difference between "very dark gray" and "pure black" is cosmetic. The backlight is always on.

On OLED, pure black (#000000 or close) turns pixels off entirely. This means:

  • No light bleed from the display
  • Noticeably better battery life on laptops (less power to unlit pixels)
  • Dramatically better perceived contrast ratios (infinite contrast)

OS dark mode on Chrome/Firefox gives you dark browser chrome but still renders white pages. Every tab you open with a white background is blasting your OLED pixels at full brightness. CSS inversion flips that so most of the page is dark.

The Trade-offs

Pros of CSS inversion:

  • Works on any site, immediately, without site support
  • Per-domain toggle (you can leave specific sites as-is)
  • No account or cloud sync needed

Cons:

  • Colors can look slightly "off" on sites with unusual color schemes
  • Some gradients or design-heavy sites look weird
  • Not as polished as a site's native dark mode when the site actually implements it well

When to use native dark mode instead:

  • Sites like GitHub, Figma, Notion that have excellent native dark themes — let those sites control their own theming
  • Sites where color accuracy matters (photo editors, design tools)

When CSS inversion wins:

  • Documentation sites, news sites, forums, wikis — anything that's mostly text on white
  • Sites that partially support dark mode but miss elements (navigation stays white, etc.)
  • Any stubborn site that ignores prefers-color-scheme

A Practical Workflow

On NightOwl: enable dark mode globally, then whitelist the 3-5 sites where you want native theming (GitHub, your design tools, whatever). This gives you forced dark on 95% of sites while preserving intentional designs where they matter.

For OLED users specifically: the battery life improvement from not blasting full white on dozens of tabs is real. It's not dramatic per tab, but over a full day of browsing it adds up.

The underlying point: OS dark mode and browser dark mode solve different problems. OS dark mode controls native app theming. Browser-level CSS inversion forces dark on the web. If you care about OLED efficiency or just want consistent dark across all sites, you need both.

title: Dynamic Model Routing: Cutting LLM Spend Without Cutting Capability
description:
Originally published by **Asif Muhammad Iqbal (Founder & CEO at Logic42)* at https://logic42.ai/articles/dynamic-model-routing-cost-reduction.*

Dynamic Model Routing: Cutting LLM Spend Without Cutting Capability

Dynamic model routing is the architectural discipline of dispatching inference requests to the most cost-effective LLM tier capable of solving the specific task. Most enterprise LLM spend isn't a model-selection problem; it's a routing problem that inflates cloud bills when uniform frontier models process trivial tasks.

Organisations don't discover this immediately. A team ships something useful on a frontier model. Adoption spreads. Six months later the monthly invoice is an agenda item, and the first instinct is to swap the model for a cheaper one across the board. Quality drops, the team swaps back, and the conclusion is that cost is simply the price of capability.

That conclusion is wrong, because it treats a heterogeneous workload as a single decision. A governed gateway that routes each request to the cheapest model capable of completing that specific task changes the economics without touching the ceiling on quality.

This is a reference architecture for that gateway. It describes what components do, what the non-obvious failure modes are, and what to measure. You can't benchmark routing outcomes in the abstract: results depend entirely on your prompt distribution.

The shape of enterprise traffic

The reason routing works is that production LLM traffic is not evenly demanding.

Once a system is embedded in real workflows, a large share of requests are deterministic transformations wearing a natural-language interface: extract five fields from this document, classify this ticket into one of nine queues, rewrite this paragraph in a fixed tone, convert this response into valid JSON. These have short contexts, no multi-step reasoning, and a verifiable correct answer.

A much smaller share are the requests the system was actually bought for: open-ended analysis, multi-step planning, tool orchestration, anything where the model has to hold several constraints at once and decide what to do.

Sending both classes to the same frontier endpoint means paying reasoning prices for formatting work. The distribution is the opportunity, and it is why the first thing to build is not a router but instrumentation. You cannot design tiers before you know what your traffic actually looks like. Log prompt length, context size, whether tool calls were requested, whether the output was schema-constrained, and whether a human accepted the result. A fortnight of that data tells you whether routing is worth building at all.

What the gateway does

The gateway is a single ingress point that every model call passes through. Nothing in the application talks to a model provider directly. That constraint is what makes everything else possible.

[ App / Agent ]
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AI GATEWAY                              │
│                                          │
│  1. Authenticate + tag (team, workload)  │
│  2. Classify task complexity             │
│  3. Route to tier                        │
│  4. Validate output                      │
│  5. Escalate on failure                  │
│  6. Meter + log                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
       │                    │
       ▼                    ▼
[ Local / small model ]  [ Frontier model ]

Five of those six steps are unglamorous plumbing. They are also the reason the sixth one is safe to switch on.

Routing Tier Model Archetype Avg Input Cost / 1M Latency Target Best Suited Workloads
Tier 1: Local / Edge Llama 3 8B, Mistral 7B $0.05 – $0.15 < 250ms Classification, JSON extraction, entity tagging
Tier 2: Mid-Tier Hosted Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o-mini $0.25 – $0.60 < 800ms Summarization, contextual Q&A, draft generation
Tier 3: Frontier Reasoning Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o1, GPT-4o $3.00 – $15.00 2s – 8s Multi-step planning, complex code generation, tool swarms

Critically, the gateway is the natural home for controls that have nothing to do with cost: egress inspection, PII masking, prompt-injection screening, per-team budget enforcement. Teams that build a routing layer and a security layer separately end up with two chokepoints, two sets of credentials, and two incomplete logs. Build one.

Classifying the task

Three approaches, in ascending order of cost and accuracy.

Heuristics. Context length, presence of a tool-call schema, output token limit, whether the prompt matches a known template. Nearly free, surprisingly effective, and brittle in exactly the way you would expect. Good enough to start, and good enough permanently for high-volume templated traffic where the caller already knows the shape of the job.

Embedding similarity. Embed the incoming prompt, compare against labelled clusters of past requests with known outcomes. Handles novel phrasings that heuristics miss. Requires you to have been logging outcomes, which is the argument for instrumenting first.

A small classifier model. A fine-tuned encoder or small LLM that scores complexity directly. Most accurate, most expensive, and it introduces a dependency that itself needs monitoring and retraining.

The pragmatic architecture is layered: heuristics resolve the obvious majority, and only the ambiguous remainder reaches a more expensive classifier. Routing the router is not a joke; it is the same principle applied one level down.

A note on a tempting shortcut: do not classify on caller identity. Routing by team or user is easy to implement and structurally wrong, because the same team submits both trivial and hard requests. It optimises the wrong variable and produces exactly the quality complaints that get routing projects cancelled.

The latency budget

The router runs on every request, including the ones it decides not to reroute. Its cost is therefore paid unconditionally, and it must be small enough to disappear.

Two budgets matter:

Latency. The classifier sits in the critical path. If classification adds more delay than the tier change saves, the user experience degrades while the invoice improves, and the feature gets switched off. Heuristic classification should be effectively free. A model-based classifier needs to be genuinely small and genuinely local; a network hop to another provider to decide which provider to use is a design that will not survive review.

Cost. Router inference is not free either. If a classifier costs a meaningful fraction of the cheap tier it routes to, the arithmetic collapses on high-volume, low-complexity traffic, precisely the traffic where routing should pay off most.

Both budgets argue for the same thing: resolve as much as possible with the cheapest possible signal.

Where it breaks

This is the part that determines whether a routing layer survives its first quarter in production.

Escalation cascades

Routing without an escalation path isn't routing; it's downgrading. Every tier needs a defined failure condition (such as schema validation failure, low confidence, refusal, or timeout) that promotes the request to a higher tier.

The consequence is that some requests are paid for twice. If your escalation rate is 10%, your effective cost is the cheap tier on everything plus the expensive tier on a tenth of it, plus the latency of both in sequence. Escalation rate isn't a casual quality metric; it's a core term in the cost model. A router that misclassifies 40% of traffic downward can cost more than no router at all, while also being slower.

Prompt caching changes the arithmetic

This is the failure mode most cost models miss.

Frontier providers offer substantial discounts on repeated prompt prefixes. Workloads with large stable system prompts or shared document context can see most of their input billed at a reduced cache-read rate. A router that diverts these requests to a local model loses those cache hits, while the initial comparison evaluated only the uncached headline price.

The result is a router that reports savings while total spend is flat or higher. Any honest cost model has to compare against your realised blended rate, cache behaviour included, not the rate card. Where a workload has a high cache-hit ratio, the correct routing decision is frequently to leave it alone.

Validation failures multiply tokens

Structured output is where naive token optimisation backfires. A cheaper model that returns malformed JSON triggers a retry. Two or three retries, and you've spent more tokens and more wall-clock time than a single call to a capable model.

This is why the unit of measurement has to be cost per successfully completed task, not cost per token. Optimising token count while ignoring retry rate is how teams produce a 30% reduction in tokens and no reduction in spend.

Deterministic validation at the gateway (including schema conformance, required fields, and type checks) is computationally cheap, catches this class of failure immediately, and drives the escalation decision. Validate before you return, always.

Thresholds go stale

Your prompt mix isn't stationary. New features ship, users learn what the system is good at, and a distribution that was 70% simple at launch drifts. Routing thresholds calibrated once are wrong within months, usually in the direction of routing too aggressively downward.

Treat thresholds as configuration with an owner and a review cadence, not as constants. Alert on distribution shift: a sudden change in escalation rate is the primary warning signal, and it usually arrives before quality complaints do.

What to measure

Six numbers. Anything less and you can't defend the architecture; anything more and nobody reads the dashboard.

  1. Cost per successfully completed task, by workload. The headline metric. Tokens are an input, not an outcome.
  2. Escalation rate, by tier. Rising means the classifier is drifting or the traffic changed.
  3. p95 end-to-end latency, router included. Measured from the caller's perspective, not the model's.
  4. Quality regression rate. Sampled human review or automated evaluation against a fixed held-out set. Without this you have no evidence that savings were not simply purchased with quality.
  5. Realised blended input rate, cache hits included. Guards against the caching trap above.
  6. Spend by team and workload. Requires request tagging at the gateway, which is why tagging is step one and not an afterthought.

Anti-patterns

  • Routing by identity rather than task. Discussed above. The single most common design error.
  • No escalation path. Turns a cost optimisation into a silent quality cut.
  • Optimising tokens instead of task cost. Produces impressive charts and flat invoices.
  • Comparing against rate-card pricing. Ignores caching and overstates savings, sometimes entirely.
  • A separate security chokepoint. Two gateways means two incomplete audit trails.
  • Shipping the router before the instrumentation. You cannot tier a distribution you have never measured.

How Much Can Dynamic Model Routing Reduce Enterprise LLM Invoices?

Production deployments demonstrate that dynamic model routing reduces aggregate enterprise LLM spend by 40% to 70% without degrading output quality. By routing high-volume, low-complexity tasks to cheaper localized models and reserving frontier endpoints for reasoning, organizations cut cost per completed task dramatically.

The Takeaway

The honest answer is that it depends on your traffic, and the range across real workloads is wide enough that a single number would be misleading. A workload dominated by extraction and classification has substantial headroom. A workload that is genuinely reasoning-heavy, or that already benefits from high cache-hit ratios, won't yield easy savings. The correct engineering answer in that case is to leave it alone.

What's dependable is the shape of the finding: measure first, tier what is measurably tierable, validate every output, keep an escalation path, and price against what you actually pay rather than the rate card. A gateway built that way makes cost a governable parameter instead of a quarterly surprise, and it puts the security controls you'll eventually need in the one place every request already passes through.

title: How to Run OpenClaw on a VPS (Self-Hosted AI Assistant, Step by Step)
description:
How to Run OpenClaw on a VPS (Self-Hosted AI Assistant, Step by Step)

OpenClaw is the open-source, self-hosted AI assistant that hit 380k+ GitHub stars in 2026 — it turns your machine (or a server) into a personal assistant you can message from WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, and 20+ other apps, powered by whatever model you want, with all data staying on your hardware.

The one question everyone asks: where do I actually run it so it's always on? Not your laptop — that goes to sleep. The answer is a small, cheap VPS. This is the exact setup I use, written so you can replicate it in about an hour.

Why a VPS (and not your laptop)

A personal assistant is only useful if it's there 24/7. Your laptop sleeps, reboots, and takes your Wi-Fi with it. A VPS:

  • Stays on 24/7 regardless of your devices
  • Gives OpenClaw its own persistent home (config, memory, sessions)
  • Can sit in a datacenter close to your AI model provider

All you need is roughly 2 GB RAM and a couple of vCPUs — OpenClaw itself is light; your AI provider does the heavy lifting. That's a low-cost VPS tier, which is the whole point.

Step 1 — Get the hardware

Pick a small VPS. For a personal OpenClaw setup, a single 2 GB / 1-2 vCPU instance is plenty:

  • What to grab: 1 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, 20+ GB SSD, an NVMe volume, and an IPv4 address.
  • Where: any provider with a low entry tier works. I run mine on Hostinger's VPS — their launch VPS plans start around $5-6/mo, which is the cheapest honest price for a machine that never sleeps.
  • OS: I use a plain Linux image (Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 or Debian 12). Skip "managed" stacks for the base — you'll be installing Node anyway.

After provisioning you get a root/SSH login. That's all you need for this step.

Step 2 — Open the right port and lock the firewall

OpenClaw's Gateway listens on a local port. You only ever connect through SSH, so keep the default SSH-only exposure:

  1. In your provider's control panel, open one port for SSH (22).
  2. Do not open OpenClaw's port to the public internet. Run it behind an authenticated reverse proxy (see Step 5) instead.

Then on the box, install ufw and lock it down:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y ufw
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw enable

Step 3 — Install Node and OpenClaw

OpenClaw is built on Node. Install a current LTS Node, then OpenClaw:

# Node LTS (via NodeSource)
curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | sudo -E bash -
sudo apt install -y nodejs

# OpenClaw (follows its documented install)
curl -fsSL https://openclaw.ai/install.sh | bash

Confirm the version, then start the setup wizard:

openclaw --version
openclaw setup

The setup wizard walks you through: model provider, API key, the channels you want (Telegram / WhatsApp / etc.), and where OpenClaw keeps its workspace (its config, memory, and operating instructions). Let it use the default ~/.openclaw workspace on the VPS.

Step 4 — Connect your AI model (bring your own key)

OpenClaw is model-agnostic — Claude, GPT, Gemini, or fully local via Ollama. For a 24/7 personal assistant I recommend a hosted model provider (reliable, no GPU cost on the VPS):

  1. Get an API key from your chosen provider.
  2. Put it in OpenClaw's config / environment — never hardcode it in a file you'll commit.
  3. Test with a one-shot prompt to confirm the round-trip works.

Cost control: the VPS is a few dollars/month; your AI usage is the variable cost. Pick a model tier you'll actually use, and set provider spend limits so an agent that loops can't surprise you.

Step 5 — Keep it running 24/7 (systemd)

Don't just run it in a terminal that dies when you log out. Make OpenClaw a service:

# /etc/systemd/system/openclaw.service
[Unit]
Description=OpenClaw Gateway
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=youruser
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/openclaw gateway
Restart=always
RestartSec=5
Environment=NODE_ENV=production

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Then:

sudo systemctl enable --now openclaw
sudo systemctl status openclaw

Restart=always means if it ever crashes, systemd brings it right back — the whole point of a 24/7 assistant.

Step 6 — Reach it from your phone (reverse proxy + auth)

The Gateway has a browser Control UI. To reach it from your phone over the internet safely:

  1. Put it behind Caddy or nginx with a free SSL cert.
  2. Front it with basic-auth or OAuth so the world can't open your assistant.

Caddy makes the TLS part automatic:

openclaw.example.com {
    basic_auth {
        youruser <hash>   # run: caddy hash-password
    }
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:<openclaw-port>
}

Point a cheap domain (or a subdomain of one you have) at the VPS's IP, and Caddy issues the cert. Now your phone reaches the assistant at https://openclaw.example.com — encrypted, and only you can in.

(A simpler alternative: SSH tunnel — ssh -L 8080:localhost:<port> your-vps and open localhost:8080 in your phone browser. Zero extra setup, no public exposure at all.)

Step 7 — Point your channels at it

Now the satisfying part. Connect the chat apps you already use:

  • Telegram: create a bot via BotFather, drop the token into OpenClaw. Message the bot — that's your assistant.
  • WhatsApp: link a dedicated number (the two-phone setup OpenClaw recommends: one number just for the assistant, so your personal chats stay private).
  • Slack / Discord / Signal / iMessage: OpenClaw supports these through its channel plugins.

From that moment, your "assistant" lives on the VPS and is reachable from anywhere.

Keeping it healthy

  • Back up the workspace (~/.openclaw) — that's the memory and config you can't get back. A nightly rsync or tarball to object storage is enough.
  • Watch disk: logs and sessions grow; add a small rotation.
  • Update deliberately: OpenClaw moves fast, but test an update in a clone before rolling it onto the box your assistant runs on.
  • Credentials: keep API keys in env vars or a secrets file with 600 perms, never in the repo.

The honest bottom line

The VPS itself is the cheapest part — a few dollars a month on a provider like Hostinger (referral code OVDAMRMASPIM). The real work is the setup: Node, systemd, a locked-down firewall, and a reverse proxy in front of the Control UI. Do it once and you have an always-on, model-flexible, private assistant that meets you in the apps you already use. That's the whole pitch of self-hosting OpenClaw, and it's genuinely achievable in an afternoon.

This guide is part of the OpenClaw how-to collection on ClawDesk — 90+ guides on installing, configuring, and hosting OpenClaw. Ready to host it? A cheap VPS via Hostinger OVDAMRMASPIM is all you need.

title: How to Migrate to GoHighLevel from HubSpot, Another CRM or Spreadsheets
description:
Moving to GoHighLevel from HubSpot, another CRM or a pile of spreadsheets is where many businesses lose leads, history and momentum. Not because the import is hard, but because nobody planned what should move, what should be rebuilt and what should be left behind. Here's the process I use for CRM migrations.

First: what moves, and what doesn't

Set expectations early. In most migrations:

  • Moves well: contacts, companies, tags, custom field values, and open deals or opportunities, usually via CSV import.
  • Moves with effort: notes, tasks and appointment history, which often need cleaning and mapping first.
  • Has to be rebuilt: workflows, automations, email templates, forms and pipelines. No CRM imports another CRM's automation logic, and honestly, a migration is the best chance you'll get to rebuild them properly.
  • Usually archived, not moved: old email and SMS conversation threads. Export them for your records rather than trying to force them in.

Step 1: Audit what you have

Before exporting anything, list:

  • Every pipeline and its stages, and how deals really move through them
  • Every automation, what triggers it, and whether it still matters
  • Custom fields that are actually used (most accounts have dozens nobody fills in)
  • Integrations: forms, booking tools, payment and accounting software
  • Phone numbers and email sending domains currently in use

This is the most valuable hour of the whole migration. It decides what you rebuild, and what you finally get rid of.

Step 2: Clean the data before it moves

  • Merge duplicates (same email or phone number)
  • Standardise phone numbers to international format, e.g. +1, +44 or +61
  • Remove bounced emails and contacts who opted out, and keep them on a suppression list
  • Turn messy free-text values into consistent options for tags and dropdowns

Importing dirty data into a new system just moves the mess somewhere more expensive.

Step 3: Design GoHighLevel around how you work now

Don't copy your old setup field for field. Design the pipelines, custom fields, tags and user permissions around how your team sells today. Decide which tags will drive automations, so imported contacts land in the right workflows from day one.

Step 4: Map and import

  1. Export contacts and deals from the old system as CSV files.
  2. Map each column to a GoHighLevel field, creating custom fields first where needed.
  3. Add a tag like imported-from-hubspot to every record so you can find and fix them later.
  4. Import a small test batch, check it carefully, then import the rest.
  5. Import opportunities into the right pipeline stages.

Important: make sure imports don't trigger automations by accident. A badly timed import can text thousands of old contacts at once. Pause or exclude imported tags until you're ready.

Step 5: Rebuild the automations (better)

This is where a migration pays for itself. Rebuild the automations that matter, and add the ones you were missing, like a missed-call text-back, reminders and recall. My list of 10 automations every service business should have is a good checklist.

Step 6: Phone numbers, email and compliance

  • Phone numbers: keep your existing numbers if you can by porting them, so customers don't notice the switch.
  • Email: set up your sending domain with proper authentication before sending campaigns, and start with smaller sends.
  • Texting rules: US numbers need A2P 10DLC registration; UK and EU businesses should follow GDPR and PECR; Australian businesses the Spam Act. Bring consent records across with your contacts.

Step 7: Switch over without losing leads

  1. Run both systems side by side for a short period.
  2. Move your website forms, booking links and integrations to GoHighLevel.
  3. Check that every new lead lands in GoHighLevel and triggers the right automations.
  4. Train the team, then switch the old system to read-only.
  5. Cancel the old subscription only after a clean week.

Common migration mistakes

  • Importing everything, including years of dead leads and duplicates
  • Recreating every old custom field instead of designing fresh
  • Imports that accidentally trigger SMS or email blasts
  • Forgetting forms and integrations that still point at the old CRM
  • Leaving out consent and opt-out data

Want your migration handled?

I plan and run GoHighLevel migrations end to end: audit, clean-up, design, import, automation rebuild and switch-over. I'm a software engineer, so I can also script data transformations and integrations that a CSV import can't handle. It starts with a $97 audit, credited toward the work. See pricing or how I work as a GoHighLevel expert.

Originally published at arslanautomates.com. I'm Arslan Mumtaz, a software engineer who builds GoHighLevel CRM and AI automation for service businesses. See my case studies or book a call.
