title: NestJS vs Express vs Fastify in 2026: a practical comparison
description:
Originally published on devanddeliver.com.

Introduction

Raw throughput benchmarks make NestJS look slow - but 17,000 requests per second is 1.5 billion requests a day, and the real question is whether your codebase can handle your team. We ran the benchmarks ourselves and made the case for NestJS as the professional default for Node.js backends in 2026.

Versions covered: Express 5.2.1 · Fastify 5.8.5 · NestJS 11.1.24
Benchmarks: Node.js 24.15, Apple Silicon, 100 connections, 20s
Last verified: May 2026

The short version

NestJS is the right default for professional backend work in Node.js in 2026. It is the only one of the three that gives you a complete application framework - dependency injection, module system, guards, interceptors, lifecycle hooks, and a testable architecture out of the box. Every serious team building a multi-module API in TypeScript will be better served by NestJS than by assembling the same things manually from Express middleware.

Fastify is the right choice when raw throughput is a first-class requirement - IoT ingestion, public APIs handling tens of thousands of requests per second per instance, or anything where cold start time matters (serverless, edge). It is an excellent HTTP server. It is not an application framework.

Express is the right choice when you are prototyping, maintaining an existing codebase, or need a thin layer with zero opinion. It is the foundation the Node.js ecosystem was built on. In 2026 it is still the right tool for small, focused services.

The mistake is comparing all three on throughput benchmarks and concluding NestJS is the slowest. NestJS trades a portion of raw req/s for something more valuable at scale: a consistent, testable, team-friendly application architecture. If your server is handling 20,000 requests per second, it is serving over 1.7 billion requests a day. The question is not whether NestJS can handle your load. It almost certainly can. The question is whether your codebase can handle your team.

First, understand what each one is

Express is a routing layer with middleware. That is almost all it does - deliberately. It gives you (req, res, next) and gets out of the way. Express v5 (the current stable) arrived in late 2024 after years in beta and fixed the most common footgun: unhandled promise rejections now propagate to your error middleware automatically. Everything else is largely the same as it has been for a decade. That is partly a strength: the Express mental model is universal, its middleware ecosystem is enormous, and there are no surprises.

Fastify optimises for throughput. Its two architectural choices - a compiled JSON serializer and AJV-based schema validation baked into the router - make it the fastest mainstream Node.js HTTP framework. It uses a plugin system with encapsulation rather than Express's flat middleware chain. The result is a framework that is opinionated about performance and relatively unopinionated about everything else: you still compose your own structure, your own testing patterns, your own cross-cutting concerns.

NestJS is an application framework that runs on top of Express or Fastify and solves the problems those frameworks leave to you. It brings Angular-style architecture to the backend: a dependency injection container, a module system, decorators for controllers and services, guards for auth, interceptors for cross-cutting logic, exception filters for consistent error handling, and a TestingModule API that makes unit testing injectable services trivial. NestJS does not compete with Express or Fastify on throughput. It uses them as its HTTP layer and adds everything a production application actually needs on top.

NestJS v11 defaults to the Express v5 adapter. It supports the Fastify adapter natively via @nestjs/platform-fastify.

Framework snapshots

Express 5.2.1 Fastify 5.8.5 NestJS 11.1.24
Node.js minimum 18+ 20+ 20+
TypeScript Optional Optional First-class
DI container ❌ ❌ ✔️
Module system ❌ ❌ ✔️
Built-in validation ❌ JSON Schema (AJV) class-validator / Pipes
Auth pattern Middleware Plugin hook Guard (composable, testable)
OpenAPI / Swagger Manual / plugin Manual / plugin Auto-generated from DTOs
Testing utilities None built-in None built-in TestingModule built-in
Microservices support ❌ ❌ (gRPC, Kafka, RabbitMQ)
Weekly npm downloads 107M¹ 7.9M 10.7M
GitHub stars ~69k ~33k ~67k

¹ Express downloads are heavily inflated by transitive dependencies - NestJS itself pulls Express under the hood. The intentional install numbers are closer to 10-15M per week.

What NestJS gives you that the others do not

Before the code comparison and benchmarks, it is worth being explicit about what you are actually getting with NestJS. These are not marginal conveniences - they are the reason teams choose it.

DEPENDENCY INJECTION AND TESTABILITY

In Express or Fastify, services depend on each other through imports, globals, or manual wiring. In NestJS, every service declares its dependencies and the DI container wires them at startup. The payoff is in testing:

// Test a service in complete isolation - no real database, no HTTP server

const module = await Test.createTestingModule({
  providers: [
    UsersService,
    {
      provide: PrismaService,
      useValue: { user: { findUnique: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(mockUser) } },
    },
  ],
}).compile();

const usersService = module.get<UsersService>(UsersService);

Three lines to swap the real Prisma client for a mock. This pattern works across your entire application - any service, any dependency, no special wiring required. Achieving equivalent test isolation in Express means passing dependencies through constructors manually everywhere or introducing a third-party DI library yourself.

A MODULE SYSTEM THAT SCALES WITH YOUR TEAM

NestJS organises code into modules with explicit import/export boundaries. UsersModule exports UsersService. AuthModule imports UsersModule to access it. If AuthModule does not import UsersModule, it cannot access UsersService - the DI container enforces the boundary at startup.

This matters less on a solo project. It matters a lot when four developers are working on the same codebase and "which service can I use from this module" has a clear, enforced answer instead of "just import the file and hope nothing breaks."

GLOBAL CROSS-CUTTING CONCERNS - WRITE ONCE, APPLY EVERYWHERE 

// main.ts - configure once

app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true }));
app.useGlobalGuards(new JwtGuard());
app.useGlobalFilters(new AllExceptionsFilter());
app.useGlobalInterceptors(new LoggingInterceptor());

Every route in the application now validates input, enforces JWT auth, formats errors consistently, and logs requests - without touching a single route handler. In Express, the equivalent requires adding middleware to every router, trusting that someone remembered, and hoping the chain is in the right order.

Individual routes can opt out or add their own guards without disturbing the global defaults:

@Get('health')
@Public() // custom decorator to skip JwtGuard on this route
healthCheck() { return { status: 'ok' }; }

OPENAPI DOCUMENTATION GENERATED FROM YOUR DTOS

Install @nestjs/swagger, add a few decorators to your DTOs, and NestJS generates full OpenAPI documentation automatically. No separate schema file, no manual sync, no risk of docs drifting from the actual API:

import { ApiProperty } from '@nestjs/swagger';

export class CreateUserDto {
  @ApiProperty({ example: 'Alice' })
  @IsString()
  name: string;

  @ApiProperty({ example: 'alice@example.com' })
  @IsEmail()
  email: string;
}

The same DTO that validates incoming requests also documents the API endpoint. One source of truth.

THE BROADER ECOSYSTEM

NestJS ships first-party packages for the things every real backend eventually needs: @nestjs/config (configuration with environment validation), @nestjs/schedule (cron jobs), @nestjs/bull (queues via BullMQ), @nestjs/event-emitter (in-process events), @nestjs/microservices (gRPC, Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS with the same Guards/Interceptors pattern as HTTP). These are all maintained by the NestJS core team, follow the same conventions, and require no architectural rethinking to introduce into an existing app.

Mental model: how a request moves through each

Express:

request → middleware A → middleware B → route handler → response

Everything is a function with (req, res, next). You own the chain.

Fastify:

request → onRequest hooks → JSON Schema validation → handler → serialization → response

Validation runs at the framework level before your handler. Invalid bodies are rejected automatically.

NestJS:

request → middleware → guards → interceptors (before) →
  pipes (transform + validate) → controller → service →
    interceptors (after) → exception filters → response

Each layer has one job. Guards decide whether a request is allowed through. Pipes transform and validate the body. Interceptors handle logging, caching, response shaping. Exception filters handle every possible error in one place. You configure each layer once globally, then override per-route only when you need to.

Code comparison: CRUD + validation

The same endpoint in each framework - create a user, list users, get by ID, delete by ID. TypeScript throughout.

EXPRESS V5 + ZOD 

// app.ts
import express, { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import { z } from 'zod';

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const users: { id: number; name: string; email: string }[] = [];
let nextId = 1;

const CreateUserSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string().min(1),
  email: z.string().email(),
});

app.get('/users', (_req: Request, res: Response) => {
  res.json(users);
});

app.post('/users', (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const result = CreateUserSchema.safeParse(req.body);
  if (!result.success) {
    return res.status(400).json({ errors: result.error.flatten() });
  }
  const user = { id: nextId++, ...result.data };
  users.push(user);
  res.status(201).json(user);
});

app.get('/users/:id', (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const user = users.find(u => u.id === Number(req.params.id));
  if (!user) return res.status(404).json({ message: 'User not found' });
  res.json(user);
});

app.delete('/users/:id', (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const idx = users.findIndex(u => u.id === Number(req.params.id));
  if (idx === -1) return res.status(404).json({ message: 'User not found' });
  users.splice(idx, 1);
  res.status(204).send();
});

// Express v5: async errors now propagate to error middleware automatically
app.use((err: Error, _req: Request, res: Response, _next: NextFunction) => {
  res.status(500).json({ message: err.message });
});

app.listen(3000);

FASTIFY V5 (BUILT-IN JSON SCHEMA) 

// server.ts
import Fastify from 'fastify';

const app = Fastify({ logger: false });

const users: { id: number; name: string; email: string }[] = [];
let nextId = 1;

const bodySchema = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['name', 'email'],
  properties: {
    name:  { type: 'string', minLength: 1 },
    email: { type: 'string', minLength: 3 },
  },
  additionalProperties: false,
};

app.get('/users', async () => users);

app.post('/users', { schema: { body: bodySchema } }, async (request, reply) => {
  const body = request.body as { name: string; email: string };
  const user = { id: nextId++, ...body };
  users.push(user);
  return reply.status(201).send(user);
});

app.get<{ Params: { id: string } }>('/users/:id', async (request, reply) => {
  const user = users.find(u => u.id === Number(request.params.id));
  if (!user) return reply.status(404).send({ message: 'User not found' });
  return user;
});

app.delete<{ Params: { id: string } }>('/users/:id', async (request, reply) => {
  const idx = users.findIndex(u => u.id === Number(request.params.id));
  if (idx === -1) return reply.status(404).send({ message: 'User not found' });
  users.splice(idx, 1);
  return reply.status(204).send();
});

app.setErrorHandler((error, _request, reply) => {
  reply.status(error.statusCode ?? 500).send({ message: error.message });
});

app.listen({ port: 3000 });

NESTJS V11 (CLASS-VALIDATOR + VALIDATIONPIPE) 

// users/dto/create-user.dto.ts
import { IsEmail, IsString, MinLength } from 'class-validator';

export class CreateUserDto {
  @IsString()
  @MinLength(1)
  name: string;

  @IsEmail()
  email: string;
}

// users/users.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Post, Delete, Param, Body, HttpCode } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CreateUserDto } from './dto/create-user.dto';
import { UsersService } from './users.service';

@Controller('users')
export class UsersController {
  constructor(private readonly usersService: UsersService) {}

  @Get()
  findAll() {
    return this.usersService.findAll();
  }

  @Post()
  create(@Body() dto: CreateUserDto) {
    return this.usersService.create(dto);
  }

  @Get(':id')
  findOne(@Param('id') id: string) {
    return this.usersService.findOne(+id);
  }

  @Delete(':id')
  @HttpCode(204)
  remove(@Param('id') id: string) {
    return this.usersService.remove(+id);
  }
}

// main.ts - register ValidationPipe globally once; every route gets it automatically
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({
    whitelist: true,              // strips unknown properties automatically
    forbidNonWhitelisted: true,   // returns 400 on unknown properties
  }));
  await app.listen(3000);
}
bootstrap();

What the comparison shows: Express and Fastify require you to choose and wire validation per route or per router. NestJS's ValidationPipe with DTOs applies to every endpoint globally. As the application grows from 4 routes to 40, this difference compounds. No new developer can forget to add validation to a new route - the framework prevents it.

Code comparison: JWT auth

EXPRESS - MIDDLEWARE 

import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import jwt from 'jsonwebtoken';

export const jwtMiddleware = (req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {
  const token = req.headers.authorization?.split(' ')[1];
  if (!token) return res.status(401).json({ message: 'Unauthorized' });
  try {
    (req as any).user = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET!);
    next();
  } catch {
    res.status(401).json({ message: 'Invalid token' });
  }
};

FASTIFY - PLUGIN HOOK 

import fastifyJwt from '@fastify/jwt';

app.register(fastifyJwt, { secret: process.env.JWT_SECRET! });

app.get('/protected', {
  preHandler: async (request, reply) => {
    try {
      await request.jwtVerify();
    } catch (err) {
      reply.send(err);
    }
  }
}, async (request) => {
  return { user: request.user };
});

NESTJS - COMPOSABLE GUARD 

// auth/jwt.guard.ts
import { Injectable, CanActivate, ExecutionContext, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import * as jwt from 'jsonwebtoken';

@Injectable()
export class JwtGuard implements CanActivate {
  canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const req = context.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const auth = req.headers['authorization'];
    if (!auth?.startsWith('Bearer ')) throw new UnauthorizedException();
    try {
      req.user = jwt.verify(auth.slice(7), process.env.JWT_SECRET!);
      return true;
    } catch {
      throw new UnauthorizedException();
    }
  }
}

// Composing multiple guards on a single route is one line:
// @UseGuards(JwtGuard, RolesGuard)
// @Roles('admin')
// @Delete(':id')
// remove(@Param('id') id: string) { ... }

// Unit testing a guard requires no HTTP server:
// const guard = new JwtGuard();
// const context = createMockExecutionContext({ authorization: 'Bearer valid-token' });
// expect(guard.canActivate(context)).toBe(true);

The NestJS guard model pays off when you need to compose auth logic: JWT check, role check, rate limit check, feature flag check. In Express, that is four middleware functions you must apply in the right order to the right routes and remember to test each combination. In NestJS, it is @UseGuards(JwtGuard, RolesGuard) and each guard is independently unit-testable.

Performance benchmarks

These numbers were run on Apple Silicon, Node.js 24.15.0, using autocannon, 100 concurrent connections, 20-second runs. No external I/O, in-memory data.

GET / - BARE JSON RESPONSE

Framework req/s p50 p99
Fastify 5.8.5 100,301 <1 ms 1 ms
Express 5.2.1 53,400 1 ms 3 ms
NestJS 11 + Fastify adapter 41,159 1 ms 7 ms
NestJS 11 + Express adapter 33,344 2 ms 11 ms

POST /VALIDATE - JSON BODY PARSE + FRAMEWORK-NATIVE VALIDATION

Fastify: built-in JSON Schema (AJV).
Express: manual field checks.
NestJS: class-validator + ValidationPipe.

Framework req/s p50 p99
Fastify 5.8.5 42,720 1 ms 7 ms
Express 5.2.1 28,764 3 ms 7 ms
NestJS 11 + Fastify adapter 19,693 4 ms 14 ms
NestJS 11 + Express adapter 17,432 4 ms 22 ms

POST /QUERY - VALIDATE + 10MS SIMULATED DATABASE CALL

Same validation as above, with a 10ms async wait added to simulate a real indexed database query. This is what production throughput actually looks like.

Framework req/s p50 p99
NestJS 11 + Express adapter 8,812 11 ms 16 ms
NestJS 11 + Fastify adapter 8,929 11 ms 13 ms
Express 5.2.1 8,770 11 ms 13 ms
Fastify 5.8.5 8,612 11 ms 16 ms

All four frameworks converge to the same throughput - within margin of error, in the same order as random noise. The theoretical ceiling with 100 connections and 10ms I/O is 10,000 req/s; every framework reaches ~88% of it. The 2.5× gap from the pure-CPU benchmark disappears completely.

COLD START AND IDLE MEMORY

Framework Cold start Idle RSS Idle heap
Express 5.2.1 83 ms 62 MB 8 MB
Fastify 5.8.5 137 ms 68 MB 11 MB
NestJS 11 (Express adapter) 570 ms 95 MB 21 MB
NestJS 11 (Fastify adapter) 550 ms 95 MB 21 MB

READING THE NUMBERS HONESTLY

The pure-CPU benchmarks (GET, POST /validate) show a real gap. Fastify handles 2.5× more requests per second than NestJS when there is nothing else to wait on. That number is accurate and worth knowing.

It is also largely irrelevant to the decision.

The moment you add a database - even a fast indexed query at 10ms - every framework converges to the same throughput. The bottleneck becomes I/O wait time, and the 2-4ms of framework overhead NestJS adds per request disappears into the noise. In production, behind a real database, NestJS and Fastify deliver the same throughput.

NestJS at 17,000 req/s (pure CPU) is already handling 1.5 billion requests per day on a single server. With a real database in the picture, all four frameworks land around the same number, and that number is determined entirely by your database latency and connection pool, not by your choice of Node.js framework.

What you are actually trading by choosing NestJS: some CPU-bound throughput headroom that your server will almost certainly never fully use, in exchange for DI, testability, module boundaries, composable guards, global validation, automatic Swagger generation, and a first-party ecosystem for queues, crons, microservices, and everything else a real backend eventually needs.

The cold start story is different. NestJS's ~570ms startup is the DI container initialising, decorators resolving, and modules wiring. For a long-running API server it is paid once at deploy. For serverless or short-lived containers where cold start affects every request, it is a genuine cost. Fastify at 137ms and Express at 83ms are significantly better in those environments.

Switching to the Fastify adapter inside NestJS gives you around 20% better throughput on CPU-bound routes. With I/O in the picture, that 20% gap is barely measurable. The Fastify adapter is still worth using on greenfield projects  but "for performance" is the wrong reason. The right reason is that Fastify is a better underlying HTTP engine.

On benchmarks you will find elsewhere: One widely cited comparison claims NestJS outperforms Express on throughput. Our numbers - and the architectural reality - do not support that. NestJS's Express adapter runs on top of Express; it cannot be faster. If you see NestJS above raw Express in a benchmark, look closely at what is being measured.

NestJS project structure

A production NestJS project follows a consistent, predictable shape that any NestJS developer can navigate immediately:

src/
  main.ts                       # bootstrap - global pipes, guards, filters, interceptors
  app.module.ts                 # root module
  common/
    filters/                    # AllExceptionsFilter
    guards/                     # JwtGuard, RolesGuard
    interceptors/               # LoggingInterceptor, TransformInterceptor
    decorators/                 # @CurrentUser(), @Public(), @Roles()
  modules/
    users/
      users.module.ts
      users.controller.ts
      users.service.ts
      dto/
        create-user.dto.ts
        update-user.dto.ts
    auth/
      auth.module.ts
      auth.service.ts
      strategies/               # JWT strategy
  prisma/
    prisma.service.ts           # extends PrismaClient, implements OnModuleInit
    prisma.module.ts

A new developer joining the project knows exactly where to look for any piece of logic. common/guards/ has the auth guards. modules/users/ has the users domain. The structure is the documentation.

DATABASE: PRISMA (RECOMMENDED) VS TYPEORM

In 2026 most new NestJS projects reach for Prisma:

// prisma/prisma.service.ts
import { Injectable, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client';

@Injectable()
export class PrismaService extends PrismaClient implements OnModuleInit {
  async onModuleInit() {
    await this.$connect();
  }
}

TypeORM remains common in established codebases and still works well with NestJS. The main 2026 consideration: TypeORM's synchronize: true setting auto-migrates schema at startup and should never be enabled in production.

GLOBAL EXCEPTION FILTER 

// common/filters/all-exceptions.filter.ts
import { ExceptionFilter, Catch, ArgumentsHost, HttpException, HttpStatus } from '@nestjs/common';

@Catch()
export class AllExceptionsFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  catch(exception: unknown, host: ArgumentsHost) {
    const ctx    = host.switchToHttp();
    const res    = ctx.getResponse();
    const status = exception instanceof HttpException
      ? exception.getStatus()
      : HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR;
    const message = exception instanceof HttpException
      ? exception.getResponse()
      : 'Internal server error';
    res.status(status).json({ statusCode: status, message });
  }
}
// Register once in main.ts: app.useGlobalFilters(new AllExceptionsFilter());

Every unhandled exception in the application now returns a consistent JSON shape. No try/catch in individual route handlers, no risk of raw error objects leaking to the client.

NestJS patterns worth knowing

These are not gotchas - they are architectural decisions NestJS makes explicit that other frameworks leave implicit.

Circular module dependencies surface at startup, not runtime

If UsersModule imports AuthModule and AuthModule imports UsersModule, NestJS throws at bootstrap:

Error: Nest can't resolve dependencies of UserService (?)

This is NestJS catching a circular dependency before your application takes a single request. The fix is forwardRef(), or - better - rethinking whether the two modules should be split differently. Express would silently handle this until something breaks at runtime.

class-validator and the validation performance trade-off

class-validator uses TypeScript reflection metadata, which has runtime cost. Our benchmarks show it reduces throughput on a three-field POST from ~28k to ~17k req/s compared to Express with manual validation. What you gain is automatic, consistent, globally applied validation across every endpoint - no per-route Zod schema, no forgotten validation on a new route, no inconsistent error shapes. For most APIs the trade-off is straightforwardly worth it.

If you hit a specific endpoint where validation is genuinely a throughput bottleneck, you can bypass ValidationPipe on that route and use a custom pipe backed by Zod or raw AJV instead. The framework supports this without requiring architectural changes.

RequestScoped providers: a deliberate choice, not a default

@Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST })
export class RequestContextService {}

Request-scoped providers recreate the injection subtree on every request, which is expensive. The default is singleton scope (the right choice for almost everything). Request scope exists for cases where you genuinely need per-request context - distributed tracing with request-scoped loggers, per-request tenancy in multi-tenant systems. Use it intentionally.

Lifecycle hooks have a defined order

OnModuleInit fires per-module during initialisation. OnApplicationBootstrap fires once after all modules are ready. If your Prisma service connects in OnModuleInit and another service depends on it during initialisation, use OnApplicationBootstrap in the dependent service to guarantee the connection is established first.

The adapter choice: Express vs Fastify under NestJS

Workload NestJS + Express NestJS + Fastify Gain
GET / 33,344 req/s 41,159 req/s +23%
POST /validate 17,432 req/s 19,693 req/s +13%
Cold start 570 ms 550 ms negligible
Idle RSS 95 MB 95 MB same

The Fastify adapter consistently delivers 15-23% more throughput. The catch: some Express-specific middleware does not work under the Fastify adapter. Older Passport strategies, certain session packages, and any middleware that directly modifies the Express req/res objects will need Fastify equivalents (@fastify/passport, @fastify/session).

For a new greenfield project with no Express dependencies: use the Fastify adapter, accept the marginal tradeoff in ecosystem breadth, and get the performance headroom. For an existing project with established middleware dependencies: stay on Express adapter and save the migration effort for something with more impact.

Picking your framework

NestJS is the right default for backend work in Node.js when:

  • You are building a real application - auth, modules, services, repositories, business logic
  • More than one developer will touch the codebase
  • You need unit-testable services
  • You want consistent patterns across every module, not just the ones the original author wrote
  • You are thinking beyond HTTP: queues, scheduled jobs, microservices, event-driven architecture - the NestJS ecosystem covers all of it with the same mental model

Fastify is the right choice when:

  • Throughput is a primary constraint - IoT ingestion, high-frequency trading, event processing at scale
  • You are writing a single-purpose HTTP service with a small surface area
  • Cold start time matters (serverless, edge functions)
  • You want schema-validated endpoints with near-zero validation overhead

Express is the right choice when:

  • You are prototyping or scoping
  • You are maintaining an existing Express codebase where the migration cost outweighs the benefit
  • You need deep compatibility with a specific Express-only library
  • The service is genuinely small enough that framework structure adds noise, not clarity

What's next: NestJS v12 (planned Q3 2026)

NestJS v12 is expected in Q3 2026 with three changes worth tracking:

  • Native ESM - CommonJS workarounds in monorepos become unnecessary
  • Vitest as the default test runner - replacing Jest in the scaffolded template
  • Standard Schema / Zod in decorators - class-validator may no longer be the only first-class DTO validation option. If this lands, the validation performance story changes: Zod's runtime cost is lower and its TypeScript inference is tighter

If you are designing an application today that will be in production in 12 months, keep DTO validation encapsulated. The ValidationPipe pattern is stable; the underlying validator may swap.

Agency take

NestJS is our default for client backend work. Not because it is the most performant, but because it is the one that holds up when the project gets handed to a new developer six months later, when the team grows from two to five, when you need to write tests for a feature built by someone else. The structure NestJS enforces is the kind you would build yourself in Express eventually - it just starts from day one instead of after the first painful refactor.

We reach for Fastify when a service has an explicit throughput requirement or when serverless cold start matters. We reach for Express when scope is tight and structure would be overhead rather than investment.

The throughput gap in the synthetic benchmarks is real. Once you add a real database - even a fast one - all four frameworks in these benchmarks land within a few percent of each other. The bottleneck is I/O, not the framework. We measured it: at 10ms simulated query time, Fastify, Express, NestJS on Express, and NestJS on Fastify all hit ~8,700–8,900 req/s. The 2.5× synthetic gap becomes noise.

Pick the framework your team can build on confidently. That is NestJS for most teams doing serious backend work in 2026.

Need help with this in your product? Our senior team builds NestJS and Node.js back ends, and you can hire our Node.js developers to join your own team. See how we helped Speeki grow to 100+ enterprise clients, or book a free 15-minute call.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use.

Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases.

Our goals for Python on Vercel

Ten months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications. We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions:

  • Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async/await, and context managers.

  • A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together.

  • Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on.

The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run.

Deploying Python applications on Vercel

We’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv, and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN.

For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them.

For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies.

Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructure

A Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language:

These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application.

Start building with Python on Vercel

Whether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services.

To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code.

The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN.

Here’s how the main parts connect:

  • Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. The browser connects directly to Jupyter, while mounted Drives provide the Python dependencies and workspace files.

  • Saving and publishing: The browser periodically sends the current notebook to FastAPI. FastAPI saves the source in PostgreSQL, renders changes as HTML, and uploads the result to Blob, so people can read published notebooks through the CDN without starting a Python kernel.

  • Sharing updates: After publishing a change, FastAPI sends a message through Vercel Queues. Each backend instance with connected browsers receives the notification and sends updated notebook listings over WebSockets, so people see changes without reloading.

  • Assisting with code: The agent uses AI SDK for Python and runs inside Vercel Workflows, which saves execution state and retries failed steps. Chat history stays in PostgreSQL, while notebook editing and execution tools work through the connected browser, which sends results back through FastAPI to resume the workflow.

The source code on GitHub includes the complete application and its deployment configuration. You can use it to explore these integrations or as a starting point for your own Python application.

Investing in the Python community

Last December, the Gel Data team, led by me and Elvis Pranskevichus, joined Vercel to build Python support and continue our open-source work.

At the same time, we announced our sponsorship of the Python Software Foundation and committed to funding one year of Serhiy Storchaka’s CPython maintenance through the foundation. Serhiy has authored over 600 commits to CPython’s main branch so far in 2026.

We also sponsored PyCon US and EuroPython this year, where the team and I met Python developers and heard where they were getting stuck. Those conversations help us figure out what to fix next.

We also published PEP 827, which, if accepted, would add type manipulation features that could help frameworks such as FastAPI offer simpler APIs with less boilerplate and more precise type checking.

What’s next for Python on Vercel

We’re continuing to improve Python SDKs, runtime performance, and development workflows for both people and coding agents. If you run into a deployment issue or find something missing in the Python SDKs, share your feedback in Vercel Community so the team can use it to guide that work.

Resources

  • Point your agent at our Python guides in the Knowledge Base

  • Deploy an eve agent in Python in one click

title: Optimal Explicit and Implicit Regularization Strengths in High-Dimensional Continual Linear Regression
description:
arXiv:2610.20804v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study continual linear regression in a high-dimensional regime, where a learner observes a sequence of tasks and updates its parameters sequentially. In this setting, we derive an explicit closed-form expression for the generalization loss of a model trained with gradient descent for a fixed number of steps per task, which holds for arbitrary teachers. We prove that the optimal fixed step size decays nearly inversely with the number of tasks, specifically as $\ln T / T$, for a single teacher and, more generally, i.i.d. teachers. Under this scaling, we show that the resulting generalization loss is asymptotically equivalent to that achieved by optimally tuned L2 (isotropic) regularization. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to generalized ridge regression with diagonal regularization matrices, obtaining a closed-form characterization of the generalization loss and identifying necessary and sufficient conditions under which the optimal regularizer is isotropic. Finally, we identify a regime where the optimal step size remains finite even as the number of tasks tends to infinity, thus revealing a non-trivial tradeoff between task variability and implicit regularization, in contrast to the i.i.d. teacher scaling. Our theoretical predictions are corroborated by experiments on both linear models and neural networks, providing practical guidance for the design of continual learning systems.

title: AI acceptable use policy for employees: what works
description:
Somewhere in your organisation this morning, someone pasted a client contract, a candidate CV or an unreleased financial projection into a personal ChatGPT account. This is not a hypothetical risk to manage next quarter: 66% of office professionals admit using AI tools at work even when they believed their employer did not permit it. The reflex response, a blanket ban, does not work. It simply pushes confidential data onto personal smartphones and unmonitored home networks. This article sets out the working alternative for a 20 to 200 person firm: a two-page AI acceptable use policy you can write this week, a sanctioned tool under company accounts, and a private gateway for the work that must stay inside your perimeter. With the numbers.

An effective AI acceptable use policy for employees sets clear data classification boundaries, specifies sanctioned corporate tools, and establishes a no-blame incident reporting path. Rather than attempting an outright ban, a workable policy gives staff approved, low-friction alternatives so confidential company and client data never enters public AI models. For a 20 to 200 person organisation, this means combining a two-page policy document with company-managed accounts and a self-hosted private gateway for sensitive workloads.

The urgency is driven by frontline behaviour. A PagerDuty survey published in June 2026 found that two-thirds (66%) of office professionals have used AI tools at work despite believing it was not permitted under company policy (PagerDuty). The same survey found 88% have shared work-related information with public AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini: 43% shared emails, 40% meeting notes, 34% customer data, and 31% financial information or confidential company documents.

If your instinct as a leader is to issue a strict ban or block AI domains at the perimeter firewall, the evidence suggests that the ban has already failed. Worse, it actively increases your exposure. When staff need to summarise twenty pages of meeting notes before a 2:00 PM executive call, they do not abandon the technology; they open ChatGPT on a personal smartphone, tether to a 5G hotspot, or forward the document to a personal webmail address.

Here is what actually works, what it costs, and how a 20 to 200 person organisation can put a working system in place within 30 days.

Why do employees ignore AI bans and leak company data?

The PagerDuty Shadow AI Survey was conducted by Wakefield Research among 1,250 office professionals in non-IT roles at organisations with annual revenue of USD 500 million or more, across the United States, United Kingdom, Australia and Japan (PagerDuty). While your organisation in the UAE or GCC is likely smaller, there is no evidence that staff behaviour differs when deadlines loom. The direction of travel is unambiguous.

Two operational figures matter most to technical and business leadership:

First, the volume of confidential material entering public models is accelerating rapidly. Figures compiled by Unio Digital from vendor security research put the share of corporate data entering AI tools that is sensitive at 34.8%, up from 10.7% two years earlier (Cyberhaven, 2025). The same review highlights that 77% of employees paste data directly into generative AI prompts, and 82% of those pastes originate from personal accounts rather than corporate workspaces (LayerX, 2025).

Second, the financial and operational cost when that exposure triggers a security incident is severe. IBM's Cost of a Data Breach 2026, as compiled in the Unio Digital review, found that security incidents involving shadow AI had more than doubled to 43% of organisations, averaging USD 5.39 million per incident (Unio Digital).

The lesson for a mid-market firm is not that you will necessarily face a USD 5.39 million breach bill; those samples skew towards multinational enterprises. The immediate takeaway is that shadow AI use is near-universal, it directly involves your most sensitive commercial material, and it is happening right now through unmanaged personal channels that your IT and security teams cannot audit.

Why do blanket AI bans fail in practice?

Blocking external AI domains at your office firewall feels decisive during an executive committee meeting. In practice, it creates a dangerous illusion of security.

Start with how your team actually works. Because 82% of corporate data pastes into generative AI tools originate from personal accounts (Unio Digital), the corporate network perimeter is largely irrelevant. Consumer ChatGPT accounts retain chat history by default and use prompt inputs to train and refine foundation models unless an individual user navigates deep into settings to opt out. A consumer account is not covered by your master service agreements, your non-disclosure agreements, or enterprise data protection commitments.

Furthermore, consumer account credentials represent an active secondary risk. Over 225,000 OpenAI credentials captured by infostealer malware were listed for sale on dark web illicit marketplaces in 2024 (Unio Digital). When an employee uses their personal account on an unmanaged personal device, any paste containing client confidential data sits inside an account that may already be compromised by infostealer malware. A firewall ban does not remove the data from these insecure environments. It simply removes your security team from the conversation, pushing usage to mobile browsers and home Wi-Fi networks where data loss prevention (DLP), conditional access, and audit logging cannot reach.

Bans also inflict direct damage on talent retention. In the PagerDuty study, 77% of office professionals stated that their employer's AI restrictions limit their professional growth, while 75% said they would be likely to look for a new role that offered better AI skills development (PagerDuty). Forcing high-performing analysts, software engineers, and project managers to work with one hand tied behind their backs creates resentment.

The practical alternative is not unconstrained permission. It is a three-part operating model: a concise, practical acceptable use policy, an approved commercial tool provisioned under company accounts, and a self-hosted private gateway for the sensitive workloads that cannot leave your perimeter.

How to write an AI acceptable use policy for employees

An AI acceptable use policy for employees should never be a 40-page legal dissertation. Lengthy governance manuals are rarely read, harder to remember, and virtually impossible for frontline managers to enforce. A policy that works must fit on two pages, present a clear mental model, establish a sanctioned path that is more convenient than personal workarounds, and provide a clear procedure for when someone makes a mistake.

The policy should centre on a strict three-tier classification model that tells staff exactly where different types of data may go:

  • Red (Restricted): Client personal data, Emirates ID numbers, bank details, unreleased financial projections, payroll files, intellectual property, and anything covered by an NDA. This tier must never be submitted to a hosted multitenant AI tool. It is routed exclusively to your internal private gateway.
  • Amber (Internal): Internal strategy memos, project roadmaps, non-sensitive source code, and business context that contains no personal identifiers or confidential financial metrics. Hosted commercial tools under corporate accounts are permitted only after redaction.
  • Green (Public): Public marketing collateral, standard boilerplate text, generic coding syntax queries, synthetic test data, and general brainstorming. Any sanctioned corporate tool is approved.

Below is a functional policy template. Customise the bracketed operational fields, keep the length under two pages, and issue it immediately:

ACME AI Acceptable Use Policy (v1.0, dated DD Month YYYY)

1. Purpose. This policy defines how we use artificial intelligence tools
   at work. Its goal is to enable productive, safe AI adoption, not to
   prohibit it.

2. Sanctioned tools. Staff may use AI exclusively via corporate accounts:
   - ChatGPT Business (under the ACME corporate workspace)
   - Microsoft Copilot Chat (authenticated with your corporate Entra ID account)
   - The ACME Internal AI Gateway at https://ai.internal for Red and Amber data
   Using personal accounts, consumer logins, or unapproved third-party AI
   extensions for company work is strictly prohibited.

3. Data classification rules. Before submitting information, classify it:
   RED: Client PII, national identity numbers, financial records, HR files,
   unreleased company metrics, NDA-governed material. Gateway only.
   AMBER: Internal memos, architectures, source code. Sanctioned hosted
   tools permitted ONLY after redacting identifiers.
   GREEN: Public content, generic drafting, open syntax questions.
   Sanctioned tools permitted freely.

4. Redaction protocol. When preparing Amber content for hosted tools:
   replace client and employee names with placeholders such as [Client A];
   strip account numbers, phone numbers, and addresses; retain only the
   abstract structure required to complete the task.

5. Human accountability. You remain personally responsible for deliverables.
   Verify all facts, calculations, statutory citations, and code outputs
   before sharing with clients or deploying to production.

6. Transparency. Inform clients or counterparties when AI has generated a
   substantial part of a deliverable whenever contracts or regulations require it.

7. No-blame incident reporting. If you inadvertently paste Red data into an
   unapproved or hosted tool, notify [Head of IT] within 24 hours. Prompt
   reporting carries no disciplinary sanction. Concealing a known data leak
   is a disciplinary offence.

8. Governance. This policy is reviewed quarterly by [Head of IT].

Two operational principles ensure this policy succeeds:

First, your sanctioned path must deliver superior performance: low-latency models, generous usage caps, and zero friction. If the internal gateway is slow or difficult to access, staff will revert to consumer accounts.

Second, enforce network boundaries pragmatically. Block consumer AI login pages on managed laptops via your secure web gateway or endpoint management profile. Configure endpoint DLP rules to detect patterns like UAE Emirates ID numbers (784-XXXX-XXXXXXX-X) and international bank account numbers (IBANs) in browser clipboard events. You cannot control personal mobile devices directly, but you can remove friction from the corporate path and maintain an auditable record of compliance.

Which AI tools should your company policy sanction?

The fastest risk-reduction step an organisation can take is migrating employees from unmanaged personal accounts to a corporate workspace. The contractual and technical differences between consumer and enterprise tiers are fundamental.

OpenAI does not use data submitted to ChatGPT Business, ChatGPT Enterprise, or the OpenAI API to train its models by default (OpenAI enterprise privacy). Workspace administrators retain administrative oversight, user provisioning, and retention controls, with deleted conversations purged from OpenAI operational systems within 30 days. ChatGPT Business is priced at USD 25 per seat per month on monthly billing, or USD 20 per seat per month on annual billing, with an upgraded Premium seat at USD 125 monthly or USD 100 annually, specifically accommodating organisations sized from 2 to 200 seats (OpenAI Business pricing).

For organisations running on Microsoft 365, Microsoft Copilot Chat accessed via an Entra ID corporate account provides commercial data protection at no additional cost (Microsoft Learn). Prompts and responses do not cross the Microsoft 365 tenant boundary, are not inspected by humans, are not used to train foundation models, and inherit corporate audit logging and eDiscovery retention policies.

When developing custom internal tooling using the OpenAI API, inputs have not been used for model training by default since 1 March 2023 (OpenAI platform data controls). API operational logs are retained for abuse monitoring for up to 30 days, and organisations handling highly regulated workloads can apply for zero data retention (ZDR).

Route Direct cost Used for model training Governance and controls
Personal accounts (status quo) USD 0 direct Yes, by default unless opted out Zero administrative visibility; personal email logins
ChatGPT Business USD 25/seat monthly; USD 20/seat annual No, by default Central admin console, SSO, seat lifecycle, 30-day purge
Microsoft Copilot Chat (work account) Included with Entra ID corporate plans No, protected M365 tenant boundary, corporate audit logs, eDiscovery
OpenAI API (custom applications) Usage-based token pricing No, default policy since March 2023 30-day abuse monitoring logs; zero retention on approval
Private self-hosted gateway GPU compute leasing Never, runs isolated weights Complete data residency, raw prompt audit logs, local weights

A critical constraint for GCC organisations to evaluate: major providers such as OpenAI do not offer an in-country UAE data processing boundary for these software-as-a-service plans. For standard drafting and day-to-day administrative tasks, this trade-off is often acceptable when paired with strict Amber redaction rules. However, for sensitive client files, national identity data, and regulated records, cross-border data transfer without explicit legal grounds introduces significant compliance exposure.

When is a private AI gateway worth paying for?

Consider a typical GCC operational structure: an 80-person professional services consultancy in Dubai operating on Microsoft 365. The organisation comprises advisory, marketing, and client delivery teams. Approximately 25 staff members routinely handle Red or Amber material: financial models, audit schedules, M&A due diligence files, and human resources records. The remaining 55 staff members conduct general analysis, drafting, and research.

A private gateway consists of dedicated GPU hardware running open-weight inference models behind a unified reverse proxy. The proxy handles user authentication, per-department token allowances, and immutable local logging. Your staff interact with standard web interfaces or internal scripts, but the inference processes execute on private hardware hosted within a local data centre. Prompts and responses remain strictly within your controlled perimeter.

We deploy and manage these environments for clients within our AI infrastructure service, placing FastLLM Proxy in front of model instances. FastLLM Proxy acts as an OpenAI-compatible gateway that centralises request routing, enforces department quotas, and manages access controls across private GPU instances and external hosted endpoints.

Three triggers indicate that your organisation requires a private gateway:

  1. Data residency mandates: Client agreements, public sector contracts, or regional data protection statutes requiring that personal and financial information never leave the UAE.
  2. High volume of confidential data: When sensitive workflows are executed daily, human redaction discipline inevitably slips under pressure. Technical segregation prevents leaks by design.
  3. Regulatory auditability: Regulated entities in financial services, legal, and healthcare sectors must produce verifiable audit trails detailing who issued each prompt, what model generated the response, and where the compute was located.

To evaluate the operational expenditure, consider indicative pricing from GPU providers. Using Hyperstack published rates as an industry benchmark:

  • NVIDIA L40 (48 GB VRAM): USD 1.00 per hour on demand, translating to approximately USD 730 per month running 24/7 (roughly AED 2,700). An L40 runs OpenAI's open-weight gpt-oss-20b model (requiring approximately 16 GB VRAM) or high-performance 32B parameter models in 4-bit quantisation with ample headroom.
  • NVIDIA H100 (80 GB VRAM): USD 2.50 per hour on demand, amounting to roughly USD 1,825 per month (approximately AED 6,700), or from USD 1.75 per hour on reserved terms (roughly USD 1,280 per month). OpenAI's deployment guidelines show that gpt-oss-120b requires approximately 60 GB of VRAM, running on a single H100 instance (OpenAI cookbook).

The production inference layer is powered by vLLM, an open-source, Apache 2.0 licensed serving engine featuring continuous batching, PagedAttention memory management, and an OpenAI-compatible API structure supporting hundreds of model architectures.

The service commands for standard open-weight architectures illustrate the operational simplicity:

# Launch gpt-oss-120b on a single 80 GB GPU instance (requires ~60 GB VRAM)
vllm serve openai/gpt-oss-120b --max-model-len 32768

# Launch gpt-oss-20b on an L40 instance (requires ~16 GB VRAM)
vllm serve openai/gpt-oss-20b --max-model-len 32768

Internal developers and chat user interfaces connect to the gateway by modifying the base URL in the standard OpenAI client:

import os
from openai import OpenAI

# Direct internal tools and agent workflows to the secure internal gateway
client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://ai.internal/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["AI_GATEWAY_KEY"],  # Department-specific key with proxy budget enforcement
)

Now compare the direct operational cost across potential setups for this 80-person firm:

Architecture Monthly compute cost Model training risk Data residency Audit logging control
Unmanaged personal accounts USD 0 direct High: default training enabled No control None: inaccessible to IT
ChatGPT Business (80 seats) USD 1,600 (annual billing) Zero: enterprise commitment SaaS cloud boundary Enterprise console metadata
Private gateway (L40 48 GB) ~USD 730 hosted Zero: self-hosted instance UAE perimeter Full prompt and response logs
Private gateway (H100 80 GB) ~USD 1,825 on demand Zero: self-hosted instance UAE perimeter Full prompt and response logs

The strategic approach is a blended model: provision ChatGPT Business seats for the 55 employees engaged in public or generic research (55 seats at USD 20 equals USD 1,100 monthly), while directing the 25 sensitive-work analysts to the private gateway (USD 730 to USD 1,825 monthly).

For a total monthly budget between USD 1,830 and USD 2,925, the firm eliminates shadow AI, provides high-speed tooling for general staff, and guarantees that sensitive client data never leaves an audited, local GPU instance. Compared against the IBM benchmark cost of USD 5.39 million per shadow AI incident (Unio Digital), the business case is clear.

How do you roll out an AI policy in 30 days?

Deploying this framework across a mid-sized organisation requires an orderly progression over four weeks:

Week 1: Policy sign-off and baseline tooling

Finalise your organisation's two-page acceptable use policy using the template provided. Secure executive sign-off from legal, operations, and IT leadership. Procure an initial pool of five to ten ChatGPT Business seats or confirm Microsoft Copilot commercial protections in your Entra ID tenant. Implement standard web filtering rules blocking consumer generative AI sign-up pages on managed endpoints, and configure endpoint DLP to alert when UAE Emirates ID numbers or IBAN strings appear in web paste events.

Week 2: Private gateway staging and integration

Spin up your dedicated GPU instance. Deploy vLLM with your chosen open-weight model weights and configure the reverse proxy layer. Configure departmental API keys with strict monthly token quotas, log retention policies, and rate limits. Onboard the 25 staff members handling sensitive workflows to test latency, prompt responsiveness, and usability.

Week 3: Departmental practical training

Policy adoption fails when training is limited to mass email announcements. Conduct one-hour interactive sessions with each department. Review real-world emails and documents from their daily workflow, demonstrating how to categorise items into Red, Amber, and Green. Teach practical redaction techniques, verify that users can access their sanctioned accounts, and reiterate the non-punitive incident reporting policy.

Week 4: Production cutover and exception management

Decommission ad-hoc developer access and unapproved API trial accounts. Move the remaining corporate staff onto their sanctioned commercial accounts. Publish the official directory of approved AI tools on the intranet alongside the two-page policy, and schedule the first quarterly governance review. The audit logs generated by your gateway and administrative consoles now form your operational compliance baseline.

UAE AI compliance: what does the PDPL require by 2027?

For organisations operating in the United Arab Emirates, establishing AI governance is no longer just a cybersecurity best practice; it is an immediate statutory requirement.

Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on the Protection of Personal Data (PDPL) requires full compliance by 1 January 2027 (WCR Legal). The UAE PDPL is a consent-first framework. Unlike the European Union General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the UAE federal statute does not recognise "legitimate interests" as a lawful basis for processing personal information.

Relying on informal assumptions while employees feed client or employee data into public machine learning systems exposes the organisation directly to statutory sanctions. Administrative fines under the PDPL reach up to AED 5 million (approximately USD 1.36 million) for severe violations, and regulatory compliance guidance explicitly instructs organisations processing UAE personal data at scale to maintain documented AI usage policies covering approved tools and permitted use cases (WCR Legal).

In financial free zones, strict supervision is already in effect:

  • DIFC: DIFC Data Protection Regulation 10 has been active since January 2026, establishing mandatory requirements for AI impact assessments, transparency disclosures, and rigorous record-keeping for high-risk data processing, backed by statutory fines between USD 25,000 and USD 50,000 per violation (WCR Legal).
  • ADGM: The Data Protection Regulations 2021 (DPR 2021) closely mirror international standards, requiring strict technical safeguards, documented transfer mechanisms, and verifiable audit trails for automated processing.

A practical corporate posture recognises that the two-page acceptable use policy, commercial workspaces, and a private inference gateway are not separate initiatives. Together, they constitute the exact compliance package an auditor or regulatory authority will examine: a defined policy, sanctioned tooling, boundary protections against unauthorised processing, and verifiable logs demonstrating where data was processed.

What should your organisation do next?

Take these operational steps immediately:

  1. This week: Adapt the acceptable use template to your organisation's reporting lines and get it approved. Enable commercial data protection in your Microsoft 365 environment or purchase a starter tier of ChatGPT Business seats. Review your standard client engagement contracts to identify existing data processing restrictions.
  2. This month: Evaluate your sensitive data exposure. If contractual data residency, high-volume confidential processing, or regulatory compliance mandates apply to your firm, evaluate your private gateway deployment. Size your compute capacity using published rates: an L40 at USD 1.00 per hour for standard models, or an H100 at USD 2.50 per hour for 120B parameter architectures (Hyperstack pricing).

Our own team in the UAE does the consulting, the deployment and the support for our clients, configuring local GPU infrastructure and integrating reverse proxy software to establish secure, audited AI endpoints. If you need a fully compliant, private AI gateway operating within your perimeter, explore our AI infrastructure services to begin.

title: Range-Over-Func Iterators for People Who Miss LINQ
description:
The most common complaint in the comments on this series, and the first item in what I miss from C#, is LINQ. That post shows this:

var activeUsers = users
    .Where(u => u.IsActive)
    .OrderBy(u => u.Name)
    .Select(u => new { u.Id, u.Name })
    .ToList();

and then the for loop and the sort.Slice call you wrote instead. Go has had range-over-func iterators since 1.23, the standard library has been growing functions that return them in every release since, and Go 1.27 removed the one language restriction that made a fluent chain impossible. This post is the honest side by side. Every snippet runs.

What an iterator is in Go

In C#, IEnumerable<T> is a pull model. The consumer holds an enumerator and calls MoveNext() until it says no. A yield return method is compiled into a state machine that implements that interface for you.

Go went the other way. An iterator is a function that takes a callback:

type Seq[V any] func(yield func(V) bool)

The iterator pushes values into yield, and yield returns false when the consumer wants to stop. The for range statement knows how to drive one:

func Naturals() iter.Seq[int] {
    return func(yield func(int) bool) {
        for i := 0; ; i++ {
            if !yield(i) {
                return
            }
        }
    }
}

for n := range Naturals() {
    if n > 3 {
        break   // yield returns false, the iterator returns, nothing leaks
    }
    fmt.Println(n)
}

That is the whole mechanism. The body of your for loop becomes the yield function. break becomes yield returning false. There is no state machine and no interface, which is why the compiler can inline simple cases and why the design went through so many rounds before it shipped.

There is also iter.Seq2[K, V] for pairs, which is what maps.All and slices.All return, and iter.Pull for the rare case where you really do need MoveNext() semantics, at the cost of a goroutine-like coroutine behind the scenes. You will almost never want it.

What the standard library gives you

Sources and sinks, mostly. No adapters.

slices.Values(s)        // iter.Seq[E]
slices.All(s)           // iter.Seq2[int, E]
slices.Backward(s)
slices.Chunk(s, n)
maps.Keys(m)
maps.Values(m)
maps.All(m)
strings.Lines(s)        // Go 1.24
strings.SplitSeq(s, sep)
strings.FieldsSeq(s)

slices.Collect(seq)     // []E
slices.Sorted(seq)      // []E, sorted
slices.SortedFunc(seq, cmp)
maps.Collect(seq2)      // map[K]V

So the first thing LINQ people reach for already works:

keys := slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))

That line replaced a nine line function in half the Go codebases I have worked in.

What is missing is Where, Select, Take, First and friends. The proposal to add them as x/exp/xiter was withdrawn after a long argument about whether adapters encourage over-abstraction. There is a decent chance they come back once the community has settled on idioms. For now you write them, and they are short.

Writing Where and Select 

func Where[T any](seq iter.Seq[T], keep func(T) bool) iter.Seq[T] {
    return func(yield func(T) bool) {
        for v := range seq {
            if keep(v) && !yield(v) {
                return
            }
        }
    }
}

func Select[T, U any](seq iter.Seq[T], f func(T) U) iter.Seq[U] {
    return func(yield func(U) bool) {
        for v := range seq {
            if !yield(f(v)) {
                return
            }
        }
    }
}

Each one is a function that returns a function. The !yield(v) check is the only line that matters: it is what lets a break three layers up stop an infinite source at the bottom.

func First[T any](seq iter.Seq[T]) (T, bool) {
    for v := range seq {
        return v, true
    }
    var zero T
    return zero, false
}

first, _ := First(Where(Naturals(), func(n int) bool { return n > 100 }))
// 101, and Naturals stopped at 101

Lazy, composable, early-terminating. All three properties the "what I miss" post said Go did not have.

The example, rewritten

With those two helpers and slices.SortedFunc, the LINQ query from the top becomes:

active := slices.SortedFunc(
    Select(
        Where(slices.Values(users), func(u User) bool { return u.IsActive }),
        func(u User) UserSummary { return UserSummary{u.ID, u.Name} },
    ),
    func(a, b UserSummary) int { return cmp.Compare(a.Name, b.Name) },
)

It does the same thing. It is lazy until the sort. And it reads inside-out, which is the complaint everyone has about it within five minutes. In C# the pipeline reads top to bottom because Where and Select are extension methods on the sequence. In Go, up to 1.26, there were two reasons you could not do that:

  1. You cannot define methods on a type from another package, so nothing can hang off iter.Seq directly. You need your own named type.
  2. Methods could not have their own type parameters, so even on your own Query[T] type, a Select that returns Query[U] was impossible to declare. That is the one that killed every attempt at a fluent LINQ in Go.

The first restriction is permanent and the workaround is one line. The second one is gone.

Go 1.27 and generic methods

As of August 2026 a method can declare type parameters of its own. So this is now legal:

type Query[T any] iter.Seq[T]

func From[T any](s []T) Query[T] { return Query[T](slices.Values(s)) }

func (q Query[T]) Where(keep func(T) bool) Query[T] {
    return func(yield func(T) bool) {
        for v := range q {
            if keep(v) && !yield(v) {
                return
            }
        }
    }
}

func (q Query[T]) Select[U any](f func(T) U) Query[U] {
    return func(yield func(U) bool) {
        for v := range q {
            if !yield(f(v)) {
                return
            }
        }
    }
}

func (q Query[T]) OrderBy(cmp func(a, b T) int) Query[T] {
    return From(slices.SortedFunc(iter.Seq[T](q), cmp))
}

func (q Query[T]) ToSlice() []T { return slices.Collect(iter.Seq[T](q)) }

And the query reads the way your C# brain wants it to:

active := From(users).
    Where(func(u User) bool { return u.IsActive }).
    OrderBy(func(a, b User) int { return cmp.Compare(a.Name, b.Name) }).
    Select(func(u User) UserSummary { return UserSummary{u.ID, u.Name} }).
    ToSlice()

Type inference fills in U from the function you pass, so you never write Select[UserSummary]. The two caveats from the release notes: an interface still cannot declare a generic method, and a generic method cannot satisfy an interface. For a query type that is irrelevant. For anyone hoping to write IQueryable, it is the end of the road, and honestly good.

Whether you should build this is a separate question. The Go answer is still that a pipeline of three steps is a for loop with three lines in it, and the loop is easier to debug. Where Query earns its keep is the same place LINQ does: when the pipeline is the point, when it is reused, or when the source is lazy and you want First to stop it.

What it costs

Each stage of the pipeline is an indirect function call per element. The compiler inlines the simple cases but not a chain of closures. Filtering and projecting a hundred thousand structs on Go 1.25, three runs each:

ns/op allocs/op
for loop with append 500,000 23
Collect(Select(Where(Values(...)))) 920,000 33

Roughly double on a benchmark that does nothing but iterate. In a real handler the database round trip dwarfs it. It is the same trade LINQ makes against a foreach, and the same answer: write the pipeline, profile before you unroll it.

The honest table

LINQ Go now Notes
Where write it, 8 lines or Query.Where on 1.27
Select write it, 8 lines generic method needs 1.27
OrderBy slices.SortedFunc materialises, same as LINQ
First / FirstOrDefault write it, 6 lines returns (T, bool)
Take / Skip write it easy, counter in the closure
Any / All / Count loop or write it three lines each
ToList slices.Collect
ToDictionary maps.Collect from a Seq2
Distinct slices.Sorted + slices.Compact or a map, if order matters
GroupBy write it, returns map[K][]T no lazy grouping
Zip / Join iter.Pull on one side ugly, write the loop
Aggregate loop a fold is a loop
SelectMany nested range in a closure fine
IQueryable nothing and nothing coming

Everything in the "write it" column is under ten lines and lives in one file in your module. There are third-party packages that have already written them, and the lo library the old post mentioned now has an it subpackage built on iter.Seq, but a dependency for forty lines of code is a bad Go instinct and the standard library may yet absorb them.

What I would say now

The "what I miss" post said Go's approach "lacks the expressiveness" of LINQ. In 2024 that was fair. In 2026 the laziness and composition are there, the standard library sources and sinks are there, and generic methods mean the fluent form is a type definition away. What is still missing is the adapters in the box and the convention that everyone uses the same ones, which is the thing that makes LINQ readable across codebases rather than just within one.

So: less missing than I said. Not gone. Write the eight lines, keep the loop for the simple cases, and do not import a query language.

title: GBase Database Server Sizing: How to Choose the Right Hardware Tier
description:
Choosing hardware for GBase Database (GBase 8s) isn't about buying the most expensive server. It's about matching resources to your workload.

A practical starting point is to evaluate three deployment tiers: development, small-to-medium workloads, and large-scale enterprise systems.

1. Three GBase Database Hardware Tiers

The following specifications are illustrative planning references. Verify them against the official hardware requirements for your GBase 8s version and target platform before deployment.

Tier Typical workload CPU Memory Storage
Minimum Development and debugging 2 × 2-core CPUs, 2.0 GHz 4 GB 100 GB+
Mid-range Fewer than 100 concurrent users; TPS below 50; data under 100 GB 4 × 4-core CPUs, 3.0 GHz 16–64 GB ECC 1 TB+ enterprise SSD
High-end More than 1,000 concurrent users; TPS above 500; data at least 1 TB 64+ cores 128 GB ECC 2 TB+ SSD; dedicated storage as needed

Important: These tiers are starting points, not universal sizing guarantees. Actual performance depends on transaction complexity, workload mix, indexing, availability requirements, and storage architecture.

2. Three Principles for Database Capacity Planning

First, estimate concurrency and transaction throughput.

Concurrent sessions and transactions per second (TPS) help determine CPU capacity and memory requirements. Benchmark representative workloads rather than relying on user counts alone.

Second, size storage for both capacity and performance.

Data volume determines baseline storage needs, but transaction workloads also depend on IOPS, latency, log-write performance, and growth forecasts. Storage requirements should reflect measured workload characteristics.

Third, leave room for peak demand and growth.

Plan for peak concurrency, data expansion, maintenance operations, and recovery requirements. Sizing a server at its minimum capacity can leave little room for unexpected workload spikes.

3. Why Memory Matters for GBase Database

For an OLTP database such as GBase Database, memory configuration affects caching, concurrency, and overall workload performance.

Insufficient shared memory can prevent instance initialization or constrain workload capacity. However, simply adding RAM doesn't guarantee better performance: shared-memory parameters must also be configured appropriately for the operating system and GBase 8s instance.

Final Takeaway

Effective GBase Database server sizing starts with workload metrics, not hardware price tags.

Estimate concurrency, TPS, data volume, I/O requirements, and future growth. Then validate your proposed configuration through workload testing before production deployment.

How does your team size database servers: workload benchmarks, vendor recommendations, or previous project experience?

title: Connect devices, sensors and custom hardware to business workflows
description:
Connected hardware is most valuable when it supports a clear operational response. A sensor reading, button press or machine state becomes useful when the platform knows which asset it belongs to, whether the information is current and who should act when something needs attention.

The project should therefore begin with the workflow, not a catalogue of devices.

Define the event and response

Write down what needs to be observed or controlled. Examples include temperature leaving an agreed range, a tank reaching a threshold, an asset arriving at a site or a manual inspection being confirmed.

Then define the response. Who receives the information? Is acknowledgement required? What evidence closes the event? What happens outside business hours? This turns a reading into an operational requirement.

Reuse existing equipment where practical

An older asset may already expose a relay, serial port or industrial protocol. An off-the-shelf product may provide an API or export. Assess the supported interface, documentation, ownership and maintenance implications before adding new hardware.

Where no suitable interface exists, an external sensor or custom gateway may bridge the gap without replacing the asset. The design should respect warranties, electrical isolation, environmental conditions and safe installation.

Treat connectivity as variable

Sites may have weak mobile coverage, restricted networks or periods without power. Decide what the device should do while offline, how much information it stores and how duplicate events are prevented after reconnection.

Show the last contact time in the platform. A missing reading should not be displayed as a normal value. For important processes, create a separate alert for loss of communication and retain a manual check.

Identify every device and asset

Use stable identifiers for the physical unit, installed asset and site. Record commissioning, firmware, calibration and maintenance information where relevant. If hardware is moved or replaced, preserve the history without assigning new readings to the wrong asset.

Avoid using a network address or user-entered label as the only identity. Both can change.

Secure the full path

Limit each device to the services and actions it needs. Protect credentials, rotate them where supported and plan how a lost or retired device is disabled. Validate incoming data and record the source and receipt time.

Remote control requires additional safeguards. Separate monitoring from control, confirm the current state and require appropriate approval for consequential commands.

Connect readings to work

A graph can help with investigation, but daily users often need an exception queue, assigned task and response history. Link the device event to the asset, site and responsible team. Suppress repeated notifications for the same unresolved condition while preserving the underlying readings.

Managers can then review recurring issues and response performance. Leadership can see trends across an asset portfolio without losing the source evidence.

Pilot in the real environment

Test power loss, connectivity loss, invalid readings and physical conditions. Confirm installation and replacement procedures. Establish a baseline and run the connected workflow alongside the current check until the team trusts it.
